Issue summary:
Finovia reports intermittent 403s from the admin API and scheduled worker jobs when requests are routed through their SSH bastion using SOCKS5 dynamic forwarding. Direct requests (not going through the SSH tunnel) succeed.

Impact:
- Immediate: Several scheduled consumer jobs fail with 403 for ~12 hours during business hours, causing backlog in payment reconciliation.
- Scope: All API calls that traverse the customer's SSH bastion (SOCKS5/SSH -D) path to the private deployment. Web console sessions from corporate network appear unaffected.

Environment:
- Private deployment in us-east-1, customer-managed bastion host, NLB -> edge-proxy (customer VPC) -> Redwood private control plane.
- Edge Proxy version: v1.14.3 (customer fork).

Steps to reproduce (customer-provided):
1) ssh -D 1080 bastion@bastion.finovia.internal -i ~/.ssh/bastion_key
2) export ALL_PROXY=socks5://localhost:1080
3) curl -v -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" -H "X-Tenant-Id: finovia-prod" https://private-api.redwood.internal/v1/admin/roles
4) Observe: 403 returned. Repeat same curl without ALL_PROXY set -> 200 OK.

Relevant logs (edge-proxy access log snippet):
- Incoming request from 10.0.34.12 via TCP proxied by bastion (X-Forwarded-For present). Access log shows downstream headers: "X-Tenant-Id" missing and "Authorization" present.
- Gateway auth check: "missing tenant header -> authz denied"

Notes:
- Customer asserts this started after a bastion container upgrade to alpine:3.18 two weeks ago, though timing is approximate.
- All failing requests share path/transport characteristic: proxied via SOCKS5 dynamic forwarding.

10-Mar: Reproduced using local ssh -D to a publicly accessible test endpoint. Observed that a socks5 stream ends up being re-originated by the bastion's user-space agent, which strips non-standard headers when building the upstream HTTP request.
11-Mar: Bastion tcpdump shows the original client sends X-Tenant-Id to local SOCKS proxy; the proxy then issues a new HTTP request without X-Tenant-Id when performing the outbound connection.
11-Mar: Differences between HTTP CONNECT (preserves raw TCP) and SOCKS5 dynamic forwarding (application-level proxy) explain why header is lost only for ssh -D flows.
12-Mar: Confirmed edge-proxy correctly rejects requests with missing tenant header per RBAC rules. No misconfiguration found in RBAC policy. The root cause is header omission upstream by the customer's bastion/proxying layer.
12-Mar: Customer identifies upgrade on bastion which replaced a small helper (sproxy) with a newer default that rebuilds requests. We saw consistent reproduction with the customer's helper binary in a containerized environment.
13-Mar: Risk assessment: Long-term, many customers use SSH bastions; difference between HTTP CONNECT and SOCKS5 needs clearer documentation. Edge-proxy fallback (based on source IP mapping) can mitigate but has security implications; will implement as opt-in and logged heavily.

2026-03-13 14:02 - Engineering (Rohit Patil): Agreed to patch edge-proxy to detect missing tenant header and consult fallback tenant mapping based on source IP and configured tenant CIDR maps. Filed INT follow-up for implementation and docs update.
Workaround provided: customer switched scheduled jobs to use port-forwarding (ssh -L) or corporate HTTP proxy (CONNECT) which preserved X-Tenant-Id; scheduled jobs resumed.
Short-term mitigation: Support updated customer runbook to prefer HTTP CONNECT proxies or explicit L7 proxies that preserve headers for service-to-service calls.
Long-term fix: Engineering to implement optional "tenant-source-ip-mapping" fallback in edge-proxy to allow mapping a source IP/CIDR to a tenant when a tenant header is absent (opt-in per-customer config). INT ticket created to track the implementation and security review (INT-2201).
Follow-ups:
- INT-2201: Design + implementation of tenant-source-ip-mapping (security review required).
- Docs update: add guidance to Private Deployment onboarding about SSH bastion behaviors and recommended proxying modes (Confluence page linked).
- Post-incident: check other private customers for similar SSH-bastion upgrades and proactively notify.
Status: In Progress - short-term workaround validated by customer; engineering design in progress.

Issue summary: BrightCart observed a sharp increase in 5xx errors and token latency for requests routed to their reserved pool between 2026-03-12T09:40 and 2026-03-12T11:05 UTC. Impact: ~22% of batched requests returned 500/502 within the window, median token latency increased from ~45ms to ~420ms, and several long-running streams were terminated by the serving runtime. Environment: Dedicated capacity (reserved pool id rp-44), prod us-east-1, cluster sku: 8xA100, autoscale policy: conservative-burst-v2. Steps: See steps_to_reproduce. Logs and telemetry attached below. Initial hypothesis: sudden saturation of GPU memory/KV cache by a single noisy tenant causing eviction storms and scheduler thrashing, which cascaded to failed batch allocations and queue timeouts. Resolution summary: applied temporary isolation by moving the noisy tenant to a different pool, increased pool GPU headroom and lowered max_batch_size for affected routes, and deployed an autoscaler fix to back-pressure noisy-tenant allocation. Follow-ups: post-incident audit of tenant scheduling and new quota-based scheduling enforcement.
1) Send 100 concurrent batched requests (batch size 16) to /v1/generate on BrightCart's reserved pool rp-44 using open-7b-q4 model.
2) Observe request queue growth beyond configured max_queue_ms and increased token generation latency after ~15 minutes.
3) Repeat with a single high-memory streaming workload (long context, prefix cache hits) to replicate KV cache eviction pattern.
4) Monitor metrics: gpu_utilization, gpu_memory_used, serving_batch_alloc_errors, scheduler_queue_length.
5) Confirm 5xx error spike aligns with GPU memory OOM and batch allocation failures in logs.
2026-03-12T09:43:12Z rp-44-node-7 serving-runtime: BatchAllocError: allocation timeout after 12000ms (requested 4g, available 0g)
2026-03-12T09:43:12Z rp-44-node-7 gpu-manager: GPU memory pressure: 98% (A100-40GB), KV-cache entries evicted=3124
2026-03-12T09:44:01Z autoscaler: scale_event: prevented_scale_up pool=rp-44 reason=insufficient_gpu_headroom
2026-03-12T09:45:05Z scheduler: queue_delay_ms route=/v1/generate median=375 max=1234
2026-03-12T10:02:33Z proxy: downstream 502 from serving-runtime on rp-44-node-3 during streaming connection
Metric analysis: serving_batch_alloc_errors correlated with gpu_memory_used > 92% and KV eviction spikes. Three nodes (rp-44-node-3/5/7) showed repeated allocation timeouts.
Heap: The noisy tenant's streaming workload retained large KV caches (~8GB per worker) due to long-context inference pattern and lacked prefix caching TTL in user config.
Scheduler behavior: When allocation timeouts occurred, scheduler attempted to rebalance batches which increased queue delay and caused downstream 502s from timeouts.
Autoscaler observation: conservative-burst-v2 policy prevented immediate scale-up because it evaluates aggregated queue signal and saw transient oscillation; this created a feedback loop where allocation failures blocked scale triggers.
Customer config: BrightCart had max_batch_size=64 and aggressive prefetch settings; lowering batch size reduced per-batch memory and improved headroom.
Related incidents: SUP-51777 documented intermittent GPU availability that had similar symptoms but different root cause (eviction due to kernel memory leak). Linked for historical context.
Applied temporary tenant isolation by moving the noisy evaluation job to a separate reserved pool, increased pool headroom by adding one GPU to rp-44 for 1 hour, lowered max_batch_size for the affected routes to 16, and deployed an autoscaler patch to break the prevention loop. Customer confirmed error rate returned to baseline and median token latency dropped back under 70ms. Incident marked resolved after 30m of stable metrics.
1) Enforce per-tenant KV-cache memory quotas in the serving-runtime (Owner: Diego) - target ETA 2026-03-26
2) Add quota-based scheduling to autoscaler to avoid allocation/prevention loops (Owner: Priya) - target ETA 2026-03-19
3) Update dedicated capacity onboarding checklist to include recommended max_batch_size and prefix TTL settings for streaming workloads (Owner: Maya) - target ETA 2026-03-18
4) Run a synthetic soak test for rp-44 configuration to validate the autoscaler fix under long-context streaming patterns (Owner: SRE) - scheduled 2026-03-15
5) Customer follow-up call to review best-practices and configuration changes (Owner: CS) - scheduled 2026-03-14
Support (Maya): Customer reported recurring ~20% 5xx rate for batched routes starting ~09:40 UTC. Provided initial logs and requested SRE assistance. Link to Slack thread: #support-brightcart (slack.com/archives/C02ABC/ppp456)
SRE (Diego): Began live investigation at 09:55 UTC. Noted high GPU memory pressure across 3 nodes and repeated KV cache evictions. Hypothesis: one tenant's streaming workload retained large prefix caches causing memory blowout and preventing new batch allocations.
Customer (BrightCart - Alice Mills): Confirms a background evaluation job ramped up in the morning that cycles long-context prompts every 30s. Will pause job if that helps.
SRE (Diego): Paused suspected tenant workload at 10:07 UTC and observed immediate drop in eviction rate and allocation failures. Initiated tenant isolation and scaled rp-44 headroom +1 GPU as temporary mitigation.
Support (Maya): Notified customer of mitigation and timeline. Customer validated reduced errors after job pause.
Engineering (Priya - autoscaler): Deployed autoscaler hotfix at 10:52 UTC to prevent scale prevention loop when pool reports high allocation failures. Patch: prioritize new allocation slots over deferring scale-up when allocation failures > threshold.
SRE (Diego): Closed incident at 11:05 UTC after stabilization and rollback of temporary measures to standard config with quota enforcement enabled.
Postmortem reminder: Owner assigned for follow-ups: Priya Khatri (autoscaler), Diego Alvarez (scheduling), Maya Chen (CS liaison)

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customers (primarily OrionHealth enterprise tenant) began reporting increased 5xx responses and streaming session disconnects on the mixed chat+embedding route between 2026-03-13T16:05 and 2026-03-13T18:30 UTC. Errors spiked from baseline ~0.2% to ~8% for the route; several long-lived streaming sessions observed abrupt RSTs followed by short lived runtime restarts.

Impact:
- OrionHealth: intermittent failures while generating clinical summarizations (chat) and uploading embedding batches; user-facing errors and timeouts.
- Platform: elevated 5xx floor on the route in us-east for ~2.5 hours; increased latency and partial degradation of streaming.

Environment:
- prod:us-east (primary)
- Route: /v1/chat+embed (mixed route; hedged retries enabled)
- Models in use: open-vicuna-13b for chat, redwood-embedding-v2 for embeddings

Steps to reproduce (observed by SRE):
1) Replayed a tenant-weighted steady-state traffic mix (60% short-chat, 30% embeddings, 10% long-chat streaming) against staging priority scheduler with the same weights that were rolled to prod.
2) Increased small long-lived streaming connections to simulate real customer sessions.
3) Observed accept-queue pressure at the API gateway and concurrent hedged retries from the edge when priority weights dipped below threshold.

Observed behavior:
- API gateway returned 502/503/504 for new requests; streaming connections experienced half-open socket resets.
- Serving runtime processes logged SIGTERM sequences and then restarted on some GPU workers (graceful exit did not complete before watchdog timed out).
- Priority scheduler metrics showed negative "available slots" in the shim for a short period due to a weight normalization bug (see investigation).

Logs and artifacts:
- Sample gateway trace: trace_id=trace-20260313-6731 (attached)
- Runtime logs: gpu_worker_77: "watchdog: restart requested after accept loop stall" (attached snippet)
- Dashboard: /dashboards/ingress/priority-shed-2026-03-13 (attached)
Timeline and quick findings:
- 16:05 UTC: first elevated error alerts from routing monitors.
- 16:07 UTC: hedged-retry counter for route rose x12 over baseline, backlog in accept queue increased.
- 16:12 UTC: SRE replayed the weight calculation for the priority scheduler and found an edge case where floating-point rounding produced a transient negative "available_slot" after normalizing tenant weights when combined with dynamic burst credits. This caused the priority-shed shim to mark some low-latency routes as ineligible which triggered large-batch hedged retries from the edge.
- 16:20-17:30 UTC: multiple serving runtime processes received surge of concurrent connections; some obeyed graceful shutdown but several hit the runtime watchdog and restarted, amplifying rate of 5xx.
- Hypothesis: priority-scheduler miscalculation -> misclassification of route eligibility -> hedged retries + accept-queue overload -> runtime watchdog-triggered restarts -> elevated 5xx floor.
- Corroborating evidence: matched timestamps across scheduler logs (scheduler-2) and gateway (apigw-10); PR https://github.com/redwood-inference/priority-scheduler/pull/498 contains the normalization change deployed in the previous sweep.

Temporary mitigations tried:
- At 16:30 UTC: applied an emergency soft-cap on hedged-retry amplification in the edge (reduced hedged retry fanout for affected route) — reduced immediate pressure on accept queues.
- At 16:45 UTC: increased accept-queue depth on the API gateway for prod:us-east for the mixed route and tuned watchdog timeout on two suspect GPU worker pools. Both reduced restarts but did not fully clear the error floor.

Next steps planned:
1) Roll back the weight-normalization microchange from PR 498 in a controlled canary (SRE scheduled at 2026-03-14T02:00 UTC).
2) Add defensive clamp to priority scheduler to ensure available_slot >= 0 and log telemetry on negative occurrences.
3) Add unit tests for mixed-weight + burst-credit paths.
4) Postmortem draft and customer communication for OrionHealth.

Work-in-progress: temporary edge hedged-retry cap and accept-queue tuning reduced immediate customer impact. A rollback of the priority-scheduler normalization change is scheduled for 2026-03-14 UTC; permanent fixes include clamping, tests, and a telemetry alert for negative available_slot events. Documented followups for postmortem and retro.

Additional notes:
2026-03-13 16:35 UTC - SRE (Luca Moreno): Initial triage shows accept-queue growth and hedged-retry amplification for /v1/chat+embed. Suspect priority scheduler weight normalization. Pulling scheduler logs now.
2026-03-13 16:50 UTC - OrionHealth (customer): We've observed failed clinical summary exports at ~16:10-16:40 UTC. Any ETA on mitigation? This impacts our reporting pipeline.
Support provided temporary suggestion: switch to chat-only route as workaround (not ideal).
2026-03-13 17:05 UTC - Support (Maya Patel): Applied hedged-retry cap at edge; monitoring for error-rate drop. Customer informed; asked to validate if retries stop on their side.
2026-03-13 17:20 UTC - SRE (Luca Moreno): Hedged cap reduced 5xx from ~8% to ~1.5% over 10 minutes. Watching for runtime restarts. Opening rollback window for scheduler microchange. Linking PR 498 in investigation.
2026-03-14 02:05 UTC - SRE (Luca Moreno): Rolled back normalization change to canary subset; no negative available_slot events in canary for 30m and canary error-rate stable. Preparing full rollback and postmortem notes.
2026-03-14 08:30 UTC - Support (Maya Patel): Customer notified of temporary mitigation and rollback schedule; provided workaround guidance and committed to postmortem. Customer acknowledged and requested timeline for permanent fix.
Rollback priority-scheduler normalization change (PR 498) - scheduled 2026-03-14
Add clamp to available_slot in priority scheduler and add unit tests
Create alert for negative available_slot occurrences
Draft customer-facing incident summary and postmortem (owner: Support)

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customer BrightCart reports intermittent 30s+ request times and client-side timeouts when using structured output (JSON-mode) with streaming=true on dedicated capacity. Impact:
- Several checkout microservices experienced prolonged latency spikes during peak traffic (10:45-11:20 UTC).
- Errors are request timeouts (client sees 504) and occasional server-side 5xx.
Environment:
- Dedicated cluster: dc-dedicated-42 (us-east)
- Redwood runtime v2.7.3, api-gateway v1.4.1
- Customers are pinned to model redwood/openchat-7b-v1 with structured-json output template
Steps to reproduce:
1) Create a generation request with streaming=true and mode=json_schema with template producing ~15KB structured payload per request.
2) Fire concurrent 250 RPS from BrightCart test harness for 10 minutes.
3) Observe tail latency and errors from client side after ~5 minutes.
Observed behavior:
- Median latency is normal (~120ms) but 99.9th percentile spikes to 20-45s.
- Traces show long delays in "serialize_and_flush" spans and large CPU time in worker processes handling JSON encoding.
Expected behavior:
- Streaming JSON responses should not cause long-tail serialization delays; flushes should be constant and under SLOs.
Temporary workaround provided to customer:
- Suggested reducing streaming buffer flush interval and switching streaming=false (non-streaming) for now; customer applied non-streaming and errors subsided.

Support (2026-03-10) - Maya Chen: Customer reported spikes after enabling structured JSON mode with streaming=true. Asked for request IDs and sample payloads. Requested authorization to pull traces and CPU profiles from their dedicated pool.
Customer (2026-03-10) - Aaron Patel (BrightCart): Sent request IDs sup_req_9831..9839 and sample prompt+schema. Noted spikes correspond to peak traffic window and only for JSON-mode; plain text mode unaffected.
SRE (2026-03-11) - Diego Ramos: Pulled flamegraphs for worker processes on dc-dedicated-42. Observed synchronous JSON encoding calls that pinned a worker thread for large outputs. Opening investigation into serialization backpressure and streaming flush logic.
Engineering (2026-03-11) - Lina Park: Reproduced locally with load generator. Confirmed that when structured outputs exceed ~8KB and streaming enabled, the runtime batches and then performs blocking encoding on main worker leading to increased per-request tail latency.
Support (2026-03-12) - Maya Chen: Notified customer that we identified a likely serialization/backpressure issue and are testing a hotfix that performs async encoding off the critical I/O path. Provided ETA for patch rollout.
Customer (2026-03-12) - Aaron Patel: Thanks team; will keep non-streaming enabled until fix is rolled. Requested follow-up monitoring when hotfix is live.
03/11 - Collected pprof CPU profiles from three workers on node rwi-dc-42-worker-5. Top stack shows runtime.serializeJSON -> encoding/json.Marshal -> internalBuffer.Write blocking for 300-800ms per request at tail.
03/11 - Trace capture (trace IDs provided) shows serialize_and_flush spans accumulating in queue; backpressure appears when more than ~200 concurrent streaming frames are pending for a single worker process.
03/11 - Reproduced with load harness: switching to streaming=false keeps tail latency below 500ms. Enabling streaming + structured template reproduces 99.9th percentiles > 20s within 5 minutes at 250 RPS.
03/11 - Hypothesis: JSON-mode triggers use of full in-memory encoding for structured outputs; combined with streaming frame aggregation, large outputs cause blocking CPU work on hot threads instead of being offloaded to async workers. This creates head-of-line blocking and increases long-tail latency.
03/12 - Correlated incident with recent change in v2.7.3 that modified streaming flush coalescing and buffer threshold (PR 1168). That change increased per-frame aggregation to improve throughput but unintentionally increased worst-case encoding chunk sizes.
03/12 - Identified quick mitigation: reduce coalescing buffer threshold on dedicated clusters to avoid huge encoding work in single operation. Prepared a hotfix branch that also offloads serialization to a separate goroutine pool.
03/12 - Added observability tasks: instrument per-request serialization_time_ms, frames_coalesced_count, and cpu_ms_per_serialize. These metrics will be emitted to console and customer dashboards for affected clusters.
03/12 - Linked to PR for patch: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/1189 (adds async-serialization and config flag streaming.coalesce_max_bytes)
03/12 - Follow-ups: schedule config rollout for dedicated clusters, add safety limit on coalescing, add integration test for streaming+structured outputs to ci-load tests.
Workaround applied: customer switched to streaming=false which restored normal latency. Engineering prepared hotfix (PR 1189) that: (1) reduces default streaming coalescing threshold to 8KB on dedicated clusters, (2) offloads JSON serialization to an async worker pool to avoid blocking main serving thread, and (3) emits per-request serialization telemetry. Hotfix deployed to canary on dc-dedicated-42 on 2026-03-12 22:10 UTC, observed 99.9th latency drop from 28s->380ms under reproduction load. Plan: roll to remaining dedicated clusters on 2026-03-13 during maintenance window. Post-deploy actions: update runbook, add CI test coverage, notify customers of config option streaming.coalesce_max_bytes and guidance for schema size.
payload.summary: Streaming JSON-mode responses causing sporadic long-tail decode delays and client timeouts

payload.description:
Issue summary: Customer reports duplicate downstream tool (payment webhook) invocations after a client-side network blip during a multiplexed streaming session. Impact: duplicate payments sent to their payment processor for ~0.5% of streamed requests over a 3-hour window. Environment: Dedicated cluster in us-east, Python SDK (v1.8.3) producer, TypeScript SDK (v2.0.1) consumer, model gptx-2-large.

Observed behavior: OnyxPayments uses a batching pattern where a single streaming connection carries multiple parallel tool call requests (multiplexed). When a client reconnect occurs and the SDK resends unacknowledged batch frames, the Python SDK injects a per-action idempotency token (action_id) but also includes a per-stream idempotency header. The TS SDK's reconnect logic only replays the original request body without reattaching the per-action token, leading the service to treat the replay as new for some actions. Result: downstream tool executed twice for a subset of actions.

Why this is urgent: Customer handles financial transactions; duplicates lead to reconciliation overhead and potential regulatory exposure.
1) Start a multiplexed streaming session from SDK-A (Python v1.8.3) to Redwood Hosted endpoint with 8 parallel logical requests over one TCP stream.
2) Trigger a sequence of actions that include a tool/function call invoking an external payment webhook (sandbox).
3) Simulate a transient network disconnect that drops the TCP connection after the server has accepted some frames but before all action acks are returned (client later reconnects).
4) Allow SDK reconnect and replay of unacknowledged frames. Observe webhook receiver and Redwood request logs for duplicate invocations.
Excerpt from gateway logs (us-east-1) showing two executions for action_id 'act_7f3a' across two different request IDs: req-20260312-01 and req-20260312-01-r2. Timestamp delta: 00:00:07. Trace IDs: trace-8b2a and trace-9c3b. See attached full dump in internal link.
Initial triage: confirmed duplicate external webhook posts correlated with client reconnect window. No server-side retries configured for this route.
Reproduced in lab with SDK matrix: Python v1.8.3 (producer) + TS v2.0.1 (consumer) with intentional disconnect -> duplicates observed. When both endpoints use Python SDK or both use TS SDK, behavior differs: duplicates reproduced only when producer SDK attaches per-action idempotency differently than replaying SDK.
Hypothesis: idempotency token normalization and placement differ across SDK implementations. Service expects a single canonical idempotency key per action; if absent or mismatched on replay, server treats as new action.

Additional notes:
2026-03-12 11:18 - OnyxPayments (customer): Provided pcap and streaming session trace. Confirmed they use a sidecar proxy but it preserves headers; they also confirmed they perform per-action UUID generation client-side.
2026-03-13 08:30 - Eng (runtime): Noted that the serving runtime accepts both per-stream and per-action keys but de-duplication table TTL is 30s. If reconnect replay occurs after TTL, duplicates happen. Suggest increasing TTL for routes marked as 'external-side-effect'.
2026-03-13 12:10 - Support: Coordinating a short-term mitigation: recommend customer enable explicit per-action idempotency propagation on reconnect and enable 'strict-idempotency' flag in their Dedicated config.
2026-03-13 16:45 - Customer: Agreed to apply workaround and run for 24 hours; requested timeline for SDK patch.
Workaround applied: OnyxPayments enabled explicit per-action idempotency resend on reconnect and toggled strict-idempotency at the route level; duplicates stopped in the monitoring window. Engineering changes: SDK team to release Python and TS patches that standardize idempotency header naming and ensure per-action tokens are preserved on replay. Runtime change: evaluate increasing de-duplication TTL for routes marked as external-side-effect. Follow-ups: INT-1124 created to track SDK release and runtime config change; postmortem to be published in confluence after implementation.
payload.summary: Inconsistent idempotency scope across SDKs for multiplexed batch streaming causing duplicate tool executions after partial reconnect

payload.description:
Issue summary: FinCloud Capital uses Redwood's live audit webhook to stream tenant-scoped activity into their Splunk HEC cluster. Over the last 72 hours they observed event sequences arriving out-of-order and occasional duplicate event_ids, causing their dedupe+windowing logic to drop legitimate transactions. They want: (1) a documented guarantee of ordering semantics (per-tenant watermark or monotonic sequence), (2) per-event idempotency token behavior and TTL, (3) a small redacted sample payload set mapped to Splunk HEC fields, and (4) guidance for resuming ingestion from a resume-token if a window gap occurs.
Customer-facing: Splunk-based reconciliation reports show missing transactions for two accounts (revenue-impacting). FinCloud has paused daily reconciliation and classified this as P1 because it affects month-end reporting. Risk of regulatory reporting errors if unresolved.
1) Customer subscribes to live audit webhook for tenant T-78 using HMAC-authenticated delivery to their HTTPS endpoint.
2) Traffic profile: 1200 events/minute burst, typical sequence numbers assigned by Redwood per event.
3) Customer processes events with dedupe by event_id and time-window of 30s. They observe (a) event_id duplicates within <10s and (b) sequence numbers that jump backward by 1-3 for some windows.
4) Customer captures first_occurrence and last_received timestamps and provided them in attached logs.
5) When the customer retries delivery acknowledgement, some duplicates are reprocessed and others are dropped by their ingestion logic.
6) Customer requested sample redacted payloads and mapping table to validate field-level masking for PII-sensitive attributes.
Initial hypothesis: transient reordering caused by cross-shard retry and prefetch on delivery worker, combined with client-side processing assumptions about monotonic seq numbers.
Telemetry: broker delivery log shows duplicate handoffs for event_id evt-78-0001 with two different seq values; occurrence aligns with a consumer restart and immediate producer retries.
Ingest runtime: sequence numbers are assigned at generation time per-tenant, but ordering guarantees are best-effort per shard. When an event is retried from dead-letter or retry queue it can be re-emitted with the original seq but may arrive after later seqs if cross-shard routing happened.
Auth/HMAC: no evidence of replay attack; HMAC timestamps valid and within TTL.
Added short-term guidance to customer to widen dedupe window to 60s and accept idempotency by event_id instead of strict seq monotonicity.
Enabled per-tenant sticky routing to preferred shard for T-78 for 24 hours to reduce cross-shard retries during peak bursts.
Queued a platform change proposal to emit a resume_token with per-batch high-watermark for ordered delivery. See PR referenced above.
Workaround: Increased routing stickiness and recommended dedupe window change. Long-term plan: implement explicit per-batch resume_token + optional monotonic offset header and document idempotency semantics in the webhook API docs. Customer accepted workaround and scheduled a follow-up validation run on 2026-03-14. Escalated to Product for API doc update.
Product to update webhook API docs with: idempotency_token semantics, resume_token format, and recommended dedupe window guidance
Platform Eng to run canary for resume_token in staging and run a high-throughput soak test
CS to schedule a joint validation session with FinCloud on 2026-03-14
Close ticket after customer confirms reconciliation results for a 24h production run
payload.summary: High-frequency audit webhook: ordering guarantees, per-event idempotency, and sample redaction mapping for Splunk HEC

payload.description:
Customer (Northstar Financial) reports intermittent streaming disconnects on Hosted chat/completions and is asking how Redwood classifies them for reliability/SLO reporting.

Customer notes:
- They consume streaming via SSE.
- They observe occasional "stream ended"/disconnect mid-generation with no final message.
- They suspect some are caused by client-side timeouts/proxies, but are concerned Redwood counts these as platform errors.
- They want a clear definition of: (a) what counts as a streaming failure, (b) what is excluded as client abort, and (c) whether disconnects impact availability/error-rate SLI.

Impact:
- User-facing partial responses in their app (Hosted).
- Questions are blocking internal rollout and their security/reliability review.

Requested from Support:
- Clarify Redwood SLI/SLO accounting for streaming disconnects.
- Provide guidance on what they should log/collect to distinguish client aborts vs server-side terminations.

Internal context:
- Ongoing tiered SLO + error budget program; streaming reliability is a primary SLI with explicit exclusions (client aborts, invalid requests, rate-limited requests).
- Need to ensure external wording matches measurement reality and avoids implying Redwood is accountable for client-side network drops.
2026-02-11 (Rachel Kim, Support) — Intake
Customer says: "We see streaming responses terminate unexpectedly ~0.3–0.8% of requests (varies by hour). We cannot tell if this is our ALB/proxy or Redwood. How do you count streaming disconnects for SLO? Do these show up as 5xx?" Requested examples and asked customer for request IDs + timestamps + region.

Asked customer to provide:
- Request IDs (x-redwood-request-id) for 10–20 failures
- Timestamps (UTC) and region
- Client error message + HTTP status (if any)
- Whether they received any SSE event indicating a server error vs silent disconnect
- Their client read timeout / proxy idle timeout settings

Set priority P2 (customer rollout concern, no clear Sev1 platform incident indicators).
2026-02-11 (Aisha Bello, SRE) — Initial guidance on classification
High-level SLI semantics (internal):
- Availability / success-rate SLI uses request-level outcome at gateway: counts as success when request completes with non-5xx and (for streaming) reaches terminal completion event; 429/4xx excluded by definition; explicit exclusions for client aborts.
- Streaming reliability SLI is measured via stream lifecycle events:
  - stream_opened
  - stream_completed (terminal)
  - stream_error (terminal)
  - client_abort (terminal, excluded)

If the connection is closed by the client (e.g., client cancels request, upstream proxy drops idle connection), we attempt to classify as client_abort and exclude from SLI. If the server terminates due to internal error, upstream model server failure, or gateway timeout, it is stream_error and counts against SLI.

Potential gray area: network resets where the gateway only sees a TCP reset without clear initiator. We’ve been improving taxonomy; some resets may currently be conservatively counted as stream_error if we can’t attribute to client. We should verify with sample request IDs.

Action: once we have request IDs, check gateway logs + stream termination reason tags in telemetry to see distribution (client_abort vs upstream_reset vs gateway_timeout).
2026-02-12 (Rachel Kim, Support) — Customer examples received
Customer sent 14 request IDs across us-east and eu-west. Their client stack: Node.js fetch + corporate proxy in front of app servers. They found their proxy has a 60s idle timeout and they sometimes generate >60s responses for long prompts.

Notable: several failures occur around 58–62s wall time.

Shared internally:
- request_id list attached in Zendesk side channel (not pasted here)
- sample: prompt length ~9k tokens, max_tokens=2048, streaming=true
2026-02-12 (Sergio Costa, Eng Platform - Dashboards/Alerts) — Quick look in logs/metrics
Pulled traces for 6 of the request IDs.
Findings:
- 4/6 show termination reason=client_disconnect (gateway saw downstream close) at ~60s.
- 1/6 shows upstream model server reset (reason=upstream_reset) around 12s; gateway returned no 5xx because stream was already open; stream_error emitted.
- 1/6 shows gateway idle timeout (reason=gateway_write_timeout) at ~65s; stream_error emitted.

So: majority appear client/proxy timeout; 2 look like platform-side stream errors.

Note: For the client_disconnect cases, we are emitting client_abort terminal event and excluding those from SLI accounting. For upstream_reset and gateway_write_timeout, these count against streaming reliability SLI.

Recommendation to customer: increase proxy idle timeout and/or send keep-alive comments (if supported) / reduce max_tokens / enforce server-side max stream duration. Also capture Redwood request_id for correlation.

Internal follow-up: ensure external docs clearly state that client disconnects are excluded; ambiguous resets may count if attribution is unclear.
2026-02-13 (Aisha Bello, SRE) — Customer-facing explanation drafted
Proposed response to customer (approved by Support):
1) What counts as a streaming failure: If Redwood terminates an active stream due to server-side error (upstream reset, gateway timeout, internal exception), we count that as a streaming reliability failure.
2) What is excluded: If the client closes the connection / cancels the request / downstream proxy times out, we classify as client abort and exclude from SLO/SLI calculations.
3) How it relates to 5xx: Not all streaming failures manifest as a single 5xx status code because the stream is already established; we track these via stream terminal events (completed/error/client-abort).
4) How to troubleshoot: Provide request IDs and timestamps; check client/proxy idle timeouts; consider setting max_tokens and enforcing app-level timeouts.

Also noted (transparent): In some rare cases where we cannot reliably attribute the disconnect initiator (e.g., certain TCP resets), we may conservatively treat it as a stream error. We are improving termination attribution and taxonomy as part of the tiered SLI work.

Linked internal references:
- SLI spec: sli-specification-api-gateway-and-routing
- Tiered SLO definitions (for internal alignment): tiered-slo-definitions-hosted-vs-dedicated

Asked Sergio to confirm the two platform-side failures are not part of a broader incident (looked isolated).
2026-02-13 (Rachel Kim, Support) — Sent response + mitigation steps
Sent explanation to customer plus recommended mitigations:
- Increase proxy idle timeout above worst-case generation duration (suggest 3–5 minutes if they allow long outputs)
- Reduce max_tokens and/or use shorter prompts to avoid >60s streams
- Ensure the client continues reading from the stream; avoid buffering that can appear idle
- Log and pass through x-redwood-request-id for each request

Also offered: We can provide a short "SLO accounting" blurb suitable for their internal review; pointed them to updated docs (in progress) and offered to hop on a call with Solutions Engineering if needed.

Customer reply: acknowledged proxy timeout likely culprit; asked if Redwood can send periodic keep-alive events. We replied: currently we don’t guarantee heartbeat events on every stream; best practice is to set proxy/client timeouts appropriately and keep responses bounded.
2026-02-14 (Aisha Bello, SRE) — Resolution + follow-ups
Resolution: Clarified SLI/SLO accounting for streaming disconnects; confirmed most observed disconnects were client-side proxy idle timeouts and are excluded from SLI as client aborts. Two platform-side stream errors identified (upstream_reset, gateway_write_timeout) were isolated and did not indicate a broader incident; they would count against streaming reliability SLI.

Follow-ups:
- Docs: add explicit section in customer-facing reliability docs clarifying streaming terminal events and exclusions (tracked under redwood-docs/pr-2211).
- Telemetry: evaluate whether any ambiguous disconnect reasons are being over-counted as stream_error; if so, improve classification/tags without increasing metric cardinality (roll into ongoing tiered SLI tagging work).

Marking ticket Resolved; waiting on customer confirmation not required.
Provided definition of how Redwood classifies streaming disconnects (client abort excluded; server-side terminations count), validated sample request IDs, identified primary cause as customer proxy idle timeout, and shared mitigations + documentation references.
payload.summary: Hosted streaming disconnects + questions on SLO accounting (client abort vs server-side stream failure)

Issue summary:
Customer reports intermittent high 95/99 latency and request timeouts (HTTP 504) when using the API with the structured output / json mode enabled. Failures spike for requests that produce long structured payloads (roughly >1500 tokens) and include large arrays in the JSON schema.

Impact:
- Multiple production endpoints for Acero Health returning 504s during peak traffic windows (1–2% error rate over last 12 hours).
- Significant 99th percentile tail latency increase (from ~450ms baseline to 2.5–6s) observed in customer telemetry and our per-customer route metrics.

Environment:
- Prod, region: us-east, model: redwood-4b-structured-v1, customers on enterprise plan with pinned model version.

Steps to reproduce (customer provided):
1) Call POST /v1/generate with content-type application/json and payload containing schema request for a large list output (500+ items).
2) Ensure max_tokens ~ 2k and temperature 0.2.
3) Observe response latency and occasional 504s after 30s deadline.

Observed logs / traces:
- Request trace: trace-id=tr-0a1b2c (link: /traces/tr-0a1b2c) shows worker served tokens up to final chunk then spent ~1.8s in post-processing before returning payload.
- Runtime worker logs show repeated lines: "POST_PROCESS: starting json validation/decoding, payload_size=3.4MB" and process CPU at ~95% during that interval.
- Gateway logs show 504s for requests where downstream worker exceeded gateway deadline.

Investigation notes so far:
- Reproduced in-house with a synthetic workload that mirrors customer's schema: enabling structured-output leads to an extra synchronous JSON.parse/validate step in serving-runtime after token generation completes.
- The post-processing is executed on the inference worker main thread and blocks the event loop; decoder + validation currently uses Python's json.loads + jsonschema.validate which are CPU-bound for large payloads.
- When streaming=true, tail latency reduces significantly because chunks are flushed earlier; however many customers rely on single final JSON object for schema validation and do not enable streaming.
- Hypothesis: structured-output mode adds a CPU-bound post-processing stage that scales poorly with large structured outputs and long arrays, causing long-tail latency and occasional deadline expirations.

Workarounds provided to customer:
- Short-term: reduce max_tokens or split requests into smaller batches of items to keep final JSON < ~1MB.
- Set streaming=true where application can tolerate partial results; streaming reduces tail latency by flushing earlier.
- Use model variant without strict structured enforcement (if customer can accept looser validation) to avoid post-processing step.
- As an immediate platform mitigation, we temporarily increased worker pool size for Acero's tenant in us-east to reduce queueing (applied 2026-03-13 15:40 UTC).

Next steps / proposed fixes:
- Engineering (runtime) to offload JSON parsing/validation to a separate worker thread or a dedicated post-processing service to avoid blocking the main inference loop. Linked PR: github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/1123 (WIP).
- Add safeguards in gateway: detect large structured outputs and proactively extend downstream deadlines or route to dedicated post-processing pool.
- Add telemetry to flag requests with large structured payloads and surface in Console per-route dashboards.
- Customer follow-up: schedule 30-minute call to review splitting guidance and confirm whether streaming=true is acceptable for their workflows.

Status: In Progress — engineering has a WIP PR to make JSON validation asynchronous; SRE applied temporary capacity increase for the tenant.

Additional notes:
2026-03-12 12:02 - Customer (Acero Health - Li Chen): We're seeing production timeouts during our morning peak when generating batch summaries. Changing to streaming is non-trivial due to our ingestion pipeline expectations. Please advise.
2026-03-13 16:12 - SRE (Nina Patel): Increased Acero tenant worker pool by +30% in us-east as temporary mitigation. Observed immediate drop in error rate to ~0.4% but tail latency still elevated for largest requests.
payload.summary: High tail latency and 504s when using 'json' structured output mode on long outputs (customer: Acero Health)

Issue summary:
Customer MapFlow Analytics reports a finalized invoice line that billed their mixed-model batch embedding job at the default hosted rate instead of their negotiated per-model rate for gptx-3.7-alpha. The batch included records sent with model aliases and a single job id; they expected the gptx-3.7-alpha segments to be billed at the contracted rate ID: MR-2025-GPTX.

Impact:
- Customer saw a ~$1,250 unexpectedly higher charge on the monthly invoice (Invoice #MF-202602).
- This is blocking reconciliation for their finance team and raising concerns about rate enforcement for mixed-model jobs.

Environment:
- Production (us-east-1).
- Customer using self-serve plan with a negotiated per-model override applied to model alias "gptx-3.7-alpha" via contract MR-2025-GPTX.
- Batch job submitted via client SDK v1.9.2 on 2026-02-20, job id: batch-9876-mf.

Steps to reproduce (from customer):
1) Create a mixed-model batch with 120k records where 60% routed to rwkv-large-v1 and 40% to gptx-3.7-alpha via model aliasing in a single job.
2) Submit as a single multipart request using key X-API-Key: ak_live_mapflow_01.
3) Allow processing to complete and wait for hourly postback to billing pipeline.

Expected behavior:
- Billing should apply contracted per-model rate to tokens generated by gptx-3.7-alpha segments (rate ID MR-2025-GPTX).
- Invoice line should split or annotate amounts so negotiated portion is visible.

Actual behavior:
- The finalized invoice aggregated the entire job under the default hosted embedding tariff for self_serve plan. No per-model override lines were present.

Logs / evidence attached by customer:
- invoice_pdf: MF-202602.pdf (customer provided PDF excerpt)
- usage_export.csv: shows job id batch-9876-mf with token counts and model_alias column populated
- SDK request snippet showing model aliases and single job id

Initial hypothesis:
- Postback aggregator may have collapsed multi-model segments into a single rate bucket when requests used a single job id and model aliases, losing the per-model override key during tag propagation.

Requested outcome:
- Adjust invoice to reflect negotiated rate for gptx-3.7-alpha portion or issue a credit for the delta.
- Root cause explanation and a mitigation plan to prevent re-occurrence (e.g., ensure per-model rate tags survive batching/reconciliation).

Issue summary: During the customer's evening traffic spike (approx 19:00–20:30 local), the dedicated reserved GPU pool servicing HelixDocs experienced a ~60% drop in sustained throughput and elevated p95/p99 latencies accompanied by intermittent request timeouts (504). Impact: HelixDocs reported degraded user experience across document-summarization endpoints; several production customers timed out and opened support channels. Environment: Dedicated reservation (pool-helix-001) in prod-us-east-1 using pinned redwood-open-7b-v2. Expected behavior: Pool autoscaler should scale to meet the concurrent request load and preserve p95 latency under the target SLO. Observed: slow/insufficient scale-up, repeated GPU context thrashing, and single-tenant batch job monopolization leading to head-of-line queueing.
1) Send synthetic burst traffic matching customer's evening mix: 150 concurrent streaming chat requests plus interleaved 30 long-sequence summarization jobs over 15 minutes.
2) Ensure pool is at min_replicas=2 and autoscaler policies are default cooldown=300s.
3) Observe serving runtime queuing, per-pod GPU utilization, and request latencies via /console/dedicated/pool-helix-001/dashboard.
4) Repeat with a heavy background batch job scheduled (simulate tenant's nightly maintenance job).
2026-03-12T19:07:02Z pool-helix-001 pod/serve-3 gpu0 util=97% gpu1 util=4% kernelexec=long-batch (suspicious)
2026-03-12T19:09:10Z autoscaler: desired_replicas=6 current=2 reason=cpu_or_gpu_utilization threshold_crossed but cooldown_active=true
2026-03-12T19:09:58Z serving-runtime: kv-cache-evict spike=high p99=2.8s request_id=ab12cd
Console graph: https://console.redwood/internal/dedicated/pool-helix-001?from=2026-03-12T18:50&to=2026-03-12T20:10
Support timeline: Slack #support-helixdocs thread https://redwood.slack.com/archives/C0678/example-thread
Initial hypothesis: noisy neighbor (HelixDocs scheduled batch) combined with autoscaler cooldown prevented timely scale-up.
Metric evidence: sustained single-GPU saturation spikes on pod/serve-3 while sibling GPU on same node stayed underutilized — indicates uneven job placement and lack of MIG slice balancing.
Autoscaler behavior: observed desired_replicas increased but actual scale-up delayed due to cooldown and node provisioning lag; min_replicas=2 was insufficient for burst shape.
Routing: customer had model pinned to redwood-open-7b-v2; automatic fallback to smaller variant was disabled by their pin, so no graceful degradation occurred.
Kubernetes scheduler logs show repeated pod evictions and rebindings during 19:05–19:20 window, likely due to preemption from background batch controller.
No evidence of hardware fault; telemetry and node-exporter show stable thermal/power readings.
Comparing to baseline day: peak qps pattern has higher long-sequence jobs during this customer's evening hours (customer usage pattern change not previously flagged).
Related runbook: /confluence/runbooks/dedicated-pool-autoscale-troubleshooting referenced for mitigation steps.
Priya Nair (Support) 2026-03-12: Customer reports increased 504s between 19:05–19:25. Provided sample request IDs and timestamps. Asked for urgent triage.
Diego Marquez (SRE) 2026-03-12: Picked up. Spun up extra nodes manually to stabilize pool; requesting customer logs for scheduled jobs.
HelixDocs (Customer) 2026-03-12: Confirmed a nightly ETL-style summarization run was changed last week to include longer context documents, which aligned with spike. They can throttle or reschedule if needed.
Diego Marquez (SRE) 2026-03-13: Found repeated GPU context switching on node-12; probe suggests our scheduler placed a multi-mig job next to latency-critical pods. Opening scheduler policy follow-up (INT-14202).
Priya Nair (Support) 2026-03-13: Communicated interim workaround to customer (enable model fallback + set per-tenant concurrency cap). Customer applied fallback and saw immediate p95 improvement.
Diego Marquez (SRE) 2026-03-13: Will work with infra to add a short-term autoscale tweak (lower cooldown to 60s for this reservation) and submit change to autoscaler config PR.
Combination of (1) a tenant-deployed high-cost batch job that saturated individual GPU slices, (2) an autoscaler policy with a long cooldown and low min_replicas that delayed scale-up, and (3) scheduler placement that left uneven GPU utilization on nodes (MIG slice imbalance). These three factors produced head-of-line queueing and intermittent request timeouts.
Applied a three-step mitigation: 1) temporarily lowered autoscaler cooldown to 60s and increased desired_replicas cap for pool-helix-001; 2) enabled customer-configured model fallback to a smaller variant to reduce per-request GPU time; 3) isolated nightly batch workload by applying a per-tenant concurrency policy and scheduling window. After changes, p95 returned to SLO within 12 minutes and no new 504s observed.
1) Update autoscaler policy: consider dynamic cooldown tied to event type and allow faster scale-up for dedicated reservations with SLOs.
2) Improve scheduler placement: add MIG-awareness and per-tenant isolation heuristics to avoid GPU slice monopolization.
3) Offer customer advisory: detect and notify customers when their usage pattern shifts to heavier long-sequence jobs and recommend model fallback or concurrency caps.
4) Postmortem: complete draft on Confluence and consider opt-in autoscale profile for high-variance customers.
5) Create follow-up internal task to audit reserved pools for min_replicas values that are too low for typical burst shapes (INT-14202).

Issue summary: Customer reports intermittent control-plane authentication failures and frequent gRPC keepalive resets for their Private deployment. The failures began after a network vendor upgrade that introduced an overlay VXLAN fabric between on-prem aggregation routers and the VPC transit gateway.
1) Deploy a multi-shard model request via customer's Private deployment (region us-west-2) to trigger control-plane token refresh and model artifact streaming.
2) Observe gRPC keepalive probes between serving nodes and control-plane endpoints when under sustained 90-110 rps request load.
3) Correlate with times when upstream overlay path is used (VXLAN encapsulation) vs fallback underlay path.
4) Reproduce by toggling the overlay interface MTU on a test path (1500 -> 1400) while streaming a ~20MB model shard range request.
Expected: Stable gRPC sessions and successful token refresh/manifest fetches without transient auth errors. Observed: Periodic gRPC stream resets, token refresh failures (401), and partial shard reads (retries).
serving-node-1/grpc: keepalive timeout, last_ack=22ms, rtt=120ms
control-plane/auth: 401 token refresh error for instance i-0abcd1234 (error=stream-reset)
tcpdump: IP (tos 0x0, ttl 64, id 54321) 10.0.2.14.48814 > 10.10.1.8.443: Flags [P.], seq 1:1437, ack 1, win 29200, length 1436
tcpdump: [fragmented] outer-ethertype=0x0800 vxlan vni 100 inner IP len 1600 -> indicates inner frame larger than underlay MTU
artifact-fetch: range-request partial, server returned 206 but subsequent GET returned truncated chunk, client logged EPIPE
customers-net-device: syslog: vxlan: packet-too-large, dropped frame

Additional notes:
2026-03-01 15:28 - Customer (NetOps - Jamie Lin): Uploaded pcaps and confirmed VXLAN VNI=100 with underlay MTU 1400 after upgrade; previously underlay was 1500. Noted some devices report 'fragmentation required' errors.
2026-03-03 09:33 - Customer (Jamie Lin): Applied temporary MTU increase on underlay nodes (to 9000) and disabled TX offload on serving hosts; reported gRPC resets reduced to near-zero for a 4-hour test window.
Hypothesis 1: VXLAN encapsulation increased packet size beyond underlay MTU; fragments get dropped or reordered by intermediate devices, breaking gRPC/TLS expectations.
Hypothesis 2: Host-side TCP segmentation offload (TSO/GSO) combined with small underlay MTU leads to large offloaded segments that are fragmented by network, causing corrupted TLS record boundaries on the receiver.
Test performed: Ran tcpdump on serving-node and underlay router. Observed outer (encapsulating) packets with length > 1500 and intermediate syslog messages 'packet-too-large' on vendor gear.
Test performed: Disabled TSO/GSO on serving nodes (ethtool -K eth0 tso off gso off) and re-ran streaming tests; saw immediate reduction in keepalive resets.
Correlation: Incident windows aligned with vendor overlay rollforward which changed default underlay MTU from 1500 to 1400 and enabled VXLAN with 50 bytes overhead.
Related notes: Customer's PMTU discovery was intermittently blocked by an inline firewall which returned ICMP unreachable inconsistently, worsening the fragmentation behavior.
Observed side-effects: Partial artifact reads and retries added latency, provoking more frequent token refresh attempts that then hit race conditions during short-lived stream resets.
Short-term workaround (applied by customer): Increased underlay MTU to jumbo frames (9000) on aggregation routers and disabled TSO/GSO on serving hosts. Result: gRPC resets and token refresh 401 frequency dropped to near zero in validation window.
Root cause: VXLAN overlay encapsulation created inner packets that exceeded underlay MTU; intermediate gear dropped or mishandled fragments and ICMP PMTU messages were intermittently blocked by an inline firewall, breaking TLS/gRPC assumptions and causing token refresh races.
Permanent remediation options:
  - Preferred: Align underlay MTU to account for VXLAN overhead (increase MTU or enable jumbo frames across fabric) and ensure PMTU ICMPs are permitted end-to-end.
  - Alternative: Configure host-level MSS clamping to reduce inner packet sizes (e.g., iptables/netfilter rule to clamp MSS to 1350) and keep TSO/GSO disabled on serving hosts if hardware offload is incompatible.
  - Add monitoring: SRE recommends adding synthetic long-range artifact fetch checks and a packet-fragmentation gauge to the customer's network dashboards to detect regressions.
Action items completed: Customer implemented underlay MTU change and host TSO/GSO disable; SRE provided a short runbook for MSS clamping and PMTU verification. Follow-up scheduled to verify stability over 7 days.
Follow-up: Recommend change request with network vendor to ensure VXLAN MTU requirements documented and for firewall rule to allow ICMP 'Fragmentation needed' messages to flow.
payload.summary: Intermittent control-plane auth failures and gRPC keepalive resets from private deployment behind VXLAN overlay (MTU mismatch)

Issue summary: Starting ~2026-03-14T03:10 UTC, Veridian Health reported persistent elevated 5xx responses (mostly 502/503) for a high-volume feature that issues many short-lived generate calls (avg 120ms). Impact: ~30% of requests returned 5xx over a 2-hour window; customer-facing product degraded. Environment: production, dedicated tenant on us-west pool, tenant pinned to a large quantized model. Initial hypothesis: api-gateway retries or connection churn. Further investigation pointed to upstream serving-runtime CPU and disk IO saturation caused by concurrent prefetch/verification tasks triggered by short-lived requests for a newly pinned model artifact.
1) Tenant pinned to redwood/llama-3-70b-quant via Console. 2) Issue a high QPS of short requests (payloads ~80 tokens, per-request latency target low) with many concurrent connections that connect/disconnect per request. 3) Observe api-gateway 502/503 rates increase and backend runtimes exhibiting high system CPU and many prefetch worker processes kicking off model artifact verification. 4) Reproduce in prod-us-west with customer workload simulator at ~350 req/s.

Verification uses CPU and disk IO; when multiple verifier jobs overlap they starve request-serving threads and cause request timeouts.

Issue summary:
Customer Nimbus Analytics reported a sustained increase in 5xx responses (predominantly 502/503) on their mixed workload routes (chat + embedding bulk upload) beginning 2026-03-10 02:00 UTC. The elevated error rate correlated with a pattern of short-chat sessions interleaved with large embedding uploads from the same tenant.

Impact:
- Customer saw ~12% overall error rate on their ingestion and chat endpoints for ~90 minutes, causing failed ingestion jobs and degraded UX.
- Several upstream serving-runtime processes restarted with OOM-like termination logs; requests for the tenant repeatedly failed until runtime pods were recycled.
- Business impact: ingestion backfill jobs aborted; customer success escalated to enterprise support.

Environment:
- Redwood hosted (prod - us-east-1)
- Tenant: Nimbus Analytics (enterprise, dedicated routing)
- Routes affected: /v1/chat/stream (streaming), /v1/embeddings/upload (batch)
- Models serving: text-embed-2-large (batch), redwood-chat-v1 (streaming)

Timeline & reproduction steps observed by Support:
1) 2026-03-10 01:58 UTC - first anomaly detected by SLO alerting: 5xx rate > 5% for tenant routes.
2) 02:00-02:20 UTC - spikes of short chat sessions (~100-300ms) interleaving with large embedding multipart uploads.
3) 02:21 UTC - several runtime pods handling the tenant showed abrupt exits and restart loops.
4) 02:45 UTC - apigw backpressure increased, connection queue depth rose and further request failures observed.
5) 03:20 UTC - mitigations (rate-limit tenant burst, re-route heavy uploads to lower-priority path) applied; error rate began to decline.

Steps to reproduce (lab):
- From a tenant-shared VM, simulate 30 concurrent tiny chat sessions (short prompt) while concurrently uploading 4 large multi-part embedding payloads (~500MB each) with default route priorities.
- Observe apigw connection queues and ingress prioritizer metrics; monitor serving-runtime memory and process restarts.

Logs / metrics collected:
- apigw metrics: per-tenant accept-queue depth, stream slot allocation, hedged-retry counts.
- prioritizer traces: long-tail allocation time for streaming routes, large-scale reassignments of slots during mixed bursts.
- serving-runtime logs: abrupt SIGABRT-like exits with thread-stack traces indicating memory pressure during KV cache operations.
- k8s events: pod OOMKill and rapidly successive restarts (~3 restarts within 2 minutes).
- dashboards: tenant-level 5xx spike, ingress priority share dropped to <2% for streaming traffic while embeddings consumed >95% of active slots.

Investigation notes:
- Initial hypothesis that embedding upload size alone triggered NVMe iowait was not supported: host disk metrics were within normal bounds and IO queue depth did not correlate strongly with crash windows.
- Observed that the ingress prioritizer assigned ephemeral slots aggressively to embedding routes when multipart upload flows established many concurrent sub-connections. This left near-zero minimum share for streaming routes for that tenant.
- The prioritizer algorithm allowed long-running batch flows to saturate the route slot pool because it did not enforce a minimum per-route share when tie-breaking among similar priority classes.
- When streaming traffic was starved, apigw queued streams and attempted hedged retries; the resulting connection churn amplified backend load, causing serving-runtime to allocate larger KV caches and then hit memory pressure leading to process exits.
- Root cause: ingress prioritizer bug that fails to enforce a configured "min-share" floor for streaming routes under mixed-workload tie conditions, enabling batch flows to monopolize ephemeral slots and drive a cascade of hedged retries and runtime restarts.

Mitigation / workaround applied:
- Support applied an immediate tenant-level burst throttle for embedding uploads at 02:30 UTC (reduced concurrent upload threads) which allowed streaming slot share to recover.
- Routing rule added to demote large embedding uploads to a lower-priority lane (noisy background) to prevent slot monopolization while a permanent fix was prepared.
- Customer advised to shard uploads into smaller pieces and schedule heavy backfills outside peak windows as a short-term operational mitigation.

Fix and rollout:
- Engineering implemented PR https://github.com/redwood-inference/ingress/pull/4582 which enforces a configurable min-share floor per route and improves tie-breaking to prefer round-robin among tenants within the same priority class.
- Patch was staged to canary in us-east-1 on 2026-03-11 10:00 UTC, validated with synthetic mixed-workload tests that mimic the reported pattern.
- Full prod rollout completed 2026-03-11 15:30 UTC. Monitoring showed tenant 5xx returned to baseline (~<0.5%) within 20 minutes post-rollout.

Resolution & follow-up:
- Status: Resolved. Root cause fixed and deployed; customer confirmed successful ingestion on follow-up call.
- Runbook action: add a new observability check to detect per-tenant slot monopolization and trigger automated demotion (safeguard) if a route's share falls below configured min-share for >30s. Ticket created: INT-4402 (internal) to add the safeguard.
- Engineering follow-ups: expose min-share thresholds in tenant configuration UI and document recommended settings for mixed workloads.

Notes for CS/SRE:
- If customers with mixed batch+stream workloads report elevated 5xx, check prioritizer "effective-share" metrics first and inspect concurrent sub-connection counts for multipart uploads.
- Short-term remediation steps: throttle tenant embedding concurrency and apply routing demotion; long-term: ensure min-share and rate-limits are tuned per tenant workload profile.
payload.summary: Mixed-workload priority starvation causing elevated 5xx rate and runtime restarts for Nimbus Analytics

payload.description:
Customer NoteWave Mobile reports intermittent truncated final sentences and missing terminal metadata on long-lived SSE streams when a mobile device transitions between cellular and Wi-Fi. Issue only observed when requests route through our CDN with HTTP/3 enabled. The stream appears to resume but the final 'choice' object and terminal metadata are not delivered to the client, leaving responses incomplete.
Multiple mobile users intermittently receive partial completions which breaks NoteWave's in-app summarization flow. Incidence is ~0.6% of mobile streaming sessions for this customer during peak churn events, causing user-visible content loss and support tickets.
3) Observe stream resume behavior; sometimes the stream connection migrates and the client receives duplicated prefix tokens followed by no terminal 'choice' object and missing metadata.
Client shows partial final sentence and no closing metadata event. Server logs show QUIC CONNECTION_CLOSE / path migration events from the edge and application reports stream resumed with 'end' flag but client-side parser does not receive it.
On path migration or QUIC connection handoff, the stream should either fully resume with terminal metadata or fail-over gracefully to HTTP/1.1/WebSocket with consistent finalization semantics.
edge: QUIC_PATH_MIGRATION peer=198.51.100.23 conn_id=0x7f3ab4ff event=path_migration
app: stream_id=0x9a3f, session=notewave-usr-123, last_offset=32456, resume_attempt=1, send_end=true
client: SDK v1.4.2: recv RESET_STREAM (error_code=0x0), then new stream started with duplicate prefix tokens, no end event
cdn: cf-edge: quic_reset_count=12 over 1h window for this customer
- Reproduced in lab using simulated network handoff with HTTP/3 via our staging CDN; observed connection migration and partial reassembly in the SSE framing layer.
- Hypothesis: CDN/edge does a QUIC handoff and buffers/drops final datagrams; our streaming resume token is tied to connection-level offsets that don't map across QUIC path migrations. Client SDK assumes idempotent resume semantics which do not hold when edge discards the trailing datagram containing terminal metadata.
- Traced a sample session: incoming datagram containing terminal 'choice' arrived at edge but was marked retransmittable and not forwarded to origin before path migration; subsequent path re-establishment created a new stream lacking that datagram.
- No recent code changes in serving runtime that modify end-of-stream markers. Similar issues were not seen when HTTP/1.1 or WebSocket transport used.
Advise NoteWave to pin transport to WebSocket or HTTP/1.1 in the SDK until fix is deployed. Suggested client-side mitigation: request finalization polling (issue a short non-streaming completion at end of session) as a fallback to fetch missing terminal metadata.
In progress — engineering to add defensive resume semantics: attach a resumable terminal ACK to application-level session state and make the edge forward terminal datagrams to origin before performing QUIC path migration when possible. Also implementing server-side idempotent finalization so clients may re-request missing terminal metadata. CDN config change to disable aggressive quic_path_migration for streaming endpoints being evaluated.
1) ENG to prototype terminal ACK (PR referenced above) and run chaos test with QUIC migration scenarios (owner: Liam Patel).
2) SRE to add metric quic_reset_count per customer and alert when >0.5% (owner: Samira Gomez).
3) Customer success to onboard NoteWave to a temporary WebSocket-only configuration and collect telemetry (owner: Jordan Kim).
4) Re-run regression tests and release SDK update with opt-out for HTTP/3 (target: 2026-03-20).

Issue summary:
Customer reports that admin impersonation requests to the admin-ops endpoint are returning 403 when performed from their tenant admin console. The failure started after a proxy upgrade in the customer's private deployment. Impact: admins cannot impersonate users in tenant-scoped environments, blocking support and admin workflows for multiple teams at the customer.

Impact:
- Nimbus Health admins unable to impersonate users via /admin/impersonate (403).
- Operational impact: blocked troubleshooting and support actions for ~10 teams, estimated >2 hours/day lost productivity.
- Risk: escalation to enterprise support if not resolved within 48 hours.

Environment:
- Private deployment (customer-managed control plane) running across us-west-2 region.
- Identity stack: identity-proxy v1.12.0 (customer installed), auth-service v2.3.1, api-gateway v3.0.0.

Steps to reproduce:
1) Login as tenant admin to customer console (tenant ID: tenant-nimbus-43).
2) Open impersonation UI and attempt to impersonate a standard user.
3) Observe network request to https://api.private.nimbus.example/admin/impersonate returns 403.
4) Capture request/response headers and auth cookie.

Observed logs and headers (redacted):
- Response: 403 Forbidden {"error":"forbidden","reason":"missing_tenant_claim"}
- auth cookie: "rw_session=eyJhbGciOi..." (cookie name prefixed by "__Tenant_tenant-nimbus-43_rw_session")
- identity-proxy access log: trace_id=trc-7b2a9c, upstream_status=403, upstream_error="rbac: tenant claim not present"

Notes: The cookie name is being rewritten/prefixed at the edge to include the tenant scope (pattern __Tenant_<tenantid>_<cookie>). The RBAC layer expects an "org_id" claim in the session JWT payload. We see the JWT payload on the proxy decode contains no "org_id" claim, whereas the original session token prior to proxy rewrite included org_id.

Additional context:
- Customer recently upgraded their ingress edge component (third-party CDN/proxy) which inserts a cookie-name prefix to isolate cookies between tenants.
- This prefixing step also triggers a code path in our identity-proxy which attempts to normalize cookie names and, due to a race in header parsing, strips a small Base64 chunk from the cookie value for some prefixes. That truncated value decodes to a JWT missing the org_id claim (signature still valid).

Expected behavior:
- Cookie-name prefixing by external proxies should not modify cookie value bytes. identity-proxy should correctly locate and decode the full session token and preserve claims including org_id.

Workarounds attempted:
- Customer temporarily disabled cookie-name prefixing at the edge and impersonation succeeded immediately.
- Support suggested passing tenant id via X-Forwarded-Tenant header; customer cannot enable that pattern in their CDN.

Action requested:
- Investigate and provide code fix and backported patch for identity-proxy to avoid truncation when cookie names include tenant prefixes, add unit and integration tests covering prefixed cookie names, and provide a recommended patched binary for the customer's private deployment.
1) Authenticate as tenant admin for tenant-nimbus-43 on customer's private deployment.
2) Trigger POST /admin/impersonate with target user id.
3) Observe 403 and check identity-proxy access log for trace_id trc-7b2a9c.
4) Compare cookie value before and after edge prefixing (if accessible) or disable prefixing to confirm behavior.
identity-proxy[2026-03-10T13:42:11Z] trace_id=trc-7b2a9c method=POST path=/admin/impersonate upstream_status=403 error="rbac: tenant claim not present"
auth cookie received: __Tenant_tenant-nimbus-43_rw_session=eyJhbGciOiJI...truncated...
(original cookie before prefixing captured by customer: rw_session=eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJvcmdfaWQiOiJ0ZW5hbnQtbmltYnVzLTQzIiwidXNlcl9pZCI6IjQ1NjcifQ.SIG)

Initial hypothesis: edge prefixing mutated cookie name only; however reproduction shows cookie value truncated in a deterministic way when prefix includes tenant pattern. Team reproduced locally by adding prefix to cookie name and confirmed identity-proxy v1.12.0 normalization routine was using fixed-offset substring logic that mis-calculated start index when prefix length exceeded 12 chars. Eng (Marco) added debug logs and confirmed trim logic triggered. Related internal ticket INT-4421 tracks normalization rewrite from 2025 which introduced the bug.

- Repro on dev: yes (added integration test).
- Root cause: cookie-name normalization routine in identity-proxy uses brittle offset math when splitting name by underscores. When cookie name contains additional underscores from tenant prefix, normalization logic treated part of the cookie value as name separator and sliced the value buffer incorrectly.

Work for fix:
- Replace substring arithmetic with explicit parsing using lastIndexOf and boundary checks.
- Add test cases for prefixes with multiple underscores and long tenant ids.
- Prepare backport to v1.11.x and patch for v1.12.0.

Links: Slack thread #support (https://slack.redwood.ai/archives/C05SUPP123/p1650000000000000), runbook: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/SUPPORT/tenant-cookie-scope-runbook, internal ticket INT-4421.
Support (Aisha): Opened with customer-reported 403 on impersonation endpoint. Attached proxy logs and customer-captured cookie samples.
Customer (N. Harris, Nimbus Health): Confirmed issue began after their CDN upgrade last night. They can reproduce consistently and provided a dump of the original cookie before the CDN rewrites it.
Eng (Marco Diaz): Reproduced locally with prefixed cookie name; identity-proxy normalization routine uses fixed offsets. Preparing patch and unit tests. Blocking: need a signed backport approval for release to private deployments.
Support (Aisha): Customer requested ETA for patch and whether a hotfix binary is available. Provided temporary mitigation instructions to disable cookie prefixing and noted potential deploy window.
Eng (Marco Diaz): Patch ready in PR https://github.com/redwood-inference/identity-proxy/pull/1234. Will prepare backport PR to v1.11.x and coordinate with Release for a security-style hotfix release.
Support (Aisha): Communicated to customer that hotfix will be available and asked for preferred maintenance window. Customer requested ASAP — they will accept off-hours deploy tonight.
Fix implemented in identity-proxy: replaced brittle substring logic with robust parsing using lastIndexOf and explicit boundary checks. Backported patch applied to v1.11.x and v1.12.0 branch. Release artifacts published and hotfix binary provided to customer. Added unit and integration tests for prefixed cookie names and tenant ids containing underscores.
- PR merged: https://github.com/redwood-inference/identity-proxy/pull/1234
- Backport PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/identity-proxy/pull/1240
- Hotfix binary delivered to Nimbus Health and applied to their private cluster on 2026-03-11 22:30 UTC by their infra team.
- Post-deploy validation: impersonation requests succeeded, no more 403s observed.
- Follow-up: Add monitoring alert to detect JWT payloads missing org_id claim and a dashboard to track impersonation success rate per-tenant.
- Customer confirmed closure and requested a short postmortem; follow-up action: Support to provide one within 3 business days.

Issue summary: Around 2026-03-13 02:12 UTC we observed a sudden, sustained increase in 5xx responses (primarily 502/503) for a subset of Intellibook traffic in us-east-1. The error pattern presents as a sawtooth: short spikes of elevated 5xx over a 2–3 hour window, correlated with connection pruning events on edge proxies and aggressive keepalive trimming from the autoscaler when a tenant shift occurred.

Impact: Intellibook reported timeouts and degraded throughput for interactive chat endpoints. Estimated 25–35% of their requests that touch redwood-2.0 experienced transient failures; customer business impact: reduced availability for their live editor sessions. Only dedicated-tier tenant traffic observed; other tenants unaffected.

Environment: prod-us-east (us-east-1), affected pool: dedicated-gpu-pool-12, ingress layer: edge-apigw-v4, runtime pool: redwood-runtime-ssd-12.

Timeline (UTC):
- 02:08: autoscaler triggered a tenant shift (traffic moved from pool-12 to pool-8 for capacity balancing).
- 02:12: first 502s observed in Intellibook traces; Grafana shows accept-queue depth drop and connection pruning spikes.
- 02:14: Keepalive metrics show abrupt drop in active keepalive sessions on edge-apigw-v4.
- 02:20: Runtime pods start reporting short-lived OOM-adj warnings and increased latency; connection resets observed in proxy logs.
- 04:30: manual mitigation applied (disable aggressive connection pruning; bump keepalive window), error rates return to baseline by ~04:45.

Steps to reproduce:
1) Simulate tenant traffic shift (move 30–50% of tenant sessions from one dedicated pool to another) while running streaming chat sessions with long-lived connections.
2) Trigger autoscaler policy that performs connection pruning/route rebalancing.
3) Observe 502/503 spikes and accept queue fluctuations in ingress metrics.

Observed logs/metrics:
- Grafana dashboard: apigw.accept_queue.length spiked then collapsed; apigw.conn_prune.count increased from 0 to >120/min during bursts.
- Sample proxy log lines (edge-apigw-v4):
  "[2026-03-13T02:13:21Z] WARN conn_prune: pruning 18 keepalives for tenant intellibook (pool-12 -> pool-8)"
  "[2026-03-13T02:13:22Z] ERROR upstream: read reset by peer (downstream conn closed) status=502 request_id=..."
- Runtime logs: short-lived kv-cache lock warnings and GC feedback loops; no full runtime process crashes but transient evictions and increased latency.

Initial hypothesis: The autoscaler connection-pruning logic aggressively trimmed keepalive pools during a tenant shift, causing sudden mass connection resets. The edge API gateway then retried requests which amplified load on the target runtime pods; a subset of runtimes hit memory pressure/GC spikes (not full OOM kills) and returned 502/503. Downstreams amplified due to short retry policy and insufficient backlog headroom at the runtime side.

Temporary mitigation applied:
- Disabled aggressive conn-pruning for pool-12 at 02:22 UTC.
- Increased keepalive window on edge-apigw-v4 from 60s to 180s for Intellibook routes.
- Applied a soft cap on concurrent prefetch threads for the affected runtime pool.
Result: 5xx spike subsided within ~20 minutes; customer traffic restored.

Resolution (work in progress): Root cause appears to be an interaction between the new autoscaler pruning algorithm and the edge keepalive reuse heuristics under rapid tenant shifts. A permanent fix will require:
- Autoscaler change to perform staggered pruning with backoff and health checks.
- API gateway change to drain keepalives more gracefully and avoid immediate retries that amplify pressure.
- Runtime tuning to increase accept queue headroom during tenant rebalances.

Follow-ups: Create a postmortem, coordinate code changes across infra (autoscaler) and edge (apigw), and schedule a controlled test of tenant-shift scenarios in staging with canarying.

See description timeline. Quick repro: in staging, shift ~40% of sessions off a warmed pool while running long-lived streaming sessions; enable conn-prune policy; watch apigw.accept_queue and apigw.conn_prune metrics.
apigw.accept_queue.length: dropped from 120->10 during pruning; apigw.conn_prune.count: spike to >120/min; runtime.latency.p95 increased 2x; 5xx-rate for intellibook endpoints rose from 0.4% to ~28% during window.
- Correlated timestamps between apigw logs and runtime traces show pruning events precede 502s by ~1-3s.
- No evidence of kernel OOMs or node reboots.
- Autoscaler logs show prune job started as part of 'pool consolidation' routine after utilization metric crossed threshold.
- Linked INT-4210 contains earlier discussion about pruning algorithm concerns.
- Related PR https://github.com/redwood/infra/pull/8362 contains a change to pruning heuristics introduced two weeks ago.
Applied immediate config changes (disabled aggressive pruning, bumped keepalive), and temporarily exempted Intellibook from pool consolidation until the autoscaler fix ships.
