payload.description:
Issue summary: Customer observed duplicate external side-effects (HTTP webhook calls to their downstream job queue) after a transient networking blip during a streaming function-call session. Impact: Duplicate jobs created, downstream idempotency broken, customer had to de-duplicate resulting jobs manually for ~45 minutes. Environment: Dedicated tenant on prod us-east-1 using Go SDK v1.13.2 with default retry/backoff settings and jitter enabled. Steps to reproduce:
1) Open a streaming function-call session with a long-running tool invocation that posts to a customer webhook (their webhook acknowledges with 200 only after job is enqueued).
2) Induce a transient TCP connection interruption (short ~2s outage) between client and Redwood edge (simulated by dropping packets).
3) Client Go SDK attempts streaming resume and applies exponential backoff with jitter before reconnect.
4) On reconnect, the SDK replays buffered events; due to race between resumed ACKs from server and an in-flight webhook confirmation, two distinct funcall acceptance/ack sequences are observed by the orchestration layer. Expected behavior: At-most-once side-effect for a tool invocation when customer follows funcall confirmation pattern, or clear guidance that clients must attach idempotency tokens at tool call level. Actual behavior: Two webhook posts with different transient confirmation tokens (non-deduplicated), resulting in duplicate jobs.
Relevant logs included below and reproduced with minimal Go client sample in steps.

Create a streaming funcall session using Go SDK v1.13.2 and register a tool that posts to an HTTP webhook and waits for 200
Simulate a 1.5-3s network disconnect between client and the Redwood edge during the funcall response streaming
Allow client SDK to auto-reconnect using default backoff+jitter
Observe webhook logs: two separate POSTs within 1-4s window for the same logical funcall id
Edge request id: edge-6b2f4a9c
Serving runtime trace: trace_id=sr-9c7e-1, step=kvcache-resume, latency=17ms
Customer webhook logs: POST /enqueue jobId=null payload.job_ref=abc123 status=200 at 2026-03-12T15:03:21Z
Customer webhook logs: POST /enqueue jobId=null payload.job_ref=abc123 status=200 at 2026-03-12T15:03:23Z

Additional notes:
2026-03-12 - SRE (Riley Thompson): Confirmed transient packet drops seen on edge host edge-32 in us-east-1; serving-runtime reported resume handshake succeeded twice for same stream id.
2026-03-13 - Eng (Ethan Chen): Reproduced locally with Go SDK; hypothesis: ACK race between server-side funcall confirmation and client-side replay when jittered reconnect causes duplicated confirmation path.
2026-03-14 - Customer (Vectorly Analytics) via CS: Requested mitigation guidance and whether Redwood can enforce stricter at-most-once semantics for funcall tool side-effects.
Reproducer: local cluster test replicated duplicate POSTs when client jitter value > 300ms and server-side delayed webhook confirmation occurred during reconnect window.
Findings: Server will accept a resumed stream and re-emit pending funcall events; if the original funcall was already delivered to the tool, and tool's confirmation path is not tied to a stable idempotency token, downstreams will see duplicate side-effects.
Root cause hypothesis: Combination of (1) streaming replay semantics that re-queue pending funcall deliverables on resume, (2) client-side jittered reconnect that causes slightly different sequencing of ACKs/confirmations, and (3) lack of enforced funcall-level idempotency token by the platform for legacy tool integrations.
Edge host network glitch correlated with restart of connection worker; serving-runtime accepted new session and re-sent buffered ops without marking them as 'replay' in webhook payload headers.
Related: SUP-41209 had similar webhook duplicate symptom but in that case header mapping was the trigger; here it's replay ordering + missing idempotency token.
Workaround provided: recommend customer add a strong idempotency key in the tool payload (X-Vectorly-Job-Id or similar) and make downstream webhook idempotent. Short-term change: Go SDK patch to include per-funcall idempotency token by default on replay (PR https://github.com/redwood-inference/sdk-go/pull/512) — roll forward in canary today in us-east-1. Long-term: platform change to annotate replayed funcall events with 'X-Redwood-Replay: true' header and emit durable funcall id to allow automatic dedupe in edge and in tooling. Tracking engineering epic: ENG-STREAM-2026.
ENG: Add replay flag header and durable funcall id in serving-runtime (assigned ENG-STREAM-2026)
SDK: backport default per-funcall idempotency token to v1.13.x and v1.14 (PRs created)
SRE: add alert to detect >1 external POSTs for same funcall id within 10s window on edge hosts
payload.summary: Client backoff jitter + streaming resume leads to out-of-order funcall ACKs and duplicate side-effects

payload.description:
Issue summary: Customer runs a multi-step orchestration where the model is asked to call two external tools in sequence (1) a synchronous DB write via a webhook and (2) a long-running external job kickoff via a webhook. During streaming responses the SDK client experiences a partial-ack (ACK) for the first tool call but the final stream disconnects before the server confirms the overall request completion. Impact: The customer's webhook for step (1) receives the POST and performs a side-effect (payment capture). After the streaming reconnect, SDKs retry the request and the webhook receives a second POST, causing duplicate side-effects. This happens inconsistently and appears correlated with client reconnects from mobile networks. Environment: Production using Python SDK v1.9.3 and Go SDK v0.8.4 behind an API Gateway. Customer is on an enterprise plan with reserved Dedicated capacity in us-east.
1) Configure orchestration that issues two tool calls sequentially from a single streamed generation: first webhook A (synchronous side-effect), then webhook B (async job kickoff).
2) Use Python SDK with streaming=true and set small TCP keepalive timeouts to emulate flaky mobile network.
3) Trigger generation and forcibly interrupt the stream mid-output (simulate network blip).
4) Reconnect client and let SDK perform its default retry behavior without providing explicit idempotency keys.
5) Observe webhook A receiving duplicate POSTs and performing duplicate side-effects; webhook B sometimes receives duplicate job kickoffs as well.

Initial hypothesis: SDK retry logic resends entire user request when stream is interrupted and server does not return a final success marker; tool calls inside the generation are therefore re-executed unless idempotency metadata is included.
Observed that serving-runtime acknowledges individual tool_call dispatch to external webhook with internal logs, but the client sees only stream-level success/failure. If stream-level handshake is lost, client retries the outer request causing duplicate downstream side-effects.

Go SDK behaves similarly when configured to auto-retry; differences observed in default retry backoff timing causing varied duplication rates.
No evidence of server replay from queue/backoff — duplicates originate from client-side retry of the full generation call.

Issue summary: Sandbridge Health (dedicated customer) experienced a 20-minute period of elevated 5xx responses from the inference endpoint which coincided with a 3x billing increase and multiple duplicate completions returned to their users. Impact: customer-visible duplicate replies (same prompt returned twice with different response IDs), elevated token billing for the window, and large user-facing latency spikes. Timeline (high level): 2026-03-05T18:02Z - first 502 spike observed in us-east serving cluster; 18:05Z - Sandbridge opened a support chat and reported duplicate completions; 18:08Z - Support triaged as P0 and routed to SRE/Runtime on-call; 18:12Z - automatic fallback routing triggered from primary quantized variant to compatibility variant; 18:18Z - circuit-breaker misclassification allowed duplicated retry path; 18:22Z - mitigation (disable aggressive fallback and throttle retries) applied; 18:30Z - visible error rates returned to baseline. Steps to reproduce (customer pattern): 1) Send high-concurrency streaming generation requests pinned to redwood-open-7b-quantized with idempotency header X-Req-Id; 2) During transient kernel-selection failure the gateway returned 502; 3) Client retried at the SDK layer without preserving idempotency header; 4) Routing fallback sent retry to a different model variant, producing a second (distinct) completion. Logs and artifacts: request traces, streaming logs, and billing deltas attached on Confluence page. Investigation notes: initial hypothesis focused on autoscale latency causing 502s; deeper traces show a transient kernel-selection OOM on a subset of quantized workers leading to 502/503. The API gateway retried the request to an available host which returned a different model variant. The customer's SDK retried client-side without keeping the original idempotency X-Req-Id header, which prevented dedup logic from de-duplicating retries. Root cause: three contributing factors - (1) kernel-selection edge-case produced transient 5xxs on quantized pool, (2) gateway fallback policy routed retries to a different compatible variant, (3) client-side retry behavior dropped idempotency metadata, allowing duplicate completions to be billed. Resolution: ramped down automatic fallback policy for the quantized pool; applied a short-lived rate-limit/quick-shed to thin out retry storms; coordinated with Sandbridge to apply an SDK patch ensuring idempotency header persistence. Billing remediation: flagged the affected window for manual review and issued a credit for the excess token usage after customer agreement. Follow-up: runbook updates and longer-term fixes scheduled.

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customer NovaLabs reported a 30-50% drop in steady-state throughput and sporadic tail-latency spikes after they enabled a mixed set of per-tenant optimizer flags (per-tenant quantization profile + aggressive KV prefetch + adaptive micro-batching). The change was applied to two model variants (llama2-13b-q4_0 and llama2-13b-fp16) as part of cost-optimization testing in their Dedicated pool.

Impact:
- NovaLabs production traffic saw request throughput fall from ~1.2k rps to ~650 rps during peak periods.
- Tail latency (p99) increased from ~180ms to ~820ms for streaming requests.
- Two customer endpoints experienced increased 5xx transient errors related to internal timeouts.

Environment:
- Redwood Dedicated - us-east cluster (gpu-pool-dedicated-7)
- Tenant: nova-prod (customer_id: c-0147)
- Model variants: llama2-13b-q4_0 (quantized), fallback llama2-13b-fp16

Steps to reproduce (customer supplied):
1) Send steady concurrent streaming load via their integration: curl -N POST https://api.redwood.example/v1/generate -H "Authorization: Bearer <key>" -H "X-Redwood-Tenant: nova-prod" -d '{"model":"llama2-13b-q4_0", "stream": true, "prompt": "status check" }'
2) Observe higher latency and reduced throughput after enabling optimizer profile bundle: {quant_profile: tenant-q4, kv_prefetch: aggressive, batching_window_ms: 20}
3) Reverting kv_prefetch flag locally appeared to improve latency in a small canary run.

Logs / identifiers shared by customer:
- Example request IDs with degradation: r-20260312-1a2b3c, r-20260312-1a2b3d
- Tenant metrics screenshots attached in ticket (throughput/latency graphs)

Immediate customer ask:
- Guidance on safe emergency off-ramp to restore throughput with minimal feature interruption.
- Root cause hypotheses and recommended next steps to avoid recurrence.
Timeline and initial triage:
- 2026-03-12 09:12 (Support): Ticket opened by Customer Success after NovaLabs flag rollout.
- 2026-03-12 09:28 (SRE): Correlated spike in scheduling queue length and increased kernel preemption logs for gpu-pool-dedicated-7.
- 2026-03-12 09:45 (Eng - optimizer): Noted incompatible interaction between tenant-q4 quant profile and aggressive KV prefetch: quantized weight layout + prefetching causes increased cache churn and extra kernel memory traffic, amplifying context-switch latency under load.
- 2026-03-12 10:05 (Scheduler): Observed micro-batching window of 20ms combined with adaptive micro-batching caused larger-than-expected batch sizes, leading to slower per-token processing for quantized paths.

Hypotheses:
1) KV prefetch aggressiveness is evicting useful KV segments, causing repeated recomputation for long contexts in quantized execution paths.
2) Mixed batching policies (tenant override + global adaptive) produced suboptimal batch formation that penalizes quantized kernels.
3) Quantization profile selection without alignment to kernel-packing strategy triggered fallback code paths with higher overhead.

Repro steps executed by SRE/Eng:
- Replayed a subset of customer traffic against a staging replica of gpu-pool-dedicated-7 with and without kv_prefetch. Results: disabling kv_prefetch recovered latency to within 10% of baseline.
- Tuned batching_window_ms to 8ms in staging: improved throughput but introduced slightly more overhead per-request (acceptable for NovaLabs).

Temporary mitigation applied (approved with customer):
- Forced per-tenant override to disable kv_prefetch for nova-prod in us-east.
- Applied temporary routing rule to prefer llama2-13b-fp16 for heavy streaming endpoints for 2-hour window.
- Monitored metrics; throughput recovered to ~1.05k rps and p99 latency dropped to ~210ms within 30 minutes.

Open questions for engineering:
- Do we need an automated conflict-detection check when combining quantization profiles with KV prefetch and batching overrides?
- Should optimizer flag validation prevent applying flagged combos to Dedicated pools without a canary?

Additional notes:
Workaround implemented: disabled aggressive KV prefetch for nova-prod and routed streaming traffic to fp16 variant as temporary safe-mode. Short-term tuning: batching_window_ms reduced to 8ms for tenant to balance latency/throughput.
Planned permanent actions:
- Engineering to add config validation that prevents unsafe optimizer flag combinations (PR opened: github.com/redwood-inference/optimizer-config/pull/102).
- Add a pre-deploy canary enforcement for Dedicated flag changes: automatically require a 5% canary for 30m on the tenant's pool before full rollout.
- Create a heuristic in the serving runtime to detect excessive KV churn and auto-soft-disable kv_prefetch for affected connections until a graceful fallback is negotiated.
- Schedule postmortem with NovaLabs and internal teams; due 2026-03-18.
Follow-up tasks assigned:
- INT-88012: Implement config validation rules (owner: Priya Rao).
- INT-88400: Add canary gating to dedicated flag rollouts (owner: Diego Alvarez).
Ticket state: Customer confirmed improved performance. Leaving ticket open until validation PR merged and canary gating in place.
payload.summary: Throughput drop after mixed optimizer profiles enabled for tenant; need conflict resolution and emergency off-ramp

payload.description:
Issue summary: Customer reports intermittent increases in time-to-first-byte (TTFB) for streaming completions. The symptom is that some streaming requests return initial tokens after a 2-6s delay even though request enters the serving runtime quickly. Impact: customers see perceived latency spikes for interactive flows and partial timeouts when clients have strict idle time windows. Observed at scale across multiple backends in us-west and reproduceable in limited cases from internal synthetic tests.

Observed behavior:
- Requests accepted by API gateway and routed to serving cluster immediately (backend request logs show sub-200ms queuing).
- First chunk from serving runtime often delayed by multiple seconds before being flushed to client. Subsequent chunks stream normally after first flush.
- When we disable proxy buffering on edge (apigw/nginx) the TTFB returns to expected ~120-300ms range.

Why this is likely: preliminary triage indicates a protocol/conn-reuse mismatch between API gateway (proxy) keepalive behaviour and the serving runtime's chunking strategy. When proxy buffering is enabled and the proxy reuses a keepalive connection that previously saw a large header/tracing payload, it sometimes buffers until either (a) a buffer threshold is reached, or (b) the backend explicitly flushes by closing or hitting a chunk boundary we do not trigger. This causes the first-chunk delay but not subsequent tokens once the stream is warmed.
1) Use customer streaming API with small prompt (~80 tokens) against redwood/bison-2-7b in us-west.
2) Ensure client keeps a short idle timeout (2-5s) between request start and consuming first token.
3) Send 100 concurrent streaming requests over a reused keepalive connection from same client IP.
4) Observe distribution of TTFB; ~15-30% of requests exhibit 2-6s TTFB while others respond fast.
5) Toggle proxy_buffering off on the APIGW/nginx side and re-run; issue disappears in synthetic test.
6) Re-enable buffering and run with a clean TCP connection per request; TTFB regressions reduce substantially.
api-gateway access: 2026-03-09T18:52:12Z GET /v1/streams 200 upstream_latency=0.18s downstream_latency=2.64s conn_reuse=true
serving-runtime: 2026-03-09T18:52:12Z request_id=abc123 stage=generate first_token_emitted=2.3s kv_warmup=0.05s
load-balancer tcp: 2026-03-09T18:52:12Z conn_id=97 last_used=2026-03-09T18:50:12Z keepalive_ms=90000
edge-proxy (nginx) error: 2026-03-09T18:52:12Z buffered 1 bytes waiting for flush: proxy_buffering=on

Additional notes:
2026-03-11 - Customer (NimbleDocs): Verified turning off 'proxy_buffering' in their test environment eliminated stalls in 200/200 samples.
Hypothesis 1: proxy_buffering combined with keepalive reuse causes proxy to wait for enough data or connection-close to flush first chunk. Evidence: disabling buffering returns normal TTFB.
Hypothesis 2: large tracing headers from upstream clients sometimes change buffer allocation path and push proxy into a different flush policy. Evidence: requests with >8KB combined headers show higher probability of stalls.
Telemetry: 95th percentile TTFB for streaming endpoints jumped from ~480ms to ~2.8s for a subset of connections with conn_reuse=true between 2026-03-08 and 2026-03-09.
Reproduced locally using nginx with proxy_buffering=on and proxy_http_version=1.1 vs off; behaviour matches customer reports.
Risk: disabling proxy_buffering increases upstream load and may expose backend to small write amplification; need to tune keepalive and buffer thresholds.
Follow-ups: add a low-risk canary for proxy_buffering=false on streaming routes, add metric for 'first_chunk_delay' to per-route dashboards, and audit header size distribution for customers.
Mitigation applied: disabled proxy_buffering for streaming routes in APIGW canary (rolled to 10% of edge hosts). Also aligned keepalive timeouts between APIGW (now 120s) and load balancer to avoid reuse windows that previously exposed the bug. Permanently: engineering will add an explicit backend flush hook for first-chunk emission and add a feature flag to prefer flush-on-first-chunk for streaming models. Customer notified and accepted workaround. Postmortem planned; estimated full rollout after performance validation.
1) Instrument first_chunk_delay metric and add alert at 1.5s for streaming endpoints
2) Implement explicit flush-on-first-chunk in serving-runtime (PR opened)
3) Run load test with proxy_buffering disabled at 50% edge capacity to measure upstream load impact
4) Communicate permanent fix ETA to NimbleDocs and update docs on streaming tuning
payload.summary: Intermittent TTFB regressions for streaming completions when API gateway connection reuse interacts with proxy buffering

payload.description:
Issue summary: Customer reports repeated mid-stream silence during streaming generation for requests with very large max_tokens and a high client-side burst rate. After a prolonged quiet period (typically 18-30s, sometimes longer) the client receives an HTTP 504 / connection reset. Impact: Blocks CuraLogix nightly batch report generation job; multiple requests failing intermittently and causing downstream ETL retries and invoice-impacting SLA violations. Environment: Dedicated capacity in prod-us-east using redwood-rlhf-13b-v2; model pinned by customer to v2; traffic pattern is short bursts of 6 parallel very-large-output requests during batch windows (max_tokens between 75k-150k). Observed behavior: partial token stream arrives (~20-30% of expected tokens), then a silence gap, then connection resets/504 after ~90s. Expected behavior: steady streaming until finalization and clean 200 with stream close. Severity/Scope: reproducible in customer's nightly job; affects ~40% of batch runs in last 48 hours.
1) Use dedicated tenant in prod-us-east with model redwood-rlhf-13b-v2 pinned
2) Send 6 parallel streaming generate requests with max_tokens ~100000 and prefix length ~2k tokens
3) Observe token emission for first ~10-30s, then silence for 20-30s, then client error (HTTP 504 or ECONNRESET) around 90s total wall time
4) Repeat during peak batch window to reproduce consistently
Customer client log: "stream chunk received (partial), then socket write EPIPE at 2026-03-09T23:14:22Z"
Gateway tail: 2026-03-09T23:14:20Z GET /v1/generate STREAM id=tx-9a3c status=200 chunks=12 then no data for 24s then upstream reset (504)
Serving-runtime: trace tx-9a3c kernel-swap triggered at 23:14:21Z queue-depth=18 mem-pressure=0.78 eviction=delayed
Scheduler logs: priority inversion observed, long-running large-token job preempted synchronous finalizer on same GPU at 23:14:19Z
Telemetry: added fine-grained emit-heartbeat spans to serving-runtime to capture silence windows; initial traces show emit heartbeat not fired for 18-28s in impacted traces
Hypothesis A: adaptive batching policy attempted to coalesce large-token requests leading to head-of-queue blocking and priority inversion for finalizer tasks
Hypothesis B: KV cache compaction/eviction path paused token emission while serializing very large KV pages to disk in rare cases
Hypothesis C: streaming-proxy HTTP/2 window management stalled when a single connection carried large unacknowledged frames (need to correlate with proxy-level window metrics)
Repro test: Reduced parallelism to 2/6 in dedicated tenant replicated issue disappearance; suggests contention rather than model correctness
Trace pointers: tx-9a3c, tx-9a7f, tx-9b01 show similar silence signatures around kernel-swap events
Next steps: (1) coordinate with runtime team to add backpressure limits for extremely large max_tokens per tenant; (2) add proxy-level per-stream WINDOW_UPDATE timeouts and more aggressive keepalive; (3) consider server-side enforced soft cap on concurrent very-large-output streaming slots per GPU
Mitigations proposed and partial workarounds provided to customer. Temporary workarounds: limit concurrent very-large-output streams to <=2 during batch window, lower max_tokens to <=50k where possible, and enable small-stream-chunking (client-side) so proxy-level WINDOW_UPDATE is exercised more frequently. Runtime/infra actions: runtime team to add telemetry and a patch to avoid long finalizer preemption; proxy team to harden HTTP/2 window handling. Target follow-up for patch rollouts scheduled: runtime patch PR and proxy config change. Status: awaiting customer validation of temporary mitigations and runtime team ETA for patch.

Additional notes:
2026-03-10 11:20 CuraLogix (Customer): We can reproduce reliably when running 6 concurrent huge-output requests. Reducing to 2 concurrent requests appears to avoid the silence. We need a workaround while you investigate.

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customer Mapflow Labs (Dedicated) reports intermittent 429s beginning 2026-03-01 02:10 UTC after deploying a sidecar update to their ingress fleet. The update adds a per-request header for route-affinity (X-Route-Affinity) intended for internal routing heuristics.

Impact:
- Several realtime chat streams and background bulk ingest jobs are seeing elevated 429 rates for ~15-60s bursts, causing message loss and backoff loops in their orchestrator.
- Affects production traffic in us-west region for Mapflow's dedicated pool.
- Customer reports increased error rate in their monitoring: ~2.4% of requests returned 429s at peak (baseline <0.01%).

Environment:
- Dedicated pool: dp-mapflow-prod-usw1
- API ingress: nginx sidecar v1.6.2 -> updated to v1.7.0 at 2026-03-01 01:55 UTC
- Traffic mix: realtime websocket chat (short-lived sessions) + scheduled batch upload workers (multipart uploads)

Steps to reproduce (from customer):
1. Deploy nginx sidecar v1.7.0 with configured header rewrite: add header X-Route-Affinity: user-id
2. Start 200 concurrent short-lived websocket sessions while a batch job triggers 50 parallel multipart uploads
3. Observe 429 spikes on both websocket start requests and upload initial preflight calls

Observed behavior:
- 429 responses include headers: X-Rate-Limit-Reason: route-affinity-split, X-Rate-Limit-Remaining: 0
- In coupled bursts, websocket handshake returns 429 with inconsistent Retry-After headers (some show 3s, some missing)
- Console shows tenant token consumption spike aligning with ingress rewrite timestamps

Expected behavior:
- Route-affinity header should not change server-side token accounting, or there should be deterministic attribution to a single token bucket so mixed traffic does not double-count.

Initial logs (customer supplied):
[2026-03-01T02:08:57Z] ingress sidecar: adding header X-Route-Affinity: user-42
[2026-03-01T02:09:01Z] upstream: request start path=/v1/chat/stream api_key=redacted

payload.description:
Issue summary:
During a staggered canary rollout for rw-instruct-7b-v3 in us-east-1, NimbleApps reported ~12% of their requests being served by an older model variant despite an explicit tenant-level model pin. The behavior lasted for ~45 minutes and coincided with an autoscaler prewarm burst triggered by a traffic spike.

Impact:
- Customer reported mixed outputs and downstream feature regressions for active users (measured anomalous quality score increase and user complaints).
- Approximately 11k requests affected for the customer across the incident window.

Environment:
- Production, us-east-1, Dedicated pool for NimbleApps (reserved capacity pool id: ded-342)

Additional notes:
2025-11-04 Support (Priya Singh) -> Customer: Confirmed we are rolling a targeted hotfix that changes prewarm handshake ordering to commit pins before edge cookie rotation. Asked customer for traffic window to cutover safely.
2025-11-05 NimbleApps (Customer): Verified behaviour has ceased after cutover; provided sampling confirming no legacy outputs in a 1h window post-fix. Thanked on call for quick turnaround.
What we observed:
- Autoscaler prewarm created N new prewarm nodes at t0+12s in response to surge.
- Prewarm handshake had a non-atomic ordering: node marked healthy -> edge cookie rotation -> orchestrator snapshot commit.
- In ~9% of sampled requests, edge rotated tenant affinity cookie just before orchestrator committed the new pin mapping, causing requests to land on edge shards that still resolved the tenant to the legacy variant.
- Orchestrator snapshots showed an overlapping epoch where two different routing tables were readable by different edge shards for ~18s.
- No GPU OOMs or serving runtime crashes found. Latency remained within SLO except for slight tail increase during the handoff window.
Hypotheses considered and eliminated:
- Tokenization mismatch in the model: rejected after verifying request payloads and embeddings.
- Customer-side pinned version misconfiguration: rejected; tenant manifest showed explicit pin to rw-instruct-7b-v3 prior to rollout.
Contributing factors:
- Prewarm handshake ordering (health -> rotate cookie -> commit) is non-atomic across control-plane and edge.
- Edge cookie rotation TTL is short and coincided with the commit window during a burst.
- Canary scheduling used staggered slice times (0s, +10s, +20s) which increased overlap surface for commit windows across shards.
Immediate mitigations applied:
1) Rolled a hotfix to orchestrator to change prewarm handshake ordering: commit pin mapping before issuing edge cookie rotation. PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/orchestrator/pull/3184. Deployed to us-east-1 dedicated pools at 2025-11-04T04:00Z.
2) Increased health-probe smoothing for prewarm nodes to reduce transient epoch changes during bursts.
3) Added a guard in edge-proxy to prefer orchestrator pin mapping when epoch differences detected within a 30s window.
Rollout notes:
- Hotfix applied via canary (5% -> 25% -> 100%) over a 3-hour window for dedicated pools; monitored cohort pins and customer telemetry.
- Post-deployment checks (logs + sampling from NimbleApps) showed 0% legacy-routed requests in the 1h stable window.
Follow-ups and action items:
- Engineering to add an orchestrator unit test that asserts prewarm handshake atomicity across control-plane and edge (owner: Liam Chen, target: 2025-11-12).
- Create a capacity-surge playbook to avoid staggered slice overlap during autoscaler prewarm (owner: Product, target: 2025-11-20).
- Postmortem scheduled and linked: https://confluence.redwood.ai/postmortems/SUP-209876-postmortem
Customer communication:
- Notified NimbleApps via support and scheduled an incident review call. Customer confirmed remediation and accepted workaround as final resolution.
payload.summary: Staggered canary burst: pin inconsistency causes subset of requests to reroute to legacy variant

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customers on a reserved pool reported a midday spike where short-lived streaming requests abruptly routed to a lower-capacity fallback model variant, causing a cascade: fallback instances consumed disproportionate GPU attach slots, triggering allocator backpressure and a persistent p99 uplift across the pool. Impact is sustained for ~20-40 minutes during these windows.

Impact:
- NimbleDocs (dedicated) observed p99 latency increase from 180ms -> 860ms for short streaming calls.
- Throughput (tokens/sec) dropped by ~35% across the pool during incidents.
- Automatic fallback to quantized/low-memory model variants appears to be correlated with the start of the window.

Environment:
- Dedicated reserved pool (prod, us-east) serving redwood/gptx-13b-v2 (pinned) with automatic fallback policies enabled.
- Autoscaler: predictive + reactive with default attach concurrency of 4.

Steps to reproduce (customer-provided):
1) Send 3k short streaming requests (avg 60 tokens) over a 5 minute window.
2) Observe routing: when main nodes temporarily report KV-cache warmup >10s, the router pushes to fallback variant.
3) Fallback attaches are short-lived but allocate NVLink/slot resources and prevent main pool attach convergence, leading to queueing and higher p99.

Logs & key traces:
- Router trace: fallback decision spikes at 11:07:12 - 11:07:55 UTC (see router.trace ids in comments).
- Autoscaler events: series of rapid attach/fail/attach at 11:07:xx producing allocator contention.
- Serving runtime logs: repeated "attach_slot_timeout" and "kv-cache-miss" messages correlated with fallback attach bursts.

Observed hypothesis:
We believe a concurrency inversion occurs when the fallback variant has faster cold attach success for short streams but higher slot-churn per attach. Because the router prefers lower-latency attach for short requests, many requests temporarily route to fallback, causing many rapid attach/detach operations that fragment slot availability and delay main model prefetch/warmup. The autoscaler interprets attach failures as capacity pressure and tightens attach throttles, exacerbating the throughput drop.

Customer impact notes:
- Customer reports business KPIs affected (search indexing throughput).
- Customer requested immediate mitigation and a durable fix to avoid repeated mid-day degradations.

Additional notes:
2026-03-11 09:02 - Customer (NimbleDocs): Confirmed mitigation reduced immediate impact. Still want a long-term change to prevent fallback spike in reservation pools. Provided synthetic replay workload.
11:15 UTC: Correlated router decisions with kv-cache miss rate; main model firing prefetches but slow warmup correlated with io-wait on nvme (see infra dashboard).
11:22 UTC: Autoscaler attached/detached rapidly; attach success rate for fallback variant ~92% but average attach duration shorter (~120ms) vs main (~280ms), resulting in more frequent churn for equal request volume.
11:45 UTC: NVLink usage and slot allocation patterns show many short-duration attachments from the fallback pool fragmenting allocation windows. Evidence captured in allocator.logs (ids in related_github_prs).
Workaround applied: temporarily increased fallback attach backoff, added a routing safety gate to prefer warmed main model when recent prefetch attempts are in-flight, and increased min-attach-duration threshold for fallback variants in dedicated pools.
Immediate result: p99 reduced to ~220ms in the monitored window and throughput recovered to within 95% of baseline.
Long-term actions:
- Engineering will add a routing hysteresis to avoid mass-fallback during short cache warmup periods (tracker PR & follow-up).
- Autoscaler will be updated to better distinguish high churn short attaches vs true capacity shortage.
- Runbook update: add a dedicated-pool fallback throttle knob for customers with high short-stream traffic.
Follow-ups: see linked GH PRs and Confluence pages for implementation plan and rollout schedule.
Implement routing hysteresis RFC and land PR in autoscaler/runtime in staged rollout (owners: Platform Eng)
Add dedicated-pool fallback throttle knob to Console and expose config to enterprise customers (owners: Product + DevEx)
Schedule postmortem with NimbleDocs to review SLAs and confirm acceptance of long-term mitigation (owner: CS)
Monitor reserved pool for 72 hours post-change and report metrics to customer (owner: SRE)
Re-evaluate KV-cache warmup performance and NVMe io latency to prevent recurrence (owner: Infra)
payload.summary: Fallback-concurrency inversion causing reserved-pool burst starvation and degraded p99

Issue summary:
On 2026-03-10 during a scheduled tenant load ramp (LexaDocs dedicated pool) we observed a correlated spike in 5xx responses (predominantly 502/503) from the API gateway. Upstream serving runtime processes were intermittently crashing with OOMs tied to GPU memory fragmentation. The surge lasted ~45 minutes and affected a subset of the tenant's requests causing visible errors for customers using streaming endpoints.

Impact:
- LexaDocs reported elevated error rates and failed generation calls for ~12% of requests during the window.
- Errors were user-facing (502/503) and impacted production workloads for the tenant only (dedicated pool).
- No broad multi-tenant outage.

Environment:
- Infrastructure: Dedicated GPU pool for LexaDocs (c5g-equivalent hosts with A100s).
- Region: us-east-1 (primary).

Additional notes:
- Runtime: serving-runtime v1.8.4 (container image digest: sha256:abc123...)
1) Deploy LexaDocs traffic profile to hit throughput of 120 RPS sustained per GPU for 15+ minutes.
2) Use streaming chat endpoint with long prefix prompts (average 1.2k tokens).
3) Observe runtime memory growth pattern and GPU utilization with prefetch enabled.
4) Watch for 502/503s emitted at API gateway and connection resets upstream.
- API gateway returned 502 or 503 for a subset of requests; errors correlated with runtime container exits.
- Runtime logs show GPU allocation failures and 'out of memory' traces immediately prior to process exit.
- Autoscaler did not add capacity quickly enough due to backoff/scale-delay.
- After pod restart, the runtime recovered but fragmentation reappeared under sustained long-prefix traffic.
- runtime stderr: "[2026-03-10T14:23:12Z] ERROR serving: GPU allocation failed: cudaMalloc failed with out of memory"
- runtime trace: "kalloc: fragmentation high, unable to serve new KV cache allocation"
- apigw logs: multiple upstream reset codes and 502s between 14:22:50-15:07:10 UTC
- gpu memory metrics: sustained 98% nominal usage with spikey free blocks pattern
- autoscaler events: scale-up triggered at 14:25 but new pods not ready until 14:34 due to image pull/initialization
1) Immediate: evict and restart affected runtime pods for LexaDocs pool to clear fragmentation.
2) Applied temporary cap: reduce prefetch window for LexaDocs to 32 tokens to decrease ephemeral GPU allocation pressure.
3) Scoped traffic shaping: applied conservative token-based concurrency limits at the API gateway for the tenant.
These actions reduced 5xx rate to baseline within ~8 minutes of the first restarts.
14:20 UTC: LexaDocs SRE reported initial error spikes via #support Slack.
14:22 UTC: Support triaged, opened ticket and escalated to SRE on-call.
14:24-14:30 UTC: Correlated gateway 502 counts with runtime container OOMs; GPU free-block fragmentation pattern observed in metrics.
Hypothesis: Long-prefix streaming + prefetch + pinned model KV caches cause allocator fragmentation on the serving runtime's GPU memory arena leading to allocation failure under sustained high-RPS.
Evidence: repeated cudaMalloc failures and 'fragmentation high' runtime logs prior to crashes.
Autoscaler behavior: scale-up delay combined with image pull + model load time amplified the error window; further, the fallback policy caused apigw to route requests to unhealthy upstreams until restarts completed.
SRE reproduced locally with a synthetic load profile; reproduced allocation failures after ~10 minutes under identical prefetch + long prefix conditions.
Related: INT-3321 contains earlier notes on allocator tuning and kernel-level reclamation attempts.
Support (Aisha): 'Received a LexaDocs incident report at 14:20 UTC — they see 502s when sending long prompts via chat stream.'
SRE (Marco): 'Observing frequent cudaMalloc failures in the LexaDocs serving pool. Initiating pod restarts and lowering prefetch for the tenant.'
LexaDocs (Customer - Claire): 'We saw a spike of failed generations for about 30-40 minutes. Appreciate fast follow-up; need postmortem and assurance this won't recur.'
SRE (Nina): 'Confirmed local repro. Plan: backport allocator patch and add guardrail for prefetch + prefix length. Will schedule canary.'
Support (Aisha): 'Applied temporary rate-limit and informed customer of mitigations; monitoring error rate now trending to normal.'
Root cause: GPU memory allocator fragmentation in serving-runtime v1.8.4 triggered by sustained long-prefix streaming + prefetch and high per-GPU RPS, producing repeated cudaMalloc failures and runtime exits.
Fix applied:
1) Hotfix deployed (serving-runtime v1.8.5-hotfix) that adjusts the GPU allocator's slab sizes and introduces a compaction path to reduce fragmentation. Deployed to LexaDocs dedicated pool as a canary at 2026-03-11 02:00 UTC.
2) Configuration change: lowered default prefetch window for long-prefix streaming to 32 tokens for affected tenant and introduced a tenant-level guard that rejects prefetchs >128 tokens when token-concurrency exceeds thresholds.
3) Autoscaler tuning: reduced scale-up backoff and pre-warmed image cache to shorten cold-start for dedicated pools.
Outcome: After the hotfix and config changes, the 5xx rate returned to baseline and no further OOMs observed in monitoring for 72 hours.
Engineering: merge hotfix PR into mainline and run full integration test matrix (owner: Nina, due: 2026-03-18)
SRE/Platform: add allocator fragmentation alert to prod dashboards (owner: Marco, due: 2026-03-16)
Product/Customer Success: run remediation call with LexaDocs and offer one-week usage credit (owner: Priya, due: 2026-03-15)
Observability: add synthetic long-prefix streaming canary to detect early fragmentation (owner: Observability team, due: 2026-03-20)

payload.description:
Issue summary:
During a scheduled HSM key rotation in Polaris Logistics' private deployment (eu-west), a subset of nodes experienced failed TLS handshakes when the local sidecar attempted to retrieve rotated certificates. The control-plane orchestrator retried the rotation, which caused repeated short-lived TLS renegotiations across the pool and triggered streaming connection resets for in-flight completions.

Impact:
- Customer-visible streaming disconnects and truncated responses across approx. 12% of requests for 22 minutes during the rotation window.
- Several requests were retried by client libraries and internal retry logic, leading to duplicate completion tokens being billed. Estimated customer invoice exposure: ~€1,450 before credits.
- Temporary failover traffic to us-east increased tail-latency for some sessions (observed 95th percentile increase ~420ms).

Environment:
- Private deployment behind Polaris VPC peering, eu-west region, Redwood private control plane. HSM: vendor-managed cluster (HSM-Co) integrated via KMS proxy.
- Affected runtime: serving-runtime v3.9.1 with sidecar cert refresh.

Steps to reproduce (internal):
1) Triggered HSM rotation via rotation-operator in staging using customer-like cert chain.
2) Observed sidecar metrics: cert-refresh loop timeout at 150ms, TLS handshake failures spike.
3) Replayed rotation against a small pool of eu-west nodes; streaming reset reproduced when cert fetch returned 503 for short windows.

Logs / telemetry pointers:
- Kibana: logs.app.eu-west.stream-reset > 2026-03-10T08:12:00Z (stack: auth.tls_handshake_error)
- Datadog dashboard: private-rotation.alerts / serving-runtime.tls_handshake_failure_rate
- Billing analytics: billing.events.duplicate_token_count (SUP-100500_billing_slice)

Investigation notes:
- Root cause: race between HSM-side rotation acknowledgment and the KMS proxy's cache TTL. When HSM rotated keys, the proxy intermittently returned 503 while cache was being warmed; sidecars interpreted this as transient network failure and retried TLS negotiation. The orchestrator's retry loop re-invoked rotation on partially-updated nodes, amplifying the window of instability.
- Concurrency issue in rotation-operator: simultaneous rotation attempts allowed for overlapping rotation waves instead of a strict rolling window. We found a missing distributed lock in the rotation operator for private deployments.
- Client SDKs with optimistic retry produced duplicate completion requests with new tokens; our usage-accounting system counted both completions before de-dupe reconciliations ran.

Immediate mitigation and resolution applied:
- Emergency rollback: rotation-operator rolled back to previous key state for affected pool (completed at 2026-03-10T08:34Z).
- Temporary configuration: increased KMS proxy cache TTL and added 5s penalization on 5xx responses to avoid tight retry loops.
- Billing action: issued provisional credit of €1,450 to Polaris Logistics pending reconciliation; finance ticket INT-412 created for final invoice adjustment.
- Patch deployed: rotation-operator hotfix v1.2.3 (adds distributed locking and staggered wave enforcement) staged and promoted to private control plane at 2026-03-11T02:20Z.

Customer communication:
- Initial alert sent to Polaris CSM at 2026-03-10T08:26Z acknowledging incident and mitigation plan.
- Proactive credit and postmortem offered; customer response requested specific timing for final reconciliation and playbook changes.

Post-incident actions / next steps:
1) Root Cause Analysis (RCA) write-up: owners SRE (Sergio) + Rotation team to finalize by 2026-03-17.
2) Add automated e2e test in staging that simulates KMS 5xx windows and validates sidecar behavior. Target PR: rotation-operator #205.
3) Update private deployment runbook to require explicit rotation dry-run and leader lock for HSM rotations.
4) Billing: reconcile duplicate-token counts and issue final credit by 2026-03-18 (Finance owner: Lina Park).
5) Customer follow-up: schedule a technical review call with Polaris by 2026-03-16; include SRE, Solutions Eng, and Customer CISO.

Status summary: mitigated (rollback + hotfix deployed). Ongoing: RCA documentation and billing reconciliation.


Additional notes:
Rollback to previous keys, KMS-proxy TTL increase, rotation-operator hotfix v1.2.3 (distributed lock + staggered waves), provisional billing credit issued and finalized after reconciliation.

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customers observe short bursts (~30s-2m) of 502/503 responses originating at the API gateway when a large embedding job (approx 1.2M tokens across many small requests) runs concurrently with normal traffic. Rate of errors correlates with embedding job spikes and periods of many short-lived streaming sessions (keepalive churn).

Impact:
- LuminaSearch (dedicated) reported 15-30% request error-rate increase during bursts, impacting live search indexing.
- Errors are transient but repeatable with similar workload pattern; downstream retries amplify load.

Environment:
- Prod, us-east, Dedicated GPU pool (A100s), serving-runtime v2026.02.7, nvml driver v470.x, API gateway v1.14.3

Steps to reproduce (approx):
1) Start large embedding job: 12k concurrent small embedding requests batched by customer SDK into many parallel connections.
2) Introduce a stream of short-lived streaming sessions to simulate keepalive churn (many short connections).
3) Observe API gateway 502/503 spikes and increased watchdog restarts on runtime.

Observed logs / metrics:
- api-gateway logs show upstream reset / 502 with code "upstream connection closed" during bursts.
- serving-runtime logs contain repeated lines: "watchdog: gpu-worker-thread timeout, resetting worker pid=***" and occasional "nvml timeout waiting for response (2000ms)".
- GPU utilization shows high but not fully saturated. CPU on runtime host shows high runnable thread count in process responsible for driver IO.
- KV-cache eviction rate spikes, prefetch queue length increases.

Notes on customer session:
- Customer reported increased retrying logic in their client; they attempted backoff which reduced but did not eliminate the bursts.
- No config changes on customer side during incident window.

Initial hypothesis: driver-level stalls (nvml) or GPU-thread pool contention causing runtime watchdog to reset GPU worker threads. This triggers inflight requests to be aborted and returns 502/503 at api-gateway.

What we checked so far:
- Correlated timestamped runtime watchdog logs with api-gateway 502 windows; near 95th percentile alignment.
- Examined NVML kernel messages and dmesg for driver resets: found repeated nvml timeouts (2000ms) during bursts but no full GPU reset.
- Traced runtime worker thread stacks (coredump/stacktrace sampling) — many threads blocked on driver ioctl or on futexes in the IO path.
- Prefetch subsystem shows long queue growth and KV-cache lock contention, likely increasing number of small GPU requests and locking driver IO.
- API gateway healthchecks show upstream connection closures when worker pids are being restarted by watchdog.

Hypothesis refinement:
- Combination of (1) high-volume small embedding requests causing a large number of short driver IO ops and (2) keepalive churn preventing connection reuse leads to GPU worker threads spending disproportionate time on small serial IO, increasing latency per-op and tripping watchdog thresholds.
- Result: worker reset -> inflight abort -> api-gateway 502/503 waves.

Immediate mitigations tested in staging:
- Increase runtime watchdog timeout from 1.5s to 3s on a canary; reduced observed resets under same synthetic load (but increases time to detect real GPU deadlocks).
- Enabled coalescing of extremely small embedding ops into micro-batches on canary pathway; significantly lowered driver IO ops/sec and avoided watchdog trips in tests.
- Toggled connection keepalive reuse configuration in api-gateway (longer keepalive) to reduce churn; tests showed improved connection reuse and fewer 502s.

Additional notes:
SRE Team (2026-03-13): Observed nvml timeouts in node logs for 3 hosts in the dedicated pool. Stack samples show driver ioctl bottleneck. Suggested temporary scaling down of concurrent embedding shards for customer.
Support (2026-03-14): Communicated temporary mitigation (requesting customer to throttle concurrent embedding shards by 40%) — customer accepted while we prepare broader fix.
Deploy micro-batching feature to dedicated pool behind config flag (owner: Runtime Team)
Evaluate default watchdog timeout and make adaptive threshold based on per-tenant request size distribution (owner: Runtime Team)
Add driver-level instrumentation to correlate nvml latency per-op (owner: Infra)
Document recommended client-side concurrency limits for large-embedding jobs and add to onboarding docs (owner: DevEx)
Schedule postmortem and include customer impact summary and timeline (owner: Support)
In progress - temporary customer throttle applied while runtime micro-batching is rolled out canary->prod. If canary metrics remain stable for 48h, we'll flip flag for affected dedicated pool and update docs. Final resolution to include monitoring for nvml-op-latency and adaptive watchdog heuristics.
payload.summary: Burst 502/503s from GPU worker thread starvation during large-embedding job with keepalive churn

Issue summary:
Customer reports that when their client reconnects to an in-progress SSE stream after a short network blip, the first emitted tokens are truncated or garbled. The remainder of the stream resumes normally, but the partial/gibberish prefix corrupts downstream parsers in their product. This is intermittent (~1-2% of reconnects) and correlates with our auth token rotation window in the prod-us-east serving fleet.

Impact:
- NovusRetail reports failed order-summary displays in their storefront for ~2% of streaming requests after reconnects.
- Client-side parsers report JSON parse errors when the stream's initial tokens are corrupted.
- Business impact: some users see blank widgets; revenue impact estimated small but customer wants SLA-level mitigation.

Environment:
- Customer on Dedicated cluster in us-east (dedicated pool id: dr-prod-7).
- Client uses SSE via the public Redwood API with short-lived bearer tokens (rotation TTL 30s at their integration).

Why this is different from other streaming reconnect cases:
- Not a pure proxy fragmentation or keepalive issue — traces show a valid SSE chunk arrives but first few characters are mangled, not missing.
- Occurs only when the client's reconnect happens within ~2-5s of our auth token rotation point.
- Neither client nor edge shows TLS/TCP resets at time of corruption.
1) Customer has an active SSE session from the Redwood hosted API producing a long running generative response.
2) Induce a short network blip (client-initiated disconnect) and immediately reconnect the SSE stream within 2-5 seconds.
3) Observe that the resumed SSE stream emits a first data event where the first 2-8 characters of the tokenized text are replaced with non-UTF8 or garbled bytes, causing client JSON parsing to fail.
4) Repeat ~50-100 times to reproduce the ~1-2% occurrence window; easiest to reproduce when client performs token refresh right around server-side rotation window.
Client-side captured fragment (base64): H4sIAAAAAAAA/ytJLS4BAAx+f9gEAAAA (corrupt leading bytes) followed by valid UTF-8 tokens.
Edge proxy (nginx) access log at 2026-03-09T14:22:08Z: 200 GET /v1/streams?id=abc123 - - 0.083 - upstream_response_time:0.080
Serving runtime trace (2026-03-09T14:22:08.042Z): conn=dr-prod-7/slot-12 auth_check ok (token_id: rtk-245) rotated at 14:22:06.867Z; resume_stream resumed_kv_cache=true; emitted first_chunk size=128 bytes
Auth service audit (2026-03-09T14:22:06.860Z): rotated token rtk-246 issued; old token rtk-245 moved to grace state expires_in=30s
Hex dump of received SSE chunk: 7b 22 74 6f 6b 65 6e 22 3a 22 e2 28 9f 20 2f ... (notice e2 28 9f inserted at offset 12)
No TCP retransmit events in connection logs; no TLS renegotiate entries.
Initial hypothesis: proxy chunk coalescing or MTU split — discarded after confirming chunk size variance and presence of non-UTF8 bytes that match neither nginx nor customer client encodings.
Observed tight correlation with auth token rotation operations on the serving node (rotation grace period and immediate reauth paths).
Repro attempt with synthetic client toggling token refresh window reproduced corrupted prefix in ~3/120 trials — not deterministic but statistically significant versus baseline 0/120 when token refresh disabled.
Trace-level capture shows a goroutine in the serving-runtime that swaps auth context during resume; swapping code path copies the buffer into a reusable slab while simultaneously appending the prefix from the KV cache — race suspected between buffer zeroing and write path leading to leftover bytes in front of new data.
Memory-debugging with sanitizers on a dev replica reproduces out-of-order memory copy when auth rotation coincides with resume flow (local heap reuse observed).
Edge-level mitigation (disable immediate token rotation while resumes in-flight) removed occurrences in a small canary (dr-canary-2) for 48 hours.
A race condition in the serving-runtime resume path where an auth rotation path reuses/re-initializes a write buffer concurrently with resume write. The concurrent memory copy left stale bytes at the buffer head which are emitted as the first bytes of the resumed SSE data, producing garbled/truncated prefixes on the client.
Customer can increase bearer token TTL to >90s or defer token refresh until after stream finalization. Temporary server-side mitigation deployed to canary: hold token rotation for 10s after any resume event on that slot.
Patch merged to fix buffer reuse race (runtime PR #4123). Hotfix rolled to canary (dr-canary-*) observed zero reproductions in 72h. Rollout plan: staged deploy to Dedicated clusters in us-east over 48 hours with telemetry threshold checks. Post-deploy, recommend customer revert token TTL change or leave as-is; confirmed with NovusRetail that they will keep token TTL at 90s until full rollout completes.
1) Merge and monitor runtime fix across dedicated pools (owner: serving-runtime team).
2) Post-deploy metrics: track percentage of reconnects with non-UTF8 prefix payloads; target <0.01% over 24h windows.
3) Add a defensive unit test and fuzzing harness for resume+auth rotation interleavings (owner: runtime QA).
4) Follow up with NovusRetail after full rollout and confirm SLA closure; schedule a short postmortem with SRE and runtime engineers.

2026-03-10 09:25 UTC - Customer (NovusRetail): Sent three timestamps, sample IDs, and client SDK version 1.4.2. Confirmed this started after we switched token TTL to 30s last week.
2026-03-11 15:02 UTC - Support (Evan): We have a suspected race in our resume/auth code path. We're running a canary fix disabling token rotation during resume and will update in 24h with results.

2026-03-12 16:00 UTC - Support: Provided temporary client workaround (increase token TTL to >90s or refresh tokens only when not actively reconnecting) and timeline for code fix.

Issue summary:
Customer BrightEdge AI reports persistent 429s starting 2026-03-10 23:00 UTC for production ingestion. Errors surface during a daily mixed workload: long-lived SSE connections used for low-latency user feedback plus scheduled bulk batch uploads that run every 10 minutes.

Impact:
- ~12% of requests receive 429 over a two-hour window during nightly pipeline runs.
- User-facing SSE sessions experience reconnects, and bulk ingestion jobs time out and retry, increasing downstream cost.

Environment:
- Dedicated pool (customer-dedicated) in us-east-1.
- Ingress fronted by internal edge proxy cluster behind api-gateway.
- Ephemeral-signed-url refresh service used by BrightEdge's orchestrator to rotate short-lived auth tokens every 60s.

Steps to reproduce (provided by customer):
1) Start 40 SSE clients that hold open streams for 30+ minutes.
2) Trigger scheduled batch upload coordinator that opens 150 parallel short HTTP/1.1 POSTs to /v1/embeddings for 10s windows.
3) Observe rate of 200->429 responses on aggregated requests from the tenant.

Expected behavior:
- Background credential refreshes and health probes should not cause tenant-level token-bucket depletion for burst windows.
- SSE long-lived connections should be prioritized (low-latency) and isolated from bulk ingestion traffic.

Actual behavior:
- Token-window accounting counts ephemeral auth refresh calls and health probe requests against the same per-tenant token bucket used for user traffic.
- A sawtooth pattern in the refill window coincides with the orchestrator refresh schedule (every 60s) causing cumulative exhaustion.

Relevant logs/observations provided by customer:
- Example 429 response headers: X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0; X-RateLimit-Reset: 21s; Retry-After: 21
- Edge logs:
  [2026-03-11T00:12:00Z] tenant=brightedge worker=auth-refresh path=/v1/auth/refresh status=200
  [2026-03-11T00:12:00Z] tenant=brightedge path=/v1/embeddings status=429 route=/embeddings-bulk
  [2026-03-11T00:12:01Z] tenant=brightedge path=/v1/stream/connect status=200 conn_id=xyz reconnect=1

Notes:
- Customer added that after reducing the refresh frequency to 300s the 429 rate drops but intermittent 429s still occur during concurrent scheduler windows.

Please see comments for interactive troubleshooting and SRE findings.
2026-03-11 09:15 UTC - Support(Asha): Opened ticket after initial triage with customer. Collected sample logs, request IDs, and timestamps. Asked customer for list of IPs and exact refresh schedule.
2026-03-11 11:02 UTC - SRE(Marco): Reproduced sawtooth refill pattern in tenant accounting on internal test harness by emulating 60s auth-refresh fanout plus bulk POSTs. Noted that healthcheck probes from the edge sidecar were not being excluded from rate accounting in dedicated pool config.
2026-03-11 14:28 UTC - Support(Asha): Customer confirms orchestration uses a burst of short-lived tokens; provided additional headers and example request-ids for 2026-03-10 23:05-23:15 UTC window.
2026-03-12 03:45 UTC - SRE(Marco): Applied a non-production config on canary nodes to ignore /v1/auth/refresh and internal healthcheck endpoints from tenant token-bucket counts. Early canary shows 90% reduction in 429s for synthetic run. Preparing patch.
2026-03-13 16:10 UTC - Support(Asha): Customer accepted temporary mitigation (rate-splitting guidance) and requested timeline for permanent fix. Asked for a formal runbook update to avoid regression post-upgrade.
2026-03-14 08:05 UTC - SRE(Marco): Deployed config change to customer dedicated pool (rolling restart with safe drain). Observed improvement in production: 429s dropped from 12% -> 0.8% during next scheduled run. Monitoring watch active for 48 hours.
Hypotheses tested:
- H1: Healthcheck and orchestration refresh worker requests are counted against tenant's burst window -> confirmed in dedicated config.
- H2: Edge proxy connection reuse / HTTP/2 multiplexing incorrectly attributes background probe requests to primary API key -> some evidence in logs; correlated with shared connection pools.
- H3: Priority weighting between SSE route and embeddings-bulk route was not enforced for this tenant -> confirmed: route-weighting not applied when requests originate from internal signed-url host header.

Actions performed:
- Reproduced sawtooth refill in internal harness matching customer cadence.
- Tested excluding /v1/auth/refresh from token accounting on canary nodes.
- Adjusted route matching to respect host header for signed-url clients and applied route-weighting enforcement.
- Added a temporary token-window throttle exemption for internal-health endpoints on the dedicated pool.

Data points:
- Canary synthetic run with exemption: 429s reduced 92% compared to baseline.
- Production after rollout: 429s reduced to 0.8% during scheduled windows; SSE reconnects fell below 0.3% of total connections.

Mitigation and fix applied:
1) Exempted internal auth-refresh and healthcheck endpoints from tenant token-bucket accounting in dedicated pool config.
2) Enforced route-weighting and host-based route isolation for signed-url clients so background workers are counted against a separate low-priority bucket.
3) Rolled configuration as a safe rolling restart with drain on dedicated nodes for BrightEdge.

Customer-facing workaround communicated: stagger auth-refresh frequency (>=120s) and switch to separate service account when possible to isolate background workers.

Status: Patch rolled to production 2026-03-14 07:50 UTC; monitoring window initiated for 48h. Post-deployment follow-up scheduled.
Follow-ups and runbook updates:
- Update dedicated pool runbook: doc section 'Exclude internal health and auth-refresh endpoints from token accounting' (owner: infra-rate-team).
- Add a dashboard tile for per-tenant window refill and healthcheck accounting (owner: observability).
- Consider defaulting route isolation for signed-url origins in next major release.
- Postmortem scheduled if issue reoccurs after monitoring window ends.

payload.description:
Issue summary: Customer reports that long-lived Server-Sent Events (SSE) streaming sessions show 1) duplicated trailing token fragments after an internal load-balancer (LB) failover, and 2) 'ghost' event fragments that arrive out-of-order or without corresponding end markers. Impact: downstream application sees duplicated partial final choices and intermittent state-machine errors when stitching choices, causing incorrect UI display and occasional instruction duplication. Environment: prod-us-east, behind our regional L7 LB, customer uses persistent SSE with client-side reconnect logic (exponential backoff + resume token). Steps to reproduce: 1) Start a long streaming session (>60s) against /v1/stream with redwood-v1.3 pinned. 2) Induce a rolling restart on one of the regional edge proxies or trigger an LB failover (simulated by removing healthy instances). 3) Allow client reconnect to resume using last-offset resume token. Observed behavior: on reconnect, client sometimes receives duplicate tail fragments (e.g. last 8-12 tokens repeated) and intermittent short 'meta fragments' that contain no content but a resume-id header; occasionally a fragment arrives after an 'end' event, producing a ghosted sentence. Expected behavior: resume should continue from the last delivered token and not produce duplicates or out-of-order fragments. Logs attached and relevant traces referenced below.
Start SSE stream to https://api.redwood.ai/v1/stream with model=redwood-v1.3 and stream_timeout=180s
Generate prompt expected to produce ~40s of streaming tokens (long generation)
While streaming, remove one backend from the prod-us-east L7 pool to force LB failover (or restart edge-proxy)
Observe client logs and reconstructed output after the client reconnects using resume token
Datadog trace: trace_id=dd-0f3a2b, span=stream-session-reconnect, see https://app.datadoghq.com/traces/0f3a2b
Edge proxy error: 2026-03-13T18:42:07Z WARN lb: connection reset by peer during in-flight SSE; session_id=cs-9b3f
API gateway: 5xx spike window 18:42:05-18:42:09 (12 requests), correlate with failover event
Customer client log excerpt: Received chunk #24: "...final token" then reconnect, upon resume received chunk #24 again and chunk #25 duplicate

Additional notes:
SRE (Lina Chen) (2026-03-13): Confirmed failover event in prod-us-east at 18:42. Edge proxy restarted and health checks triggered. Observed short window of half-closed connections. Will pull tcpdump and proxy logs.
Streaming Runtime (Diego Alvarez) (2026-03-14): Found cases where session metadata race allows a buffered final fragment to be forwarded twice when resume token reconciliation occurs after a delayed end-event. Preparing a hotfix branch to add an idempotency check on fragment sequence ids.
Support (2026-03-14): Sent workaround to customer: enable 'sticky-sessions' on their LB or switch their client to wait 150ms after re-establish before resuming to reduce race. Customer applied sticky-sessions and reported initial reduction in duplicates; still seeing rare ghosts.
Hypothesis 1: Edge LB failover causes half-closed TCP connections; proxy attempts to replay buffered chunks to new backend resulting in duplicate fragments.
Hypothesis 2: Resume path in streaming-proxy does not fully reconcile last-ack offset under concurrent end-event delivery, causing a small window where the same fragment can be emitted twice.
Evidence: trace correlation shows identical fragment id and identical token checksum sent twice separated by ~120ms; client-side resume token matches server resume position but server emitted fragment again after end-event.
Mitigation tested: instruct customer to enable LB stickiness -> duplicates decreased. Also tested client-side 150ms pause before resume -> duplicates decreased in simulation.
Next steps: add idempotency by tracking recent fragment sequence ids for 1s after session end + backfill patch to avoid replay, and add extra logging to trace fragment sequence ids on production canary
Mitigation applied: Customer enabled LB sticky-sessions and temporarily reduced duplicate rate. Streaming runtime hotfix in PR (see related_github_prs) adds fragment-seq idempotency and tighter resume reconciliation; canary build scheduled 2026-03-15. Final resolution pending canary validation and full rollout.
payload.summary: Ghosted fragments and duplicated tail segments after load-balancer failover during SSE session

Issue summary: During a scheduled canary rollout for redwood-3b-v2 we observed an aborted prewarm handshake caused by a sudden health-probe spike from the edge-prober. Impact: ~12% of ByteScale tenant sessions were routed to fallback variants for ~18 minutes, causing increased latency and inconsistent outputs for batch inference jobs. Environment: Dedicated pool in us-east-1, canary slice ~5% traffic, control plane snapshot version v2026.03.09. Observed behavior: 1) Orchestrator begins prewarm for canary instances. 2) Edge health-prober issues >50 fast consecutive probes for several hosts; probe responses include intermittent timeouts. 3) Prewarm handshake for affected cohort aborts mid-way; controller marks prewarm as failed and emits prewarm-abort event. 4) Session pins were partially applied before abort, producing split pin state across edge and orchestrator leading to repeated fallback routing and opaque session duplication.
Deploy canary slice (5%) for redwood-3b-v2 to dedicated pool in us-east-1 with prewarm enabled
Simulate a burst of failed/slow health-check responses from the edge host (50+ probes within 60s)
Observe orchestrator logs for prewarm-handshake timeouts and prewarm-abort events
Send steady tenant traffic that exercises session affinity and observe routing decisions and model selection

2026-03-10T09:02:37Z edge-prober WARN Health probe timeout target=10.2.4.18 latency=1200ms attempt=18
2026-03-10T09:03:02Z route-coordinator ERROR Prewarm handshake aborted prewarm_id=pw-88a reason=probe-spike
2026-03-10T09:03:05Z orchestrator WARN Partial pin applied tenant=bytescale-77 sessions=142 applied_shards=3/8
2026-03-10T09:05:22Z router INFO Fallback routed tenant=bytescale-77 session=ses-004 variant=legacy-2 latency=2.2s count=37
Aisha Patel (Support) 2026-03-10T09:18:00Z: Confirming customer impact — ByteScale reports intermittent high latency and degraded quality for scheduled batch runs. Currently throttling non-critical background jobs for the tenant.
Marco Ruiz (SRE) 2026-03-10T10:03:00Z: Temporary mitigation applied: forced pin-resync on the cohort and pinned sessions were reissued from control-plane snapshot v2026.03.09. Observed fallback counts decreased after resync. Still seeing sporadic edge-probe timeouts.
ByteScale (Customer) 2026-03-10T10:22:00Z: Thank you — we saw throughput recover but some outputs still reflected legacy-variant tokenization mismatches. We paused job queue and will hold new batches until cleared.
Lena Thompson (Eng) 2026-03-11T08:45:00Z: Hypothesis: prewarm handshake does not atomically commit pin metadata across orchestrator and edge shards; abort leaves partial state. We'll reproduce in staging with accelerated health probes.
Initial correlation between prewarm-abort and spike in edge health-prober timeouts; edge prober configured to be aggressive for ded pool
Partial pin state recorded: control-plane shows commit for 3 shards while edge cache held different affinity tokens for same sessions
Router metrics show 1.5x fallback rate in cohort window 09:03-09:21 UTC; tokenization mismatch indicates some requests hit legacy variant
Related: SUP-412358 (stale-pin-consensus after region migrate delay) has similar partial commit symptoms; engineering linked for control-plane pin atomicity review
Repro in staging: able to trigger abort by dropping 60% of probe responses during prewarm window; observed same split pin state and fallback loop
Engineering: add atomic two-phase commit for prewarm pin application across orchestrator + edge shard registries (PR drafted)
SRE: tune edge-prober backoff and add transient-probe-gating to prewarm path to avoid aborting on short spikes
Support: coordinate with ByteScale on rolling job resume schedule and confirm tokenization-consistency tests before full traffic promotion
Follow-up: postmortem and runbook update once fix merged and deployed
workaround applied: forced pin-resync and temporary prewarm gating reduced fallback rate; engineering to deliver atomic prewarm commit to prevent recurrence

Issue summary:
Customer (Brightscribe Labs) reports that after a flurry of short websocket disconnects from a browser client behind a corporate load balancer, resumed streams sometimes contain: duplicated leading tokens (prefix repeated), and the final choice is split into two fragments where the final fragment is missing the closing punctuation and metadata. This appears most frequently when reconnects occur within 400ms of each other (rapid reconnect loop).

Impact:
- Some user-facing responses appear to have repeated prefixes which confuse downstream parsing in the customer's client.
- Final choice missing trailing punctuation/metadata causes their post-processing (choice-ranking + telemetry tagging) to fail intermittently.
- Customer is on Dedicated tier and reports this impacts a small percentage (~0.6%) of streaming responses during peak traffic.

Environment:
- Dedicated pool: us-east, GPU-backed serving nodes (A10G equivalent).
- Client: Chrome 113 in a single-page app with background auto-reconnect enabled by customer code.
- Network path: customer LB -> corporate proxy -> Redwood API Gateway -> streaming runtime.

Steps to reproduce (as reported):
1) Initiate streaming chat request via websocket.
2) Trigger rapid disconnects by toggling offline/online in browser or simulating flaky proxy (disconnects spaced ~200-400ms).
3) Allow client to auto-reconnect and resume stream using lastSeenTokenOffset semantics.
4) Observe response: sometimes prefix duplicated and final choice split/truncated.

Observed behavior:
- Reconnect resume creates an extra initial fragment that contains tokens already sent before the disconnect.
- The final choice is emitted in two separate "choice" frames: the first part appears as normal partial content, the second arrives but lacks trailing meta (no "finish_reason" and missing punctuation).
- No 5xx errors in API gateway logs during incidents; proxy logs show a flurry of CONNECT/TEARDOWN.

Expected behavior:
- Resume should stitch seamlessly without re-sending tokens already acknowledged by client.
- Final choice should be emitted complete with finish_reason and punctuation retained.

Initial hypothesis:
- Race between prefix cache eviction (KV cache) and resume reconciliation logic when reconnects happen faster than our resume window; client ack offsets may drift causing duplicated slices.
- Proxy or LB may be splitting frames or introducing micro-reordering that our websocket resume code does not currently guard against.

Attachments / links:
- Customer-provided minimal repro app (link shared to S3 in private exchange).
- Logs snapshot: s3://redwood-support-uploads/sup-99760/logs-2026-03-09-14z.txt
- Dashboard snapshots: https://grafana.redwood.company/d/sessions/resume-metrics?orgId=1&var-env=prod

Additional notes:
2026-03-11 13:22 - SRE (Jon Chu): Found a pattern: websocket keepalive timeouts at the LB were set to 30s but the proxy between LB and gateway had a 1s aggressive idle-reap for half-open sockets, which caused frequent mid-stream TCP resets when load peaked. Opening a ticket with networking to investigate policy for long-lived streams.
2026-03-11: Collected session-level event trace for affected session ids. Resume offsets in event stream show two resume attempts with overlapping token ranges (offsets 0-128 then 100-230) — indicates stale last-ack value on resume request.
2026-03-11: Verified KV cache TTL is 60s and is not expiring in observed windows. Kernel-level TCP resets from proxy cause the runtime to treat subsequent resume as new session in some code paths leading to fragment duplication.
2026-03-12: Temporarily reproduced with internal flaky-proxy and added extra guard in resume logic to dedupe overlapping token ranges — local test reduced duplication occurrences by ~95% in synthetic runs.
2026-03-12: Hypothesis refinement: two issues compound — aggressive proxy TCP teardown leading to raced resume attempts, and resume reconciliation code that appends fragments when offsets slightly overlap instead of trimming duplicates.
In progress. Short-term mitigation: advising customer to increase client-side backoff to avoid rapid auto-reconnects and coordinate with their proxy team to relax idle-reap settings. Engineering has a targeted patch (serving-runtime PR #1289) that adds defensive de-duplication for overlapping resume offsets and stricter validation of finish_reason propagation. Patch is in code review and test plan includes end-to-end repro with flaky-proxy. Next steps: land PR, deploy to canary dedicated pool, monitor resume-metrics for reduction in duplicate-prefix and missing-final-choice events. Customer notified and offered temporary guidance and higher-frequency monitoring.
Merge PR 1289 and run canary rollout to a subset of dedicated pools (target: us-east small subset)
Coordinate with Networking team to confirm proxy idle-reap behavior and recommend settings to Brightscribe (CP: Jon Chu)
Ask customer to apply client backoff patch to avoid auto-reconnect loops while we validate fix
Monitor grafana panel 'sessions/resume-metrics' for drop in duplicated-prefix rate to <0.1% for Brightscribe pool
payload.summary: Resume-after-split: fragmented final choice and duplicate leading tokens after rapid reconnect loop (websocket)
