Issue summary: During a rolling model update for a dedicated tenant (Fable Analytics) we observed a sustained increase in 5xx responses from the API gateway for ~30 minutes. Error signatures included 502/503 returned by the gateway and upstream timeouts from the serving runtime. Impact: Customer-facing requests experienced ~18% error rate on inference endpoints (text-generation and embeddings) for the tenant; internal monitoring flagged increased queue depths and long tail latencies on several runtime instances. Environment: prod-us-east, dedicated-gpu-pool-7, models involved: redwood-7b-v1 -> redwood-1.3b-quant swap. Steps to reproduce / timeline: 1) 2026-03-10 02:10 UTC: rollout-service started canary of redwood-1.3b-quant on pool-7. 2) 02:13-02:30: multiple runtime instances began reporting KV-cache invalidation events and slow prefix lookups. 3) 02:17: API gateway error rate rose; retries amplified traffic. 4) 02:20: autoscaler temporarily spun up additional replicas, which then hit the same stall. 5) 02:40: partial mitigation (traffic routing to fallback model) applied manually. Logs / metrics observed: - Serving runtime threads blocked waiting on KV cache shard locks (lock hold times spiked from <5ms to >1200ms). - Kernel and GPU metrics normal (no OOM), but per-process epoll wait counts rose. - API gateway 502/503s correlated with upstream connection timeouts and increased accept queue lengths. - Prefetch/pipeline logs show a mismatch: some workers attempted to load quantized model shards with a pipeline config that still referenced old KV-cache keys. Initial hypothesis: Rolling update introduced a pipeline configuration drift between instances (old process still serving with previous KV key namespace while new instances invalidated/rehydrated kv-shards). This caused lock contention and long-lived blocked RPCs, triggering upstream timeouts and 5xx amplification via retries. Immediate customer impact workaround: Shifted tenant traffic to a compatible fallback model and temporarily paused rollout. Follow-ups: investigate rollout-service coordination and introduce a pre-update KV namespace handshake to avoid mixed-namespaces during hot-swap.
Priya Sharma 2026-03-10T03:05Z: Initial report submitted by customer. Attached error rate graphs and sample 502 responses. Customer reports degraded experience in production; requesting ETA for fix.
Liam O'Connor 2026-03-10T04:12Z: Acknowledged. Triage started, re-routing customer to fallback model to reduce immediate error rate. Eng oncall paged for runtime and kv-cache. Linking SUP-497131 for historical context.
Mariana Ruiz (SRE) 2026-03-10T04:45Z: Observed KV-cache shard lock hold times > 1s on three replicas in pool-7. No memory or GPU pressure. Suspect namespace mismatch and cache invalidation storm. Collecting strace and runtime thread dumps.
Evan Park (Runtime) 2026-03-10T05:10Z: Thread dumps show blocked epoll wait on fd associated with cache manager; prefetch queue depth is high. Added temporary circuit-breaker to prefetch path to avoid lock storms; monitoring effect.
Liam O'Connor 2026-03-11T01:22Z: Manual mitigation (pause rollout + route to fallback) reduced 5xx to baseline. Preparing postmortem action items; scheduling a rollback to stable pipeline for the tenant until fix is merged.
Fable Analytics - Aaron Kim 2026-03-11T02:05Z: Thanks for quick mitigation. Saw errors drop after you paused rollout. Please keep us posted on root cause and long-term fix.
Collected runtime thread dumps, kv-cache logs, and rollout-service event stream. Replayed events in staging with identical config: reproduces blocked lock behavior when two versions attempt to claim same kv-namespace keys during overlapping prefetch windows. Root cause narrowed to rollout-service not performing an atomic kv-namespace migration handshake when swapping pipeline configs for mixed-quantization variants. Also observed retry storm from API gateway due to short retry backoff amplifying blocked upstreams. Created repro harness and added deterministic test to simulate overlapping prefetches.

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customer reports that after a network interruption and a client-side rotation of their session keystore, resumed Go SDK streaming sessions sometimes produce tool (webhook) calls in a different order than originally emitted. This leads to downstream jobs running out of sequence and user-visible correctness failures.

Impact:
- Sporadic data integrity issues in customer pipelines (order-dependent transforms).
- Affects production traffic for their Dedicated deployment in us-west.
- Estimated ~0.3% of resumed sessions in the last 24h exhibiting the problem per customer telemetry.

Environment:
- Redwood Dedicated, prod:us-west
- Go SDK v0.9.7 (customer reported; they requested guidance on upgrading behavior)
- Session keystore rotation occurs client-side when they refresh ephemeral signing keys every ~15 minutes.

Observed behaviour / symptoms:
- During a stream resume after an interruption, the host receives webhook POSTs for tool calls that appear re-ordered compared to the original sequence. Sequence numbers in the payload (client-provided) are present but callbacks arrive out-of-order; sometimes a later index is received before an earlier one.
- The resume path shows the server re-issuing cached KV-prefix results and then reading from the resumed request queue. Suspected interleaving between prefix/KV replay and new in-flight tokens.

Why this is unique from other idempotency duplicates:
- This is not a classic duplicate (exact same call twice); it's out-of-order execution which corrupts downstream state machines that rely on monotonic ordering.

Attachments provided by customer:
- Minimal repro harness (Go) that toggles keystore rotation, intentionally drops the TCP connection mid-stream, and then resumes.
- Webhook delivery logs with timestamps and payload sequence indices.
- SDK telemetry trace ids for several failures.

Customer asks:
1) Is this expected behavior when rotating session signing keys mid-stream?
2) What server-side guarantees exist about ordering across resume + KV-prefix replay?
3) Recommended mitigation patterns for order-sensitive workflows.

1) Start a multi-tool streaming request from Go SDK v0.9.7 against redwood-v1-large.
2) Emit 6 ordered tool calls with client sequence numbers in the payload (seq: 1..6).
3) After seq 2, force a network drop (simulate flaky mobile network).
4) On client reconnect, rotate ephemeral keystore (new signing key) and resume the stream.
5) Observe webhook receipts: sometimes seq 4/5 arrive before seq 3.

Customer also provided a small Go harness that toggles signing-key header X-Session-Key between the first and resumed connection.
Selected webhook delivery snippet (timestamps in ms):
- 2026-03-09T22:15:01.123Z POST /hooks/tool - payload.seq=1 id=abc123
- 2026-03-09T22:15:01.456Z POST /hooks/tool - payload.seq=2 id=abc124
- --- network drop ---
- 2026-03-09T22:15:03.900Z POST /hooks/tool - payload.seq=4 id=abc126
- 2026-03-09T22:15:04.010Z POST /hooks/tool - payload.seq=5 id=abc127
- 2026-03-09T22:15:04.150Z POST /hooks/tool - payload.seq=3 id=abc125

Server-side trace highlights (trace ids): trace-0a1b2c resumed-session replay began at 22:15:03.890; KV-prefix replay completed at 22:15:04.120; outbound webhook(s) started at 22:15:03.900. Logs show overlap between replay completion and outgoing webhook dispatch.
Initial hypotheses:
- When session keystore rotates on the client, the resumed connection is accepted as a separate session instance and server replay interleaves cached (prefix) events with new queued events because session identity normalization differs across resume path.
- The serving runtime's replay worker may be using a best-effort concurrency window; it publishes cached events back into the outbound queue while resumed in-flight events are already enqueued, causing ordering flips.
- Webhook-proxy has aggressive batching/backoff which can reorder requests if queued separately.

What we've replicated internally:
- Able to reproduce in a staging Dedicated cluster when we simulate a signing-key header change on resume and enable the customer's resume harness.
- Root cause points to the session-manager not strongly tying a resume token to a single linear event stream when the session authentication material differs.

Preliminary mitigations tried:
- Forcing resume to require identical session-key material (server-side) prevents the issue but breaks some legitimate client rotation patterns.
- Introducing a per-session resume-lock that serializes replay then new events eliminates reordering but adds ~30-60ms extra latency on resume.

Customer impact tradeoffs noted:
- Strict resume-key checks: correct ordering but causes failed resumes for customers that rotate keys mid-stream (breaking availability).
- Resume-lock/serialize: preserves ordering with small resume latency increase.

Next steps proposed:
- Engineering: design a resume-lock that is opt-in per-customer (Dedicated customers) via account flag.
- Short-term support mitigation: recommend customer set resume=false for order-sensitive streams (explicitly close and restart the session) or avoid rotating signing keys during active streams.
- Long-term: change session-manager to canonicalize session identity across keystore rotations if rotation metadata includes parent-key-id header.

Additional notes:
SRE (on-call): Reproduced. Root-cause points at session-manager replay concurrency. Drafting a short-term config flag to serialize replay on a per-customer basis.
Customer (NimbleScribe): We rotate keys automatically; disabling rotation during user sessions is a tough constraint for us. Would prefer a server-side opt-in that preserves ordering and keeps our rotation policy.
payload.summary: Go SDK: Out-of-order tool executions after stream resume when client rotates session keystore

Long-term fix: engineering to implement rotation-safe dedupe that ties dedupe window to stable evaluation run ids and ensures token migration backwards compatibility. Issue summary:

Between 2026-03-09 22:40 UTC and 2026-03-10 03:10 UTC several customers using the customer's dedicated pool (Finova Analytics) reported large p50/p95/p99 throughput drops and increased request queueing. The symptoms are consistent with GPUs being unable to accept new batches (slot starvation) even though node-level utilization (GPU% compute) looked moderate.

Impact:
- Finova reported ~60% drop in processed inference requests during peak window; elevated request latency and queued backlog caused failed SLAs.
- Multiple internal tenant routes observed transient 5xx spike and autoscaler thrashing (rapid spin-ups followed by immediate scale-down).

Environment:
- Dedicated pool: finova-dedicated-us-east (reserved capacity).
- Region: us-east-1.
- Model: redwood-gpt-2.7b-quantized pinned at v2026-02-28.

Steps to reproduce (observed pattern):
1) Normal traffic baseline for model routes.
2) A large number (~10k/min) of short streaming requests (mean token length 8) from a single tenant begin across many connections.
3) Autoscaler starts provisioning slots/nodes but scheduler begins to show slot allocation failures and high slot fragmentation.
4) Serving runtime reports high KV cache churn and many small active batches; new full-batch allocations are delayed, causing request queue buildup and 429/502 for some routes.

Logs / artifacts attached in telemetry:
- kube events and node allocation logs (timestamps 2026-03-09 22:35:00 -> 2026-03-10 03:15:00).
- runtime-per-request traces showing repeated small-batch dispatches and KV cache eviction messages.
- autoscaler logs: repeated scale-up then immediate reclaim cycles.

Initial hypothesis:
- A noisy (stealth) tenant generated a flood of many short-lived streaming requests that fragmented GPU slot allocation and triggered autoscaler thrash; runtime batching could not coalesce due to short contexts and high connection churn. This produced slot starvation for steady tenants and large throughput variance.

Workaround applied so far:
- Applied per-tenant short-stream rate limit (temporary) for the suspected tenant to stabilize the pool.
- Tuned autoscaler cooldown to 180s to reduce thrash.
- Enabled additional batching window (increase up-to N ms) on serving runtime for the affected pool to allow coalescing of small streams.

Next steps:
- Identify the tenant and confirm traffic pattern (DONE: suspect tenant anonymized as T-4289).
- Run targeted replay of request pattern in staging to validate batching/window change.
- Plan permanent mitigations: per-tenant soft rate limits, improved slot packing policy, and autoscaler backoff heuristics.

Additional notes:
Metric correlation: queue_length and slot_allocation_failures spike concurrently with increased small-stream connection rate from single tenant CIDR block.
Telemetry: runtime logs show 'kv_cache_eviction=TRUE' bursts and 'batch_size=1' occurrences up by 320% versus baseline for the period.
Autoscaler: observed repeated scale-up to +3 nodes followed by immediate scale-down within 30-60s (thrash). Current cooldown 30s was too low for this workload pattern.
Network: no TLS/DNS errors observed; connection churn originated from valid customer endpoints.
Hypothesis validated in staging: replaying short-stream flood reproduces queue build and slot fragmentation; increasing batching window greatly improves throughput and reduces p99.
Related tickets: see SUP-33489 (fragmented-slot-saturation) and SUP-61234 (interleaved-affinity-mismatch) for overlap in symptoms and historical mitigations.
Risk: aggressive batching window could increase latency for true low-latency clients; need knob exposed per-customer route.
Partial mitigation applied: throttled offending tenant and adjusted autoscaler cooldown; batching window increase rolled out to affected pool in a controlled manner. Customer (Finova) reports recovery to near-baseline throughput. Permanent engineering work to implement per-tenant soft shaping, scheduler slot-packing improvements, and autoscaler smarter backoff is planned (see linked PRs).
Create engineering epic for slot-packing and per-tenant shaping (owners: Serving Runtime team).
Roll out autoscaler backoff heuristics to prod with canary (owner: Autoscaler team; target: 2026-03-25).
Run postmortem and publish to Confluence (owner: Incident Commander).

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customer reports duplicated side effects (duplicate downstream webhook/tool executions) when using Redwood Go SDK streaming function-calls behind their edge gateway that uses QUIC/HTTP3. Duplicates appear correlated with client IP changes (e.g., mobile handover) and short-lived connection migrations.

Impact:
- Multiple duplicate external tool/webhook invocations observed causing billing and downstream transaction duplication (financial impact to customer).
- Occurs intermittently under normal production traffic from a subset of mobile clients.
- Customer flagged as dedicated tenant with strict correctness requirements.

Environment:
- Customer: FinGrid Labs (dedicated tenancy).
- Redwood: prod-us-west serving runtime, API gateway behind Envoy edge with HTTP/3 enabled (QUIC).
- Client: Go service using redwood-go-sdk v0.9.7 streaming function-calls + tool invocation.

Steps to reproduce (approx):
1) Start long-lived streaming session from client using Go SDK (stream uses chunked frames and keeps a persistent QUIC connection).
2) Trigger a function/tool call that results in an outbound webhook/external job (customer side effect).
3) Simulate mobile network handover / IP change to force QUIC connection migration (or use test harness that triggers connection rebind).
4) Observe server logs and downstream endpoints for duplicate invocations within ~2s window.

Observed behavior:
- Two (sometimes three) identical tool/webhook calls within 1-5s of the connection migration.
- Request logs show idempotency header values differing in length and content between the initial request and the retry. Example headers captured from prod logs:
  - X-Redwood-Idempotency: "Aq3fV1GzQ2=="
  - X-Redwood-Idempotency: "Aq3fV1GzQ"
- The shorter variant (missing padding) is treated as distinct by the runtime idempotency index, leading to duplicate execution.
- Edge proxy (Envoy) logs show header reassembly across QUIC datagrams; occasional header chunk boundaries coincide with connection bind/migration.

Expected behavior:
- Idempotent retries should resolve to the same idempotency token regardless of header chunking or transport-level migration; downstream tool invocations should not be duplicated.

Relevant logs / excerpts (sanitized):
- client-go (sdk) outbound frames:
  FRAME [idempotency: "Aq3fV1GzQ2=="] seq=124
  (migration occurs immediately after frame send)
- edge proxy (envoy) capture:
  recv headers chunk1: "X-Redwood-Idemp=Aq3fV1GzQ"
  recv headers chunk2: "2==;" (reassembled)
- runtime idempotency lookup key (as logged): "Aq3fV1GzQ"  <-- padding removed during reassembly in 2/1725 sampled requests

Investigation notes so far:
- Repro on customer traffic with controlled IP migration in staging (engineer lab).
- Root cause appears to be a combination of: (1) QUIC header chunking across frames during connection migration, (2) an intermediate edge/proxy reassembly path that normalizes/strips trailing '=' padding from header values, and (3) the runtime's idempotency store treating the header string as-is (no normalization / tolerant-matching).
- Go SDK encodes streaming idempotency tokens using base64 URL-safe encoding and includes padding; some proxies remove '=' characters when reassembling header chunks (likely due to an HTTP header normalization/concatenation bug in the edge config).
- We confirmed that matching the reassembled value to the original (by re-adding padding to length % 4 == 2/3) would have de-duplicated the requests.

Preliminary workaround provided to customer:
- Short-term: disable HTTP/3 on the edge gateway for the affected service to avoid QUIC migration path (customer confirmed reduction in duplicates).
- Client-side: send the idempotency token in both the X-Redwood-Idempotency header and in the request JSON body at top-level (e.g., {"idempotency_token":"..."}). Runtime team can be asked to check body token as fallback.
- Edge config: increase HTTP header buffer / disable header normalization that strips '=' (if configurable in their Envoy variant).

Suggested long-term fixes / engineering tasks:
- Runtime: normalize idempotency tokens on ingest (apply base64 padding normalization and compare canonical forms before creating a new execution record).
- SDKs: send canonicalized idempotency token with deterministic canonicalization (trim/encode using base64url without padding AND also include a checksum header). Consider a signed short-hash header that is resilient to truncation.
- Edge & infra: harden Envoy/edge config to preserve header characters across QUIC migration and add tests for header chunk reassembly under migration conditions.

Customer impact notes:
- Customer reports financial duplicate postings for a small percentage of transactions (they provided sample webhook payload IDs). They asked for an urgent mitigation strategy while engineering implements runtime normalization.

Attachments linked by customer: sample webhook receipts, short pcap-style trace and header dumps (uploaded to secure S3 link, provided in comment below).

-- customer provided 'webhook_receipt_20260310.json' and 'pdu_trace_20260310.txt'

Additional notes:
Disable HTTP/3 on the ingress for affected tenant OR have client include idempotency token in request body as a fallback key. We also recommend increasing header buffer / disabling header normalization on the edge proxy.
Merge runtime canonicalization PR and deploy to canary for dedicated tenants (ENG task)
Provide customer with step-by-step to disable HTTP/3 or change Envoy header settings (Support playbook)
Add e2e regression test that simulates QUIC connection migration and header chunking (QA/Infra)
Intermediate edge proxy normalizes/reassembles QUIC header chunks and strips padding characters from base64-encoded idempotency header; runtime treats the resulting string as a new token leading to duplicate executions.

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customers on a set of dedicated pools (Maply.AI - dedicated) reported sudden P50/P95 latency knees lasting ~2-6 minutes across multiple reservations during peak windows. Impact: customer-facing inference increased P95 by 2-4x and experienced intermittent 429s when client-side retrying caused backpressure.

Impact:
- Affected customer Maply.AI reported degraded SLAs for three live routes (geocode-normalize, route-summarize, labelize) between 08:12-08:20 UTC.
- Traffic patterns show many short, sub-100ms request bursts with prefetch-enabled traffic for long contexts.

Environment:
- Dedicated pools in prod - us-east, GPU family: A100-40GB heterogeneous mix (some older guests with 3xx driver).
- Serving runtime: v2.9.1; Scheduler: v1.4.2; Prefetcher: enabled with default timing window.

Steps to reproduce (observed pattern):
1) At scale, many small synchronous clients send short requests with prefetch turned on in SDK.
2) Prefetch pipeline issues KV prewarm RPCs with timing skew relative to the main request arrival, creating a wave of prefetch CPU work followed by simultaneous batch attachments.
3) Scheduler assigns fractional GPU slots to many short batches (slot dust) leaving GPUs with many tiny allocations that fail to fully amortize kernel startup.
4) Autoscaler snapshot window interprets the noisy short bursts as transient and delays provisioning, causing short-lived GPU shortages and increased batching latency.

Observed behavior:
- P50 increases modestly but P95/P99 show sharp knees.
- Short-lived 429s and client-side retries correlate with autoscaler backoff traces.
- GPU utilization shows many sub-5% occupancy intervals across nodes while queue depth spikes.

Expected behavior:
- Smooth batching with steady slot occupancy and autoscaler triggering predictable scaling without short starvation windows.

Logs/metrics attached (panels and excerpts included in investigation notes).
2026-03-13 08:26 - Support (Aisha Patel): Acknowledged with primary oncall. Customer reports repeated P95 spikes; requested request/response IDs and timeframe. Forwarded logs to SRE.
2026-03-13 08:33 - Oncall (Marcus Huang): Correlated spikes with scheduling logs. Noticed prefetch RPC spikes 100-200ms before main infer RPC. Opening investigation. Slack: #support-dedicated thread INC-20260313-07.
2026-03-13 09:05 - Customer (Maply Ops - Jordan Lee): Confirmed SDK was upgraded last week to enable prefetch=true with default timing window. They can toggle prefetch on a route to test.
2026-03-13 10:12 - SRE (Lena Ortiz): Early mitigation suggestion: disable prefetch for the affected routes on Maply's dedicated pools and observe latency for the next 30 minutes. Asked infra team for quick autoscaler profile adjustment to shorten snapshot window.
2026-03-13 10:45 - Support (Aisha Patel): Customer applied prefetch=false on two routes. Reports P95 returned near baseline within ~10 minutes. Requested to keep changes for monitoring while we investigate root cause.

Additional notes:
08:20 UTC - Grafana panel (dedicated/us-east/slots): queue_depth spike from 30 to 210 concurrent batches; GPU occupancy per node drops to 3-8% while batch attach rates increase. (panel: /d/dedicated/slot-util)
Scheduler trace: saw 18% of attach RPCs reporting 'prefetch: true' with timestamps 80-220ms earlier than main RPCs for same request IDs (trace samples attached).
Autoscaler logs: snapshot interval=60s; scale decision delayed by 1 interval due to moving-average smoothing. Several nodes entered 'pending-attach' state and were not provisioned before queue spikes hit p99 latency. (log snippet in ticket)
Hypothesis A: Prefetch timing skew produces micro-concurrency that fragments slot allocation and generates many underfilled batches ('slot dust'), reducing effective throughput despite low nominal GPU utilization.
Hypothesis B: Autoscaler smoothing parameter (scale_down/scale_up thresholds) combined with short-lived spikes leads to no immediate provisioning, creating transient GPU shortages even though overall capacity looks sufficient.
Hypothesis C: Heterogeneous GPU set includes a mix with slightly different kernel startup latencies exposed under small-batch heavy attach patterns; the older driver nodes observed higher attach latency but were not preferentially evicted, adding variance.
Evidence: Reproduced similar pattern on staging with 200 client coroutines sending small requests at 50-150 qps with prefetch=true; observed p95 knee and slot dust. When prefetch disabled, pattern disappeared and batching aggregated to larger, more efficient batches.
Related signals: small increase in NVLink attach contention counters and elevation in PCIe retry errors on 3 nodes coincident with spike windows.
Short-term mitigation: Advise Maply.AI to disable SDK prefetch for affected routes (done) or set prefetch timing window to a higher tolerance (recommendation: 350ms).
Short-term infra mitigation: Reduce autoscaler snapshot smoothing on the specific dedicated pool from 60s to 20s to react faster to short bursts (requires ops change).
Medium-term: Implement prefetch-coalescing in the serving runtime so prefetch RPCs for the same tenant are deduplicated within a 200-400ms window.
Medium-term: Add autoscaler signal from attach-rate (not only queue depth) to detect prefetch waves and pre-provision slots proactively.
Long-term: Add heterogeneous-node-aware placement to prefer nodes with consistent driver/kernel startup for low-batch workloads or route-level allocation preferences.
Monitoring: Add Grafana alert for high queue_depth + low GPU occupancy pattern (queue_depth>150 and avg_gpu_util<10% for 60s) to create early paging alerts for SRE.
2026-03-13 11:05 - Mitigation applied: Maply disabled prefetch=false for two critical routes. Observed P95 drop to baseline within ~10 minutes. No further 429s reported after 11:20 UTC.
2026-03-13 12:00 - Infra ops adjusted autoscaler snapshot window in staging; validated faster reaction to small bursts in controlled tests. Ops request for permanent config change is filed as INT-48321.
Permanent fix plan: Deliver prefetch-coalescing patch (serving-runtime PR referenced) and autoscaler attach-rate signal by end of Q2. Engineering tickets created and prioritized with product (linked INT-50312, PR: github.com/redwood/serving-runtime/pull/4891).
Customer communication: Notified Maply of short-term mitigations and the roadmap items. Customer accepted recommended SDK change and asked to be informed when runtime coalescing is available.
Post-incident: Schedule a postmortem with SRE and Runtime teams to review threshold tuning, prefetch design, and heterogeneous node placement. Tentative postmortem date: 2026-03-20.
Maply appreciative of quick mitigation; requested guidance on SDK prefetch parameters and a timeline for runtime coalescing. They requested export of per-request traces for their audits.
Create INT ticket for autoscaler snapshot config change (INT-48321)
Implement prefetch coalescing design (ENG-PRIORITY-M07)
Add alerting rule and dashboard panels (MON-7382)
payload.summary: Unbalanced prefetch timing causing transient GPU starvation and batched latency knees

Issue summary:
Customer noticed an unexpected invoice charge and autopay failure after a tenant-level tag rename that happened during a scheduled plan migration. A subset of postbacks from a large multi-region batch embed job were routed with the old tenant tag, causing those postbacks to be credited to the wrong cost center. Promotional credits tied to the customer account were not applied to the invoice (they show as applied in the console UI but not on the finalized invoice), which triggered autopay to fail on the finalized cycle.

Impact:
- Finalized invoice for billing cycle 2026-02 shows a $9,420 line item from 'staging-rate' entries and a $-1,250 provisional credit missing.
- Autopay attempted on 2026-03-01 but failed due to insufficient applied credits causing customer account to show past-due.
- Customer billing contact is on hold for audit; they request an explanation and provisional credit while we investigate.

Environment:
- Prod (us-east), tenant DocuLogix main org, affected API key domain: proj-doculogix-prod (one key flagged in the first row of postback table).
- Plan change executed 2026-02-28 22:04 UTC (migration window).

Steps to reproduce / observed sequence:
1) 2026-02-28T21:58 UTC: large batch embed job kicked off targeting us-east with mixed-models; postbacks streamed to billing collector.
2) 2026-02-28T22:04 UTC: tenant tag rename performed (console action: change tenant tag from docu-legacy to doculogix-main) as part of plan migration.
3) 2026-02-28T22:04:02 - 22:06 UTC: collector service accepted ~1,800 postbacks; ~120 were tagged with old tenant id due to a brief cache miss in the tag-mapper.
4) 2026-03-01: billing finalized; invoice lines include charges attributed to old tenant tag and promo credits not applied.

Logs / snapshots attached in backend: billing/postbacks/2026-02-28/us-east/postbacks-22-04.log (snippet shows tag header mismatch), console audit 2026-02-28 22:04 (tenant-tag-change), postback-reconciler metrics for same minute shows 15% postback rejections before retry.

Initial hypothesis:
- Tag-mapper cache TTL expired at the exact time of the rename leading to a race where some postbacks used stale mapping and were attributed to the legacy tenant id.
- Promo credits are applied at invoice-finalization by matching tenant ids; misattributed postbacks caused credits to attach to the legacy tenant (now inactive), so the live tenant invoice appears without those credits.
- Autopay failed because effective balance remained above threshold after misattribution.

Requested next steps from Support/ENG:
- Engineering: confirm postback attribution and produce reconciler run to reassign misattributed postbacks to active tenant.
- Billing ops: produce provisional credit for customer while fix is validated.
- CS: notify customer with timeline and provide temporary waiver so autopay won't disrupt services.

Additional notes:
2026-03-11 — Infra (comment via INT-2134): Tag-mapper TTL default is 60s; there was a brief cache miss while the rename propagated. No deploys at that time. Recommending reconciler replay for 120 postbacks to reassign tenant id.
2026-03-12 — Customer (DocuLogix - Maria Chen): Thank you. Please confirm that applying provisional credit won't affect our usage metrics dashboard; we need usage numbers unchanged for internal chargebacks. Also request ETA for final invoice correction.

Issue summary:
During a staged canary rollout for PrismHealth (enterprise/private deployment, us-east-1), a short-lived jitter in tenant alias synchronization caused a subset of requests to be routed to the compatibility (degraded/compat) variant instead of the pinned model. The behavior was 'transparent' to the client (no explicit 5xx or pin-clearing), resulting in slightly different generation tokenization and a downstream quality regression for ~2% of traffic for a 7 minute window.

Impact:
- Production latency within SLOs but output quality degradation for specific tenant routes (error reported by PrismHealth automated QA).
- ~2% of requests for the tenant experienced slight tokenization differences and rerouting to compat variant; no data leakage.
- Customer reported increased downstream classification mismatch in their monitoring.

Timeline (UTC):
- 2026-03-12 14:03 — Canary weight increase from 5% -> 10% started (automated rollout).
- 2026-03-12 14:07 — PrismHealth alert triggers: batch of QA prompts show tokenization drift.
- 2026-03-12 14:09 — Support Triage notified; snapshot of requests recorded.
- 2026-03-12 14:10 — Edge telemetry shows alias-sync success/fail spikes for tenant route.
- 2026-03-12 14:16 — Orchestrator replay confirms transparent fallback to compat variant for specific cohort.
- 2026-03-12 14:20 — Canary weight paused; mitigation enacted.

Observed behavior:
- Tenant routing metadata (alias -> model mapping) was read by edge-proxy with TTLs; for a small cohort the alias read returned stale compatibility mapping for 30–45s before reconciling.
- Orchestrator accepted requests against the compat variant without raising explicit pin-change events.

Expected behavior:
- Alias sync jitter should not cause silent fallback while tenant has an explicit pin; edge should prefer control-plane pinned mapping and defer to orchestration if read is inconsistent.

Temporary mitigation taken:
- Rolled back canary weight to 5% and paused automated increases.
- Forced alias-sync reconciliation for PrismHealth cohort and flushed edge alias cache for the tenant.
- Notified customer and routed their critical traffic to a pinned dedicated pool until fix.

1) Start a staged canary for a customer with tenant-level model pinning active (weight increase window).
2) Simulate alias-sync latency by delaying control-plane alias propagation to one edge shard for ~30s.
3) Send concurrent streaming requests with token-sensitive prompts.
4) Observe routing logs: some requests return compat variant id even though the tenant pin exists.

edge-proxy logs (snippet):
[2026-03-12T14:08:27Z] tenant=prismhealth alias-read cached=false status=200 mapping=compat-7b-v1
[2026-03-12T14:08:27Z] tenant=prismhealth request_id=rq_45a model_resolved=compat-7b-v1 route=degraded-stream
orchestrator logs (snippet):
[2026-03-12T14:08:28Z] tenant=prismhealth session=st-123 accept=compat-7b-v1 pin_check=skipped reason=alias_mismatch

Telemetry links:
- Canary rollout dashboard: https://console.redwood.ai/dashboards/rollouts/2026-03-12-14
- Edge alias sync latency chart: https://console.redwood.ai/dashboards/edge/alias-sync-latency
Initial hypothesis: edge cache TTL expiration + delayed control-plane snapshot commit led to alias-read returning an older compatibility mapping.
Evidence: correlated spikes in alias-read latency and control-plane commit lag at 14:07–14:09. Orchestrator accepted mapping without verification because pin-check path short-circuited when alias read returned mapping.
Further findings:
- The pin-coherence path relies on edge cache TTL and an eventual background reconcile; when alias-sync jitter happens during weight increases, the reconcile race allows compat mapping to be used for in-flight sessions.
- No memory corruption or auth failures detected.
- A replication lag on the control-plane write queue (db commit lag ~150ms but queuing added ~1.2s for a subset of shards) coincides with edge cache refresh windows.
Open questions:
- Should edge prefer last-known pinned mapping over an alias read that is older than X milliseconds?
- Is there a missing verification step in orchestrator when pin exists but alias read mismatch occurs?
Samir Rao (Support) 2026-03-12 14:12: Investigating with SRE, collecting logs and customer payloads. Notified PrismHealth that we're on it.
Elena Martinez (SRE) 2026-03-12 14:18: Found control-plane commit queue lag affecting alias propagation to shard-7. Pushing for immediate reconcile and edge cache flush for tenant.
PrismHealth (Customer) 2026-03-12 14:25: Seeing elevated QA mismatch in our monitoring. Appreciate the quick rollback — can you confirm which sessions were affected?
Elena Martinez (SRE) 2026-03-12 14:33: We recorded request IDs and replayed those against pinned variant; differences logged and provided to customer via secure share. No PII exposed.
Product (Maya Chen) 2026-03-12 15:02: Flagging for postmortem to review alias-sync logic during canary weight shifts and to update the rollout runbook.
Mitigation applied: paused automated canary weight increase and forced alias reconciliation; edge cache flush for tenant shard; routed PrismHealth to a pinned Dedicated pool as a safety measure.
Next steps (action items):
- Engineering to add a defensive check in orchestrator: if tenant has explicit pin, prefer control-plane pinned mapping for X seconds even if alias read disagrees (PR proposal: orchestrator#1842).
- Add telemetry alert for alias-read variance > 50ms during rollout weight changes.
- Runbook update assigned to Product/Platform for canary weight rollback criteria.
Status: customer routed to pinned pool; monitoring shows no further regressions since 14:22 UTC. Work in progress for code change and postmortem write-up.
payload.summary: Tenant alias sync jitter causes transparent fallback to compatibility variant during canary window

payload.description:
Issue summary:
CipherNova reported sustained p50/p95 throughput decline (~15-30% below baseline) on their dedicated pool beginning 2026-03-10 09:10 UTC. Symptoms matched a steady reduction in batched pipeline utilization with occasional short-lived recoveries. Impact affected two pinned models used by their conversational product and resulted in customer-reported slowdowns and higher queueing.

Impact:
- Customer-facing latency increase: p50 +160ms, p95 +600ms vs baseline for steady low-latency routes.
- Effective QPS drop of 18% on pinned dedicated pool during peak window.
- No token loss, but degraded throughput triggered customer throttling thresholds.

Environment:
- Dedicated pool (reserved), us-east-1, GPU type: A100-80GB mix.
- Autoscaler config: proactive with cooldown 90s, predictive disabled.
- KV/prefix caching enabled for both models.

Steps to reproduce (environment sensitive):
1) Run steady batched traffic to gptx-13b-8k with 8 concurrent clients at 200 RPS total from us-east-1.
2) Observe per-GPU pipeline utilization and batch fill rates.
3) Notice a gradual decline in batch fill and sustained single-digit drop in active pipeline streaks after ~20 minutes.

Observed logs / metrics (excerpts):
- scheduler: "lease:prefetch_incomplete=0.23, failed_handoff=12/1h"
- serving-runtime: "pipeline_streaks=0.68 -> 0.51 (20m)"
- autoscaler: "scale_decision:hold due to transient attach-failures"
- NVLink errors: none; driver stable.

Initial hypothesis:
We suspect a race between prefetch lease heartbeats and scheduler handoff when GPUs are under heterogeneous attachment churn. Some prefetch leases appear to be marked incomplete, leaving partial batches or orphaned prefetch slots that reduce effective pipeline saturation. This behaves like a noisy-neighbor but at the lease/handshake layer rather than pure compute hogging.

Customer impact and requested outcome:
Customer requests restoration of baseline throughput and mitigation so similar lease mismatches do not recur. They requested visibility into handoff failures and a short-term workaround if available.
Generate steady RPS to pinned models from us-east-1
Measure batch fill and pipeline streak over 30 minutes
Correlate scheduler lease logs with serving-runtime pipeline metrics
Prefetch_incomplete metric rose from baseline 0.02 to 0.23 during incident window.
Trace correlation shows lease author (scheduler-node-17) issued prefetch requests that never reached 'complete' state before executor moved to next batch on 3 GPUs.
Attached GPUs show no driver errors; CPU-side handshake delays of 40-120ms observed on kubelet attach path.
Autoscaler held scaling decisions due to perceived attach failures (false-positive) — this prevented adding capacity to mask the issue.
Short-term remediation: reduced prefetch handshake TTL and tuned scheduler retry backoff. Applied to pool at 2026-03-11 02:00 UTC. Observed partial throughput recovery.
Medium-term fix: runtime team to land commit that tightens lease state transitions and adds a reconciliation worker to sweep 'prefetch_incomplete' leases older than 10s. PR opened: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/4128 (testing in staging).
Follow-ups: add dashboard alert for prefetch_incomplete > 0.1 and an autoscaler exception when attach error rate is correlated with incomplete leases. Schedule postmortem runbook update and communicate to CipherNova by 2026-03-14.
Customer workaround: temporarily enable conservative burst_capacity for their dedicated pool to absorb intermittent drops until permanent fix is deployed.

2026-03-10 10:05 UTC - SRE (Ravi Kapoor): Collected scheduler and runtime traces. Observed increased prefetch_incomplete counters on several GPUs. Opening instrumented trace request to runtime team.

Additional notes:
2026-03-11 02:10 UTC - SRE (Ravi Kapoor): Deployed temporary autotuner config to shorten prefetch handshake TTL to 5s for affected pool; observed partial recovery (~8% improvement) but not full baseline.
2026-03-11 14:00 UTC - Support (Ava Martinez): Customer reports throughput improved but intermittent slowdowns persist during midday spike. Requested full root cause and permanent fix timeline.
Customer-facing summary will be drafted after root cause verification. Initial message: we identified a prefetch lease mismatch causing partial pipeline starvation; a temporary config change restored some throughput and a targeted fix is in testing.

Issue summary:
Customer requests a timeboxed forensic export covering a 3-hour window (2026-02-28T22:00Z to 2026-03-01T01:00Z) for a specific tenant. They report duplicate events arriving in their SIEM after our webhook bridge, and they require: (a) per-session reconstruction with ordering guarantees, (b) a signed delivery manifest (HMAC/SHA256 per-batch) for chain-of-custody, and (c) proof of TLS client certificate rotation timestamps used by our forwarder during that window.

Impact:
- Arcadia uses these exports for regulatory investigation. Duplicate events and missing ordering block their forensic analysis and escalate to legal/compliance. They marked this P1 / Sev1.

Environment:
- Redwood prod-us-east, customer Arcadia (enterprise) using tenant-id: arcadia-prod-42.
- SIEM: Customer-side Splunk HEC endpoint behind mutual TLS.

Steps to reproduce / customer-provided reproduction notes:
1) Customer replayed webhook ingestion of events for a 1-hour subset and observed duplicate event_ids in Splunk for specific session_ids.
2) They observed gaps in ordering for long-running sessions (>30s between tokens) that should be sequenced by our resume token.
3) Customer exported TLS logs from their edge and noted our client cert presented at 2026-02-28T22:30Z but no rotation record was available from our manifest.

Observed behavior:
- Duplicate events are present for ~0.3% of events in the sampled window. Duplicates cluster around peaks when our bridge retries (backpressure) and during a short spike on 2026-02-28T22:28-22:32Z.

- Customer requests an attestation of the client cert thumbprint(s) used by our forwarder during the target window and a signed manifest including resume tokens and per-event sequence numbers.

- Ordered, deduplicated sequence for each session with monotonic sequence numbers.
- Signed per-batch manifest (HMAC-SHA256) with resume tokens to allow deterministic reassembly.
- TLS client cert rotation proof including issuance timestamps and KID/thumbprint.

Attachments provided by customer:
- sample_splunk_dupes.csv (100 rows)
- webhook_bridge_logs_20260228-22.gz (truncated)
- customer_tls_capture.pcap

Customer asks: full export for 2026-02-28T22:00Z -> 2026-03-01T01:00Z, signed manifest with batch checksums, per-event sequence numbers and resume tokens, and TLS client cert rotation record for the forwarder that pushed to their HEC endpoint.

Additional notes:

Action: Collect raw bridge logs, look for retry spikes and outgoing certificate details.

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customer (NimbleRetail) on a dedicated cluster reports repeated p95/p99 latency spikes and a pattern of automatic routing fallbacks to a smaller/quantized model variant. The symptoms coincide with several ephemeral GPU allocations and eviction events in the same reserved pool.

Impact:
- Intermittent request-level p99 spikes to ~6-12s for generation routes that normally sit at ~400-700ms.
- ~8-12% of requests during windows are served by a lower-capacity model (redwood-13b-q8 -> redwood-13b-q4 fallback), leading to occasional content regressions.
- Customer-facing SLAs at risk for peak windows (midday US-east).

Environment:
- Dedicated capacity: pool-id: pool-prod-us-east-22 (NimbleRetail reserved)
- Region: prod-us-east (us-east-1)
- Models in use: redwood-13b-v1-q8 (pinned), fallback variants available: redwood-13b-v1-q4
- Autoscaler config: predictive+reactive hybrid, min_slots=4, target_util=0.78, burst_enabled=true

Timeline / Observed behavior:
- 2026-03-12 11:00-11:45 UTC: sustained p95/p99 growth visible in Kibana for pool-prod-us-east-22.
- 2026-03-12 11:07 UTC: autoscaler started provisioning new nodes (provisioning lag ~18s).
- 2026-03-12 11:08-11:15 UTC: multiple eviction logs and GPU attach/detach messages; scheduler logged preemptions for low-priority background jobs.
- 2026-03-12 11:12 UTC: routing policy triggered fallback to q4 variant for ~9% of requests to maintain latency SLOs.

Steps to reproduce (customer):
1. Run sustained small-stream mixed workload (many short streams, mean tokens per request ~40) with intermittent large-generation peaks (some requests >1000 tokens).
2. Observe p95/p99 latency in the tenant pool and query last 30m routing logs for 'fallback' events.

Logs / Metrics (high level):
- autoscaler-provisioner logs: repeated "node_provision_delay=18s" and "slot_attach_timeout=4s" around event windows.
- scheduler logs: "preempted_job_id=bg-checkpoint-..." and "eviction_reason=priority_reclaim"
- serving-runtime: repeated "gpu_eviction" events, "nvlink_warning" (low frequency), and batcher queue length spiking to 4x baseline.
- Kibana Dashboard: p50 stable, p95 drift to 2-6s, p99 to 6-12s at peak.

Initial mitigation applied:
- Temporarily raised pool's min_slots from 4 to 6 for NimbleRetail to reduce immediate provisioning churn (manual override).
- Applied stricter priority on tenant's allocation (temporary tag) to reduce background preemptions.
- Disabled predictive burst window for 20 minutes to let steady-state allocator rebalance.

Customer visible workaround:
- Customer noticed immediate p95 improvement after min_slots increase; still seeing occasional fallbacks during the next peak at 11:35 UTC.

Notes / constraints:
- The pool shares underlying HW with several other reserved tenants; noisy background maintenance jobs on infra side were scheduled overlapping with customer's peak.
- Fallback routing is functioning as designed but hidden to the customer; they prefer deterministic pinning and want investigation into why allocation lag is high enough to trigger fallbacks.

Desired outcome:
- Identify root cause of provisioning/attachment latency and noisy-neighbor preemptions.
- Prevent future fallback routing during customer peak windows without unbounded reserved capacity increases.
- Follow-up runbook updates and autoscaler config suggestions for tiered fairness.
Hypotheses considered: (1) predictive autoscaler over-shrunk pool during low-traffic leading to under-provisioning at burst; (2) background infra maintenance jobs or low-priority training sweeps caused eviction traffic and NVLink contention; (3) node provisioning latency due to cloud API throttling or image pull bottleneck.

Findings so far:
- Correlation between scheduled infra maintenance job (internal tag: infra-maint-2026-03-12) and eviction spikes in the same availability zone. Slack thread #infra-maint shows a maintenance kickoff at 2026-03-12T10:56:00Z.
- Provisioner metrics show an increased median 'first_ready' latency compared to baseline (18s vs baseline 6s). Attach timeouts increased during 11:05-11:18 UTC.
- Scheduler logs show preemptions targeted at background-checkpoint jobs with tag 'low-priority-batch', which explains GPU evictions.
- No consistent kernel-level hardware errors; NVLink warnings are low frequency and not primary.

Intermediate conclusion: mix of autoscaler sizing + overlapping infra background jobs produced transient scarcity. The autoscaler reacted but provisioning lag and preemptive evictions triggered fallback routing to preserve request success, creating the customer-visible regressions.
Workarounds and short-term actions taken:
- Raised NimbleRetail pool min_slots to 6 (manual override) which reduced immediate fallback rate from ~9% to ~1-2%.
- Coordinated with Infra on Slack (#infra-maint) to reschedule or throttle non-critical background jobs during major customer peak windows. Infra acknowledged and queued a controlled retry for maintenance tasks.
- Added a temporary policy to delay preemptive eviction of low-priority jobs for 60s during autoscaler provisioning windows to reduce churn.

Planned longer-term fixes:
- Autoscaler tuning: increase baseline warm slots for dedicated pools with predictable peaks; adjust predictive window to be less aggressive for customers with min_slots > 4.
- Improve provisioner resilience: investigate image caching and parallel attach improvements to reduce node_provision_delay from 18s to target < 8s. (Owner: infra/provisioner team).
- Add a fairness policy: tenant-priority-reservation flag that ensures reserved pools with 'enterprise' or 'dedicated' tiers are protected from non-critical maintenance preemptions during customer SLAs.
- Update Runbook: documented steps to identify 'fallback' routing triggers and recommended autoscaler configs for dedicated customers with mixed short/long stream workloads.

Status: In Progress. Remaining work assigned to infra/provisioner and autoscaler teams. Targeting next deployment of autoscaler tuning by 2026-03-21.
2026-03-12 12:02 - Support: Miguel Santos: Opened ticket after NimbleRetail support call. Customer included trace IDs and routing logs. Escalating to infra and autoscaler owners.
2026-03-12 12:20 - Infra: Priya Rao: Confirmed infra-maint window overlapped with customer's peak. We're pausing non-critical batch maintenance for the next 48h for affected AZs.

Additional notes:
2026-03-12 13:01 - Support: Miguel Santos: Applied temporary min_slots=6 override and saw reduction in fallback events; customer reports improved UX but requests permanent fix.
2026-03-14 10:23 - Product: Daniel Ortiz: Adding a feature request to expose a 'no-maintenance' SLA window flag for Dedicated customers to be honored by infra and scheduler.
2026-03-14 15:08 - Support: Aisha Patel: Consolidated runbook draft and scheduled working session with autoscaler and infra owners for 2026-03-16 to finalize tuning and deployment plan.

payload.description:
Customer (Northpeak Health) reports production failures in Private deployment immediately after migrating KMS key + tightening IAM. Symptoms are consistent across services that need to unwrap DEKs using customer-managed AWS KMS.

Issue summary
- Decrypt requests to customer-managed KMS returning AccessDeniedException.
- Requests that require decrypt fail fast, causing 5xx responses from Redwood services in the customer VPC.

Impact
- Customer reports ~30–40% of API requests failing (workloads hitting encrypted config/secrets + audit-log exporter).
- End-user impact: request failures + degraded availability for clinical workflow integration.

Environment
- Deployment mode: Redwood Private (customer VPC)
- Cloud: AWS
- Region: us-east-1
- KMS: Customer-managed CMK (symmetric)
- Key ARN provided by customer: arn:aws:kms:us-east-1:***:key/6c1d2c4b-****-****-****-************
- Principal used by Redwood services (per customer): arn:aws:iam::***:role/redwood-private-runtime
- Observed starting: 2025-11-01 09:15 ET

Customer report / steps to reproduce
1) Customer rotated/migrated CMK and updated IAM policies to least privilege.
2) Redwood runtime attempts to decrypt envelope key (DEK) to read encrypted material.
3) Decrypt fails with AccessDeniedException.

Logs (customer-provided excerpts)
- redwood-control-plane (private):
  "error":"kms.decrypt failed","kms_error":"AccessDeniedException","message":"User: arn:aws:sts::***:assumed-role/redwood-private-runtime/i-0f3a... is not authorized to perform: kms:Decrypt on resource: arn:aws:kms:us-east-1:***:key/6c1d2c4b-... because no identity-based policy allows the kms:Decrypt action","request_id":"7d3c3f7d-2e0a-4a9d-b8e8-8baf0d1b6b7e","region":"us-east-1"
- redwood-data-plane:
  "level":"error" "component":"envelope" "op":"decrypt" "kms_code":"AccessDeniedException" "hint":"Check key policy + IAM role permissions (kms:Decrypt, kms:DescribeKey) and encryption context conditions" "trace_id":"1a4f0e2c0a8f0e0a"

Initial hypothesis
- IAM policy for runtime role no longer allows kms:Decrypt (or condition on encryption context / key alias mismatch).
- Key policy on CMK does not trust the runtime role, even if identity policy allows kms:Decrypt.
- Region mismatch unlikely (all errors show us-east-1).

Requested info from customer
- Sanitized IAM policy attached to arn:aws:iam::***:role/redwood-private-runtime
- CMK key policy statement(s) that grant usage
- Whether they added encryption-context conditions (kms:EncryptionContext:*) during hardening
- Whether the key is in "Enabled" state
2025-11-01 09:28 ET (Kira Thompson, Support): Acknowledged. Requested IAM policy + CMK key policy excerpt. Sent customer runbook link and asked for KMS CloudTrail event snippet for failed Decrypt.

2025-11-01 10:02 ET (Customer, Northpeak Health): Provided IAM policy JSON excerpt (sanitized) and confirmed they restricted to kms:Encrypt and kms:GenerateDataKey only; removed kms:Decrypt intentionally “since we don’t want services to decrypt directly.” They expected Redwood to only encrypt.

2025-11-01 10:15 ET (Jordan Lee, Eng - Policy/permissions): Confirmed Redwood envelope scheme requires runtime decrypt for reading encrypted config/secrets and for certain audit pipeline records. For private deployments, customer KMS must allow kms:Decrypt for the runtime principal. Also noted key policy must allow the principal; identity policy alone is insufficient if key policy blocks.

2025-11-01 10:32 ET (Jordan Lee): Shared minimal required actions for runtime principal: kms:Decrypt, kms:DescribeKey, kms:GenerateDataKey (and optional kms:Encrypt for some flows). Recommended scoping to the specific CMK ARN and adding encryption context constraints rather than removing Decrypt.

2025-11-01 11:05 ET (Customer): Updated IAM policy to include kms:Decrypt and kms:DescribeKey, but still seeing AccessDenied.

2025-11-01 11:22 ET (Jordan Lee): Requested key policy. Explained common pitfall: CMK key policy lacking "Principal": runtime role. Provided example statement.

2025-11-01 12:10 ET (Customer): Updated CMK key policy to trust arn:aws:iam::***:role/redwood-private-runtime for kms:Decrypt and kms:DescribeKey. Errors reduced but not fully resolved; some pods still failing.

2025-11-01 12:24 ET (Sean Gallagher, SRE): Suggested restart/rollout to refresh assumed-role credentials + ensure no pods still referencing old key alias/ARN; check if multiple keys in play due to cutover.

2025-11-01 12:41 ET (Customer): Performed rolling restart of redwood services. Decrypt failures stopped; error rate back to baseline.

2025-11-02 09:05 ET (Kira Thompson): Confirmed stable for ~18 hours; asked customer to keep CloudWatch/KMS metrics watch and to share any remaining AccessDenied occurrences.

2025-11-04 14:20 ET (Kira Thompson): Customer confirmed no recurrence. Proceeding to resolve ticket; shared follow-up guidance and docs links.
Root cause: Customer tightened IAM and CMK key policy during KMS hardening/rotation and removed kms:Decrypt permissions for the runtime principal. In addition, the CMK key policy initially did not grant the runtime role permissions, so even after identity policy updates, KMS still returned AccessDenied.

Fix / workaround applied by customer:
1) Updated identity policy for arn:aws:iam::***:role/redwood-private-runtime to allow kms:Decrypt and kms:DescribeKey for the specific CMK ARN.
2) Updated CMK key policy to include an Allow statement granting the same principal permission to use the key.
3) Rolled restart of relevant pods/services to ensure consistent runtime behavior and clear any stale references.

Outcome: Decrypt failures ceased and production error rate returned to baseline.
Provided customer with least-privilege recommendations:
- Keep kms:Decrypt for runtime principal; restrict via resource ARN and (recommended) encryption context conditions instead of removing decrypt.
- Separate roles: one for runtime decrypt vs rotation/admin operations (break-glass).
- Validate key state (Enabled) and ensure region alignment.

Shared references:
- Confluence: KMS decrypt failures runbook (triage + common root causes)
- Confluence: Private deployment KMS integration operator guide (required permissions + validation)
- Infra baseline for IAM modules/role separation

Suggested they run the installer preflight validation after any key policy/IAM changes (once they upgrade to installer version including PR-392).
We confirmed the failures were caused by KMS permissions changes during your hardening work. Redwood Private uses envelope encryption and must call AWS KMS Decrypt at runtime to unwrap data encryption keys for read paths. Restoring kms:Decrypt (and kms:DescribeKey) for the runtime role, and ensuring the CMK key policy also grants the same principal permissions, resolved the issue. If you want to further tighten access, we recommend scoping to the specific key ARN and using encryption-context conditions rather than removing Decrypt entirely. We can also share a least-privilege sample policy/key policy snippet and help validate via the installer preflight checks on your next upgrade.
payload.summary: Private deploy: KMS AccessDenied on decrypt causing request failures (envelope decrypt)

payload.description:
Issue summary:
During a daytime traffic burst for customer BeaconApps we observed a rapid uptick in 5xx responses from the hosted API (primarily 502/504). Initial spike started 2026-03-14T10:12Z and peaked for ~8 minutes. Errors surfaced from API Gateway fronting fleet and correlated with increased connection errors to upstream runtimes.

Impact:
- BeaconApps reported increased failed generation requests (25–40% error rate for a 10-minute window).
- Other enterprise tenants on the same ingress pool saw minor elevated error rates (~3–5%).
- No data loss; requests returned 5xx and were retried by client causing additional load.

Environment:
- prod | us-east-1; ingress pool apigw-canary-12; serving-runtime pool rw-runtime-prod-7.
- Affected model types: open-llama-13b-v2, gptx-lite-7b.

Steps to reproduce (approx):
1. Replay BeaconApps tenant burst trace (provided in attached trace file).
2. Simulate many keepalive-heavy short-lived connections to /v1/streams endpoint with varied prompt lengths.
3. Observe accept queue growth on apigw-canary-12 and backlog in proxy->runtime TCP connections.

Observed behavior:
- apigw returned spikes of 502/504 along with occasional 503s.
- Upstream runtime containers reported long GC pauses (~700–1200ms) interleaved with thread scheduling spikes.
- TCP sockets at proxy layer entered CLOSE_WAIT/lingering states causing file descriptor pressure and accept-queue pileup.

Expected behavior:
- Small transient bursts should be absorbed by autoscaler and connection pooling without a high 5xx floor.

Workaround applied:
- Ingress team increased accept queue and ephemeral socket timeout for the affected pool (temp change) at 2026-03-14T10:30Z.
- Runtime team applied conservative GC tuning on one canary host (reduced pause variance) and restarted two noisy containers at 10:35Z.
- Support instructed BeaconApps to apply client-side exponential backoff and avoid aggressive short-lived keepalives while we stabilise.

Next steps/Action items:
- Engineering to roll permanent ingress proxy patch to ensure earlier socket reclamation and limit CLOSE_WAIT growth.
- Runtime team to validate GC settings across the shard and add target-level telemetry for GC pause histograms.
- Observability to add an alert for socket linger fraction > 3% and correlate with runtime GC p50/p95.
- Postmortem and changelog entry scheduled after full resolution.

Additional notes:
- This ticket references a similar historical event (SUP-421999) where keepalive pressure contributed to 5xx, but current root cause analysis shows GC pause amplification played a central role this time (different mitigations required).

Additional notes:
Correlation: timeline aligns: upstream runtime GC spikes (p99 GC pause ~950ms) co-incident with apigw accept-queue saturation.
Hypothesis: frequent short-lived connections prevent TCP keepalive reuse causing large number of sockets in TIME_WAIT/CLOSE_WAIT while runtime threads stall on GC, reducing socket servicing and causing apigw to return 502s/504s.
Evidence: strace on one proxy process shows >1200 fds in CLOSE_WAIT; netstat snapshot attached. Runtime logs show repeated Full GC cycles in host rw-runtime-prod-7a around 10:15–10:25Z.
Heap usage modest but fragmentation + JIT thread scheduling increased pause durations.
Temporary mitigation proved effective: after tunables and restarts error rate dropped to <1% within 6 minutes.
Permanent fix candidates: backpressure at ingress (limit short-lived conn rate per tenant), GC ergonomics for runtime container image, and earlier socket reclamation logic in proxy.

rw-runtime-prod-7a | 2026-03-14T10:19:01Z | GC pause=980ms | thread=main | stacktrace=attached-gc-flame.svg

Mitigated - temporary ingress tunables and runtime restart/GC tuning applied; awaiting permanent fix rollouts and postmortem.
Schedule ingress proxy patch release: ENG-PR-9276
Add GC pause telemetry dashboard and runbook update
Customer follow-up: email BeaconApps summary and recommended client backoff settings

payload.description:
Issue summary: Between ~2026-03-12 14:10 UTC and ongoing, Acme Health reported a sharp increase in p95/p99 inference latency and a rise in streaming request cancellations originating from their dedicated cluster in us-west-2. Impact: Customer-facing inference calls experienced timeouts and client-side stream disconnects; retries caused request duplication for a subset of traffic. Scope: Only Acme Health's dedicated pool in us-west-2 observed the behavior; other dedicated customers in the same region show intermittent, lower-severity spikes.
2026-03-12 14:05 UTC - First alert from Acme (support@acmehealth.com). 14:12 UTC - Automated SLO alert (p99 > 3.5s) for Acme routing shard. 14:18 UTC - Support triage; assigned to on-call SRE. 14:25 UTC - Observed concurrent increase in egress path latency and TCP retransmits on the regional egress-proxy. 15:05 UTC - Temporary policy applied to bypass recently added egress-peering route; partial improvement. 16:00 UTC - Follow-up: spike recurred when load increased; investigation continues.
1) Send streaming generate requests to customer's dedicated endpoint in us-west-2 with typical prompt size. 2) Observe initial token latency under normal conditions, then repeat under burst load (200 concurrent clients). 3) Note p95/p99 token latencies rising to >3s and stream connection resets consistent with client-side cancellations. Reproducible during the spike window.
- Grafana dashboard: https://grafana.internal/redwood/prod/egress/us-west-2 (p99 token time jumped from 850ms -> 3.9s). - nginx/egress-proxy logs: increased 502s and backend connection reset entries tied to backend IPs from peer BGP range. - tcpdump on egress-proxy: elevated retransmits and out-of-order segments. - Serving runtime traces show longer queue wait times due to upstream egress slowdowns.
A recent egress peering advertisement or route preference change caused a subset of traffic to be forwarded over a higher-latency transit path (AS-path hop increase), increasing RTT and causing streaming timeouts. The egress-proxy did not fail over cleanly between routes under burst load, exposing tail latency.
Checked recent network changes: Ops deployed egress peering change at 2026-03-12 13:58 UTC (see INT-4027).
BGP path analysis: several prefixes used by customer traffic now prefer a transit announced by partner X with 2 additional AS hops relative to previous path.
Correlation: p99 spikes aligned with periods of increased load and when the proxy chose the new path during connection establishment.
Reproduced locally by forcing route selection via traffic-engineering flags; confirmed higher latency and TCP retransmits on that path.
Workaround applied: pinned affected egress prefixes to original peer via emergency policy; immediate p95/p99 improvement observed (~40% reduction), but not fully stable under peak burst due to intermittent failover behavior.
Observability gap: egress-proxy health checks do not currently capture elevated RTTs before backend connection resets; adding latency probes to the runbook.
Related: linked to SUP-19911 where a similar pattern occurred in eu-west but with different root cause (transit saturation).

Additional notes:
Sanjay Rao (SRE) (2026-03-12 14:35): Started capturing tcpdumps on egress-proxy; initial signs point to path change. Eng paging alerted network team.
Lena Morales (Network Eng) (2026-03-12 15:00): Confirmed a change in route preference from partner peer B. Rolling back announcement should reestablish prior AS-path. Preparing rollback play.
Support (2026-03-12 15:12): Applied emergency egress pin for Acme prefixes; customer confirms perceptible improvement but intermittent failures persist at scale.
Customer (Acme Health) (2026-03-12 15:30): Noted fewer errors after policy but still seeing elevated tail latency during peak times. Requesting ETA and a durable fix.
Emergency egress pinning applied for Acme prefixes (immediate improvement).
Short-term: advise customer to stagger client reconnects and increase client-side stream keepalive to reduce amplification of retries.
1) Network: rollback peering preference for affected prefixes to original peer (scheduled 2026-03-13 02:00 UTC). 2) Engineering: patch egress-proxy connection pool to fail fast to healthiest upstreams (INT-4123). 3) Add latency-health probes and SLO alerts for egress backends. 4) Post-incident: runbook update and blameless postmortem with engineering, network, and support.
payload.summary: Unexpected egress reroute in us-west-2 causing tail-latency spikes and streaming cancellations for Acme Health

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customer NimbusAI reported a sharp degradation in throughput for their reserved dedicated pool during a 30-minute window on 2026-03-10. The pool hit ephemeral GPU depletion and automatic rollover to fallback variants was delayed, leading to elevated p95/p99 latency and 429s for the customer.

Impact:
- NimbusAI experienced 20-40% reduced throughput across pinned routes and a 5x increase in p99 latency for short-stream requests.
- Multiple customer endpoints returned 429 (throttled) and some short streams saw connection resets.
- Impacted a single dedicated pool in us-west-2; other customers on the same pool saw transient requests slowdown but not complete outages.

Environment:
- Redwood Dedicated pool "dp-usw2-42" (production), mixed GPU types (A100, H100), autoscaler enabled, default cooldowns.
- Customer pinned redwood-open-7B for route /generate-chat; some traffic uses redwood-3b-v2 for embeddings.

Steps to reproduce (observed in telemetry):
1) Customer deploys a small real-time agent that rapidly reconnects and loads model context per request (many short-lived sessions).
2) Within a 5m window traffic pattern shifts to 10k short streams/min with high session churn.
3) Allocator begins to fragment slot leases; autoscaler triggers a scale-up but allocation attach latency increases.
4) GPUs appear provisioned but are temporarily unusable due to slot fragmentation/lease contention and kv-prefetch thrashing.

Observed behavior:
- p95 latency climbs from ~80ms to 300-600ms; p99 spikes to multiple seconds.
- Autoscaler scales up but new nodes remain underutilized while attach retries increase.
- Logs show many "lease_acquire_timeout" and "slot_in_use" entries plus prefetch eviction warnings.

Expected behavior:
- Autoscaler should add capacity and allocator should attach new GPUs within SLO; short sessions should not cause pool-wide fragmentation.

Initial logs & links:
- Grafana: https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/dp-usw2-42/throughput?orgId=1 (p95/p99 graphs attached in runbook)
- Recent sidecar logs: "lease_acquire_timeout: 00:00:02" repeated ~12k times in 20m
- Console traces show increased attach latency around 2026-03-10T15:12:00Z

Initial triage summary:
Support confirmed pattern is a noisy-tenant hotspot: high short-stream fanout and rapid reconnects caused allocator and prefetch subsystems to thrash. Autoscaler responded but attach/lease contention prevented bandwidth from being realized, causing the customer-visible throughput drop. Temporary mitigation and longer-term fixes are required.
2026-03-10T12:40:00Z - Support (Aisha Patel): Acknowledged, collecting logs and requested sample request IDs and customer traffic pattern. Asked NimbusAI for a recent curl trace and SDK call timestamps.
2026-03-10T13:05:00Z - Customer (NimbusAI - Martin Liu): Provided SDK logs showing rapid session open/close every 200ms for many shards; attached request-id headers. Noted that agent reconnects are intentional for quick cold-start isolation.
2026-03-10T13:20:00Z - SRE (Liam O'Connor): Observed surge in lease_acquire_timeout and prefetch eviction metrics. Marking potential allocator fragmentation + kv-cache pressure. Spun up additional debug logs on allocator and set temporary autoscaler override to hold new nodes in warm state for 10m.
2026-03-10T14:00:00Z - Support (Aisha Patel): Applied short-term mitigation: applied a tenant-specific soft-rate limit (reduce max simultaneous short streams from 800 to 150) and enabled per-tenant connection pooling. Customer confirmed immediate improvement in new requests.
2026-03-10T16:45:00Z - SRE (Liam O'Connor): Noted that after mitigation, attach latency dropped back toward baseline and 429s decreased. We'll keep autoscaler override for 24h while engineering implements allocator fixes.
2026-03-11T09:10:00Z - Product (Sofia Martinez): Raised follow-up to product: consider exposing per-tenant session churn controls in Console and recommend SDK pooling defaults in docs.
Hypothesis A: Noisy-tenant short-stream fanout causes allocator lease fragmentation and repeated prefetch eviction, preventing newly scaled GPUs from being used immediately.
Hypothesis B: Autoscaler cooldown and our slot compaction window are too aggressive for rapid transient spikes; scale-up occurs but allocator remains stuck on busy slots, so capacity is not realized.
Telemetry evidence: lease_acquire_timeout count correlates with p99 spike window (Pearson r=.87). Prefetch cache eviction rate increased by 6x during the event.
Checked driver/host metrics: no GPU thermal throttling, PCIe errors, or OOMs recorded. Suggests logical contention rather than hardware failure.
Reproduced locally on staging with simulated churn: spinning up 5k short streams/min caused slot fragmentation and attach retry storms. Re-running with connection pooling eliminated the problem.
Potential root cause: tenant's connection pattern plus small-session allocation granularity leads to heavy slot churn; allocator lacks immediate compaction and leases are held for short durations leading to effective capacity loss.
Related historical tickets: SUP-77109 (autoscale miss-batch-saturation) and SUP-903210 (interleaved-affinity mismatch). Some common signals but different manifestation (this one is short-session churn driven).
Short-term mitigations applied (2026-03-10):
- Tenant soft-rate limit on short streams (applied via per-tenant policy).
- Enabled SDK connection pooling recommendation to customer and rolled out per-tenant connection pooling on gateway for NimbusAI.
- Temporarily increased autoscaler warm-hold period from 2m to 10m for the affected pool to avoid immediate shrink/rebalance.
Customer reported throughput recovered to ~95% of baseline within 30 minutes after mitigations were applied. 429s and p99 spikes subsided.

Medium-term engineering fixes (in-progress):
- PR #1287 for allocator: lease compaction algorithm to reduce fragmentation and a background slot consolidation worker. (See related PR link).
- Autoscaler change: add churn-detection signal to delay shrink and to prefer slot compaction before failing attach.
- Console change: Add per-tenant "session-churn" alert and a guided remediation (rate-limit / pool warm-hold toggle).
Long-term recommendations for customers:
- Prefer SDK connection pooling for high-frequency short requests.
- Use persistent sessions when possible to reduce allocation churn.
- For heavy short-stream workloads, consider a dedicated smaller pool with longer warm-hold settings.

Follow-ups:
- Engineering to validate allocator compaction in staging with churn test by 2026-03-18.
- Product to spec Console controls for per-tenant churn protection by 2026-04-01.
- Support to reach back out to NimbusAI with postmortem and SDK guidance once fixes land.
payload.summary: Tenant hotspot causing ephemeral GPU depletion and rollover delays in dedicated pool

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customer reports that during a scheduled graceful canary swap in us-east-1 their tenant sessions that had explicit model pins are suddenly served by the legacy variant and see degraded outputs. The customer uses a client which uploads prompt payloads using chunked/multipart POSTs (large prompt embedding + attachments).

Impact:
- Several customer requests routed to legacy variant; observed silent fallback (no 5xx) but responses differ (tokenization deltas).
- Streaming sessions for pinned model appear to lose pin mid-stream causing mixed-model outputs for a subset of requests (~0.8% of their traffic) for ~20 minutes during the canary window.

Environment:
- prod | us-east-1; enterprise tenant Acme Health; requests originate from their EU proxy into us-east-1 edge cluster.
- Affected model: gptx-13b-quantized-v2 (pinned at route level).

Steps to reproduce (customer):
1) Send a multi-part chunked POST containing a large prompt + binary attachment with header X-Tenant-Session and X-Model-Pin set.
2) During a canary weight ramp (10% -> 50%), observe that some requests are routed to legacy variant despite header indicating explicit pin.
3) Replaying with non-chunked single POST preserves pin consistently.

Observed logs / telemetry attached by customer (excerpt):
- edge-proxy: "WARN header_truncated: X-Tenant-Session length 512 > 256 -> dropped-suffix"
- orchestrator: "INFO route_decision: tenant=acme-health session=abc123 fallback=legacy-variant reason=missing_session_affinity"
- serving-runtime: intermittent kv-cache-miss and prewarm handshake failures for sessions that lost pins.

Notes: customer provided request IDs: req-20260310-22A, req-20260310-22B, req-20260310-31C (attached).

Additional notes:
2026-03-14 07:55 - Support (Maya): Customer confirmed reduction in incidents after mitigation but still seeing rare (~0.05%) occurrences. Requested ETA for permanent fix and clarification on workaround for their SDK.
Initial triage showed ingress was trimming long X-Tenant-Session tokens after multipart reassembly. Truncation only surfaced during canary weight shifts because the orchestrator's session affinity check runs early in the routing pipeline and falls back to variant selection when token missing/invalid. Also found a race: prewarm handshake for the new canary variant sometimes completes before the last chunk with headers is processed, which leads to request being accepted and routed without the pin. Reproducible with crafted client sending large session tokens and chunked boundaries that split header-fragment delivery.
Recommended customer temporary workarounds: 1) Switch to single-part POSTs for pinned-session traffic during canary windows. 2) Shorten session token length (<= 256 bytes) in their SDK. 3) Explicitly pass model parameter in the request body (model: gptx-13b-quantized-v2) until fix is deployed.
1) Merge and canary-deploy ingress-proxy PR to preserve headers across multipart reassembly (PR #2421). 2) Enable orchestrator feature-flag to prefer explicit request model pin over missing session affinity during staged rollouts. 3) Monitor canary (us-east-1) for 72h, compare pin-loss rate against baseline. 4) Postmortem and SDK guidance update if root cause confirmed. Engineering owners: Ingrid Park (Edge), Rahul Desai (Serving).
payload.summary: Graceful canary swap drops pinned session when client uses chunked/multipart request
