payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customer enabled split burst pools and priority lanes for their Dedicated pool to separate interactive traffic from background batch flushes. After the change, they report intermittent 429 rejections originating from background flush workers (cron-triggered) while interactive traffic remains healthy.

Impact:
- Background flush jobs (periodic object sync + embedding backfill) are receiving ~5-10% of requests rejected with 429s during scheduled flush windows.
- Visible in customer metrics and console: background job latency spikes and partial flush failures; not impacting low-latency interactive calls but causing backlog growth for nightly batches.

Environment:
- Dedicated pool: dp-ndl-001 (us-east-1)
- Pool config: split_burst_pools = true, priority_lanes = [interactive, background], smoothing_window = 8s, burst_capacity = 200 tokens/sec (background), 1000 tokens/sec (interactive)
- Client: Nimbus internal orchestrator using short-lived ephemeral keys scoped to background queue

Steps to reproduce (observed pattern):
1) Enable split burst pools and create two priority lanes with the configuration above.
2) Kick off a scheduled background flush (concurrent workers 12).
3) The background coordinator issues many short concurrent connections (HTTP/2 multiplexed) with ephemeral keys and performs small embedding calls.
4) After 30–90s, a subset of background requests receive 429 with header X-RateLimit-Reason: token_window_exhausted.
5) Interactive traffic remains within expected latencies and does not show 429s.

Logs / Evidence:
- Sample 429 response headers captured by customer: X-RateLimit-Policy: background_lane, X-RateLimit-Reason: token_window_exhausted, Retry-After: 2
- Edge traces: https://telemetry.redwood.local/trace/nd-ff34 (redacted) show background worker connection fanout at T+45s.
- Console: per-route token accounting shows background lane consumed a burst credit spike coincident with ephemeral key refresh events.

Hypotheses already considered by Support/CS:
- Ephemeral key churn from orchestrator correlates with many short sessions, causing refill misalignment between edge and origin windows.
- Small-request pattern from background flush (many short calls) triggers smaller token-bucket windows leading to sawtooth refill exhaustion even when aggregate tokens should be sufficient.
- Split pools configured with tight smoothing_window (8s) leads to aggressive refill behavior that disadvantages background lane during multiplexed bursts.

Workarounds attempted by customer:
- Reduced concurrent background workers from 12 to 4 -> reduced 429s but increased total flush time unacceptably.
- Added jitter to job start times -> partial improvement.
- Temporarily increased background burst_capacity to 400 -> reduced 429s but customer concerned about long-term cost and fairness.

Requested next steps / ask from Engineering:SRE:
- Confirm whether burst credit accounting for split pools can double-count short-lived ephemeral sessions when they reuse pooled IPs/HTTP2 connections.
- Review token-bucket refill alignment between edge and origin for priority-lane separation; propose a config knob or recommended default for background-heavy workloads.
- Recommend safe tuning guidance (smoothing_window, burst_capacity, concurrency limits) for orchestrators that use ephemeral keys + short-lived requests.

Acceptance criteria / Desired outcome:
- Deterministic explanation for 429 pattern seen by customer (root cause or combination of factors).
- Short-term config changes Support can advise (concrete values) to mitigate 429s without large cost increase.
- Engineering action item if necessary (bug, telemetry improvement, or default config change for dedicated pools running split burst pools).

Additional notes:
2026-03-12 08:13 - Support (Maya): Sent recommended temporary mitigations: increase background_burst_capacity to 350, add jitter to worker start times, and set concurrency cap to 6. Customer to test and report back.
payload.summary: Intermittent 429s on background flush after enabling split burst pools and priority lanes

payload.description:
Issue summary:
High-frequency, small-payload request pattern from NoteWell AI caused sustained growth of the API gateway accept queue which resulted in increased 5xx responses and a cascade of upstream runtime watchdog restarts on dedicated pool nodes.

Impact:
- Customer: NoteWell AI (dedicated) reported 30-40% error rate on inference calls for ~45 minutes during midday bump.
- Symptoms: Elevated 5xx rate from apigw, streaming sessions dropping, runtimes reporting watchdog-triggered process exits and immediate hot restarts. Latency for successful requests increased ~2.5x.

Environment:
- prod-us-east, dedicated GPU pool (pool-id: ded-us-e-18)
- Traffic signature: large number of concurrent short requests (~30-150ms payloads, high qps from a small set of IPs)
- Models in use: redwood/opt-13b and open-llama-7b pinned for the tenant

Steps to reproduce (observed in traces):
1) NoteWell AI traffic ramp: dozens of clients issuing many short chat-completion calls with small prompts concurrently.
2) apigw accept-queue length climbs; accept latency increases and TCP backlog moves to CLOSE_WAIT spikes.
3) apigw begins returning 502/503 to a growing fraction of requests as upstream connections queue and time out.
4) Upstream runtimes see increased connection churn and elevated thread contention; some processes hit runtime watchdog thresholds and SIGABRT or are OOM-killed, triggering restarts.
5) Restarts temporarily reduce capacity causing more apigw rejections and a feedback loop.

Observed logs & metrics (snippets):
- apigw: "accept_queue_len=254 backlog_wait_ms=1280 upstream_conns_active=632"
- runtime(nvme3): "watchdog: process exceeded soft cpu/latency limit -> killing pid=4221 SIGABRT"
- k8s pod events: "OOMKilled container=runtime-replica restartCount=3"
- sfx trace: percent_5xx: 0.37 during 12:05-12:50

Temporary mitigations applied:
- On-call SRE enabled conservative priority-shed on the apigw route for the tenant to cap burst qps (apigw route weight -> 0.6) which reduced immediate 5xx rate.
- Scaled dedicated pool by +2 replicas (manual) and drained a hot pod with repeated restarts.
- Applied connection-timeout tuning on apigw for short-lived sessions (reduce upstream idle timeout from 60s -> 15s) to improve turnover.

Current hypothesis:
- The workload pattern consists of high qps of tiny requests which defeats our usual batching optimizations and causes accept-queue saturation. Saturation increases head-of-line blocking inside apigw and produces connection churn that the runtime can't absorb, tripping the watchdog and causing restart loops. The feedback between reduced serving capacity and apigw rejections amplifies the error spike.

Next immediate actions:
- Create a targeted rate-limiter on the tenant route to enforce small-request QPS ceilings (SRE task).
- Instrument apigw accept-queue and runtime-conn-reuse metrics for finer-grained SLO dashboards (Observability).
- Add tenant-specific heuristic to prefer longer-lived connections and encourage client-side batching in support guidance (Customer Success + Docs).

Request from customer:
- NoteWell asked for a short-term whitelist increase if we can stabilize their beam; they reported the traffic originates from a scheduled collection job they can throttle if advised on safe limits.

Additional notes:
2026-03-13 12:40 - SRE (automated): Scaled pool ded-us-e-18 +2 replicas; drained pod runtime-4221 due to repeated watchdog kills.
2026-03-13 12:55 - Customer (NoteWell AI lead): Confirmed traffic pattern is a nightly scraping job they misconfigured to run at midday today. They can throttle within 30 minutes if we provide target QPS guidance.
2026-03-14 11:22 - Support (Lina Gomez): Customer confirmed they throttled the job and saw stable traffic. Requesting written guidance and a follow-up to add client-side batching best-practices.
Conn-tracking shows >70% of new connections from three source IP blocks tied to the NoteWell job; packet capture shows SYN bursts followed by half-open handshakes during peak.
Runtime memory and thread metrics indicated increased context switches and GC pauses during the window; not a straightforward memory leak but overload-induced instability.
Autoscaler did not react fast enough because the metric for scaleup is average CPU over 60s; consider adding an accept-queue-based scale signal.
We found a recent apigw change to accept-loop batching that may reduce fairness under many tiny requests (PR 981). Rolling back or gating on request-size may help.
Short-term: rate-limiter applied, priority-shed reduced inbound burst, scaled pool and drained dead pods. Customer throttled job per guidance; service stabilized.
Medium-term: Evaluate apigw accept-loop change (PR 981) and add adaptive shedding for short-payload high-qps flows. Implement accept-queue length as an autoscaler signal for dedicated pools.
Customer CS action: provide NoteWell AI with a recommended per-tenant QPS ceiling and client-side batching examples. Schedule follow-up rollout with them to avoid future mis-schedules.
Postmortem owner: Ethan Brooks. Target postmortem published to Confluence within 72 hours and includes runbook updates for accept-queue saturation.
payload.summary: High-frequency small-payload requests overload accept-queue causing apigw 5xxs and runtime restart spiral

payload.description:
Issue summary: Customer reports that after an ingress upgrade, some users in their private VPC lose access to the Redwood Console. The requests succeed to the edge but are denied by RBAC when mapped roles are empty. Impact: Admins and some service users at Aurelia Systems cannot access the console or start scheduled workers; intermittent but reproducible for ~12% of sessions. Environment: Aurelia private deployment (VPC peered), prod region eu-west-1, using our identity-proxy behind customer-managed ingress. Observed behavior: Inbound SAML assertions / OIDC upstream headers arrive at identity-proxy with the expected role attributes documented in the tenant mapping, but the attribute ordering occasionally changes and a downstream header rewrite strips the attribute value when it appears after a different namespace header. Expected behavior: Identity proxy should parse role attributes regardless of ordering; RBAC should map roles consistently. Business impact: Customer-facing admin operations blocked; requested high-priority investigation and temporary mitigation.
1) Use customer-provided test tenant in Aurelia private VPC
2) Initiate SAML SSO login via customer IDP with role attribute set in assertion (roles: admin,devops)
3) Repeat login while toggling ingress rewrite module (http2-to-http1 conversion enabled)
4) Observe identity-proxy request headers and console access outcome
2026-03-09T14:07:21Z identity-proxy INFO incoming assertion: NameID=... roles=(admin,devops)
2026-03-09T14:07:21Z ingress DEBUG rewrite applied: moved header X-Tenant-Meta after X-Forwarded-Proto
2026-03-09T14:07:21Z identity-proxy WARN parsed-roles: [] -- role header empty after rewrite
2026-03-09T14:07:22Z rbac DENY principal=svcacct-123 reason=missing-role
2026-03-09 13:45 UTC - Aurelia reports intermittent console 403s via #support-private channel
2026-03-09 14:00 UTC - Support gathered cookie/session traces and reproduced locally using customer ingress config
2026-03-09 15:10 UTC - SRE reproduced header-order dependent strip on a staging ingress image
2026-03-10 09:30 UTC - Scoped mitigation deployed: temporary ingress rule to preserve attribute ordering for Aurelia cluster
Initial triage showed the identity-proxy receives a header H: X-Redwood-Roles. In successful flows the header arrives before X-Tenant-Meta; in failing flows the order is reversed. Our header-merge code in the ingress conversion path performs an efficient concatenation but uses a regex that can drop header values when a subsequent header with a similar prefix is present. Reproduced this with an http2-to-http1 conversion case where multiple pseudo-headers are collapsed. Hypothesis: ingress rewrite rule and proxy header normalization interact producing a zero-length value for X-Redwood-Roles when ordering is reversed. Also observed that some client libraries in the customer's on-prem rewrite strips trailing null bytes which amplify the issue.
Applied a targeted ingress patch to preserve original assertion header order for Aurelia's load balancer. In addition, recommended customer to reconfigure IDP to send roles in a namespaced single header (X-Redwood-Roles) rather than multiple headers. Temporary ACL rule added to whitelist known admin service accounts so operational access can continue while fix is being validated.
1) Patch ingress header-merge regex to correctly preserve multi-valued headers even when ordering changes (PR opened: identity-proxy#2843). 2) Add unit/integration tests covering http2->http1 conversion cases and header reordering. 3) Release hotfix to private deployments and coordinate scheduled rollout with Aurelia. 4) Post-deploy monitor for 72 hours and validate with customer-provided login sweep.
Asha Patel (Support) 2026-03-09: Received initial report from Aurelia via support@. Customer says admin console returns 403 for ~12% of SSO logins.
Liam O'Connor (SRE) 2026-03-09: Reproduced locally with customer ingress config. Suspect ingress rewrite; capturing packet traces.
Marta Ruiz (Identity) 2026-03-10: Found regex in header-merge that trims values when a namespaced header follows. Preparing fix PR.
Aurelia Systems (Customer) 2026-03-10: Confirmed ingress rule patch restored console access for initial users. Will validate at scale tomorrow.
Patch merged to identity-proxy main and hotfix branch. Hotfix deployed to Aurelia staging and validated with full SSO sweep; production rollout scheduled 2026-03-13 02:00 UTC. Post-rollback plan prepared. Follow-up ticket created to add integration test coverage: INT-872. Customer notified with workaround and timeline.
- INT-872: Add header-ordering integration tests in CI
- Update runbook: ingress header rewrite checklist
- Outreach: provide post-mortem to Aurelia and add monitoring alert for spike in role-empty RBAC denies

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customer wants a clear statement of the platform's data residency guarantees when a customer pins traffic to a specific region (eu-west) and how cross-region fallback behaves when that region has capacity constraints. They are specifically worried about: whether any customer PII or unredacted request payloads may leave the pinned region during fallback, what controls exist to prevent cross-region routing, and the expected latency implications if fallback to another region occurs.

Requested outcome:
- A precise explanation (for compliance) of whether request bodies, logs, or cache artifacts can be transferred to another region during fallback.
- Documentation pointers and console settings that enforce strict in-region residency (if available).
- Typical latency delta numbers for eu-west -> us-east fallback for streaming and non-streaming generation at 256/1024 token lengths.

Customer quote: "We need to demonstrate to our security team that pinning to eu-west prevents exfiltration of EU data except under a documented and auditable fallback that we control. Also need guidance on perf expectations in case fallback happens."
Customer compliance team is delaying integration sign-off until residency/fallback behavior is documented. Potential revenue delay for Dedicated/private deployment. No active outage reported but business approval blocked.
1) Customer configured project with region pinning=eu-west in Redwood Console.
2) Sent test generation requests (streaming and non-streaming) from EU client.
3) Observed occasional 429s and backend routing debug entries showing 'fallback-route' in request trace.
4) Customer requests confirmation about payload routing and persistence when fallback occurs.
Excerpt from request trace (redacted):
- trace_id=tx-9a12e, route_attempts=[eu-west-primary, eu-west-burst, fallback-us-east-1], status=200, note=successful-on-fallback
- Console audit entry: user=devops@Nimbus, action=update:region_pin=eu-west, time=2026-03-08T14:04:22Z
Full traces linked in related_confluence_pages.
- Initial triage: routing logic is honoring 'pin=eu-west' preference but Smart Routing allows controlled fallback to compatible regions when local capacity is exhausted or when latency SLO cannot be met.
- Confirmed with routing team (see Slack thread #support-routing) that request bodies are not 'replicated' proactively to other regions; fallback involves executing the inference in the fallback region using the received request.
- KV/prefix cache: in-region cache entries are not automatically streamed to fallback region; a cache miss in eu-west will result in inference executed in fallback region without prior transfer of cached state.
- Logs and audit records: request traces and console audit logs may be stored centrally depending on tenant settings; for Private deployments customers can enable local-only audit sinks (KMS/HSM controls).
- Performance check: measured p95 generation latency delta for eu-west -> us-east fallback during a short test (internal synthetic): non-streaming 256 tokens ~ +120ms, non-streaming 1024 tokens ~ +340ms, streaming tail increases vary (client RTT dominates) — these are lab numbers and depend on instance sizing.
- Compliance note: current behavior implies request payloads are processed in fallback region (i.e., data will be present in the fallback region transiently for the duration of the inference).

Additional notes:

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customer performed a tenant migration that moved their Private deployment into a different subnet in us-east. After the migration they report intermittent high p95 latency spikes for inference calls that are supposed to be region-pinned to us-east.

Impact:
- NimblyHealth chat UI: message delivery delays seen by end-users (observed client-side timeout retries).
- Measured p95 increased from ~220ms baseline to 1.8s–2.4s on ~8–12% of requests during the window.
- Customer is enterprise (compliance-sensitive) and requires region residency guarantees.

Environment:
- Redwood private deployment (customer-managed VPC) migrated on 2026-03-09 at ~22:30 UTC.
- App layer: rw-instruct-7b for short prompts, gpt-4o-mini for assistant flows.
- Observations from prod traces and packetflow capture between 2026-03-09 22:45 - 2026-03-10 03:00 UTC.

Steps to reproduce (observed by customer / replicated by Support):
1) Send 1,000 inference requests pinned with residency: {region: "us-east", strategy: "soft-pin"}.
2) Sample traces and flow logs with X-Trace-Id header.
3) Notice ~10% of flows egress through eu-west NAT; TLS handshake time and cross-region RTT contribute to high p95.

Observed behavior:
- Control plane shows pin assignment for the tenant to us-east (pin metadata present).
- Data plane traces show an intermittent subset of connections resolved to eu-west egress IPs (reverse DNS and BGP origin).
- TTLs on the residency cache look updated but some proxies still route to legacy NAT.

Expected behavior:
- All requests with a us-east pin should remain within us-east egress paths unless a strict failover or capacity fallback is triggered.

Logs / evidence (high-value links):
- Sample trace IDs: trace-0a3f2c, trace-0b19d7, trace-0c88a1 (links included in customer logs).
- Packet capture excerpt: s3://redwood-support-artifacts/SUP-623457/pcap-20260310-001.pcap (access granted to SRE).
- Console chart: https://console.redwood.ai/customer/nimblyhealth/metrics/egress-paths?from=2026-03-09T22:00Z&to=2026-03-10T04:00Z

Investigation notes so far:
- Hypothesis 1: NAT gateway / route table associated with the new subnet still contains a stale reference which leads to asymmetric egress through eu-west under specific hash-based load balancing.
- Hypothesis 2: A subset of dataplane proxies used by this private VPC returned an old residency cache (sticky mapping) that was not invalidated during the migration; control plane indicates correct desired pin but a stale dataplane mapping led to wrong egress.
- SRE checked route tables and saw a secondary route pointing at a peering connection used previously for warm failover; that peering connection has eu-west NATs behind it.
- DNS TTLs for the dataplane egress boundary were 30s; however some long-lived connections and keepalives meant sessions continued to use the old path past the migration window.
- There were no 5xx errors observed in model servers, only increased TLS handshake time and cross-region latency on affected flows.

Temporary mitigations applied:
- Support instructed customer to toggle strict_residency=true for the tenant (forces fail closed to same-region or immediate error). This reduced cross-region egress to ~0.2% for the next hour but affected burst capacity.
- SRE invalidated residency cache entries for the tenant on the dataplane proxies (rolled patch to refresh mapping).

Next steps / recommended remediation:
1) SRE to verify and remove the legacy peering route that points at eu-west NATs from the customer's new subnet route table (actioned, pending confirmation).
2) Engage Networking (ENG-NET) to add a control-plane hook to invalidate dataplane residency caches when a tenant's VPC/subnet mapping changes.
3) Add telemetry to flag when control-plane pin != dataplane egress region for live alerts.
4) Follow up with customer to schedule a low-risk re-test and monitor p95 for 24h post-change.

Customer communications:
- We told the customer the immediate mitigation options and requested permission to invalidate caches and re-run a controlled traffic test. Customer accepted cache invalidation and temporary strict_residency toggle.

Resolution notes (work in progress):
- Cache invalidation and temporary strict residency reduced the failure mode. Networking team prepared a PR to remove legacy peering in the customer's route table. Awaiting confirmation after PR deploy and two-hour observation window.


Additional notes:
2026-03-10 01:30 UTC — SRE (Marta Ruiz): Found a peering route in customer's new subnet that points at an older peering connection. Possible asymmetric egress. Initiating route removal in staging, will coordinate with Networking for prod windows.
2026-03-10 03:10 UTC — Networking (Arjun Patel): Confirmed route table entry referencing peering-47; peering-47 has eu-west NAT. Preparing PR to remove peering-47 from customer's route table after a 60-minute maintenance window consent from customer.
2026-03-10 04:22 UTC — Customer (NimblyHealth - Sarah Kim): Confirmed maintenance window for 2026-03-10 05:30–06:00 UTC. Approved cache invalidation and route change. Reported reduced latency immediately after strict_residency toggle.

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customer reports that after performing a graceful shutdown of their client process (signal-driven shutdown with drain window) and then reconnecting shortly afterwards, tool/function invocations that were issued before shutdown are observed to be interleaved with new invocations issued after reconnect. This results in unexpected ordering of side-effecting tool calls (webhook posts and DB writes) and occasional duplicate downstream outcomes.

Impact:
- Hummingbird Analytics sees ordering violations in their transactional pipelines (out-of-order writes to downstream DB) for ~0.5% of requests during a rolling deploy.
- Potential data integrity issues and duplicate notifications to their downstream partners.
- Customer is blocked on a rollout to production until ordering guarantees are understood.

Environment:
- Languages: Python SDK v1.8.2 and TypeScript SDK v1.6.0 (both used across different services in their stack).
- Deployment: Hosted Redwood API (prod-us-east), model gpt-redwood-v1.
- Pattern: clients use streaming sessions with per-session nonce and an application-level sequence number. Clients perform graceful shutdown by stopping intake, waiting 2s, and then closing connections. On reconnect they resume the same session token.

Steps to reproduce (as provided by customer):
1) Start a streaming session from Python service A and issue tool calls T1 -> T2 -> T3.
2) Trigger graceful shutdown of service A (SIGTERM, drain 2s) during T2 processing.
3) Service A restarts and reconnects using the same session token; meanwhile a TypeScript service B also issues tool calls U1 -> U2 on the same session.
4) Downstream systems observe ordering like: T1, U1, T2, U2, T3 (expected: T1, T2, T3, U1, U2)

Expected behavior:
- Tool/function calls from a single session should preserve the order in which the client emitted them (session-scoped ordering), or at minimum provide deterministic ordering semantics and dedup semantics to avoid side-effect duplication.

Actual behavior:
- Calls that were emitted before the graceful shutdown are being re-queued and merged with calls from other clients/services on reconnect, leading to interleaving and possible duplication.

Logs / snippets (customer supplied):
- "session_id=abc123 event=emit seq=42 source=python-service-a"
- "session_id=abc123 event=disconnect reason=SIGTERM"
- "session_id=abc123 event=reconnect source=python-service-a"
- Downstream webhook timeline shows U1 arriving between T1 and T2.

Notes from customer: they rely on per-session sequencing + application-level monotonic sequence numbers and expect the platform to not reorder cross-client events for the same session token. They are open to either a platform-side ordering guarantee or recommended application-level compensating transactions/patterns.
2026-03-12 11:02 - Support (J. Patel): Confirmed receipt of ticket. Requested sample request IDs, client logs, and which services used Python vs TS. Asked for a HAR of the reconnect window.
2026-03-12 13:45 - Customer (H. Lin, Hummingbird): Attached logs (session_id=abc123) and timestamped webhook receipts. Clarified that both Python and TS services can share the same session token intentionally for their orchestration layer.
2026-03-12 16:10 - Support (A. Khan): Reproduced locally with a short script using Python SDK v1.8.2. Observed reordering when using session-resume with same session token plus a concurrent writer. Opened ticket with Eng for deeper investigation (linked SUP-927411).
2026-03-13 09:30 - Eng (C. Mendes): Initial hypothesis: race between reconnect replay queue and interleaved incoming requests in the serving gateway. Suggested test toggles: (1) disable client-side session resumption to force new session IDs; (2) enable server-side strict per-session FIFO queueing for a test run.
2026-03-13 14:50 - Customer (H. Lin): Performed test 1 (new session IDs) and saw expected ordering. Will run test 2 if Eng provides a feature flag or guidance.
2026-03-14 10:05 - Eng (C. Mendes): Deployed a temporary gateway flag to enable per-session FIFO replay in staging, reproduced interleaving with flag off and ordering preserved with flag on. Collected flame traces and queue metrics; uploaded to linked PR for review.
2026-03-14 15:20 - Support (A. Khan): Notified customer of staging test results and provided mitigation guidance (short-term: avoid session resumption across services, or ensure single writer per session during deploy; medium-term: Eng will propose server-side enhancement).
2026-03-13 - Root cause hypothesis: When a client reconnects with the same session token, the serving gateway merges the client's replay buffer into an existing session queue without an ordering watermark, allowing concurrent new requests from other clients to interleave before the replay buffer drains.
Observed behavior in gateway logs: replay_enqueue and incoming_enqueue operations processed by different worker threads without a strict FIFO merge operation. Metrics show replay buffer drain latency spikes during reconnects.
Python and TS SDKs both allow session resumption; customer pattern intentionally shares session IDs across services which increases interleaving risk.
Workaround (short-term): Customer to avoid reusing the same session token across independent services during rolling restarts; perform handoff using a single-writer promotion step, or use new session IDs on restart. Provided example patches for Python and TS SDK to auto-generate new session tokens on reconnect.
Mitigation (platform): Eng implemented a temporary gateway feature-flag (per_session_fifo_replay=true) which enforces a merge that drains replay buffers before accepting new interleaved requests for the same session. Flag verified in staging with customer test case.
Next steps: Eng to land PR https://github.com/redwood-inference/sdk/pull/2018 to add opt-in server-side FIFO guarantee and a config knob in Dedicated/Private for stricter session semantics. Product to evaluate making this opt-in flag documented as a recommended setting for transactional workloads.
Estimated ETA for GA changelist: 2 weeks (pending security review and load testing).
Follow-up: CS to run a controlled rollout with Hummingbird Analytics and confirm no latency regression with FIFO enabled. Create an RFC for session-resume semantics to publish recommended patterns.
payload.summary: Tool invocation order interleaves after graceful client shutdown + reconnect across Python/TS SDKs

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customer reports that scheduled alerts and ad-hoc alert evaluations on several dashboards stop returning series and their tracehook links are removed when users run an ad-hoc timeshift (e.g., -1d, -7d) AND the query contains a planner hint comment in the SQL-like query (customer uses a query hint to force a snapshot plan).

Impact:
- Multiple scheduled alerts for KindredHealth AI were suppressed between 2026-03-12T22:00 and 2026-03-13T02:30 UTC for several org-level dashboards.
- Tracehook links in dashboard panels (the blue "Open trace" link) disappeared for the affected series, preventing click-through to raw trace context.
- Customer reported missed paging events that their on-call relied on; business impact: delayed incident response.

Environment:
- Customer: KindredHealth AI (dedicated)
- Region: us-east (primary)
- Console version: 4.12.3
- Alerting service: rwd-alerts-v2
- Query planner component: query-planner-v1.9

Steps to reproduce (minimal):
1) Login as a user with dashboard editor access on the customer org.
2) Open dashboard "Pipeline Health" -> Edit panel -> Switch to SQL query mode.
3) Insert a planner hint comment at top of query: /*+ snapshot(true) */
4) Run the query for standard time range (last 1h) to confirm results returned.
5) Use the chart timeshift control to apply a -1d timeshift and re-run.
6) Observe that evaluation returns 0 series in panel and tracehook "Open trace" link disappears.
7) Re-run after removing the planner hint comment; series and tracehook link reappear.

Expected behavior:
- Applying a timeshift with planner hints should not suppress series or drop tracehook URLs. Alerts evaluating the same query should still produce series and maintain tracehook metadata for linking.

Actual behavior:
- Ad-hoc timeshift + planner hint triggers an internal query planner path that results in an empty resultset for the timeshifted evaluation; alert eval engine treats this as no-data and suppresses alerts. Tracehook enrichment step is skipped, so UI links are removed.

Logs / evidence:
- Dashboard panel query_id: dshb-77a4; console request_id: req-6f7b9c.
- Alert eval logs (rwd-alerts-v2) show: "planner: snapshot-hint path chosen -> transformed PlanType=SnapshotDelta; resultset row_count=0" around 2026-03-13T00:12:03Z.
- Tracehook enrichment logs show a skipped enrichment event with reason "no-series" for the same request_id.
- Customer-provided screenshot attached (screenshot-03013.png).

Workaround tried by customer:
- Removing the planner hint from queries restores behavior immediately.
- Running the same query in Explore (non-dashboard) with timeshift returns expected results (suggests dashboard alerting pipeline diverges).

Notes:
- This reproduces reliably on the customer org and we have a failing reproduction in a staging clone of the customer (staging-kindred-2026-03-13).
- Not observed in orgs that do not use planner hints.

Initial triage by support shows alerting pipeline treats some planner-hint-induced plan transforms as 'no-data' for time-shifted windows. SRE confirmed query-planner v1.9 introduced an optimization in commit 7c3b2f that rewrites some snapshot hints into SnapshotDelta plans. Hypothesis: SnapshotDelta path toggles a fast-path that bypasses series metadata population required by tracehook enrichment.

What we've checked so far:
- Replayed alert eval in staging with debug logging enabled; confirmed plan type flip coincides with zero-row result.
- Confirmed tracehook enrichment is a downstream step that uses series fingerprints which are only populated for standard PlanType flow.
- Confirmed removal of hint restores older plan selection and fixes both series and tracehook.

Next steps:
- Query-planner owners to add guard to SnapshotDelta path to preserve series metadata for timeshifted evaluations (ENG-ops assigned).
- Add defensive enrichment check so tracehook enrichment will attempt to reconcile series using raw request context if series metadata missing.
- Add unit/regression test exercising timeshift + planner hint on alert eval runner.

In Progress - ENG owners (query-planner) investigating patch. A candidate fix is under review in PR #4321 to preserve series metadata on SnapshotDelta path. Support has provided customer with a short-term mitigation: remove planner hint or add a wrapper condition so alert rule uses a copy of the query without hints. We scheduled a maintenance patch rollout to staging for 2026-03-16.

Planned permanent resolution steps:
- Merge PR preserving metadata and apply to alert-eval runner.
- Add e2e regression tests.
- Postmortem and follow-up: consider telemetry to detect "planner-hint + timeshift" silent-suppression events and alert SRE.

Additional notes:
2026-03-13 08:30 - Customer (Priya Menon, KindredHealth AI): Confirmed that removing comment fixes dashboards. This caused missed alert on 2026-03-13 00:45 which delayed paging. Asking for ETA to fix as this affects production monitoring.
1) Remove planner hint comments from dashboard/alert queries.
2) Create a duplicate alert panel specifically for scheduled evaluations with hints stripped (short-term).
3) If you need assistance automating hint stripping, Support can help generate a sanitized query copy for scheduled alerts.
- ENG: Merge PR to preserve metadata on SnapshotDelta path (blocked on code review).
- QA: Add regression test for timeshift + hint case.
- Support: Notify customer when patch is deployed and validate alerts for a 24h window.
- Obs: Add telemetry rule to detect alert eval runs that return zero series immediately after plan-type change.
payload.summary: Alert evaluation and tracehook links drop when query planner hint used during ad-hoc timeshift

payload.description:
Issue summary: Starting 2026-03-08 09:42 UTC PineTrack reported elevated p99 latency and repeated autoscaler shrinks in their dedicated pool during a scheduled usage window. Impact: sustained p99 from ~220ms -> 1.2s for text-generation routes and intermittent 503 errors for higher-concurrency sessions. Users saw degraded throughput and dropped streams for ~40 minutes. Environment: Dedicated pool (prod-us-east), customer pinned to redwood/compat-13b, autoscaler policy: aggressive scale-down (idle_threshold=30s).
1) Route steady multi-tenant load to dedicated pool with concurrent short streams (50-100 streams/s). 2) In same pool, schedule a background artifact-scanner (IO heavy) to perform frequent NVMe reads/writes. 3) Observe p99 and kernel latency on serving hosts, autoscaler perceives reduced effective throughput and initiates scale-down. 4) After scale-down, load remains high and p99 spikes further, autoscaler then ramps back up causing oscillation.
Support logs: host/gpu metrics show PCIe transfer latency spikes correlated with artifact-scanner start (logs: /logs/pinetrack/2026-03-08/pci-latency-0942.log). Autoscaler events: scale-down at 09:45 UTC (decision: low-util), scale-up at 09:48 UTC, repeated twice. Kernel traces: increased DMA wait times and NVMe queue depth jumps. Monitoring graphs: https://grafana.redwood/s/teams/pool/dedicated-us-east?from=2026-03-08T09:30Z&to=2026-03-08T10:30Z
Initial hypothesis: noisy tenant causing GPU compute stalls. Collected perf counters (PCIe DMA latency) and NVMe IO metrics; found tight correlation between background-scanner IO bursts and GPU DMA tail latency. Autoscaler logic evaluated endpoint throughput and decided to scale down because of apparent drop in processed requests; scale-down window too aggressive for transient IO noise. SRE replayed scaled-down decision on historical metrics and reproduced oscillation. Tenant isolation layer allowed heavy NVMe IO within same node, contributing to PCIe contention. Cross-checked with disk-IO QoS metrics: absent for dedicated pool nodes. No kernel panics or GPU driver crashes found. Related change identified: a recent infra rollout (PR infra/rg-autoscaler#4123) reduced scale-down hysteresis to improve cost; this made the pool susceptible to transient drops.
Mitigation applied (2026-03-08 10:02 UTC): 1) Temporarily pinned PineTrack traffic to a warm sub-pool with IO-QoS enforced. 2) SRE disabled aggressive scale-down (increase idle_threshold to 120s) for the affected dedicated cluster. 3) Requested customer to postpone artifact-scanner runs while we validated isolation fixes. Permanent fixes: 1) Rollout IO-QoS enforcement on dedicated pool nodes to limit NVMe burst impact (PR infra/rg-qos#119). 2) Update autoscaler to incorporate PCIe and IO anomaly signals into scale decisions (ticketed as INT-331220). 3) Add runbook entry for noisy-IO detection and automated temporary routing. Customer notified and confirmed service returned to baseline by 10:35 UTC. Follow-ups: monitor for 72 hours and coordinate downtime window to deploy QoS kernel parameters.

Additional notes:
2026-03-08 10:12 UTC - PineTrack (customer): Confirmed they had a nightly scanner scheduled that overlapped the peak. Agreed to pause for 1 hour while Redwood applies isolation.
payload.summary: PCIe I/O noise from co-tenant workload caused autoscaler shrink oscillation in dedicated pool

Issue summary: Customers report sporadic long-tail latency (final token delay of 2-8s) for responses emitted in structured JSON mode. Impact: Several request streams for a single enterprise customer (TextFlow AI) time out at the client after finalization delay, causing failed ingestion of generated JSON payloads. Environment: Dedicated pool in us-east; affected across two model variants. Observed behavior: majority of tokens stream normally but final chunk stalls unpredictably, often when the decoded output contains backslash escape sequences (\n, unicode escapes).
1) Create a structured output request with mode=json and schema validation enabled.
2) Use a prompt that requests multi-line JSON with escaped characters (e.g., user text that includes newlines and quotes).
3) Send requests at production QPS seen from customer (burst of concurrent requests ~60).
4) Observe streaming response: last event is delayed by multiple seconds before finalization event and content-length header closure.
2026-03-12T15:11:02Z request_id=abc123 model=redwood-v1-13b stream_chunk=...
2026-03-12T15:11:10Z request_id=abc123 decoder: emit final chunk delayed by 6.2s
gateway: downstream client disconnected after 7.5s waiting for stream end (client timeout)
serving-runtime: KV-cache hit rate normal; no CPU/GPU contention reported in metrics window

Additional notes:
SRE Oncall (SRE): Initial traces show decoder loop re-entering escape-unmarshal path. Suspect backpressure in JSON postprocessor when encountering long escaped sequences.
Hypothesis: JSON-mode postprocessing holds a lock while performing validation/unescaping which blocks the streaming finalizer under burst load.
Telemetry: p99 finalization latency spikes correlate with requests that contain more than 40 escape tokens in final 200 characters.
Reproduction: Deterministic repro in staging by issuing 50 concurrent requests with payloads containing repeated \uXXXX unicode escapes; reproduces 80% of runs.
Checks performed: GPU/CPU and network metrics show no resource saturation; kernel traces show blocking in decoder postprocess call stack.
Workaround tested: Disabling schema validation in JSON mode removes the long-tail delay in staging; however not acceptable for customer's production schema needs.
Workaround applied: temporarily route TextFlow AI's traffic to a canary variant with escape-sequence fast-path enabled (serving-runtime PR #2048). Root cause: JSON-mode unescape+validate path held a mutex while performing regex-based unescape on long escape-heavy tokens, causing finalization backpressure under concurrency. Permanent fix: landed and merged PR to break unescape into lock-free streaming pipeline and added unit + integration tests covering heavy escape sequences. Rolling out to dedicated pool in us-east with monitoring for p99 finalization latency. Customer notified and will monitor for 48 hours before closing. Follow-ups: add a regression test to CI and update runbook with mitigations.
payload.summary: Long-tail latency in JSON output mode after escape-sequence tokens cause finalization backpressure

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customer reports noticeably slower chat responses where there is a visible pause before the assistant emits the first token. This started shortly after our runtime 1.5 rollout combined with a new smart-router policy that prefers model variants with 'cost-optim' labels in low-cost cells.

Impact:
- Several production chat flows at Acme Fintech have median initial-token latency increase from ~220ms to ~1.1s and p95 ~2.4s.
- Affects user-facing chat widgets for ~18% of requests that route through the new policy.
- Higher perceived lag causing customer support escalations and potential user churn risk.

Environment:
- Redwood prod, us-east-1 region, Dedicated pool for Acme Fintech.
- Runtime version: 1.5.0 (rolled 2026-03-09 02:00 UTC).
- Smart-router policy: prefer-cost-variants v2 (rolled 2026-03-09 01:50 UTC).

Steps to reproduce:
1) Make a ChatCompletion request with streaming enabled using model redwood/gptj-6b-qat-v2 pinned for customer account on the dedicated pool.
2) Observe full connection establishment; monitor time between request acceptance and first streamed token.
3) Repeat ~50 times to sample distribution.

Expected behavior:
- First token emission should be ~200-300ms median for this model and dedicated pool.

Actual behavior:
- Median initial-token latency observed ~1.1s, p95 ~2.4s for affected requests. Not consistent across all requests — correlates to requests routed to specific low-cost variant shards.

Logs / traces (excerpt):
- access-log: request_id=6f9b3a start=2026-03-09T02:12:07.123Z accept=2026-03-09T02:12:07.130Z first_token=2026-03-09T02:12:08.302Z
- serving-trace: kernel_warmup=480ms, load_model_variant=180ms, kv_cache_lookup=40ms, queue_wait=200ms, grpc_handshake=30ms
- router-log: chosen_variant=cheap-variant-34 reason=policy:prefer-cost-variants v2

Attachments: performance traces and flamegraphs uploaded to customer-support S3 (s3://redwood-support/sup-13724/).
03/09 04:20 - Initial triage: Support confirmed impact and escalated to SRE. Captured traces and customer repro steps.
03/09 06:05 - SRE observed correlation between higher initial-token latency and requests routed to 'cheap-variant-*' shards that use a different kernel selection and aggressive quantization profile.
03/09 08:10 - Eng hypothesis: slow 'kernel warmup' path triggered when runtime routes to variants that haven't been hot for the current sequence-length distribution. Warmup cost ~400-600ms per request leading to median shift.
03/09 09:30 - Additional hypothesis: smart-router's new 'prefer-cost-variants' policy increases traffic to underutilized nodes, causing higher cold-start rates and queue_wait spikes (~150-300ms).
03/09 10:45 - Experiment: force-route 200 sample requests to 'low-latency' variant; median initial-token latency returned to ~230ms. Confirms routing + variant-warmup as root factors.
03/09 11:20 - Identified related change in PR router#187 that adjusted scoring weights; linked PRs for follow-up. Also flagged PR serving-runtime#4213 that changed kernel selection ordering for qat quantized models.

Issue summary: Customer reports that reranking results show unexpectedly low similarity scores after upgrading their client integration. Impact: Production rerank calls for BrightSearch search pipeline are returning highly divergent orderings; search latency spikes from baseline ~120ms p50 to 800-1200ms, and some requests fall back to a CPU-based compatibility path causing 503s. Environment: Production API (us-east-1), embed-large-v2 model. Initial hypothesis: mismatched binary embedding serialization (endianness or float32 vs float16 byte layout) on the client side causes the server to detect incompatible vector signatures and trigger a slow code path which includes extra validation and CPU normalization.
1) Customer uses custom client to serialize embeddings as raw little-endian floats into a binary protobuf payload and POSTs to /v1/embeddings
2) Server accepts embedding payload but logs a "signature-mismatch" for vector checksum at ingestion stage (no immediate 4xx)
3) Rerank call with those embeddings hits serving-runtime compatibility check, triggers CPU fallback normalization, then executes similarity computation on a fallback path leading to increased latency and sometimes 503s under load
4) Replacing client serialization with Redwood official SDK (which sends base64-encoded big-endian float32 array) produces expected rerank ordering and restored latency

2026-03-10T14:03:12Z ingestion: embedding_checksum=0x7fa3 (expected-format=be32) -- warning: checksum mismatch, falling back to permissive parser

Support reproduced locally by serializing float32 in little-endian vs SDK big-endian: big-endian base64 payload reproduces expected scores; little-endian raw binary triggers checksum warning and CPU path
Checksum routine expects network byte order (big-endian) for historical reasons; permissive parser exists for backward compatibility but incurs slower path and extra normalization steps
Observed that legacy permissive-parser also performs element-wise NaN/Inf checks and converts to host float format on CPU which is expensive under high QPS
No model weight or inference graph changes on back-end; this appears purely input-serialization compatibility issue
Potential for customers to silently degrade quality if they use custom serialization without matching Redwood's expected layout
2026-03-10 15:02 - Support (Aisha Patel): Hi BrightSearch team — thanks for the report. Can you confirm which client library and serialization method you're using to send embeddings? Also please include a sample base64 payload if possible.

2026-03-12 11:55 - Customer (BrightSearch / Dev): Applied SDK-based serialization; rerank ordering restored and latency returned to baseline. Thanks for triage. Please advise on long-term roadmap as we may keep custom pipeline for other reasons.
Workaround provided: revert to Redwood official SDK serialization or explicitly encode float32 arrays as big-endian/base64 when sending embeddings. Customer confirmed recovery after applying workaround.

Issue summary:
Customer NovaScale seeing progressive loss of usable GPUs in their Dedicated pool (prod-us-west) across the afternoon of 2026-03-10. Symptoms: p50 throughput steady, p95/p99 latency climbing and allocatable GPU count decreasing until autoscaler triggers fallback to lower-capacity tier. Impact: customer reports degraded throughput for high-fanout chat routes; business impact is request throttling and elevated latency for a portion of customer traffic.

Impact:
- ~6 GPUs in the reserved pool became unusable over ~3 hours for the customer cluster, causing 30-45% throughput reduction on affected routes.
- Autoscaler reacted but misclassified the pattern as capacity pressure and increased scale, which failed because leaked CUDA contexts prevented new attach operations.

Environment:
- Dedicated capacity, prod-us-west, reserved pool id: rp-7321 (customer-visible).
- Sidecar version in use: sidecar-1.2.2 (customer image).
- Serving runtime: rwd-infer-2.7.

Steps to reproduce (observed pattern):
1) Customer runs high-throughput short-stream workload with many short lived containers connecting through the sidecar.
2) Over time nvidia-smi shows an increasing number of GPU process entries with identical command lines but different PIDs associated with the tenant sidecar.
3) New inference attach attempts fail with kernel-level allocation errors (CUDA_ERROR_OUT_OF_MEMORY) even though aggregated memdb still reports free memory (indicating leaked contexts).
4) Autoscaler observes rising attach failures and attempts to add capacity; new capacity remains unusable until host-level sidecar restart clears contexts.

Logs / telemetry excerpts:
- rwd-telemetry: gpu_attach_failures spike at 2026-03-10T15:18:34Z (rate: 84/min)
- host metrics: GPU SM util low (~5%) but process table shows 18 sidecar processes holding contexts on GPU0.
- dmesg (host): repeated messages: "cuda: context leak detected for PID 23211" (custom sidecar runtime log emitted).
- nvidia-smi (snapshot): multiple processes with identical container ids and small resident set sizes but preventing new CUDA contexts.
Initial hypothesis: noisy tenant creating short-lived contexts that are not destroyed due to JVM-native binding bug in sidecar wrapper
Observed that sidecar-1.2.2 creates a persistent global context per attach but fails to call cudaDeviceReset on abnormal disconnects
Autoscaler logic only considers allocation latency and mem pressure; it does not count number of active CUDA contexts. This led to false positive scale-up when leakage was present
Reproduced locally with load test harness: reproduced leak within ~1500 attach/detach cycles using sidecar-1.2.2
Hosts where sidecar restarted returned GPUs to healthy state immediately (indicating leak is process-local and cleared on process exit)
No evidence of hardware errors or driver faults; NV driver version: 525.85 confirmed compatible
2026-03-10T15:18:34Z rwd-telemetry gpu_attach_failures=84/min pool=rp-7321
2026-03-10T15:19:02Z host-01 dmesg: cuda: context leak detected for PID 23211
snapshot nvidia-smi: Processes: 18 sidecar entries (cmd: /opt/sidecar/bin/sidecar --tenant nova-314), GPU0 mem: total 48GB, in-use by leaked contexts: ~2GB fragmented
Immediate mitigation: rolling restart of sidecar process on affected host(s) to reclaim leaked contexts. Prevent autoscaler from scaling up the pool for rp-7321 until sidecar version is upgraded (set pool annotation 'suppress-autoscale: true' temporarily).
Hotfix shipped in sidecar-1.2.4 (2026-03-12): explicit cudaDeviceReset on all disconnect/error paths; emits cuda_context_count metric. Autoscaler logic patched to consult 'cuda_context_count' and treat high context counts as non-scaling condition. Deployed to canary (us-west-2) and then rolled to customer cluster; observed reclaim of leaked contexts and restoration of attach success. Follow-ups: add automated alert when cuda_context_count per-GPU > 5 for > 5 minutes, and harden sidecar unit tests to include forced-exception detach scenarios.
2026-03-10T16:00Z - Support (Asha Patel): Logged detailed traces and escalated to SRE channel #sre-dedicated. Customer notified; asked for immediate mitigation steps.
2026-03-10T16:22Z - SRE (Diego Ramirez): Per-host workaround: run 'systemctl restart rwd-sidecar' on affected nodes to free contexts. Scheduling rolling restarts to clear pool. Avoid global pool scale-up until leak mitigated.
2026-03-10T18:10Z - Customer (NovaScale): Confirmed temporary restart restored throughput to baseline for two hosts; asked if long-term fix available.
2026-03-11T09:05Z - Eng (Sofia Andersson): Identified offending JNI code path where exception path skips cudaDeviceReset(); patch PR created (see related_github_prs).
2026-03-12T11:30Z - Eng (Liam O'Connor): Hotfix build sidecar-1.2.4 including explicit context cleanup and additional metrics emitted for 'cuda_context_count' pending deploy to canary
Push sidecar-1.2.4 to remaining regions: schedule rollout waves with canary verification
Add 'cuda_context_count' into our autoscaler decision tree and adjust threshold defaults
Create alerting runbook and add to on-call rotation: guide for immediate detection and remediation of CUDA context leaks
Coordinate with NovaScale to confirm stability for 72h post-deploy and close ticket after customer confirmation

Issue summary: Verdant Health reports intermittent 403 responses and aborted streaming when private deployment nodes attempt to download model artifacts and when customer-facing streaming requests go through their corporate TLS inspection appliance. Impact: model pulls fail (~15% of attempts) and streaming calls frequently abort mid-response causing application errors for end users. Environment: private deployment in customer VPC peered to Redwood control plane; customer uses inline TLS inspection (corporate proxy) that terminates and re-establishes TLS.
1) Place a VM inside customer's private VPC that uses the corporate TLS inspection appliance for egress.
2) Attempt to curl a Redwood presigned artifact URL from the VM: curl -v -H "Range: bytes=0-" "<presigned-url>"
3) Observe HTTP/403 responses intermittently and check returned headers.
4) Initiate a streaming completion request from an app behind the same TLS inspection appliance and observe aborted streams / early EOFs.
Control plane log excerpt (artifact-fetch): GET /artifact/pull?object=llama-3-70b 403 X-Request-ID=4d2f: error="invalid-auth-header" details="Proxy-Authorization header present"
Packet capture (tcpdump) from customer egress shows injected header: Proxy-Authorization: Basic ZGVtbzpwYXNzd29yZA==
Edge nginx access log (streaming endpoint): client=10.2.3.45 - - "POST /v1/streams HTTP/2.0" 499 - "-" "Proxy-Authorization: Basic ..."
Application error sample: streaming aborted: io.EOF after 3.1s, underlying status: UNAUTHENTICATED (code 16)
Support reproduced 403s by proxying requests through customer's TLS inspection appliance in their staging environment; observed Proxy-Authorization header injected on outgoing connections.
Control plane has a defensive header validation that rejects incoming requests containing Authorization-like headers when authentication is via signed presigned URLs; this is triggering 403s when the Proxy-Authorization header is present.
Tcpdump and proxy logs show the appliance rewrites SNI to an internal inspection hostname and injects Proxy-Authorization for its own backend auth; the presigned URL validation on Redwood treats the extra header as an authentication attempt and fails validation.
Streaming aborts appear correlated to header injection + TLS re-termination causing HTTP/2 connection reuse to fail (proxy reuses connection for multiple streams and inserts auth header intermittently).
Morgan Chen (Support) 2026-03-10: Initial intake from Verdant Health. They saw 403s for artifact fetches and aborted streams since 2026-03-08; provided sample presigned URL and packet captures.
Verdant Health (Customer) 2026-03-11: Confirmed corporate TLS inspection is handled by SecureGate v3; they have a policy that injects Proxy-Authorization for backend chaining. They can add rewrite rules but asked if Redwood can tolerate the header.
Ravi Patel (SRE) 2026-03-12: Reproduced locally by standing up SecureGate in lab. Confirmed Proxy-Authorization header present and control plane code path returns 403 with reason 'invalid-auth-header'.
Elena Ruiz (Product) 2026-03-13: Requested impact numbers and whether this can be safely stripped at ingress; noted potential risk if proxies inject arbitrary auth headers and how that interacts with presigned URLs and mTLS.
Verdant Health 2026-03-14: Willing to add a temporary rewrite rule to remove Proxy-Authorization from egress to Redwood if we provide recommended header filters. Asked for guidance and a patch timeline.
Workaround (customer): Verdant Health to add a reverse proxy rule to strip Proxy-Authorization for traffic destined to Redwood control plane and S3-compatible artifact endpoints.
Short-term product mitigation (planned): Add ingress header sanitization that drops Proxy-Authorization / Proxy-Authenticate / X-Proxy-Auth headers for requests authenticated via presigned URLs. Target patch: 2026-03-20 for staging rollout.
Long-term: Update docs and private deployment checklist to call out proxies that inject auth headers and include recommended proxy rewrite rules. Add a flag in Private control-plane config to toggle aggressive header stripping for customers that request it.
Post-incident: Create an internal runbook for diagnosing header-injection issues (linked in related_confluence_pages) and add automated checks in onboarding that detect injected auth headers during test artifact pulls.

Issue summary: Customer (MapleAI) observed recurring p95/p99 throughput jitter and transient request timeouts from their dedicated pool between 2026-02-24 23:40 UTC and 2026-02-25 02:10 UTC. The pattern looks like repeated slot reclamation and rapid autoscaler activity tied to a short-lived tenant that produced high NVLink and PCIe I/O, not purely GPU compute.

Impact: Affected customer's production endpoints (~10 routes) experienced p99 latency spikes from ~180ms to 2.8s and a measurable drop in tokens/sec throughput (~28% at peak). No model-level errors; errors manifested as 502/504 and occasional kernel queue timeouts. Customer reported user-facing failures for ~80% of requests during the 30-minute worst window.

Observed behavior: Dedicated pool showed oscillating allocation counts (slot add/remove churn), autoscaler logs show rapid scale-up then immediate shrink with many short-lived GPUs entering the pool. Host-level telemetry recorded high NVLink utilization and PCIe retransmits on a subset of hosts hosting the noisy tenant. Prefix cache metrics remained stable.

Hypothesis: A tenant issued a mix of many short, high-concurrency streams with heavy tensor copy / I/O patterns (large prompt attachments and streaming checkpoint writes) that caused host-level IO saturation and caused our scheduler to evict or reassign slots rapidly. Autoscaler interprets the temporary increase in queue length as demand and spins up more capacity, which then collapses as eviction/IO fails, causing oscillation.

Timeline: 2026-02-24 23:36 UTC - first p50/p95 drift noted in customer telemetry. 23:40 UTC - cluster autoscaler triggered +6 GPUs for pool. 23:46 UTC - NVLink errors spike on hosts 3/7/11. 23:48 UTC - scheduler reports 12 slot preemptions in 8 minutes. 00:10 UTC - customer reports 502s. 01:05 UTC - autoscaler attempted a second scale-up; short lived. 02:15 UTC - transient return to baseline after noisy tenant ramp-down.

Attachments: collection of p99 graphs, autoscaler event log, sample gc/daemon logs will be added to ticket attachments section.
1) Route heavy mix of short-request streams (>200 concurrent short streams/sec) to a dedicated pool route pinned to small-batch service profile.
2) Include large client-side request bodies that require host-side staging (e.g., long attachment or embedded context >1MB).
3) Observe host NVLink/PCIe counters and scheduler autoscaler events within 5-30 minutes of sustained burst.
4) Verify that CPU and GPU compute utilization remain moderate while host I/O metrics saturate.

[2026-02-25T23:46:03Z] host-monitor host=gpu-h03 nvlink_err=41 pcie_retries=12

Tokens/sec (peak impact): 8,900 (-28%)
p99 latency baseline: 0.18s

Note: We intentionally did not roll back any kernel changes and preserved logs for postmortem.
Workaround applied: In coordination with MapleAI we temporarily limited route concurrency to 60 streams per second and increased autoscaler stable-window to 90s for the dedicated pool. This stopped the rapid add/remove oscillation and restored p99 near baseline.
Next actions: 1) Engineering to add an I/O-saturation detector to the scheduler to avoid treating IO-backed queue growth as compute demand (ticket created: infra-io-detector). 2) Consider adding per-tenant IO quotas for dedicated pools. 3) Run targeted repro with infra+runtime to validate fixes.

payload.description:
Customer (Northpeak Search) reports that after Redwood Support adjusted their tenant burst limit, the Dedicated Console still shows the previous limit value.

Issue summary
- Tenant: northpeak-prod (Dedicated, eu-west)
- What changed: burst.max_gpu_ratio and burst.max_burst_gpus were increased via control plane admin tooling.
- Expected: Console "Burst capacity" panel updates within a few minutes.
- Actual: Console continued to display the old limit for ~45 minutes; API behavior appeared to follow the new limit (fewer 429s at previous cap).

Customer impact
- Customer confusion during a planned indexing run; they were trying to verify the new cap before starting the job.
- No production outage; burst admission and metering appeared correct.

Environment
- Console: prod
- Region: eu-west

Steps to reproduce (internal)
1) Update burst limits for a tenant via control plane admin endpoint.
2) Immediately open Console -> Dedicated -> Burst capacity.
3) Observe limit values sometimes remain stale even though the underlying control plane read API returns the new config.

Initial hypotheses
- Console backend caching tenant config too aggressively (Redis + in-process cache) and not invalidating on writes.
- CDN caching on the Console BFF endpoint.
- Read replica lag for the tenant config store (write goes to primary; Console reads from replica).

Evidence collected
- At 2025-06-10 16:18 UTC, control plane read API (/v1/tenants/{id}/burst-config) returned the updated values.
- Console BFF endpoint continued returning the previous values until 2025-06-10 17:03 UTC.
- Console UI was not hard-refreshing the limit state when the page was already open (customer had the page open before the change).

Acceptance criteria for fix
- Post-change, Console reflects updated burst config within 5 minutes (p95).
- If values are older than 5 minutes, Console should display a "Refreshing…" indicator or surface last-updated timestamp.
- Ensure change events are audit logged (already required) and can be used for invalidation hooks.

Customer-facing note (what we told them)
- The burst limit change is active immediately in the control plane; Console display can lag due to caching.
- As a workaround, hard refresh and/or wait ~10 minutes; Support can confirm the live config via API readback.

Additional notes:
Customer quote: "We see fewer 429s already, but the Console still says our limit is 8. Can you confirm 16 is actually applied?"
Next: confirm whether this specific tenant key existed prior to change and when it will expire; consider targeted invalidation.
Related: we discussed cache invalidation for burst config in #eng-platform when adding Console endpoints; not implemented yet.
Mitigation: I can manually delete Redis key for the tenant to unstick immediately while we implement proper invalidation/shorter TTL.
Action item: create follow-up engineering ticket to implement write-through invalidation using audit event stream.
Also adding last-updated timestamp to API response so UI can display staleness.
Will coordinate with Logan Wright on event consumption patterns. Targeting patch before broad GA enablement in eu-west.
Notes: if audit event pipeline is delayed, TTL still bounds staleness. Added safe guard to bypass cache when request header X-Force-Refresh is set (internal only) for Support debugging.
Follow-ups: ensure this behavior is covered in GA readiness checklist; update internal onboarding checklist to mention expected propagation (< 5 min) and support workaround if event stream is degraded.
Fixed in Console BFF: burst config is now cached separately with short TTL and invalidated on burst config write events (audit stream). Support workaround (internal): purge tenant cache key or use force-refresh header. Customer confirmed Console reflects updated limit within ~1 minute post-fix.

2) Start a retention backfill job that triggers tracehook token rotation for org-scoped tokens (internal job id RBX-BF-2026-03).
3) In Console > Dashboards, open a saved query and use 'Copy Query as Permalink'.
4) Paste permalink into incognito browser or send to another account.
5) Observe 404 response when loading the permalink and missing tracehook anchor in the UI.
Permalink should resolve to the saved query state and include a valid tracehook token or reference that is available even if token rotation occurs during export/backfill.
Received 404 page and console shows 'tracehook token invalid or expired' in network response. Permalink metadata references a tracehook token value that was rotated mid-export by retention backfill process.
Console network trace (trimmed):
- GET /permalink/abcd1234 -> 404 {error: "tracehook_token_not_found"}
- Tracehook service logs around 2026-03-10T03:21:xxZ: rotation triggered (job RBX-BF-2026-03), replaced org-token v2 -> v3
- Export agent log: permalink payload included org_token:v2 (stamped 2026-03-10T03:20:58Z) but rotation completed at 2026-03-10T03:21:12Z
Reference logs: s3://rbx-exports/brightloop/2026-03-10/permalink-abcd1234.json
Hypothesis 1: Permalink generator reads current tracehook token and embeds it directly in the permalink metadata; if a rotation runs between read and registration, the token will be absent.
Hypothesis 2: Backfill/retention job rotates org-scoped tracehook tokens without also updating or invalidating in-flight export metadata.
Findings: Reproduced locally by triggering a rotation during export agent run. Permalinks created in the 14-second window between token read and registration point to the now-rotated token.
Temporary mitigation attempted: updated export agent to fetch token after registration step, but that caused race with registration API (needs atomic fetch+register).
Relevant PRs/CI: github.com/redwood/tracehook/commit/1f9a2 introduced faster rotation logic (2026-02-28).

Additional notes:
SRE Lead (Maya Patel): Noted that rotation window is expected but permalinks should reference a stable identifier (token id) rather than raw token. Suggests changing permalink to reference a token id that can be resolved to current token server-side.
Eng (Tracehook) (Liam O'Connor): Identified code path in export-agent where we read tracehook.getCurrentToken() and inline it into permalink payload before permalink is registered. Proposed fix: switch to server-side token resolution by storing token_id instead of raw token and resolving at permalink read-time.
Customer (BrightLoop contact: Nora Singh): Provided list of affected permalinks and confirmed external teams could not access reports during a critical compliance window. Asks for ETA/rollback option.
In progress - code fix landed in tracehook service to accept token_id in permalink payload and resolve current token at read time. Hotfix PR created for export-agent to include token_id rather than raw token.
Action items executed:
- PR tracehook#4872 merged to add token_id lookup and keep backward compatibility for existing permalinks.
- Export agent PR opened (console-ui#4872) to stop inlining raw tokens and instead register token_id with permalink registry.
- Deploy plan: rollout tracehook service change to prod us-east behind feature flag, then deploy export-agent change, enable feature flag, monitor for 10 minutes, then remove flag.
- Customer notified with interim workaround: If you share permalinks created during 2026-03-10T03:19Z-03:23Z, Support can re-register links using new resolution endpoint. Manual re-registration completed for 8 of 12 links so far.
ENG-Tracehook: Instrument token rotation to emit mapping events to permalink-registry (issue ENG-TR-532)
CONSOLE: Add unit/integration tests to simulate rotation during export and assert stable permalink resolution
SRE: Run backfill window test in staging with canary export-agent to validate fix before full rollout
CS: Send final status update to BrightLoop and provide CSV of re-registered permalinks

Issue summary: Starting 2026-03-11 09:15 UTC Vendora Labs reported intermittent streaming request timeouts and elevated p95/p99 reply latency. Impact: customer-facing chat sessions experienced 10-30% error rate (timeouts) and p99 latency increased from ~450ms to 3-6s, causing user-facing failures and several support escalations. Environment: Hosted Redwood API (prod), regional routing to us-east, model pinned to redwood-7b-v1. Expected: steady p95/p99 under 600ms for this workload. Actual: recurring p95/p99 spikes and 504 timeouts correlated with high continuous-batcher queue depth.
1) Use customer workload profile (many short prompts, sequence length ~64 tokens) against /v1/generate with model redwood-7b-v1 in us-east
2) Send sustained 120 rps with bursts to 300 rps over 10 minute windows
3) Observe service-level metrics: request latency distribution and continuous-batcher queue depth
4) Reproduce observed behavior: p95/p99 spikes when batcher aggregates many small requests into large batches and KV cache misses appear
2026-03-11T09:21:42Z [serving-runtime] request_id=rid-8a7f23 queue_depth=42 batch_size=64 latency=5120ms status=timeout
2026-03-11T09:22:10Z [scheduler] warn: continuous_batcher_window expanded to 40ms due to mis-estimated inter-arrival; effective batch_size=128
2026-03-11T09:23:05Z [api-gateway] 504 response returned upstream_timeout after 5s to client_id=vendora-123
Baseline p95=420ms p99=610ms before incident. During spikes p95=1.8s p99=5.6s, error rate (504) increased to 12% for affected routes. Continuous-batcher queue_depth peaked at 320 concurrently on a single serving pod; max_batch_size observed at 256 on several hosts.
Initial hypothesis: model update or kernel selection caused token-level slowdown — ruled out. Found strong correlation between batcher window expansion and p99 spikes. Sequence profile for Vendora workload is high-frequency short sequences; continuous batcher heuristics expanded batching window when inter-arrival jitter increased (likely due to upstream client burstiness and a transient scheduling delay on a subset of GPU hosts). Larger batches for short sequences increased end-to-end tail latency due to scheduling and KV cache cold misses. Also observed CPU contention on the host handling RPC dispatch leading to delayed batch dispatch. Reproducible in staging by introducing jitter and raising inter-arrival variance. Related evidence: scheduler logs showing adaptive window growth, PRAGMA telemetry showing increased kernel launch latency when batch_size > 128 for this model. Linked to regression in batcher heuristics introduced in INT-3789 (internal change last week).
Short-term mitigations applied 2026-03-11 11:02 UTC: 1) Locked continuous-batcher max_window_ms to 8ms for enterprise routes and for redwood-7b-v1 in us-east to prevent automatic over-aggregation. 2) Reduced max_batch_size to 96 for affected serving pools. 3) Deployed per-customer low-latency routing for Vendora to non-batched pool while fix rolled out. 4) Increased CPU request for RPC dispatcher on hot-serving hosts. Long-term fix: reverted the aggressive adaptive-window algorithm in INT-3789 and implemented a guardrail to bound batch_size growth for short-sequence-heavy tenants; added a new histogram-based estimator for inter-arrival variance. Patch PR merged and rolled out 2026-03-12 (see related_github_prs). Monitoring: added an automated alert (label: continuous-batching-tail) when batch_size>128 coincides with p99>2s. Customer notified and validated reduction in timeouts; final validation by Vendora completed 2026-03-13.
2026-03-11 09:35 - Support (Aisha): Customer reports increased 504s on chat. Collected request_ids and example payloads. Escalating to SRE oncall.
2026-03-11 09:48 - SRE oncall (Lukas): Observed batcher window growth and high queue_depth on 3 pods in us-east. Temporarily throttling batching for vendora-123 token. Will test guardrail.
2026-03-11 11:10 - SRE (Lukas): Mitigations applied: lock window_ms and reduce max_batch_size. Error rate falling to ~1%. Keeping route pinned; rolling patch to revert heuristic now.
2026-03-12 16:20 - Eng (Maya Chen): Reverted adaptive-window algorithm in mainline, PR #1624 merged. Added histogram estimator and unit tests. Scheduling full rollout tonight with canary 10%.
2026-03-13 08:05 - Support (Aisha): Vendora confirms normal behavior restored; no further timeouts observed in daily run. Closing incident after post-deploy verification.
payload.summary: Batch scheduler backlog causing p95/p99 spikes and request timeouts for production streaming

Issue summary: At ~2026-03-13T14:22Z we observed a sustained surge of 5xx responses from the API gateway for QuantEase tenant during an embedding upload. The gateway reported accept-queue growth leading to upstream runtime errors and a cascade of retries. Impact: customer reports ~35% of embedding requests returning 502/503 and elevated latencies for unrelated traffic for ~25 minutes. Environment: prod-us-east, dedicated pool (tenant id qte-9922). Observed behaviour: accept-queue depth on edge proxies increased rapidly, ephemeral proxy keepalive exhaustion, upstream serving-runtime CPU threads spiking and frequent runtime restarts. Expected behaviour: short-lived spikes handled by autoscaler and backpressure without customer-visible 5xx floor.
Customer-facing: QuantEase observed failed embedding uploads and downstream application retries. Business impact: batch ingestion job for search indexing failed, delayed production sync. Platform impact: transient elevated 5xx floor across several routes in the same dedicated pool; internal SLOs degraded during the window.
1) Customer performed an async bulk embedding upload split into ~4k small chunks with client-side aggressive retries on 429/timeout. 2) Several clients retried in parallel (concurrent clients ~80). 3) Gateway accept-queue filled with half-open connections from ephemeral proxies. 4) Serving runtime started shedding connections and returning 502/503 under pressure. Note: replication attempt in staging with smaller load reproduced accept-queue growth within 2 minutes.
Edge proxy logs: repeated 'accept queue full' entries at 2026-03-13T14:23:02Z; apigw metrics: accept_queue_length increased from 5 -> 320 within 3 minutes; runtime logs: 'watchdog: worker restart due to thread pool saturation' and 'kvcache lock contention' around 14:25Z. Example stack traces and truncated logs linked in related_confluence_pages. -- Request IDs: r-qte-14f3, r-qte-14f7, r-qte-15a2.
Hypotheses: (a) customer-side retry storm amplified by partially successful chunk uploads leading to retransmit hot loop; (b) ephemeral proxy keepalive depletion prevented normal connection reuse, increasing accept queue; (c) kvcache prefetch thrash in dedicated serving runtime caused increased CPU and runtime restarts. What we checked: - Ingress metrics, accept queue histograms, proxy keepalive pool size (saw slots approaching zero). - Tenant telemetry (concurrent streams and active connections spiked). - Serving runtime thread and GPU metrics show CPU-bound scheduling spikes prior to OOMs. Partial findings: a correlated pattern of small embedding chunks with HTTP/2 streams re-opened on retries; many retransmits within 200-800ms. Linked to an older client library that uses exponential backoff with capped jitter that in practice created synchronized retry waves. Cross-references: see SUP-314159 for similar accept-queue patterns during bulk embedding traffic.
2026-03-13T14:28Z - Asha Patel: Customer opened via support channel; provided timeline and sample request IDs. Notified SRE on-call.
2026-03-13T14:33Z - Miguel Torres: Acknowledged, collecting traces and metrics. Asked customer for SDK version and full request headers. Escalated to runtime team.
2026-03-13T14:50Z - SRE (Priya Rao): Observed accept_queue growth on edge-proxy nodes servicing qte-9922. Pushed temporary priority-shed rule for that tenant to free queue slots.
2026-03-13T15:10Z - Runtime eng (Leo Nguyen): Noted kvcache eviction storms and increased prefetch latency; bound to high connection churn. Investigating whether a previous kernel change affected HTTP/2 stream reuse.
2026-03-13T15:45Z - Miguel Torres: Deployed emergency mitigation: tenant-level rate throttle for small-blob embedding route and increased proxy keepalive slots on a subset of nodes. Error rate subsided within ~7 minutes.
2026-03-13T16:05Z - Customer (QuantEase Ops): Confirmed uploads resumed; reported partial completion of their ingestion job. Asked for a permanent fix so scheduled nightly job can complete reliably.
2026-03-13T16:30Z - Miguel Torres: Noted that mitigation prevented further runtime restarts; drafting follow-up actions and client-side recommendations. Creating postmortem action items.
2026-03-14T09:00Z - Miguel Torres: Adding follow-up: outreach to SDK team about retry/backoff defaults and to runtime team about improving kvcache resilience under connection churn.
Workaround applied: tenant-level short-term throttling for small-blob embedding route and increased ephemeral proxy keepalive capacity on affected nodes. Outcome: 5xx rate returned to baseline within 10 minutes. Permanent fixes planned: 1) Add a server-side adaptive ingress-shedder that detects retransmit amplification and applies queuing/backoff for high-frequency small-chunk uploads. 2) Improve runtime kvcache locking to avoid prefetch lock amplification during high churn. 3) Customer guidance: update SDK to v2.4.1 which includes jittered exponential backoff and reduced chunk concurrency. Rollout notes: Ingress shedder design will be prototyped in staging (ticket INT-1202), runtime kv fix targeted for next minor (runtime) release. Postmortem scheduled on 2026-03-18; action owner list will be added to the incident RCA.
Owners: Miguel Torres (ingress mitigations), Leo Nguyen (runtime fix), Priya Rao (SRE operational runbook). Tasks: SDK outreach, automated detection rule, increase default proxy keepalive threshold for dedicated pools, KPI monitors for accept-queue growth. Target completion: 2026-03-31.
This incident highlights interaction between customer client behavior (aggressive retries + small chunking) and platform connection handling. Recommend adding more tenant-specific telemetry to detect retransmit amplification earlier.
When contacting the customer: recommend using updated SDK with fixed backoff, suggest batching strategy changes (larger chunk sizes, lower concurrency). If similar spike observed, apply temporary tenant priority-shed and throttle small-blob embedding route while notifying runtime on-call.
payload.summary: Ephemeral accept-queue flood from async embedding retransmit causing API 5xx cascade
