payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customer reports that long-running SSE streams (chat responses with lists/bulleted conclusions) sometimes arrive with the final paragraph missing after a brief network hiccup. Client uses our JS SDK behind a Chromium-based electron app with a service worker that implements a fetch handler to buffer/resume requests.

Impact:
- Occurs intermittently (estimated ~4% of sessions during heavy egress) for BlueWave Health's private deployment.
- Final paragraph or last bullet list sometimes absent — downstream UI shows a completed stream but content stops abruptly.
- Customer workflow relies on complete clinical-summary paragraphs; missing tails are high-impact.

Environment:
- Private deployment (VPC) in us-east-1, API fronted by customer-managed proxy + our api-gateway.
- Client: electron 20+ with service worker registration and custom fetch replays.
- Models: rw-instruct-7b (primary), fallback rw-compat-16k.

Steps to reproduce (observed by customer):
1) Start streaming completion (SSE) for prompt that returns 3-4 paragraph summary with trailing bullet list.
2) After ~18-45s, client triggers an optimistic retry due to internal socket timeout (client-side) while service worker is attempting to replay an earlier fetch.
3) SDK reopens/resumes SSE connection and server sends resume frames.
4) Playback shows duplicated prefix fragments but the terminal paragraph/bullets are missing on the final stitched output.

Observed behavior:
- Stream resumes and finalization marker is sent by our runtime (logs show terminal event emitted).
- Client-visible assembled stream lacks the last paragraph; server-side emitted tokens appear in logs but are not present in reconstructed SSE delivered to app when the service worker replay path is used.

Expected behavior:
- Resumed SSE should deliver entire token stream including terminal paragraph and finalization metadata regardless of client-side optimistic retry or service worker replay.

Temporary workaround provided to customer:
- Disable the service worker fetch-replay for long-poll/SSE endpoints (workaround reduces occurrence to ~0%).
- Increase client-side socket timeout to avoid optimistic retry during transient jitter.

Logs sample (server):
- runtime-session-id=rs-9a7f4e: terminal_event_sent=true, last_token_seq=842, bytes=73
- gateway: resume.window=1, resume.offset=840->842, response-code=200
- auth-proxy: connection-handoff=client-ephemeral-ipa->edge-ipa, keepalive=reset

Notes: customer captured HAR + service worker console traces and attached them in the ticket (see comments).
2026-03-13 18:45 - Customer (BlueWave Support): Attached HAR + SW logs. Noticed that console shows SW replay event immediately before final newline disappears.
2026-03-13 19:10 - Support (Ava Martinez): Acknowledged receipt, escalating to runtime/SRE. Asking for SDK/service-worker repro steps.
2026-03-13 19:40 - SRE (Darren Ng): Reproduced in staging with SW-enabled test harness. Observed both connections claiming resume token; terminal frame emitted by runtime but only consumed by first in-order stream. Second attach path appears to see prefix only.

Additional notes:
2026-03-14 09:05 - Support (Ava Martinez): Sent workaround steps (disable SW replay, bump client timeout). Customer applied workaround and confirmed fix for their immediate production impact.
03-13 18:20 UTC: Replayed customer HAR — saw duplicate CONNECT from client with identical client-id header within 300ms
03-13 19:05 UTC: Reproducer run in staging with a synthetic service-worker replay reproduced missing tail when fetch handler replays the request while SDK issues retry
Hypothesis: service-worker replay path causes browser-level response stream to be intercepted and reconstituted; SDK resume/rewind logic expects monotonic single socket handshake and can drop terminal fragments when two parallel connection sequences race to attach to same session token
Correlation: similar linkage to SUP-314159 (session rotation) where handoff races caused trailing-frame loss
Workaround accepted by customer: disable service worker fetch-replay for SSE endpoints and increase client socket timeout
Engineering proposed fix: make resume attach idempotent and ensure terminal buffer flush is gated on finalization flag rather than attach order (PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/982)
Planned rollout: hotfix to staging channel 2026-03-15, canary to private deployments 2026-03-16, full rollout after 48h monitoring windows
Complete runtime PR and add unit/integration tests for dual-attach resume race
Coordinate with SDK team to detect SW replay path and emit a warning in console (SDK PR #173)
Follow up with customer 2026-03-16 to validate hotfix in their private deployment
payload.summary: Client retry race and service-worker replay silence final paragraph on SSE resume

Reranker then runs compatibility checks and sometimes runs CPU sync path if variant mismatch detected. Adding instrumentation to header validation.

2026-03-12T15:40:00Z Liam O'Connor: Deployed hotfix branch to guard against mismatched precision headers (PR referenced). Also tuned serving-runtime to prefer async GPU similarity fallback instead of CPU sync. Monitoring for regressions.

payload.description:
Issue summary: Customers are seeing non-deterministic rerank order (top-k swings) and spikes in rerank latency for batch-based rerank calls. The behavior started after a capacity event where GPUs in the embed pool entered reduced-memory mode and some embedding requests were served from a high-precision fallback path.

Impact: BrightSearch reports incorrect search ordering for a subset (~2-3%) of queries and end-to-end rerank latency increased from median 85ms to 420ms during incidents. Business impact: noticeable user-facing ranking regressions and increased error budget for the Dedicated tenancy.

Environment: prod/us-east, dedicated embed pool for BrightSearch. Affected model: redwood-embed-1024-q8 (primary) with fallback route to redwood-embed-1024-fp32 under memory pressure.

Steps to reproduce (observed pattern):
1) Send a mixed traffic pattern that includes heavy long-sequence embedding requests concurrently with normal requests (BrightSearch synthetic trace attached).
2) During GPU memory pressure, runtime triggers precision fallback for a fraction of in-flight embeds to FP32 path.
3) Reranker receives embeddings with slightly different normalization/scale and detects dimension metadata headers as identical.
4) Rerank pipeline sometimes routes similarity computation to CPU synchronous fallback (observed in logs), adding ~300-500ms.
5) Observed results: similarity scores off by small epsilon; ties and ranking flips appear for edge-cases; some requests time out or return 504.

Observed behavior: inconsistent top-k across repeated queries, occasional 504s, and latency spikes correlating with precision-fallback events. Logs show alternating embed headers with identical dims but different precision flags.

Expected behavior: deterministic similarity ordering for same input when model pinned, and graceful performance without synchronous CPU fallback.

Attachments/Logs: Inlined log snippets below and attached BrightSearch payload sample.
- trace_id=ts-20260311-7a8f: "embed:pool=dedicated-bs mem_state=constrained precision=fallback->fp32 kernel=quantized_scalar"
- rerank: "sim-compute fallthrough=cpu_sync reason=kernel_unavailable latency=372ms"
- api-gateway: "429 adaptive-throttle embed_pool=dedicated-bs concurrency=128"

Notes: Customer has temporarily pinned to redwood-embed-1024-fp32 which stabilizes ordering but increases cost. They request a root cause and fix so they can return to the efficient q8 quantized model without ranking regressions.

Additional notes:
2026-03-11 12:05 - SRE (Marta Gomez): Observed GPU OOM pressure on dedicated-bs pool between 09:10-09:45 UTC. Several embedding pods toggled health->drain. Found logs indicating precision fallback for ~3% of requests.
2026-03-12 09:21 - BrightSearch (J. Moore): Confirmed we see timing windows when results flip and occasionally return 504. Workaround of pinning to fp32 is effective but costs us ~2.5x. Need a non-costly fix.
Kernel selection trace shows path: q8_embed -> (mem_low) -> fp32_fallback -> header_propagated_as_q8 -> rerank_kernel_mismatch -> cpu_sync_fallback.
Reproduced locally by toggling embed pod mem_limit and forcing fallback; saw same small cosine differences (1e-4 to 1e-2) that change top-5 in edge cases.
Adaptive throttler increased 429s temporarily when concurrency > 100; this interacts with customer's retry logic causing bursts that exacerbate memory pressure.
Metric correlation: precision-fallback events spike concurrently with pod restarts and GC events on the embed pool.
Related internal issue INT-4022 contains earlier notes about kernel-tag propagation; likely a follow-on for proper header/tagging refactor.
Mitigation applied: 1) Hotfix to validate and normalize precision metadata at embed service boundary so reranker never receives ambiguous headers. 2) Prefer async GPU similarity fallback path where possible; avoid CPU synchronous fallback. 3) Temporarily increased embed pool reserve to avoid memory-driven fallback for BrightSearch while we rollout permanent fix. Customer unpinned and confirmed significant reduction in both latency and rank flips. Next steps: full refactor of kernel-precision tagging (INT-4022) and improved autoscaler heuristics.
2026-03-12 14:55 - Hotfix deployed to prod us-east embed pool (canary->100%).
2026-03-12 15:10 - Increased pool reserve for BrightSearch to reduce fallback probability.
2026-03-12 16:00 - Enabled async GPU fallback for similarity compute in reranker for dedicated pools.
Monitoring: Added precision_fallback metric and dashboard (confluence link above).
payload.summary: Intermittent similarity score swings and high rerank latency when embedding precision falls back under memory pressure

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customers using a combination of long-lived HTTP/2 connections with aggressive keepalive and high-volume background bulk uploads are seeing intermittent 429s on low-latency requests routed to the same API key. Impact appears correlated with connection reuse and the server-side token accounting window.

Impact:
- Sporadic 429 responses for realtime chat calls while large background embedding uploads are running.
- User-visible latency spikes and retry waves causing degraded UX for LuminaSearch support users.

Environment:
- Dedicated pool (LuminaSearch dedicated-01) in prod-us-east.
- Traffic mix: ~30% realtime chat (short requests), 70% bulk embedding batches (multipart uploads).
- HTTP/2 enabled on client side with connection multiplexing and frequent keepalive PINGs.

Steps to reproduce (customer):
1) Start a batch embed job with parallel multipart uploads (16 workers) across persistent HTTP/2 connections that reuse a small pool of connections.
2) Simultaneously start interactive chat sessions sending frequent short requests.
3) Observe 429s on chat routes after a period (~3–7 minutes) of sustained bulk activity.

Observed behavior:
- 429s include standard throttle headers: X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining appear to be decreasing even for chat requests.
- Console shows tenant-level quota nearing exhaustion despite dashboard reporting available credits.
- TCP connection stats show reuse with a small set of origin IPs and many concurrent streams.

Expected behavior:
- Route-level separation (realtime vs bulk) to prevent bulk background jobs from causing 429s on low-latency chat traffic when separate priority pools are configured.
- Throttle headers reflect per-route accounting for interactive routes.

Logs and artifacts provided by customer (attached links):
- tcpdump snippets and HTTP/2 stream counts (link: s3://lumina-logs/prod/keepalive-dump-2026-03-06.pcap)
- API traces: trace-2026-03-06T14-04.gz (shows correlation between PINGs and stream resets)
- Console screenshot showing tenant credits: https://lumina.example/screens/tenant-credit-dump.png
Support (Maya Singh) 2026-03-07: Customer reported first seen 2026-03-06 14:00 UTC. They attached pcap and traces. Asked for initial triage and whether keepalive behavior could be counted against tenant burst credit.
SRE (Diego Ramos) 2026-03-07: Acknowledged. Assigning to ingress/ratelimit owners to check token-counting for multiplexed HTTP/2 streams. Requesting sample API key and timestamped logs.
Customer (LuminaSearch - Alex Chen) 2026-03-07: Provided API key (redacted) and additional traces. Noted that reducing parallel workers reduces 429 frequency but doesn't eliminate it.
Ingress owner (Priya Kapoor) 2026-03-08: Initial check: healthchecks and PING frames are not intended to count as requests. Observed many concurrent active streams and repeated preflight-like OPTIONS calls from the uploader. Need deeper accounting checks in rate-limiter.
Rate-limiter (Ethan Boyd) 2026-03-09: Found a quota aggregation edge where connection-level attributes (client IP + connection id) were mapped to a shared token window. When many streams on same connection had rapid connect/disconnect, refill logic misattributed refill credits causing short-term overcounting for interactive routes.
Hypothesis 1: HTTP/2 multiplexing + connection reuse causes background upload streams to be grouped and counted against a shared refill window leading to tenant credit depletion visible to realtime routes.
Hypothesis 2: Keepalive PINGs combined with probe endpoints are being misclassified as billable preflight requests by the ingress normalization layer (path normalization discrepancy).
Telemetry: token bucket logs show bursts aligned with upload worker start times. Refill window snapshots show transient negative Remaining values before automatic smoothing kicks in.
Reproduced in staging by simulating multiplexed HTTP/2 uploads with same API key and 12 parallel streams. Observed chat route 429s after ~5 minutes. Confirmed local repro consistent with customer report.
Short-term mitigation (applied 2026-03-09): Recommended customer reduce per-connection worker count to avoid overloading single-connection token accounting; customer applied and saw immediate reduction in 429 frequency.
Applied a rate-limiter config patch in staging to avoid counting PING and OPTIONS probe endpoints as billable requests (PR linked).
Long-term fix: rate-limiter change to separate per-route token windows when priority lanes are configured for dedicated pools. Scheduled rollout to canary next week (related PR https://github.com/redwood-inference/rate-limiter/pull/412).
Follow-up tasks: implement connection-fingerprint awareness to split refill accounting across routes for multiplexed connections; update docs on recommended worker-per-connection defaults for HTTP/2 clients.
Recommend isolating bulk embedding workers onto separate API key or enabling dedicated priority lane for bulk ingest. As immediate customer workaround, reduce parallel workers per connection to 4 and enable exponential backoff on embed retries.
Coordinate canary rollout of rate-limiter patch with infra (target: 2026-03-16).
Create a short KB entry for customers about HTTP/2 connection reuse, keepalive, and worker-per-connection guidance.
Monitor LuminaSearch dedicated pool post-mitigation for 72 hours and update ticket with telemetry summary.
payload.summary: Keepalive + HTTP/2 connection reuse causing intermittent 429s under mixed bulk/realtime traffic

Issue summary:
Customer receives integrity / checksum failures for binary artifacts returned from function-calling outputs when the request is retried by the Python SDK. Failures only appear in production on the customer's Private deployment after an API retry path (client-side backoff) and when the runtime returns a gzipped binary blob as part of a funcall response payload.

Impact:
- Arbor Analytics ETL pipelines intermittently report corrupted attachment contents and raise exceptions.
- A subset of requests (~0.3% of funcall responses) get invalid checksums leading to failed downstream processing and manual re-ingest.
- Customer is on Enterprise plan and on a Private deployment with HSM-backed key rotation enabled.

Environment:
- Redwood Private deployment (customer-managed control plane)
- Region: us-east-1
- Python SDK v1.8.3 (pinned)
- API gateway: HTTP/2 fronting internal gRPC to serving runtime
- Serving runtime: redwood-llm-v2-large with gzip content compression enabled for funcall outputs
- HSM: periodic API key rotation during nightly window (03:30-04:00 UTC)

Steps to reproduce (reported by customer):
1. Submit a funcall request that returns a binary attachment (e.g., generated report.tar.gz encoded in base64 inside funcall result).
2. Simulate transient network error on the client so the SDK applies its retry/backoff (observed during short 502/timeout).
3. On retry, the response sometimes decodes to binary with invalid checksum when written to disk by the customer's consumer.

Observed behavior:
- The Python SDK logs show a retry and a subsequent 200 response.
- The funcall.response.body appears to contain base64 that decodes but the binary is corrupted (tar fails to extract).
- SRE traces show the first attempt returned compressed payload with Transfer-Encoding: chunked over HTTP/2; second attempt response path shows identical content-length but different content encoding header.

Expected behavior:
- Retries should result in identical, bit-exact payloads for the same logical response or the retry should be detected and ignored if dedup semantics are used. No corruption should occur as a result of retries.

Logs and artifacts provided by customer (sanitized):
- SDK debug trace (attached) showing request id and retry sequence: req=arbor-req-9982 attempt=1 -> timeout, attempt=2 -> 200
- Base64 strings from both attempts (hex diff attached in support bundle)
- Serving runtime request trace: trace-id 2c3f6a showing gzipped payload returned on attempt 1 and attempt 2 with differing content-encoding headers in the edge layer.

Hypothesis (initial):
- Edge/ingress layer is performing header normalization on retry paths (HTTP/2 connection reuse + proxy rewriting) and occasionally drops or reorders content-encoding headers for chunked gzip responses.
- The SDK's retry path assumes idempotent raw body bytes and directly decodes base64 without validating content-encoding consistency across attempts.
- HSM key rotation timing may cause subtle changes in how binary is streamed (observed correlation with nightly rotation window), but not the primary cause.

Temporary workaround provided to customer:
- Customer disabled gzip compression for funcall outputs in their Private runtime config; this mitigated the corruption rate in their environment to near zero.
- Recommended short-term: upgrade to Python SDK preview v1.9.0 (contains additional validation) and enable SDK-level content-encoding sanity checks as a stopgap.

Next steps (investigation):
- SRE to check ingress proxy (internal Edge) logs for header mutation on connection reuse and retries.
- SDK team to add decoding-time content-encoding validation and optional conservative retry semantics for funcall binary payloads.
- Runtime team to evaluate whether we can ensure stable content-encoding across retries (avoid rewriting headers on retried requests).

References:
- Customer-provided support bundle: arbor-560412-bundle.tar.gz (stored in support ticket attachments)
- Related internal note: INT-2215 (ingress header-rewrite experiments)

Additional notes:
Edge layer reproduced header drop when multiplexed streams used and chunked transfer encoding combined with gzip; implemented guard to copy content-encoding header from original upstream response to replayed response.
SDK change will: add content-encoding check between attempts, fall back to not decoding if enc mismatch, log error, and surface non-idempotent warning to customer.
Customer private deploy had HSM rotation during incident window but root cause appears independent; still coordinating with infra to ensure key rotation does not affect streaming semantics.
payload.summary: Binary payload integrity errors after SDK retry with gzipped function outputs

Issue summary: Customer reports that when their client applies aggressive client-side backpressure (pause/resume on the streaming socket) while the SDK/edge is in the middle of a function/tool call, the tool acknowledgement gets lost. Impact: downstream systems observe either duplicate side-effects after replay or never-observed confirmations, leading to billing ambiguity and customer data inconsistencies.

Environment: Prod, dedicated deployment for Nimbus Health in us-east. Python SDK 1.8.2 used from a serverless worker behind an in-house proxy.

Steps to reproduce:
1) Start long-lived streaming session via Python SDK to call external tool via function-calling feature.
2) Trigger a tool execution that emits a confirmation webhook synchronously from the tool handler.
3) Simulate client backpressure by pausing the TCP read loop for ~500-1500ms intermittently (server in CPU-constrained environment).
4) Resume the stream; SDK reconnects/flows may replay inflight events.

Expected behavior: SDK/edge should preserve tool acknowledgement idempotently and surface a single confirmed execution to the customer; replays should be deduplicated by idempotency keys.

Actual behavior: In ~30% of runs, the webhook confirmation is not recorded in the session state; later replay either re-invokes the tool (duplicate side-effect) or the system marks the execution as unknown.

Logs/observations:
- Edge logs show 'ack-window-timeout' correlated with paused reads at timestamp ranges.
- Kinesis traces show the outbound webhook was accepted (200 OK) but the confirmation event did not reach session persistence due to a write timeout to Redis during the pause window.
- Customer observed two charges for the same tool call in billing logs for one replayed invocation.

Customer impact: Potential duplicate side-effects and billing disputes. Requires mitigation guidance and a reliable long-term fix.
Hypothesis A: Client-side pause causes edge to drop in-flight ACK update RPCs to session-store (Redis) due to connection pooling exhaustion under backpressure.
Hypothesis B: SDK replays inflight messages without strictly replaying tool confirmation idempotency headers leading to new invocations.
Ran a repro in staging with identical pause pattern; observed Redis write timeouts (avg 1200ms) and edge logs 'inflight-ack-dropped'.
Found related code path in streaming coordinator where confirmation propagation is async and not gated behind durable write acknowledgement.
Short-term mitigation: recommend customer set SDK client to use 'ack_mode: confirm_before_close' and increase socket-read buffer to avoid pausing the stream.
Also suggested configuring dedicated deployment autoscaling to avoid CPU starvation during proxy bursts.
Follow-up: engineering to add sync-level persistence for tool confirmations or a confirmation-resend handshake on resume.
2026-03-10 | Ava Chen: Captured initial report from Nimbus Health. Customer provided sample repro script and billing trace. Marked P1 due to billing impact.
2026-03-10 | Rohan Patel (Support): Acknowledged and requested full SDK logs and proxy config. Also asked for precise timing of pause/resume.
2026-03-11 | Nimbus Health (Customer): Uploaded repro script showing pause intervals and sample webhook server logs (200 responses).
2026-03-11 | Linh Nguyen (SRE): Confirmed Redis timeouts in our staging repro. Suggested increasing connection pool and adding telemetry for ack-write-failures.
2026-03-12 | Rohan Patel (Support): Provided temporary workaround to customer: enable 'confirm_before_close' and set env var REDWOOD_STREAM_READ_TIMEOUT=3000. Customer to test and report.
2026-03-12 | Nimbus Health (Customer): Applied workaround; initial verification shows no duplicate charges in two-hour test window.
Temporary workaround recommended and validated by customer: enable client-side 'confirm_before_close' mode and increase stream read timeout; also advised scaling edge proxy and increasing Redis connection pool. Engineering to implement durable confirmation persistence and a resume-handshake to ensure confirmations are reconciled on reconnect. Track fix in runtime PR #4021 and follow up with customer once deployed to dedicated cluster.

Issue summary: Customer reports intermittent failures when the private deployment requests large model artifact ranges via presigned S3 URLs. Downloads fail partway through with HTTP/2 RST_STREAM from the serving node, leading to corrupted artifacts or repeated range retry loops. Impact: Model pulls for new model versions fail ~15% of the time on artifact range requests >8MB, causing slower rollouts and serving node restarts in the customer VPC environment. Environment: Private deployment (customer-managed egress) in us-east-1. Occurs from multiple serving nodes and during peak concurrency windows.

Observed behavior:
- GET range requests to presigned S3 URLs start successfully and transfer multiple megabytes.
- After a short period the client side sees HTTP/2 RST_STREAM (stream error) and the TLS connection remains up.
- Artifact downloader retries with shifted range offsets; sometimes the reassembled object fails checksum.

Why we think it's networking-related:
- Failures correlate with higher concurrent download fan-out (many parallel range requests).
- tcpdump from a serving node consistently shows the server and S3 peer offering SACK in TCP options, but packets observed on the customer egress path lack SACK and occasionally show altered TS and WS values.

Customer impact and ask: Customer requests either a configuration bypass for the firewall to allow SACK/TCP options or guidance on recommended download parameters and a short-term mitigation we can apply on the serving node side.
1) Deploy private agent in customer's us-east-1 VPC with default artifact fetcher config.
2) Trigger a model rollout that requires the serving nodes to download a large model artifact (>200MB) that our downloader splits into concurrent ranged GETs (default parallelism = 8).
3) Observe client-side downloader logs and capture tcpdump on the serving node and at the customer egress NAT/edge device.
4) Reproduce under moderate concurrency (30-60 parallel pulls across nodes) to increase likelihood of suppression by stateful egress device.
[2026-03-10T09:14:22Z] downloader: GET /artifact.part (range: bytes=0-8388607) => 200, received 8,388,608 bytes
[2026-03-10T09:14:23Z] downloader: GET /artifact.part (range: bytes=8388608-16777215) => started
[2026-03-10T09:14:23Z] http2: RST_STREAM id=15 code=INTERNAL_ERROR - remote

tcpdump snippet (serving node egress): TCP Options: MSS=1460,SACK_PERM,TS val 34567890 ecr 12345678,WS=7
tcpdump snippet (captured on customer edge): TCP Options: MSS=1460,TS val 34567890 ecr 12345678,WS=7 (SACK_PERM missing)
2026-03-10 Priya (Support) - collected tcpdumps and downloader traces; customer confirms managed NGFW in egress path (inline).
2026-03-10 Jordan (SRE) - observed consistent SACK stripping between serving node and egress capture; S3 <-> serving side shows SACK, customer edge shows SACK absent. Hypothesis: inline NGFW is normalizing TCP options (dropping SACK), causing retransmission/reordering to be handled differently and breaking http2 stream reassembly under our concurrent range strategy.
Checked server kernel: tcp_sack enabled on serving nodes (net.ipv4.tcp_sack = 1). Serving nodes show fast retransmits on missing SACK information which can lead to out-of-order ACKs surfaced to HTTP/2 layer as stream errors.
Tried reproducing using a single-threaded download (parallelism = 1): no RST_STREAM observed in 50/50 test runs - supports parallelism + SACK-stripping interaction hypothesis.
Customer firewall vendor reports a default "TCP option normalization" feature enabled for traffic inspection; vendor doc references SACK-stripping in certain throughput-protection modes.

Additional notes:
2026-03-10 11:30 - Mariner NetOps (customer): We use an inline NGFW (vendor: Oakridge Networks) and have not enabled TLS inspection for the presigned S3 host. We'll provide packet captures from the edge tomorrow morning local time.
2026-03-12 09:20 - Mariner NetOps: We're willing to test a policy change to preserve TCP options for traffic to S3 endpoints. Awaiting exact hostnames/IP ranges to whitelist.
1) Short-term: Set artifact fetcher parallelism to 1 or 2 to avoid concurrent range reassembly sensitivity. This was validated in-house and reduced failure rate to <1% in tests.
2) Customer-side: Configure NGFW to preserve TCP options (disable TCP option normalization / SACK stripping) for traffic to presigned S3 hostnames or IP ranges. This requires a rule change on their appliance.
3) Serve-side patch: engineering proposes adding a downloader mode 'sequential-range-with-retries' (slow-path) for private deployments as a safety for customers behind aggressive middleboxes.
In Progress - temporary mitigations applied: customer set downloader parallelism to 2 and observed immediate reduction in failures. Customer will test NGFW policy change to preserve TCP options for S3 traffic; Eng to schedule prioritized implementation of a sequential-range download mode for private deployments if policy change is not possible.
1) Support to coordinate with customer to apply NGFW whitelist for S3 hostnames and validate with packet captures (owner: Priya).
2) Engineering to scope and estimate sequential-range downloader mode and a configuration flag for private deployments (owner: Elena, ETA: 2026-03-20).
3) After customer confirms NGFW rule change, run 24h soak with normal parallelism and capture tcpdumps to validate SACK preservation and no RST_STREAMs (owner: Customer + Jordan).

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customers using the Python SDK (v1.4.2) with short idempotency tokens observed cross-session response reuse and occasionally mismatched tool invocation arguments under high concurrent load. PromptlyAI reports that distinct user sessions got back responses (and downstream tool outputs) originating from other sessions. This appears to be a collision / normalization problem with idempotency keys used by the SDK

Impact:
- Incorrect function/tool outputs returned to clients (data leakage between sessions).
- Confusing application-level behavior: tools returning values not matching the local prompt/context.
- High business risk for customers that have side-effectful tool integrations (webhooks, downstream job creation).

Environment:
- Python SDK v1.4.2 (customer reports wrapper that generates compact keys via uuid.uuid4().hex[:8])
- Production (us-east) serving via hosted Redwood API
- Models in use: redwood/decoder-xl-1.0 and openlm/llama-3-7b

Steps to reproduce (customer-provided):
1) Create a lightweight client that sets an idempotency key using uuid.uuid4().hex[:8].
2) Start 200 concurrent requests across two distinct user sessions that call a function/tool with side effects (e.g., create_job webhook).
3) Observe some responses containing tool outputs originating from other sessions.
4) Server logs show repeated use of the same idempotency key and cached responses being returned.

Observed behavior:
- API responses are returned with X-Idempotency-Key headers matching the short keys.
- In logs, different request IDs map to the same idempotency key and the backend treats them as retries (response reuse).
- Resulting tool outputs sometimes reflect arguments from the other session, indicating request conflation.

Expected behavior:
- Different sessions/requests without an explicit, fully-unique idempotency key must not collide; server should treat them as independent requests unless a true identical idempotency key is provided by the caller.

Quick workaround suggested to customer:
- Stop using truncated idempotency keys (avoid first-8-bytes pattern). Instead provide a full 32-char uuid4 hex string (uuid.uuid4().hex) or set an application-unique prefix per session.
- Pin SDK version to v1.4.3 once published (contains immediate mitigation).

Logs (redacted):
- Request A: request_id=req_0a3f, X-Idempotency-Key=1a2b3c4d, returned cached_response_id=cache_7
- Request B: request_id=req_b7c2, X-Idempotency-Key=1a2b3c4d, returned cached_response_id=cache_7 (originated from Request A)

Notes: this ticket focuses on the case where customer-side short keys + SDK/server normalization can produce collisions under scale. We are treating this as a customer-impacting bug and prioritizing an SDK and server-side mitigation.
2026-03-12 - Customer (PromptlyAI): We're seeing occasional responses that contain tool outputs from other users. We audit our wrapper and saw we used uuid4().hex[:8] to shorten keys. Can you confirm if that could cause collisions?
2026-03-12 - Support (Alex Chen): Thanks for the report — we're investigating. Please stop the short-key generator and switch to full uuid.uuid4().hex for now. We'll look into SDK behavior as well.
2026-03-13 - Engineering (Marina Patel): Initial reproduction in staging confirms collisions when idempotency keys are restricted to 8-hex chars. We also saw a legacy normalization step in sdk-python that lowercased + truncated for header compatibility. Opening patch to emit full uuid by default.
2026-03-13 - Security (Diego Ruiz): Possible information leakage risk since tool outputs can contain user-scoped data. Recommend immediate advisory to affected customers and patch priority elevated.
2026-03-14 - Engineering (Marina Patel): Deployed server-side namespacing change to avoid global de-dup across customer sessions (infra PR merged). SDK patch landed as 1.4.3 to stop compacting keys. Asking PromptlyAI to upgrade and confirm.
2026-03-14 - Customer (PromptlyAI): Upgraded to SDK v1.4.3 and replaced key generator with full uuid. Initial tests against prod show no further cross-session reuse. We'll monitor and report back.
2026-03-14 - Support (Alex Chen): Marking as in-progress until we confirm two follow-ups: (1) confirm no other SDKs have similar truncation behavior (TS/Go sweep), and (2) add a confluence note + customer advisory template.
2026-03-14 - Engineering (Marina Patel): Follow-ups: create test harness for idempotency collision injection, add SDK validation that warns when supplied idempotency keys are < 16 hex chars, and schedule release note entry.
2026-03-14 - Ops (Ravi Singh): Deployed transient metric to counts of idempotency key reuse per customer namespace; will keep for 7 days to detect regressions.
What we did:
- Reproduced locally using a simple client that supplies uuid4().hex[:8]. Under 200 concurrent requests we saw ~0.6% request conflation.
- Instrumented api-gateway and found a legacy normalization path in sdk-python that attempted to keep idempotency headers compact for a CLI use-case; that path intentionally shortened new keys to 8 bytes for readability but did not include namespacing.
- Confirmed server treats identical idempotency keys as a retry of the same logical request and will re-use cached response / skip re-execution of side-effectful tools. This caused the observed response reuse/leakage.
- Verified that upgrading to full uuid prevents collisions at observed load.
- Also reproduced a second, rarer scenario where a proxy stripped characters from longer keys (non-ASCII or padding) — ops added a normalization-safety shim to the ingress to preserve keys.

Root cause summary:
- Customer code + SDK compatibility path led to truncated idempotency keys (8 hex chars).
- Truncated keys have non-negligible collision probability at high QPS and across many sessions.
- Server-side de-dup logic treated collisions as retries, leading to cross-session response reuse.

Mitigations done:
- Short-term: communicated workaround to customer and asked to use full UUIDs.
- SDK: removed compacting/truncation behavior in sdk-python default path; added warning when provided key length < 16 hex chars. Patch released as v1.4.3.
- Infra: namespaced idempotency cache by account/session where possible and fixed proxy normalization that could strip trailing chars. Added metric to detect unexpected reuse rates.

Next steps:
- Audit TS and Go SDKs for similar compacting/truncation heuristics (owners assigned).
- Add docs guidance and a confluence security advisory template for customers using short keys.
- Add unit+load tests to catch collisions in CI harness.
Actions completed:
- SDK patch v1.4.3 published (removes truncation and adds validation/warning).
- Infra change: idempotency namespacing by account applied to prod (reduced global collisions).
- Ops added a metric alert for idempotency key reuse rates per tenant and a proxy shim to preserve long headers.
- Customer upgraded to v1.4.3 and replaced uuid4().hex[:8] with full uuid.uuid4().hex; initial verification shows no further incidents.

Follow-ups (open):
- ENG: Sweep TS/Go SDKs for similar behavior (INT-4521).
- DOCS: Publish advisory + add best-practice snippet in SDK quickstarts.
- SECURITY: Run audit to ensure no PII leakage occurred; customer asked to provide sample logs for retention scope.

Ticket status: Keep open (In Progress) until TS/Go sweep complete and audit closed.
payload.summary: Truncated idempotency keys in Python SDK causing cross-session response reuse and tool-argument leakage under high concurrency

Issue summary: Customer reports sporadic end-to-end latency spikes and downstream 504/502 timeouts when invoking sequences that call two or more external adapters (connectors) within a single request. Impact: Live production workloads for ScaleSky Labs experiencing ~10-30% request timeouts during peak traffic windows, resulting in failed transactions and user-visible errors. Environment: prod-us-east-1, dedicated pool (dedicated-tier-us-east-1-ss-03). Observed behavior: Requests that orchestrate 2+ adapter calls show an additional ~80-250ms per adapter for synchronous schema/metadata lookups in the adapter-proxy path; some requests exceed client timeout (120s) or hit internal 30s gateway timeouts. Expected behavior: Adapter metadata/schema checks should be cached or performed asynchronously so per-request added latency is minimal (single-digit ms) and not compounded across chained adapters.
1) Using customer's integration, send a multi-stage orchestration request that triggers adapter A (external data fetch) then adapter B (post-processing). 2) Ensure streaming responses are enabled and payloads include large prompt context (~8k tokens). 3) Observe end-to-end timing and any gateway timeouts. 4) Compare request traces with and without adapter chaining (single adapter).
trace_id=6b9d4f2a-1a2c-4f7e-90b1-2c9f8ab3c4de: gateway->adapter-proxy handshake took 120ms, adapter-introspect schema call 95ms, adapter-invoke 30ms; total extra hop ~225ms. sample_error: upstream 502 from adapter-proxy (502 Bad Gateway) at 2026-03-09T18:42:12Z. client-timing: total_e2e=3420ms, adapter_hops=3, per_adapter_avg=110ms. logs_link: https://logs.redwood.internal/trace/6b9d4f2a
03/10 - Initial triage: Support reproduced elevated p95 latencies for multi-adapter flows in customer's dedicated pool. Single adapter flows show nominal latency.
03/10 - SRE traced pattern to adapter-proxy layer making synchronous metadata/schema validation calls to adapter endpoints prior to execution — validation was not cached for adapters flagged as ephemeral.
03/11 - Engineering hypothesis: recent change in adapter-proxy (PR 312) added an eager schema negotiation step to prevent mis-typed payloads; combined with cold adapter endpoints this yields additional network hops per adapter call.
03/11 - Observed that streaming + large prompt contexts amplify time spent in adapter handshakes due to blocking validation I/O on the request path.
03/12 - Verified that enabling a short-lived adapter metadata cache reduces added latency from ~95ms to ~8-12ms per adapter in staging.
03/12 - No indications of noisy neighbors or GPU contention in dedicated pool; serving-runtime timings are normal when adapter-proxy is bypassed.
03/12 - Risk: naive caching could mask schema drift; need TTL and cache invalidation on adapter deploy events.
Aisha Patel [Support, 2026-03-10]: Customer reported ~15% of requests with 504s during peak (window 18:30-19:15 UTC). Attached traces and cURL reproducer.
ScaleSky Labs (customer) [2026-03-10]: We can reproduce reliably by chaining our 'lookup' then 'enrich' adapters; sending reproducer to support@redwood.
Miguel Torres [SRE, 2026-03-11]: Reproduced in staging. Confirmed adapter-proxy performs sync introspect call (schema negotiation) per adapter invocation. Opening INT ticket to track runtime change.
Lina Cho [Eng, 2026-03-11]: PR 312 introduced an explicit sync validation to avoid silent failures; propose moving to async validation + optimistic execution with background verification.
Miguel Torres [SRE, 2026-03-12]: Deployed metadata caching patch to staging (TTL=5m). Reduced per-adapter added latency to ~10ms in tests. Planning limited prod rollout tonight during low-traffic window.
Aisha Patel [Support, 2026-03-12]: Notified customer of planned workaround and requested confirmation window for production rollout.
1) Increase client-side timeout to 180s and gateway timeout for affected routes to 90s (temporary). 2) For immediate mitigation, ask customer to reduce adapter chaining depth (combine logic into a single adapter) or use batched adapter calls. 3) For dedicated customers: enable 'adapter-metadata-cache' feature flag on their pool to short-circuit repeated schema checks.
Hotfix released: adapter-proxy v1.8.4 introduces short-lived metadata caching with TTL=5m, and a configuration flag to opt into optimistic execution (perform schema validation async post-invoke). Staged rollout: deployed to staging 2026-03-12; canary to 10% of prod traffic 2026-03-12 23:00 UTC; full prod rollout after 6h verification if no regressions. Post-deploy verification showed p95 e2e latency for multi-adapter flows dropped from ~1.9s to ~1.2s and timeout rate fell to <0.1% for the customer's traffic pattern.
1) Merge follow-up PR to add cache invalidation hooks on adapter deploys and webhooks from adapter registry (INT-8821). 2) Add integration test for multi-adapter streaming flows to catch regressions (tracking in ENG backlog). 3) Monitor customer-specific telemetry for 72h and schedule a post-incident review with ScaleSky Labs. 4) Update adapter runbook with guidance on feature flag usage and rollout checklist.

Issue summary: Customer noticed a negative hourly usage line for 2026-03-09 on their provisional invoice and a missing compensating credit that should have nullified the negative delta. Impact: VectorSearch.ai saw an unexpected -1,842 token delta (negative usage) in the hourly accumulator for their org during the 03/09 02:00-03:00 UTC window. The invoice preview did not include the expected compensating credit; accounting reports show a missing credit-line which will drive a customer support SLA escalations if not corrected before month-end.

Environment: production, dedicated capacity in us-west-2, edge collectors enabled for region-level ingestion.

Steps to reproduce / observed sequence: 1) Edge collector A in us-west-2 reported postbacks for org 67890 at 02:02, 02:07, 02:12 UTC. 2) Regional collector B replayed delayed postbacks with earlier timestamps (01:58, 02:01) due to a short SQS requeue incident. 3) Ingestor applied the late postbacks out-of-time with the hourly accumulator which first recorded higher usage then received older smaller deltas, producing a net negative hourly delta of -1,842 tokens. 4) The automated credit engine detects negative accumulator deltas and normally generates a 'compensating credit' job; in this case the job was suppressed by a heuristic that filters sub-hour late-arrival corrections to avoid double-credits. 5) Result: negative usage persisted in hourly table and did not appear as a zeroed line with a credit on the invoice preview.

Expected behavior: Late-arriving postbacks should be reconciled to the hourly accumulator and, if they produce a negative delta, the billing pipeline should either normalize the delta to zero and emit a compensating credit line or route the correction to the retroactive-credit pipeline so the customer's invoice reflects no negative usage without manual intervention.

Actual behavior: Negative delta remains and compensating credit is missing on invoice preview. Accounting export and customer-facing invoice diverge.

payload.description:
Issue summary:
BrightLedger reported sudden elevated 502/5xx responses concentrated on streaming endpoints during a customer-driven concurrency spike. Errors follow a repeating pattern aligned with horizontal pod autoscaler (HPA) scale-out events and coincident long-lived stream drains.

Impact:
- ~18% of streaming requests returned 502 over a 15-minute window for this tenant only.
- Observed transient latency spikes and client aborts causing user-visible failures in V1 of BrightLedger's chat integration.
- No billing discrepancy reported, but high customer impact (dedicated tier).

Environment:
- Tenant: BrightLedger (dedicated pool)
- Region: us-east-1 (prod)
- Routing: edge -> api-gateway (http2) -> runtime-proxy -> serving-runtime
- Models: redwood/llama-2-13b-quant (streaming), rdw/stream-embed-v1 (embedding fallback paths)

Steps to reproduce / observed pattern:
1) Customer initiated a high concurrency ramp (10x baseline) at 10:12 UTC.
2) Autoscaler triggered scale-out by adding ephemeral runtime pods between 10:13-10:15 UTC.
3) During pod termination/replace/keepalive drain windows, a subset of streaming sessions attempted hedged reconnects and kept sockets open while the runtime drained KV cache and flushing buffers.
4) At ~10:14 and 10:16 we observe short bursts of 502s originating at api-gateway with upstream code 502/503 and runtime proxy reporting "stream-drain-timeout" and "upstream-reset" in logs.

Logs / telemetry excerpts:
- api-gateway: increased 502 ratio => 18% (10:12-10:27)
- runtime-proxy: repeated 'drain timeout for active stream' and 'failed handshake during graceful-close'
- node metrics: keepalive connection count per worker rose sharply, ephemeral port usage climbed near kernel limits on some hosts
- autoscaler logs: rapid add/remove of pods due to conservative HPA cooldown configured for this dedicated pool

Initial hypothesis and investigation notes:
- Hypothesis A: Keepalive/session mismatch during concurrent drain caused connection handoffs to hit an edge case in runtime-proxy, producing upstream resets and triggering 502s at the api-gateway.
- Hypothesis B: HPA rapid churn plus long-lived streams exhausted ephemeral ports on a small subset of nodes, leading to transient handshake failures and upstream resets.
- Preliminary heap/oom checks: no OOMs on serving-runtime; CPU and GPU metrics nominal for the period.
- NVMe and network io latencies normal. Kernel ephemeral port exhaustion metrics show short-lived high ephemeral_port_used bursts on 2/12 hosts hosting this tenant.
- Reproduced locally with synthetics by creating many long-lived streaming connections and scaling pods: observed similar reconnect races and 'drain timeout' logs when autoscaler added pods while existing ones were still draining active sessions.

Workaround in place:
- Support temporarily raised tenant's autoscaler cooldown and increased keepalive window for the dedicated pool to reduce simultaneous drain+scale events. Applied at 10:40 UTC — 502 ratio dropped to ~1.2% within 5 minutes.
- Customer was advised to stagger large bursts while we investigate.

Next steps (owned by SRE/Infra):
- Short term: stabilize by tuning HPA cooldown, increase ephemeral port reservation on affected hosts, and extend keepalive drain grace for streaming workloads. (in progress)
- Medium term: add explicit handoff logic in runtime-proxy to accept re-routed streams during drains and reduce ephemeral port reuse. (engineering ticket planned)
- Long term: autoscaler improvements to detect high long-lived-stream counts and prefer warm-pool scaling instead of aggressive new pod churn.

Status update summary:
- Mitigations applied reduced customer-visible errors.
- Root cause likely a combination of keepalive/stream drain races and ephemeral port resource pressure exposed by aggressive HPA churn.

Resolution notes (draft):
- Final fix requires runtime-proxy change and autoscaler heuristics; backlog ticket created for engineering. Follow-up communication scheduled with BrightLedger for revalidation after full fix rollout.

Additional notes:
2026-03-13 12:22 UTC - Customer (BrightLedger, Sam Ortiz): We saw the errors and applied client-side retry logic, but it's causing duplicate operations. Appreciate a mitigation asap.
payload.summary: Concurrent stream drain causing repeated 502 pattern during HPA-induced capacity surge

Issue summary:
Customer reports that after rotating multiple API keys across subaccounts, usage for some requests was billed to the parent org and not the originating subaccount. This resulted in incorrect invoice line items and auto-applied credits to the wrong billing entity.

Impact:
- VeraHealth saw ~18k token usage attributed to parent org over a 6-hour window on 2026-03-09.
- Invoices and credit memos were generated for the parent account, customer-facing billing dashboard shows different totals than internal metering.
- Customer unable to reconcile month-to-date spend; potential accounting impact for month close.

Environment:
- Dedicated deployment (dedicated customer pool), prod - us-east-1
- Affected models: redwood-llm-13b (primary), openllama-3b (fallback)

Steps to reproduce (as reported by customer):
1) Rotate API keys for subaccount A and subaccount B via Console -> API Keys.
2) Reconfigure service to use new keys for microservice behind a load balancer.
3) Make 1000s of inference requests in canary then full traffic.
4) Notice billing dashboard shows a spike on parent billing org while subaccount counters do not reflect corresponding consumption.

Observed behavior:
- Token usage appears on parent org ledger and invoices; subaccount usage counters lag or remain unchanged.
- Credits issued by finance for an unrelated rate correction landed on the parent invoice.

Expected behavior:
- Rotated keys should attribute usage to the issuing subaccount. Credits/adjustments should apply to the same billing entity associated with the usage.

Initial logs/IDs:
- Customer provided request IDs: req_20260309_us_01 -> multiple 5xx and 200 traces observed.
- Billing snapshot times: 2026-03-09T02:00Z - 2026-03-09T08:00Z
- Customer console screenshot attached in ticket (not included here).
2026-03-10 09:12 - VeraHealth (Priya R.) : We rotated keys at 01:45 UTC and saw the parent invoice reflect the spike. Please help — finance is asking for corrections.

Additional notes:
2026-03-10 10:02 - Priya R. (VeraHealth): Subaccount IDs: sub_acc_4499, sub_acc_4500. Sample request IDs: req_20260309_us_01, req_20260309_us_02. Screenshot of invoice lines attached.
Hypothesis 1: Key rotation endpoint for dedicated customers temporarily creates a parent-scoped key mapping while propagating subaccount mappings to the serving-edge cache.
Query run against metering DB: SELECT sum(tokens) FROM bill_events WHERE timestamp BETWEEN '2026-03-09T02:00Z' AND '2026-03-09T08:00Z' AND org_id = 'parent_vera' -> returned ~18,243 tokens; corresponding subaccount events missing for same request_ids.
Edge cache (auth-cache) TTL observed at 5s but propagation lag in dedicated SQS queue was ~7 minutes for rotating keys on that day due to a backlog (see infra PR #1892).
Found fallback behavior: when auth lookup timed out for subaccount mapping, the request auth library fell back to parent-org credential mapping rather than rejecting. This produced misattribution in the metering pipeline.
Correlated with commit https://github.com/redwood-inference/infra/commit/4a7d1e which changed fallback in auth library to tolerate missing subaccount mappings (intended to reduce 401s).
Mitigation applied 2026-03-11 18:40 UTC: rolled back tolerant fallback in auth library on dedicated edge (hotfix) and cleared auth-cache entries for impacted keys. Backfill process launched to reassign events: a controlled job will reprocess the affected bill_events for the window 2026-03-09T02:00Z to 2026-03-09T08:00Z and rewrite org_id to correct subaccounts where request_id matches. Finance notified; a temporary credit hold placed on parent invoice to avoid double charges. Follow-ups: (1) postmortem scheduled and linked to INT-4112; (2) add unit/integration tests for key-rotation propagation; (3) increase monitoring around dedicated SQS backlog thresholds. Customer asked for expedited credit memo by 2026-03-15.

Issue summary:
During a staged rollout where ByteScale pinned a subset of customer sessions to gptx-3.7-instruct-v2:2026-03-09-rc2, some pinned sessions began receiving responses from the canary variant (gptx-3.7-instruct-v2-canary) after an autoscaler-driven instance warmup completed and the prefix KV cache populated.

Impact:
- ~12% of pinned sessions observed model mismatch over a 45-minute window (not all user requests, intermittent).
- Generates semantic diffs on downstream QA checks for ByteScale; customer-facing features degraded for targeted users.

Environment:
- Redwood Dedicated pool in us-east (prod).
- Customer pinned route: route-id bx-auth-nyc-041.
- Autoscaling triggered due to traffic spike between 10:05-10:20 UTC.

Steps to reproduce (approx):
1) Customer pins session affinity to model gptx-3.7-instruct-v2:2026-03-09-rc2.
2) Simulate traffic ramp to the pinned route to trigger autoscaler scale-up.
3) Observe serving instances initializing KV prefix cache and batching warmup.
4) After cache warmup, certain requests for pinned sessions are routed to canary variant (same family but different tag).

Observed behavior:
- Request logs show session cookie/session-id present. Routing decision at the gateway indicates the request matched the pinned policy, but downstream instance instrumentation shows model binary id differs (canary).
- Affected requests have no 5xx; response tokens valid but model outputs vary.
- Routing trace shows fallback policy executed with reason code: FALLBACK_CACHE_MISS then FALLBACK_CANARY (unexpected).

Expected behavior:
- Pinned sessions remain pinned to the specified model tag until explicit unpin or TTL expiry.
- Canary should only receive traffic as dictated by rollout weights or an explicit fallback when all pinned instances are unavailable.

Logs / traces attached (excerpt):
- gateway-trace 2026-03-10T10:12:33Z route=bx-auth-nyc-041 session=usr-7b9c: matched_pin=true routed_to_pool=dedicated-us-east pool-instance=i-0fabc123 model_tag=2026-03-09-rc2
- runtime-metrics 2026-03-10T10:12:34Z instance=i-0fabc123 kv-cache=warming state=ready selected_model=gptx-3.7-instruct-v2-canary kernel=quant-fast
- fallback-log 2026-03-10T10:12:34Z reason=FALLBACK_CACHE_MISS candidate_pool=canary weight=0.05

Workaround observed by Customer:
- Customer temporarily disabled autoscale burst for the dedicated pool while we investigated; pinned routing stabilized until capacity adjustments resumed.

Current hypothesis:
- A race between KV prefix cache population and routing table entry propagation causes the routing decision to mark the session as pinned locally, but the serving instance's model selector resolves to a compatible canary binary when its prefix cache is still incomplete.
- There may be an ordering bug where new instances register as "ready" before their local cache indicates pinned model availability, triggering fallback logic that prefers a compatible canary.

Immediate next steps (in progress):
- SRE to correlate instance readiness timestamps with cache-population events (Diego).
- Add additional routing telemetry to record the pin owner at decision time vs selected instance model tag (Maya).
- Reproduce in staging with controlled autoscale and instrumentation (assigned to eng on-call).
- Prepare a temporary server-side guard to defer "ready" state until critical prefix cache has downloaded (if confirmed).

Additional notes:
- Customer billing or quota unaffected.
- No 5xx errors observed; root cause expected to be ordering/race in warmup/registration.


Additional notes:
2026-03-12 08:35 - Customer (ByteScale): Confirmed workaround (disable burst autoscale) reduced occurrence; asking for ETA on permanent fix and any recommended rollout best practices.
Checked routing-service logs: pin lookup returned owner route consistently; however instance-level model selection can differ if instance reported model variants set includes 'canary' as compatible variant.
Checked autoscaler events: scale-up produced 3 new instances between 10:05-10:15 UTC. All reported ready before kv-cache completion for ~40% of cases.
Verified no config changes to rollout weights or pin TTL during window. Canary weight remains 0.05 for this customer.
Observed fallback_reason tag: FALLBACK_CACHE_MISS present in all affected traces.
Staging repro indicates race condition reproducible by making cache download artificially slow.
Complete readiness-guard patch review and canary rollout to internal staging (Eng).
If patch validated, schedule hotfix to Dedicated control plane during low-traffic window and notify affected customers.
Document recommended pin-safe autoscale configuration for customers (Support + Docs).
Postmortem and follow-up runbook item to add explicit telemetry for pin_owner vs model_selected to speed future triage.

payload.description:
Issue summary:

Customers observed intermittent high p99 token latency and occasional 504 / streaming timeouts when sending repeated chat prompts that reuse a short prefix. The problem started at ~2026-03-10T09:20Z for LexiChat (dedicated pool in us-east) and correlated with spikes in backend KV fetch volume and backend RPC retry errors.

Impact:
- LexiChat: multiple users reported stalled streaming responses and 504s during repeat prompts; visible in their app as long delays between the first and subsequent tokens (p99 > 5s).
- Other dedicated customers in us-east experienced elevated p99s but fewer 504s.

Environment:
- prod/us-east dedicated serving pool (shared backend kv-store)
- affected model: redwood-chat-13b for LexiChat routes

Steps to reproduce (customer-provided):
1) Create a chat session and send an initial prompt to warm a prefix (e.g., "Summarize the following chat ...").
2) Send 12–20 short follow-up prompts that reuse the same prefix/context within ~2 minutes.
3) Observe streaming token arrival: first prompt completes quickly; subsequent prompts sometimes stall for multiple seconds or return 504 after timeout.

Observed logs / telemetry:
- Serving runtime traces show a burst of KV prefix read RPCs per request when stall occurs (miss rate for prefix cache jumps from ~2% baseline to ~45% during incidents).
- kv-store TCP errors (ECONNRESET) and elevated RPC retry counters in the same window.
- Streaming sessions show prolonged backpressure inside the serving worker while waiting on KV fetch completion; worker-level queue length climbs and triggers request-level timeouts.
- No immediate correlation to model GPU exhaustion or scheduler throttling.

Investigation notes:
- Initial hypothesis: prefix cache eviction (thrashing) causing cold KV reads.
- Deeper trace: per-shard TTL values for prefix entries were inconsistent after a config push on 2026-03-09 that updated TTL algorithm thresholds. Some shards had shorter effective TTLs due to an off-by-one unit conversion between config bundles and runtime readers.
- Resulting behavior: when a shard's TTL expired slightly earlier, many simultaneous requests for the same hot prefix caused a cache refill stampede. The refill path performs a small but blocking CP-heavy KV aggregation call that can take ~30–300ms; when many such calls occur concurrently it exacerbates latencies and increases the probability of RPC retries to the kv-store, leading to backpressure and timeouts in the streaming pipeline.
- The cache-warmer background job that normally smooths refills had been disabled in the affected pool (flagged as part of an earlier experiment) which magnified the effect.
- Repro on staging: reproduced by artificially desyncing TTL between two replica groups and disabling warmers; observed same p99 spike and streaming stalls.

Temporary mitigations applied:
- Re-enabled cache-warmer flag on LexiChat's dedicated pool (rollout completed 2026-03-10T12:00Z).
- Increased per-prefix soft TTL floor on the affected shards to prevent micro-evictions (applied as emergency config 2026-03-10T12:30Z).
- Added a per-prefix in-flight request coalescing gate in front of the KV refill path to ensure only one refill RPC per prefix per short window (hotfix PR referenced below).

Customer-facing workaround provided:
- Advised LexiChat to add a lightweight client-side micro-batching of repeat prompts (delay 50–100ms) to avoid synchronously hammering the same prefix while we roll fixes.

Longer-term fixes and follow-ups:
- Root cause fix merged to ensure consistent TTL encoding across config bundles and runtime readers (PR github.com/redwood/re-runtime/pull/487).
- Permanent gating + smarter jitter for cache-warmers to avoid coordinated refills (PR github.com/redwood/re-runtime/pull/492).
- Improve observability: add a serving-runtime metric for per-prefix refill concurrency and a sentinel alert for refill storms.
- Runbook update: add steps to quickly re-enable warmers and apply TTL-floor if refill storm detected.

Resolution notes (in-flight):
- Immediate mitigations reduced incidents for LexiChat; we observed the prefix cache miss rate fall back to baseline within ~45 minutes of the emergency changes.
- SRE and runtime teams are scheduling the TTL encoding fix and the coalescing logic for early-week production deploy (target: 2026-03-14).

References/links:
- Incident Slack thread: #incidents • thread:IC-2026-03-10-kv-ttl-desync
- Staging replication steps: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/ENG/KV+TTL+Desync+Repro
- Related tickets: SUP-23918 (prefetch race), SUP-22109 (kv shard collisions)

Maya Chen (Support) - 2026-03-10: Initial report from LexiChat attached; customer reports repeated short prompts stall. Opened incident and assigned to SRE.
Oliver Patel (SRE) - 2026-03-10: Identified per-shard TTL inconsistency after config push. Re-enabled cache-warmer and applied TTL floor. Monitoring for regression.
Aria Gomez (Runtime Eng) - 2026-03-11: Confirmed desync bug reproduced in staging; preparing PR for consistent encoding. Added coalescing gate prototype (benchmarks look promising).
LexiChat Support Contact (customer) - 2026-03-11: Noted improvement after mitigation; still occasionally sees single-user stalls during peak traffic. Asked for ETA on permanent fix.
Oliver Patel (SRE) - 2026-03-12: Merged hotfix to gate refills and increased TTL floor; scheduled full rollout with canary.
Applied emergency mitigations (re-enabled warmers, enforced TTL floor, added refill coalescing). Root cause: config encoding mismatch causing per-shard TTL desync and cache-refill stampedes. Permanent fixes merged and scheduled for rollout; follow-up observability and runbook updates planned.
Deploy TTL-encoding fix across regions (PR #487) and validate with chaos tests
Deploy coalescing gate and warmers improvements (PR #492) with canary in us-east
Add refill-concurrency metric and alert to the SRE dashboard
Update KV cache runbook with mitigation steps and customer notification template
Follow up with LexiChat post-rollout and confirm SLA closure
payload.summary: Intermittent p99 latency / 504s for repeat-chat prompts due to per-shard KV TTL desync and cache refill storms

Issue summary:
Customer observes missing attachment metadata and truncated final sentence when streaming via SSE after a short burst of traffic and a subsequent auth cookie rotation. The stream returns partial content (final paragraph missing) and the separate attachment metadata envelope is not delivered.

Impact:
- Several end-user documents from AcmeSlides are missing the final bullet/attachment link in ~2-4% of streams during peak traffic windows.
- Customer reports production impact for editors embedding generated attachments (images/PDF links).

Environment:
- Dedicated account on prod (us-east-1) using Redwood Dedicated pool RG-07.
- Client: custom browser app (Chrome 112) using SSE fallback with auth cookie rotation every 30s.

Steps to reproduce (reported by customer):
1) Initiate long-form generation with attachments enabled (attachments metadata emitted as separate envelope after final chunk).
2) Generate under synthetic high QPS (burst to ~160 rps against dedicated shard).
3) After ~20–40s, rotate auth cookie (client refresh) causing SSE rebind.
4) Observe stream completes but final paragraph and attachment metadata absent.

Expected behavior:
- Stream completes with final paragraph and a distinct attachments metadata envelope.

Observed behavior:
- Stream ends with what appears to be a graceful final chunk but the terminal marker for the attachments envelope is not received. The last sentence is truncated in ~2–4% of trials.

Initial customer-supplied trace IDs:
- trace: us-east:trace/4a7d9c2b
- session_id: acme-xyz-20260310-11

Notes:
- Customer confirmed non-streaming (polling) requests for the same task return attachments and full text consistently.
- Issue seems correlated with high burst and auth rotation timing.

sample server logs (redacted):
[2026-03-10T11:02:15Z] RG-07 worker-12: stream start session=acme-xyz-20260310-11 trace=4a7d9c2b
[2026-03-10T11:02:33Z] gateway-5: auth-cookie-rotate user=acme-slides session=acme-xyz-20260310-11
[2026-03-10T11:02:33Z] gateway-5: sse-rebind attempt session=acme-xyz-20260310-11 code=200
[2026-03-10T11:02:33Z] worker-12: late-ack-window start session=acme-xyz-20260310-11
[2026-03-10T11:02:33Z] worker-12: emit-final-chunk session=acme-xyz-20260310-11 bytes=1200
[2026-03-10T11:02:33Z] worker-12: scheduled-attachments-envelope session=acme-xyz-20260310-11 state=queued
[2026-03-10T11:02:33Z] gateway-5: keepalive-ack delayed by 220ms session=acme-xyz-20260310-11
[2026-03-10T11:02:33Z] worker-12: attachments-envelope dropped (client-ack-window-expired) session=acme-xyz-20260310-11

03/10 11:30 - Reproduced locally using a dedicated dev shard with synthetic burst and auth rotation script; observed identical symptom when rotation aligned with final-chunk emission.
Hypothesis: during SSE rebind the gateway's re-ack window (late-ack or keepalive delays) can allow the final-chunk to be delivered but the subsequent attachments envelope to be considered out-of-window and dropped by the gateway-side flow control component.
Observed that worker emits final chunk and then enqueues attachments envelope. If gateway experiences a transient ack/backpressure delay, the envelope passes the gateway's per-session out-of-order/time-window heuristic and is not forwarded to client.
No evidence of payload corruption at worker level; worker logs show 'queued' then 'dropped by gateway' for attachments envelope.
Reviewing recent change: gateway flow-control heuristic PR merged 2026-02-28 (PR 1836) modified ack window policy for rebind cases. Candidate for regression.
Heap/sockets during repro show ephemeral increase in epoll backlog at gateway (~300ms spikes).
Support (2026-03-10T12:05) - Aisha: Thanks for the reproduction steps and traces. We've escalated to infra and will attempt to replicate in a staging Dedicated pool.
Customer (2026-03-10T12:22) - Jordan (AcmeSlides): We've isolated it to times when users rotate auth while the model emits the last paragraph. Happy to run a longer replay if you need more traces.
SRE (2026-03-10T14:10) - Marcus: Reproduced in staging with a 10k-run harvest. Gateway is dropping the post-final envelope when rebind occurs within 250ms window after final chunk emission. Opening INT ticket for gateway flow-control rollback test.
Eng (2026-03-11T09:03) - Priya Shah: Found the PR that tightened drop thresholds for rebind edge-cases (PR 1836). The policy change did not consider attachments-as-separate-envelope pattern. Preparing hotfix branch to relax policy when envelope-type=\"attachments\".
Support (2026-03-12T08:30) - Aisha: Customer notified that we have a mitigative rollback on staging and are scheduling a canary rollout to Dedicated pools tomorrow.
Temporary mitigation: increase client-side resilience by including attachments inline in the final chunk (client setting: attachments.inline=true) OR delay auth cookie rotation until stream completion. We provided client-side snippet to hold rotation until server 'stream_end' event received.
1) Finish hotfix branch to adjust gateway ack-window heuristic for attachment envelopes (ENG). 2) Canary deploy to one Dedicated pool and monitor stream success rate (SRE). 3) If canary passes, schedule rollout and communicate to affected customers. 4) Postmortem to review why PR 1836 didn't include this pattern (PM/ENG).
payload.summary: SSE late-ack window gap causes truncated final segment and missing attachment metadata

payload.description:
Customer reports TS SDK streaming chat intermittently freezes after ~20-30 minutes of continuous use (many conversations). They use the browser build with EventSource transport. No error; onmessage stops firing. Workaround is full page refresh.
Support (Vanessa): Collected browser version, memory profile, and a minimal repro that creates many EventSource instances.
Eng (Dylan): Found we were leaking EventSource handles when consumers stop iterating early; should close() when iterator is GC'd/aborted.
Eng (Dylan): Implemented explicit .return() handler on async iterator to close EventSource; added docs for always breaking the loop with try/finally. Released 2.4.2.
Support (Vanessa): Customer confirmed freeze no longer occurs with 2.4.2.
payload.summary: TypeScript SDK: EventSource-based streaming chat freezes in long-running sessions
