payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customer reports intermittent 504 gateway timeouts and increased tail latency for long-running chat completions. Issue appears correlated with clients sending chunked transfer requests and very large tracing/correlation headers (X-Trace-Baggage). Impact:
- ~12% of requests from NimbleDocs in us-west-2 are failing with 504 or returning after >30s delay.
- Affects production inference for redwood/gpt-7b-v2-quant used in assistant completion flows.
Environment:
- Prod, us-west-2, Hosted API (edge -> API Gateway -> NLB -> serving pool)
- API Gateway: AWS ALB in front of Nginx proxy instances (managed by infra team)
- Customer client uses chunked transfer with streaming and attaches large tracing baggage headers (~9–12 KB)
Observed behavior:
- Requests with headers >8KB frequently trigger proxy buffering in Nginx and cause the ALB to hit idle timeout waiting for backend bytes; ALB returns 504. Other cases show 502 when header truncation occurs upstream.
- When using small headers or non-chunked uploads, errors drop to baseline.
Expected behavior:
- Chunked streaming requests with reasonable tracing headers should proxy through with streaming responses and not hit the ALB idle timeout.
1) Use client that sends a chunked POST to /v1/streams with streaming body and large X-Trace-Baggage header (~10KB).
2) Initiate a completion that takes >8s of backend processing before first bytes of response are flushed.
3) Observe ALB logs for target: response_code 504 and note ELB status code vs target status code.
4) Repeat removing trace header (or reducing to <2KB) and observe success and streaming behavior.
- ALB access log extract (2026-03-12T08:33:21Z): request_processing_time=0.002 target_processing_time=31.214 elb_status_code=504 target_status_code=504
- Nginx error log: "[error] 12345#0: *987 client aborted request, client: x.x.x.x, server: api, request: \"POST /v1/streams HTTP/1.1\""
- Nginx proxy_buffering debug: wrote 8192 bytes to proxy temporary file
- Serving runtime trace: request received, processing started, first token sent at +28s (but connection already reset)
- Packet capture (attached) shows client -> ALB sends headers then small body chunks; ALB establishes backend connection but does not forward until certain conditions due to buffering config.
Hypotheses:
- Large request headers exceed proxy_buffer_size and proxy_buffers in Nginx, forcing buffering to disk; combined with chunked transfer and backend delayed flush causes ALB to perceive idle connection and close.
- ALB idle timeout (configured at 60s) interacts poorly with Nginx buffering behavior; if Nginx doesn't forward first backend bytes promptly ALB times out.
Findings:
- Reproduced in staging by sending 10KB X-Trace-Baggage header with artificial 25s delay before first backend write -> ALB returned 504 consistently.
- Reducing header to 1.5KB or tuning Nginx proxy_buffer_size to 16k eliminated buffering and restored streaming.
- No evidence of serving-runtime CPU slowness; the delay was artificial in tests, but production shows similar timing during heavy KV-cache warmups.
Next steps:
- Short-term workaround: ask customer to trim tracing baggage below 4KB and enable periodic early flush (send an initial chunk) to avoid ALB idle.
- Mid-term: infra to evaluate increasing proxy_buffer_size and adding ALB connection_draining/longer idle timeout for streaming routes; consider disable proxy_buffering for /v1/streams.
- Add defensive metric: count requests that trigger proxy temporary file writes and correlate with 5xx rate.

2026-03-12 10:03 - SRE (Marcus Patel): I reproduced in staging with large headers + delayed backend flush. Nginx proxy_buffering sent to disk after 8KB which delayed backend handshake to ALB. Suggest temporary patch: disable proxy_buffering on stream endpoint.
2026-03-12 11:45 - Customer (NimbleDocs, Elena Rossi): We can trim the header size, but SDK change is org-wide and not easy to revert. Requesting a server-side fix.
2026-03-13 08:22 - Infra (Priya Kumar): Ran a config experiment on canary Nginx to increase proxy_buffer_size to 16k for streaming route. Preliminary tests show reduced proxy temp file writes and no 504s in replicated scenario.
2026-03-14 07:55 - Support (Ava Chen): Notified customer of workaround (trim trace header to <4KB) and that infra is testing canary config. Customer accepted workaround temporarily. Keeping ticket open while canary runs.
Workaround provided: customer to trim tracing headers and add initial chunk flush. Infra to deploy canary change to increase proxy_buffer_size for streaming routes and disable proxy_buffering for /v1/streams if stable. payload.description:
Issue summary:
Quantiva Security Ops team is evaluating the SIEM-ready audit export beta (Splunk/S3) and asked for (a) the definitive category taxonomy for Audit Event Schema v2, and (b) concrete filter examples they can use to limit exported events to what their SOC needs (and minimize PII).

Customer questions (verbatim-ish from call + follow-up email):
1) “What are the exact category values, and are they stable?”
2) “Can we filter to only admin/console actions and exclude model inference traffic?”
3) “Can we do an allowlist for a few actions (e.g., workspace.user.invite, api_key.create) and denylist everything else?”
4) “Can we filter out fields like source_ip / user_agent, or at least exclude events where those are present?”
5) “Do you support filtering by actor email / resource name / prefix match?”

Impact:
Blocking customer from finalizing filter configuration for beta rollout. They need written guidance for internal change control.

Environment:
Prod (EU). Beta flag not yet enabled for tenant.

Request:
Provide category taxonomy + recommended “starter filters” with explanation of tradeoffs (compliance vs volume vs PII). If docs are missing/unclear, publish an authoritative list and examples we can share during beta.
2025-05-07 (Liam O'Rourke, Support): Created ticket from Quantiva thread. Assigning to Colin for SE-style guidance; looping Security/PM for canonical taxonomy + doc link we can share externally.
2025-05-07 (Colin O'Donnell, Solutions Engineer): Acknowledged. I can provide practical examples, but we need Marcus/Kevin to confirm the canonical category list + stability guarantees. Also need to be careful: we don’t currently support filtering that inspects presence of specific fields (e.g., “exclude events with source_ip present”).
2025-05-08 (Kevin Osei, Security Eng): Category values are intended to be stable (additive changes only during beta, no renames). Source of truth is Audit Event Schema v2 + taxonomy mapping. High-level buckets we’ve been using: auth, access, admin, data, model, billing, security, system. Some actions are also grouped under these.
PII: source_ip and user_agent are only populated for certain event types; we do not support filtering by presence of those fields today. If they need strict minimization, recommended approach is to filter out entire categories/actions that tend to include network context.
Also confirm: filtering is evaluated on event metadata (category/action + selected actor/resource fields), not on free-form payloads; this is intentional for safety and performance.
2025-05-08 (Naomi Feldman, PM): +1. We should publish a customer-shareable “Category taxonomy + example filters” section as part of beta docs/FAQ. Important clarifications:
- Filters are about what is exported, not what is retained in Redwood.
- During beta, categories/actions may expand but we’ll avoid breaking changes.
- Non-scope: regex / prefix match on arbitrary strings; no filtering on request bodies/prompt content.
I’ll track doc update separately; for now, Support can send a short list + examples with beta disclaimers.
2025-05-09 (Colin O'Donnell, Solutions Engineer): Draft response to customer (for Support to send):

1) Category taxonomy (Audit Schema v2)
We group audit events into stable categories used for filtering + SIEM mapping:
- auth: login/logout, SSO/SAML events, token/session lifecycle
- access: permission checks, membership changes (may overlap with admin depending on action)
- admin: workspace/org administration (settings, invites, role changes)
- security: key/secret lifecycle, export config changes, policy changes
- model: model access/config changes, routing policy changes (NOT per-request inference content)
- data: dataset/connectors (if applicable), artifacts metadata operations
- billing: plan/entitlement changes
- system: internal service operations relevant for compliance (rarely used in customer filters)

2) Filtering capabilities (beta)
Supported predicates:
- allowlist/denylist on category
- allowlist/denylist on action (exact match)
- resource.type + resource.id (exact match)
- actor.type (user/service) + actor.id (exact match)
- time window controls for backfill/replay

Not supported (beta):
- regex / prefix / contains matching on actor email, resource name, user_agent
- filtering on presence/absence of optional fields (e.g., source_ip)
- filtering on request payloads / prompts / generated text (prohibited)

3) Example “starter filters”
A) Admin-only (recommended first pass)
- allow categories: [admin, security, access]
- deny categories: [model, data, billing, system] (optional)

B) Narrow actions allowlist (high signal)
- allow actions: [workspace.user.invite, workspace.user.remove, workspace.role.update, api_key.create, api_key.revoke, audit_export.create, audit_export.update]
- deny categories: [system]

C) Exclude SSO chatter
- allow categories: [admin, security]
- deny categories: [auth]

Notes:
- Delivery is at-least-once; downstream should deduplicate by event_id.
- Category expansion may occur; if you need strict control, prefer an allowlist.

I’ll ask Docs to add these examples to the Splunk/S3 beta guides + FAQ so this is not tribal knowledge.
2025-05-10 (Liam O'Rourke, Support): Sent customer response using Colin’s draft + added disclaimer: “category list is authoritative for beta but may expand; no renames planned.” Customer asked one follow-up: can they export ONLY “audit_export.*” events to monitor changes to export config itself. I told them yes via action allowlist (exact match), pending confirmation from Eng on action strings.
2025-05-10 (Jordan Lee, Policy Eng): Confirmed: action filtering is exact match on action string. For export config audit events, action names are:
- audit_export.create
- audit_export.update
- audit_export.delete
- audit_export.rotate_credentials
- audit_export.test_connection
(Names are in schema v2; ensure customer understands rotate_credentials may be admin-only).
2025-05-13 (Colin O'Donnell, Solutions Engineer): Quantiva confirmed this meets their needs. They will start with allowlist of [audit_export.* actions + workspace role changes]. Reminder: they still want to minimize PII. We reiterated we can’t redact per-destination fields via filtering; redaction is applied at event emission per policy. If they need stricter controls, we should discuss category/action selection and confirm which events include IP/UA.
2025-05-14 (Liam O'Rourke, Support): Closing as Resolved. Outcome: provided taxonomy + examples; PM will incorporate into docs/FAQ. Next step is INT enablement ticket once they finalize destination settings.

payload.description:
Issue summary:
- Repeated autoscaler scale-down/up cycles on customer's private cluster coinciding with increased model shard download failures and 5xxs on long-running streaming calls.

Impact:
- Intermittent request 5xxs for live inference traffic (~3-7% of requests during window), elevated p95/p99 latency, and downstream application retries. Several jobs reported cache/KV eviction leading to higher token costs.

Environment:
- BrightBank private deployment (VPC peered to Redwood control plane), prod, us-east-1. Customer uses an on-prem egress appliance that forwards to a NAT gateway; VPC Flow Logs are enabled with sampling on the appliance by their SOC team.

Steps to reproduce (observed in customer's environment):
1) Start large concurrent batch of embeddings/generation that triggers parallel model shard downloads from S3 via presigned range requests.
2) Observe egress appliance generating sampled flow logs and connection tracking reports.
3) Around the same time, serving nodes report TCP resets, HTTP/2 RSTs and repeated short-lived connection failures.
4) Redwood autoscaler interprets multiple transient failures as pod/node underutilization and triggers scale-down, then immediate scale-up when traffic continues.

Observed behavior:
- High conntrack churn metrics on customer's appliance (conntrack deletions spike).
- Broken keepalives and ephemeral port re-use warnings in serving logs.
- Autoscaler events: scale-down triggered while healthy requests are still inflight, followed by scale-up.

Expected behavior:
- Stable conntrack state during large transfers with graceful transient failures handled by retries and no autoscale thrash.

Attachments/Artifacts:
- Flow log excerpts, conntrack metric graphs, autoscaler event timeline, serving node logs (attached in ticket).
Correlated timestamps across flow logs, conntrack counters and autoscaler events; timeline aligns within 500ms windows.
PCAP shows mid-stream FIN/RST from appliance to SGN (serving node) rather than from remote S3; suggests local conntrack deletion or NAT pool exhaustion.
conntrack table on appliance configured with aggressive timeout and periodic pruning script (cron) that runs under high connection-count conditions.
Autoscaler treats a burst of connection-level errors as low-utilization signal due to our current healthcheck sampling; debounce threshold too low for transient network-induced failures.
No evidence of S3 throttling or model artifact corruption; retries succeed after ephemeral failures.
Customer's flow-logs sampling interacts poorly with appliance heuristics (sampling triggers housekeeping that prunes flows aggressively when log export backlog grows).
Aggressive conntrack pruning on customer's egress appliance (triggered by VPC Flow Logs sampling/backpressure) caused premature deletion of in-flight NAT entries during concurrent ranged shard downloads. This led to TCP resets and short-lived failures that the autoscaler misinterpreted, producing scale-down/up cycles.
Mitigation (applied by customer):
- Disabled aggressive conntrack pruning cron job.
- Increased conntrack_max and per-flow timeouts on egress appliance.
- Temporarily reduced flow-logs sampling rate.
Result: serving-node RSTs dropped to baseline and autoscaler stopped thrashing.

Follow-up actions (persisted):
- INT-4021 created to add autoscaler debounce logic when healthchecks show transient network errors.
- Ops runbook updated (PR #2142) with recommended conntrack/timeouts and presigned range concurrency guidelines for private deployments.
- Recommend formal change window for customer's SOC to validate new config and re-enable controlled flow-log sampling.

Owner: BrightBank networking + Redwood SRE.
1) Schedule joint change window with BrightBank to validate permanent config and re-enable flow-logs at reduced sampling.
2) Deploy autoscaler debounce PR (INT-4021) to staging and run canary on private clusters.
3) Add monitoring alert for rapid conntrack deletion spikes tied to autoscaler events.
4) Follow up in 1 week to confirm stability and close ticket.

Additional notes:
2026-03-11 - BrightBank Eng (customer): Furnished tcpdump (pcap) and appliance config dump. They confirmed sampling of VPC Flow Logs enabled with 1:100 sampling ratio and an internal process that prunes conntrack aggressively.
2026-03-12 - BrightBank Eng (customer): After disabling aggressive pruning and increasing conntrack_max, immediate reduction in conntrack deletions and serving-node resets observed. Autoscaler stabilized. Customer requests recommended config and a follow-up change window for permanent fix.
2026-03-09T14:12:33Z serving-node-3 warning: HTTP2 RST_STREAM id=15 code=INTERNAL error=reset by peer
2026-03-09T14:12:33Z egress-appliance debug: conntrack_delete: 1243 entries removed in 5s window
2026-03-09T14:12:34Z autoscaler info: scale-down triggered target-replicas=4 current=6 reason=low-utilization-metric
(Customer repro is environment-specific)
1) Replay high-concurrency shard downloads simulating production traffic (range requests, >16 concurrent connections per node).
2) Enable flow-logs sampling on egress appliance to match observed SOC config.
3) Watch conntrack and ephemeral-port metrics while measuring serving-node TCP/reset counts and autoscaler triggers.

payload.description:
Issue summary: NimbusHealth reports intermittent 416 Range Not Satisfiable and partial shard corruption when Dedicated serving nodes perform parallel shard downloads during nightly rolling updates.

Impact: Several production model endpoints for the customer become degraded for short windows (10-30s) causing retries, extra token spend, and occasional application-level errors for end-users.

Environment: Private deployment (VPC peered to Redwood control plane) in us-east-1. Model shards are stored on presigned S3 URLs (us-east) fetched by serving nodes via VPCE and corporate DNS forwarder which uses DNS-over-TLS (DoT) to upstream resolver.

Observed: Control-plane logs show DNS resolution of the presigned host resolving to an older CNAME occasionally (points to an archived bucket/object snapshot). The presigned URL generated by control-plane is valid but points to an object with a different byte-length than serving nodes expect. When the node issues ranged GETs in parallel, S3 responds 416 (Range Not Satisfiable) or returns a different content-length causing a range-to-byte-offset mismatch and partial shard corruption.

Initial hypothesis: The customer's DoT resolver intermittently responds with a truncated/truncated-EDNS0 UDP reply (TC bit set) which is ignored by the forwarder; fallback to TCP is inconsistent, causing occasional return of stale/A record due to resolver cache sharding. This leads to control-plane selecting the stale host and generating a presigned URL for a different artifact version.

1) Deploy a dedicated serving group in customer VPC pegged to us-east.
2) Trigger a model rollout that causes serving nodes to download 32 parallel shard ranges per node.
3) On the customer DNS forwarder, enable verbose DNS-over-TLS logging and watch for UDP truncation/TC flags.
4) Correlate timestamps of any truncated DoT responses with control-plane DNS cache entries and the presigned URL hostnames returned.
5) Reproduce by forcing the forwarder to drop TCP fallback to observe increased rate of 416 responses.

Occasional 416 responses from S3 during parallel ranged GETs; serving node logs show Content-Length mismatch and 'shard validation failed: expected 10485760 got 524288'. Control-plane DNS cache showed a different CNAME for the presigned host for a ~20s window around the failures. Customer DoT logs show 'truncated response' events at the same timestamps.
Presigned URLs generated by control-plane resolve consistently to the correct S3 host/object. DoT resolver should gracefully fallback to TCP on EDNS0/UDP truncation and not serve stale cached CNAME/A records. Parallel ranged GETs should succeed without 416s or content-length mismatch.
[serving-node-1] 2026-03-12T02:14:22Z shard_fetch range=bytes=0-524287 status=416 content-length=524288 expected=10485760
[control-plane] 2026-03-12T02:14:22Z dns-resolve presigned.host -> cname=old-artifact-2026-02-05.s3.amazonaws.com
[dns-forwarder] 2026-03-12T02:14:21Z dot-upstream tcp-fallback=false response=TRUNCATED tc=1
[dns-forwarder] 2026-03-12T02:14:23Z dot-upstream tcp-fallback=true response=OK cname=new-artifact-2026-03-12.s3.amazonaws.com

- Support reproduced the issue in a controlled staging repro by toggling TCP fallback on the customer's forwarder; when TCP fallback disabled we saw >90% repro rate.
- Packet captures show EDNS0 UDP responses with TC set from the DoT upstream resolver. Forwarder version 1.4.2 ignored TC flag and did not retry over TCP in ~30% of cases due to a bug in DoT implementation.
- Control-plane caches DNS answers for 30s; when the forwarder returned a stale CNAME on the first UDP response, control-plane cached the stale entry briefly and generated presigned URLs pointing to wrong object versions.
- Correlated timestamps with customer's nightly batch causing heavy DNS parallelism which increased probability of UDP truncation at upstream resolver.
- SRE confirmed S3 objects exist and are intact; the mismatch is purely due to URL pointing at wrong object version.

Additional notes:
2026-03-12 - NimbusHealth (Customer): We're running vendor DNS forwarder v1.4.2 with custom caching. We'll open a ticket with vendor but need a short-term workaround.
Partial mitigation applied 2026-03-13: control-plane cache TTL reduced for presigned artifact hostnames for affected customer and presign flow updated to detect immediate content-length mismatches and re-issue presigned URLs once. Customer's vendor released DNS forwarder patch v1.4.3 that ensures TCP fallback on DoT UDP truncation. Full remediation requires customer to apply vendor patch and schedule forwarder restart.
1) Apply vendor patch v1.4.3 to DNS forwarder to ensure TCP fallback on DoT truncation.
2) If patch cannot be applied immediately: throttle parallel shard fetches to 4 concurrent ranged GETs per node and add a short jitter between presigned URL generation and first fetch.
3) Temporary control-plane TTL reduction already applied for affected customer.
- Engineering to add automatic detection: if presigned artifact fetch returns 416 or content-length mismatch, control-plane should automatically re-resolve and re-issue presigned URL and surface a diagnostic.
- Documentation: add recommended DoT configuration and a KB article for customers running DoT forwarders.
- Ops: add an alert for surges in DNS 'truncated' events from customer forwarders.
payload.summary: Intermittent DoT resolver truncation returns stale CNAME -> leads to obsolete presigned URL and 416 on shard range fetch

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customers report sudden long-tail inference latency and intermittent timeouts starting 2026-03-09 18:00 UTC. Root cause appears to be client SDKs issuing coordinated retry bursts that exhaust per-connection HTTP/2 stream limits at the API gateway, causing effectively serialized requests and elevated p95/p99 latency for affected tenants.

Impact:
- Tabletop Analytics observed 30-40% requests with latency spikes >5s and ~2% timeouts (request-level).
- A subset of other enterprise tenants show similar patterns during peak load windows.
- Errors observed primarily as 429 on gateway, then downstream stalls as clients retry synchronously.

Environment:
- Prod API gateway fronting hosted inference clusters in us-east-1.
- Customer using SDK v1.4.2 via pooled worker threads in their microservice.
- SDK config: maxConnections=6, maxStreamsPerConnection not set (defaults to HTTP/2 peer limits), retries=5, baseBackoffMs=300, exponentialBackoff=true, jitter=false.

Steps to reproduce (customer-provided):
1) Spin up 40 threads each sending concurrent short generation requests (avg 120 tokens) at steady QPS that previously worked.
2) Induce transient upstream 429 (e.g., reduce backend capacity or add artificial throttling).
3) Observe client logs: threads issue retries without jitter, aligned backoff windows.
4) Gateway reports "stream allocation" warnings and 5xx throttling spikes.

Expected behavior:
- SDK should apply randomized jitter to retry windows to avoid synchronized retry storms.
- Gateway should gracefully reject beyond stream capacity with clear guidance and metric tags.

Actual behavior:
- Retries from many client threads align and queue on limited HTTP/2 streams per TCP connection, causing effective serialization of requests and greatly increased request latency.
- Network traces show connection pool fully utilized while application-level concurrency remains waiting for an available stream.

Logs and supporting artifacts:
- Customer attached client-side excerpt: repeated identical retry timestamps across threads (attached in ticket).
- API gateway logs show repeated 429 entries from same tenant between 2026-03-09T18:02:10Z and 18:03:45Z and then a surge of downstream 503s.
- Packet captures indicate many clients reuse few TCP connections (HTTP/2 multiplexing) and attempt new streams past server-permitted limits.

Temporary mitigation suggested to customer:
- Reduce per-process worker threads to keep concurrent streams under 50 while we investigate.
- Patch SDK to enable jitter (workaround patch recommended below).

Timeline:
- 2026-03-09 18:30 UTC: Customer reported spike.
- 2026-03-09 19:00 UTC: Support confirmed identical retry timestamps in client logs; escalated to infra.
- 2026-03-10 02:10 UTC: SRE reproduced pattern in staging using load script that mimics customer's thread pool.

Findings:
- SDK default retry behavior (v1.4.2) uses deterministic exponential backoff without jitter. With multiple threads initialized at the same time and similar failure timing, retries align.
- API gateway enforces a soft limit on concurrent HTTP/2 streams per connection; when exceeded clients experience stream queuing or resets depending on upstream implementation.
- Many customer deployments reuse a small connection pool (maxConnections=6) across dozens of threads, which forces many logical requests to compete for a small number of physical streams.
- Correlated retries cause brief oversubscription of backend bearer tokens and request queues, amplifying retry storms.

Hypothesis validated by staging run: enabling randomized jitter and increasing maxConnections per process eliminated the synchronized bursts and reduced p99 by ~65% in the experiment.

Next steps planned:
- Backport SDK hotfix to 1.4.x that turns on jitter by default and documents recommended pool sizing for common thread pool sizes. PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/sdk/pull/4512 (in review).
- Update SDK docs to include guidance: (1) prefer more connections with lower per-connection streams when client will create many simultaneous goroutines/threads, (2) enable jitter, (3) cap retries for short requests.
- Add gateway metric exposing per-connection stream saturation and a per-tenant tag to help diagnostics.
- Outreach: schedule a 1:1 with Tabletop Analytics to apply temporary config recommended and plan rollout of SDK fix.

2026-03-10 00:12 - Support (Aisha Patel): Received initial report from Tabletop Analytics. Asked for client logs and config; customer provided samples and described thread pool architecture.
2026-03-10 01:45 - SRE (Marco Chen): Reproduced high p99 in staging with a 40-thread worker sim similar to customer. Observed aligned retry timestamps and gateway stream warnings. Moving to In Progress and looping in SDK team.
2026-03-10 07:20 - SDK Eng (Priya Rao): Noted SDK v1.4.2 uses deterministic exp backoff. Preparing patch to add randomized jitter and a config flag to limit retries for short requests. Opening PR #4512.
2026-03-11 11:03 - Customer (Tabletop Analytics - ops@tabletop): Applied temporary reduction of concurrent threads as requested; immediate improvement in error rate but still seeing intermittent p95 spikes during traffic bursts. Asking ETA for SDK patch.
2026-03-12 09:30 - Support (Marco Chen): SDK patch merged to main; backport PR opened for 1.4.x. Recommended customer to upgrade to patched 1.4.x release once backport completes and to temporarily increase maxConnections to 12 and enable jitter flag via runtime config.
2026-03-12 15:47 - Support (Aisha Patel): Added runbook link to ticket and scheduled follow-up call with customer on 2026-03-13 to assist with rollout and monitor metrics.
Workaround and permanent fix applied:
- Short-term: Customer increased maxConnections to 12 and limited worker threads. Observed immediate reduction in timeouts and p99 latency.
- Medium-term: Backported SDK patch to enable randomized jitter by default and added explicit guidance for connection pool sizing for thread-heavy clients (PR https://github.com/redwood-inference/sdk/pull/4512). Backport PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/sdk/pull/4520.
- Platform: Instrumentation added to gateway to surface per-connection stream saturation (rolled out to prod us-east on 2026-03-12 04:00 UTC).
- Documentation: SDK quickstart updated to include retry/jitter guidance and recommended defaults for enterprise thread pool patterns.

Follow-ups:
- Owner: Priya Rao (SDK) for tracking backport rollout and release notes.
- Owner: Marco Chen (SRE) to monitor gateway stream metrics and add alerting for per-tenant stream saturation.
- Customer follow-up call scheduled and ticket will be closed after 72h of stable metrics.
payload.summary: Client SDK retries align across threads causing HTTP/2 stream exhaustion and long-tail inference latency

Customer BrightLedger is undergoing a third-party vendor security audit in two weeks and requested: (1) a full export of account-level audit events for calendar year 2025, (2) SIEM-compatible delivery (Splunk CEF or NDJSON with timestamp + sig fields), and (3) signed evidence for control assertions (AUP acceptance confirmation, KMS usage for log encryption, and log retention/immutability statements). Impact: audit deadline is 2026-03-24. Customer requires chain-of-custody metadata and statement of retention policy.

Environment / scope:
- Customer account: brightledger-prod-001
- Region: us-east-1
- Time range: 2025-01-01 to 2025-12-31 UTC
- Record types requested: API request/response events, token usage metadata (anonymized IDs), auth events (login, token create/revoke), model-inference start/stop events, audit config changes, and SIEM-relevant metadata (user_agent, src_ip when available).

Requested output/format options (customer preference):
1) NDJSON, one event per line, ISO8601 timestamp in top-level field "@timestamp", fields: event_type, user_id (hashed), resource, region, request_id, outcome, signature_hash.
2) Splunk CEF mapping (field mappings provided by customer).

Customer also attached a security questionnaire section (they highlighted need for: KMS key usage logs, rotation cadence, HSM-backed key statements, and evidence of immutable object storage for audit logs).
Initial triage: Support verified the customer's account, confirmed they have Enterprise contract and allowed export rights. Checked audit-export service health dashboard — no service incidents in us-east in the requested window. Located a recent export job template PR in infra repo that added NDJSON output and checksum manifest (PR#8421).

Open blockers:
- Need explicit signed AUP attestation from Redwood Security lead (CS to route).
- Customer requested logs with src_ip; our PII policy redacts full IPs by default — need legal/CS approval to provide truncated/partial IPs or hashed IPs. Linked INT-4120 for policy approval.
[2026-03-10] Maya Patel (Support): Logged request and opened SUP-71902. Customer provided security questionnaire PDF and Splunk CEF field mapping. Requested timeline: complete export and deliver signed evidence by 2026-03-17 to allow auditor prep.
[2026-03-10] Customer (BrightLedger - Audit Team): Attachments: BL_audit_q1_2026.pdf. Customer confirms they need both NDJSON and CEF, but NDJSON is the minimum acceptable format.

[2026-03-12] Carlos Vega: Confirmed we can accept a salt via secure upload and will produce salted IP hashes. Preparing export job for full year; estimated export size ~120GB compressed. Will provide presigned S3 URLs in encrypted zip, with manifest and signed attestation PDF attached.

Issue summary:
Customer reports a sudden and sustained decrease in billed token usage for multiple daily jobs starting 2026-03-09 07:00 UTC after we recommended a quantized model variant. Usage in their dashboard shows ~60% lower token consumption vs expected; invoices show lower charges and the customer is requesting a credit for the under-billed period.

Impact:
- NimbleDocs batch pipelines process document summarization for paying users; lower billed usage appears to correlate with fewer tokens recorded on invoices (customer claims revenue leakage).
- Customer requests audit logs + provisional credit while investigation proceeds.

Environment:
- Dedicated pool in us-west-2, autoscaling enabled, config applied via customer reserved capacity.
- Rollout applied: model variant switch from redwood-mini-v2 -> redwood-mini-v2-quantized-8bit on 2026-03-09 06:40 UTC (canary then full for their org).

Steps to reproduce (as reported by customer):
1) Customer runs daily batch at 06:50 UTC (starts at 06:45–07:10 window).
2) Before rollout, dashboard matched expected token counts and invoiced amounts.
3) After rollout, dashboard shows reduced token counts while generation outputs are functionally equivalent per customer's QA.

Observed behaviour:
- Metering dashboard shows 55–65% less billed tokens for the affected org for all jobs that hit the quantized variant.
- Streaming vs non-streaming aggregation difference visible in internal logs for the org: streaming token metric missing KV-cache prefix accounting.

Expected behaviour:
- Token metering should reflect generated tokens across variants identically (billing-exposed tokens may differ slightly due to quantization tokenization edge cases but not this magnitude).

Request:
- Full audit of metering pipeline for the org between 2026-03-09 and 2026-03-11.
- Provisional invoice credit for underbilled delta if confirmed.
- Root cause and mitigation to prevent future occurrences.

Additional notes:
2026-03-10 10:02 - Customer (NimbleDocs Support): Provided representative request IDs and pair of job run IDs: job-nd-20260309-0648, job-nd-20260310-0647. Attached CSV with per-shard token counts.
2026-03-11 08:12 - Eng (runtime): Initial hypothesis: a prefix/KV-cache accounting change in the quantized path omitted counting cached tokens in the billing aggregation job when streaming was enabled. Investigating aggregator lambda that collapses per-chunk counts.
2026-03-12 12:30 - Support: Informed customer that engineering has identified a metering attribution gap and we are preparing a remediation plan. Requested permission to apply provisional credit while fix is rolled out.
Metering replay: compared raw model responses to billing-aggregator input; found consistent undercount for cached prefixes when streaming=true and model path quantized-8bit.
Root cause hypothesis: runtime emitted metric key 'token_count_stream' only on non-cached generation path; metric ingestion job expects 'token_count' and ignores token_count_stream for billing aggregation due to legacy rename.
Code areas touched: serving-runtime/kernels/quantized_streaming_adapter.go, telemetry/producer/metrics_emitter.go, metering/aggregator/ingest_transformer.py
Related change: infra PR github.com/redwood-inference/infra/pull/2145 merged 2026-03-09 05:50 UTC adjusted streaming hook identifiers for quantized path (introduced rename regression).
Scope: initial estimate affects dedicated orgs using quantized variants + streaming enabled; estimated impacted window 2026-03-09 06:40 UTC -> 2026-03-12 10:00 UTC (fix rollout started 2026-03-12 09:50 UTC).
Estimated undercount: aggregate replay suggests ~0.58x billed tokens vs real tokens for NimbleDocs during affected runs. Need final delta after full re-ingestion to confirm credits.
Workaround applied: Billing ops approved provisional credit equal to 80% of the preliminary delta subject to adjustment after full re-ingestion. Engineering patched metric emitter to include 'token_count' for cached streaming path and deployed hotfix to canary 2026-03-12 09:50 UTC and full rollout by 2026-03-12 13:10 UTC. Follow-ups: (1) re-ingest affected range and compute final delta; (2) issue invoice adjustment and credit note to NimbleDocs; (3) add automated regression test for metric name coverage across streaming/cached/quantized paths. Ticket remains open until re-ingestion and invoice adjustment complete.

Issue summary:
Customer reports intermittent failures for long-lived gRPC streams and control-plane authentication loops on their private deployment. Failures started after they deployed a corporate TLS termination appliance in their egress path.

Impact:
- Multiple production endpoints intermittently fail to maintain gRPC multiplexed streams (observed as stalled requests and increased grpc-go 'RST_STREAM' from client).
- Control-plane mutual-TLS authentication occasionally fails during renewals, causing agent reconnection churn.
- Customer reports increased 5xxs and degraded throughput for chat streaming features.

Environment:
- Private deployment (customer-managed VPC) in us-east-1
- Redwood agent v2.8.1, control-plane v1.21.0, serving-runtime build 2026-02-18
- Customer egress path terminator: 'AcmeReverseTLS v3' (in-line TLS terminator/proxy)

Steps to reproduce (observed by customer / SRE):
1) From within customer's subnet, initiate long-lived gRPC stream to Redwood serving node using grpcurl or a streaming client.
2) Observe intermittent stalls after 30-120s; the TCP and TLS sessions remain up but application-level messages stop.
3) Run openssl s_client and tshark concurrently to capture ClientHello/ServerHello.
4) Capture shows ALPN extension containing duplicate tokens (e.g. "h2,h2" or "http/1.1,h2") inserted by the egress terminator.

Relevant logs / snippets:
- grpc client side (snippet):
  time=2026-03-09T21:03:12Z level=warn grpc: failed to read frame: rpc error: code = Unknown desc = stream terminated
- agent auth renewals (control-plane):
  2026-03-09T21:04:07Z WARN agent connector: tls handshake failed: remote error: TLS handshake failed (alpn mismatch)
- Wireshark/TShark capture (decoded extension):
  ClientHello ALPN: [h2]
  Observed on wire after proxy: ALPN: [h2, h2]
  ServerHello picks first token -> negotiation ambiguity in some clients; others pick later token resulting in mismatched TLS state.

Initial hypotheses / investigation notes:
- The egress terminator is duplicating or rewriting the ALPN extension, which can create ambiguity for some TLS stacks (esp. grpc-go + native HTTP/2 implementations), leading to partial negotiation or incorrect stream state.
- Some gRPC implementations treat duplicate ALPN tokens as signaling different preference ordering; if the proxy rewrites order or duplicates entries, server/client may disagree on multiplexing behavior.
- mTLS renego and session resumption code paths appear brittle when ALPN tokens are modified mid-connection, causing the control-plane's cert verification layer to interpret the session inconsistent and drop auth.
- Observed behavior is intermittent and depends on exact request timing and which proxy worker handles the flow.

Attachments provided by customer: packet capture (pcap), proxy config excerpts, tcpdump, and timestamps for failing requests.

Suggested next steps (short term):
- Ask customer to enable TLS passthrough (L4) on the terminator for Redwood backend hosts as a temporary workaround.
- Request a full pcap (pcapng) including ClientHello/ServerHello from a failing transaction; SRE will confirm duplicate ALPN tokens and annotate packets.
- If passthrough is impossible, ask customer to configure the terminator to preserve original ALPN contents without duplication or to update to vendor firmware that respects ALPN.
- Add server-side defensive handling to log ALPN arrays length and token duplication on handshake for future diagnostics.

Longer-term remediation items (engineering):
- Add explicit ALPN validation to control-plane and serving-runtime that warns on unexpected duplicates and surfaces a clearer metric in Console.
- Consider rolling a minor compatibility change in the agent's TLS stack to be tolerant of duplicate ALPN entries when semantics are equivalent (after security review).

Resolution notes (provisional):
- Customer applied temporary L4 passthrough for redwood endpoints at 2026-03-11 18:40 UTC. Immediate reduction in gRPC stalls observed.
- Customer vendor (AcmeReverseTLS) acknowledged a bug in their ALPN rewriter and provided a vendor patch planned for 2026-03-15.
- Redwood SRE created a short runbook for private-deploy customers that includes ALPN verification steps and packet capture guidance.

Follow-ups:
- Engineering to review potential defensive telemetry changes (ALPN duplication metric) and estimate effort (ENG-6187).
- Customer success to schedule a postmortem call after vendor patch and full regression testing.

2026-03-10 09:18 - Support (Asha Patel): Triage created after customer escalation. Asked for pcap and configuration of terminator. Assigned to Diego.
2026-03-10 11:04 - Customer (Rajiv Menon, FinOptima): Uploaded pcap and proxy config. Noted that failures started after patching AcmeReverseTLS on 2026-03-08.
2026-03-10 13:22 - SRE (Diego Morales): Confirmed duplicate ALPN tokens observed in pcap. Recommending L4 passthrough as workaround. Adding control-plane log hooks to capture ALPN arrays.
2026-03-11 19:05 - Customer (Rajiv Menon): Enabled L4 passthrough for redwood endpoints; initial monitoring shows reduced error rate. Vendor issued a hotfix ETA 2026-03-15.
2026-03-12 07:10 - Support (Asha Patel): Added runbook draft link and scheduled follow-up with customer success on 2026-03-16. Marking ticket for monitoring until vendor patch is verified.

Customer AuroraFinTech requests a deterministic per-tenant SIEM export snapshot (one-hour window) with an allowlist of fields, a per-field redaction mapping for PII, and a packaged response to their SOC2-style security questionnaire.

Impact:
- Customer needs the artifact for an upcoming auditor review on 2026-03-20.
- Unable to validate field-level pseudonymization and non-repudiation proof without delivered snapshot and manifest.

Request details:
1) Deliver a chrono-anchored NDJSON snapshot (2026-03-01 14:00:00Z to 15:00:00Z) for tenant aurora-fintech-01 with:
   - Fields: timestamp, event_type, tenant_id (pseudonymized), user_id (hashed/pseudonymized), api_key_id (masked), request_path, response_status, model_id, token_cost
   - For user_id and tenant_id: HMAC-SHA256 pseudonymization using rotating KEK (provide KEK rotation window and key-id used).
   - Provide per-batch SHA256 manifest and signature (Ed25519) for each file delivered.
2) Provide a human-readable per-field redaction mapping table (CSV) showing original field -> transformed field -> transformation method and rationale for SOC2 evidence.
3) Answer security questionnaire items (attached) related to log integrity, key rotation, access controls, and retention.

2) Apply the customer's allowlist and pseudonymization rules and export to S3 staging bucket provided by customer (presigned URL).
3) Produce manifest + signature and attach CSV redaction map.

Issue summary: Between ~2026-02-25T01:15:00Z and 2026-02-25T03:10:00Z OrbitPay experienced repeated streaming stalls (clients received truncated or paused server-sent streams) and duplicate final completions for payment confirmation flows. Impact: merchant confirmation endpoints intermittently produced duplicate events, causing client retries and risk of double-charging. Customer escalated immediately due to live transactions failing.

Initial impact estimate: ~3% of streaming requests in the US-East population; severity high because paths touch payment confirmation flows. Incident declared P0 and escalated to on-call SRE and Support leadership.

Observed behaviour: streams cut mid-response (no terminal DONE frame), client reconnects and receives the completion again; spikes in streaming-reset metric and 5xx for streaming endpoints. Tail latency (p99) for streaming endpoints increased by ~340ms during peak.

Relevant external references: internal Slack thread #support (link: slack://channel/support/archives/p0123xxxxx), status page incident ID incident-20260225-orbitpay.

Customer communication summary: initial acknowledgment within first response SLA; bridge call with OrbitPay product and engineering teams held 2026-02-25 02:30 UTC. Regular status updates provided every 20 minutes during mitigation window.
Invoke /v1/chat/stream with OrbitPay production API key and a payment-confirmation prompt payload (~1.2k tokens) under sustained load (~250-400 rps).
Observe client receives partial stream chunks then silence (>10s) without DONE frame, client reconnects and final completion is returned again (duplicate).
Reproduce probability increases when server-side concurrent KV-cache hits and kernel-selection churn occur (observed during rolling deployment).
2026-02-25T01:16:05Z router-abc123 WARN stream-reset session_id=ox-19 reason=client-silence source=serving-runtime
2026-02-25T01:16:07Z runtime-xyx987 ERROR kvcache-mismatch shard=5 request=0x23fa4 error=cache-corruption-detected
2026-02-25T01:22:49Z router-abc123 WARN backpressure high conn_pool=us-east pool_util=0.94
2026-02-25T01:31:22Z autoscaler INFO scale-event pool=us-east-dedicated delta=+3
2026-02-25T02:05:11Z observability INFO alert firing=streaming-resets threshold=5m window=1m value=62
Triage: SRE validated elevated streaming-reset and duplicate-completion counters aligned with OrbitPay requests (prod-us-east).
Hypothesis 1: KV-cache shard drift during a kernel-selection/rolling update caused inconsistent prefix state; reconnects re-evaluated prefixes and emitted final completion twice.
Hypothesis 2: Router session affinity mismatch after a partial rollout of PR #2987 introduced a window where streaming connections lost their server-side session marker and were reattached to a new runtime which replayed final completions.
Telemetry: tracing shows same request_id served by two different runtime instances for ~45s windows; KV cache mismatch logs present in same timeframe.
Reproduction: load test with controlled kernel-selection churn reproduced truncated streams and duplicate completions locally; disabling the canary rollout removed the duplication in test cluster.
Root cause (determined): a regression in the serving runtime's backpressure and session-resume logic introduced in runtime PR #2987 that, under high concurrency and during kernel selection, could drop the stream terminal event and allow a replay path on reconnect.
Contributing factors: rolling deployment timing, higher-than-expected concurrency from OrbitPay during a scheduled marketing event, and insufficient early-warning telemetry for session-affinity drift.
2026-02-25 02:40 UTC: Scoped mitigation - increased router sticky-session timeout and applied temporary connection backpressure cap for OrbitPay token bucket.
2026-02-25 03:10 UTC: Hotfix rollout - reverted runtime PR #2987 on prod-us-east and disabled ongoing canary. Immediate reduction observed in duplicate completions and stream resets.
2026-02-25 03:45 UTC: Full rollback completed and monitoring confirmed normalization of streaming metrics by 04:00 UTC.
2026-02-25 05:00 UTC: Customer update: OrbitPay confirmed reduced failures and resumed normal operations; Offer of invoice credit and support-led replay audit initiated.
Root cause fix: revert of runtime PR #2987 and patch backported with improved session-resume checks that ensure terminal events are idempotent. Patch deployed to prod-us-east 2026-02-25 03:10 UTC; follow-up verification completed 2026-02-25 04:15 UTC.

Customer remediation: Applied proactive reconciliation support for OrbitPay transactions during the incident window; finance and CS coordinated an invoice credit for impacted transactions (agreement logged).

Preventative actions (post-incident):
- Add kernel-selection and session-affinity end-to-end tests to the CI harness.
- Introduce an alert for 'tracing:request_id_seen_on_multiple_runtimes' to catch session splits earlier.
- Tighten canary rollout gating for backpressure or session-related changes.
- Run a targeted capacity burn test ahead of known OrbitPay traffic spikes; publish guidance to customers for planned marketing events.

Follow-ups assigned and due dates: INT-4411 (engineering postmortem) assigned to SRE team, due 2026-03-04; SUP-772000 (customer compensation and audit) assigned to CS, due 2026-03-01.

Additional notes:
2026-02-26 10:00 - CS Team: OrbitPay follow-up call scheduled to review reconciliation results and credit terms. Customer requested audit log export for 01:00–04:30 UTC; exported and delivered 2026-02-26 15:00 UTC.
INT-4411: Full engineering postmortem — include timeline, root cause analysis, and regression test plan (owner: Ravi Patel, due: 2026-03-04).
SUP-772000: Customer compensation and audit package — finalize reconciliation and invoice credit (owner: Leah Martinez, due: 2026-03-01).
Implement CI tests for session-affinity and kernel-selection interactions (owner: Runtime Eng, due: 2026-03-18).
Add alert and dashboard for cross-runtime request_id detection (owner: Observability, due: 2026-03-11).
Document planned pre-warm guidance for high-traffic customers and add to onboarding checklist (owner: Solutions Engineering, due: 2026-04-01).

Issue summary:
We observed a sharp increase in 5xx responses for long-lived streaming endpoints beginning ~2026-03-14T01:10Z on the us-east production fleet serving dedicated customers. Errors are concentrated on streaming routes ("/v1/chat/stream") and manifest as rapid connection rejects (502/503) and occasional 500s from the serving-runtime process prior to connection teardown.

Impact:
- Customer Acme Analytics reported elevated error rates (~18% of streaming sessions failing) and multiple downstream user-facing timeouts in their production integration.
- Latency for successful streams increased by ~120ms p50 and p95 latency rose substantially.
- A few runtimes show worker exits (OOM-like symptoms) correlated with the same timeframe.

Environment:
- Prod (us-east), Dedicated tenant pool for Acme Analytics, tagged cluster: ded-cluster-17
- Affected models: redwood-open-v2-7b (primary), fallback open-chat-7b
- Client side: Acme updated SDK to redwood-js v2.3.1 at ~2026-03-14T00:55Z (they confirmed rollout to a small percentage of hosts internally).

Steps to reproduce (observed pattern):
1) Start a long-lived streaming session with a large initial context (>8k tokens).
2) Observe initial prefix prefetch / KV warmup activity from runtime (spikes in NVMe I/O).
3) Client-side hedged-retry (new default in SDK v2.3.1) issues aggressive parallel requests on perceived slow first-byte from the gateway.
4) Load balancer closes one of the half-open sockets (ALPN/TLS subtle downgrade observed), triggering client to reissue requests and the gateway to enqueue more accept connections.
5) Accept queue and ephemeral worker pool grow; runtime performs additional prefetches causing KV eviction thrash and occasional worker OOM / process restarts.
6) Elevated 5xx and streaming disconnects are reported.

Observed behavior:
- Grafana: spike in apigw 5xx rate at 2026-03-14T01:10Z (from baseline <0.2% to 8% over 10 minutes).
- Datadog: serving-runtime process in affected nodes shows memory growth followed by restart traces, NVMe iowait spike, and increased prefetch queue length.
- Access logs: multiple concurrent requests with identical payloads (hedged retries) from same client IP ranges.

Expected behavior:
- Long-lived streams should be stable; hedged retries should not cascade into resource thrash or trigger runtime restarts.

Temporary mitigation applied:
- At 2026-03-14T02:00Z support applied a temporary ingress circuit-breaker for Acme's tenant pool limiting concurrent hedged attempts to 1 (effectively disabling parallel hedged retries at apigw level). This reduced 5xx to ~1.1% in the next 25 minutes.
- Notified Acme to pause their internal SDK rollout to the rest of their fleet (they acknowledged at 2026-03-14T02:12Z).

Next steps / proposed remediation:
- Short term: roll apigw rate limiting rule to other dedicated clusters to throttle parallel hedged attempts for streaming routes until a safer retry policy is deployed.
- Medium term: add accept-queue backpressure signals from runtime to gateway to avoid creating excess ephemeral workers when prefetch backlog is high.
- Long term: update SDK guidance and release a server-side header to inform clients of server-side perceived first-byte latency to avoid aggressive retries.

References / links:
- Grafana: https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/apigw/streaming-5xx?from=now-1h&to=now (internal)
- Datadog process traces: https://app.datadoghq.com/processes?runtimes=ded-cluster-17
- Slack thread: #support (https://slack.redwood.ai/archives/C04SUPPORT/p1626234000000)
- Confluence runbook (draft): https://confluence.redwood.ai/runbooks/streaming-hedged-retry-incident-handling

2026-03-14T01:22Z - Aisha Banerjee (Support): Customer alerted to elevated streaming errors; collected logs and confirmed SDK rollout window. Asked for immediate sampling of request traces.
2026-03-14T01:39Z - Marcus Lee (SRE): Noted spike in NVMe iowait and prefetch queue length on nodes hosting ded-cluster-17. Opening investigation into hedged retries as possible amplification vector.
2026-03-14T01:58Z - Emily Torres (Eng - Runtime): We've seen similar KV-eviction thrash patterns when parallel prefetches are issued for the same prefix across concurrent ephemeral workers. Suspect parallel hedged retry is issuing duplicate prefetches. Attaching initial trace IDs in related_prs.
2026-03-14T02:05Z - Aisha Banerjee (Support): Applied apigw temporary rate-limit rule for Acme tenant pool (rule id: rl-8332). Customer paused SDK rollout. 5xx dropped significantly in the first 20 minutes. Customer will run tests and provide telemetry.
2026-03-14T02:30Z - Acme Analytics (Customer): Confirmed error rate relief after pausing rollout. Requesting timeline for permanent fix and whether SDK guidance will be updated.
Correlation between SDK v2.3.1 hedged-retry default and 5xx spike confirmed via request fingerprints and user-agent strings.
Accept-queue depth increased 6x during the spike; we observed ~2x ephemeral worker spin-up rate compared to baseline.
Runtime logs show repeated prefetch requests for the same prefix across concurrent workers leading to KV cache invalidation and increased memory pressure.
Hypothesis: aggressive hedged retry + transient TLS/ALPN handshake flakiness at load balancer causes duplicate inflight work that the runtime cannot coordinate, leading to resource thrash and occasional process exits.
Reproduced locally in staging by running synthetic hedged-retry client against a long-prefetch model; saw accept queue growth and sustained I/O.
[2026-03-14T01:11:05Z] apigw: conn_accept from 34.198.12.45 path=/v1/chat/stream user_agent=redwood-js/2.3.1 hedged=true
[2026-03-14T01:11:05Z] runtime: prefetch_start model=redwood-open-v2-7b prefix_tokens=8200 trace_id=tx-7a9f
[2026-03-14T01:11:12Z] runtime: nvme_iowait=78% node=ded-node-17-03 prefetch_queue=84 mem_rss=12.3GB pid=4421
[2026-03-14T01:11:20Z] runtime: worker_exit pid=4421 reason=oom_like_eviction trace_id=tx-7a9f
[2026-03-14T01:12:00Z] apigw: returning 503 to 34.198.12.45 path=/v1/chat/stream reason=upstream_unavailable
Temporary apigw rule (rl-8332) applied to throttle parallel hedged attempts for streaming routes in Acme tenant pool. Customer paused SDK rollout. Engineering to implement a server-side backpressure signal and coordinate with SDK team to change the default hedged-retry policy for streaming routes. Follow-up action: create a short-term deploy to add a server header (X-Server-FirstByte-Latency) and a roadmap ticket with runtime changes to gate prefetch concurrency by tenant and prefix. Target ETA for medium-term runtime gating: 2 weeks.
Create SDK advisory and publish recommended retry policy for streaming (assigned: Developer Experience team).
Implement runtime tenant+prefix prefetch coalescing to avoid duplicate prefetches across ephemeral workers (assigned: Runtime team).
Expose an accept-queue/backpressure metric to apigw for proactive rate limiting (assigned: Ingress team).
Add automated test in staging that simulates hedged-retry client against long-prefix workloads to catch regressions.

Issue summary:
Customer Streamlyr reports intermittent 429 throttles affecting scheduled webhook callbacks for their ingestion workers after we migrated SSL termination for the us-east edge pool. The pattern looks like short, repeatable 429 bursts at the top of scheduled windows (cron-aligned webhooks).

Impact:
- ~20% of webhook callbacks from Streamlyr in prod-us-east receive 429s for 2-10s bursts during scheduled job start windows.
- Jobs retry but the customer reported duplicate processing and longer completion times for nightly pipelines.

Environment:
- Redwood: hosted dedicated pool (Streamlyr dedicated tenant), prod-us-east edge pool, rate-limiter v3.2.1
- Customer: Streamlyr ingestion workers, scheduled cron at :00 and :15, long-lived webhook connections with short parallel fanout (10-40 concurrent connections).

Steps to reproduce (provided by customer):
1) Configure scheduled worker to issue 40 parallel callbacks to Redwood webhook route at exact minute boundary (:00)
2) Observe short 429 spikes lasting ~5s at start of window (seen in customer telemetry and our ingress logs)
3) Repeat after toggling SSL termination to origin (customer observed fewer 429s)

Observed behavior:
- Edge proxy shows refill-window offset for a subset of persistent connections after SSL termination migration (timestamps misaligned by 1s-3s across edge/ingress accounting).
- Rate-limiter token accounting appears to double-debit for around 2-3s for some connections (edge counted request, origin also counted during NAT/conn handover), causing tenant token bucket exhaustion and 429s.

- Guidance on configuration to avoid short windows of throttling without sacrificing throughput.

payload.description:
Issue summary:
BrightBank is building a long-running orchestration service that fans out a single user request to multiple Redwood function/tool calls over 30–90 seconds. They run two identical orchestrator replicas (for high availability) that can pick up work from a shared persistence layer. Customer wants a robust, language-agnostic confirmation pattern that ensures each external tool/webhook is invoked at-most-once across the cluster, even when:
- an orchestrator replica crashes mid-call,
- network partitions cause retries and reconnects, and
- SDKs (Python/TS/Go) perform automatic request retries for 5xx/429 with exponential backoff.

Impact:
Duplicate charges and duplicate downstream side-effects (e.g., payment submissions) have occurred in a staging run. Customer cannot tolerate duplicates in production. They are asking for explicit, tested guidance and sample patterns across our SDKs.

Environment:
- Redwood Dedicated (eu-west),
- API version: 2026-03-01,
- SDK versions: python 2.3.1, go 1.8.0, ts 1.5.4,
- Orchestrator: two replicas reading job state from Postgres and Redis lease,
- Webhooks target external payment processor (idempotency supported on their side), but BrightBank wants to avoid relying on downstream idempotency for compliance.

Steps to reproduce (high-level):
1) Start two identical orchestrator replicas connected to the same job queue.
2) Enqueue a task that will: (a) call Redwood function A (transform), (b) call external webhook W via a tool/function call from Redwood, (c) call Redwood function B to finalise.
3) Introduce a mid-call failure by killing the orchestrator process after step (b) request has been sent but before confirmation is recorded.
4) Restart replica so automatic retry logic triggers; observe whether webhook W receives a duplicate POST.

Observed behavior:
- In staging runs we observed duplicate webhook POSTs for ~5% of test tasks when orchestrator crashed between sending the tool call and recording a local confirmation flag. SDK automatic retries and background token refreshes made reproductions nondeterministic.

Expected behavior:
- Guidance and patterns that allow BrightBank to implement at-most-once semantics without requiring changes to Redwood server, using current SDKs and small application-side bookkeeping.

Customer asks for:
- Concrete, per-SDK sample snippets showing how to: create stable per-invocation idempotency tokens, persist confirmations atomically with local state transition, and reconcile inflight confirmations on startup.
- Advice on how to configure SDK retry policies and timeouts for long-running tool calls.
- A recommended durable confirmation store pattern (Redis vs Postgres advisory locks vs lightweight state machine) and guidance on race windows to avoid.
- Any SDK features we can expose (or short-term workarounds) to simplify this pattern.

Run two orchestrator replicas reading from same job queue and persistence
Enqueue test task that triggers a function call + external webhook tool call + finalizer
Kill replica after sending tool call but before persisting confirmation
Restart replica and allow SDK to retry; observe webhook target for duplicate POSTs
Example truncated logs from orchestrator run:
[2026-03-12T14:02:01Z] INFO Sending tool_call id=job-20260312-0001 tool=payment_post
[2026-03-12T14:02:01Z] DEBUG SDK outgoing headers: Idempotency-Key: job-20260312-0001; nonce=v1
[2026-03-12T14:02:01Z] INFO Persisting state: awaiting_confirmation
[2026-03-12T14:02:01Z] ERROR Process killed (SIGKILL) while awaiting confirmation persistence (simulated)
-- replica restarted --
[2026-03-12T14:02:30Z] INFO Orchestrator restart: reconciling inflight jobs
[2026-03-12T14:02:30Z] WARN No confirmation record for job-20260312-0001; resending tool_call
[2026-03-12T14:02:31Z] DEBUG SDK retry: attempt=1 reason=connection-reset
[2026-03-12T14:02:33Z] INFO Tool call completed (downstream payment POST accepted)

Downstream received 2 POSTs in rapid succession at 14:02:01 and 14:02:33
Provide a pattern where the orchestrator can safely distinguish between 'call sent but unconfirmed' and 'call not sent' without relying entirely on remote idempotency. Ideally persistent confirmation should be written atomically with an acknowledgement/receipt from the SDK or server.
When orchestrator crashes between send and local confirm, restart logic resends call. SDK retries and token refresh can cause duplicate HTTP attempts; without a persisted confirmation persisted during the send window there is a race that causes duplicates.
Support reproduced locally by simulating SIGKILL between send and local DB write (non-deterministic due to timing).
Observed that SDK provides automatic retries for transient errors; this is configurable but the core race (send vs local record) remains application-level.
Confirmed external payment processor had idempotency-key dedupe but BrightBank cannot rely solely on that for audit compliance.
Checked server logs: Redwood gateway returns 202 Accepted immediately for forwarded tool calls; confirmation of side-effect success comes asynchronously via webhook callback in some flows — complicates atomic persist.
Discussed options with SRE: advisory locks reduce split-brain resend but add complexity during replica crash recovery.
Support (Marcus Hale): Thanks for the clear reproduction. We're primarily able to provide application patterns — the send vs persist window is a classic at-most-once challenge when the client is responsible for confirmation. Will loop in SDK team for snippets.
BrightBank (Elena Rivera): We prefer a solution that doesn't require complicated distributed locks across services; a simple contract like 'persist confirmation after tool-call response' would be ideal but the problem is the call can be acknowledged by Redwood before downstream side-effect completes.
SDK Engineer (Jin Park): Suggestion: use a two-phase confirmation pattern: (1) create a durable 'intent' record with stable idempotency_token before sending; (2) send tool call with that idempotency_token and mark state to 'sent'; (3) on receipt of confirmation from webhook or server-side callback, atomically transition intent -> done. On restart, agent checks intent state to decide whether to resend. We'll provide code examples for Python/Go/TS.
SRE (Olivia Chen): For redis vs postgres: Postgres transactional upserts with unique constraint on idempotency_token give atomicity guarantees. Redis can work with SETNX but needs TTL management and careful crash recovery handling.
Support (Marcus Hale): ETA for sample snippets: 2 business days. Linking to internal runbook and small reference PR.
BrightBank (Elena Rivera): Thanks — also would like recommended retry policy values (max attempts, backoff base) for long-call webhooks that may take tens of seconds.
Suggested pattern (high level):
1) Before sending, persist an 'intent' record in Postgres with columns (idempotency_token, job_id, state=INTENT, created_at). Ensure unique constraint on idempotency_token.
2) Send tool/function call using the same idempotency_token in headers/payload.
3) After receiving immediate 2xx/202 from Redwood SDK/server, update intent state to SENT within a transaction that records the outbound attempt metadata (attempt_id, timestamp). If the process crashes before this write, the intent remains INTENT and restart logic will attempt send.
4) Rely on an external confirmation webhook or server acknowledgement to transition state to DONE atomically. If confirmation doesn't arrive within timeout, orchestrator retries but consults intent state to avoid blind duplication.

Per-SDK notes:
- Python: use context manager + transactional upsert. Show example with asyncpg + aiohttp wrapper around SDK call.
- Go: use sql.Tx for upsert then send; on restart, a reconciler loop scans for INTENT older than N seconds and replays with rate limiting.
- TS: recommended local durable queue (e.g., PG-backed) + AbortController to gracefully cancel if duplicate detected.

Retry policy guidance:
- For long-running webhooks (30–90s): set SDK max_attempts=3, initial_backoff=1s, max_backoff=10s, and overall operation timeout ~120s. Use jitter to avoid thundering herd.

Short-term SDK improvements suggested:
- Expose send-and-wait-for-server-confirm helper that atomically returns a send-receipt ID that can be persisted.

Workarounds provided to customer: detailed per-SDK code snippets (draft) and a recommended Postgres intent pattern; SRE suggested Postgres unique constraints as the simplest durable store. Customer acknowledged and will pilot the pattern in staging. SDK team will evaluate adding a 'durable-send' helper in next sprint. No server changes required at this time.
payload.summary: Guidance: safe confirmation patterns for concurrent orchestrators and long-running function/tool calls across Python/Go/TS SDKs

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customer NovaCart reports recurring p95/p99 latency spikes and intermittent 504s for inference requests from a small subset of clients on their Dedicated pool. Spikes started 2026-03-09 23:00 UTC and have reoccurred in short bursts. Impact: production inference errors (504) and request timeouts affecting storefront personalization and cart-loading flows.

Impact:
- ~2-5% request error rate during bursts for affected tenants (customer-reported).
- Elevated p95/p99 from normal ~120ms to 800-1800ms during bursts.
- Some client connections abort streaming responses (observed aborted_count increase).

Environment:
- Dedicated capacity (single-tenant pool) in us-west-2.
- Runtime: redwood-serving v3.7.1.
- Batch/coalescing config: coalescing_window_ms = dynamic (adaptive), continuous-batcher enabled, per-connection KV cache warmup enabled.

Steps to reproduce (customer):
1) Send steady low-QPS requests from ~150 concurrent clients pinned to dedicated pool.
2) Observe occasional clustered p99 spikes and 504s that last 30-120s.
3) Spikes correlate with small bursts of 10-30 requests followed by timeouts on subsequent requests.

Observed behavior:
- Scheduler logs show irregular micro-batch sizes (1-3 then 20-30) within short windows.
- Coalescing window appears to occasionally expand by an order of magnitude causing head-of-line delays for earlier-arriving requests.
- TCP connection resets and aborted streams observed in proxy metrics during spike windows.

Expected behavior:
- Stable coalescing window with micro-batches sized predictably by QPS and configured thresholds, avoiding long tail latency.
- Streaming responses should not abort due to scheduler-induced queue delays.

Workaround (customer):
- Customer temporarily throttled client concurrency and reduced per-connection keepalive, which reduced spike frequency but is not viable long-term.


Initial observations:
- Correlated spikes with bursts of small micro-batches and then a large coalesced batch; pattern suggests timer/skew in coalescing window algorithm rather than model execution time.
- No obvious GPU saturation during windows (GPU utilization stable).
- Host CPU on serving nodes shows short-lived scheduler thread CPU spikes coincident with tail latency.
- Autoscaler events for the pool were quiet; no scaling activities at incident times.

Hypotheses tested so far:
1) Adaptive coalescing window mis-estimation under low-QPS fanout causing occasional over-waiting for batch members -> reproduced locally by toggling adaptive thresholds.
2) KV cache warmup stalls causing head-of-line delays for first few requests in a batch -> partial correlation but not root cause.
3) Network-level queuing (proxy) introducing jitter -> proxy metrics show concurrent resets but timing aligns after coalescing delays.

Data collected/links:
- Serving runtime flamegraphs during spike: s3://redwood-logs/serving/flame/2026-03-09_spike/
- Scheduler metrics dashboard: https://console.redwood.io/d/serving/scheduler?from=2026-03-09T22:55&to=2026-03-09T23:10
- Proxy aborted/connection metrics: https://console.redwood.io/d/proxy/aborts?pool=dedicated-novacart

Immediate mitigation attempted by Eng:
- Rolled a configuration change in a canary pod to force a hard cap on coalescing_window_ms = 8ms (was adaptive). Canary reduced tail latency in 1 pod.
- Increased per-tenant queue isolation to prevent cross-tenant micro-batch merging.

Next steps planned:
- Reproduce with a deterministic load generator that mimics NovaCart traffic shape (short bursts + low sustained QPS).
- Instrument coalescing timer events with high-resolution timestamps and add sampling traces in runtime (PR linked).
- Patch candidate to fix adaptive window backoff and land in runtime PR #4123.
- Add alerting for coalescing_window_stddev per pool.

Mitigation in progress: Eng enabled a temporary config to cap coalescing_window_ms at 8ms on dedicated pool for NovaCart which reduced p99 spikes and 504s during verification window. Customer applied temporary client-side concurrency limit as a stopgap.

Planned permanent fix:
- Merge runtime PR #4123 which stabilizes adaptive coalescing algorithm and adds defensive guardrails when thread scheduling jitter detected.
- Deploy enhanced telemetry (coalescing timer histograms) and an alert rule for stddev spikes.
- Follow-up: run extended soak in dedicated canary and roll to remaining nodes if stable.

Post-incident actions:
- Update batch coalescing runbook with troubleshooting checklist and quick toggles.
- Create a support playbook entry for coalescing_window caps for dedicated customers experiencing similar symptoms.

2026-03-10 09:15 - Customer (NovaCart SRE - Jordan Lee): Provided request IDs and observed time window. Noted that issue started after a client rollout on 2026-03-09 morning.
2026-03-10 10:05 - Eng (Liam O'Connor): Confirmed reproducible pattern in staging with synthetic workload. Attempted canary change to cap coalescing_window_ms.
2026-03-11 02:30 - SRE (Ravi Singh): Observed decreased 504s after canary; collecting longer-term metrics overnight.
2026-03-12 11:00 - Support (Maya Patel): Updated customer with temporary mitigations and ETA for runtime patch. Customer requested postmortem once fix is in prod.
2026-03-12 16:25 - Eng (Sofia Martinez): Linked runtime PR #4123 and requested QA validation schedule.

Issue summary:
Customer NovusChat reports repeated mid-day throughput lulls in their Dedicated pool (prod-us-west) that coincide with a high volume of short-lived streaming requests. The symptom is a sudden P99 and P95 throughput drop for routes pinned to dedicated capacity, lasting 3–8 minutes before partial recovery.

Impact:
- Intermittent user-facing latency increases for NovusChat users (p99 latency up 4x).
- Background request queueing observed; some requests hit client-side timeouts.
- Business impact: degraded chat responsiveness during peak local hours.

Environment:
- Dedicated cluster: prod-us-west (reserved capacity for NovusChat).
- Customer tier: Dedicated/enterprise.
- Models: redwood/open-compat-13b and openlm/turbo-8k.
- Autoscaler config: min_replicas=4, max_replicas=24, scale_window=120s, short_stream_heuristic_enabled=true.

Steps to reproduce (customer-provided):
1) Send 300-600 concurrent short streaming sessions (1–3s per stream, frequent restarts) distributed across 20 tenants on the same dedicated pool.
2) Observe scheduler allocations and autoscaler decisions via the Console.
3) See throughput collapse on pinned routes and elevated request queueing.

Observed metrics & artifacts:
- GPU allocation saturation spikes on a subset of hosts (nvlink contention + high PCIe IO).
- Autoscaler shows delayed pod spin-up: mean time-to-ready increased from 35s -> 90s during events.
- KV cache eviction rate increases sharply; cache miss ratio climbs from 2% -> 18% within event window.
- Per-tenant slot utilization shows uneven hot-spotting: a small number of tenants consume many small slots, causing slot fragmentation.
- Monitoring screenshots and Prometheus query outputs attached in PR above.

Issue summary: During a staged canary rollout for redwood-llama-7b-v2 in us-east, ~3% of BrightHealth AI traffic was unexpectedly routed to the secondary variant (quantized fallback) despite an explicit tenant model pin. Impact: customer reported mixed responses in production affecting 12 tenant sessions (chat flows). Symptoms observed at 09:21 UTC: inconsistent model outputs from the same session-id, and increased token latency (p50 -> p95).

High-level hypothesis: orchestrator snapshot application lag caused a partial control-plane commit where edge proxies had stale routing snapshots while the central router had already committed a canary weight update. This led to a redispatch path where requests that should have be pinned were re-evaluated by a reconciliation step and dispatched to the secondary variant.

Requested outcome: restore full pin coherence for affected tenant(s), identify root cause in orchestration snapshot propagation, and add guardrails to avoid redispatch during staged commits.
1) Trigger a staged canary rollout for redwood-llama-7b-v2 with a small traffic weight (5%) in us-east.
2) Simulate a brief orchestrator leader failover during commit window (kill leader API process for ~6s) to force snapshot re-application.
3) Send long-lived chat sessions with pinned model headers for a tenant and observe routing headers and model ids returned by edge proxies.
4) Notice that some requests with the pinned header are returned from the quantized variant and show different model-id in response metadata.
5) Reproduce using traffic mirror to replay customer traffic against staging cluster to validate behavior.
2026-03-12T09:21:12Z edge-proxy[edge-01] INFO route-resolve tenant=brighthealth session=f2a9 model_pin=redwood-llama-7b-v2 -> route_v2 commit_idx=4123
2026-03-12T09:21:13Z orchestrator[leader] WARN snapshot-apply duration=6.4s commit_idx=4124
2026-03-12T09:21:13Z router[ctrlplane] INFO reconciliation tenant=brighthealth resolved_variant=redwood-llama-7b-v2-quant reason=redispatch requeue=true
2026-03-12T09:21:14Z serving-runtime[worker-7] ERROR request=3f9a token-latency-ms=432 model=redwood-llama-7b-v2-quant mismatch_pin=true
Ava Chen (Support) [2026-03-12T10:03Z]: Customer observed mixed responses starting at ~09:20 UTC. Collecting session IDs and example payloads. Escalating to SRE and Orchestratorowners.
SRE (Priya Nair) [2026-03-12T10:17Z]: Early look suggests snapshot apply on orchestrator leader took 6.4s due to compaction GC. Edge nodes pulled older snapshot concurrently causing transient routing divergence. Repro steps drafted.
Mateo Alvarez (Assigned) [2026-03-12T11:02Z]: Running replay of affected session traffic on staging mirrored cluster to reproduce redispatch. Noted that reconciliation path triggers when commit_idx mismatch and session lease renewal coincides with healthprobe backoff.
BrightHealth (EMMA) [2026-03-12T11:26Z]: We saw 12 sessions with garbled summaries; thanks for the quick response. We need fix and mitigation — customer requests rollback to previous canary immediately if pin coherence cannot be guaranteed.
Priya Nair (SRE) [2026-03-12T13:40Z]: Mitigation performed: paused the canary rollout, increased snapshot propagate timeout, and added a temporary edge-side check to prefer control-plane pin header until snapshot commit confirmed. Monitoring for re-occurrence.
Mateo Alvarez (Engineering) [2026-03-13T08:12Z]: Patch landed to add a short-term reconciliation guard (PR linked). Next: follow-up to remove guard after we verify orchestration GC tuning and snapshot apply times are within threshold.
Hypothesis A: orchestrator snapshot apply delay due to compaction/GC caused inconsistent commit_idx across control-plane replicas.
Hypothesis B: edge-proxy healthprobe backoff triggered reconnection which invoked a reconciliation flow that re-evaluates model pin and allowed fallback routing when commit metadata was ambiguous.
Finding: reproduce on staging by forcing leader restart during commit window; replication delay & edge pull of older snapshot leads to short window where reconciliation code path marks session lease expired and redispatches to fallback variant.
Metric evidence: commit_idx skew observed between leader and follower at time-of-incident (leader=4124, follower=4119). Snapshot pull latencies increased from baseline ~120ms to ~6.2s during event.
Risk note: behavior affects long-lived sessions that renew leases during commit windows; short-lived requests less likely to hit redispatch flow.
Next steps: tune snapshot compaction GC to avoid long pause, add commit-confirm handshake to edge to avoid reconciling pins while snapshot mismatch present, add unit/integration tests for staged canary under leader failover.
Mitigation applied on 2026-03-12: paused canary rollout and deployed edge guard to prefer explicit model_pin header until commit confirmation. Engineering landed a short-term patch to prevent reconciliation-triggered redispatch during commit_idx skew (PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/2891). Longer-term fix: orchestration GC tuning + commit-confirm handshake. Customer BrightHealth AI notified and will monitor for 72 hours; ticket will be closed after 72h with no regression.
Runbook references: OPS/Canary-orchestrator (linked). Follow-up action: schedule postmortem and create a task to add integration test coverage for orchestrator failover during staged canary (INT ticket to be created).
