payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customer reports streaming chat responses that gradually slow token delivery over ~10-40s and then stop without an explicit 5xx. The client eventually sees a socket close after its internal timeout. Impact: several long-running conversational sessions with >8k token histories for the customer experience silent pauses then disconnects.

Impact:
- Intermittent but reproducible for this customer on prod us-east-1 for long-context chats.
- Affects users on both web client and SDK behind corporate VPNs.

Environment:
- Redwood hosted API (prod) region us-east-1
- Customer uses enterprise tenant with Dedicated routing to shared pool
- Observed with redwood-1-large and gptx-like-13b model variants
1) Start a streaming chat session via SSE with a long prompt/history (>8k tokens).
2) Continue a back-and-forth for several messages until total context length >~10k tokens.
3) Observe generated tokens streaming for ~20-60s; notice per-token latency creeping up from ~80ms to >600ms.
4) After a period of slow delivery there is a ~5-15s silence and then client-level socket close due to application timeout.
5) Repeat; issue occurs more frequently when autoscaling or worker compaction runs concurrently.
Selected logs/timestamps pulled from customer session (redacted):
- 2026-03-09T14:12:31.109Z request-id=req-9f8a stream-start tokens_sent=0
- 2026-03-09T14:12:39.194Z req-9f8a token-100 latency=85ms
- 2026-03-09T14:12:55.721Z req-9f8a token-600 latency=430ms
- 2026-03-09T14:13:05.102Z req-9f8a token-900 latency=780ms
- 2026-03-09T14:13:12.980Z WARN serving-runtime: starting kv-cache-checkpoint compaction (worker=wn-34)
- 2026-03-09T14:13:17.311Z req-9f8a stream-silence duration=12s client-timeout=15s
- 2026-03-09T14:13:29.872Z connection-closed by client socket-err=ECONNRESET
Diagnostic links:
- Console trace: https://console.redwood.ai/trace/req-9f8a
- Logs: https://logs.redwood.ai/query?request=req-9f8a
Initial hypothesis: progressive token latency tied to a backend compaction/checkpoint operation causing worker-side write stalls and backpressure that reduces token emission bandwidth. Edge proxy (Fastly/our edge) was also observed to coalesce small chunked responses occasionally resulting in silence from the client perspective.

What we checked:
- Worker traces show KV checkpoint tasks trigger within the same worker's scheduling window causing CPU spikes and brief network stall.
- No 5xx from runtime; stream remained open but tokens were not flushed to socket.
- Edge proxy config set to buffer up to 32KB per chunk for TLS reassembly; combined with client TCP delayed-ACKs on some VPNs, small incremental token chunks were coalesced into longer pauses.
- Autoscaler events correlated: new worker warmup and concurrent checkpoint compaction increased host load.

Hypotheses refined:
1) KV checkpoint compaction triggered synchronous writes/locks that inhibited async token flushes on affected workers.
2) Edge buffering + small chunk emission pattern created client-observable silence during those spikes.

Evidence supporting root cause:
- Correlation between 'starting kv-cache-checkpoint compaction' log and immediate latency spike to >500ms and then silence.
- Reproduced in a controlled staging run by forcing checkpoint compaction while streaming a long conversation; observed same token deceleration then silence.

Additional notes:
2026-03-11 13:40 - LearnWave Labs (customer): Can confirm after our test with the patch we saw steady token flow and no disconnect for sessions that previously failed. Thanks!
Fixes applied: 1) Runtime: checkpoint compaction reworked to use non-blocking cooperative coroutines and yield to token-flushing path. 2) Runtime: periodic keepalive SSE comment tokens emitted if no tokens for >4s. 3) Edge: disabled aggressive chunk coalescing for streaming endpoints. Rollout: staged to prod us-east-1 on 2026-03-12 08:00 UTC, monitored for 48 hours. Customer validated with long-context sessions; no reproductions afterward.
Follow-ups:
- Add a metric 'streaming-pauses-during-checkpoint' and alert if rate > 1/hr per tenant.
- Backfill mitigation to ensure dedicated pools run checkpointing on separate worker threads by default.
- Postmortem: https://confluence.redwood.ai/postmortems/SUP-846215-postmortem
If customer reports recurrence: request affected request-id and timestamps; check worker for concurrent 'kv-cache-checkpoint' log entries; verify edge coalescing flags and runtime keepalive emission. Escalate to Runtime Eng and Edge team if pattern matches.
payload.summary: Progressive stream deceleration followed by silent cutoff during KV checkpointing on long chats

Issue summary:
Customer dashboards and alerting for DataSynth Labs show gaps and a complete silence for a specific metric series (route.client_version) after we deployed a schema deprecation that removed the legacy 'client_version' ingestion field. The pipeline mapping replaced the field with 'client_release' but older aggregated rollups still expect the old field name which causes the alerting eval to drop the series.

Impact:
- Multiple critical alerting rules for the customer did not fire between 2026-02-27 23:40 and 2026-02-28 02:10 UTC.
- Dashboard panels that pivot on client_version show empty series.
- Billing/usage rollups are intact but per-route breakout metrics appear suppressed.

Environment:
- prod ingestion (us-east), org: DataSynth Labs, project: analytics-ingest-prod
- Console version: 2026.02.1

Observed behavior:
- Per-route time-series that previously had series keyed by client_version now show no series at all.
- Alerts that reference the client_version dimension evaluate to zero-series and end up in a suppressed state (no notifications).

Expected behavior:
- Console should either translate legacy client_version->client_release or generate a series with a fallback label so alerts continue to evaluate.

Customer notes:
- Customer deployed a new SDK which drops client_version and emits client_release on 2026-02-27. They expected a transition window.

1) Ingest an event set where the 'client_version' field is removed and a new 'client_release' field is present.
2) Wait for aggregation rollup window (hourly).
3) Query console dashboard panel that groups by 'client_version' dimension for last 4 hours.
4) Inspect alert rule that uses group-by client_version to evaluate for spikes.

Expected: panel shows fallback series or a migration mapping; alert evaluates on groups containing 'unknown' or 'legacy'.
Actual: panel returns empty series and alert eval returns no groups.
Observed: silent series, missing alerts. Expected: graceful fallback/mapping or explicit migration path documented.
Note: this is different from an ingest-loss (events exist) — raw events with client_release are present in logs; the console aggregation layer is dropping the series because of schema mismatch during rollup compacting.
- On initial triage (Aisha) found raw events in the fast-path Kafka topic containing client_release payloads for DataSynth between 2026-02-27T23:30 and 2026-02-28T01:00 UTC.
- Aggregation job logs show a schema mismatch warning: 'missing field client_version, group-by key skipped'.
- Rollup path uses persisted rollup-schema v1 which enumerates 'client_version' as a grouping key; migration to accept 'client_release' was staged but not enabled in prod.
- Quick check of the aggregation mapping PR (platform PR #2248) shows migration steps but the feature flag 'rollup-schema-v2' is still false in prod in us-east.
- Support forwarded to infra with request to toggle flag for DataSynth org to enable v2 mapping while we coordinate with customer for a controlled cutover.
- SRE (Marco) ran a targeted backfill test on staging: enabling rollup-schema-v2 restored series with fallback labels 'migrated:client_release' and alerts evaluated correctly.
- Kafka topic lsr-ingest-us-east partition 12 offsets 1243220-1245400 contain events with 'client_release' present.
- Aggregator logs (aggregator-7-logs): 2026-02-28T00:05:12 WARN Missing group key: client_version for org=DataSynth id=3421
- PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/platform/pull/2248 (schema migration and mapping).
- Dashboard snapshot: https://app.redwood.io/dash/snapshot/DS-20260228-001 (internal link, expires 7 days).
- Slack thread: #support (link: https://redwood.slack.com/archives/C02SUPPORT/p1677510000000)

2) As long-term: schedule a migration window and run a backfill for rollups covering 2026-02-27T20:00 to 2026-02-28T03:00 UTC.
3) Customer should continue to send client_release and we will keep mapping enabled for 48 hours before flipping off legacy acceptance.
In progress: SRE prepared a safe rollout that gates on a per-org flag. No permanent fix deployed globally without change window. Backfill job queued and monitoring will validate alert evals. Planned next update 2026-03-01 after backfill completes.
- SRE to enable feature flag for DataSynth (Marco) and confirm alerting behavior (ETA 2026-03-01 02:00 UTC).
- Run backfill for affected rollup buckets (Ops runbook: RB-0423).
- Update migration docs in Confluence and add explicit console migration guide for schema-deprecation events.

Action links: https://github.com/redwood-inference/platform/pull/2248, https://redwood.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/OPS/pages/alerts+and+ingest+schema+changes

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customer reports truncated streaming responses and missing attachments when the client does an immediate reconnect (retry loop) after a short network hiccup. The client uses our SSE endpoint and sends an idempotency token; attachments (binary frames encoded as base64 envelope in our stream) are occasionally interleaved into the JSON delta stream on resume and the final JSON array is truncated by the client-side parser.

Impact:
- Intermittent data loss for long streaming responses that include attachments (images/embeds).
- Customer-facing feature (real-time document generation) produces corrupted outputs ~2-3x/day for KiteAI in us-east.

Environment:
- Production (prod us-east).
- KiteAI using our JS SDK v1.14.0 behind a corporate proxy + CloudFront in front of our API.
- Client opens SSE, gets ~30s of stream, experiences a short transient (TCP reset), reconnects immediately with same session id and idempotency token.

Steps to reproduce (as supplied by customer and reproduced in staging):
1) Start a long generation that returns alternating JSON delta events and base64-encoded attachment envelopes.
2) Mid-stream, induce a connection drop (tcpkill or simulate client network flap).
3) Client performs immediate reconnect (no randomized backoff) and sends same session id + idempotency token.
4) Observe resumed stream: some binary attachment frames appear between JSON array items. Client parser throws a JSON parse error or drops trailing array items.

Observed behavior:
- Resumed stream frequently includes small binary envelope chunks that are not correctly labeled as attachments (boundary markers dropped) and appear before the closing JSON array. The client-side parser sees a malformed JSON stream and stops processing; the final chunk(s) are not applied.
- Server logs show two resume attempts for the same session within 100ms and duplicated system messages. Upstream (CloudFront) reports TLS record coalescing and HTTP/2 connection reuse for the same origin.

Expected behavior:
- Resume should preserve event boundaries: JSON deltas first, then attachment envelopes properly wrapped. Duplicate system messages should be deduplicated; final JSON array must not be truncated.

Relevant logs / excerpts (sanitized):
- client: "SSE reconnect session=ks_72ef idempotency=tok-19 start=2026-03-09T22:15:03.123Z"
- gateway: "incoming resume: session=ks_72ef from=203.0.113.45 via CloudFront-ELB"
- serving-runtime: "write: delta[...]{JSON chunk} | write: attach[base64 chunk fragment] | write: delta[...]{JSON chunk}"
- client error: "SyntaxError: Unexpected token B in JSON at position 13412"

Notes about uniqueness of this failure:
- The issue appears when three conditions align: immediate client reconnect (no jitter), upstream connection coalescing (CloudFront/edge merges small TLS records), and mixed-surface responses (JSON delta + binary-style attachment envelopes). We have many SSE truncation reports; this one differs because the binary attachment fragment is being injected into the JSON stream (boundary marker lost), not simply missing final bytes.

Additional notes:
2026-03-11 09:33 - SRE Team (Automated): Added Grafana dashboard link: https://grafana.redwood.internal/d/streams/resume-errors (error spike at 2026-03-09T22:15UTC).
2026-03-12 08:55 - Customer (KiteAI): Applying client-side workaround for now (enable reconnectBackoff setting). Will monitor and report if any residual errors after server patch rollouts.
Hypothesis: Upstream (CloudFront / corporate proxy) is combining small write fragments into fewer TLS records during the reconnect handshake. Our streaming stack relies on explicit boundary markers between JSON events and attachment envelopes; when record coalescing occurs, the gateway path occasionally drops or merges the boundary token ("--ATTACH--") into the previous TLS fragment. On immediate reconnects, the server replay/resume code path does a fast-forward of buffered fragments which exposes the merged binary fragment in the middle of a JSON array.
What we tested:
- Reproduced in staging with CloudFront-like proxy and no reconnect jitter.
- Confirmed that toggling client-side reconnectBackoff to 200-500ms reduces failure rate.
- Canary gateway change that disables record coalescing of small writes reduced, but didn't eliminate failures when CloudFront is present.
- Confirmed that inserting an explicit escape wrapper around attachments prevents the client parser from failing (temporary mitigation).
Next investigation steps:
- Add server-side resume reassembly guard to enforce event-boundary checks before emitting to clients.
- Add deduplication on duplicate system messages for same session id within 500ms window.
- Engage CDN/CloudFront engineers to check configuration that might cause TLS record coalescing for small writes.
Workaround provided to customer: enable reconnectBackoff (200-500ms) in SDK and set stream.attachBoundaryStrict=true to preserve envelope markers.
Fix work completed / rollout notes:
- PR #2891 (serving-runtime): added boundary-preservation layer in api-gateway that marks attachment envelopes and refuses coalescing rewrite. Canary rolled in staging 2026-03-11.
- PR #2903 (serving-runtime): added resume sanity-check to drop out-of-order binary envelopes and log a resume-mismatch (deployed to us-east on 2026-03-12 11:00 UTC).
- Added short client-side dedupe window to ignore duplicate system messages for same session (SDK v1.14.1 issued to KiteAI).
Status: Patch rolled to prod us-east; monitoring metrics. Customer reports no new truncation incidents in 24h after rollout and client-side workaround.
Follow-ups / action items:
- Engineering: add unit/integration test for mixed JSON+attachment resume scenarios (owner: serving-runtime team).
- Ops: monitor Grafana panel for replay errors and resume-mismatch logs for next 7 days (owner: SRE).
- Product: document reconnectBackoff recommendation in SDK quickstart for streaming heavy-attachment workloads.
This ticket documents a corner-case resume race where upstream TLS/HTTP/2 coalescing combined with immediate client reconnects can surface binary envelope fragments inside JSON streams. Root cause is a combination of network path behavior + resume reassembly assumptions. Mitigations applied across SDK, gateway, and serving runtime. Recommend including reconnect jitter as a best practice in SDK defaults for streaming endpoints.

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customer observed that long responses which embed an inline image (markdown ![alt](data:image/png;base64,....)) are truncated when an SSE disconnect occurs mid-stream. On resume the client receives a stream that ends with a broken markdown image tag (missing closing parenthesis) and the rendered output in the customer's app shows a broken image.

Impact:
- Affects a subset of long streaming responses that include inline base64 image blobs or very long image URLs.
- Customer-visible content corruption: broken markdown image tags and missing embedded images.
- Occurred intermittently for customer sessions behind a corporate proxy during a short transient network blip; customer reports this happened ~3 times in the last 24h across multiple users.

Environment:
- Redwood hosted prod, us-east region, public API.
- Customer: Polaris Assist (self_serve).
- Model: open-chat-7B-v1.

Steps to reproduce (attempted):
1) Create a prompt that instructs the model to include a small inline image as a base64 data URI in markdown (example: ![diagram](data:image/png;base64,<long-payload>)).
2) Start SSE streaming request with client that supports resume tokens.
3) During large payload emission (image blob chunking), force a short disconnect at the edge (we tested by dropping the connection on a local reverse proxy).
4) Reconnect/resume session.
5) Observe the final assembled stream on the client — in failing cases the closing ")" of the image markdown and the tail of the base64 payload are missing.

Observed logs / traces:
- Edge proxy (customer side) shows TCP FIN and immediate reconnect within ~2s.
- Load balancer logs: upstream returned 200 OK then connection close; no 5xx.
- Serving runtime trace (request-id: req-20260312-9a2b): last sent SSE chunk ends inside a base64 data URI; resume window applied new chunks but server-side resume framing omitted last buffer flush.
- Client console shows lastChunk: "!...data:image/png;base64,AAA..." (truncated), parsing error when client attempts to decode.

Hypothesis / initial analysis:
- When SSE chunk boundaries fall inside a large token (base64 blob), our streaming resume logic sometimes fails to emit a final flush of the pending buffer for that token after a reconnect race.
- The edge-proxy or client reconnect sequence may result in the server replaying only up to the last committed resume offset; the final partial buffer that contains the closing parenthesis is lost if it was not checkpointed.
- The issue surfaces more often with very large inline payloads (image data URIs) than with plain text because chunk boundaries split binary-like base64 runs and the parser on the client expects a complete markdown token.

Workarounds / mitigation attempted:
- Advised customer to avoid embedding base64 images inline in streaming responses; instead provide a signed URL returned after generation. Customer confirmed this avoids the corruption.
- We tested forcing more frequent resume checkpoints on a staging runtime and saw reduced occurrence, but this is not yet safe for prod without load testing.

Next steps / action items:
- Engineering (Serving-Runtime) to add unit test that simulates streaming a large base64 data URI with mid-stream disconnect and validate final flush semantics. (Assigned: @ethan-zhao)
- Short-term: add conservative flush on resume boundary in the edge proxy path to ensure any pending chunk is emitted to the client (hotfix candidate).
- Product: update streaming resume guidance in docs to warn about large inline media in streaming responses.
- Support: notify Polaris Assist of recommended pattern (use upload-to-storage + link) and provide ETA for fix.

Resolution notes (in progress):
- Reproducer built in staging that consistently hits the condition when chunk size set to 8KB and the base64 payload spans multiple chunks.
- Patch candidate under review that ensures resume triggers buffer flush-of-current-token; still measuring performance impact.

Additional notes:
2026-03-12 21:30 - Support (Priya): Shared mitigations—recommend switch to URL-based images; customer accepted temporary workaround and requested timeline for fix.
2026-03-13 15:45 - Customer (Polaris Assist): Confirmed workaround works for now, asked whether there will be any change to API contract or additional latency. Support replied that API contract remains the same; change is internal to streaming reliability.
Fix candidate created and under perf testing; customer advised workaround (use external image URL). Will update when PR lands and rollout begins.

payload.description:
Issue summary: BrightWrite reports a sudden, sustained increase in 5xx responses (502/503) from their dedicated tenant beginning ~2026-03-13 09:22 UTC. The spike coincides with a large embedding upload + mixed small chat traffic. Impact: Customer-facing upload jobs failing, automated ingestion retries, and visible latency spikes for downstream queries. Environment: Dedicated tenant on prod - us-east with reserved capacity. Steps to reproduce: 1) Upload a large embeddings batch (~120k vectors) via embeddings endpoint 2) Simultaneously send small chat requests to the same tenant 3) Observe API gateway 502/503 errors and runtime restarts/logged backoffs. Recent changes: no customer model pin changes; autoscaler applied a scheduler backoff tweak earlier today. Logs: see attached SRE logs and proxy traces referenced in investigation notes.
Correlation: 09:22 UTC aligns with scheduler config sweep (auto-rollout) that changed backoff reset window for prewarm probes in us-east cluster.
api-gateway metrics: accept_queue_length increased 8x; 502s originate from upstream connection resets and proxy workers reporting 'watchdog: worker exited (signal 9)'.
"nvml logs" show transient GPU memory fragmentation and a sequence of quick model prefetches from embeddings shard coordinator which coincided with high ephemeral-proxy CPU. (see github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/issue/987)
ephemeral-proxy behavior: high concurrency embedding uploads created many concurrent long-lived connections; scheduler backoff oscillation attempted rapid prewarm then backed off, resulting in connection pile-up and thundering-herd of ephemeral proxies trying to recover.
Heap/oom: Several runtime proxy workers exhibited OOM-like exit traces; container restarts caused upstream to drop connections, amplifying 502s at API gateway.
Hypothesis A: Scheduler backoff parameter change reduced the damping on prewarm probes, amplifying concurrent prefetches and causing ephemeral-proxy CPU/memory thrash leading to worker exits.
Hypothesis B: Embedding bulk upload pattern interacts poorly with streaming chat traffic (mix of long-lived and short-lived connections) causing accept-queue head-of-line blocking and upstream resets.
Short-term mitigations executed: tenant ingress rate cap applied; advised customer to reduce embedding upload concurrency; cleared prefetched KV cache entries for affected shard to reduce spike load.
Monitoring: set alerting on accept_queue growth (>200) and proxy worker exit rate (>5/min).

Additional notes:
2026-03-13 10:05 - SRE on-call (Ava Chen): Observed scheduler backoff oscillation when prewarm requests slowed; ephemeral-proxy thread count spiked then crashed with OOM-suspected logs. Collecting heap and nvml stats.
2026-03-13 11:15 - Support (Priya Patel): Sent workaround to customer: throttle embedding upload concurrency to 8 and retry with exponential backoff. Customer confirmed temporary throughput improvement.
2026-03-14 08:30 - SRE (Ava Chen): Pushed hotfix to scheduler that reduces aggressive backoff resets and staggers prewarm probes. Monitoring for 24h.
2026-03-14 12:00 - Customer (BrightWrite): Reporting reduced error rate; embedding upload completed after lowering concurrency. Requesting postmortem and permanent mitigation.
Workaround: Ingress rate cap and temporary concurrency limit on BrightWrite's tenant allowed embedding uploads to complete with <2% 5xx within 3 hours.
Fix deployed: Scheduler hotfix rolled back the aggressive backoff reset and added jitter to prewarm probe start times (deployed 2026-03-14 08:30 UTC).
Runtime changes: Runtime team updated ephemeral-proxy to better cap memory per-worker and added soft-limits to avoid hard OOM exits (deployed canary 2026-03-14 09:50 UTC).
Follow-ups: 1) Create a dedicated runbook for mixed-traffic (embedding + streaming) tenant patterns. 2) Increase accept_queue default sizing for dedicated pools and revisit autoscaler thresholds. 3) Add test that simulates large embedding upload + chat traffic for regression testing. Owner: Diego Morales / Runtime team. Deadline: 2026-03-21.
Customer communication: Support committed to a postmortem and permanent mitigations; customer acknowledged and requested timeline for runbook and autoscale improvements.

payload.description:
Issue summary
- Northstar Healthcare pilot (Private/VPC) is seeing intermittent DNS failures from workloads running in private subnets.
- Symptoms: sporadic resolution failures for both internal cluster names (kubernetes.default, CoreDNS upstream lookups) and AWS service domains (ecr.*, sts.*, logs.*) when VPC endpoints/private DNS are in play.
- Impact: cluster add-ons and Redwood Private installer pods occasionally fail to pull images / reach AWS APIs; some core services restart due to readiness/liveness probe failures when upstream lookups time out.

Impact
- Customer reports that failures appear in bursts (5–20 minutes), then self-resolve.
- During bursts:
  - Image pulls intermittently fail (i/o timeout, no such host)
  - Installer preflight checks sometimes fail on STS/CloudWatch Logs reachability
  - Internal service discovery occasionally fails (CoreDNS returns SERVFAIL)
- Customer severity: blocking stable POC validation; they cannot proceed to the next security gate until stability is demonstrated.

Customer environment
- AWS: us-east-1
- EKS: private subnets across 3 AZs
- VPC endpoints enabled for ECR (api + dkr), S3 gateway endpoint, STS, CloudWatch Logs (and others per our alpha guidance)
- No direct internet egress from private subnets (very strict egress controls); NAT exists but is not used for most traffic per customer policy
- Customer DNS: Route 53 Resolver is default; they also have conditional forwarding requirements to on-prem (future state), but for this pilot they stated no active Resolver rules should be affecting *.amazonaws.com

Timeline (customer-reported)
- 2025-07-07: first observed during cluster bootstrap
- 2025-07-08: escalated to Redwood during pilot standup; ticket opened
- 2025-07-10: joint troubleshooting session; captured CoreDNS + node-level logs
- 2025-07-15: mitigation validated; customer reports no further bursts for 72 hours

Steps to reproduce (as observed)
1) Deploy standard cluster add-ons and Redwood Private prerequisites in private subnets.
2) Run parallel image pulls from ECR and make repeated DNS queries from pods (dig/nslookup) to:
   - kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local
   - ecr.api.<region>.amazonaws.com
   - sts.<region>.amazonaws.com
3) During burst windows, observe intermittent failures:
   - nslookup returns SERVFAIL or times out
   - curl to AWS APIs fails with "Could not resolve host" from within pods

What we checked (investigation notes)
- Confirmed issue reproduces from multiple nodes across AZs; not isolated to a single node.
- CoreDNS:
  - Metrics showed spikes in upstream query latency and timeouts during burst windows.
  - CoreDNS logs included intermittent: "plugin/errors: 2 <domain> A: read udp <pod_ip>:<port>-><upstream_dns>:53: i/o timeout".
- Node / VPC resolver path:
  - Verified /etc/resolv.conf inside pods points to the cluster DNS service (typical).
  - Verified CoreDNS upstream configured to use VPC resolver.
  - Confirmed VPC attributes enableDnsSupport/enableDnsHostnames are enabled (customer had enableDnsHostnames = false initially; they flipped it during troubleshooting per Victor’s request).
- Network controls:
  - Customer NACLs are restrictive; one NACL rule set did not include ephemeral return traffic for UDP 53 flows from private subnets to the VPC resolver.
  - Observed that when NACLs were loosened temporarily, DNS bursts reduced significantly.
- VPC endpoints + private DNS:
  - Noticed customer enabled private DNS on endpoints but had not enabled the corresponding endpoint security group ingress from all node/pod CIDRs (they were allowing from node SG only).
  - During some bursts, DNS would resolve to private endpoint IPs, but follow-on connections would fail, creating the impression of DNS instability.
- EKS add-on posture:
  - CoreDNS was deployed at default replica count for their cluster size; during transient network issues, CoreDNS became a bottleneck.

Working hypothesis
- Primary driver: restrictive NACL + missing ephemeral return rules leading to intermittent UDP/53 failures between CoreDNS and the VPC resolver, exacerbated under bursty lookup load.
- Secondary contributors:
  - Endpoint SG allow-listing was too narrow (node SG only), which broke traffic from some pods (depending on CNI/pod IP allocation).
  - CoreDNS capacity too low and retry behavior amplified the issue during partial packet loss.

Evidence / logs (sanitized)
- CoreDNS (during burst):
  - "plugin/errors: 2 ecr.api.us-east-1.amazonaws.com. A: read udp 10.20.34.18:38842->10.10.0.2:53: i/o timeout"
  - "SERVFAIL" responses for external names, intermittent
- Pod-level:
  - "nslookup: can't resolve 'sts.us-east-1.amazonaws.com'"
  - "docker login" / image pull errors: "lookup <ecr-host> on <cluster-dns-ip>:53: no such host"

Mitigation applied (confirmed with customer)
1) NACL updates (customer-owned)
- Ensure NACL rules allow:
  - Outbound UDP/TCP 53 from node/pod CIDRs to VPC resolver (VPC+2 address) within VPC
  - Return traffic for ephemeral ports (1024-65535) for UDP/TCP response flows
- Customer implemented recommended ephemeral allow rules scoped to VPC CIDR.

2) VPC resolver / VPC attributes sanity
- Confirmed VPC attributes:
  - enableDnsSupport = true
  - enableDnsHostnames = true
- Confirm DHCP option set uses AmazonProvidedDNS (no custom DNS servers for pilot).

3) Endpoint SG allow-listing
- Updated endpoint security groups to allow inbound from:
  - EKS node security group
  - Pod CIDR(s) if pods have routable VPC IPs (AWS VPC CNI), or relevant source CIDRs
- This addressed the “DNS resolves but connect fails” confusion for AWS API endpoints.

4) CoreDNS resiliency
- Increased CoreDNS replicas (customer changed from 2 -> 4) and enabled anti-affinity across AZs.
- Added request/limits to prevent CPU starvation.

Additional notes:
Outcome
- Customer reports no further DNS bursts for 72 hours after changes.
- Redwood installer preflight checks and image pulls stabilized.
Redwood follow-ups (docs/modules)
- Action: update alpha Terraform module docs to make DNS/NACL expectations explicit.
  - Add a dedicated “DNS prerequisites and failure modes” section (CoreDNS upstream to VPC resolver, NACL ephemeral returns, VPC attributes).
  - Clarify that VPC endpoints SGs must allow pod CIDRs when using AWS VPC CNI.
  - Add a troubleshooting checklist: verify enableDnsSupport/enableDnsHostnames, DHCP options, NACL ephemeral rules, and endpoint SG sources.
- Proposed doc updates to land in: vpc-terraform-modules alpha deployment guide + reference architecture.
  - Owner: Kira Thompson to draft; review by Victor Alvarez + Sean Gallagher.
Notes / cross-links
- Related support pattern: missing endpoints and private DNS misconfig causing ECR failures (see SUP-28411).
- Installer improvements: PR-19110 adds stronger preflight messaging for endpoint/DNS prerequisites; not a full fix for NACL issues but reduces time-to-diagnosis.
Comments (condensed)
- 2025-07-08 (Colin O'Donnell, Support): "Customer reports intermittent DNS in private subnets; installer pods failing 'no such host' for STS/ECR. Requesting Infra/Networking eyes."
- 2025-07-08 (Victor Alvarez, Infra): "Please confirm VPC enableDnsHostnames and NACL rules for ephemeral return; seen this manifest as intermittent UDP 53 loss. Also check endpoint SG sources include pod CIDR if using VPC CNI."
- 2025-07-10 (Sean Gallagher, SRE): "CoreDNS metrics show upstream timeouts; recommend scaling CoreDNS and checking for CPU throttling. If packet loss persists, consider NodeLocal DNSCache."
- 2025-07-11 (Colin O'Donnell, Support): "Customer found NACL missing ephemeral return. Applied scoped allow rules + endpoint SG widened to pod CIDR. Monitoring."
- 2025-07-15 (Colin O'Donnell, Support): "72h stable post-change; customer unblocked. Closing as resolved; capturing module doc follow-ups."
Customer updated NACL to allow UDP/TCP 53 + ephemeral return within VPC CIDR, enabled VPC DNS hostnames, corrected VPC endpoint SG sources to include pod CIDRs, and scaled CoreDNS. DNS instability stopped; installer/image pulls stabilized. Redwood will update alpha module documentation to call out DNS/NACL prerequisites and endpoint SG source guidance.
Docs: add DNS/NACL prerequisites + endpoint SG source guidance to alpha deployment guide and reference architecture (owners: Kira Thompson + Victor Alvarez).
Terraform docs: add a troubleshooting section for intermittent DNS and a validation checklist for pilot readiness.
Support playbook: link SUP-28458 pattern under Private/VPC troubleshooting alongside SUP-28411.
payload.summary: Private VPC pilot: intermittent DNS resolution in private subnets impacting core services (EKS/CoreDNS, VPC endpoints)

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customer (MailFold) reported a rapid increase in 5xx responses and long tail streaming disconnects starting ~2026-03-13T18:12Z. API gateway returned a mix of 502/503 and short-lived 504s. Upstream serving runtimes for the customer's dedicated pool experienced worker restarts and OOM-like exits during the same window.

Impact:
- MailFold observed ~15-20% of requests failing with 5xx across chat and embedding routes for ~12 minutes.
- Streaming sessions dropped mid-stream; clients hit reconnect/retry loops.
- Customer-facing SLA alerts triggered; customer reported production user impact (message delivery failures).

Environment:
- prod (us-east-1), MailFold dedicated GPU pool (dedicated customer tenant).
- Rate-limiter backed by Redis (cluster B) and a local in-memory fallback.
- Autoscaler: dynamic HPA with prewarm policy.

Steps to reproduce (observed pattern):
1) Simulated Redis master failover occurred (external DB event at 18:10Z).
2) Rate-limiter client fell back to local token-bucket with conservative defaults.
3) Sudden retry/replay behavior from upstream client SDKs (hedged retries + prefetch churn) produced a high burst of simultaneous requests.
4) Serving-runtime prefetch workers attempted aggressive KV prefetch and hit kvcache lock contention; several runtime workers were OOM-killed by the watchdog.
5) API gateway started returning 502/503 as upstreams became unhealthy.

Observations / Logs / Metrics:
- apigw: 502/503 rate peaked at 18:14Z -> 19:00Z; customer 5xx% ~18.7% (per-route).
- runtime: repeated SIGABRT and watchdog restarts; kernel logs show out-of-memory events on several GPUs (nvml messages correlated).
- rate-limiter: Redis client reported connection timeouts and 'READONLY' during failover; fallback tokens depleted rapidly.
- kvcache: lock_wait_count increased 20x; eviction_rate spiked.

Relevant log excerpts (sanitized):
[2026-03-13T18:12:30Z] rate-limiter: redis timeout: IOERR: Connection reset by peer
[2026-03-13T18:13:02Z] serving-runtime[worker-14]: kvcache: lock_wait=132ms key=tenant-123/prefetch
[2026-03-13T18:13:47Z] runtime[worker-7]: OOM killer invoked: process_exit_status=137 nvml: memory allocation failed
[2026-03-13T18:14:02Z] apigw: upstream unhealthy for route /v1/chat/stream tenant=mailfold status=502

Current status:
- Incident declared and triaged by Support. SRE investigating runtime crashes and Redis failover correlation. Mitigation steps applied (see comments).

2026-03-13T18:16Z - Support (Liam O'Neill): Received initial alert from MailFold; gathered request IDs and sample call IDs. Opened ticket and escalated to SRE channel #sre-support.
2026-03-13T18:22Z - SRE (Riley Chen): Observed Redis failover at 18:10Z in cluster B; client SDK fell back to in-memory limiter which quickly drained. KVCACHE lock contention correlated with prefetch-heavy queries. Marking as likely backpressure + rate-limiter fallback amplification.
2026-03-13T18:30Z - Engineering (Priya Desai): Deployed temporary throttle on MailFold tenant at the API ingress to shed excess retries and disabled aggressive prefetch for that tenant. Noted immediate drop in 502s from 18:31Z. Preparing a more stable config roll-forward.
2026-03-13T19:05Z - Customer (MailFold support): Customer confirms request success rate improving after throttling; still seeing sporadic dropped streaming frames. Asked for timeline and permanent fix plan.
2026-03-13T20:10Z - SRE (Riley Chen): Applied longer-term mitigation: increased local token-bucket refill and added short circuit-breaker for prefetch queue depth. Monitoring for recurrence.
Primary hypothesis: Redis master failover triggered a degraded rate-limiter fallback that did not backoff retries aggressively, producing a burst that amplified prefetch and KV lock contention in serving-runtime.
Supporting evidence: timestamps of Redis failover, rate-limiter timeouts, kvcache lock_wait spikes and runtime OOM logs all align within a 2-3 minute window before 5xx surge.
Contributing factors: MailFold's SDK hedged retry pattern (2 fast retries), combined chat + embedding mixed workload created high memory pressure on dedicated pool. Autoscaler prewarm thresholds didn't spin up capacity quickly enough under lock contention.
Dashboards referenced: https://monitoring.redwood.com/d/infra/apigw-5xx?orgId=1&from=now-2h&to=now, kvcache heatmap at https://monitoring.redwood.com/d/runtime/kvcache-locks.
Related: suspected link to existing issues SUP-421999 (tls-session-cache corruption) and SUP-271999 (handoff thundering); these provide context on upstream health amplifiers.
Temporary mitigations validated: ingress shedding + disabling aggressive prefetch for tenant reduced 5xx rate to <1% within ~3 minutes of change.
Mitigation applied (temporary) on 2026-03-13: ingress-level request-shedding for MailFold and disabled tenant-specific aggressive prefetch. Increased in-memory token-bucket capacity and introduced a short-duration circuit-breaker for prefetch queue depth. Engineering to roll a safer fallback path when Redis is unavailable (ensure exponential backoff + jitter and avoid immediate replay).

Planned follow-ups:
- Patch rate-limiter client to use exponential backoff + jitter on Redis failover (PR referenced). Owner: Priya Desai. ETA: 2026-03-20.
- Autoscaler tuning: reduce HPA cooldown for dedicated pools and add a reactive prewarm when kvcache lock_wait spikes. Owner: Platform SRE. ETA: 2026-03-22.
- Post-incident review and runbook update to include graceful Redis-failover behavior and tenant-specific prefetch caps. Postmortem scheduled on 2026-03-16.
- Customer-facing summary to be sent to MailFold by CS with timeline and follow-ups.
payload.summary: Sudden 5xx surge: apigw returning 502/503 and upstream runtime OOMs during Redis rate-limiter failover

payload.description:
Issue summary: Customer reports a ~24-hour provisional overcharge after a production incident where requests for their dedicated pool were transparently routed to hosted fallback. Impact: NimbleRetail observed a ~12% increase in token charges on their provisional invoice; charges split across multiple invoice lines (reserved and hosted) and one negative correction line appeared later. Environment: Dedicated pool (dedicated-nyc-3), prod-us-east serving a high-throughput streaming chat workload. Steps to reproduce: 1) Simulate dedicated pool saturation by throttling two GPUs via load-shedding test harness in staging. 2) Trigger fallback policy to hosted pool (policy: latency-first). 3) Use the streaming chat API for a 2k token conversation and then finalize with non-stream aggregation. Observed behavior: Metering pipeline recorded both streaming deltas and the final non-stream token aggregation for the same request; when fallback occurred mid-stream, tokens were attributed to hosted at host rate and also kept under reserved accounting, creating double-counting. Expected behavior: Token usage should be de-duplicated and attributed to the final serving target; fallback should not cause parallel metering records. Logs & artifacts: referenced logs at s3://redwood-logs/support/SUP-550321/ and kube pod logs in #support Slack thread. Customer-provided timestamps and preliminary invoice excerpts attached in ticket attachments.
2026-03-10 | Aisha Patel (Support): Opened ticket after customer provided provisional invoice and sample request IDs. Asked for request IDs and timestamps for three sample sessions.

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customer NovaChat on a Dedicated cluster in eu-west reported sustained end-to-end latency regression (p50 from ~80ms to 600-1200ms) and intermittent request timeouts (504) for production inference routes. The degradation started during a traffic spike on 2026-03-12 morning and persisted despite autoscaler activity.

Impact:
- Multiple production customer-facing endpoints experienced increased latency and ~3-7% of requests returned 504 over a 90-minute window.
- Affected ~4 apps belonging to NovaChat; business impact: degraded user experience and some failed chat sessions.
- Not a global outage; limited to the customer's dedicated pool in eu-west.

Timeline (local times):
- 2026-03-12 08:14 UTC: NovaChat alerts to Support via portal; included sample request IDs and stack traces.
- 2026-03-12 08:20 UTC: Support triaged, escalated to SRE and Serving-Infra.
- 2026-03-12 08:35 UTC: Observability shows sustained GPU utilisation hotspots on 3 hosts, prolonged kernel scheduling delays, and elevated queue length in request-router.
- 2026-03-12 09:05 UTC: Temporary mitigation applied: pinning affected routes to standby pool and increasing min replicas for NovaChat; partial improvement.
- 2026-03-12 10:10 UTC: Root-cause hypothesis updated after heap of traces: single tenant job producing very large continuous batches and a model variant triggering inefficient CUDA kernels causing slot contention.

Steps to reproduce (dev environment):
1) Deploy a dedicated pool with similar instance types and driver versions (NVIDIA 545.xx).
2) Send a steady stream of concurrent requests with artificially large prompt sizes to one tenant route emulating NovaChat peak traffic (200 concurrent requests, ~1.2k token prompts).
3) Observe serve-runtime metrics: kernel latency, queue length, and host-level GPU metrics.

Observed logs / snippets:
- router: "request-queue-time=512ms route=novachat-chat pool=eu-west-dedicated queue-length=46"
- serving-runtime: "kv-cache-lock-wait=120ms host=gw-eu-03 gid=0"
- node-exporter: "nvidia_gpu_utilization=98%, smi_pending_cmds=27, pcie_rx_errors=0"
- nginx: "upstream timed out (110: Connection timed out) while reading response header from upstream"

Hypotheses considered:
- Noisy tenant: single customer workload producing oversized batches and long-running kernels blocking GPU scheduling.
- Mis-sized autoscaler: autoscaler configured with conservative scale-up window and low max burst capacity, causing reactive scaling lag.
- GPU driver/kernel mismatch on 3 hosts (gw-eu-01/02/03) leading to degraded kernel preemption behaviour.

Immediate actions taken:
- Support pinned NovaChat routes to a separate standby pool at 09:05 UTC to relieve contention (workaround).
- Increased min-replicas for NovaChat in Dedicated config to keep buffer capacity during spikes.
- Temporarily disabled cross-tenant packing on affected hosts.
- Added a short-term autoscaler override (faster scale-up) for the customer's pool.

Desired state / success criteria:
- Latencies return to baseline (p50 < 150ms) and request success rate > 99.7% for NovaChat routes.
- No recurring contention events across the dedicated fleet.

Notes on customer communication:
- Customer notified at 09:20 UTC of mitigation and advised of ongoing investigation.
- Follow-up scheduled for 2026-03-13 11:00 UTC with NovaChat account team to review permanent mitigations.

2026-03-12 08:22 - Support (Aisha Patel): Acknowledged. Escalating to SRE and Serving-Infra. Customer provided request IDs: r-4637, r-4640, r-4652.
2026-03-12 08:41 - SRE (Daniel Kim): Observed 3 hosts with >95% GPU util and long kernel wait times. Queue length correlated with host hotspots. Spinning up investigation on driver versions and kernel preemption settings.
2026-03-12 09:07 - Support (Aisha Patel): Pinned routes to standby pool; customer reports partial recovery.

Additional notes:
2026-03-12 11:02 - Customer (NovaChat - ops@novachat.com): Thanks for the quick mitigation, would like a permanent fix. Please share follow-up actions and ETA.
Metric correlation: high request-queue-time aligns with spikes in smi_pending_cmds and GPU SM utilization >95% on 3 hosts (gw-eu-01/02/03).
Serving runtime trace showed long-running kernel launches for specific op kernels in model 'mistral-7b-v2' when input sequence length >1k tokens; these runs block subsequent CUDA streams on same device.
Autoscaler logs show scale-up actions triggered at 08:38 UTC but new nodes became healthy only at ~08:55 UTC due to conservative readiness checks and slow instance boot times.
Temporary mitigation: pinned NovaChat routes to standby pool and increased min-replicas; result: throughput restored to acceptable levels, error rate fell to <0.3%.
Medium-term fixes planned before 2026-03-20: (1) driver upgrade to NVIDIA 555.xx across eu-west fleet to improve preemption, (2) autoscaler policy change to reduce scale-up cooldown and increase burst capacity, (3) implement per-tenant soft-QoS limits to cap maximum aggregate batch size/throughput.
A follow-up INT ticket (INT-409) opened to schedule the driver rollout and change autoscaler policy. Serving-Infra PR drafted: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/4382.
Action items assigned to infra and platform: Daniel Kim (infra) and Lina Ortega (serving-infra).
INT-409: Schedule staged driver upgrade for eu-west hosts and validate preemption improvements (owner: Daniel Kim).
ENG-OPS-1721: Implement per-tenant batching guards and cross-tenant packing limits with throttling policy (owner: Lina Ortega).
OPS-245: Review and adjust autoscaler readiness checks and reduce scale-up window for dedicated pools (owner: Maya Singh).
Customer follow-up: 2026-03-13 11:00 UTC review call with NovaChat to confirm permanent mitigation plan (owner: Aisha Patel).

payload.description:
Issue summary:
During a staged canary (weight 8%) for model open-code-7b-v1, several tenant sessions for AuroraDocs observed sudden routing to a degraded legacy variant for 30–90s. Behavior correlated with a shadow-reconciliation job that runs asynchronously after the primary canary commit.

Impact:
- Customer-facing: ~12 tenants at AuroraDocs intermittently received degraded-model outputs causing downstream formatting regressions.
- Latency: affected streams experienced ~2x tail latency for the window.
- Billing: increased debug fallback invocations and duplicate warmups increased token cost for the customer.

Environment / context:
- Deployment: Dedicated pool (reserved capacity) servicing AuroraDocs tenant ID AD-1179 in us-east-1.
- Canary config: staged rollout, weight 8%, prewarm enabled, shadow-reconcile enabled (async).
- Pinning: AuroraDocs had explicit tenant pin to open-code-7b-v1 for certain routes (chat-stream).

Steps to reproduce (observed pattern):
1) Schedule canary weight increase from 0 -> 8% with shadow-reconcile ON.
2) Canary commit completes; traffic begins hitting canary.
3) 30–90s after commit an async reconcile job writes snapshot updates to control plane and triggers an edge-epoch bump.
4) During reconcile window, tenant sessions that were pinned to open-code-7b-v1 intermittently route to legacy variant for a short duration and then return to pinned behavior.

Logs / traces observed:
- Edge-proxy logs show header rewrite + short-lived connection reset (PROXY_RET 502) followed by request routed to fallback cohort.
- Orchestrator snapshot delta includes a second, small write from the shadow-reconcile worker 28s after commit.
- Serving-runtime metrics: kvcache misses spike, prewarm allocations duplicated for same model instance.

Current hypotheses investigated so far:
- Race between pin-affinity reconciliation and edge-epoch propagation: async reconcile writes cause an ephemeral mismatch that fails the pin-coherence check on a subset of edge nodes.
- Shadow-reconcile path does a partial route rewrite that omits tenant pin metadata header under specific payload shapes (multipart attachments).
- Connection resets at the edge trigger fallback fast-path which ignores pin-state in favor of fastest-available variant (safety behavior).

Temporary mitigations applied:
- Support temporarily disabled shadow-reconcile for AuroraDocs canary jobs (manual toggle) which eliminated the observed fallback within two test cycles.
- Increased prewarm dedup window to reduce duplicate allocations.

Requested next steps / owner tasks:
- (Eng - Orchestrator) Validate atomicity of snapshot writes from shadow-reconcile worker and add a pin-consistency flag (Owner: Miguel).
- (Edge) Add defensive check to preserve pin metadata header on header-normalization path for multipart. (Owner: Priya Menon).
- (SRE) Add alert for edge-proxy PROXY_RET spikes correlated with reconcile windows (Owner: Ben Cooper).
- (CS) Confirm with AuroraDocs whether any specific request patterns (attachments) reproduce more frequently and collect sample request IDs (Owner: Aisha).

Acceptance criteria for closure:
- No tenant experiences unplanned fallback for same canary flow after shadow-reconcile re-enabled in a staged test for 24h.
- Root-cause change merged and rolled to staging with observability checks.

Notes:
- This ticket touches behavior similar to previous pinned routing incidents but the distinguishing factor is the asynchronous shadow-reconcile writer. See linked SUP-3141592 for snapshot merge context.

Additional notes:
2026-03-12 10:02 - AuroraDocs (CS rep): Customer confirmed that disabling shadow-reconcile removed the issue during their afternoon traffic window. They asked for timeline for a permanent fix.
payload.summary: Async pin override observed during canary shadow reconciliation causing sporadic fallback to degraded variant

payload.description:
Issue summary
GovLab Research is preparing an air-gapped Redwood Private upgrade. Their internal security team requested a formal, step-by-step process for using the installer “break-glass” override if signature verification blocks the install, including:
- Who at Redwood must approve (and what evidence we provide)
- What the customer must record locally (commands/logs/audit events)
- How to remediate after the emergency install to return to normal verification

Context
- Customer is in a strict air-gapped environment with controlled media transfer and change-management gates.
- They anticipate possible verification failure due to: time skew, trust store not yet updated after key rotation, or media transfer corruption.
- They do NOT want a generic ‘use --insecure’ instruction; they need a documented, auditable exception path.

Customer request
1) Provide the official Redwood approval path for break-glass verification override.
2) Provide required logs and artifacts to capture for audit.
3) Provide a follow-up checklist to restore normal verification (including trust store update and re-validation).

Notes
This is guidance-only (no active install failure reported yet). Customer wants this before their change window next week.

Proposed guidance to provide (draft)
A) Preconditions (before considering break-glass)
- Confirm bundle integrity on the staging workstation BEFORE transfer (sha256 checks on the bundle archive and manifest).
- Run installer inspect/verify commands to capture failure reason.
- Attempt standard remediations: correct clock/time source, update trust store, re-transfer media, re-extract with supported tools.

B) Break-glass approval path (Redwood)
- Support opens SUP ticket + attaches verification output and customer change window timeline.
- Required Redwood approvals:
  - Security Eng sign-off: Marcus Lin (or delegate) confirms failure mode and that break-glass is appropriate.
  - GRC/Policy sign-off: Olga Petrov (or delegate) confirms exception logging requirements.
  - Exec sponsor for exceptions (as needed): Dr. Aisha Rahman for high-risk or repeated exceptions.
- Support/SE provide customer a written statement documenting: reason, scope (bundle build id/version), timeframe, and required follow-up.

C) Break-glass execution (customer)
- Run installer preflight in verbose mode and capture output.
- Run install with the policy-gated break-glass flag (exact flag name depends on installer version; customer must be on the minimum installer version that supports auditable override).
- Ensure local audit log retention is enabled; verify the override emits an explicit audit marker event.

D) Required artifacts/logs to capture (customer)
- Full output of:
  - bundle inspection/verify command
  - preflight command
  - install command (with flags; redact tokens if any)
- Installer logs from the documented log path
- Generated support bundle (must include bundle metadata + verification status)
- Local audit events for:
  - bundle_verification_failed (with reason)
  - bundle_verification_break_glass_used
  - install_started/install_completed

E) Follow-up to restore normal verification
- Update installer trust store to include current signing root(s) (air-gapped transfer) and confirm key IDs.
- Re-run verify against the same bundle offline; confirm signature validates without override.
- For the next upgrade, block using break-glass by default (policy reset) and document closure of the exception in change records.

Acceptance criteria for closing this ticket
- Customer confirms they received:
  - Approval matrix + escalation contacts
  - Required logs list
  - Post-exception remediation checklist
- Support has an internal checklist ready to reuse for similar requests.

Additional notes:
Provided customer-facing break-glass override procedure including: (1) preconditions and standard remediation steps before override, (2) Redwood approval path (Support + Security Eng + GRC; exec review if repeated/high risk), (3) required logs/support bundle/audit events to capture locally, and (4) follow-up checklist to restore normal signature verification (trust store update + re-verify without override). Customer confirmed the process satisfies their change-management requirements.
If GovLab experiences an actual verification block during the change window, open a new SUP ticket and attach: bundle verify output, installer logs, and support bundle. Route to Security Eng if break-glass is requested for an “unknown key” reason; prefer trust store update and re-verify. Track repeated break-glass usage for exec review per policy.
payload.summary: Request: guidance on break-glass override for offline bundle signature verification (air-gapped Redwood Private install)

Issue summary: Customer requests a daily incremental handoff of tenant-scoped audit events to their SIEM vendor with per-file HMAC anchors, resume tokens, and a field-level pseudonymization mapping for PHI-sensitive fields. Impact: Medoria ingests Redwood audit events into a regulated analytics pipeline; missing cryptographic anchors and inconsistent redaction mappings block their legal team from accepting the feed. Request: 1) Signed manifest per export containing SHA256 checksums and HMAC anchor using a customer-provided KEK; 2) Per-record pseudonymization for specified fields (user.email, user.phone, payment.card_last4) with reversible token mapping held by customer; 3) Resume token in each file for deterministic replay; 4) UTC canonicalization of timestamps and consistent timezone normalization; 5) Delivery via S3 with server-side encryption and lifecycle 365d. Desired acceptance criteria: artifacts include manifest.json, data-part-00000.ndjson.gz, resume.token, and hmac.anchor; all checksums and HMACs validate against the KEK and field mappings match the provided specification.
1) Customer configured tenant export in Console → Integrations → Audit Exports with destination s3://medoria-redwood-exports/prod/
2) Selected 'incremental daily' and uploaded KEK public key for HMAC anchors
3) Expected files to include manifest.json + hmac.anchor + resume.token. Actual: data files present, manifest.json missing 'hmac_anchor' field, some timestamp fields in local tz, and user.email appears unhashed for a small subset (approx 0.2%).
[2026-03-09T23:00:12Z] export-runner start job_id=exp-20260309-77a
[2026-03-09T23:00:13Z] partition write s3://medoria-redwood-exports/prod/data-part-00000.ndjson.gz size=6.1MB items=18432
[2026-03-09T23:00:14Z] manifest generated manifest_id=man-20260309-77a fields=checksum,timestamp
[2026-03-09T23:00:14Z] hmac anchor generation skipped reason=keystore-mismatch
[2026-03-09T23:00:15Z] resume token written resume=tok-20260309-77a
[2026-03-09T23:00:15Z] export-runner completed duration_ms=3402

Initial triage by SRE (Miguel): reproduced export for tenant medoria-prod. Observed manifest.json schema v2 produced by exporter includes 'checksums' and 'timestamp' but 'hmac_anchor' field is only present if keystore alias matches internal naming convention. Customer uploaded KEK with alias 'medoria-kev-2026' while exporter expected pattern 'tenant-{tenant_id}-export-kek' causing conditional skip. Further, small percentage of records had 'user.email' emitting plaintext due to a race in the pseudonymization pipeline when the token cache miss path fell back to passthrough; high concurrency at time of run (~500 parallel writes) surfaced the bug. Hypothesis: conditional keystore lookup plus race in tokenization cache leads to missing HMAC and sporadic unhashed fields. Next steps: 1) Offer immediate workaround to regenerate artifacts with a temporary internal HMAC anchor signed by Redwood-approved service (customer consent obtained); 2) Patch exporter to accept arbitrary KEK aliases and fall back to provided public key; 3) Fix tokenization cache race (PR drafted).
Support (2026-03-10) - Aisha: Opened with initial request and provided customer's field mapping CSV + KEK public key. Asked for validation checklist and expected artifact example.
Customer (Medoria Security, 2026-03-10) - Elena Park: Confirming KEK alias used during upload: 'medoria-kev-2026'. We cannot re-upload keys quickly due to internal change control, need workaround on your side.
SRE (2026-03-11) - Miguel: Reproduced the export and observed keystore alias mismatch which caused hmac_anchor omission. Small number of user.email values unhashed — collecting sample rows to share privately.
Support (2026-03-11) - Aisha: Proposed two options: (A) Redwood generates and signs hmac_anchor with internal signing key and provides attestation (requires customer approval), (B) Customer re-uploads key with expected alias. Waiting on Medoria approval for A.
Customer (Medoria Security, 2026-03-11) - Elena Park: Approve option A for short-term. Please include signed attestation and a note we will rotate to our own KEK for long term.
SRE (2026-03-12) - Miguel: Created hotfix branch to accept explicit public key and to harden tokenization cache; running CI and internal export test. PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/platform/pull/1287
Support (2026-03-12) - Aisha: Provided instructions for validating anchor when we upload signed_hmac_anchor.tar.gz to S3. Awaiting acceptance testing from Medoria.
Customer (Medoria Security, 2026-03-12) - Elena Park: Downloaded artifacts and validated checksums. HMAC anchor validated against Redwood attestation. Noted one remaining timestamp in data-part-00000 had 'America/Chicago' tz — requesting canonicalization sweep for that file.
Workaround applied: Redwood produced signed hmac_anchor using internal attestation key and uploaded signed_hmac_anchor.tar.gz to customer's S3 path per their DPA. Customer accepted temporary artifact on 2026-03-12 after validation. Long-term fix: exporter patched to accept explicit KEK public key regardless of alias and to canonicalize timestamps to UTC during export; tokenization cache race fix merged in PR#1287. Release plan: staged rollout to prod exports on 2026-03-17 (canary tenants 10% -> 50% -> 100%). Post-deployment actions: run a backfill for medoria for exports 2026-03-01..2026-03-09 with canonicalization and reissued hmac anchors; generate confluence postmortem and send SOC evidence bundle to Medoria security. Follow-up owner: Miguel Ortega.

payload.description:
Issue summary: Customer reports periodic spikes of 429 responses for background ingest jobs immediately after a release of a sidecar orchestrator. Impact: Background pipeline (bulk embeddings) sees 10-15% request failures for ~5-10 minutes; interactive traffic unaffected but customer sees requeue/backoff failures in their orchestrated workers. Environment: Dedicated pool in prod-us-west, private VPC peered with AtlasData. Suspected area: token accounting / proxy fanout interaction with ephemeral workers and healthcheck/heartbeat requests.
1) Deploy orchestrator sidecar with ephemeral worker pool enabled (replica factor 8).
2) Kick off bulk embedding job (concurrent worker count ~120).
3) Observe burst of small keepalive/heartbeat requests from ephemeral agents to control plane.
4) After ~30-90s, many client requests begin to receive 429 from rate-limiter for tenant namespace.
5) When ephemeral pool reduces, 429s stop within ~5-10 minutes.
Excerpt from nginx edge (prod-us-west) showing early 429s:
[2026-03-12T17:21:03Z] atlasdata/worker-42 POST /v1/embeddings 200 128ms
[2026-03-12T17:21:04Z] atlasdata/ephemeral-heartbeat GET /health 204 5ms
[2026-03-12T17:21:04Z] atlasdata/worker-43 POST /v1/embeddings 429 3ms x-rate-reason=tenant_quota_exhausted
[2026-03-12T17:21:05Z] atlasdata/ephemeral-heartbeat GET /health 204 4ms
[2026-03-12T17:21:05Z] atlasdata/worker-44 POST /v1/embeddings 429 2ms x-rate-reason=tenant_quota_exhausted
(Full logs uploaded to support bundle: s3://redwood-support-bundles/SUP-575575/2026-03-12.tar.gz)
Initial hypothesis: heartbeats from ephemeral agents were being attributed to the same tenant token bucket as embedding requests because healthcheck path was not excluded by the rate-limiter attribution layer after the orchestrator change. Evidence: spike in small GETs coincident with 429 wave; token refill metric for tenant shows rapid drain during same window.
What we looked at:
- Ingress traces (edge -> auth -> rate-limiter) show healthcheck requests carrying same api-key header as workers (ephemeral agents reuse short-lived credentials).
- Rate-limiter bucket metrics: tenant_token_count dropped to zero at 17:21:05Z; refill rate unchanged.
- Orchestrator telemetry: orchestrator introduced a pooling optimization that increases heartbeat frequency to 1s under high fanout.
- No changes in billing/credits that would cause depletion.
Interim conclusion: combination of short-lived credentials + increased heartbeat frequency produced a burst of token accounting events that the rate-limiter counted against tenant quota, leading to background ingest 429s. Interactive routes were on higher-priority lane and preserved.
2026-03-12 18:00 UTC - Support: Thanks for the report — we see the same spikes and are investigating. Could you confirm whether your workers and sidecar share the same API key or use separate service accounts?
2026-03-12 18:15 UTC - AtlasData: Workers use the same service account; orchestrator creates ephemeral processes that use short-lived tokens minted from the same account.
2026-03-13 09:30 UTC - Support: We've identified a likely accounting skew; working on a mitigation and will follow up with a patch timeline.
2026-03-14 14:10 UTC - Support: Rolling a config change to isolate healthchecks from tenant quota in staging for validation.
Support (Carlos): Added initial triage, flagged to infra-sre.
Infra-SRE (Leah O'Connor): Reproduced locally with orchestrator v2.3.4; heap of 1s heartbeats causes ~2.5x token-cost due to our pre-auth path incrementing token counters on connection accept.

Additional notes:

Issue summary:
FinVerve Bank is onboarding Redwood audit exports into their internal SIEM. They require a per-tenant, append-only audit stream where each delivered batch is anchored with a SHA-256 chain hash (customer-provided anchor token) that they can independently verify. They also require a live redaction sample demonstrating row-level pseudonymization (PII fields masked reversible under HSM) and a small mapping document showing how Redwood audit fields map to their SIEM schema.

Impact:
FinVerve intends to use the stream for regulatory evidence and will not complete production onboarding until they receive cryptographic anchoring + a live redaction sample. Onboarding delay affects a scheduled go-live for a payments feature in two weeks.

Request / Deliverables:
1) Specification for per-batch hash anchoring format (SHA-256 over canonicalized UTF-8 JSON payload, canonicalization rules included).
2) Example signed manifest for a nightly delta with anchor token reference and manifest signature metadata.
3) Live 1-hour redaction sample (subset of events) with reversible pseudonymization applied and HSM attestation header.
4) Field mapping CSV (Redwood audit fields -> FinVerve SIEM fields) and a sample webhook configuration (headers, cert pinning) for their ingestion.

Attachments provided by customer: sample SIEM mapping, compliance questionnaire, and internal policy notes.

1) Customer configured tenant export to webhook endpoint in Console (prod, us-east) with default envelope.
2) Customer attempted to pull delta bundle via S3 mirror; received payload but cannot verify integrity because there is no anchor token or canonicalization metadata.
3) Customer requested a reversible pseudonymization sample but received a masked sample without HSM attestation headers.

Observed result: payloads arrive but cannot be independently verified by customer; compliance team block on acceptance.
Expected result: each delivered batch should include an anchor reference + canonicalization metadata and reversible pseudonymization sample should include HSM attestation header so FinVerve can map to their evidence requirements.

Checked export pipeline: manifest generator attaches batch_id, timestamps, and delivery signature but anchor field is only populated for 'signed-ledger' export mode; FinVerve export was configured as 'delta-mirror' (no anchor).
Engineering hypothesis: 'delta-mirror' pipeline omitted anchor by design for performance; adding anchor is low-risk but requires schema bump and a short rollout to Dedicated mirror path.
Tests run: created a dev tenant export in 'signed-ledger' mode and delivered sample manifest to FinVerve. Verified SHA-256 anchor generation and verification reproducible locally. Confirmed reversible pseudonymization pipeline can emit HSM attestation headers when 'hsm-pseudonymize=true'.

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Ephemeral proxy nodes in the us-east-1 ingress fleet exhibited rate jitter under a small-payload, high-QPS tenant workload causing a sustained elevation in 5xx error-rate across the tenant's requests (~2% -> 12%).

Impact:
- BrightForms (dedicated) observed widespread 5xx responses for short/fast embedding and chat calls between 11:20-12:40 UTC on 2026-03-12.
- Affected surface: REST generation and streaming endpoints for small payload requests (<200 bytes).
- Business impact: degraded UX and retries from the customer leading to amplified load.

Environment:
- Prod, us-east-1 region, dedicated capacity pool for BrightForms.
- Ingress path: api-gateway -> ephemeral-proxy -> runtime pool (dedicated GPU nodes).
- Autoscaling and prefetch enabled for the customer's model variants.

Steps to reproduce (observed pattern):
1) Send ~3000 small POSTs/min (100-200B payload) across multiple connections with short TTL keepalives.
2) Ephemeral proxy acceptor queues occasionally backpressured (spiky accept latency) causing upstream hedged-retry logic to fire.
3) Hedged retries combined with apigw backoff mis-calibration produced request duplication leading to transient runtime overload and 5xx responses.

Logs/metrics snippets collected:
- apigw.ingress.accept_latency.p90: spiked from 8ms -> 120ms at 11:25 UTC.
- ephemeral-proxy.retry_count: +250% correlated with windowed accept latency spikes.
- runtime.request_5xx.rate: baseline 2% -> sustained 10-14% during peak.
- Sample error from runtime: "upstream-cancellation: capacity-exceeded"
- Kernel traces on runtime nodes showed increased context-switches and io wait during the spike.

Initial customer report:
- BrightForms sent a support email at 11:30 UTC reporting intermittent 500s during embedding uploads and chat completions at high QPS.

Observed differences vs a classic prefetch-thrash:
- This incident did not coincide with a model sync or prefetch invalidation window.
- Root cause appeared upstream in the ingress/ephemeral proxy path where jitter and hedged retry interactions amplified load rather than a pure runtime OOM or NVMe hotspot.

Timeline of investigation:
- 11:35 Support acknowledged and opened ticket; routed to SRE on-call.
- 11:45 SRE identified correlated spikes in ephemeral-proxy.retry_count and apigw.accept_latency.
- 11:55 Confirmed hedged-retry policy triggers under accept latency >50ms; found a recent canary tweak to hedged-retry backoff on 2026-03-11 (PR 119) that shortened the secondary retry window.
- 12:05 Replica set of ephemeral proxies in front of BrightForms showed uneven connection distribution (50% of connections funneled into 3 pods due to a transient routing hash change).
- 12:20 Implemented temporary mitigation: disabled hedged-retry for this tenant at apigw edge and increased accept queue size on affected ephemeral-proxy pods.
- 12:35 Error-rate began to fall; by 12:50 rates returned to baseline.
Hypotheses tested and results:
- Hypothesis A: Runtime OOMs caused 5xx -> disproved (no OOM/panic logs, memory stable).
- Hypothesis B: Prefetch invalidation caused thrash -> disproved (no prefetch sweeps in logs).
- Hypothesis C: Hedged retry + acceptor jitter amplified requests -> supported by correlated metrics and timeline.
Evidence and artifacts:
- Ingress routing logs showing connection-affinity shift at 11:22 UTC (investigation trace id: trace-20260312-1122).
- apigw and proxy traces (link to internal cycle-storage): /mnt/logs/ingress/2026-03-12/trace-1122.gz
- Heap and kernel traces on runtimes: /mnt/diag/runtime/brightforms/2026-03-12/

Short-term actions applied (12:20-12:50 UTC):
- Disabled hedged-retry behavior for BrightForms at apigw gateway until hedged policy is tuned.
- Increased ephemeral-proxy accept queue depth on affected pods (nodes auto-healed/restarted to pick config).
- Applied routing fix to rebalance connections across ephemeral proxies (removed stale route-hash canary).

Long-term fix and follow-ups:
- Reverted the hedged-retry canary change in proxy (PR 119 rolled back) and opened follow-up PR 482 in gateway to add jitter and exponential backoff to hedged-retry.
- Add an admission check so connection hashing changes require a gradual drain window (Confluence: acceptor-queue-tuning-playbook).
- Update playbook to include a knob to disable hedged-retry per-tenant and automated detection alert when retry_count grows >100% within 5min.
- Run a targeted load test (small-payload high-QPS) with new hedged-retry settings before re-enabling.

Resolution notes:
- Ticket resolved after error rate returned to baseline and BrightForms confirmed acceptable behavior at 13:10 UTC.
- Post-incident monitoring window scheduled for 72 hours.

Additional notes:
2026-03-12 12:40 - BrightForms (Customer): Confirming improved success rate; still seeing occasional 502s but much reduced. Thanks for the quick action.

Issue summary:
Customer (Narrato AI) reported periodic p95/p99 latency cliffs on streaming generation starting 2026-03-12 morning. Spikes affect short lived streaming calls (single prompt -> immediate close) used by their products for ephemeral assistant responses.

Impact:
- Intermittent p99 latency spikes up to 4s (baseline ~220ms) for streaming endpoints.
- Client-side perceived timeouts and some 504s for requests that hit top of the long-tail.
- Affects a portion of requests for this dedicated tenant (~5-8% of traffic during peak).

Environment:
- prod | us-east-1 dedicated pool for Narrato AI
- Serving runtime version: 2026.02.1
- Continuous-batcher config: adaptive-linger enabled (min_linger_ms=2, max_linger_ms=120, target_batch_tokens=2048)

Steps to reproduce (observed + synthetic):
1) On prod, observe Narrato's route during peak window (08:00-10:00 UTC) for p95/p99 graphs.
2) Synthetic repro: spawn 2000 short streaming connections (single short prompt, client closes after stream) across 250 clients with ~10 QPS each for 3 minutes.
3) Measure p95/p99 for streaming responses; watch batcher metrics (linger_ms distribution, batch_size distribution, flush_count).

Observed metrics and traces:
- Periodic ~7 minute cadence in p99 cliffs correlated with spikes in batcher_linger_samples and an uptick in 'linger_entropy' metric (internal).
- KV-cache sync latencies also show small coincident increases (~5-20ms) during cliffs.
- Traces show many small requests being buffered and then flushed together causing queueing at the head-of-line for short streams.
- No increase in GPU saturation or host-level CPU/mem during events.

Initial hypothesis:
Adaptive-linger algorithm is reacting to short-stream dominated traffic by inflating its linger window for longer than expected (linger hysteresis), which causes transient accumulation of short requests into larger flushes and results in periodic tail latency cliffs. The algorithm's state seems to drift under oscillatory traffic patterns; once linger inflates, it takes a few cycles to decay.

Investigation notes:
- Correlated Datadog dashboard: dashboards/datadog/streaming-batcher/narrato-p99-20260312 (internal link in comments).
- Flamegraphs from sampled traces show queueing time as dominant contributor to p99.
- Checked rollout history: adaptive-linger config change rolled via config-service 2026-02-28 for all dedicated pools. No code deploys coincident with first reported date.
- Reproduced locally with synthetic harness; toggling adaptive-linger off prevents cliffs.

Temporary mitigation applied:
- For Narrato's dedicated pool we set adaptive-linger.enabled=false and applied static linger_ms=8 on 2026-03-12 13:20 UTC. Immediate reduction in p99 observed within 60s during next flush cycles.
- Alert rule created to detect 'linger_ms > 50ms for >30s' on customer pools.

Follow-up / next steps:
- Engineering to add a decay cap to adaptive-linger (max_decay_ms) to limit hysteresis. (ENG-PR planned)
- Add regression test in synthetic harness simulating high-count short streams to catch oscillatory cases.
- Consider tenant-aware adaptive parameters (short-stream-heavy tenants get conservative defaults).
- Postmortem and design doc update scheduled.

Resolution notes (temporary):
- Workaround applied at 2026-03-12; customer confirmed improvement in follow-up call. We have not rolled the change cluster-wide. Will coordinate broader fix after engineering design review.

2026-03-12 11:30 UTC: Reproduced locally with synthetic harness (2000 short streams) — adaptive-linger reproduces p99 cliffs.
2026-03-12 13:10 UTC: Confirmed config-service rollout on 2026-02-28 included adaptive-linger defaults.

Temporary mitigation: adaptive-linger disabled for customer pool and static linger_ms=8 applied. Customer verified improvement. Engineering to implement decay cap and add regression tests before re-enabling adaptive-linger cluster-wide.

2026-03-13 15:02 - Eng (Miguel Torres): Drafting PR to add max_decay_ms and tenant-aware min_linger_ms. Will include synthetic test coverage and canary plan. PR: https://github.com/redwood/realtime-batcher/pull/412
