Issue summary: BeaconAI reported a sudden increase in 95th and 99th percentile latency and a small but rising fraction of 5xx errors after enabling an aggressive combined config: async batching enabled (max_batch_size=256), prefix KV prefetch enabled, and a new quantization profile (int8-fast). Impact: customer-facing inference latency up ~2.2x 95p, request failures ~0.6% (5xx), sustained for ~20 minutes with intermittent recovery. Customer traffic is on a Dedicated pool. They requested prescriptive rollback steps that minimize user-visible disruption and guidance to harden snapshot restores to avoid recurrence.
1) On dedicated pool tenant BeaconAI, apply optimizer profile 'int8-fast-agg' which sets async_batching=true, max_batch_size=256, kv_prefetch=true, quant_profile=int8-fast
2) Route production traffic (baseline 1200 rps) to the tenant pool with normal token length distribution (avg 280 tokens).
3) Observe latency and error metrics over the next 5-30 minutes: 95p and 99p increase, occasional 5xx spike correlated with GPU memory pressure events and KV misses.
2026-03-10T09:12:15Z WARN serving-runtime: batch overflow, allocated_batches=193, max_batch_size=256, observed_latency_ms=360
2026-03-10T09:12:42Z ERROR model-loader: quantized-kernel OOM attempt, spilled to CPU, traceback=...
2026-03-10T09:13:01Z WARN kv-cache: eviction-threshold reached for tenant=BeaconAI, proactive-evict=true
Request IDs sampled: rQf9-0a2b, rQf9-0a2c, rQf9-0a6d -> first byte delays 120-430ms; 5xx codes 502/504 observed
Initial telemetry shows correlation between enabling async batching with very large max_batch_size and the quant_profile. Hypothesis A: int8-fast uses a kernel that increases GPU memory working set for long sequences and causes occasional OOM spills to CPU which amplify latency. Hypothesis B: aggressive batching caused large variance in sequence grouping leading to KV prefetch thrash and eviction storms. We validated via heap snapshots (linked PR) that memory footprint rose ~18% after profile change. No infra-level GPU hardware faults were reported. We flagged a candidate quick mitigation: reduce max_batch_size -> step down async batching -> revert quantization to conservative int8-balanced, while preserving some batching benefits.

Additional notes:
2026-03-10T11:05 SRE Ops (R. Diaz): Recommend we set circuit-breaker for this tenant to 1.5s token latency and 0.5% error before doing any large-scale config ops. We can gate by route.
2026-03-12T09:30 BeaconAI-Customer (support@beacon.ai): Thank you — we'll accept staged rollback with traffic split. Please confirm expected downtime (should be zero).
Workaround applied (in-progress): executed staged rollback with zero-downtime traffic-split to old optimizer profile. Sequence executed: 1) deploy profile gate: create 'BeaconAI-safe' profile copy with async_batching=true, max_batch_size=96, kv_prefetch=true, quant_profile=int8-balanced; 2) set routing policy: 80% live -> safe profile, 20% live -> previous aggressive profile for 10 minutes; 3) monitor 95p/5xx for 30 minutes; 4) if stable, shift to 100% safe profile; 5) capture final serving snapshot and tag snapshot with timestamp and profile metadata. We also hardened snapshot restores by adding a preflight check that verifies the quant kernel compatibility and available GPU memory headroom before completing restore (implementing a soft-fail to block restores that would trigger eviction storms). Outcome: after shift to safe profile, BeaconAI 95p returned to baseline within 18 minutes and 5xx rate dropped to baseline. Follow-up actions: a) propose an automatic pre-deploy memory smoke-test for aggressive quant profiles, b) add optimizer guardrail that caps max_batch_size by observed average sequence length per tenant, c) update canary checklist in Confluence page linked. Ticket will remain open until the guardrail PR is merged and canary metrics confirmed for 48h.
payload.summary: Live tenant 95p latency spike and intermittent 5xx after aggressive batching+quant profile; request safe rollback + snapshot hardening

Issue summary: Customer BrightVoice AI reports an unexpected increase on a finalized invoice for a multi-hour batch embedding job run on 2026-03-05. The invoice line shows a higher per-embedding unit price (price floor applied retroactively) for hours in which the job was initially billed at the self-serve reserved rate.

Impact: Billing overcharge for one finalized invoice (invoice #BV-20260305) affecting a single dedicated tenant. Customer is requesting an explanation and a credit if the charge is incorrect. Customer reports the delta is ~USD 3,420.

Environment: Dedicated pool (dedicated-nyc-gpu-pool-3) with fallback to hosted when reserved nodes temporarily saturated. Batch embedding controller: batch-runner-v5 (image: runner:2026-02-28).

Steps to reproduce (customer reported):
1) Upload CSV of ~1.2M rows to start a single batch embedding job at 02:10 UTC on 2026-03-05.
2) Job runs across a 7-hour window with autoscaling and a fallback window between 04:00-05:10 UTC when some reserved workers hit capacity and requests routed to hosted fallback.
3) Final invoice shows higher per-embed unit price for entire job, not only the fallback window.

Expected behavior: Only tokens/embeddings routed to hosted fallback should be billed at hosted rates and any reserved-capacity pricing should remain unchanged for hours served by dedicated capacity. Retroactive price floors should not be applied after invoice finalization.

Actual behavior: The billing pipeline applied a price floor rule retroactively to the whole job, increasing unit price for all hours. Customer email thread indicates they saw correct provisional estimate before finalization but were surprised by final invoice.

Logs / evidence attached (referenced): invoice BV-20260305 (PDF), provisional_estimate_BV-20260305.csv, batch-runner logs (s3://bv-embeds/logs/2026-03-05/), billing-postback dump (s3://billing/postbacks/2026-03-05/finalized).

Start a batch-embed job on a dedicated tenant with autoscaling that triggers hosted fallback
Allow fallback to host for ~1 hour mid-job
Observe postback ordering and final invoice aggregation
[2026-03-05T04:02:13Z] batch-runner: routed 124K requests to hosted-fallback (fallback-reason=reserved-exhausted)
[2026-03-05T04:02:17Z] billing-postback: queued postback id=pb-98a1 for tenant=bv-tenant
[2026-03-05T05:15:02Z] billing-aggregator: applied price_floor=0.000040 to rate_group=embed_standard for tenant=bv-tenant (trigger=price-floor-policy-v2, effective_start=2026-03-05T00:00:00Z)
[2026-03-05T06:00:12Z] invoice-service: finalize invoice BV-20260305 total=3420.72
We saw a provisional estimate of ~$1200 but the finalized invoice jumped to ~$4600. We only used hosted fallback for ~1 hour; why would the whole job be marked up? We need a credit or a clear explanation to pass to finance.
Support (Maya): Acknowledged receipt and opened ticket; asked for provisional estimate and invoice PDF (2026-03-10).
Customer (BrightVoice billing contact - Elena Rovira): Uploaded invoice PDF and provisional estimates; requested urgent credit assessment (2026-03-10).
Billing eng (Tomas): Assigned to investigate pricing rule application and postback ordering (2026-03-10).
SRE (Anand Patel): Noted there was a brief control-plane partition at 04:00 UTC that may have affected postback ordering; flagged for triage (2026-03-11).
Billing eng (Tomas): Found runs where price-floor rule evaluation used job-level aggregation instead of per-postback granularity; investigating rollback (2026-03-12).
Initial hypothesis: price-floor-policy-v2 incorrectly keyed on job_id aggregation produced an effective_start that backfilled earlier hours when a hosted-fallback event was present.
Postback ordering: billing-postback messages for fallback hours arrived later than dedicated-hour postbacks; aggregator deduplicated and rekeyed resulting in job-level price application.
Config: price-floor-policy-v2 was rolled 2026-02-25 and includes 'job-level' override to prevent undercharging when fallback occurs; test coverage missed multi-postback ordering cases.
SRE note: during 04:00 UTC there was a short control-plane API latency spike (observed in metrics cluster-api: 120s P95) which delayed hosted postbacks by ~30 minutes.
Estimate of incorrect charge: aggregator applied higher unit_price to 100% of job tokens (1.2M rows * 1 embed each) instead of only 124K fallback items; delta =~ $3,420.
Related repo change: commit ab12cd34ef introduced the job-level aggregation accidentally; PR 4823 reverted local test but not deployed to production at the time of job.
Hold on finalizing billing credits pending approval from billing manager
Create refund/credit memo draft for BrightVoice (approx USD 3,420) if investigation confirms pipeline fault
Schedule hotfix to change aggregator granularity from 'job' -> 'postback' and add ordering-tolerant merging (track as INT-4382)
Add automated regression test covering delayed-postback ordering to price-floor policy test suite
Notify customer of expected timeline (targeted 2026-03-14 for credit posting)
Coordinate with finance to apply credit and notify customer with invoice adjustment
Investigation confirmed a bug in billing-aggregator where price-floor policy was keyed at job-level and retroactively applied to full job after receiving a delayed hosted-fallback postback. Billing team to issue a credit memo for the overcharge (USD 3,420). Hotfix scheduled and PR created to rekey aggregation by postback window and add tolerance for out-of-order postbacks. Credit to be posted to customer account by 2026-03-14.

Issue summary:
A customer (EchoMail, dedicated pool in us-west-2) reported a sharp throughput collapse and p99 latency spike beginning ~2026-03-13T09:20 UTC. Symptoms include rapid GPU attach failures, high allocator queue length, and autoscaler failing to add capacity (scale stuck). Pattern: a tidal wave of many short-lived streams from multiple tenants caused slot fragmentation and amplifier effect from a noisy tenant using many tiny streaming connections.

Impact:
- EchoMail: observed ~70% throughput drop for batched routes and p99 latency increase from 120ms to 3.2s on chat generation.
- Other tenants in same dedicated cluster: intermittent timeouts and elevated p95/p99.
- Operational: alert storm for attach_lag and allocator_backpressure in us-west-2.

Environment:
- Deployment: dedicated reserved pool (cluster: dp-west-42) in us-west-2
- Runtime: serving-runtime v1.23.0, allocator v0.9.5, autoscaler v2.18.1
- Networking: standard VPC (no customer-side VPN changes reported)

Steps to reproduce (observed reproduction pattern):
1) High-fanout traffic pattern with many short streams (<= 3s) arriving concurrently, mostly from a single tenant cohort.
2) Each short stream requests warmup/prefetch; allocator issues many small allocations and NVLink/KV-cache warmups.
3) Slot fragmentation prevents coalescing into efficient batches; GPU memory pressure grows and thin-slicing increases attach latency.
4) Autoscaler sees transient attach latency and oscillating metrics and enters a cooldown state instead of provisioning, leaving cluster below target capacity.

Observed metrics and logs (selected):
- allocator.attach_latency.p95 (us-west-2): baseline 80ms -> spike 1.8s at 2026-03-13T09:23 UTC
- allocator.queue_depth: 5 -> sustained 230 during burst window
- GPU utilization: uneven across hosts; several nodes at 98% while others idle (slot hoarding pattern)
- autoscaler.log: repeated "scale suppressed: cooldown_policy" messages from 09:24:00 -> 09:40:00
- serving-runtime stderr: repeated kernel queue rejects with "KV cache cold start" during fanout

Initial mitigation applied:
- Support temporarily applied tenant-level rate-limit (throttle) at the gateway for the noisy tenant cohort at 09:45 UTC which immediately reduced short-stream arrival rate by ~85% and allowed allocator queue to drain.
- Manually increased autoscaler max burst limit for the cluster (temporary override) at 09:52 UTC which allowed 2 additional GPU nodes to be provisioned and restore aggregate throughput to ~85% of baseline.

Investigation notes:
- Hypothesis 1: Noisy-tenant with many short streams causes repeated prefetch/kernel warmups, creating NVLink/KV-cache thrash and preventing efficient batching. Evidence: high rate of small allocate/release cycles in allocator logs keyed to tenant id T-echo-308.
- Hypothesis 2: Autoscaler heuristics are overly conservative for very high-frequency short-stream workloads and enter cooldown due to perceived instability. Evidence: autoscaler metrics show multiple scale decisions suppressed during the peak window; scale recommendation was positive but suppressed by cooldown.
- Hypothesis 3: Slot fragmentation and affinity mismatch between multiplexed short streams leads to some GPUs being "hot" while others remain underused. Evidence: host-level GPU utilization skew and logs showing connection affinity stuck to a subset of nodes.

Next steps / action items:
- Short term (SRE + Support): keep tenant-level throttle in place for noisy cohort and monitor for 24 hours. (Owner: Support)
- Mid term (Infra): deploy a targeted autoscaler tweak to relax cooldown sensitivity for clusters experiencing sustained attach_latency (experiment rollout in staging first). (Owner: Mateo Ruiz)
- Mid term (Runtime): add a diagnostic histogram for per-tenant short-stream rate and slot fragmentation to help automated routing decisions. (Owner: Runtime team)
- Long term (Product + Solutions): work with EchoMail to introduce client-side batching or aggregated keepalive to reduce connection churn. (Owner: Solutions)

Notes: customer was kept updated during triage and accepted the temporary throttle as acceptable under dedicated SLA.
payload.summary: Tidal burst of short streams in us-west-2 causing regional GPU starvation; autoscaler stuck failing to scale and noisy-tenant amplification

Issue summary:
Customers running long-lived streaming sessions over HTTP/2 occasionally observe duplicate executions of downstream function/webhook calls after an in-stream reconnect. The duplicates occur only when the client reconnects within ~3s after a network hiccup and seem correlated with large idempotency header values (base64-encoded blobs) being split across HTTP/2 HEADERS/CONTINUATION frames.

Impact:
- Nimbus Forms reported 5 duplicate webhook executions in the last 48 hours causing duplicate order submissions and triggering billing edge-cases.
- Affects enterprise customers using Python and Go SDKs with streaming + function calling enabled.
- Leads to data integrity issues for customers that rely on at-most-once semantics for external side effects.

Environment:
- Redwood prod us-east-1 (api-gateway fronted by ALB -> http2-enabled proxies -> backend runtime)
- Customer uses Python SDK v1.12.3 (streaming), Go SDK v0.9.1 also observed similar behavior
- Model: gpt-redwood-2-xl; request pattern: streaming chat with function_call = "auto" and idempotency token set by SDK per-session

Steps to reproduce (approximate, intermittent):
1) Start a streaming chat session from the Python SDK with a long idempotency token (~220 bytes base64).
2) Trigger a function call that results in an outbound webhook (customer's endpoint).
3) Introduce a short network interruption (e.g., TCP RST / client reconnect) while the client is still streaming (observed radius: within 1-5 seconds of first function call emission).
4) Client reconnects and resumes the stream. Server accepts the resumed stream and replays the last chunk(s).
5) Downstream webhook receives a second invocation for the same logical function-call id.

Observed logs/attachments (sanitized):
- api-gateway access logs show two POSTs to the webhook endpoint within 1s of each other with different X-Request-Id values.
- Runtime debug trace: idempotency-header present on initial HEADERS but truncated on reconnect HEADERS; header value differs by a suffix of 8-12 bytes.
- Client-side SDK log (Python): "reconnect: resuming stream, sending HEADERS with idempotency-token: <truncated>"

Notes:
- Reproduction rate is low (roughly 0.02% of streams for this customer), but impact is high due to billing and side-effects.
- Hypothesis from Nimbus: internal proxy or ALB is re-chunking headers on reconnect and dropping continuation bytes for very long header values.

Request:
- Investigate whether our HTTP/2 handling path accepts header continuations correctly on resumed streams and if any ingress proxies (ALB / sidecar) truncate long headers across reconnects.
- Determine mitigations (e.g., enforce idempotency token length limit, normalize tokens to a short stable hash at gateway, or adjust SDK to send a compact token).
2026-03-12 | Aisha Khan (Support): Initial report from Nimbus. Attached sanitized webhook payloads and gateway access logs. Customer requests urgent mitigation options.
2026-03-12 | SRE Triage: Assigned to Benito. Noted correlation with long header sizes. Added labels and requested packet captures from customer network path.
2026-03-13 | Benito Marsh (SRE): Collected ALB logs and tcpdump from internal proxy. Observed HEADERS frame split where CONTINUATION frame never reached runtime in ~3 spurious reconnects. Opened SDK issue to add shorter default session token: https://github.com/redwood-inference/sdk-python/pull/842
2026-03-13 | Nimbus (customer): Confirmed they can reproduce by forcing a reconnect with large token; willing to test a gateway-side patch or SDK change. Asking about rollback risk.
2026-03-14 | Engineering (Runtime): Noted a rare edge in our HTTP/2 parser where header continuation frames arriving post-stream-resume could be dropped if connection state was not fully rebuilt. Working on a patch to make continuation assembly tolerant to reconnects. ETA for patch: 2026-03-17.
2026-03-14 | Support (Aisha): Suggested interim mitigation: reduce idempotency token length (SDK change) and enable a short-term duplicate-suppression window in the webhook consumer. Customer agreed to test SDK alpha tomorrow.
Packet capture (internal): shows HEADERS (frame length ~160) followed by CONTINUATION (frame length ~64) during initial stream; on reconnect only HEADERS arrives, CONTINUATION missing due to proxy-level reset.
ALB config review: http2 enabled; no known bug reports, but our sidecar unit tests didn't cover very long header sequences across reconnects.
SDK behavior: current SDKs generate per-session idempotency tokens as base64 of 128 random bytes. This produces headers up to ~172 characters before encoding; some proxies resegment headers differently leading to splitting across frames.
Runtime parser: previously assumed a single HEADERS frame for tokens under 512 bytes; partial parsing logic didn't maintain a continuation buffer across stream-resume boundary.
Customer reproducibility: high when token >= 160 chars and reconnect is forced within 5s. Lower token lengths (<80 chars) did not reproduce duplicates in tests.
Edge case in HTTP/2 header continuation handling: when long idempotency headers are split into HEADERS+CONTINUATION frames, a reconnect path could drop continuation frames due to connection/resume state reconstruction in our HTTP/2 pipeline, leading to truncated token being processed as a different idempotency value and causing duplicate downstream function calls.
Immediate mitigations: 1) Engineering patched runtime HTTP/2 parser to buffer and assemble CONTINUATION frames across stream-resume states; patch merged to canary on 2026-03-14. 2) Released SDK hotfix to compute a compact token (sha256 hex of random bytes) by default in v1.12.4-alpha to keep header length < 64 chars; link: https://github.com/redwood-inference/sdk-python/pull/842. 3) Support recommended customer deploy a short dedupe window on webhook consumer for 10s until runtime patch fully rolled out.

Rollout notes: patch on canary 2026-03-14; planned gradual rollout to prod us-east-1 on 2026-03-16 after smoke tests. SDK hotfix published as alpha 2026-03-14; GA planned 2026-03-18.

Follow-ups: add integration test for long idempotency headers across reconnects, document recommended max token length in SDK docs, and add monitoring alert for unexpected duplicate function invocations (rate > 0.01% per customer).
payload.summary: Intermittent duplicate function calls when client reconnects over HTTP/2 — idempotency header truncated across frames

Issue summary: After a planned reparent operation that moved two high-volume subaccounts under a new org umbrella, DataPulse began seeing opaque 429s affecting both realtime chat streams and nightly bulk-embedding jobs. This appears correlated with the reparent window (2026-03-11 03:00-03:10 UTC).

Impact: Multiple DataPulse services had a significant portion of requests rejected with 429 for ~40 minutes, causing downstream backlog for their batch pipeline and user-facing latency spikes for realtime features. Customer reports 18% failure rate on embed backfills and sporadic 429 for low-rate chat sessions.

Timeline:
- 2026-03-11 02:58 UTC: orchestration triggered subaccount reparenting (internal operation id orch-2026-311-77).
- 2026-03-11 03:04 UTC: first customer report of 429 surge.
- 2026-03-11 03:25 UTC: engineering rollback of a non-critical flag; 429s persist.
- 2026-03-11 03:45 UTC: support engaged; initial triage points to quota accounting.

Environment: prod-us-east (dedicated pool: dp-dedicated-03), mixed HTTP2 websocket and REST ingest.

Steps to reproduce (customer):
1) Start concurrent embed backfill (1000 concurrent workers) for subaccount A.
2) Simultaneously run realtime chat load (50 concurrent websockets) on subaccount B (now under same parent).
3) Observe intermittent 429 responses with X-RateLimit headers showing token window near zero.

Observed behavior: 429s show as "rate limit exceeded" but total tenant quota in console still shows available burst credits. Token window counters on several ingress nodes show inconsistent attribution where short-lived auth tickets were counted against the pre-reparent subaccount mapping.

Relevant logs / metrics (samples):
- ingress-proxy logs (03:03:59 UTC): "token_bucket_check: key=subacct-A:worker-77, counted=1200, window=60s, remaining=0"
- rate-limiter debug (03:04:19 UTC): "burst_pool_lookup: parent_org=org-X, subaccount_id=subacct-B -> burst_pool_id=pending-reassign-9001"
- billing/credits service (03:05:02 UTC): "credit_balance: org-X total=1.2M, subacct-A=800k, subacct-B=400k"

Notes: X-RateLimit headers were present but sometimes omitted on websocket handshake rejects; customer SDK did not surface consistent retry-after values.

Customer asks: immediate mitigation to avoid lost requests, and explain what caused burst-credit accounting to be out-of-sync after reparenting.

Desired outcome: restore stable request acceptance for both realtime and batch traffic while preserving correct burst allocation; implement reconciliation to avoid recurrence.

Impact: Compliance exposure for VerdantCare; customer escalated to legal and compliance teams and requested immediate evidence and remediation.

Issue summary: During a weighted canary promote for rw-gpt-3.2-compat, we observed tenant sessions losing their model pin and being routed to the fallback/degraded variant. This appears correlated with edge multipath preflight probes that create two concurrent handshake flows to the orchestrator.
Impact: Several BrightWave customers reported mixed model outputs and a spike in 5xx routing to degraded variant for a subset (~4%) of requests. Customer observed increased latency and model-output inconsistency during the 10:45–11:20 UTC canary window. Environment: Production, us-east1, Dedicated pool for BrightWave Analytics. Steps to reproduce: 1) Start a gradual canary promote with weight 10% on rw-gpt-3.2-compat. 2) Enable multipath/connection-reuse at edge (simulate flaky TCP path multiplexing). 3) Replay tenant traffic with streaming sessions and interleaved keepalives. 4) Observe pin commit races where a preflight handshake on Path A commits a canary pin but Path B carries a stale control-plane snapshot that overwrites/evicts the pin. Observed behavior: - Mixed routing where subsequent requests from the same session hit legacy/degraded variant. - Edge logs show two preflight handshakes within 200ms for the same session token. - Orchestrator logs show conflicting commit order: "commit_pin tenant=brightwave session=abc123 variant=canary seq=402" then later "commit_pin tenant=brightwave session=abc123 variant=legacy seq=399" (seq numbers indicate stale snapshot on second flow). Expected behavior: Preflight handshakes should establish deterministic pin commit ordering; stale snapshots should not overwrite a later commit for the same session. Initial hypothesis: Edge multipath causes duplicate preflight handshakes to reach different orchestrator replicas with diverging epoch/snapshot states. Orchestrator currently accepts commit if snapshot_seq >= last_seen_seq per replica, but there is a window where a stale replica's write can arrive after a newer commit from another replica and be accepted, producing pin rollback. Temporary mitigation applied: - Support throttled BrightWave traffic to 5% of peak to reduce multipath pressure. - Hotfix deployed to edge-proxy to clamp preflight retries for known keepalive reconnect patterns. Investigation notes: - Snapshot sync lag between orchestrator replicas observed on tracing spans (max lag ~350ms under load). - Prewarm agent sometimes forwards preflight probes directly to worker nodes bypassing orchestration caching layer, increasing exposure to stale state. - No model quantization or serving changes during window. Next steps: 1) SRE to patch orchestrator commit acceptance to use monotonic commit tokens (in-flight patch PR referenced). 2) Engineering to add idempotent commit guard at edge-proxy for preflight flows. 3) Plan a controlled canary replay with multipath enabled in staging to validate fix. 4) Postmortem to be prepared and shared with BrightWave.

orchestrator-1[2026-03-12T10:46:02Z] INFO commit accepted tenant=brightwave session=abc123 seq=402
edge-proxy[2026-03-12T10:46:02Z] WARN preflight session=abc123 path=2 commit_pin seq=399 variant=legacy

~4% of BrightWave traffic experienced transient routing to legacy/degraded variant during canary window; increased latency and mismatch in outputs reported by customer; potential billing discrepancy flagged due to unexpected variant execution.
Clamped preflight retries at edge and temporarily reduced traffic weight for BrightWave canary cohort. Advised customer to retry affected sessions; prepared manual pin re-assertion tool for urgent rebinds.

Engineering - Daniel Kim (2026-03-12 12:03 UTC): Deploying edge-proxy clamp for preflight duplicates (hotfix deployed to canary edge fleet). Opening PR to make commit acceptance monotonic and idempotent: https://github.com/redwood-inference/orchestrator/pull/2410

SRE - Miguel Alvarez (2026-03-13 09:01 UTC): Patch validated in internal staging with simulated multipath; initial results show no rollback with seq-monotonic guard. Planning rollout to prod orchestrator replicas during low-traffic window (2026-03-14 03:00 UTC).

Issue summary: Between 2026-03-10 11:50-12:55 UTC Nimbus Freight reported a rapid increase in in-flight request counts and duplicate completions. Customer observed increased token billing (3x baseline) and duplicated responses for ~35% of requests. Impact: customer-facing endpoints for fulfillment chat and webhook completions experienced elevated latencies and duplicated responses causing downstream reconciliation failures and invoice exposure. Environment: Dedicated GPU pool (nimbus-dedicated-01), prod-us-east, autoscale enabled, custom retry middleware at customer side. Immediate symptoms: spike in inflight metrics, autoscaler repeatedly adding capacity then quickly shedding, many requests retried at client causing duplicated completions. This ticket covers investigation, mitigation, root cause, and post-incident action items.
2026-03-10T11:46Z - Nimbus alert: elevated token usage; 11:50 - Support received first customer message; 11:55 - Observed inflight counter rising from 1200->4300 across pool; 12:02 - Stream duplicates confirmed by replay; 12:10 - Canary fallback configured to route to warm backup pool; 12:25 - Autoscaler policy adjusted to increase min nodes and hold scale for 10m; 12:55 - Duplicate completions rate dropped below 1%; 13:30 - Billing mitigation credit issued; 2026-03-12 - Root cause patch deployed to scheduler and customer-facing middleware recommendations published.
Hypotheses evaluated: 1) noisy neighbor - low signal. 2) model kernel regression - not correlated with model change. 3) control-plane epoch/timestamp drift after a DST/time-sync event - strong correlation. Findings: an internal maintenance job that adjusts scheduling epochs for internal metrics executed a cron job intended for a different timezone and applied a +3600s drift to the scheduler's epoch bucket for nimbus-dedicated-01. The scheduler's inflight accounting uses epoch-based lease ids; when the epoch shifted mid-flight some inflight leases were double-acknowledged by worker nodes leading to double-counting and premature ACKs that allowed client retries to re-enter the system. The autoscaler reacted to inflated metrics causing capacity thrash; duplicated processing occurred for requests that were retried by the customer within the retry window. Cross-reference: Slack thread #support-nimbus (https://slack.redwood.ai/support-nimbus/p12345), PR fixing epoch drift handling (github.com/redwood-inference/scheduler/pull/4217).
Short-term: 1) Applied emergency config to freeze epoch updates on dedicated pools (11:58). 2) Increased autoscaler stabilization window and bumped min_nodes to prevent thrash (12:25). 3) Configured temporary dedupe filter at api-gateway for requests with identical client-provided id for 1 hour (12:30). 4) Issued billing credit covering estimated overage while investigation ongoing (12:40). Long-term: deploy scheduler patch to ignore unintended epoch deltas and add validation, add stronger prechecks for cron timezone context, and publish recommended client-side idempotency guidance.
Root cause: scheduler epoch drift caused by maintenance job applying a timezone-shifted epoch to the scheduler control-plane for dedicated pool nimbus-dedicated-01. Fix: merged scheduler patch that validates epoch deltas and enforces monotonic leases (merged PR #4217 and deployed 2026-03-12 02:10 UTC). Added api-gateway dedupe as safety net. Customer outcome: duplicate completions reduced to <0.5%, autoscaler stabilized, and billing credit issued for anomalous token consumption (credited on 2026-03-11 invoice). Ticket status moved to Resolved after verification period and customer acceptance.
1) Scheduler: add epoch delta safety guard and integration test for DST/timezone edgecases - owner @infra-scheduler, due 2026-03-17
2) Runbook: create 'epoch drift' playbook and checklist for maintenance jobs - owner @sre, due 2026-03-16
3) Autoscaler: add hysteresis and backoff when inflight counters change >30% in 2m - owner @autoscaler-team, due 2026-03-19
4) Docs/SDK: publish idempotency header guidance and recommend client-generated request_id best practices - owner @developer-experience, due 2026-03-18
5) Billing: finalize credit calculation and confirm invoice adjustment with customer - owner @finance, due 2026-03-13

Additional notes:
2026-03-11 09:20 - Customer (Nimbus ops lead, Elena Verma): Confirmed service stability and accepted billing credit proposal. Requested post-incident summary and recommendations.

Issue summary: Beginning 2026-03-12 09:10 UTC, a subset of streaming inference requests from customer Streambean Analytics experienced elevated p95/p99 tail latency and occasional streaming stalls. Initial symptoms looked like cross-region egress to eu-west for sessions that normally use us-east, increasing TTFB and triggering client-side timeouts.

Impact: Affects ~4% of Streambean's traffic on their dedicated pool; observable p99 increase from ~220ms to ~1.6s for streaming start, and intermittent partial payloads/stream reconnects. Customer reports user-visible delays in live transcript and webhook timeouts.

Environment: Production, dedicated capacity for Streambean Analytics (customer_id sbn-224). Edge nodes in us-east showed healthy health checks; routing decisions show repeated selection of eu-west egress for some account-tagged requests.

Requested action: Triage routing decision logic, confirm rollback or mitigation, provide ETA for permanent fix and post-incident action items.
Customer-facing latency regressions on streaming endpoints leading to transcript delays and occasional client reconnects. Business impact: degraded demo/live usage for Streambean (dedicated).
1) Use Streambean account token (account tag sbn-224) to open streaming chat session against streaming endpoint using model gpt-open-13b-v1.
2) Send initial prompt with ~80 token system and call stream; observe TTFB and streaming start time in client.
3) Repeat across 100 sessions around 2026-03-12 09:00-10:30 UTC time window. ~4% of sessions will show >1.2s TTFB and occasional stalled chunk after first 3-5 tokens.
4) On platform side, query route decision logs for request IDs; look for route_score and selected_egress_region fields.
2026-03-12T09:13:21Z request_id=req-8f3a route_score_primary=0.4999 route_score_secondary=0.5001 selected_egress=eu-west latency_connect=760ms streaming_start=1.42s
2026-03-12T09:17:03Z request_id=req-b1c2 route_score_primary=0.5000 route_score_secondary=0.5000 selected_egress=us-east latency_connect=210ms streaming_start=0.22s
2026-03-12T09:21:55Z request_id=req-cc4d route_score_primary=0.4998 route_score_secondary=0.5002 selected_egress=eu-west latency_connect=1.02s streaming_start=1.60s
Edge proxy metrics: us-east egress success rate 99.98%, eu-west success rate 99.95% (no health alarms).
Tracing sample: route-eval-v2 module returned floating score values; downstream selection picks highest score with no stable tie-breaker.
Initial hypothesis: path/flap causing normal tie-break behavior to favor eu-west. Network team found no BGP or peering anomalies during window.
Observability: rolling deployment of 'route-eval-v2' change went live 2026-03-11 22:00 UTC with a code change that moves scores from integer buckets to normalized floats and updated rounding logic in router.
Reproducible pattern: accounts with high short-burst session rate produce route_score values that land very close to 0.5, and the new rounding exposed a bias that prefers secondary when scores are tied within floating epsilon.
Confirmed by sim: running production traffic samples through local routing binary reproduces ~3.8% misrouted-to-secondary ratio matching customer percent.
Observability gap: no explicit metric for 'tie_break_bias', added temporary histogram for route_score delta distribution and egress selection ratio per account.
Lucas Ortega (Support) 2026-03-12: Notified customer and created ticket. Provided workaround: pin account to us-east by setting account routing override. Customer accepted temporary workaround.
SRE (Evan Ross) 2026-03-12: Verified network paths and peering; no network-level cause. Pointed to recent routing-service change. Linking PR for review.
Routing Eng (Priya Patel) 2026-03-13: Identified tie-breaker rounding change as root cause. Proposed two options: 1) hotfix to deterministic tie-break (prefer primary when delta < 1e-6), 2) rollback to integer-bucket behavior.
Hotfix deployed 2026-03-13 18:30 UTC: routing-service v2.1.7 patched to include deterministic tie-break rule (prefer primary when score delta < 1e-5) and metric instrumentation added. Immediate effect: Streambean misroute ratio dropped to <0.1% and streaming p99 returned to baseline within 30 minutes.

Follow-ups assigned: ENG-ops ticket to add automated canary gating for routing logic changes (backlog item), alert rule for route selection skew >0.5% on account-level, and postmortem documenting rollout gap and observability shortfall. Customer compensated per SLA and notified.

Issue summary: Multiple customers (initial report: ThinkInk Labs) observed a short-lived but high-rate 5xx spike on websocket-based routes between 2026-03-13T08:10Z and 2026-03-13T08:27Z. Errors surface as HTTP 502/503 from the api-gateway; upstream runtime instances report GPU watchdog timeouts and rapid process restarts.

Impact: Intermittent failures for streaming/chat sessions for ThinkInk Labs (dedicated cluster). Estimated ~80% of websocket sessions opened during the window failed to establish or dropped mid-stream. No data loss reported but significant UX disruption for the customer.

Environment: prod-us-east, dedicated pool for ThinkInk Labs, model variants pinned to gpt-backend-v1. Autoscaling disabled for dedicated pool (customer preference).

Steps to reproduce (customer-provided):
1) Open 40 concurrent websocket streaming sessions that immediately send a 1–2 token handshake followed by a short prompt.
2) Maintain steady creation rate of ~6 connections/sec for 3 minutes.
3) Observe ~30–70% session drop / 502 return from API gateway after a few seconds.

Observed logs & outputs:
- api-gateway logs: repeated upstream "502 Bad Gateway" with upstream reset / connection refused.
- ingress-sidecar: connection spike + "accept queue full" traces around 08:12Z.
- runtime logs on affected instances: repeated "GPU watchdog timeout: kernel stalled" and immediate process SIGABRT/restart.
- Prometheus traces: runtime per-process GPU utilization near 98–100% with kernel preemption events; per-request latency spikes before watchdog.

Customer notes: The workload is websocket-first small-handshake, then short generation. Customer asserts this pattern used to be supported at this scale until last week (they have unchanged client behavior).
2026-03-13 08:20Z — Triage: Support triaged to SRE. Correlated api-gateway 502s with runtime watchdog alerts on the dedicated cluster.

Timeline & correlation:
- 08:10–08:12Z: incoming websocket connection rate increased (ThinkInk warmup).
- 08:12Z: ingress-sidecar accept-queue growth; api-gateway begins to return 502s as upstream sockets refuse.
- 08:12–08:18Z: affected runtime pids show GPU watchdog timeouts; nvml logs show repeated kernel preemption and driver recoveries.

Hypotheses considered:
- H1: sudden fanout of websocket handshakes is saturating runtime event loop and triggering kernel watchdog on GPUs due to synchronous prefetch/initialization path.
- H2: ingress-sidecar accept-queue pressure is causing many half-open handshakes, which amplify latency and cause them to queue on a small set of warmed runtimes, producing hot GPU contention and watchdog timeouts.
- H3: a recent runtime library change (PR 1829) altered kernel launch parameters for small prompt shapes leading to less cooperative scheduling on our GPU drivers under high connection churn.

Evidence:
- Heatmap of requests -> small-sequence launches correlated to failed pids.
- Runtime stack traces show stalls inside memory allocation + cuBLAS init paths prior to watchdog.
- The rate of 5xx decreases when we artificially throttle ingress accept-rate or when we route websocket handshakes to a warm standby pool.

Temporary mitigations tried:
- Lowered websocket accept rate at api-gateway layer for ThinkInk pool (reduces client concurrency). Result: immediate reduction in watchdog hits and 5xx.
- Applied local routing to shift new handshakes to warm standby runtimes with prewarmed KV cache; reduced per-runtime burst.

Next steps planned:
- Roll back or patch runtime PR 1829 in a testbed to measure kernel launch behavior under websocket churn.
- Implement a long-term fix: move init/prefetch off hot GPU thread or add a cooperative init path for small handshake prompts.
- Add an ingress-sidecar backpressure metric alert and an automated soft-rate-limit for websocket handshake fanout.

Additional notes:
Jordan Kim (SRE) (2026-03-13T09:18Z): Correlated api-gateway 502s with runtime GPU watchdogs. I throttled handshake accept at the gateway for ThinkInk pool — error rate dropped immediately. Continuing investigation into runtime startup path.
Marta Alvarez (Runtime Eng) (2026-03-13T10:05Z): Noted PR 1829 changed cuBLAS workspace sizing on small token launches; reproducing locally with websocket-fanout harness. Suspect cooperative scheduling regression under heavy connection churn.
Customer (Anil Rao, ThinkInk Labs) (2026-03-13T10:30Z): We saw a 60% failure rate during our morning batch. Thank you for the throttle — can you confirm no data was lost? We prefer no broad rate limits but will accept temporary mitigation.
Jordan Kim (SRE) (2026-03-13T11:00Z): Confirmed no generation outputs lost — failing requests did not complete. Providing a short-lived retry guidance to client: exponential backoff starting at 250ms for handshake retries. Documented in ticket.
Marta Alvarez (Runtime Eng) (2026-03-13T14:20Z): Runbook item: add a soft prewarm path that performs cuBLAS init on a background thread before accepting a streaming handshake. Experiment scheduled in staging today.
Priya Shah (Support) (2026-03-14T02:10Z): Customer confirmed improved experience after gateway throttle; requesting ETA for permanent fix and whether we can disable the throttle after patch.
Jordan Kim (SRE) (2026-03-14T03:05Z): SRE to coordinate canary of patched runtime in staging, then promote to a subset of dedicated pools. Tentative ETA 48–72 hours pending test results.
Mitigation applied: Gateway handshake-rate throttle for ThinkInk dedicated pool and routing new handshakes to a warm-standby runtime group. Immediate reduction in 5xx observed. Engineering hypothesis points to recent runtime PR 1829 affecting small-launch kernel behavior under connection churn.
Planned permanent fix: Implement background cooperative init for cuBLAS/cuDNN on handshake and test reverting PR 1829 variants. Add ingress-sidecar soft-backpressure and an automated handshake throttling mechanism.
Follow-up actions:
- Eng to run canary with patched runtime (assigned to Marta Alvarez).
- SRE to add new alert for websocket accept-queue growth and GPU watchdog rate (assigned to Jordan Kim).
- Support to coordinate customer communication and remove temporary throttle only after successful canary.
Ongoing: mitigation successful; root cause not yet fully confirmed. Canary and postmortem to be scheduled. Customer updated and monitoring continues.

Issue summary: After the recent HTTP/2 stream refactor in api-gateway (rolled 2026-03-11), several long-running orchestrations that rely on ordered function/tool calls are observing out-of-sequence tool executions. This manifests as earlier tool side-effects being executed after later ones, or occasionally skipped and replayed, causing user-visible duplication or missing state updates.

Impact: Customer AtlasWorks reports inconsistent downstream state for production workflows (payment+fulfillment orchestration). Behavioral impact includes duplicated webhook posts, undo/redo races in their order pipeline, and one customer workflow that resulted in delayed invoice creation. Affects a small cohort (estimated 3% of requests for that tenant) but high-risk for financial flows.

Environment: Dedicated pool for AtlasWorks in prod us-east-1. SDKs in customer stack: python-sdk v0.12.0, ts-sdk v0.9.6. Redwood components implicated: api-gateway HTTP/2 connection pool and http2-proxy path that recently changed stream multiplexing heuristics. Serving runtime shows normal token latency.

Steps to reproduce (high level):
1) Customer provides a streaming orchestration: model calls that issue tool/function invocations in a sequence (authorize -> reserve -> capture).
2) Client opens a single HTTP/2 stream multiplexed across several multiplexed logical channels (or uses SDKs that multiplex).
3) Mid-stream the connection receives a stream-level RST (simulated network blip) and the SDKs perform a reconnect + retry using the platform backoff policy.
4) On resume, function-call acknowledgements are reconciled; however, ordering is not preserved and callbacks/tools are dispatched out of original sequence.

Expected behavior: After reconnect/resume, function/tool calls from a single logical session should be delivered and/or deduplicated in the original order, preserving transactional sequence semantics where the customer relies on ordered side effects.

Actual behavior: Some tool invocations are delivered out-of-order: later tool runs appear to complete before earlier ones, and occasional duplicates occur when the client-side retry and gateway-level retry both re-dispatch the same logical call. Evidence shows request IDs preserved but the delivery ordering across multiplexed channels changes.

Logs / Observed traces (sanitized):
- gateway: stream-reset for stream_id=4823 cause=GOAWAY; reconnect window start=2026-03-11T15:22:10Z
- customer webhook logs: POST /webhook/orders 2026-03-11T15:22:13Z (capture) then 2026-03-11T15:22:12Z (reserve) -> ordering inverted
- serving-runtime trace: request_id=atlas-ord-7f3 token_latency=42ms model=gpt-redwood-13b serve_node=gpu-12
- sdk-python debug: retry_attempts=2 backoff_ms=[150, 500] resume_session_id=sess-993

Attachments: Customer provided minimal reproduction harness and request transcripts in a private S3 link (shared with support).

Additional notes:
2026-03-13 11:03 - AtlasWorks (Customer): Provided transcript and sample orchestration. Noted that issue reproduces ~1 in 30 runs under load. Impact is business-critical for invoicing pipeline.
2026-03-14 12:05 - Support (Aisha): Communicated mitigation workaround to customer (disable multiplexing / fall back to per-request connections) while fix in progress.
Hypothesis 1: New stream owner selection algorithm in http2-proxy can dispatch queued messages from resumed streams in a different ordering across logical channels when stream reset and resume occur concurrently.
Hypothesis 2: SDKs apply local retries and re-emit function calls on reconnect; gateway-level replay/forwarding and SDK retries both send the same call with same request_id but different sequence timing, causing perceived reordering due to race windows.
Reproduction: Created a staging harness that mirrors customer multiplexing pattern (python-sdk v0.12.0 streaming client) and injected RST after 1200ms. Observed ordering inversion in 7/100 runs.
Logs: Gateway queue timestamps show dispatch order changed on resume: queued[callA@15:22:11, callB@15:22:12] -> sent[callB, callA] after resume. SDK ack reconciliation sees both delivered and marks later one first because of channel affinity switch.
Short experiment: Disabling channel-affinity patch in gateway restores ordering in our harness. This narrows scope to the refactor in PR #1892.
Impact matrix: Only multiplexed streaming sessions using per-session resume (not simple request/response) are affected. Dedicated customers with per-request patterns unaffected.
Workaround provided (2026-03-14): Instructed AtlasWorks to disable multiplexed session reuse in SDK (setting SDK_MULTIPLEXING=off) or use per-call connections for critical flows. Both options reduce throughput but preserve ordering.
Short-term fix (in progress): Gateway engineering to revert or mitigate the stream-owner selection behavior introduced in PR #1892. Patch branch created: revert/stream-owner-affinity-1892. Running integration tests against customer harness.
Long-term action items: 1) Add explicit ordering-preservation tests for multiplexed resume scenarios to CI. 2) Add an opt-in header for customers that require strict in-order delivery during stream resume. 3) Update SDK docs with recommended resilience patterns and idempotency token guidance for orchestrations.
Follow-up: Schedule postmortem and customer-facing incident note after fix rollout. Coordinate with AtlasWorks to validate in their dedicated staging before prod rollout.
payload.summary: Misordered function-call delivery after HTTP/2 stream refactor causing out-of-sequence tool side-effects

Issue summary:
Customer reported a sudden increase in tail latency and streaming timeouts starting ~2026-03-13 09:40 UTC. A subset of inference requests originating from Fillmore Health's US-west region are being routed through a remote eu-west hop, adding ~250-500ms extra handshake/TTFB and causing streaming sessions to frequently abort with 504/stream-cancel errors. Impact: elevated p95/p99 for both synchronous generation and streaming endpoints; several production user-facing failures.

Impact:
- Fillmore Health: ~20% of requests during window experienced >1s TTFB and 8% saw streaming disconnects/timeouts.
- Symptoms reported: increased p50->p99 gap, disconnected streams mid-response, client-side retries.

Environment:
- Prod (us-west-2) edge -> Redwood API -> serving runtime pool (dedicated capacity for customer).
- Customer is on enterprise tier with Dedicated capacity and geo-affinity pinned to us-west-2.

Observed behavior:
- Traces show unexpected next-hop: requests from edge proxy in us-west-2 are being forwarded to an intermediate egress proxy in eu-west-1 before reaching the serving runtime.
- TCP RTT for affected flows: ~120ms baseline vs ~420ms when redirected. TLS handshake durations correspondingly larger.
- Streaming protocol aborted at server-side with error: HTTP/1.1 504 Stream Timeout after prolonged TLS handshake.

Expected behavior:
- Requests should maintain local egress path to the serving runtime in us-west-2 with p50/p95 latency within expected SLOs.

Immediate mitigation performed so far:
- Support temporarily pinned customer route to local-pop via account routing tag which reduced affected fraction to <1% within 12 minutes.

1) Use Fillmore Health API key and send continuous streaming generation requests to /v1/stream endpoint from client in us-west-2.
2) Observe p99 and streaming disconnect rate over 10-minute window.
3) Correlate traces (x-request-id) to edge logs and inspect next-hop egress proxy reported in X-Edge-Egress header.
4) Reproduce by forcing account to use global egress policy (simulated) to observe redirection behavior.
[2026-03-13T09:41:12Z] edge-proxy us-west-2 request_id=req-7a2f X-Edge-Egress: pop-eu-west-1-02; tls_handshake_ms=380; status=stream_cancel 504
[2026-03-13T09:41:13Z] serving-runtime us-west-2 request_id=req-7a2f accepted; kv_warm=false; recv_bytes=1024; process_ms=120
[2026-03-13T09:43:48Z] account-routing: Fillmore-acc (tag: enterprise-dedicated) -> routing-decider assigned egress pop-eu-west-1-02 due to transient route score flip

Aisha Kapoor (Support) 2026-03-13T09:45:00Z: Customer reported ~30% of streaming sessions timed out. Collected sample request ids and escalated to SRE. Pinning customer to local-pop reduced errors during test window.
Connor Lee (SRE) 2026-03-13T10:02:00Z: Initial hypothesis: BGP community-based failover policy caused a temporary preference for eu-west egress for certain prefixes. Pulling network telemetry now. Not seeing capacity pressure on us-west serving pool.
Morgan Chen (Network) 2026-03-13T10:15:00Z: Confirmed transient route advertisement from a partner transit caused prefer-eu community to be attached; rolling back community filters for affected prefixes should stop redirects. Applying mitigation now.
Aisha Kapoor (Support) 2026-03-13T10:28:00Z: Informed customer of temporary mitigation; monitoring for residual impact. Customer acknowledged and requested postmortem.
Traces show consistent X-Edge-Egress header set to eu-west-1 for affected requests; correlation with netflow shows outbound AS path included partner-as-64521 during window.
No evidence of serving-runtime CPU/GPU saturation; KV cache warmup unaffected; increased latency coincides with extra cross-region hop and TLS handshake timeouts.
Routing-decider logs: recent weight recalculation at 2026-03-13T09:39:54Z applied transient penalty to us-west-2 due to a measured upstream health probe failure (false-positive) from partner network.
We observed higher connection churn on the partner peering session; partner has an upstream route flap which attached a prefer-eu community onto our prefixes for a short window.
Mitigation: network team rolled back partner community filter and enforced local-pop preference for account routing tags. Support pinned Fillmore Health to their Dedicated us-west-2 pool until the routing-decider policy is updated.
Long-term fixes: 1) Update routing-decider to require multi-probe confirmation before applying inter-region penalties for prefixes with Dedicated affinity. 2) Add synthetic egress health probes to detect false-positive probe failures earlier. 3) Create automated rollback if cross-region egress rate for affinity-bound accounts exceeds threshold.
Customer communication: notified Fillmore Health about root cause and mitigations; provided timeline for permanent fix and agreed to formal postmortem.
payload.summary: Out-route redirection causing long-tail inference latency and streaming timeouts for enterprise account

Issue summary:
Brightline Insurance Security team requested detailed clarification on (a) the audit log export format/schema and (b) retention controls for Redwood Dedicated / Redwood Private. They want an example payload and a clear statement of what is/is not included (e.g., prompts, generated text, keys, PHI).

Impact:
Blocking completion of their security questionnaire and internal auditability review. This is a gating item for advancing from security review to procurement.

Customer questions (verbatim-ish):
1) “Do you provide an audit log export? What format (JSON/CSV/SIEM) and can it be streamed?”
2) “Please provide the schema/fields and a sample event.”
3) “What is the default retention period? Can we configure retention (e.g., 7/30/90/365 days) and do we control where logs are stored?”
4) “Do logs include prompt / completion content or customer data?”
5) “Can we export to our SIEM (Splunk/Datadog/CloudWatch) and how often?”

Context:
- This came up during Brightline’s regulated-workloads security review.
- Brightline indicated strict auditability requirements (access/auth events, admin changes, config changes, and request metadata correlation).

Requested output:
- Provide customer-facing answer (approved language) + sample payload reference.
- Confirm retention knobs and what’s plan-dependent vs. generally available.
- Track follow-ups for Docs + evidence pack index update.

Links:
- Slack: #sales thread “brightline insurance security review asks” (ref: sources/slack/sales/1746490044-brightline-insurance-security-review-asks.json)
- Related security FAQ: sources/confluence/sales-enablement/security-faq/regulated-workloads-security-faq.json
- Evidence pack index: sources/confluence/security-and-compliance/compliance-evidence/abm-pilot-security-evidence-pack-index.json
2025-05-16 (Naomi Feldman, Reporter): Creating ticket to track Brightline’s audit log export + retention questions. They asked for schema + sample event and whether logs contain prompt/completion content. Need response by early next week to keep them on track for June procurement window.
2025-05-16 (Olga Petrov, Assignee): Acknowledged. I’ll draft a customer-safe response for Naomi/AE and validate retention + export capabilities with SE + Security. Looping in Docs for a durable artifact we can reuse across regulated accounts.
2025-05-17 (Markus Klein, Solutions Engineering): From prior regulated deep dives: audit logs are available for Dedicated + Private. For Private deployments, customers can configure export destination (e.g., customer-owned object storage / SIEM forwarder depending on deployment). We should be explicit that content logging (prompts/completions) is NOT part of platform audit logs. Audit logs focus on access/admin/config + request metadata. Recommend referencing the audit log export example once the snippet is merged.
2025-05-17 (Dr. Aisha Rahman, Security): Please avoid hard-coding “default retention = X days” unless we confirm per offering. We can state: retention is configurable and can be set per tenant/policy; options may vary by deployment mode and contract. Also confirm language: Redwood does not include prompt/completion bodies in audit logs by default. We should say that customers can choose what to log in their own application layer, but Redwood platform audit logs are separate.
2025-05-18 (Olga Petrov): Draft response (for review):
- Export formats: JSON Lines (newline-delimited JSON) available; CSV can be provided for limited event types on request; integrations for SIEM via scheduled export or forwarding agent (Private) depending on environment.
- Delivery: batch export on a schedule (hourly/daily) and on-demand export supported; streaming/real-time forwarding is available in Private deployments where the customer manages the log forwarder.
- Scope: events include authentication events, user/admin actions, policy/config changes, key management configuration changes, and request metadata (request_id/trace_id, model identifier, timestamp, status code, tokens counts when available). Does NOT include prompts/completions or customer payload bodies.
- Security: logs are encrypted in transit; at rest encryption depends on deployment mode (Hosted/Dedicated vs Private). For Private, customer controls storage + encryption keys (KMS/HSM integration supported per deployment).
- Retention: configurable retention windows; exact ranges depend on plan and deployment. Customers can export logs to their own storage for longer retention.
Asking SE to sanity check fields + sample payload.
2025-05-19 (Evan Scott, Solutions Engineering): Sanity check: include these common fields we’ve shown in deep dives: event_time, event_type, actor (user/service), actor_ip, auth_method, tenant_id, resource_type, resource_id, action, outcome, request_id, trace_id, region, user_agent (where applicable). For request metadata events: route, model, token_counts (prompt_tokens, completion_tokens), latency_ms, status_code. We should be careful: token counts/latency are present for API requests; admin events won’t have them.
2025-05-20 (Kira Thompson, Docs): I can add a short doc section “Audit logs: export + schema (high level)” and link from the regulated workloads landing page + security FAQ. Need final approved language from Security (Aisha/Naomi) and a sample payload. If we can reference the examples repo snippet, that’s best. Target: end of week.
2025-05-21 (Olga Petrov): Sent customer-facing response to Naomi/Avery for delivery to Brightline (pending final sign-off from Security). Included:
- Audit logs do not contain prompts/completions by default.
- Export available (JSONL) with example event.
- Retention is configurable; for long-term retention export to customer-controlled storage.
Also noted: If Brightline needs a specific Splunk HEC format, we can provide guidance but they may implement transform in their forwarder.
2025-05-22 (Naomi Feldman): Delivered response to Brightline security contact. They asked one follow-up: “Can you confirm whether request metadata includes end-user identifiers?” I responded that Redwood logs identify the calling API key/service principal and tenant; end-user identifiers are customer-defined and not inherently present unless the customer includes them in headers/metadata and chooses to log them on their side.
2025-05-27 (Daniel Carter, Compliance Support): Evidence pack update suggestion: add a one-page appendix listing audit log event categories + sample JSON (redacted). Also add a note on retention being policy-driven and export for extended retention. I can update the evidence pack index once Docs publishes the canonical page.
2025-05-29 (Olga Petrov): Marking resolved. Brightline confirmed this satisfies their questionnaire section. Remaining items are general (SOC 2 request handled separately). Follow-ups created for Docs + evidence pack index.
Provided Brightline Insurance a customer-facing explanation of audit log export formats (JSONL), high-level schema/fields, and retention/export approach. Shared/pointed to a sample payload (redacted) and clarified that platform audit logs do not include prompt/completion content by default. Created follow-ups for Docs and evidence pack index to make the answer durable for other regulated prospects.
payload.summary: Brightline Insurance: Audit log export schema + retention controls questions (regulated security review)

Issue summary:
Aurelius Health reports a sustained elevation in 5xx responses (502/504) on their embedding bulk upload route starting ~2026-03-13 10:45 PDT. Errors surface at the API gateway with upstream resets.

Impact:
- Customer embedding ingestion failing for ~40% of requests during peak upload window (10:30-11:20 PDT).
- Affects a single dedicated tenant pool for Aurelius Health; customer reports failed uploads in production, blocking nightly ETL.

Environment:
- Dedicated pool: ded-pool-az2-usw2 (GPU nodes: A100-80GB, driver image: nvidia-driver:525.89)
1) Customer issues large embedding batch (multipart/streamed) of ~250k vectors via /v1/embeddings:batch endpoint
2) Requests stream concurrently from 8 worker processes (concurrency ~64), each using keepalive connections
3) After ~10-15 minutes of sustained throughput, API gateway begins returning 502 and 504s; upstream runtime logs show NVML reset messages and abrupt worker exits
Sequence of events observed in metrics and logs: (a) api-gateway accept queue grows; (b) keepalive timeouts increase; (c) serving-runtime reports 'NVML: GPU reset' and 'watchdog: runtime exit' followed by rapid restarts; (d) Autoscaler attempts to replace failed pods but new pods receive the same uploads and also fail, amplifying 5xx rate.
apigw: 502 spike at 2026-03-13T17:02:11Z; request_id x-az2-9982
runtime stderr: 'NVML: GPU reset detected on device 0'
node dmesg: 'GPU hang: ch 0 faulted; forced reset'
serving-runtime: OOM not observed; CPU steady ~70%, but GPU reset correlates with 99th latency spikes
netstat: listen backlog rising from 128 -> 1024 within 90s during the event
keepalive/conn metrics: active keepalive count drops; handshakes increase 5x
1) Throttled customer's ingestion to concurrency 16 and reduced per-worker streams to 2 (immediate reduction in 5xx to <5%).
2) Temporarily routed Aurelius Health traffic to warm spare dedicated pool (ded-pool-az2-usw2-spare) with older driver image (nvidia-driver:520.78) — success for short window.
3) Customer committed to staggering uploads (5 minute cooldown between batches) pending root cause fix.
Hypothesis A: Recent nvidia driver 525.89 has a regression under sustained multi-process CUDA context churn with large streaming uploads leading to GPU hangs and NVML resets.
Hypothesis B: Combined effect of high accept-queue/backlog on API gateway + immediate fanout to busy GPUs causes increased PCIe contention and triggers existing driver corner case.
Checked: No kernel OOMs, no container OOMs. NVML resets present in kernel logs across 4 different node instances in the pool. Memory fragmentation on GPU observed after ~12 minutes of sustained upload in stress tests.
Repro: Synthetic load runner reproduces GPU reset after ~9-12 minutes when running 64 concurrent small-stream embedding inserts on driver 525.89; not reproducible on 520.78 under same load.
Related PR: runtime change to gate immediate routing of queued requests to newly created pods is proposed (see PR https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/4871) to reduce stampede.
Telemetry: Trace shows keepalive churn increases TLS handshake rate 4x before resets — indicates connection churn may exacerbate driver behavior due to sudden new cuda contexts.
Short term: We applied per-tenant throttling and migrated Aurelius Health to a spare pool running driver 520.78 which restored normal success rates. Medium term: Scheduled driver rollout to driver 520.78 on ded-pool-az2-usw2 during maintenance window 2026-03-15 02:00 UTC. Long term: Runtime PR to implement ingress-queue drain and backoff on pod replacement merged and staged for canary (PR #4871). Postmortem and driver upgrade verification runbook linked. Customer asked for confirmation once stable; CS to follow up post-maintenance.
1) Perform staged driver downgrade on ded-pool-az2-usw2 in maintenance window (2026-03-15).
2) Canary PR #4871 in non-customer dedicated pools and observe accept-queue and pod-replacement behavior under synthetic load.
3) Create KB article for customers advising recommended ingest concurrency limits for large embedding uploads and the option to use spare pools if available.
4) Schedule postmortem with runtime/driver/infra teams and share to Aurelius Health within 48h of completion.
Maya Chen (Support) 2026-03-13T11:12:00Z: Initial report received from Aurelius Health. Asked for request IDs, timestamps, and whether uploads are compressed/multipart. Escalated to SRE due to GPU reset logs.
Luis Ortega (SRE) 2026-03-13T11:28:00Z: Observed NVML reset traces on 3 different runtime nodes in ded-pool-az2-usw2. Correlation window matches customer's bulk ingestion. Opening investigation; tagging runtime/driver teams.
Priya Nambiar (Runtime Eng) 2026-03-13T12:05:00Z: Noted driver image 525.89 in pool. Past incidents showed intermittent hangs under heavy pci-bandwidth + multipart streaming. Spun up spare pool with 520.78 for repro.
Aurelius Health (Customer) 2026-03-13T12:22:30Z: Confirmed reduced concurrency workaround improved success rate for recent batch. Requesting ETA for permanent fix and whether this will recur.
Luis Ortega (SRE) 2026-03-13T13:40:00Z: Autoscaler behavior contributed to amplification: new nodes immediately received queued uploads and hit the same driver hang. Plan: implement short ingress-queue drain + retry-backoff to avoid stampede during restarts.
Maya Chen (Support) 2026-03-14T09:15:00Z: Customer notified of temporary mitigations and scheduled maintenance window for driver upgrade on 2026-03-15 02:00 UTC. Provided checklist and expected downtime ~3-5 minutes per node.
payload.summary: Embedding bulk upload causing elevated 5xx (502/504) from API gateway; correlated with GPU driver resets and keepalive drops

Issue summary:
Customer reports a one-time spike on their provisional invoice for a nightly batch embeddings job. The provisional invoice shows an overage line but the expected provisional credit (hourly buffer / warmup credit) was not applied. The timing coincides with a scheduled tokenizer micro-upgrade that changed token counts for the affected dataset.

Impact:
- Vertex Analytics saw a provisional overage charge of ~USD 1,200 on 2026-03-09 provisional invoice.
- Customer is on Dedicated plan with reserved capacity; unexpected overage caused an autopay failure alert.
- Customer requests explanation and provisional credit reconciliation prior to final invoice.

Environment:
- Customer org: Vertex Analytics (dedicated)
- Region: us-west-2 production
- Job: nightly-batch-embed-v2 (approx 1.2M documents, microbatching)
- Model variants: openlm-embed-3b (quantized variant served during fallback)

Steps to reproduce / Observed sequence:
1) 2026-03-09 01:45 UTC: Tokenizer micro-upgrade (deploy ID: tok-2026-03-09-01) rolled to us-west staging then promoted to prod at 02:10 UTC.
2) 2026-03-09 03:00 UTC: Vertex starts nightly-batch-embed job hitting dedicated endpoints.
3) 2026-03-09 03:05–03:45 UTC: Batch processor reports slightly higher token counts per document (+8% on average) and several files were re-tokenized due to new normalization rules.
4) 2026-03-09 04:00 UTC: Metering postbacks for batch show increased token counts to billing pipeline.
5) 2026-03-09 05:00 UTC: Billing provisional invoice generated without applying the hourly buffer/warmup provisional credit for this job.
6) 2026-03-10: Customer noticed provisional overage and opened support ticket.

Logs / Attachments:
- Attached: sample-postback-entries-2026-03-09.csv (from customer)
Deploy tokenizer vX to prod (tok-2026-03-09-01)
Run nightly-batch-embed-v2 with same input set
Inspect metering postback token counts and compare to pre-upgrade baseline
Check postback windowing and hourly-buffer credit application logs
Batch job token counts increased after tokenizer micro-upgrade and provisional invoice reflected overage without the expected warmup/hourly buffer credit being applied.
Tokenization changes should update token counts in metering but provisional credits (hourly buffer / warmup) should still be applied to eligible jobs; final invoice should reconcile any provisional overage if mitigation is applied.

Additional notes:
2026-03-10 11:20 - Customer (Vertex Analytics - Sara Kim): Provided sample-postback-entries-2026-03-09.csv and clarified that they expect warmup credits for the first 2 hours of the job per their dedicated contract.
2026-03-10 16:00 - SRE (Liam O'Connor): Confirmed duplicate postbacks (3xx/5xx retry loop) observed for postback shard 17 between 03:07–03:20 UTC; de-dupe worker lagged behind due to GC event. Filing INT-391 for de-dupe worker fix.
2026-03-11 12:10 - Support (Aisha): Notified customer we are investigating and asked patience; promised provisional hold decision within SLA window.
2026-03-12 09:00 - Finance (Maya Singh): Approved provisional hold for final invoice pending reconciliation; requested documented delta and proposed credit amount before release.
Initial hypothesis: Tokenizer upgrade increased token counts which caused legitimate higher usage — requires customer-facing explanation.
Secondary hypothesis: Duplicate postbacks during re-tokenization window caused inflated metering leading to overcharge; de-dupe lag observed in logs and linked to GC pause on de-dupe-worker-17.
Metering analysis: Aggregated postbacks for job nightly-batch-embed-v2 between 03:00–04:00 UTC; total tokens reported: 13,480,912. Pre-upgrade baseline average for same job historically: 12,400,000 (+8.7%).
  - Duplicates identified: ~748,000 tokens (approx 5.5% of reported), confirmed by identical postback fingerprints re-ingested with new token counts after re-tokenize pass.
  - Tokenizer delta: ~332,000 tokens (approx 2.5%) attributable to changed normalization (emoji decomposition + new punctuation rules).
Billing pipeline: Hourly buffer/warmup credit calculation triggers during ingestion window; check shows credit was not attached because the postback aggregator marked the job as 'non-eligible' for buffer due to a transient job-tag metadata mismatch introduced by the batch-processor update at 02:58 UTC.
Root causes (combined): 1) Duplicate postbacks during re-tokenization due to de-dupe-worker GC pause; 2) Batch-processor metadata tag rename (tag: warmup_elig -> warmup_eligible) resulted in missing eligibility flag for credit application; 3) Tokenizer change contributed small natural token increase but not the majority of overage.
Mitigation steps taken (2026-03-12):
1) Billing placed provisional hold on final invoice for Vertex Analytics pending reconciliation (Finance approval).
2) Issued a provisional credit of USD 720 to offset the duplicate-postback portion while full reconciliation completes.
3) Hotfix deployed to de-dupe worker to prevent GC-induced re-ingestion (INT-391 linked).
4) Batch-processor tag mapping rollback applied to restore warmup eligibility for reprocessed postbacks; re-run of aggregator scheduled for 2026-03-12 22:00 UTC.
Planned follow-ups:
- Re-run postback aggregation for the 2026-03-09 window and recompute final token totals (Owner: Diego Morales) by 2026-03-13.
- Generate formal reconciliation statement and proposed final credit (Owner: Finance - Maya Singh) by 2026-03-13.
- Add monitoring alert for de-dupe-worker GC pauses and tag-mapping drift (Owner: SRE).
- Communicate outcome to customer with breakdown and final invoice adjustment or waiver as appropriate.
Customer communication:
- 2026-03-12 15:00 Support informed customer of provisional credit and hold; they acknowledged and requested final reconciliation.
Final invoice will be adjusted to remove duplicate-induced tokens and reapply eligible warmup/hourly buffer credits; customer to receive full reconciliation report and either invoice adjustment or waiver depending on final delta.

payload.description:
Issue summary:
- Customer on Dedicated (Summit AI) reported a sudden throughput drop (tokens/sec) and elevated queueing during a scheduled window.
- We correlated the drop with internal FP8/INT8 benchmark jobs that inadvertently consumed capacity in the same H100 node pool used for the customer’s Dedicated deployment.

Customer impact:
- Time window: 2026-02-16 02:10–03:05 UTC
- Symptoms: lower sustained throughput, increased p95 latency, intermittent request timeouts at peak concurrency.
- Scope: Summit AI Dedicated H100 pool in us-east.

Environment:
- Dedicated cluster/pool: dedicated-prod-use1-h100
- Region: us-east

Detection:
- Customer email to Support + Console screenshots showing throughput reduction.
- SRE saw increased scheduler queue depth for the dedicated namespace and elevated GPU utilization from non-dedicated workloads.

Issue summary: After a CSV upload via the Console ingest flow, the customer sees frequent rerank quality regressions and intermittent 5xxs. Impact: ~12% of search queries return inverted top-k (relevant doc falls out of top 10) and ~4% of rerank requests return 500/502 when embedding dims are detected as mismatched. Environment: LexisSearch production account (enterprise tenant), ingest via Console CSV upload from EU office that uses Latin-1 default encoding. Steps to reproduce:
1) Upload sample CSV with CRLF line endings and ISO-8859-1 (Latin-1) encoded file via Console -> Ingests -> CSV import.
2) Trigger a rerank API call on the newly ingested dataset (route: /v1/rerank with reranker-v1).
3) Observe rerank scores and API responses.
Observed behavior: Some CSV rows are parsed with an extra leading invisible character (0xA0 / non-breaking space) in the first field, which causes the ingest preprocessor to treat that row as a new batch boundary. This shifts the mapping between embedding vectors and document IDs for a subset of the batch. The embeddings-service detects a dimension mismatch (expected 768, got 769 after an accidental padding conversion) and triggers a CPU fallback path, causing elevated latency and occasional 500s when the fallback queue is saturated. Expected behavior: Console should normalize charset to UTF-8 and strip leading invisible chars so row-to-id mapping remains stable. Embedding dim should remain consistent and fallback should not be triggered unless model actually emits different dims.
Initial hypothesis: Latin-1 encoded CSV + CRLF combined with a trim-sanitizer that only runs on UTF-8 input caused an extra non-printable insertion during ingestion. Batching logic uses a row delimiter heuristic that is charset-sensitive, resulting in off-by-one index alignment between doc metadata and embedding vector batch.
Relevant logs (redacted):
[2026-03-09T18:02:13Z] ingest-csv: file_open: charset=ISO-8859-1, line_ending=CRLF, rows=12, columns=6
[2026-03-09T18:02:13Z] preprocess: normalize_line_endings -> applied: false (file not flagged as UTF8)
[2026-03-09T18:02:14Z] batcher: grouping rows -> batch_size=8 -> boundary_indexes=[0,4,8,12]
[2026-03-09T18:02:15Z] embed-service: accept_vectors -> expected_dim=768, received_dim=769 -> queue_fallback=triggered
[2026-03-09T18:02:20Z] reranker: request_id=abc123 -> status=500 -> error="embedding-dim-mismatch"
2026-03-10T09:12:00Z - Aisha Patel (Support): Customer reports search relevance regressions after CSV ingest. Initial triage: ask for sample CSV and request run of a debug upload with UTF-8 enforced.
2026-03-10T10:03:22Z - Marcus Liu (SRE): Received sample CSV. Observed non-breaking spaces at row starts (0xA0) when file decoded as Latin-1. Reproduced locally by saving file as ISO-8859-1 and uploading via Console. Creating ingest debug trace.
2026-03-10T14:40:11Z - Nisha Rao (Eng, embeddings): Instrumented embedding ingress to log raw byte lengths. Found one vector padded with a null byte after conversion; looks like sanitizer returned different length when decoder encountered 0xA0. Adding hypothesis to investigation notes.
2026-03-11T08:55:00Z - LexisSearch (Customer): Provided example query IDs and before/after rankings. Confirmed that a specific document jumps from rank 1 to outside top 20 for multiple queries. Will provide full CSV with PII stripped.
2026-03-12T16:23:45Z - Marcus Liu (SRE): Deployed temporary mitigation: force UTF-8 decode on Console ingest path and log occurrences. Early results: the rate of inverted top-k dropped from ~12% to ~1.5% for new uploads. However historical datasets still show regressions; plan follow-up migration.
2026-03-13T11:30:02Z - Aisha Patel (Support): Notified customer of the temporary mitigation and asked if they can re-upload as UTF-8 for immediate relief. Customer requested permanent fix and dataset migration guidance.
Findings summary:
- Root trigger: Console CSV importer did not force UTF-8 decoding. When ISO-8859-1 files contained non-breaking spaces (0xA0) or high-bit characters, the preprocessor that strips whitespace failed to recognize them, leaving invisible bytes at field boundaries.
- Side effect: Batcher heuristic that detects row boundaries for multiplexing relied on a sanitized delimiter index; the invisible bytes changed tokenization length heuristics causing an off-by-one alignment between metadata array and embeddings array.
- Embedding pipeline: The embedder runtime applied a conversion step that, when encountering certain byte patterns, appended a padding byte (0x00) to align vector proto. This caused a single-vector dim mismatch (769) which triggers CPU fallback and sometimes overflow in fallback queue -> 500/502s.
- Mitigation proof-of-concept: Forcing UTF-8 decode + NFKC normalization at ingest eliminates the garbage byte and prevents batch misalignment.
- Risk areas: Existing datasets already ingested with Latin-1 remain misaligned in vector-store; re-ingest is required to correct mapping. There is risk of similar issues for other one-off encodings (Windows-1252).
- Links: Slack thread #support-lexissearch, runbook: confluence/pages/INGEST-CHARSET-NORM, debug PR: github.com/redwood/ingest/pull/499 (draft).
Temporary mitigation: Forced UTF-8 decode and NFKC normalization in Console ingest pipeline rolled out to us-west-2 on 2026-03-12 (hotfix). This reduced new-uploads regressions by ~87%.
Permanent plan: Engineering will ship a hardened sanitizer that: (1) detects file charset and coerces to UTF-8, (2) normalizes line endings and invisible whitespace, (3) validates row-to-vector counts before committing batch, and (4) rejects uploads with mixed encoding with a clear customer-facing error recommending re-save as UTF-8. Target for permanent fix: 2026-03-20.
Customer remediation: Offer LexisSearch one-time bulk re-ingest using a migration tool that re-decodes historical CSVs to UTF-8 and re-submits to embeddings pipeline in a safe dry-run mode. Also providing credits for rerun.
Follow-ups: Create an automated audit to scan existing vector-store for dim outliers and mismatched metadata counts. Add an alert to detect embed-service CPU fallback rate > 0.5% in a 5m window.
