payload.description:
Issue summary: Customers (FinTrove) report that alert webhook payloads sent from Console occasionally arrive at their downstream automation with the tracehook parameters missing or truncated. The tracehook parameter contains a route token and trace_id that downstream systems use to correlate alerts with traces. When truncated, the customer's automated triage removes the link to the trace and human investigation becomes manual.

Impact: Enterprise customer FinTrove experiences loss of trace links for a subset (~6-7%) of alerts during high-cardinality alerting windows. This increases MTTR since on-call must manually search traces. The problem appears intermittent and correlates with alerts that include long route tokens or extra context in the alert payload.

Observed behavior: Console sends webhook POSTs where the body is truncated at ~8192 bytes (observed) and the "tracehook" parameter is partially or completely missing on the receiving side (customer webhook endpoint logs). Alerts otherwise show as delivered (no retry).

Expected behavior: Webhook POSTs should include the full JSON payload or form payload including tracehook params so downstream automation receives trace links reliably.
1) Create a console alert that includes expanded context and uses a route_token that is ~2.5k chars (simulated long base64 token).
2) Configure webhook notification to point at a test endpoint that logs raw request bodies (customer provided curl server).
3) Trigger alert by firing synthetic events that match the alert rule, ensuring payload size will exceed 8kb after url-encoding metadata fields.
4) Observe test endpoint logs and compare to the payload shown in Console 'Delivered' audit trail.
edge-proxy (us-east-1) request_id=abc123 - upstream POST to customer webhook started: 2026-03-10T16:12:02Z
console-webhook-dispatcher dispatcher_id=wd-77 - payload_length=8144 bytes before encoding, encoded_length=10238 bytes
customer-endpoint logs - received body length: 8192, tracehook param truncated after 3k chars
nginx error: client intended to send too large body: 8192 bytes (observed on staging repro proxy)
Initial hypothesis: encoding/transfer mechanism used by Console webhook sender switches to application/x-www-form-urlencoded for legacy alerts and percent-encoding expands token size causing upstream proxy to drop/truncate body.
Reproduced in staging by sending alert with long token - observed truncation at ~8192 bytes in test endpoint captured with tcpdump and confirmed by comparing with dispatcher payload copy stored in S3 (partial).
Edge NGINX config uses default large_client_header_buffers and client_body_buffer_size that result in rejection/truncation for large encoded form payloads when combined with long headers and query params.
Console audit shows 'Delivered' status because the webhook sender received a 200 from the proxy before the proxy forwarded truncated body to the customer endpoint (proxy returned success on chunk 1).
Workaround confirmed: switching webhook to application/json POST (not form-encoded) preserves tracehook field and avoids truncation in our staging repro.
Risk: several customers and internal default alert templates still use the legacy form-encoded path for webhooks; rollout must not break smaller payloads and must preserve backward compatibility.
Maya Chen (Support) 2026-03-10: Customer reported 17 alerts overnight with missing trace links. Provided request captures and suggested temporary change to JSON webhooks but customer asked for a more permanent fix.
Rafael Ortega (SRE) 2026-03-11: Confirmed repro in staging. Suspect nginx buffer limit + percent-encoding expansion. Filed infra task to validate nginx buffers in edge-proxy clusters.
Elena Park (Customer Success) 2026-03-11: Escalated to account exec. Customer requests ETA for fix; prioritized due to enterprise SLAs.
Rafael Ortega (SRE) 2026-03-12: Created PR to switch console webhook sender to always POST application/json and use chunked transfer-encoding for large payloads. PR: github.com/redwood-inference/console/pull/4826. Running canary in staging 2/3 nodes.
Workaround provided to customer: update notification endpoint configuration to 'POST JSON' in Console (Settings > Alerts > Notification Methods) as interim. Documented steps and sample payload provided.
Short-term fix: update edge-proxy nginx config to increase client_body_buffer_size and large_client_header_buffers in us-east-1 to handle encoded payloads during migration window.
Long-term fix: switch webhook sender to application/json + chunked transfer to avoid url-encoding expansion. PR created and under review (see related_github_prs).
Follow-up: add automated e2e test covering large alert payloads and add telemetry to track webhook payload size and downstream truncation events.

payload.description:
Issue summary: Starting 2026-03-12 06:20 UTC, LinguaFlow reported higher first-byte latency (FBT) and intermittent 504 stream disconnects for identical 'replay' chat turns that previously hit the hot prefix cache. Impact: User-facing slowdown on conversational replay flows; p99 FBT increased from ~300ms to ~2s for identical prompts, with ~0.6% of requests hitting 504 stream timeouts during micro-bursts. Environment: Dedicated customer cluster in us-east running gptx-13b-v1 model variants. Observed pattern: The regression affects sequences where the client resends an identical prompt (replay/undo-redo UX) within 5–20s of the prior turn. Instead of a hot-key KV cache hit, some requests take a cold-path multi-shard lookup, increasing token-generation startup time and occasionally triggering the streaming connection to disconnect. This appears correlated with background shard metadata refreshes and a prefetch worker window that briefly returns stale or partial shard maps.
1) Use LinguaFlow replay workload (identical 512-token prompt) with concurrency 8 from us-east. 2) Send same prompt twice with 10s gap. 3) Observe streaming latency for second request. 4) Repeat across 50 iterations to reproduce p99 spikes. Expected: second request should hit KV prefix cache hotpath and have FBT similar to first. Actual: occasional fallback to cold lookup with FBT jump and sometimes 504 if downstream streaming buffer times out.
Sample logs (abridged):
[2026-03-12T06:21:17.842Z] request_id=rf-4a9 shard_map_version=v17 cache_lookup=partial-miss prefetch_worker=busy route=hot-path->fallback fbt=2137ms stream=closed(504)
[2026-03-12T06:21:27.120Z] request_id=rf-4a9 shard_map_version=v17 kv_index_shards=[s1,s2,-] kv_lookup=multi-shard cold_path=true
[2026-03-12T06:22:01.009Z] request_id=rf-7f2 shard_map_version=v18 cache_lookup=hit fbt=312ms stream=ok
Observability notes: most partial-miss events have 'kv_index_shards' containing a '-' placeholder indicating missing shard mapping; these cluster around times when the shard-metadata agent logs a reindex cycle (v16->v18).
Initial hypothesis: a short-lived race between the shard metadata update and the kvcache prefetch worker can create a mapping hole for certain prefixes. When the mapping hole is observed the request falls back to a cold-path multi-shard lookup (synchronous) rather than the async hot prefix fetch, increasing FBT and sometimes exceeding streaming timeouts. Evidence: correlated timestamps between 'shard-metadata:reindex' events and spike windows; traces show additional 1.2s spent waiting on sequential shard lookups. Alternative hypotheses considered: noisy neighbor GPU stalls, network packet loss, or client-side retries — none correlated with observed windows. Reproduction proved deterministic when we forced a metadata refresh during warm cache conditions. Additional note: impact disproportionately affects replay (identical) flows because they expect hot prefix KV hits and have tighter client-side streaming timeouts.

Additional notes:
Customer (LinguaFlow - Support Contact): Noted immediate improvement after workaround. Asked for permanent fix timeline and postmortem.
Workaround: temporarily blocked metadata swap until in-memory index build completed (deployed 2026-03-12 12:40 UTC) and applied conservative prefetch backoff on affected nodes. Root cause: race between shard metadata publication and local index application produced partial shard mappings for some prefixes; requests hitting those partial maps fell back to synchronous multi-shard cold lookups, increasing FBT and causing stream timeouts. Fix: runtime change to make metadata swap atomic (ensure index built then flip), plus safety check that rejects published mapping that would create '-' placeholders. Patch PR created and under review: github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/5172. Rollout plan: canary to 10% of dedicated clusters 2026-03-14, full rollout 2026-03-17 after validation. Postmortem and follow-ups: add canary metric, improve alerting for 'partial-miss' rate, update KV cache runbook.
payload.summary: Partial KV shard metadata gap forces cold-path lookup for identical replay requests, causing FBT/regression and occasional timeouts

payload.description:
Customer reports duplicated external side-effects (multiple webhook posts and duplicated DB writes) when using ephemeral API keys that are chained across long-running multi-tool calls. Pattern observed only when (1) client performs mid-request ephemeral key rotation/refresh, (2) a long-running function/tool call is in-flight, and (3) the SDK retries the request after a transient 5xx or connection drop. Customer uses a hybrid workflow: initial orchestration in TypeScript (serverless) then delegates to a Python worker to run a long tool chain that performs external webhooks and enqueues background jobs. They see duplicate downstream actions ~10-30% of the time during scale tests.
1) Create an ephemeral API key with 30s TTL and configure SDK to auto-refresh via delegated token endpoint.
2) In TypeScript serverless, start a streaming chat that invokes two tools sequentially: (A) outbound webhook POST to third-party, (B) enqueue job to internal queueing service.
3) Hand off session metadata (ephemeral token + idempotency token) to a Python background worker that invokes the same Redwood function chain (tools executed in-process).
4) During the Python worker execution, simulate a transient backend 502 on the final acknowledgement (or close the socket mid-chunk) to trigger SDK retry behavior and a token refresh.
5) Observe whether the webhook receives duplicate POSTs and whether the queue service shows duplicate enqueued jobs.
6) Repeat with variable TTLs (15s, 30s, 60s) and with/without explicit per-tool idempotency keys.
2026-03-10T18:11:32.423Z INFO ts-orch: starting session session_id=sn_94a3 ttl=30s ephemeral_key=ek_...
2026-03-10T18:11:35.990Z DEBUG py-worker: received handoff, idemp_token=idt_12345 tools=[webhook_post, enqueue_job]
2026-03-10T18:11:38.120Z WARN py-worker:webhook: remote 502 on POST https://external.vendor/api/orders 502 Bad Gateway
2026-03-10T18:11:38.121Z ERROR sdk:stream - connection reset by peer during final ack; client will retry; token refresh starting
2026-03-10T18:11:38.450Z INFO auth-service: issued new ephemeral ek_... (chained refresh) for session sn_94a3
2026-03-10T18:11:38.768Z INFO sdk:retry - replaying last chunk with idemp idt_12345; resulted in second webhook POST
2026-03-10T18:11:39.032Z INFO external-webhook: Received POST order_id=ord_99 payload=...
2026-03-10T18:11:39.345Z INFO external-webhook: Received POST order_id=ord_99 payload=...
Initial hypothesis: idempotency token scope is tied to ephemeral key lifetime; when token is reissued mid-flight the SDK normalizes the idempotency header differently between TS orchestration and Python worker leading to a mismatch on server-side dedupe.
Reproduced locally with a synthetic 502 injected into the last chunk. Observed that TypeScript client includes header 'X-Idemp: idt_12345' in handoff metadata, but the Python worker SDK re-encodes it as 'X-Idemp: idt_12345::ek_<new>' when it refreshes/attaches new ephemeral key. Server dedupe uses exact header match, so second replay is treated as distinct request.
Checked server logs: two distinct request IDs processed for the same logical operation within 500ms; dedupe keys did not match due to appended ephemeral key tag in the dedupe hashing path.
Edge-case: if the initial ephemeral key expires before the final ack, the runtime attaches 'auth-chain' baggage to outgoing tool calls; baggage serialization varies by SDK (python vs ts), causing inconsistent normalization across services.
Verified that disabling auto-attach of token metadata in the Python SDK avoided duplication (workaround), but this is not ideal for customers relying on seamless key rotation.
2026-03-10 | Aisha Romero (Customer): We consistently see duplicates when running our k6 scale test. Can you confirm whether the idempotency key should survive an ephemeral key refresh?
2026-03-10 | Ben Carlson (Support): Thanks Aisha — we are triaging. Can you share a small repro? Preferably a minimal TS orchestrator and Python worker snippet and access to a webhook endpoint we can hit during repro.
2026-03-11 | Aisha Romero (Customer): Uploaded repro gist to private GitHub link and opened temporary webhook at https://hook-repro.novaapps/example (valid for 24h). TTL used was 30s. We also tried 60s with same behavior.
2026-03-11 | Eng (runtime): Observed SDK header normalization bug — Python SDK appends ephemeral auth tag to idempotency header during implicit refresh. TS SDK does not. Filing INT follow-up to normalize behavior across SDKs.
2026-03-12 | Ben Carlson (Support): Confirmed repro internally. Workaround documented below; planning SDK patch and server dedupe fallback to normalized base idempotency key.
1) Create INT ticket to align SDK idempotency header serialization across languages (python/ts/go).
2) Implement server-side fallback dedupe that canonicalizes idempotency keys by stripping ephemeral auth suffix for a short grace window (30s).
3) Ship patch to Python SDK to avoid appending ephemeral key to idempotency header when SDK performs implicit refresh; add opt-in behavior toggle.
4) Notify customer when workaround & patch lands and advise on short-term mitigations (explicit per-tool idempotency keys or disabling token auto-attach).
Customer impact: duplicates of external webhook and queue writes leading to idempotency protection failures on third-party systems. Priority elevated given production-scale tests failing.

Issue summary: BrightPost reports a dramatic throughput inversion and sustained tail-latency increase after a staged optimizer push that enabled aggressive continuous batching + KV-prefetch for their tenant. Impact: Several routes for the tenant returned >95th percentile latency spikes (2000-3500 ms) and a sustained decrease in successful QPS despite increased offered load; customer-facing outages for low-latency endpoints were observed for ~45 minutes. They requested immediate guidance to mitigate and a safe stepwise demote plan that preserves session continuity for long-lived conversations.

Environment: Dedicated pool (d-prod-e5), tenant: brightpost-prod, model: redwood/open-7b-v2 pinned at v2026-03-08-optA. Autoscaling policy: aggressive-cpu-driven with continuous-batching enabled and kv-prefetch=true.

Customer request: 1) Immediate mitigation to restore latency SLOs. 2) A low-risk rollback/demote checklist that can be executed during business hours without data loss. 3) Post-incident recommendations to avoid recurrence.
1) Deploy optimizer profile 'optA' to tenant brightpost-prod with continuous_batching=enabled, max_batch_size=256, kv_prefetch=true, quant_profile=dynamic-int8.
2) Ramp traffic in a canary-to-100% pattern over 15 minutes using steady arrived RPS (customer traffic pattern includes many long chat sessions with tokens per session >1000).
3) Observe scheduler increasing batch aggregation window to maintain throughput; KV-prefetch begins preloading large prefix caches leading to memory pressure and eviction churn.
4) Observe token latency tail rising and overall successful QPS dropping as requests are retried or timed out downstream.
2026-03-10T13:42:08Z serving-runtime WARN tenant=brightpost-prod kv_cache_evictions=124532 memory_pressure=0.82
2026-03-10T13:44:02Z scheduler INFO tenant=brightpost-prod avg_batch_size=187 batch_wait_ms=68
2026-03-10T13:45:12Z api-gateway ERROR route=/v1/chat generate 504 downstream_timeout latency_ms=3120
Link to Alertboard: https://redwood.inc/alerts/AB-2026-03-10-1128
Related grafana: https://grafana.redwood.internal/d/serving/tenant-brightpost?from=2026-03-10T13:30:00Z&to=2026-03-10T14:30:00Z
BrightPost Support (2026-03-10 13:48) - 'We started seeing errors and slow responses around 13:35 UTC after the optimizer rollout. Can you roll back to yesterday's behavior? Production impact is ongoing.'
Support (Aisha) (2026-03-10 13:52) - 'Acknowledged. We're triaging. Please keep traffic steady and do not retry bursts. Can you share the last snapshot id from your console snapshot feed?'
SRE (Tom) (2026-03-10 13:58) - 'Initial hypothesis: continuous batching has widened aggregation windows under this workload pattern, and kv-prefetch is causing aggressive memory usage and eviction churn which in turn increases disk/ram I/O. Will attempt a per-tenant throttle and staged demote.'
BrightPost (2026-03-10 14:05) - 'Snapshot id s-2026-03-09-brightpost-001 attached in console. We need a plan that keeps long chat sessions intact.'
Support (Tom) (2026-03-10 14:12) - 'Applying temporary per-tenant max_batch_size=64 and disabling kv-prefetch for brightpost-prod now. Will monitor for 10 minutes then recommend next steps.'
Telemetry shows avg_batch_size jumped from ~24 to ~187 in the 8-minute window after optA rollout. The scheduler's adaptive window increased due to sudden per-tenant token arrival variance.
KV cache metrics: thrash rate increased by 7x; resident set exceeded expected footprint causing host memory_pressure>0.8 and swap activity on some nodes.
Quant_profile dynamic-int8 did not show immediate accuracy regressions on sampled outputs, but may increase model memory footprints in this implementation causing additional GC pressure in the serving runtime.
Confirmed that disabling kv-prefetch and constraining batch size reduces tail latency rapidly in a controlled pilot for 5% shadow traffic.
Mitigation executed (2026-03-10 14:15): Applied per-tenant overrides: continuous_batching=enabled, max_batch_size=64, kv_prefetch=false, batch_wait_ms_target=40. Immediate effect: 95p latency dropped from ~2600ms to ~420ms within three minutes for the pilot group.
Demote plan executed (staged, 2026-03-10 14:30-15:00): Step 1: Create optimizer snapshot of current optA (snapshot id s-2026-03-10-optA). Step 2: Roll traffic to optA-light profile for 25% traffic for 10 minutes (optA-light = continuous_batching=enabled, max_batch_size=48, kv_prefetch=false, quant_profile=static-int8). Step 3: If metrics stabilise, expand to 60% then 100% over 10-minute windows. We followed this staged plan and reached 100% at 15:00 UTC with stable latencies and restored QPS.
Communication: Notified BrightPost via support channel at each step; scheduled post-mortem and follow-up engineering review to harden gating.
Permanent action: Created follow-up PR to implement a per-tenant batching circuit-breaker (see PR #7123) and added conservative defaults for kv-prefetch on dedicated tenants with long-session profiles.
1) Engineering to add a telemetry-derived soft-circuit-breaker that auto-bounds max_batch_size when kv_cache_evictions > threshold for 60s.
2) Product to update optimizer rollout checklist to require a tenant profile classification (long-session vs short-session) and to default kv_prefetch=false for long-session tenants unless explicitly validated.
3) Support to create a tenant-level alerting playbook that surfaces 'batch_size inversion' and recommends immediate per-tenant override commands.
4) Schedule a 2026-03-14 post-incident review with BrightPost and Engineering to validate changes and capture action owners.
payload.summary: Runaway batching cascade: mitigation and tenant demote checklist

Issue summary:
Customer ClariTech reports that when their iOS/Android app is backgrounded for >12s and then resumed, SSE streams frequently reconnect but the final 'terminal' metadata for responses is missing or duplicated, resulting in truncated JSON chunks and client-side parse errors. Impact: multiple end-user sessions see incomplete answers or repeated prefix text.

Impact:
- Several customers in the enterprise account experienced truncated model responses in the UI during mobile app resume flows.
- Affects chat and long-form generation routes using streaming SSE.

Environment:
- Customer mobile app (React Native wrapper + native WebView on Android 13 and iOS 16)
- Production Redwood hosted API, us-east region
- Customer using dedicated capacity with pinned model version

Observed behavior:
- App backgrounded ~15–90s, resumed -> client SDK performs incremental reconnect. Server accepts resume token but final 'end' metadata event (" + end-of-stream metadata + ") never delivered; downstream client eventually times out and attempts full reconnect which yields duplicate prefix tokens.

Expected behavior:
- Resume should reattach and deliver any missing terminal metadata or else perform a clean restart with no duplicated content.

Temporary workaround:
- Customer set SDK to disable resume-on-background (force full reconnect) and increased client-side reassembly timeout to 8s. This reduces truncations but increases perceived latency on resume.

1) Open ClariTech mobile app and start a streaming chat request to Redwood hosted endpoint (SSE enabled).
2) Wait for ~20s of streaming output to begin, then background the app (home button / screen lock).
3) Keep the app backgrounded for 15–90s (observed window).
4) Resume the app — SDK attempts transparent SSE resume using stored session token and sequence number.
5) Observe client logs: resume accepted but final terminal metadata event not emitted; client reassembly times out or later sees duplicated prefix after a fallback full reconnect.
client: resume_request token=rt_XXX seq=243 time=2026-03-10T18:22:37Z
proxy: 200 resume OK -> upstream session id=us-east-7-AB12 seq=243
serving-runtime: stream-chunk id=us-east-7-AB12 seq=243 payload=""
serving-runtime: missing terminal event detected - last-seen-seq=242; no terminal metadata after resume window
client: reassembly_timeout after 8500ms -> performing full reconnect
client: new_session token=rt_YYY seq=0 -> receives duplicate prefix tokens from seq 0..20
03/10 - initial triage by Support: reproduced with ClariTech build v3.4.1 on Android 13 emulator when using RN WebView keepalive/pause behavior.
03/11 - SRE/Serving looked at proxy logs: saw resume accept followed by no terminal event emission from worker; worker reports an in-memory session state flagged as 'thawed' but with pending terminal batch lost during OS-level socket suspension.
03/11 - Hypothesis: client-side background suspend causes TCP/OS stack to drop in-flight keepalive/FIN; intermediate transparent streaming proxy marks original connection stale and upstream worker performs partial flush and frees terminal metadata before client rebinds, so resume is accepted but terminal marker is gone.
03/11 - Additional discovery: client SDK monotonically increments seq before suspend in RN layer; on resume the SDK sends seq+1 which can cause off-by-one acceptance and duplicate prefix on fallback.
03/12 - Reproduced on prod-like staging with a mobile suspend harness; able to trigger missing terminal metadata consistently when background >12s and resume within a 60s window behind our Edge proxy.
Support (Aisha): Logged initial report and requested full HAR and client SDK logs from customer. Asked them to try disabling resume-on-background as a short-term mitigation.
Customer (ClariTech - eng): Sent SDK logs and confirmed workaround reduced truncations but unacceptable UX (longer reconnect). Provided additional traces showing duplicate prefix after fallback.
SRE (Luca): Confirmed resume acceptance in edge logs with no terminal event emitted. Created a staging harness to reproduce using Android emulator. Marking for eng attention.
Eng (Marta R.): Identified that worker flush code treats socket tear as completion and frees terminal metadata if connection has no pending ACKs for >10s. Suggested we make terminal metadata persisted to resume log for 30s to allow client rebinds.
Eng (Luca): Proposing two-part fix: 1) server-side change to retain terminal metadata for short TTL post-flush and accept out-of-order resume within a delta window; 2) client SDK patch to avoid seq increment on suspend and to fall back faster to full reconnect without retransmitting prefix tokens.
Support (Aisha): Scheduled a coordinated release window with ClariTech for the SDK patch + server side change. Customer requested ETA and asked for rollback plan if latency increases.
SRE (Luca): Will roll server-side change to canary (staging -> 5% prod) and monitor stream-tail error rate and duplicate-prefix rate. SDK patch will be cut to customer as pre-release for testing.
In progress: mitigation applied (customer disabled resume-on-background). Engineering patch scoped: server will persist terminal metadata for 30s post-flush and accept resume with seq tolerance ±1; client SDK will be patched to avoid pre-suspend seq bump and quicker full-reconnect fallback. Plan: canary server change 03/13, SDK pre-release to ClariTech 03/13, full rollout pending canary metrics.
payload.summary: Mobile app background suspend causes SSE session thaw reorder and loss of terminal metadata

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customer reports Python SDK streaming calls do not respect configured timeouts. Non-streaming requests time out as expected, but streaming can hang indefinitely when the connection stalls mid-stream (no bytes received) or when the proxy buffers.

Customer impact:
- Production worker processes hang, consuming concurrency slots.
- Customer sees elevated end-to-end latency and occasional request pileups.
- They are hesitant to enable streaming broadly until timeouts are reliable.

Customer context:
- Company: Northwind AI (enterprise)
- Networking: behind corporate egress proxy (TLS intercept) + occasionally slow upstream
- Observed: most frequently when stream starts but then stops emitting chunks for >60s

SDK / environment:
- redwood-sdk-python version: 0.17.2 (per customer)
- Python: 3.11
- HTTP client: httpx (via SDK)
- Deployment: k8s, us-east

Expected behavior:
When user configures a timeout (e.g., 10s overall), streaming generator should raise a timeout exception and abort underlying connection when no data is received within the configured window (or when overall timeout elapses).

Actual behavior:
Streaming generator continues waiting for bytes (appears to block indefinitely) even though `timeout` was passed to the client.

Steps to reproduce (customer repro, adapted):
1) Configure the SDK with a short timeout.
2) Initiate a streaming chat completion.
3) Simulate a stalled stream (customer sees this behind proxy; we reproduced with a local proxy that accepts upstream, sends initial headers + a partial chunk, then stops sending bytes).
4) Observe Python iterator blocks without raising a timeout.

Repro snippet (customer-provided, sanitized):
```python
from redwood import Redwood

client = Redwood(api_key="<redacted>", timeout=10)  # seconds

with client.chat.completions.stream(
    model="rw.chat.v1",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Write a long answer about caching."}],
) as stream:
    for event in stream:
        print(event)
```

What customer sees:
- In certain cases, iteration blocks on `for event in stream:` and never returns.
- No exception is raised.
- Killing the process is the only way to reclaim capacity.

Logs / evidence:
- Customer supplied request IDs where available (they often cannot get request_id when stuck because no terminal event):
  - request_id: rwreq_01HRQJ9Z2W6J6M7KEXAMPLE
- When it does fail, they occasionally see `httpx.ReadTimeout` on non-streaming endpoints, but not on streaming.

Initial hypothesis:
Timeout is being applied to initial connect / request send, but streaming read loop is not enforcing read/overall timeouts consistently. Potentially an httpx streaming iterator path where read timeouts aren’t triggered if the socket is kept open but yields no bytes, or the SDK isn’t passing the timeout config into the streaming context / iter loop.

Requested outcome:
- Confirm whether this is a known issue/regression.
- Provide a workaround (customer needs something they can deploy this week).
- Provide an ETA for a fix release and link to the PR(s) for tracking.
2026-01-17 09:12 PT — Owen Phillips (Support)
Thanks for the detailed repro. A couple of quick questions so we can reproduce precisely:
1) Can you confirm whether you set `timeout` on the Redwood client vs per-request?
2) Do you see the hang after *any* tokens are streamed, or can it also hang before the first event?
3) If you can share, do you have a proxy vendor/name (Zscaler, Netskope, etc.)?

In the meantime, as a mitigation, can you wrap the streaming loop in your own overall timeout (thread/alarm/async cancellation depending on your setup) so you can abort the worker if it stalls? We’ll look for an SDK-level fix so you don’t need to maintain that long-term.
2026-01-17 10:03 PT — Customer (Northwind AI)
1) We set `timeout=10` on the client (constructor). Not per-request.
2) Mostly after some tokens. It starts streaming, then stalls and never resumes.
3) Zscaler (TLS inspection enabled). We can’t change this.

We already have a crude watchdog that kills the pod if a request exceeds 120s, but that’s disruptive (drops in-flight jobs). We need the SDK to throw a timeout so we can retry or fail gracefully.
2026-01-17 11:28 PT — Owen Phillips (Support)
Got it. Looping in the Python SDK owner (Sabrina) + SDK parity TL (Ibrahim). We’ve seen a few proxy-related streaming stalls; we’ll confirm whether our configured timeout is enforced during the streaming read.

Next update by EOD Monday with either workaround guidance or an identified fix path.
2026-01-20 09:41 PT — Sabrina James (Python SDK)
Confirmed repro internally using a local “stalling proxy” (accepts connection, sends headers + first SSE event, then stops sending bytes).

Findings (0.17.x):
- The client-level `timeout` is mapped to httpx request timeout for request setup.
- In the streaming path, we were not consistently applying an overall timeout guard around the event iterator.
- With certain proxy/socket behaviors, httpx doesn’t raise `ReadTimeout` in our loop because we’re effectively waiting on the streaming response iterator without a bounded read window in a way that triggers the configured timeout.

Plan:
- Implement the standardized timeout model for Python (connect/read/overall) and enforce overall timeout for streaming iteration.
- Ensure cancellation closes the underlying response and surfaces a typed SDK timeout error that includes `request_id` when available.

Tracking PRs:
- PR-850 (timeout model plumbing)
- PR-854 (streaming disconnect handling + error typing)

Workaround (immediate):
Until the fix ships, wrap the stream consumption in an application-level overall timeout and explicitly close the stream on timeout. If you’re using sync code, you can do this with a watchdog thread that calls `stream.close()` and aborts the request; for async, use `anyio.fail_after` / `asyncio.wait_for` around the stream consumption.

We’ll provide a concrete snippet once we confirm the best pattern with minimal side effects.
2026-01-20 14:12 PT — Ibrahim Khan (SDK parity TL)
Adding: this is in-scope for the cross-language timeout standard. The new default model is:
- connect timeout
- read timeout (max time between bytes/events)
- overall timeout

Streaming will primarily enforce read + overall. We’ll also add a conformance fixture so TS/Go/Python all fail fast on stalled streams the same way (and with consistent error fields).
2026-01-21 08:37 PT — Owen Phillips (Support)
Customer-facing workaround snippet (sync) proposal — please confirm, Sabrina:

```python
import time
import threading

MAX_SECONDS = 30

with client.chat.completions.stream(...) as stream:
    deadline = time.time() + MAX_SECONDS

    def watchdog():
        while time.time() < deadline and not stream.closed:
            time.sleep(0.25)
        if not stream.closed:
            stream.close()

    t = threading.Thread(target=watchdog, daemon=True)
    t.start()

    for event in stream:
        # handle event
        pass
```

This is not perfect but better than killing the pod.
2026-01-21 10:05 PT — Sabrina James (Python SDK)
Confirmed the snippet is directionally OK. Two notes:
1) Encourage customers to set MAX_SECONDS > their expected generation time, and treat this as “overall timeout”.
2) After `stream.close()`, the iterator should exit; some environments may raise an exception depending on where the underlying socket is. They should catch and treat as timeout.

Fix status:
- PR-850 updated to support an explicit overall timeout wrapper for streaming consumption.
- We’ll surface a `RedwoodTimeoutError` (typed) with fields: `request_id` (if known), `timeout_ms`, and `phase` (connect/read/overall).

ETA:
Targeting python sdk 0.18.0 early next week pending CI + review.
2026-01-27 16:22 PT — Sabrina James (Python SDK)
Fix merged and released in redwood-sdk-python 0.18.0.

Release notes (high level):
- Streaming now enforces overall timeout consistently.
- Read timeout is applied to stalled streams (no bytes) where possible.
- Streaming timeout errors are typed and include request_id when available.

PRs:
- pr-850-timeout-model-connect-read-overall
- pr-854-streaming-disconnect-handling-and-errors

Also added conformance fixtures coverage in pr-857 (includes a stalled-stream test).

Docs:
Migration notes updated to clarify the timeout behavior and config names.
2026-01-28 09:02 PT — Owen Phillips (Support)
Sent customer upgrade guidance:
- Upgrade to redwood-sdk-python >= 0.18.0
- Set explicit overall timeout (example: `timeout={"overall": 30, "read": 10, "connect": 5}` depending on their config format)
- Log `request_id` from errors/events for Support triage

Asked them to confirm behavior in their Zscaler environment.
2026-02-03 15:18 PT — Customer (Northwind AI)
We upgraded to 0.18.0 and deployed to a subset.

Results:
- Previously hanging streams now terminate with a timeout exception around ~30s as expected.
- We can catch and retry safely in our job runner.

One note: when it stalls after tokens, the exception doesn’t always include request_id (makes sense because it’s mid-stream and we don’t always have it). But this is still a big improvement.

You can close this ticket.
2026-02-04 09:11 PT — Owen Phillips (Support)
Closing as resolved. Follow-up: we should ensure request_id is emitted in the initial streaming response headers/events consistently to maximize chance of capturing it before a stall (linking to INT-1182 request_id visibility work).
Resolved by shipping redwood-sdk-python v0.18.0 with standardized timeout model and explicit enforcement of overall/read timeouts for streaming consumption. Provided workaround (application-level watchdog + stream.close()) for pre-upgrade mitigation. Customer confirmed fix in production subset and requested closure.
payload.summary: Python SDK: streaming requests appear to ignore configured timeouts (hangs indefinitely on slow/stalled stream)

Issue summary:
AtlasDocs reported a gradual but persistent drop in throughput for their dedicated reserved pool during repeated short-stream bursts (many concurrent 50–500ms streaming requests) beginning 2026-03-12 09:15 UTC. Total requests succeed but effective tokens/sec and slot utilization decline over a 6–20 minute window until either traffic subsides or a manual pool drain/reshuffle is performed.

Impact:
- Customer sees 30–70% reduction in delivered throughput on affected routes, p95 latency increases from ~180ms to ~700ms for batched endpoints.
- No 5xx errors observed; requests are delayed/queued at allocator attach and occasionally hit model-fallbacks.
- Affects AtlasDocs dedicated pool (reserved) and one other self_serve test tenant intermittently.

Environment:
- prod/us-east-1, dedicated cluster: pool-id rp-atlasdocs-03
- Serving runtime v2.9.1 with scheduler v1.4.0
- API gateway edge nodes us-east-1a/b/c

Steps to reproduce (customer):
1) Fire many short streaming generation requests (prompt size ~40 tokens, expected completion ~30 tokens) at high QPS (200–350 qps) from multiple client connections with keepalive off.
2) Observe sustained throughput degradation after 6–15 minutes: token/sec drops, slot attach latencies rise, allocator heartbeat count for pool controllers decreases.

Observed logs / metrics snippets:
- allocator.attach.latency.p50: increases from 120ms -> 420ms over 8 minutes
- pool.slot_utilization: 82% -> 34% over same window
- api.gateway.conn_state.syn_recv: spikes of ephemeral connections (thousands/min)
- sidecar.metrics: "heartbeat_missing_count": incrementing for pool controller pods
- no driver crashes, no OOMs, kernel logs clean

Initial hypothesis:
- Small, frequent streaming connections are creating ephemeral socket fanout at the API layer that pushes connector/backpressure into the scheduler/allocator, causing heartbeat suppression and delayed GPU attach.
- Connector (edge) connection churn causes sidecar to queue too many short-lived streams; this backpressures the allocator's health checks which then reduce preference for warm slots leading to cooler slot utilization and slower batch formation.

Customer-provided artifacts:
- Sample curl-based repro that mirrors their traffic generator (attached to ticket): atlas_repro_v2.tar.gz
- Grafana snapshots for rp-atlasdocs-03 (token/sec, attach latencies, connection churn)

Start a traffic generator that opens many independent HTTP/2 streaming sessions without connection reuse at 250 qps; each stream sends a short prompt and closes within 200-800ms.
Observe allocator.attach.latency and pool.slot_utilization in Grafana for rp-atlasdocs-03 over 10-20 minutes.
Run a controlled test with connection reuse (keepalive enabled, multiplexed streams) and compare slot utilization trajectory.
2026-03-12T09:20:11Z pool-controller[rp-atlasdocs-03] INFO heartbeat_missing_count=3; attach.latency=230ms
2026-03-12T09:24:01Z api-gateway[edge-17] WARN ephemeral_conn_open=1042; ephemeral_conn_close=1010
2026-03-12T09:27:49Z scheduler WARN pool-reshuffle triggered by attach_backoff

2026-03-12 10:02 - Support (Maya Chen): Acknowledged receipt. I've escalated to SRE/scheduler team and requested immediate telemetry dumps for pool rp-atlasdocs-03.
2026-03-12 11:14 - SRE (Diego Ramos): Early signal: api-gateway shows high SYN/connection churn; sidecar reporters show reduced heartbeat frequency for pool controller. Suspect connector saturation is starving the allocator's reconciliation loop.
2026-03-12 13:40 - Support (Maya Chen) -> Customer: Can you try enabling HTTP/2 connection reuse / keepalive on your generator for a 30-minute window? This has reduced reproduction in similar cases.
2026-03-12 14:05 - Customer (AtlasDocs, Rachel Lee): We enabled keepalive and observed throughput stabilized; tokens/sec returned to baseline in ~5 minutes. We'll keep running a longer test and report back.
Checked scheduler logs between 09:10-09:40: several 'heartbeat_suppressed' marks when api-gateway reported >800 ephemeral_conn/sec.
Heap and CPU on pool controller pods normal; however the reconcile loop shows latency spikes when sidecar queue length > 1200.
Reproduced locally with small traffic generator: replication succeeds when connection reuse is disabled. Multiplexed streams did not reproduce the suppression.
Hypothesis refined: connector backlog (many short TCP streams) causes sidecar to prioritize connection processing; health pings for allocator are delayed, the scheduler marks nodes as less preferred and batch formation becomes sporadic leading to apparent throughput evaporation.
Related: small overlap with SUP-271998 (tenant-shadowing) but root cause here is connection-level fanout, not tenant CPU hogging.
Ask AtlasDocs to enable HTTP/2 keepalive / connection reuse (we provided code snippets).
Apply temporary edge-side rate limiting on ephemeral connections for rp-atlasdocs-03 to keep connector backlog < 500.
Manually trigger pool reshuffle / drain and warmup when sustained connector churn is detected (operator-runbook step).
(ENG) Implement backpressure propagation from edge connectors into allocator to avoid heartbeat suppression (ticket backlog assigned).
(SRE) Add a detector that alerts when ephemeral_conn_open rate > threshold and auto-apply soft connection-mitigation rules for dedicated pools.
(DEVX) Publish best-practice guidance for customers on streaming connection reuse and example SDK configs that lower connector churn.
(ENG) Evaluate improving sidecar accept loop scheduling to ensure allocator reconcile/pings maintain high priority.
Follow-up review with AtlasDocs after rollout of mitigations.
2026-03-13 - Workaround accepted by customer: enabled connection reuse; throughput recovered in ~5 minutes during test window.
2026-03-14 - SRE applied a temporary soft-rate-limit at edge for pool rp-atlasdocs-03 during peak hours to prevent recurrence while long-term changes are scoped.
Pending: ENG work items to harden allocator resiliency and sidecar scheduling (linked PRs and tickets).

comments: 2026-03-14T00:00:00Z Elena Martinez: Ticket created from Mapline support email. Attached gateway logs and a short curl-based repro script from the customer.
2026-03-14T00:00:00Z Ravi Shah: Acknowledged. Assigned to SRE on-call. Kicking off preliminary trace aggregation and rate-limiter metric review.

2026-03-14T00:00:00Z Mapline Ops: Provided additional pcap and proxy config (connection_pool: keepalive, max_conns: 4) and confirmed token TTL = 30s. Noted that issue started immediately after proxy rollout.

2026-03-14T00:00:00Z Ravi Shah: Found correlation: 429 spikes align with windows when many unique auth tokens are observed over the same backend connection. Asked engineering to check whether per-connection accounting logic is applied in edge rate-limiter shortcut code path.
payload.description:
Issue summary:
Mapline started seeing sustained 429 responses for a subset of API requests after switching their edge architecture to a pooled HTTP/2 reverse-proxy (for connection reuse) and reducing token lifetime to 30s (short-lived tokens issued by their auth service). The increased 429s began immediately after the deployment and affect both streaming and non-streaming generation routes.

Impact:
- ~18% of requests from Mapline's production hosts returned 429s over a 20-minute window during a traffic spike.
- Customer reports user-visible latency spikes and failed batches for embedding imports.
- Affects dedicated GPU pool (Mapline has reserved capacity) in us-west.

Environment:
- Customer: Mapline (dedicated)
- Redwood deployment: hosted control plane, dedicated serving pool in us-west
- Edge: pooled HTTP/2 reverse-proxy (internal to customer's infra)
- Auth: short-lived tokens (30s TTL) issued per request by Mapline's token service

Steps to reproduce (as provided by customer):
1. Configure a client to obtain a fresh token per request (short TTL).
2. Send 100 concurrent generation requests over a small number (2-4) of long-lived HTTP/2 connections via the pooled proxy.
3. Observe 429 responses in ~15-25% of requests during sustained concurrency.

Observed logs/traces (customer supplied):
- Example trace IDs: trace-usw-1073, trace-usw-1098
- API gateway logs show many distinct API keys/auth headers observed on a single backend connection.
- Rate limiter metrics show high per-connection token accounting increments rather than per-api-key accounting for a subset of calls.

Customer asks:
- Why did switching to a pooled HTTP/2 proxy + short-lived tokens result in more 429s?
- Is there a recommended config to avoid this without increasing token TTL?

Requested priority: P1 (production impact).

Additional notes:
2026-03-14 - Eng (runtime-team): Requested full API gateway logs and an example token header. Also asked for exact repro script to replicate under our test harness.
Hypothesis 1: Proxy is multiplexing many short-lived tokens over a few HTTP/2 connections. Rate-limiter code path that runs on the gateway was attributing token consumption to connection buckets in fast-path, leading to double/mis-counting when tokens change frequently on the same connection.
Hypothesis 2: Client-side behavior (one token per request) increases cardinality and triggers backend per-key sharding hot spots; combined with connection reuse this surfaces a race where counters are incremented on the wrong shard for a short window.
What we checked: Cross-referenced api-gateway logs with rate-limiter counters; noticed bursts of 'conn_bucket_increment' events tied to the same remote IP and connection_id while auth header changed between requests.
Trace: pulled request-level sampling for trace-usw-1073. Sequence shows tokenA -> tokenB -> tokenC on same stream id; 2xx responses followed by 429s as per-connection window exhausted.
Reproduction in our lab: Used local HTTP/2 proxy that reuses 2 connections and rotated short-lived tokens per request. We reproduced elevated 429 rate when token TTL <= 30s and connection reuse enabled.
Eng finding: Fast-path optimization in gateway treats consecutive requests on same stream as same-account for performance; it fails to re-evaluate auth header on token rollover immediately leading to stale accounting until next sync tick (~100ms). Under high concurrency this produces token accounting skew and temporary overdraws.
Risk assessment: P1 for Mapline (dedicated pool). Broader impact low but customers with similar short TTL + connection pooling pattern could be affected.
Related: opened internal bug INT-4321 to track gateway fast-path fix and a follow-up to add test coverage for high-cardinality short-lived tokens on multiplexed connections.
Mitigation applied (2026-03-14): Instructed Mapline ops to either increase token TTL to >=120s or configure their proxy to avoid aggressive token-per-request fanout (option: set max_conns to connection-per-backend-host 8+ or disable token rotation for pooled clients).
Temporary server-side tweak (rolled at 2026-03-14 19:20 UTC): Enabled conservative auth re-eval on gateway fast-path for Mapline tenant to force per-request auth header validation (adds ~0.5ms p99 but prevents miscounting). Monitoring showed 429 rate dropped from 18% -> 0.8% within 5m.
Permanent fix plan: Engineering will land INT-4321 to correct fast-path to re-check auth header immediately when Authorization changes on a stream; add unit+load tests. Target PR and canary next week (ETA 2026-03-21).
Follow-ups for customer: Provide guidance doc with recommended proxy configs and examples for token TTL trade-offs; offer assisted rollout for them to test longer-lived tokens vs proxy settings in a staging copy of their cluster.
Customer accepted workaround: Mapline opted to increase token TTL to 2 minutes and throttle client token requests; they will evaluate full patch when available.

Issue summary: Customer reports a ~3x increase in time-to-first-token (TTFB) for chat completions after we rolled out runtime 1.5.0 and a model variant swap for redwood-instruct-2.7.

Impact: Multiple production teams at Harmonia Health observe initial token latency rising from ~120ms to 350-450ms for short prompts (<=64 tokens). This impacts UI perceived responsiveness for chat features and has triggered degraded user experience.

Observed start: After a coordinated push on 2026-03-09 (runtime 1.5.0 + model variant routing tweak) — spike aligns with deploy timestamps.

Temporary status: Customers routed to fallback variant sometimes see normal latency; however, most requests to primary routing path hit the elevated TTFB consistently.

Additional notes: No 5xx spike was observed; throughput and downstream token emission remain normal. Symptoms are specifically elevated latency before the first token is emitted (TTFB).
1) Create a chat completion request using the redwood-instruct-2.7 model in prod-us-west
2) Use short prompts (~10-50 tokens) and request streaming responses with default timeout
3) Observe initial token arrival time in client telemetry (compare to baseline collected prior to 2026-03-09).
4) Repeat routing request header to prefer primary variant vs fallback variant to compare times.

2026-03-09T18:02:13Z DEBUG pool-primary-27: session open, kv-cache warm: true

agent-telemetry: ttfb_p50_preupgrade=120ms ttfb_p50_postupgrade=375ms
Initial hypothesis: kernel selection/quantization path in 1.5.0 may introduce an extra compilation or memory migration causing first-token stalls.
Checked autoscaler logs: no cold-start spikes on nodes; GPU utilization steady. Not a capacity shortage.
Compared routing traces: requests routed to fallback variant (older model binary) do not show the delay -> points to variant-specific runtime behavior.
Heap and GPU memory snapshots show more frequent allocation churn during initialization for primary variant under runtime 1.5.0.
Investigated recent PRs: runtime PR #981 modified kernel cache eviction heuristics; model-registry PR #412 changed variant tag ordering for routing (can alter kernel choice). Both merged 2026-03-09.
Reproduced locally in staging by forcing runtime 1.5.0 + primary variant: captured a 300-500ms stall in serve startup for first request in a session when KV cache warm but kernel rebind occurs.
1) Short-term customer workaround: add header variant_preference=fallback to route away from affected primary variant.
2) Ops: rollback runtime 1.5.0 on the affected us-west pool if multiple enterprise customers confirm impact (pending Prod runbook approval).
3) Engineering: revert runtime PR #981 kernel cache eviction change on a canary pool and measure TTFB impact.
Action taken: Eng team prepared a canary revert of the kernel eviction heuristic (PR rollback) and deployed to a small subset of primary pools in us-west on 2026-03-11.
Result: Canary pools showed TTFB p50 reduced from ~370ms to ~130ms for redwood-instruct-2.7, aligning with fallback behavior. No other regressions observed in throughput.
Customer communication: On 2026-03-11 18:00Z, we coordinated with Harmonia Health to route their production traffic to the reverted pool; customer confirmed improved UX.
Permanent follow-up: Engineering will land a focused fix to kernel selection logic that avoids rebinds at first request and update runtime 1.5.1. A post-deploy validation will include a synthetic TTFB smoke test for pinned short prompts.
Root cause: unsafe kernel cache eviction in runtime 1.5.0 combined with new model-variant ordering caused kernel rebinds on first token for certain model binaries, producing a 300-500ms initial stall.
Action item 1: Add TTFB synthetic check to pre-deploy canary health tests for all runtime upgrades (owner: SRE, due 2026-03-19).
Action item 2: Engineering to implement lazy rebind and preserve warmed kernel handles for variant swaps (owner: Serving Runtime, PR tracked).
Action item 3: Update rollout runbook to include explicit verification of short-prompt p50 TTFB across affected regions before fully promoting runtime.

2026-03-10T11:44Z - Customer (Harmonia Health): Provided three example request_ids and client-side timings. Confirmed issue started after midnight on 2026-03-09.

Issue summary:
Customer reports a ~€9,300 charge on finalized invoice for a long-running batch-embed job. The job was expected to be billed under batch pricing (per-batch rate) but appears to have been charged at the chat/streaming per-token rate for a ~12-hour run. In addition, a €210 provisional credit for a scheduled kv-cache warmup was missing from the finalized invoice; the customer says the credit was visible in the billing preview before finalize.

Impact:
- LuminaDocs reports a one-off ~€9,300 unexpected charge (customer-visible line item) and a missing provisional credit of €210. Total delta ≈ €9,510.
- Customer is enterprise, in EU (eu-west) private deployment, and is now asking for a credit and root cause to avoid revoking autopay.

Environment:
- Private deployment connected to Redwood control plane (private fallback enabled).
- Primary job submitted from LuminaDocs org via dedicated endpoint; when capacity was low, traffic routed to hosted fallback in eu-west.
- Job invoked tool-calls in streaming responses to serialize metadata; original job type: batch-embedding (async job) with large microbatches.

Steps to reproduce (customer-provided):
1) Submit large async batch job for 1,200 documents using embed pipeline with tool-call metadata serializer enabled.
2) During peak, dedicated pool saturated -> requests routed to hosted fallback using fallback model variant.
3) Hosted runtime treats incoming requests as streaming/chat due to tool-call header and the model variant capability flags; meter records tokens under streaming/chat rate-class.
4) Invoice finalized on next billing cycle; provisional credit for scheduled cache warmup was not applied due to currency rounding logic that reclassified small credits after conversion to EUR.

Logs / attachments provided by customer:
- billing_line_item_2026-02-28.pdf (customer copy)
- job-uuid-3f9b7f-log.txt (contains routing headers and fallback decision timestamp)
- sample-request-headers.json (shows X-Redwood-Tool-Call: true and X-Job-Mode: batch)

Additional notes:
2026-03-13 — SRE (automated): Link to trace: https://traces.redwood.ai/trace/0f5a9c — shows dedicated pool saturated at 03:20 UTC; routing policy fallback triggered to hosted eu-west. Kernel selection differences noted (fallback variant set 'supports_streaming:true').
2026-03-13 — LuminaDocs (Customer): Provided signed invoice PDF and confirmed they used the 'metadata-tool' toggle for serialization. Customer requests a provisional credit and refund for misbilled tokens if confirmed.
Investigation summary:
- Routing: At 03:20 UTC dedicated pool reached saturation. Smart routing selected hosted eu-west pool as fallback (expected behavior).
- Model variant selection: Fallback chose a variant flagged 'supports_streaming' because it offered lower-latency kernel for small sequences. The presence of X-Redwood-Tool-Call and streaming-capable variant led the meter classifier to route token accounting into 'streaming/chat' buckets rather than 'batch' buckets.
- Metering classifier: Token classification is feature-gated; current gate logic prioritized 'tool-call=true' over 'job.mode=batch'. This was intentional historically for interactive workloads but is incorrect for async batch jobs that include tool-call metadata.
- Currency rounding: The bill preview uses a short-running FX snapshot; finalization uses EOD FX and applies a smoothing rule that eliminates sub-euro provisional credits if total credit < €2 after re-aggregation. The €210 was above threshold, but due to an earlier rounding bug in aggregator, the kv-cache warmup credit was split across two micro-lines, each < €1 after conversion and subsequently dropped.
- Repro: We replayed a sanitized client request (same headers) in staging with dedicated saturation simulated; the meter logged 'rate_class:streaming' for chunks originating from requests that contained tool-call headers.
Next steps:
- Immediate: create provisional credit adjustment and one-off invoice correction for LuminaDocs (billing).
- Short-term fix: Update metering classifier to prefer job.mode=batch for async jobs where job metadata indicates batch semantics even if tool-call flag is present; roll canary in staging and eu-west hosted pools. (ENG-3210)
Workarounds and resolution plan:
1) Temporary credit: Issued provisional credit of €9,510 to LuminaDocs account pending formal invoice adjustment. (Billing actioned 2026-03-14)
2) Patch: Metering classifier change submitted (PR github.com/redwood-inference/ingest-service/pull/872) to bias toward job.mode when present. Canary rollout scheduled for 2026-03-16 to eu-west hosted fallback pools. Linked INT follow-up for private deployment docs update.
3) Currency reconciliation: Filed bug with finance team to stop splitting small credits across micro-lines during FX conversion (FIN-452). A hotfix will prevent sub-euro line splitting during finalize.
4) Communication: Drafted customer-facing message explaining the root cause, the immediate credit, and planned fixes. Offered LuminaDocs a 3-month billing guard (manual review) for enterprise trust.
Status: provisional credit applied; engineering patch in review. Pending post-canary verification (due 2026-03-20) and final invoice reissue.

Issue summary: Acme Analytics reported a spike in request p99 latency and a surge of 504s starting 2026-03-12 12:10 UTC. Root cause suspected: routing policy sent a fraction of steady-state traffic from their us-west deployment to an eu-west sparse/quantized variant that was initializing, causing KV cache coldness and long model warmups.

Impact: Approximately 12% of requests experienced >5s p99; customer reported user-facing timeouts and increased error rates on production ingestion endpoints. No data loss, but severe degradation of SLAs for the affected routes.

Environment: Dedicated capacity for Acme Analytics in prod (us-west primary). Canary and fallback policies allowed cross-region failover to eu-west when local autoscaler briefly marked several us-west replicas as constrained.

Observed behavior: Routing decision machine selected the sparse-quantized eu-west variant because it satisfied the cost/latency policy at policy-eval time, but the target replicas were still initializing and had disabled KV caching. Requests sent there were subject to cold KV misses and model cold-starts leading to serialization of warmup and high tail latency (and some 504s when request deadlines exceeded).
1) In a dedicated prod deployment with traffic pinned to us-west, induce an autoscaler event that marks 2/6 local replicas as constrained (simulate heavy compute).
2) Ensure routing policy allows cross-region fallback for 'cost-savings' threshold.
3) Trigger steady request stream at typical customer QPS for ~10 minutes.
4) Observe routing logs; a percentage of requests will be diverted to eu-west sparse variant which is in 'initializing' state.
5) Measure p50/p95/p99 and 504 count on affected route.

[2026-03-12T12:10:22Z] serving-runtime: replica eu-west-variant-23 state=initializing kv_cache=disabled
[2026-03-12T12:10:23Z] request=xyz took=5184ms status=504 upstream=eu-west-variant-23
[2026-03-12T12:11:05Z] metrics: route=/v1/generate p99=5.4s p95=1.1s errors=42
Links: https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/alerts/route-acme-p99?panelId=7
[2026-03-12 12:25] Support (Leah Park): Triage: customer reports intermittent timeouts; opened internal escalation to SRE. Notified customer that we are investigating and suggested a temporary pin to their primary variant.
[2026-03-12 12:40] SRE (Mateo Ruiz): Observed routing decisions sending ~13% of traffic to eu-west sparse-quantized variant which is in initializing state. Investigating autoscaler decision that flagged local replicas as constrained.
[2026-03-12 13:05] Engineering (Sofia Chen): Confirmed kv_cache disabled on new eu-west replicas due to a config drift in image v2.3.4; replicas warmup serialized. Proposed immediate mitigation: disable cross-region fallback for this customer and pre-warm eu-west replicas if we plan to route there.
[2026-03-12 13:30] Support (Leah Park): Applied temporary pinning on customer's routing policy to force local-us-west variants. Customer reports latency return to normal; errors reduced to baseline.
[2026-03-13 09:10] Engineering (Mateo Ruiz): Deployed routing gate fix that prevents routing to initializing replicas; also hot-fixed config drift in eu-west image to enable KV caching by default.
[2026-03-14 11:45] Support (Leah Park): Followed up with customer to confirm post-fix behavior. Customer accepted resolution and requested notes on preventing recurrence.
Initial hypothesis: autoscaler scaled down local capacity or marked replicas constrained, triggering cross-region fallback policy.
Telemetry shows routing evaluation picked eu-west sparse variant due to transient score improvement (cost + nominal latency) but did not account for replica readiness state in final decision.
Replica logs show 'kv_cache=disabled' and model warmup RPCs queued; cold KV misses observed on first token requests, causing long tail latency.
Observed config drift: image tag v2.3.4 built on 2026-03-05 had an opt-in flag for KV cache not set; recent eu-west rollout used that image and left replicas without prefix caching.
Related to known fallback risk (see SUP-33421) but this occurrence included cross-region network penalty plus cold start, making impact larger.
Short-term mitigations applied: 1) Temporarily disabled cross-region fallback for Acme Analytics routing policy; 2) Pinned traffic to us-west variants for safe period; 3) Contacted customer and advised to validate during scheduled traffic window.
Engineering fixes rolled out: 1) Hotfix to image v2.3.4 to enable KV cache by default and restart eu-west replicas; 2) Routing change to respect replica readiness (state != initializing) as a hard precondition for variant selection; 3) Add gating metric in policy eval to penalize variants with 'kv_cache=disabled' until warmup completes.
Result: After mitigation p99 decreased to baseline within 20 minutes and 504s dropped to zero for the pinned routes. No further cross-region diversions observed for the customer after gating introduced.
Update rollout checklist to include KV cache flag verification for all quantized images (owner: Sofia Chen, due: 2026-03-20)
Add a prewarm/auto-warm policy for cross-region variant activation (owner: Mateo Ruiz, due: 2026-04-01)
Create monitoring alert that fires when routing decisions send >5% traffic to replicas in 'initializing' state (owner: Infra Observability, due: 2026-03-22)
Review routing policy scoring to include explicit readiness penalties and network region penalty (owner: Routing Team, due: 2026-03-28)
Share incident summary with customer and internal postmortem link (owner: Leah Park, due: 2026-03-16)

payload.description:
Issue summary: Customer reports spikes in tail latency and intermittent fallback to a degraded variant while a tenant was pinned to a promoted model during a canary window. Impact: A subset of requests for NimbusDocs (~0.6% of traffic) observe token-level latency spikes from ~40ms median to 400-700ms 99th, and ~1 in 2000 requests were routed to the fallback variant for ~2 minutes. Environment: Dedicated pool (d-5g), prod us-west-2, pinned model redwood/open-instruct-v1 pinned by tenant override. Steps to reproduce: 1) Pin tenant to promoted model variant. 2) Trigger prewarm / prefetch on the variant from console (simulate prewarm load). 3) Run an artificial traffic spike with 95/5 short/long sequences. 4) Observe health-probe preflight and edge-side prefetch requests interleaving with live tenant requests. Observed behavior: Health-probe and prefetch jobs intermittently hold edge-connection slots and inject KV-warmup traffic that extends per-request scheduling latency; this causes the routing layer to mark a small number of backend workers as slow and trigger fallback routing for tenant sessions still under pin. Expected behavior: Prewarm/prefetch probes should not affect live pinned sessions' latency or provoke fallback routing. Temporary workaround: Pause prewarm jobs for the tenant and increase canary health thresholds to tolerate brief probe-induced latency increases.
Create a dedicated tenant in us-west-2 and pin it to redwood/open-instruct-v1 via the Console pin API
Configure prewarm jobs to run with aggressive concurrency (prefetch concurrency = 16) against the same variant
Send mixed short/long request traffic at ~120 rps from the edge for ~5 minutes
Observe edge and orchestrator logs for interleaved probe/prefetch entries and routing decisions
edge-proxy [2026-03-09T21:04:12Z] INFO request_id=abc123 route=tenant-42 backend=worker-7 latency=512ms probe=true
orchestrator [2026-03-09T21:04:13Z] WARN worker=worker-7 health_check_latency=480ms mark_slow=true
routing-mesh [2026-03-09T21:04:15Z] INFO tenant=tenant-42 decision=fallback target=degraded-variant reason=slow_backend

Additional notes:
2026-03-12 - Customer (NimbusDocs) via CS: Applied temporary pause of prewarm jobs and saw immediate reduction in fallbacks. Asking for permanent fix timeline.
Probe: orchestration health checks and console-initiated prewarm jobs share the same worker scheduling window and contribute to connection saturation.
Worker telemetry shows KV cache warming tasks increase first-token completion time which the health-check smoothing algorithm interprets as degraded worker health.
Routing policy currently treats worker marked slow for >300ms as candidate for fallback; short bursts from prewarm can exceed this threshold and trigger reroute.
Repro repo: tests added in serving-runtime perf harness replicating 99th percentile spike when prewarm concurrency > 8 and tenant pinned sessions concurrently active.
Edge behavior: edge-proxy does not annotate prewarm requests in a way that downstream can treat them as non-customer-affinitive leading to incorrect affinity accounting.
Short-term: Add a flag to prewarm/health-probe requests (edge header X-Prewarm: true) to deprioritize scheduling and exclude from slow_backend health metrics (hotfix).
Short-term: Update canary health thresholds for pinned tenants to use conservative smoothing during active pin windows.
Medium-term: Refactor scheduler to isolate prewarm jobs into separate soft-pool with bounded concurrency per node.
Long-term: Add pin-aware QoS where pinned tenant streams have preemptive scheduling priority and probe traffic is shunted to background lanes.
Run a controlled canary of the hotfix in us-west-2 with NimbusDocs before broad rollout.
2026-03-12 - Hotfix deployed to edge-proxy and orchestrator: prewarm requests now carry X-Prewarm header and are deprioritized by scheduler (PRs 219, 4521).
2026-03-12 - Observed results: fallback rate for NimbusDocs dropped to baseline within 10 minutes of hotfix, 99th latency returned to <120ms for pinned traffic.
Follow-up: Medium-term work item created in backlog (INT-10077) to implement dedicated prewarm soft-pools and pin-aware QoS. Customer will be notified and offered a review call.
Workaround documented: If customers plan large prewarm runs during active pins, schedule prewarm off-window or reduce concurrency until soft-pools are implemented.
Mitigated with hotfix; root cause is scheduling interference from prewarm/health probes. Medium-term scheduler isolation is recommended to prevent recurrence.

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customer reports that threshold alerts attached to a dashboard panel did not fire during multiple spikes visible in the panel. The panel uses a custom bucketing scheme (5m buckets) and the dashboard timezone set to Auto (detect from browser). The alerts are configured as simple threshold alerts (metric > 0.8) with evaluation window 10m and for: 2m.

Impact:
- Customer missed 3 alerting events over a 4 hour period on 2026-03-12 which they rely on to autoscale downstream services.
- Potential business impact: delayed incident response and over-provisioning while investigating.

Environment:
- Customer: ByteFrame Analytics (dedicated cluster, us-east region)
- Console version: web-frontend v2.11.3
- Alerting-service: alerts-api v1.9.7, evaluator v1.9.7
- Timeseries store: tsdb v3.4.2 (bucketed rollups enabled)

Steps to reproduce (customer-facing):
1) In their dedicated console, open a dashboard with a timeseries panel that uses 5m bucketing and dashboard timezone set to Auto.
2) Create a threshold alert on the panel: condition metric > 0.8, evaluation_window=10m, for=2m.
3) Wait for a metric spike that appears in the panel (they observed spikes at 08:05, 09:15, 11:40 UTC).
4) Observe that the panel shows the spike but no alert notification is generated.

Observed logs and artefacts provided by customer:
- Panel screenshot (attached in ticket) showing spike at 2026-03-12T09:15:00Z and no alert hit.
- Customer query history: query id q-20260312-9a4e
- Alert evaluation logs (from alerts-api):
  [2026-03-12T09:16:10Z] eval: alert_id=bf-73 rule=threshold eval_window=10m buckets=[2026-03-12T09:10:00Z,2026-03-12T09:15:00Z] result=NO_DATA
  [2026-03-12T09:16:11Z] query-engine: query_id=q-20260312-9a4e time_range=[2026-03-12T09:06:00Z-2026-03-12T09:16:00Z] buckets=5m returned_points=1
- Console audit log shows dashboard view at 2026-03-12T09:16:05Z using browser TZ=Europe/London (BST).

Notes: The customer provided a session replay and the timeline indicates the dashboard panel bucket visually aligned with the spike, but the alert evaluation considered an earlier set of bucket boundaries and returned NO_DATA for the expected buckets.

Additional notes:
2026-03-14 12:00 - ByteFrame Support Contact (customer): Confirmed that applying the workaround stopped missing alerts for subsequent spikes but asked for permanent fix and timeline.
Summary of findings:
- Reproduced with synthetic data on dedicated stack using same tsdb rollup config.
- alerts-evaluator evaluated time windows aligned to UTC bucket boundaries by default. When a dashboard/panel uses a non-UTC timezone or 'auto' browser TZ, the query-engine requests bucket boundaries shifted by local offset.
- This produced a 5-minute misalignment: evaluator checked buckets [09:10,09:15] while query-engine returned points for visual buckets [09:12,09:17] due to rollup bucket offseting logic.
- Logs show evaluator returned NO_DATA for the buckets it evaluated even though data existed in the shifted buckets.
Hypothesis: regression introduced in alerts-evaluator v1.9.4 where timezone offset was dropped when converting evaluation window to rollup-aligned boundaries.
Evidence: git bisect points to commit 7f2b1c2 in alerts-evaluator that changed window alignment code to use time.FixedZone incorrectly. Related PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/platform/pull/1348
Telemetry: added debug logs for evaluator boundary calculation (enabled for customer's dedicated cluster) to capture future events.
Workaround (customer-facing):
- Short term: Set dashboard timezone to UTC for affected dashboards or change alert evaluation window to use a fixed lookback (e.g., evaluation_window=12m) so boundaries overlap with rollup buckets. We validated this prevented missed alerts for subsequent spikes.
- Medium term: Patch PR merged (https://github.com/redwood-inference/platform/pull/1348) that ensures evaluator uses tsdb bucket offset when calculating boundaries. Patch currently under canary rollout to staging and one dedicated customer cluster.
- Permanent fix: PR includes unit tests and adds an integration test that exercises non-UTC dashboard timezone with rollups. SRE to monitor canary for 48 hours before wider rollout.

Issue summary: Customer reports a sudden drop in reranker recall and low-scoring top-k candidates for certain queries. Symptoms started after a proxy config rollout. Impact: ClearDocs production pipelines see ~18% drop in top-5 recall and elevated rerank tail latency due to retries. Environment: Dedicated tenant on us-east, using rwd-open-embedding-001 served via edge proxy (version 2026.03.08).

Observed behavior: - Embeddings arriving at rerank service sometimes show reduced dynamic range (values clustered near 0), causing cosine similarity suppression. - Proxy logs contain periodic serialization warnings about 'unsupported numeric bit-depth' near the same timestamps. - Re-running the same payload directly against the serving runtime (bypassing proxy) returns expected float32 embeddings and restores rerank quality.

Urgency: Customer production degradation, P1 expected response.
1) Send the customer's sample batch (attached) through the repro proxy route via POST /v1/embeddings with content-type application/json.
2) Observe embedding vector numeric ranges in response and compare against direct runtime endpoint (/private-runtime/embeddings).
3) Run rerank job using supplied vectors and check top-5 recall.
4) Compare proxy logs for serialization warnings at timestamps.

Notes: Repro was intermittent (~1/6 batches) but consistent when proxy used; bypass reliably produces correct vectors.
[2026-03-09T18:12:04Z] proxy-frontend WARN serialization: unsupported numeric bit-depth: 16 -> falling back to approximate encode
[2026-03-09T18:12:04Z] proxy-frontend DEBUG payload-size=12kb tenant=cleardocs route=/v1/embeddings
[2026-03-09T18:12:04Z] rerank INFO cosine_top5=0.12 (expected ~0.62) latency=142ms
[2026-03-09T18:12:05Z] runtime DEBUG embed-response dtype=float32 first_val=0.12345
[2026-03-09T18:12:05Z] proxy DEBUG downstream-encode dtype=uint16 sample_first_val=3

Initial hypothesis: Recent proxy optimization introduced a ‘bit-depth ramp’ that attempts lower-bit quant storage for in-flight embeddings to save bandwidth. Evidence: proxy logs explicitly mention 'unsupported numeric bit-depth: 16' and downstream encode shows uint16 values. Direct runtime returns float32.
Actions taken: - Reproduced locally with customer's payload and confirmed proxy-encoded embeddings are effectively quantized to uint16 in wire format, losing sign and magnitude. - Confirmed rerank algorithm expects float32 normalized embeddings; quantization without proper dequant/scale leads to compressed vectors near zero. - SRE examined last proxy rollout (2026-03-08) which included middleware change 'embed-compress' to enable bandwidth savings for large tenants.
Open questions: Was embed-compress intended to be tenant-gated? Why did telemetry not flag drift earlier?

2026-03-10 10:05 - SRE - Priya Desai: Repro'd locally. Proxy was applying uint16 pack for embeddings > 4kb. Added temporary rule to bypass embed-compress for tenant cleardocs. Will monitor results.

2026-03-12 16:20 - Eng - Liam Patel: Hotfix rolled to prod (proxy v2026.03.12-hotfix-embed). Embed-compress now tenant-gated and includes X-Embed-Scale header. Observability dashboards updated to alert on embed dynamic range anomalies.

Workaround: Temporary bypass rule added for tenant 'cleardocs' on proxy (2026-03-10 10:12) which restored expected embedding values.
Fix: Hotfix deployed to proxy (v2026.03.12-hotfix-embed) with three changes: 1) feature flag scoping to ensure embed-compress is tenant-gated; 2) include X-Embed-Scale header and dtype metadata to allow downstream dequantization; 3) validation to reject quantized payloads without scale header.
Rollout notes: Hotfix rolled to us-east prod first; metrics show top-5 recall recovered to baseline within 20 minutes.
Postmortem actions: - Create Confluence runbook 'Embedding Serialization Runbook' (link added). - Add alert for embedding dynamic-range drop in Console (token-level). - Audit ClearDocs traffic for the past 72 hours and offer support for any affected rerank jobs. - Add integration test covering proxy encode/decode roundtrip for embeddings.
