Issue summary:
Customer CartoScale Inc. invoices contain a new line item labeled 'Warmstart optimization premium' for multiple hourly windows during February billing cycle. Customer says they did not opt into any premium feature and their reserved dedicated pool should be covered by their contract rate.

Impact:
- Unexpected charge ~ $1,230 on February invoice line items.
- Customer asks for immediate provisional credit and explanation.
- Affects finance reconciliation at month close.

Environment:
- Dedicated capacity pool: cartoscale-prod-dedicated (us-west-2)
- Contract: Annual reserved capacity (4x A100 equivalent), billing tier enterprise-annual-2025
- Observed on finalized invoice INV-2026-02-789 (PDF snippet attached by customer)

Steps to reproduce (what customer did):
1) Customer ran normal production workload in us-west-2 during Feb 2–6 and Feb 18–19.
2) They viewed invoice and noticed multiple small warmstart premium line items aggregated to $1,230.
3) Opened support ticket requesting clarification and credit.

Expected behavior:
- No warmstart premium charges should apply to committed reserved capacity hours under enterprise-annual-2025 contract.

Actual behavior:
- System generated a per-hour surcharge labelled 'Warmstart optimization premium' for certain warmup windows during dedicated autoscaling events and a few scheduled warm-cache maintenance tasks.

Invoice snippet (customer-provided):
- 2026-02-03 02:00 UTC — Warmstart optimization premium — $210.00
- 2026-02-18 19:00 UTC — Warmstart optimization premium — $320.00
- 2026-02-19 03:00 UTC — Warmstart optimization premium — $700.00

Attachments provided by customer: invoice PDF page (redacted), timestamped job IDs, sample request IDs.

Additional notes:
2026-03-11 — CartoScale (Customer): Uploaded invoice PDF and list of job IDs spanning suspected windows. Confirms reserved capacity should cover these hours per contract. Requests full reversal if error confirmed.
2026-03-11 — SRE (internal): Found warm-cache maintenance jobs initiated by autoscaler at 2026-02-18 19:00 and 2026-02-19 03:00. Labels on metrics pipeline show a new pricing_tag 'warmstart_premium' on those windows. Investigating origin of tag.
Query run: SELECT tags, job_id, start_ts, billing_tag FROM scheduler_job_events WHERE pool = 'cartoscale-prod-dedicated' AND start_ts BETWEEN '2026-02-02' AND '2026-02-20' — returned three warm-cache maintenance jobs with billing_tag='warmstart_premium'
Hypothesis 1: A recent autoscaler release (PR #4821) introduced optional warmstart optimization. During rollout the feature defaulted to 'on' for certain dedicated pools; billing system treated it as billable add-on and applied 'warmstart_premium' tag to job events.
Hypothesis 2: Contract override logic for enterprise-annual customers failed to match pricing_tag when job events included both 'reserved_hour' and 'warmstart_premium' flags; reserved-hours discount pipeline dropped and surcharge remained.
Cross-checks: Looked at contract pricing rules for enterprise-annual-2025 — confirmed policy explicitly waives warmstart surcharges for committed reserved hours, but billing service only sees 'reserved' tag when job attribution pipeline runs; race condition found between tag enrichment and pricing rule evaluation.
Findings: Race condition introduced in scheduler tagging enrichment after deploy of PR #4821 led to transient windows where scheduler emitted warmstart_premium before reserved_tag enrichment completed. Downstream pricing engine evaluated tag set without reserved_tag and applied surcharge.
Root cause: rollout of warmstart optimization feature (PR #4821) inadvertently changed tag ordering for scheduler job events causing a short race window where 'warmstart_premium' was visible to billing without the 'reserved' attribution. Fix deployed: reorder enrichment so reserved attribution happens before any optional premium tags and added a guard in pricing evaluator to consider historical reserved contracts for matching pools.
Action taken:
- Provisional credit of $1,230 applied 2026-03-12 (CR-2026-03-110555).
- Billing team to regenerate adjusted invoice and issue corrected INV-2026-02-789-rev1 by 2026-03-15.
- Scheduler team rolled back the tag-order change and shipped fix (hotfix release 2026.03.12-hotfix-7).
- Added unit and integration tests to prevent tag-evaluation race; created INT-9001 for postmortem and follow-ups.
Customer follow-up: CartoScale confirmed provisional credit acceptance and asked for confirmation when finalized invoice is posted. Billing will email finalization and include memo referencing CR-2026-03-110555. Ticket closed after invoice revision posted.
We identified a tagging/order race introduced during a warmstart optimization rollout that caused short windows where a billable 'warmstart premium' tag wasn't paired with the reserved-hours contract attribution. We applied a provisional credit and issued a corrected invoice. Engineering has shipped a hotfix to prevent recurrence and added tests. If you see any further unexpected invoice lines, please reopen or open a new ticket.
payload.summary: Unexpected 'Warmstart optimization premium' line on monthly invoice — explanation and credit request

Issue summary: Between 2026-03-12 02:10–02:34 UTC customers (notably Acme Analytics on a dedicated pool) experienced a rapid rise in 5xx responses (502/504) from the API Gateway. Impact: Short-lived spike produced ~18% error rate for embedding requests (small payloads) from the customer, causing job failures and increased retries client-side. Environment: prod (us-east) Dedicated capacity pool id: dp-45. Observed behavior: API Gateway returned 502/504 while downstream runtimes showed frequent process restarts and repeated nvml driver resets. Metrics: upstream runtime restart rate spiked from baseline ~0.02/min to ~2.4/min; GPU reset errors (nvml) increased by ~120x; Python GC pause time histograms showed a large increase in long pauses. Steps to reproduce: 1) Concurrent embedding bulk of small requests (payload ~120 bytes) fan out to many replicas. 2) Prefetch layer coalescing disabled for this tenant due to earlier config; 3) Runtimes experienced increased memory churn during KV cache updates leading to GC activity and eventual process watchdog triggers. Logs/snippets: "runtime: restarted by watchdog: nvml: GPU reset (code 43)"; "gc: pause 1286ms - major collection"; "apigw: upstream closed connection (reset)". Expected behavior: No sustained 5xx floor during short-request bursts; graceful queuing and batching or backpressure rather than upstream restarts.
2026-03-12 02:18 - Support (Anika): Customer reports 18% failures for embedding uploads, provided request IDs and example payloads.
2026-03-12 02:25 - SRE (Liam): Observed correlated spikes in runtime restarts and nvml errors. Opening investigation; attaching live dashboards: https://dashboards.redwood.ai/d/embeddings/rg-45?from=2026-03-12T02:00Z&to=2026-03-12T03:00Z
2026-03-12 03:05 - Engineering (Priya): Kernel-level trace shows repeated GPU driver resets triggered within the runtime after long GC pauses. Suggest throttling concurrency for the tenant as a stop-gap.
2026-03-12 04:10 - Support (Anika): Applied temporary rate cap and enabled coalescing flag for Acme; error rate dropped to <1% within 20 minutes.

Additional notes:
2026-03-13 10:00 - Customer (Acme SRE): Confirmed issue alleviated; requesting postmortem and prevention plan.
Initial hypothesis: simple apigw overload - ruled out by low CPU on API gateway and no accept queue saturation.
Found root trigger: a cluster of very small embedding requests caused extreme KV cache churn in runtime (many small updates), increasing Python object churn and triggering frequent full GC cycles.
Full GC pauses (p99) increased from ~25ms baseline to ~1.3s during spike; these pauses overlapped with NVML calls leading to driver timeouts on some GPUs.
NVML stacktrace shows driver reset originated while runtime held GPU context during a long blocking GC; watchdog interpreted as unresponsive and restarted process.
Autoscaler behavior: when one worker restarted, load briefly redistributed causing other warm workers to hit similar GC patterns and cascade into multiple restarts (crashchain).
Mitigation validated: enabling request coalescing + tenant concurrency cap prevented the KV-churn pattern and reduced GC pressure. Temporary kernel pin (quantized variant) used to reduce nvml interaction frequency.
Related internal ticket for autoscaler behavior: INT-2042 (queued).
Applied immediate mitigations: (1) Enabled per-tenant coalescing for small-embedding requests; (2) Temporarily capped concurrent embedding requests for Acme to 60 RPS; (3) Deployed runtime GC tuning (increase young-gen threshold, reduce frequency of full GCs) and updated watchdog window to tolerate longer GC pauses; (4) Rolled back a recent aggressive autoscaler policy that simultaneously recycled workers. After mitigations error rate fell to <1% and runtime restarts returned to baseline.
Permanent change: Implement request-size-aware batching and automatic coalescing for embed workloads (tracking ticket: ENG-7182).
Autoscaler: Add staged recycle to avoid synchronized worker restarts (ENG-7150).
Monitoring: Add GC pause alerts tied to downstream NVML driver resets and automatic short-circuiting of NVML calls during extended GC pause (SRE-402).
Docs: Update runbook to include detection pattern (GC pause spike + nvml resets -> apigw 502s) and immediate mitigations.

Issue summary: Beginning ~2026-03-13 09:20 UTC BrightBank observed a sustained elevation in 5xx responses on production chat endpoints. Initial spikes coincided with a keepalive sweep and an internal autoscaler activity window. Impact: Customers reported increased 502/503/504 rates and frequent streaming disconnects for long-poll sessions. Escalation: Customer-facing SLA impact for enterprise BrightBank. Environment: prod-us-east (multiple apigw frontends + regional serving runtime pool).
Approximately 6% error-rate elevation for chat generation routes (route /v1/chat/*). Peak window 09:20-10:05 UTC, ~1200 requests/min for the tenant. Several long-lived streaming sessions experienced resets and subsequent retries leading to upstream overload. Internal metrics show apigw worker process CPU saturation and kernel cgroup throttling events on a subset of nodes.
1) Simulate BrightBank tenant traffic profile: 1k rps steady with ~5% long-lived streaming sessions using keepalive pings.
2) Trigger a keepalive sweep across apigw frontends (internal test harness: infra/loadgen/keepalive-sweep v2).
3) Observe apigw worker CPU / cgroup throttling counters and downstream 502/503 responses to client.
4) Reproduce on staging with same autoscaler topology to validate behavior.

Hypothesis: a noisy background job + keepalive sweep caused host-level CPU contention, triggering cgroup throttling on apigw containers; throttling pushed request queues to the runtime, some runtime processes hit watchdog/timeouts and exited (SIGTERM chain), resulting in 502/503/504 amplification.

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customer attempted to upgrade Redwood Private in their AWS VPC environment using the new installer preflight checks. Upgrade is blocked with a hard failure: insufficient storage headroom on one of the required volumes (PVC backing Postgres + platform state). Customer expected the upgrade to proceed; they were not aware of the headroom requirement.

Impact:
- Upgrade window paused; customer cannot proceed with planned maintenance.
- No production outage, but customer is blocked from security/feature release.

Customer request:
- Clarify why the check is blocking vs warning.
- Provide concrete remediation steps and thresholds (how much free space is required) and how to verify.

Environment:
- Deployment mode: Private (VPC)
- Region: us-east-1
- K8s: EKS
- Storage: EBS CSI
- Installer: redwood-private-installer v0.31.0 (as provided in 1.19.0 upgrade bundle)
- Attempted upgrade: Redwood Private 1.18.3 -> 1.19.0

Steps to reproduce:
1) Run: redwood-private upgrade plan --target-version 1.19.0
2) Run: redwood-private upgrade precheck --plan ./upgrade-plan.json
3) Observe hard failure on StorageHeadroomCheck

Observed output (customer-provided):
[Precheck: StorageHeadroomCheck] FAILED (blocking)
- pvc: redwood-postgres-data (ns=redwood-system)
- capacity: 500Gi
- used: 468Gi
- available: 32Gi
- required_available: 75Gi (or 15% of capacity, whichever is higher)
Remediation: Expand the PVC/underlying volume or free disk space. See runbook: "Private upgrade prechecks".

Additional notes:
Customer also reported they have historical backups/snapshots retained longer than needed; they suspect this is consuming volume capacity.

Ask for Engineering:
- Confirm thresholds + whether required_available calculation is correct.
- Confirm if any temporary migration/backup steps require additional ephemeral disk during upgrade.
- Provide recommended remediation path (EBS resize vs cleanup) and any gotchas for Postgres PVC resizing on EKS.
2025-06-18 09:12 (Dev Patel, Support): Customer (Cascade Financial Group) reports upgrade blocked by "StorageHeadroomCheck". They are in a 4-hour change window and need guidance ASAP. Added logs/output in description. Requesting Infra/SRE guidance on remediation + confirm threshold behavior.
2025-06-18 09:26 (Irene Choi, Infra): The check is intended to be blocking. During upgrade we can (a) take a snapshot/backup depending on config and (b) run DB migrations that may create temporary files + WAL growth. We’ve seen failures mid-migration when disk is <10% free. Current threshold in the precheck spec is max(15% of PVC capacity, 75Gi). The customer has ~6% free (32Gi on 500Gi) so this is a correct block.

Recommended remediation for EKS + EBS CSI:
1) Expand the PVC by increasing requested storage (e.g., 750Gi or 1Ti) and ensure the StorageClass supports allowVolumeExpansion.
2) Verify filesystem resize completes on the postgres pod.
3) Re-run prechecks.

Alternative: Free space by reducing retention of local artifacts/logs on that volume (if any), but for postgres it’s safer to expand.
2025-06-18 09:41 (Rafael Mendes, SRE): +1 blocking. We should not advise overriding; rollback reliability depends on having enough headroom too. Customer-facing explanation: this prevents partial upgrades / DB corruption risk.

Verification commands:
- kubectl -n redwood-system get pvc redwood-postgres-data
- kubectl -n redwood-system exec deploy/redwood-postgres -- df -h /var/lib/postgresql/data

If they do PVC expansion, confirm EBS volume modification completes (AWS console/CLI) and the node filesystem reflects the new size.
2025-06-18 10:05 (Dev Patel, Support): Sent customer remediation steps: increase PVC size (recommended) and provided verification commands + rationale why check is blocking. Asked for their StorageClass name and whether allowVolumeExpansion is enabled.
2025-06-18 11:22 (Customer via Support): StorageClass is gp3, allowVolumeExpansion is true. They can expand during window. Asking what target size to set to be safe, and whether the installer backup step increases usage substantially.
2025-06-18 11:37 (Irene Choi, Infra): For 500Gi PVC, required is 75Gi free (15% is 75Gi). They currently have 32Gi free. If they expand to 750Gi, 15% is 112.5Gi; required becomes 112.5Gi. If their used remains ~468Gi, free would become ~282Gi which passes comfortably. 700Gi would also be fine. Installer backup: depends on their configuration; snapshots are not stored on the PVC, but migrations can create temporary tables/WAL churn. Recommend 750Gi to avoid flirting with the threshold.
2025-06-18 12:10 (Dev Patel, Support): Relayed recommendation: expand PVC to ~750Gi (or 700Gi minimum) to satisfy precheck and reduce risk. Clarified snapshots are not stored on the PVC; headroom is for DB operations + safety.
2025-06-19 08:54 (Dev Patel, Support): Customer expanded PVC to 750Gi, filesystem resized successfully. Prechecks now PASS. They are proceeding with upgrade plan execution.
2025-06-19 10:33 (Dev Patel, Support): Customer completed upgrade to 1.19.0 successfully. No rollback required. They asked for a documentation link to ensure storage headroom is validated ahead of future windows.
2025-06-19 10:45 (Rafael Mendes, SRE): Please point them to the Private Upgrade Runbook section "Prechecks -> Storage headroom". Also recommend adding a recurring check/alert for PVC usage >80% on postgres PVCs.
2025-06-20 09:18 (Dev Patel, Support): Provided runbook link and suggested monitoring: alert when postgres PVC >80% used. Customer confirmed receipt and closed the loop.
Resolved via customer-side remediation (expanded postgres PVC from 500Gi -> 750Gi; re-ran prechecks; upgrade succeeded). No product change required.

Follow-ups:
- Support: add a snippet to customer comms template reminding operators to validate PVC headroom before scheduling a maintenance window.
- Eng/SRE: consider publishing a short "capacity planning for upgrades" note (linking to existing precheck spec) and recommending a standard alert for postgres PVC utilization in Private deployments.
payload.summary: Private upgrade blocked: preflight check fails due to insufficient storage headroom (cluster PV/PVC)

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customer reports that long-running SSE streams used by their in-product assistant occasionally end with an incomplete final sentence when an auth cookie rotation occurs mid-response. On client reconnect the stream resumes but the client observes a duplicated prefix and a second 'continuation' fragment that does not align with the original final tokens. This leads to corrupt JSON metadata ordering in the last event and missing closing punctuation in prose outputs.

Impact:
- Several customers in Acme Financial Services (enterprise) observe truncated regulatory text at the end of streamed generation; in one case a closing legal clause was dropped and later duplicated as an out-of-order continuation.
- User-facing impact: incorrect or malformed final output; downstream JSON parser errors in the customer's UI.

Environment:
- prod-us-east (edge -> api-gateway -> serving-runtime)
- Customer traffic through corporate WAF and an enterprise SSO that performs cookie rotation for session renewal
- Observed on redwood-1.2 model variant with streaming SSE client using standard SDK

Steps to reproduce (customer-provided):
1) Start a long-running streaming generation (prompt length > 2k tokens, expected stream duration > 60s) from a browser behind enterprise SSO that performs 5m cookie rotation.
2) Trigger a token refresh (auth cookie rotation) during the middle-to-late phase of generation.
3) The browser's SSE connection briefly reconnects (0.5-2s), then resumes via SDK resume logic.
4) Observe the final chunk: last sentence missing punctuation, JSON metadata arrives as a separate "end_metadata" event after EOF, followed by a duplicate prefix fragment.

Observed behavior:
- Upstream logs show an HTTP 401 (auth) at the gateway at time of rotation followed by successful re-auth and a new cookie set.
- Serving runtime logs show a slow drain of the old connection's output buffer (multiple small flushes) and then a resume of a second session with a slightly different stream_id. KV-cache priming from the resumed session contains the previous prefix, causing duplicate prefix tokens.
- Client sees: partial final sentence (no final period), then an out-of-order JSON metadata event, and then a duplicate continuation that repeats the end of the previous fragment.

Expected behavior:
- Auth rotation should not cause missing terminal tokens; resume should attach to an idempotency boundary or include explicit end-marker that prevents duplicate prefix replay. Final metadata should be ordered before connection termination.

Relevant logs & traces (sanitized):
- api-gateway request_id=bb3a9c2e-8f1b-4c2b-aeab-0f8d9b7a12dd 401 at 2026-03-12T15:10:37Z, Set-Cookie: session=rotated; Path=/; HttpOnly
- serving-runtime stream_id=st-9f2a drain_flushes=6 last_flush=2026-03-12T15:10:38.112Z resume_session=st-9f2a-2
- trace: edge_conn=conn-8345 -> gateway(bb3a9c2e) -> runtime(st-9f2a)

Temporary workaround used by customer:
- Increase client-side buffer timeout and wait 2s before reconnecting to allow slow drain to finish (reduces duplicates but not reliable).
- Customer downgraded to non-rotating session for a narrow user subset as emergency mitigation.

Notes on severity & rollout impact:
- This impacts finality of streamed outputs (legal/regulatory text) and JSON metadata consumers; therefore classified as Sev1 for the affected customer.
- Not observed on short streams or when cookie rotation occurs early in the generation.

Additional notes:
Hypothesis: Cookie rotation causes the gateway to treat the handshake as an auth error which triggers a half-close on the old socket; the serving runtime drains incrementally and the client reconnects quickly, creating a resumed session that re-primes the KV cache with the final prefix. The race between drain completion and resume leads to duplicate prefix + missing final punctuation due to small flush boundary falling between tokenization units.
Evidence: Multiple drain_flushes entries in runtime logs and two different stream_ids observed in a single logical request. The later stream includes KV cache primed with last 64 tokens from previous session. The end_metadata event is emitted as a separate event after the runtime emitted an end-marker on the first connection but before the second session completes its priming.
Repro steps validated in staging with a synthetic SSO that performs cookie rotation every 30s: failure reproduced ~70% of the time when rotation aligns with last 20% of generation time.
Telemetry: Add an analytics counter for stream resume events that include previous_stream_id != resumed_stream_id and record drain_flushes count.
Short-term patch: Increase gateway drain grace window for authenticated SSE streams by 2s (staged and under canary).
Medium-term fix: Modify serving-runtime to include explicit end-of-stream idempotency token in final event so resumed sessions detect terminal events and suppress duplicate prefix replay.
Long-term: Update SDK resume logic to wait for an explicit terminal marker or an adjustable grace period before priming KV cache on resumed sessions. Add config for enterprise customers behind SSO/WAF.
Customer communication: Draft post-incident note + recommended client-side backoff guidance.
In progress: gateway grace window increased in canary (PR: github.com/redwood-inference/gateway/pull/314). Serving-runtime PR for end-of-stream idempotency token created: github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/5421 (under review). SDK change proposed to add configurable resume-backoff; design doc linked in Confluence. Customer notified of canary change and asked to test on their staging SSO. Follow-up: monitor telemetry for 48h after canary and then schedule rollout to prod if duplicates drop below 0.5% of resumed streams.
If you see duplicate prefix on resume: increase client SDK resume delay to 1500-2000ms to allow prior connection drain to finish.
For enterprise SSO customers: if feasible, delay cookie rotation window for long-running assistant sessions or scope rotation to re-auth flows that do not interrupt SSE paths.
Customer can pin a non-rotating session token for regulatory flows until platform fix is rolled out.

payload.description:
Issue summary: Customer Arcadia Labs reports recurring 429 throttles during steady-state ingestion runs from a fleet of short-lived uploader workers. They see 429s even when token usage looks within expected monthly/rolling quotas.

Impact: Intermittent failed uploads (10-25% of requests during 1–2 hour ingestion windows), delays in downstream indexing, and elevated retry traffic causing secondary waves of throttles. No billing disputes opened, but customer is concerned about reliability for nightly syncs.

Environment: self_serve tenant in prod (us-east primary, eu-west failover). Workers spawn ephemeral API keys (lifetime ~5–10 minutes) and open 20–50 concurrent connections per worker process. Ingestion pattern: steady sustained throughput ~120 requests/s for 90–120 minutes, with microbursts when workers restart.

Steps to reproduce:
1) Create N ephemeral keys and fan out 300 worker processes across 3 hosts.
2) Each worker initiates 20 parallel streaming sessions to /v1/generate for small prompts (avg 64 tokens).
3) Start all workers within a 90 second window (simulates a deployment rollout).
4) Observe 429 responses beginning ~30s after start; persists intermittently for the ingestion window.

Expected behavior: Smooth sustained throughput with occasional short-lived bursts handled by token bucket bursting.

Actual behavior: Tenant-level quota tokens are exhausted and 429s appear despite per-key buckets showing available tokens for some keys. 429s correlate with worker restarts and the fanout of ephemeral keys.
1) Provision 300 ephemeral keys (5m TTL) and assign to uploader processes. 2) Start processes within a short window so many keys become active simultaneously. 3) Each process makes 20 concurrent streaming starts to the same route (/v1/generate). 4) Monitor 429 rate and token-bucket metrics in the console and edge logs.
Edge metrics (2026-03-10 02:14:xx - 02:20:xx): tenant_token_exhaustion_count=482, per_key_429s=variable, route_concurrency_exhausted=312. Example trace id: trace-6b3f9a2c -> 429 reason=TOKEN_BUCKET_EXHAUSTED tenant_id=arcadia-001 window_ms=60000. Gateway logs show many short-lived connections closed/reopened: "connection reset by peer" during the warmup. No 5xx spikes observed on serving-runtime endpoints.

Additional notes:
2026-03-12 14:56 - SRE (A. Patel): Pulled edge metrics. Observed synchronized increase in active keys and a matching steep drop in tenant burst tokens. Provided links to Grafana panels and request traces. Suggested test with staggered worker start and longer-lived keys.
2026-03-13 10:08 - Support (Jordan Blake): Proposed mitigations: increase worker key TTLs to reduce fresh-key fanout, stagger rollouts over 10+ minutes, and implement jittered backoff on 429s. Asked customer to try a small experiment with staggered start and to share results.
What we looked at: token bucket traces (tenant and per-key), edge proxy connection lifecycle, console quota charts, and gateway + serving runtime metrics. Findings: 1) Tenant burst bucket is shared and seeded infrequently relative to key churn; when many short-lived keys activate simultaneously the effective burst capacity is consumed quickly. 2) Per-key buckets can show availability because they are provisioned independently, but tenant-level accounting triggers 429s once tenant windows/credits are exhausted. 3) Worker restart storms (many processes starting within the same 60–120s) produce microbursts that outpace the refill rate. 4) No evidence of misbilling or token double-counting. 5) No serving-runtime overload; 429s originate at gateway/rate-limiter.
Hypotheses tested: staging replay of customer pattern with staggered vs simultaneous starts showed stagger reduces 429s significantly. Increasing simulated refill rate reduced 429s but is not available to self_serve tenants via console. Verified that route-level quotas are supported on Dedicated and can be used to isolate heavy ingestion routes from interactive routes.
Workarounds provided: 1) Reduce API key churn — prefer reusing longer-lived keys (10–60m) for uploader pools. 2) Stagger rollout/warmup of worker processes over several minutes (introduce randomized start offsets). 3) Implement exponential backoff with full jitter on 429s (suggested initial backoff: 200ms -> 2s, max 8s) and limit aggressive retry concurrency when receiving 429s. 4) Group uploads into slightly larger batches (amortize connection overhead). 5) If using ephemeral keys for security reasons, pre-warm keys one at a time before starting concurrent streams to avoid simultaneous token seeding.
Product/longer-term suggestions (for internal follow-up): 1) Add a console-visible "burst budgeting" indicator for self_serve tenants showing tenant-level burst credit and estimated refill. 2) Consider exposing a configurable burst window or paid add-on for high-sustained ingestion patterns (similar to Dedicated reserved capacity but for burst smoothing). 3) Document best practices for ephemeral-key patterns and provide a short runbook template.
Customer outcome: After applying recommended changes (stagger, reuse keys, jittered backoff), Arcadia Labs reduced 429s from ~15% to <3% and accepted the tweaks as immediate mitigation. They're evaluating a Dedicated trial for larger nightly syncs; sales notified.
payload.summary: Configuring sustained vs burst quota for multiplexed ingestion workers to avoid 429s

Issue summary:
NimbleDocs reports repeated 429 responses for end-users during sustained interactive sessions. The customer upgraded to per-user ephemeral tokens to enforce end-user quotas on top of their org-level subscription. Console shows both user and org quota available, but API requests are being throttled.

Impact:
A subset of end-users receive 429s during high-concurrency workflows (document preview + realtime summarization). Customer-facing sessions degrade; several users report timeouts and retries. No full org outage but user-level UX severely impacted.

Environment:
Dedicated account on prod (us-east-1). Using Redwood SDKs with ephemeral tokens minted by customer auth service. Tokens have TTL of 15 minutes. Traffic peak simulated at ~120 concurrent end-users per org.

Observed behavior:
- Requests using ephemeral token appear to be consumed from both the per-user bucket and the org-level tenant bucket simultaneously.
- Console shows user bucket with headroom while tenant bucket is exhausted (429s returned with X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0).
- Throttles occur even though console recently reflected a billing upgrade that should have increased tenant quota.

Expected behavior:
- Ephemeral tokens minted for end-users should be charged only to the intended bucket (user-level) and counted against the org pool per configured policy, not double-counted.

Additional notes:
- Customer moved to ephemeral tokens last week and rotated parent API key on 2026-03-11.
- They use a token-creation service that attaches metadata headers to identify parent_key_id and user_id.

1) Configure a dedicated account with org API key and enable per-user ephemeral tokens.
2) Use NimbleDocs token minting flow to request ephemeral tokens (TTL 15m).
3) Start 100+ concurrent short-lived streaming sessions using ephemeral tokens.
4) Observe 429s and check response headers for X-RateLimit-Remaining and X-RateLimit-Scope.
5) Compare console quota readouts for user and tenant during the spike.

Reproduction notes: reproducible in staging when token-creation service omits parent_key_id header during minting.

Sample snippets from proxy/access logs (redacted):
2026-03-13T09:12:05Z | req_id=abc123 | token_id=ephemeral-7a2f | parent_key_id=NULL | X-Forwarded-For=35.201.22.11 | status=200 | latency=120ms
2026-03-13T09:12:06Z | req_id=abc124 | token_id=ephemeral-7a2f | parent_key_id=NULL | status=429 | quota_scope=tenant | X-RateLimit-Remaining=0
2026-03-13T09:12:07Z | req_id=abc125 | token_id=ephemeral-9b3c | parent_key_id=org-993 | status=200 | latency=95ms

Auth service trace (customer-provided):
- Token mint call returns ephemeral token with header `x-parent-key-id: org-993` in some flows but missing in rotated flow.

Timeline and diagnostics:
- 2026-03-13 10:00 UTC: Support received report from NimbleDocs (CS AE: Marco Ruiz).
- 2026-03-13 10:12 UTC: Support captured request/response headers and observed parent_key_id null for many ephemeral tokens.
- 2026-03-13 11:00 UTC: Replicated in staging by removing parent_key propagation from token mint path — reproduced identical 429 pattern.
- Quota-service metrics show tokens with missing parent_id are being charged against a fallback accounting path that currently increments both user and tenant buckets for safety (legacy behavior introduced in 2024-auth-fallback change).
- Console refresh occasionally shows tenant quota increase (billing upgrade), but enforcement layer still uses in-memory token-bucket snapshots that lag ~30s under strong churn.

Hypothesis:
1) Missing parent_key metadata on ephemeral tokens triggers fallback code path which increments both user and tenant counters to avoid orphaned tokens (legacy safety).
2) Combined with high concurrency and shard-snapshot lag, tenant bucket gets exhausted leading to 429s even though console shows nominal headroom.

Evidence:
- Repro in staging with parent_key omitted.
- Quota-service logs show double increment events flagged with tag `legacy_fallback_charge`.

Immediate mitigations tried:
- Instructed customer to enable a minting path that ensures parent_key header is always set (workaround).
- Increased quota-service token refill smoothing temporarily for this org to reduce transient 429s.

Short-term (applied 2026-03-14):
- Deployed hotfix to quota-service to stop double-incrementing when parent_key is missing; instead mark token as 'orphaned' and count only against user bucket until token is reconciled. (PR: github.com/redwood-inference/platform/pull/4021).
- Updated enforcement path to prefer persisted parent_key mapping in DB if header absent (failsafe).
- Released guidance to NimbleDocs: ensure token mint flow includes `x-parent-key-id` header; SDK patch v1.12.4 validates mint response.

Long-term actions (backlog / post-incident):
- Add robust instrumentation for fallback charge events across quota shards (owner: quota-team).
- Migrate legacy fallback behavior to a reconciliation job that runs asynchronously and does not increment tenant bucket synchronously. (TICKET: INT-3301).
- Improve console -> enforcement consistency with short-lived snapshot windows and write-through invalidation on billing changes.

Customer communication:
- Notified NimbleDocs 2026-03-14 09:10 UTC of hotfix and recommended steps. They confirmed reduced 429s in a 2-hour validation window.
payload.summary: End-user ephemeral tokens being double-counted against org and user buckets causing 429s for NimbleDocs

Issue summary:
Customer BrightChat Labs (dedicated) reported a sudden increase in 5xx responses and long-tail tail latency on streaming and short-sync generation routes starting during the 09:15-09:45 UTC window in us-east. Impact: several production endpoints returning 502/503 and occasional 504, increased first-byte times up to 8s for affected requests.

Impact:
- BrightChat experienced degraded UX across chat and batch embeddings; multiple customer sessions timed out and retried.
- Platform-level metrics show API gateway threadpool saturation and a correlated spike in upstream runtime connection churn.

Environment:
- prod | us-east; affected routes: /v1/chat/stream and /v1/embeddings/bulk.
- Customer on dedicated capacity pool: shard dc-dedicated-45.

Steps to reproduce (observed pattern):
1) Send burst of mixed streaming and embedding requests (small payloads, high concurrency) to BrightChat tenant.
2) After ~20s, several ephemeral runtimes start failing health checks and drop connections.
3) API gateway threads queue up and return 502/503 when backpressure exceeds threadpool limits.

Observed behavior:
- Heartbeat misses from ephemeral scheduler to proxy; runtimes flagged unhealthy and removed from routing.
- Rapid reconnect attempts from many clients cause socket churn and keepalive exhaustion.

Expected behavior:
- Ephemeral scaler should maintain stable heartbeat windows during scale-up and not trigger mass eviction. Runtimes should warm gracefully without overloading the API gateway.
Issue observed during mixed streaming+embedding burst against BrightChat tenant in us-east
Synthetic reproduction: 200 concurrent short streaming sessions + 10 parallel bulk-embed uploads over 30s
Monitor api-gateway threadpool, ephemeral scheduler heartbeats, and runtime health events during the burst
[09:16:21] scheduler: heartbeat timeout for runtime r-0c12 (last seen 2026-03-12T09:16:02Z)
[09:16:22] proxy: mark runtime r-0c12 unhealthy (consecutive misses=3)
[09:16:23] apigw: threadpool queue full -> returning 502 to tenant brightchat (route=/v1/chat/stream)
[09:16:24] runtime: reconnect failure: dial tcp: connection reset by peer
[09:16:30] scheduler: prewarm trigger + scale-up to 4 ephemeral instances for tenant brightchat
Support (Aisha): Customer noticed an uptick in 5xx starting ~09:15 UTC; they captured SDK logs and retry traces. Asked for immediate triage and suggested temporary rate limiting.
SRE (Tomás Rivera) 2026-03-12 10:03: Observed synchronized heartbeat misses from the ephemeral scheduler across >60% of pool nodes for dc-dedicated-45. Correlated with a config sweep to scheduler.timeout_ms that landed at 09:12 UTC.
Eng (Elena Brooks) 2026-03-12 11:10: Confirmed heartbeat window drift after config sweep — value decreased from 12000ms -> 4000ms in the control plane; some warmup tasks exceed new window leading to false negatives and eviction.
SRE (Tomás) 2026-03-12 11:35: Applied mitigation: rolled back scheduler.timeout_ms to 12000ms for dc-dedicated-45; manually re-added evicted runtimes to routing; observed error rate drop within 7 minutes.
Customer (BrightChat CSM) 2026-03-12 12:05: Customer verified restored traffic and reported improved response behavior; will keep monitoring for regressions.
Timeline and findings:
- 09:12 UTC: control-plane config sweep pushed a new scheduler heartbeat timeout (4000ms) to several dedicated pools as part of a normal rollout.
- 09:15 UTC onward: workloads with mixed streaming and embedding caused ephemeral runtimes to exceed the tighter heartbeat window during scale-up/warmup.
- False unhealthy markings produced mass evictions; clients retried, driving socket churn and apigw threadpool exhaustion.
- Metrics: apigw threadpool utilization peaked at 98%; runtime connection churn increased by 8x; evicted count peaked at 52 instances for dc-dedicated-45.
- Root cause: too-aggressive heartbeat timeout combined with prewarm tasks that block the scheduler event loop briefly (IO-bound checkpointing on some runtimes).
- Secondary contributing factors: default keepalive pool size for apigw was near threshold for this tenant's historical burst pattern, leaving little headroom during reconnection waves.
Short-term mitigations completed:
1) Rolled back scheduler.timeout_ms to 12000ms for affected dedicated pools (dc-dedicated-45).
2) Manually reintroduced healthy runtimes and triggered a staggered prewarm to avoid sync eviction.
3) Applied temporary tenant-level client QPS throttle for BrightChat (set to 75% of baseline) until rollout fully validated.
4) Increased apigw keepalive pool soft limit by 20% for us-east edge to absorb reconnect spikes.

Longer-term actions (tracked as follow-ups):
- Engineering will harden rollout gating for scheduler control-plane changes (PR linked) to include canary traffic patterns and an automated rollback if unhealthy evictions exceed threshold.
- Adjust default prewarm behavior to reduce blocking IO on warmup paths; add non-blocking checkpoint stream.
- Add an alert rule: sudden cluster-wide heartbeat miss rate >5% triggers immediate rollback and alert.
- Ownership: Autoscaler team to deliver patch in runtime repo and a scheduled canary to validate in staging with synthetic mixed workload.

Workaround for customers: use per-tenant rate limiting or stagger client-side reconnection with exponential backoff.

Issue summary:
Customers on BeaconHealth's dedicated deployment report duplicated external tool/webhook invocations and missing ack visibility when clients use the SDK prefetch/buffered-sender feature combined with long-running streaming sessions.

Impact:
- Duplicate side-effects observed in customer systems (double POSTs to downstream tools) for ~0.8% of streaming sessions that were active >30s.
- Billing noise due to re-executed tool work.
- Customer has temporarily disabled prefetch, impacting throughput and latency.

Environment:
- Dedicated pool in us-west (customer-owned capacity).
- SDKs in use: go (v1.11.0), python (v2.0.4), ts (v0.9.7); all using client-side prefetch/buffering with background token refresh enabled.
- Model: redwood/gptx-8k-v1 pinned in routing policy.

Steps to reproduce (customer-provided):
1) Start a long-lived streaming session with a chain of function/tool calls (external webhook that creates an order).
2) Enable client prefetch/buffer of 10 messages and enable background token refresh.
3) Simulate a short network hiccup or proxy 503 (edge) causing reconnect and resume.
4) Observe duplicate POSTs to downstream webhook within seconds of the resume.

Observed behavior:
- On reconnect, some SDKs re-sent buffered messages but the idempotency header (X-Idempotency-Key) was either missing or truncated on one of the resend attempts, resulting in the server accepting the call as a new invocation.
- Acknowledgement tokens from our runtime (funcall ack) were sometimes applied to the resumed session but did not de-duplicate the downstream side-effect because the idempotency key didn't match.

Expected behavior:
- SDK should preserve per-action idempotency metadata across reconnects and replays, or the server should suppress duplicate downstream executions when the request body/hash matches within a short dedupe window.

Relevant logs/traces (samples):
- trace_id: 9f7a2e03-usw-2026-03-09-02:15:37 (shows reconnect and two POST attempts to customer webhook: 200 then 201).
- gateway logs: edge-proxy returned 503 at 02:15:36, client resumed at 02:15:38.

Additional notes:
2026-03-11 - BeaconHealth (Customer): Attached sanitized headers for the two POSTs. Noted X-Idempotency-Key present on first POST but missing on second. Shared SDK config: prefetch=10, background_refresh=true.
2026-03-12 - BeaconHealth (Customer): Confirms workaround effective; requested guidance for permanent fix and whether runtime dedupe window will be tuned for dedicated clusters.
Findings:
- Root cause appears to be interaction between client prefetch buffering and our chunked request/resume path. When buffered frames are re-emitted after a reconnect, a header boundary can be lost if the client re-chunks messages differently, resulting in either missing or truncated X-Idempotency-Key.
- Affected paths: streaming resume with buffered frames + background token refresh that triggers a simultaneous connection reset and resume.
- Reproducible across go and python SDKs (TS less frequent due to different internal buffering).
Hypotheses tested:
- Proxy edge 503 triggers immediate reconnect -> yes.
- SDK re-chunking behavior leads to header boundary loss -> confirmed in go repro.
- Server dedupe on body-hash would have prevented side-effect duplication in many cases, but we currently rely primarily on X-Idempotency-Key for tool dedupe.
Action items created:
1) SDK engineering: backport header-preservation fix to go/python/ts clients (PR linked). Priority: high.
2) Runtime: evaluate short dedupe-by-body/hash window (120s) for function/webhook invocations to catch cases when idempotency header is absent due to client-side truncation.
3) Support: surface clear guidance in SDK docs about prefetch implications and recommend per-action idempotency keys.
Workaround and fix rollout:
- Short-term: Customer disabled prefetch buffer; implemented webhook-side dedup using X-Idempotency-Key and body-hash fallback. Support validated reduction in duplicates.
- Medium-term: SDK patch landed in go and python (PR https://github.com/redwood-inference/ssr-sdk/pull/6789). We released go v1.11.1 and python v2.0.5 candidate to BeaconHealth's dedicated cluster for validation on 2026-03-12.
- Long-term: Runtime team will prototype a 2-minute body-hash dedupe for tool/webhook invocations in dedicated environments; design doc link: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/ENG/Runtime+tool+dedupe.
Follow-ups:
- SRE/Runtime to run gradual rollout of body-hash dedupe to dedicated clusters and monitor false-positive suppression rates (owner: Lara Gomez). Target ETA: 2026-04-02.
- SDK team to publish release notes and upgrade guide; add explicit docs about prefetch and token refresh interactions (owner: Marcus Li). Target ETA: 2026-03-18.
- Support to update KB article and notify customers with streaming+prefetch use patterns.
Status: In Progress (customer validated workaround; patches deployed to staging and a dedicated canary cluster; production rollout pending runtime dedupe decision).
payload.summary: Client-side prefetch queue + reconnects causing missed idempotency header and duplicated funcall acks across SDKs

Issue summary:
Customer DocuSynth reports that long SSE streams intermittently terminate with the client receiving an EOF immediately after a short silent period that follows the handshake. The server later shows a batched heartbeat message emitted by the gateway and the final choice content appears in logs, but the client never receives the terminal delimiter.

Impact:
- Some generation requests for document summarization stop 2–8 seconds before the expected end, returning partial content.
- Customer says ~3% of streaming sessions in us-east time window 09:00–18:00 are affected.
- Symptoms cause downstream UI to show "incomplete result" and trigger a retry loop.

Environment:
- DocuSynth account on Dedicated cluster in prod-us-east.
- Affected model: redwood-1-large pinned v2026-02-28.
- Edge: customer routes through their NLB -> our streaming-gateway -> edge-proxy -> serving-runtime.

Observed behavior:
1) Client completes normal SSE handshake and starts receiving tokens.
2) After final choice is about to be sent, a 3–6s quiet period occurs (no chunks to client).
3) Client receives an EOF/connection-close without a "event: end" delimiter.
4) Server logs show a batched heartbeat emitted at the end of the quiet period and then the final choice entry in the serving-runtime logs, but no matching SSE end event to the socket send trace.

Expected behavior:
- Short quiet periods are acceptable, but the terminal choice must be sent and the SSE end marker must be delivered before connection close.

Steps to reproduce (customer-provided):
1) Use customer SDK with keepalive=10s, send a long prompt (1200–2200 tokens output).
2) Reproduce on prod-us-east under normal load; issue surfaces intermittently.
3) Captured a failing session trace id: sess-ea4f7b2c.

Notes:
- Affected only for sessions that pass through a particular version of the customer's NLB (they confirmed two NLBs; one shows no failures).
- Client-side metrics show socket close reason as 1006 in some cases (abrupt close).
- No billing impact reported.

Client performs SSE handshake against streaming endpoint with keepalive=10s
Request large generation (expected >1000 tokens) with redwood-1-large pinned
Observe 2–8s quiet period near end of generation followed by immediate EOF without end event
Capture server-side trace (sess-ea4f7b2c) and gateway logs for comparison
[2026-03-10T14:22:05Z] gateway[sess-ea4f7b2c] -> tokens streamed up to choice N-3
[2026-03-10T14:22:08Z] gateway[sess-ea4f7b2c] -> quiet window begins (no send operations)
[2026-03-10T14:22:11Z] gateway[sess-ea4f7b2c] -> emitted batched-heartbeat {batch_id: hb-117}
[2026-03-10T14:22:11Z] serving-runtime[sess-ea4f7b2c] -> final-choice stored to log (choice_index: N)
[2026-03-10T14:22:11Z] edge-proxy -> socket closed by remote (client) code=1006

Additional notes:
2026-03-11 09:43 - DocuSynth (Customer): Provided a pcaps and confirmed affected NLB is Azure NLB with aggressive idle-timeout custom setting (20s). Also supplied SDK session id sess-ea4f7b2c.
Hypothesis 1: Edge NLB is performing a late TCP rebind/keepalive that interferes with timely ACK of the final SSE bytes, causing client to RST and our gateway to close before end-event is delivered.
Hypothesis 2: Gateway heartbeat coalescing optimization batches heartbeat and final choice into one kernel send; if the client closes mid-coalesced-send the SSE end event may never be observed by the client.
Evidence: pcap shows server FIN followed by client RST in 2 reproductions. Kernel send queue shows coalesced 14KB payload containing heartbeat + final chunk in traces where failure occurred.
Temporary test: added explicit flush and 50ms delay after end-event in canary. Reproduction rate dropped but not eliminated under heavy synthetic load.
Shared workaround with customer: increase SDK keepalive to 30s and enable explicit per-chunk flush option (available in the beta SDK).
SRE to open PR to make 'flush-after-end-event' default in gateway with conservative 50ms grace window and a config toggle. PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/streaming-gateway/pull/5021
SRE and Edge teams to run load test with simulated NLB behavior to validate fix; target rollout to canary on 2026-03-14.
If fix reduces failures <0.1% in canary, schedule full rollout to prod-us-east with a 24-48 hour monitoring window.
In progress: Provided workaround and deployed canary instrumentation. Code change drafted to flush after end-event; load testing pending. Customer accepted temporary SDK workaround and will monitor.

Issue summary:
Between 18:10-19:05 PDT on 2026-03-12, QuillEdge reported sustained throughput collapse on their reserved capacity pool (P50 and P95 tokens/s dropped by ~65%). Customers experienced increased queueing and elevated p99 latency for short-lived streaming requests.

Impact:
- Customer production workloads degraded for ~55 minutes during evening traffic ramp.
- Automated fallbacks to hosted routes triggered for some requests.
- No data loss; inference responses were delayed or routed to lower-capacity fallbacks.

Environment:
- Dedicated reserved pool in us-west-2 (cluster id: rp-west-22).
- Customer model pin: redwood-instruct-7b-v2, concurrency config: 12 per slot.

Timeline (high-level):
- 18:08: first alerts — increased queue length and attach latencies.
- 18:12: customer open ticket with support; observed p99 spikes.
- 18:20: platform metrics showed repeated GPU PGFAULT events on 3 nodes in pool.
- 18:25: autoscaler reacted by shrinking pool (hysteresis window causing several slot drains).
- 18:30-19:00: throughput remained depressed while evicted slots cycled and KV cache warmups repeated.
- 19:02: mitigation rollout (driver patch + autoscaler threshold tweak) applied to pool.
- 19:05: observed recovery to baseline.

Steps to reproduce (internal repro notes):
1. Seed reserved pool with mixed short-lived streaming client (avg token length 50) and background prefetch batchers.
2. Induce sudden increase of small-stream connections (~3x baseline) over 2 minutes.
3. Force a simulated GPU driver memory pressure to produce page fault spikes (test harness only).
4. Observe autoscaler decision path under current hysteresis (cooldown 90s) and slot drain behavior.

Observed metrics & logs (high level):
- GPU PGFAULT count: nodes gpu-ww-004/006/009 ~120-220 faults in 10m window.
- Kernel OOM/eviction logs: repeated TDR-like driver resets reported but driver recovered without full node reboot.
- Autoscaler actions: 3 slot shrinks starting 18:24, completed by 18:28.
- KV cache miss rate spiked from 4% to 42% during slot churn.
- Request fallback/incidence: ~1.8% routed to hosted fallback for some tenants.

Hypothesis:
Primary cause is transient GPU memory pressure that manifested as driver-level page-faults on a subset of GPUs serving QuillEdge. The autoscaler interpreted the degraded attach/heartbeat signals and initiated scale-downs due to conservative hysteresis thresholds. The resulting slot churn forced repeated KV cache rebuilds and increased per-request cold cost and latency, compounding the throughput collapse. We also observed that a background snapshotter process on the same nodes increased NVMe IO, amplifying driver latency under the small-stream-dominated workload.

Investigation notes:
- Reproduced elevated PGFAULT counts on staging when running mixed small-stream + snapshotter IO.
- Driver logs indicate late-page reclamation stalls prior to recoveries (no fatal crashes).
- Autoscaler logic currently uses attach-latency + heartbeat-drop windows (90s cooldown) which, combined with immediate reactive shrink, created a feedback loop.
- KV cache warmup time for these models is non-trivial and magnified throughput impact after slot changes.

- 18:40: Provided initial engineering update and temporary mitigation (increase pool min-size and enable fallback routing threshold).

Issue summary:
Customer reports a sharp drop in dedicated pool throughput starting ~2026-03-10 11:30 UTC impacting PrismHealth's production routes. Symptoms include elevated p95/p99 latency, increased queueing, and requests falling back to lower-tier models. The degradation recovers only after operator intervention (restarting allocator processes).

Impact:
- PrismHealth observed 3x increase in p99 for text-generation routes and ~40% drop in throughput for pinned model redwood-small-ops-3b.
- Multiple retries and client-side fallback to hosted models triggered higher token costs.
- User-facing slowdowns during midday window for the US-East reserved pool.

Environment:
- Dedicated capacity (reserved pool id: rp-89c2)

- Region: us-east, prod
- Customer tier: dedicated
- Affected services: serving-runtime, allocator, autoscaler, scheduler

Steps to reproduce (observed):
1. Heavy mix of long-lived streaming and many short-lived inference requests during midday traffic spike.
2. Allocator shows steadily increasing average slot age and queue depth.
3. New short streams are queued behind aged allocations; autoscaler does not scale fast enough because allocator believes pool is saturated.
4. Throughput drops and p99 latency increases; requests begin failing over to fallback routing after configured timeouts.

Relevant logs / traces (excerpts):
- allocator WARN 2026-03-10T11:38:21Z "slot_age_skew > threshold (mean=98s, p95=420s)"
- scheduler DEBUG 2026-03-10T11:39:05Z "assign_attempts=3; queued_short_streams=172; active_long_streams=43"
- autoscaler INFO 2026-03-10T11:40:12Z "scale_decision=hold; signal=low_free_slots; reason=allocator_reports_high_util"
- serving-runtime ERROR 2026-03-10T11:41:00Z "prefetch_latency=1.8s; kv-cache-growth=+18% in 10m"

Notes: allocator aging refers to the distribution of allocation ages (how long a GPU slot has been occupied). We observed a skewed distribution where many slots are long-lived and not releasing quickly (old streaming sessions + pinned prefetched contexts), while short-lived bursts pile up and are starved. This is different from classic noisy-tenant GPU hogging — allocator metrics suggested internal bookkeeping that caused late-stage allocation reordering and a conservative free-slot estimate to be published to the autoscaler.

Issue summary: Starting ~2026-03-13 11:05 UTC we observed a rising 5xx rate on a subset of routes serving FolioAI's dedicated tenancy. Errors were primarily 502/503 from API gateway and upstream runtime connection resets. Impact: customer observed ~18% of requests failing with 5xx over a 50-minute window; some streaming sessions dropped mid-response leading to customer-visible feature regressions. Environment: prod/us-east, dedicated pool for FolioAI. Steps to reproduce: 1) Initiate 50 parallel multipart/chunked embedding uploads with small (2-8KB) chunks and artificially delayed chunk pacing (50-200ms between chunks). 2) Keep connection open until all chunks delivered. 3) Observe gateway accept-queue growth and incremental increase in upstream runtime worker 'stalled-parser' goroutines. Observed logs: - apigw: "accept_queue_depth=512 route=fio-embed status=503 upstream=reset" - proxy: "read_timeout: client stalled during chunked body; backlog=498" - runtime: "worker: stalled_parser_count=34, mem_heap_alloc=7.8GB, goroutine=1720" - autoscaler: "scale_decision: insufficient CPU headroom; recent_p95_latency=820ms" First-response SLA missed for a portion of affected requests. Temporary mitigations: rate limiting on customer route, diversion to warm fallback variant, and mass-reject policy for slow-chunked uploads applied at 11:25 UTC.
2026-03-13 11:12 UTC - Support (Aisha): Customer reported increased 5xx affecting embedding uploads. Collected traces and forwarded to SRE. Requested immediate mitigation options.
2026-03-13 11:18 UTC - SRE (Marco): Initial metrics show accept_queue latency rising and a correlated increase in 'stalled_parser' workers in runtime. Hypothesis: a pathological client upload pattern holds socket resources while leaving runtime parse tasks blocked, amplifying backpressure to apigw.
2026-03-13 11:26 UTC - Support (Aisha): Applied temporary route-level rate limit (concurrent_uploads=8) and enabled reject-on-slow-body policy. 5xx rate reduced from 18% to ~4% within 6 minutes per dashboards.
2026-03-13 12:05 UTC - Customer (FolioAI contact: Maya Torres): Confirmed partial recovery but requests intermittently hit 5xx during peak bursts. Shared sample client logs and request IDs.
2026-03-13 16:20 UTC - Engineering (SRE): Deployed parser timeout patch (PR#2398) to staging for validation. Observed improved early-reject behavior on slow-chunked bodies without impacting normal traffic.
2026-03-14 08:40 UTC - Engineering (Marco): Hotfix rolled to prod; removed emergency rate limit for FolioAI, replaced with tuned slow-body reject and adjusted apigw accept-queue threshold. Monitoring shows stable 5xx baseline.
2026-03-14 09:05 UTC - Support (Aisha): Customer validated that embedding uploads are now completing and 5xx rate returned to prior baseline. Marking incident resolved; follow-up items added.
Timeline: 11:05 UTC - first signal in SRE dashboards; 11:18 UTC - support escalation; 11:25 UTC - emergency rate limit applied; 16:20 UTC - staging patch; 08:40 UTC (next day) - prod hotfix roll.
Root cause hypothesis: Slow-chunked client uploads were holding API gateway connections open and causing a head-of-line resource starvation within the serving-runtime's request parsing pipeline. The runtime's parser would block awaiting chunk completion, causing goroutine accumulation and increasing memory retention which amplified autoscaler and worker churn.
Why this manifested as 5xx: With accept_queue growth and many blocked parser workers, the proxy started returning 502/503 when it could not forward to healthy upstreams. Backpressure then caused some runtimes to hit resource thresholds and reset connections, leading to 5xx.
Evidence: Correlation between slow_body_duration metric and accept_queue_depth (pearson r=0.87). Stack samples showed repeated syscall.SIGPIPE and stalled read loops in parser codepath. Heap profiles showed temporary allocations from buffered chunk assembly.
Scope: Affected only dedicated tenancy for FolioAI due to their client pattern (small-chunk, slow-pacing uploads). Other tenants with bulk uploads using standard chunk sizes not impacted.
Workarounds tested: - Route-level concurrent upload limit (reduced incidents but customer throughput constrained) - Divert to fallback variant (increased latency) - Early-reject on slow-body (best balance).
Deployed parser timeout and early-reject behavior controlled by configuration (runtime flag: slow_body_timeout_ms=1200). Updated API gateway accept-queue thresholds to fail fast earlier for slow uploads and added a route-level policy to surface client-side guidance (recommended chunk size and pacing). Hotfix PR merged: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/2398. Rollout notes: staged to 10% (staging) -> 50% -> 100% with monitoring checks between waves; observed no regression for normal traffic. Post-incident actions: (1) add automated synthetic test that simulates small-chunk slow uploads against dedicated pools, (2) update runbook to include early-reject and rate-limit playbook, (3) notify Product about potential UI guidance for customers performing bulk embedding uploads.

Customer BlueArc Commerce reported persistent elevated 5xx responses on the /v1/embeddings/upload and streaming embedding endpoints during a planned data migration. Errors began after a sustained concurrency spike and appeared correlated with client-side hedged retries. Customer's large-batch embedding uploads intermittently fail; multiple downstream features (search indexing, personalization pipeline) reporting partial failures. Estimated affected requests: ~50k over a 3-hour window. Customer SLAs at risk for dedicated contract.
1) Use a client that issues hedged requests (client issues duplicate requests to reduce tail latency) to /v1/embeddings/upload with 4x parallel hedges per request.
2) Send steady concurrent upload traffic from a single tenant: 300 concurrent connections, average payload ~10MB per request.
3) Observe apigw metrics: elevated 502/503/504 rates; watch runtime logs for prefetch/pipeline errors and process restarts.
[runtime-01] 2026-03-10T18:12:33Z ERROR serve: panic: nil pointer dereference at runtime/prefetch.go:214
[nvml] 2026-03-10T18:12:34Z WARNING: GPU 0 reset detected
[apigw] 2026-03-10T18:12:34Z WARN: upstream returned 502 after retry amplification (hedged fanout=4)
[autosc] 2026-03-10T18:13:05Z INFO: launched 3 new runtimes due to CPU pressure; immediate OOM on one pod
Initial hypothesis: apigw hedged requests multiplied concurrent work against the same model shard and caused prefetch lock contention and KV-cache thrashing.
Reproduced locally in staging by replaying tenant traffic with hedged fanout=4; observed serialized prefetch being bypassed by parallel code path added in runtime PR #1842.
Core dumps show panic in prefetch cancellation path where a prefetched buffer pointer is accessed after premature free (stack traces attached to GH issue).
Autoscaler reacted by spinning up additional runtimes which further increased pressure on NVMe and GPU memory, causing GPU resets and intermittent OOMs.
Alerting/monitoring: apigw spike in upstream_5xx_rate, runtime process restart_count, nvml_reset_count all spiked within seconds of the hedged flood.
1) Temporarily disabled hedged retries for BlueArc tenant via rate-limiter rule in apigw (reduced fanout from 4 to 1).
2) Applied circuit-breaker on embedding upload route to limit parallel in-flight requests per tenant to 80.
3) Rolled back runtime change from PR 1842 to restore serialized prefetch behavior while a fix is prepared.
4) Increased observability retention for affected runtime nodes and enabled core-dump collection for a full window.
5) Notified customer and advised to pause large bulk uploads until resolved.
Patch committed to runtime to guard prefetch buffer lifetime and add per-tenant prefetch serialization (runtime PR 1857). API Gateway updated to cap hedged fanout at 2 and enforce per-tenant concurrent upload limits. Changes rolled to canary then prod in us-east-1 on 2026-03-12 03:20Z. 5xx rate returned to baseline (~0.4%) for the tenant. Customer confirmed resumed uploads succeeded. Ticket closed after verification window.
A) Load-test hedged-retry scenarios with quantized models under NVMe/GPU saturation and publish runbook.
B) Add a prefetch serialization unit test and fuzz buffer lifetime edge cases.
C) Introduce an apigw metric for hedged_fanout per-route and tenant and set alert threshold at >2 for sustained 5m.

Customer observed intermittent routing to a compatibility variant (compat/llama-compat-1.0) for specific tenant sessions that had an explicit model pin to redwood/falcon-v2-7b-llm-v2.1.3. The divergence began during a scheduled dedicated pool preemptive rebalance tied to an autoscaler prewarm and regional cutover.

Impact:
- Several tenant sessions returned responses from the compat variant for ~15-30 minutes intermittently across us-east and eu-west.
- Customer reported increased token bill for compatibility variant (estimated +32% token cost) and user-facing quality regressions for high-value workflows.
- Streaming connections remained connected; issue primarily observed on requests that included function-calling metadata and custom headers.

Environment:
- Tier: dedicated
- Dedicated pool: atlas-dedicated-gpupool-3 (us-east primary, eu-west standby)
- Model pinned by tenant via API: redwood/falcon-v2-7b-llm-v2.1.3
- Time window: 2026-03-10 02:12 - 2026-03-10 02:47 UTC

Steps to reproduce (as provided by customer):
1) Create tenant session with explicit model pin to redwood/falcon-v2-7b-llm-v2.1.3
2) Send streaming chat requests with function-calling enabled and headers: X-Tenant-ID, X-Request-Origin, X-Client-Trace (customized by customer edge)
3) Trigger a heavy load ramp (~2x baseline) or wait for autoscaler rebalance during a geo cutover window
4) Observe intermittent responses from compatibility variant and sudden per-token billing delta

Observed behavior:
- Pin metadata (pin cookie/lease) is present on the client but routing occasionally returns compat variant responses.
- Edge logs show header rewriting/stripping events occurring near the same timestamps as the first fallback.
- Orchestrator shows a short-lived preemptive rebalance in the dedicated pool that killed a subset of prewarm workers.

Expected behavior:
- Tenant sessions with an explicit model pin should continue to route to the pinned variant or use the configured fallback policy (explicitly configured to prefer pinned or failover gracefully without switching to compat).

Attachments / Logs:
- Customer supplied request IDs: [r-20260310-7a1e, r-20260310-7a2c, r-20260310-7b90]
- Edge log excerpts and sample response bodies included in attachments (uploaded to ticket).

Noted that when X-Client-Trace was truncated by our edge normalizer the affinity key used by the router was missing, causing fallback to compatibility variant. Opening investigation notes.

2026-03-12 11:03 - Customer (Atlas Eng - Maya Singh): Patch validated on our side for the 24h window; no further unexpected compat responses observed. Waiting on long-term fix timeline and confirmation on billing adjustment options.
Edge telemetry: header_normalizer component evidence shows 18 stripping events across the window where X-Client-Trace and X-Request-Origin were shortened to a tokenized form. The router affinity key is derived from X-Tenant-ID + request-hash; when secondary header is missing TTL fallback occurs.
Orchestrator timeline: preemptive rebalance initiated at 2026-03-10 02:05 UTC. Two prewarm workers terminated in eu-west, causing traffic to shift and some sessions to be routed via edge replay to us-east. Rebalance coincides with spike in fallback rates.

Hypothesis 2: Orchestrator prewarm worker termination created a short window where the route snapshot did not include the tenant's pinned binding on the active shard (race between snapshot publish and worker termination).

Mitigation applied: tenant-scoped edge rule bypass for affinity headers. Short-term: continue bypass for 72h while orchestration team implements 'pin-handshake-resilience' change to snapshot publication order and adds a prewarm draining grace window to avoid simultaneous worker termination and snapshot republish. Long-term: RFC to make router affinity derive from signed pin cookie (server-validated) rather than mutable edge headers. Billing: CS to coordinate credit review with Finance for the 0.8 hour window where compat model billing was higher; engineering to provide verification of fallback duration.

Issue summary: Multiple customer requests (VirtuDocs) observed ~5-15% of repeated prompt requests hitting long tails (p99 > 6s, some 30s timeouts) when sending identical conversation prefixes. Impact: Customer facing increased latency on repeat user prompts causing timeouts and degraded UX during peak hours. Environment: Dedicated pool in us-east-1, serving-runtime v1.14.2 with kvcache async-prefetch enabled. Observed behavior: repeat prompts that previously returned <300ms now occasionally take multiple seconds or time out (30s). Expected behavior: cached prefixes should result in sub-500ms latencies for short contexts.
1) Use a repeat prompt sequence: send prompt A, then follow-up identical prompt A after short interval (5-15s)
2) Repeat at moderate concurrency (10-30 qps) against dedicated endpoint in us-east-1
3) Observe latency distribution on the Redwood API (token-level breakdown).
03/09 16:00 - Support: Received VirtuDocs report, escalated to SRE with p99 histograms and example request ids.
03/09 16:20 - SRE: Confirmed spike in p99 for prefix-heavy traffic pattern on dedicated pool; correlation with async-prefetch flip on 2026-02-28 deploy.
03/09 17:10 - Eng (runtime): Reproduced locally by simulating concurrent repeat prompts; saw duplicate origin fetches and lock timeout on kvcache prefetch pipeline.
Hypothesis: The async-prefetch coordinator introduced in v1.14.0 does not correctly deduplicate in-flight prefetches when shard-mapping is rebalanced concurrently, leading to double origin fetches and delayed cache population. This increases per-request latency and occasionally triggers upstream timeouts under load.
Tests performed: A/B test with async-prefetch disabled returned p99 back to baseline; injected artificial shard rebalances to reproduce duplication; added extra instrumentation to measure outstanding prefetches per key.
A race condition in the async prefetch coordinator of the kvcache introduced by the shard remapping optimization (v1.14.0). When shard mappings change mid-prefetch, the deduplication key used by the coordinator could differ, causing two concurrent origin fetches for the same logical prefix. The duplicate fetches increased origin load and delayed the first successful cache population, causing p99 latency spikes and occasional 30s upstream timeouts.
Mitigation (hotfix): Disabled async-prefetch on the affected dedicated pool and reverted the shard-key normalization change via rollback in config (rolled 2026-03-10 02:00 UTC).
Immediate workaround for customer: Enabled synchronous prefix retrieval (config toggle) for VirtuDocs dedicated endpoint; this eliminated the race and brought p99 down to baseline within 15 minutes.
Permanent fix: Engineering created PR #7642 to make deduplication use a stable logical prefix id that survives remapping and added additional unit/integration tests. PR merged to main and scheduled for v1.14.3 rollout (2026-03-12).
Follow-up actions: Add dashboards for outstanding prefetch counts, add alert when duplicate origin fetch rate > 1% for >5m, and add a canary to exercise shard-remap scenarios before global rollouts.

Issue summary: Customer FastLogix reports a sudden wave of 429 responses across multiple services after they triggered a staged rollout of our new priority-shard feature in their dedicated pool. Impact: Customer reported ~20% of interactive chat requests rejected with 429 over a 45 minute window; several business-critical webhooks also saw rejections causing downstream backpressure. Environment: dedicated pool in us-west-2, priority-shard rollout toggled via feature-flag 'priority-shard-v2' to 25% of routes, orchestrator version 1.12.3, ingress-proxy sidecar 2.3.1. Steps to reproduce: 1) Enable feature-flag for subset of routes (priority-shard-v2=25%) 2) Start orchestrated workers (100 parallel processes) performing mixed bulk + realtime calls to /v1/chat and /v1/embeddings 3) Observe 429s spike within ~3 minutes 4) Toggle feature flag off and observe gradual recovery Observed behavior: 429s include header X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0 and X-RateLimit-Reset: ~30s. Console shows per-route quotas decreasing for both new-shard and legacy routes simultaneously. Logs show many requests attributed to the same tenant but counted against multiple route buckets (duplicate token accounting). Expected behavior: rollout should route traffic to the new shard without double-counting tokens and without causing cross-route burst exhaustion. Attachments/links: Slack thread #support-fastlogix: https://slack.redwood.com/archives/C12345/p1670000000000, Ratecontroller PR referenced above, customer-provided request traces (attached to ticket).
Customer reported degraded user experience for interactive chat widgets across their SaaS customers (approx 15-25% failed calls) and delayed webhook delivery for low-priority background jobs. They are on a dedicated reserved pool and require predictable throughput; this incident caused a business-impacting degradation and triggered their internal incident process.
1) In dedicated console, set priority-shard-v2=25% for org FastLogix 2) Launch 100 orchestrated worker processes which multiplex small chat calls (avg 40 tokens) and intermittent embedding calls 3) Monitor /v1/chat responses and rate-limit headers 4) Observe surge of 429 rejects within ~3 minutes
Sample 429 response headers captured from customer traces: Date: Tue, 10 Mar 2026 18:02:11 GMT
X-RateLimit-Limit: 120000
X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0
X-RateLimit-Reset: 29
X-RateLimit-Policy: per-route,tenant
Request-ID: rq_8a7f3c1
Ingress proxy logs: proxy-2.3.1 reported 'x-forwarded-for rewrite' messages concurrent with feature-flag toggle. Orchestrator traces: worker-74 emitted heavy preflight checks and warmup probes during rollout.
- Initial hypothesis: rollout introduced per-route bucket split but token accounting not yet synchronized between edge and origin, causing duplicate decrement.
- Observed correlation between feature-flag toggles and a spike in preflight/warmup traffic from orchestrated workers.
- Edge (ingress) was rewriting X-Forwarded-For and normalizing path prefixes; discovered recent proxy change (NGINX sidecar 2.3.1 -> config 'strip-route-prefix' enabled) that altered route fingerprinting.
- Ratecontroller logs show simultaneous debit to tenant and route buckets for same request ID in ~12% of sampled traces (duplicate-charge pattern).
- Related PR (ratecontroller#789) touched refill epoch rounding logic and priority-splatting; rolling re-deploy occurred earlier today and overlaps with customer's staged toggle.
- Reproduced in a canary by toggling feature-flag with a small orchestrator replica set; confirmed duplicate counting when proxy path normalization and shard split are enabled together.
- Confirmed that disabling 'strip-route-prefix' or disabling staged feature-flag prevents double-counting in the canary.
2026-03-10 17:58 UTC - FastLogix toggled priority-shard-v2 to 25%
2026-03-10 18:01 UTC - First wave of 429s reported by customer to support channel
2026-03-10 18:08 UTC - SRE triage; reproduced in canary
2026-03-10 18:22 UTC - Temporary mitigation recommended (disable feature-flag)
2026-03-10 18:28 UTC - Customer disabled flag; partial recovery observed
2026-03-11 09:15 UTC - Engineering issued patch PR to add stronger route fingerprinting and atomic debit guard
2026-03-12 03:40 UTC - Patch deployed to ratecontroller canaries for expanded testing

Additional notes:
2026-03-10 18:25 - FastLogix (Customer): We disabled the flag as requested. Noticed reduced 429s but still seeing occasional rejects. Would like rollback guidance if issue persists.
A timing and attribution mismatch between ingress route fingerprinting (changed by sidecar config) and the ratecontroller's shard-splitting debit logic. When the priority-shard rollout was toggled, some requests were attributed to both legacy and new route buckets due to path normalization differences and a refill-epoch rounding race, causing tenant-level burst credits to be double-counted and producing 429 rejects.
Short-term mitigation: advised customer to disable the feature-flag (priority-shard-v2) and temporarily revert the sidecar 'strip-route-prefix' change if safe. Opened a hotfix PR that: 1) adds an atomic debit guard preventing the same request ID being debited twice across route shards, 2) strengthens route fingerprinting to use route-id + normalized-path digest, and 3) aligns refill epoch rounding to wall-time boundaries to avoid split-window debits. Deployed patch to canary cluster; after validation will schedule staged rollout across dedicated pools. Suggested customer configuration changes: route-isolation=true for priority lanes during rollout, and reduce orchestrator parallelism with a 10s splay between worker starts.
- Engineering to merge and roll out ratecontroller patch to production after full canary validation (owner: Priya Nair).
- Update runbook 'priority-shard-rollout' with explicit preflight checks (ensure ingress path normalization compatibility).
- Add automated canary test that simulates orchestrator fanout + feature-flag toggle to catch duplicate-debit regressions.
- Operations to notify dedicated-pool customers about best practices when enabling per-route sharding (support article / KB).
This ticket will be updated when the patch is promoted to production and FastLogix confirms stable behavior. For immediate avoidance steps: do not combine path-normalizing proxy changes with priority-shard toggles; if unavoidable, use a 1% canary and monitor X-RateLimit headers closely for duplicate debit signatures.
