Issue summary:
Customer reports a noticeable increase in p99 latency for requests originating in EU (eu-central-1) after they enabled the 'strict data residency' toggle for their account. Traffic traces show some requests egressing to us-west-2 before returning to eu-central model hosts.

Impact:
- Customer-facing latency spikes: p50 ~120ms (unchanged), p95 ~240ms (slight), p99 up from ~620ms to ~1.6s on 2026-03-08 14:00-16:30 CET.
- Affects payment auth microservice calling Redwood for chat completions (sensitive data policy requires EU residency).

Environment:
- Customer environment: prod | eu-central, account on enterprise plan with private tenancy flag enabled.
- Models in use: redwood-rlm-13b (pinned), fallback set to open-llama-7b.

Steps to reproduce (as provided by customer):
1) Toggle strict residency ON in Console for account FinServeX.
2) Send completion requests from application region eu-central using pinned model redwood-rlm-13b.
3) Observe p99 via application monitoring and traces (Datadog).

Logs / traces attached by customer (excerpt):
- trace: /traces/finservx/2026-03-08/14:22:11 -> route decision: prefer eu-central but capacity_degraded -> selected fallback node host-uw2-12.us-west-2.redwood -> egress hop count: 2 -> model host: eu-central-rlm-13b-5 (final)
- tcpdump snippet: SYN/ACK exchange across igw-eu -> peering-usw -> igw-usw reported in packet capture.

Customer asks:
- Why are requests leaving EU when strict residency is ON?
- What causes the multi-hop to us-west and how can we prevent it?
- Mitigation to restore p99 while preserving residency guarantees.

Initial hypothesis: strict residency toggle enforces data-at-rest restrictions and causes control-plane to prefer nodes with verified residency attestations. If eu pool capacity is temporarily degraded, routing policy attempted a compatible fallback (same model version) hosted in another region but preserved ephemeral data residency by returning final compute to EU — causing an extra proxy/egress hop for KV/cache synchronization.

What we checked so far:
- Router decision logs (smart-routing) show policy 'residency_strict' with fallback_policy: allow_cross_region_buffered_fallback = true.
- Capacity metrics for eu-central dedicated pools showed a short degradation window 2026-03-08 14:05-14:36 with GPU utilization hitting burst thresholds (no autoscale able to spin within 30s).
- Batching/worker assignment logs indicate a fallback read from us-west replica for prefix cache (KV cache global shard) for ~12% of requests in the window.
- Network traces corroborate egress through peering links (higher RTT path).

Interim hypothesis conclusion: Not a policy bug — expected behavior when strict residency is interpreted as 'final model compute must be in EU' but non-critical cache/coordination reads may touch other regions if fallback flags allow. This yields multi-hop and increases p99.

Next steps planned:
- Verify account-level residency flag semantics with Product (confirm whether cross-region cache reads are allowed under "strict residency").
- Patch routing policy to add optional residency_strict:disallow_cross_region_control_reads for enterprise tenants pending legal approval.
- Add capacity guardrail: prefer local queueing for short windows instead of cross-region fallback if p99 latency impact exceeds threshold.

Related signals and links:
- capacity dashboard: /dashboards/capacity/eu-central-2026-03-08
- routing logs: s3://redwood-routing-logs/2026/03/08/finservx-ead3.log

Support (Aisha Kumar) 2026-03-09: Escalated to SRE; customer provided Datadog traces and tcpdump. Requested immediate mitigation options.
SRE (Marco Alvarez) 2026-03-09: Confirmed short capacity degradation in eu-central. Reproduced multi-hop path in staging using residency toggles. Marking for engineering routing-policy review.
Product (Leila Chen) 2026-03-10: Product notes: 'strict residency' was shipped with nuance: allows non-sensitive control-plane reads from region mirrors. We should document this more clearly. Agreed to evaluate disallow flag for Enterprise.
Customer (FinServeX - Ops contact Jonas Meyer) 2026-03-10: Accepting temporary mitigation if it preserves residency guarantees; requests ETA for a configuration switch or rollback.
SRE (Marco Alvarez) 2026-03-11: Implemented temporary rule on routing table for FinServeX: disable cross-region cache reads for their account. Monitoring p99 now.
Workaround applied: for customer FinServeX we set account-level routing override to disallow cross-region cache/control reads (effective 2026-03-11 09:12 UTC). Immediate result: p99 reduced from ~1.6s -> ~680ms within one hour; p95 unchanged.

Planned permanent fixes:
1) Product will add explicit residency options in Console (strict vs strict+control-disallow) and update docs.
2) Routing-engine patch to prefer local queueing for short capacity shortages where acceptable to reduce multi-hop latency.
3) Improve autoscaling responsiveness for eu-central dedicated pools to avoid fallback triggers.

Follow-ups:
- ENG-3421 (routing-engine) to implement config flag (ETA 2 sprints).
- DOCS-818 update residency docs and Console copy (ETA next week).
- Monitor FinServeX for 72 hours and then close ticket if p99 remains stable.
payload.summary: Higher p99 after enabling strict egress residency — multi-hop routing to us-west observed

Issue summary: Customer LexaHealth reports repeated invocations of an external webhook/tool when using our TypeScript SDK streaming API. The app uses function-calling (tool invocation) to run side effects; after a transient network blip the SDK reconnects and appears to replay the tool call, causing duplicate downstream actions (duplicate patient notifications).

Impact: Production impact for a single customer — duplicate notifications sent to end users. Potential regulatory sensitivity for health-related notifications. Happened intermittently across several requests; not a full outage but high customer impact.

Environment: Redwood TS SDK v1.5.3, Node 18, prod region us-east, using dedicated capacity (customer-managed routing rules). Tool call performed via function-calling API with a customer webhook target.

Steps to reproduce (as provided by customer):
1. Start a streaming chat session with function-calling enabled and provide an idempotency token only on the top-level request (not on the function call payload).
2. Trigger an input that results in a function call by the model (tool name: notify_patient).
3. Simulate a transient disconnect (customer reported a brief WebSocket disconnect at ~300ms into response). SDK auto-reconnects and resumes.
4. Observe two outbound POSTs to the customer's webhook within ~1s of each other.

Expected: Single invocation of notify_patient per model decision. SDK should avoid replaying tool calls after reconnect unless the model explicitly re-issues them.

Actual: The SDK's reconnect path replays the last tool invocation payload to the server which results in the serving runtime invoking the tool again. This appears correlated with streaming reconnect + SDK-side retry/backoff interaction.

Logs (customer-provided):
- SDK client reconnect record: "ws disconnect code=1006, reconnecting, attempt=1"
- Outbound webhook traces: POST /webhooks/notify_patient 2026-03-10T14:22:31.102Z -> 2026-03-10T14:22:31.453Z and POST 2026-03-10T14:22:31.712Z
- SDK request id: req-lexa-9a7f

Additional notes: Customer does not pass an explicit idempotency-key for function invocation (they rely on top-level request id). They use the TypeScript SDK streaming convenience which hides some of the low-level frames. They are on a dedicated pool that has routing fallback enabled.

Additional notes:
2026-03-10 16:10 - LexaHealth (Customer): Provided logs and a minimal repro snippet using SDK v1.5.3. Confirmed duplicate webhooks only appear when network blip is introduced. Asked for urgent mitigation; duplicated notifications affect patient workflow.
2026-03-12 08:17 - Support (Elena): Sent mitigation steps to LexaHealth: (1) Add a function-level idempotency token in the function payload (suggested key: lexahid). (2) Update SDK usage to enable "suppressReplayOnReconnect" flag (temporary internal flag available in v1.5.4-beta). Customer requested timeline for stable fix.
2026-03-12 10:00 - LexaHealth (Customer): Implemented function-level idempotency and reports no duplicate notifications in two hours of synthetic load. Requests a request for permanent SDK fix and a postmortem style note.
Client behavior: TS SDK 1.5.3 queues outgoing frames and on reconnect re-emits any frame not acked by server. No special-case for function_call frames.
Server behavior: serving-runtime executes function_call frames idempotently only at request boundary; no sub-operation dedupe currently. We observed two executions with identical payload & signature within the same request id.
Hypothesis: combination of streaming reconnect + lack of sub-operation idempotency results in duplicate tool execution. Deduping on server-side by payload signature within a small window reduces duplicates but does not address root SDK ergonomics.
Risk assessment: Medium - happens only when stream reconnects mid-response. For high-volume customers or those with side-effectful tools this is high impact.
Customer implemented function-level idempotency token in the function payload and saw immediate mitigation. Short-term server-side dedupe PR created (see related PR). Recommend customer keep the token until SDK v1.6.0 is released.
Merge server-side sliding-window dedupe (PR #289) and deploy to staging for canary testing.
Implement SDK change to propagate sub-operation id and opt-out replay flag; include tests for reconnect scenarios.
Create an SDK docs guide for "Function-calling & idempotency" with code examples for TS/Python/Go.
Prepare a short post-incident note for LexaHealth outlining root cause, mitigation, and timeline for permanent fix.

payload.description:
Issue summary:
During a midday burst (11:40–12:10 UTC) the customer's dedicated pool in us-east experienced a sudden attach thinness: new inference attaches failed with timeouts and a spike in p99 latency. Customer (NimbusMaps) reported degraded throughput for both embeddings and short generation routes.

Impact:
- NimbusMaps (dedicated customer) saw ~70% reduction in successful attach rate for short-lived connections and a p99 latency increase from ~220ms -> ~2.8s for embedding requests.
- Platform autoscaler delayed scale-up by ~90s due to noisy telemetry aggregation. Other tenants in the same reserved pool observed transient p50 degradation.

Environment:
- Redwood Dedicated pool: reserved-pool-usc-east-7a (GPU A100s mixed NVLink)
- Customer plan: reserved monthly; pinned model open-embed-2.1 and redwood-3b-quant-v2 for some routes

Steps to reproduce (observed in telemetry):
1) Customer started a large batched embedding job with 100 concurrent short streams at ~11:35 UTC across 10 worker processes.
2) Several of these streams created long-lived pinned KV caches due to repetitive long-context inputs (>= 4k tokens) and prefetch hints in SDK v2.3.1.
3) New attach requests during the burst were queued; some timed out with 504s from the attach proxy.
4) Autoscaler metric window aggregated noisy heartbeats from sidecars and suppressed scale decision until the next smoothing window (~90s later).

Observed behavior:
- Attach timeouts (attach proxy 504) and attach latency spikes in scheduler logs.
- A small cohort of connections held persistent GPU slot reservations via a long-lived prefetch cycle (observed by slot-tracker logs).
- Telemetry sidecar emitted high-frequency heartbeat metrics (50–200/s per sidecar) which overwhelmed the autoscaler rate-limiter and led to delayed reactions.

Expected behavior:
- Autoscaler should recognize sustained attach failure and trigger scale-up or fallback in <30s.
- Long-lived streams should not prevent fair attach distribution across the reserved pool.

Initial mitigation applied:
- Support temporarily increased attach proxy timeout to 8s for the customer's routes and bumped autoscaler smoothing sensitivity for the pool.
- SRE evicted two long-lived slot reservations identified in slot-tracker (manual eviction) to free slots for pending attaches.

Notes on customer impact and business risk:
- Customer reported reduced embeddings throughput at a high-traffic time for a product demo. Risk to renewal if recurrence occurs.

Additional notes:
2026-03-13 12:25 - NimbusMaps (Customer): Confirmed partial recovery after eviction. Throughput improved but intermittent p99 remains elevated. Asked for root cause and permanent fix.
Slot-tracker logs show 3 sessions with persistent slot reservations: session_ids s-5781, s-5782, s-5783; s-5781 and s-5782 were evicted at 11:48 UTC.
Autoscaler metrics: heartbeat_ingest_rate spiked to 1.6k/s for pool window; smoothing window prevented scale-up because noise exceeded threshold for burst detector.
Prefetch behavior: SDK v2.3.1 prefetch auto-enabled when input pattern includes long-context markers; this produced repeated KV cache growth without releasing slots.
Scheduler traces: attach queue length rose from 2 -> 110 in ~90s; attach proxy started returning 504 after queue hit configured max_wait.
Telemetry pipeline: sidecar flood bypassed local debounce because of a malformed batch encoding introduced in sidecar v1.12. Confirmed in sidecar logs: repeated POST /heartbeat with identical payload IDs.
Potential root causes: aggressive SDK prefetch + malformed sidecar batching + autoscaler smoothing parameters too conservative for this failure mode.
Risk vector: repeated long-context embedding jobs from any tenant could reproducibly trigger the same attach-thinness if not mitigated platform-side.
Workarounds and fixes in progress: 1) Rolling deploy of a sidecar patch (v1.12.1) to fix batching and add local debounce (PR #6420). 2) Autoscaler tuning: reduce smoothing window for reserved pools during attach-failure events (config change). 3) SDK advisory and hotfix to change default prefetching behavior for embedding routes (coord with developer relations). Customer notified; SRE applied short-term heartbeat rate-limit. Postmortem and permanent remediation targeted by 2026-03-16.
1) Complete sidecar patch rollout to all reserved pools (target 2026-03-15 18:00 UTC). 2) Autoscaler config change validated in staging and schedule production push. 3) Draft SDK advisory and release patch with guidance to disable aggressive prefetch for large embedding batches. 4) Postmortem with customer and update runbook to detect heartbeat floods earlier.

payload.description:
Issue summary: Customer reports duplicate downstream webhook POSTs and duplicate function/tool executions when using the streaming Python SDK behind their corporate connection pool proxy. The customer uses short base62 id tokens (12 characters) for per-tool idempotency. Observed behavior appears only when a streaming request is retried after a transient network reset from the proxy. Impact: Duplicate side-effects in customer systems (duplicate invoice creation and duplicate file-processing jobs). Customer blocked from using streaming tool-calls safely in production until root cause is addressed.
1) Customer opens a streaming create call via Python SDK with function calls that include 'X-Redwood-Idempotency' header set to a 12-char base62 token.
2) Payload includes a multipart file attachment (content-type: multipart/form-data) and a tool invocation 'create_record'.
3) Customer's corporate proxy uses connection pooling and rewrites some headers for long-lived connections.
4) During large uploads (>5MB) the proxy resets the client connection once; client SDK retries streaming request per default backoff.
5) Downstream webhook (customer endpoint) receives two POSTs for the same tool call with different idempotency tokens, and both result in created records.
On a retry, the SDK or gateway should preserve the original client-provided idempotency token (X-Redwood-Idempotency). Downstream webhooks should only see one effective tool invocation when the same idempotency token is used, preventing duplicate side-effects.
The proxy strips or rewrites the customer-provided X-Redwood-Idempotency header for the retried streaming request. The SDK then generates a new short base62 id for the retry path, resulting in two distinct idempotency tokens and duplicate webhook deliveries. Additionally, because tokens are short (12 chars), we observed at least one collision in customer logs where different requests mapped to the same short token in their datastore, exacerbating duplicates.
Customer-provided logs (sanitized):
- 2026-03-09T14:12:03Z StreamStart request-id=cli-7f3a
- 2026-03-09T14:12:06Z Proxy reset connection (RST) while chunked upload in progress
- 2026-03-09T14:12:08Z SDK retry initiated new-idempotency=Xk9bZ7aP3qLt
- 2026-03-09T14:12:09Z Webhook POST /hooks/fn returned 200 for id=Xk9bZ7aP3qLt
- 2026-03-09T14:12:11Z Webhook POST /hooks/fn returned 200 for id=Yc1dM2nQ4rSz
- Duplicate create_record processed in customer's DC.
Attached proxy logs show header drop for 14:12:06-14:12:09 window.
2026-03-10 - Initial triage by Support: Confirmed duplicates in customer logs and matched timestamps to proxy reset events in customer firewall logs.
2026-03-10 - Reproduced in-house behind a local envoy pool by simulating connection reset at 5MB chunk boundary; observed SDK retry path generated new short id when server-side header not echoed.
Hypothesis A: Edge/proxy dropped 'X-Redwood-Idempotency' header on retry when connection reused/pooled, causing the gateway to treat retry as a new request and generate a fresh id.
Hypothesis B: SDK short-id generation (12-char base62) increases collision risk for heavy customers; customer's internal datastore index is not globally namespaced, allowing collisions to surface.
Additional finding: The gateway respects 'x-forwarded-*' but will only trust downstream idempotency headers if they arrive in the initial CONNECT stream; when headers are missing, gateway auto-assigns 'rw-id' and includes in downstream webhook payload.

Additional notes:
SRE (Maya Kim) (2026-03-12): Found gateway code path that generates rw-generated id when incoming request lacks X-Redwood-Idempotency. Edge proxy config patch candidate prepared to preserve custom headers across retries (PR referenced).
Customer (Frostline Health, Ops) (2026-03-12): Confirmed workaround works in staging when they disable connection pooling; request guidance for permanent mitigation.
Support (2026-03-13): Recommended short-term mitigations and next steps (see resolution).
Temporary workaround: Customer disabled connection pooling and configured proxy to forward custom headers for streaming endpoints; this prevented new id generation in retries.
Planned fix: Edge team will land a gateway change to prefer and persist client-provided X-Redwood-Idempotency across streaming reconnects and retries. Patch PR ready (edge-preserve-idempotency-457); rollout scheduled canary 2026-03-17 then full rollout 2026-03-22.
Longer-term: Recommend customers use 20+ char idempotency tokens (RFC-compliant UUID v4 or namespaced UUID) to reduce collision risk; SDKs will be updated to default to 20-char base62 tokens for enterprise tier and include a warning when customers configure tokens shorter than 16 chars.
Follow-up actions: Create a KB article describing proxy settings and recommended idempotency token length. Owner: Arjun Patel. Target close date: 2026-03-23.
1) INT-33211 - Edge gateway: ensure X-Redwood-Idempotency header preservation on retries (owner: Maya Kim).
2) SDK-1894 - SDKs: increase default idempotency token length to 20 chars for enterprise builds and add validation (owner: SDK team).
3) KB-article: Write 'Streaming behind corporate proxies' guidance and include sample Envoy config (owner: Docs).
payload.summary: Connection-pool proxy strips client id header on streaming retry causing duplicate multipart function calls and short-id collisions

Issue summary:
FluxHealth reports large increase in perceived inference latency and frequent client-side timeouts for their production routes starting 2026-03-10 11:12 UTC. Customer sees 5–20x slower tail latency and many requests fail client-side before any server error is returned.

Impact:
- All FluxHealth production routes in us-east show user-visible slow responses for ~45 minutes.
- Business impact: downstream patient-facing feature degraded; customer flagged as Sev1.
- Traffic volume for this tenant is ~2.5x normal during window; Spike correlated with batch job from FluxHealth but their team says job is within expected parameters.

Environment:
- Redwood Hosted API (prod) in us-east
- Customer account: fluxhealth-prod (enterprise)
1) Customer sends steady traffic from fluxhealth-prod to text-generation route using redwood-13b-v2.
2) When rate limits hit (429s) the FluxHealth client SDK performs immediate retries with short exponential backoff (base 200ms).
3) Retries amplify traffic and cause the gateway rate limiter to throttle more aggressively, appearing as increased latency and client-observed timeouts.
4) Can be reproduced in staging by replaying FluxHealth traffic trace with same client retry config and enabling strict rate limiter on gateway.
- Gateway logs: surge of 429 responses from rate-limiter at 2026-03-10T11:12:34Z (see grafana panel: https://grafana.redwood/internal/d/surge/fluxhealth-429)
- Serving runtime logs: increased queue depth and batching spikes; head-of-line blocking observed on several pods.
- Datadog traces: delayed service entry spans on api-gateway -> router (trace id sample: 2f7a3b)
- Example log lines copied to S3: s3://redwood-support/fluxhealth/SUP-91561/logs-11-12-2026.txt
- Initial triage (Aisha): confirmed customer-side timeouts correlate with a burst of 429s from gateway.
- Observed pattern: client does aggressive immediate retries for 429s; these retries arrive as fresh requests (not recognized as retries by gateway) and contribute to sustained higher load.
- Hypothesis: combined effect of tenant-level quota enforcement + client retry behavior caused transient overload and queueing in serving runtime, increasing p95/p99 token latencies.
- Confirmed by replay: after simulating client retry loop, p99 token latency increased from ~300ms to ~2.1s and 429 rate rose by 3x.
- Checked recent deploys: no serving-runtime deploy at the incident start time; api-gateway PR #451 (rate-limiter tuning) deployed 4 hours earlier but config unchanged for this tenant.
- Related internal ticket INT-412 tracks gateway rate-limiter observability gaps.
Short-term: coordinated with FluxHealth to throttle their retry behavior — asked them to switch client SDK to exponential backoff with jitter and increase initial backoff to 800ms. This immediately reduced retry amplification.
Medium-term: implement token bucket hold-back and retry-aware headers at gateway so retries are recognized and treated with lower priority, and introduce per-tenant cooldown windows for quota throttling.
Immediate operational action taken: enabled conservative rate-limiter policy for fluxhealth-prod for 30 minutes starting 2026-03-10T12:05Z to allow backlog to drain.
Workaround for customer: patched SDK (v1.2.7) with jittered backoff and retry budget; FluxHealth deployed patch at 2026-03-10T12:22Z and reported error rates dropping by ~80%.
Pending longer-term work. Owner: Rate-limiter team (Miguel). Planned follow-ups: PR to add X-Client-Retry header propagation and priority handling, add tenant retry budget metrics to syslog, and update customer runbook for recommended SDK retry settings. Target ETA for fixes: 2026-03-24.

Additional notes:
2026-03-10 12:30 - FluxHealth (Emily Chen): Deployed SDK patch with increased backoff; initial signs show fewer timeouts. Sending follow-up metrics in 15m.
2026-03-11 09:05 - SRE (Hiro Tanaka): Created INT-412 to add metrics for 'retry-origin' and edge headers. Assigned to gateway team.
payload.summary: Cascading client retries causing apparent inference latency for FluxHealth production traffic

comments: 2026-03-13T13:25:00Z Observation: Large embedding worker triggered high outbound connections to runtimes while streaming connections kept many fds open (keepalive misconfiguration).
2026-03-13T13:27:00Z Hypothesis A: Ephemeral proxy reached OS soft FD limit resulting in EMFILE and failing accept() calls -> api-gateway returned 502s.
2026-03-13T13:28:00Z Hypothesis B: Serving runtime watchdog restarted GPUs due to increased NVME IO from embedding checkpointing, compounding upstream restarts.

2026-03-13T13:31:00Z Evidence: dmesg and proxy logs show EMFILE; runtime restarts coincident but error traces point at connection drops rather than OOM in runtime. More likely proxy accept failures first.

Mitigated: scaled proxy replicas, increased per-host nofile soft limit, and applied tenant connection cull and client-side rate limiting. Error rate returned to baseline by 13:48 UTC. Root cause appears to be ephemeral-proxy file descriptor exhaustion driven by long-lived streaming connections combined with high-concurrency embedding bursts. Upstream runtime restarts were secondary, caused by connection churn.
payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customer (Acme AI, dedicated) reported a sudden increase in 502/503s on their chat+embedding mixed route between 13:12-13:40 UTC. Symptoms: short-lived streaming sessions intermittently fail with 502; concurrent embedding bulk uploads receive 503s and large tail latencies.

Impact:
- ~12% error rate spike (502/503) observed for tenant traffic for ~25 minutes.
- Affected production customers using mixed streaming + embedding workflows; high user-visible error rate for chat features.

Environment:
- prod us-east-1, dedicated pool for Acme AI.
- Ingress via api-gateway -> ephemeral-proxy -> serving-runtime (tenant-shared).

Steps to reproduce (approximate):
1) Start a steady stream of long-lived streaming connections (1s keepalive interval) from many clients (~200 concurrent).
2) Trigger a large embedding bulk upload (~8k vectors, multiplexed into a few large requests) simultaneously.
3) Observe apigw accept-queue growth, ephemeral-proxy FD counts rising, followed by upstream runtime resets and 502/503 propagation.

Logs / Observations at time of spike:
- api-gateway metrics: accept_queue_depth > 800, connection_accept_latency p95 increased from 4ms -> 220ms.
- ephemeral-proxy process (proxy-ephemeral-12) reported file descriptor count ~62k (soft limit 65k) and transient EMFILE errors in logs.
- kernel dmesg showed repeated "too many open files" on ephemeral proxy host during peak.
- serving-runtime logs show watchog-triggered restart messages and "upstream connection reset by peer" prior to 502s.
- netstat/lsof snapshots captured large number of CLOSE_WAIT and LONG_ESTABLISHED websockets tied to a small set of client IPs.

Immediate customer-visible impact: 502/503s and increased first-byte latency for mixed-route calls.

2026-03-13 13:20 UTC - Support: Customer reported elevated 502s on mixed-route; collected request IDs and sample timestamps.
2026-03-13 13:22 UTC - SRE: Pulled apigw accept-queue, proxy fd usage, and runtime restart counts. Accept queue overflow correlated with FD saturation on ephemeral proxy node 'proxy-ephemeral-12'.

Additional notes:
Tools/commands used: ss -s, lsof -p <proxy_pid> | wc -l, /proc/<pid>/limits, kubectl logs proxy-ephemeral-12, apigw metrics dashboard (AcceptQueue, p95_accept_latency).
Metric snapshots: ephemeral-proxy fd_usage 96% at 13:24 UTC, accept_queue_depth spike between 13:20-13:30 UTC, serving-runtime restart_count +6 within 10 minutes.
2026-03-13 13:26 UTC: Scaled ephemeral-proxy replicas +3 in us-east to relieve accept queue. Immediate partial reduction in accept queue depth.
2026-03-13 13:30 UTC: Applied temporary connection culling rule to drop idle streaming connections > 350s for Acme tenant to free FDs.
2026-03-13 13:33 UTC: Increased OS soft ulimit (nofile) on affected ephemeral proxy hosts from 65536 -> 131072 as emergency mitigation.
2026-03-13 13:40 UTC: Applied backpressure to embedding ingestion (rate limit client-side via edge) to reduce burst concurrency. Error rate fell back to baseline over ~8 minutes.
Customer communication: Sent interim update and workaround steps at 13:36 UTC; customer acknowledged and applied client-side rate limiting for bulk upload.
Maya Patel (Support) - 2026-03-13 13:18 UTC: Customer reported sudden chat failures and embedding timeouts. Collecting logs and request IDs.
Liam O'Connor (SRE) - 2026-03-13 13:24 UTC: Seeing high fd usage on proxy-ephemeral-12 and EMFILE in proxy logs. Scaling proxies now.
Diego Morales (Platform Eng) - 2026-03-13 13:29 UTC: Noted runtime restarts but stack traces indicate connection resets. Prioritizing proxy remediation and ulimit bump.
Maya Patel (Support) - 2026-03-13 13:36 UTC: Customer applied temporary client-side rate limiting; errors decreasing. Customer asks for postmortem and permanent fix timeline.
Liam O'Connor (SRE) - 2026-03-13 14:10 UTC: Confirming stabilized metrics after mitigation; monitoring for recurrence. Will open follow-ups for hardening.
Create infra ticket to add heuristics for automatic culling of stale streaming connections when FD usage exceeds threshold (INT-xxxxxx).
Permanent change: Raise default ephemeral-proxy nofile limits via bootstrap and add alert when fd_usage > 75% (owner: infra).
Add admission control for large embedding bulk uploads that detect concurrent long-lived streaming sessions and automatically stagger or queue requests (owner: serving-runtime).
Runbook update: Document mixed-workload acceptance criteria and emergency mitigation steps in Confluence runbook.
Postmortem: Draft and link a short postmortem summarizing timeline, root cause, and permanent remediation, target completion 2026-03-20.
This incident surfaced an operational gap where long-lived websocket/streaming sessions together with DoS-ish embedding bursts can exhaust FD capacity on proxy nodes. Consider prioritizing work that adds headroom and smarter shedding for mixed routes.
payload.summary: Unexpected 502/503 surge caused by ephemeral keepalive FD exhaustion during mixed embed+chat burst

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customer reports that several users who should have tenant-admin privileges in their private deployment are only seeing read-only views in the Redwood Console. This started after a recent IdP configuration change (rolled by the customer) where their IdP began emitting a new claim named "roles_v2" as an array of objects instead of the legacy "roles" string list.

Impact:
- Multiple DataSentry users cannot perform admin actions (create API keys, manage billing visibility, manage dedicated pools) despite being marked as admins in the IdP.
- Customer-facing admin workflows are blocked for a small group (~6 users) in prod us-west-2.

Environment:
- Private deployment (VPC) for DataSentry Inc.
- Console version: 3.4.2
- Identity proxy version: 2.8.1

Steps to reproduce (as provided by customer):
1) Login with affected user via customer IdP through private Console URL (https://console.datasentry.example).
2) Observe Console: top-right shows expected tenant and username.
3) Attempt to access Organization -> Admin settings -> Manage API keys -> button is disabled/hidden.
4) Call Admins API (GET /v1/orgs/{org_id}/members) with bearer token from affected user; response shows role: member.

Expected behavior:
- Users with admin roles emitted by IdP should be mapped to tenant-admin role in Redwood RBAC and have full admin capabilities.

Actual behavior:
- The identity proxy ignores "roles_v2" claim; downstream role-mapping logic only reads "roles". As a result, users are treated as non-admins.

Logs / traces included by customer (redacted):
- Identity proxy authn debug: "claim roles missing; fallback to empty role list"
- Customer SAML response excerpt (redacted): "roles_v2": [{"name":"tenant-admin","scope":"org:12345"}, {"name":"billing-admin","scope":"org:12345"}]

Additional notes:
- Customer confirmed they intentionally switched to a richer claim structure for future-proofing.
- This began on 2026-03-09 after IdP config change.

Additional notes:
2026-03-10 10:02 - Customer (DataSentry): Provided redacted SAML assertion, confirmed 6 affected users, and shared that legacy 'roles' claim is now absent.
Hypothesis: Identity proxy only deserializes 'roles' as []string; structured arrays under 'roles_v2' are ignored by claim normalizer.
Reproduction: Created test IdP response with roles_v2 as array of objects: identity-proxy returned no roles to RBAC pipeline; console served 'member' role.
Observed metrics: authz decision logs in prod show 'role_count=0' for affected tokens between 2026-03-09T14:12 and 2026-03-09T14:30 UTC.
Cause: Schema mismatch; customer changed to object-based role claim without coordinating mapping change in identity-proxy config. No prior validation blocked ingest of non-legacy claim names.
Risk assessment: Low risk to platform but high product impact for this customer (admin tasks blocked). Other private deployments could have similar custom claims.
Workaround validated: IdP transformation (copy roles_v2[*].name -> roles[]) restores expected behavior immediately.
Planned fix: Add configurable claim mappers to identity-proxy to support nested arrays and custom claim names; include a default compatibility layer that will map detected roles_v2 -> roles for a 2-release window.
Workaround: Customer applied an IdP transformation to copy roles_v2[*].name into legacy roles[] claim; verified by Support that admin privileges restored for affected users. Engineering created PR https://github.com/redwood-inference/identity-proxy/pull/478 to add configurable claim mappers and a compatibility heuristic for common 'roles_v2' structures. payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customer reports that when their service (using Go SDK v1.12.3 and Python SDK v2.4.0 concurrently) experiences transient connectivity errors and performs exponential backoff with jitter, subsequent reconnects in a multiplexed client session sometimes produce tool confirmations that arrive out of order or cause downstream orphaned side-effects (duplicate downstream job triggers).

Impact:
- Intermittent duplicated downstream jobs for a small subset of user requests (~0.3% of total calls during a 30m window).
- In some cases, confirmation/ack messages for tool calls arrive after a later tool call has already been executed by the customer backend, leading to out-of-order state transitions and manual reconciliations.
- Customer uses Dedicated capacity and has strict SLA for correctness; this behavior risks data integrity for orchestrations triggered by tool calls.

Environment:
- Dedicated cluster in prod-us-east.
- SDKs: Go v1.12.3 (multiplexing enabled), Python v2.4.0 (background reconnect enabled).
- Client pattern: long-lived multiplexed websocket session; per-request idempotency tokens generated by client; backoff performed client-side on network error codes (5xx, connection reset).
- Routing: sticky sessions to the same serving node where possible but fall back to other nodes on reconnect.

Steps to reproduce (customer-provided):
1) Open multiplexed stream with 8 concurrent logical channels.
2) Send a tool-invoking request that triggers a webhook to their job worker. Include client-generated idempotency token.
3) Simulate short network flaps (tcp reset) for the websocket connection while the request is inflight.
4) Client performs exponential backoff with jitter and re-establishes multiplexed session; some logical channels resume, others are recreated.
5) Observe downstream system receiving two executions for the same logical operation or receiving confirmations that map to earlier logical operations (out-of-order).

Expected behavior:
- Retries / reconnects should never cause duplicate downstream side-effects when a per-request idempotency token is supplied and honored by the platform.
- Tool confirmations should be delivered in a way that preserves per-channel ordering or provide a clear mechanism to correlate confirmations with original logical requests.

Actual behavior:
- Duplicate downstream job execution (duplicate webhook POSTs) in ~0.3% of observed flows.
- Late confirmations referencing a previously-sent request arrive after a different request has already progressed, causing out-of-order state transitions.

Attachments / logs provided by customer:
- Partial websocket capture logs (redacted) showing rebinds and channel reassignments.
- Downstream worker logs showing two nearly identical job runs with the same client-side idempotency token.
- SDK versions and sample code snippets.

Temporary workaround suggested by customer:
- Reduce multiplexing concurrency to 1 per process (mitigates but not acceptable for throughput).
- Add stronger dedup/idempotency verification on the job-worker side (works, but customer expects platform to guarantee at-most-once when token provided).

Additional notes:
2026-03-10 13:02 - GammaApps Support (customer): Uploaded websocket capture and example worker logs. Reiterated that tokens are unique UUIDv4 strings. Reported issue persists across both Go and Python clients.
2026-03-11 09:05 - Eng (streaming-proxy): Noted that sticky session hinting is advisory; on node failover we reassign logical channels and migrate inflight state. Hypothesis: channel-level sequencing metadata is not fully durable across reconnects causing confirmations to be correlated to wrong logical request under certain timing/jitter patterns.
2026-03-11 12:22 - Support: Provided customer with a mitigation flag to disable multiplexed channel reuse on reconnect (server-side toggle). Customer applied to small subset and reported duplicate rate dropped to zero in that cohort.
2026-03-12 08:40 - Eng (sdk team): Reproduced duplication with Go SDK v1.12.3; older Go SDK v1.10.9 did not resurface the issue due to different channel rebind behavior. Planning a patch that improves channel resurrection handshake to ensure per-channel sequence tokens are negotiated after reconnect.
2026-03-12 15:03 - GammaApps Support (customer): Agreed to 4-hour canary window next Friday. Requested ETA for Python SDK compatibility changes as well.
Summary of findings:
- Reproduction confirms that certain reconnect timing + multiplexed channel reuse leads to mismatch of channel sequence state between client and server.
- Cause looks like a race where the server-side streaming-proxy restores channel routing before sequence/token reconciliation completes, allowing late confirmations to be attached to the wrong logical channel.
- Observed that client idempotency tokens are sent as opaque baggage but platform may rely on in-memory channel mapping for correlation during reconnect; if channel mapping shifts, token correlation can be lost and webhook may be retried without dedup check.
Hypotheses tested:
- Disabling channel reuse prevents the issue (confirmed).
- Forcing strict post-reconnect sequence handshake prevents duplication (local test success).
Next steps:
1) Implement a critical patch in streaming-proxy to require sequence handshake after reconnect before accepting confirmations.
2) Backport safer reconnect behavior to Go SDK to avoid optimistic channel reuse on reconnect.
3) Add additional server-side dedup guard using client idempotency tokens persisted across short-lived reconnect windows (fast path cache + LR policy).
4) Run canary on customer's dedicated cluster and monitor duplicates metric.
Mitigation applied:
- Temporary server-side toggle to disable optimistic channel reuse was applied for the affected customer cohort; duplicates dropped to zero for that cohort.
Planned fixes:
- streaming-proxy: require explicit per-channel sequence handshake on reconnect (PR #1442).
- sdk-go: update reconnect logic to await handshake and not reuse channel IDs until confirmed (PR scheduled).
- server dedup cache: lightweight idempotency cache for 120s to catch races during reconnect windows.
Follow-ups:
- Coordinate canary with GammaApps on 2026-03-19 (4-hour window).
- Postmortem + runbook update to include: recommended client flags for multiplexing, and platform-side configuration default change to safer handshake behavior.
Customer communication:
- Customer notified of workaround and upcoming patch schedule. Will update ticket with canary results and close after successful canary and postmortem.
payload.summary: Out-of-order tool confirmations and orphaned side-effects after client exponential backoff + multiplexed reconnects

Issue summary: Customer LexiconHealth reports server-sent events (SSE) chat streams silent-pausing mid-token when the platform performs a priority escalation and swaps the request routing to a dedicated GPU pool. Impact: Multiple in-flight streaming chats for a small percentage (~0.6%) of requests into LexiconHealth's tenant stall for 6-20s of silence followed by either resumed stream or silent close. Environment: prod, us-east-1, dedicated tenant, observed on redwood-chat-3.5-dedicated and open-llama-7b-v2. Steps to reproduce: 1) Send long-form streaming chat with chunked SSE enabled and per-request priority flag set to high. 2) Trigger autoscale/priority escalation by issuing several concurrent high-priority requests from same tenant. 3) Observe stream silence between SSE chunks during routing transition. Expected behavior: Stream should continue with minimal interruption or graceful handoff. Actual behavior: Stream pauses mid-token for many seconds without TCP FIN or SSE keepalive events; sometimes client reports connection still open but no data. Preliminary hypothesis: During priority escalation the routing layer performs an in-flight route-swap to a dedicated serving pool. The swap path currently moves the connection state asynchronously; a gap occurs where the worker continues generation but the SSE proxy stops forwarding chunks due to connection pinning with the previous router. NGINX/edge keepalive/proxy connection reuse prevents immediate reconnection, producing silent periods instead of errors. Additional factors: KV-cache pinning and staged worker eviction observed on nodes with heavy batching.
logs: router-A 2026-03-12T14:18:12.412Z request=rid:abcd1234 chunk=12 -> forwarded; router-A recorded route-swap to router-B at 14:18:12.419Z
traces: distributed trace shows worker continued generating tokens (token 13..18) but SSE proxy at router-B did not forward until 14:18:20.592Z
tcp captures: no FIN/RST during gap; keepalive pings continued on TCP connection; kernel retransmits negligible. Indicates application-layer stall rather than TCP drop.
heap/kv-cache: small eviction noted on worker node 7 around same timeframe; likely unrelated but worth investigating interaction with pinned KV state during handoff.
nginx config: connection reuse enabled via upstream keepalive; swap created a mismatch in backend connection mapping causing buffered data to sit at old proxy writer thread.
load: incident clustered around autoscale events (scale-up to dedicated pool) between 14:15-14:25 UTC; similar minor regressions seen in Canary on 2026-03-09.
attempted fixes: forced proxy flush on swap in staging removed the silent gap but introduced 1-2s latency spike; need a smoother approach.

Additional notes:
2026-03-12 10:05 - Support (Liam): Requested tcpdump, client logs, and full request IDs; asked if customer is behind a corporate proxy (they are not).
2026-03-12 13:40 - Customer (LexiconHealth): Shared three request IDs and client-side timing: heartbeat frames continue but no SSE lines arrive for ~8s. No reconnect triggered by client.
2026-03-13 02:12 - SRE (Priya): Correlated request IDs to router logs. Observed route-swap events and a sequence where router A forwards first chunks then hands off to router B with no explicit proxy-level flush. Noted NGINX keepalive reuse between A and B.
2026-03-14 07:30 - Eng (Marco): Recreated in staging with controlled route-swap; observed identical silent gap when route pinning is released mid-generation. Proposed mitigation: serialize route handoff or stream proxy flush on swap.
2026-03-14 12:10 - Support (Liam): Applied temporary mitigation for LexiconHealth by disabling priority-escalation path for their tenant and forcing in-place worker processing. Customer reports no further stalls in 3 hours of monitoring.
2026-03-14 14:05 - Customer (LexiconHealth): Acknowledged mitigation and requested ETA for permanent fix and rollback plan.
Mitigation applied 2026-03-14: disabled priority-escalation route for LexiconHealth tenant and adjusted router config to avoid asynchronous connection pin release during swap. Immediate customer impact mitigated; monitoring confirms zero stalls in 4h post-mitigation. Next steps: engineering to implement atomic handoff (server-side stream relay) or graceful stream-forwarding with explicit flush on swap. Scheduler team to review autoscale handoff ordering and ensure KV-cache pin/unpin ordering. Target permanent fix in serving-runtime v1.14.2 with canary rollout 2026-03-21.

payload.description:
Issue summary:
StreamFlux runs a mixed workload that interleaves low-latency chat requests with large batch uploads (embedding jobs). After enabling an ingress-side smoothing flag in their orchestrator, they observed repeated 429 rejects against the dedicated pool for the last 36 hours.

Impact:
- ~10% of chat requests returned 429s during daytime peak windows, causing user-facing errors in their product.
- Bulk embed jobs were often throttled mid-upload and had to be retried, extending job completion times by 2–4x.

Environment:
- Customer uses a Redwood Dedicated pool with route-level weights and two priority classes (interactive, background).
- Ingest orchestrator runs parallel workers that fan out short-lived signed uploads followed by post-upload callbacks.

Steps to reproduce (customer-provided):
1) Start 200 concurrent chat sessions (avg 2s per request) targeted at api/chat with priority=interactive.
2) Kick off 8 parallel backfill embedding jobs (multipart uploads) using api/embed with priority=background.
3) Enable orchestrator smoothing flag: "burst_compaction=true" and set refill_interval_ms=250.
4) Observe 429s and increased retry loops in client telemetry.

Expected behavior:
- Interactive traffic should receive >99% success under provisioned Dedicated pool capacity; bulk jobs should backpressure gracefully to background lane without causing chat 429s.

Actual behavior:
- Dedicate pool token accounting shows bursts compacting into refill windows that temporarily exceed interactive lane allocations. Health-check probes and signed callback retries appear to be counted against the same burst budget and cause sticky throttles after scale events.

Attached logs/traces:
- Customer sent a sampling of request_ids: rq_20260312_1122_{A,B,C} and a flamegraph from their orchestrator.
- Ingest logs show many short-lived connections (conn < 1s) with identical API key multiplexing.

2026-03-12 09:14 - StreamFlux (customer): We're seeing chat 429s after enabling compaction to reduce token churn. We thought compaction would smooth bursts, not trigger rejects — can Support advise configuration best-practices?

Additional notes:
2026-03-12 10:10 - StreamFlux: Health probes and callback workers use a service account that shares the primary key. Attached console snapshot: showing refill spikes aligning with the background job start times.
2026-03-13 12:40 - Support (Priya): Proposed immediate mitigations and recommended config changes provided in resolution notes. Will follow up on whether customer wants us to open a private VPC run for deeper traces.
Checked dedicated-pool metrics from 2026-03-12T10:00–11:00: CPU/memory normal, token bucket shows periodic large refills coinciding with orchestrator fanout bursts.
Observed that signed callback workers reuse the interactive API key; each callback attempt generates a preflight and a small POST which the rate controller counts as independent tokens — aggregated by compaction into a single refill window.
Autoscaler log showed a scale-up at 10:03 but scale-down at 10:05; short-lived scale events plus compacted refills led to a refill accounting edge-case where per-route soft-limits were momentarily exceeded and the global token pool issued 429s for lower-weighted routes.
No evidence of serving-runtime errors (5xx) — this is quota accounting behavior at the rate-limiter layer combined with route weighting and short connection fanout.
Correlation with SUP-3141596 (refill-window anomalies during mixed workloads) suggests a similar token accounting interaction but our customer's burst_compaction flag and shared key pattern make the symptom more acute.
Test harness results: isolating callbacks onto a separate key or bumping refill interval to >=1500ms removed 429s under equivalent load.
Short-term mitigation (customer applied):
- Create separate API key for health checks and callback workers (do not share primary interactive key).
- Set burst_compaction=false temporarily to revert to baseline behavior.
- Increase refill_interval_ms to 1500 for the route used by background uploads.
Observed result: chat 429s dropped to <0.5% in next 6-hour window.
Recommended long-term config guidance:
- Isolate long-running or high-fanout background jobs into a dedicated route with its own quota/burst pool (route-level isolation).
- Use separate API keys for background workers and interactive users so token accounting is not multiplexed.
- For hybrid workloads, prefer larger refill intervals (>=1s) when short-lived multiplexed connections are common; tune priority weights so interactive lane has guaranteed steady capacity.
- If using Dedicated pools, consider reserving a dedicated burst lane for interactive traffic with stricter soft limits on background lanes to avoid burst bleed-over.
- Monitor the console token heatmap and enable the "show per-key refill traces" toggle for at least 24 hours during a candidate config change.
Engineering follow-up (internal):
- Create a short-run RFC to add a rate-limiter metric that surfaces per-key multiplexing counts (tickets: INT-1023).
- Product consider an orchestration flag that marks signed-callbacks as exempt from interactive refill compaction when they use a service account (nice-to-have).
- Documented recommended settings added to the confluence runbook linked above.
Customer acceptance: StreamFlux confirmed improvement and requested a call to review permanent isolation and an enterprise best-practices checklist. Support to schedule postmortem call and optionally assist with key separation rollout.
payload.summary: Configure rate-smoothing and burst compaction for hybrid realtime + bulk ingest pipeline

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customer (Arcadia Health) reports intermittent but repeatable p95/p99 spikes for short streaming requests from a dedicated pool. Spikes present as sudden waves lasting ~30-90s where p95 jumps ~200-600ms and p99 spikes to multiple seconds (observed up to 6.1s). Impact: user-facing timeouts and a small increase in 504 errors during waves.

Impact:
- Multiple mid-sized customers experienced degraded experience for short chat turns (1-3 tokens per chunk) during windows.
- Billing and SLAs affected for dedicated pool customers during events.

Environment:
- Dedicated GPU pool (dgx-4 node type) in prod-us-east serving gptx-13b-quant-v2.
- Continuous/coalescing batcher enabled with tenant-priority weighting and adaptive linger.
- Observed primarily on nodes with mixed short-stream and long-stream traffic.

Observed behavior:
- Regular traffic baseline latency p95 ~120ms. During event windows p95 climbs to 400-800ms, p99 to 2-6s.
- Traces show many short streaming requests being held for additional linger periods and then flushed together, producing a burst of long flush time.
- Metrics show batch sizes increasing suddenly (from ~4->40) aligned with flush events.

Expected behavior:
- Continuous batcher should maintain smooth flush cadence for short streams without accumulating large micro-batches that cause long-tail spikes.

1) Route mixed traffic (short streaming turns interleaved with longer streams) through a dedicated pool with continuous batcher enabled.
2) Use a steady low-QPS short-stream workload (50-200 r/s) with occasional long streams present.
3) Observe p95/p99 over a 30-90 minute window and correlate batcher flush metrics (batch_size, flush_interval, queue_depth).
4) Compare behavior with/without tenant-priority weighting and with different min_flush_period settings.
[2026-03-10T14:18:12Z] node-03 batcher: queued short-stream request id=abcd1234 seq=2 dwell=115ms
[2026-03-10T14:18:12Z] node-03 batcher: flush triggered by alignment window; batch_size=38 flush_latency=1634ms
[2026-03-10T14:18:13Z] trace: request abcd1234 timed out after 5000ms (client-level)
[2026-03-10T14:19:35Z] exporter.metrics: p95=0.79s p99=3.21s 504s=12 (window 60s)
Support (Ayesha): Customer reported first seen 2026-03-09 evening. Attachting initial traces and Grafana snapshots. Asked for exact traffic pattern and whether any pool config changed.
Customer (Arcadia Health): Confirmed no config changes on their side. Pattern seems to happen more during QPS drops followed by small bursts.
SRE (Liam): Noticed batch_size surges and aligned flush timestamps across several hosts. Scheduling an investigation into host timer behavior and scheduler alignment logic.
Eng (Nia, runtime team): Suggested testing with monotonic clock usage and disable tenant-priority weighting to reproduce. Also asked for kernel and NTP status on affected nodes.
Hypothesis 1: Flush timing alignment across hosts causes simultaneous coalescing of many short requests -> large micro-batches -> p99 waves.
Hypothesis 2: Host-level timer jitter (observed on node-03 and node-07) due to kernel frequency scaling (intel_pstate) caused drift in the software timer used by the coalescer.
Action: Pulled Grafana dashboards for batch_size, flush_interval, and per-host timer drift. Found correlation between hosts with higher timer jitter and stronger p99 spikes.
Experiment: Switched the batcher to use CLOCK_MONOTONIC_RAW in a canary pool and disabled tenant-priority weighting for 2h. Result: p99 tail reduced by ~45% during similar traffic windows and alignment events were fewer.
Logs/links: https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/streams/continuous-batcher?orgId=1&from=now-2h
Kernel logs: node-03: dmesg shows frequent CPU frequency transitions at time of events.
Mitigation applied: rolled out a change to use a monotonic raw clock for the batcher timer and added randomized jitter to the flush alignment window to avoid cross-host synchronization.
Hotfix deployed to prod-us-east dedicated pool (rolling update across nodes) on 2026-03-12 03:00 UTC. Observed immediate reduction in event amplitude; p99 decreased from ~3.2s to ~1.4s in subsequent windows.
Permanent fix PR: github.com/redwood-inference/realtime-scheduler/pull/1109 — uses monotonic clock and introduces smoothing to adaptive linger calculation.
Workarounds for customers: temporary disable tenant-priority weighting or increase min_flush_period to smooth batching. Provided CLI examples to Arcadia Health.
Follow-ups: (1) Add per-host timer-jitter telemetry and alerting, (2) Update Continuous Batcher runbook with steps to diagnose alignment events, (3) Schedule kernel tuning audit for dedicated host images to reduce frequency scaling jitter.
payload.summary: Misaligned flush timing in continuous batcher causing sudden p99 latency waves

Issue summary:
During the late-afternoon window on 2026-03-10 we observed a sustained drop in throughput for a reserved dedicated pool in us-west-2 serving NimbleDocs (dedicated). Symptoms included elevated attach/slot acquisition latency, increased 429s on batched routes, and an observed decline in concurrent GPU allocations for the affected pool.

Impact:
- Customer-facing: ~12% increase in end-to-end p95 latency for their batched text generation routes between 14:10-15:05 PST; intermittent 429s and throttled requests.
- Platform: allocator reported temporary reduction of available attachable slots; autoscaler did not spawn new nodes due to perceived low utilization.

Environment:
- Prod, us-west-2, dedicated pool id: rp-2831 (NimbleDocs reserved cluster).
- Serving runtime: 1.8.3-release
- Allocator: v0.22.1
- Snapshotter-sidecar: v0.9.6

Steps to reproduce (observed pattern):
1) Start sustained small-stream workload (many short streaming sessions) against customer's pinned model.
2) At ~14:00, background snapshot flush job (system task) triggered high NVMe/io-write on a subset of hosts in the reserved cluster.
3) Shortly after, attach latency p95 jumps and new session attaches start failing with timeouts; queued requests build up and autoscaler does not react as expected.

Observed behavior and telemetry:
- attach_latency_p95 for cluster rp-2831 rose from ~18ms baseline to ~320ms within 4 minutes.
- gpu_attach_failures increased and correlated with nvme_write_latency spikes on 6/24 hosts in the pool.
- autoscaler metrics showed allocation_decision_rate steady but available_slots metric dropped; allocation decisions aborted due to sidecar attach hang.
- Sidecar logs include repeated errors: "snapshotter: flush delay > 120s, initiating write-back" and socket-level write timeouts.

Initial hypotheses:
- Snapshotter-sidecar flush induced NVMe IO pressure causing host-level stalls that prolong attach handshake (noisy sidecar).
- Small-stream heavy fanout from tenant amplifies the attach overload and causes queue serialization on allocator.
- Autoscaler logic misinterpreted temporary attach stalls as low demand, delaying scale-up.

Investigation notes:
- Collected dmesg and nvme SMART logs from affected hosts (links in comments).
- Confirmed that background maintenance job launched by orchestration-runner at 14:05 produced concurrent GC/flush on reserved hosts.
- Heap profile from snapshotter shows a large flush batch size change pushed in last config rollout (PR referenced below).
- Kernel stack samples show context-switch stalls during nvme write spikes.

Workarounds applied to mitigate customer impact:
- Support routed small percentage (~10%) of traffic to fallback region eu-west temporarily for high-concurrency routes to reduce pressure.
- RPM: throttled snapshotter-sidecar flush interval on affected hosts to reduce IO concurrency.
- Applied transient throttling on batch concurrency for the NimbleDocs routes from the console to reduce attach churn.

Next steps / Action items:
- Engineering (allocator + runtime) to add backoff for attach retries so autoscaler distinguishes between attach stall and low demand (owner: Ravi).
- Snapshotter team to revert the recent aggressive flush batching change or gate it behind host IO checks (owner: Maria Lopez).
- SRE to add NVMe write-latency alerting tied to allocator decisions to trigger automatic routing to alternate pools.
- Postmortem and runbook update: include "snapshot-flush" as a noisy-neighbor vector and mitigation checklist.

Resolution notes (so far):
- Immediate customer impact reduced after snapshotter throttle and traffic re-routing. Root cause still being validated across full fleet.
- A temporary patch was rolled to decrease flush concurrency on us-west-2 reserved hosts; full revert or safe rollout planned after verification.

payload.description:
Issue summary: Customer reports intermittent model load failures for private deployment behind a corporate egress HTTP proxy. Serving nodes fail to fetch multiple model shards; some shard downloads return 200 OK (full object) or 403 when the serving runtime requested a Range GET, leading to shard checksum/offset mismatch and model load aborts.

Impact: Multiple production instances in the customer's us-east private deployment fail model initialization at scale during rolling restarts. Impact is intermittent but reproducible under high shard-parallelism. Several customer services degraded; they escalated to P1.

Environment: Private deployment (VPC + VPCE) with an on-premise egress appliance/proxy that the customer's networking team manages. Artifact storage is S3 via a VPCE endpoint; serving nodes use presigned range GETs over HTTP/1.1 keepalive to fetch model shards in parallel. Problem appears only when multiple consecutive shard requests reuse the same upstream connection.

Observed behavior: Serving runtime logs show repeated errors: 'shard checksum mismatch' or 'unexpected content-length' followed by model load failure. HTTP traces from the serving node show second or later requests on the same connection had either missing Range headers or an incorrect Host header forwarded upstream. On the artifact side we see 200 responses where 206 expected, and occasionally 403 with S3 denying the request due to Host mismatch.

Expected behavior: Each Range GET should be forwarded unchanged; upstream S3 should respond with 206 Partial Content for valid presigned Range requests and the data should match the requested byte ranges.

1) Deploy a private cluster behind the customer's egress HTTP proxy.
2) Start a serving node that downloads shards using presigned S3 range GETs over HTTP/1.1 keepalive.
3) Configure parallel shard downloads that re-use the same persistent connection (default keepalive).
4) Observe that some subsequent requests on the same TCP connection arrive at S3 without Range or with wrong Host header.
5) Reproduce reliably when egress proxy connection pool latency < 50ms and when more than 4 shards are fetched in <2s window.
Selected snippets from serving node (trimmed):
- [2026-03-06T21:12:03Z] fetch_shard(12) presigned_url="https://s3-vpce.example.amazonaws.com/bucket/object?X-Amz-Signature=..." Range: bytes=0-1048575 => 206 OK
- [2026-03-06T21:12:03Z] fetch_shard(13) presigned_url=... Range: bytes=1048576-2097151 => 200 OK (received full object size)
- [2026-03-06T21:12:04Z] shard checksum mismatch for shard 13

Packet capture (serving node -> egress): second GET includes Range header. Packet capture (egress -> s3): Range header absent; Host header changed to the first request's host header value. Full tcpdump attached to ticket (redacted).
- Reproduced in lab by placing Nginx-based connection pool proxy in front of S3 and enabling aggressive connection reuse. When pool reuses a connection the proxy reused request-line/headers from first request in buffer due to a bug in header handling under pipelined/keepalive workload.
- Collected request/response traces from serving node and from egress appliance. Serving node always sends Range and correct Host. Egress logs show missing Range or Host rewritten to previous value prior to upstream write.
- Hypothesis: Egress proxy uses an optimization to avoid reconstructing headers on connection reuse; under specific timing it replays a stale header block. The issue only manifests for rapid sequential range GETs that multiplex over a shared upstream connection.
- Confirmed that switching serving runtime to disable HTTP keepalive (connection per request) eliminates the problem; also confirmed that disabling connection pooling on the egress appliance eliminates it.
- Customer's egress proxy is a third-party appliance (version 8.2.1) with connection pool rewrite feature. Vendor has acknowledged a similar bug in older firmware but required a packet capture for confirmation.

Additional notes:
2026-03-09 - Support (Liam OConnor): Requested egress proxy logs and asked customer to temporarily disable keepalive on a canary serving node to test. Provided reproducer instructions and a curl-based test script to exercise sequential range GETs.
2026-03-10 - Customer NetOps (Raj Patel): Confirmed that disabling keepalive on one node mitigated the issue. We collected proxy traces and opened a vendor ticket (case #VN-99821). Vendor requests our tcpdump and indicates potential fix in 8.3.x.
2026-03-11 - Support (Liam OConnor): We reproduced locally with an Nginx connection pool configuration and filed an internal bug for 'presigned-range-pipelining' to the infra team (INT-90721). Recommended workaround to customer: set 'Connection: close' or disable pooling for S3 endpoints in egress proxy. Also recommended vendor upgrade plan.
2026-03-12 - Customer (Raj Patel): Applied temporary egress-proxy ACL to force new upstream connections for s3-vpce.example.amazonaws.com and reports 24 hours of stability so far.
2026-03-13 - Support (Liam OConnor): Marking investigation complete; vendor patch scheduled. Documenting long-term mitigation and follow-up items below.
Third-party egress proxy connection-pool implementation could reuse an upstream TCP connection while incorrectly reusing or omitting per-request header blocks (Range/Host) under rapid pipelined requests. This leads to incorrect responses (200 instead of 206) or Host mismatch causing 403 from S3, triggering shard corruption and model load failure.
1) Configure serving runtime to disable HTTP keepalive for presigned shard downloads (connection per request) until vendor patch is applied.
2) On the customer's egress appliance: disable connection pooling or add an exception for S3 VPCE hostnames so each presigned URL gets its own upstream connection.
3) As an immediate mitigation, decrease shard parallelism to reduce chance of reuse.
Vendor acknowledged bug and provided a candidate firmware 8.3.0-rc with header-handling fix. Customer applied an egress ACL to disable pooling for S3 endpoints and observed stabilization. Support recommends vendor upgrade to 8.3.0 when available and applying the documented proxy exception as permanent config. Ticket to remain open until vendor upgrade is completed and verified in production.
Follow-ups:
- Customer to schedule vendor upgrade (owner: Raj Patel).
- Support to validate post-upgrade in staging before closing (owner: Liam OConnor).
- Docs: add troubleshooting note to Confluence about proxy pooling and presigned ranges.
1) Customer: schedule upgrade to egress appliance 8.3.0 and share upgrade window.
2) Support: run post-upgrade smoke tests using the provided reproducer script and one-week monitoring.
3) Engineering: consider adding a safeguard in the serving runtime to verify Content-Range/Content-Length for each shard and retry with a new connection if mismatch detected. (Refer to INT-90721).
payload.summary: Intermittent egress proxy connection-reuse scrubs Host/Range on pooled connections causing sharded artifact fetch failures

comments: 2026-03-10T10:45:00Z Aisha Patel: Case opened after DataFerry flagged production 429s affecting ingestion. Collected initial logs, asked customer to capture edge-proxy debug logs and rate-limiter snapshots.

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customer DataFerry reports intermittent 429 responses for a subset of long-lived SSE subscribers and concurrent gRPC ingestion streams after they performed a subaccount reparent operation (moved streaming workload from subaccount A -> B) in their Private VPC deployment. Impact: multiple production ingestion workers and real-time dashboards were rate-limited causing data lag and backlog.

Impact:
- ~12% of SSE connections observed 429s over a 2 hour window during nightly export; gRPC clients report sporadic rejections for otherwise identical requests.
- Business impact: delayed analytics pipelines, elevated error rates on dashboards, escalated by on-call.

Environment:
- Deployment: Private (customer-managed VPC) behind their NAT gateway + customer edge LB -> Redwood edge-proxy (v2.4.1).
- Region: prod-us-west.
- Relevant components: ingress-proxy, edge token windowing rate-limiter, route-weighting for streaming lanes, subaccount reparent event executed at 02:10 UTC.

Steps to reproduce (as performed by customer):
1) Start mixed workload: 300 SSE subscribers to /events and 60 concurrent gRPC streaming workers to /v1/streams using the same top-level API key but different subaccount-scoped keys.
2) Trigger subaccount reparent via Console API (move workload from subaccount A to B).
3) Observe connection churn as clients re-auth; ~30% of clients reconnect within 90s due to orchestration.
4) Customer sees a wave of 429s affecting ~40% of reconnecting SSEs and a smaller subset of gRPC calls.

Observed behavior:
- Rate-limiter records show the same physical API token being charged twice across two different route fingerprints for a short epoch, then a sudden token-window depletion and subsequent 429 rejects.
- Edge-proxy logs contain many reconnects with changing TLS session fingerprints and repeated preflight probes from health-check sidecars.
- Customer's NAT gateway has limited ephemeral ports and exhibits high NAT churn at the time of the reparent.

Expected behavior:
- Reparent/migration should not double-count tokens or cause persistent 429 waves for reconnecting clients; reconnects should be accounted idempotently or allowed a short grace window for migrating sessions.

Samples / logs provided by customer (sanitized):
- Edge-proxy snippets showing token_id=ak_*** charged at 02:11:17 and again at 02:11:19 with different connection_fingerprint values.
- Rate-limiter debug: refill_epoch=1617 drifted on 2 of 3 nodes; duplicate_count spikes coincide with NAT port churn.
- Client-side traces: SSE reconnects show 100-300ms jitter, health-check probes every 10s during reconnect window.

Additional notes:
- Customer had a background bulk-export that increased preflight traffic during the same window.
- They are on a private deployment with some ingress controls (their load balancer terminates TLS, rewrites headers).

Additional notes:
2026-03-10 13:02 - Customer (DataFerry): Provided sanitized edge-proxy logs and NAT utilization graph. Confirmed subaccount reparent occurred at 02:10 UTC.
2026-03-11 16:03 - Eng (Rate-limiter): Found refill_epoch drift on one rate-limiter replica (node rl-3). Replica was slow to apply epoch commit, causing a brief window where the same token was allowed on two nodes. Correlated with high reconnect rate.
2026-03-12 08:22 - Customer: Confirmed they had a sidecar health-check that aggressively probed reconnecting clients. They agreed to temporarily disable health-checks for the SSE service during migration.
Hypothesis 1: NAT port churn + edge TLS session changes lead to different connection fingerprints for the same API key; fingerprinting logic caused duplicate accounting across two route-buckets.
Hypothesis 2: One rate-limiter replica (rl-3) had epoch commit delay (observed GC pause) which, combined with reconnect burst, resulted in transient double-count of token until leader commit reconciled.
Evidence: rate-limiter logs show duplicate charge events with identical token_id and separate connection_fingerprint values within the same refill epoch window. NAT gateway metrics show ephemeral port exhaustion events at the same timestamps.
Action taken: pulled rate-limiter token ledger for rl-1/rl-2/rl-3, edge-proxy reconnect traces, and customer's NAT port usage charts.
Reproduction attempts in staging: triggered coordinated reconnects + short epoch commit introduced artificially on one replica; reproduced duplicate charge pattern and transient 429 wave.
Short-term mitigation applied (2026-03-12): Redwood support granted a temporary quota bump for DataFerry for 6 hours and disabled aggressive preflight counting for SSE routes in the ingress-proxy for this tenant. Customer disabled health-check sidecar during their reparent operations per our suggestion.
Medium-term fix planned: rate-limiter patch to dedupe token charges across connection fingerprints within the same refill epoch and to add a configurable grace window for subaccount reparent operations (PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/rate-limiter/pull/140).
Customer recommendations provided: increase NAT ephemeral port pool on their LB, avoid aggressive health-check probes during large reconnect waves, and configure isolated burst pool for long-lived SSEs vs bulk-export workers.
Monitoring/follow-up: created alert rule to detect refill_epoch drift and a dashboard for per-tenant duplicate-charge counts. Follow-up owner: Marco Ruiz. Postmortem scheduled and linked to INC-2026-331.
Status: keeping ticket open until rate-limiter patch deploys to Private VPCs and customer's configuration changes are validated in their next migration window.
payload.summary: Intermittent 429s for mixed SSE + gRPC streams after subaccount reparent in Private VPC

They require verifiable proof of outbound network egress for audit events, a one-time SFTP snapshot delivery with IP-allowlisted presigned URLs, and completed responses to a 120-question security questionnaire.

Impact: Customer expects this evidence to be ingested by their compliance team by 2026-03-18. Missing items or unverifiable checks will delay regulatory audit and may require contract escalation.

Environment: prod/us-east, tenant: northbridge-prod, audit stream: activity-events-v2.

Requested deliverables:
1) A signed (ED25519) manifest SHA256 of an exported delta snapshot covering 2026-03-01T00:00:00Z to 2026-03-09T23:59:59Z. Manifest must include per-file checksums, UTC canonical timestamps, and a Redacted/Unredacted file map.
2) Network egress proof: VPC flow logs and egress_nic tagging showing outbound connections used by the snapshot delivery, with destination_asn, destination_ip, TLS SNI, and socket-level TLS cipher. payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customer NimbleAssist noticed a reserved credit line (~$1,200) appearing on their March invoice after our multi-region cutover on 2026-03-11. The reserved credit references free-tier buffer allocation and shows as a provisional hold (Line 3B: 'reserved_free_buffer_us-east').

Impact:
- Invoice shows a reserved credit reducing available balance; customer cannot auto-pay until hold resolved.
- Customer reports unexpected "missing" free-tier consumption (tokens appear unconsumed in dashboard), and alerts triggered for sudden reduction in available credits.
- Business impact: NimbleAssist (enterprise) blocked on monthly billing reconciliation for procurement.

Environment:
- Production tenant for NimbleAssist, primarily routed through us-east after cutover. Some async postbacks landed in eu-west during flow.

Steps to reproduce / observed behavior:
1) Cutover process applied new region tags and billing_tag rewrite for multi-tenant reconciler at 2026-03-11T02:10Z.
2) Customer ran regular batch evaluation and streaming traffic between 2026-03-11T04:00Z and 2026-03-11T08:30Z.
3) Billing reconciler created provisional hold lines referencing reserved_free_buffer_us-east and did not consume tokens; aggregator shows two different tag values for the same API key.
4) Invoice generation job picked up provisional holds on 2026-03-12T00:45Z.

Expected behavior:
- Free-tier buffer allocation should be applied and consumed immediately on usage or released if unused; no provisional reserved credit should be left on finalized invoice.

Observed behavior:
- Reserved credit persisted and blocked autopay; customer-facing dashboard shows token usage but billing postbacks show offset to a separate pseudo-org tag.

Logs / evidence attached:
- Billing reconciler logs snippet: reconciler.job: 'tag_rewrite: applied override to api_key *******abcd -> billing_tag: neo-us-east-archive' (attachment: reconciler_logs_20260311.txt)
- Invoice snapshot: invoice_2026-03-12_nimbleassist.pdf (line showing reserved_free_buffer_us-east)

Additional notes:
Reconciler tag rewrite produced a shadowed billing namespace: some postbacks kept old tenant_tag while reconciler created a new reserved_bucket entry under new tag. This left tokens visible in usage dashboard but unclaimed by billing namespace.
Out-of-order postback replay from eu-west queue (delayed by ~18 minutes) meant reconciler ran twice for same logical usage with different tags: one consumption record and one reservation record.
Rate-limiting on postback consumer caused backpressure and duplicate reconciliation attempts; consumer backoff retries had idempotency key mismatch for patched tag formatting change.
Affected customers appear to be those with hybrid-hosted + private routing that touched both regions during the cutover window; estimated impacted invoices ~10-12 customers with combined provisional holds ~$8k.
Related code change: https://github.com/redwood-inference/reconciler/pull/4321 altered billing_tag normalization to include region suffix which interacted badly with legacy postbacks.
Workaround: billing-admin released reserved holds for NimbleAssist and issued credit memo CM-5698. We set invoice to adjusted and enabled autopay. Long-term fix: rollback tag normalization change in reconciler (PR 4321) and deploy idempotency key safeguard for postback consumer. Follow-ups: INT ticket to run a scan and release remaining orphaned reserved_free_buffer_* holds for impacted customers; add additional helm readiness gating for reconciler during region cutovers.
INT- cleanup run: run audit script to find reserved_free_buffer_* holds created between 2026-03-11T01:50Z and 2026-03-11T03:30Z and auto-release or queue for manual review (owner: Ethan Morales)
Revert PR 4321 or patch: add idempotency on tag normalization and add integration test to cover cross-region postback ordering (owner: Lina Berg)
Communicate to affected customers: send tailored update emails and sticky credits where appropriate (owner: CS team)
Add postmortem to Confluence and link to status page event if more than 5 customers impacted (owner: Ops)
We discovered that a recent reconciler change during the region cutover caused a provisional reserved credit line to be created for your account. We released the hold and issued a credit memo so autopay can proceed. Our engineering team will follow up with a permanent fix and will notify you when a postmortem is available.
2026-03-14 NimbleAssist finance confirmed invoice updated and autopay successful; requested written confirmation and root cause within 48 hours.
