payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customer reports a spike in end-to-end inference latency and client-side timeouts when sending large batched inference requests (bulk job of ~25 concurrent requests per client). The SDK appears to serialize retries and produces long head-of-line delays rather than distributing retry attempts across healthy connections.

Impact:
- Several customers on Dedicated capacity experienced perceived timeouts and increased median latency for batched/parallel inference.
- Client-side metrics show heavy retry activity and a single active TCP connection per SDK process during peak bursts.
- Affects production workloads for PromptCraft (dedicated allocation).

Environment:
- Redwood Dedicated (prod us-east-1)
- Customer SDK: redwood-sdk-js v2.3.0 (custom config)
- Load pattern: ~25 parallel connections from a single process batching 16 prompts per request

Observed behavior:
- Burst of requests -> SDK initiates retries but retry jitter misconfiguration causes uniform backoff windows (no randomness), leading to synchronized retry waves.
- SDK default maxConnections overridden to 1 in customer's init script (corporate template), leading to serialized HTTP requests.
- API gateway reports many concurrent queued requests from the same tenant but only one open upstream connection, producing head-of-line blocking and increased latency.
- Clients observe socket-level timeouts and then exponential retries in lockstep, which appear as repeated long latencies rather than occasional failed calls.

Expected behavior:
- SDK should spread retries across connections with randomized jitter so retries are staggered, and clients should use a higher connection pool for parallel workloads.

Steps to reproduce:
1) Start a single-node test client using redwood-sdk-js v2.3.0 with maxConnections set to 1 and backoff config: initial=200ms, multiplier=2, jitter=0 (explicitly disabled).
2) Fire 25 parallel request tasks, each sending a batch payload of 12 prompts to redwood-7b-v1 on prod us-east-1.
3) Induce a transient upstream 503 on serving-runtime (simulate slow node or canary drain) for ~3s.
4) Observe client-side request queueing, repeated retries all happening in same time-window, and increased p95/p99 latencies.

Logs / traces collected:
- API gateway trace id: agw-us-east-20260301-7f9a2c (attached in ticket)
- Client logs show repeated "Retrying request (attempt 3) after backoff=1200ms" with identical timestamps across multiple tasks.
- Serving-runtime logs show spikes of queued requests from tenant PromptCraft and repeated 502/503s during the window.

Notes:
- Customer applied an internal SDK wrapper that set maxConnections=1 for connection pinning to their telemetry proxy. That policy combined with disabled jitter caused serialized retry storms.
- Not a server-only regression: reproduces locally with the customer's SDK config.

Install redwood-sdk-js v2.3.0 with custom config (maxConnections=1, jitterDisabled=true)
Run a client that submits 25 parallel tasks each sending batched payloads of 12 prompts
Simulate a transient upstream 503 for ~3s and observe retry timing and connection counts
[client] 2026-03-01T14:22:10Z Retry attempt=2 backoff=800ms task=17
[client] 2026-03-01T14:22:10Z Retry attempt=2 backoff=800ms task=19
[agw] 2026-03-01T14:22:10Z queuedRequests=42 tenant=PromptCraft upstreamConnections=1
Initial hypothesis: server-side throttling or scheduling causing timeouts. Ruled out after reproducing locally using customer's SDK config.
Observed SDK config disables jitter and pinches connection pool to 1 — causes serialized head-of-line blocking under concurrency.
Network captures show repeated SYN/ACK on same connection and long HTTP/1.1 keepalive queues, not parallel connections.
Serving-runtime shows normal healthy kernel; error spikes align with synchronized client retry waves, not underlying model slowness.

Additional notes:
SRE (Maya Singh): Gateway shows per-tenant queued counts spiking; will add temporary rate-throttle rule to protect shared resources.
Customer (PromptCraft CS): We've reverted wrapper to default connection pool and are rerunning load test; will report back.
Workaround provided 2026-03-02: set maxConnections>=16 for this workload and enable randomized exponential jitter (enableJitter=true) in SDK config.
Temporary mitigations: SRE added a per-tenant soft concurrency cap to avoid cascading queueing while customer rolled back the wrapper.
Root cause: customer-side SDK configuration that disabled jitter combined with an overly small connection pool (maxConnections=1) which serialized retries and created apparent service timeouts.
Fix planned: SDK change in v2.4.1 will emit a startup warning when maxConnections < recommended for detected concurrency, and will default to enabling jitter unless explicitly set to false. PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/sdk/pull/842
Follow-up: create a support doc (KB) about safe SDK connection/backoff defaults and recommend templates for high-parallelism bulk workloads.

2026-03-02: Workaround recommended and applied by customer; SRE applied temporary gateway cap.
2026-03-03: Engineering reproduced locally and opened SDK PR for warning behavior.
2026-03-05: Customer confirms restored latency after rollback to defaults. Preparing closure notes.
Mitigated — customer rolled back the custom wrapper and enabled jitter; SDK warning landed in PR for v2.4.1. Recommend closing after follow-up KB published.
Publish KB: 'SDK connection pool and backoff best practices' with code examples for Node and Python clients
Add SDK telemetry metric for effective maxConnections and jitterEnabled to alert on risky configs
Review Dedicated onboarding template to ensure recommended pool defaults for bulk workloads are prominent
payload.summary: SDK exponential backoff jitter misconfiguration causing serialized retries and apparent inference timeouts for bulk requests

Issue summary: Ledgerly reported a sustained increase in 5xx errors for streaming API calls beginning 2026-03-10 09:12 UTC. The errors manifest as 502/503 responses from the API gateway for new requests while long-lived streaming sessions remain active. Impact: ~18% error rate for streaming endpoints for Ledgerly's tenant; only observed in us-east region. Customer-facing impact: degraded UX for live chat and transcript streaming, increased client retries.
- Affects Ledgerly (enterprise customer using dedicated tenant in us-east)
- Error types: 502 Gateway, 503 Service Unavailable, occasional 504 for long polling
- Estimate: 14-22% of streaming requests failed between 09:12–11:35 UTC on 2026-03-10 (rolling metrics)
- No billing discrepancy reported; primarily availability/latency degradation
Prod (dedicated tenant) on cluster us-east-a. Customer had multiple long-lived streaming sessions with high token output (average response sizes > 25k tokens per session) and clients using older HTTP/2 client library with small TCP write windows.
1) Create a long-lived streaming session to redwood-v2-large in us-east.
2) Simulate a slow client writer: send initial headers, then throttle data frames to 10 KB/s (small write window).
3) Open 40 concurrent short-lived streaming requests from a different client identity while the slow session is active.
4) Observe new requests returning 502/503 from API gateway after connection pool exhaustion and proxy timeouts.
[2026-03-10T09:21:05Z] apigw[edge-01] WARN conn_pool: tenant=ledgerly sockets_in_use=120 max=128 waiting=42
[2026-03-10T09:21:08Z] apigw[edge-01] ERROR upstream: got 503 from upstream (upstream_timeout) request_id=abc123

[2026-03-10T09:23:07Z] orchestrator INFO restart: worker pid=33412 restarted (same host)
- Initial hypothesis: simple connection-pool exhaustion at API gateway due to high number of long-lived streams.
- Confirmed that ledgerly had multiple streams that did not perform regular client-side flushing (slow writers) which held socket slots open for >2 minutes.
- Deeper trace: runtime threadpool metrics show a single worker with a telemetry flush (background telemetry aggregator) intermittently taking CPU and blocking scheduling of small tasks; combined with runtime's per-worker max concurrency, short-lived requests queued up, waiting on worker availability.
- The blocked thread combined with blocked sockets at the proxy produced head-of-line conditions: new requests could not get a free connection and the gateway returned 502/503 after its internal timeout.
- Recreated locally with slow-client simulator and observed identical error pattern and threadpool blocking in runtime logs.
- Related to INT-7682 (previous threadpool tuning experiment) — regression likely introduced by the telemetry-flush change that reduced fairness for incoming RPCs under heavy long-lived stream load.

2026-03-10 09:46 UTC - Customer (Ledgerly - S. Nguyen): Provided session IDs and client library version (http2 v0.9.1). Noted that streams were open for up to 14 minutes on large outputs.

Mitigation performed 2026-03-10 10:15 UTC: adjusted per-tenant connection pool soft limits (reduced long-lived socket reservation), increased API gateway internal socket timeout to avoid premature upstream failure, and applied emergency restart to the single runtime worker exhibiting telemetry-flush pinning. Deployed runtime patch (commit a9f3d2) to move telemetry flush to low-priority cooperative task to prevent thread starvation.
Workaround provided to customer: upgrade HTTP/2 client library to v0.9.3 and enable periodic small-frame flush (every 2s) to avoid holding sockets indefinitely.
Current status: error rates for Ledgerly returned to baseline (~<1%) by 2026-03-10 11:05 UTC. Monitoring alerts created for head-of-line socket hold and runtime blocked-thread ratio.
Update streaming runbook: add detection for slow-client head-of-line and recommended mitigation steps (contrib: Diego)
Add integration test: simulate slow-client writes + concurrent short requests to verify fairness under real config (owner: runtime team)
Revert/tune telemetry-flush schedule if further regressions seen and instrument thread run-queue metrics (owner: infra-observability)
Consider per-tenant long-lived-stream reservation token to prevent aggressive pool exhaustion (owner: api-gateway)
Follow up with Ledgerly to confirm client patch rollout and collect post-fix telemetry (owner: CSM)

This incident highlights an intersection failure mode: slow client writers can create resource starvation when combined with a single-threaded blocking pattern in the runtime. Fix includes both customer-facing guidance and a platform change to reduce scheduling priority of telemetry and other background work.
Investigigation complete. A small number of tenants experienced elevated 5xx for streaming endpoints due to long-lived client connections combined with background thread scheduling interactions; mitigations rolled out and fixed for impacted tenants. Full postmortem to follow.

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Support received multiple reports from StreamlineAI (Dedicated) about a sudden rise in server errors during peak morning traffic window (09:00-10:30 UTC). Error rate rose from ~0.2% to ~12% for the tenant's routes. Customers observed intermittent HTTP 502/503/504 returned by the API and streaming sessions disconnecting.

Impact:
- StreamlineAI saw increased request failures and stream disconnects affecting production availability for a 15-minute window.
- Elevated token retry and hedged-retry activity from SDK clients.
- Latency for successful requests increased by ~120ms median and p95 by ~450ms.

Environment:
- Redwood Dedicated pool (tenant pinned).
- Region: us-east.
- Models serving: gptx-4-onnx-quant pinned.
- Autoscaler: enabled, burst policy set to allow ephemeral warmup.

Steps to reproduce (observed pattern):
1) Tenant sees a steady small-payload burst from many short-lived connections (keepalive churn).
2) API gateway keepalive pool begins recycling sockets aggressively when ephemeral worker count spikes.
3) Accept queue depth grows; proxy begins returning 502s for new connections.
4) Upstream runtimes experience high prefetch and KV cache thrashing, GPU utilization oscillates and triggers watchdog resets for a subset of workers.

Logs / snippets:
- apigw: "ERROR tcp_accept: accept queue backlog exceeded: backlog=512 -> dropping"
- proxy: "WARN upstream_health: stale-keepalive detected, closing 42 sockets"
- runtime: "GPU_WATCHDOG: worker 128 killed - NVML reset observed; oom=false; kernel_swap=true"
- metrics snapshot (09:12 UTC): request_error_rate=12.1%, accept_queue=490, ephemeral_workers=240 -> baseline ephemeral_workers ~40

Initial customer report excerpt:
> "We saw a sudden wave of failures around 09:10 — streaming sessions disconnect and simple chat completions returning 502. No change on our side. Our traffic is short-lived connections (mobile SDK)."

Additional notes:
2026-03-13 Support (Priya): Customer confirms mobile SDK v2.1.3 with hedged retry enabled; telemetry shows backoff disabled in their config. Requested they temporarily disable hedged retry; customer agreed and applied a config change at 09:40 UTC.
2026-03-13 StreamlineAI (Customer): After disabling hedged retries we saw immediate drop in error rate to ~0.8% and streaming disconnects reduced. However sporadic 502s remain.
2026-03-14 StreamlineAI (Customer): Confirmed that errors returned to normal levels after both client-side hedged retry disable and server-side keepalive headroom increase. Asked whether Redwood can recommend SDK config defaults to avoid this class of problem.
Timeline correlation: accept queue and ephemeral_workers spike co-occurred with API error spike (09:08-09:22).
Root correlation: short-lived mobile connections with hedged retry created repeated connection churn, causing keepalive pool to recycle sockets at high rate.
Proxy behavior: closing stale keepalive sockets en masse increases downstream cold-connects; cold connects hit runtime prefetch path which triggers KV cache invalidations and GPU kernel swaps.
NVML resets: subset of runtime workers experienced NVML soft-resets likely due to driver-level kernel swaps under high context-switch pressure (observed on 5 out of 60 workers in host-group).
Mitigations validated: disabling hedged retries on client reduced amplification immediately; server-side keepalive headroom prevented accept queue exhaustion and reduced cold-connection rate.
Risk: Without runtime prefetch guards, similar tenant traffic patterns could cause repeated GPU thrashing and intermittent worker restarts during other tenant bursts.
A feedback amplification loop between aggressive client hedged retries (short-lived connections), proxy keepalive recycling, and runtime prefetch/kv-cache activity which caused accept-queue exhaustion and triggered NVML soft-resets on a subset of GPU workers.
Short-term: Coordinated mitigation with customer (disable hedged retry) + server-side increase in keepalive pool headroom and accept-queue tunables in us-east. Medium-term: merged PR to add runtime-side prefetch concurrency limits and a proxy change to stagger keepalive socket closures (PR linked).
1) Ship runtime prefetch guard (PR 1632) to canary across all regions in next maintenance window. 2) Update dedicated runbook and add automatic tenant-level prefetch throttling during accept-queue pressure. 3) Update SDK recommended defaults to have hedged retries off for mobile scenarios in the docs and publish guidance to customers. 4) Monitor StreamlineAI for 72h and then move ticket to Resolved if stable.
Error rate stable below 1% for 72 hours for StreamlineAI and no NVML resets in affected host group. Follow-up runbook updates merged into ops-runbooks.

Impact: CloudCanary reporting degraded realtime summarization performance and increased latency; automated retries caused client-side backoffs and user-visible errors. Scope: Affected a subset of dedicated customer capacity pools using redwood-7b-v1; roughly 8% of requests in us-east and spillover into us-west via cross-region fallback. Immediate customer impact documented by CloudCanary support logs and error samples attached below.
1) Use CloudCanary dedicated credentials against prod-us-east endpoint (same routing policy used by customer). 2) Issue a sustained mix of streaming and non-streaming requests at moderate concurrency (~50 concurrent sessions) with 16k context windows. 3) Observe API Gateway 502/504 rates rising after ~20 minutes, upstream connection resets on runtime-proxy, and runtimes report half-open sockets in metrics.

Initial hypothesis: autoscaler warmup caused short-term capacity gap — ruled out after autoscaler metrics show no scale-down events in the window.

Issue summary: NimbusAnalytics observed repeated midday throughput collapses in their dedicated GPU pool. Impact: p99 latency spiked to >30s for batched routes, sustained loss of throughput for ~10-30 minute windows causing user-facing errors and retries. Initial triage indicated GPU attachments were delayed and autoscaler returned fewer slots than expected. Hypothesis: background snapshotter process is generating NVMe IO bursts on hosts used by the dedicated pool, causing IO wait and delaying GPU attach syscalls which the autoscaler interprets as node unavailability.
Customer-facing inference requests experienced 20-70% throughput reduction during affected windows; timeouts increased and errors surfaced in SDKs. Billing/usage accuracy impacted for the window. Customer SLAs at risk.
1) Run sustained small-stream batched workload against dedicated pool (NimbusAnalytics tenant) during midday window
2) Trigger a background snapshot job (internal snapshotter) that performs concurrent nvme writes on the same host set
3) Observe increased GPU attach latency and autoscaler reducing attaches/failing to meet demand
4) Reproduce p99 latency spike and throughput drop within 5-15 minutes of snapshot start

2026-03-12T12:04:09Z node/host-7 kernel: blk_update_request: I/O error, dev nvme0n1, sector=...
2026-03-12T12:04:10Z autoscaler: evaluate_pool(dedicated-nimbus) => desired=8, available=4, note='attach-latency>threshold'
2026-03-12T12:05:30Z serving-runtime: batch_worker: failed_to_pin_gpu timeout=25000ms request=rb-334
Customer trace id: nimbus-req-20260312-8a2b
SDK: Retry 3/5 after timeout from /v1/generate (err=AttachTimeout)
Support (Aisha): Initial triage suggests correlation between snapshotter background runs and observed attach latencies. Opened host-level IO dashboard (dash/host-io) and alerted infra.
SRE (Marco): Confirmed NVMe write stalls on host-7 and host-8 coinciding with the window; kernel iowait jumped to 78%.
Customer (Nimbus Ops - Raj): We started seeing spikes around 11:55 and it impacted multiple inference endpoints. We can schedule maintenance windows if snapshotting needs throttling.
Support (Aisha): Applied temporary mitigation: throttled snapshotter job parallelism for Nimbus tenant and pinned them to a different host-affinity group. Monitoring for stabilization.
SRE (Marco): Creating PR to add rate-limiter to snapshotter and to feed nvme/io-wait metric into autoscaler as a soft-signal (see PR #4821).
Host IO dashboard shows repeated 20-40s spikes in nvme latency during snapshot windows; these align with attach syscall latencies recorded by scheduler.
Sampler traces from serving-runtime show batch workers blocked on cudaDevicePrimaryCtxRetain for durations that match kernel-level IO wait spikes — suggests attachment blocked by host-level resource contention.
Autoscaler currently only watches attach errors and node health; it treats prolonged attach latency as node absence which triggers conservative shrink decisions causing shortfall.
Noise isolation: the snapshotter runs were scheduled on the same GPUs' hosts due to affinity packing; other tenants on the same pool experienced collateral throughput loss (noisy-neighbor).
Background snapshotter jobs performed unthrottled NVMe writes on dedicated pool hosts. The resulting IO saturation produced kernel iowait spikes which delayed GPU attach operations. The autoscaler misinterpreted attach latency as reduced capacity and reduced attaches, creating a feedback loop and customer throughput collapse.
Immediate mitigation (2026-03-12 13:00Z): Reduced snapshotter parallelism for NimbusAnalytics and moved active snapshot jobs off the customer's dedicated host affinity set. Observed restoration of attach latency to baseline within two attach windows and throughput returned to 95% within 12 minutes.
Short-term follow-up (planned rollout 2026-03-15): Deploy snapshotter rate-limiter and introduce host-tagging to avoid co-scheduling heavy snapshot IO with latency-sensitive dedicated pools.
Long-term fix (roadmap Q2 2026): Feed host-level nvme/io-wait metric into autoscaler heuristic so the autoscaler distinguishes slow attach due to IO from actual node loss; improve scheduler backoff policy to avoid aggressive pool shrinking on transient attach latency.
Throttle snapshotter parallelism to 1 job per host for tenants in latency-sensitive pools
Temporarily change NimbusAnalytics host-affinity tag to 'isolated-snapshot-avoid'
If immediate relief needed, move tenant to a warm spare dedicated pool with different host set
1) Merge PR #4821 to add snapshotter rate-limiting and backpressure (owner: Marco)
2) Create autoscaler change to incorporate nvme/io-wait as a soft-signal (owner: infra/auto-scale team)
3) Update runbook: 'dedicated-pool-noisy-io' with playbook steps to identify and mitigate snapshotter collisions
4) Schedule a capacity isolation policy review for Q2 to reduce shared host IO between snapshot-heavy workloads and low-latency pools
Notify NimbusAnalytics when PR is merged and when autoscaler change is staged; schedule a 1:1 postmortem with customer and infra for April capacity planning.
Mitigation applied and customer throughput stabilized. Engineering working on PR for snapshotter rate-limiter; autoscaler heuristic change scoped and planned. Monitoring active for 72 hours.

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customer using the Go SDK with a custom retry middleware (wraps SDK stream client to implement exponential backoff + local batching) observes duplicate external tool executions (webhook posts and DB writes) after stream resume following transient network disconnects.

Impact:
Intermittent duplicate side-effects in production for a small subset of long-running chat sessions (~0.2% of sessions). Customer reports duplicated webhook payloads and duplicate order rows in their downstream DB leading to reconciliation work and customer complaints.

Environment:
- Redwood Dedicated pool (dedicated tenant), prod us-east
- Go SDK v0.12.3 with custom RetryMiddleware v1.0 (in-house)
- Model routes pinned to redwood-alpha-2b, fallback to open-llama-13b enabled

Steps to reproduce (customer repro):
1) Start a long-lived streaming chat session that triggers two sequential function/tool calls: (a) external webhook POST to create a ticket, (b) internal DB write confirmation. The SDK client sends both functool frames in a short window.
2) During the second token window, simulate a brief network disruption (TCP reset / client Internet flaps).
3) Client retry middleware closes and then re-establishes the SDK stream. On resume the middleware attempts to replay the buffered frames but in some runs reorders the buffered batch (due to sorting by retry-time heuristics) so the DB write appears before the webhook confirmation frame.
4) Redwood serving runtime processes the resumed stream; because the model fallback path returns a shorter prefix cache (KV cache divergence) the server accepts the replayed frames as new, causing the webhook to be executed again. DB write also happens a second time in the interleaved order.

Observed logs & artifacts:
- Customer provided debug trace: https://slack-redwood.slack.com/archives/C012XYZ/p1640000000
- Customer reproduction capture: s3://slatemaps-repro/trace-20260313.tar.gz (contains SDK trace, local middleware logs)
- Server logs around the time show two separate funcall-request ids: funcall_id=fc_9a7b... and fc_9a7b...-r2; timestamps separated by ~1s.
- Serving runtime trace shows fallback to open-llama-13b during resume with shorter kv_cache.sequence=42 vs original 46.

Initial hypothesis:
- The customer-side retry middleware mutates ordering of buffered functool frames during resume which, combined with a model fallback that results in shorter prefix/KV cache at the server, prevents the runtime from matching the replay to the original in-flight execution. Without a canonical dedup token preserved across resume and fallback, the server treats the replay as a new request and re-executes side-effects.

Investigation notes so far (support/SRE):
- Reproduced a minimal repro locally by running the Go SDK with the customer's middleware that reorders based on a last-attempt-first heuristic. Confirmed duplicate webhook post in dedicated staging.
- Checked server-side dedup windows: dedup tokens are scoped to per-model-version + kv_cache.sequence range; when fallback occurs the dedup lookup can miss if kv_cache.sequence decreased.
- Confirmed SDK does send an idempotency header for funcalls in normal flows but the middleware code rewrites headers during replay (it drops the original idempotency-baggage and generates a new short token).

Immediate mitigations suggested to customer:
- Hotfix: stop mutating idempotency baggage on replay and preserve the original funcall idempotency token across retries/resume.
- Workaround: disable in-client batching/reordering for long-running sessions (recommended until server-side tolerance fix is in place).

Next steps / action items:
- Support: Confirm customer has patched middleware to preserve idempotency baggage and test for duplicates (assigned to Liam Chen).
- SRE/Runtime: Evaluate changing dedup lookup policy to include broader kv_cache ancestry window when checking for previous funcall executions across model fallback boundaries (engineering task; create RFC).
- Product: Consider adding guidance to SDK docs about not reordering functool frames and an SDK helper to preserve idempotency baggage across retries.

Priority rationale:
Customer is on Dedicated plan and experiencing production-side duplicates; P1 chosen due to business impact and potential data integrity issues.

Additional notes:
2026-03-14 11:18 - Customer (SlateMaps) engineer - maya@slatemaps.com: We shipped a quick patch to preserve the original idempotency_token on replay and have not observed duplicates in 2 hours of traffic. Will monitor and report after 24h.
Mitigation in progress - customer patched middleware to preserve original idempotency token; Support to monitor. Engineering task created to harden server dedup across fallback.

payload.description:
Issue summary: Customer reports that exporting a dashboard panel to CSV returns an empty file (0 data rows) when the panel's filter uses OR conditions that include a tracehook parameter. Impact: BrightCart's scheduled digest relied on the CSV to attach tracehook links to alerts; missing rows caused alerts to be delivered without context and a missed escalation. Environment: prod (us-east), BrightCart org ID 8162, dashboard id db-94a1. Example export job id: export-20260313-8162-77.

Observed behavior: The console UI shows matching rows in the panel preview, but the bulk export job completes successfully and the CSV contains only headers (no data rows). This happens reproducibly when the filter contains OR conditions mixing tracehook tokens and other predicates (e.g., tracehook.session_id = "abc" OR route = "payments"). Exports that use only AND conditions or that omit tracehook tokens succeed.

Notes: Customer first noticed at 2026-03-13 15:22 PDT when scheduled report delivered an empty attachment. They attached a screenshot of the panel preview and the CSV.

1) Login to BrightCart org (org id 8162) in prod us-east.
2) Open dashboard db-94a1 and locate panel 'Payments session activity'.
3) Set panel filter to: tracehook.session_id = "abc123" OR route = "payments".
4) Click 'Download CSV' (bulk export).
5) Observe exported file CSV has headers but zero data rows.
6) Modify filter to use AND instead of OR or remove tracehook clause and repeat export -> CSV contains rows.
CSV export should include the same rows that are shown in the panel preview for the given time range and filter (including when the filter has OR conditions referencing tracehook tokens).
Export job returns 200 and a CSV file with headers only. Panel preview shows data rows for the same filter.
export-service logs (prod us-east) for export-20260313-8162-77:
[2026-03-13T22:22:11Z] INFO export.request received org=8162 user=svc-reports job=export-20260313-8162-77
[2026-03-13T22:22:12Z] DEBUG query-sanitizer: input_filter=tracehook.session_id = 'abc123' OR route = 'payments'
[2026-03-13T22:22:12Z] DEBUG planner: rewrite=OR_simplify -> (tracehook.session_id = 'abc123') OR (route = 'payments')
[2026-03-13T22:22:12Z] DEBUG planner: chosen_plan=streaming-join-prefetch
[2026-03-13T22:22:13Z] WARN result-set size=0 rows=0
[2026-03-13T22:22:13Z] INFO export.complete job=export-20260313-8162-77 duration_ms=1205 status=success size_bytes=102
Investigation timeline:
- 2026-03-13 22:40 UTC: Reproduced against BrightCart prod org from support console using their dashboard and a synthetic tracehook token -> export returns empty CSV but UI preview shows rows.
- Confirmed export-service v1.9.4 running in us-east.
- Captured SQL/IR emitted by query planner: when OR is present and one side references a tracehook-augmented column (nullable string), the sanitizer performs an incorrect boolean normalization that rewrites the OR into an expression with IS NOT NULL checks that can be optimized away by the planner when a partial index on tracehook metadata exists.
- Root cause hypothesis: query-sanitizer component incorrectly hoists or collapses OR branches involving tracehook tokens during boolean simplification. This interacts with the planner's partial-index-aware predicate pushdown, producing a plan that returns zero rows for combinations that are valid in the preview path (preview uses an alternate execution path that evaluates filters at the application layer after enrichment).
- Reproduced with a minimal test case against staging; created unit test demonstrating sanitizer rewrite mismatch.

Patch deployed: export-service v1.9.5 that fixes boolean-simplifier to preserve OR branches referencing nullable tracehook columns and avoid hoisting IS NOT NULL checks. Patch includes unit tests and an integration test that mirrors the panel preview path.
Rollout: Canary started 2026-03-14 01:40 UTC at 5% -> 25% -> 100% by 02:10 UTC in us-east. All subsequent reproduction attempts now return expected rows in exported CSV.
Workaround (prior to patch): Instruct customer to either (a) change OR to explicit parentheses and avoid using tracehook token on one side (e.g., (route = 'payments') OR (tracehook.session_id IS NOT NULL AND tracehook.session_id = 'abc123')), or (b) use the panel's 'Download visible rows' feature which uses the preview path.
Customer communications: CS issued a one-week service credit for missed digest delivery and coordinated a re-run of the scheduled export.
Follow-ups: Add a cross-check in export CI to run integration tests against typical tracehook filters; add dashboard-level telemetry to surface export-preview divergence.

Issue summary: Starting 2026-03-13 11:12 UTC we observed a sustained increase in 5xx responses from the edge for a subset of streaming and synchronous generation requests. Error spike correlates with large numbers of short-lived connections that enter an ephemeral-proxy sleep state then thaw simultaneously, amplifying priority-pool evictions and causing upstream serving-runtime error cascades.

Impact: ~8-14% overall 5xx rate for affected tenant traffic window (BrightDocs production traffic); streaming sessions experienced frequent disconnects and reconnect storms. Several customer requests failed with 502/503 and intermittent runtime restarts.

Environment: production (us-east-1), BrightDocs tenant routed to dedicated priority pool (reserved-dedicated-02). Affected model: redwood/gptx-8k-v1.

Steps to reproduce (observed pattern):
1) Create sustained set of short streaming sessions (~1-2s messages, high churn) from a single tenant.
2) Observe ephemeral proxy lifecycle: many proxies enter sleep (idle) with TCP keepalive enabled.
3) When tenant traffic flares, proxies thaw concurrently and attempt to re-establish backend connections.
4) Priority eviction logic attempts to free slots in ephemeral pool, triggering connection pruning and OOM-like resource pressure in a few serving-runtime processes.

Observed behavior: repeated 5xx responses at API edge, increased runtime allocation/restart counts, longer p95 latencies for streaming handshake. Trace IDs: trace-ff12ac, trace-bb98d1 (sampled).

Expected behavior: Thawing should be smoothed (staggered) and connection reuse should avoid mass eviction. No tenant-visible 5xx spike.

Logs and artifacts: attached sampling of runtime stderr from two processes (startup / OOM-like entries), api-gateway access logs showing 502/503 burst window 11:12-11:40 UTC, Prometheus graphs for ephemeral-proxy pool size and eviction rate, Grafana link: https://grafana.redwood.local/d/ephemeral/pool-overview?from=2026-03-13T11:00:00Z&to=2026-03-13T12:00:00Z
Initial hypothesis: sleep->thaw synchronization in ephemeral proxy combined with priority-pool eviction produces a feedback loop that starves serving-runtime threads.

What we checked:
- Confirmed spike in ephemeral-proxy wake events around 11:12 UTC (ephemeral-proxy/wake_rate metric).
- Observed concurrent backend connection churn in api-gateway connection tracker (conn_reuse_miss spike).
- Heap/alloc patterns on two serving-runtime pods showed rapid memory pressure, followed by watchdog restarts; cores show increased pagefaults.
- Autoscaler logs show no immediate scale-up due to short-lived nature of connections.

Partial findings:
- Reproduced locally by simulating many 1-2s streaming sessions: when ephemeral proxy sleep timeout set to default 45s, concurrent thaws lead to 100-200 connection tear/establish events in 10s window.
- Priority eviction algorithm favors rapid free-up over backoff, causing a loud eviction cascade when many proxies return at once.

Hypotheses:
1) Sleep timeout + synchronized client reconnect behavior creates temporal locality that overwhelms limited ephemeral pool.
2) Priority eviction aggressiveness should be rate-limited to avoid cascade.

Next steps being executed:
- Applying immediate mitigation (see resolution)
- Instrumenting throttle on eviction decision and adding jitter to proxy wake scheduling
- Preparing a controlled canary of a config change to ephemeral-proxy (disable aggressive sleep for priority pools)
- Longer-term: tune default sleep timeout and add adaptive staggers based on pool pressure metrics

Mitigation applied: disabled ephemeral-proxy sleep for affected BrightDocs route (ephemeral-proxy.sleep_timeout=0) to avoid synchronized thawing. Immediate effect: 5xx rate reduced to baseline.
Planned permanent fix: merge PR #1289 which adds randomized wake jitter and a rate limiter on priority eviction decisions, followed by a staged canary across priority pools. Expected timeline: canary 2026-03-15 10:00 UTC, full rollout pending canary success.

Issue summary:
Customer LexiDocs reports intermittent high tail latency (p95->p99) and occasional 504 gateway timeouts on text generation endpoints. Problem appears during low-burst workloads (short bursts of small requests) and began after the serving-runtime 2026-03-03 rollout.

Impact:
- Multiple user-facing requests returned 504s and saw p99 latency > 2.5s (baseline ~250ms).
- Affects production traffic for LexiDocs dedicated capacity in us-east.
- Business impact: user-facing timeouts for document previews in product.

Environment:
- Dedicated pool: lexidocs-dedicated-us-east
- Serving runtime version: 2026.3.03-canary (rolled to prod 2026-03-03)
- Autoscaler: configured reserved + burst policy

Steps to reproduce (synthetic):
1) From a client in us-east, send bursts of 10 concurrent small-completion requests (max_tokens=64) at 1 QPS sustained for 5 minutes, with random inter-burst idle intervals of 10-30s.
2) Observe p95/p99 and error rates on the route.

Observed behavior:
- p50/p75 stable; p95 shows periodic bumps and p99 spikes to 2-3s every ~20-40s.
- Gateway logs show internal timeouts and downstream "504 read timeout" entries correlated with serving-runtime worker queue wait exceeding 1.5s.
- Continuous-batcher metrics report increases in "idle_wait_ms" and a growing "pending_batch_window" metric right before spikes.

Expected behavior:
- Small bursts should batch quickly with max_wait ~10-30ms and produce stable p99 < 500ms.

Relevant logs & metrics (excerpts):
- grafana: https://grafana.redwood/prod/lexidocs/d/perf/continuous-batching?from=now-2h&to=now
- Sample serving-runtime log lines:
  [2026-03-10T14:22:31Z] INFO batcher: created batch id=0x7f3c wait_ms=12 size=8
  [2026-03-10T14:23:14Z] WARN batcher: idle_threshold_adjusted from=15ms to=400ms reason=observed_low_rps
  [2026-03-10T14:23:14Z] WARN batcher: pending_batch_window=420ms size=2
  [2026-03-10T14:23:16Z] ERROR api-gateway: upstream read timeout after 1500ms route=/v1/generate

Temporary workaround applied:
- Increased request-level timeout at gateway from 1500ms -> 3500ms for lexidocs routes (mitigates 504s but increases client-visible waiting).
- Rolled back serving-runtime to 2026.2.28 on one pool for validation; observed improvement in p99 during rollback windows.

Notes:
- Behavior appears correlated with a heuristic that increases the continuous-batcher "idle_threshold" when observed RPS drops; in this workload the heuristic over-adjusts and leaves batcher waiting longer for additional requests.
- Rollback to prior serving-runtime improves tail but we need a targeted fix or config knob.
- Customer requests a timeline for a permanent fix and whether dedicated pools require manual config changes.

Initial hypothesis: a regression in the batcher idle-threshold heuristic introduced in 2026-03-03 rollout.
What we checked:
- Release notes: a change to adaptive batching heuristics (PR #2107) adjusted idle_threshold dynamic scaling.
- Metrics: increased idle_threshold coincides with low inter-burst RPS; pending_batch_window and idle_wait_ms spike preceding p99 events.
- Node-level: no obvious CPU/GPU saturation; autoscaler not thrashing during observed window.
- Clock skew: slight NTP drift found on one worker (-120ms) but not consistently correlated.

Current hypothesis: adaptive idle_threshold logic uses a moving-average window that underestimates inter-arrival variance for low-burst patterns, causing transient over-increase of idle wait and producing long tail waits and timeouts.
Next steps:
- Reproduce in staging with the exact dedicated pool config and RPS pattern (assigned to Liam).
- Instrument batcher with trace IDs to follow per-request wait lifecycle (temp PR to add debug counters).
- Prepare a config flag to cap idle_threshold at 120ms and test with canary traffic.
- If confirmed, prepare hotfix revert or config change to be rolled to lexidocs pool only and then broader rollout.

Issue summary: After an automated geo-failover triggered during a regional maintenance window, TellusSearch began receiving an elevated rate of 429 responses (soft throttles) from our multi-region Dedicated pool. Impact: ~10% of streaming sessions from TellusSearch were receiving intermittent 429s; customer reports degraded UX and elevated error rates in US-east users. Timeline: 2026-03-10 03:05 UTC - scheduled route drain in eu-west; 2026-03-10 03:12 UTC - automated failover completed; 2026-03-10 03:15 UTC - TellusSearch alerts and ticket opened. Expected behaviour: failover should preserve token-bucket state and not cause sustained soft throttles. Observed behaviour: sustained elevated 429 rate for ~90 minutes localized to requests routed from eu-west into us-east serving pool. This appears correlated to token-bucket counters and lease timestamps not reconciling post-failover.
1) Use a dedicated API key attached to a multi-region customer pool (TellusSearch setup). 2) Initiate geo-drain or failover on eu-west while active streaming clients remain connected. 3) Observe 429 spike within 5-10s and elevated soft-429 rate for subsequent 30-120 minutes as token-bucket balances do not re-sync between region proxies.
429 rate increased from baseline 0.2% to 6.4% for TellusSearch between 2026-03-10T03:12Z and 2026-03-10T04:45Z. Error signature: 'rate_limit_exceeded: token_bucket_drift' seen in api-gateway logs. Sample trace ids: trace-122334-03, trace-122334-11. Token-bucket counter snapshots: us-east proxy reported remaining_tokens=0 at 2026-03-10T03:13Z while eu-west proxy reported remaining_tokens=5200 and a last_reset_ts earlier than us-east, resulting in double-debit protection kicking in on requests routed to us-east. CPU/memory on serving nodes normal; scheduler logs show rapid host reassignments during the drain window.
Initial hypothesis: token-bucket lease timestamps are not synchronized across region-edge proxies during failover, which allows tokens to be counted separately and then reconciled causing negative balance on target proxy. Verified: edge-proxy metrics show mismatch in last_reset_ts across regions up to 120s. Checked NTP skew: host clocks within 50ms. Checked pubsub event reorder: observed out-of-order route update event processed by us-east proxy ~3s after eu-west, but reconciliation logic expects eventual consistency and has a race. Looked at scheduler: host reassignment triggered immediate re-route without waiting for token-bucket state delta propagation. Related PR modifying fast-route-rollout path merged 2026-03-08 (runtime PR #4521) may have reduced reconciliation window. Hypothesis: new fast-rollout path reduced token-bucket reconciliation window causing temporary negative effective tokens on the receiving proxy, leading to soft throttles instead of graceful fallback.
03/10 03:20 UTC - Sent initial acknowledgement and mitigation plan to TellusSearch (M. Alvarez). We explained we were investigating a failover-related throttle spike and provided guidance to temporarily stagger client reconnects. 03/10 05:10 UTC - Follow-up with ETA for mitigation (config rollback + hotfix) and recommended a safe retry/backoff pattern in their uploader. Customer requested postmortem and prevention plan.

Additional notes:
1) Apply hotfix to routing service to force immediate token-bucket reconciliation on cross-region route transfers (PR referenced). 2) Add integration test for geo-failover token-bucket handoff. 3) Backfill monitoring: create a dashboard alert for region-to-region token_reset_ts delta > 50s. 4) Share postmortem with TellusSearch and update runbook for scheduled maintenance to include safe reattach window. 5) Consider rate-limit behavior change to prefer graceful degraded throughput rather than immediate soft-429 during reconciliation.
In progress - temporary rollback applied for affected customer allocation and per-customer mitigation recommended. Hotfix development in progress; aiming for deployment 2026-03-13. Pending postmortem and runbook updates.
payload.summary: Geo failover caused token-bucket drift and sustained soft 429s for multi-region dedicated pool

Customer (NimbleDocs) observed that during a staged canary rollout of redwood/gptx-13b-v2 some requests from the same tenant returned responses from both the old and new variants. Issue appears correlated with a control-plane orchestrator leader rotation that happened mid-rollout. Symptoms include mixed quality outputs for a small percentage of sessions, elevated 500 responses from the edge for ~7 minutes, and a billing spike due to duplicate request replay.
Intermittent mixed-model responses for ~2% of requests for a subset of tenant sessions; increased 5xx errors for 7 minutes; customer-reported degraded user experience and unexpected usage billing spike. A single enterprise customer (dedicated) affected; potential risk to other rollouts if not fixed.
1) Start a staged rollout for model redwood/gptx-13b-v2 with 10% initial cohort.
2) Induce an orchestrator leader rotation by restarting the primary control-plane replica during the first 3 minutes of rollout.
3) Send a mixture of pinned and non-pinned requests for the same tenant session (streaming and non-streaming) and observe model variant in responses.
4) Observe routing snapshots and cohort assignments via /debug/route-snapshot for the tenant during rotation window.

2026-03-12T14:03:01Z orchestrator[leader->follower]: leader lost, new_leader_id=3, detected_epoch_skew: follower_epoch=1247 leader_epoch=1249
2026-03-12T14:03:05Z control-plane: reconcile retry: snapshot mismatch for tenant=nimbledocs-ten-42 expected_epoch=1248 found_epoch=1247

2026-03-12T14:03:08Z edge-proxy: route-resolve tenant=nimbledocs-ten-42 snapshot_version=2026-03-12T14:03:04Z -> variant=redwood/gptx-13b-v2-canary (new)
2026-03-12T14:09:20Z billing: duplicate-request-detection: 128 doubled requests from tenant nimbledocs-ten-42 during 14:03-14:10 window
Initial hypothesis: routing snapshot TTL and leader rotation created transient snapshot divergence across control-plane replicas leading to different route decisions at edge proxies.
Confirmed that two distinct route_snapshot versions (timestamps separated by ~52s) were concurrently considered authoritative by different edge nodes.
Observed orchestrator publish logic allows a new epoch to be published before all followers confirm last snapshot ack; followers that lagged kept serving older snapshot -> cohort split.
No evidence of KV-store corruption; manifests and snapshots present but epoch sequence gaps visible in orchestrator logs.
Customer traffic pattern (long-lived pinned sessions with streaming) amplified the symptom because session-affinity cached an edge-resolved variant for the duration of the stream.
Aisha Patel (Support) 2026-03-12: Customer reported mixed outputs and billing spike, provided sample request IDs and timestamps. Asked SRE to triage.
Marcus Chen (SRE) 2026-03-12: Confirmed epoch mismatch in orchestrator logs; reproducer created in staging to validate leader rotation behavior.
Lena Rodriguez (Control-plane Eng) 2026-03-13: Found that follower ack path has a race where leader increments epoch and publishes snapshot before follower acks; pushing a hotfix PR to gate publish on ack quorum.
Marcus Chen (SRE) 2026-03-14: Deployed emergency configuration to increase route_snapshot_ttl and forced snapshot resync across all edge nodes for affected region; monitoring shows routing stabilized.
Customer (NimbleDocs) 2026-03-14: Confirmed user-facing errors reduced and quality inconsistencies resolved.
1) Temporarily pinned NimbleDocs tenant to the legacy variant until stable snapshot resync completed.
2) Forced global snapshot resync command for us-east-1 edges and control-plane replicas at 2026-03-13T22:00Z.
3) Rolled back the canary for NimbleDocs and paused other staged rollouts until fix validated.
4) Merged hotfix (github.com/redwood/control-plane/pull/7890) that gates epoch publish on follower ack quorum; hotfix deployed to prod 2026-03-14.
5) Issued a billing credit estimate to NimbleDocs for duplicated requests; finance ticket created (linked INT-90421).
Control-plane orchestrator could publish a new route snapshot epoch before a quorum of follower replicas acknowledged the previous epoch, producing epoch skew across replicas and resulting in inconsistent route resolution at edge proxies during leader rotation.
1) Add end-to-end guardrails: control-plane should expose a snapshot-consistency check that edges can query before committing route decisions.
2) Add automated canary hold if any epoch_gap > 1 detected during staged rollouts.
3) Improve metrics/alerts: track epoch divergence count and set a PagerDuty escalation at >0 for enterprise rollouts.
4) Postmortem and runbook update: document leader-rotation mitigation and resync steps; publish to confluence (add to related_confluence_pages).
5) Follow up with NimbleDocs CS for formal credit and communicate permanent fixes and timeline.
payload.summary: Orchestrator epoch skew causes staged-rollout cohort divergence and mixed variant routing

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customers on a private VPC (Acme Financial) are observing intermittent 403 responses for API requests that re-use long-running browser sessions or background jobs (jobs that hold a session for >10 minutes). The failures began after a scheduled maintenance window where the customer's PKI and monitoring appliances were updated.

Impact:
- Several production workflows failed intermittently for ~20% of requests that rely on cached SAML assertions.
- Affects user-facing dashboards and automated batch jobs that maintain session cookies for extended periods.
- Customer reports the issue as blocking (financial reporting jobs).

Environment:
- Redwood Private deployment in customer VPC (prod:us-east-1).
- IdP: Customer-hosted SAML IdP (Shibboleth 4.2).
- Identity proxy: redwood-identity-proxy v1.9.3 (private package).
- Assertion cache TTL: 5 minutes (configured at proxy).

Steps to reproduce (observed pattern):
1) User logs in and obtains SAML assertion via browser SSO.
2) User triggers a background task that re-uses session cookie / assertion within 6-15 minutes.
3) Approximately 10-30% of attempts return 403 with authorization denied.
4) Re-authenticating via SSO immediately restores access.

Observed behavior vs expected:
- Expected: cached assertion remains valid for TTL (5m) and proxy should refresh or revalidate automatically without producing 403s.
- Observed: intermittent assertion validation failures and RBAC lookup returns no role bindings because assertion intake shows NotBefore/NotOnOrAfter outside expected window for ~1-3s on affected requests.

Relevant artifacts attached below (logs, counters, links).
2026-03-10 12:04 - Support (Aisha Khan): Acknowledged. Escalating to SRE and Eng. Opening incident channel #support-private-sso.
2026-03-10 12:30 - SRE (Miguel Santos): Confirmed spikes of 403s in customer logs. Sample auth-proxy trace: 'Assertion validation failed: Assertion conditions indicate NotOnOrAfter timestamp 2026-03-10T12:17:03Z < current time 2026-03-10T12:17:05Z'.
2026-03-10 14:02 - Customer (Jane O'Leary, Acme): Noted scheduled update of their NTP servers and PKI at 2026-03-10T11:55Z. They saw transient time adjustments. Provided IdP logs and node time drift report.
2026-03-11 09:18 - Eng (Priya Nambiar): Hypothesis: assertion cache TTL boundary combined with ~1-2s NTP drift causes assertion to be considered expired at the moment of proxy revalidation. Working on reproducer locally with clock skew injected.
2026-03-12 17:45 - SRE (Miguel Santos): Deployed temporary mitigation: increase assertion cache grace window to 5s and added a 2s jitter to revalidation timing. Monitoring for reduction in 403s.
2026-03-13 10:11 - Customer (Jane O'Leary): Reports that incidence dropped to ~1% after mitigation; still seeing occasional failures during heavy job schedules.
2026-03-13 13:02 - Eng (Priya Nambiar): Preparing PR to implement configurable clock-skew-tolerance and persistent assertion re-fetch fallback. See PR linked.
Timeline and findings:
- 12:00-13:00: initial spike observed in prod metrics (403 rate for Acme tenant from 0.5% to 22%).
- Correlated with customer maintenance window where their IDP NTP was stepped by ~1.5s due to NTP pool rotation; IdP logs show assertion timestamps shifted by +/-1-2s immediately after maintenance.
- Proxy assertion cache TTL boundary is 300s. When a request arrives near the TTL expiration, proxy attempts to validate assertion timestamps vs local clock. If the IdP-provided timestamps and the proxy clock differ by >1s, the assertion is intermittently treated as expired, which causes RBAC to skip role-binding lookup and return 403.
- Evidence: auth-proxy traces show 'condition check failed: notOnOrAfter < now' for requests that otherwise had valid signatures. The 'now' value in the trace was ahead by 1-2s compared to IdP timestamp.
- Reproducible in QA by artificially skewing IdP or proxy clock by 1-3s and hitting an assertion cache boundary.
- Related to assertion cache refresh behavior: proxy tries to refresh only when TTL expired, otherwise uses cached assertion; during refresh window the timing is brittle to small clock drift.
- No evidence of token signature or role mapping corruption. Not a RBAC policy bug, but validation timing edge-case combined with caching.
auth-proxy[pid=4211] WARN Assertion validation failed: NotOnOrAfter 2026-03-10T12:17:03Z < now 2026-03-10T12:17:05Z (drift detected)
idp-shib[2026-03-10T12:17:03Z] INFO Issued assertion for user: uid=oleary.j; NotBefore=2026-03-10T12:12:03Z; NotOnOrAfter=2026-03-10T12:17:03Z
proxy-clock-check: local_time=2026-03-10T12:17:05Z; ntp_offset=+1.8s
Combination of small NTP time-step on customer's IdP and assertion cache TTL boundary in identity proxy. The proxy's validation had a strict comparison without sufficient clock-skew tolerance for cached assertion refreshes, so 1-2s drift triggered NotOnOrAfter rejections and skipped RBAC role-binding lookup.
Rolled out two-step mitigation to Acme private deployment: 1) Increased assertion cache grace tolerance to accept up to 5s skew for cached assertions, and 2) Implemented an immediate re-fetch fallback when validation fails near TTL (proxy will attempt to re-request metadata/assertion once before rejecting). Deployed temporary config change at 2026-03-12 17:45Z. Created PR to make skew tolerance configurable and to add automated tests for clock drift scenarios (https://github.com/redwood-inference/auth-proxy/pull/982).
Advise customer to ensure NTP & time sync across their IdP nodes are stable during maintenance windows. Short-term: set IdP to step gradually (slew) rather than step time during scheduled updates, or schedule maintenance during low-traffic windows. We applied server-side grace window to reduce impact while a permanent fix is merged.
Merge PR for configurable clock-skew-tolerance and automated regression tests (owner: Priya Nambiar).
Backport fix to stable private branch and schedule controlled rollout to other customers with similar configuration.
Create monitoring alert to surface sudden changes in average auth-proxy NTP offset and to correlate with increased 403 rates (owner: SRE).
Add runbook section for 'time-sync induced assertion failures' to Confluence page and link it in incident response templates.
payload.summary: Intermittent 403s for long-running private sessions due to SAML assertion TTL + NTP drift and assertion cache expiry

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customer EchoCart reports recurrent 429 throttles during a nightly job that sends batched GraphQL requests to generate personalized product descriptions. The same job concurrently triggers webhook callbacks to a third-party image service which issues short-lived signed callbacks back to EchoCart, which in turn call our generation endpoint.

Impact:
- >50% of batch runs (approx 80k queries over 30 minutes) see mid-job 429s, causing retries and partial output.
- Client reports higher than expected token consumption for the window; customers see increased latency due to retries.

Environment:
- Dedicated tenant on prod in us-east-1; Dedicated pool id: ded-echo-07 (customer provided).
- Traffic pattern: orchestrated workers (8 parallel) submit GraphQL batch requests (size 64) while receiving webhook callbacks that immediately fire follow-up generation calls.

Steps to reproduce (customer-provided):
1) Start 8 parallel workers that submit GraphQL batched generate requests every 5s with batch_size=64.
2) Configure webhook endpoint that replies with a signed short-lived callback to the worker that triggers an immediate follow-up generate of up to 4 small prompts.
3) Observe throttling after ~6-8 minutes into the run and sustained 429s until token buckets refill.

Observed behavior:
- Server returns 429 with X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0.
- Rate-limit headers show a short refill window (30s) and a per-route concurrency window that appears to be shared across the route and the webhook callback path.

Expected behavior:
- Batch generation and webhook-driven follow-ups should be accounted under separate route isolation or under tenant burst windows without mutual exhaustion.

Customer-provided artefacts:
- Sample request IDs: req-echo-20260310-11, req-echo-20260310-47
- Timestamps: 2026-03-09T03:12:04Z to 2026-03-09T03:45:00Z
- Representative raw headers and X-RateLimit- headers attached in ticket (snippets pasted below).

Additional notes:
2026-03-11 - Customer (EchoCart support): Provided ded-echo-07, curl snippets, and sample worker orchestration script. Noted throttle starts after multiple webhook callbacks overlap with main batch window.
2026-03-13 - SRE (J. Morales): Added tracing hooks to ded-echo-07 to collect per-route accounting for the next customer run. Suggested workaround: configure callbacks to use a dedicated route or ephemeral key with isolated quota, or increase burst credits on tenant for nightly window.
Collected tenant accounting snapshots for ded-echo-07 during repro window; found two active route keys with identical route tags. Both keys counted against the same per-route concurrency window and shared burst credits.
Rate limiter config for the tenant uses a short refill window of 30s and a small burst bucket intended for interactive traffic; this pattern is incompatible with large concurrent batch windows plus many small follow-ups.
Observed that webhook callbacks come in with the same Authorization header (client reuses API key) and are therefore attributed to the same route ledger; this causes the batch request stream and callback micro-requests to compete for the same token bucket.
No evidence of proxy duplication or double-counting from our edge logs; counting appears correct but the allocation policy is suboptimal for this workload.
Relevant traces: tracing.redwood/trace/req-echo-20260310-11 and trace/req-echo-20260310-47.
Customer temporary mitigation: route webhook callbacks through a separate dedicated route key or use a secondary API key for callbacks so traffic is accounted separately. Alternative short-term fix: increase tenant burst credits for nightly window or increase refill window to 2m.
Recommend config change: create route-level isolation for webhook callback endpoint (route tag: echo-webhook-cb) and assign a separate quota/burst profile.
Product: evaluate default refill windows for dedicated tenants running mixed batch+realtime patterns; consider adaptive refill for bursty batch windows.
SRE: monitor ded-echo-07 in next scheduled run and collect per-route bucket histograms; correlate with latency and retry counts.
Follow-up: if customer prefers product-side change, open INT ticket to propose a new quota profile for mixed batch workloads.
Partial workaround applied by customer (separate route key for callbacks) and confirmed immediate improvement in subsequent short runs. Ownership: SRE to validate in scheduled nightly full run before closing. No code change required yet.
EchoCart reports that after applying the separate callback key the 429s dropped from ~60% of jobs to <5% during short tests; they will run full nightly cadence and report back.
Consider adding a docs note for dedicated customers describing common pitfall: shared API key across primary batch route and synchronous webhook callbacks can exhaust short-window burst quotas. Recommend adding an example config in the console templates for separating callback traffic.
payload.summary: Unexpected throttling during concurrent GraphQL batch requests and webhook callbacks

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customers report streaming completions abruptly terminate after roughly 60–70s when the client uploads the request body slowly (chunked). The connection shows ALB sending FIN and the upstream edge proxy returning 499/connection-reset symptoms. This started after the recent SSL reconfiguration that enabled session resumption and an internal change that surfaced more per-request tracing headers (baggage/traceparent rotation).

Impact:
- Multiple users of Papertrail Analytics' integration observed incomplete responses during longer-generation workflows (not every request; intermittent at ~2-5% of long streams).
- Visible customer-visible failures for live chat and transcript-generation features.

Environment:
- Redwood hosted API (api.redwood.ai) -> regional ALB -> edge-proxy cluster -> serving-runtime pool running redwood/gpt-large-v1 on dedicated capacity for the customer.
- Affected region: us-east-1.

Steps to reproduce (customer-provided):
1) Start a streaming completion using chunked upload with a large initial context (~120KB) and a periodic client heartbeat that appends small cookies/trace headers every 10–15s.
2) Observe TTFB is normal but after ~60–70s the stream terminates mid-completion with a connection reset.
3) Re-run with same payload but send body faster (single request) — stream completes normally.

Observed logs & signals:
- ALB connection logs show remote_close with FIN from ALB at ~65s.
- Edge-proxy metrics: per-conn send buffer high watermark triggered, proxy logged "write failed: connection reset by peer" around same time.
- Access logs carry growing Header-Length values between initial request and last chunk (from ~1.2KB up to 9.8KB).
- TLS session logs show a successful session-resumption path for affected clients.
- No direct application 5xx; serving-runtime reported no model OOM or CPU spike.

Initial hypothesis:
- Combination of slow client chunked uploads + incremental header/baggage rotation causes header size to grow mid-request, triggering proxy buffer growth and eventually exhausting the proxy send buffer or hitting ALB idle/send-timeout behavior. SSL session resumption path appears to change TCP/TLS timing such that proxy flush behavior is impacted, exacerbating the window where no bytes are sent to the ALB and triggering idle close.

Files and links shared by customer:
- pcap excerpt (sensitive) uploaded to secure case attachment.
- Example request id: req-20260301-7f2a4c.
- Slack thread: #support-papertrail (link provided).

Additional notes:
2026-03-02 09:30 Engineering (Priya Menon): We validated that enabling session resumption changes TLS record timing; combined with repeated Set-Cookie/trace header growth we observed HPACK-like expansion on our HTTP/1.1 proxy (we're terminating TLS at the edge). Drafting a short-term mitigation: cap header size per request and drop non-essential tracing headers mid-stream.
Edge proxy (nginx-flavor) configuration: proxy_buffer_size 8k; proxy_buffers 4 8k. Observed effective header bytes exceed configured buffer across some requests, triggering extra allocations and stalls.
ALB idle timeout: currently 60s for upstream idle-send; ALB will send FIN when no bytes flow for 60s despite client still uploading slowly (writes held by proxy buffer).
"Hypothesis validated in staging by synthetic client that streams body at 100B/s while rotating traceparent every 12s — reproduced identical FIN timing."
Collected metrics: proxy send buffer fill ratio, TLS record timings, header-length histogram per request.
Workaround applied (2026-03-02): added temporary proxy rule to drop/strip non-essential tracing baggage and set conservative header-size cap for streaming routes. ALB idle-timeout raised to 120s for affected dedicated customer pool as an intermediate mitigation. Customer reported immediate reduction in truncated streaming.
Long-term fix: engineering to ship proxy buffer reconfiguration (increase proxy_buffers and enable chunked passthrough without header reassembly) and evaluate moving header enforcement earlier in the stack. Also propose a runtime change to avoid reattaching large tracing headers mid-stream. Target rollout in next maintenance window (2026-03-09).
payload.summary: Intermittent streaming completions cut at ~65s — ALB FIN and proxy send buffer fill correlating with SSL resumption + header growth

comments: 2026-03-12T14:22:00Z Marcus Chen: Acknowledged. I see the customer's route table snapshot includes /32s learned by TGW. Asking NETOPS to validate whether traffic is being ECMP'd to wrong ENI.

2026-03-13T09:12:00Z Marcus Chen: Provided verification steps: 1) Confirm route withdrawal in TGW route table 2) Re-run artifact pulls 3) Check VPC flow logs for symmetric src/dst ENI mapping 4) Watch for repeated advertisements. Also opened INFRA-412 for console flagging.

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customer (FintechCo - private deployment) reports intermittent hangs when Redwood serving nodes attempt to download model artifacts using presigned S3 URLs. The control plane shows long-lived TCP sessions without TLS application progress (TLS '0-RTT' or zero-window events observed). Artifact fetches appear to succeed sometimes but intermittently hang in a half-open state for ~30-90s and then recover when connections are retried.

Impact:
- Artifact fetch failures during model start/scale cause model-pull timeouts and degraded request throughput for the customer's private cluster.
- Affected traces show long tail cold-start times and increased request latency.
- Customer-facing: some inference requests returned 502/504 during scale events.

Environment:
- Private deployment (customer-managed VPC peered to Redwood control plane via TGW/VPC peering).
- Region: us-west-2.
- Customer network: on-prem router advertises host-routes into their cloud VPC via BGP over Direct Connect.
- Serving nodes: g4dn-like instances in private subnet behind ENIs.

Steps to reproduce (observed pattern):
1) Trigger model scale-up (deploy new model version or restart serving process).
2) Serving node downloads artifact via presigned S3 URL from Redwood artifact storage (control plane presigned URL).
3) TCP connection established, TLS client hello observed from serving node.
4) Server responds; however, return packets for that TCP flow are routed to a different ENI (same AZ but different instance) and do not reach the original socket.
5) Original connection stalls (zero window / retransmits), artifact download times out after retries.
6) If customer BGP peer withdraws the leaked host-route or a quick route flap occurs, flow returns to expected ENI and downloads complete.

Observed behavior / logs / metrics:
- tcpdump from serving node: initial SYN, SYN-ACK, Client Hello, then ACKs continue but no TLS application data progress. Retransmits and duplicated ACKs observed.
- VPC flow logs: packets for response path show destination ENI different from source ENI for the flow hash.
- Control plane log: presigned URL access attempts show CONNECT events with long round-trip and then final timeout at ~45s.
- Customer's edge router BGP table snapshot attached via support upload: shows /32 host routes for specific on-prem IPs leaked into their VPC CIDR.
- Cloud route table snapshot: route priority shows host-routes learned via TGW which take precedence over instance primary subnet routes.

Initial investigation notes:
- Hypothesis A: On-prem BGP speaker is leaking /32 host routes that overlap the ephemeral source addresses used by serving nodes or the artifact endpoints. When those host routes are installed in the VPC/TGW route table, return traffic for specific flows is sent to the on-prem path (or to a different ENI implementing that route) instead of the originating ENI, causing asymmetric routing and TCP stalls.
- Hypothesis B: ECMP/hash interaction with TGW and host-routes causes inconsistent flow steering; the underlay forwards responses to a different instance which lacks the matching socket, leading to RST or retransmits.
- We reproduced asymmetric return path in lab by advertising a /32 host route from a BGP speaker and observing identical stalled TLS behavior.

What we've tried so far:
- Confirmed via tcpdump and VPC flow logs that responses were misrouted to a different ENI.
- Asked customer to temporarily withdraw the leaked host-route; artifact fetches resumed normally.
- Applied temporary iptables DNAT on serving instance to force return path through same ENI (workaround proof-of-concept) — mitigated the stall in short term but not a long-term solution.
- Requested edge team to show BGP config; discovered an automation script leaking host-specific routes for internal monitoring IPs.

Workaround / Mitigation provided to customer:
- Immediate: Withdraw the leaked /32 host route(s) on the on-prem BGP speaker (customer confirmed). Downloads and model pulls recovered within 2 minutes after withdrawal propagated.
- Short-term: Customer to add route-policy on border router to prevent advertising host-prefixed routes into the cloud VPC (explicit deny on /32 / host ranges).
- Temporary: If withdrawal is not possible, configure instance-level source/destination check adjustments plus a NAT gateway path for artifact fetches to ensure symmetric return via NAT. (Documented caveats: may increase cost and change source IP in presigned URL access checks).

Resolution plan / next steps:
- Customer action (required): Implement BGP export filters to block /32 host-route advertisement into their cloud VPC and test route stability for 24 hours.

Issue summary: Customer running large multi-region ingestion pipeline (split into short-lived worker sessions) started seeing persistent 429s for the /v1/embeddings endpoint after migrating parts of the workload to a Dedicated pool. Impact: Ingestion throughput dropped ~70%, backlog of files accumulated, downstream vector updates delayed. Environment: Dedicated pool -> dedicated-us-east-2, Hosted control plane, token-based auth, multiplexed short-lived API keys created by the customer's orchestration layer.

Observed behavior: Despite account quota appearing available in the Console and token-bucket metrics, the client receives high rate of 429 responses with Retry-After headers between 5-12s. Throttling persists even when total tenant token usage is below committed capacity. Customer suspects per-session accounting or a stale window aligning with their split-session worker pattern.

Expected behavior: Short-lived worker sessions that sequentially call the embeddings endpoint should be able to consume available tenant quota under standard burst smoothing settings without sustained 429s unless overall tenant capacity is exceeded.

Customer runs 200 parallel short-lived worker processes that each obtain an ephemeral API key from their orchestration service.
Each worker opens a connection and immediately POSTs a 128-item embeddings batch to /v1/embeddings and closes after completion.
Workers are sharded across two regions (us-east-2 and eu-west-1) that both route to the same Dedicated pool via smart-routing.
After ~3-5 minutes the clients start receiving 429s with Retry-After 5-12s despite per-tenant token counters showing available capacity.
Scaling down parallelism by 50% reduces 429 frequency, but not eliminating them entirely.
2026-03-10T15:12:03Z ERR throttle=tenant_quota_exceeded tenant_id=lyra-123 api_key=ephemeral-zz123 route=/v1/embeddings status=429 retry_after=8
x-rate-limit: 1000; window=60; remaining=180; tenant_remaining=2200
gateway-trace: route=dedupe->quota-checker->router host=dedicated-router-8
observed: spike pattern aligned to ephemeral key TTL refresh; health-check probes from pool surfaced in tenant accounting during the same window
Initial hypothesis: per-key token-bucket misattribution causing small ephemeral keys to hit low per-key windows while tenant window remains healthy.
Checked Console usage graphs: tenant-level tokens not exhausted; per-route metrics show high per-key rejection counts but no clear single noisy neighbor.
Correlation found between ephemeral key churn (high fanout of keys created and destroyed) and 429 onset. Suspect bucket reset/aggregation logic in edge proxies incorrectly mapping short-lived keys to the same internal bucket slice leading to hot-slot contention.
SRE ran replay of customer request pattern in staging with 300 short-lived keys; reproduced ~15% 429 rate with default burst windowing. When using long-lived key (single key), no 429s reproduced at same aggregate rate.
Added debug flags to quota-service to log internal bucket assignment for ephemeral keys; logs show multiple ephemeral keys being hashed to same shard during TTL boundary.
Related config: customer uses aggressive key TTL of 10s and orchestration spawns keys per worker start for easier isolation.

Additional notes:
2026-03-11 09:12 - LyraSearch (Customer): Our workers create keys with TTL=10s and spawn ~200 processes every minute. We did this to ensure per-file isolation and easier retry semantics. Can we change anything on our side while you investigate?
2026-03-11 15:45 - LyraSearch (Customer): Increased TTL to 5m in staging; large decrease in 429s observed during a 20-minute run. Preparing change for prod tomorrow morning.
Workaround applied by customer (increased ephemeral key TTL to 5m). Engineering tracking short-term fix INT-42088 and longer-term resilience improvement in quota-service to avoid shard-hotting for high-churn key patterns.
Customer saw immediate improvement in staging and applied TTL change in prod; throughput returned to expected levels with residual <2% 429s. Engineering to deploy fallback pooled-accounting behavior in next patch (refer to linked PR) and follow up with ETA. Postmortem scheduled after fix rollout.

Export must be delivered as an immutable Azure Blob (WORM) container with a manifest that includes SHA-256 checksums, per-file HMAC using a customer-provided KEK, and an RFC3161 timestamp token for the manifest. Customer also requires PII tokenization for specified fields (email, ssn, account_id) using our tenant-scoped reversible tokenization keys, plus a mapping schema CSV that aligns fields to their SIEM names. Impact: This is a legal compliance request with potential regulatory review; customer cannot proceed without notarized timestamp and integrity proofs. Timeline: requested delivery within 48 hours. Acceptance criteria: (1) Immutable Azure container URL + SAS read-only link and retention locked for 365 days; (2) Manifest.json with SHA256 checksums and base64-encoded RFC3161 timestamp token; (3) HMAC envelope proofs for each file using KEK id provided by customer; (4) Tokenization map CSV and sample verification script; (5) Audit trail of export operation including operator identity, runbook step IDs, and job duration.
Potential legal/regulatory exposure if notarized export not delivered. Customer's downstream auditors will block verification and escalate to legal. Blocking customer production processes that rely on archive confirmation.
1) Customer initiated legal-hold request via compliance portal and uploaded KEK id and PII field list. 2) Support attempted standard 'bulk-audit-export' job for tenant ql-trading. 3) Export job failed policy validation due to missing RFC3161 signing step in current export pipeline. 4) Manual attempt to produce artifacts created blobs but without WORM retention and without timestamp token.
Export job id: export-20241112-ql-78. Storage account: rw-audit-prod. Error captured: 'pipeline:timestamp-step: not implemented' at 2024-11-12T18:42:03Z. Blob creation events: PutBlob x 12. Refer to logging link: https://grafana.redwood.internal/d/exports/export-jobs?orgId=1&var-job=export-20241112-ql-78

Hypothesis 2: WORM retention requires storage account-level immutability policy — our automation path currently creates blobs but does not set immutability policies for tenant-scoped exports. Evidence: worker logs show 'timestamp_disabled=true' flag for tenant ql-trading. Partial workaround tested: post-process runner added RFC3161 token by calling TSA (openssh-rfc3161 proxy) and uploaded manifest; however this was manual and did not set retention lock. Next steps: (A) Implement export-runbook change to call external TSA service and embed the returned timestamp token in manifest. (B) Add storage account immutability step that sets a temporary legal-hold or immutability policy as allowed by customer's Azure subscription. (C) Validate HMAC generation against customer's KEK in HSM (we requested wrapped key artifact).
