Issue summary:
Customer QuantizeAI reports repeated short-duration collapses in sustained throughput on their Dedicated GPU pool in us-west. Over the last 36 hours they observed 3–8 minute drops where tail latency spikes and throughput falls to ~20% of provisioned capacity despite apparently healthy GPU memory and normal average utilization.

Impact:
- Customer report: production batch inference jobs degrade intermittently, affecting SLAs for their end users (timeouts and retries).
- Observable: request success rate drops, streaming connections get disconnected during drops, error rate (5xx) increases by ~4–6x during events.

Environment:
- Dedicated pool: d-pool-quantize-01 (reserved), region us-west, GPU type A100-80GB (mixed instance types), model pinned to gpt-large-v1.
- Autoscaler: adaptive mode with min_replicas=4, max_replicas=12, scale_window=30s initially.
- Routing: tenant routing with per-tenant queueing and fallback to compatible variants.

Steps to reproduce (customer-facing):
1) Run a steady stream of small requests (avg request size ~150 tokens) from multiple clients across tenants.
2) Add an intermittent burst generator that sends 400 short requests over 30s every 90s.
3) Observe throughput and tail latency in Grafana panels (Serving -> per-pool QPS/latency).

Logs / observations attached to ticket:
- Grafana snapshot: throughput_spike_and_drop_2026-03-09.png (linked in comments).
- Traces show long scheduling wait times in front of the runtime (scheduling.latency).
- Node metrics: GPU memory stable (~60–70%), gpu_utilization variable; host CPU load shows short spikes coincident with throughput drops.
- Autoscaler logs show frequent scale-down followed by scale-up cycles during events (allocation churn).

Initial hypothesis:
- Short, high-frequency bursts from one or more tenants cause rapid fluctuations in the scheduler's queue length metric. The autoscaler interprets this as sustained change, leading to micro-scale down/up decisions and allocation churn that temporarily starves steady traffic (microthrottling).
- Alternatively, a co-tenant workload is causing driver/kernel-level context thrash or short-lived device resets that are not surfaced as GPU OOMs but increase host-side latency.

Requested customer impact data:
- Time windows when customer saw impact (provided): 2026-03-08 22:12–22:20 UTC, 2026-03-09 03:41–03:48 UTC, 2026-03-09 12:17–12:24 UTC.

Next steps planned:
- SRE to reproduce in staging using a burst generator (assigned to Marco).
- Apply temporary mitigation in prod: increase autoscaler min_replicas to 6 and add a 90s debounce to scale-down to prevent immediate eviction on short spikes.
- Add tenant-level QoS cap to limit burst concurrency for tenants that exceed X rps for > Y seconds.
- Instrument more fine-grained scheduler metrics and add alert on allocation-churn > threshold.

Additional notes:
2026-03-10 QuantizeAI (support contact - Nina Cho): Provided additional logs and a recording of their load generator showing bursts at ~90s intervals. Confirmed model pinned to gpt-large-v1 and no recent config changes on their side.
Repro in staging: running two tenants (steady stream tenant + burst tenant) reproduced throughput collapse within 2 cycles. Profiling shows scheduler allocation requests spike then cancel frequently.
Autoscaler logs: recorded scale-down decisions occurring ~15s after a short quiet period, followed by immediate scale-up when burst resumes; scale_window=30s too aggressive for bursty workloads.
Scheduler traces: allocation-granularity set to per-pod with <1s reconciliation loop; leads to high API churn during burst patterns.
Node telemetry: no GPU ECC errors or memory OOMs; host CPU and kubelet metrics show short-lived CPU saturation on nodes hosting the burst tenant which increases container scheduling latency.
Affected workload pattern identified: small, high-frequency requests (150 tokens) in bursts of ~400 requests over 30s every ~90s from a single tenant. This pattern amplifies scheduler churn.
Temporary mitigation applied: min_replicas bump and scale-down debounce. Immediate effect: fewer oscillations, median throughput restored; some residual latency spikes remain during bursts.
Longer-term fixes proposed: 1) scheduler change to batch allocation decisions with 60–120s window for dedicated pools; 2) autoscaler algorithm change to weigh recent volatility and ignore transients <Xs; 3) tenant QoS enforcement feature (per-tenant concurrency caps) to prevent single tenant from causing pool-level churn.
Related PRs: serving-runtime fix to expose additional scheduling metrics (PR #812), scheduler debounce and reconcilation changes (PR #410).
Mitigation applied in prod 2026-03-13: increased autoscaler min_replicas to 6 and enabled a 90s scale-down debounce for the affected pool. Customer reports visible improvement; monitoring period set to 48h. Next actions: implement scheduler batching and autoscaler transient-guard patch (linked PRs), roll out tenant QoS cap as opt-in for dedicated pools, and schedule postmortem with QuantizeAI. Owner for permanent fixes: Marco Ruiz (scheduler) and Priya Desai (autoscaler).
Schedule postmortem with customer and internal teams (owner: Aisha Patel) - due 2026-03-20
Merge scheduler batching PR and roll out to canary - owner Marco Ruiz - target 2026-03-25
Autoscaler transient guard PR (weight volatility) - owner Priya Desai - target 2026-03-22
Add per-tenant QoS cap feature to product backlog and prioritize for dedicated customers - PM: Zoe Tan
payload.summary: Cross-tenant microthrottling causing intermittent throughput collapse in Dedicated pool (us-west)

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customer is following the Hosted API quickstart and consistently receives HTTP 401 with error "invalid_api_key". Root cause appears to be using the wrong API key value (copied from the wrong Console context) and/or setting an incorrect environment variable name, resulting in the SDK sending an empty/incorrect Authorization header.

Impact:
Blocks time-to-first-success (TTFS). Customer cannot complete the first request step and is at risk of churn.

Customer report (verbatim-ish):
"We’re using the Python quickstart, but every request returns 401 invalid_api_key. We copied the key from the console and set it as an env var. Not sure what we’re missing."

Environment:
- Hosted API (prod)
- Region: us-east
- Python SDK quickstart (customer did not specify exact version initially)
- Running locally (MacOS)

Steps to reproduce (from customer + internal repro):
1) Create API key in Console
2) Export env var
3) Run the Python quickstart snippet
4) Observe 401 invalid_api_key

Observed error:
- HTTP status: 401
- Body: {"error":{"type":"invalid_request_error","code":"invalid_api_key","message":"Invalid API key"}}

Initial hypotheses:
- Key copied included leading/trailing whitespace or line break
- Env var name mismatch (e.g., REDWOOD_APIKEY vs REDWOOD_API_KEY; OPENAI_API_KEY used by mistake)
- Shell export not applied to the process (e.g., running in IDE without env)
- Using an org/team-scoped key from a different workspace than the one selected in Console

Notes:
This matches a top onboarding failure pattern: wrong key / wrong env var / wrong header. Recommend guardrails in checklist + docs improvements:
- Checklist step: "Create an API key and set env vars" with a validation snippet and explicit header format
- Console: show a copy button that includes the exact export command per shell + key prefix hint
- SDK: when key is empty/missing, throw a local error before making network call (avoid opaque 401)

Support asks / desired outcome:
- Provide immediate troubleshooting steps to unblock customer
- Capture doc + product follow-ups for onboarding checklist guardrails

Additional notes:
1) The env var name you set (exact spelling/case)
2) Whether you’re using Redwood Python SDK directly or the OpenAI-compatible endpoint
3) The first 6 chars of the key prefix (do not paste the full key) and whether it’s from the same workspace you’re testing in the Console
Quick checks:
- Run `python -c "import os; print(bool(os.getenv('REDWOOD_API_KEY'))); print(os.getenv('REDWOOD_API_KEY','')[:6])"`
- Ensure no quotes/newlines in the key: `echo -n $REDWOOD_API_KEY | wc -c` (should be a stable length; avoid trailing newline)
- If using OpenAI-compat, confirm you set `OPENAI_API_KEY` to the Redwood key AND are targeting the Redwood base URL.
2025-03-07 10:02 PT — Customer (Bluepeak AI): We set `REDWOOD_APIKEY` (no underscore) in our shell profile and ran the snippet. We also tried setting `OPENAI_API_KEY` because the code looked similar to OpenAI examples. Key prefix starts with `rw_`.
Can you try:
1) `export REDWOOD_API_KEY="<your key>"`
2) New terminal session (or source your profile)
3) Re-run the snippet
If you prefer OpenAI-compat:
- Set `OPENAI_API_KEY` to the same Redwood key
- Set `base_url` / `OPENAI_BASE_URL` to the Redwood endpoint from our docs
Also double-check you copied the key from the correct workspace/project in the Console (top-left workspace switcher).
2025-03-07 10:44 PT — Customer (Bluepeak AI): Using `REDWOOD_API_KEY` fixed it. We also had the key copied with a trailing space in one attempt. Now getting 200s. Thanks.
- Add explicit note in quickstart: exact env var names per SDK + OpenAI-compat differences
- Add troubleshooting callout: "If you see 401 invalid_api_key, verify env var name and that your process sees it"
- Add copy-paste-safe export commands in Console (bash/zsh/fish/powershell)
Creating follow-up in onboarding checklist content: step should include a validation command + warning about whitespace and workspace mismatch.
- ENG-5831 (Docs + quickstart updates): add env var name table and 401 troubleshooting
- PM-742 (Guided onboarding checklist): include guardrail acceptance criteria for API key step
- INT-3307 (Support tools): ensure checklist state helps us quickly identify incomplete API key step once feature is live
Customer had set the wrong environment variable name (REDWOOD_APIKEY instead of REDWOOD_API_KEY) and one attempt included trailing whitespace in the key. After setting REDWOOD_API_KEY correctly in the active shell session, requests succeeded (HTTP 200). Follow-up actions captured for docs/checklist guardrails.
Root cause was the API key not being picked up by the SDK due to an env var name mismatch (and in one attempt, trailing whitespace in the copied key). Setting `REDWOOD_API_KEY` (with underscore) to the exact key value and rerunning the quickstart resolved the 401. If you use the OpenAI-compatible flow, ensure `OPENAI_API_KEY` is set to the Redwood key and the base URL points to Redwood.
Pattern matches Q1 onboarding analysis: 401/403 auth mistakes are top driver of early tickets. Add checklist step guardrail + SDK preflight (missing/empty key) if feasible. Also ensure gateway emits onboarding event for API key creation vs first 401 (for funnel attribution and support troubleshooting).
payload.summary: New user quickstart fails with 401 "invalid_api_key" (wrong API key or env var name)

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customer NoteWell reports that rerank results appear consistently suppressed (low similarity scores) and the rerank endpoint is exhibiting elevated tail latencies and occasional 503s for bulk batch requests. The customer is on a Dedicated cluster in us-east.

Impact:
- Production query throughput impacted for NoteWell search product (~5-10% traffic routed to Redwood rerank).
- p95 latency for rerank increased from ~120ms to ~2.3s for their bulk requests; p99 spikes to 6s on retries.
- Customers see degraded top-k recall and missing expected hits (low score mass).

Environment:
- Dedicated pool: d-prod-wn-12 (us-east)
- SDK: notewell-internal/0.8.1 (custom wrapper) sending precomputed embeddings
- Embedding model: text-embed-3-small (client-side encoder)
- Reranker service: rerank-v2 (running on GPU with CPU fallback under backpressure)
1) Use NoteWell's batching pipeline to send a batch of 512 precomputed 768-d float32 embeddings to /v1/rerank endpoint with Content-Type: application/json and no normalization header.
2) Observe rerank response scores are an order of magnitude lower than same queries generated server-side with Redwood SDK defaults.
3) Repeat with SDK v1.9.3 client-side l2-normalization enabled: scores align and tail latency returns to baseline.
4) Replay customer traffic in staging against dedicated shard simulator to reproduce queued CPU normalization fallback and 503s.
[2026-03-10T14:22:11Z] rerank-request id=af3b2e status=queued fallback=cpu-normalize queue_ms=1520 rt_ms=2350 -> 503
[2026-03-10T14:22:11Z] embed-ingest id=af3b2e sample_scale=1.0e+02 dtype=float32 header:x-embed-normalization=absent
[2026-03-10T14:22:12Z] rerank id=af3b2e scores=[0.001,0.002,0.0005,...] expected ~[0.72,0.68,0.64]
Initial hypothesis: mismatch in embedding normalization between NoteWell's client pipeline and Redwood rerank expectations. Customer-side embeddings were not L2-normalized and did not include the optional x-embed-normalization header.

What we observed:
- Reranker assumes unit-length embeddings by default; absence of header previously routed to a legacy CPU normalization path for backward compatibility.
- Under large batches (>=256), CPU normalization caused worker saturation and queued requests; when queue depth exceeded threshold, requests hit 503s or triggered GPU->CPU fallback leading to increased tail latency.
- Score distributions showed scale collapse (values near zero) when raw embeddings had larger magnitude; after client L2-normalization scores restored.

Telemetry and dashboards:
- Trace: #support channel thread: <https://slack.redwood/#support/C055N8X1> (see thread ts 16123344)
- Grafana: rerank-p95-prod (d-prod-wn-12) jump from 120ms -> 2.3s at 2026-03-10T14:20Z
- Correlated spike with NoteWell deploy of their embedding pipeline at 2026-03-10T14:18Z

Partial repro in staging using NoteWell payloads. Attached simulated workload and scripts saved to internal S3: s3://redwood-support/repro/SUP-864210/

Additional notes:
NoteWell SE (A. Chen): Provided batch payload and confirmed their encoder emits raw dense vectors without normalization. They were relying on server-side normalization historically. 2026-03-10
NoteWell SE: Confirmed: enabling SDK-side L2 normalization normalizes scores and brings p95 back to ~140ms. Still seeing occasional 503s for historical queued requests. 2026-03-12
Client embeddings were not L2-normalized and requests omitted the normalization header. Redwood's legacy server-side CPU normalization path becomes a bottleneck for large batches, causing GPU fallback/queueing and score scale mismatch when normalization is delayed or skipped.
Short-term workaround: Instructed NoteWell to upgrade to Redwood SDK v1.9.3 (or apply client-side L2 normalization) which sets x-embed-normalization=l2 and pre-normalizes embeddings; this restores score ranges and eliminates CPU normalization overhead.
Medium-term fix: Engineering to harden server-side validation and fast-path: 1) Add a lightweight input validation that rejects unnormalized embeddings with an explicit error when batch size >128 (PR 2784). 2) Implement parallelized CPU normalization fallback and telemetry to avoid single-thread saturation (INT-4021). 3) Add a deprecation notice for relying on implicit server-side normalization and update docs/runbook.
Rollout plan: PRs merged to canary 2026-03-14, staged to dedicated clusters 2026-03-16, full prod rollout 2026-03-18 after performance verification.
payload.summary: Client-sent non-normalized embeddings causing suppressed rerank scores and elevated tail latency

Issue summary:
BrightLens contacted Support reporting that their March 1-7 provisional invoice shows no hourly buffer credit for two windows where their Dedicated pool saturated and requests fell back to hosted. Impact:
- Missing hourly buffer credit on provisional invoice causing apparent overage for customer
- Customer concerned invoice will finalize without expected credit applied
Environment:
- Dedicated pool org-id: org-brightlens-01 (dedicated)
- Region: us-east-1
- Timeframe: 2026-03-02 01:40 - 2026-03-02 02:15 UTC and 2026-03-05 22:05 - 2026-03-05 22:55 UTC
Steps to reproduce / Observed behavior:
1) Dedicated pool saturated -> smart routing sent traffic to hosted fallback variant
2) Serving runtime returned hosted responses; postbacks were emitted with fallback_tag:hosted and original_queue:dedicated
3) Billing postback reconciler processed hosted usage but did not apply the org-level hourly buffer credit for those fallback intervals
Expected behavior:
- When dedicated traffic falls back to hosted, hourly buffer credits tied to the consumer org should still be consumed/applied for the fallback usage (per pricing policy)
Actual behaviour:
- Hosted usage lines present, but hourly buffer credit lines missing for those intervals. Finance shows a provisional overage for BrightLens.
Attached logs and artifacts:
- sample postback JSONs (postbacks_redacted_20260302.ndjson)
2026-03-10 10:12 - Support (Priya): Customer reports missing hourly buffer credits after fallback. Attached provisional invoice and sample postbacks. Requested urgent investigation and provisional credit hold.

Additional notes:
2026-03-10 14:22 - SRE (Ethan): Found postback entries with fallback_tag=hosted and original_queue=dedicated. Reconciler filters hourly_buffer eligibility by queue tag; looks like filter excludes fallback records. Hypothesis: filter uses queue==dedicated strictly instead of original_queue field.
2026-03-11 09:30 - Support (Priya): Customer acknowledged and asked whether a provisional waiver can be issued while we fix the reconciler. Also asked for a short-term manual adjustment timeline.
2026-03-12 17:30 - SRE (Ethan): Provided CSV of 1,124 affected postback ids and estimated buffer credit = $1,872. Next step: deploy reconciler patch to include original_queue and rerun postback ingestion for affected window.
Initial triage: confirmed hosted usage lines present in provisional invoice; no matching buffer credit entries for the two outage windows.
Hypothesis: billing reconciler eligibility check uses queued_queue attribute, not original_queue, therefore fallback events tagged as hosted lost the dedicated-buffer attribution.
Ran local reconcile replay on a snapshot: when feeding postbacks with original_queue=dedicated the buffer credit algorithm emitted expected credit line. When original_queue absent or ignored, no credit was emitted.
Found code path in invoice-reconciler where fallback_tag logic not populating billing_queue in normalized record. Edge-case when request routed by Smart Router -> hosted variant done at gateway layer and gateway prepends fallback_tag but does not set billing_queue field.
Root cause: mismatch between Smart Router fallback metadata and reconciler normalization contract. Reconciler expects billing_queue field; gateway sets original_queue but an earlier normalization step dropped it for hosted postbacks.
Risk assessment: low risk to runtime; only affects postback processing path. Fix impacts reconciler ingestion and replay pipeline.
Workaround and fix plan:
1) Short-term: Billing will apply provisional manual credit of $1,872 to BrightLens while fix is deployed (Finance note FIN-2026-03-BL-01).
2) Fix: deploy reconciler patch to propagate original_queue into normalized billing_queue for fallback-tagged postbacks. PR #873 created and reviewed.
3) Re-run ingestion for affected windows and regenerate provisional invoice lines; postback replay job scheduled for 2026-03-13 02:00 UTC.
4) Post-deploy validation run against sample postbacks and customer confirmation.
Follow-ups:
- Add unit tests covering fallback metadata paths.
- Update Smart Router -> Reconciler contract doc in Confluence.
- Monitor next billing run for similar anomalies and create alert on mismatch between fallback_tag counts and buffer credit lines.

payload.description:
Issue summary:
BrightLexa reports recurring incomplete final events and short resume gaps when their clients rapidly rotate websocket/SSE client IDs during heavy fan-out. Impact: users observe missing closing choice/token and occasionally two partial final fragments (one live, one after resume) which cannot be stitched. This breaks downstream transcript consumers and causes duplicate billing events.

Impact:
- ~20% of large streaming responses for this customer have a missing terminal choice or produce an orphaned trailing fragment after resume.
- Affects production us-east serving for dedicated cluster.
- Customer workflows that rely on exactly-one final event fail validation.

Environment:
- Dedicated capacity cluster: redwood-dedicated-us-east-1
- API: streaming SSE + websocket fallbacks for clients behind CDNs
- Client behavior: aggressive client-id rotation on reconnect (30–90s TTL), many short-lived connections in <1s bursts from edge fleet behind a custom proxy.

Steps to reproduce (customer-provided):
1. Create a streaming chat request pinned to gpt-redwood-3b on dedicated region us-east.
2. Simulate 150 concurrent clients that each open a stream for 45–120s and then rotate client-id and reconnect immediately (bursty rollover).
3. Introduce a proxy-level short TCP FIN/RESET during one reconnect window (can be reproduced using a flaky proxy).
4. Observe some sessions where the client receives a final token chunk but the server later emits a resume fragment that contains overlapping/truncated metadata and no explicit end-event.

Observed behavior:
- Client receives an apparently-complete final fragment (content tokens + metadata end flag) then on reconnect receives another fragment containing the last 20–50 tokens (partial overlap) without end-event.
- In some traces, the original final-event is accepted by API gateway but connection tombstone is not removed promptly; subsequent route to a different serving node replays cached tail fragment.
- Logs show HTTP/2 RST_STREAM or short-lived h2 stream resets correlated with these customer reconnect bursts.

Expected behavior:
- When a client reconnects and resumes, the system should either deliver a single canonical terminal fragment or clearly emit a resume boundary and the end-event exactly once. No duplicate or orphaned final fragments.

Logs / snippets (redacted):
[proxy] 2026-03-14T15:02:12Z client-id=cli-42 FIN recv; upstream h2 RST 0x1c
[api-gateway] 2026-03-14T15:02:12Z session=ses-8ac accept final-choice seq=184 end=true
[serving-runtime] 2026-03-14T15:02:13Z session=ses-8ac tombstone=true node=node-7 cached-tail-seq=184
[router] 2026-03-14T15:02:13Z session=ses-8ac route->node-3 resume request id=res-1
[serving-runtime] 2026-03-14T15:02:13Z session=ses-8ac emit tail seq=168 partial=true end=false

Temporary workaround provided to customer:
- Increase client-id TTL so reconnects are less bursty (client-side change).
- Enable shorter cache eviction on dedicated cluster nodes (ops knob) to avoid stale tombstones while we investigate.

Additional notes: customer provided packet captures and proxy logs; we have permission to reproduce on a staging clone of their traffic pattern.
Simulate 150 concurrent streaming clients with client-id rotation TTL 30-90s behind a proxy that injects short TCP resets
Pin requests to gpt-redwood-3b on dedicated us-east cluster
Introduce a short h2 RST during reconnect window and observe duplicate/orphaned final fragments

Additional notes:
2026-03-14 17:05 UTC - Eng (runtime): Reproduced on a dedicated staging cluster with a proxy fault injector. Observed cached-tail emission from node if tombstone removal delayed >300ms. Created instrumented trace PR to add tombstone TTL metrics: github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/8842.
2026-03-14 18:22 UTC - Support (Aisha): Shared temporary workaround with customer; they validated that increasing client-id TTL reduced incidence from ~20% to ~2%.
2026-03-14 20:12 UTC - Eng: Deployed tracing patch to staging; captured a deterministic replay showing race between gateway ACK and tombstone GC causing a second fragment emission when route changed nodes.
Hypothesis 1: Tombstone GC window too long allowing router to consider session active on another node and re-send cached tail when a new handshake arrives
Hypothesis 2: HTTP/2 RST on the upstream path sometimes leaves gateway in 'accepted final' state while runtime still has cached partial result; resume flow lacks strong idempotency checks for terminal fragments
Found: tombstone removal currently runs on a soft timer (500ms) and is not immediately observable by router; router relies on session metadata staleness check that uses last-seen timestamp only
Found: some proxies in customer path inject FIN before ACK which generates a short race and h2 RST observable in logs
Work in progress. Immediate mitigation: customer-side TTL increase and ops knob to lower tombstone TTL rolled to experiment. Engineering changes planned: (1) add explicit terminal-fragment idempotency token and server-side dedupe on resume flow, (2) instrument tombstone lifecycle with high-cardinality traces and metrics, (3) add fast-path tombstone invalidation on gateway when it sees an accepted final event. payload.description:
Issue summary: DataScout reports sudden waves of 429 responses from Redwood's hosted API affecting mobile users performing network handoffs (cell->wifi and wifi->cell). Impact: ~8% of realtime chat requests from mobile clients are rejected with 429 during short windows after a connection migration; user-facing symptoms include failed messages and client-side exponential backoff loops. Environment: Dedicated tenant on prod/us-west, traffic class prioritized for realtime low-latency streams.

Observed behavior: when mobile clients reconnect using HTTP/3 (QUIC) after NAT or path change, we see duplicate accounting against the tenant token bucket and an elevated rejection rate localized to recently migrated connections. Expected behavior: connection migration should not cause double-counting or immediate quota exhaustion for short-lived reconnections; requests should be debited only once per logical session.

Customer urgency: P1 because this impacts DataScout's mobile product stability for paying customers on Dedicated. They requested temporary mitigation and root cause analysis and asked for recommendations for client configuration and dedicated-pool tuning.
1) Provision a dedicated tenant with a priority 'realtime' route and small burst pool (DataScout config).
2) Start ~150 mobile clients established on HTTP/3 to the same API route; maintain low per-client request rate (interactive chat).
3) Simulate network handoffs for a subset of clients (NAT rebinding / switch network) causing QUIC connection migration and immediate reconnects.
4) Observe responses and rate-limit headers from the API; monitor token_bucket metrics on dedicated-pool dashboards.
Excerpt from edge-proxy access logs (prod/us-west):
2026-03-08T09:12:23Z client=10.4.12.9 conn_id=qc_7f3a path=/v1/chat model=rwdxl-v1-large status=200 tokens=34 tenant_id=ds-011
2026-03-08T09:12:27Z client=10.4.99.24 conn_id=qc_9b2d path=/v1/chat model=rwdxl-v1-large status=429 tokens=0 tenant_id=ds-011 reason=quota_exhausted
2026-03-08T09:12:27Z token_window_refill=0.0 tenant_tokens=3 tenant_bucket_capacity=50
2026-03-08T09:12:27Z note=conn_migration_detected old_conn=qc_7f3a new_conn=qc_9b2d ttl_ms=420
Relevant rate-limiter trace: rate_limiter.request_id=rl-3345 decision=reject reason=window_exceeded counted_against=tenant ds-011 related_conn_ids=[qc_7f3a,qc_9b2d]

Initial hypothesis: QUIC connection migration triggers a new logical connection id at the edge which is being treated as a distinct active session for token accounting; a mismatch in the 'coalesce by session' key caused the rate-limiter to count both old and new requests within the same short refill window.

What we checked:
- Reviewed edge-proxy connection lifecycle code path for HTTP/3 handoffs and the mapping to token bucket keys.
- Correlated tenant token_bucket metrics on dedicated-pool (dashboards: /dashboards/tenant/ds-011/token-usage).
- Replayed customer traffic in staging with simulated NAT rebinding; reproduced the early 429s when connection migration frequency > 1/min.

Findings:
- Edge assigns per-connection IDs for QUIC; rate-limiter uses connection_id + tenant_id to key temporary per-connection accounting for short-lived windows. On migration we saw both old and new connection IDs counted within the same refill window.
- The intended behavior (coalesce on stable client fingerprint when available) is not executed for certain mobile IP-change patterns because a fallback client fingerprint was empty (client didn't send alt-svc/connection hints).
- Token refill timing and burst allocation in Dedicated small burst pools exacerbates impact: low bucket capacity means double-counting results in immediate rejection.

Next steps planned:
- Engineering will implement guard to deduplicate immediate migration events by consulting recent-connection map for the same client-fingerprint and defer double-counting for a short grace interval.
- Provide temporary mitigation guidance to DataScout (client-side and config changes) while fix is rolled out.

Support (Aisha): Customer observed ~8% of mobile chat messages failing with 429 after switching networks. Attached customer traces and access-log snippets. Asked for priority triage and suggested temporary workarounds.
SRE (Diego): Reproduced locally in staging with QUIC migration simulation. Confirmed double-counting of migrated connections in rate-limiter trace. Raising to Eng for fix. Filed INT-80512 for implementation planning and linking runbook.
Customer (DataScout, Ops - Maya Chen): Thanks for the quick triage. We can roll a client update if that helps; prefer an edge-side fix but want a short-term config we can toggle. Please advise on safe settings for dedicated pool to avoid impacting latency.
Support (Aisha): Suggested temporary options: 1) widen dedicated pool burst capacity (increase tenant_bucket_capacity) during mobile migration windows, 2) configure client to prefer connection reuse and add small randomized jitter on reconnects, 3) fallback to HTTP/2 for mobile clients as a stopgap. Customer asked for specific commands for console.
Temporary mitigations recommended to DataScout: increased dedicated tenant burst capacity by +30% for a 24h window (provisioned 2026-03-09), instruct mobile client to add 250-750ms jitter to reconnect attempts and enable HTTP/2 fallback in their SDK (customer committed to patch release 2026-03-11).

Engineering fix: small dedupe guard merged to edge-proxy (PR #1289) to suppress duplicate accounting on immediate QUIC connection migrations. Change scheduled for canary deploy 2026-03-13 to prod/us-west; monitoring dashboard created and linked.

Follow-ups:
- Post-deploy: monitor tenant ds-011 token rejection rate for 72 hours.
- Add unit test for migration dedupe and a conformance test for clients that do not provide fingerprint hints.
- Customer success to verify mobile client patch rollout and report remaining 429 rate by 2026-03-16.
payload.summary: Early 429s observed for mobile HTTP/3 (QUIC) connection migrations during client network handoff

Issue summary: Customer reports intermittent p99 request timeouts (504/timeout) on hosted inference endpoints. Pattern appears during sustained, but uneven traffic from multiple tenants on a single dedicated shard. Impact: Several production API calls for NarrativeAI returned timeouts over a 3-hour window, resulting in visible errors to end users and an SLA incident. Environment: prod, dedicated shard srv-ded-11, us-east-1, serving-runtime v2.8.3, continuous-batcher enabled with default tenant weights. Observed behavior: p95 stable, p99 spikes and occasional stream disconnects correlate with periodic bursts of small requests from one high-frequency tenant followed by quiet periods from others. Hypothesis: Continuous batcher is becoming "entrained" (synchronized) to tenant burst cycles when tenant-level burst controls and KV-cache miss sequences align, causing batch windows to flush simultaneously and produce tail latency spikes. This is exacerbated when tenant burst smoothing is disabled and when KV-cache misses force model cache warms within the batch flush window. No evidence of GPU OOMs or scheduler backpressure in the observed period.
1) Provision a dedicated shard with continuous-batcher enabled and default tenant weights.
2) Generate sustained uneven traffic: Tenant A emits many short requests (avg 20 tokens) in tight bursts for 30s on/off cycles; Tenant B/C emit sparse long requests.
3) Observe per-tenant p99 latency on inference routes for 15-60 minutes using the Console traces and request logs.
4) Toggle tenant burst smoothing to ON and re-run to compare tails.
2026-03-09T09:12:11Z srv-ded-11 router: trace_id=... p99_latency=1.42s status=504 tenant=NarrativeA
2026-03-09T09:12:15Z serving-runtime: batcher: flush_window=12ms batch_size=32 tenant_mix=[A:22,B:6,C:4] kv_cache_miss_rate=0.42
2026-03-09T09:12:16Z model-server: warmup=0.003s token_throughput_ok
2026-03-09T10:45:02Z router: rate_limit=ok queue_depth=73 stream_disconnects=3
Support (Maya Chen) 2026-03-09: Opened with customer-provided traces and Console links. Customer reports ~3% error rate during 09:00-12:00 window. Asked for sampling config and recent config changes.
SRE (Liam O'Connor) 2026-03-10: Initial triage shows batcher flushes clustering at ~12ms windows with high batch sizes during tenant A bursts. No scheduler level throttles. Hypothesis: temporal alignment between tenant A bursts and batcher linger causes large microbatches and KV cache miss amplification. Requesting reproducer workload from customer and enabling debug traces on shard.
Engineering (Priya Reddy) 2026-03-11: Added instrumentation to measure per-tenant arrival phase and batch flush timestamp jitter. Observed >85% of p99 spikes occur when two conditions met: (1) tenant burst on ramped in <200ms and (2) per-tenant KV cache miss rate >30% in same window.
Support (Maya Chen) 2026-03-12: Applied temporary workaround: enabled tenant burst smoothing on NarrativeAI dedicated shard and lowered per-tenant max_burst_tokens from 10k -> 4k. Customer reports reduction in observed errors during monitoring period.
Customer (NarrativeAI Ops) 2026-03-12: Confirmed decreased end-user errors after smoothing and lower burst limit. Asked for permanent mitigation plan.
SRE (Liam O'Connor) 2026-03-12: Scheduling a controlled A/B rollout of two mitigations: 1) tenant-burst smoothing by default and 2) prewarming KV-cache for tenants exhibiting >20% miss rate during bursts. Target: next maintenance window 2026-03-18.
- Batcher trace histograms show multimodal flush intervals aligning with tenant burst cadence.
- KV-cache miss amplification: many small requests force model path cold-starts inside same microbatch leading to slightly longer per-token times that add up at p99.
- No indication of hardware contention (GPU metrics normal), suggests scheduling/queueing dynamics are root cause.
- Similar pattern reported in SUP-27654 but that focused on cross-tenant batch merging; here root cause is entrainment to a single tenant's burst pattern on a dedicated shard.
- Reproducer created using wrk-style driver that simulates on/off 30s bursts with 20-token short requests shows p99 >1s when smoothing disabled and KV miss rate high.
Temporary: enabled tenant burst smoothing and reduced per-tenant max_burst_tokens on affected shard (applied 2026-03-12). Customer observed immediate reduction in errors. Planned permanent fix: engineering to implement two changes: (1) adaptive batcher jitter to de-synchronize flush windows across tenant arrival phases, and (2) proactive KV-cache prefetch for tenants that exhibit bursty small-request patterns. A/B rollout scheduled for 2026-03-18 with monitoring dashboards and alert thresholds. Follow-up: update continuous-batcher runbook and add a checklist for dedicated shard placement of high-burst tenants.
payload.summary: Intermittent p99 timeouts correlated with continuous-batcher entrainment under skewed tenant arrival patterns

Issue summary: Over the evening window we observed a sustained elevation in 5xx responses from the hosted API for a single dedicated-tenant (CodaHealth) which correlates with heavy prefetch/concurrent-stream traffic. Impact: ~6-9% of requests return 502/503/504 during the 18:30-21:00 UTC window; multiple live streaming sessions report abrupt disconnects and retries. Expected behavior: error rate should be <0.5% and p99 latency under SLOs. Environment: production US-East cluster serving dedicated pools for CodaHealth. Customer notes that traffic pattern changed to more aggressive prefetch and long-context prompts around the same time.
1) Tenant pins rw-13b-instruct-v2 and enables aggressive prefetch (concurrency=12) with long prompts (avg 2k tokens)
2) Drive sustained request rate ~150 req/s for 20+ minutes simulating customer workload
3) Observe API gateway 5xx rate, runtime logs for OOMs or eviction churn, and autoscaler activity
Error-rate: baseline ~0.4% -> spike to 6.8% between 18:35-19:40 UTC. p50 latency 210ms -> 430ms; p99 latency 2.4s -> 7.1s. Serving-runtime observed KV-cache eviction rate increase x18 and frequent prefix cache misses. GPU utilization steady ~92% but host NVMe iowait rose to 45% on affected nodes. API gateway queue depth increased by ~3x and connection resets correlated with worker restarts. Dashboards: https://grafana.redwood/prod/d/tenants/codahealth-prefetch and logs: https://logs.redwood/prod?query=SUP-830555
Initial hypothesis: prefetch concurrency + long contexts saturating KV cache and causing runtime thrash leading to retries and upstream 5xx
Checked runtime logs: several ephemeral worker processes restarted due to watchdog timeout after repeated prefix load stalls (watchdog traces attached)
Autoscaler behavior: warmup lag observed — new nodes provisioned but joined after 60-90s, creating a period of insufficient serving capacity
Network: no VPC-level packet loss or TLS errors recorded; API gateway shows accept-queue growth and backpressure metrics rising
Reproduced a smaller-scale load on staging with same model and prefetch settings; observed similar elevated eviction churn but fewer 5xx due to larger staging cache capacity

Customer reduced prefetch concurrency from 12 to 4 and limited concurrent streaming sessions. Support enabled fallback routing to spare capacity pool for the tenant during warmup periods.
Mitigation confirmed: reducing aggressive prefetch reduced eviction churn and 5xx rate. Engineering to deploy autoscaler warmup improvements and a prefetch backpressure mechanism; follow-up rollout scheduled. Ticket remains In Progress until permanent changes are deployed and validated.

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customer (NimbusApps, dedicated) reports significantly longer wait for the first token on chat completions and occasional streaming disconnects following the coordinated model ABI and serving runtime migration on 2026-03-09. Impact is customer-facing: chat flows stall for 2–6 seconds before the first token, and ~1% of sessions see an immediate stream termination (504/502) within first 5s.

Impact:
- Increased TTFB (first-token latency) observed across small and medium prompts; baseline ~80–120ms → observed 2,000–6,000ms.
- Intermittent streaming cutouts resulting in 5xxs for a small subset of sessions.
- Affects conversational UX: typing indicator freezes, client-side timeouts.

Environment:
- Dedicated cluster in us-east-1 assigned to NimbusApps.
- Serving runtime v2.7.0 deployed 2026-03-09 03:10 UTC alongside model pin to redwood/gptx-7b-v2-q4_0 (ABI change applied).
- Router version 1.14.2 with affinity routing and prefetch enabled.

Steps to reproduce (customer):
1. Start a new chat session via /v1/chat/completions using model redwood/gptx-7b-v2-q4_0 with streaming=true and small prompt (~20 tokens).
2. Observe client-side wait until first onDelta event or first token chunk appears.
3. Some sessions return 504/502 within first 5s.

Expected behavior:
- First token emitted within ~100–200ms for small prompts; stable streaming connection for entire session.

Observed behavior:
- First token latency spikes to 2–6s for 70–80% of requests during peak; median increased from 120ms to ~2.3s.
- ~0.8–1.2% sessions abort with 5xx within first 5s.

Recent changes (relevant):
- 2026-03-09 03:10 UTC: Serving runtime v2.7.0 rolled to dedicated cluster; included ABI change to KV cache layout and a kernel selection tweak for Q4 quantized models.
- 2026-03-09 03:15 UTC: Router prefetch policy enabled for low-latency customers; affinity rebalancing applied.

Logs / metrics snippets (support capture):
- Customer-reported session IDs: nimbus-req-5a7c3, nimbus-req-5a7c7, nimbus-req-5a7d1.
- Metrics (cluster: nimbus-dedicated-01, window 03:00–06:00 UTC): first_token_latency p50 120ms -> 2.3s, p95 350ms -> 4.8s.
- Serving logs show transient "cache miss, rehydrate kv" events aligned with slow requests.
- Router logs show occasional 504 routed back from streaming-proxy for connections aged <5s.

Initial triage / investigation notes:
- Verified customer is pinned to Q4 variant and cluster received the v2.7.0 runtime; reproducer built against the same config shows similar elevation in first-token latency.
- Heap and GPU utilization within normal range; no evident OOM.
- Observed increased frequency of cold-KV rehydrates on ABI-swapped models: new ABI requires migration of prefix/KV layout causing synchronous rehydrate path on first request post-upgrade.
- Router prefetch appears to sometimes emit an additional warmup RPC to a fallback path, delaying main request by ~1.2s in some traces.

Hypotheses:
1) ABI change introduced a synchronous migration step on first model invocation which blocks token emission until KV rehydrate completes.
2) Router prefetch/warmup sequence adds a serialized handshake before the primary request reaches serving runtime for pinned customers due to affinity rules.
3) In rare cases a misconfigured health-probe in streaming-proxy returns early 502/504 when the handshake overlaps with the KV migration window.

Priority and impact rationale:
- P1 / Sev1: Dedicated customer-facing regression impacting user experience and risking churn if not mitigated.

Immediate mitigation steps performed:
- Rolled back router prefetch toggle for NimbusApps to false at 2026-03-10 04:30 UTC (confirmed by router logs).
- Deployed a patch to serving runtime to avoid synchronous KV rehydrate on the critical token-emission path as an opt-in flag for affected clusters (canary) at 2026-03-11 01:10 UTC.
- Applied temporary client-side guidance to increase streaming handshake timeout to 10s.

Customer-visible workaround:
- Advised customer to pin to q4 fallback model variant redwood/gptx-7b-v2-int8-fallback (no ABI migration) or keep pre-upgrade runtime (if feasible) until fix is verified.

Next steps / action items:
- Eng (runtime): confirm whether KV migration can be made async or parallel to token emission; PR #582 is the current branch. (Owner: Rafael Costa).
- Eng (router): audit prefetch/warmup path for serialized RPCs; consider making warmup parallel or no-op for pinned customers. (Owner: Priya Shah).
- SRE: run extended canary for patched runtime across 48h on one dedicated cluster and monitor first_token_latency and 5xx rate. (Owner: Marcus Nguyen).
- CS: follow up with NimbusApps with ETA and temporary credit offer; collect additional logs if any more 5xx occur. (Owner: Aisha Patel).

Resolution notes (ongoing):
- 2026-03-11 01:10 UTC: Opt-in async-kv flag deployed to nimbus-dedicated-01; immediate median first_token latency improved to ~220ms in canary traffic.
- 2026-03-11 04:00 UTC: Router prefetch rollback confirmed; some additional improvement in p95 observed.
- Monitoring: canary shows p50 ~240ms, p95 ~380ms, 5xx rate back to baseline for canary flows.
- Full cluster rollout pending completion of integration tests for async-KV path and router warmup changes.

Follow-up / retrospective items:
- Add automated test for ABI migrations that simulates KV rehydrate and asserts token emission is not blocked.
- Update runtime upgrade runbook to include a staged ABI migration and telemetry to flag synchronous rehydrates.
- Improve observability: add a span/tag for 'kv_rehydrate_sync' to quickly correlate with TTFB spikes.

Issue summary:
When viewing a dashboard with a high-cardinality 'series' facet, users report that the ordering of the series list becomes effectively randomized each time the live panel refreshes. This causes the drilldown links for popular series to change position and, in some cases, the exported drilldown link points to the wrong series.

Impact:
- OrbitAnalytics (dedicated customer) reports recurring user-facing confusion and incorrect drilldowns on three production dashboards used by their analysts.
- Analysts rely on stable facet ordering to validate alerts and run ad-hoc investigations; incorrect drilldowns lead to wasted time and occasional incorrect conclusions.
- Reproducible for the customer on multiple browsers and appears to affect dashboards with >500 unique series in the time window.

Environment:
- Redwood Console (hosted) serving OrbitAnalytics dedicated org
- Region: us-east
- Dashboards: traffic-anomalies-weekly, model-inference-attribution
- Time window: last 7 days, auto-refresh enabled (30s)

Steps to reproduce:
1) Login as OrbitAnalytics user and open 'traffic-anomalies-weekly' dashboard.
2) Expand series facet in the left rail and observe top N series ordering.
3) Toggle auto-refresh on (30s) and let it run 2-3 cycles.
4) Observe position changes in the series list.
5) Click drilldown on a top series immediately after a refresh; the drilldown sometimes navigates to a different series than the label clicked.

Observed behavior:
- Facet list order changes on each refresh for customers with high-cardinality series (>=500).
- Drilldown links sometimes carry an index-based param (series_index=42) that no longer matches the label at that index after reordering.

Expected behavior:
- Series facet ordering should be stable between refreshes (consistent sort key) and drilldown links should resolve to the label the user clicked regardless of reordering or refresh timing.

Temporary workaround:
- Customer disabled auto-refresh and uses manual refresh when needed; this limits but does not eliminate the issue because other users occasionally trigger re-render flows.

2026-03-10: Reproduced in prod with OrbitAnalytics account. Frontend shows non-deterministic ordering after refresh cycles on dashboards with >500 series.
2026-03-11: Hypothesis: client-side facet rendering relies on iteration order of a JS Set/Object created from backend map; when backend emits series in streaming chunks the client appends without a stable sort. Also found index-based drilldown parameter creation that assumes stable ordering.
2026-03-11: Backend confirmed that series payload arrives in streaming batches; no explicit sort key is enforced by the server for high-cardinality response to avoid extra compute. See Slack: #support thread <#support/console-ops> (link: https://slack.redwood.ai/archives/C04SUP12345).
2026-03-11: Frontend prototype: enforced sort by 'count desc, label asc' eliminates reordering in local repro. Created PR to add deterministic sort and switch drilldown to use series_id instead of series_index.
2026-03-12: Confirmed that switching drilldown to series_id addresses incorrect navigation even if ordering changes. Patch prepared in frontend (PR 4829) and a companion backend change to include stable series_id in the streaming payload is required.
Related artifacts: related_github_prs and confluence debugging page added to ticket. Linked to SUP-61234 which has a separate saved-query timeout that surfaced during reproductions; also cross-referenced SUP-781409 which previously dealt with missing trace links after retention operations.

Attached screenshots and a short Loom.
2026-03-10 - Support (Avery Chen): 'Thanks Samir — we've triaged and can reproduce on your org. We're escalating to frontend and putting the dashboard into read-only for a short window if we need to test changes. ETA initial findings 24h.'

Additional notes:
2026-03-12 - Support (Avery Chen): 'Applied temporary mitigation: disabled client-side population of index-based drilldown for the OrbitAnalytics org. This prevents incorrect navigation for now while we roll the fix. Please verify on your side.'
2026-03-12 - OrbitAnalytics (Samir Patel): 'Confirmed that drilldowns now point to the correct series. Ordering still visually moves but drilldown correctness is acceptable for our workflow. Thanks — please advise when full fix lands.'
Mitigation applied: client-side index-based drilldown generation disabled for affected org while fix rolls out. Hotfix PR submitted to console-ui to enforce stable sorting and to change drilldown to use series_id; backend change to include series_id in streaming payload opened. Next steps: roll frontend hotfix through staging, run e2e with high-cardinality fixture, and deploy to prod. Issue summary: Starting 2026-03-10 03:40 UTC we observed a sustained elevation in 5xx responses from the API gateway for traffic belonging to PaperTrail Labs' dedicated tenant. Errors manifested as HTTP 502/503 from the gateway and abrupt streaming session terminations. Impact: Customer-facing failures for PaperTrail's realtime chat product (multiple streams dropped, reconnect storms). Scale: Affected roughly 6% of the tenant's requests during the spike window (~10:30-11:15 PDT), with short bursts peaking at ~18% error rate. Business impact: user-facing errors and automated client retries resulting in support escalations. Timeline: - 2026-03-10 03:37 UTC: Monitoring alert triggers (gateway 5xx rate increased). - 2026-03-10 03:40 UTC: Support opened ticket; customer reports streaming disconnects. - 2026-03-10 04:05 UTC: On-call SRE and ingress engineer pulled into Slack (#support and #incidents). - 2026-03-10 04:20 UTC: Initial mitigation applied (per-route rate cap lowered, soft-evict enabled). - 2026-03-10 05:00 UTC: Errors reduced but intermittent reconnect spikes continued. Observed behavior: - Connection drops reported by clients (RST/ERR stream close). - Gateway logs show short-lived upstream 502/503 with runtime returning 'upstream closed' and 'watchdog timeout' traces. - Traffic pattern: mix of short streaming sessions and frequent small inference requests; many clients retried within short backoffs. Steps to reproduce: see steps_to_reproduce field. Immediate mitigation: temporarily reverted a recent per-tenant throttler tuning deployed 2026-03-09 and increased keepalive pool size for the tenant's route. Result: immediate drop in 5xx rate to baseline, but long-tail reconnect churn persisted. Root cause hypothesis: A feedback loop between the gateway per-route token-bucket throttler and the serving-runtime backoff behavior. When the throttler began rejecting bursts, clients retried aggressively; those retries congested the ingress priority-shedder and caused rapid ephemeral connections that pushed runtimes into kernel-level timeouts and watchdog restarts under memory pressure. Secondary contributors: - Slightly aggressive throttler hysteresis (reduction window too large) introduced oscillation. - Autoscaler thresholds for the dedicated pool were tuned high for CPU (not socket backlog), so scale-up lagged. - A recent runtime patch changed reconnection jitter behavior, reducing effective jitter and concentrating retries. Current status: Mitigations in place; monitoring and customer observing. Next steps: - Engineering to introduce jittered exponential backoff in runtime client retry logic (PR created). - Tune token-bucket parameters to shorter window and lower reject penalty. - Adjust autoscaler to consider accept-queue length and open socket count. - Post-incident follow-up: write a runbook entry and bake tests for throttler hysteresis. Escalation: On-call SRE (Diego) and Platform Eng (Lina Park) engaged.
1) Use a PaperTrail Labs dedicated API key and open N concurrent streaming sessions (N ~ 250 in us-east) with short keepalive and frequent small messages (simulate chat heartbeats).
2) Interleave small non-streaming inference calls at a QPS spike to create mixed workloads (example: 500 QPS of 100-token generation calls).
3) Observe gateway return rates and runtime logs as load ramps quickly over ~60s.
4) Trigger client-side retry within 200-500ms (aggressive retry) to emulate observed client behavior and look for accept queue growth and 502/503 patterns.

Checked Grafana dashboard: /d/platform/ingress?var-tenant=papertrail -> saw correlated spikes in accept-queue length and gateway 5xx around 03:40 UTC.
Datadog traces show many short lived connections; p95 connect time spiked from 12ms -> 480ms during the window.
Replayed load in staging with identical throttler params reproduced downstream watchdog timeouts when client retry jitter < 100ms.
Heap and GPU metrics on dedicated pool were in normal range; issue reproduced without GPU pressure, pointing to socket/backlog and scheduler pressure as proximate cause.
Reviewed recent deploys: ingress throttler tuning rolled 2026-03-09 (PR https://github.com/redwood-inference/ingress/pull/1192) and runtime retry jitter patch 2026-03-08 (PR https://github.com/redwood-inference/platform/pull/4567).

Additional notes:
PaperTrail Support Rep (customer): Confirming their SDK had default retry 300ms with no jitter; asking whether recommended SDK changes exist.
Temporary fix: rolled back ingress throttler parameter change and increased per-route keepalive pool; advised customer to enable client-side jittered exponential backoff (recommended SDK patch v2.3.1).
Patch delivered: PR https://github.com/redwood-inference/platform/pull/4589 introduces 20-300ms randomized jitter in runtime retry logic and guards against concentrated reconnects.
Autoscaler change: follow-up ticket created to add socket/accept-queue as an autoscaling signal (INT-332101).
Follow-up: schedule postmortem and runbook update; add chaos test in staging to validate throttler hysteresis behavior under mixed streaming+short-call workloads.

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customer reports receiving 429 responses for a subset of requests even though the X-RateLimit-* headers returned in prior responses implied available quota. The workload is a mix of long-lived websocket streams (chat-style) and short-lived HTTP POST chunked uploads for document ingestion.

Impact:
- Intermittent 429s for streaming clients after a period of bulk ingestion (customer-visible errors).
- Clients report header values (X-RateLimit-Remaining/X-RateLimit-Reset) that do not match subsequent immediate 429 status.
- Customer cannot reliably separate streaming vs bulk traffic due to tenant-level token accounting; this threatens their SLA for real-time features.

Environment:
- Dedicated pool (customer-dedicated GPU farm) in us-east.
- Traffic through Redwood edge-proxy fronting HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and websocket upgrades on the same IPs.
- Mixed API key usage: single API key reused by ingest workers and streaming clients.

Observed behavior:
1) Start ~20 long-lived streaming websocket sessions (low token rate).
2) Kick off concurrent multipart HTTP uploads from ~50 short-lived workers.
3) Within 30–120s some streaming clients receive 429s with headers indicating non-zero Remaining tokens in previous responses.

Expected behavior:
- Rate headers should reflect per-tenant accounting and be coherent with immediate acceptance/rejection decisions.
- Streaming sessions should not see sudden 429s when tenant-level tokens are sufficient or when headers indicate remaining allowance.

Workaround requested: guidance on configuration and mitigations until root cause is fixed.
1) Using dedicated tenant on us-east, open 20 websocket streaming sessions to /v1/chat/stream with same API key.
2) Start 50 parallel HTTP/2 POST multipart uploads to /v1/ingest with same API key; each upload does 10 concurrent chunks.
3) Observe client-side logs for any 429 responses on websocket connections and check X-RateLimit-* headers on both accepted and rejected requests.
4) Repeat with separate API keys for streaming and uploads to compare behavior.
[2024-10-15T14:03:22Z] edge-proxy: conn=0x7f34 accept POST /v1/ingest tenant=helio-42 tokens_before=1200 tokens_after=1140
[2024-10-15T14:03:22Z] serving-runtime: serve request id=abc123 model=open-llama-13b-v2 tokens=60
[2024-10-15T14:03:22Z] edge-proxy: websocket conn=0x7f20 send event=chat.token tenant=helio-42 X-RateLimit-Remaining=1040 X-RateLimit-Reset=1697375000
[2024-10-15T14:03:50Z] edge-proxy: websocket conn=0x7f20 receive error=429 tenant=helio-42 decision=reject tokens_available_cache=980 actual_accounting=0
[2024-10-15T14:04:02Z] rate-limiter: debug tenant=helio-42 policy=tenant-window window_ms=10000 bucket=standard_accounting local_count=5 remote_count=5
Support (Maya): Logged ticket after initial report from customer. Asked for request IDs and timeline. Provided immediate mitigations: recommend separating API keys for streaming and bulk ingestion and reducing chunk parallelism.
Customer (HelioSearch): Confirmed separation decreased but did not eliminate 429s. Provided pcap and a list of request ids where headers reported Remaining>0 shortly before 429s.
SRE (Arjun): Triaged and pulled edge-proxy traces and rate-limiter metrics. Noted an aggregation mismatch in request attribution between HTTP/2 connection-level counters and per-request accounting.
SRE (Arjun): Requested an experiment window to turn on detailed per-request accounting in prod for the tenant for 1 hour to collect fine-grained traces.
Initial hypothesis: per-connection accounting for HTTP/2 + websocket upgrade was being cached at the edge and not reconciled with per-request token consumption, causing stale X-RateLimit-Remaining headers to be emitted.
Trace analysis: correlation between 429 events and connection reuse across multiplexed streams (HTTP/2) showed that the edge code path emitted headers from a connection-level snapshot that wasn't updated after concurrent chunked POSTs finished.
Metric evidence: spikes in metric edge.rateheader.stale_count coincident with customer bulk-ingest windows. CPU and serving-runtime metrics normal. No model OOMs or GPU shortages found.
Repro attempt: using a local cluster with HTTP/2 multiplexing we reproduced header mismatch when a health-check thread and chunked uploads incremented the same connection-level counter between header emission and final accounting commit.
Related artifacts: slack thread #support-helio (https://slack.redwood/support-helio), dashboard: https://grafana.redwood/tenant/helio-42/rate-accounting, and traces: https://jaeger.redwood/trace/abc123
Linked code area: edge-proxy header cache and rate-limiter attribution (see pr link below).
Mitigation applied: turned off connection-level header caching and switched the tenant to per-request authoritative accounting for the 2-hour experiment window. Immediate effect: streaming clients no longer observed 429s in the test window.

Short-term recommendation to customer:
- Use separate API keys for streaming vs ingestion (we provided a script to rotate keys).
- Reduce parallel chunk concurrency to 4 per worker for now.
- Implement client-side exponential backoff with jitter as documented in our SDK guidelines.

Planned long-term fix: patch edge-proxy to decouple header emission from cached connection snapshots and add atomic commit semantics so headers reflect post-accounting consumptions. Patch submitted: PR #9876. QA plan: canary release to 10% of edge-proxy fleet, verify metrics edge.rateheader.stale_count drops to 0 and no regression in latency.

Follow-up: monitor for 72 hours and schedule a postmortem with HelioSearch; include changes in rate-limiter runbook.
payload.summary: Inconsistent rate-limit headers and apparent token double-counting during multiplexed websocket + HTTP upload workload

payload.description:
Issue summary:
During routine verification after a configuration change to the customer's IdP, Citrine reported that scheduled background workers using service tokens could access model execution routes, but their web console users received 403 when performing the same actions. This started after an IdP update that began including an alternate tenant alias in the JWT 'aud' claim.

Impact:
- Scheduled ingestion and reconciliation workers (CRON jobs) continued to execute successfully (no failures observed in job runner logs).
- Interactive web console operations for tenant admins and engineers (model pinning, rollout checks) are intermittently denied 403.
- Customer reports failed UI operations during business hours causing operational disruption.
- Potential risk: audit logs show different principal identity for worker vs console actions which complicates compliance auditing.

Environment and scope:
- Customer: Citrine Payments (private deployment)
- Region: eu-west
- Redwood Private deployed in customer-managed VPC with ingress/proxy in front of control plane
- IdP: On-premise SAML/OIDC broker that emits JWTs via a federation gateway
- Affected components: ingress-proxy audience validation, RBAC name-matching, scheduled worker token handling

Steps to reproduce (customer supplied):
1. Trigger a scheduled worker job that uses the service account token (job runs on customer side and calls Redwood private API).
2. Confirm job completes and model invocation logs show success.
3. Login to Redwood Console as the same tenant admin (interactive OAuth SSO via same IdP).
4. Attempt to perform model-rolling operation or view admin-only route; observe 403.
5. Capture IdP JWT from both flows and compare 'aud' claim content.

Observed behavior:
- Worker JWT 'aud' includes canonical tenant UUID only (example: "tenant-0123-uuid").
- Console JWT 'aud' includes both canonical tenant UUID and legacy tenant alias (example: ["tenant-0123-uuid","tenant-acme"]).
- RBAC evaluation pipeline appears to match principal->tenant bindings against a single expected aud value, causing the console JWT with multi-valued aud to fail name-based matching in the RBAC sanitizer.

Expected behavior:
- Multi-valued 'aud' containing a canonical tenant identifier + alias should be normalized by the ingress/auth layer and evaluated as equivalent to the canonical tenant. Both scheduled workers and interactive sessions should receive the same effective RBAC identity.

Logs / artifacts provided by customer (sanitized):
- Worker request trace: 2026-03-09T03:20:11Z POST /v1/models/run 200 token.sub=svc-ingest-42 token.aud=["tenant-0123-uuid"] trace_id=tr-9f8
- Console request trace: 2026-03-09T12:02:07Z GET /console/apps 403 token.sub=user:alice token.aud=["tenant-0123-uuid","tenant-acme"] trace_id=tr-2b3
- Ingress proxy debug dump (snippet): "aud_checker: token has multiple audiences, canonical_match=false, reject=false?=true"

Initial hypothesis and findings:
- Hypothesis A: The ingress/aud validation code path treats multi-valued aud as ambiguous and applies a strict exact-match check against tenant binding table, causing alias-containing tokens to miss matches.
- Hypothesis B: RBAC sanitization pipeline contains a legacy code path that flattens aud into a single string for scheduled workers (service tokens) but not for interactive tokens, leading to asymmetric behavior.
- Hypothesis C: The customer's IdP began emitting a namespaced alias that conflicts with an internal tenant namespace normalization rule (whitespace/case normalization).

Investigation steps taken by Redwood support so far:
- Replayed customer console JWT in staging auth proxy: reproduced 403 when multi-valued aud present.
- Compared RBAC principal resolution logs for service vs interactive tokens: found different sanitizer branch.
- Created a local test token with aud=[canonical] + [alias] and saw identical fail.
- Confirmed that scheduled workers succeed because their tokens are canonical-only.

Temporary workaround suggested to customer:
- Short term: Configure IdP to stop emitting the legacy alias in the 'aud' claim for interactive sessions (if feasible) until a platform fix is in place.
- Workaround for console users: Use service account impersonation for the time being if operations need to be performed programmatically.

Next steps / action items:
- Engineering: add normalization step in ingress/audience validator to collapse multi-valued aud and prefer canonical tenant UUIDs (ENG-#A-4832).
- Product/Support: Add a logging flag to surface tokens with multi-valued aud for faster triage.
- Security/Compliance: Evaluate the audit log identity differences and note in compliance tracker for Citrine.
- Follow-up: schedule a short maintenance window to deploy a fix to staging, validate with Citrine, then roll to prod.

Acceptance criteria:
- Tokens with multi-valued aud containing canonical tenant UUID are accepted and map to correct tenant identity for RBAC evaluation.
- Console users no longer see 403 for tasks that previously failed.
- Audit log shows consistent principal mapping across worker and interactive actions.


Additional notes:
Reproducible in staging. Root cause appears to be unhandled multi-valued 'aud' tokens hitting an exact-match RBAC sanitizer. Both ingress and RBAC modules require coordinated change to normalize aud while preserving audit trail.
Engineering fix in progress; staging validation scheduled. Customer offered short-term IdP config change as a stopgap. Will not close ticket until post-deploy validation confirms consistency across audit logs.
payload.summary: Private deployment: tenant-alias in 'aud' claim allows scheduled worker token but blocks interactive console access

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customer (ClariData) reports a mismatch between expected discounted hourly line items and the finalized invoice after they performed a reserved-capacity swap (moved workload from an older reserved pool to a new reserved pool within the same billing cycle). Impact: customer sees an under-applied discount on 6 hours of reserved usage and an unexpected separate 'hosted fallback' line.

Impact:
- Invoice overcharge of ~$2,180 for billing period ending 2026-03-11 as reported by customer finance team.
- Affects one dedicated tenant during a reserve swap/zone migration.

Environment:
- Prod, us-east regional billing batch.
- Customer using Dedicated reserved capacity (contract ID RC-2025-CLARIDATA).

Observed behavior:
- During the reserve swap at 2026-03-10T18:20Z, postback ordering caused subset of traffic to be attributed to the old reserved tag for part of the hour and to hosted fallback for remaining requests. The hourly-tier discount rule matched only the new reserved tag for that hour, leaving a gap.

Expected behavior:
- Pricing tier logic should aggregate hourly usage across the swap window and apply the reserved hourly-tier discount pro rata, avoiding separate hosted fallback lines when traffic has a valid reserved mapping.

Requested outcome from customer:
- Reconciliation of the month invoice lines and application of compensatory credit for the under-applied discount.

Relevant account identifiers and billing metadata:
- Account: clari-data-prod (acct_0CLARIDA)
1) Perform a reserved capacity reassignment on a dedicated tenant during an hourly boundary (swap old-reserve -> new-reserve at 18:20Z).
2) Generate steady inference traffic to rw-13b-v2 from 18:00Z to 19:00Z to exercise hourly aggregation window.
3) Let billing postbacks run and finalize hourly aggregation job.
4) Compare resulting invoice lines to expected prorated reserved discount for 18:00-19:00 hour.
2026-03-10T18:19:59Z POSTBACK Received: tenant=acct_0CLARIDA tag=reserve_old usage=1200 tokens
2026-03-10T18:20:05Z POSTBACK Received: tenant=acct_0CLARIDA tag=reserve_new usage=800 tokens
2026-03-10T18:20:08Z POSTBACK Received: tenant=acct_0CLARIDA tag=hosted_fallback usage=400 tokens
Billing batch query (hourly_agg): SELECT sum(tokens) FROM postbacks WHERE tenant='acct_0CLARIDA' AND hour='2026-03-10T18:00Z' GROUP BY tag;  -- returned three groups (reserve_old, reserve_new, hosted_fallback)

Additional notes:
2026-03-13 - Customer (Emma Soto, ClariData Finance): Can you provide estimated credit amount? We need that for our month-end close.
Hypothesis: Hourly aggregation logic treats tags atomically; when multiple tags appear in the hour aggregation it does not merge into a single prorated reserved line. This interacts poorly with reserve swaps that occur mid-hour.
Checked reconciler logs for hour 2026-03-10T18:00Z: three groups detected; discount_applier skipped pro rata computation because group_count > 1. See reconciler log pointer: /var/log/reconciler/2026-03-10/agg-18.log lines 412-436.
Ran local SQL to simulate desired pro rata: computed expected reserved_discount = (tokens_with_reserved_tags / total_tokens) * reserved_hourly_rate_discount -> results matched customer's expected reduction (~$2,180).
Related code paths: billing/discount_applier.py -> function apply_hourly_tier_discount; edge-case gating at line where groups>1 -> early return. Patch proposed to compute weighted prorate when groups are compatible (reserve_old + reserve_new + hosted_fallback where hosted_fallback had reserve mapping within 10s).
Potential side-effects: need to ensure we do not incorrectly apply reserved discount to true hosted traffic. Proposed guard: only merge groups if there is a matching reserve contract active for the tenant during hour and if hosted_fallback tag was observed only during overlap window and followed by reserved tag within X seconds.
Temporary actions: provisional credit of $2,180 applied on 2026-03-14 to clari-data-prod account (credit ID CR-2026-171). Long-term fix: billing team to land reconciler PR to compute prorated reserved discounts across tag-boundary windows; target ship in next weekly billing patch (related PR: github.com/redwood-inference/reconciler/pull/927). Follow-ups: add a unit test for mid-hour reserve-swap and add a metric (billing.prorate_merged_count) to monitor how often we merge groups. Customer notified and will confirm acceptance of provisional credit before final invoice adjustment.
1) Merge reconciler PR with guard conditions and run staging billing run against synthetic swap data (owner: Arjun Patel, ETA 2026-03-18).
2) Run full reconciliation for March period and compute final credit amount; if different from provisional, issue balancing credit or invoice correction (owner: billing team, ETA 2026-03-20).
3) Add alert for unusual postback tag churn during hourly windows (owner: Observability team, ETA 2026-03-25).
4) Update runbook Confluence page with explicit guidance on reserved swaps and expected billing artifacts (owner: Billing PM, ETA 2026-03-22).

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Fleetware reports intermittent checksum mismatches and 'shard corrupt' errors when their private deployment fetches large sharded model artifacts using presigned URLs. The failures appear only for range requests that happen across resumed TLS sessions (session reuse / session ticket). Observed behavior is a 200 OK returning a full object or merged byte ranges instead of a 206 Partial Content for one or more Range requests, leading to validator checksum mismatch.

Impact:
- Nightly retrain/model-push jobs failing intermittently (10-30% of runs).
- Automated serving rollbacks triggered due to shard validation failures.
- Customer reported increased latency and manual intervention to re-fetch shards.

Environment:
- Fleetware private deployment (Redwood Private) via VPCE interface endpoint + internal NLB in us-west-2.
- Serving nodes run latest 2026.02 runtime.
- Artifact store: S3 presigned URLs served via internal cache/proxy in customer network (corporate accelerator).

Steps to reproduce (customer):
1) Deploy a model with sharded artifacts (custom-13b-sharded).
2) Start a fetch that requests shard ranges (Range: bytes=0-5242879 then subsequent ranges).
3) Allow the underlying TLS session to be resumed (application-level keepalive / session ticket).
4) Observe on ~2/10 attempts that the client receives HTTP 200 for a range request or receives merged byte ranges that fail checksum validation.

Observed logs / headers (sanitized):
- TLS: Session-Resumed=true, Ticket-Age=0; ALPN offered: h2; negotiated: h2 -> later response shows http/1.1
- NLB/VPCE: Set-Cookie: stickysess=AZb; X-Forwarded-Proto: https
- Response: HTTP/1.1 200 OK
  Content-Length: 5242880
  Content-Range: missing or ranges merged
- Runtime: shard-validator: checksum mismatch for shard-12 (expected XYZ, got ABC)

Temporary workaround (customer tried):
- Disabled application-layer cache on corporate accelerator: reduced failure rate but not eliminated.
- Disabled TLS session reuse on the serving node client: eliminated failures (diagnostic) but unacceptable for perf.

Request from customer:
- Root cause analysis: is VPCE/NLB or the corporate accelerator rewriting ALPN or coalescing range responses across session resume?
- Permanent mitigation guidance and recommended configuration defaults for Redwood Private NLB/VPCE to avoid this class of corruption.

2026-03-12 13:22 - Customer (Ops lead, Fleetware): Uploaded sanitized tcpdump and sample headers to the ticket. Noting that failures spike during their cross-AZ failover window.
2026-03-13 09:05 - SRE (Martin O'Neill): Observed ALPN downgrade in captured headers (h2 -> http/1.1) and Set-Cookie stickiness coming from a VPCE proxy appliance. Hypothesis: proxy is terminating TLS then re-establishing to S3, and its range handling combined with session-resume/pipelining is merging responses.
2026-03-13 15:40 - Support (Priya Kapoor): Suggested diagnostic: toggle NLB TLS mode to TCP (pass-through) and test. Customer to try this in canary AZ.
2026-03-14 08:12 - Customer (Ops lead, Fleetware): Confirmed toggling NLB to TCP mode removed the merged-range responses in 200/200 tests. Will schedule a controlled test to disable VPCE proxy stickiness next.
2026-03-14 11:30 - SRE (Martin O'Neill): Noted that runtime should be defensive; opened linked GH PR to add range-revalidate fallback when Content-Range missing or Content-Length mismatches (see related PR).
Captured tcpdump shows TLS session resume between client <-> VPCE-proxy and a separate TLS session between VPCE-proxy <-> S3 (double-termination).
ALPN negotiation differs across the two legs; proxy is downgrading to http/1.1 for backend, while client sends h2. This mismatch correlates with merged responses.
VPCE-set cookie indicates cookie-based session stickiness is configured on the customer appliance/NLB which may coalesce multiple range requests into single backend request for optimization.
Changing NLB to TCP mode eliminates proxy termination in-path and reproductions dropped to 0/30 in customer's canary test — strong signal that TLS termination + app-layer caching is culprit.
Runtime currently trusts 206/Content-Range headers; there is no defensive re-request on missing Content-Range, which allows silent data corruption to propagate to shard validator failure instead of triggering a re-fetch.
Potential contributing factor: HTTP/2 multiplexing semantics at proxy boundary when converting to HTTP/1.1 on backend might be collapsing or concatenating ranges for performance, leading to server returning 200 with merged content.
Workaround applied: Customer disabled NLB cookie-based stickiness and switched NLB to TCP (pass-through) for the VPCE interface. Immediate effect: merged-range responses stopped, production shard fetch success rate returned to baseline.
Code mitigation: Merged PR https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/4187 that implements a defensive revalidate path: if Content-Range is missing or content-length doesn't match expected range, runtime will re-request the offending range(s) rather than accepting merged response. Backported to 2026.03 runtime patch.
Operational guidance: Document recommending 'VPCE/NLB: use TCP pass-through for artifact fetch endpoints' and 'disable application-layer response coalescing for presigned range downloads' added to Confluence and the VPCE runbook.
Follow-ups: Customer to run a 48-hour soak with NLB TCP mode; SRE to monitor artifact fetch error-rate and validate patched runtime behavior in staging. Ticket to remain open until soak completes (target close 2026-03-16).
