Issue summary: BrightDocs reported interleaved user sessions where chat generation calls returned outputs from the canary variant while embedding calls for the same session were still pinned to the stable variant. This led to semantic mismatch (embeddings from v-stable but generated text from v-canary) causing downstream scoring failures and data skew.

Impact: Affects ~3% of requests for the BrightDocs tenant since rollout began; causes elevated error rates in their downstream similarity service and increased support tickets. Customer-facing incidents: search relevance dropped for certain cohorts.

Environment: Dedicated cluster in us-east (tenant-dedicated-42) running a weighted canary (10% traffic) for redwood/gptx-13b-quant-v2. Embedding service rolled as a separate route to redwood/embed-1 pinned to v-stable by customer config.

Steps to reproduce (observed):
1) Customer opens a chat flow that calls /v1/chat.generate then calls /v1/embeddings.create immediately after.
2) Repeat for a user with session cookies and an affinity token present.
3) In ~3% of attempts, chat.generate returned responses traced to canary hash and embeddings.create returned the stable model outputs.

Logs/observations:
- Edge request traces show identical session-affinity tokens attached to both requests.
- Routing decision logs show chat.generate went through route/variant: gptx-13b-quant-v2@canary-2026-03-09 while embeddings.create resolved to embed-1@stable-2026-02-21.
- Canary coordinator logs show an in-flight promote commit for the chat route at 2026-03-10T14:23:11Z overlapping with prewarm health probes for the embedding route that scheduled cache rewrites at 14:23:12Z.
- No obvious auth header mutation at the proxy level; however sidecar telemetry shows duplicate health probe responses for some edge nodes.

Initial hypothesis: An interleaving between the canary promote window and route-specific cache prewarm/healthprobe processing caused the routing table to transiently accept variant metadata for one service call but not the other for the same session token. This produced mixed-variant servicing within a single logical user transaction.

Support (Alex Chen) 2026-03-10: Ingested customer report and validated traces. Customer provided three example trace IDs and timestamp ranges. Opened initial triage in #support-ops and requested SRE help.
SRE (Samir Patel) 2026-03-10: Noted overlapping timestamps of canary commit and prewarm. Requested edge logs and coordinator timeline. Assigned to Priya for routing deep-dive.
Engineering (Priya Nair) 2026-03-11: Reproduced routing discrepancy in internal test with synthetic affinity tokens by speeding up canary commit window; observed same mixed-resolution when prewarm cache rewrite collides with commit ack path. Created reproducer script and recorded deterministic failure at ~1:100 run rate in the test harness.
Customer (BrightDocs - Evan Morales) 2026-03-11: Confirmed that the reproducer mirrors production behavior. Provided additional batch of user traces and timeline for their scheduled traffic surge (2026-03-09 to 2026-03-11).
Support (Alex Chen) 2026-03-12: Coordinated temporary mitigation: recommend customer pin both chat and embedding routes explicitly to the same variant until rollback/patch is deployed. Customer applied pin to embed route; observed immediate reduction in mismatch reports.
Engineering (Priya Nair) 2026-03-12: Drafted a fix to the coordinator commit path to make route updates atomic across co-located route-sets and to add a short quiesce window to prewarm operations. Posting PR to edge-proxy and canary-coordinator. See related PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/edge-proxy/pull/4392.
Reproducer: deterministic when promoting with artificial 50ms delay in commit-ack path and simultaneous prewarm cache writes—causes route metadata divergence for calls that happen within the window.
Root cause: coordinator promoted chat route variant and broadcasted route-change event; some edge nodes applied new variant metadata immediately while embedding route prewarm path performed an idempotent cache rewrite that re-registered old variant mapping for embeddings.create binding due to non-atomic update ordering.
Race vector: non-atomic route update + asynchronous prewarm acknowledgement + per-route sticky-affinity table updated independently for different route namespaces (chat vs embeddings). Affinity token is global but per-route sticky mapping applied in separate codepaths.
Observed that forcing a TTL bump on affinity tokens temporarily reduced occurrence (likely because it forced refreshes and re-resolution to current mapping).
Related: SUP-302118 noted similar session divergence when health probes overlapped with rollout windows; recommend cross-checking prior mitigation history.
In progress - temporary mitigation accepted by customer (explicit pin to same variant across chat+embed). Engineering to merge atomic-commit patch to canary-coordinator and edge-proxy that serializes route updates across co-located route groups. Patch will also add a 250ms quiesce window where prewarm cache writes are deferred until commit completes. Plan: ship hotfix to staging 2026-03-13, promote to prod us-east 2026-03-14 during low-traffic window. Post-deploy: monitor mismatch rate and rollback if >0.5% within 30 minutes.
Merge PRs and schedule hotfix deploy: edge-proxy PR 4392, canary-coordinator PR 1187
Add automated unit/integration test that simulates concurrent canary commit + prewarm and asserts strong consistency across multiple routes for same affinity token
Update runbook: add 'quiesce prewarm on commit' step and include diagnostic query for mixed-variant traces
Coordinate with BrightDocs to remove temporary pin after validation window and collect 48h of telemetry

Issue summary:
Customer reports repeated long stalls (20-90s) during model initialization and intermittent streaming resets for sessions served from their private deployment in us-east-1. TLS handshakes for model pull and streaming channels complete but token streaming often stalls; eventually client receives a final gRPC status=UNAVAILABLE. Customer noticed the problem roughly after a corporate firewall firmware change that same morning.

Impact:
- Affects AtlasHealth production traffic: ~15% of sessions see >20s stalls, ~3% see full disconnects.
- Impacts both model artifact fetch and live token streaming for redwood-3b-v1 and gpt-medic-2.1.
- Customer is on a privacy-sensitive private deployment (private control plane + VPC peering).

Hypothesis: a middlebox (corporate NGFW) is stripping or disabling TCP Window Scaling option (RFC 7323) and/or clamping TCP options, degrading throughput on long-lived TLS streams and causing the streaming layer to hit stalls or retransmit timeouts. This primarily affects flows with large RTT and sustained throughput requirements (model pulls and streaming token paths).
1) From a client in the customer's corp network, start a streaming generation against the private deployment endpoint (gRPC).
2) Observe initial TLS handshake completes; streaming begins but stalls after ~3-10 tokens for some sessions.
3) Capture packets with tcpdump on the path between customer host and private deploy egress.
4) Repeat test from a host outside the corp firewall (bastion in customer VPC) to compare behavior.

Commands used during repro:
- grpcurl -proto api.proto -d '{"prompt":"Hello"}' -v customer-private.redwood:443
- sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -w /tmp/stream.pcap tcp and port 443

Expected: steady token streaming with small per-token latency. Observed: stalls of 20-90s, retransmits, and final gRPC UNAVAILABLE in some sessions.
Support traces and packet captures attached in Confluence page. Key excerpts:

- tcpdump (client->server): TCP options in SYN missing Window Scale (no WS option), MSS present; later ACKs show tiny advertised window (~64KB) and repeated zero-window probes.
- wireshark summary: One-way RTT ~ 45ms, but throughput stalls correlating with receive-window shrink to 0 followed by long zero-window probes.
- Server logs: streaming session id=abc123 reported repeated backpressure; runtime emitted 'streaming_chunk_timeout' at 16s, 34s. No TLS ALERT observed.
- Console traces: per-route token latency spikes align with the customer's private IP blocks.

Packet excerpt (client->server SYN):
  Flags [S], seq 0, options [mss 1460,sackOK,TS val 123456 ecr 0], (notice: no wscale option)
- Reproduced issue from a workstation behind customer's NGFW; not reproducible from bastion inside VPC (bypassing corp egress).
- tcpdump shows absence of TCP Window Scale option in SYN -> remote host is not advertising scaling; further packets show advertised receive window clamping to small values and long zero-window probes.
- Support tested with iperf3: throughput limited to ~6-8Mbps despite available bandwidth, consistent with small RWND.
- Customer confirmed a firewall policy change/firmware update at 08:15 on 2026-03-10.
- SRE ran an experiment: enabled conservative streaming chunking on a subset of servers (decrease in stalls but degraded user-perceived throughput).
- No certificate/TLS handshake failures; TLS records continue but are segmented into smaller fragments.
- Hypothesis validated: middlebox appears to be stripping TCP WS option or applying TCP MSS/Wscale clamp resulting in poor flow control behavior for long-lived TLS streams.
- Risk: other customers behind similar middleboxes may exhibit the same pattern; this is specific to environments that perform deep TCP option normalization.

Additional notes:
2026-03-10 13:20 - AtlasHealth-Eng (Customer): Confirmed change to NGFW profile at 08:15; security team says they enabled 'legacy TCP normalization' for compliance. Will attempt temporary rollback on a small subnet for validation.
Workaround (recommended to customer):
1) Disable 'legacy TCP normalization' or ensure 'TCP Window Scaling' option is permitted/untouched on the NGFW for outbound traffic to the Redwood private-control-plane and model-serving IP ranges.
2) If firewall change cannot be made quickly, enable the temporary runtime mitigation on the customer's private deployment: reduce_stream_chunk_size=true and set max_inflight_tokens=64. This reduces stalls but increases per-token latency/cost.
Permanent fix / follow-up actions:
- Customer to roll firewall policy change during maintenance (scheduled).
- INT-2091 created to add detection: server-side alert when SYNs for a connection lack WS option and token streaming stalls exceed threshold.
- infra PR #5123 (linked) includes a runtime flag to automatically fall back to conservative chunking and emit a clear alert.
Status: Customer applied temporary rollback on test subnet and saw immediate improvement. Awaiting full rollout confirmation. Marked P1 until rollout completes.
- Create an internal runbook for networking teams detailing how to triage TCP option normalization issues (assigned to Liam O'Connor).
- Add automatic runtime metric + alert for 'missing_tcp_window_scale_and_streaming_stalls' (INT-2091).
- Update onboarding checklist for private deployments to include a firewall policy template that explicitly permits TCP Window Scaling and does not normalize TCP options.
payload.summary: TCP window scaling disabled by corporate firewall causes long TLS handshake and streaming stalls on private deployment

Issue summary:
Arkadia Finance (Optimize Suggestions beta) reports that the “Risk: Low/Medium/High” label in the Console Suggestions view is being interpreted by internal stakeholders as security/compliance risk (or “chance Redwood is wrong”), rather than “likelihood of latency/reliability regression if you apply the recommended batching/caching change.” They requested clearer, shareable language for governance review and change-management tickets.

Impact:
- Slows adoption of Suggestions recommendations (internal approvals blocked)
- Increases back-and-forth with platform governance/security teams
- Risk of miscommunication: stakeholders assume “High risk” implies security risk

Where this shows up:
- Suggestions list table risk badge tooltip
- Details drawer “Risk” section copy
- Beta docs page (glossary / definitions)

Customer request:
1) Rename/clarify what “risk” means (performance/reliability risk, not security)
2) Add a short explanation that can be pasted into an internal change request
3) Provide guidance on how to safely validate a suggestion (rollout controls, canary, monitor p95)

Customer context:
- Using Suggestions for batching/caching recommendations on 2 high-traffic routes
- Stakeholder group includes platform governance and security reviewers

Notes:
This is not a product defect; it’s primarily UX/copy + docs clarity. Customer asked for near-term mitigation while we consider longer-term labeling changes (e.g., “Performance risk”).
2026-02-22 09:18 (Dev Patel, Support) — Ticket created from CS escalation. Customer quote: “Our security review board flagged ‘High risk’ as a compliance concern. We need wording that clearly states this is performance risk only, and what we should monitor.”
2026-02-22 11:02 (Miguel Santos, Customer Success) — Confirmed on call with Arkadia: They’re screenshotting the Suggestions page into internal approval docs. They want a one-liner definition + a second line with concrete guardrails (e.g., canary rollout, watch p95 + error rate). Asked if we can add a doc link directly in the tooltip/drawer.
2026-02-22 12:10 (Marissa Cole, Product - Console) — Agree this is a priority for beta trust. Proposed copy direction: explicitly say “Performance & reliability risk” and add a tooltip line: “Not a security/compliance risk.” Also add “How we calculate risk” deep-link to docs. Looping in Design + Docs.
2026-02-23 10:41 (Kenji Nakamura, Design) — Reviewed current tooltip. It only says “Likelihood of negative impact” which is too vague. Suggest: 1) Rename section header in drawer to “Performance risk” (if feasible without re-layout), 2) Tooltip: “Estimates likelihood of latency or error-rate regression when applying this config change. Not a security risk.” 3) Add examples in the drawer: “Why this is Medium: traffic is bursty; batching could increase p95.”
2026-02-23 14:06 (Sana Farid, Risk/Confidence DS) — +1. Also recommend we avoid implying quality risk since beta scope is batching/caching. We can mention “reliability (timeouts/queueing)” and “latency (p95)” but not “model output quality.” If we mention quality at all, it should be phrased as “No expected output-quality change for batching/caching; monitor as usual.”
2026-02-24 09:32 (Elliot Price, Docs) — Drafted docs additions: a short glossary entry and a ‘How to roll out safely’ section with concrete steps (canary, compare baseline, watch p95/p99 + 5xx/429 + timeouts). Will also add a note: “Risk labels are conservative and based on observed traffic patterns; not guarantees.”
2026-02-25 16:20 (Nora Ahmed, Console UX Eng) — Implemented copy updates behind the existing Suggestions beta flag. Proposed UI changes:
- Tooltip title: “Performance & reliability risk”
- Tooltip body: “How likely applying this suggestion is to increase latency or error rate for this route. Not a security/compliance risk.”
- Drawer: added “What to monitor” bullets (p95 latency, timeouts/5xx, queue depth if available).
Pending PM/Design final approval.
2026-02-26 10:05 (Miguel Santos, Customer Success) — Shared the updated wording with Arkadia for review (screenshot + text). Customer responded that this resolves their governance confusion and asked for the docs link they can reference in change tickets.
2026-02-27 13:48 (Dev Patel, Support) — Closing loop: Doc updates merged and Console copy queued for next beta patch rollout. Provided customer with a pasteable definition + rollout checklist (see Resolution).
Resolution:
1) Console UX copy/tooltip update (beta):
- Clarified that “Risk” refers to performance & reliability risk (latency/error-rate regression likelihood) when applying the suggested batching/caching change.
- Explicitly stated: “Not a security/compliance risk.”
- Added “What to monitor” guidance in the details drawer.

2) Documentation update:
- Added a “Risk level” definition section and a short rollout checklist (canary + monitor p95 latency, 5xx/timeouts, and traffic changes).
- Added language that estimates and risk labels are conservative and not guarantees.

Customer-facing mitigation shared:
Pasteable language for Arkadia’s internal change request:
“Risk level indicates the likelihood that enabling this batching/caching configuration will negatively impact performance (e.g., p95 latency) or reliability (e.g., timeouts/5xx) for the selected route based on observed traffic patterns. It does not represent security or compliance risk. Apply via a canary rollout and monitor p95 latency, timeouts/5xx, and request volume during the change window.”

Follow-ups / references:
- Copy guidelines tracked in risk-level definition spec and the Suggestions beta docs page.
- If we continue to see confusion, PM will consider renaming the label globally to “Performance risk” (requires design sign-off and potential table column rename).
Monitor additional beta feedback for ongoing confusion about “risk” semantics; if repeated, evaluate renaming the column header to “Performance risk” in the list view.
Add the docs deep-link in the UI where feasible without clutter (tooltip/footer link), subject to design review.
Ensure Support macros include the pasteable definition above for future tickets.

comments: 2026-03-10T09:02:00Z Aisha Patel: Reproduced with AcmeAI proxy settings. Captured 2 request IDs (rwd-9091, rwd-9092) where payload identical but X-Idempotency-Key differed. Sent example logs to SRE.

payload.description:
Issue summary: Customer reports that when using a delegated service account pattern (AcmeAI proxies requests through their tenancy router), long-running function/tool calls occasionally complete but downstream side-effects (webhook calls, database writes) are executed twice or partially applied. The duplicate/partial side-effects appear only when the request path traverses AcmeAI's multi-tenant reverse proxy which injects a Delegated-Id header and rewrites some incoming headers.
1) Customer sets up a delegated-service flow: client -> AcmeAI tenancy-proxy -> Redwood API (prod/us-east) using a delegated service key.
2) Client issues a streaming function-call that triggers an external webhook (tool) with idempotency metadata set at the request scope (X-Idempotency-Key).
3) Proxy rewrites headers (normalization step) and attaches Delegated-Id and X-Account-Tenant headers. Proxy also base64-url encodes a portion of the id when forwarding to Redwood.
4) Intermittently, SDK (python/node) retries the call after transient network hiccup; Redwood serving-runtime accepts and runs the tool but webhook receives either duplicated POSTs or a single POST with duplicate side-effect application (e.g., two partial DB upserts).
5) Observe server logs and webhook endpoint traces for duplicate deliveries correlated with a modified idempotency key seen at Redwood's ingress.
Expected: A single external side-effect per idempotent request regardless of proxy header rewrites or delegated key flows.
2026-03-09T15:23:11Z redwood-api-gateway INFO incoming request key=acct:acme:1234 x-idempotency-key=client-8f3a (received) delegated-id=proxy-B64-Q2FjZQ==
2026-03-09T15:23:12Z serving-runtime INFO accepted request; mapped idempotency-scope=request:client-8f3a-normalized
2026-03-09T15:23:14Z webhook-acme INFO POST /events 200 idempotency-key=client-8f3a
2026-03-09T15:23:15Z webhook-acme INFO POST /events 200 idempotency-key=client-8f3a__proxy-B64 (duplicate)
Proxy logs (AcmeAI) show header-rewrite event at 15:23:10Z: normalized idempotency key truncated to 16 chars and suffix added: client-8f3a__proxy-B64
Initial hypothesis: header normalization at customer proxy mutates idempotency key namespace so Redwood treats retried attempt as a distinct idempotency scope.
Observed that some proxies truncate long Id keys and append a tenant suffix; this leads to two distinct keys arriving at the API depending on where truncation occurred in the call path (client vs proxy).
SDK behavior: python SDK will reattach the original X-Idempotency-Key when retrying, but if the proxy has already rewritten the header on first request, subsequent attempts may traverse a different internal path (edge cache vs direct) and be rewritten differently, producing two unique keys at the gateway.
Serving-runtime dedup semantics are per-normalized-key + model-route. If the normalization differs mid-flight, dedup cannot correlate the two attempts.
We confirmed one reproduction with curl via AcmeAI proxy that reproduces duplicate webhook deliveries when proxy truncation limit < 24 bytes and appends tenant suffix.

Additional notes:
2026-03-10 13:22 - Customer (AcmeAI): We cannot remove tenant suffix addition due to our routing requirements. Looking for guidance on preserving single-delivery semantics without changing our platform.
2026-03-11 16:40 - Product (Riley Chen): Note: must validate that canonicalization does not collide across true distinct requests in multi-tenant environments. Add tests for cross-tenant collisions and audit logs for normalization events.
Workaround provided: instruct AcmeAI to configure SDK to send Idempotency-Scope header (client-generated UUID) and avoid relying on proxy-modified X-Idempotency-Key. Short-term ingress patch added to gateway to strip recognized proxy-suffix patterns for delegated flows; patch deployed to prod/us-east behind a feature flag. Follow-ups: write automated tests to ensure canonicalization safety, add telemetry to detect future normalization mismatches, coordinate with customer to evaluate removing tenant suffixing or using a fixed client-side idempotency header. Pending code PR #2893 for permanent ingress normalization and SDK convenience helpers.
1) Merge and roll out PR https://github.com/redwood-inference/sdk/pull/2893 which adds SDK helper to set Idempotency-Scope header in python/ts SDKs.
2) Complete gateway canonicalization review and add robust dedup tests across tenant-suffix edge cases (owner: Marcus).
3) Schedule 30-minute sync with AcmeAI engineering to discuss proxy header behavior and long-term mitigation (owner: CS lead).
4) Add an alert to console when incoming request idempotency keys vary across retry attempts for the same client request ID (observability owner).
payload.summary: Delegated idempotency scope normalization mismatch via multi-tenant proxy causing partial tool side-effects

payload.description:
Issue summary:\nCustomer reported sudden p99 and throughput collapse in their dedicated pool during a midday window. The degradation started with normal traffic but escalated over ~10 minutes until requests were queuing and autoscaler reported GPU shortages.\n\nImpact:\n- DocuServe experienced ~70% drop in sustained throughput for the reserved pool for 12 minutes.\n- Several short-lived streams from the customer were left in a stalled state; other tenants on the same pool saw p99 increases and request retries.\n- No permanent model eviction reported, but multiple GPU attach/detach events and prefetch failures logged.\n\nObserved behavior (summary):\n- Large uptick in KV-prefetch memory for a small set of long-context requests from the customer.\n- Autoscaler decreased headroom after underestimating memory trajectory, leading to late scale-up and many requests stuck waiting for slots.\n- A set of silent, long-lived streaming connections kept GPU slots reserved while their actual token generation paused ("silent-stream slot hoarding").\n\nWhy this is unique: the incident combines a fast-ramping per-tenant KV cache footprint (memory surge) with silent streaming session behavior that prevents the scheduler from reclaiming slots, producing a cascading GPU shortage and throughput loss.
1) Create a dedicated tenant on a small reserve (2 GPUs) and pin a model with long KV cache behavior (e.g., redwood-7b-quant-v2).
2) Open many short streams that send initial long-context prompts triggering full KV prefetch. Ensure requests include intermittent pauses after initial tokens (simulate human typing).
3) Observe autoscaler memory telemetry and GPU allocation while gradually increasing concurrent short-stream count.
4) Notice that when streams pause after initial prefetch, scheduler does not reclaim the slot until explicit idle timeout, leading to slot hoarding and reduced effective capacity.
2026-03-12T14:07:12Z [serving-runtime] WARN prefetch: tenant=docuserve-42 kv_size=1.9GB expected=150MB
2026-03-12T14:09:05Z [autoscaler] INFO scale-decision: pool=dedicated-docuserve desired_gpus=6 current_gpus=2 reason=memory_ramp
2026-03-12T14:09:47Z [scheduler] ERROR attach: gpu_attach_timeout tenant=docuserve-42 slot_wait=83s
2026-03-12T14:10:31Z [metrics] p99_latency_ms=1200 p50=90 throughput_tpm=320 (normal baseline 1050 tpm)
2026-03-12 14:20 UTC - Initial triage: Confirmed elevated per-tenant KV growth tied to a small cohort of streams. Dashboards: /d/pool/dedicated-docuserve/kv-heap shows step change at 14:06.
Found scheduler state where connections were in STREAM_OPEN but token output paused for >30s; slot still marked active. Idle-timeout was 60s (configured for this pool).
Autoscaler logs show memory prediction model used historical per-request averages; short-lived high-memory prefetch patterns were treated as outliers and not weighted, so reactive scale-up lagged ~3m.
Hypothesis: combination of long-context prefetch and human-typed pauses created a repeatable pattern where slots are reserved but not utilized, and autoscaler's smoothing underestimates required memory headroom.
Cross-ref Slack: #support thread "SUP-821970-docuserve-kv-surge" contains traces and customer repro. Engineering alerted runtime team and scheduler on-call.
Aisha Kaur (Support) 2026-03-12 14:25: Customer reports 70% throughput drop starting 14:06. I'm attaching initial logs and asking for priority routing to scheduler/infra.
Diego Martinez (SRE) 2026-03-12 14:32: Noted. Investigating autoscaler predictions and idle-timeout behavior. Pushing temporary config change to reduce idle-timeout for this pool to 15s as an experiment.
Evan Lee (Runtime) 2026-03-12 14:40: Observed KV cache ramp; runtime emits prefetch_size metric. Proposing to add per-tenant prefetch cap and to surface prediction signals to autoscaler.
Customer (DocuServe) 2026-03-12 15:05: Confirmed throughput recovering after reported config change; however concerned about recurrence under normal workload.
Mitigation applied (short-term): reduced idle-timeout on the affected dedicated pool from 60s to 15s to allow scheduler to reclaim silent streams and free slots; increased autoscaler memory smoothing sensitivity for the next 30 minutes to trigger earlier scale-up.\n\nWorkaround for customer: client should use explicit session-close on user pause events or reduce prefetch window for interactive prompts. Recommended temporary client-side change: set streaming keepalive lower during pauses.\n\nPlanned long-term fixes:\n- Add per-tenant KV-prefetch caps or adaptive prefetch that respects current pool headroom.\n- Augment autoscaler memory predictor with tail-aware features that weight recent high-memory events more heavily.\n- Expose scheduler idle signals to the console and add an automated policy to preempt stalls when pool saturation crosses threshold.\n- Follow-up PR created to runtime: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/1198 (adds prefetch cap and new metric).
INT-4042: Create autoscaler model update ticket to include tail-weighting and short-burst detection.
SUP-821965: Customer follow-up to validate client change and collect post-mitigation metrics for 48h.
ENG: Implement per-tenant prefetch cap and publish config knob in release notes.
OPS: Add console alert when pool idle-slot-reserve ratio exceeds 25%.
payload.summary: Dedicated pool throughput collapse from rapid KV-prefetch memory surge and silent-stream slot hoarding

2. Trigger ephemeral worker warmup/thaw while rolling a model variant to the same serving pool.

- Circuit-breaker configs were marginally tuned for steady-state and did not handle simultaneous thaw+swap well.

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customer (DataSense Labs) observed recurring soft-429s during a 5–10 minute window that coincides with a nightly background sweep job and our token refill boundary. They are running a mix of low-latency synchronous generation (short-chat requests) and a fleet of long-lived background workers that poll/generate periodically for embeddings and telemetry.

Impact:
Intermittent 429 responses for short-lived interactive traffic at ~00:00 local time for the tenant. Customer reports user-facing failures for ~3–8% of requests during the window; page reload/backoff mitigates but impacts latency and UX.

Environment:
- Dedicated pool (reserved GPUs) in prod-us-west (us-west-2)
- Single tenant with route separation configured but shared burst/baseline refill windows
- Background sweep job (internal orchestrator) runs every night at 00:00 local and fanouts ~150 workers performing periodic embeddings and health checks
- Rate-limiter configured with a burst pool and sustained window; background jobs use the same API key scope as interactive routes

Steps to reproduce:
1) Schedule background sweep to run at top-of-hour (00:00) with 150 parallel workers doing short API calls (200–500ms each).
2) Send steady low-latency interactive traffic at ~10 req/s from 50 concurrent clients.
3) Observe response headers and 429s returned for interactive requests during the refill boundary.

Observed behavior:
- X-RateLimit-Remaining drops to 0 for tenant-level keys during the window.
- 429 responses show headers: X-RateLimit-Limit: 60000, X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0, X-RateLimit-Reset: 61s (approx).
- Token refill logs show a refill epoch at 00:00 with heavy background-worker accounting inflating immediate consumption.

Expected behavior:
- Background sweep should not spike tenant-visible consumption in a way that causes interactive requests to receive 429s; or the platform should allow isolation of background vs realtime lanes (burst pool separation) so interactive traffic remains unaffected.

Attachments:
- Customer provided request timeline and sample headers (attached in ticket).
- Server-side refill trace snippets and rate-limiter logs pulled by Support (see investigation_notes).

Additional context:
Customer requests prescriptive guidance and short-term workarounds (no infra changes on their side ideally), plus recommendations for long-term config patterns for dedicated pools mixing background sweep jobs and interactive traffic.

Additional notes:
2026-03-01 - Support (Diego Alvarez): Thanks for the report — we need three things to triage: 1) sample request IDs/time ranges for the 429s, 2) the schedule for your background sweep (timezone + concurrency), and 3) confirmation whether the background workers use short-lived ephemeral keys or the same long-lived API key. We'll pull refill and rate-limiter traces for the tenant once we have those.
Also: background workers perform a keepalive ping every 30s during the sweep window for orchestration reasons.
2026-03-02 - Support (Diego Alvarez): Shared initial findings: refill epoch at 00:00 sees a large instantaneous accounting from the background sweep and keepalive pings. This consumes burst credits and leaves interactive routes without burst capacity for ~60–120s while refill smoothing catches up. Recommending immediate mitigations and a long-term isolation plan (see investigation_notes and resolution_notes).
2026-03-03 - SRE (Priya Nair): Investigation confirms that keepalive pings and readiness probes from k8s health checks were counted against tenant quota. Also observed minor clock skew (~2s) between some edge proxies causing small refill window drift; combined with fanout the effect is amplified. Proposal: 1) exempt internal health-check endpoints from rate accounting via route-level policy, 2) schedule sweep outside of refill boundary or use staggered startup, 3) configure dedicated burst pool for interactive routes or separate API key scope for background workers.
2026-03-05 - Support (Diego Alvarez): Marking resolved after customer confirmed success. Follow-up: submitted INT ticket to infra to add a runbook for dedicated pools about 'refill alignment and background-job isolation' and a console UX suggestion to show per-route burst pool usage.
Pulled token-refill logs for tenant_id: ds-778; saw epoch spikes at 00:00 PDT on 2026-03-01 and 00:00 PDT on 2026-03-02 correlating with customer request IDs.
Observed a burst of ~150 concurrent short requests (50–200ms) plus ~150 keepalive pings within the first 30s of the refill epoch.
Rate-limiter accounting currently counts readiness/healthcheck endpoints; these were being called by orchestrator during the sweep and incrementing tenant token usage.
Edge proxy traces show ~2s clock skew between two ingress clusters which caused some refill-window misalignment; when combined with fanout this produced near-simultaneous accounting across shards.
No anomalies found in autoscaler logs for the dedicated pool; GPU availability and serving-runtime latency were normal during events.
Temporary mitigation (customer applied): staggered worker startups + disabling keepalive reduced immediate burst; observed falloff from ~6% 429 to <0.5% in subsequent runs.
Long-term configuration options evaluated: route-level burst isolation, separate API key scope for background workers, scheduling sweeps outside refill epoch, platform-side smoothing of refill epochs for dedicated pools, and explicit exemption rules for health-check endpoints.
Filed INT follow-up to consider default docs/console guidance for dedicated customers mixing background jobs and interactive lanes.
Workaround applied and validated by customer: staggered sweep startup + disable keepalive during sweep reduced 429s to <0.5%. Recommended short-term actions for customer: 1) create a separate API key scoped to background workers to isolate accounting, 2) schedule sweep to start off-boundary from tenant refill epoch, or stagger worker start times by group. Recommended platform-side / long-term actions (internal): 1) provide an option to exempt health-check/keepalive endpoints from tenant token accounting via route policy, 2) add a console warning when a tenant's refill epoch coincides with a scheduled high-fanout job, 3) consider smoothing refill boundaries across shards for dedicated pools to reduce epoch-amplification on fanouts.
Follow-ups: INT-330 created to track runbook/doc updates and PR#2210 opened to prototype a route-exempt flag for health-check paths. Customer confirmed resolution on 2026-03-05 and is scheduling separate API keys as a durable fix.
INT: Update dedicated-pool runbook with guidelines for mixing background workers and interactive lanes (assigned INT-330).
Engineering: Evaluate and prototype route-level exemption flag for health-check endpoints (PR#2210 reference).
Support/CS: Draft short KB article for customers on 'Avoiding refill-boundary spikes' with recommended config snippets and sample curl/route examples.
Customer: Implement separate API key for background workers and schedule future sweeps off-refill-window; Support to verify after change.
payload.summary: Advice on configuring dual-refill windows for sync API and long-lived background workers to avoid late-window 429s

Issue summary:
Customer (Finexia Payments) reports intermittent control-plane authentication failures originating from nodes in their VPCE-backed private deployment. Failures correlate with short windows (30s-2m) every 10-30 minutes where model requests fail with TLS auth errors and gRPC 14 (UNAVAILABLE) on control-plane RPCs.

Impact:
- API calls that trigger model pulls or route-metadata requests fail briefly, leading to 5xx responses for user-facing inference requests.
- Affects production inference for two model families; observed retries succeed after short interval. No permanent data loss but elevated error rate and failed transactions for time-sensitive workflows.

Environment:
- Private (VPCE) deployment for Finexia Payments (enterprise).
- Region: us-east-1.
- VPCE type: Interface endpoint + ALB in front of control-plane NLB. Split-horizon DNS used by customer to resolve internal VPCE aliases.

Steps to reproduce:
1) From a customer subnet behind their firewall, establish long-lived gRPC streaming session to Redwood control-plane (auth + route info).
2) Observe occasional TLS handshake failures on the control-plane connection.
3) Trigger model pull request; some requests return gRPC UNAVAILABLE with TLS alerts (handshake failure or bad_certificate).

Logs / Observations:
- Serving node logs show TLS handshake errors: "tls: remote error: illegal parameter" and "handshake failure: sni mismatch" for a subset of control-plane peers.
- Customer packet captures show alternation between two backend IPs behind their LB where Server Name in ClientHello is rewritten to an alias by their DNS resolver for certain subnets.
- VPCE flow logs show short-lived TCP resets timed with the failure windows.
- No recent changes on Redwood control-plane cert chain. Customer rotated an internal ALB alias policy two days prior.

Initial hypothesis:
- Split-horizon DNS plus ALB aliasing results in client resolving to an alias that maps to a backend that expects a different SNI (internal cert name). The ALB (or customer LB) sometimes advertises a cert chain that does not match the SNI sent by the Redwood client, causing TLS auth failure for control-plane RPCs. The VPCE interface endpoint and ALB health probing may force backend flips mid-handshake.

Temporary workaround applied:
- Customer configured their DNS to prefer the canonical control-plane hostnames for affected subnets (bypassing alias). Error rate dropped in observed windows.

Next steps / investigation planned:
- Support to validate whether Redwood control-plane accepts the alias SNI (review cert SANs and virtual host mapping).
- SRE to correlate backend ALB health-check timing with failure windows.
- Request customer to attach tcpdump of failing handshake and ALB access logs for the 10:00-12:00 UTC window.
- Create a short-term routing recommendation for the customer (pin control-plane fqdn or add VPCE DNS override).

Desired resolution criteria:
- Confirm root cause and produce runbook actions for customers using split-horizon DNS + ALB aliasing.
- Implement any server-side toleration if safe (e.g., accept alias SNI when cert SANs permit) or document unsupported configuration.

2026-03-12 14:05 - Support (Aisha Patel): Opened ticket after customer reported repeated 5xxs; asked for packet captures and ALB logs.
2026-03-12 15:22 - Customer (Finexia NOC): Provided tcpdump showing ClientHello SNI equals 'control.internal.finexia' while DNS returned alias 'rwd-cp-alias.finexia.local' for certain subnets.
2026-03-12 16:10 - SRE (Marco Ruiz): Observed matching TLS handshake errors in our ingress logs; asked infra team to pull ALB access logs and health-check timing.
2026-03-12 18:45 - Customer: Temporarily added DNS override to resolve canonical host for control-plane; error rate visibly reduced during test window.
2026-03-13 09:05 - SRE (Marco Ruiz): Correlated ALB backend rotation and short health-check flaps with failure windows. Preparing summary and proposed runbook entry.
Customer applied DNS override to prefer canonical control-plane hostname; reduces failures until permanent fix is applied.
Ongoing investigation. SRE to recommend configuration guidance and evaluate allowing alias SNI in control-plane cert mapping if secure. Update expected: 2026-03-15.

Issue summary:
Customers using long-lived multiplexed connections to the embeddings endpoint observe intermittent 'holes' in rerank results (missing top candidates) and elevated tail latency during short bursts. Problem started after a recent proxy roll (2026-03-10) and affects multiplexed HTTP/2 + h2c request flows on the api-gateway.

Impact:
- Findly.ai reports 2-5% of requests return fewer candidates than expected, causing user-visible search regressions.
- Tail latency for rerank end-to-end increases to >2s during 5-10s bursts.
- Occurs intermittently (~once per 5k requests) but reproducible with a crafted multiplexed test harness.

Environment:
- prod, us-east region, api-gateway behind envoy proxy, HTTP/2 multiplexing enabled, client: internal multiplex test harness / real Findly traffic.
- Affected models: open-embed-v2-384 (embeddings), open-rerank-lite (reranker service).

Steps to reproduce:
1) Open 8 simultaneous HTTP/2 streams over one connection to /v1/embeddings (multiplexing enabled).
2) Send a mix of short and long payloads: 30% long (2K tokens), 70% short (<= 128 tokens) across streams in interleaved order.
3) Wait for responses and pass embedding vectors into reranker in the same submit order.
4) Observe occasional missing candidates and higher tail latency when a long request completes while other streams are queued.

Observed behavior:
- When a long stream finishes, a small number (~1-2) of following short-stream embeddings arrive with incorrect ordering metadata (stream-id mismatch) at the reranker, which causes candidate sets to be dropped by the reranker service and triggers client retries.
- Proxy metrics show burst queue depth spikes in envoy and increased stream reset (RST_STREAM) counts correlated with missing candidates.

Expected behavior:
- Multiplexed streams should preserve per-request ordering and metadata mapping. Embeddings responses should be attributed to the correct request and delivered to the reranker without loss.

Logs / traces (sanitized snippets):
- envoy: "stream 42 RST_STREAM reason=REFUSED_STREAM" followed by "stream 43 response completed, stream_id=42-mismatch detected" (seen in proxy logs).
- serving-runtime: "received embed response for request_id=dy8jf1, client_stream=8, mapped_request=dy8jf2" (mapping inconsistency).
- reranker: "drop: candidate_batch_id=cb-998 missing_vectors=1".

Notes:
- This ticket is customer-facing; Findly is blocking a production rollout. They are on enterprise with SLA.
- Appears after proxy roll 2026-03-10; suspect interaction between envoy's connection-level flow control and our per-request metadata tagging layer when streams complete out-of-order.
2026-03-12 11:02 - Support acknowledged and collected pcap + proxy logs from Findly (Leah K)
2026-03-12 13:12 - Reproduced locally with multiplex harness. Observed stream-id reuse and mapping mismatch in adapter layer (Marco A)
2026-03-12 15:40 - SRE runbook check: no infra CPU/GPU pressure. Envoy upgrade to 1.35.2 rolled 2026-03-10 is primary delta (Ilya P)

Additional notes:
2026-03-13 09:30 - Staging test with artificial delay reproduces 100% once stream metadata object pool size < 16. Without pooling, no mismatches observed (Marco A)
2026-03-13 11:10 - Confirmed envoy RST_STREAM behavior with flow-control window shrink under burst; this interacts with adapter's retry path causing duplicate/shifted mapping (SRE: Ilya P)
Enabled detailed per-stream diagnostics in staging and prod for a subset of traffic (feature flag: stream-diagnostics)
Temporarily increased adapter metadata pool size to 128 in staging to reduce reuse races
Applied a canary config to envoy to disable REFUSED_STREAM optimization for 10% traffic in staging
Coordinated with Customer success to collect reproducer harness and traffic patterns from Findly
Short-term mitigation: disable HTTP/2 multiplexing for the customer's connection (api key level) or set client to open one request per connection. This prevents the interleaving scenario while we fix the adapter. We provided instructions to Findly and applied a temporary per-customer mux-disable flag.
Race condition in the adapter layer's stream metadata pool combined with envoy's REFUSED_STREAM behavior under bursty flow-control; metadata object reused while a prior stream's completion callback still in-flight, causing misattribution of embedding responses to requests.

payload.description:
Customer (Northstar Health Systems) is planning an on-prem / air-gapped upgrade of Redwood Private and is requesting a clear, operator-friendly rollback procedure that can be shared internally for change control.

Request details (from customer):
- They need step-by-step rollback instructions suitable for an IT ops runbook, including what is and is not supported (e.g., Helm rollback vs restore-from-backup).
- They require clarity on expected downtime/RTO and what artifacts must be preserved (offline bundle, chart versions, container images, DB backups, PV snapshots).
- They have strict constraints:
  - Air-gapped environment (offline bundle only, no outbound registry/chart repo access).
  - Change windows are short (2 hours max) with a hard stop where they must revert.
  - Audit/compliance requires evidence of backups taken and a deterministic rollback path.

What they are upgrading:
- Redwood Private control plane + data plane via Helm in their own Kubernetes cluster.
- Current version: customer reports they are pinned to an N-1 release (exact patch TBD; they mentioned 2.9.x in email).

Customer questions to answer:
1) If the upgrade fails mid-way (e.g., DB migration or control plane rollout), what are the exact steps to revert?
2) Is a Helm rollback supported? If not, what is the supported rollback mechanism?
3) What preconditions must be met to roll back safely (snapshots, dumps, stopping components, etc.)?
4) What data can be lost (if any) and how to verify system health post-rollback?

Support goal:
- Provide an accurate rollback procedure based on current GA capabilities (not aspirational), while aligning with the upcoming upgrade/rollback work so the customer does not build an incorrect internal process.
2025-05-29 09:14 PT — Dev Patel (Support) — Ticket created after customer asked for rollback guarantees and a written procedure for on-prem upgrades. Customer explicitly asked for something they can attach to their CAB/change request.
2025-05-29 10:02 PT — Owen Phillips (Support Escalation SME) — Acknowledged. Key point to set expectations: today, rollback is supported via restore-from-backup taken immediately before upgrade (DB + config + PV snapshots), not via Helm rollback. Will draft customer-facing steps and validate with SRE/Release Eng.
2025-05-29 12:21 PT — Rafael Mendes (SRE) — Confirming: Helm rollback is not considered safe once DB migrations run. If any migration step has executed, the only supported rollback is full restore (DB restore + PV snapshot restore as applicable) to the pre-upgrade point-in-time. Also recommend pausing data plane rollouts first to reduce blast radius.
2025-05-30 08:37 PT — Connor O'Brien (Release Eng) — For air-gapped: ensure they retain the full pre-upgrade offline bundle (charts + images + manifests) and checksums. If they overwrite their mirror with new tags, rollback becomes hard. Recommend immutable, versioned directories in their artifact mirror (e.g., /redwood-private/2.9.3 and /redwood-private/2.10.0).
2025-05-30 11:05 PT — Michael Nguyen (Migrations) — Add guidance: if upgrade fails during migration, do not attempt a "downgrade" by running older pods against a migrated DB. Restore the DB from the pre-upgrade backup. For Postgres, prefer pg_dump/pg_restore for logical backup (or a storage snapshot if their storage backend supports consistent snapshots).
2025-06-02 09:18 PT — Owen Phillips (Support) — Sent customer a draft rollback procedure (below) and asked them to confirm their current versions (installer + chart + platform) and storage backend.

Draft rollback procedure (customer-facing, current GA):
A. Before upgrade (required to have a rollback path)
1) Ensure you have the full pre-upgrade artifact set stored offline:
   - The offline bundle for the currently running version (charts + images + manifests).
   - Checksums/signature file if provided.
2) Take backups immediately before running the upgrade:
   - Control plane database backup (Postgres logical dump) and verify you can restore it.
   - Snapshot persistent volumes for stateful services (where supported) or capture storage-level snapshots.
   - Export cluster config relevant to Redwood (Helm values, secrets references, cert material references).
3) Record current versions:
   - Chart version(s), Redwood Private version, and installer version.

B. When to rollback
- Rollback is recommended if:
  - Control plane does not become Ready after upgrade within your maintenance window.
  - DB migrations error or exceed your change window.
  - Auth/OIDC integration breaks and cannot be remediated quickly.

C. Rollback steps (supported)
1) Stop further change:
   - Halt any automation applying charts.
   - If data plane rollout is in progress, pause/stop it first.
2) Restore to pre-upgrade backups:
   - Restore the control plane DB from the backup taken immediately before upgrade.
   - Restore PV snapshots (or storage snapshots) for stateful components if they were mutated during upgrade.
3) Re-deploy the previous version artifacts:
   - Re-apply the previous chart(s) and manifests from the pre-upgrade offline bundle.
   - Ensure your image registry points to the pre-upgrade image set.
4) Post-rollback verification:
   - Confirm control plane health checks.
   - Confirm data plane routing works.
   - Confirm audit logs and auth integrations.

D. Explicitly not supported / cautions
- Helm rollback is not supported once DB migrations have applied.
- Do not run older control plane pods against a DB that has been migrated forward.

Also offered a 30-min call to tailor this to their storage backend and their change window.
2025-06-03 14:44 PT — Dev Patel (Support) — Customer replied: they use CSI-backed storage with snapshot support, and want a single PDF-like doc. They also asked: "Is there a way to do a rollback without restoring PVs, just DB?"
2025-06-04 09:27 PT — Irene Choi (Infra) — Answer: depends on which PVs are used and whether any stateful components store upgrade-time state outside DB. Conservative guidance: assume PV restore is required unless we can confirm components are stateless or only cache. For model cache PVs: usually can be cleared/rebuilt, but we should not present that as universal without confirming their deployment topology.
2025-06-05 10:11 PT — Owen Phillips (Support) — Responded to customer: DB-only rollback may be possible if PVs contain only rebuildable caches, but safest supported rollback remains DB restore + PV restore for stateful services. Asked them to provide which PVCs they have and what components are stateful in their install (control-plane DB PVC, object store, model cache).
2025-06-06 16:03 PT — Kenji Nakamura (UX) — FYI: upcoming installer work will include a first-class rollback command that consumes stored upgrade state and runs deterministic hooks. Not GA yet; do not promise timelines to customer. Point them to the current runbook excerpt and we can update once GA.
2025-06-07 09:41 PT — Owen Phillips (Support) — Final: Provided a cleaned-up rollback procedure (same content as draft, reworded as a runbook) and linked the relevant Redwood internal/external-aligned docs section for upgrades + troubleshooting. Marking as Resolved; follow-up task: convert to customer-facing doc snippet once docs PR lands.
Provided customer with a supported rollback procedure for current GA behavior: restore-from-pre-upgrade backups (DB + PV snapshots as applicable) and re-deploy prior version artifacts from the pre-upgrade offline bundle. Set expectations that Helm rollback is not supported once DB migrations have applied. Offered a tailoring call and requested storage/PVC details to refine DB-only vs DB+PV guidance for their topology.
Do not oversell the upcoming rollback command. Customer-facing language must remain: supported rollback is restore-from-backup. If customer presses for guarantees, route to Solutions (Markus Klein) + PM (Vivek Kulkarni) for contract/SLA language. Consider adding a short, sanitized "Rollback (On-Prem)" section to external docs once aligned with: rollback semantics page + private upgrade runbook + backup/restore strategy. Ensure we align with auditability requirements (backup evidence + timestamps) and offline bundle immutability guidance.
payload.summary: Request: documented rollback procedure for Redwood Private (on-prem / air-gapped) upgrades

Issue summary: LuminaHealth reported a sudden per-token cost increase (~3x) and elevated 5xx rates for a specific tenant after enabling a combined optimization bundle (dynamic batching bump, aggressive KV prefetch, int8 quant profile). Impact: production traffic for LuminaHealth faced degraded tail latency, increased cost, and user-visible errors for ~15% of sessions. Environment: Dedicated capacity, prod-us-east, tenant id TLN-998. First observed: 2026-03-10 09:12 UTC. Customer timeframe: they enabled the optimizer bundle via Console feature flags during a morning deployment window.
1) On a dedicated tenant using redwood/open-7b-int8-v2, enable: (a) dynamic_batching.max_batch_size=2048 (b) kv_prefetch.enabled=true (c) quant_profile=aggressive-int8-v2. 2) Ramp traffic to steady QPS similar to LuminaHealth (~1.8x baseline). 3) Observe a spike in per-token CPU/GPU churn, KV eviction spikes, and increased 5xx/timeouts. Note: issue reproduces within 10-20 minutes for this workload distribution.
- spikes in serving-runtime OOM-ish evictions: eviction_rate tenant TLN-998 +420% at 09:19 UTC. - tail latency (95/99p) rose from 160ms/320ms to 480ms/1.9s. - backend 5xx rate increased from 0.2% to 3.7% for the tenant. - KV cache miss ratio jumped when prefetch collided with async evictions. - Billing spike: estimated per-token compute cost x2.9 for the affected window. Relevant logs: /logs/prod/us-east/serving/TLN-998/2026-03-10-09*.gz
Customer rolled the toggle back once but re-applied the optimizer bundle with a slightly higher batch size; reported inconsistent results. They captured a short recording and A/B traffic split showing the degradation tied to the combined flags rather than any single change.
Initial hypothesis: interaction between aggressive batching, int8 execution path, and KV prefetch created contention for memory and CPU/GPU transfer resources leading to eviction churn and excessive kernel fallback. Checks performed: - Confirmed tenant-specific snapshot of optimizer flags via Console. - Queried runtime traces: saw frequent kernel re-selection for int8 paths and repeated KV cache eviction events. - Checked autoscaler: no global shortage but per-gpu memory pressure for tenant-scheduled pods. - Confirmed no infra-level network errors in the window. Correlation: pattern matches previous incidents where mixed aggressive quant + prefetch caused oscillation (see linked SUP-96122).
1) Applied immediate per-tenant throttling: rate cap lowered by 30% for TLN-998 at 09:34 UTC. 2) Forced routing to fallback model variant redwood/open-7b-fp16 for the tenant at 09:40 UTC. 3) Disabled kv_prefetch for the tenant at 09:42 UTC. 4) Snapshot restore: rehydrated last known-good optimizer snapshot (2026-03-09) to ensure baseline flags. Effects: 5xx rate reduced back toward baseline within 8 minutes; tail latency normalized after model fallback and kv_prefetch disable.
The primary cause appears to be a resource contention feedback loop: aggressive batching increased per-request resource footprint on the int8 path; concurrent KV prefetch increased memory pressure and eviction churn; the runtime's kernel selection fell back intermittently causing amplification in latency and compute. The combination produced a cost/throughput regression not seen when any single optimization was enabled alone.
Resolved for the immediate incident by: (a) enforcing temporary tenant throttles, (b) switching tenant traffic to fp16 variant, (c) disabling kv_prefetch, and (d) restoring last-known-good optimizer snapshot. Customer confirmed service returned to acceptable latency and cost profile by 2026-03-10 09:53 UTC. Status: mitigated, monitoring for recurrence.
1) Add per-tenant safety gates that prevent enabling aggressive quant + kv_prefetch + high batch_size simultaneously without staged rollouts. 2) Implement a runtime circuit-breaker metric (combined memory-eviction + kernel-fallback) to auto-demote to conservative profile. 3) Create a Console preflight check that simulates resource impact for a tenant using representative traffic. 4) Update docs with explicit matrix of compatible optimizer flags and recommended staging steps. 5) Schedule a follow-up E2E test with LuminaHealth traffic patterns in staging.
Create per-tenant optimizer gate (ENG-optimizer #1228)
Add circuit-breaker metric and automation (ENG-runtime #1299)
Confluence: publish optimizer compatibility matrix
Run staging replay for LuminaHealth workload 2026-03-15
Customer notified of mitigations and agreed to staged re-test under Support supervision. Engineering to own follow-up tasks; Support will keep the ticket open until the automation and gating are in place and tested with the customer.

2026-03-10 09:33 - SRE (Ravi Singh): Applied temporary rate cap and pushed fallback routing to fp16 variant; monitoring for improvements.
2026-03-10 09:44 - Customer (LuminaHealth - Priya Desai): Noted latency improved after fallback; asked for recommended safe re-enable steps.
2026-03-11 11:02 - Eng (Marco Li): Confirmed kernel fallback pattern; suggested lowering dynamic_batching.max_batch_size to 512 and testing incremental kv_prefetch with pre-warm windows.

Issue summary: Since 2026-03-09 ~18:00 UTC Noteable Analytics (dedicated deployment in us-east) reports large increases in end-to-end request latency and intermittent request timeouts when tool/function calling is enabled. Impact: user-facing endpoints for document enrichment and extraction see tail latency spikes from ~200ms to 6–15s, and some requests hit the platform 30s request timeout. Preliminary hypothesis: schema validation and an extra validation/proxy round-trip introduced when tool calls are enabled is adding synchronous network hops under certain request paths, magnifying tail latency under bursty traffic. Environment: Dedicated pool, single model pinned redwood-v2-13b, API route /v1/generate with tool_call enabled and schema_validation=on. Reproducibility: intermittent; correlates with bursts and requests that include tool_metadata and complex tool schemas.
1) On a dedicated deployment with model pinned (redwood-v2-13b), enable tool_call and schema_validation flags for a route.
2) Send a mix of short and long prompts (100–800 tokens) that trigger a function/tool call (tool metadata schema attached).
3) Increase concurrency to 80–120 RPS to simulate production burst from the customer.
4) Observe end-to-end latency and streaming behavior; some requests time out at ~30s and streaming disconnects occur.
5) Toggle schema_validation to false and re-run the same load to compare latency distribution.

Synchronous control-plane schema validation performed by function-proxy for every request that includes dynamic tool schemas. Under bursty traffic, schema-validator service threadpool and control-plane networking became saturated, adding 200–1200ms per request and causing occasional retries/timeouts which amplified tail latency.
Workarounds: 1) Customer disabled schema_validation for hot routes (verified reduction in tail latency). 2) Recommend increasing API request timeout to 60s for long-running jobs as a temporary mitigation. Permanent fix: Runtime team approved schema caching in function-proxy and an async validation flow for known schemas (PRs created). Plan: deploy schema-cache v1 to staging 2026-03-14 and to us-east prod canary 2026-03-16 followed by a full rollout.

Issue summary:
Customer reports intermittent 429 responses for interactive chat calls routed through their Dedicated pool after we applied a route weight reallocation. The errors appear opaque (429 with minimal throttle headers) and affect a small subset of API keys for the account. Behavior began immediately after a background reweight job ran at 2026-03-12T02:00:00Z.

Impact:
- Customer's low-latency chat flow experiences ~5-10% request failures (429) for a 90-minute window during the reweighting activity.
- Customer is on a committed Dedicated pool and requires predictable throughput for business-critical chat sessions.

Environment:
- Deployment: Dedicated pool (tenant: triton-analytics-dedicated-01)
- Region: us-west-2
- Routes: chat-stream (priority class: low-latency), ingest-bulk (background warmup)

Expected behavior:
- Route weight changes should not cause opaque 429s; throttle headers should indicate remaining tokens and refill schedule.

Actual behavior:
- Intermittent 429 responses lacking consistent X-RateLimit-Remaining and X-Refill-Timestamp values.
- Errors correlate with background route weight shift and autoscaler warmup traffic spikes.

Steps to reproduce (from customer):
1) Schedule a route weight reallocation that increases weight for background ingest route by 3x for 10 minutes.
2) Simultaneously run steady interactive chat traffic from 10 workers (session token reuse).
3) Observe occasional 429 responses on chat-stream requests during the weight change window.

Notes: customer provided a small client replay and traced timestamps (see logs).
Trigger a route weight reallocation that boosts background route weight for a short period
Maintain low-latency chat traffic concurrently from multiple worker processes
Monitor for 429s and inspect throttle response headers and console token-window graphs
2026-03-12T02:03:12.123Z ERROR 429 /v1/chat  key=ak_live_XXXX - missing X-RateLimit-Remaining header
Grafana: rate_limiter.token_window_usage{route="chat-stream",tenant="triton-analytics"} spike at 2026-03-12T02:01:50Z
Sentry: repeated 429 traces with parent request id and no throttle metadata; sample id: 9f2c4a
Initial hypothesis: token refill orchestration lag between route-weight controller and rate-limiter leading to temporary misallocation of burst credits
Observed: dedicated-pool autoscaler issued warmup traffic on the background route during the same time window (confirmed in autoscaler logs). Warmup traffic appears to have been counted against tenant burst pool in addition to route-level bucket.
Rate-limiter code path review: there is a smoothing/refill pass that runs on a per-route schedule; route weight updates are applied asynchronously and may not be atomic with refill window alignment
Correlated metrics show token-window counter decrement on chat-stream while ingest route weight increased — suggests cross-route accounting when burst pools are shared
Throttle headers are missing when the gateway path returns an internal shortcut 429 path (we found a code path that returns early when shared-burst pool is marked exhausted)
Reproduction in staging: We reproduced a smaller-scale 429 surge when programmatically triggering a weight reallocation and simultaneously pushing background warmup traffic; headers were present there, pointing to partial metadata propagation in prod path (edge proxy to origin header rewrite suspected)

Marta Gonzales (SRE) (2026-03-12): Confirmed autoscaler warmup events at 2026-03-12T02:00:45Z. Extracted ingress logs; found some requests returned by edge without throttle headers. Added a high-priority trace to follow header propagation.

Ship hotfix to edge-proxy to populate throttle headers on early 429 exit path (PR ready: edge-proxy/pull/241)
Deploy route-weight controller change to apply weight and trigger a refill alignment event atomically
Add an automated canary test that replays weight changes while generating mixed background and interactive traffic
Add dashboard panel showing per-route burst pool attribution during reweight events
Document recommended operator practice: perform weight reallocation with background route in paused warmup mode or staggered windows

payload.description:
Issue summary: After a customer-installed BPF-based flowlog/monitoring agent was deployed in their private VPC, several serving nodes in the customer's private deploy began exhibiting transient gRPC stream resequencing. Symptoms included repeated token-cache misses, partial model shard re-fetches, and application-layer 5xxs on long-lived streaming requests. Impact: Customer reports elevated request latencies and a ~12% increase in failed streaming sessions for production traffic to the Llama2-13B-v2 model in us-east-1. This is customer-impacting for their production workload.
1) Deploy the customer's BPF flowlog agent with default config (includes packet capture + promiscuous flag enabled) on hosts in the private VPC.
2) Start sustained production workload hitting streaming chat endpoints using pinned model 'llama2-13b-v2'.
3) Observe gRPC stream retransmits and application-layer retries within 2-10 minutes.
4) Collect tcpdump and ethtool/RPS counters on the affected ENI node.
- Initial hypothesis: packet duplication or reordering at kernel/driver level due to promiscuous-mode BPF hooks interacting with NIC Gro/Gso and RPS/RFS steering.
- Customer confirmed they deployed a third-party flowlog agent (v2.1.4) which uses kernel BPF tc/ingress hooks and enables promiscuous mode to capture mirrored traffic.
- Observed elevated rx_packets twice as high as expected on affected ENI.
- Kernel RPS/RFS CPU masks show non-uniform steering after agent install; many packets steered to a CPU not running serving process leading to out-of-order handoff between RX and processing cores.
- gRPC traces show out-of-order sequence numbers and occasional retransmits; KV cache invalidations correlate with retransmit windows.
- No changes in our serving runtime or model artifacts detected in same window.
- Reproduced locally in customer's staging by toggling agent's promiscuous option: with promiscuous off, symptoms disappear in 3m; with on, resequencing and 5xxs return.
- /var/log/agent/flowlog.log: 'interface eth0: set promiscuous mode ON' at 2026-03-09T22:14:05Z
- kernel ring buffer snippet: 'eth0: GRO: packet reordering detected: rps rcpu mismatch' repeated
- tcpdump (sample): see packet timestamps showing small out-of-order delivery across same TCP connection (captured pcap attached by customer: ds_flowlog_bpf_0310.pcap)
- serving runtime logs: 'kvcache: shard-read mismatch; initiating re-fetch' and 'grpc: stream reset due to duplicate-seq'
- agent metrics: flowlog_agent.capture.packets_total spike from 1.2M -> 2.6M per minute after deploy

Additional notes:
2026-03-10 14:30 - Customer: Provided BPF agent config and confirmed promiscuous_mode = true.
2026-03-12 10:05 - Networking team (SRE) joined call; suggested temporary mitigations and kernel tunables to pin RPS masks and disable GRO on affected ENI.
Third-party BPF-based flowlog agent enabled promiscuous mode which changed packet processing path and interacted with NIC/GRO and kernel RPS/RFS CPU steering. This caused micro reordering of packets handed to the serving process, leading to gRPC-level resequencing/retransmits and subsequent KV-cache coherence failures in the serving runtime.
Customer-side immediate mitigations applied: 1) Set flowlog agent 'promiscuous_mode' = false (agent config change). 2) Set sysctl net.core.rps_sock_flow_entries=32768 and pin rps_cpu masks for ENI to CPUs hosting serving processes. 3) Disable GRO for eth interface: 'ethtool -K eth0 gro off' if acceptable for their throughput. These reduced errors to baseline in staging and prod when applied carefully.
In progress: agreed mitigation path with customer. Customer has rolled agent config change (promiscuous_mode=false) and applied RPS pinning on 60% of affected nodes; error rate fell to <2% above baseline. Engineering action items: (a) add detection in agent healthcheck to flag promiscuous mode BPF installs; (b) create a runbook for customers describing recommended kernel tunables when using BPF capture; (c) add serving-runtime guard to tolerate brief resequencing windows without cache invalidation. PR opened: https://github.com/redwood-inference/agent/pull/1786 (adds warning and config validation).
ENG: Add RPS/RFS detection telemetry to serving nodes (ticket INT-5010)
DX: Update private-deploy checklist to call out BPF/promiscuous interactions (owner: Product Ops)
SRE: Formalize GRO disable guidance for high-capture workloads
payload.summary: Customer private deploy: BPF-based flowlog agent enabling promiscuous mode -> RPS/RFS CPU steering change causing gRPC packet resequencing and KV-cache divergence

Issue summary:
Customer BrightLens reported a production tail-latency regression after a combined rollout that changed the quantization profile and enabled aggressive prefix/KV cache prefetching for several dedicated pools. The change was deployed as a single staged rollout targeting the dedicated us-east pools; after the rollout completed, a subset of requests began to show 2--5x tail latency increases and intermittent 502s for long streaming responses.

Impact:
- User-facing: slow responses and occasional failed streams for ~9% of requests in the affected pools.
- Business: impacts BrightLens' inference SLAs for their internal quota-bearing tenant.

Environment:
- Dedicated GPU pool: brightlens-prod-us-east (NVIDIA H100, 8 gpus per node)
- Serving runtime: 2026.02.2-build
- Config service snapshot: snap-2026-03-10-21:18

Steps to reproduce (observed on prod metrics):
1) Send a 2k token streaming request to the chat endpoint pinned to vicuna-13b-v1 for the brightlens tenant.
2) Observe initial streaming tokens, then a stall where latency for token N+1000 increases dramatically compared to baseline.
3) Check request logs and see 502 or incomplete stream in ~1 out of 12 failing traces.

Expected behavior:
- No substantial change in P95/P99 latency for streaming long-context requests after optimizer/profile rollout.
- No 502s introduced by optimizer changes.

Actual behavior:
- P95 increased from ~180ms to ~480ms; P99 up to ~1.8s on large-context streaming requests in affected pool.
- 502s appear tied to internal timeouts during KV-cache prefetch + quantized kernel path for certain shard placements.

Immediate ask:
Guidance for a safe rollback plan that avoids data loss (preserve warmed KV cache where possible), minimizes customer downtime, and provides verification steps. Customer specifically requests a recommended sequence because quant profile and KV-cache toggles were interleaved in one change set.

Additional notes:
2026-03-11 14:28 - SRE Oncall (Priya Singh): Confirmed transient pod restarts in brightlens-prod-us-east starting 2026-03-11T13:40Z. Noticed elevated kernel fusion stall counters on nodes hosting model shard group G-3. Pinning network I/O looked normal.
Hypothesis 1: Quantization profile changed kernel selection causing a slow path at long attention windows on certain devices (H100 firmware + selected GEMM kernel mismatch).
Hypothesis 2: KV cache prefetch aggressive setting increased memory pressure and concurrent IO which amplified kernel stalls, leading to internal timeouts in the streaming pipeline.
Metric evidence: Correlation between hosts where quant profile flip occurred and elevated 'attention_kernel_slow' counter. Hosts with both quant flip and prefetch enabled showed highest error rates.
Log excerpts: timeouts in stream-writer: "write timeout after 120s"; serving-runtime stack traces show stalled kernel invocation during decode loop for sequence positions > 1024.
A/B rollback sanity check: Reverting only quant on a small subset returned P99 to baseline; reverting only KV-cache prefetch reduced 502s but did not fully restore P99. Suggests interaction effect.
1) Take a config snapshot: config-service create-snapshot --pool brightlens-prod-us-east --tag pre-rollback-2026-03-13
2) Phase A - Quant profile soft rollback: use gradual traffic split to move 30% of traffic off new quant profile to previous profile for vicuna-13b-v1. Command: redwoodctl rollout traffic --pool brightlens-prod-us-east --model vicuna-13b-v1 --from-profile quant-new-2026-03-10 --to-profile quant-stable-2026-02-28 --percent 30 --wait 60s
3) Monitor P95/P99, kernel stall counters, and 5xx rate for 15 minutes. If P99 reduction observed, continue to 60% then 100% in 20m increments.
4) If quant rollback alone does not fully resolve 502s, Phase B - KV cache pref instead of full flush: disable aggressive prefix prefetch at pool level (toggle to conservative prefetch) to avoid flushing warmed caches: redwoodctl config set --pool brightlens-prod-us-east --kv-prefetch conservative
5) If disabling prefetch is insufficient, perform controlled KV cache eviction on a single node to ensure a clean warm path: redwoodctl node evict-kv --node <node-id> --pool brightlens-prod-us-east, then observe behavior for that node before wider action.
6) Avoid doing both full-quant rollback and full cache flush simultaneously. Prefer quant rollback first, then conservative prefetch toggle, then targeted node-level evictions if needed.
7) Post-rollback validation: run a standardized set of long-context streaming synthetic requests (provided in runbook) and confirm P95/P99 are within 10% of baseline for 30 minutes; inspect streaming completeness and absence of 502s.
8) After verification, create a postmortem runbook item and schedule a follow-up config change that separates quant profile changes from cache prefetch toggles in future rollouts (no interleaved changes).
Workaround applied: Gradual rollback of quant profile to stable for vicuna-13b completed at 2026-03-13T03:12Z. P99 on rolled hosts dropped back to baseline within 2 minutes.
Customer-facing outcome: BrightLens confirmed improved response latency and reduced failed streams during their peak across the affected pool segments.
Permanent fix path: Recommend splitting future optimizer rollouts into two distinct steps with canary windows: (A) quant/profile changes validated on isolated shards; (B) KV-prefetch changes applied after at least 24h stable telemetry. Engineering to add a preflight check for 'kernel_slow' counters before promoting quant profiles.
Follow-up: ENG-OPS action item created to add health-check gating in the config-service for combined optimizer changes. Scheduled change review with BrightLens on 2026-03-18.
ENG: Implement kernel-slow preflight check in config-service (owner: @marcus). Target ETA: 2026-03-20.
SRE: Add automated alert that fires when 'attention_kernel_slow' counter increases > 3x baseline in a pool for 10m (owner: @priya).
CS: Coordinate BrightLens verification window and sign-off (owner: @ava).
PM: Update rollout playbook to disallow interleaved optimizer and cache changes in the same config snapshot.
