payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customer reported sustained request timeouts and streaming stalls during their nightly bulk shipment tokenization job (batch window 02:00-03:30 ET). A subset of requests experienced tokenization timeouts at the serving-runtime layer which cascaded into streaming stalls and client-side disconnects. Impact: ~18% of Cygnus production requests in the window returned 504/timeout and ~12% stream sessions closed without final chunk, impacting order confirmations and downstream workflows.

Impact:
- Customer reported order processing delays and duplicate background retries triggered by the client after streaming stalls.
- Temporary spike in token and request counts due to retries produced a billing exposure; Cygnus flagged for credit review.

Environment:
- prod, us-east-1, customer using enterprise account with pinned model redwood-open-3b and quantized variant for cost-sensitive routes.

Steps to reproduce (observed in-incident):
1) Customer submits parallelized batch tokenization job (500k short prompts) using streaming chat API with allow_partial=true.
2) Backend pressure on KV cache eviction increases due to skewed prefix distribution.
3) Tokenization workers fall back to slower kernel path for quantized model leading to high tail latency and internal timeouts.
4) Streaming connection resets observed in ~20s window after initial tokenization delay.

Relevant logs / signals:
- Serving-runtime trace IDs: sr:20260310:us-e-0a:trace:* (attached to incident folder).
- Autoscaler events: repeated scale-up/scale-down cycles between 02:12 and 02:36 (spike in instance churn).
- KV cache evictions increased 12x baseline; miss rate grew from 3% -> 35%.
- Router returned 504s with message "tokenizer_timeout" and streaming disconnects with ECONNRESET logged at edge.

Customer quote (initial):
"Large batches started failing mid-window. Streaming stopped giving final chunk and our retry logic duplicated jobs. We need assurance this won't happen at scale."

Additional notes:
Hypothesis 1: Kernel selection rollout (PR #1187) aggressively shifts quantized runs to new fast path without accounting for skewed prefix distributions; when prefix cache misses spike, execution falls back to a slower kernel inducing tokenization timeouts.
Hypothesis 2: Autoscaler reacts to increased per-instance CPU/memory by rapidly scaling up, but scale-down was triggered too aggressively when latency briefly improved, causing cold-start pressure and additional cache churn.
Data points: KV cache miss rate rose to 35% and TTL evictions increased. Correlated traces show tokenization step timeouts aligning with misses. The rollback at 03:00 reduced timeouts to baseline within 10 minutes.
Customer behavior: large parallel batch submitted with high prefix similarity causing hot keys and poor cache locality; allow_partial=true meant clients retried on timeout leading to duplicate downstream requests and billing spike.
Reproducibility: Synthetic test with same batch profile reproduced elevated tail latency when kernel-selection flag enabled; reproducer located in infra/tests/issue-240999-runbook.
Related items: linked INT-412 (autoscaler smoothing investigation) and SUP-70012 (previously similar failover pattern for dedicated capacity under quantized fallback).
Hotfix: Rolled back the kernel-selection thresholds (PR revert of serving-runtime PR #1187) and applied a temporary increased KV cache allocation for Cygnus' route to reduce evictions. Autoscaler policy adjusted to increase scale-down cooldown from 30s to 5m to avoid thrash. Customer received immediate mitigation; error rates returned to baseline by 03:20. Billing team approved a retroactive credit to cover duplicated jobs and retry-induced token counts. Incident bridge closed once success rate stabilized.
ENG-1221 (Runtime): Implement safe-guard for kernel-selection that rejects fast-path when KV miss-rate > 15% (owner: Ravi Patel) - target 2026-03-27
OPS-909 (Autoscaler): Add hysteresis and longer cooldown windows for scale-down during high-variance workloads; create canary for 48-hour monitoring (owner: Priya Nambiar) - target 2026-03-20
DX-77 (Docs/SDK): Update guidance for customers on large parallelized batch patterns: recommend prefix sharding and client-side jitter to avoid hot-keying (owner: Nadia Wallace) - target 2026-03-19
SRE-archive: Add Cygnus reproducer to incident runbooks and include telemetry dashboard with KV miss-rate + kernel path breakdown (owner: Elena Gomez) - target 2026-03-17
Finance: Finalize customer credit amount and close billing dispute (owner: Carla Ruiz) - target 2026-03-15
This incident was triggered by an aggressive kernel-selection rollout that did not account for a pathological request distribution from the customer's parallel tokenization job. The immediate rollback and cache allocation prevented further user-visible impact. Long-term mitigations include kernel-selection guards, autoscaler hysteresis, and customer-facing guidance to avoid hot-keying. All high-priority follow-ups assigned with owners and due dates. Customer expresses measured satisfaction with the response and accepted the credit offer.
Estimated duplicate-token exposure: ~650k tokens billed during incident window. Finance approved provisional credit; final reconciliation pending.

payload.description:
Issue summary: Customer sees intermittent truncated streamed responses and JSON parse failures when using SSE through their corporate reverse proxy. The client receives fragments (partial JSON objects) that never conclude with the terminal 'end' event. In many cases the final closing bracket and metadata are missing, causing the client's parser to throw and drop the response. Impact: End-user chat sessions sometimes render only partial paragraphs; escalated by Parcelly because this affects confirmation messages for shipments (~5-8% of streaming sessions during peak).
1) Customer environment: browser client opens SSE to our /v1/stream endpoint via an on-prem reverse proxy (corporate appliance) that applies aggressive idle timeouts (60s) and HTTP/1.1 to HTTP/2 conversion.
2) Start a long streaming generation (~>500 tokens) targeting redwood-open-13B pinned on dedicated capacity.
3) Simulate idle by pausing client network (background tab or manual pause) for ~70s to trigger proxy idle teardown.
4) Resume network and let client reconnect (SSE reconnection logic kicks in). Observe client logs: parser errors and missing terminal 'event: end' chunk; server logs show trailing bytes sent prior to connection close.
5) Repro with curl from within their network: `curl -N -H 'Accept: text/event-stream' https://api.redwood.example/v1/stream -v` and watch for truncated last event after proxy RST during idle timeout.
Excerpt from customer-provided client console: 'SSE parse error: Unexpected end of JSON input at position 243' — Upstream server logs (correlated) show 'connection half-closed: wrote tail bytes after FIN' and edge-proxy shows 'idle timeout: closed connection (RST)'. Packet-level capture (pcap) from customer shows server FIN then proxy RST while server still had buffered chunks to send.
2026-03-10 14:10 - Reproduced in staging with NGINX reverse proxy configured to idle_timeout 60s and proxy_buffering on. Observed race where backend wrote final streaming fragments while proxy was already closing on idle; proxy forwarded an RST to client and then the client's reconnection created a fresh session where resume logic attempted to stitch but missing terminal marker caused finalization to be skipped.
Hypothesis: The proxy idle teardown (RST) can occur *while* the serving-runtime flushes trailing chunks. Those trailing bytes end up in proxy buffers and may be dropped or delivered as a partial fragment on a new connection depending on how the proxy converts conn state (HTTP/1.1 <-> HTTP/2). Resume logic expects a clean end-event; seeing a stray mid-fragment or missing end leads to parser error and client drop.
Checked codepath: resume token/offset mapping in session-store marks streams terminal only on receipt of explicit end event. If bytes are lost at socket boundary, there is no fallback to 'force-terminate' based on connection close metadata. The edge currently does not synthesize a terminal event on socket RST from the proxy.
Observed that turning off proxy_buffering and increasing keepalive/idle timeout reduced rate of occurrences in staging to near zero.
SRE note: cloud provider LB also has an idle probe (120s). Customer appliance's tighter 60s window exposes the race more frequently than typical cloud LBs.
Severity assessment: customer-visible and user-facing UX regression; P1/Sev1 justified because Parcelly has high volume flows relying on guaranteed final output for confirmations.
Interplay between aggressive proxy idle teardown (RST) and server-side streaming flush: partial trailing fragments are dropped or reattached incorrectly across connection handoffs, and server-side resume logic does not synthesize/force terminal events on abrupt socket teardown.
Short-term for customer: increase proxy idle timeout to >= 180s OR disable aggressive proxy_buffering for SSE endpoints. If changer not possible, configure the client to treat parse errors as retriable and trigger a fresh non-resume request to fetch final summary (non-streaming fallback).
Client-side mitigation: add tolerant JSON reassembly logic that waits ~500ms for trailing bytes before failing; accept partial+retry flow for confirmation messages.
Server-side quick mitigation: enable explicit chunk delimiter payloads ('__STREAM_END__') emitted on connection close path (temporary flag rollout) so that some proxies pass through an identifiable closing marker.
In progress - mitigation applied and customer confirmed reduced failure rate. Engineering epic created to harden resume logic and add a server-side guard that force-closes sessions with a synthesized terminal event when upstream socket RST is detected.
2026-03-11: Support applied temporary mitigation guidance to Parcelly. They increased proxy idle timeout to 300s; incidents dropped in production from ~6% to ~0.3%.
2026-03-12: Engineering Triage -> created GH issue gh:redwood-inference/serving-runtime#2231 to implement: (A) detect upstream connection RST and mark stream terminal; (B) best-effort retry to deliver missing terminal marker to client on resume or synthesize end event in session-store.
2026-03-13: Staging test with synthesized terminal event logic shows deterministic recoveries for previously failing repros. Plan: release patch to edge+serving-runtime in next canary (target 2026-03-18) and monitor 48h before broader rollout.
Follow-ups: Update runbook Confluence:Runbooks/SSE-connection-handoff with proxy config recommendations and add an observability dashboard for 'sse-terminal-missing' metric.

Additional notes:
2026-03-10 12:05 - Support (Ava Moreno): 'Thanks — investigating. Can you confirm proxy vendor and if you can temporarily lift idle timeouts? Also can you share client SDK version and whether you see parser errors in the browser console?'
2026-03-10 16:10 - SRE (Kai Patel): 'Reproduced in staging with NGINX config similar to their appliance. Hypothesis: proxy RST racing with backend flush. Recommend increasing idle timeout as immediate mitigation.'
2026-03-12 10:03 - Eng (Maya Chen): 'Created GH issue gh:redwood-inference/serving-runtime#2231. Will add server-side RST detection and end-event synthesis. ETA for canary: 2026-03-18.'
2026-03-14 08:15 - Support (Ava Moreno): 'Tracking progress with engineering; keeping ticket open until patch is in canary and Parcelly validates in staging. Parcelly has been added to the canary cohort.'

Issue summary: Starting ~2026-03-10 00:20 UTC we observed a slow, persistent increase in 5xx responses for a subset of tenant traffic in prod-us-west. Impact: customer-facing errors (502/504) at 3-8% sustained with short spikes to ~18% on small bursts. Impacted customers included BrightMarket Labs (dedicated). Environment: prod-us-west, API gateway fronting multiple serving-runtime pools, prefetched KV caching enabled for affected workloads. Steps to reproduce: 1) Send steady stream of concurrent streaming generate calls (concurrency 40-60) to tenant endpoint pinned to rw-llama-13b-v2. 2) Observe error rate slowly increase over 30-90 minutes, not an immediate spike. 3) When error rate climbs, confirmed that only a subset of runtime hosts also show increased process restarts and accept backlog growth. Observed behaviour: - API gateway logs show a rise in upstream: "connection reset by peer" and "upstream timed out" over hours. - Runtime hosts with issues show accept queue length growth (netstat backlog > 1024) and rapid fd table usage approaching ulimit. - Runtime process (worker) restarts seen in k8s events correlating with accept queue saturation rather than OOM. - Autoscaler did not immediately add capacity because node-level health checks remained green until the accept backlog crossed kernel thresholds. Expected behaviour: Stable error rate <0.1% for similar workload. Logs/metrics: - apigw logs sample: "[2026-03-10T01:42:13Z] upstream error: connection reset by peer (upstream: http://10.4.22.13:8080) request_id=..." - runtime host syslog: "nf_conntrack: table full, dropping packet" (host-10-4-22-13) - netstat excerpt: "tcp        0      0 10.4.22.13:8080       0.0.0.0:*               LISTEN      12345/process (backlog=2048)" - k8s events: "Backoff restarting failed container" Investigation hypothesis: The pattern is slow drift (not a sudden surge) which suggests a connection lifecycle misbehavior. Initial hypothesis: a change in container base image (rolling update two days prior) altered libuv/tcp keepalive handling -> accumulation of sockets in TIME_WAIT/half-open state and accept queue backlog growth. Secondary hypothesis: intermittent kernel-level conntrack pressure combined with a small regression in the edge-proxy causing uneven connection distribution (SO_REUSEPORT skew) leading to a subset of runtimes receiving disproportionate new connections and hitting fd limits. Workaround applied: 1) Increased accept backlog and ulimit for affected PODs via daemonset patch (temporary) and rolled a new edge-proxy config to enable shorter keepalive on upstreams. 2) Bumped autoscaler to be more aggressive for the tenant pool to move traffic to healthy hosts. Follow-up required: revert the base-image change or apply fix in runtime to avoid half-open socket retention, tune conntrack and iptables settings for short term, and add guardrails in autoscaler to detect accept-queue saturation.

Findings: - Hosts that hit the state had 2.5x higher new connection counts compared to peers. - fd_table utilization was at 92% on problematic hosts; no OOMs. - Kernel conntrack metrics showed short bursts of table-full events leading to dropped packets. Evidence: logs and netstat excerpts uploaded to internal S3 (link posted in comments). Next steps: 1) Validate and merge runtime fix in PR #5941 to ensure sockets are closed promptly (owner: infra/serving). 2) Add accept-queue and fd watermark alert to SRE monitoring. 3) Add an autoscaler probe for accept-queue/backlog to prefer healthy hosts sooner. 4) Run a canary of base-image rollback vs runtime patch to confirm root cause.

Root cause under patch: regression in runtime socket handling combined with conntrack pressure and uneven load distribution from edge-proxy. Candidate permanent fixes: runtime patch (PR #5941) to close accept-side sockets earlier, edge-proxy change for more even distribution, and autoscaler change to detect backlog saturation. Action items: - Merge and deploy PR #5941, monitor for 48 hours. - Add monitoring alert for accept backlog > 1024 and fd_util > 85% to trigger autoscaler policy. - Schedule post-mortem and update runbook.

Issue summary: During a midday burst window on 2026-03-10, MapleAI's dedicated pool experienced a transient GPU shortfall that manifested as elevated p50/p99 latency across multiple routes. The allocator created uneven GPU assignments when a mix of long-lived and high-concurrency short streams arrived concurrently, which allowed a noisy tenant's lightweight short streams to throttle batch progress for other tenants.

Impact: Customer-facing latency degradation and increased timeout errors for MapleAI production workloads. Affected endpoints: text-generation and embeddings for two pinned models. No data loss reported.

Environment: Dedicated cluster pool: dp-prod-42 (us-east-1). Autoscaler configured with predictive window and prewarm enabled. Pool uses mixed-instance heterogeneous GPU shapes.

Timeline:
- 2026-03-10 11:42 UTC: MapleAI reports spike in p99 and backend 504s.
- 2026-03-10 11:45 UTC: Support triage, alerted SRE (#support-alerts).
- 2026-03-10 11:53 UTC: Observed sudden drop in available GPU slots, allocator logs show rapid short-lease churn.
- 2026-03-10 12:05 UTC: SRE applied short-term soft-cap on noisy tenant and increased prewarm count for affected pool.
- 2026-03-10 12:30 UTC: Latency improved; MapleAI confirmed fall-to-normal behavior.

Steps to reproduce (best-effort):
1. Create mixed streams to the same dedicated pool: a) many small short streams (~100-200ms per request, high concurrency) and b) several long-lived large-context generation streams (single request >10s).
2. Ensure predictive autoscaler prewarm remains near baseline (no aggressive prewarm).
3. Observe allocator's slot assignment behavior under concurrent burst and long-held leases.

Observed behavior: The allocator favored assigning small short streams to GPU slots, causing batch fragmentation and preventing efficient packing of long requests. Autoscaler did not expand quickly enough because the telemetry pulse was dampened by many short-lived leases; prewarm counts were insufficient due to mixed-instance placement heuristics. Result: transient GPU slot scarcity and p99 latency bleed across tenants.

Expected behavior: Autoscaler and allocator should maintain isolation such that a burst of short streams does not reduce effective throughput for long-context batched routes; predictive prewarm should provide headroom for mixed bursts.

Temporary workaround applied: SRE applied a tenant-scoped soft cap (rate limit and small concurrency cap) against the noisy route, forced an immediate prewarm increase for dp-prod-42, and temporarily adjusted the allocator affinity to prefer colocating long requests onto larger-instance GPUs.

Next steps: follow-up investigation (below) and schedule an RCA with Allocator and Autoscaler owners.
[2026-03-10T11:52:41Z] allocator.INFO: lease_acquire failed: available_slots=3 requested=6 pool=dp-prod-42
[2026-03-10T11:52:42Z] autoscaler.DEBUG: predictive_window_score=0.31 threshold=0.6 pool=dp-prod-42
[2026-03-10T11:52:42Z] serving-runtime.WARN: batcher.fragmentation_ratio=0.74 route=/v1/generate tenant=mapleai
[2026-03-10T11:52:50Z] allocator.INFO: short_lease_churn=127 window=60s pool=dp-prod-42
[2026-03-10T11:53:05Z] metrics.ERROR: p99=1.42s baseline_p99=0.23s route=/v1/embeddings tenant=mapleai
Initial hypotheses: 1) Mixed workload (many short streams + few long streams) exposed an allocator packing regression that prefers filling slots with short requests, fragmenting GPU batch slots. 2) Predictive autoscaler telemetry smoothing hid rapid bursts of short leases, delaying expansion. 3) Heterogeneous GPU shapes caused affinity mismatches so long-context requests landed on smaller-instance GPUs, reducing efficient batching.

What we checked:
- Correlated allocator logs and slot metrics (short_lease_churn spikes aligned with p99 increases).
- Autoscaler telemetry shows low predictive score despite high instantaneous concurrency due to smoothing window of 60s.
- Placement traces show long-context requests were assigned to T4-equivalent nodes while larger A10 nodes were consumed by high fanout short streams.

Partial findings:
- Short-lease churn (127 in 60s) is >3x baseline for the pool.
- Fragmentation ratio >0.7 on batchers for affected routes.
- Autoscaler prewarm count was at baseline 2; increasing to 6 reduced immediate latency.

Hypothesis prioritized: Improve short-lease awareness in autoscaler and allocator and introduce tenant-level soft isolation heuristics to avoid cross-tenant bleed.

Additional notes:
2026-03-12 18:00 - MapleAI (Customer): Appreciative of quick mitigation. Requesting summary and any recommended best-practices to avoid reoccurrence.
Workaround: tenant soft cap and forced prewarm restored service. Permanent fix in progress: allocator heuristic update to prefer packing for overall batchability, autoscaler smoothing window override on short-lease churn, and a tenant-isolation configuration flag for Dedicated pools.
Rollout notes: allocator PR will be canaried on dp-prod-42 with 5% traffic shift, monitor fragmentation_ratio and p99 for 48h. Autoscaler change will be deployed in feature-flag mode with telemetry gates.
Follow-ups assigned:
- Allocator owner (Ethan Cole): land PR and run canary (ETA 2026-03-18).
- Autoscaler owner (Serena Park): implement smoothing override and telemetry alert (ETA 2026-03-22).
- Support (Priya Iyer): send post-incident summary to MapleAI and schedule a sync.
RCA pending: link to final postmortem will be attached to this ticket when complete.
1) Complete PR review and canary allocator changes on dp-prod-42. 2) Implement autoscaler threshold override for short-lease churn. 3) Create a dedicated-runbook section for mixed-workload bursts including recommended per-tenant soft caps and prewarm defaults. 4) Postmortem and customer-facing summary by 2026-03-23.
This ticket focuses on a cross-cutting allocation/auto-scaling interaction exposed by mixed short/long workloads. Consider adding a metric 'short_lease_churn' to pool dashboards and a prewarm-insufficiency alert to avoid recurrence.

Issue summary: Customer reports that when a streaming session reconnects after a short network flap, the final (terminal) fragment of the response is missing. The session appears to have completed server-side, but the client never receives the terminal 'end' chunk. Impact: Several of Neptune Analytics' production inference pipelines are returning incomplete reports to end users; customers are seeing truncated paragraphs or missing final sentences. Observation: Logs indicate reconnect attempts where the session sequence number wraps (increments overflow) and the session-manager accepts the reconnect but logs an overlapping seqnum window; downstream delivery to the websocket/SSE channel omits the 'terminal' event. This is reproducible under a high-frequency reconnect pattern and has been seen with both SSE and websocket clients.
1) Create a long-running streaming call to /v1/streams using gpt-redwood-3b with streaming=true.
2) Simulate periodic network drops (150-500ms) from the client every ~12-20s until the model emits final tokens.
3) Allow the client to automatically reconnect using the session token and resume mechanism.
4) Observe that sometimes the server-side logs show the stream completed, but the client never receives the terminal 'end' chunk and the payload is truncated.
Notes: issue appears more likely when reconnects happen frequently and when the session sequence counter on session-manager crosses a 32-bit boundary (wrap).
2026-03-10T14:22:31.123Z session-manager[pid=1254] INFO Accept reconnect: session_id=abc123, client_seq=4294967294
2026-03-10T14:22:31.126Z serving-runtime[pid=4321] DEBUG Delivering chunk seq=4294967294 -> client
2026-03-10T14:22:31.284Z session-manager[pid=1254] INFO Reconnect recognized, incremented server_seq -> 4294967295
2026-03-10T14:22:31.587Z serving-runtime[pid=4321] INFO Model finished generation, terminal_chunk_seq=4294967296
2026-03-10T14:22:31.589Z session-manager[pid=1254] WARN Sequence wrap detected: server_seq wrapped to 0 (previous 4294967296). Overlap window=8
2026-03-10T14:22:31.590Z api-gateway[pid=210] ERROR Dropping outbound terminal event for session_id=abc123: seq_out_of_window
2026-03-10 15:05 - Support (Aisha Kapoor): Customer provided pcap and browser logs; they show successful reconnect handshake and resume requests but no final 'end' event on the client. Asked for account_id and full request IDs.
2026-03-10 16:30 - SRE (Martin Lowe): Reproduced locally by forcing client seq to 0xFFFFFFFF and reconnecting. Server logs show a seq wrap handling edge-case where terminal event is mapped to wrapped value and then considered out-of-window by outbound multiplexer.
2026-03-11 09:12 - Customer (Neptune Analytics): Impact is ~7% of their streaming calls during morning burst; business-critical dashboard reports are missing final conclusions. They requested ETA for fix or a safe workaround.
2026-03-12 10:40 - Eng (Lina Chen): Proposed mitigation: change session-manager to use 64-bit monotonic counters internally and treat seq wrapping as benign. Also suggested immediate mitigation: increase replay window on outbound multiplexer for the session_id to account for wrap offsets.
2026-03-12 11:02 - Support (Martin Lowe): Shared a temporary config patch for Neptune to apply to their Private deployment (session.replay_window=32bit+8) and recommended client-side fallback to request a fresh session if resume_count > 10 within 30s. Customer applying patch now.
2026-03-12 11:45 - Customer (Neptune Analytics): Applied patch to staging and reported initial reduction in truncated cases; will run overnight for production approval.
Hypothesis: 32-bit unsigned sequence counter overflow causes server-side session-manager to wrap to 0. Outbound multiplexer computes a relative window to decide whether to emit events; the wrapped terminal event falls outside the computed window and is dropped.
Reproduced: Yes, in local cluster by artificially incrementing client_seq to 2^32-2 and triggering a reconnect during the final token emission.
Scope: Affects both SSE and websocket transports because session-manager sequence handling is transport-agnostic. Likely triggered only for very long-lived sessions or extremely frequent reconnect patterns. Observed for gpt-redwood-3b and open-llama-7b (models that produce long outputs).
Risk: Low to medium frequency but high customer impact when it occurs (final conclusion missing). Could affect other customers with high reconnect rates in older clients that reuse 32-bit counters.
Next steps: (a) implement 64-bit counters and roll out; (b) add unit test that simulates wrap; (c) add metric for seqwrap events and outbound-drops-by-reason.
Workaround applied (customer-private): increase session.replay_window to 96 and enable 'seqwrap_tolerant' flag in session-manager. Neptune reports initial mitigation effective.
Planned fix: roll internal libs to use 64-bit monotonic sequence counters for session-manager and outbound multiplexer. Will include compatibility shim for older persisted session tokens.
Rollout plan: Patch in canary (low-traffic region) by 2026-03-18, full rollout over 7 days after smoke tests. Metric: monitor 'terminal_event_dropped:reason=seq_out_of_window' to target < 1/week per 100k streams.
Follow-up: engineering to produce a small compatibility note for SDKs describing client-side guidance (fresh session if >10 reconnects in 30s).

Issue summary: Starting 2026-03-10 09:12 UTC we observed a sustained p99 latency spike and reduced reserved GPU attach rates in CobaltAI's dedicated pool in us-west-2. Impact: Customer reports 40-60% reduction in throughput for batched routes and 5xx spikes for streaming requests. Autoscaler did not provision additional GPUs during the event, and several tenants experienced throttling.

Environment: Dedicated pool (cust-reserved-44), production, us-west-2, customer tier=dedicated.

Steps to reproduce: 1) Customer runs multi-tenant inference with mixed short/long-streams using SDK v2. 2) Background analytics sidecar scheduled a high-frequency sample upload sweep. 3) Within minutes, batch queue lengths grew and attach latency to GPUs increased. 4) Autoscaler cooldown prevented new allocations for ~6 minutes.

Observed behavior: Sudden burst of small sidecar uploads coincided with a large number of short-lived connections from customer workers. This created ephemeral connection fanout, noisy-prefetch IO on NVMe, and elevated CUDA attach times. Autoscaler heuristics misclassified the signal as transient and did not scale, causing regional GPU thinness and cross-tenant contention.

Expected behavior: Autoscaler should detect sustained queue growth and schedule capacity or fallback earlier; sidecar I/O should be rate-limited to avoid platform-wide attach penalties.

Relevant logs/metrics: See linked graphs for attach_latency, allocator_pending, gpu_attach_failures, nvme_io_wait. Affected routes show increased serialization and batch fragmentation.

Customer impact & timeframe: Intermittent throughput collapse for ~25 minutes during the morning window; customer batch jobs saw tail-loss and multiple retries.

Temporary workaround: Apply sidecar client throttling and enable short-lived-conn coalescing on client side. Support suggested immediate rate-limit rule on customer's analytics sidecar to reduce connection rate by 80%.

Hypothesis: sidecar upload threads saturate host IO and induce GPU driver attach latency; autoscaler rules need an additional 'attach_latency' metric to trigger earlier scale-up.
2026-03-11 | CobaltAI (Customer): Confirmed they rolled a temporary throttling policy and saw immediate improvement in throughput. Asked for permanent mitigation and guidance to avoid future regressions.
2026-03-12 | Jonas Reed (Eng): Deployed temporary autoscaler rule change to lower cooldown from 60s to 30s for this reserved pool; monitoring for noise amplification. Planning a hotfix to add attach_latency to autoscaler feature gating.
Correlation: Attach latency spike co-occurs with NVMe io_wait and increased small-file uploads from customer's sidecar process.
Autoscaler behavior: Smoothing+cooldown prevented scale-up despite growing pending queue; threshold tuned for medium-length jobs, not short-stream fanouts.
Root causes: (1) Noisy sidecar causing host IO pressure; (2) attach_latency not included in autoscaler decision signals; (3) batcher fragmentation due to short stream interleaving increased effective GPU occupancy per tenant.
Mitigation tested: Applying rate limits on sidecar reduces attach_latency within 90s and restores attach rate. Lowering autoscaler cooldown to 30s triggers scale-up within 60-90s in tests but risks reacting to true transient spikes.
Telemetry links: slack thread #support-cobaltai, grafana panels (attach_latency, allocator_pending, nvme_io_wait), and trace ids: trace-20260310-12ab.
Related: partial overlap with SUP-3141592 (cohort coldstart burst) and SUP-531020 (microbatch saturation) — added as linked issues for cross-reference.
Mitigation performed: 1) Customer applied sidecar upload rate-limits (recommended at 80% reduction); 2) Temporary autoscaler cooldown change applied to the specific reserved pool; 3) We scheduled a targeted hotfix to incorporate attach_latency into autoscaler signals and added a guard to ignore pure-IO transients. Customer throughput restored to expected levels after rate-limiting.

Follow-ups: Implement autoscaler signal change (ENG-2079), add a platform-side I/O backpressure policy for high-frequency uploaders, and update the dedicated runbook with sidecar throttling guidance. Plan verification window for 72 hours post-deploy.

payload.description:
BrightCart reports repeated duplicate executions of a downstream payment webhook (charge_customer) after their orchestrator workers are restarted as part of scheduled rolling updates. Duplicates occur intermittently when a restarted Go worker reuses the same OS PID as the previous process, and our Go SDK's ephemeral idempotency seed (pid + timestamp-derived salt) collides with the prior in-flight requests, causing the serving runtime to accept a retry as a new request and re-run the function call.
1) Deploy BrightCart's Go orchestrator on Private Redwood in eu-west. The worker uses SDK-Go v0.34 which derives ephemeral idempotency seeds using `fmt.Sprintf("%d-%d", os.Getpid(), time.Now().UnixNano())` for session-scoped idempotency.
2) Start a long-running orchestration that triggers an external `charge_customer` function call (external webhook) and does not immediately receive the webhook callback (delayed ack pattern).
3) Trigger a graceful restart of the worker (kubectl rollout restart or systemd restart) while the orchestration is in-flight so the original process exits and a new process starts quickly.
4) If PID is recycled by the OS and the new process generates an ephemeral idempotency seed identical to the previous (rare but possible under high churn), Redwood's serving runtime treats the incoming replay/new connection as a new idempotent scope and does not match the original confirmation token. The SDK sends a retry and the function executes again, leading to duplicate side effects (double charge).
Expected: SDK/server should deduplicate by a stronger request identifier (UUID or persisted session id) rather than ephemeral PID to avoid collisions across process restarts.
2026-03-09T21:14:12.673Z INFO orch_worker.go:342 starting orchestration run=brc-ord-2304 pid=2143 idempotency_seed=2143-1615383426730000000
2026-03-09T21:14:45.912Z INFO http_client.go:142 webhook outbound POST /charge_customer status=202 body="accepted"
2026-03-09T21:14:50.001Z INFO systemd: main process exited pid=2143 code=0
2026-03-09T21:14:50.210Z INFO orch_worker.go:77 new process started pid=2143 idempotency_seed=2143-1615383426745000000
2026-03-09T21:14:50.315Z WARN sdk-go retry.go:58 no confirmation received; scheduling retry; seed=2143-1615383426730000000
2026-03-09T21:14:50.420Z ERROR serving-runtime func_exec.go:211 function=charge_customer run=brc-ord-2304 duplicate_execution_detected=false -> executing again
Support reproduced locally with a controlled PID recycle using a small container pool: when the worker process restarts quickly, the SDK's seed generator can produce identical seeds because it uses PID + time-snap; race window small but observed under rapid restarts.
Serving runtime uses idempotency key namespace that included the SDK-provided seed. Because seed collides and the confirmation token path relies on per-connection confirmation events, the runtime cannot correlate the original ack with the retry coming from a new connection context.
Hypothesis: root cause is weak entropy in SDK seed + short-lived session scoping for function confirmations. The Private deployment environment (low PID entropy in small k8s node pool) increases probability of collision.
We inspected other customers (dedicated/hosted) and do not see wide impact; likely specific to small on-prem clusters with rapid orchestrator rollouts.
Customer used SDK-Go v0.34; later SDK versions include UUID-based session ids (v0.35+).

Additional notes:
2026-03-10T11:12:03 - BrightCart (Customer): We saw 3 duplicate charges across 2 customers during a rolling update. We've reverted the rollout to stop churn but need a root cause and fix before resuming.
2026-03-11T08:22:47 - SRE (Emma Torres): Private eu-west k8s nodes have small PID allocation ranges due to ephemeral container reuse on their host images. This increases PID recycling speed vs public clouds.
2026-03-12T15:03:59 - Eng (Liam O'Connor): Draft PR to SDK-Go to switch default ephemeral seed to RFC4122 UUIDv4 and to persist session id to a file descriptor across graceful restarts when possible. PR: github.com/redwood-inference/sdk-go/pull/482 (pending review).
2026-03-12T16:20:10 - Support (Aisha): Sent mitigation steps to customer (see resolution). Customer agreed to test SDK patch in staging before stable rollout.
Workarounds provided: 1) BrightCart rolled back the aggressive restart window to ensure PID reuse window is avoided; 2) Short-term: set environment variable REDWOOD_IDEMPOTENCY_SALT to a stable per-process random UUID at process bootstrap (customer applied and validated in staging). Engineering changes: merged SDK-Go PR to use UUIDv4 for ephemeral seeds (v0.35.0). Serving runtime safe-guard added to treat exact-seed collisions from different connection contexts as potential replays and prefer confirmation matching by request-level request_id when present (deploy rollout planned to private eu-west on 2026-03-16).
1) Engineering to backport UUID seed change to v0.34.x branch for customers who cannot upgrade; timeline: 3 business days.
2) SRE to recommend node image update to increase PID entropy for Private customers; documentation update in Confluence runbook.
3) Product to notify other private customers with small node pools about recommended SDK upgrade and env var mitigation.
4) Postmortem to be prepared if customer confirms duplicates in wider window; due date 2026-03-20.

Issue summary: While handling sustained high-burst traffic from customer LexiChat (dedicated pool), streaming chat connections (SSE and WebSocket) are being reset mid-generation. This typically occurs 20-90s after generation start and results in partial output (tokens missing) and the client receiving a connection reset or silent stall.

Impact: Multiple LexiChat customer sessions see mid-response disconnects or permanent stalls; affects revenue-critical chat features. Reported as repeatable during peak bursts of concurrent streaming sessions (~600 concurrent streams). Estimated ~12% of streaming sessions for this customer are impacted during bursts.

Environment: prod-us-east, dedicated cluster lexichat-ded-3, routing via streaming-proxy v2.9.1 and api-gateway v1.14. Serving runtime: gpt-redwood-XL-v1 pinned, model variant q4o.

Steps to reproduce: 1) Start sustained load test mimicking LexiChat traffic profile (burst QPS spikes to 600, average response length ~350 tokens). 2) Open streaming sessions via WebSocket and SSE clients with keepalive heartbeats disabled on client side. 3) Observe sessions for 3+ minutes; failures reproducible after ~20-90s in a subset of streams.

Observed behavior: - Client sees: ECONNRESET or abrupt socket close; for SSE the event stream terminates without a final close event. - Server logs: streaming-proxy reports repeated "write: broken pipe" and "connection reset by peer" entries; api-gateway logs show 502/523 spikes. - Metrics: streaming-proxy CPU threads spike and ephem FD count climbs just before failures; per-instance network TX stalls reported. - No consistent model-side OOMs in serving-runtime; KV cache hits stable.

Expected behavior: Streaming sessions should remain open until generation completes or a clear error with a retry/fallback policy is applied. No mid-generation silent drops.

Initial hypotheses: 1) streaming-proxy or its connection pool hits FD limits / thread starvation under burst causing RSTs. 2) A proxy-level timeout or TCP half-close race on long-lived streaming connections triggered by aggressive upstream retries. 3) Keepalive/heartbeat mismatch between client and proxy causing proxy to recycle sockets.

Logs and traces: See Grafana panels (streaming-proxy CPU, FD count): https://grafana.redwood/internal/d/streaming?orgId=1&var-cluster=lexichat-ded-3. Sentry events: https://sentry.redwood/issue/STREAM-5342. Example proxy log snippets attached (s3 link): s3://redwood-support/logs/SUP-136478/proxy-logs-0310.txt.

Temporary workaround provided to customer: - Reduced concurrent streaming concurrency to max 250 per instance and enabled client-side keepalive heartbeats (30s) which reduced but did not eliminate failures. - Recommended moving a subset of high-length responses to polling (non-stream) endpoints as fallback until mitigation rolled out.

Next steps requested: - SRE to review FD limits and ulimit/tcp parameters on streaming-proxy layer and increase if necessary. - Engineering to repro in staging with identical connection churn and run strace on proxy during repro. - Add more granular streaming-proxy metrics (per-connection age, open FDs per worker) and correlate with failure windows. - Consider backpressure changes or graceful draining logic in streaming-proxy to avoid abrupt RSTs.

Additional notes:
2026-03-10 11:02 - SRE Triage (Miguel Santos): Observed FD spike on two proxy instances during reported window. Tentatively increased ulimit on staging for repro. Assigned to Liam for deeper investigation.
2026-03-12 15:22 - Engineering (Evelyn Chen): Hypothesis: proxy retry/backoff mis-handles half-closed streams when upstream serving-runtime has transient latency. Adding defensive checks and backlog throttling. Creating PR to add per-connection age metric and to limit concurrent streaming handoffs. PR: github.com/redwood-inference/streaming-proxy/pull/211.
2026-03-13 09:30 - Support (Aisha Patel): Customer acknowledged workaround and asks for ETA on permanent fix; requested status update and any necessary config changes on their side.

Issue summary:
Customers on Private deployment intermittently see 401 Unauthorized errors during token refresh flows. The errors are observed only from SDKs that reuse long-lived HTTP/2 connections (stream multiplexing), and only when the client retries the token-refresh request after a 401/401->retry sequence.

Impact:
- Token refresh failures cause transient auth lapses for control-plane API calls and artifact downloads, resulting in model load failures and degraded inference requests for a subset (~2-4%) of sessions.
- Affects Valence HealthTech's private VPC deployment in us-east-1; incident window 2026-03-01 03:00–10:30 UTC.

Environment:
- Redwood Private deployment (customer-managed egress) in us-east-1
- SDK: redwood-sdk-go v0.9.12 and redwood-js v2.3.1
- Serving runtime: 2026-02-14 build
- Egress path: customer NGFW -> corporate HTTP/2 reverse proxy -> outbound NAT

Steps to reproduce (observed):
1) Long-running client establishes HTTP/2 connection to control-plane (token endpoint).
2) Access token expires; SDK issues POST /v1/tokens/refresh using same pooled connection.
3) Initial refresh attempt receives 401 from control-plane (valid case if token already revoked), SDK retries refresh after short backoff reusing same HTTP/2 connection.
4) Second request arrives at corporate proxy but Authorization header is missing on the retried request. Control-plane rejects with 401 and client starts a cascade of retries or fails the request.

Logs & snippets:
- Client side trace (timestamped): "POST /v1/tokens/refresh stream-id=5 -> 401; retry stream-id=9 missing Authorization"
- Control-plane access logs show second request with empty Authorization header and x-forwarded-for preserved.
- tcpdump from a serving node (pcap excerpt) shows Authorization present on bytes for the first stream, absent on the second.

Initial hypothesis:
- Egress proxy or NGFW is performing HTTP/2 stream-level inspection and rewriting that drops sensitive headers on retried streams or strips headers when connection-level state indicates a new stream without a fresh header frame.

Workaround (temporary):
- Customer configured the SDK to disable HTTP/2 connection reuse (force HTTP/1.1) which eliminated the intermittent 401s.
2026-03-01 04:15 UTC — Support (Ava): Acknowledged ticket, requested packet captures and control-plane access logs. SLA acknowledged.
2026-03-01 06:20 UTC — Customer (Valence SRE): Uploaded tcpdump and proxy config excerpt (corporate-proxy v3.2.7). Observed that proxy has custom header-filter rules. Link: https://slack.redwood/support-valence/PCG3J4K
2026-03-01 09:00 UTC — SRE (Jordan): Reproduced locally by instrumenting corporate proxy in dev: disabling header-filter preserves Authorization on retried HTTP/2 streams. Filed INT-1124 for internal proxy rule audit.
2026-03-02 11:30 UTC — Eng (Maya Patel): Confirmed SDK HTTP/2 retry uses new stream id but relies on connection-level header continuation; proxy rule matched and removed 'Authorization' on subsequent streams. Preparing mitigation patch for SDK to always include credentials on retry. Reference PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/platform/pull/4821
2026-03-03 14:05 UTC — Customer: Applied temporary workaround to force HTTP/1.1 in SDK; observed no more 401s during 24h smoke tests.
2026-03-05 09:45 UTC — Support (Ava): Deployed SDK patch v0.9.13 with explicit Authorization-on-retry; requested customer to revert HTTP/2 change and monitor. Customer confirmed stable. Closing follow-up monitoring in 48h.
2026-03-05 10:30 UTC — Customer (Valence SRE): Verified revert and stability; no errors in 72h. Thanks for quick turnaround.
Captured full pcap from serving node and from customer egress gateway during incident window; compared Authorization header bytes across initial and retried streams.
Reproduced behavior in lab by standing up corporate-proxy v3.2.7 with header-filter rules that drop sensitive headers on non-first stream frames; reproduction confirmed only for HTTP/2 multiplexed connections.
Hypothesis validated: proxy's header-filtering module considered retries as "new transactions" and stripped Authorization unless the request carried explicit per-request headers (some frameworks rely on implicit continued headers via connection reuse).
Customer proxy vendor (AceroProxy) notes: default security profile includes 'suppress-auth-on-subsequent-streams' to prevent credential replay across multiplexed clients; option is configurable in profile 'strict-reuse-block'.
Tested two mitigations: 1) configure proxy to allow Authorization passthrough for defined upstream (requires vendor change), 2) SDK change to always attach Authorization on every retry even when connection reused. SDK change was quicker to ship and minimally invasive.
Root cause: customer egress proxy was stripping Authorization header on retried HTTP/2 streams due to a security profile setting ('suppress-auth-on-subsequent-streams'). Fix path: 1) short-term: shipped SDK update (redwood-sdk-go v0.9.13 and redwood-js v2.3.2) to attach Authorization header explicitly on retry attempts even when reusing HTTP/2 connections; 2) recommended long-term: customer to update proxy profile to allow passthrough for Redwood control-plane endpoints or add an allowlist for upstream token endpoints.

Action items completed:
- Deployed SDK patch and published release notes with migration guidance. (PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/platform/pull/4821)
- Customer reverted HTTP/1.1 workaround and monitored for 72h with no recurrence.
- Internal INT-1124 opened to track proxy rule guidance and add a knowledgebase article.

Follow-up:
- Create KB article for private-deploy customers describing known proxy profiles that strip per-request headers on multiplexer protocols and recommended patterns. (Confluence: https://redwood.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/ENG/pages/5643/egress+proxy+policy+runbook)
- Consider SDK telemetry that warns when retries occur over HTTP/2 without explicit per-request headers.

Issue summary: Multiple customers (largest: StreamlineAI) reported short-lived waves of 5xx responses on streaming and embedding endpoints. Impact: customer requests during bursts receive 502/503/504 with high variance in first-byte times; some long-lived streaming sessions drop mid-stream. Environment: prod us-east serving dedicated fleet for StreamlineAI (reserved capacity). Observed pattern: errors occur in short pulses lasting ~30-120s, often in evenings, correlated with a small subset of upstream runtimes cycling and API gateway accept-queue growth.
1) Run sustained mixed traffic: many long-lived streaming connections (keepalive HTTP/2) interspersed with embedding upload batches from a small client pool.
2) Introduce a client behavior that sends delayed window updates and occasional tiny payload bursts (simulates slow consumer with sporadic writes).
3) Observe apigw accept-queue length and backend handshake times; monitor for 5xx pulses on edge and runtime restarts.
Mar 10 18:21:12 apigw-44ab accept_queue=193 peer=svc-ephemeral-12 result=queued
Mar 10 18:21:35 runtime-ephemeral-12: SIGTERM triggered due to watchdog timeout during prefetched-model lock (nvml reset)
Mar 10 18:22:01 apigw-44ab proxy: upstream 10.0.12.8 reset while reading response header (502)
Mar 10 18:22:15 apigw-44ab accept_queue=28 drain=fail reason=connect_timeout
Mar 10 18:22:32 srx-scheduler: backpressure=on prefetch_thrash=high
Initial triage: Pattern suggests accept-queue growth at apigw followed by short upstream restarts (watchdog timeouts) rather than a single sustained overload.
SRE observation: CPU on apigw hosts spikes concurrently with keepalive churn; fd usage climbs but not full exhaustion. Accept queue length correlates with 5xx pulse start times.
Runtime logs: One runtime process hit a GPU driver reset and triggered a local restart; subsequent reshuffling of ephemeral workers increased connection handoffs.
Hypothesis 1: Slow-client windowing causes partial reads at the proxy, leaving sockets tied up and causing accept-queue pressure; when accept queue backpressure increases, the apigw amplifies retries to upstreams causing transient overload and runtime watchdog timeouts.
Hypothesis 2: Small number of long-lived streaming sessions from StreamlineAI are unevenly distributed across apigw nodes; when a node experiences runtime restart, the rebalancing amplifies ephemeral load onto neighbors, creating a short 5xx pulse.
Observed mitigations tried: temporarily shifting customer route weight off the hot apigw hosts decreased pulse frequency; adding a short client-side keepalive threshold on StreamlineAI reduced connection churn in testing.
Support (Aisha): Customer reports 5xx pulses ~18:20-18:25 local time yesterday. They provided a sample timeseries and a pcap of a single streaming session (attached to ticket). Asked SRE for initial log sweep.
SRE (Diego): Pulled apigw host metrics and runtime logs. Found accept_queue spikes and a runtime GPU reset on runtime-12. Suspect prefetched model lock contention contributed to watchdog timeouts. Investigating fd leak hypothesis.
Eng (Marta Novak): Noted a recent ingress-proxy tweak (PR #7891) changed the read timeout semantics for half-closed streams. Will review if this increased partial-read retention. Linking PR: github.com/redwood/pr/7891
Support (Aisha): Customer confirmed they perform periodic tiny writes from an SDK under poor network conditions (mobile). They can try increasing their client-side keepalive frequency for a test window.
SRE (Diego): Scoped mitigation: increased apigw accept-queue cap on the affected AZ and temporarily diverted 30% of StreamlineAI traffic to a healthy pod group (route weight change). Monitoring for recurrence.
Eng (Ethan Shaw): Adding a short-term circuit in the ingress to penalize connections that emit long tail windowing behavior. Drafting patch (WIP) and load test plan.
Workaround: shifted StreamlineAI route weights away from three saturated apigw nodes and applied a temporary ingress policy to drop half-closed idle streams after 45s. Customer applied a conservative SDK keepalive fix during the window. Result: 5xx pulses frequency dropped to zero during the monitoring window. Next steps: eng to land ingress PR to tighten partial-read retention and backpressure handling; SRE to add alerting threshold for accept-queue growth and autopurge policy. Postmortem scheduled.

payload.description:
Issue summary: LexaHealth observed a rapid elevation in 5xx responses across their dedicated eu-west capacity during a large multipart upload + mixed chat/embedding workload. Errors appear as 502/504 from API Gateway and intermittent 5xx from upstream runtimes.

Impact: Multiple production endpoints returning ~8-18% 5xx rate for a 45-minute window. Customer reports degraded UX for in-flight uploads and streaming chat sessions. This is a paying Dedicated customer with high SLAs.

Timeline (high level):
- 2026-03-13 03:07 UTC: sustained upload begins from customer automation ingest (large batching of multipart embedding uploads + chat bursts).
- 03:10 UTC: api-gateway 502/504s spike; latency increases.
- 03:12-03:35 UTC: error rate peaks, internal dashboards show routing queue length and accept-queue growth on specific apigw hosts.
- 03:40 UTC: initial mitigation (rate limiting ingress for that tenant) reduced error rate but not fully resolved.

Observed symptoms:
- API Gateway logs show repeated "502 Upstream handoff timeout" and occasional "504 keepalive read timeout".
- Serving runtime logs show short-lived runtime restarts correlating with kube hotplug events (GPU hotplug / container reattach) at the same time as heavy prefetch invalidations.
- Prefetch/KV cache invalidation counts spike; kvcache lock waiters increase.
- Route planner shows fanout reorder events where requests were redirected between ephemeral runtime nodes instead of queued at stable backends.

Why this is unique/different from other 5xx patterns: The signal combines a) large multipart upload pressure, b) ephemeral runtime hotplug sequence (hotplugging GPUs into the node pool), and c) a routing handoff path that attempts immediate fanout to new ephemeral nodes rather than queuing or applying admission-control backpressure. The immediate fanout combined with kvcache invalidations caused upstream runtimes to become transiently overloaded and drop connections rather than serving requests, amplifying 5xxs across the customer's shard.
1) Use a dedicated tenant on eu-west with model redwood-open-7b pinned
2) Begin large multipart embedding uploads concurrently with several streaming chat sessions (simulate LexaHealth ingestion: 4 parallel upload clients + 12 concurrent streaming chat clients),
3) Trigger a simulated ephemeral node hotplug (scale-out + immediate attach of new GPU-backed runtimes) while prefetch is enabled and kvcache TTL is low
4) Observe API Gateway 502/504s and upstream runtime restarts in a monitoring window ~2-10 minutes after start
apigw-eu-west-03: 2026-03-13T03:11:02Z ERROR http2: 502 Upstream handoff timeout tenant=lexahealth request_id=01A2B3C
runtime-eu-west-07: 2026-03-13T03:11:05Z WARN prefetch: kvcache invalidation burst=1.2k locks_waiting=54 shard=embed-12
runtime-eu-west-09: 2026-03-13T03:11:06Z ERROR runtime: received SIGTERM during attach; graceful shutdown elapsed=2s reason=gpu-hotplug-attach
apigw-eu-west-03: 2026-03-13T03:12:30Z WARN accept-queue: depth=28758 host=apigw-eu-west-03 tenant=lexahealth
Initial alert from SRE flagged apigw accept-queue growth and high 502 rate for tenant shard.
Correlated runtime attach/hotplug events from the cluster autoscaler logs within the same 120s window as start of 5xx spike.
Observed kvcache invalidation rate and a backlog of prefetch ops; kvcache compaction was running concurrently on the same nodes.
Hypothesis A: Routing attempted immediate fanout to newly attached runtimes which had cold KV caches and were still initializing kernel selection; heavy prefetch + invalidation created CPU/io pressure and triggered watchdog restarts.
Hypothesis B: Admission control did not apply granular per-tenant shed when accept-queue exceeded threshold because hotplug events altered host health signals, causing misrouted requests.
Checked linked metrics: per-tenant request concurrency jumped to 600 concurrent inflight sockets; apigw worker threads saturated and returned upstream handoff errors rather than queueing to stable backends.
Cross-referenced Slack thread #support-lexahealth and channel #incidents-eu where customers posted stacktraces and we confirmed tenant-specific traffic pattern.
03:18 UTC - Support applied emergency tenant-level ingress rate limit to LexaHealth to cap concurrency and reduce immediate 5xx impact.
03:25 UTC - SRE disabled aggressive prefetch for affected shard as a temporary measure to reduce kvcache invalidation pressure.
03:40 UTC - Routing team rolled out a quick server-side tweak to delay fanout to newly attached runtimes by 250ms during attach window (canary on 2 hosts) to test hypothesis.
03:55 UTC - Observed partial reduction in 5xx after rate limiting + prefetch disable; full recovery pending routing change validation.
We collected full logs and heap/disk metrics and attached to this ticket for postmortem.
1) Routing: implement and promote controlled fanout policy (hold new-node fanout until kvcache warm or use admission throttle) — owner: Alex P — high priority.
2) Runtime: add guard to defer SIGTERM during attach until in-flight prefetches drain or mark node as not-ready in route planner during attach — owner: Priya S.
3) SRE: run a replay load test in staging that reproduces large-multipart upload + streaming mix with simulated node hotplug to validate fix — owner: SRE team.
4) Follow-up postmortem to update runbooks and add a metric-driven automated tenant-level admission control for sustained accept-queue growth — owner: Support/Eng.
5) Notify LexaHealth with timeline and mitigation plan; schedule a joint verification window once a fix is staged.
Estimated ETA for codefix canary: 48-72 hours; full rollout pending test results.
(In Progress) Temporary mitigations (tenant ingress-rate cap, disabling aggressive prefetch) reduced immediate 5xx rate. Engineering is preparing routing & runtime fixes to prevent immediate fanout to hotplugged nodes and to make attach events safer for heavy prefetch workloads. Final resolution pending code rollout and verification.
Support (Maya Chen) 2026-03-13T03:22Z: Notified customer of temporary ingress rate limit and that we're investigating routing + runtime attach correlation.
SRE (Ravi Kapoor) 2026-03-13T03:28Z: Confirmed hotplug logs on runtime-eu-west-09/07; prefetch compaction was scheduled in same minute — pausing prefetch for shard now.
Routing (Alex Patel) 2026-03-13T03:42Z: Pushed a 250ms hold-on-fanout on canary apigw hosts; seeing a 3x reduction in immediate 502s on canary route.
Customer (LexaHealth Ops) 2026-03-13T04:05Z: Thanks — we see improved stability but will keep ingest paused until you confirm a permanent fix.
Support (Maya Chen) 2026-03-14T09:17Z: Created this tracking ticket for engineering workstreams and scheduled a verification window with LexaHealth for 2026-03-16 UTC.
Customer impacted: LexaHealth (dedicated eu-west). Temporary mitigations applied; full fix pending engineering rollout. Not publicly posted to status page yet as incident is tenant-scoped.
If customer asks: root cause appears to be a combination of routing fanout to newly-attached runtimes + heavy prefetch invalidations causing upstream overload and watch-dog restarts.

payload.description:
Issue summary: Customer reports sudden exhaustion of tenant token budget (429s) during an orchestrated ingest job that runs many short-lived worker tasks in parallel. Problem appears only after a recent change to their orchestrator which stitches multiple short-lived upload workers together into waves.

Impact: Intermittent 429s for interactive routes and bulk ingest pipelines for NimbleAI; visible around the top of each orchestrated wave. Client reports degraded throughput and a spike in retries. No model-level errors observed.

Environment: Dedicated pool in prod-us-west; tenant pinned to dedicated lease. Ingest job spawns 120 workers, each opening short-lived streaming sessions and issuing small embed/chat requests.

Steps to reproduce (provided by customer):
1) Trigger nightly orchestrated backfill with 120 parallel workers.
2) Each worker opens a new short-lived API connection, completes a 6-12 request burst, then terminates.
3) Observe tenant-level 429s starting ~60s after wave start, continuing until refill stabilization.

Observed logs (snippets):
[2026-03-09T02:14:32Z] auth-service: token-grant OK tenant=nbl-231;
[2026-03-09T02:14:59Z] rate-limiter: REJECT tenant=nbl-231 window=60s tokens_left=0 reason=burst-window-exhausted;
[2026-03-09T02:15:01Z] gateway: 429 path=/v1/embeddings size=512 host=ingest-worker-77;

Additional context: Customer recently enabled orchestrator-level parallelism optimization (stagger disabled) and moved orchestration to a single coordinator to reduce scheduling churn. They also requested a single burst pool for both low-latency chat and large background batches to reduce operational complexity.

Why this is unique: The patterns indicate a shed/"shearing" effect where many short-lived sessions align to refill boundaries and create transient window collisions that exhaust tenant burst credits faster than steady-state smoothing anticipates. This is different from long-lived SSE or healthcheck-induced 429s because the traffic is high-cardinality, short-duration, and aligned with the orchestrator's wave timing.
Hypotheses: 1) Refill window alignment lets multiple workers consume the same refill credit slice; 2) Token slicing at API-gateway is attributing requests twice on worker restart; 3) Dedicated-pool refill lag during autoscaler scale-up is delaying credit replenishment.

Telemetry collected:
- Rate-controller histograms show refill bursts at t+0s and t+60s for the tenant; cumulative consumption spikes when worker start times are within the same 10s bucket.
- Dedicated pool autoscaler logs show scale-up completed but serving nodes not fully warmed; kernel-level warmup delays add ~200ms per connection.
- Gateway logs confirm ephemeral worker connections are reusing different source IPs (NAT pool), increasing header fingerprint variance and preventing per-connection affinity counting.

Notes from quick checks:
- Reproduced in staging with a synthetic orchestrator using 100 short-lived workers; 429 pattern matches production traces.
- Turning on stagger (small jitter on worker start) reduces peak token drain by ~40% in staging.

Relevant dashboards:
- https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/rate-ctrl/tenant-consumption?orgId=1&var-tenant=nbl-231
- https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/infra/dedicated-pool-warmup?orgId=1

Next investigative actions: capture exact refill window alignment, check gateway token attribution code path for worker reconnects, and reproduce varying stagger/jitter to quantify mitigation.

Additional notes:
Logs: s3://nimble-logs/ingest/2026-03-09/trace.log
Short-term: enable small start jitter (200-1000ms) for orchestrated workers to spread token consumption across refill windows; separate background-batch tenant route into a dedicated burst pool (request via console -> create burst pool). Both actions reduced 429s in staging.
Customer-applied config: NimbleAI enabled 500ms jitter and created a background-batch route assigned to a separate burst pool; reported immediate throughput improvement.
Mitigation provided (stagger + route separation) and engineering patch under review to make gateway token attribution idempotent for ephemeral connections. Pending: PR for edge-proxy session-tagging (https://github.com/redwood-inference/edge-proxy/pull/879) and a follow-up to expose 'orchestrator-jitter' recommendations in Console docs.
Follow-up tasks: 1) Merge and roll PR to staging and run full repro; 2) Add a Console toggle for 'orchestrator jitter' recommendations under dedicated-pool best practices; 3) Document guidance for splitting burst pools for mixed-latency workloads (assigned to Diego Chen).
If customer cannot apply jitter, consider temporarily increasing tenant burst-window size for dedicated lease (admin action) and coordinate with billing (burst credit implications). Use rate-controller debug mode to watch per-window attribution.
Explained root cause hypothesis (window collision from many short-lived worker starts), provided two low-friction mitigations (start jitter + separate burst pool), and delivered short-term improvement. Customer is awaiting platform-side fix for safer ephemeral-session handling.
payload.summary: Tenant token drain caused by rate-window collisions during orchestrated ingest workers

payload.description:
Issue summary
- Customer reports Dedicated burst capacity did not activate during predictable traffic spikes. Throughput capped at baseline replicas, causing queueing and elevated p95/p99 latency.
- Customer expectation: burst should add temporary replicas within 2–5 minutes when utilization/queue depth crosses threshold.

Impact
- 2026-02-12 17:05–18:20 UTC: sustained elevated latency and intermittent 5xx from upstream timeouts due to request queue buildup.
- Customer-visible symptoms:
  - Latency increase: p95 from ~850ms to ~4.8s (chat), p99 up to ~9–12s.
  - RPS capped at baseline; queue depth increased and stayed elevated.
  - No visible scale-out events in their Console view.

Customer / Tier
- Northstar Payments (Dedicated)

Environment
- prod, us-east
- Dedicated pool: northstar-prod-gpu-pool (A100-80GB)

What we expected
- Burst capacity should temporarily scale above reserved baseline up to configured burst_max_replicas when triggers are met, subject to regional capacity availability.

What happened (initial observation)
- Autoscaling policy evaluation occurred, triggers met, but scale-out did not proceed beyond baseline max.
- System logged repeated 'scale_out_blocked' events with reason: 'pool_max_replicas_reached' and later 'no_capacity_in_cell'.

Steps to reproduce (customer)
1) Run scheduled batch + interactive traffic at top of hour (17:00 UTC).
2) Observe utilization > 75% and queue depth > 300 for > 5 minutes.
3) Expect scale-out; instead replicas remain at baseline.

Triage checklist (Support)
- Confirmed request IDs provided by customer; sampled across the spike window.
- Confirmed region: us-east, dedicated deployment.
- Confirmed customer config changed earlier this week: raised baseline_min_replicas; no explicit change to burst settings.

Investigation notes (SRE + Platform)
- Reviewed autoscaling policy for pool:
  - baseline_min_replicas=12
  - baseline_max_replicas=12
  - burst_enabled=true
  - burst_max_replicas=20
  - scale_out_metric=queue_depth (threshold=200, window=3m)
  - scale_down_cooldown=15m
- Found two separate blockers:
  1) Config/guardrail interaction: pool-level max_replicas remained pinned to baseline_max_replicas=12. The burst_max_replicas was set, but the scheduler respected pool max as a hard cap due to an older policy schema path still in effect for this tenant.
  2) Regional capacity constraints: even after manual override to raise pool max, only 4 additional GPUs were available in the assigned cell; requests to allocate beyond that returned 'no_capacity_in_cell'.

Key signals checked
- Dedicated autoscaler events: scale_out_requested present, scale_out_applied absent during the window.
- Scheduler allocation logs: 'cap_exceeded: max_replicas' followed by 'insufficient_capacity'.
- Cluster capacity dashboard (internal): us-east cell use1-gpu-c3 at 96–99% A100 utilization.
- Customer-facing metrics (Support-safe quick view): queue depth and throttle indicators aligned with reported symptoms.

Mitigation
- Immediate:
  - Rafael (SRE) applied manual scale to 16 replicas (within available capacity) and raised pool max cap for this tenant to allow burst to exceed baseline.
  - Advised customer to temporarily reduce max_tokens and enable client-side exponential backoff for non-interactive traffic until burst stabilizes.
- Short-term (same day):
  - Reserved additional capacity in adjacent cell (use1-gpu-c4) and adjusted placement to allow up to 18 replicas during peak hours.

Customer communications
- Followed Dedicated SLA cadence per playbook: acknowledgement within 30 minutes; updates hourly during active mitigation.
- Shared explanation:
  - A configuration cap prevented burst from scaling above baseline.
  - Even after lifting the cap, us-east cell capacity limited burst headroom; we increased available capacity and will add guardrails to prevent silent non-activation.

Root cause
- Primary: legacy policy schema path treated baseline_max_replicas as a hard cap, ignoring burst_max_replicas for this tenant.
- Contributing: us-east A100 cell saturation reduced burst headroom during the customer’s spike window.

Resolution
- Burst now activates above baseline for this tenant after pool max cap correction.
- Capacity increased to provide headroom for expected peaks (target: +6 replicas available during scheduled spike windows).

Issue summary:
Customer reports that after a proactive capacity rebalance on Dedicated pool 'dp-usw-2' their sessions lost model-version affinity and were routed to the fallback variant mid-request. This caused two user-facing failures: an aborted streaming response and a degraded generation quality for multi-turn chat flows.

Impact:
- BrightPath Health observed ~0.6% of requests (sampled from their edge logs) diverted to fallback variants over a 12-minute window.
- Several long-running streamed calls were terminated with a 502 when KV cache mismatches were detected.
- Customer production workload (SLA tier: Dedicated, critical) experienced increased latency and a handful of user-visible regressions.

Environment:
- Dedicated pool: dp-usw-2 (proactive rebalance at 2026-03-10T21:14:05Z)
- Edge region: us-west (primary), failover to us-east observed
- Models: redwood/rw-instruct-13b-quant-v2 pinned on tenant route; fallback: redwood/rw-chat-7b

Steps to reproduce (observed in customer traffic):
1) Customer pinned route to rw-instruct-13b-quant-v2 and validated affinity for 48 hours.
2) Autoscaler triggered proactive rebalance to migrate GPUs in dp-usw-2 for maintenance.
3) Edge control-plane initiated graceful drain on 4 nodes; routing tokens were reissued.
4) A subset of long-lived sessions (session_cookie present) resumed across the new node and received a routing decision referencing the fallback model variant.

Expected behavior:
- Pinned sessions maintain version affinity across proactive capacity changes, or are gracefully failed with a clear error to the application.

Actual behavior:
- A subset of pinned sessions lost affinity and were silently routed to fallback variants midstream. Streaming connections returned 502/5xx for some connections where KV cache state mismatch was detected.

Immediate customer-visible workaround applied:
- Support temporarily set an edge-route-level policy to 'force-pin: true' for BrightPath to prevent rebind during subsequent rebalances.

Notes:
- This reproduces only for long-lived sessions that cross a node migration boundary while the edge-router is applying routing token rotations.
- We observed header mutation in the sidecar for some requests that correlates with affinity loss.

Pin route to target model and run multi-turn streaming sessions for >300s
Trigger proactive rebalance / simulate node drain on dedicated pool
Observe whether resumed sessions receive original pin or fallback decision
Check edge-router logs for token rotation and header mutations

Issue summary: Starting 2026-03-12 09:10 UTC, NoteStream reported recurring high tail latency (p95/p99) and intermittent request timeouts for short, single-turn text-generation calls. The spikes present as long-tail latency increases without corresponding CPU/GPU saturation, and are concentrated on a small percentage of requests during periods of low-to-moderate QPS with bursty microbursts.

Impact: Customers using the dedicated pool (NoteStream) are observing 5–10% of requests hitting p95/p99 spikes up to 3–4x baseline, causing frontend timeouts and user-facing slowdowns. There are business-impacting errors for NoteStream's editors flow (timeouts at 8s).

Environment: Dedicated pool in prod:us-east (d-htx-a cluster), model variants: redwood-mini-v1 and a quantized llama-2-13b variant. Autoscaling configured with min 2, target 8 gpus. Batching mode: continuous batching enabled with default max_batch_delay=20ms; adaptive window growth enabled.

Observed behavior: During short bursts (spikes of 10–50 concurrent single-token or short-prompt requests), the scheduler appears to increase batch window to coalesce small requests; however measured batch wait times for the affected batches jump to 60–120ms in the p99, and some requests subsequently hit application-level timeouts at 8s due to head-of-line waiting through multiple batches. Throughput and GPU utilization remain healthy overall.

Expected behavior: Continuous batching should maintain low per-request wait time for short requests by constraining max_batch_delay or capping adaptive-window growth; p95/p99 should remain close to baseline under low-to-moderate QPS.

Temporary workaround suggested to customer: Switch to fixed strict batching profile (max_batch_delay=5ms) or disable adaptive-window growth for their dedicated pool, which reduces observed p99s to near baseline in canary tests.
1) Use dedicated pool with continuous batching enabled (default config).
2) Send many short single-turn requests in microbursts (10–50 qps bursts, 10–30s duration).
3) Observe p95/p99 for end-to-end request latency (client->response) rising during bursts even though GPU utilization remains under 60%.
4) Toggle batching to strict (max_batch_delay=5ms) and repeat; p99 drops significantly in our tests.

2026-03-12T09:12:03.115Z runtime[pid=8910] WARN request_id=abc123 latency_ms=4120 stage=queued_for_3_batches
2026-03-12T09:12:03.118Z gpu-metrics cluster=d-htx-a util=58% mem=64%
Grafana: https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/latency/serving?panelId=12&from=2026-03-12T09:00:00Z&to=2026-03-12T09:30:00Z
Tracing: https://traces.redwood.ai/trace/abc123 (shows multiple consecutive batch-queue spans)
2026-03-12 10:00 UTC - Initial triage by Support (Aisha): collected traces, customer timing, and config; reproduced on staging with dedicated pool replica.
2026-03-12 11:10 UTC - SRE (Diego) reproduced tail latency in canary; isolated to continuous/adaptive batching path where window growth allowed successive small batches to accumulate head-of-line requests.
Hypothesis A: Adaptive window growth is over-aggressive for workloads with short, bursty requests; the algorithm increases delay to hit amortized throughput targets, increasing tail latency for those requests.
Hypothesis B: KV-cache warmup interacts with batch coalescing: first-context requests cause longer kernel selection / mem-copy latencies that cascade into subsequent batched requests under the same time window.
Mitigation tests: reducing max_batch_delay to 5ms and disabling adaptive growth reduced p99 by ~65% in canary. Increasing min throughput per-batch (min_batch_size=2) reduced head-of-line waiting but increased overall latency for tiny requests—tradeoff noted.
Next actions: (1) Recommend customer apply temporary config change to strict batching; (2) engineering to add telemetry for per-batch 'adaptive-window' growth events and correlate with tail latencies; (3) evaluate quick patch to cap window growth per-tenant.
Support (Aisha) 2026-03-12T10:05Z: Reached out to NoteStream, collected sample traces and their pool config. Reproduced in staging with same traffic pattern.
Customer (NoteStream - Mark Liu) 2026-03-12T10:20Z: We saw editors timeout during heavy usage window at 09:12 UTC. App side reported 8s timeouts. Happy to try config changes; prefer non-disruptive ones.
SRE (Diego) 2026-03-12T11:15Z: Ran canary with strict batching (max_batch_delay=5ms) — p99 dropped from 1.2s to 380ms for the short requests. Will prepare telemetry patch.
Eng (Priya Rao) 2026-03-12T14:30Z: Noted possible interaction with kernel selection on first requests; opening INT-1287 to investigate warmup penalties. Recommend backport small cap on adaptive-window growth as short-term fix.
In progress. Short-term mitigation recommended: customer apply strict batching profile (max_batch_delay=5ms) or disable adaptive-window growth. Engineering to deliver telemetry and a cap-on-growth patch (tracked in INT-1287). Follow-up scheduled with NoteStream for 2026-03-14 to validate changes.
Customer reported editors flow timeouts at 8s; affects ~12k daily active editors. Critical for product adoption this quarter.
Customer willing to accept temporary config change outside business hours; prefers minimal model changes.

- screenshot showing 401 from trace link (attached)
