payload.description:
Customer reports repeated p99 latency spikes and sustained throughput degradation in their Dedicated GPU pool starting 2026-03-10 03:40 UTC. Symptoms coincide with a morning traffic pattern where thousands of short streaming requests (100-500ms each) from the AtlasLearn mobile SDK fan out rapidly. The Dedicated autoscaler does not appear to add capacity in time; GPUs show frequent small allocation/eviction cycles and kernel queue stalls. This ticket captures the investigation into allocation churn, autoscaler responsiveness, and whether scheduling heuristics are unfairly favoring large-batch jobs, enabling slot fragmentation and transient starvation for small streams.
1) Use AtlasLearn mobile client simulation script to open 4k concurrent streaming sessions over 2 minutes: python tools/sim_client.py --concurrency 4000 --stream-duration 0.2 --payload-size 1kb
2) Target the customer's Dedicated pool route: POST /v1/generate?pool=atlaslearn-dedicated with streaming SSE
3) Observe per-GPU allocation events via internal allocator endpoint: GET /internal/allocations?pool=atlaslearn-dedicated
4) Correlate with GPU queue depth and kernel errors from /metrics and NVidia dmon logs
- p99 generation latency from 400ms baseline to 2.8s during peak fanout.
- Autoscaler adds 0 or 1 GPUs (insufficient) while allocator shows dozens of short-lived slot allocations and evictions.
- GPU metrics show high context switch rate, small batch utilization (low GPU occupancy), and repeated 'allocation_timeout' traces.
- Some requests receive 429/503 when allocator can't satisfy short-lived slot requests.
- Autoscaler should provision additional GPUs to maintain latency SLOs for customer Dedicated pool during predictable fanout spikes, or the runtime should coalesce short streams to avoid allocation churn.
- No sustained kernel queue stalls or high eviction rate for small streaming jobs.
2026-03-10T03:42:12Z [allocator] slot_alloc start tenant=atlaslearn token=abc123
2026-03-10T03:42:12Z [allocator] slot_alloc evict tenant=atlaslearn token=abc123 reason=short_lived
2026-03-10T03:42:12Z [gpu-0] kernel_queue depth=127 occupancy=12%
2026-03-10T03:42:13Z [autoscaler] evaluated=1 desired=3 current=2 last_scale=2026-03-10T03:39:01Z
2026-03-10T03:42:14Z [nginx] 503 POST /v1/generate (upstream timeout)
Initial hypothesis: high fanout of tiny streams causes allocator to create many ephemeral GPU slots, increasing scheduler overhead and preventing effective batching.
Metric evidence: per-GPU small-batch ratio jumped from 8% to 62% during spike (grafana: grafana.redwood/internal/d/alloc?panel=small_batch_ratio).
Observed allocator churn: average slot lifetime dropped to 210ms; eviction rate spiked to 38% (trace logs).
Autoscaler behavior: scaling loop has 30s evaluation window and requires >70% sustained utilization to scale — too coarse for sub-minute spikes. See scheduler autoscale SLOs in runbook.
No NVidia ECC errors or hardware faults found; noisy tenant behavior confirmed by tenant-level allocation heatmap.
Potential scheduling bug: recently landed change to 'short_stream_preemption' (runtime PR #4418) may prefer evicting older small-stream slots to free memory for larger batches, causing thrash under many small streams.

Additional notes:
Partial mitigation applied: temporary tenant-level throttle on slot creation plus autoscaler sensitivity adjustment. Root cause appears to be a combination of (1) client-side behavioral change producing many short streaming requests and (2) runtime policy that aggressively evicts small-stream slots under memory pressure, which, under high fanout, produces allocation churn and starvation. A runtime code change (revert PR #4418) has been drafted and is planned for quick rollout to staging for validation.
- Customer can enable SDK batching (client-side) to group small prompts into fewer long-lived streams.
- We've applied a tenant rate cap (max_inflight_streams=1000) and lowered autoscale threshold for the Dedicated pool as an immediate mitigation.
Deploy revert of short_stream_preemption (runtime PR #4446) to staging and run AtlasLearn simulation suite.
Implement multiplexing/coalescing feature to allow many tiny streams to reuse existing slots (spec PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/specs/pull/89).
Add an autoscaler mode for rapid transient fanout events: evaluate 10s windows and allow temporary burst capacity.
Add customer-facing guidance in AtlasLearn onboarding to prefer SDK batching or multiplexed streams for mobile use-cases.
Postmortem to be authored and linked to this ticket within 7 days.

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Aurelia Financial is requesting a machine-parseable delivery format and a small test harness for a compact, ordered activity ledger. Requirements include: gzipped NDJSON with per-event canonical UUID, UTC-normalized timestamps, deterministic deduplication seed, per-batch JWT-signed manifest (signed with Redwood KMS key-id), and delta resume tokens to support resumable playback after cross-region failover. They also want a minimal test harness that can simulate a cross-region burst/failover and demonstrate how resume tokens are used to resume without duplication or gaps.

Impact:
Customer reports intermittent gaps in their analytics during regional failover testing. Business impact is "near-real-time" fraud detection misses for a small subset of transactions; they requested evidence and a reproducible example for their internal audit/legal teams.

Environment:
- Production exports to customer-owned S3 ingestion bucket (aurelia-prod-ingest-us-east)
- Redwood delivery pipeline: audit-archiver v2.1 -> gzip-ndjson -> per-batch manifest signer (kms) -> s3-put with resume-token metadata
- Regions observed: primary us-east-1, failover eu-west-1

Observed behavior / steps customer ran:
1) Triggered a cross-region failover test by disabling us-east-1 delivery for 30s during a low-traffic window (2026-03-04T02:15:00Z).
2) Their S3 ingestion observed a gap: sequence offsets 10542-10560 missing; subsequent batch resumed at 10561, but a subset of events reappeared later as duplicates.
3) Customer used their internal consumer which relies on resume tokens to dedupe; they observed resume tokens mismatched expected offsets after the failover.

What customer is requesting:
- A sample gzipped-ndjson batch package (3 batches) with: canonical-uuid, event_ts (UTC), resume_token, per-batch JWT manifest (kid, alg, signature) and an example verification snippet.
- A short playbook (1page) describing how Redwood generates resume tokens and guarantees monotonic ordering across cross-region failover.
- A minimal test harness (Python) that: a) replays the sample batches, b) simulates a failover at a configurable offset, and c) demonstrates correct resume and dedupe behavior.
- Export of the exact manifests and a signed timestamped evidence bundle for auditing.

Logs / pointers we have collected:
- Delivery trace: https://console.redwood.ai/deliveries/logs/DEL-20260304-9842 (internal)
- S3 put traces for their bucket: s3://redwood-delivery-archive/us-east/2026-03-04/batch-10561.gz
- KMS signing key used: arn:aws:kms:us-east-1:123456789012:key/abcd-ef01-2345 (we will provide attestation)

Expected behavior:
Resume tokens should deterministically indicate the last-seen position and allow a replayer to continue without creating duplicates or leaving gaps, even when a failover occurs mid-batch. Per-batch manifests should be verifiable by the customer's auditors.

Priority reasoning:
Customer is enterprise, fraud-detection use-case, regulatory audit scheduled. They requested a short evidence package and a reproducible harness for their SOC and legal teams.

Next steps requested from Support/Eng:
- Provide sample export package and verification example.
- Explain resume-token format and guarantees in plain language suitable for auditors.
- Deliver the test harness and instructions for running cross-region failover scenarios locally against the sample package.

Additional notes:
2026-03-05 - Customer (Olivia Martins, Aurelia): Provided requested time window and attached minimal consumer logs (consumer_offsets.log). Customer confirms they do not filter events upstream; they rely on our ordering guarantees.
Link to internal slack: https://slack.redwood.ai/archives/CINCIDENTS/p164679
2026-03-07 - Support (Maya Chen): Sent interim response to customer with proposed token spec and ETA for the sample package (2026-03-09). Asked customer if they prefer RSA or ECDSA-signed manifests for auditor compatibility.
Checked delivery runtime: audit-archiver v2.1 showed a retry loop at 2026-03-04T02:15:12Z when primary region link timed out; failover path promoted eu-west writer which used same batch-id namespace but a different highwater origin.
Observed resume_token schema variants in historical deliveries; some older deliveries used monotonic sequence only (not region-scoped). Need to standardize to include region prefix.
KMS signing verified for batch-10561 manifest; signature valid using key arn:aws:kms:us-east-1:123456789012:key/abcd-ef01-2345. Will include signed manifest sample in deliverable.

payload.description:
Issue summary:

Customer DataSilo AI reported intermittent 429 responses across several API routes following a scheduled scale-down of their dedicated GPU pool. The pattern started immediately after the autoscaler removed a node while route-weight redistribution (reshuffle) was in progress.

Impact:
- Customer observed ~8-12% of requests returned 429 over a 7-minute window across mixed workloads (embeddings + chat).
- Errors affected production workflows for multiple customers in the same dedicated pool; DataSilo reported failed ingest jobs and degraded user-facing chat latency.
- Business impact: downstream job retries caused backpressure on orchestrators and transient SLA breaches.

Environment:
- Redwood Dedicated pool: pool-id dp-88-west
- Region: us-west-2 (prod-us-west)
- Customer tier: dedicated, reserved capacity 4xA100 nodes (quantized models enabled)
- Traffic mix: 60% chat low-latency, 40% batch embeddings

Steps to reproduce (observed in customer logs / can be simulated):
1. Configure a dedicated pool with route-weighting across 3 routes (chat-high, chat-low, batch-embeds).
2. Schedule policy-driven scale-down (remove 1 node) during light traffic but with ongoing route-weight reshuffle enabled (weight change in Console).
3. Observe: autoscaler drains pod(s), routing layer triggers route-weight rebalance, some in-flight sockets are reassigned.
4. Within 30s of node removal, edge proxies report increased 429 responses for short sessions and for connections which had been reassigned mid-request.

Observed logs / traces (representative):
- gateway: "429 quota_exceeded route=chat-high pool=dp-88-west session_id=..."
- rate-limiter: "token_window_decrement failed: target_node_not_ready during rebalance"
- serving-runtime: "cache-miss + reconnect: kvcache invalidated during host-swap"
- autoscaler: "drain complete node=node-7; trigger route-weight reassign; 3 active sessions migrated"

Initial hypothesis:
- During node removal the route-weight reshuffle briefly double-counts or drop-counts tokens for sessions mid-migration, resulting in transient token-window exhaustion at the logical tenant level.
- Edge proxy connection handoff plus delayed healthcheck reporting caused the token refill scheduler to see an inconsistent view of active connections, producing a local backlog -> 429s.

Mitigation attempted (customer + support):
- Temporarily paused scheduled scale-down to allow gradual manual drain (customer) — mitigated further 429 waves.
- Support toggled route-weight reshuffle to "deferred" in control plane for dp-88-west (temporary) to prevent automatic reassign during active drains.
- Applied short-term smoothing: increased per-route burst window for chat-high by 2x for 15 minutes.

Requested by customer:
- Explanation for root cause and a durable fix to prevent 429s on scheduled maintenance/scale actions.
- Guidance on safe autoscale/drain settings and recommended route-weight change practices for Dedicated pools.

03-11 09:14 PDT: Reproduced in staging with same pool config when simulating node removal and simultaneous console route-weight update; observed 5-9% 429s for short-lived sessions.
Token accounting trace showed a ~20s window where route-layer emitted duplicate decrement events for some session ids during reassign handshake.
Healthcheck lag on drained node reported 12-18s before proxy dropped connection from routing tables; this mismatch corresponds to first 429 spike.
KV cache eviction during host swap caused extra upstream retries which incremented token counts on retry paths (possible double-charge).

Issue summary:
Customer BrightWrite reported a sudden sustained increase in 5xx responses between 18:35-19:40 PDT on 2026-03-13. Errors correlate with a large tenant burst (long-lived streaming sessions) and a concurrent increase in ephemeral socket churn at the API gateway. Upstream serving-runtime instances experienced GPU watchdog restarts and OOM-like behavior during the window.

Impact:
- BrightWrite (dedicated) observed ~40% of their requests returning 5xx intermittently; streaming sessions were frequently disconnected.
- Error spike affected their production us-west region only.

Environment:
- prod-us-west, dedicated cluster pool RB-ded-42
- Affected model routes: redwood-instruct-13b and llama3-70b-mixed pinned for the customer

Steps to reproduce / observed sequence:
1) Customer performed a scheduled internal campaign that opened ~1.8x baseline concurrent streaming sessions starting at ~18:30 PDT.
2) API gateway ephemeral connection count (socket ephemeral port usage) increased and hit threshold on some edge nodes.
3) API gateway began returning 502/503 for new streams and started TCP resets for existing keepalives.
4) Serving-runtime backends received bursts of partial connections leading to heavy KV cache thrash and increased GPU memory volatility.
5) GPU watchdog restarts observed on several runtime pods; some restarted multiple times causing transient 5xx floor.

Observed logs/metrics (high level):
- apigw.edge.sockets.ephemeral_in_use spike to 98% on 3 nodes (normal <= 45%)
- apigw.errors.5xx increased from baseline 0.5% -> 22% (customer routes)
- runtime.gpu.watchdog_restarts: 6 events in 30m across 4 pods
- runtime.kvcache.evictions spike and prefetch queue length growth

Expected behavior:
- API gateway should gracefully queue/route without triggering connection resets; runtime should not enter watchdog restart loops under transient socket pressure.

Attachments:
- selected apigw and runtime logs (attached to ticket)
- Cloud metrics graphs (links in comments)

2026-03-13 19:02 - Support (Aisha): Initial triage performed. Collected logs and elevated to SRE. Informed customer we're investigating and requested exact timeframe and any recent config changes.
2026-03-13 19:18 - SRE (Diego): Noted socket_ephemeral_in_use spike on edge nodes edge-17/19/23. Correlated with increased long-lived streaming sessions from BrightWrite tenant. Opening infra-side investigation into accept queue sizing and keepalive behavior.
2026-03-13 19:45 - Customer (BrightWrite - Ops): Confirmed they kicked off a heavy streaming-promotional job at 18:28 PDT and saw disconnects. Asked for ETA/mitigation.
2026-03-13 20:05 - SRE (Diego): Temporarily increased per-node ephemeral port window on impacted edge nodes and applied connection drain smoothing for BrightWrite route. Observed drop in 5xx rate to ~3% within 6 minutes. Not a permanent fix.
2026-03-14 08:30 - Support (Aisha): Follow-up to customer with interim mitigation and next steps (runtime config change + infra patch scheduled). Customer satisfied with workaround but requested full root cause and timeline for permanent fix.
Edge analysis: accept queue and ephemeral port exhaustion on a subset of edge nodes. Edge software did not gracefully throttle long-lived streaming accept rate; new connections triggered resets when ephemeral pool depleted.
Runtime analysis: sudden surge of half-open/short-lived connections increased memory fragmentation in serving-runtime and generated KV cache thrash; combined with large batch of streaming prefix tokens caused GPU memory pressure and watchdog restarts.
Hypothesis: combination of aggressive customer streaming concurrency + apigw accept/keepalive policy produced connection churn that amplified to runtime, causing GPU watchdog restarts (not a model bug).
Dashboards/links: apigw-graphs-2026-03-13 (link), runtime-watchdog-timeline-2026-03-13 (link)
Related historical tickets: SUP-214890 (stale keepalive proxy reuse), SUP-472901 (connection thrashing causing bridge 502s) — behavior similar but root cause here more focused on ephemeral socket exhaustion at edge layer.
Short-term mitigation (completed 2026-03-13 19:55): increased ephemeral port allocation and smoothing, applied temporary route-level throttle for BrightWrite to limit concurrent streaming sessions. Result: 5xx rate reduced to ~2-4% for customer traffic.
Planned fix (scheduled): update API gateway to backpressure new long-lived streaming accepts earlier and add adaptive keepalive reclamation (patch PR https://github.com/redwood-infra/agent/pull/2345). Update serving-runtime to harden KV cache eviction under high connection churn (PR https://github.com/redwood/serving-runtime/pull/987).
Customer follow-up: engineering SLOs and suggested client-side exponential backoff for streaming reconnects. Support scheduled a postmortem meeting with BrightWrite for 2026-03-16.

- Runtime: improve watchdog telemetry and avoid restart loops under transient memory pressure (owner: Serving Runtime team)
- Support: update runbook and add proactive alert for apigw.ephemeral_in_use > 80% (owner: Support)

payload.description:
Issue summary:
During a scheduled rolling migration of a customer-pinned model variant into Acme AI's dedicated pool (prod/us-west), we observed intermittent GPU-attach handshake failures for a subset of new worker attachments. Those failures caused automatic fallback to a smaller quantized model variant for some requests, which in turn led to cascading throughput collapse (p50->p95 regression) for Acme's high-throughput routed endpoints.

Impact:
- Customer Acme AI experienced ~60% drop in request throughput for ~40 minutes during the migration window.
- Elevated latency: p50 increased from 48ms to 220ms, p95 increased from 230ms to 1.8s for affected routes.
- Some requests returned fallback model outputs (smaller quantized variant) unexpectedly.

Environment:
- Dedicated pool: acme-dedicated-prod-uswest (GPU types: A100-80GB mixed with A100-40GB)
- Model rollout: acme-domain-tuned-mistral-7b -> mistral-7b-v1 (rolling across 24 workers)
- Time window: 2026-03-12 14:10 UTC -> 2026-03-12 14:50 UTC

Observed behavior / Timeline:
1) 14:10 UTC: Rollout started, controller scheduled replacements of ~2 workers/min.
2) 14:15 UTC: Metric spike in allocator attachment_time_ms and attach_failures.
3) 14:18 UTC: Autoscaler began conservative throttles due to transient attach latencies; some routes hit fallback policy (model_variant: mistral-quant-7b).
4) 14:20-14:45 UTC: Throughput degraded and p95 spiked; multiple attach handshake errors correlated with a subset of hosts showing increased NVMe IO wait.
5) 14:50 UTC: Rollout paused; manual mitigation applied (drain + reattach on different shard).
6) 15:05 UTC: Throughput recovered to baseline after forced evacuations and targeted worker restarts.

Steps to reproduce (non-deterministic):
- In dedicated pool with mixed GPU SKUs, start a rolling replace of 20-30 workers with model variant swap.
- Simultaneously generate sustained short-stream traffic (small batched requests) from a tenant with many small concurrent streams (Acme load generator used 3500 streams @ 5rps each).
- Observe allocator attach latencies, NVMe IO wait, and attach handshake timeouts.

Logs / Evidence:
- Allocator logs: repeated "attach_handshake_timeout" entries from hosts 10.2.41.12, 10.2.41.18 between 14:16-14:28 UTC.
- Metrics: attach_time_ms P90 jumped to 12.3s; attach_fail_rate 4.7%; worker_nvme_io_wait P95 increased 8x on affected hosts.
- Console traces: route-level fallback events showing automatic switch to mistral-quant-7b at 14:19 UTC.
- Slack thread: #support -> thread t12345 (https://slack.redwood.io/archives/C02/support/p16423).
- Related dashboards: Dedicated Pool -> acme-dedicated-prod-uswest (link in related_confluence_pages).

Hypotheses / Initial investigation notes:
- Hypothesis A: Mixed GPU SKU placement + heavy short-stream fanout caused NVMe IO contention on placement hosts during worker attach, slowing the attach handshake.
- Hypothesis B: The attach handshake backoff is too aggressive on attach latency, causing the router to trigger fallback to quantized variant prematurely.
- Hypothesis C: A noisy tenant (Acme's own high concurrency pattern) amplified attach latency and evicted local caches, increasing NVMe pressure.

Temporary mitigations applied:
- Paused the rollout to stop creating new attachments.
- Per-host restarts of the serving sidecar on 5 affected machines.
- Manually increased handshake timeout to 25s for this rollout via feature flag.
- Routed Acme traffic away from two noisy workers to reduce concurrent short-stream fanout.

Recommended next steps / action items:
- SRE to reproduce in staging with mixed GPU SKUs and high small-stream concurrency (assigned: Diego).
- Adjust attach-handshake timeout and backoff policy to better tolerate transient NVMe IO spikes (short-term flag, long-term config).
- Add allocator-level NVMe pressure alerting and per-host attach-rate limiting to avoid cascading failures.
- Eng: evaluate whether worker pre-warming can reduce new attach IO (ticket to follow).

Resolution notes (work in progress):
- Rollout paused and partial recovery achieved via restarts and routing mitigations.
- Root cause not yet confirmed; follow-ups scheduled.

payload.description:
Issue summary:
BrightCart's dedicated reservation started seeing sustained p95 latency degradation and recurring 504 upstream timeouts during their nightly ingestion bursts (approx 23:45–00:30 UTC). The behavior began 2026-03-12 and persisted across multiple bursts. Impact: user-facing generation requests time out or take >> expected latency, downstream job retries amplify load and cause throughput collapse.

Impact:
- Customer reports elevated p95 from ~120ms to 800–1200ms and intermittent 504s.
- Total successful tokens/sec reduced ~45% during the window.
- Affects business-critical ingestion route and small interactive queries simultaneously.

Environment:
- Dedicated pool (BrightCart-resv-01) in prod-us-east backed by A100-like instances.
- Autoscale configured with step increments of 2 GPUs, min=2, max=12, cooldown=5m.
- Workloads: mixed short-chatty seqs (~64 tokens) and short burst long-seq inference (~1024 tokens) from the same tenant.

Steps to reproduce (from customer):
1. Trigger nightly ingestion with concurrency ~120 concurrent requests across many short sequences.
2. Observe p95 drift 5–15 minutes into burst and 504s at 10–20 minutes.
3. Stopping ingestion and leaving only chat traffic returns p95 to baseline within 7–10 minutes.

Observed behavior:
- p95/p99 climb and sustained 504s.
- Autoscaler does add GPUs but in steps too large to match transient burst profile, causing oversubscription and context thrashing on existing GPUs during scale events.
- Internal runtime logs show repeated kernel preemption and frequent NVMe page faults on a subset of pods at the time of peak.
- KV-cache hit-rate drops by ~30% concurrent with latency spike (cache eviction thrash suspected).

Expected behavior:
- Autoscale should react smoothly to sustained increase and maintain latency SLOs; transient bursts should be absorbed by batching and KV cache without causing timeouts.

Logs/metrics to review (provided by customer and RBX observability):
- Pod-level GPU utilization heatmap: shows two pods at >95% utilization while others idle.
- Scheduler traces: several pods moved and new pods scheduled during the spike window.
- Runtime logs: repeated "cudaStreamSynchronize timeout" and "kv_cache_eviction" events.
- Token throughput dashboards: tokens/s down ~45% during incident windows.

Initial hypotheses:
1) Noisy-neighbor effect from mixed workload causing inefficient packing onto GPUs; short vs long sequence mix amplifies context switch overhead.
2) Autoscaler step size (2 GPUs) and cooldown mean we overshoot or react too slowly; scheduling decisions cause hot pods to form and create temporary hotspots.
3) Underestimated microbatching thresholds lead to small batch sizes for long-seq jobs increasing per-token overhead.
4) KV cache eviction thrash due to cache being partitioned per-pod and new pods not warming their cache quickly.

Immediate impact mitigation performed:
- Support asked BrightCart to temporarily reduce ingestion concurrency to 60 and stagger the burst; they observed immediate p95 reduction to ~200ms.
- Increased autoscaler cooldown temporarily to avoid oscillation while we investigate.

Next steps we are taking (engineering action plan):
1) SRE/serving to review bin-packing logs and GPU-affinity allocation for BrightCart-resv-01 to detect misallocation (assigned to Marco Ruiz).
2) Runtime team to analyze kv_cache eviction logs and provide cache-warmup heuristics or shared-prefix warm cache options.
3) Autoscale team to test a smaller granularity autoscale (1-GPU step + predictive ramp) on a staging replica using a replay of BrightCart burst trace.
4) Observability team to add a short-lived dashboard focused on per-pod KV hit-rate, kernel preemption counts, and page-fault spikes for the next 48 hours.
5) Coordinate with BrightCart on a controlled burst test window (proposed 2026-03-14 23:30–00:00 UTC).

Workaround for customer:
- Stagger ingestion windows and reduce concurrency to avoid simultaneous long-seq batches co-located with short-seq chat traffic.
- Pin ingestion routes to a separate dedicated pool where possible to avoid mixed-job interference.

Attachments provided by customer:
- Snapshot links: https://rbx.observability/brightcart/resv-01/2026-03-12/23:40 (heatmaps and pod logs).
- Local capture of client retries and timestamps attached to ticket (sensitive).

2026-03-12 02:22 - Customer (BrightCart SRE - Priya Shah): Reduced concurrency to 60, staggered starts; p95 dropped from ~900ms to ~200ms. Still occasional 504s at peak. We can run a controlled test if you need it.
2026-03-12 03:05 - Support (Aisha Patel): Thanks, Priya. Asking infra team to look at autoscale config and per-pod GPU allocation. Tagging Marco Ruiz.

Additional notes:
2026-03-14 01:05 - Support (Aisha Patel): Coordinating controlled test window with BrightCart for 2026-03-14 23:30–00:00 UTC. Asked customer to route debug logs and enable request tracing header for the window.
2026-03-14 11:55 - Customer (Priya Shah): Agrees to test canary routing for ingestion next maintenance window. Appreciative of workaround guidance.
2026-03-14 12:30 - Support (Aisha Patel): Marking ticket In Progress. Next milestone: run canary in prod with autoscale adjustments and runtime batch-timeout patch. Will update post-canary.
Pod allocation pattern suggests packing algorithm favored minimizing pod counts over balancing GPU utilization across pods, which interacted poorly with mixed short/long sequence workloads.
KV cache is currently sharded per-pod; new pods after autoscale events start uncached, causing a warmup period where long-seq jobs hit cold cache and trigger heavier GPU work and page faults.
Kernel preemption traces correlate strongly with periods of high long-seq job arrival while GPU was handling other contexts — indicates contention rather than a single faulty pod.
Autoscaler step size of 2 GPUs + 5m cooldown is too coarse for BrightCart's high-frequency short bursts; predictive scaling or 1-GPU steps improve reaction shape in staging.
No evidence of hardware failure on GPUs; NVMe page faults appear correlated with pod context switches rather than disk errors.
Workaround and mitigation: Customer to stagger and reduce concurrency for immediate relief; will provision a canary change to autoscaler (1-GPU step, shorter cooldown, predictive ramp) and deploy runtime batch-timeout patch to reduce kernel preemption during mixed workloads. Engineering to follow up with a plan to implement shared KV-cache warmup or global prefix cache in future release. After successful canary, schedule rolling change for BrightCart-resv-01 with post-deploy metrics watch. Ticket will be updated with canary results and final rollout notes.

Monitor temporary dashboards and alerts for 48 hours post-canary (owner: Samir Desai)

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customer reports persistent 429 responses originating from their dedicated ingest pool during a rolling bulk ingest job. Throttles begin well before expected refill boundaries, causing partial failures and retries in their orchestrator.

Impact:
- 20-30% of ingestion worker tasks receive 429s during a 2h rolling import window.
- Jobs retry and extend total import time by ~3x.
- Customer-facing syncs downstream are delayed; revenue-impacting for nightly ETL.

Environment:
- Dedicated capacity (customer-managed pool), pool id: dsp-7e1a
- Region: prod-us-west (single AZ failover configured)
- Ingest orchestrator: DataStreamX uploader v2.3 (uses short-lived ephemeral keys per worker)
- Rate config: split-burst pool enabled with priority lanes; route affinity on

Steps to reproduce (as provided by customer):
1) Start rolling bulk ingest across 50 workers with ephemeral key fanout
2) Warmup phase runs parallel preflight requests to pin model variants
3) After ~6 minutes into the job, intermittent 429s appear across many workers, intensifying as the job proceeds and more ephemeral keys are minted

Expected behavior:
- Throttling should respect burst credits and sustained refill windows; early 429s should not occur during initial warmup if within burst allocations.

Actual behavior:
- 429s observed consistently before refill boundary; console shows burst credit balance dropping faster than tokens consumed at origin.

Collected artifacts (attached by customer):
- Ingest job logs (timestamps, worker ids), HTTP response headers from throttled requests, ephemeral key creation timeline
- Console screenshot showing per-route and pool-level token balance at time of incident

2026-03-12 10:02 - Support (Aisha): Acknowledged receipt. Asked customer for request/response headers and list of ephemeral key timestamps. Escalated to SRE for early triage.
2026-03-12 11:18 - SRE (Mark): Noted odd drift between edge token windows and origin refill. Requested edge proxy logs (edge-proxy-usw-3) and rate-limiter debug metrics for epoch window overlapping at 10:57-11:05.
2026-03-12 13:42 - Customer (Elena, DataStreamX): Uploaded logs and a short trace of worker key creation; called out that workers create ephemeral keys approximately every 30s during the first 10 minutes.
2026-03-12 16:01 - Support (Aisha): Confirmed we have artifacts; running local replay against a staging rate-limiter to attempt reproduction. Noted link to runbook and will update when SRE has metrics.
2026-03-13 09:22 - SRE (Mark): Reproduce attempt on staging using similar ephemeral-key cadence reproduced early 429 pattern. Hypothesis posted to ticket. Planning controlled config change in staging to validate fix.
Hypothesis: A synchronization gap exists between edge-level token accounting and origin refill epochs when ephemeral keys are created rapidly and route affinity shifts mid-window. Edge proxies appear to attribute token consumption to ephemeral key buckets before central refill has reconciled, causing perceived early exhaustion.
Observed: In staging replay, edge-proxy counters incremented ahead of origin by 2-4s during high fanout; refill window boundaries at origin align to minute epoch while edge had slight drift due to NTP jitter and proxy batching behavior.
Metric evidence: rate-limiter.checkout_latencies and token_delta metrics show spikes at worker-fanout events; per-route burst_credit_balance at edge drops while origin reports pending refill. Related dashboard: https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/rl/edge-refill-drift?orgId=1&from=now-30m
Triage action: opened PR to add conservative debounce on edge-side accounting and to tag ephemeral keys with ingestion-session id so origin accounting can coalesce counts before rejecting. See PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/ratelimiter/pull/879
Risk assessment: Low-to-medium risk to change; affects only dedicated pools with short-lived-credential fanout and split-burst enabled. Requires canary rollout in prod-us-west to validate.
Coordination note: Need customer to enable short canary run window; suggested to run gradually with 10% worker concurrency for first validation.
Workaround (short-term): Instructed DataStreamX to increase ephemeral key TTL to reduce churn (from 30s -> 300s) and to apply client-side jitter on key creation to avoid synchronized fanout. This immediately reduced 429 occurrence in their next test window.
Mitigation (mid-term): Deployed staging fix that adds a 200ms edge-level debounce and tags ephemeral sessions to batch accounting. Staging replay shows 85% reduction in early 429s. PR referenced above contains tests and metrics links.
Planned rollout: Canary rollout scheduled for prod-us-west with 10% of dedicated pool traffic on 2026-03-16, monitored by SRE and on-call. Full rollout contingent on 48h canary results.
Follow-ups: 1) Add diagnostic console panel to show edge-origin token drift per-pool. 2) Update docs with recommended ephemeral key TTL and jitter guidance for dedicated pools. 3) Create a small runbook for customers running high-fanout rolling ingests.
Status: Pending canary. Customer notified of workaround and will validate TTL change in nightly import.

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customer BrightAssist reports that after an HA proxy failover in their environment, SSE streams used for chat completions resume but the final choice is truncated and the client receives duplicated trailing fragments. This causes the customer application to fail JSON parsing for structured responses and to show incomplete assistant messages.

Impact:
- Multiple production requests (15-30/min for a single customer pod) end with malformed final choices leading to downstream app exceptions.
- Customer reports increased error rate and user-visible truncations during a recent network maintenance window.

Environment:
- Dedicated customer deployment, hosted in us-east-1 on Redwood Dedicated.
- Fronted by customer's HAProxy cluster (two-tier: edge -> internal LB -> customer nodes).
- SDK: JS browser client using EventSource (SSE) with Last-Event-ID resume logic.
- Models: redwood/chat-deployment-v2.

Steps to reproduce (customer-provided):
1. Start a long-running chat generate request which streams 200-400 tokens.
2. Force a HAProxy edge failover (reload/restart) during token stream generation.
3. Client reconnects and passes Last-Event-ID to resume.
4. Observe final fragments: duplicate trailing fragments interleaved and the end event missing or the choice body truncated.

Observed behavior:
- Client receives duplicate chunks that contain trailing token fragments (e.g., ",\"metadata\":{...}" appears twice).
- A terminal 'event: end' is sometimes missing after resume, or arrives but with sequence offsets that cause the client to drop the final token batch.
- Some resumed streams contain a short garbled fragment appended to the previous choice, producing invalid JSON in structured outputs.

Expected behavior:
- After reconnect/resume the stream should continue without duplication or truncation; the final 'end' event should be delivered exactly once and the choice body should be intact.

Relevant logs (customer excerpts):
- "edge: connection reset by peer; replaying Last-Event-ID=6734"
- "internal-lb: 502 during upstream shutdown, resume requested with id=6734"
- A sample fragment sequence the customer saved (sanitized) shows duplicated trailing suffix lines with identical token offsets.

Workarounds tried by customer:
- Forcing full restart instead of resume avoids duplicated fragments but increases latency.
- Using long-polling instead of SSE avoids the issue but is not acceptable for UX.

Notes:
- Customer is on a paid dedicated contract and is impacted for multiple production users.

Support reproduced a variant of the issue in staging by simulating TCP connection close during SSE stream and replaying Last-Event-ID; observed truncated final chunk intermittently.
Hypothesis 1: HAProxy or intermediary is buffering and splitting SSE event boundaries; on failover re-inserted fragments cause the server/runtime to re-emit overlapping token ranges leading to duplicate trailing fragments.
Hypothesis 2: Last-Event-ID resume logic expects monotonic offset acknowledgement from client; proxy-induced reordering of small TCP fragments causes the resume offset to point to a byte boundary inside a multi-byte token, producing truncated JSON on reassembly.
Hypothesis 3: The serving-runtime may commit and stream a final 'end' event before all socket buffers are flushed; a mid-flight failover can cause a partial 'end' event emission that the resume path doesn't canonicalize (idempotency gap).
Collected traces: request IDs and event offsets from customer; shared a trace dump via secure link with SRE team (internal ticket attached).
Reproduced in our lab using HAProxy 2.6 config with 'option http-server-close' toggled; duplication frequency increased when proxy had response-buffering enabled.
SRE note: Node-level TCP FIN+RST timing correlates with missing 'end' events; suggests race between socket teardown and application flush path.

Additional notes:
2026-03-10 14:02 UTC - BrightAssist (Customer): Uploaded sanitized SSE capture and HAProxy logs (link provided). They confirm the issue occurs after planned network maintenance window when the edge proxy is reloaded.

Issue summary: Customer reports intermittent 429s from a dedicated pool while running orchestrated worker fanouts that multiplex many short-lived sessions. The customer suspects token-slicing and atomic refill semantics are causing groups of parallel workers to collide on refill boundaries.

Impact: Roughly 8–12% of requests are receiving 429s during scheduled flush windows for their background ingest and the rate spikes are correlated with their orchestrator job starts. This is causing delays in their pipeline and some time-sensitive webhook retries to fail.

Environment: MetricFlow dedicated pool in prod-us-west, traffic originates from a fleet of orchestrator workers that open ephemeral sessions and use API keys rotated every 6 minutes. Workload pattern: bursts of ~200 short sessions that call streaming start then immediately push small chunks (~1-3k tokens).

Observed behavior: 429s come in tight waves aligned to the orchestrator job start times. Throttle headers show remaining=0 and x-refill-epoch points to a refill event that applied to a group of sessions simultaneously. Customer believes refill is being computed atomically per-namespace and token-sliced windows allow momentary negative bursts.

Steps to reproduce (customer provided):
1) Create a dedicated pool and provision 2 workers per orchestrator shard.
2) Rotate ephemeral keys every 6 minutes and fanout 200 workers to start within a 30s window.
3) Each worker starts a streaming session and immediately emits a small payload.
4) Observe 429s concentrated within the first 90s of the job.

Request: Customer asks for an explanation of refill semantics when many short-lived sessions start together and guidance on configuration to avoid synchronized 429 waves. They also ask whether splitting refill epochs or changing token-slicing granularity will help and what recommended knob changes are safe for a dedicated pool.
2026-03-12 10:20 UTC - Received initial ticket with customer logs and sample traffic pattern (200 workers, ephemeral keys).
Checked tenant rate limiter logs: refill events recorded at epoch boundaries with batch size consistent with configured burst budget. Noted a cluster of token grants followed by immediate consumption and subsequent remaining=0 for many sessions.
Hypothesis A: Atomic refill per-tenant combined with synchronized session start leads to token allocation granularity causing short-lived sessions to contend and exhaust micro-budgets simultaneously.
Hypothesis B: Token-slicing uses coarse-grain shards (N=8) for this tenant; when many sessions map to same slice the refill appears atomic and causes seen 429 wave. Consider reducing slice size or enabling random jitter on refill mapping.
Observed metric: token_grants_per_epoch spiked from baseline 1200 to 18k during job window; per-slice utilization showed 60% of allocations hitting two slices.
Console trace: route-level latency spiked 5x during event; no 5xxs from serving runtime—rejections are explicit rate rejects.
Customer token rotation pattern (6m TTL) is causing many ephemeral keys to align with refill boundaries due to orchestrator scheduling; recommend reviewing key rotation schedule as well.
Checked linked issue SUP-3141596 for similar refill alignment cases; that ticket implemented refill jitter experiments on staging with positive results.
Action taken so far: increased customer's burst allowance temporarily by +20% for their dedicated pool to provide immediate relief while we evaluate config changes.
Telemetry snapshot saved: s3://redwood-support/telemetry/SUP-527890/epoch-snap-20260312.json (access granted to eng on request).

Additional notes:
MetricFlow - Ops (2026-03-12T11:37Z): Provided sample requestIDs and job-start timestamps for two windows (2026-03-11T23:00Z and 2026-03-12T03:00Z). Noted pattern: starts are scheduled by cron jobs in their orchestrator which align closely with system clocks across shards.
Ethan Chen (SRE) (2026-03-12T13:10Z): Observed per-slice hot-spotting. Tentative plan: run a controlled experiment to change slice_count from 8 to 32 for this tenant in staging and add random refill jitter of up to 30s to epoch boundary. Asking Product if jitter change is safe for SLA window accounting.
Product (2026-03-12T14:05Z): Jitter change acceptable at customer-level for non-critical low-latency lanes. For higher tiers would need rollout notes. Suggest start with orchestrator/background lane only.
MetricFlow - Dev (2026-03-12T15:22Z): We can stagger cron starts by introducing per-shard random delay up to 45s. But we'd prefer config guidance on the server side so we don't have to change many orchestrators across fleets.
MetricFlow - Ops (2026-03-14T12:01Z): Thank you, please proceed with background-lane change during our maintenance window 2026-03-15 02:00-03:00 UTC. We'll monitor.
Temporary burst allowance increased +20%; staging experiment with slice_count=32 and refill_jitter=20s reduced 429 wave amplitude by ~70%. Planned staged rollout to customer background lane during maintenance window. Final resolution pending production rollout and 48h monitoring.
payload.summary: Clarify atomic refill and token-slicing interactions for multiplexed orchestrator causing intermittent 429s

Issue summary:
Silverline Health (private deployment in prod-us-east) experienced intermittent connection flaps beginning 2026-03-10 08:12 UTC that resulted in 5xx responses and session resets for streaming and non-streaming requests. Errors observed by customer were TLS handshake failures and abrupt HTTP/2 stream resets. This ticket documents the escalation, short-term mitigation, and post-incident follow-up actions.

Impact:
- Customer-facing production traffic experienced ~12% error rate during peak window (08:12–10:03 UTC).
- Streaming sessions dropped mid-response; several business-critical flows retried and saw increased latency.
- Customer single-tenant private control plane hosting their dedicated gateway was affected; no hosted tenants impacted.

Timeline (high level):
- 2026-03-10 08:12 UTC: Silverline CS reports increased 5xx and streaming disconnects via support@ and opens escalation.
- 2026-03-10 08:28 UTC: Triage call with SRE, Private deployment ops, and Silverline network engineer.
- 2026-03-10 08:45 UTC: SRE identifies bursts of TCP connection churn and TLS handshake errors on control-plane VMs.
- 2026-03-10 09:10 UTC: Short-term mitigation applied: increased NLB idle-timeout from 60s -> 300s and temporarily disabled TLS session resumption on control-plane proxy to prevent stale cache reuse.
- 2026-03-10 09:35 UTC: Error rate falls to <1%; customer confirms nominal traffic and accepts workaround.
- 2026-03-11–2026-03-12: Root cause investigation and repro in staging cluster.
- 2026-03-12 17:00 UTC: Deploy permanent control-plane patch rolling TLS session cache eviction fix and bumped connection pool thresholds.
- 2026-03-13 10:00 UTC: Customer acceptance testing complete; ticket moved to Resolved.

Steps to reproduce (internal notes):
1) On a private control plane with NLB configured to default idle timeout (60s), run a bursty client that opens many short-lived connections and reuses TLS sessions.
2) Observe TLS handshake failures and occasional HTTP/2 RST_STREAM when the control-plane proxy's session cache evicts entries under memory pressure.
3) Reproduce was easier when a scheduled batch job from customer peaked at 08:00–08:20 UTC, causing ephemeral connection churn.

Logs / Artifacts / Dashboards:
- Control-plane proxy logs: tls: handshake error: local error: tls: bad record MAC (sampled at 2026-03-10T08:40Z).
- NLB metrics: connection_count spikes and increased connection resets (link to dashboard).
- Packet capture (sanitized) shows client attempting session resumption followed by full handshake failures.
- Customer-provided application logs indicating retries and increased end-to-end latency.

Initial mitigation and communications:
- Applied NLB idle-timeout increase and disabled TLS session resumption temporarily on control-plane proxies; documented change and timeline to customer.
- Proactively opened a dedicated Slack channel (#support-silverline-private) for live updates and arranged an executive escalation bridge for the first 2 hours.
- CS notified customer of potential brief restarts during patch rollout; provided rollback plan.

Root cause hypothesis:
- Combination of (a) control-plane proxy TLS session cache evictions under memory pressure and (b) aggressive upstream client connection churn (customer batch job) caused increased TLS full handshakes and transient handshake failures. The problem was amplified by a low NLB idle timeout which led to more frequent connection reestablishment and pressure on the proxy session cache.

Resolution summary:
- Short-term: increased NLB idle timeout and disabled session resumption to avoid stale cache lookups; temporarily increased control-plane proxy memory limits to reduce evictions.
- Long-term: patch to TLS session cache logic that avoids returning partially-evicted entries, connection pool tuning, and an infra automation change to detect sudden connection churn and automatically raise NLB timeout for private deployments.

Post-incident follow-up items (see remediation_actions):
- Coordinate a runbook update for private-control-plane networking and TLS settings.
- Validate similar private deployments for the same signal and schedule proactive configuration changes for high-burst customers.

Attachments: links to logs, packet captures, and the root-cause analysis doc archived in Confluence.
[2026-03-10 08:20 UTC] Maya Chen (Support): Customer reports widespread streaming disconnects and 5xx. Opening escalation, paging SRE and Private Ops. Silverline reports that the incidents started after a scheduled batch job at 08:00 UTC.
[2026-03-10 08:31 UTC] Priya Nair (SRE): Observed TLS handshake errors and elevated connection churn on control-plane proxy. Starting live capture and increasing log level for proxies behind NLB-43.
[2026-03-10 08:50 UTC] Jordan Alvarez (Private Ops): Applied NLB idle-timeout change (60s -> 300s) and disabled session resumption on proxies in a canary group (2/6 hosts). Monitoring metrics for 10 minutes before wider rollout.
[2026-03-10 09:20 UTC] Luca Romano (Customer Success, Silverline): Customer confirms error rate dropped to baseline after mitigations. They request confirmation that this won't recur before their nightly batch at 02:00 local time.
[2026-03-11 14:05 UTC] Anika Bose (Applied ML / Infra): Reproduced session-cache eviction in staging with smaller memory limits. Preparing code patch to ensure atomically-valid session entries are returned by cache API.
[2026-03-12 16:55 UTC] Jordan Alvarez (Private Ops): Rolling deploy of TLS session cache fix complete across control-plane. Increased proxy memory and connection pool thresholds. No errors reported in final overnight validation. Notifying customer for acceptance testing.
[2026-03-13 09:45 UTC] Luca Romano (Customer Success, Silverline): Customer completed acceptance tests against their nightly batch; no errors observed. They marked incident as resolved on their end and thanked the team for quick remediation.
[2026-03-13 10:12 UTC] Maya Chen (Support): Marking ticket Resolved. Follow-ups scheduled: runbook update (owner: Jordan), cross-check other private tenants for similar config (owner: Anika), customer post-incident review call scheduled 2026-03-16 16:00 UTC.
[2026-03-16 16:05 UTC] Post-incident review note (Jordan Alvarez): Action items reviewed on call; Silverline requested an optional health-check webhook for their control plane which we agreed to prioritize in Q2 roadmap.
Control-plane TLS session cache bug fixed and deployed; NLB idle timeout increased; proxy memory and connection pools tuned. Customer validated fix during acceptance testing. Runbook updated and scheduled automation for detecting connection churn drafted. No further recurrence in 72-hour observation window.
A race in the control-plane TLS session cache caused partially-evicted entries to be returned during high churn; combined with a low NLB idle timeout and customer-side bursty connection patterns this produced handshake failures and stream resets.
short_term_workaround: Increase NLB idle timeout to 300s and disable TLS session resumption on affected proxies.
medium_term_fix: Patch TLS session cache to only return fully-valid entries and increase proxy memory limits and connection pool thresholds.
long_term_action: Add infra automation to detect abrupt connection churn signals and auto-tune NLB/timeout settings for private deployments; add health-check webhook for customer request.
runbook_update: Update private-control-plane runbook to include detection queries and escalation checklist used during this incident.
payload.summary: Silverline Health private deployment: intermittent connection flaps causing 5xx and session resets (major incident escalation)

Issue summary:
Customer (NimbusDocs, dedicated) reported a slow, progressive throughput degradation in their reserved GPU pool over ~90 minutes. P50 stayed stable but p95/p99 and overall completed requests / second trended downward while queue length and batch serialization increased. No large traffic spike from the customer. This ticket collects the operational investigation, telemetry excerpts, mitigation steps, and next actions.

Observed behavior:
- Gradual throughput decay (~20-40% reduction over 1.5 hours) starting at 2026-03-10T09:12:00Z.
- Concurrent rise in kv-prefetch pending queue length and prefetch_ack_latency (tail).
- Autoscaler observed transient CPU/memory signals, initiated small scale-up, then scaled down as signals stabilized causing slot churn.
- Several short-lived evictions and increased batch serialization (many tiny batches).

Why unique/different from prior tickets:
Pattern is not an instantaneous noisy-tenant flood but a coordination timeout between prefetch subsystem and allocator/sidecar that slowly reduces effective throughput as batches serialize and allocator misinterprets heartbeats as slots released. Existing issues cover classic noisy tenants and snapshot I/O — this one points to prefetch ack path timing and sidecar telemetry jitter as root contributors.
Customer-facing requests experienced lower overall RPS and elevated tail latency (p99 up from ~230ms to ~1.1s). Several API calls returned 429-like throttling on client backpressure as their local queueing grew. Customer reported degraded user experience for their interactive summarization flow. Billing or invoicing unaffected.
2026-03-10T09:12Z - first alert from internal throughput monitor. 09:18Z - customer reported via in-app ticket. 09:22Z - Support triaged and engaged SRE. 09:35Z - initial hypothesis: noisy tenant. 10:05Z - SRE observed kv-prefetch pending queue growth in cluster metrics. 10:40Z - temporary mitigation applied (increase autoscaler min allocation & raise prefetch timeout). 11:10Z - partial recovery in throughput; monitoring continues. 2026-03-12 - engineering patch for sidecar prefetch ACK race merged to main and scheduled for canary deploy.
1) Customer runs steady low-latency interactive workload (many short streaming requests) pinned to dedicated pool in us-west.
2) After ~30-90 minutes of normal traffic, observe kv-prefetch pending queue steadily grow in the tenant's shard metrics.
3) Scheduler begins issuing attach/detach cycles as it perceives slot churn; small batches increase in frequency and batch size drops.
4) Autoscaler sees transient signals (sidecar telemetry jitter) and scales up then down, causing additional slot churn.
5) End-to-end throughput declines and p99 latency increases without a single large noisy burst from other tenants.
2026-03-10T09:21:59Z serving-runtime[allocator]: INFO slot_release candidate slot=slot-3 tenant=nimbusdocs reason=prefetch_ack_timeout latency=620ms
2026-03-10T09:22:03Z sidecar-telemetry: WARN prefetch_ack delayed tenant=nimbusdocs request_id=abcd-1234 ack_ms=658
2026-03-10T09:35:12Z autoscaler: INFO scale_event min_desired=8 -> 10 reason=cpu_burst transient=true
2026-03-10T09:37:41Z scheduler: INFO attach slot=slot-12 tenant=nimbusdocs result=success
2026-03-10T09:40:03Z serving-runtime: WARN small_batch_frequency=0.72 threshold=0.5 tenant=nimbusdocs
Key metric deltas during window (09:10-10:10Z): throughput RPS -30%, p99 latency +380%, kv-prefetch_pending +420%, attach/detach ops +250%.
Checked historical baselines for the dedicated pool: no scheduled maintenance or hardware degradation events during window.
Correlated sidecar telemetry traces with allocator logs and found repeated prefetch ack latencies clustered around the same tenants/shards.
Heap/driver-level GPU errors were absent; GPU utilization remained within expected bounds, but effective batch packing dropped dramatically.
Autoscaler decision logs show a small scale up (reactive) followed by scale down when telemetry smoothing removed the spike — this oscillation amplified slot churn.
Can reproduce internal repro in staging by artificially injecting 400-700ms delays into prefetch_ack path which triggers similar attach/detach churn and throughput drop.
No customer-side SDK change; traffic patterns consistent with standard short-stream interactive usage.
Related telemetry points to a recent sidecar telemetry bump (v2.19.1) rolled out to a subset of nodes two days prior — timing and canary overlap with affected hosts.
Primary: A regression in sidecar telemetry/prefetch ACK handling introduced tail ack latency. This causes the allocator to interpret prefetch failures/timeouts as slot release or livelock, increasing attach/detach ops and creating many small batches (batch serialization).
Secondary: Autoscaler smoothing and aggressive scale-down combined with transient telemetry spikes to create a feedback loop that magnified throughput loss.
Tertiary: Edge cases in prefetch timeout configuration (short default) make dedicated pools with many short streams particularly sensitive.
1) Immediate: Increased autoscaler min capacity for NimbusDocs dedicated pool by +2 to reduce impact from transient scale-downs (applied 10:40Z).
2) Immediate: Raised prefetch_ack timeout from 250ms -> 1000ms in pool-level config for affected pool (temporary guardrail).
3) Short-term: Rolled back sidecar telemetry v2.19.1 on the small canary subset pending root cause analysis (decision at 10:55Z).
4) Medium-term: Engineering prepared a fix to make prefetch ack path resilient to delayed telemetry messages instead of timing out slot leases.
In-progress: Temporary config changes produced partial recovery. Engineering has merged a patch to the sidecar and runtime to avoid prefetch ACK races (PRs referenced above). Plan: canary rollout 2026-03-12 18:00Z -> region roll forward pending metrics. Follow-ups: add alert for prefetch_ack_latency > 500ms, tune autoscaler smoothing to avoid aggressive scale-down when prefetch_pending > threshold, and run a focused postmortem after full rollout.
1) Canary deploy sidecar/runtime patch to 5% hosts in us-west and monitor kv-prefetch_pending and attach/detach ops for 60m (owner: Miguel Santos).
2) Create a dedicated alert (SLO/monitoring) for sustained prefetch_ack_tail > 500ms and kv-prefetch_pending growth (owner: Observability team).
3) Revisit default prefetch timeout across dedicated pools and document recommended pool-level overrides for short-stream workloads (owner: Platform Product).
4) Postmortem write-up and customer-facing summary for NimbusDocs (owner: Support/Product).

Issue summary: BrightLens reported intermittent p50->p99 spikes and request failures for reserved dedicated pool during a 30m window on 2026-03-10. Impact: customer-facing degraded throughput and ~15% of requests returning 504/attach-timeout for short-lived streams, causing elevated error rates in their production app.

Observed timeline: 2026-03-10 09:10-09:40 UTC saw a shortwave burst of many short-lived coldstart streams (median 700ms) from a BrightLens job. Autoscaler did not provision additional slots quickly; allocator logs show slots temporarily held by background prefetch and one noisy tenant. Result was transient GPU attach timeouts and cascading retries.

Why this is customer-impacting: Dedicated pool expectation for BrightLens (reserved) is predictable throughput and low failed attach rate. The combination of a sudden high fanout of short sessions plus delayed attach/eviction recovery led to perceived capacity loss and increased latency.
1) In a reserved pool with mixed long and many short streams, script a shortwave burst of 8k short-lived streams over 5-10 minutes targeting a single tenant slot group.
2) Ensure background KV-prefetch sweep runs concurrently.
3) Observe allocator attach latencies, autoscaler decisions, and per-tenant slot occupancy.
4) Measure p50/p99 token latency and failed attach rate.

Notes: Reproduction requires reserved GPU pool and ability to create many short sessions. We reproduced in staging with a simulated tenant.
Selected excerpts: allocator.log[2026-03-10T09:12:14Z] WARN attach_timeout tenant=brightlens slot_id=pool-23-7 delta=3.1s; autoscaler.log[2026-03-10T09:12:20Z] INFO scale_down_candidate window_mean=0.02 but burst_detected=true; prefetcher.log[2026-03-10T09:11:58Z] INFO kv_prefetch hold_slot=pool-23-7 duration=4.2s. Stacktrace snippets around attach timeouts included socket timeout during nvlink handshake and repeated backoff. Full logs on internal S3: s3://redwood-ops/logs/SUP-358642/
Initial triage: Support reproduced a short-lived p99 spike in staging by simulating the exact burst profile. Observed that autoscaler smoothing window (30s) suppressed aggressive scale-up because recent average appeared low. Meanwhile, a noisy tenant's prefetcher held several slots for 3-5s each, leading to slot attach queueing.

Hypothesis A: Autoscaler smoothing + cooldown prevented timely scale-up during shortwave bursts.
Hypothesis B: Background prefetch and a noisy tenant's long-lived connection pattern caused ephemeral slot blocking rather than true GPU exhaustion.

Telemetry: Correlated allocator queue depth increase with prefetch sweeps and a single tenant (tenant-842) that had a burst of healthcheck/logging connections. No evidence of driver crashes or GPU OOM. NVLink latencies briefly increased but within acceptable ranges.

SRE action: Instrumented autoscaler to emit burst_detected flag and added a high-frequency probe on attach queue length. Confirmed that enabling burst detection would have triggered an earlier scale-up in the reproduced scenario.

Additional notes:
2026-03-10 13:40 - Tomás Rivera (Backend): Observed a noisy tenant in the same reserved pool emitting frequent small connections; asked CS to check whether BrightLens had changed traffic pattern. Also noted a related autoscaler PR that improved burst detection (github.com/redwood-inference/autoscaler/pull/312).
2026-03-11 09:12 - BrightLens (Customer): Confirmed they ran a new ingest pipeline at 09:00 UTC that creates many ephemeral chat sessions. They asked if dedicated pools can be protected from their own background jobs.
A confluence of autoscaler smoothing (designed to avoid oscillation) and slot-holding background work from a noisy tenant caused short-lived attach queueing. The autoscaler did not register the shortwave burst quickly enough to add capacity, resulting in temporary GPU attach failures and elevated p99 latency. No hardware or driver faults detected.
Immediate: Applied temporary capacity bump for the customer's reserved pool (added 2 GPU equivalents) and throttled prefetcher tasks for the noisy tenant. Customer reverted their ingest job to a slower ramp as an interim measure.
Mitigation deployed: temporary pool bump + prefetch throttle. Engineering merged autoscaler change to reduce smoothing sensitivity for detected shortwave bursts (PR github.com/redwood-inference/autoscaler/pull/314). A permanent autoscaler improvement and a tenant-side guidance doc were scheduled. Awaiting postmortem and customer acceptance before closing.
Ship autoscaler burst-detection feature and default to more aggressive short-burst scale-up in reserved pools (owner: autoscaler team, ETA: 2026-03-24)
Add allocator metric alert for 'attach_queue_length > 5 for >30s' in reserved pools (owner: SRE, ETA: 2026-03-18)
Create customer-facing guidance for BrightLens on safe ingest ramp patterns and recommend using dedicated warmup windows (owner: Solutions Eng, ETA: 2026-03-17)
Investigate limiting prefetcher slot hold time or making it preemptible in reserved pools (owner: serving-runtime, ETA: 2026-04-01)
Postmortem doc and TL;DR to runbook (owner: Incident Lead, ETA: 2026-03-20)
Confirm metrics and monitor for 72h after autoscaler change in prod-us-west (owner: SRE, ETA: ongoing)
Customer follow-up call scheduled 2026-03-17 15:00 UTC (owner: CSM), include rollout checklist and acceptance criteria
This ticket highlights an operational edge case for reserved pools: heuristics that intentionally damp autoscaler reactivity can interact badly with short, high-fanout coldstart patterns and background system tasks. Consider policy parity between dedicated/private pools for aggressive short-burst handling.
payload.summary: Autoscaler starve window during shortwave burst + tenant coldstart causing transient GPU attach failures

payload.description:
Issue summary:
NimbleDocs is seeing duplicated downstream tool executions (webhook target receives same tool invocation twice) when a streaming generation triggers a function/tool call. The Go SDK client receives a transient signature verification error from the webhook endpoint on the first delivery, performs a retry, and the webhook ends up executing the side effect twice.

Impact:
- Intermittent duplicate processing of invoices in customer's system (customer reports ~2-3% of requests duplicating over the past 48h).
- Affects production traffic on their Dedicated cluster in us-west-2.

Environment:
- Customer using Redwood Go SDK v0.8.3 with streaming and func_call support enabled.
- Dedicated deployment (customer-owned VPC) with API Gateway + edge proxy (third-party WAF) in front of customer webhook.

Steps to reproduce (as reported by customer):
1) Start a stream with a tool call that posts to https://hooks.nimbledocs.com/rdw-callback
2) We observe the SDK sending callback with headers: X-Redwood-TS, X-Redwood-Signature (HMAC-SHA256).
3) The customer's WAF strips millisecond precision from the timestamp header (X-Redwood-TS: 1678901234 -> 1678901234).
4) Customer server calculates HMAC using original timestamp (with ms) and signature validation fails.
5) Server returns 401 -> Redwood SDK performs immediate retry for callback delivery -> server accepts second delivery and executes tool action.

Expected behavior:
- SDK retries should not cause duplicate side effects for non-idempotent endpoints if the first delivery might have actually been processed (or should include guidance to make webhooks idempotent).

Actual behavior:
- Some webhook endpoints reject the first callback because of timestamp rounding/truncation by intermediaries, causing client retries that lead to duplicate downstream side effects.

Relevant logs (sanitized):
- SDK outbound attempt 1 headers:
  X-Redwood-TS: 1678901234.789
  X-Redwood-Signature: sha256=ab12...
- Edge/WAF observed header rewrite:
  X-Redwood-TS: 1678901234
- Customer server log: "signature mismatch: calculated=cd34... received=ab12..." -> returns 401.
- SDK outbound attempt 2 (retry) headers:
  X-Redwood-TS: 1678901235.102
  X-Redwood-Signature: sha256=ef56...
- Customer server accepts and processes the callback on attempt 2.

Attachments: customer provided packet capture showing header truncation and sample SDK trace token.
2026-03-12 10:22 - Support (Aisha): Opened with initial triage and requested packet captures and example webhook logs from customer.
2026-03-12 14:05 - Customer (NimbleDocs): Uploaded packet capture showing WAF middleware truncating X-Redwood-TS. Confirmed duplicates occur ~2% of calls.
2026-03-13 09:10 - Eng (Marcus): Reproduced locally by inserting a proxy that truncates timestamp header; observed identical signature verification failure followed by retry leading to duplicate POSTs to origin.
2026-03-13 11:40 - SRE (Lin): Noted that SDK currently includes full-ms timestamp and server-side validation expects exact match — there's no replay cache for callbacks at customer endpoint by default.
2026-03-14 08:12 - Support (Aisha): Proposed mitigations to customer and engineering follow-ups (see investigation notes and resolution).
Reproduction steps performed in internal staging: Go SDK v0.8.3 streaming client -> local proxy that truncates X-Redwood-TS to seconds -> origin validates signature with ms precision -> origin returns 401 -> SDK retries with new timestamp -> origin accepts second call. Result: duplicate execution observed.
Root cause: mismatch between the timestamp canonicalization expected by customer's HMAC verification and header mutation by an intermediary. The SDK sends a fresh signature tied to the precise timestamp; if intermediary mutates timestamp before the origin, origin will reject first attempt even though SDK signed original value. SDK then retries and issues a second signed attempt which origin accepts. No deduplication layer on customer's webhook means side effect occurs twice.
Edge case: clock skew on origin could cause legitimate rejections; however packet capture shows clock aligned — truncation is the trigger. WAF (third-party) is rewriting headers for normalization/compatibility and dropping fractional seconds.
Potential SDK behavior change: include an idempotency token in callback body/headers separate from HMAC that downstream can use for deduplication; maintain short-lived replay cache on our callback delivery subsystem (danger: extra state and memory on Redwood side).
Customer constraints: they cannot add a replay cache on origin side easily because their processing pipeline is third-party-managed. They prefer guidance to harden webhook validation logic to tolerate timestamp normalization.
Related internal links: linked SUP-473901 (retry-scope-enforcement-mismatch) may have useful context on header normalization patterns.
Workaround provided to customer (2026-03-14):
1) Update webhook signature validation to allow for a configurable timestamp tolerance and to validate HMAC against both raw and truncated timestamp variants when the request originates from known proxies. Example pseudo-logic: accept if HMAC matches signature(timestamp_ms) OR signature(timestamp_seconds).
2) Implement idempotency check on webhook consumer using X-Redwood-Callback-Id header (we recommended customer check this header when deciding whether to execute side effects).
3) As short-term, whitelist Redwood delivery IPs on their WAF or configure the WAF to preserve X-Redwood-TS header without truncation.
Engineering follow-up (internal):
- Action item ENG-11273: Evaluate adding an X-Redwood-Callback-Id header to all SDK callback deliveries (low-risk), targeted for SDK v0.9.x.
- Action item ENG-11274: Investigate a transient dedupe cache in the callback delivery path; document operational cost/limits.
- Action item DOCS-5568: Add guidance to webhook best practices for handling timestamp normalization and idempotency patterns (include signature verification tolerant patterns and sample code for Go/Python/TS).
Status: Workaround accepted by customer. Engineering tickets created and tagged for Q2 prioritization. Keeping this support ticket open while ENG checks feasibility and until docs are published.
Final customer note: NimbleDocs implemented header-tolerance logic and reported a drop to ~0.05% duplicates over 24h after change (2026-03-14 18:30).
payload.summary: Go SDK streaming tool-callback: webhook HMAC signature mismatch after proxy timestamp truncation causing duplicate tool executions on retry

Issue summary: Customer runs a mixed workload where each interactive chat request is preceded by a lightweight 'preflight' safety/scoring check. After enabling a preflight microservice, FinSight started seeing persistent 429 throttles for low-latency interactive chat traffic. Impact: end-users get immediate 429s for short chat requests despite overall tenant usage being within expected bounds. The customer reports that each chat interaction produces two quota decrements in the console: one for preflight and one for the actual generation.

Expected behavior: preflight checks are lightweight and should either be exempt from tenant token accounting (internal preflight) or billed at a small fixed cost, not double-counting the real generation request. Observed behavior: preflight + generation both decrement tenant token buckets as full requests, leading to tenant quota exhaustion and 429s that affect production chat traffic.
Customer-facing interactive experiences are intermittently blocked with 429s during normal usage peaks. Several paying enterprise customers have reported degraded UX and one internal partner escalated to SRE due to SLA concerns.
1) Customer has preflight service calling /v1/preflight followed immediately by /v1/chat.completions
2) Send 1000 paired preflight+chat requests over a sustained 2 minute window from a single API key, mixed concurrency (50 concurrent connections),
3) Watch tenant token ledger and rate-limit counters in Console, observe two decrements per end-user interaction,
4) Continue until tenant hits quota and subsequent chat requests receive 429s with X-RateLimit-* headers showing depleted tokens
2026-03-10T14:05:02Z EDGE route=/v1/preflight key=acct-FIN-01 inc=token_count:512
2026-03-10T14:05:02Z EDGE forwarded /v1/preflight -> origin cluster=preflight-us-east (status=200)
2026-03-10T14:05:02Z ORIGIN route=/v1/chat.completions key=acct-FIN-01 inc=token_count:512
2026-03-10T14:05:03Z RATE-LIMITER tenant=FIN-01 tokens_remaining=0 reason=window-exhausted
2026-03-10T14:05:03Z CLIENT 429 response returned to api-key acct-FIN-01 request_id=ff12ab34
Initial triage (Support): Confirmed client is issuing a preflight request prior to each chat call and both show up in customer Console usage charts as full requests.
SRE check: Rate-limiter metrics show identical per-request accounting for /v1/preflight and /v1/chat.completions (both increment tenant token counters by the estimated token count).
Edge routing hypothesis: /v1/preflight should have been marked as an internal/exempt path but the recent edge routing change (edge config v22.4) introduced a path-level header rewrite that removed X-Redwood-Internal, causing preflight to be treated as a normal billed request.
Correlation: the timing of customer enablement of preflight + our edge config rollout matches the start of reports (2026-03-09 22:00 UTC).
Repro on staging: Reproduced paired accounting in staging by sending preflight+chat and watching ledger increments. Adding X-Redwood-Internal:true on the preflight request causes it to be ignored by tenant accounting (workaround).
Risk assessment: High customer impact (enterprise chat UX), quota exhaustion can cascade to other tenants if shared pool misconfiguration present.
Ava Chen (Support) 2026-03-10: Raised by FinSight support engineer. Asked for request samples, API keys, and timestamps. Provided initial guidance to throttle preflight frequency.
Diego Marquez (SRE) 2026-03-10: Confirmed double-counting in rate-limiter metrics. Noted edge config change v22.4 as likely root cause. Requested edge logs for affected time range.
FinSight-Eng (customer) 2026-03-10: Provided sample request pair and said disabling preflight reduces 429s immediately but is not an acceptable long-term solution.
Diego Marquez (SRE) 2026-03-11: Workaround validated — adding header 'X-Redwood-Internal: true' to preflight requests prevents billing. Preparing patch to restore internal-header preservation in edge routing.
Workaround (prod): Customer instructed to set X-Redwood-Internal:true for preflight requests until server-side patch is deployed. Support provided a curated nginx sidecar snippet for their SDK to add the header.
Short-term fix: Reverted the edge config change that stripped internal header from preflight paths in us-east canary (edge rollback v22.4->v22.3.1). Canary observed for 6 hours with no new double-counting reports.
Permanent fix: Edge PR github.com/redwood-inference/edge/pull/7821 includes tests to ensure /v1/preflight and /internal/* paths preserve internal headers and are exempt by default; target merge and staged rollout 2026-03-13.
Post-action: Added automated e2e test to CI that simulates preflight+generation flow and asserts only generation increments tenant ledger. Added a console note explaining preflight accounting behavior and a recommended SDK header for internal calls.
Follow-up: Postmortem scheduled and linked; SRE to review edge routing change process to add a gate for internal-header preservation.
Merge and roll out PR to edge (priority): Diego assigned to coordinate canary rollout and monitor rate-limiter metrics in us-east.
Customer comms: Support to send an incident summary and expected timeline for the fix to FinSight by 2026-03-12.
Billing check: Finance to validate whether any overbilling occurred due to the double-counting and if credits are required (cc: billing@redwood).
