Issue summary: NovaCare reported intermittent inference requests that either time out or return very slow responses starting 2026-03-10 09:15 UTC. Initial customer observation suggested a latency regression in the serving stack. Impact: production traffic for NovaCare's chat endpoint experiences degraded throughput and increased user-perceived timeouts leading to support tickets and rollbacks in their client. Environment: NovaCare is on a Dedicated cluster in us-east using model gpt-like-2.7b-quant with client-side retries implemented in their SDK.
1) Issue observed at 2026-03-10 09:15 UTC during peak window for NovaCare (daily digest).
2) Customer client issues 20 concurrent streaming generate calls with their normal retry policy (immediate retry + up to 3 attempts, no jitter),
3) Several calls receive 429/QuotaExceeded responses from our gateway; customer SDK treats these as failures and retries immediately,
4) Retries rapidly increase request rate, causing rate-limiter to apply broader per-tenant throttling,
5) Result: many requests either hang until timeout on client side or return delayed responses once the token-bucket recovers.
2026-03-10T09:15:21Z gateway ERROR tenant=novacare code=429 quota=burst_limit remaining=0
2026-03-10T09:15:21Z serving-runtime WARN request_id=xxx latency_ms=1500 queued=true
2026-03-10T09:15:22Z gateway INFO tenant=novacare token_bucket=0.00 refill_rate=1.0
2026-03-10T09:15:23Z api-gateway INFO tenant=novacare incoming_rate=420rps retry_rate=310rps
Observed pattern: initial set of requests legitimately exceeded configured burst quota; gateway returned 429s with no Retry-After header in some code paths (legacy rate-limiter behavior).
Customer SDK (v1.2.3) treats all non-2xx as candidate for immediate retry; no exponential backoff and no parsing of Retry-After. This produced a retry amplification factor ~4x during peak window.
Token-bucket algorithm: burst tokens drained in <3s under amplified load; refill_rate insufficient to service immediate back-to-back retries. The serving runtime queued some requests which increased tail latency (observed 95th percentile jump from 180ms to 1.2s).
No model-side performance regression was detected when isolating single requests; CPU/GPU metrics remained within expected baselines for the model. Latency-only when request burst persisted.
Short-term mitigations applied (2026-03-11 02:00 UTC):
- Gate change: gateway now returns Retry-After header for quota 429s (PR: github.com/redwood-inference/infra/pull/2471) to encourage client backoff.
- Emergency throttling rule tuned to add randomized jitter on server-side retries to reduce sawtooth load.
Customer guidance provided to NovaCare (on 2026-03-11):
- Update SDK to >=1.2.5 which treats 429 as rate-limited and implements exponential backoff with full jitter. Link to patch: https://github.com/redwood-inference/rdw-sdk/releases/tag/v1.2.5
- Short-term capacity option: increase dedicated burst quota for NovaCare for the daily digest window while they roll out SDK changes.
Longer-term actions (backlog):
- Add automatic Retry-After generation for all quota enforcement paths and ensure header includes recommended backoff values (OWNER: infra/rate-limiter).
- Add per-tenant adaptive throttling that considers retry amplification signals and temporarily reduces per-IP retry acceptance (OWNER: serving/runtime).
- Improve observability: add retry_ratio and effective_throttle_ratio panels to per-tenant dashboard (OWNER: console).
Status: Customer observed restored latency after SDK update + temporary quota increase. Monitoring for recurrence; ticket will be closed after 48h of stable metrics.

Additional notes:
2026-03-11 Product (Maya Singh): Recommend quick mitigation: send Retry-After on 429 and add response header indicating quota type (burst vs sustained).

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customers using BrightWrite Labs (dedicated tenant) reported a sudden increase in 5xx errors during a high-concurrency burst from their mobile clients. Errors started ~2026-03-12 11:18 UTC and persisted intermittently for ~90 minutes.

Impact:
- Elevated 5xx rate (~18% of requests for tenant) across short-streaming and small-chat routes.
- Customer reported degraded user experience for ~2k active users during the window.

Environment:
- Production (dedicated pool) in us-east
- Tenant pinned to redwood-open-7b-v1

Steps to reproduce (customer):
1. Rapidly open 500 short streaming sessions (50 concurrent bursts) from mobile SDK with keepalive disabled in some versions.
2. Send short prompts (~20-40 tokens).
3. Observe ~10-20% of sessions receiving server 502/503.

Observed behavior:
- API gateway returning 502/503 with upstream error message: "upstream handshake timeout" or "upstream reset during handshake".
- Some runtime instances (ephemeral pool) restarted with SIGABRT and TLS handshake logs showing timeouts.

Initial logs (excerpt):
- apigw: "ERROR upstream handshake timeout tenant=brightwrite session_id=..."
- proxy: "tls: accept failed: EOF while waiting for client hello"
- runtime: "panic: unexpected EOF during accept (tls handshake)"

Temporary workaround requested by customer:
- Customer throttled client-side connection ramp (reduced concurrency by 80%) which reduced observed 5xx rate.

Attachments:
- link to Grafana tenant error-rate panel: https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/tenant/brightwrite/error-rate
- support logs bundle: s3://support-logs/sup-365999/2026-03-12.zip

Additional notes:
2026-03-12 11:42 - SRE (Marcus Nguyen): Observed handshake timeouts on ephemeral proxy and TLS accept failures on several runtime shards. Opening investigation in #support and #infra-ephemeral.
2026-03-12 12:10 - Ops (Leah Kim): Looked at accept-queue metrics; accept backlog spiked just before handshake timeouts. Possible half-open connection stampede from mobile SDK variant.
2026-03-12 12:45 - Eng (Ravi Desai): Identified runtime goroutine watchdog logs correlating with "tls: handshake timeout" followed by forced restarts from the health manager. Suspect connection handling regression in new accept loop optimization.
Timeline:
- 11:15 UTC: observed tenant throughput ramp from client-side telemetry
- 11:18 UTC: API gateway error-rate climbs from baseline 0.5% to 18%
- 11:20-11:35 UTC: accept queue depth grows; apigw logs report 'upstream handshake timeout'
- 11:30 UTC: several runtime shards restarted by health manager (SIGABRT)
Findings:
- Root correlation appears to be a mobile SDK bug that disables keepalive for a subset of clients, causing many short-lived TCP connections with incomplete TLS handshakes under high concurrency.
- The runtime accept path had an optimization that assumed short handshake latencies; under half-open client behavior it hit an unexpected EOF path and triggered a panic in the TLS accept handler. That panic surfaced to process exits on some runtime replicas.
- Ephemeral proxy was not applying backpressure early enough; the accept queue filled and API gateway observed upstream timeouts, returning 502/503 to callers.
- No evidence of GPU OOM or model kernel faults; serving runtime CPU usage increased modestly due to TLS work and goroutine churn.
Diagnostics collected:
- tcpdump traces from proxy replicas showing many SYN packets with no full TLS ClientHello follow-up
- runtime core dumps indicating panic in tls_accept.go: line ~142 (EOF during read)
- Grafana dashboards: accept_queue_size, apigw.upstream_handshake_timeouts, runtime.uptime_restarts
Hypothesis validated:
- Reproduced locally by disabling keepalive and ramping connection open/close at scale — caused identical handshake-timeout patterns and runtime panics.
Short-term mitigations applied:
1) Raised ephemeral proxy accept_queue_size and tuned handshake retry/backoff to shed connections earlier. Deployed the change 2026-03-13 09:00 UTC.
2) Customer applied client-side throttling as a stop-gap and confirmed reduced errors.
3) Rolled out runtime patch (PR-9982) that guards against EOF during accept and converts the path to graceful handshake failure instead of panic. Backported to dedicated branch and deployed 2026-03-14 02:00 UTC to low-traffic nodes.
Long-term follow-ups (tracked as action items):
- TASK-1204: Improve accept-queue autoscale policy to proactively rate-limit handshakes on sudden connection ramps.
- TASK-1205: Add an SLI for 'handshake failure rate' and alert at 1% per-tenant sustained for 5m.
- DOCS-88: Publish recommended mobile SDK connection guidance (keepalive enabled, exponential backoff).
Customer outcome:
- BrightWrite Labs confirmed normal traffic patterns on 2026-03-14 and observed error rate returned to baseline (~0.4%). Customer thanked support for patch and advised to wait 48h of stability before closing.
We identified and fixed a runtime handshake edge-case that, combined with a client-side connection ramp, caused elevated 5xx rates for one tenant. We deployed mitigations and a runtime patch; customer error rates returned to baseline. We are adding monitoring and documentation to prevent recurrence.
payload.summary: Intermittent upstream runtime handshake failures during tenant burst causing elevated 5xx rate

payload.description:
Issue summary
- Customer reports Go SDK does not respect Retry-After on 429 responses. Instead it retries immediately (or with minimal delay), causing rapid repeat 429s and increased load.

Impact
- Customer sees prolonged periods of throttling and elevated request volume from their clients during 429 bursts.
- Risk of “retry storm” / thundering herd when many workers hit 429 simultaneously.
- Inconsistent behavior vs TS/Python expectations (customer has mixed-language services).

Customer report (Northwind AI)
- Workload: ~200 goroutines sending chat completions for background enrichment jobs.
- Behavior: when rate limit kicks in, Go clients retry too fast and never recover until they reduce concurrency manually.
- Expectation: SDK should honor Retry-After header and back off.

Environment
- Prod, us-east
- Go SDK version: v0.9.6 (per customer)

Steps to reproduce (internal)
1) Use Go SDK with default retry settings.
2) Send burst traffic until gateway returns 429.
3) Observe retry timing. Expected: delay >= Retry-After (plus jitter). Actual: delay appears ~0–200ms and repeats.

Evidence / logs
- Customer-provided snippet (redacted):
  - 429 responses include header: Retry-After: 8
  - request_id present in body but not surfaced by SDK error

- Internal repro (from Support):
  - curl shows Retry-After header is present on 429 from api.redwoodinference.com:
    - HTTP/2 429
    - retry-after: 10
    - x-request-id: req_01JH9P7K9X2R2D5RZK...
  - Go SDK debug output shows retry loop delay does not incorporate Retry-After.

Notes
- This aligns with ongoing SDK parity initiative for standardized retries/timeouts.
- Need to confirm whether the Go SDK parses both Retry-After formats:
  (a) integer seconds
  (b) HTTP-date

Requested outcome
- Go SDK should:
  - Treat 429 as retryable by default (already does)
  - Respect Retry-After if present (seconds or date)
  - Clamp to a sane max (per standard) and apply jitter around the chosen delay
  - Surface request_id on the raised error for triage

Suggested fix (high level)
- In Go retry middleware, when response status == 429:
  - Parse Retry-After header:
    - If integer seconds: sleep that duration
    - Else attempt HTTP-date parse and compute delta from now
  - Use max(parsed_delay, exponential_backoff_delay) to avoid retrying sooner than policy
  - Apply jitter (full jitter or equal jitter per standard) without going below parsed_delay

Gateway/header verification
- Verify gateway emits Retry-After consistently on 429 for both streaming and non-streaming paths.
- If missing in some cases, coordinate with platform to add it (but initial checks show it exists).
2026-01-29 09:18 (Owen Phillips, Support) — Ticket opened from customer escalation. Customer says Go SDK retries “immediately” on 429 even though they see Retry-After in response headers via a proxy log. Asking for: SDK version, sample request_id(s), and whether they’re using streaming.

2026-01-29 10:02 (Northwind AI, via Support summary) — Confirmed Go SDK v0.9.6. Non-streaming chat completions. They run ~200 concurrent workers. Provided 3 request_ids where 429 occurred (req_01JH9P7K..., req_01JH9P7M..., req_01JH9P7Q...). They see Retry-After: 8 or 10 seconds in their edge logs.

2026-01-29 10:25 (Owen Phillips, Support) — Reproduced with a burst script. curl shows gateway returns Retry-After on 429 in prod us-east. Go SDK retries much sooner than the header value. Attaching repro notes to internal Slack thread #support (ref: 1768110400).

2026-01-29 11:10 (Mateusz Zielinski, Go SDK) — Acknowledged. Quick scan: current retry loop uses exponential backoff only and does not consult Retry-After. Will patch to parse both numeric seconds and HTTP-date. Will align with parity retry standard (max attempts, jitter) as part of ongoing work.

2026-01-29 11:28 (Allison Grant, SRE) — +1 to respecting Retry-After. Please ensure jitter does not reduce below Retry-After delay (avoid synchronized retries). Also recommend clamping extreme Retry-After values (e.g., >60s) per standard and surfacing retry_count for logs.

2026-01-30 14:05 (Mateusz Zielinski, Go SDK) — Implemented fix on branch. Behavior: on 429, compute baseDelay = max(expBackoff, retryAfterDelay). Apply equal-jitter around baseDelay but never below baseDelay. Also propagating request_id into error type when present.

2026-02-03 09:42 (Owen Phillips, Support) — Verified gateway Retry-After presence using both:
- /v1/chat/completions (non-streaming)
- /v1/chat/completions?stream=true (streaming)
Observed retry-after present on 429 in both cases. x-request-id present.

2026-02-04 16:20 (Mateusz Zielinski, Go SDK) — PR opened: redwood-sdk-go#612 “retry policy standardization” includes Retry-After parsing + tests. Also includes conformance fixture for 429 + Retry-After=3s.

2026-02-06 13:15 (Owen Phillips, Support) — Sent customer workaround while fix is pending release:
- Reduce concurrency during 429 bursts
- Implement external rate limiting and/or honor Retry-After in application-level retry wrapper
- Temporarily disable SDK retries and handle 429 manually (customer requested this option)

2026-02-10 10:05 (Mateusz Zielinski, Go SDK) — Fix released in Go SDK v0.10.0. Release notes mention: “Respect Retry-After on 429; improved request_id in errors.”

2026-02-10 11:30 (Owen Phillips, Support) — Customer confirmed improved behavior after upgrading to v0.10.0: retry cadence now matches Retry-After and they recover without manual intervention. Closing.

Resolution
- Shipped fix in redwood-sdk-go v0.10.0 (PR: redwood-sdk-go#612)
- Confirmed gateway already emits Retry-After for 429 in prod.

Follow-ups
- Ensure conformance suite includes 429 + Retry-After cases across Python/TS/Go.
- Track request_id propagation consistency (linked: INT-1182).
payload.summary: Go SDK ignores Retry-After on 429 and retries too quickly (rate limit / thundering herd risk)

Issue summary:
Finova Payments (enterprise customer) has requested a signed delivery proof and a field-level retention mapping for Redwood's live SIEM connector. They need artifacts for a scheduled third-party penetration test and their internal compliance team.

Impact:
Customer cannot complete their pen-test and compliance attestation without a verifiable export and documentation showing field retention and ability to pause/replay deliveries. This blocks their go/no-go for production rollout to a set of regulated tenants.

Request details (what customer asked for):
1) A sample delivery bundle (one hour of prod audit events) delivered via their SFTP endpoint and an accompanying signed manifest (HMAC + RFC3161 timestamp) proving all files were exported and delivered in order.
2) Field-level retention mapping document that lists each audit event field, type, retention default, and whether it is redacted/pseudonymized by default (including examples).
3) Demonstration of ordered delivery and at-least-once semantics for the SIEM connector (replay steps and idempotency guarantees).
4) An on-demand replay runbook and a capability to pause delivery for a single tenant for a defined time window.
5) Evidence of key rotation history used to sign manifests (last 3 rotations) and KMS audit log excerpt showing signing operations.

Acceptance criteria (customer):
- Received signed bundle with manifest and RFC3161 timestamp.
- Field mapping PDF with redaction examples and retention policy statements.
- Console runbook or SRE-validated steps to trigger replay and to pause/resume delivery for a tenant.
- KMS proof showing signing operations for the manifest files.

Issue summary: Customer FinLedger reported intermittent 401 Unauthorized responses and a burst of duplicate events in their Datadog HTTP Logs intake after performing a scheduled API key rotation. Impact: Duplicate billing concerns and noisy alerts in Datadog, potential GDPR PII leakage risk during replay windows. Environment: Dedicated tenant on prod (us-east-1). Customer expects per-tenant rotating keys to apply without interruption to active webhook delivery and wants confirmation of at-most-once delivery semantics and a sample replay-proof payload. Request: provide root cause analysis, immediate mitigation, configuration change to ensure rotation applies atomically, sample payloads showing idempotency headers, and a short evidence package they can forward to their security/compliance team.
1) Customer rotated tenant API key via Console > Security > Tenant Keys. 2) Backend webhook proxy started sending logs to Datadog using new key but some proxy instances used old key due to stale tag on config rollout. 3) Datadog returned 401 for the old-key requests; client retried and eventually succeeded with new-key requests, creating duplicates because retry policy retried without idempotency token. 4) Customer observed 401 spikes starting 2024-10-28T03:12Z and duplicates clustered at 03:20-03:45Z.
2024-10-28T03:12:04Z webhook-proxy[proxy-7] WARN HTTP 401 POST https://http-intake.logs.datadoghq.com/v1/input - tenant=finledger key=xxxx - response="Unauthorized"
2024-10-28T03:13:09Z webhook-proxy[proxy-3] INFO HTTP 200 POST https://http-intake.logs.datadoghq.com/v1/input - tenant=finledger key=yyyy - event_id=ev_20241028_0001
2024-10-28T03:20:21Z webhook-proxy[proxy-7] INFO Retrying event ev_20241028_0001 after 401 - retry=1
2024-10-28T03:20:22Z webhook-proxy[proxy-9] INFO HTTP 200 POST - event_id=ev_20241028_0001 - dedup_check=false

Additional notes:
2024-10-28 13:48 - SRE (Jordan Lee): Initial hypothesis: config rollout used label selector 'tenant-id:finledger' but some proxy pods were labeled 'tenant:finledger' causing rollout skip for ~20% of proxies. This left stale instances using the old key, producing 401 and triggering client-side retries.
2024-11-01 14:07 - FinLedger (Sophie Martin): Confirmed duplicates dropped after patch; requested evidence bundle and a replay-proof sample payload to show compliance team.
- Replicated rotation flow in staging by rotating tenant key and observing rollout. Found 3 of 15 webhook-proxy instances retained old config because of mismatched k8s label key. - Retry policy in proxy attempted immediate retries without sending event id header, causing Datadog to accept subsequent identical events as new. - Datadog HTTP intake provides no server-side deduplication unless client provides a unique identifier per event. - Root cause chain: human-triggered rotation -> config rollout selector mismatch -> stale proxies -> 401 responses -> immediate retry logic without idempotency header -> duplicates in Datadog.
1) Emergency mitigation: deployed v1.3.4 to webhook-proxy that accepts old+new keys for 5 minutes post-rotation, and injects X-Redwood-Event-Id header into all outbound log POSTs when absent. 2) Updated rotation workflow in Console to perform a rolling key swap with an automated 5-minute dual-key acceptance window. 3) Added idempotency support: clients now include X-Redwood-Event-Id and we log event hashes for 48 hours for dedup checks. 4) Fixed label mismatch in k8s deployment and added a pre-rotation validation check that verifies all proxy replicas have correct labels. 5) Provided FinLedger: (a) sample payload with X-Redwood-Event-Id and dedup instructions, (b) evidence bundle (signed delivery manifest, sample headers, timeline), and (c) Confluence runbook for compliance. 6) Created follow-up internal work items for GA feature: permanent dedup index and per-tenant replayproof manifest.
INT-10234: Add pre-rotation cluster validation to rotation service (owner: infra-team)
INT-10311: Implement persistent dedup index for audit exports (owner: serving-runtime)
INT-10420: Add telemetry for dual-key acceptance window usage (owner: monitoring)
We have reviewed the evidence bundle and the duplicates stopped after your patch. We need a short note to share with our compliance team summarizing the fix and confirming that retained logs during rotation are available for audit. Please include the exact time window when dual-key acceptance was active.
Dual-key window for FinLedger rotation executed at 2024-10-28T03:12:00Z - 2024-10-28T03:17:00Z. Provided signed manifest and sample headers. Customer confirmed receipt on 2024-11-01. Ticket closed after confirmation and internal follow-ups created.
Resolved: Per-tenant Datadog HTTP ingest experienced duplicates during API key rotation. Fixes include a short dual-key acceptance window, idempotency headers (X-Redwood-Event-Id), and pre-rotation validation to prevent stale proxies. Evidence bundle and replay-proof sample payload delivered to customer.
payload.summary: Datadog HTTP logs ingest: per-tenant key rotation failing, causing 401/duplicate events and missing deduplication

Issue summary: ParcelFlow reports scheduled alerts linked to a dashboard fail to evaluate on schedule. The scheduler marks the job as timed out, and the alert window is missed. Impact: Customers on dedicated capacity miss alert notifications for production SLOs; manifests as no Slack/webhook messages and alert state not updated in console. Environment: prod (us-east), dedicated tenant for ParcelFlow. First seen: 2026-03-09 22:40 UTC; recurring each day around the scheduled 02:00 UTC rolling window. Steps to reproduce: 1) Create a dashboard with multiple panels including a single 'JSON / Debug' panel that contains a ~12MB inline JSON payload (copy/paste from logs). 2) Attach an alert to a panel on that dashboard with evaluation window aligned to the dashboard's time range and enable 'Evaluate on schedule'. 3) Schedule the alert to run at 02:00 UTC. 4) Observe scheduler logs and alert state after scheduled run. Expected: scheduled alert evaluates, updates status, and sends notifications if triggered. Observed: scheduler worker reports evaluation timeout after 45s (scheduler configured timeout = 30s), alert status remains stale, no notifications sent. Additional notes: ad-hoc manual evaluation via console works when the inline JSON panel is removed. The same dashboard with smaller JSON payloads (<1MB) evaluates normally. Logs/trace snippets: "scheduler.job[alert-eval].time=2026-03-09T02:00:12Z status=timeout duration=45s reason=panel-renderer-hang trace_id=tr-93abf". Attachments: dashboard-export.json (redacted), scheduler logs excerpt (attached to ticket).

Additional notes:
2026-03-10 10:05 - Support Engineer Marco Li: Acknowledged. I've reproduced locally on staging using a 10MB inline JSON panel; scheduler worker logs show worker blocked in panel rendering step and then hit the 30s evaluation timeout. Assigning to infra-alerting team for deeper analysis.
2026-03-11 14:42 - SRE Priya Nair: Initial hypothesis: dashboard renderer runs synchronously in the alert evaluation path, and large panels can block the evaluation event loop. Experimented with isolating 'render-only' panels in a separate headless renderer process and saw evals complete. Opening an internal ticket to decouple heavy panel rendering from alert evaluation.
2026-03-12 16:30 - Engineering Lead Aisha Patel: Planning a short-term mitigation and a medium-term fix. Short-term: increase scheduler per-job timeout for tenants affected by large-panel dashboards and add a rendering time budget. Medium-term: move heavy panel rendering to async pre-render pipeline and cache rendered artifacts so alert evals can operate on cached outputs.
Checked scheduler logs (prod-us-east) for affected tenant: multiple consecutive eval timeouts aligned to customer's schedule window.
Reproduced on staging by pasting a 11.8MB JSON into a dashboard JSON panel; ad-hoc manual evaluation works if run interactively but scheduled job times out consistently.
Profiling of alert-eval worker shows 85% CPU spent inside dashboard-renderer.parseAndRender() for large JSON panels; stack traces point to synchronous JSON pretty-print and DOM-to-image conversion blocking the worker thread.
Confirmed removing the large panel or replacing it with a reference to a lightweight saved query returns evaluation latency to normal (<5s).
Verified existing retention/compaction jobs unaffected; this is unrelated to retention layer but interacts with scheduler because rendering uses cached query results that are larger when retention window increases.
Related PR identified that introduced synchronous rendering in eval path: github.com/redwood-inference/console@commit/9b7e4f3 (linked above).
Short-term mitigation rolled out 2026-03-12 20:00 UTC to prod-us-east for affected dedicated tenants: scheduler per-job timeout increased from 30s to 60s and a rendering time budget guard was added to fail fast on heavy panels. Nightly monitor added to watch for increased eval durations.
Medium-term plan: implement async pre-render pipeline for heavy panels and a cache keyed by panel hash + time window. Target ETA for staged rollout: 2026-04-20. Issue tracked internally in INT-33012.
Customer communication: ParcelFlow informed of short-term mitigation and asked to remove large inline payloads; they accepted and confirmed alerts resumed. Follow-up scheduled for 2026-03-18 to validate metric stability.
Post-deploy verification: two scheduled runs observed post-mitigation with durations 9s and 12s; no timeouts and alerts evaluated as expected.
Follow-ups: (1) Add console UI warning when saving panels with inline payloads >2MB recommending saved queries or attachments; (2) Add alerting doc note about heavy panels impacting scheduled evaluations.

comments: 2026-03-14T03:45:00Z Runtime Eng: Found repeated cudaFree failures on worker x86-prod-rt-14; fragmentation metric rose quickly. Hypothesis: frequent KV cache allocate/free due to ephemeral streaming sessions.
payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customers (Glassline Analytics, dedicated) observed a sustained elevated 5xx error rate beginning 2026-03-14 02:15 UTC. Symptoms include API gateway returning 502/503 and upstream runtimes reporting OOMs and repeated worker restarts.

Impact:
- Multiple customer endpoints intermittently returning 5xx, affecting production inference for short-streaming requests and small-payload embed calls.
- Error rate peak ~14% of requests for a 30-minute window, downstream retries caused increased load.
- Customer reports degraded throughput & timeouts for real-time event enrichment pipeline.

Environment:
- Region: us-east (prod)
- Tier: Dedicated capacity pool (tenant pinned to model redwood/open-4b-int8)
- API surface: streaming API and short request text generation (avg payload 80 tokens)

Steps to reproduce (internal reproduction):
1) Run a synthetic load generator sending many concurrent short-lived streaming sessions (50ms per connect, ~2000 sessions/min) to the tenant's route.
2) Observe apigw accept queue growth and many ephemeral TCP connections.
3) Observe runtimes allocate KV cache for new sessions and free frequently; GPU memory fragmentation increases and NVML reports cudaFree warnings.
4) After ~5-10 minutes, runtimes hit OOM watchdog -> worker restart -> upstream 5xx responses.

Observed behavior:
- apigw logs: repeated 502/503 for tenant routes with "upstream reset" and "no healthy upstream" bursts.
- runtime logs: repeated "GPU memory allocation failed" and "watchdog: OOM -> restarting worker" entries.
- metrics: GPU memory fragmentation metric increases from baseline ~8% to ~42% during spike; runtime restart count +10 in 10 minutes.
- kvcache: high eviction rate and frequent cold-shard reloads.

Expected behavior:
- Short-lived streaming sessions should be multiplexed onto healthy long-lived workers; backpressure should be handled by ingress prioritizer without causing kernel-level GPU OOMs.

Temporary mitigations performed so far:
- Support adjusted apigw keepalive and connection reuse policy for the tenant to prefer longer pooled connections (rolled config at 2026-03-14 02:42 UTC).
- Reduced tenant concurrency cap from 600 -> 300 while we investigate.
- Applied emergency rate-shed rule to small-payload streaming route to reduce fan-in to runtimes.

Next steps (action items):
- Engineering to correlate NVML traces to runtime memory allocator activity and evaluate fragmentation pattern.
- Verify ingress prioritizer fairness settings and fix misapplied small-stream classification rule.
- Consider KV cache warmup persistence for tenant to avoid repeated allocations.
- Post-incident: follow-up runbook updates to catch short-connection storm patterns and automatic tuned rate-shed thresholds.
2026-03-14 03:05 UTC - Support (Ayesha Patel): Customer reported increased errors; opened ticket and applied initial throttles. Notified SRE channel #incidents.
2026-03-14 03:28 UTC - SRE (Diego Rios): Observed accept-queue spike on apigw (rt_accept_queue > 1200) and large number of NEW TCP connections from customer's ASN. Investigating runtime NVML logs.

Additional notes:
2026-03-14 04:12 UTC - Support (Ayesha Patel): Applied temporary lower concurrency cap for tenant and adjusted keepalive pooling. Error rate dropped to ~3% from 14% after change.
2026-03-14 04:30 UTC - Customer (Glassline Analytics - Erin Cho): Noted reduced errors but slower throughput. Asking for ETA on permanent fix.
Initial hypothesis: small short-lived streaming sessions bypassing connection reuse cause frequent KV cache allocations, inducing GPU memory fragmentation and OOMs. Evidence: NVML logs show multiple cudaMalloc/cudaFree cycles coincident with kvcache eviction spike. Correlated metrics: runtime_worker_restarts, gpu_memory_fragmentation, apigw_accept_queue_depth. We validated by replaying a short-stream load in staging and reproduced fragmentation pattern. Apigw config had 'short_stream_threshold' at 40ms for this tenant incorrectly set to 0, which prevented multiplexing into pooled streams. Also saw priority classifier mis-tagging these sessions as low priority, causing them to get scheduled onto ephemeral workers rather than warm pool. Logged related stack traces and attached NVML snippets to PR referenced in related_github_prs.
Workaround applied: adjusted apigw pooling/keepalive settings and temporarily lowered tenant concurrency cap which reduced error rate. Engineering plan: fix short_stream_threshold classification bug and update ingress prioritizer to prefer pooling for <200 token sessions. A hotfix PR (runtime/pull/4216) created to persist small-session KV cache and reduce allocate/free churn; target rollout to canary 2026-03-15 02:00 UTC, full rollout after verification. Post-incident action: add automated synthetic test that simulates high-rate short streaming sessions and alert when fragmentation > 25%.
payload.summary: Sustained 5xx spike from small streaming connection fan-in causing runtime OOMs and gateway backpressure

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customer runs a Dedicated GPU pool serving a mixed workload: a small fleet of long-lived streaming sessions (low qps but persistent) for realtime dashboards and periodic high-throughput bulk embedding uploads from backfill workers. After enabling a 'smoothing' rollout, they started seeing tenant-scoped 429s and P50 latency regressions for the streaming sessions during bulk upload windows.

Impact:
- Streaming sessions (real-time dashboards) experience occasional token-level 429s and truncated streaming responses during bulk ingest windows.
- Bulk uploads see unpredictable retries and longer completion times.
- Customer wants guidance to configure Dedicated pool rate-sculpting to protect low-latency streams while preserving throughput for background bulk ingest.

Environment:
- Dedicated pool (reserved), autoscaling disabled, fixed 16xA100s.
- Prod us-east region.
- Tenant configured with shared route for both streaming and embedding API keys (same tenant key).

Steps to reproduce (approx):
1) Start 20 long-lived streaming connections, each sending ~1 request per 10s (small messages, expecting low latency).
2) Kick off 50 parallel bulk embedding workers (multipart uploads) that submit batches repeatedly for 30-60 minutes.
3) Observe increase in 429s on streaming connections and higher P50 token latency immediately after bulk workers start.

Observed behavior:
- Tenant-level token window gets consumed rapidly at bulk start.
- Streaming token windows appear to be shared and depleted by background workers, causing early 429s and truncated streams.
- Rate-limiter headers (x-rw-rate-limit-*) show bursts attributed to the same tenant key without per-route separation.

Expected behavior:
- Ability to isolate low-latency streaming traffic from bulk background flushes via an easy to configure per-route or per-traffic-class sculpting policy on Dedicated pools.
- Guidance about recommended thresholds (burst credits vs sustained), smoothing window, and any Dedicated-specific knobs (e.g., route weights, priority lanes, isolated burst pools).

Temporary mitigation customer applied:
- Reduced concurrency of bulk workers by 60% (manual throttling) which reduced immediate 429s but is not acceptable for nightly backfills.
- Added exponential backoff in workers to reduce retry storms.

Request:
1) Explain how Dedicated pool rate-sculpting works when tenant traffic mixes long-lived low-qps streams and short high-qps bulk uploads. Are there priority lanes or route-based isolation options that operate strictly within a Dedicated pool?
2) Provide recommended config: suggested per-route burst credits, sustained token rates, and smoothing window values for the customer's pool size (16xA100s) to avoid stream truncation during backfills.
3) If per-route isolation isn't supported in this mode, recommend a reliable configuration pattern (separate API keys, priority lanes, or split burst pools) and the operational tradeoffs.
4) Any runtime flags or console settings they should enable (e.g., enable_per_route_quota, priority_lane_thresholds) and how to validate via headers/metrics.

Customer attached logs (excerpt) and trace IDs: 2026-03-11 22:04:12 UTC - stream-session-abc123 - x-rw-rate-limit-remaining: 0; trace: trace/ff12a0; bulk-worker job id: bulk-3872.

Additional notes:
2026-03-12 - Support (Priya Nair): Thanks Morgan — assigning to rate-limiter oncall. Can you confirm whether streaming and bulk use the exact same API key/route? Also paste a sample 'x-rw-rate-limit-*' header from both traffic classes if possible.
2026-03-13 - SRE (Daniel Kim): Hypothesis: tenant-level window is shared by default on Dedicated. We can protect streams by splitting keys or enabling route isolation. We'll propose a safe config for a 16xA100 pool. Following up with recommended values.
2026-03-14 - Support (Priya Nair): Suggested interim config in discussion: create a dedicated API key for streaming, assign it to a high-priority lane with a smaller smoothing window (e.g., 5s) and higher burst credit per-connection; configure the bulk key with a separate lower-priority lane and larger smoothing window (30s). Pending formal guidance and console steps from infra team.
Initial guidance: recommend creating separate API keys for interactive vs background traffic, map streaming key to a priority lane with per-route isolation enabled, and limit bulk workers' concurrency. Infra to provide exact console steps and recommended numeric thresholds for burst credits and smoothing windows based on pool size. Follow-up: infra PR to add a 'dedicated-priority-lane' preset for common pool sizes (tracked in linked PR).

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customer reports that when resuming Server-Sent Events (SSE) streams after a transient network blip, the final chunk is arriving truncated (partial bytes/partial token) and the usual finalization/stream-end event ("[DONE]" / end-of-stream marker) is not emitted. Output appears complete when the connection remains stable, but any resume via Last-Event-ID or client reconnect produces a response that never finalizes and leaves the application waiting for completion.

Impact:
- Affects FlashWrite's production service that uses streaming completions for real-time user previews.
- Users see partial sentences with no end-of-stream; front-end spinner never goes away.
- Errors surface as occasional duplicates and also aborted completions leading to retry storms from client logic.

Environment:
- Customer on Dedicated plan, using Redwood hosted API fronting dedicated capacity in us-east.
- SSE clients use Last-Event-ID to resume.
- Models observed: redwood-mix-1 (primary), gptx-13b (fallback).

Steps to reproduce (provided by customer):
1) Start a streaming SSE completion request with client-side Last-Event-ID handling enabled.
2) Induce a short network interruption (e.g., toggle mobile data or simulate transient TCP reset).
3) Client reconnects with Last-Event-ID set to last received event id and requests resume.
4) Server responds: stream resumes but final payload is truncated ~20-80 bytes and no finalization event is sent.
5) Client application hangs waiting for end-of-stream; retry logic triggers additional requests.

Observed behavior:
- Truncated final tokens (partial UTF-8 codepoints in a few cases).
- No explicit stream-complete event; connection eventually closed by client timeouts.
- Some resumed streams include duplicate tokens earlier in the transcript, but duplicates are less frequent than truncation.

Expected behavior:
- Resumed SSE stream should re-send missing chunks from resume point and emit normal finalization marker once generation completes.
- No partial-token truncation; server should ensure resumed content boundaries align with token boundaries (or use base64 framing).

Relevant logs and traces (customer-sent):
- Request IDs: req-usr-ff7e1a (failed resume), req-usr-ff7e1b (stable no-resume).
- Gateway trace shows 101->200 flicker on reconnect; backend generation logs show generator session restarted at offset 0 instead of resume offset.
- Application logs show client Last-Event-ID header present and matching server EIDs for earlier chunks.

Investigation notes (initial):
- SRG (support) reproduced a variation in staging: when resume header is present, router sometimes routes to a different replica that does not have session KV (KV cache not warmed) and the backend starts fresh but signals a resume-success without full payload, causing no finalization token.
- Hypothesis A: resume routing mismatch -> backend believes session already finalized and returns a short heartbeat.
- Hypothesis B: streaming gateway acknowledges resume prematurely to client while backend is still spinning up model runtime, leading to truncated first/last chunk.
- Identified an edge in streaming proxy code where Last-Event-ID is validated but not consistently forwarded to the serving-runtime when cross-node routing occurs.

Temporary mitigation/workarounds suggested to customer:
- Disable client auto-retry on truncated responses and surface a soft error allowing user to request a fresh completion (avoids retry storms).
- Configure client to prefer short backoff before immediate resume to increase chance of hitting warmed replica.
- For critical flows, prefer websocket streaming (where resume semantics are currently sticky to connection) until fix deployed.

Next steps / Owner actions:
- SRE to add enhanced logs for resume headers propagation and replica selection (Diego Morales, in progress).
- Runtime team to patch streaming proxy to forward Last-Event-ID consistently and add verification that backend acknowledges resume offset before sending resume-confirm to client (owner: Priya Shah, ticketed).
- Product to schedule a short communication to all dedicated customers describing known SSE resume caveats and recommended client-side retry behavior.

Resolution notes (pending):
- Not resolved yet. Patch planned and test cases to validate: cross-node resume, token-boundary preservation, explicit finalization event delivery.

Aisha Patel (Support) 2026-03-04: Opened ticket after receiving report from FlashWrite support contact (ticket channel/#support). Attached customer logs and sample Last-Event-ID header values. Marking as P1 due to production impact and retry storms.
Diego Morales (SRE) 2026-03-04: Investigating routing logs. Early reproduction in staging; I can reproduce truncation when router routes across availability sub-pools. Adding additional debug flags to streaming proxy to capture forwarded headers and target replica id.
FlashWrite Support (Customer) 2026-03-04: We can provide network capture for one of the failed sessions (packet capture) and a small synthetic client that consistently triggers the issue. We're available for a quick call if needed.
Diego Morales (SRE) 2026-03-05: Confirmed case where Last-Event-ID header is *sometimes* omitted by proxy when a weighted routing rule triggers cross-pool failover. Raising to runtime owners; linking to PR that will add header-preservation test and a health-check hook for warmed KV cache: github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/8123.
Priya Shah (Runtime) 2026-03-06: Draft patch created to forward resume offsets reliably and to delay resume-ack until backend confirms session offset. Adding unit/integration tests for token-boundary consistency and UTF-8 safe chunking. ETA for staging deployment: 2026-03-10.
Aisha Patel (Support) 2026-03-06: Shared temporary mitigation guidance with customer and requested acceptance testing window once patch lands. Customer acknowledged and will test in staging with dedicated capacity isolated.)
Test plan includes: (1) automated cross-node resume test harness, (2) fuzzing resume offsets to validate no partial UTF-8 emissions, (3) smoke test for finalization event in SSE and WS flows. Post-deploy follow-up scheduled with FlashWrite for verification.

Issue summary: BrightCart reports intermittent waves of 429s during peak traffic windows (03:15–03:35 UTC) that correlate with their long-lived SSE connections and a background batch-flush pipeline. Impact: Several storefront workers see 10–30% of streaming sessions rejected with 429s for short (~30s) pulses, causing user-visible refresh failures and increased retry noise. Environment: Dedicated pool (BrightCart dedicated lease) in prod-us-west, mixed traffic: persistent SSE sessions from browsers and periodic batch worker flushes that open/close short connections. Steps to reproduce: 1) Start 2k long-lived SSE sessions that send keepalive heartbeats every 30s. 2) Run batch flusher that issues 250 concurrent short POSTs every 15s. 3) Observe rate-limiter token-window and 429 count. Observed logs/metrics: - 429 spike timestamps: 2026-03-09T03:18:22Z, 03:21:07Z, 03:24:19Z - Token bucket utilization shows transient exhaustion of burst credits at the route layer for 8–12s windows. - Edge-proxy access logs show many keepalive probe requests counted as regular tokens (no special header) and concurrent short connections incrementing per-route counters. - Console quota view shows burst pool refill leveling that lags by ~10s relative to observed pulse. Expected behavior: Long-lived SSE heartbeats should either be accounted against a low-cost keepalive pool or excluded from burst accounting so short-lived high-concurrency flushes do not exhaust active burst credits. Customer expects guidance on configuration options and an actionable short-term workaround.
2026-03-10 09:03 UTC - BrightCart (Claire from BrightCart) - 'We're seeing sudden refresh failures on our product feed during the early-morning batch jobs. Looks like 429s spike for ~10 seconds and then recover. Can you help us tune rate limits?'
2026-03-10 09:18 UTC - Support (Aisha) - 'Thanks Claire — filing this internally. Can you confirm heartbeat frequency and whether the batch jobs originate from a single host or a pool? Also share any request IDs from a recent spike.'
2026-03-10 09:27 UTC - BrightCart (Claire) - 'Heartbeats: 30s. Batch flushers: 250 concurrent requests from 8 hosts. Example request-id: req_3f9a2e8c. We'll keep reproducing while you investigate.'
2026-03-11 14:06 UTC - Eng (Marco) - 'Seeing correlated token-bucket dips in metrics. Asking SRE to pull kube-proxy traces and edge logs. Temporary mitigation: enable isolated-burst-pool for their tenant and exempt known internal probe path — we can flip this from console if approved.'
2026-03-12 08:45 UTC - Support (Aisha) - 'Workaround available: enable split-burst-pool for BrightCart and set heartbeat path exemption. We need customer approval to apply tenant-level policy. Engineering patch to rate-limiter to ignore probe header is in review.'
03/10: Pulled token-bucket histogram for tenant brightcart-001; burst credits drop to 0 at the same 10s windows as 429 spikes.
Observed pattern: long-lived SSE sessions generate periodic HTTP GET keepalive probes that are currently accounted at full token cost by the route-layer limiter. When batch flushers start, their short-lived concurrent POSTs consume a large portion of the same burst pool causing immediate rejections for new streams.
Edge logs: several keepalive requests lack x-client-probe header; originates from customer SDK version 2.1.0 — recommend asking customer to upgrade to include probe header (opt-in) as short term.
Dashboards: https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/rl/tenant-burst?orgId=1&var-tenant=brightcart-001 (snapshot id: s-20260310-burst), console trace link: https://console.redwood.ai/tenants/brightcart-001/requests?from=2026-03-09T03:10Z
Hypothesis: refill smoothing interval mismatch + shared burst pool for SSE and batch is causing transient starvation. Reproduced locally by running 2k SSE clients + periodic batch fanout; replicated 429 pulses after ~18 minutes of run time on medium-sized dedicated pool.
Temporary mitigation tested in staging: enabling isolated-burst-pool for SSE (separate token bucket) eliminated 429 pulses in reproduce run; CPU/throughput unaffected.
Workaround provided: (1) Applied temporary tenant policy to split burst pools (SSE vs batch) for BrightCart and enabled heartbeat-path exemption on 2026-03-12 09:12 UTC. (2) Recommended customer upgrade SDK to include x-client-probe header to avoid full-cost accounting for keepalives. Engineering: rate-limiter PR #858 (ignore x-client-probe when present) merged to staging; rollout to prod planned after one-day soak. Follow-ups: - Product task to add 'split burst pool' toggle in Console (P0 product ticket). - Engineering to add metrics for 'probe-exempted tokens' to console and alerting.

Issue summary:
Customer performed a paid-tier upgrade late 2026-03-10 (self-serve to enterprise commit). Immediately after the upgrade completed, bulk ingesters reported widespread HTTP 429s across upload and streaming routes.

Impact:
- ClipStream ingestion pipelines saw >80% of requests return 429 for ~18 minutes.
- Business impact: delayed CDN metadata indexing; billing spike concern.

Observed behavior:
- Requests originating from the new enterprise key started receiving 429s despite console showing quota increased.
- Console usage graphs show quota refresh but gateway counters still indicated old token-bucket state.
- 429 rate-limit headers show X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0 and X-RateLimit-Reset far in the future (seems to be stale refill window).

Expected behavior:
- Quota/limit should take effect immediately after paid upgrade, with token bucket refill aligning to the new limit and console reflect the same live counters.

Workaround applied (customer):
- Customer rotated API key to create a fresh token; some traffic resumed but large upload jobs still hit limits due to connection reuse.

Notes on scope:
- Affects a single org/account (ClipStream) in us-east. Not seen across other customers during same window.
1) Start with a self_serve key under heavy ingestion (concurrent upload workers ~200).
2) Upgrade account to enterprise via console (spend/commit) without changing API key.
3) Immediately resume upload workers.
4) Observe a high volume of 429 responses and stale X-RateLimit-* headers from edge.

(Observed consistently when we replayed with a staging upgrade path.)

2026-03-10T23:25:12Z - Aisha Patel (Support): Received initial report from ClipStream. Confirmed upgrade event at 2026-03-10T23:17Z. Reproduced 429s in staging when replaying upgrade path. Escalating to SRE for token-bucket investigation.

Issue summary:
ClearVoice Media reported intermittent 429 throttles impacting a critical realtime reranking route during morning traffic window on 2026-03-10. The tenant is on a Dedicated pool (eu-central) with autoscaler enabled and custom healthcheck probes configured on the ingress sidecar.

Impact:
- ~15% of requests for reranker route returned 429 over a 30-minute window (no increased error rate in downstream models).
- Customer-visible user retries and increased latency as client retries applied backoff.
- Occurred during scheduled nightly-to-day warmup handover and autoscaler eviction window.

Environment:
- Dedicated pool: clearvoice-dedicated-euc-01
- Ingress: nginx-sidecar v1.12.3 behind LB (pooled IPs)
- Realtime route pinned to redwood-3-x-highthroughput (model variant)

Steps to reproduce (customer minimal repro):
1) Run sustained short-chat style requests at ~250rps for 10 minutes against their routed model (route: /v1/chat/realtime-rerank)
2) Trigger rolling healthcheck (customer uses 10s interval) and a simulated autoscaler eviction event (scale-down) during steady traffic.
3) Observe occasional 429 responses correlating with healthcheck bursts and node TTL drain.

Observed logs/snippets (sanitized):
- ingress-proxy: "healthcheck probe flood from 10.0.3.14: accepted 150 req/s"
- rate-limiter: "token_refill_epoch=2026-03-10T07:00:00Z window=60s tenant=clearvoice credits_before=120 credits_after=0"
- serving-runtime: "queue-length spike during host-eviction: 42 -> reject(429)"

Initial hypothesis:
1) Healthcheck probe fanout during node drain produced a short-lived burst which was attributed against tenant burst budget by the edge (pooled ip path), causing token exhaustion in the refill epoch.
2) Simultaneous autoscaler eviction / host TTL reset triggered a refill-window realignment between origin and edge token accounting (refill-drift), producing a sawtooth that made the tenant appear to consume credits faster than expected.
3) Because the Dedicated pool route uses strict per-tenant route weighting, background probe traffic was not isolated from interactive lanes and was counting against the same burst pool.

Customer-provided metrics attached (console screenshots referenced in comments).

03/10 07:12 UTC: Support validated customer logs and confirmed 429 spikes align with healthcheck bursts.
03/10 09:01 UTC: Infra reproduced locally by running sidecar probe flood + simulated scale-down; observed token bucket depletion in rate-limiter service during epoch boundary.
03/11 11:30 UTC: SRE measured 2s–6s refill offset between edge and origin during host eviction on dedicated pool; this matches refill-drift hypothesis.
03/11 13:20 UTC: Confirmed ingress pooled IPs can amplify probe fanout when many replicas share same nat/egress mapping (customer uses pool size 3).
Current prioritized mitigation: isolate healthcheck probe path from tenant burst pool (config change) and recommend smoothing refill window across edge/origin; evaluating rollback risk for autoscaler timing changes.
Aisha Gomez (Support) 2026-03-10: Received initial customer report. Collected request IDs and console screenshots. Escalated to SRE due to dedicated pool involvement.
Liam O'Connor (SRE) 2026-03-10: Reproduced locally with probe flood harness. Attaching reproduction script and captured rate-limiter trace. Marking as in-progress.
Customer (ClearVoice) 2026-03-11: Can you confirm whether healthchecks should count against burst credits? We didn't expect internal probes to affect user traffic.
Liam O'Connor (SRE) 2026-03-11: By default probes on the same ingress path will count. We're preparing a targeted config patch to add a probe-exemption header that will exclude known healthchecks from tenant accounting on dedicated pools.
Aisha Gomez (Support) 2026-03-12: Provided customer a temporary mitigation: reduce probe concurrency to 1 and stagger probe timing across replicas. Customer acknowledged and will apply changes tonight for verification.
Engineering (Rate-Limiter) 2026-03-12: Opened INT-4120 to track core rate-limiter change to support configurable probe exemption and cross-layer refill smoothing.
Customer reduced healthcheck concurrency from 3 -> 1 and staggered probe schedule (10s offsets). Also temporarily increased route burst pool size on their Dedicated config to tolerate warmup waves. Result: 429s dropped to baseline within 45 minutes.
- Short term: release config toggle to annotate ingress probes as 'probe-exempt' for dedicated pools (hotfix).
- Medium term: schedule rate-limiter refill window smoothing in origin-edge contract to avoid epoch drift during autoscaler events.
- Long term: provide console option to separate probe/background lanes from interactive lanes for dedicated customers.
[ingress] 2026-03-10T07:05:14Z -> healthcheck flood: 150 req/s from 10.0.3.14
[ratelimiter] 2026-03-10T07:06:00Z token_refill_epoch boundary credits_before=80 credits_after=0 tenant=clearvoice
[serving] 2026-03-10T07:06:03Z queue_rejects=27 host=clearvoice-node-03 eviction=true
Workaround applied and validated. Hotfix for probe-exemption is targeted for 2026-03-18 pending code review. SRE will monitor dedicated pool for 72 hours post-rollout and then advise next steps.
1) Ship probe-exempt toggle (INT-4120). 2) Coordinate with ClearVoice to roll their probe settings back to default once hotfix is deployed. 3) Follow up to revise docs and add a dashboard tile that surfaces probe traffic vs interactive token consumption.
2026-03-12: Sent status update to ClearVoice. Included mitigation steps and planned patch timeline. Customer accepted workaround and requested notification when hotfix lands.

Issue summary: At 2026-03-10 02:18 UTC we observed a rapid increase in 5xx errors and 429s for customer ArborBank leading to slowed payment verification flows. Traffic analysis showed per-request amplification (fan-out) from the API gateway to multiple backend serving shards, which created token emission backlogs and triggered per-customer rate-limiting. Impact: ArborBank experienced ~40% request slowdowns for payment path calls over a ~35 minute window; non-payment traffic (other customers) saw elevated tail latencies but significantly fewer errors due to per-customer circuit breakers. Timeline and key events are in the timeline field below. This ticket captures the immediate mitigation and longer-term follow-ups.
2026-03-10 02:05 UTC - ArborBank CS reported increased latency for payment verification via #support-arborbank in Slack.
2026-03-10 02:12 UTC - Automated alerts: api-gateway 5xx rate increased, multiplexer queue depth > 1200.
2026-03-10 02:18 UTC - Incident declared (Sev0). Initial triage started by on-call.
2026-03-10 02:23 UTC - Temporary per-customer fanout cap of 4 requests applied in gateway (hotfix), immediate reduction in new amplification observed.
2026-03-10 02:28 UTC - Autoscaler attempted to add serving nodes but collided with a tagging mismatch; manual scale-up performed.
2026-03-10 02:40 UTC - Rate limit tripping reduced to baseline; ArborBank payment flows returned to normal by 02:50 UTC.
2026-03-10 03:15 UTC - Root cause identified; rollback of recent multiplexer routing-splat change completed.
2026-03-12 10:00 UTC - Post-incident follow-up meeting; action items assigned and scheduled.
1) Send a single request to the /v1/generate endpoint with header X-Routing-Mode: fanout and an upstream client that sets batch=all. 2) Observe that the gateway expands the request into N downstream multiply-targeted calls when routing-splat config is enabled. 3) Under high concurrency this causes multiplexer queue depth to grow and backend 5xxs as token emission backlog increases.
Gateway logs show header 'X-Routing-Mode: fanout' being respected by a new routing-splat rule introduced in routing PR #782 which incorrectly treated missing shard filters as wildcard targets.
Serving runtime reported increased KV cache evictions while queue depth > 900 which amplified per-token latency.
Autoscaler failed to label new instances due to a tag name mismatch introduced in an unrelated infra change (INT-5021).
Billing observed spike in per-token charge for ArborBank during the incident window; finance notified to suppress anomalous charges pending review.
A recently deployed routing-splat configuration (PR #782) allowed wildcard expansion when a per-request shard filter was omitted. Combined with an ArborBank client header pattern that set batch=all, the gateway expanded individual requests into multiple downstream calls (fan-out). The multiplexer and serving runtime were not configured with a per-customer fanout cap, which permitted amplification until per-customer rate-limits and autoscaler interventions kicked in. An unrelated autoscaler tagging regression (INT-5021) slowed scale-up, worsening the backlog and causing backend 5xxs.
1) Hotfix: applied gateway guardrail to cap per-request fanout to 4 targets at 2026-03-10 02:23 UTC. 2) Rolled back the routing-splat change to the previous stable config at 2026-03-10 03:15 UTC. 3) Manually scaled serving cluster for ArborBank to add capacity while autoscaler tag bug was fixed. 4) Suspended anomalous billing for ArborBank during incident window.
Hotfix and rollback restored normal behavior; ArborBank confirmed payment flows recovered. Incident closed after verification of traffic stabilization for 30 minutes and no recurrence in following 24 hours. Customer follow-up call held on 2026-03-11. Root cause and remediation plan communicated to ArborBank CSM.
Apply persistent gateway validation to reject ambiguous routing headers (owner: gateway team, due: 2026-03-20)
Add per-customer fanout cap as a configurable policy (owner: routing team, due: 2026-03-24)
Fix autoscaler tagging regression and add CI check to prevent future tag name mismatches (owner: infra team, due: 2026-03-18)
Create synthetic test that exercises batch=all + routing-splat combinations in staging (owner: qa, due: 2026-03-16)
Finance to issue credit for anomalous token charges and confirm completion (owner: finance, due: 2026-03-15)
Update runbook with fanout detection and mitigation steps (owner: SRE, due: 2026-03-14)
2026-03-10 02:09 - ArborBank (Alice Jensen): 'We're seeing payment verification requests stuck in processing. Can you confirm if anything is going on?'
2026-03-10 02:15 - Support (Aisha Kapoor): 'Hi Alice, investigating now. We've triggered an on-call alert and will update within 15 minutes.'
2026-03-10 02:25 - On-call (Marcus Lee): 'Applied temporary fanout cap at gateway. Observed immediate fall in amplification. Scaling now.'
2026-03-10 03:20 - Engineering (Priya Nandakumar): 'Root cause confirmed: routing-splat wildcard expansion. Preparing rollback and a follow-up PR that adds explicit validation.'

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customer reports a ~50-250ms increase in end-to-end latency for requests using function/tool calling after a runtime change that introduced a preflight schema serialization/validation hop. This appears to affect only requests that include tool schemas and function signatures.

Impact:
- End-user API latency increased (median +60ms, 95th +180ms) for function-enabled routes for the GloboCommerce account (dedicated pool).
- Customer-facing pages load slower for chatbot flows that call external tools; some timed out after 1.5s.
- Regression began after a canary rollout of schema-validator v1.4.0 on 2026-03-09.

Environment:
- Prod, us-east, Dedicated pool #GCU-42
- API: POST /v1/chat/completions with "functions" schema present
- SDK: redwood-js v0.9.16 (customer-integrated)

Steps to reproduce:
1) Send a chat completion request that includes a tool definition and function schema.
2) Observe higher request latency compared to identical request without functions.
3) Capture trace (X-Trace-Id header) and inspect spans between api-gateway -> schema-validator -> function-proxy -> serving-runtime.

Observed logs / traces (examples):
- Trace ID: trc_20260310_7f9a3b; total server time 410ms; span breakdown: api-gateway 18ms, schema-validator RPC 130ms, function-proxy 9ms, serving-runtime 240ms. Schema-validator shows multiple blocking calls to serialization routine and an auth handshake to function-proxy.
- Datadog traces show schema-validator had a 2-hop RPC: -> schema-serializer -> signature-normalizer -> back. Each hop ~40-70ms.

Initial hypothesis:
- v1.4.0 of schema-validator introduced synchronous schema normalization and a cross-service handshake to verify tool signatures which causes additional RPC hops on the hot path.
- No batching/caching for repeated schema hashes; every request with a schema triggers the full synchronous path.

Investigation notes (timeline):
- 2026-03-10 09:12 UTC: Customer opened ticket reporting latency spikes after deployment.
- 2026-03-10 09:30 UTC: Support captured sample traces and escalated to SRE/Runtime team (Slack #support -> #sre-runtime thread).
- 2026-03-10 11:00 UTC: SRE confirmed elevated RPC counts from api-gateway to schema-validator for function-enabled requests (metrics: rpc_per_request increased from 1.02 to 1.98).
- 2026-03-10 14:25 UTC: Runtime engineer reproduced locally by deploying schema-validator v1.4.0 and measured avg extra latency ~85ms per request.
- 2026-03-11 02:10 UTC: Temporary mitigation tested: enable local LRU cache keyed by schema hash in api-gateway, avoiding round trip for repeated schemas. Measured reduction in median extra-latency to ~18ms for cached flows.

Root cause (current understanding):
- v1.4.0 implements a synchronous, canonical serialization + signature verification step that lives in the schema-validator service. It performs a call to a normalization microservice for backward-compat checks. That normalization call is on the hot path and is not cached. For customers with repetitive tool schemas (common for SDK-driven product integrations), this adds an entire RPC hop per request.

Workaround / customer guidance:
- For affected customers on Dedicated: set request field "tool_validation": "off" (temporary flag supported by gateway) to bypass preflight validation for known-good schemas. Note: this reduces safety checks; use only with trusted schemas.
- For immediate improvement without turning off validation: request that the customer upgrade to runtime client that caches schema hashes locally (redwood-js >= 0.9.18 suggested).

Planned remediation and timeline:
- Short-term (2026-03-12): deploy LRU cache in api-gateway for schema hashes across prod us-east (mitigation rollout completed 2026-03-12 03:20 UTC).
- Medium-term (2026-03-18): change schema-validator to async normalization path (fire-and-forget for known schemas) and introduce per-instance in-memory cache. PR: github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/4271 (merged, staged).
- Long-term: add integration test for schema-validator that asserts no more than one outbound RPC for canonical schemas and instrument a dashboard alert for rpc_per_request regression.

Follow-ups / action items:
- SRE: add Datadog monitor for api-gateway -> schema-validator RPC count per request (alert if >1.2 baseline).
- Runtime: ship async normalization and add strict cold-start caching behavior.
- Support/CS: notify GloboCommerce of mitigation and recommend SDK upgrade; schedule a postmortem with customer on 2026-03-20.


Additional notes:
Mitigation applied: added api-gateway LRU cache for schema hashes and enabled cached path for repeated schemas in prod us-east (2026-03-12 03:20 UTC). PR for async normalization merged (runtime/pull/4271); full rollout planned and monitored. Follow-up: monitor rpc_per_request, add integration test, schedule postmortem with customer.

payload.description:
Issue summary: During a customer-triggered burst of inference traffic from EdgeShop's dedicated reservation on prod-us-east we observed a sustained throughput drop and elevated tail latency for ~2 hours. Impact: customer-facing endpoints returned increased p95/p99 latency (p95 from ~220ms to ~1.8s; p99 spikes up to 6s) and intermittent 504 gateway timeouts. Several streaming sessions dropped mid-response. Environment: Dedicated reserved pool (reservation-id: rsv-77a9), prod-us-east, serving-runtime 2.14.1, autoscaler policy 'reserved-default-v2'. Steps to reproduce: 1) Millisecond-scale burst of mixed short & long sequences from ~20 tenants simultaneously hitting the pool (simulated by EdgeShop load test). 2) Observe queue depth and GPU utilization on the pool. 3) Notice per-pod request queues and increasing context-switching on GPU. Observed behavior: Autoscaler did not scale up quickly enough (scale-up step size set to +1 pod per 60s), some pods exhibited GPU-binding skew where NV_link-local bindings caused one GPU to reach >95% active CUDA context while sibling GPU on same node sat at ~40%. This caused head-of-line queueing, frequent preemption of KV cache transfers, and a rise in tail latency and 504s. Expected behavior: Reservation should sustain burst with autoscaler adding capacity before significant tail latency increases; GPU binding should balance across sockets and CUDA contexts to avoid single-GPU hotspots. Initial hypothesis: Combination of autoscale step-size too small for multi-tenant burst and a recent kernel upgrade (serving-runtime 2.14.1) changed CUDA stream scheduling leading to GPU bind skew. Attachments/logs: links to dashboards and flamegraphs below.

Additional notes:
2026-03-10 11:45 UTC - Customer (EdgeShop): Confirmed they were running a multi-tenant burst test across 20 services. Impact described as intermittent timeouts, some user sessions dropped.
2026-03-12 16:05 UTC - EdgeShop CS Rep: "Thanks, latency stayed within SLA during our overnight soak. We'll keep monitoring and will reopen if we see regression."
Pulled pod-level GPU metrics from prometheus: nvml_utilization_gpu for node n-prod-12 showed [GPU0: 96%, GPU1: 42%] averaged across affected window.
Servicing logs show repeated context rebinds and increased memcpy from host to device during KV cache warms, correlating with latency spikes.
Autoscaler logs: scale events were rate-limited by default step size and cooldown (60s cooldown). During burst the backlog grew faster than step size could compensate.
Reproduced locally in a staging mirror by replaying EdgeShop trace: enabling balanced-affinity in runtime prevented GPU skew and eliminated the p99 spikes.
Runtime diff between 2.13.x and 2.14.1 includes changed CUDA stream priority handling (PR 4011) which can alter context distribution under multi-tenant loads.
No evidence of hardware alarms or ECC errors. NVidia driver versions consistent across nodes (525.xx).
Hotfix deployed to impacted region: runtime rollback/patch (serving-runtime 2.14.1 -> 2.14.1+patch1) that forces balanced GPU affinity when reserved pools detect uneven context distribution.
Autoscaler policy for reserved pools updated: increased maximum step size to +3 pods/minute for large reservations and reduced cooldown to 30s when backlog > 250 requests.
Added a protective routing policy: when per-pod GPU imbalance > 25% for >2m, route new short-sequence requests to alternate compatible pool to avoid head-of-line blocking.
Customer (EdgeShop) validated with a 2-hour soak; p95/p99 stayed within expected ranges and 504s ceased.
Linked INT-4120 opened to track a thorough postmortem and a long-term autoscaler redesign.
Communicated RCA and mitigation to customer and internal channels.
Temporarily increased autoscale step size and enabled GPU-affinity fallback on the reservation; recommended customer to stagger burst windows until autoscaler changes were applied.
INT-4120: Conduct full postmortem and timeline; include SLO/alert tuning recommendations.
Autocaler redesign ticket to evaluate predictive scaling based on request queue growth rate and sequence-length mix.
Runtime team to add a regression test in CI that replicates multi-tenant burst with mixed sequence lengths to catch GPU affinity regressions.
Add dashboard alert: 'reserved-pool gpu-imbalance' to trigger before p95 exceeds threshold.
Update customer runbook to include steps to request emergency scaling for large reserved bursts.

Issue summary:
ScribeLabs reported a ~65% drop in throughput for their dedicated pool in us-west during a midday burst window. The regression coincided with the autoscaler entering a cooldown/hysteresis window after a short spike. Multiple customer routes experienced serialized short-stream batches and p99 token latency moved from ~180ms to ~1.2s.

Impact:
- Customer-facing routes degraded across three production services (increased latency, tail tokens lost to timeouts).
- Observed sustained lower batch concurrency for ~14 minutes until autoscaler recovered.
- No error 5xx spike, but elevated application-level timeouts and queued requests.

Environment:
- Dedicated capacity, us-west, reserved pool for ScribeLabs (tier: dedicated).
- Model traffic: mix of short streaming chatlets and medium-length embeddings.

Steps to reproduce (observed):
1) Induce short burst from a separate tenant in same reserved pool (simulated by load test).
2) Autoscaler scales up then immediately enters cooldown window.
3) A long-lived replica from an adjacent tenant retains a GPU slot with a persistent background KV-prefetch process; slot not released quickly.
4) Batcher serialization appears as short streams are queued behind the pinned slot and throughput collapses.

Observed behavior:
- GPU slot held by process pid=22311 from tenant `edge-analytics` for ~12 minutes (continuous CUDA context reported).
- Prefetch/KV cache writer logged periodic heavy io; sidecar logs show repeated keepalive + minor page faults.
- Autoscaler did not trigger an immediate additional allocation because cooldown prevented scale-out for ~90s intervals, causing sequential allocation attempts and transient underprovisioning.

Expected behavior:
- Short-lived background processes should not prevent GPU slot lease reclamation during autoscale events.
- Autoscaler cooldown should be adaptive to clear evidence of held-but-idle slots to avoid prolonged underprovisioning.

Initial triage summary:
- Hypothesis: noisy neighbor (long-lived background replica) + conservative autoscale cooldown produced a window of slot starvation and batch serialization.
- Evidence: GPU allocation traces, sidecar logs, and allocator-heartbeat metrics align with the hypothesis.

Attachments: links to monitoring snapshots and a small log excerpt are in investigation notes.
2026-03-10 09:42 - Support (Aisha): Ticket created after ScribeLabs report of production throughput drop. Customer provided p50/p99 charts and route IDs.
2026-03-10 10:05 - SRE (Devon): Collected allocator and GPU attach traces from us-west reserved pool. Noted a continuous attach from tenant edge-analytics (pid 22311) holding an NVML handle for 12m.
2026-03-10 11:18 - Support (Aisha): Informed customer that we're investigating noisy-tenant interaction and autoscaler hysteresis as likely causes. Requested permission to correlate customer traffic windows with pool telemetry.
2026-03-10 12:40 - SRE (Devon): Temporary workaround applied: forced soft-eviction of the long-lived replica in the pool to free the slot; observed throughput return to baseline within 90s. Noted we must coordinate eviction to avoid customer impact for the neighbor tenant.
2026-03-11 08:22 - Eng (Linnea): Added an autoscaler param experiment to reduce cooldown hold-time when allocator reports held-but-idle slot counts > 0. Will run in canary for us-west reserved pools.
2026-03-12 14:09 - Support (Aisha): ScribeLabs confirmed degradation resolved after workaround and observed no further regressions during subsequent spike window. Customer requests a permanent mitigation plan and postmortem.
2026-03-12 15:35 - SRE (Devon): Marking follow-ups: runbook update, autoscaler tuning, and detection alert for long-held slots (alert: allocator_slot_held > 30s + cooldown active).

Telemetry snapshots: allocator/attach traces: https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/alloc/us-west?orgId=1&from=2026-03-10T16:30:00Z&to=2026-03-10T16:50:00Z
Sidecar logs snippet: [us-west/pool-72] 2026-03-10T16:36:12Z pid=22311 keepalive prefetch_writer: bytes_written=12.3MB io_wait=18ms NVML_handle=1
GPU NVML timeline shows continuous handle present from 16:35:40 -> 16:47:55. During this window allocator reported pending batchers=3 but available_slots=0.
Autoscaler timeline: scaled +2 at 16:34, then entered cooldown. Next scale decision evaluated at 16:36 and 16:38 but conservative policy suppressed allocation due to cooldown hysteresis flag. Canary tweak proposed to add override when allocator reports 'held_slots' > 0.
Hypothesis validated by repro: replayed neighbor background prefetch in staging along with short chatlet bursts; when we force-evicted the pinned replica, throughput recovered and batches parallelized.
Related Slack threads: #support (ScribeLabs) https://slack.redwood.ai/archives/C08S9K1T4/p167846... and #sre-uswest https://slack.redwood.ai/archives/C1SRE1234/p167847...
Potential root causes: (1) background prefetcher not yielding GPU access when idle, (2) autoscaler cooldown too coarse-grained to detect held-but-unused slots, (3) allocator lease timeout longer than expected under mixed short/long streams.
Risk assessment: Without mitigation, similar short bursts can create repeated 5-15 minute throughput cliffs for other dedicated tenants sharing pools.
Next steps in investigation: capture per-tenant NVML hold events, instrument allocator with held_slot count metric, and add test case for background replica eviction in our CI loadbench.
Runbook links: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/OPS/Slot+Eviction+Procedure
Workaround applied: performed a controlled soft-eviction of the noisy neighbor replica which freed the GPU slot and restored throughput. Autoscaler cooldown experiment (reduced strictness when held_slots>0) has been deployed to canary in us-west.

Planned permanent fixes:
- Add allocator metric 'held_slots' and an alert when > threshold during cooldown.
- Implement autoscaler override to allow immediate scale-out if held_slots prevents utilization.
- Add a probe to sidecar that detects long-running prefetche/writer loops and signals lease release earlier.
- Follow-up postmortem to be created and shared with ScribeLabs; schedule a customer-facing RCA meeting next week.
Owners: Devon Carter (SRE) for eviction/runbook updates, Linnea Svensson (Infra) for autoscaler tuning, Aisha Patel (CS) to coordinate customer RCA.
Timeline: deploy canary change fully to us-west by 2026-03-15 if canary shows no regressions.
Communication: prepare short incident summary for customer by 2026-03-13 and schedule RCA call 2026-03-16.
Testing: add CI loadbench case that runs mixed short/long streams plus background prefetch to validate no slot pinning.
Follow-up ticket to track autoscaler param rollout: INT-21045

Issue summary:
Customer reported a sudden elevation in 5xx responses for a subset of streaming and short-poll routes after a large webhook delivery retry storm from their downstream service. The API gateway returned a mix of 502/503/504 and we observed multiple serving runtimes hit OOMs and restart loops.

Impact:
- Multiple production tenants saw increased 5xx rate and elevated latencies for 30+ minutes.
- Noteable Analytics (enterprise) experienced degraded availability for inference routes used by their ingestion pipeline.

Environment:
- Prod cluster: us-east (api-gateway fronted)
- Deployment: Hosted Redwood API (shared pool) with pinned model variant for customer routes

Steps to reproduce (reliable on load):
1) Customer resubmitted ~1200 webhooks within a 1-minute window (retry storm).
2) Each webhook triggers a short inference request and a streaming acknowledgement.
3) Apigw accept-queue and handshake concurrency spiked; hedged/async retries amplified load.
4) Serving runtimes started showing KV-prefetch timeouts followed by GPU memory growth and eventual OOM kills.

Observed behaviour / Logs / Metrics:
- Apigw metrics: accept_queue_depth rose from ~50 to >1200 in 40s; 5xx rate jumped from 0.2% to 8.6%.
- Runtime logs: repeated "OutOfMemoryError: GPU memory exceeded" from runtimes handling customer shard; then process restart.
- Autoscaler: delayed scale-up due to short-lived ephemeral worker churn.
- Traces: significant hedged-retry amplification on routes with 3xx/4xx observations.
- Customer supplied delivery logs: bulk resend timestamps and webhook headers attached in the ticket.

Links:
- Dashboards: https://grafana.redwood.internal/d/ops/apigw-accept-queue?from=now-1h&to=now
- Runtime logs (sample): https://logs.redwood.internal/query?query=SUP-1184723

Immediate customer-facing workaround provided:
- Support recommended customer to disable aggressive webhook retries and enable exponential backoff (they confirmed temporary pause).
- We applied a temporary route-level concurrency cap and increased apigw accept-queue throttling for the affected route to prevent further runtime OOMs.

Observed acceptance queue and apigw threadpool saturation correlating with customer retry window.
Runtime stack traces indicate repeated allocations in attention cache path leading to GPU memory fragmentation over repeated short sessions.
Hedged retry configuration on the gateway amplified inflight requests for slow handshake routes, contributing to burst multiplication.

No evidence of model bug; load pattern and retries were primary driver.
