payload.description:
Issue summary: BrightLogix (dedicated customer) reports intermittent multi-second pauses at the start of streamed responses. Customers see an apparent model hang for 3–8 seconds at stream initiation; after the pause either the stream resumes normally or the client issues immediate retries. Impact: user-facing latency spikes in production UI, elevated request counts and 429 responses, and customer concerns about model regression. Environment: prod-us-east serving dedicated pool (tenant brightlogix-dedicated). Steps to reproduce:
1) Use BrightLogix client in production traffic pattern (concurrent short-chat sessions, many small tokens).
2) Start streaming request (chat/completion) to the streaming endpoint pinned to redwood-open-7b-v2.
3) Observe initial delay between connection and first data frame, then either recovery or immediate client retry behavior.
Observed behavior: 3–8s pause at stream start in ~0.8% of sessions during traffic peaks; follow-up retries amplify request rate and quickly trigger soft rate-limiter enforcement returning 429s. Expected behavior: streams should begin delivering tokens within 200–800ms under normal load. Initial hypothesis: windowed soft-quota enforcement at per-tenant rate limiter is deferring requests without explicit Retry-After, combined with SDK/client immediate retry behavior causing amplification.
Logs and traces: attached traces show long wait inside streaming-proxy queue (trace IDs: trace-20260312-1405-79a, trace-20260312-1412-cf3). Rate-limiter logs for tenant show bursts reaching soft_quota_window limit and then a short enforced delay (soft_defer) rather than immediate 429; downstream clients interpret socket pause as a timeout and retry. No model-side OOMs or GPU saturation observed.
Impact notes: Because BrightLogix is on a dedicated pool, increased retries temporarily increased tail latency for co-located tenants by consuming the limited burst tokens in the shared per-pool limiter.
Attachments: excerpted proxy trace, rate-limiter event log, sample client SDK logs (obfuscated).
2026-03-12 17:00 — Reproduced locally with a synthetic load generator that opens many short-lived streaming sessions; observed identical 3–6s pause at stream start under bursty arrival patterns.
2026-03-12 19:10 — Rate-limiter configuration for dedicated pools uses a 'soft_quota_window' of 10s with a deferred accept path that causes the streaming-proxy to keep the connection open while tokens are delayed; no Retry-After header was previously emitted for deferred requests.
2026-03-12 20:50 — SDK default backoff (1s fixed) causes many clients to retry quickly; retries arrive within the same soft_quota_window and exhaust available burst tokens, flipping enforcement to hard 429s.
2026-03-13 11:30 — Serving runtime metrics: no increased GPU utilization or model-level latency regression; tail latency source is queuing in streaming-proxy and rate-limiter decision path.
2026-03-13 15:00 — Hypothesis validated: when the proxy delays initial data frames due to soft_defer semantics, clients interpret the stall as a failure and retry; combined effect results in ephemeral 429 storms and perceived inference timeouts.
2026-03-14 09:00 — Proposed immediate mitigations tested in staging: (1) emit Retry-After header on 429/deferred responses, (2) reduce soft_quota_window from 10s to 2s for short-session workloads, (3) add per-stream token accounting to avoid long-held reservations.
2026-03-14 11:20 — Observed that temporary bump of BrightLogix tenant burst reduced visible incidents; confirms rate-limiter as root contributor rather than model regression.
2026-03-14 13:00 — Identified infra PR (https://github.com/redwood-inference/infra/pull/2843) that implements Retry-After and short-window config with feature flag for canary rollout.

Additional notes:
2026-03-12 16:01 — BrightLogix (Elena, eng lead): We see a pause right after the connect frame; our frontend retries immediately after 1s by default. This started after last week's traffic spike. Key urgency: impacts user UX and sometimes results in duplicate messages.
Mitigation applied: short-term — increased per-tenant burst allocation for brightlogix-dedicated and advised the customer to configure SDK to use jittered exponential backoff (documentation snippet and example provided). Short-term change reduced incidents immediately. Medium-term — merged infra PR to emit Retry-After on 429/deferred responses for streaming endpoints and reduce soft_quota_window for short-session detection; canary rollout started in us-east on 2026-03-14. Long-term actions — implement per-stream token accounting to avoid long-lived holds, instrument per-tenant streaming proxy queue depth and expose alerting, and update SDK defaults to jittered exponential backoff for streaming connection errors. Follow-ups: 1) Ops to monitor canary for 72 hours and report metrics (owner: Diego Martinez). 2) SDK team to ship minor release v0.12.4 with backoff default changes and sample config (owner: Lina Park). 3) Postmortem and runbook update to be published under linked confluence page (owner: Asha Patel).

payload.description:
Issue summary:
- Customer reports a sudden increase in tail latency (p95/p99) beginning ~2025-12-08 09:40 PT on their Dedicated H100 pool (orbit-h100-prod, us-east).
- No customer-side deploy at that time. Customer correlates onset with Redwood runtime config update/rollout.

Customer impact:
- Primary impact: p95 end-to-end latency for chat completions increased from ~650–800ms to ~1.3–1.6s for their typical workloads.
- Secondary impact: increased request timeouts on their side (they enforce a 2.0s upstream timeout for non-streaming calls); customer reported ~0.6% timeout rate during spike.
- Business impact: degraded UX in their analytics assistant; customer requested immediate mitigation and RCA.

What changed:
- Suspected: H100 hardware tuning profile pack enabled (scheduler preset + kernel heuristics) in orbit-h100-prod pool.
- Change window aligns with staged rollout for runtime profile selection and H100 presets.

Environment:
- Dedicated: orbit-h100-prod
- Region: us-east
- GPUs: H100 (mixed SXM/PCIe per fleet notes; exact mix unknown at time of report)
- Model: llama-3.1-70b-instruct pinned
- Traffic: mixture of streaming and non-streaming; concurrency bursts at top of minute (customer cron-driven workloads)

Requested by customer:
- Immediate rollback/disable of new profile if confirmed.
- Evidence: graphs before/after + explanation of expected behavior/trade-offs.

Attachments/logs requested:
- Customer request IDs and timestamps around spike (pending at ticket creation).
Timeline (all times PT):
- 2025-12-08 10:02: Ticket created from #support escalation. Customer reports p95 doubled.
- 2025-12-08 10:10: SRE (Sean Gallagher) checks Dedicated pool deploy history; sees runtime config rollout completed ~09:37–09:45.
- 2025-12-08 10:18: Observability review: new dashboard panels segmenting latency by selected_profile indicate orbit-h100-prod switched from profile=default to profile=h100/balanced.
- 2025-12-08 10:25: Runtime debug endpoint confirms effective config drifted vs prior defaults. Notable deltas:
  - scheduler.prefill_decode_fairness_mode = "strict" (previously adaptive)
  - scheduler.queue_limit increased
  - scheduler.target_batch_tokens increased
  - backpressure thresholds shifted (more throughput-oriented)
- 2025-12-08 10:33: Hypothesis: new fairness/queue settings improved throughput at moderate concurrency but worsened tail latency under customer’s bursty arrival pattern and long-ish prompt tail.
- 2025-12-08 10:41: Quick mitigation plan agreed: disable H100 profile for this pool via per-pool override (set profile_selection_override=default; restart canary slice first).
- 2025-12-08 10:58: Canary slice (10%) shows p95 recovering within ~15 minutes (back to ~700–850ms), timeout rate returns to baseline.
- 2025-12-08 11:30: Rollback expanded to 100% of orbit-h100-prod.

Data checked:
- Dedicated pool latency dashboard (p50/p95/p99) for /v1/chat.completions.
- Scheduler metrics: queue depth, time-in-queue, batch formation wait.
- GPU metrics: SM utilization stable; no thermal throttling signals; memory headroom acceptable; no OOM spikes.
- Error metrics: 5xx unchanged; timeouts observed were customer-side.
- Profile selection metrics: selected_profile and override_source changed at rollout time.

Most likely cause:
- H100 balanced preset increased batching aggressiveness + stricter prefill/decode fairness. Under bursty traffic with mixed sequence lengths, queueing delay increased for a subset of requests, pushing p95/p99 up.

Notes:
- This matches earlier internal signals from H100 validation about tail-latency regressions tied to prefill/decode fairness (see runtime PR notes and internal Slack thread on suspected fairness regression).
- No evidence of kernel mismatch; tokens/sec improved slightly during high concurrency, but customer’s SLO is tail latency, not max throughput.

Additional notes:
We identified that a runtime configuration change enabled a new H100 tuning profile in your Dedicated pool around the time the latency spike began. That profile increases batching aggressiveness and adjusts scheduler fairness behavior; in your workload shape (bursty concurrency + mixed prompt lengths), it caused higher queueing delay and worsened tail latency.
We rolled back the profile for your pool (returned to prior defaults), and latency returned to baseline within ~30 minutes. We’ll keep the profile disabled for your pool until an updated H100 preset is validated against this workload pattern. We can schedule a controlled re-enable window with canary monitoring and an immediate rollback switch.
We will follow up with a short RCA summary and the guardrails we’re adding to prevent this regression class from escaping canary again.
Mitigation applied:
- Disabled H100 tuned profile for orbit-h100-prod via per-pool override (forced selected_profile=default).
- Performed staged restart (10% canary -> 100%).
Result:
- p95 latency returned to baseline band (~700–850ms) and customer timeouts cleared.
Root cause (working):
- Tail-latency regression introduced by H100 scheduler preset (prefill/decode fairness + batching/queue defaults) under bursty request arrival + mixed seq-len distribution.
Status:
- Customer stable on default profile.
- Pending: runtime preset adjustment + additional perf-canary coverage for bursty workloads before re-enabling.
Add explicit guidance in H100 tuned profile reference: workload envelope + known trade-offs (throughput vs tail latency) and recommended opt-out for strict p95 SLOs until latency-first preset is available.
Ensure perf-canary includes bursty arrival patterns and mixed seq-len buckets for H100 (tie to workload matrix runner).
Add automated guardrail: if queue_time_p95 exceeds threshold after profile enablement, auto-disable profile at pool level (requires product/infra sign-off).
Coordinate with Support to standardize customer comms template: 'expected behavior' vs guarantees.

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customer LumenLogic reports that their March invoice (invoice_id: INV-2026-03-07-LL) has two near-identical credit line items totaling $12,400, which produce a negative balance. The credits are labeled as 'hourly-smoothing-credit' and 'promotional-rate-override-credit' but each appears twice with the same amounts and reference metadata.

Impact:
- Customer billing shows negative line item; finance cannot finalize month-end.
- Customer is on Dedicated and expects predictable reserved-rate billing.
- Customer requests immediate explanation and provisional reversal to finalize their internal accounting.

Environment:
- Dedicated pool: redwood-dedicated-us-east-2 (LumenLogic org id: org_0xLL)
- Billing pipeline: postback-ingest -> postback-processor -> charge-apply job -> invoice-generator
- Peak activity window: 2026-03-07 01:47:00 - 01:59:00 UTC (microburst batch embed job resumed)

Steps to reproduce (as reported by customer):
1) Resume previously paused batch embedding job at 2026-03-07T01:47:12Z.
2) Job emits burst of 130k tokens and multiple postbacks.
3) At 01:48:20 UTC their reserved pool experienced a brief failover to eu-west for some routing requests.
4) Invoice generated on 2026-03-07 contains duplicate credit lines.

Customer-provided evidence:
- Invoice excerpt (sanitized): two entries each 'hourly-smoothing-credit' $6,200 and two 'promo-rate-override' $0.00 (promo displayed but duplicate credit applied).
- Postback ids (sample): pb_9a1f7c_01, pb_9a1f7c_02, pb_9a1f7c_02-replay
- Slack thread: #support-lumenlogic (link provided in private)

Requested outcome:
1) Explanation for why credits were duplicated.
2) Immediate provisional correction or invoice adjustment to allow customer to close month-end.
3) Permanent fix to prevent repeat occurrences and a timeline for reconciliation.

Additional notes:
2026-03-12 - LumenLogic Billing Contact: Approved provisional adjustment; asked for permanent fix ETA and assurance this won't reoccur during their next batch window.
Query of postback-ingest table (producer_ts between 2026-03-07T01:46:50Z and 2026-03-07T01:49:00Z) returned three distinct records with identical event_id but different region_tag fields (us-east, eu-west, us-east-replay).
postback-processor logs show dedupe check used key: concat(org_id, '|', floor(request_timestamp/60)) which groups by minute bucket and misses exact event_id collisions when replays shift timestamps by <60s.
charge-apply job is idempotent when presented with same postback_id; however, replayed messages used a suffixed postback_id (pb_..._replay) and bypassed idempotency, re-triggering credit path.
Billing code path: promotional-rate-override logic applied after smoothing-credit calculation; the second run re-evaluated smoothing and issued another credit because the first credit had been marked 'applied' but not yet reconciled to invoice when replay arrived.
Reproduction locally: simulated a replay with modified region_tag and postback_id variation results in duplicate credit generation. Patch hypothesis: strengthen dedupe key to include event_id and idempotency token (postback_id canonicalization).
2026-03-12 - Provisional action: Billing created manual adjustment invoice line (ADJ-642579) reversing the duplicate credits totaling $12,400 so the customer's invoice is balanced. Customer notified and provided adjusted PDF.
2026-03-12 - Hotfix deployed (billing-recon v1.2.3): postback-processor dedupe now uses canonical_event_id + org_id + region_shard to avoid minute-bucket collisions and normalizes postback_id suffixes to respect idempotency. Patch merged: github.com/redwood-inference/postback-processor/pull/745
Permanent reconciliation plan (next steps): Run full retro reconciliation for 2026-03-07 across affected dedicated pools and generate converse adjustments for any other orgs impacted. Billing to run job by 2026-03-15 and publish report to linked Confluence page.
Monitoring: Added a transient alert that triggers when more than one credit of the same type and amount is applied to the same org within a 2-minute window. Alert routed to #billing and on-call SRE.
Customer follow-up: LumenLogic confirmed adjusted invoice and accepted provisional reversal. They requested confirmation after retro reconciliation that there will be no net unexpected debit.

payload.description:
Issue summary: NimbusDocs reports intermittent p99 latency spikes and occasional 504s for short streaming requests originating from their us-east dedicated cluster. Impact: customer-facing application experiences brief user-facing freezes (~5-20s) multiple times per hour, causing support tickets and reduction in session throughput. Environment: prod, dedicated pool for NimbusDocs (tenant id: nimbus-47), serving runtime 1.8.2, coalescer service v0.9.1. Observed window: first seen 2026-03-11 22:10 UTC; recurring through 2026-03-12.

Steps to reproduce:
1) Customer exercises short streaming completions (prompt length ~10 tokens, expected response ~30 tokens) at sustained 12 rps per connection across 120 concurrent connections.
2) A mix of shorter single-turn and occasional long-turn (>512 tokens) requests present.
3) Intermittent p99 spikes observed in per-route dashboards and SLO alerts.

Observed behavior:
- p95 stable ~120ms, p99 jumps to 2.5s-7s for brief epochs (~30–90s).
- Streaming sessions show delayed first-chunk arrivals and sporadic 504s.
- Batch size distribution shows sudden microbatching where many 10-token requests are held until a long request arrives.

Expected behavior:
- Continuous coalescer should maintain sub-300ms first-chunk latency for short streaming requests under this load profile.

Logs/metrics/attachments:
- Grafana panels: per-tenant p99, batch-size histogram, coalescer flush latency.
- Traces: sample trace ids attached in comments.
- Customer provided client logs showing client-side time-to-first-chunk latency spikes.

Notes: customer is on Dedicated and has strict SLA requirements. They reported the issue via support chat and attached a short repro script that simulates their traffic mix.

Additional notes:
2026-03-12 12:28 - NimbusDocs (Customer): Provided repro harness and client logs. Observed that spikes often occur when a long request from internal QA runs concurrently with a burst of short streaming requests. Asked if a temporary workaround is possible.
2026-03-13 09:10 - Engineering (Serving): Added note: KV cache warmup path was observed to hold shard locks during prefix-merge, blocking coalescer flush under specific sequence length heterogeneity. Raised a PR to release lock earlier in the warmup path. See related PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving/pull/2145
Correlation: p99 windows align with spikes in coalescer.flush_delay_ms and a sudden shift in batch-size histogram where many small requests are held until a long request arrived.
Hypothesis A: Prefetching policy for long requests triggers prefix-merge behavior that holds coalescer flush longer than configured linger_ms under certain interleavings.
Hypothesis B: Tenant weight misalignment caused the coalescer to treat the tenant as higher-priority and wait for larger batch composition, increasing head-of-line latency for short streams.
Observed: KV cache warmup path acquires a shard-level mutex while priming prefixes; when long request arrives it holds the mutex and stalls short-request flush callbacks on same coalescer thread.
Repro: Reproducer provided by customer reliably triggered p99 spikes when a single long request was injected every 25s into a steady stream of short requests at 12 rps across 100 connections.
Canary change: reduce coalescer.linger_ms and disable long-request prefetching reduced p99 at canary nodes from 2.7s -> 480ms.
Code change proposed: release KV warmup shard lock after prefix data is enqueued to coalescer instead of after synchronous priming completes (PR #2145).
Workaround applied: temporary coalescer config changes (linger_ms=5, disable prefetch_long_requests) rolled out to tenant nimbus-47; immediate p99 improvement observed. Root cause: interaction between prefix-merge/prefetching logic and KV cache warmup holding shard locks caused head-of-line delays for short streaming requests. Fix: merged PR to adjust KV warmup locking and updated coalescer flush logic to honor tenant short-stream priority. Deployed serving v1.8.3 with fix on 2026-03-14. Post-deploy monitoring shows p99 stable <500ms. Follow-ups: create automated regression test for mixed short/long workload, update runbook with recommended per-tenant defaults, add alerting on coalescer.flush_delay_ms anomaly. Customer notified and provided post-incident report.
payload.summary: Intermittent p99 latency spikes traced to prefix-merge lag in multi-tenant coalescer

payload.description:
Issue summary: Over a 30-minute window on 2026-03-12 the customer observed a sustained drop in p50/p95 throughput (approx 40-60% reduction) on their dedicated pool. Traffic pattern: many short-lived streaming connections (median duration ~1.2s) from a small set of upstream services. Impact: customer-facing inference latency increased and queue lengths rose causing client timeouts and repeated retries.

Impact: Critical for NimbusDocs production workflows: timed-out document summarization jobs, 15% of requests returned 504 within the window. Customer reports heavy business impact (batch run failures).

Environment: Dedicated pool (tenant-id: nimbus-42) in prod-us-west, reserved capacity 8 GPUs (A100 equivalent). Autoscaler configured with predictive window=60s, min_replicas=2, max_replicas=10, burst_capacity enabled. Prefetcher and KV-cache configured with small_stream_threshold.

Steps to reproduce (observed):
1) Customer's ingestion service opens many short streaming connections concurrently (50-200 short streams/sec) for partial-chunk decoding.
2) Each stream schedules a small inference job which the scheduler places across GPUs with strict tenant affinity.
3) Scheduler places small short-lived tasks across many slots causing slot fragmentation and affinity mismatch.
4) Autoscaler sees steady aggregate GPU utilization (40-60%) and queue depth within predictive thresholds and does not scale.
5) Meanwhile many slots are occupied by transient streams that hold batchers/prefetch resources preventing larger batched requests from forming.
6) Larger requests queue behind these ephemeral streams leading to queue lock and effective throughput collapse.

Observed behavior: p50 latency doubled, p95 latency spiked x3, queue length metric 'rpc.queue_length' rose to sustained 120+, GPU utilization remained moderate but effective batch formation rate dropped by ~70%. No driver-level GPU OOM or kernel crashes.

Expected behavior: Autoscaler or scheduler should detect slot-level fragmentation/short-lived-stream ratio and either consolidate streams or trigger scale-up to avoid starvation of batched work.

Logs/metrics referenced:
- /dashboards/dedicated/nimbus-42/throughput (shows drop at 2026-03-12T14:21Z)
- traces: trace-ids: 8f4f3a1e, 8f4f3a2b (sample short-stream traces showing rapid connect/disconnect)
- serving logs: many "stream open"/"stream close" events with no KV-cache hits reported during window

Attachments: CPU/GPU perf snapshots, scheduler placement dump (sched-dump-2026-03-12-14-25.txt), and a sample pcap of short-stream traffic (attached to ticket).
Initial hypothesis: noisy ephemeral streams from customer's ingestion service are causing slot-level fragmentation that is invisible to the autoscaler's aggregate GPU utilization heuristics.

What we've checked:
- Verified no underlying driver or node failures in the pool during timeframe.
- Confirmed autoscaler logs show no scale decisions during the window; predictive model input (arrival rate) stayed within configured bounds.
- Scheduler placement dump indicates >70% of active slots were occupied by streams with lifespan <5s.
- KV-cache growth is low; prefetcher counters show many small prefetch attempts being serialized.
- SRE replicated similar pattern in staging by launching 200 short streams/sec; observed identical throughput collapse.

Hypotheses considered: affinity misallocation, autoscaler not weighting fragmentation metric, prefetcher holding locks on slots, slot lease timeouts too long for short streams.

Quick tests run:
- Shortened slot lease time in staging by 50% -> improved consolidation and throughput partially recovered.
- Applied a temporary throttle on new short streams (server-side) for NimbusDocs -> immediate p50/p95 recovery observed.

Root cause (working theory): combination of (a) high concurrent short-lived streams creating slot fragmentation, (b) autoscaler heuristic relying on aggregate GPU utilization and queue length but not on short-stream ratio or slot hold-time, (c) prefetcher/kv-cache acquiring per-slot resources that block batch formation.

Next investigative actions:
- Add short_stream_ratio metric to autoscaler input vector (POC).
- Review scheduler placement policy for consolidation thresholds.
- Confirm if tenant affinity policy can be relaxed for ephemeral streams to enable packing.
- Run a canary autopatch in staging to adjust slot lease TTLs for short streams and observe stability.

References: Slack thread #support (https://slack.redwood.com/archives/C0123ABC45F), internal incident TIM-2026-43 (related), and SRE test harness repo commit id abcdef123.
2026-03-12 15:02 - Support (Lina Cho): Acknowledged. Escalating to SRE for immediate investigation. Notified customer of P1 response and temporary mitigation options.
2026-03-12 15:18 - SRE (Miguel Ortega): Reproduced in staging with synthetic short-stream load. Confirmed slot fragmentation. Trying reducing slot lease TTL as a mitigation.
2026-03-12 16:05 - Support (Asha Patel): Customer applied temporary client-side burst limiter (30 concurrent short streams) and reported throughput return to normal levels. Asking for platform-side fix timeline.
2026-03-12 18:10 - Engineering (Priya Nair): Preparing autoscaler change to include 'short_stream_ratio' in decisioning. Also raising scheduler consolidation tweak as low-risk canary. PR: github.com/redwood/inference/pull/4213
2026-03-13 09:30 - SRE (Miguel Ortega): Canary deployed to staging adjusting slot lease TTL and adding additional telemetry. Early results promising: batch formation rate recovered by ~50% under synthetic load.
Workaround applied: customer enforced a client-side burst limiter and we applied a temporary throttle rule at the edge to cap ephemeral streams per-tenant. Short-term platform mitigation: reduced slot lease TTLs on a targeted canary pool and enabled more aggressive placement consolidation for ephemeral stream class.

Planned permanent fixes:
- Autoscaler: incorporate 'short_stream_ratio' and 'avg_slot_hold_time' into scale decision model (target: merged PR and canary by 2026-03-20).
- Scheduler: implement packing/consolidation policy for ephemeral streams to avoid cross-slot fragmentation (RFC opened, PR in progress).
- Runbook: add detection alert 'ephemeral_stream_fanout' that triggers automated mitigation (throttle + notify SRE).

Follow-ups:
- Postmortem scheduled (owners: Miguel Ortega, Priya Nair), to be published in Confluence after customer notification.
- Customer-facing summary and remediation timeline to be sent by CS by 2026-03-15.

Ticket state: In Progress — engineering working on autoscaler update.
payload.summary: Ephemeral connection fanout + affinity mismatch causes autoscaler deadlock and throughput collapse

payload.description:
Customer reports a sustained increase in time-to-first-token (TTFB) for chat completions immediately after the runtime 2.1.0 bridge and a model revision roll-forward to rwd-v2-pp. The issue manifests as a 300-1500ms additional delay before the first chunk is streamed in interactive sessions; subsequent token throughput is normal. Affects multiple customer sessions and elevated request timeouts for some long-prompt chats.
1) On dedicated cluster in us-east, pin runtime 2.1.0 and model rwd-v2-pp-rev3
2) Start a new chat session with a 250-400 token system+user prompt (interactive streaming enabled)
3) Observe the initial streaming handshake and measure TTFB (time until first chunk arrives)
4) Repeat across several instances to reproduce variability; compare against sessions pinned to runtime 2.0.3 + rwd-v2-large
Customer-provided curl: POST /v1/chat/completions -> request_id: cst-92b1, latency: 1324ms to first chunk, 3xx total tokens streamed
Proxy logs (elb-us-east-3): 2026-03-10T14:07:22Z request_id=cst-92b1 upstream_connect_time=0.026 upstream_response_time=1.31 status=200
Serving node logs (node-rt-7): runtime-init: model_load=0.28s kernel_probe=0.41s compile_sync_block=1.02s trace=alloc_sync()
Prometheus snapshot (us-east): inference_start_latency_seconds{quantile="0.99"} increased from 0.45 -> 1.8 between 2026-03-09T23:00 and 2026-03-10T02:00
Initial triage: Pattern correlated with runtime 2.1.0 bridge rollout and model revision that uses new kernel selection paths.
Hypothesis A: Synchronous graph/kernel compilation on first client request introduced blocking on the serving thread (evidence: compile_sync_block entry in node logs).
Hypothesis B: Scheduler affinity change caused cross-node routing that added an extra network hop (evidence: sporadic upstream_connect_time spikes in ELB logs for affected requests).
Collected metrics: increased 95/99p TTFB for chat-start spans, no corresponding increase in per-token generation time once streaming begins.
Reproduced internally on staging by forcing runtime 2.1.0 + rwd-v2-pp; median handshake latency rose ~450ms vs 2.0.3 baseline.
Node-level trace shows: model load path now triggers deferred kernel prefetch only after first request; a recent allocator change caused compile to run inline when prefetch misses occur.
Related code: runtime change introduced in github.com/redwood-inference/runtime@commit a7c3f9d and PR #4589 altered allocator behavior and compile blocking semantics.
Linked internal ticket INT-33412 opened to coordinate hotfix and infra rollout.
Customer impact: Several BrightLens AI streaming-only chat flows hit client-side 2s timeouts and saw degraded UX; no token corruption or wrong outputs observed.
2026-03-10 - Support (Luis Ortega): Acknowledged to customer, requested request_ids, sample prompts and worst-affected session timestamps; escalated to SRE.
2026-03-10 - SRE (Hannah Park): Identified compile_sync_block events on node logs matching customer request_ids; marked as likely root cause and started rollback plan for allocator change.
2026-03-11 - Eng (Maya Patel): Prepared runtime 2.1.1 hotfix that defers kernel compilation off request thread and adds a pre-warm path during model activation; PR: github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/4621.
2026-03-11 - Support (Luis Ortega): Applied temporary mitigation by pinning affected customer's routes to runtime 2.0.3 and model rwd-v2-large; customer reported immediate improvement in handshake latency.
2026-03-12 - SRE (Hannah Park): Deployed 2.1.1 to us-east canary, monitored TTFB 99p drop from ~1.8s to ~0.48s across canary traffic; scheduled full rollout.
2026-03-12 - Customer (BrightLens AI - Alex Kim): Confirmed that pinned route restored expected behavior and that post-hotfix testing showed improved TTFB; closing the ticket after stabilization period.
Hotfix deployed in runtime 2.1.1 that defers kernel compilation off the serving request path and adds proactive kernel prefetch during model activation. Immediate customer mitigation: pinned their routes to runtime 2.0.3 until canary and full rollout validated. Monitoring shows TTFB back to baseline in us-east. Follow-up: revert allocator synchronous compile default and add a pre-warm CI test for handshake latency.

payload.description:
Issue summary
- Customer reports Redwood Private on-prem installer blocks upgrade due to signature verification failure: "Unknown signing key" / "untrusted key id".
- Triggered immediately after Redwood signing key rotation for offline bundle releases.

Customer / Impact
- Customer: GovLab Research (Private, air-gapped environment)
- Impact: Upgrade blocked in preflight; customer cannot proceed with planned maintenance window. No production outage yet, but upgrade window at risk.

Environment
- Deployment: Redwood Private (on-prem), air-gapped
- Installer: redwood-private-installer v1.12.3 (customer-reported)
- Bundle: redwood-private-offline-bundle 2026.01.0 (customer-reported)
- Transport: bundle moved via offline media (external drive)

What happened
- Redwood rotated the offline bundle signing key as part of scheduled rotation.
- Customer environment has a pinned trust store containing the previous Redwood public signing key only.
- New bundles are signed with the new key; the installer correctly fails closed when the signer key is not in the local trust store.

Error (customer-provided)
- Preflight output:
  - "Signature verification failed: UNTRUSTED_SIGNING_KEY"
  - "Key ID: redwood-release-signing-2026q1 not found in trust store"
  - "Install blocked. Update trust roots or contact Support."

Repro steps (support)
1) In an environment with an outdated trust store (previous key only), run:
   - redwood-private-installer preflight --bundle /mnt/offline/redwood-private-2026.01.0.bundle
2) Observe failure during bundle verification with unknown/untrusted key.

Triage notes

Issue summary:
Customer Brushwell Analytics reports sustained p99 inference latency increase (from ~350ms to 2.5–4s) and occasional request timeouts for requests routed to apac-east.

Impact:
- Production inference for multiple endpoints degraded for Brushwell (dedicated account).
- Client sees increased API latency and intermittent 504s; affects real-time scoring pipelines.

Environment:
- Redwood hosted, dedicated capacity for Brushwell in apac-east region.
- Observed across multiple model variants pinned to redwood-v2-medium.

Steps to reproduce (from customer):
1) Send streaming chat completion requests to customer key scoped to apac-east.
2) Observe p95/p99 token latencies and occasional streaming disconnects after 2–4s.
3) Repeatedly repros ~20% of requests during window between 2026-03-12T02:10Z and ongoing.

Observed logs / telemetry snippets:
- API gateway traces show requests routed to edge-proxy instance apac-proxy-07 then immediately retried to apac-proxy-03 with sticky cookie mismatch.
- Serving runtime shows queue depth spikes on a small subset of hosts (gpu-pool-03) concurrent with increased KV cache miss rate.
- No elevated 5xx coming from model pods; time lost in proxy handoff and connection re-establishment.

Customer-provided example request IDs:
- req_brush_20260312_00123
- req_brush_20260312_00456

Additional notes:
2026-03-14 09:10 UTC — Customer CS: Brushwell reports degradation mostly mitigated for live endpoints after temporary workaround; requesting postmortem and permanent remediation timeline.
Chronology: problem surfaced 2026-03-12. Initial traces show proxy sticky-session cookie TTL mismatch introduced by an edge config change (PR#712) made during a canary; some proxies returned Set-Cookie with shorter expiry causing clients to drop affinity and immediately fall back to alternate proxies. Fallback path triggers a connection reuse failure (TLS session not resumed) which causes short-lived TCP teardown and re-establishment. This increased head latency on a subset of GPU hosts because the request arrives without warmed KV cache and is queued behind active requests.
Findings:
- Edge config change altered cookie domain/path TTL for apac proxies.
- Fallbacks were concentrated on gpu-pool-03 (single rack), indicating non-uniform capacity distribution and insufficient burst headroom.
- No model compute errors; root time lost in proxy handoff + KV cold starts + short TCP handshake.
Diagnostics run:
- Collected pcap and proxy logs for samples; correlated with api-gateway traces.
- Verified PR#712 changed cookie TTL from 1h to 30s for certain routes.
- Checked autoscale metrics for gpu-pool-03: surge in queue depth (x6 baseline) and sustained CPU on proxy host.
Mitigation applied 2026-03-12: rolled back cookie TTL change for all apac proxies and applied a temporary sticky-affinity tolerance (grace window) to prevent immediate fallback on cookie expiry. Provisioned short-term burst capacity to gpu-pool-03 and moved a subset of Brushwell traffic to neighboring GPU hosts to drain queue.
Permanent remediation plan:
1) Revert PR#712 and add unit/regression tests for cookie TTL parity across canary groups. (Edge team) 2) Adjust routing policy to avoid concentrating fallback traffic to a single gpu pool; implement randomized fallback selection with capacity-awareness. (Routing) 3) Add monitoring alert for rapid proxy-fallback rates and queue-depth hotspots with automated temporary capacity assignment. (SRE)
Status: Customer-facing impact mitigated; workaround deployed. Follow-up tasks assigned as internal tickets INT-4281 (routing policy change) and INT-4310 (edge config test coverage). Postmortem to be published after full remediation.
- Complete INT-4281 and INT-4310; target completion 2026-03-21.
- Publish customer-facing postmortem and RCA by 2026-03-18.
- Monitor Brushwell SLAs for 72 hours and report telemetry to CS every 12 hours.

Issue summary: Customers observed a sustained increase in 5xx responses from the hosted API beginning ~2026-03-13T12:10Z. The spike correlated with a large embedding bulk ingest from a dedicated customer (Acme Analytics) targeting us-east-1. API gateway returned 502/503 to many tenants while serving runtimes experienced GPU preemption and driver resets.

Impact: ~12% of requests to embedding endpoints returned 5xx over a 45-minute window, several dedicated customer requests hit SLA thresholds. Real-time dashboards showed runtime GPU utilization spikes followed by preemption events and subsequent kernel restarts.

Environment: prod-us-east-1, Dedicated pool for Acme Analytics, momentary cross-tenant traffic mixing via bridge-proxy layer.
1) Simulate a high-concurrency embeddings bulk upload to the dedicated tenant (multipart upload of 100k small items) targeting the embedding route.
2) Ensure parallelism across 200 concurrent streams from same tenant.
3) Observe bridge-proxy queue growth and delayed handoff to serving runtime.
4) Watch for GPU driver hot-reset and runtime SIGTERM followed by 502s from API gateway.
Snippet from apigw: [2026-03-13T12:15:22Z] upstream 502 bridge-proxy timeout handoff_id=0x7f3a; bridge queue length=512.
Runtime log: [2026-03-13T12:16:01Z] GPU preempt requested by OS (NVML) - driver reset event.
Scheduler: [2026-03-13T12:16:02Z] evicted runtime worker pid=83421 due to nvml_reset.
Bridge-proxy: [2026-03-13T12:15:45Z] hold_count spike -> accept backlog observed, tcp_accept backlog=1024.
- Initial hypothesis: embedding bulk overwhelmed bridge-proxy accept/handoff path, causing long-held connections and backpressure.
- Observed tight coupling: when bridge queue exceeded threshold, runtime short-lived overload triggered GPU preemption via driver OOM/hard-reset.
- Secondary amplification: autoscaler attempted to spin up more runtimes but hit host-level GPU allocation limits and NVML indicated thermal/driver thrash.
- Cross-tenant impact occurred because bridge-proxy momentarily multiplexed requests while draining; priority isolation didn't fully engage under this pattern.
- No recent infra deploys in the 2 hours prior. Related PR noted for bridge-proxy queuing improvements but not yet rolled out (github.com/redwood-inference/proxy/pull/1029).
1) Immediately applied emergency rate-limiter for large embedding upload routes for the affected tenant (Acme Analytics) to cap concurrent streams.
2) Drained and restarted bridge-proxy replicas with increased accept_queue tuning (net.core.somaxconn and proxy internal backlog).
3) Temporarily increased dedicated pool capacity for Acme tenant to reduce autoscaler churn.
4) Rolled kernel NVML driver soft-restart on hosts reporting preempt events to stabilize GPU drivers.
Rate-limiting reduced error rate to baseline within ~12 minutes after application. Bridge-proxy restart and backlog tuning prevented immediate recurrence. Engineering is performing a deeper postmortem and will schedule a follow-up runbook update. Customer notified with initial update and workaround steps.
Workaround applied: tenant-specific ingestion rate cap and bridge backpressure thresholds adjusted. Long-term fix planned: proxy handoff refactor to avoid long-lived accept queue saturation and enforce tenant-level early-shed. Planned follow-ups include: code change (proxy PR 1029), autoscaler caps for dedicated GPU pools, and NVML driver health monitoring alerting. No permanent customer data loss.
- ENG-ops: implement proxy handoff refactor (owner: @l.oconnor) target sprint 2026-03-20.
- Infra: add NVML thermal/driver-reset alert with 5m burn rate detection.
- Product: tighten tenant ingestion default quotas for embeddings for dedicated tier.
- CS: outreach to Acme Analytics with postmortem and compensation if SLA breach validated.

payload.description:
Issue summary: Customer reports that when using the TypeScript streaming SDK with multiplexed user sessions to drive a Python webhook-based tool, some tool invocations complete only partially (side-effect applied once) when the client reconnects and retries the streaming request. Impact: Duplicate or partial side-effects observed in downstream systems (orders partially created, one of two downstream webhooks fired). Customer is on a dedicated deployment in us-east and has pinned model redwood/gpt-compat-8k. Environment: prod (dedicated), SDK versions: sdk-js@2.8.1 (streaming + multiplex), sdk-py@1.4.0 (webhook handler), ingress via api-gateway v1.3.2. Steps to reproduce (customer-provided): 1) Open a multiplexed streaming connection from the TS client and start two concurrent sessions on the same connection. 2) For session A, trigger a function call that posts to the customer's Python webhook (POST /tools/charge) with an idempotency header X-Redwood-Idempotency: <session-level-id>. 3) Mid-stream, simulate transient network loss (client reconnect/backoff) while the server has already accepted and forwarded the first tool call. 4) Client reconnects and resends the in-flight messages without attaching per-action idempotency metadata (only session-level id attached). 5) The Python handler performs a partial side-effect (writes to cache and schedules a downstream job) before the request fails; on the retried call the webhook sees the session id and treats it as the same logical session but is unable to detect per-action duplicates, leading to partial re-execution or missing compensations. Expected behavior: When the streaming client retries, downstream tool webhooks should either receive a stable per-action idempotency key so the webhook can deduplicate at action granularity, or the Redwood runtime should guarantee at-most-once forwarding semantics for accepted tool invocations. Actual behavior: Partial duplicate side-effects and orphaned downstream jobs for a subset (~3/50) of retried tool calls under customer load. Customer included request/response traces and webhook logs showing different request IDs but identical session id header. Logs/Trace snippets: - TS client reconnect log: "stream: reconnect attempt=1 inflight=2 session_id=usr-92ab" - Gateway forwarded request id: gw-20260310-8471 for first attempt, gw-20260310-8472 for retry - Webhook handler log: "received charge call action_id=None session_id=usr-92ab; started processing; wrote cache key order-123.tmp; error: upstream job enqueue timeout" - Later: "retry received action_id=None session_id=usr-92ab; enqueue succeeded; downstream job duplicate with partial state" Additional notes: Customer's Python handler relies on action-level idempotency token (X-Action-Id) but the TS client only attached session-level id for multiplexing optimization. The customer asks whether this is expected SDK behavior and how best to avoid partial side-effects.

Additional notes:
2026-03-10 11:02 - Support (Oliver Chen): Acknowledged. Asked for SDK versions and the exact header set the client sends. Requested a minimal reproduction or a redacted trace with full headers.
2026-03-10 13:45 - Acme AI (supporting engineer: Jordan Price): Provided additional traces and sample TS multiplexing code. Confirmed they only set one idempotency header per session for multiplex savings. Noted the webhook cannot generate deterministic per-action id without client help.
2026-03-11 08:29 - SRE (Priya Rao): Noted that on Dedicated we saw transient reconnects due to autoscaler node drain events around 2026-03-10T02:00Z. Asked for correlation with gateway request IDs.
2026-03-11 15:12 - Runtime eng (Diego Morales): Asked whether the runtime preserves and forwards per-action metadata during resends or if the client is expected to reattach per-action keys after reconnect. Also requested raw HTTP headers for the two forwarded requests.
2026-03-12 09:05 - Support (Oliver Chen): Uploaded suggested mitigation: have TS client attach X-Action-Id per tool invocation (even in multiplex), and recommended server-side webhook to persist and check X-Action-Id before mutating downstream state. Requested customer to test with a small canary.
2026-03-12 11:27 - Acme AI (Jordan Price): Will test change this afternoon and report results. Asked if Redwood runtime can add a guard for session-level-only idempotency in streaming to warn clients.
2026-03-12 14:44 - Support (Maya Patel): Filed follow-up feature request to product for runtime-side warning and docs clarifications (linked PR & confluence page).
Checked gateway logs for gw-20260310-8471 / gw-20260310-8472; both forwarded to different runtime worker ids. No immediate evidence of duplicate forwarding suppression at runtime for session-only idempotency headers.
Observed Dedicated autoscaler activity and worker recycle that correlated with reconnect window. Worker A forwarded initial tool call to webhook; Worker B forwarded retry attempt after reconnect. Runtime does not currently synthesize per-action tokens when the client omits them.
Reproduced locally with sdk-js@2.8.1 multiplex example: when attaching only X-Session-Id, reconnect+resend results in two separate gw request ids and webhook sees two distinct attempts with same session id but no per-action id.
Reviewed Python webhook handler: it attempted to be idempotent using a composite key session_id + (action payload hash) but the payload hash differed because partial writes changed state between attempts leading to mismatched dedupe keys. This made dedupe fragile.
Hypothesis: The root cause is a combination of multiplexing optimization (clients omitting per-action ids), midstream worker handoff (due to autoscale/drain), and webhook dedupe strategy relying on mutable payloads rather than stable client-supplied action ids.
Severity assessment: P1 due to monetary side-effects but low frequency; recommend short-term mitigations and medium-term runtime/client improvements.
Correlated linked tickets for similar symptoms: SUP-29871 (stream replay duplicates), SUP-41209 (confirmation-token patterns).
Short-term mitigation provided to customer (03/12): 1) Update TS client to attach X-Action-Id per tool invocation (UUID v4) even when using multiplexed streams; 2) Webhook handler to persist seen X-Action-Id in a small atomic DB row before any mutable downstream changes; on duplicate attempts, return success without re-executing side-effects. Implementation guidance and example code snippet provided in reply.
Customer validated canary with 5000 requests and observed zero partial duplicates after adding per-action idempotency tokens. They will roll this change to production this week.
Medium-term product follow-ups opened: - Add runtime warning/logging when session-level-only idempotency header is detected on a streaming connection; - Docs update explaining per-action idempotency is required when using multiplexed streams that may reconnect; - Investigate runtime-level per-action id synthesis when client includes deterministic sequencing metadata (RFC/PR created).
Related PRs and docs: https://github.com/redwood-inference/sdk-js/pull/2410 (example to attach X-Action-Id in multiplex client), https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/INFR/Idempotency+and+Retries+Runbook (updated section draft).
Follow-ups: Product to triage feature request in next planning cycle; Engineering to evaluate runtime guard complexity and false positives. Support to close ticket when customer confirms prod roll-out and no regressions after 72h.
Status: Waiting on customer rollout verification (target close if green by 2026-03-15).

payload.description:
Customer (Northbridge AI Platform) requested a consistent, publishable post-incident summary format they can forward internally after any customer-impacting incident.

Context:
- During their enterprise evaluation, they referenced recent incidents where the status page incident updates were helpful but the final resolution lacked a standardized summary they could reuse for leadership / risk documentation.
- They specifically cited the 2025-11-07 US-East streaming degradation as an example where they wanted a short, non-sensitive summary quickly after resolution.

Request (customer requirements):
1) A standard summary template that is consistent across incidents (not bespoke).
2) Publish timing expectation: ideally within 48 hours of incident resolution (or a “preliminary summary” within 24 hours, with a final summary later if needed).
3) Content they need in each summary:
   - Clear impact statement: what was affected (capability + component), who was affected (by region / product surface), and the user-visible symptom.
   - Start/end timestamps of customer impact (UTC) and any residual monitoring window.
   - Scope: affected regions, API routes/capabilities (e.g., Chat vs Streaming vs Embeddings), and whether Dedicated/Private was impacted.
   - Mitigations taken during incident (what we did to restore service), including whether fallbacks were enabled.
   - Prevention / follow-ups: concrete actions with target timelines (no sensitive internal details, but enough to show we are reducing recurrence).
   - Root cause classification: a short category (e.g., “capacity/queuing”, “deployment regression”, “dependency outage”, “control plane”, “network”), without disclosing proprietary internals or customer-specific capacity.
4) Confidentiality constraints:
   - Must not include customer-specific identifiers.
   - Must not disclose sensitive capacity shortfalls, vendor details, or security-sensitive architecture.

Customer question:
- “Can Redwood commit to a consistent post-incident summary format and publish it on the status page for incidents?”

Requested deliverable for this ticket:
- Provide customer with Redwood’s standard post-incident summary format and confirm how/when it will be published going forward (hosted vs dedicated/private caveats).

Additional notes:
Provided customer with Redwood’s standardized post-incident summary format (publishable, non-sensitive) including: Impact, Timeline (UTC), Affected components/regions, Mitigation, Root cause class, Customer actions (if applicable), and Follow-ups. Confirmed intent to publish/link these summaries from status incidents as part of the ongoing status page transparency upgrades, with Dedicated/Private summaries handled at appropriate granularity.
Track publication + linking behavior under the status page transparency upgrades rollout; ensure Support macros reference the new summary format; validate that summaries are posted within the agreed internal targets (preliminary within 24h where possible; final within 48h) without over-promising customer-specific SLA.
payload.summary: Request: consistent publishable post-incident summary format (impact + mitigations + prevention) for enterprise reporting

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customer's Private deployment nodes fail to download model artifacts during provisioning. Control-plane and runtime log repeated TLS handshake failures showing certificate name mismatch. Customer runs a dual-stack VPC with DNS64/NAT64 enabled for IPv6-only worker subnets.

Impact:
- New workers fail to provision (stuck in 'model-pull' phase).
- Ingest and inference traffic on affected hosts intermittently falls back and triggers restarts; customers report degraded availability for pinned models.

Environment:
- Private deployment (customer-controlled VPC) in us-west-2
- Dual-stack VPC with customer-managed DNS64/NAT64 appliance
- Model artifacts hosted on redwood-artifacts.prod.redwood.internal (served by our artifact CDN TLS endpoint)

Steps to reproduce:
1) Bring up a worker in an IPv6-only subnet using the customer's VPC resolver (DNS64 enabled).
2) Start the redwood runtime that attempts to fetch artifacts from redwood-artifacts.prod.redwood.internal.
3) Observe runtime logs and TLS handshake failures.

Observed behavior:
- System resolves redwood-artifacts.prod.redwood.internal to an AAAA via DNS64 (synthesized).
- TLS client uses SNI equal to the resolved IPv6 literal (synthesized) or the resolver returns AAAA-only, causing the outgoing TLS handshake to not include the expected hostname and server responds with cert for artifact host; client interprets this as CN mismatch and terminates the connection.
- Logs show: "tls: handshake failure: x509: certificate is valid for redwood-artifacts.prod.redwood.internal, not [2001:db8::abcd]"

Expected behavior:
- Client should present correct SNI (artifact host) or resolver should provide A record so connection goes over IPv4 path without SNI mismatch. Artifacts should download successfully.

Attachments:
- Excerpts from runtime logs (see investigation_notes)
- Packet capture provided by customer (sftp link in comments)


Additional notes:
2026-03-01 10:05 - Customer (Pinebank Health - infra team): Uploaded pcap and dig output to s3://pb-support-uploads/SUP-691234/pcap1.pcap. Provided resolver config showing DNS64 enabled
2026-03-02 08:30 - Customer: Confirmed they can modify resolver for a test node. Will try creating a test node with custom /etc/hosts mapping artifact host to IPv4 address and report back.
2026-03-03 11:17 - Customer: Test node with /etc/hosts mapping to IPv4 completed. Model pulled successfully. Customer requests permanent remediation guidance.
2026-03-06 09:55 - Customer: Will implement VPC endpoint and test in staging this week. Asked Redwood for a short runbook to share with their network team; support provided links to Confluence page.
Observations from logs and pcap:
- dig +short AAAA redwood-artifacts.prod.redwood.internal -> 2001:db8::abcd (synthesized by DNS64 appliance). dig +short A returns nothing from customer's resolver.
- Runtime TLS client uses SNI = 2001:db8::abcd in ClientHello in several traces (we suspect our runtime's getaddrinfo path returns numeric form when AAAA-only present).
- Server certificate CN/SAN contains redwood-artifacts.prod.redwood.internal (no IP SAN for the synthesized IPv6). TLS negotiation fails with x509: certificate is valid for redwood-artifacts.prod.redwood.internal, not [2001:db8::abcd].
- Packet capture shows IPv6 flow to appliance then NAT64 translating to IPv4 to our CDN edge; server returns certificate for hostname as expected. Client rejects because SNI did not match the cert name.
- Workaround test: adding an /etc/hosts entry pointing redwood-artifacts.prod.redwood.internal -> 54.210.12.34 (IPv4) forced the client to use IPv4 and TLS handshake succeeded.
Hypothesis:
- Customer DNS64 synthesizes AAAA only; runtime is resolving to numeric address and populating SNI with the numeric form rather than the original hostname. On AAAA-only resolution, SNI should still be set to the original hostname; failure stems from client behavior or glibc resolver variant.
Recommendations tried:
- /etc/hosts override (successful test).
- Creating VPC endpoint to keep artifact traffic on IPv4 (customer to test).
- Suggested customer to enable split-horizon so artifact host resolves to A record for their VPC subnets.

Workaround and next steps:
- Short-term workaround: Customer added /etc/hosts mapping to an IPv4 artifact edge on test nodes which allowed provisioning to proceed.
- Medium-term remediation: Customer will create a VPC endpoint and/or configure split-DNS to return A records for redwood-artifacts.prod.redwood.internal from their resolver for worker subnets (planned this week).
- Redwood follow-up: INT-33045 created for engineering to add detection when resolver returns synthesized AAAA and to prefer original hostname as SNI or attempt IPv4 fallback before failing TLS.
- Follow-up actions assigned:

  - Support: Provide runbook for network team (link shared in comments).

payload.description:
Issue summary: Customer reports duplicated external webhook (third-party accounting webhook) invocations and duplicated tool/function runs when their web app uses the Redwood TypeScript/browser SDK in combination with a service worker background sync. Impact: Duplicate side-effects in third-party systems (double invoices) leading to customer outage of their payment workflow.

Environment/Context: SaaSify is using Redwood TS SDK v1.8.2 in a single-page application deployed on Netlify. They register a service worker that implements Background Sync to retry failed POSTs when the device regains connectivity. Users often have the web app open in multiple tabs on mobile devices with flaky cellular connectivity. The SDK is configured to auto-retry failed streaming requests and to use optimistic local retry logic in the UI.

Observed behavior: When network blips produce 502/504 from the Redwood API or the edge proxy, the browser app performs a local retry and also enqueues a background sync entry via the service worker. If a user has multiple tabs open, each tab enqueues its own background sync event and the service worker dispatches POSTs (containing function/tool call payloads) after the device reconnects. The third-party webhook receives duplicated requests 2–3 times for the same logical action.

Customer expectation: Single effective tool/webhook invocation per user action; guidance on SDK patterns and config to avoid duplicate side effects from client-side background replay and multi-tab scenarios.
1) Deploy Redwood TS SDK v1.8.2 in an SPA with a registered service worker that uses Background Sync to re-send failed POSTs.
2) Open the SPA in two browser tabs on a mobile device (or in two desktop tabs simulating mobile network flakiness).
3) Trigger a function/tool call that results in a webhook POST (e.g., create-invoice tool).
4) Simulate a brief network outage so the initial request fails with a 502/504.
5) Allow the SDK to perform its client-side optimistic retry while the service worker enqueues a sync event for background retry.
6) Restore network connectivity. The service worker background sync runs and replays the POSTs from each tab, while the SDK retry from the main thread also completes, producing multiple webhook deliveries.
7) Observe duplicate webhook receipts on the third-party endpoint.
HTTP trace (abbreviated):
2026-03-10T14:03:12.124Z - GET /v1/streaming - 502 from edge-proxy (net::ERR_CONNECTION_RESET)
2026-03-10T14:03:12.130Z - sdk-js retry (client-side) attempt=1 idempotency-key=none
2026-03-10T14:03:14.500Z - ServiceWorker backgroundSync.register(tag=create-invoice:xyz) (tab A)
2026-03-10T14:03:14.507Z - ServiceWorker backgroundSync.register(tag=create-invoice:xyz) (tab B)
2026-03-10T14:03:20.800Z - backgroundSync fired -> POST /callbacks/invoice (tab A payload) -> 200 OK third-party
2026-03-10T14:03:20.805Z - backgroundSync fired -> POST /callbacks/invoice (tab B payload) -> 200 OK third-party
2026-03-10T14:03:21.000Z - sdk-js client retry completes -> POST /callbacks/invoice -> 200 OK third-party

Note: client logs show no Idempotency-Key header being set by application code. SDK v1.8.2 leaves idempotency to caller by default in browser streaming mode.
Support reproduced the pattern locally by installing a simple service worker that queues failed POSTs and replaying from two tabs. We confirmed that the browser SDK did not inject an Idempotency-Key header in the outbound tool-calling POSTs in the customer's configuration. Edge logs show three distinct POSTs within ~1s with slightly different client-side timestamps. We verified the service worker queue produced one entry per tab, and the SDK optimistic retry produced a third POST.

We reviewed the current JS SDK behavior: in browser/streaming mode the SDK avoids automatic idempotency header injection to reduce accidental long-lived stored tokens in client storage; in Node it auto-generates per-request Idempotency-Key unless the developer sets one. This design choice reduces risk of persisting keys on disk for server apps but leaves browser devs responsible for idempotency when they use background replay mechanisms.

We also checked that the third-party webhook endpoint accepted identical payloads and had no dedup facility on their side.
Duplicate invocations are caused by the combination of: (a) absence of per-action idempotency key in the client payload, (b) multiple independent background-sync queue entries (one per tab), and (c) concurrent optimistic retries by the main thread. With no cross-tab coordination or shared idempotency token, each replay is treated as a fresh request by Redwood and by the downstream webhook.
Short term suggestions provided to customer:
- Configure the client to generate and attach a stable per-action idempotency token (Idempotency-Key) at the moment of user action and include it in the tool call payload or an Idempotency-Key header. Persist that token in sessionStorage and share via the BroadcastChannel API across tabs to avoid multiple independent background-sync entries.
- Disable optimistic client-side automatic retries in the browser SDK while relying on background sync to replay requests once (SDK config: retries=0 in browser).
- On the webhook/third-party side implement idempotency detection keyed by a user+action+client-token so duplicate POSTs are ignored server-side.

We provided a small sample snippet (TS) demonstrating generating a UUID per user action, saving to sessionStorage, and broadcasting it to other tabs. This was included inline in the support reply.
Support provided a two-part resolution on 2026-03-12:
1) Customer action: SaaSify implemented a per-action Idempotency-Key stored in sessionStorage and shared across tabs via BroadcastChannel. They also disabled SDK optimistic retries in the browser (set clientRetry=0) and relied on single background sync replay. After deployment, duplicate webhook deliveries stopped.
2) Product/SDK change: Engineering opened github.com/redwood-inference/sdk-js/pull/842 to add opt-in browser automatic idempotency behavior (generate a cryptographically random per-action Idempotency-Key when app supplies a stable action_id or when developer enables 'autoBrowserIdempotency=true'). The PR includes warnings in README and avoids persistent disk storage; auto keys live per-action only and can be surfaced to service workers via a documented BroadcastChannel pattern.

We verified with the customer that the fix eliminated duplicate side-effects for their test cases. Ticket closed after confirming no further duplicates reported for 48 hours.

Additional notes:
2026-03-11 18:33 - SaaSify Support Contact (Marta Lopez): Implemented sessionStorage + BroadcastChannel approach in staging and confirmed de-duplication. Asked for recommended SDK config to avoid re-enabling optimistic retries.
payload.summary: Duplicate external webhook/tool executions when TS browser SDK + service worker background sync replays retries across tabs

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customers in a subset of dedicated pools observed sustained P99 and P50 throughput regression beginning 2026-03-10 09:20 UTC. Root trigger: a tenant running many long-lived low-CPU, high-GPU attention streams (chat sessions) produced persistent KV cache growth which pushed allocator heartbeats and evicted small-stream slots. The allocator and autoscaler reacted by delaying new GPU attaches, which amplified queueing for other tenants in the same reserved cluster.

Impact:
- NebulaApps (dedicated) experienced 30-45% reduction in effective throughput for batched routes and a p99 latency spike from ~120ms to ~1.2s for ~40 minutes.
- Automatic fallback routed some requests to lower-capacity variants causing increased cost and degraded outputs for a brief window.
- No data loss; requests were delayed but eventually completed.

Environment:
- prod us-west-2 dedicated cluster pool-az3-resv-09
- Affected model variants: redwood/gptx-14b-quant (multi-tenant) and redwood/opt-6.7b-int8 pinned by customer routes

Steps to reproduce (internal):
1. Recreate long-lived client streams with many simultaneous keepalive connections that emit sparse token output (simulate 1k concurrent sessions, 1 token/15s).
2. Configure the tenant's route to pin gptx-14b-quant with batch-size=32 and keepalive windows enabled.
3. Observe KV cache growth on serving nodes (kv-cache size monotonic increase) and allocator attach delays.
4. Measure throughput and p99 latency across co-located tenants.

Observed artifacts and logs:
- Serving runtime logs show repeated KV cache pin warnings: "kv_cache: growth=+1.2GB/min, eviction-latency=120ms"
- Allocator metrics: "slot_attach_delay" increased from ~30ms to 800ms during peak.
- Autoscaler telemetry: delayed scale-up due to aggregated attach failures and a conservative cooldown window.
- Console trace: sudden rise in per-route queue depth for NebulaApps routes between 09:22-09:58 UTC.

Initial mitigation applied:
- 09:40 UTC: Temporarily enforced per-tenant connection throttle on NebulaApps to limit long-lived sessions to their committed concurrency.
- 09:45 UTC: Evicted stale KV cache entries on a subset of serving nodes after coordination with runtime team, reducing memory pressure.
- 09:50 UTC: Increased autoscaler aggressiveness for the affected reserved pool (shorten cooldown and increase attach retry attempts) to bring attach latency back to normal.

Notes on customer communication:
- Customer reported through support channel at 09:30 UTC and was updated at 09:42 UTC with the temporary throttle plan. Customer accepted the throttle and confirmed improved p50 after throttle enforcement.

Next steps documented here and follow-up tasks captured in investigation notes below.

Additional notes:
2026-03-10 10:05 UTC - NebulaApps (Customer): Confirmed observed latency improvements post-throttle; asked whether this will recur and requested a follow-up explaining root cause and permanent mitigations.
Hypotheses considered:
- Noisy tenant with long-lived sessions causing KV cache growth and eviction pressure (primary).
- NVLink or PCIe contention causing attach latencies (ruled out by host-level telemetry).
- Autoscaler misclassification due to heartbeat silence from overloaded allocators (contributing factor).
Findings:
- KV cache metrics correlated tightly with slot_attach_delay and allocator evictions. One tenant's session footprint grew >1TB aggregate across the pool, causing eviction thrash.
- Autoscaler cooldown (120s) plus conservative attach retry logic meant cluster did not immediately scale for transient attach failures.
- Scheduler heartbeat lag increased by 40-60ms which pushed small-stream slots into eviction path.
Relevant links:
- Grafana: https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/allocator/kv-growth?orgId=1&from=2026-03-10T09:00:00Z&to=2026-03-10T11:00:00Z
- Logs: https://logs.redwood.ai/nebulaapps/2026-03-10/attach-failures
- Slack thread: #incidents - https://slack.redwood.ai/archives/INC12345
Temporary mitigations tried and outcome:
- Per-tenant connection throttle: immediate p50 improvement, reduced KV growth rate by ~70% in 15m.
- Targeted KV prune: reclaimed ~2.1GB/node; reduced eviction latencies.
- Autoscaler tweak: improved attach recovery but needs a longer-term change to avoid oscillation.
Short-term (applied):
- Enforced tenant-level connection limits for NebulaApps until policy hardening is complete.
- Forced KV prune and node restart sequencing to avoid simultaneous eviction spikes.
- Tuned autoscaler cooldown and retry thresholds for the affected reserved pool (deployed to prod 2026-03-12 03:00 UTC).
Long-term (in progress / backlog):
- Implement per-tenant KV quotas and auto-trim policy to prevent a single tenant from growing KV state unbounded.
- Add a KV-growth signal to autoscaler as an input (RFC opened and linked PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/autoscaler/pull/402).
- Improve console alerts to detect long-pulse shadowing patterns earlier (runbook update scheduled).
Customer follow-up and closure notes:
- NebulaApps accepted the temporary throttle and requested a post-incident writeup. Postmortem draft created: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/INC/Incident+2026-03-LongPulse+Postmortem.
- Ticket closed after 48h stable metrics and customer confirmation.
Follow-up owner: Marco Rivera (SRE). Backlog epic: INT-900112 (KV quotas and autoscaler signal).
payload.summary: Long pulse shadowing: sustained long-lived streams causing KV cache growth and transient GPU credit drain in dedicated pool

payload.description:
Issue summary: Acme Health reports sporadic presigned artifact validation failures during model shard downloads on their private deployment. Failures align with short windows when control-plane requests show duplicate DNS A answers returned to serving nodes. Impact: ~3-5% of shard fetches fail with HTTP range validation errors causing inference retries and increased latency for customer traffic. This affects live production traffic in us-east and causes customer-visible 5xxs in application logs.

Observed behavior: During the reported windows, serving nodes log back-to-back connections to the same artifact host with identical client IP but different ephemeral source ports; TLS sessions appear to be established twice in quick succession for the same logical request. Downstream S3-presigned range validation occasionally rejects the second connection due to non-monotonic byte-range delivery (range hash mismatch).

Expected behavior: Normal artifact fetches should use a single TLS session and stream consistent byte ranges. DNS queries to the control-plane should return a single authoritative A record.

Environment: Private deployment (VPC peering + corporate egress), prod us-east. Customer uses an on-prem corporate edge that performs NAT reflection for internal resolver queries.

1) Trigger high-rate model shard downloads from a serving node behind customer's corporate egress
2) Observe DNS responses captured from node (tcpdump -n port 53) during failure window
3) Correlate duplicate A responses to artifact hostnames with presigned URL validation failures in serving-node logs
4) Reproduce by running a DNS query loop against corporate forwarder while issuing concurrent artifact GETs to produce race conditions
Mar 10 09:12:01 serving-node-7 fetcher[3241]: GET /shard?r=abc range 0-524287 200ms
Mar 10 09:12:01 serving-node-7 fetcher[3241]: TLS session established to presigned.artifacts.acme.net (srcport=49156)
Mar 10 09:12:01 serving-node-7 fetcher[3241]: duplicate DNS A response received: 10.10.5.8 (orig TTL=30) then 10.10.5.8 (reflected)

Mar 10 09:12:01 serving-node-7 fetcher[3241]: GET /shard?r=abc range 0-524287 502 range-validate-failed
Support replicated presigned range hash mismatch locally using captured pcap and presigned URL (see attached pcap snippet).
pcap shows two DNS A answers within 30-50ms for the same query ID originating from customer's forwarder IP and from corporate edge NAT (duplicate source).
Hypothesis: Corporate edge is reflecting or replaying DNS replies (NAT reflection / asymmetric forwarding) causing the serving node resolver library to process duplicate responses and re-open TLS connections while previous TCP stream is still establishing, leading to partial-range delivery observed by S3 backend.
We observed that re-use of ephemeral ports combined with conntrack entries at the egress appliance can cause second connection to be associated with same logical session but different TCP 4-tuple, confusing presigned range validation when ranges overlap.
SRE ran a controlled test: disabling forwarder caching at customer forwarder removed the duplicate-answer window and eliminated validation errors during the test session.
Maya Chen (Support) [2026-03-10]: Customer reported increased 5xxs from model inference; initial triage points to artifact fetch failures. Collected pcaps and application logs. Escalating to SRE for network analysis.
Ravi Patel (SRE) [2026-03-11]: Observed duplicate A answers in pcap. Requesting customer's network team to run tcpdump on their forwarder and confirm whether NAT reflection is enabled on the edge appliance.
Customer (Acme Health) [2026-03-11]: Confirmed edge appliance (vendor: NetEdge) has a feature called 'resolver reflection' enabled for internal recursion; will test disabling for a short maintenance window tomorrow morning.
Ravi Patel (SRE) [2026-03-12]: Temporary mitigation applied on our serving nodes: increased validation buffer on fetcher and added stricter TLS session reuse checks to avoid immediate reconnect on duplicate DNS responses. This reduced customer 5xxs in monitored window.
Customer (Acme Health) [2026-03-12]: After disabling reflection, errors dropped to baseline. We'll coordinate to keep feature off pending permanent fix.
Workaround implemented: customer disabled 'resolver reflection' on edge appliance; platform-side mitigations deployed to serving nodes (stricter session reuse logic and a small debounce on duplicate DNS answers). Root cause: corporate NAT/reflection of resolver replies causing duplicate DNS answers and rapid TLS reconnects that triggered presigned range validation failures. Next steps: (1) Customer to keep reflection disabled in production (done), (2) Engineering to land permanent serving runtime guard to ignore duplicate A answers from different source IPs within query window (PR #4892), (3) Postmortem and network guidance doc will be added to Confluence. Related PR and runbook linked above.
ENG: Complete PR to add duplicate-DNS-debounce to fetcher (https://github.com/redwood-inference/platform/pull/4892) - owner: @rpatel - due 2026-03-20
DOCS: Add 'resolver reflection' note to Private Deploy networking pitfalls runbook - owner: @mchen - due 2026-03-18
SRE: Monitor customer error rate for 72 hours post-change - owner: @rpatel - due 2026-03-15

payload.description:
Issue summary: Customer observes duplicate downstream webhook side-effects when using a chained function/tool workflow (generate -> parse -> call-outbound-webhook) with client-side retries enabled. Impact: Duplicate charges and duplicated external notifications for a subset of user requests.

Context: ScribeAI uses a multi-step orchestration where the model generates a structured payload, the SDK executes a local handler that calls an external payment webhook, and the customer has configured the SDK to retry on timeouts with per-request idempotency tokens at the top-level. They reported duplicates only when network blips occurred during the tool-call step or during streaming reconnects.

Observed behavior: When the SDK performs an automatic retry of the overall request, the top-level idempotency token is preserved, but the per-action metadata header that the customer's webhook expects (X-Action-Idempotency) is sometimes regenerated by their orchestration layer or dropped during streaming reconnect. The external service receives two distinct idempotency tokens for the same logical action and accepts both, resulting in duplicate side-effects.

Expected behavior: For chained tool/function calls initiated by one SDK request, any per-action idempotency metadata used to deduplicate downstream side-effects should be stable across retries and reconnects, or SDK documentation should clearly state where responsibility lies for preserving per-action nonces across retries.
1) Customer runs a chat session using SDK (python or go) with a handler that invokes an external webhook from within a function/tool call.
2) Configure SDK retry policy: 3 retries on timeout/backoff with exponential backoff; enable streaming with reconnect enabled.
3) Trigger a request that causes the function call to reach out to the external webhook (payment capture endpoint).
4) Simulate a transient network blip: drop connection when function call is in-flight or cause streaming reconnect on the SDK client side.
5) Observe the external webhook receiving two different idempotency headers for what the customer expects to be a single logical action.
2026-03-09T17:23:12Z request_id=req-3f7a2c stream_conn=conn-990 drop_reason=timeout handler=payment_capture action_nonce=act-9d2a (first attempt)
2026-03-09T17:23:14Z request_id=req-3f7a2c retry=1 stream_conn=conn-991 handler=payment_capture action_nonce=act-7b5f (retry attempt; nonce differs)
Customer-side outbound webhook logs show two POSTs within 2s: X-Action-Idempotency=act-9d2a and X-Action-Idempotency=act-7b5f; both returned 200.

Additional notes:
2026-03-11 - ScribeAI (customer): Attached stripped logs and a simplified python handler that calls requests.post to the payment endpoint. Note: We generate a new action nonce inside the function call code on every handler invocation. We assumed top-level retry would not re-run the handler if the top-level idempotency token matched.
2026-03-12 - Support (Jordan Lee): Reproduced locally with a test harness. Hypothesis: SDK retry triggers re-execution of the function/tool handler in the customer process for some failure modes (stream reconnects), so any per-action nonce generated inside the handler will be different across attempts. We recommend either: a) move nonce generation to before the handler invocation and pass it into the handler so it's stable across retries, or b) have the SDK surface a per-action stable idempotency header when re-invoking handlers during reconnects.
2026-03-13 - Eng (Riley Chen): We've captured pcap and server-side trace for req-3f7a2c. The serving-runtime saw a reconnect and a resumed session that resulted in the handler being invoked twice. The runtime did not attach or require a per-action idempotency token; it treats handlers as user code. Filing an internal task to add a best-effort propagation hook into SDKs.
Initial hypothesis: Duplicate side-effects due to handler re-execution on SDK-initiated retry or streaming resume.
Confirmed by local repro: when handler generates nonce at invocation time, retry paths produce different nonces and downstream systems accept them.
Relevant traces: trace_id=trace-7c2a8 (attached in internal logs), pcap shows streaming reconnect at 17:23:13Z and two handler invocations within 2s window.
SDK behavior: python SDK v0.14.2 and go SDK v0.9.1 re-invoke user handlers when the server signals a resumed request; JS SDK behavior varies by streaming client implementation. Documented behavior is currently vague about per-action nonce responsibilities.
Risk assessment: High for customers that perform side-effectful operations inside handlers (payments, emails). Estimated incidence: <1% of requests but high business impact when it occurs.
Temporary mitigation tested: customer moved action nonce generation to a request-scoped store (generated before calling into the model/function orchestration) and duplicates stopped in repro.
Workaround: Customers should generate action-level idempotency nonces outside of the handler invocation so the same nonce is used across retries. Support updated the SDK troubleshooting guide to add a 'per-action nonce' section and example for python/go/js.
Planned product follow-up: Engineering to evaluate adding an optional stable per-action header propagation in SDKs and an explicit note in streaming/reconnect docs. PRs opened for SDK docs + small SDK helper to attach a stable action_nonce across retries.
Status: Waiting for Engineering prioritization for SDK change; customer applied workaround and confirmed no further duplicates in validation tests.
payload.summary: Per-action idempotency token not propagated for chained function/tool calls resulting in duplicate webhook side-effects
