payload.description:
Issue summary: Customer Lumina Health plans to sunset an experimental optimizer flag (async-prefix-prefetch) across several tenant pools but does not have snapshot backups for the feature-state. They requested a backstop strategy that does not rely on snapshot restore to ensure safe rollback and no customer-visible regression. Impact: potential 95p/99p latency increase and token cost changes during sunsetting; possible transient 5xx for tenants with mixed-optimizer-profiles. Environment: Dedicated GPU pool (prod, us-east) serving gpt-3.5-redwood-v2 and gpt-4-lite. Steps to reproduce/context: 1) Toggle optimizer flag off via console feature toggle for a small subset of tenants. 2) Observe latency and error metrics for the next 15 minutes. 3) Gradually expand toggle to remaining tenants. Observed behavior: Customers report small but sustained 95p latency increase (200-350ms) and occasional 524 timeouts for long-streaming sessions after flag removal. Expected behavior: Controlled change with minimal latency regression; ability to return to pre-change behavior quickly without snapshot restore. Logs & telemetry pointers: linked APM traces in Datadog (service:redwood-serving, trace-ids included in investigation notes), console audit logs for toggle operations, metric dashboards at https://console.redwood/dash/ops/optimizer-sunset.
Hypotheses: 1) Removing async-prefix-prefetch disables aggressive KV prefetching, increasing per-request token computation and causing tail latency spikes for long-sequence streaming. 2) Mixed tenant routing causes some requests to land on nodes with warmed KV cache and others on cold nodes, amplifying variance. 3) Autoscaler reaction lag for certain worker types can increase queueing when traffic pattern shifts. Findings so far: - Correlated tail latency spikes to nodes that lost both prefetch and had recent model cold-starts (see trace cluster IDs). - No evidence of model binary change or kernel regression; CPU/GPU utilization increases modestly. - Rolling disable in small cohort shows transient spikes lasting ~10-20 minutes per pool. Temporary mitigations applied: enabled traffic-splitting to keep 10% traffic on optimized variant, throttled background batch jobs, increased per-worker concurrency limit to reduce queueing. Next hypotheses to validate: test controlled drain + staggered worker recycle to allow KV warmup without snapshot restore.

Additional notes:
Planned backstop strategy (not yet executed): 1) Pre-create traffic-split routes and guard rails in Console for tenant pools; 2) Run a Canary sequence: start at 5% optimized-disabled, monitor 95p/99p latency, error-rate, kv-cache-hit. Hold for 30 minutes at each step. 3) If 95p delta > 150ms or errors > 0.5%, immediately revert traffic-split to 100% optimized variant; 4) Use staggered worker drain (5min between hosts) for warmup instead of snapshot restore. Follow-ups: - Create a one-click Console backstop button for future sunsetting (task created for product team). - Add automated hold points into the Console Canary workflow (linked feature request: ENG-FT-2301). - Draft post-window telemetry checklist for Lumina Health. Owners: Diego (SRE) and Maya (Support). Expected rollback time SLA: <= 15 minutes to fully re-route traffic back to optimized variant.
1) Finalize and share customer-facing checklist and prepared scripts (by 2026-03-15). 2) Product to estimate Console automation (ENG-FT-2301) and return to customer with ETA. 3) Schedule dry-run with Lumina in staging on 2026-03-16. 4) Execute production sunsetting during Lumina's window (2026-03-18) with SRE on-call watching metrics. Assigned: Diego Alvarez (action owner), Maya Patel (customer coordination).
payload.summary: Guidance for safe backstop and feature sunsetting of optimizer flags without snapshot restore

payload.description:
Issue summary: Customers (BrightDocs) observed repeated short bursts of 5xx responses (502/503) lasting 10-30s, recurring ~3-4 times per hour. Impact: user-facing API calls failed or retried, latency spiked and client-side retries amplified the error bursts. Root pattern appears to correlate with rapid prefetch cancellation events followed by connection teardown on the API gateway which triggers serving-runtime GPU context swaps and worker eviction.

Impact: A subset of requests during bursts returned 502/503, some long-lived streaming sessions dropped. Customer reported interrupted batch-processing jobs and increased error budgets.

Environment: Production cluster in us-east servicing BrightDocs dedicated tenant on reserved pool.

1) Rapidly send a mixed workload to the tenant: 60 short chat requests/sec + 8 concurrent long streaming sessions.
2) Trigger a client-side prefetch cancellation pattern by issuing prefetch requests then immediate cancels (simulate BrightDocs client behavior).
3) Observe gateway connection teardown events and increased keepalive churn.
4) Watch for runtime worker eviction logs and GPU context swap around the same timestamps.

Relevant logs snippets aggregated from 2026-03-12T09:12:14Z - 2026-03-12T09:15:00Z:
- apigw: conn-teardown: fd=3187 rc=0 reason=client-cancel (rapid)
- apigw: keepalive-pool: exhaustion=0.86 threshold=0.8 stall=250ms
- runtime: worker-evict: id=87 reason=gpu-context-swap active_requests=3
- runtime: watchdog: OOM-guard triggered kernel-swap for model=redwood-7b-v2 seq=1024
- runtime: reply: 502 upstream-unavailable (evicted-worker)
- metrics: request_5xx_rate{tenant="brightdocs"} spike from 0.001 -> 0.12
- perf: nvml GPU memory fragmentation increased by ~12% at the same times

Initial hypothesis: client prefetch cancellations lead to connection churn which stresses the keepalive connection pool at the API gateway. High churn triggers frequent short-lived connections and forces the serving-runtime to reallocate GPU contexts. During context reallocation there are transient resource constraints leading to worker eviction and 502/503 responses.

What we checked:
- Correlated apigw conn-teardown timestamps with runtime worker-evict logs (matching timestamps within 100-300ms).
- Verified tenant was on a non-prewarmed GPU pool; requests with large seq lengths increased memory pressure.
- Confirmed client pattern from BrightDocs logs: heavy prefetch+cancel behavior during their batch indexing job.
- Reproduced a smaller-scale version in staging by simulating the cancel pattern; observed elevated keepalive reuse failures and occasional evictions.

Hypotheses refined: two interacting factors required to trigger bursts: (1) connection churn causing apigw keepalive pressure and (2) memory/fragmentation hotspots in runtime during kernel swap or model loading that can't absorb a sudden rebind of contexts.

Short-term mitigation (applied 2026-03-12 11:00 UTC):
- Increased API gateway keepalive pool soft-limit for this tenant by 30% to reduce teardown amplification.
- Added temporary rate-limit throttle on prefetch endpoints for BrightDocs (soft block for the next 48h).
- Applied runtime config change: delay kernel-swap guard to wait for request quiescence (reduces eviction hysteresis).

Long-term action items (backlog / engineering):
- Runtime: implement graceful kernel swap path that drains active KV cache and queues new requests instead of evicting workers. (PR drafted: https://github.com/redwood/rev/pull/1893)
- Gateway: expose tenant-level keepalive tuning knobs and adaptive backpressure when churn detected.
- Product: advise customers with heavy prefetch behavior to use staggered prefetch windows or dedicated prewarmed pool.
- Postmortem to be drafted and linked to confluence page above.

Current status: mitigations removed burst pattern in prod during 24h monitoring window. Engineering change PR in review.

2026-03-12 09:45 - BrightDocs support: 'We're seeing ~15% of calls return 5xx during our indexing stage. It began at ~09:12 and recurred every ~20 minutes.'

Additional notes:
2026-03-12 10:42 - SRE (Darren Mills): 'Confirmed correlation between conn-teardown and runtime-evict logs. Reproduced in staging with prefetch-cancel script. Increasing keepalive soft-limit as a stopgap.'
2026-03-12 11:12 - Ops: 'Applied keepalive soft-limit increase and temporary prefetch throttle for tenant. Monitoring metrics show 5xx rate decreased to baseline.'
2026-03-13 14:30 - Runtime eng: 'Submitted PR for guarded kernel-swap. Tests added for simulated churn. Requesting review from infra team.'
payload.summary: Rapid 5xx bursts tied to prefetch cancellation + connection teardown leading to runtime evictions

payload.description:
Issue summary: Customer sees intermittent but persistent 429s for low-latency chat sessions while large background embedding imports run concurrently. They are on a dedicated pool and want recommended configuration to avoid disrupting interactive sessions and to support graceful degradation for bulk workers. Impact: user-facing chat latency spikes and aborted responses; bulk jobs repeatedly throttle and backfill slowly. Request: guidance on splitting burst pools, refill intervals, priority lanes, and a recommended graceful-degradation strategy (fallback routing, soft-rejects) to keep chat alive during large ingestion windows.
1) In prod-us-west, start a background embedding import (multipart) at 300 concurrent upload streams using open-embed-large model from SynapticMaps' ingesters.
2) Launch 50 parallel low-latency chat clients that maintain persistent SSE/websocket streams using gpt-4o-mini with prompt length ~120 tokens and average reply 40 tokens.
3) Observe 429 response spikes on chat sessions within 5-15 minutes after ingest starts; embedding uploads see repeated 429s and long backoff cycles.
4) Reproduce consistently by toggling the ingest concurrency between 100 and 400 and observing correlation with chat 429 rates.
sample 429 response headers: x-rate-limit-policy: tenant-burst; x-refill-window-ms: 60000; x-tenant-remaining: 0; x-tenant-reason: burst-credit-exhausted
trace: trace_id=usw-prod-01:7f8e2a9b-cf1e-4b2e-9a2f-1a0b2c3d4e5f; route=chat-priority; host=edge-usw-03
edge-proxy logs show: keepalive probe requests counted against tenant burst bucket from k8s healthchecks at ~1 req/s per node
ingest coordinator logs: multipart upload workers performing preflight checks counted as requests prior to upload chunking; spike correlates with refill window boundary.

Additional notes:
2026-03-10 10:04 - Support (Liam Chen): Acknowledged. Can you share sample request IDs and the ingest orchestration pattern? Also please confirm whether healthchecks/sidecars are enabled on same tenant network.
2026-03-10 11:30 - Customer (SynapticMaps, Ops): Provided traces and said they use an orchestrator that ramps workers quickly for hourly backfills. Healthchecks are enabled; sidecars perform preflight and telemetry pings.
2026-03-11 08:45 - SRE (Rina Morales): Initial hypothesis: burst-credit exhaustion due to un-isolated background workers + counted preflights and health probes. Suggest split burst pools and configure priority lanes for SSE chat to be isolated from bulk ingress. Will test staged config on their dedicated pool.
2026-03-12 14:22 - Support (Liam Chen): Implemented temporary mitigation: decreased ingest concurrency to 120 and enabled 'priority:interactive' header on chat clients. Customer reports fewer chat 429s; bulk jobs slower but proceed. Planning recommended permanent changes below.
Hypothesis #1: Unsplit burst token pool — both chat and embed workers draw from same tenant burst bucket leading to exhaustion when ingest spikes.
Hypothesis #2: Preflight/healthcheck requests counted as full request units causing continuous drain across refill windows.
Observed: x-tenant-remaining often transitions to zero aligned with ingest worker ramp boundaries and refill window boundary (60s).
Temporary proof-of-concept: adding 'priority:interactive' header caused router to weight chat requests to priority lane which had separate small burst reserve; chat 429s decreased by ~80% during POC.
Workaround applied: reduced ingest concurrency and added priority header for interactive services. This is not a long-term fix for customer.
Recommended config changes for dedicated pool (actionable):
- Configure split burst pools: create two tenant burst lanes: 'interactive' (small high-frequency reserve) and 'bulk' (large but low-priority reserve).
- Set refill windows: interactive refill window = 250ms token smoothing for low-latency; bulk refill window = 60s for large imports.
- Exempt internal healthchecks/preflight pings from tenant accounting (or route through internal service account with separate quota).
- Enable soft-degradation policy on interactive route: when 'interactive' lane is near exhaustion, route to a lighter model (gpt-4o-mini -> gpt-4o-small) rather than immediate 429, and fall back to cached prefix responses for repeated prompts.
- Recommend 'priority' request header and server-side enforcement in their client stack; document client SDK snippet to add header for real-time requests.
- Rollout plan: stage changes in a canary dedicated pool, monitor x-tenant-remaining and 429 rate for 48h, then promote.
Follow-ups: Create a product docs task to surface these recommended configs in Console; suggested Confluence/KB page created for customer-specific runbook.
1) Ops: Schedule dedicated-pool canary to test split burst lanes (SRE - Rina Morales) — target 2026-03-15.
2) Support: Provide SDK snippet + priority header guidance to customer (Liam Chen) — done.
3) Product: Open doc task to add Console guidance and presets for 'interactive vs bulk' burst pools — assigned to Product Docs.
4) Follow up ticket: verify long-term metrics after canary and close this ticket once metrics stable.
payload.summary: Advice requested: slice burst pools and implement graceful degradation for mixed realtime-chat + bulk-embed workload

payload.description:
Issue summary: Customer reports intermittent 403 Forbidden responses from Redwood Private endpoints for certain users immediately after SCIM-driven group membership changes. The failures resolve after ~30–90 seconds.

Impact: Affects ~5% of authentication attempts for affected users immediately after admin changes; blocks customer admins from testing role changes and causes automated workflows to fail briefly.

Environment: Private deployment in customer's VPC (prod-us-east). IdP: Okta (SAML), SCIM provisioning enabled from Okta -> Redwood SCIM endpoint. RBAC model uses group->role bindings.

Steps to reproduce:
1) In Okta, add a user to the 'data-scientists' group which maps to 'model-infer' role in Redwood.
2) Wait until SCIM push completes (Okta shows success).
3) Immediately have user call the hosted API via Private endpoint. Observe 403 for first few calls.
4) Repeat: after ~30–90s the same calls succeed without token refresh.

Logs / Observations:
- Support logs show 403s with authz failure cause 'entitlement-not-found' and no 'role' claim in our authz cache within first minute after SCIM event.
- SCIM logs show 200 OK from Okta and successful provisioning events.
- Audit trail in RBAC service shows group change processed, but internal 'entitlement-index' timestamps lag behind SCIM event by 20–70s.
- No errors in SCIM connector; network latency to customer's VPC averages 45ms.

Preliminary hypothesis: SCIM provisioning is processed by the SCIM worker and writes memberships to the RBAC store, but the entitlement indexer (asynchronous) has a processing delay under load which causes authz checks to consult stale index until the indexer catches up. This race leads to transient 403s for newly added entitlements.
2026-02-18 09:12 - Customer (Jay Patel): 'We see users denied immediately after we add them to groups. Waiting a minute always fixes it.'
2026-02-18 10:05 - Support (Ava Chen): 'Thanks — can you confirm whether users refresh tokens or reuse existing sessions when testing? Also, can you provide the Okta SCIM event ids for a failed attempt?'
2026-02-18 10:22 - Customer (Jay Patel): 'We re-used existing sessions. Here's one SCIM event id: 8a7f3b.'
2026-02-19 14:40 - Eng (Diego Morales): 'We observed entitlement-index lag spikes correlated with bursty SCIM writes. Reproduced locally with load test hitting SCIM 200r/s — indexer queued events and processed in batch with delay.'
2026-02-24 11:03 - SRE (Priya Raman): 'Dashboard shows indexer CPU saturation during customer's daily user provisioning window. Queue depth reached 18 for ~3 minutes.'
2026-02-28 16:15 - Support (Ava Chen): 'We will schedule a maintenance window to deploy a hotfix that reduces index batching window. ETA for rollout: 2026-03-02.'
2026-02-19: Added synthetic test simulating Okta SCIM push + immediate auth call; failure reproduced consistently when index queue depth > 0.
2026-02-20: Profiled rbac-service indexer: default batch window 60s or when queue length >25; customer bursts hit queue lengths 10–20 causing window timeouts.
2026-02-22: Correlated indexer lag with GC pauses in Java process on a dedicated box; tuned JVM flags reduced tail latency in staging.
2026-02-25: Confirmed that token caching at auth-proxy prevents token refresh from forcing re-eval — users with stale tokens rely on server-side entitlement index until refresh TTL.
2026-02-27: QA validated hotfix branch reducing batch window to 5s and lowering threshold to flush at length >=5; unit and e2e tests pass.
Hotfix deployed: indexer batch window reduced and flush threshold lowered to reduce propagation lag in private deployments.
Rollout notes: Gradual rollout to customer on 2026-03-02 during low-traffic window. Monitored queue depth and authz 403 rate for 48 hours.
Result: Post-rollout, transient 403 rate dropped from ~5% to <0.1% during provisioning bursts. Customer confirmed resolution on 2026-03-04.
Follow-up actions: Add permanent metrics for entitlement propagation latency, include runbook step to monitor indexer queue depth, and consider back-pressure to SCIM connector if queue persistently grows.

payload.description:
Issue summary:
- On 2025-11-12 09:03 UTC SundialHealth began seeing partial conversation responses: first chunk delivered, subsequent chunks truncated or duplicated across parallel streams. Some sessions produced duplicate follow-ups (same assistant message sent twice) and others showed missing closing tokens causing downstream truncation in customer UI.

Impact:
- Affected ~4% of requests from SundialHealth between 09:03 and 10:24 UTC.
- High business impact: clinical note-generation workflows failed reconciliation checks; SundialHealth reported patient-facing delays and raised an executive escalation.

Environment:
- Production (us-west). Requests routed to Dedicated pool (dedicated-gpu-pool-12). Models: redwood-open-34b-v1 (primary), redwood-open-8b-quantized (fallback).

Steps to reproduce (internal):
1) Replay customer session trace ID sundial:20251112:09:17:34 with streaming=true, chunk_size=4096.
2) Observe first event with tokens stream, then duplicate chunk with identical token ids on second websocket connection.
3) Repeat under high concurrency (~250 rps) to reproduce amplification.

Observed behavior:
- Streaming proxy forwarded the same chunk twice to the client in ~0.8% of total streams and dropped final termination event in ~3.2% of sessions.
- Router logs show rapid rebinds for affinity keys X-Session-ID in a 30s window.

Expected behavior:
- Each session should see a single ordered stream of token chunks; termination event should arrive once per completion.

Attachments/logs:
- Link to request traces and CloudWatch dashboards in comments and confluence page.

Additional notes:
2025-11-12 09:45 — SRE (Jordan Patel): Initial hypothesis: streaming-proxy/broker replay loop when backend reconnection occurs during KV cache warmup. Spun up additional traces and retention of per-session socket state.
2025-11-12 10:05 — Eng (Priya Nair): Observed router rebind spikes tied to leader election events in serving-runtime; coincident with quantized fallback activation. Added feature-flagged patch to disable eager reconnection on affinity mismatch and started canary.
2025-11-12 10:28 — Support (Mei Alvarez): Notified customer of mitigation attempt: temporarily pinned traffic to primary model and disabled quantized fallback for SundialHealth. Customer confirmed reduced duplicates but reported two remaining truncated sessions.
2025-11-12 11:10 — Eng (Priya Nair): Deployed coordinated rollback of recent streaming-proxy change (PR 4682) that altered session rebind semantics; monitoring shows duplicates dropped from ~0.8% -> 0.02% and truncations resolved.
2025-11-12 13:00 — CX (Rohan Gupta): Sent incident status update to SundialHealth execs; offered 30% bill credit for impacted hour window and arranged a technical deep-dive on Nov 14.
2025-11-18 09:12 — SundialHealth (Elena Morales): Confirmed customer satisfied with mitigation and requested timeline for permanent fix and improved preflight checks on canary rollouts.
Timeline and findings:
- 09:03 UTC: error rate spike in streaming-proxy logs for pool dedicated-gpu-pool-12.
- 09:04-09:30 UTC: multiple leader-election events in serving-runtime coincident with autoscaler rebinds; router initiated reconnection logic that re-emitted pending chunk messages when backend ack state was missing.
- 09:15 UTC: quantized fallback was triggered due to a scheduled capacity shift; fallback handler had slightly different session-ack semantics and did not clear inflight chunk marker, enabling duplicate emission on reconnection.
- Traces: repeated token block IDs (trace evidence) and websocket closure_without_termination events.
- Reproducible locally by forcing router reconnection during inflight streaming and toggling fallback.
Hypotheses validated:
1) Combination of leader-election-induced reconnection + mismatch in fallback session-ack semantics produced duplicate chunk replay and occasional missing terminal event.
2) Canary for streaming-proxy change (PR 4682) increased sensitivity to rebind events and surfaced long-tail condition.
Immediate actions performed:
- Rolled back streaming-proxy change (PR 4682) cluster-wide at 10:05 UTC.
- Temporarily disabled model-fallback for SundialHealth and pinned requests to primary model until fix validated.
- Added rate-limit backoff on router reconnection path to avoid immediate replay of inflight chunks.
- Issued customer communication and credit proposal.
Deployment/fix status:
- Hotfix deployed 2025-11-13: harmonized session-ack semantics between primary and fallback handlers and added an idempotency guard for chunk emission.
- Regression tests added to CI for simulated reconnection flows.
- Monitoring alerts tightened to detect duplicate chunk IDs and missing termination events.
A timing/regression issue caused by the intersection of a streaming-proxy change (PR 4682) that altered reconnection semantics and differing session-ack handling between primary and quantized fallback model handlers. Leader election/autoscaler rebind events triggered immediate reconnections which allowed inflight chunks to be emitted twice and, in some cases, prevented terminal events from being delivered.
1) Engineering: complete full patch rollout to all pools and run a 72-hour observation window (owner: Priya Nair).
2) QA: extend CI reconnection scenario coverage and add fuzzing for websocket disconnect/rewind (owner: QA team).
3) Product/Support: schedule a technical postmortem with SundialHealth on 2025-11-14 and finalize credit in billing system (owner: Rohan Gupta).
4) Ops: add synthetic streaming checks in us-west to detect duplicate chunk ID rate > 0.05% (owner: Jordan Patel).
5) Release: document change-control checklist for streaming-proxy rollouts to require canary traffic > 24h for reconnection-sensitive patches.
- Duration: ~1h20m (09:03 - 10:24 UTC) with residual degraded behavior until rollback at 10:05 but validation continued until 11:30.
- Percent of customer requests affected: ~4% peak, total impacted sessions ~1.9k.

Issue summary: During a scheduled cross-region tenant migration for Vectra Health (dedicated pool), multiple ephemeral API keys were created by the customer's migration utility. The rate-limiter observed duplicate registrations for logically identical ephemeral sessions which caused the tenant's token-account to be over-counted, resulting in intermittent 429 throttles for short-lived streams and small embedding batches.

Impact: Several of Vectra's ingestion workers experienced short (1–3 minute) bursts of 429 responses during the migration window on 2026-03-10, causing queue backpressure and retries. No data loss observed; impact was degraded ingest throughput and elevated client error rates (5–7% of requests during spikes).

Environment: prod-us-east (dedicated pool), edge proxies in us-east-1 and failover path to us-west-2. Affected models include redwood/gpt-large-v1 for streaming and redwood/embedding-encoder-v2 for embedding batches.

Observed behavior: Edge token accounting and central quota-engine counters became briefly inconsistent after a Redis replica promotion during the migration. The migration tool (tenant-migrator v2) opened ephemeral sessions with fresh keys while the edge cache had stale token-bucket state; when the central quota reconciler ran it double-counted the new keys as additional concurrent usage, pushing the tenant over the short-term concurrency window and emitting 429s.

Why this is different from a normal quota spike: This is not a pure traffic surge — the same number of logical sessions existed, but registration of duplicates across edge and control-plane caches caused the accounting delta. It manifested as short bursts tied to the migration steps (key issuance + cache invalidate).
Initial hypothesis: traffic surge from customer workers — disproved: client-side logs show steady ingest rate, bursts align with migration steps.
Found correlation between Redis replica promotion (2026-03-10T11:02:58Z) and spike in duplicate ephemeral key registrations in edge cache.
Edge cache TTL reset allowed new key registration to skip dedupe path; central reconciler counted both old and new registrations during its 60s reconciliation window.
Temporary mitigation: increased reconciliation dedupe window and added a short-lived suppressor (30s) to ignore immediate duplicate registrations from the same client IP during migrations.
Long-term fix: patch quota-engine to detect ephemeral key lineage and perform idempotent registration (PR linked). Scheduled follow-up: infra PR to add stronger idempotency headers from tenant-migrator v2.
Observed after mitigation: 429 spikes reduced to <0.2% for a subsequent migration test run.
Related telemetry: token-bucket-compare dashboard (confluence link attached) shows the pre/post delta and time alignment with Redis failover events.
Asha Patel (Support) 2026-03-10T11:15:00Z: Contacted Vectra engineer and requested exact migration steps + version of tenant-migrator. Asked for client-side worker logs and approximate concurrency.
Lina Chen (Vectra) 2026-03-10T11:28:34Z: Confirmed we ran tenant-migrator v2 and promoted a replica right before starting an ingestion wave. Attaching worker logs (uploaded to support bundle).
Diego Morales (SRE) 2026-03-10T12:02:10Z: Deployed temporary suppressor to quota-engine to fold immediate duplicate registrations. Also increased reconciliation safety window from 60s -> 90s. Monitoring impact.
Marco Ruiz (Backend Eng) 2026-03-11T09:40:00Z: Opened infra PR to add idempotency token for ephemeral key registrations. Linked PR: github.com/redwood-inference/infra/pull/4021
Asha Patel (Support) 2026-03-12T08:05:00Z: Customer verified ingestion throughput recovered during a staged migration. Requested follow-up RFC for migration best-practices to reduce edge/control-plane race.
Diego Morales (SRE) 2026-03-12T14:12:00Z: Moving ticket to In Progress; permanent fix scheduled for next deploy window (2026-03-19).
Mitigation applied: reconciliation dedupe window increased and a short suppressor was added to reduce immediate duplicate registration counts. Permanent fix: quota-engine idempotency patch (PR 4021) to be rolled out in next deploy. Follow-up: publish migration best-practices doc and add a small delay/retry in tenant-migrator to avoid simultaneous key issuance during Redis failover.
1) Merge and deploy PR 4021 for idempotent ephemeral key registration
2) Add a telemetry alert that fires when edge/central token count delta > 20% for >30s
3) Publish a short runbook for customers performing tenant migrations recommending staggered key issuance and a 45s quiesce window during Redis promotions
4) Coordinate with Vectra to validate the fix during their next scheduled migration

Issue summary: High p99 latency and intermittent 429s observed on Flowly AI's dedicated pool starting 2026-03-10 09:12 UTC. Symptoms correspond with gradual GPU allocation failures and autoscaler failing to add capacity fast enough.

Observed impact: Customer reports increased request timeouts and error spikes for their production chat endpoint. Multiple model routes degraded concurrently in us-west-2.

Initial detection: Alerting (p99 latency > 900ms and allocation-failures > 5/min) triggered on our production observability pipeline at 2026-03-10 09:18 UTC.
Flowly AI (dedicated) experienced ~30% increase in p95/p99 latency and transient 429s across two model routes. Throughput dropped by ~25% during hot windows. Business impact: customer-reported degraded UX and elevated error rates for paying customers.
1) Route traffic to the affected dedicated pool in us-west-2. 2) Start synthetic steady small-stream workload that keeps many long-lived keepalives open (simulates chatlet fusion). 3) Run background sidecar process on a tenant VM that emits high-frequency metrics to our sidecar endpoint (~10k metrics/min). 4) Observe allocator logs and autoscaler decisions over 10-20 minutes. Expected: autoscaler should add capacity and allocations succeed; Observed: allocator marks GPUs as temporarily busy and autoscaler remains conservative.
[2026-03-10T09:16:12Z] allocator: attach_request(id=abc123) -> timeout after 1.5s
[2026-03-10T09:16:13Z] serving-runtime: nvlink_io_wait=0.28s, dma_queue=high, gpu_attach_retries=3
[2026-03-10T09:17:02Z] autoscaler: candidate_addition=0 (policy: conservative), pending_queue=14
[2026-03-10T09:17:05Z] allocator: observed_bank_busy(gpu=GPU-75, bank=2) repeated=7
[2026-03-10T09:18:03Z] sidecar-metrics: recv_metrics(rate=10200/min) from tenant=flowly-sidecar-3
[2026-03-10T09:18:10Z] error: 429 route=flowly-chat model=gpt-3o-redwood-v1

Initial hypothesis: a tenant sidecar emitting a very high cardinality metrics stream is saturating the allocator's NVLink / PCIe servicing path and causing per-GPU bank busy signals. This produces intermittent attach failures which the autoscaler interprets as transient and does not scale quickly.

What we checked: allocator attach/fail counters, NVLink PCIe backlog metrics, kernel logs on affected hosts, autoscaler decision logs, and Flowly's sidecar process (customer-provided) traffic. Cross-referenced with host-level iostat and nvidia-smi dmon.

Findings:
- The allocator showed repeated bank_busy signals localized to a subset of GPUs on three nodes.
- Network/IO saturation coincides with sidecar metric bursts (approx 10k/min) from Flowly's VM.
- Autoscaler has a smoothing window (cooldown 90s) and a conservative threshold for attachments failing (requires sustained failure rate) which delayed capacity additions.
- No driver crashes or CUDA OOM; NVLink latency elevated and DMA queues backed up during burst windows.

- Throttled Flowly sidecar metric ingestion by applying per-tenant ingress rate limit at the sidecar proxy (temporary).
- Manually triggered autoscaler to add two GPU slots to the dedicated pool in us-west-2 (immediate relief).
- Marked three affected nodes for deeper hardware IO analysis and temporarily drained low-priority pods.
- Engaged infra team to evaluate allocator NVLink handling and to add finer-grained bank_busy telemetry.

Applied per-tenant metrics ingestion caps (rate-limited sidecar requests). Customer reverted their sidecar config to emit aggregated metrics (1k/min) which reduced NVLink backlog and restored normal attach rates. Manual scale-up restored throughput while long-term fix is planned.
PENDING - engineering is implementing two fixes: 1) allocator change to de-prioritize sidecar metric IO on GPU hosts during attach windows; 2) autoscaler tuning to consider attach failure patterns and allow fast-path scale-up for noisy-tenant signatures. Patch PR opened and under review (runtime PR #4512). After patch merge and controlled rollout, we will remove temporary ingress caps and validate for 48 hours.

Follow-ups: runbook update to include noisy-sidecar detection, and discuss quota enforcement for metric streams from tenants.

2026-03-10 09:40 — SRE (Elena Garcia): Observed bank_busy on GPU-72/73/75. Suspect high sidecar IO. Temporarily rate-limiting metrics ingestion for Flowly. Requesting customer to reduce metric cardinality.
2026-03-10 10:05 — Customer (Flowly AI - Rajiv Menon): Confirmed sidecar was recently upgraded to verbose telemetry. Rolling back to aggregated metrics now. Appreciated manual scale-up.
2026-03-10 11:12 — Infra (Marcus Li): Spun up diagnostic captures on nodes gpu-node-14/15/16. No NVidia driver anomalies; DMA queue lengths spike correlated with sidecar bursts.

Additional notes:

2026-03-12 12:00 — SRE (Elena Garcia): Marking ticket In Progress until allocator PR merges and autopilot tuning deployed.

Issue summary: Starting 2026-03-10 14:05 UTC GridForms reported sustained p99/p50 latency increases and intermittent attach failures for requests routed to their dedicated pool. Impact: customer requests see 10-30s attach delays and ~6% 5xx rate for short-lived streams; overall throughput for the reserved pool dropped ~28% during the window. Environment: dedicated pool (reserve-id: gforms-prod-west), prod, us-west-2, model redwood-3b-v2. Observed behavior: periodic bursts of ephemeral healthcheck connections from tenant sidecars (aligned with heartbeat jitter) appear to throttle allocator attach operations, triggering parallel attach retries and a thundering attach pattern that starves batchers and stalls prefetch. Expected behavior: healthchecks should be rate-limited and not interfere with attach/slot allocation; allocator should queue and throttle without cascading client-side retries.
Customer-facing latency regression: p50 increased from ~120ms to 1.1s, p99 spiked to 11s. Throughput dropped by ~28% for the dedicated pool during peak of the event. Several production tenants on the same physical cluster experienced head-of-line effects until autoscaler rebalanced. Business impact: GridForms reports user-facing timeouts and automated failover triggers in their app; revenue-affecting incidents if not resolved.
1) Target the customer's dedicated endpoint with many short-lived streams (1-5s inference) from multiple client hosts.
2) Introduce jittered healthcheck probes from a sidecar process every 5-15s across hosts (simulate ephemeral flapping).
3) Observe allocator attach latencies, prefetch queue depth, and batcher slot utilization in the reserved pool dashboard.
4) Compare with baseline where healthchecks are disabled or strictly rate-limited.
Initial triage (Ayesha): correlated increased attach latency with a rise in short TCP connections from customer's sidecars around 14:00 UTC; snapshotter IO and prefetch metrics remained nominal.
SRE (Liam): allocator logs show attach request queue growth and attach-retry storms (attach attempts per slot > 12/min) during the window. Kernel-level traces show rapid connect/close cycles causing NVMe io random writes, but not full saturation.
Hypothesis: jittered healthcheck probes from the customer's sidecar are creating ephemeral TCP sessions that coincide with attach scheduling. Client-side retry/backoff absent -> simultaneous attach attempts cause the allocator to escalate allocation, which interacts poorly with batcher windowing and triggers slot starvation.
Telemetry: increased small-stream fanout metric + elevated attach_retries_count. Prefetch lease churn increased 3x. Autoscaler attempted to add nodes but cool-down settings delayed effective capacity expansion, prolonging impact.
Cross-reference: similar symptom pattern to SUP-314159 but root cause there was background snapshotter noise; here the dominant signal is ephemeral healthcheck flapping from tenant sidecars.
2026-03-10 15:02 - Support (Ayesha): Reached out to GridForms to confirm any recent sidecar or agent upgrades. Asked for their sidecar config and samples of healthcheck timing.
2026-03-10 15:37 - GridForms (customer): Confirmed a rollout of a new monitoring agent at 13:50 UTC which added fast liveness checks; provided sidecar logs showing probes every 7-12s from ~30 hosts.
2026-03-10 16:10 - SRE (Liam): Deployed temporary rate-limit on attach requests at the allocator edge for the affected pool to dampen thundering. Early telemetry shows attach retries drop by ~65% and p99 latency receding.
2026-03-11 09:20 - Support (Ayesha): Advised GridForms to patch sidecar to exponential backoff on probe retries and to enable randomized healthcheck offsets; provided a recommended delta config.
2026-03-12 11:05 - SRE (Liam): Working on a safer allocator backpressure strategy and a circuit-breaker for ephemeral-connection storms; opened PR to add attach-rate limiter and jitter-aware scheduling.
Workaround applied: edge-level attach rate limiting for the affected dedicated pool reduced attach storms and restored throughput to ~92% of baseline within 40 minutes of deployment.
Customer mitigation: GridForms rolled back the monitoring agent and patched their sidecar to add randomized probe offsets and a 2-8s exponential backoff; confirmed on 2026-03-11 that their retries stopped correlating with attach spikes.
Long-term actions: (1) Implement allocator attach-rate limiter and jitter-aware scheduling (PR referenced). (2) Update dedicated-pool runbook with guidance for tenant-side healthchecks and recommended rate limits. (3) Add autoscaler cooldown tuning for rapid short-lived fanouts to reduce delayed capacity response.

payload.description:
Issue summary: Customer enabled a bundled inference tuning profile (async batching enabled, KV prefix prefetch enabled, quantization profile q4_0) during a feature rollout. Within ~2 hours they started seeing transient but repeatable issues: elevated 95p and 99p tail latency, a small but growing rate of 5xx streaming disconnects, and a set of correctness regressions (higher hallucination/repetition on a standard prompt set).

Impact: Affects ~5 nodes in BrightHealth's dedicated pool. Reported as production impact for several user-facing features (conversational summarization). Error rate ~3% (baseline ~0.2%), 95p latency increased from ~220ms to ~800ms for the affected tenant traffic. Customer is requesting a safe, low-risk off-ramp and verification checklist to restore baseline behavior while preserving telemetry for root cause analysis.

Environment details: Dedicated pool: dhp-nyc-2, tenant_id: th-bha-91, model pinned: rw-infer-13b-q4_0 (rolled from rw-infer-13b-q8_0), rollout method: staged-split 80/20 then 100%. Observed during peak US-East window.

Logs & telemetry references: See dashboard humdinger: https://grafana.internal.redwood/boards/d/tenant-th-bha-91/optimizer-health; traces: trace ids 9a3f7c2a..9a3f8b1c (sample streaming trace), slack thread #support-brighthealth (link: slack://channel/support-brighthealth/PLATFORM-4581), and recent commit for the tuning package: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/commit/8fb2c3e (opt-pack: add q4_0 profile).
1) Tenant config used: apply tuning profile 'aggressive-infer-pack' (async_batching=true, kv_prefetch=true, quant_profile=q4_0) via PATCH /v1/tenants/th-bha-91/config
2) Send representative production prompt set (see attached sample_prompts.json) at target QPS (production ramp to 20 rps / worker)
3) Observe 95p/99p latency in tracing and 5xx streaming disconnects in the API logs
4) Run the monthly eval prompt set for accuracy regression detection and compare token-level perplexity/delta
Initial hypothesis: q4_0 quantization combined with aggressive async batching changes internal numeric stability causing token-level drift for some prompts (observed in eval diffs).
Observed increased scheduler queue depth on dedicated nodes correlating with 95p spikes — suggests batching interactions with kv-prefetch eviction/thrashing.
KV-prefix hits dropped by ~40% for affected tenant after enabling kv_prefetch (possible mismatch in cache key computation after quantization change).
No memory OOMs on the nodes; CPU (worker threads) and NVLink metrics show elevated utilization coincident with latency spikes.
Reproduced a reduced repro in staging by enabling the same profile and running the long-form summarization prompts; staging showed similar hallucination deltas but at lower magnitude (staging smaller workers).
Step 0 (safety snapshot): Create a tenant config snapshot: POST /v1/tenants/th-bha-91/config/snapshot -> snapshot_id=ss-20260312-01 (store snapshot id in ticket).
Step 1 (non-disruptive toggle): Disable KV prefix prefetch for tenant via PATCH /v1/tenants/th-bha-91/config { "kv_prefetch": false } and monitor 30 minutes for 95p latency and prefix hit-rate recovery.
Step 2 (conservative batching): If Step 1 insufficient, change async_batching policy to 'conservative' (reduce max_batch_size and batch_wait_ms) via PATCH and split 90/10 live traffic to the conservative config for 10 minutes.
Step 3 (quantization rollback): If latency or correctness not restored, revert quant profile to the last known-good (q8_0) by PATCH /v1/tenants/th-bha-91/config { "quant_profile": "q8_0" }. This is expected to be more impactful but restores numeric behavior.
Step 4 (worker drain/restart): If 5xxs persist after config rollbacks, perform a rolling restart of the affected serving nodes in the dedicated pool (coordinate with SRE; drain connections, restart agent).
Step 5 (traffic gating): If still degraded, gate tenant to lower concurrency (traffic-split to bypass dedicated pool to hosted) as emergency fallback and engage Eng for a post-mortem.
Owners: Support (Marco Diaz) to coordinate Steps 0-2; SRE (Lydia Chen) to execute Step 4; Eng (Ravi Kapoor) to own rollback to q8_0 if needed and validate model artifacts.
Note: All changes should be performed with monitoring alerts open (95p latency, 5xx rate, prefix-hit-rate, eval-accuracy). Keep snapshots and logs for post-incident analysis.
Run the monthly eval prompt set (eval-v1) before and after each step and record token-level similarity and hallucination metrics.
Confirm 95p latency returns to baseline within 30% of pre-change values for two consecutive 15-minute windows.
Confirm 5xx streaming error rate returns below 0.5% and no new unique error classes are introduced.
Validate prefix-hit-rate and scheduler queue depth metrics improved compared to the peak window.
Customer acceptance: Customer PKG engineer confirms conversational quality restored on a small representative subset (5 golden prompts).
Work in progress: Steps 0-1 applied. KV prefetch disabled at 2026-03-13T16:42Z; initial 30-minute monitor shows 95p latency dropped ~35% but token-level correctness regressions persist for a small subset. Proceeding to Step 2 (conservative batching) with 10% shadow traffic now.

payload.description:
After the customer's IdP changed SAML NameQualifier values during a maintenance rollout, CloudLedger's service account assertions no longer map to the expected tenant identity in our private deployment, resulting in consistent 403s for admin/service operations.
Issue summary:
Customer reports 403 responses for admin API calls and service account flows shortly after their IdP (on-prem ADFS + cloud proxy) pushed a configuration change that normalizes NameID/NameQualifier values. Impact:
- Admin console access is blocked for service workflows (automated backups, key rotations).
- Several scheduled jobs fail and trigger downstream errors in the customer's product.
Environment:
- Private deployment (VPC) with tenant-scoped RBAC and ingress path rewrite enabled.
- Requests flow through customer-managed IdP proxy -> Edge ingress -> private control plane.
Expected behavior:
- SAML assertions from the IdP map to tenant-scoped service-account identities and are accepted.
Actual behavior:
- SAML assertion subject contains NameID and a NameQualifier that does not match the tenant prefix in our tenant resolution logic; our auth layer rejects the assertion as unmapped, returning 403.
Notes: this started immediately after the IdP maintenance window and affects all service accounts that rely on SAML subject mapping.

1) Customer triggers a service account token exchange via SAML assertion (SAML response generated by IdP with new NameQualifier).
2) Request traverses customer IdP proxy -> edge ingress; ingress rewrites path and forwards assertion to private control plane auth endpoint.
3) Auth layer attempts tenant resolution by concatenating tenant prefix + NameQualifier -> fails mapping lookup -> returns 403.
4) Reverting IdP to previous NameQualifier restores normal mapping and clears 403s (reported by customer).
Excerpt from private control plane auth logs (sanitized):
[2026-03-11T09:12:04Z] auth.evaluated_assertion tenant_lookup="tenant-prefix:acme-corp" expected_namequal="https://idp.acme.com/tn1" actual_namequal="https://idp.acme.com/tn1-v2" result=NOT_FOUND status=403 request_id=req_0a7f

<Subject>
  <NameID NameQualifier="https://idp.acme.com/tn1-v2">service-account-automation@acme</NameID>
</Subject>
03/11 10:00 - Support triage: reproduced 403 in staging by rewriting NameQualifier on test SAML response; tenant resolution routine does strict equality match (prefix + NameQualifier) and fails.
03/11 13:35 - Confirmed customer IdP maintenance changed NameQualifier semantics; they applied a namespacing update to multi-tenant proxy (adds -v2 suffix for proxy routing).
03/12 08:20 - Ingress team validated that path rewrite is not stripping NameQualifier but does perform header normalization; nothing dropped in transit.
03/12 14:50 - Hypothesis: tenant resolution should tolerate NameQualifier suffix changes (semantic namespace variations) or consult IdP metadata alias list.

Additional notes:
Customer (CloudLedger): Confirmed change history: added namespacing to NameQualifier to support routed IdP proxies. They can rollback but prefer a platform-side tolerant mapping to avoid future disruptions.
SRE (Ingress): Verified request body unchanged, base64 SAML response reaches auth endpoint. No TLS or proxy errors observed.
Tenant resolver currently performs strict concatenation of tenant prefix and NameQualifier. IdP introduced a variant NameQualifier (suffix -v2) for proxy routing. Resolver should consult IdP metadata aliases or perform normalized prefix match when mapping service-account NameID to tenant; otherwise legitimate assertions are rejected.
1) Ask customer to rollback NameQualifier change in IdP while we prepare patch (fastest immediate mitigation).
2) Temporary allowlist: add explicit mapping for NameQualifier variants in tenant metadata (requires customer-provided list).
3) Implement tolerant matching in tenant resolver (see long-term fix).
Workaround applied: customer rolled back NameQualifier change during support window which restored service workflows (confirmed 2026-03-12 02:17 UTC). Auth engineering implemented a short-lived configuration option to map the new NameQualifier variant to the existing tenant mapping (deployed to private customer control plane 2026-03-13).
Long-term: auth team will implement alias-aware tenant resolution (RFC created, PR link below) that reads IdP metadata aliases and supports controlled suffix normalization. Follow-up action: schedule patch for private deployments and add automated test coverage for NameQualifier variants.

payload.description:
Customer observed repeated short streaming disconnects around 03:24-03:46 UTC that produced partial duplicate completions and a token accounting mismatch which inflated billed token counts. Major incident (P0) declared; mitigations applied and follow-up plan documented.
Issue summary: On 2026-03-10 between ~03:24-03:46 UTC Granary Finance observed multiple user sessions where streaming responses were truncated then resumed producing duplicate partial completions. Downstream client reassembly created repeated token sequences and resulted in an apparent increase in billed tokens and unexpected repeated completions.

Impact: Multiple production customers under the Granary account reported increased token usage (up to 2.7x for some sessions) and duplicate outputs for conversational flows. Business impact: degraded user experience for core banking assistant flows and an invoice discrepancy flagged by the customer.

Environment: Hosted Redwood API (prod), region us-east-1, customer using enterprise workspace with model pin rwd-chat-3b and fallback redwood-quant-v1. Traffic passed through streaming-proxy pool sp-us-east-2 which had a recent kernel selection rollout.

Steps to reproduce (observed pattern):
1) Start long-form chat session (prompt length ~600 tokens) over streaming endpoint.
2) At ~20-40s into generation, connection sees repeated small TCP retransmit spikes (network-level); streaming-proxy returns chunked frames with overlapping offsets.
3) Client replays or resumes and receives an overlapping chunk which the client app re-concatenates into the transcript, creating duplicated token subsequences.
4) Billing pipeline consumes chunk delimiter events and double-counts resumed token ranges when chunk offsets are non-monotonic.

Observed behavior: duplicate partial completions, non-monotonic streaming chunk offsets in proxy logs, and billing meter reports showing >100% token counts for affected sessions.

Expected behavior: streaming frames emitted with strictly increasing offsets; resumed frames should indicate resume tokens that prevent re-counting; billing pipeline should deduplicate resumed ranges.

Logs / evidence:
- Streaming-proxy logs (sp-us-east-2) show interleaved chunk IDs and offset regressions: sp-log-2026-03-10-03-26.gz (attached to ticket).
- Router trace: trace-id 0be7f330-us-east-03: shows fallback to quantized variant at 03:25:12 which coincided with increased prefix cache miss.
- Billing meter dump: billing-sample-granary-2026-03-10.csv shows token delta mismatch correlated to trace-ids.

Timeline (abridged):
- 03:22 UTC: first noisy-neighbor autoscale event in GPU pool gp-09 triggers brief kernel re-selection path.
- 03:24 UTC: customer reports first truncated stream via #support-escalations Slack.
- 03:26 UTC: SRE opens incident INC-2026-0310-71 and pages on-call.
- 03:30 UTC: mitigation: route Granary traffic to standby streaming-proxy pool sp-us-east-3; immediate reduction in truncations observed.
- 03:46 UTC: customer confirmed major reduction in duplicate outputs.
- 03:50 UTC: billing team started sample reconciliation; initial anomaly confirmed.

Mitigation applied: immediate routing to healthy streaming-proxy pool and temporary pinning of model variant to rwd-chat-3b (avoid fallback path). Short-term billing credit agreed and applied to affected invoice.

Root cause (summary): a combination of two factors: (1) an aggressive kernel-selection rollout introduced a short-lived code path in the streaming-proxy that emitted non-monotonic chunk offsets when an upstream runtime raced with the proxy's resume logic; (2) the billing ingestion service did not robustly deduplicate resumed token ranges when offsets decreased. The combination produced duplicated transcript segments and double-counted tokens.

Resolution/rollback: hotfix merged to streaming-proxy to enforce monotonic offsets and add a resume-marker header (PR github.com/redwood-inference/streaming-proxy/pull/233). Billing ingestion patched to deduplicate by (trace-id, client-session, offset-range) and deployed to prod billing pipeline (PR github.com/redwood-inference/billing/pull/704). Post-deploy validation run 2026-03-12 passed with no further duplicate token events in sampled traffic.

Customer communication and outcome: Support and CS coordinated with Granary Finance (contacts: Lila Mercer, Head of Platform) — provided a timeline, an explanation of root cause, and a one-off invoice credit for the impacted billing period. Granary accepted the remediation and requested follow-up on monitoring and SLA guardrails.

Post-incident follow-up actions (work items):
- (A1) Add a streaming-chunk-monotonicity alert to prod observability (owner: Owen Park, due 2026-03-20).
- (A2) Add deduplication unit tests to billing ingestion and create a synthetic replay harness (owner: Samira Chen, due 2026-03-18).
- (A3) Add canary gating for kernel-selection rollouts that touch streaming-proxy resume logic (owner: Elena Kovalenko, due 2026-03-25).
- (A4) Run a 72-hour reconciliation job for billing using historical traces for Granary account and report variance (owner: Billing Ops, due 2026-03-17).
- (A5) Customer-facing post-incident summary and slide deck delivered to Granary (owner: CS - Maya Singh, delivered 2026-03-13).

Notes: This ticket consolidates the customer-facing summary, technical RCA, and the post-incident action tracker. Billing credit details are recorded in finance ticket FIN-4492 (internal).
Hotfix applied to streaming-proxy enforcing monotonic chunk offsets and billing ingestion deduplication deployed. One-off invoice credit issued to Granary Finance. Monitoring and canary processes updated. Ticket closed after customer sign-off.
Race between streaming-proxy resume logic and upstream runtime kernel-selection path introduced non-monotonic chunk offsets; billing ingestion lacked dedupe on offset regressions causing double-counting.
Priya Desai (Support) 2026-03-10 03:28 UTC: Customer Lila Mercer reports truncated responses and duplicate text. Escalating to SRE. Posted initial logs and sample transcript.
Owen Park (SRE) 2026-03-10 03:33 UTC: Paging on-call and routing Granary to sp-us-east-3 as immediate mitigation. Confirmed reduction in truncations after routing switch.
Samira Chen (Billing) 2026-03-10 04:12 UTC: Billing sample shows token delta ~2.1x for some sessions. Pausing automated invoice finalization for affected account and starting reconciliation.
Elena Kovalenko (Infra) 2026-03-11 09:05 UTC: Root cause reproduction validated locally with kernel-selection canary; submitting patch to streaming-proxy to add resume-marker and enforce monotonic offsets (PR #233).
Maya Singh (CS) 2026-03-12 17:30 UTC: Delivered proactive slide deck and credited customer. Granary confirms acceptance and requests weekly reconciliation updates until next billing cycle.
Owen Park (SRE) 2026-03-13 11:20 UTC: Post-deploy validation complete — sampled traffic for 24h shows no duplicate token events. Closing incident and moving work items to respective owners.
A1: add streaming-chunk-monotonicity alert (owner: Owen Park, due: 2026-03-20)
A2: add dedup unit tests & synthetic replay harness for billing (owner: Samira Chen, due: 2026-03-18)
A3: require canary gating for kernel-selection rollouts affecting streaming-proxy (owner: Elena Kovalenko, due: 2026-03-25)
A4: run 72-hour billing reconciliation for Granary traces (owner: Billing Ops, due: 2026-03-17)
A5: weekly reconciliation updates to customer until next invoice (owner: Maya Singh, cadence: weekly)

comments: Priya Nair: Customer reported 2x duplicate webhooks for function calls originating from their TS client. Attached initial logs. Asking SRE for edge-config review.
Marcus Lee: Confirmed cookie trim at edge-proxy. Working on a canary config to prioritize header idempotency canonicalization. Will coordinate SDK team for backwards-compatibility patch.
Elena Ruiz: We'll ship a TS SDK patch that ensures client will always send X-Idempotency-Key header and will not rely on cookies. Also add a defensive header-only dedupe rule on the runtime.
payload.description:
Issue summary: Customer reports duplicated external webhook/tool invocations when their app sends long-running function calls through Redwood hosted API. The duplication happens intermittently after client retries. Impact: repeated downstream work and billing surprises for the customer. Hypothesis: idempotency token getting truncated or re-encoded by our edge proxy when transmitted as part of a session cookie leading retries to be treated as new requests.
Customer observed 2–3 duplicated webhook/tool invocations for 8% of long-running funcall requests during peak, causing ~USD 1.2k of extra downstream work over 24 hours.
1) Customer SDK (Python and TS) initiates a streaming function call with an idempotency token set in client metadata. In this integration the token is attached both as X-Idempotency-Key header and mirrored into a session cookie by an intermediary service.
2) Network path: client -> CDN edge (customer-managed) -> Redwood edge-proxy -> Redwood API -> serving-runtime.
3) Simulate intermittent latency by delaying the upstream ack (long-running function, >5s). Client-side SDK triggers retry logic (after 4s timeout) and reconnects using same idempotency token but cookie value now appears truncated at the edge.
4) Observe two tool/webhook calls on the customer's downstream service for the same logical operation.
5) Reproduction is flaky; requires specific cookie length (~>900 bytes) and chunking behavior at the customer CDN.
Retries are accepted as new requests (no dedupe). Downstream tooling receives duplicate HTTP POSTs with different idempotency token values (truncated vs full). SDKs show success for both attempts.
Retries with the same logical idempotency key should be de-duplicated by Redwood runtime regardless of intermediary cookie rewrites. Idempotency canonicalization should prefer X-Idempotency-Key header over cookies and normalize encoding.
edge-proxy (2026-03-12T14:03:21Z) INFO incoming request: client_ip=52.12.34.56 path=/v1/functions/execute headers={Cookie: session=eyJpZGVudGl0eS1rZXkiOiAiYWJj...<truncated>}
edge-proxy (2026-03-12T14:03:25Z) WARN cookie-length-exceeded: len=1026 limit=1024; trimming applied
serving-runtime (2026-03-12T14:03:25Z) INFO funcall-start id=fn-abc123 idempotency_key=abcde12345fgh (note: header X-Idempotency-Key present)
serving-runtime (2026-03-12T14:03:30Z) INFO funcall-start id=fn-abc124 idempotency_key=abcde123 (truncated in cookie representation)
Initial triage by Support: customer trace shows two separate requests reaching our runtime with differing idempotency token values despite client sending the same token header.
Edge SRE found edge-proxy config that rewrites cookies for session stitching and enforces a 1024 byte cookie header limit; when the cookie value exceeds the threshold the proxy performs a truncate operation without promoting the canonical X-Idempotency-Key header.
Customer-confirmed: their upstream CDN mirrors metadata into a large session cookie (contains additional JWTs and metadata), which is sometimes chunked into multiple Set-Cookie headers; our edge-proxy concatenation logic then performs a silent trim.
SDK behavior: Python SDK gracefully sends X-Idempotency-Key header. TS SDK (older pinned version) relied on cookie propagation for idempotency in their custom integration and did not retry with header fallback.
Hypothesis: when the edge truncates the cookie it leaves the X-Idempotency-Key header intact for some requests but not for others because of upstream connection reuse; in the truncated cases our request normalization code prefers cookie-derived idempotency and overwrites header value with cookie-derived normalized token, resulting in mismatch and therefore duplicate processing.
Repro script: provided a curl + header + cookie replication and able to reproduce 2/10 attempts locally when cookie size crosses 1024 bytes and CDN introduces chunking.
Risk assessment: High for integrations that mirror idempotency to cookies or that embed long metadata in cookies. Low for customers following header-only idempotency best practices.
Related issues: SUP-824000 (edge-proxy cookie-limit behavior) — linked for edge config context.

Additional notes:
Customer (FathomAI - A. Chen): Can you confirm hotfix ETA? We're seeing duplicates every 10–15 minutes during peak traffic windows. This is impacting customer invoices.
Marcus Lee: Target hotfix for edge-proxy config rollout at 2026-03-13 03:00 UTC to prefer X-Idempotency-Key and log any cookie-derived overrides for 48h. SDK patch scheduled for 2026-03-14.
Priya Nair: Added mitigation steps for customer — temporary workaround to remove idempotency mirror from their CDN or reduce cookie size below 900 bytes.
Partial fix applied: edge-proxy config updated to canonicalize idempotency from X-Idempotency-Key header and ignore cookie-derived tokens when header present. Canary rolled out to 10% of edges on 2026-03-13 03:00 UTC. TS and Python SDK guidance updated; TS SDK patch v1.4.3 published to explicitly set X-Idempotency-Key and avoid cookie mirroring. Customer applied temporary workaround.
Canary metrics show duplicate toolcall rate dropped from 8% -> 0.3% on canary edges. Full rollout scheduled 2026-03-14 02:00 UTC after 24h canary validation. Follow-up: add linting rule in Console to warn when customers mirror idempotency into cookies and update docs.
1) Complete full rollout of edge change and monitor duplicate rates for 72h.
2) Release TS SDK patch to all channels, notify customers via release notes.
3) Create a Console lint/warning for cookie-mirrored idempotency usage.
4) Postmortem note and customer-facing RCA to be published after full rollout.

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customer BrightGov sees their provisional invoice for 2026-02-24 underreport usage for the 18:00-19:00 UTC hour. Internal metering shows usage was posted late by ~12 minutes and the provisional invoice aggregation window omitted the late postback. This looks tied to the hourly postback aggregation job experiencing elevated lag (backpressure from the microbatch queue) during that window.

Impact:
- Customer-facing provisional invoice subtotal is ~32% lower for the affected hour, causing an alert on their finance side and potential downstream reconciliation failures.
- No permanent overcharge reported yet, but risk of surprise adjustments on final invoice when late postbacks are applied.

Environment:
- Production metering pipeline in us-east-1, hourly aggregation service (meter-agg-v2), provisional invoice generator (proinv-service).
Customer provisional invoice underreports one hourly bucket; finance team escalated and paused automated charge reconciliations.
1) Simulate sustained microbatch backlog by sending parallel batch-embed jobs from a dedicated customer token for 90s.
2) Force a delayed postback by introducing 10s processing delay in the embed worker.
3) Trigger hourly aggregation window at :00 UTC.
4) Observe provisional invoice subtotal and compare to raw postback records.

(Engineering note: reproducer included to validate aggregation logic when postbacks arrive after window close but before invoice snapshot.)
meter-agg-v2 logs (2026-02-24T18:00:00Z - 19:15:00Z):
- 18:59:48Z INFO received postback (customer=brightgov, events=124)
- 19:00:00Z WARN window-close triggered, pending-postbacks=0
- 19:00:12Z ERROR late-postback detected, postback-arrival=00:12 after-window-close, decision=drop-from-provisional
- 19:00:30Z INFO reconciliation-job enqueued

Postback service traces: trace_id=trc_brightgov_0291 latencies peaked at 7200ms for commit to s3 cache.
Metric spikes: meter.postback.queue_latency p90=6.8s, meter.agg.window_skipped=1
Confirmed provisional invoice snapshot excludes postbacks arriving > window_grace (config default 5s).
Observed transient queue buildup in microbatch workers from 18:58:30Z to 19:00:20Z related to a concurrent large batch-job from a different enterprise customer which consumed worker slots.
Config check: window_grace configured to 5s for proinv-service in prod; postback retries arrive up to 120s after initial attempt.
Hypothesis: Provisional snapshot timing + conservative grace window meant legitimate late postbacks were excluded. Long-term fix may need to be more tolerant for provisional calculations or replay into provisional aggregator.
Cross-ref: similar pattern in SUP-912345 where late stream commits affected daily smoothing.
Support (Lena Torres): Thanks for filing, Marcus. We've validated the discrepancy and escalated to Billing Ops. I'll coordinate with Metering infra to capture the late postbacks and hold final invoice adjustments while we investigate.
Customer (Aaron Patel, BrightGov): We rely on provisional invoices for internal monthly estimates — can you confirm if this will affect our March budget report? We need a workaround if not fixed within 48 hours.

Additional notes:
Support (Lena Torres): Temporary workaround applied: set feature-flag proinv.grace=30s for us-east for the next 24 hours to capture late postbacks while we patch scaling behavior. Customers impacted have been notified.
Applied feature-flag proinv.grace=30s in us-east for 24h to include late postbacks in provisional aggregation.
Billing Ops to generate an amended provisional invoice for BrightGov and flag the change with explanation to their finance contact.
If customers need deterministic hourly estimates, recommend using event-level usage reports (raw_postbacks_export) until permanent fix.
Hourly aggregation dropped legitimate postbacks that arrived just outside the configured grace window (5s) during a transient microbatch worker saturation event. The grace window was insufficient given observed postback delivery latencies under load.
Temporarily increased provisional grace window for us-east and scaled postback workers to reduce queue pressure. Billing Ops issued an amended provisional invoice to BrightGov and marked the change as non-billable for final invoice reconciliation to avoid double-billing. Monitoring configured to alert on meter.postback.queue_latency > 3s during hourly close.
Ship meter-agg-v2 patch to auto-extend window_grace when queue_latency > 2s (dev sprint 2026-03-05).
Increase default proinv.window_grace to 30s for enterprise customers while we monitor impact (ops runbook update).
Add canary test that simulates late postbacks in pre-prod to validate provisional snapshots before rollout.
Convene postmortem with SRE, Billing Ops, and Customer Success to review communication cadence for provisional invoice adjustments (owner: Rhea Singh, due 2026-03-04).

payload.description:
Issue summary: BrightRetail contacted support reporting a mid-cycle reduction in available billing credits and multiple split line items on their latest provisional invoice. The customer says credits allocated at the start of the billing period (reserved buffer + promotional uplift) dropped unexpectedly over 48 hours, and invoice lines show the same hourly window split across two ledger namespaces. Impact: Customer-facing order-processing jobs experienced throttling alerts when their buffer reached zero; revenue-impact monitoring flagged an SLA breach risk. Environment: prod us-west, org-id: org-BR-994, account uses Dedicated reserved capacity with hybrid fallback to hosted in us-west. Observed between 2026-03-08 02:00 UTC and 2026-03-10 11:30 UTC.
1) Reconcile hourly postbacks for org-BR-994 between 2026-03-08T00:00Z and 2026-03-10T12:00Z. 2) Filter postbacks by tag namespace; note entries with both 'tenant:brightretail' and a transient 'tenant:br-old' prefix. 3) Run billing replayer against the same window to reproduce split invoice lines and credit allocation changes. 4) Compare ledger snapshots pre- and post-2026-03-08T02:00Z for namespace ownership changes.
Initial hypothesis: a deploy of the postback-processor introduced a regression that allowed stale tenant prefix headers to override canonical tenant namespace for a subset of postbacks. Evidence: logs from postback-processor pod postback-processor-7f6b show repeated warnings about "prefix_mismatch" and a transient code path that maps legacy prefixes to new tenant IDs. Query of raw postbacks table (postbacks_raw) returned ~4.2k entries with legacy prefix br-old between 2026-03-08T01:55Z and 2026-03-09T05:10Z. Correlation: the ledger rehydration job ran at 2026-03-09T04:00Z and produced an intermediary aggregation that split buffer credits across two namespaces, which the invoicing run interpreted as separate lines. Temporary mitigation applied: blocked the legacy-prefix mapping in the postback-processor and manually requeued ambiguous postbacks into the canonical namespace. Work left: night-run ledger re-aggregation with dedup and canonicalization, and an account-level credit reconciliation to restore BrightRetail's reserved buffer.

payload.description:
Issue summary:
On 2026-03-10 between 11:42-12:05 UTC NimbleDocs observed high 95/99th percentile generation latency (spikes from ~200ms to up to 3.8s) and intermittent streaming disconnects for chat endpoints. Customer reported increased user-facing errors and slow responses during a high-traffic campaign window. Customer traffic is on a Dedicated pool in us-west and eu-central with routing policy that prefers full-precision variants and falls back to quantized variants when capacity-constrained.

Impact:
- Customer-facing chat UX degraded; several sessions timed out and streaming sessions disconnected (estimated 8% of active sessions during window).
- Billing and SLA risk for a paying Dedicated customer.
- Customer opened an escalation to Support and threatened reduced traffic to Redwood if not remediated.

Timeline (condensed):
- 11:40 UTC: NimbleDocs spike begins (campaign). Autoscaler begins evicting/creating pods to match load.
- 11:42 UTC: Observability shows routing layer started failing to bind requests to primary FP instances for short windows and routed ~22% of traffic to quantized variants.
- 11:45 UTC: Latency 95/99p increases recorded in prod-us-west and eu-central; streaming disconnects spike.
- 11:50 UTC: Support engaged SRE; immediate mitigation actions started (traffic steering and rollbacks).
- 12:03 UTC: Temporary routing policy rollback completed; traffic returned to FP variants and tails normalized by 12:05 UTC.

Investigation notes / Observations:
- Autoscaler churn: we saw frequent node-level evictions within the Dedicated pool triggered by a transient GPU driver patch (we had pushed a scheduled driver update to a subset of hosts in us-west earlier in the day). This produced short windows where advertised FP capacity dropped.
- Routing decision code (router) has a fallback threshold that will flip traffic to quantized variants if observed FP availability < 85% for 30s. Due to autoscaler churn, the router flipped and then stayed in fallback for additional cycles because the health check windowed metric used for promotion back to FP had a 3-minute smoothing window.
- Quantized runtime exhibited higher tail latency under the specific prompt length distribution of NimbleDocs (long chat histories + streaming tokens), because KV cache handling in the 8-bit path interacted poorly with streaming prefetch heuristics.
- Observed a small memory leak in the quantized path that caused a few instances to hit an OOM threshold and restart during the window, which extended the fallback period.

Steps to reproduce (internal):
1) Simulate traffic pattern: high concurrency with long chat histories (median context 2.5k tokens, tail 6k).
2) Force FP pool availability to drop below 85% for ~1 minute via controlled instance draining.
3) Observe router flip to quantized variants and measure 95/99p latencies for streaming endpoints.

Logs & links:
- Kibana: logs/session-errors?#time=2026-03-10T11:40:00Z-2026-03-10T12:10:00Z
- Grafana: dashboard/redwood/dedicated-pool/us-west?from=2026-03-10T11:30Z&to=2026-03-10T12:10Z
- Router traces: https://traces.redwood.com/trace/SUP-53122

Workaround applied:
- Immediate: temporarily lowered router fallback sensitivity and forced routing to FP variants for NimbleDocs Dedicated pool. This required a config toggle to bypass the 3-minute re-promotion smoothing window.
- Short-term: pinned NimbleDocs to a committed subset of warm FP instances while SRE investigated the quantized runtime leak.

Resolution summary:
- Reverted the routing re-promotion smoothing window to allow faster switchback to FP when observed availability recovered.
- Rolled back the morning GPU driver patch from the small subset of hosts that were experiencing instability; autoscaler churn stopped.
- Deployed a fix to the quantized runtime that reduces KV cache prefetch contention and prevents the observed OOM (~patch 1892).
- Post-fix monitoring showed 99p latency return to baseline within 20 minutes of full rollback.

Customer communication:
- Support sent interim updates at 11:55 UTC and 12:10 UTC while mitigation steps were underway.
- Final post-incident summary and root-cause explanation was shared with NimbleDocs on 2026-03-13. Customer accepted remediation and requested follow-ups (below).

Support (Aisha Kapoor) - 2026-03-10T11:52Z: Initial triage: confirming impact with SRE, gathering request IDs and affected endpoints from customer. Escalated to on-call SRE.
SRE (Liam Chen) - 2026-03-10T11:58Z: Observed router flip to quantized variants. Starting emergency rollback of router smoothing config for NimbleDocs. Investigating autoscaler churn and driver patch footprint.
Customer (NimbleDocs - Jenna Park) - 2026-03-10T12:01Z: We are seeing many users stuck on loading state; please advise ETA. This window is critical for our campaign.
SRE (Liam Chen) - 2026-03-10T12:04Z: Forced routing to FP variants completed. Please verify. Continuing root-cause analysis and preparing postmortem.
Support (Aisha Kapoor) - 2026-03-13T09:15Z: Shared detailed RCA and mitigation plan with customer. Customer acknowledged and requested confirmation of follow-up items. Marking incident resolved pending follow-ups.
Engineering (Priya Nair) - 2026-03-13T14:40Z: Patch 1892 merged to address quantized KV prefetch contention and memory leak; will monitor for 72h for regressions.
Mitigations: rolled back driver patch on affected hosts, reverted router re-promotion smoothing, deployed quantized runtime fix (PR 1892). No further customer impact observed after rollbacks. NimbleDocs confirmed user experience recovered. SLA credits evaluated and offered per policy; customer accepted credit and will maintain Dedicated contract.
Primary contributor was operational churn (driver patch evictions) that temporarily reduced FP capacity. Router fallback logic and re-promotion smoothing amplified impact by keeping traffic on quantized variants longer than necessary. Secondary contributor was a quantized runtime memory leak that extended instance churn. Root cause spans infra (driver rollout), router policy tuning, and quantized runtime robustness.
Action-1: Update runbook to include immediate toggle for router re-promotion smoothing (owner: SRE, due: 2026-03-20)
Action-2: Add canary gate for GPU driver rollouts to Dedicated pools to prevent parallel evictions (owner: Infra, due: 2026-04-01)
Action-3: Improve quantized path e2e tests with long-history streaming scenarios (owner: Runtime Team, due: 2026-03-28)
Action-4: Create metric alert for rapid FP availability drops (>10% drop in 60s) tied to automated paging (owner: Observability, due: 2026-03-22)
Action-5: Schedule a dedicated-customer review with NimbleDocs to discuss workload characterization and recommended model/quant profiles (owner: Customer Success, due: 2026-03-25)
Action-6: Postmortem document published and shared with CS & Engineering (link in related_confluence_pages).

Issue summary:
Northstar Search asked for a "compatibility matrix" that clearly states which Quantization Profile types are supported per model and per GPU SKU, including any max context/sequence-length constraints and whether support differs across Hosted vs Dedicated.

Customer request:
- Provide a public-facing table (or equivalent docs page) for: Model variant → supported quantization profiles → supported hardware (H100/A100/L40S/A10) → constraints (max context, batch size caveats).
- Clarify behavior when a profile is enabled but incompatible (will it hard fail vs silently fallback?).
- They want something they can hand to their platform team before enabling profiles on production routes.

Impact:
- No outage; blockers for rollout planning and internal approvals.
- Customer is evaluating beta enablement on a Dedicated cluster and wants predictable behavior + documentation.

Notes from intake call/email:
- They saw the Console toggle but could not find a definitive reference that lists what is supported. They specifically asked about INT8 (W8A8) vs FP8 mix paths and whether A10 is supported.

What we know today (internal):
- Compatibility is enforced via policy evaluation + runtime guardrails. If incompatible, the request should safely fall back to baseline precision (and emit fallback metrics + log annotations). Console/API surfaces warnings/errors depending on the operation (enablement validation vs runtime resolution).
- We have an internal serving standard page (Confluence) but customer wants a public doc artifact.

Requested outcome:
- Public docs update that includes (a) how to check compatibility for a given model/profile/hardware, (b) current supported GPU classes at GA/beta, and (c) explicit fallback behavior and how to detect it.
