Issue summary: MedAssist reports increased 95p and 99p tail latency for text-generation routes after they enabled a combined optimizer profile (async batching + aggressive quantization + KV prefetch) during a controlled rollout on 2026-03-13. Impact: customer-facing API latency spikes causing several calls to miss SLOs and user-facing timeouts for workflows that require sub-500ms tail latency. Environment: prod (us-east), dedicated enterprise account, pinned model rw/gpt-large-1.2B-finetuned. Steps to reproduce: 1) Use customer's route and tenant config (attached snapshot) 2) Send steady traffic at customer's distribution (joined sample CSV) 3) Observe 95p/99p across 1 hour window and streaming disconnect counts. Observed behavior: after config flip at 2026-03-13T13:20Z 95p latency increased from ~310ms to ~920ms and 99p from ~620ms to ~2.1s. Error traces show increased queuing and occasional model-worker GC/eviction chatter. Expected behavior: modest tail regression for small latency gains; not SLO-violating. Attachments: customer's config snapshot, compressed pprof samples, APM traces, and traffic sample CSV.
Summary of findings: - Timeline: config applied (optimizer profile id opt-ff32-agg-batch-kv) at 2026-03-13T13:20Z; latency jump aligned to rollout window. - Telemetry: batching histogram shows async_batch_size target increased from 4->12 for long sessions; KV prefetch hit ratio dropped for this tenant causing repeated cache misses and extra KV RPCs. - Quantization: quant fallback events logged for ~7% of requests (runtime fell back to higher-precision kernels under memory pressure). - Resource signals: GPU utilization stable, but host-side CPU and io_wait increased on several serving hosts processing this tenant. - Hypothesis: combined increase in async batching plus aggressive kv-prefetch unexpectedly changed request inter-arrival distribution, leading to larger per-batch assembly delays and cache churn; quant fallback amplified CPU/host latency and caused tail amplification. Dashboards: https://dashboards.redwood/internal/d/latency/tenant-MedAssist; trace example: https://apm.redwood/trace/9a7b3c
Immediate safe-demote plan executed as a staged operation: 1) Traffic-split 10% canary -> reduce async_batch_target to 6 and disable kv-prefetch for that canary route 2) Monitor 95p/99p and error-rate for 15 minutes 3) If improvement >30% at 95p, expand to 50% traffic-split and keep telemetry capture enabled 4) For remaining traffic, set per-route override to quant_profile: balanced (instead of aggressive). Implementation commands: - route override via Console > Routes > MedAssist-TextGen > Overrides - API: PATCH /v1/routes/{route_id}/overrides {"async_batch_target":6, "kv_prefetch":false, "quant_profile":"balanced"} 5) Keep snapshot of current optimizer profile (snapshot id saved) and do not purge until full validation. Monitoring hooks: 95p/99p, quant-fallback count, kv miss rate, host CPU iowait. Safety gates: auto-rollback to prior snapshot if 99p > 2s for two consecutive 5-min windows.
In progress: support and SRE applied the staged demote for 10% canary at 2026-03-13T16:05Z per workaround. Early results: 95p for canary dropped from 910ms -> 380ms within 12 minutes; quant-fallback reduced to 1.1% from 7%. Customer agreed to expand to 50% at 2026-03-13T16:30Z. Next steps: - complete 50% expansion and re-evaluate after 30m - schedule controlled full rollout reversal if stable - prepare postmortem runbook entry and update optimizer profile recommendation for this workload to avoid simultaneous aggressive batching and kv-prefetch for long-session distributions. Follow-up action item: SRE to open INT ticket to add an automated preflight check that flags high kv miss rate when async_batch_target > 8.
2026-03-13T13:32Z - Laura (MedAssist): We flipped the optimizer profile as part of our perf test. End users started seeing timeouts immediately. Sharing config snapshot and traffic CSV.
2026-03-13T14:05Z - Aisha (Support): Acknowledged. Triage assigned to Luca. Collecting telemetry and snapshots; requesting permission to run canary overrides.
2026-03-13T15:10Z - Luca (SRE): Correlated dashboards; suspect interaction between async batching and kv-prefetch. Drafting staged demote plan. See trace: https://apm.redwood/trace/9a7b3c
2026-03-13T16:10Z - Aisha (Support): Executed 10% canary demote. Initial telemetry attached (canary-results-10pct.csv).
2026-03-13T16:35Z - Laura (MedAssist): Confirmed improved UX for subset of users. Approve 50% expansion.
2026-03-14T09:00Z - Luca (SRE): 50% expansion completed. Monitoring shows stable 95p ~360-400ms. Preparing changeset to update optimizer recommendation for this model/workload. Will follow up with a concise config guideline for MedAssist.
2026-03-14T12:10Z - Aisha (Support): Noted customer happy with interim improvement; keeping ticket open for closure after full validation and runbook updates.

Issue summary: Customer BrightAI reports repeated sessions where SSE connections experience a TCP/TLS-level reset during mid-stream. When the client attempts to resume, the server accepts the resumed handshake but several fragments (partial JSON chunks and metadata tuples) are delivered to the wrong client session. The affected conversation does not receive an explicit end/closure event and the UI shows a hung 'generating' state.

Impact: Several BrightAI users see incomplete conversations (no closing metadata) and duplicated prefix fragments appearing in unrelated sessions. This leads to user-visible truncation or noise and breaks transcript integrity. Observed in ~0.3% of long-running streams (>60s) in us-east.

Environment: Production (dedicated cluster in us-east), edge fronted by customer NGINX sidecar at VPC egress; client using browser SDK v1.4.2 with SSE fallback.

Steps to reproduce:
1) Start a long-running chat generation (expected duration >60s) from BrightAI private network.
2) At ~40s, force a TCP reset on the client connection (simulate NAT refresh / ephemeral proxy drop).
3) Client reestablishes SSE with resume token and sends resume request with last-event-id.
4) Server accepts resume and continues emitting fragments.

Observed behavior: On resume, some emitted fragments are delivered to other active sessions (session-id mix), and the original session does not receive the closing 'done' metadata. Some fragments are replayed as prefixes in other sessions.

Expected behavior: Resume should atomically continue the original session only, deliver missing fragments to the correct session, and emit terminal metadata event so client can mark completion.

Relevant logs / correlation IDs:
- Customer-provided trace: trace_id=trace-Bright-9f3a
- Server request IDs observed: req=ri-7c3f2, ri-7c3f3, ri-7c3f4
- Edge error sample: "HTTP/2 stream reset (0x10)" in nginx-sidecar logs at 2026-03-09T15:23:41Z
- Serving runtime log sample: "resume: accepted token token=rt-1a2b3; session_shard=5; resume_offset=2738" followed by "dispatch: session-mismatch detected for fragment seq=2740"

Attachments: HAR-style dump, minimal reproduction script provided by customer (see comments).
Start a long SSE generation (>60s)
Simulate client TCP/TLS reset during streaming (e.g., NAT refresh)
Client reconnects and sends resume token/Last-Event-ID
Observe fragments delivered to other sessions and missing terminal event
Timeline: Reproduced in staging by simulating connection resets with short delay between resume and server-side shard rebalancing. Key findings: (1) resume token validation and session binding occur in separate async tasks; (2) there is a narrow window where the binding is visible to the resume handshake but subsequent fragment dispatch uses the new routing table before binding is fully propagated across the shard proxy; (3) fragments have seq numbers that cross-verify to original session, but dispatch resolves to session by lookup on volatile map which may have been modified. Dashboards: streaming-dispatch-errors spike metric correlated with NAT churn events. Repro script and logs uploaded to internal gist for engineer repro.
Workaround: Advise customers to implement a client-side 'resume backoff' (recommended 250-500ms pause after TCP/TLS handshake before resending resume frames) and upgrade SDK to 1.4.3 when released. Temporary server mitigation: enabled a short (500ms) guard window during which resume binds are held on original shard until dispatch confirms binding across proxies (rollout applied to us-east dedicated cluster 2026-03-11 22:30 UTC).

Permanent fix: Engineering to refactor resume binding to be atomic and synchronous across shard proxies; PR opened: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/7821 — target for rollout 2026-03-20 with canary on 2026-03-18.

Follow-up actions: Create a dedicated e2e test for resume race (INT ticket INT-2207), update client SDKs with automatic resume backoff, add monitoring alert for resume-mismatch-rate >0.1%.

Status: Partial server mitigation deployed; customer reports immediate improvement but full fix pending.
2026-03-10 09:12 - BrightAI (customer): 'We've seen this consistently in two of our test users. After our NAT refresh script we sometimes see earlier parts replayed in other open sessions.'

Additional notes:
2026-03-11 08:45 - Eng (runtime): 'Hypothesis: when a resume arrives with a recently rotated ephemeral session allocator, fragments emitted while shard remap is in flight can be enqueued to the new session routing table leading to misdelivery. Reproduction attempt succeeded in staging with enforced small remap window.'
payload.summary: SSE connection reset with no client ack leads to misrouted fragments and incomplete conversation closure

Issue summary: Starting 2026-03-10 09:15 UTC, FinQuick reported a sustained elevation of 5xx responses (502/503) from the Redwood API for their dedicated tenant. Impact: multiple customers endpoints experienced request failures and streaming session drops; customer reported lowered throughput and user-facing errors in prod. Environment: Dedicated capacity pool in us-east-1 serving mixed chat + large multipart embedding workloads. Observed behavior: API gateway returned 502/503s at ~8-12% error rate for 30+ minutes; apigw logs show upstream timeouts and connection resets. Serving runtime pods behind the route showed a backlog spike and several pods entering CrashLoopBackOff after NVML driver resets. Expected behavior: < 0.1% 5xx and graceful fallback to lower-capacity variants when runtime overloaded.
1) Customer replayed a high-throughput embedding upload (multipart, ~150 files, 2-4MB each) against their dedicated route
2) Simultaneously sent 200 small chat requests per second (concurrent sessions) to the same tenant route
3) Observe apigw error rate and runtime pod queues within 5 minutes of ramp

09:55 UTC - Hypothesis A: large multipart embedding upload created heavy disk I/O and NVMe latency on ephemeral storage, slowing runtime cold loads -> longer model kernel selection -> upstream timeouts backpressure apigw

payload.description:
Customer BeaconAI reports intermittent increases in p95 and p99 inference latency for their dedicated pool. Spikes appear as short-lived waves (5-20 minutes) where p99 climbs from baseline ~200ms to 1200-1800ms and some requests time out. Affected traffic pattern is a skewed mix of very short single-turn prompts and occasional long multi-turn streams that resume KV cache usage. Suspected tie to continuous-batcher flush behavior under asymmetric sequence-length distributions.
1) Use BeaconAI ded pool in us-east-1 and replay a trace with 85% short (<=8 tokens) single-request calls and 15% long (>=512 tokens) streaming sessions interleaved.
2) Observe request latency distribution in metrics/per-tenant dashboards.
3) Look at continuous-batcher flush_size/flush_interval and per-tenant queue depth.
4) Re-run with only short requests or only long requests as control; spikes do not reproduce consistently outside mixed workload.
2026-03-12T12:04:21Z [lb-prod-us-east-1] INFO incoming req tenant=beaconai seq_len=6 route=/v1/generate
2026-03-12T12:04:21Z [batcher-3] DEBUG enqueue tenant=beaconai conn=72842 queue_depth=12
2026-03-12T12:04:21Z [batcher-3] WARN flush_delay_ms=34 flush_size=3 policy=adaptive linger_ms=12
2026-03-12T12:04:22Z [serving-runtime-gpu-7] ERROR model=redwood-instruct-3b request_id=9a7f timeout after 1500ms
2026-03-12T12:04:22Z [metrics] gauge inter_batch_interval_p99=450ms
2026-03-12T12:04:22Z [kv-cache] INFO cache_miss tenant=beaconai prefix=conversation-12
(Full logs attached in internal S3: s3://redwood-support/beaconai/SUP-33121/logs.tar.gz)
Observations: (a) p99 correlates strongly with spikes in inter_batch_interval_p99 and spikes in small flush_size counts (many small micro-flushes followed by large flush) rather than steady batch sizes. (b) Tenant queue depth oscillates: short request bursts reduce linger, triggering early micro-flushes; long streams later cause larger batches that stall GPU worker for longer and amplify downstream queueing for short requests.
Hypothesis: Continuous-batcher adaptive policy uses recent mean sequence length and queue depth to decide linger. Under rapidly changing short->long mixtures this control loop under- or over-shoots, producing a resonant effect: clusters of small flushes then a large flush that creates head-of-line blocking and inflight KV cache warmups, causing 5xx/timeouts.
Also observed increased CPU steal on a subset of GPU nodes (host-7a, host-7b) coincident with spikes; possible noisy-neighbor exacerbation.
Data/metrics checked: per-tenant flush_interval histograms, per-connection latency traces, gpu_utilization, host_cpu_steal, kv_cache_miss_rate, request_size_percentiles.
Preliminary root-cause: control-loop oscillation in adaptive linger combined with mixed short/long sequence workloads and occasional host resource contention.
1) Temporary per-tenant override pushed: set tenant.batch_override.max_linger_ms=6 and tenant.batch_override.disable_cross_tenant_coalesce=true for BeaconAI — deployed 2026-03-12T14:05Z.
2) Rerouted a fraction (10%) of BeaconAI traffic to an isolated dedicated subpool to limit noisy neighbor effects.
3) Encouraged customer to smooth request pattern if possible (short-request batching window).
Effect: within 10 minutes p99 dropped from ~1450ms to ~240ms and error rates returned to baseline. Monitoring continues.
Workaround applied and holding. Long-term fixes proposed: (A) Update continuous-batcher control loop to incorporate sequence-length variance and add anti-resonance jitter in linger adaptation. (B) Add per-tenant detection that automatically applies short max_linger for high short/long variance workloads. (C) Investigate node-level scheduling to reduce CPU steal/noisy-neighbor exposure for dedicated pools.
Owners: serving-runtime (PR GH#12860) for algorithm change, infra scheduler for host placement. Targeted rollout: canary 2026-04-02, full rollout 2026-04-16. Follow-up task INT-4189 created for scheduler investigation.
2026-03-12T12:30Z - Maya Patel (Support): Customer reported p99 spikes and timeouts. Attached sample traces and quantified impact. Asked for priority review; customer is on dedicated plan so escalated to P1.
2026-03-12T13:05Z - SRE Triage (Ethan Romero): Reproduced pattern in staging using replay; confirmed inter-batch interval oscillation. Collecting host-level metrics and scheduler logs. Will attempt conservative per-tenant override as mitigation.
2026-03-12T14:12Z - Ethan Romero (SRE): Applied tenant.batch_override (max_linger_ms=6, disable_cross_tenant_coalesce=true). BeaconAI p99 returned near baseline. Placed temporary hold on auto-scaling that would move their pods until follow-up. Monitoring set for 24h.
2026-03-12T15:40Z - BeaconAI (Customer): Confirmed customer-side reduction in timeouts and thanked team. Customer asked for timeline for permanent fix and whether similar mitigation could be made automatic.
2026-03-13T09:10Z - Product (Lina Zhou): Requested cost/latency tradeoffs for per-tenant overrides and asked engineering for telemetry to detect high short/long variance automatically. Adding to roadmap for Optimize feature set.
2026-03-13T11:45Z - Ethan Romero (SRE): Scheduled follow-up change to batcher control loop (GH#12860) and created INT-4189 for scheduler host placement. Will update customer with planned canary dates.

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customers on a Private deployment report intermittent gRPC streaming failures where client streams hang in a half-open state (server side sees FIN/ACK without proper close). This appears during high-concurrency inference bursts and correlates with short-lived connection resets from serving nodes.

Impact:
- Real customer impact: user-facing streaming responses stall for ~5-30s then recover; some sessions require retrying prompts.
- Affects real-time chat and streaming completion use-cases for Acme Health (HIPAA-regulated workload).
- Intermittent, not constant: ~0.5–3% of streams in high concurrency windows.

Environment:
- Private deployment (customer-managed K8s cluster) running Redwood Private v0.9.8 agent.
- Node OS: Ubuntu 22.04; CNI: Calico v3.25; iptables backend.
- Serving runtime: redwood-serving v1.14.2 on GPU pool in us-east-1.
- Observed with model gpt-neox-20b pinned for route redwood:chat-realtime.

Steps to reproduce (customer-provided test):
1. Create 250 parallel streaming requests to the hosted endpoint from a pod inside the customer cluster using a short prompt loop.
2. Observe ~0.5–3% of streams transition to "stall" state in SDK and never emit additional tokens until connection reset.
3. Server-side logs show socket-level FIN/ACKs followed by immediate reconnect from client.

Logs & evidence:
- Serving node tcpdump snippet (timestamps aligned): "[S] -> [C] PSH, ACK ... [C] -> [S] FIN, ACK" followed by client reconnect within 200–700ms.
- Customer conntrack dump from node: many entries with state=ESTABLISHED, but multiple entries with orig-port in ephemeral range flagged as "DENY" by iptables egress chain (policy id 9802).
- Calico policy YAML attached by customer (snippet): egress rules only allow destination ports 443, 80, 853 and a narrow set of IP ranges; ephemeral high ports were not explicitly permitted.
- K8s pod-level logs show sidecar (security proxy) rewriting conntrack marks intermittently.

Initial hypothesis:
1) Customer's default-deny Egress NetworkPolicy blocks return-path ephemeral ports used by long-lived streaming connections (Redwood uses high source/ephemeral destination ports for chunked gRPC streams when behind NAT).
2) A security sidecar rewrites conntrack marks causing conntrack entries to be aged prematurely leading to TCP resets/half-close behavior.
3) Calico with iptables backend + conntrack combined with customer egress ACLs produces asymmetric policy enforcement during bursts.

Investigation notes (Redwood):
- Reproduced a similar failure in a staging cluster by applying a strict egress policy that only allowed 443 and 80: gRPC streaming degraded and conntrack showed "RELATED" entries aged out faster when ephemeral ports were blocked.
- Packet captures show initial TLS handshake completes successfully, but subsequent streaming packets from server to client land on ephemeral ports that the customer policy blocks for return traffic, triggering RST/FIN behavior at the host firewall.
- Confirmed sidecar (customer-managed) was running a security egress proxy that performs L7 inspection and occasionally inserts iptables rules per flow which shortens conntrack lifetime for flows it touches.
- Kernel conntrack timeout for ESTABLISHED TCP is default; however, iptables connmark manipulations combined with policy reloads led to reclassification and early drop on some flows.

Temporary workaround provided to customer:
- Relax egress policy to explicitly allow the ephemeral port range used by client-source ports (32768-61000) to Redwood control plane and serving node IP ranges.
- Disable sidecar conntrack mark rewriting for streaming pods (customer accepted this as a targeted change for the redwood namespace).
- Deploy a short-lived nftables rule on nodes to accept established RETURN traffic for those ephemeral ranges while investigation continues.

Next steps / action items:
- (Assigned to Marco Ruiz) Validate whether Redwood Private agent can be enhanced to pin source ports or reuse a narrow port range for streaming to avoid needing large ephemeral allowances.
- (Assigned to Networking team) Create knowledge-base article describing required egress allowances and recommended NetworkPolicy examples for Private deployments streaming workloads.
- (Customer action) Customer to adjust Calico policy in redwood namespace as temporary mitigation.
- Collect longer packet captures and conntrack dumps during next high-concurrency window.

Customer communication plan:
- Acknowledge issue and mitigation steps (done).
- Provide temporary policy snippet and recommend sidecar configuration change.
- Target follow-up with engineering proposal for port-pinning or agent behavior change by 2026-03-19.
1) From a pod inside the customer's K8s cluster, fire 250 parallel streaming requests against the redwood endpoint.
2) Observe SDK-level stalls in ~0.5-3% of connections.
3) Correlate timestamps with node conntrack and packet captures showing FINs from client side after server PSH packets.
Extracts:
- server-tcpdump.log: '... .PSH, ACK ...' then '... FIN, ACK ...'
- conntrack-dump.txt: multiple entries showing DROP on egress chain policy id 9802 for ports 33000-34000
- kube-calico-policy.yaml: egress: to ports 80, 443 only

- Reproduced in staging by applying strict egress rules: confirmed behavior.
- Sidecar conntrack-mark rewriting accelerates ageing for touched flows.
- Not an application-level TLS bug; lower-level network policy/conntrack interaction.
- Related internal ticket INT-4112 created for agent port-pinning feasibility study.
Customer has applied a temporary egress allow for ephemeral range 32768-61000 for redwood control and worker IPs and disabled conntrack marking in the streaming namespace. This reduced observed failures to <0.1% during next test window.
TBD - engineering to propose agent-level mitigation (port pinning / fixed source port pool) and KB write-up. No permanent patch yet.

Additional notes:
2026-03-12 16:40 - Customer (Laura Chen): Confirmed next-day load test reduced error rate; asked for written guidance for security team to approve permanent policy changes.
payload.summary: K8s egress NetworkPolicy denies ephemeral ports causing gRPC half-open streaming failures on Private deployment

payload.description:
Issue summary:
BrightCart is receiving repeated latency alerts on their production route despite live request latencies being within expected bounds. Alerts are triggered by the console's trace-based alerting rule which relies on sampled traces. Investigation shows sampled traces are landing in the tracing index with significant delay (up to 8-12 minutes), causing the alerting engine to evaluate stale, higher-latency buckets and generate false positives.

Impact:
- BrightCart has ~15 customer-facing endpoints affected; they received ~30 false alerts between 2026-03-12 14:00 and 2026-03-12 18:00 UTC.
- Customer experienced unnecessary on-call escalations and temporary degraded confidence in platform observability.
- No request denial or data loss observed; metric pipelines (statsd/metrics) appear healthy.

Environment:
- Redwood hosted prod (us-east)
- BrightCart dedicated capacity: dedicated-gpu-pool-7
- Console alert: "route.latency.p95 > 800ms over 5m evaluated from sampled-traces"

Steps to reproduce (approx):
1. Enable the trace-sampling rule on a high-throughput route (sampling rate 1%).
2. Generate sustained load for 10 minutes.
3. Observe that sampled traces appear in tracing UI after a delay >5m and that trace-derived percentile cards (p95) spike transiently when backfill occurs.
4. Check alert history -> alerts coincide with trace backfill windows.

Observed behavior:
- Sampled traces are ingested by collector but appear in the trace index with ~8-12 minute delay intermittently.
- Alert engine evaluates trace-derived windows and fires on the stale high-latency samples.

Expected behavior:
- Sampled traces should be indexed and available within <60s for accurate real-time alerting.
- Alert engine should not consider trace samples older than evaluation window or stale backfills.

Logs / links / evidence:
- Customer-provided alert snippets and timestamps attached in comments.
- Tracing ingestion logs (tracing-service) show spikes of queueing delays around 2026-03-12T14:10-14:30Z: https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/traces/tracing-ingestion?from=...
- Related internal alert: INT-408 (ingestion queue pressure detected).

Temporary workaround applied:
- Support temporarily disabled the trace-based alerting rule for BrightCart and opened a duplicate internal ticket to elevate ingestion worker capacity.

Notes for triage:
- This is likely an ingestion/indexing throughput issue (queueing at the collector or indexing pipeline) tied to bursty sampling traffic and retention compaction. Need SRE to confirm whether indexing backlog or ElasticSearch shard bottleneck caused the delay.

Additional notes:
2026-03-12 15:18 - BrightCart (Customer): Provided alert history and example request IDs; confirmed that real-time API telemetry (metric p95) stayed below thresholds during the alerts.
2026-03-13 09:30 - Ops (Indexing Team): Increased indexing worker pool size for us-east and started controlled backfill. Monitoring shows reduced delay from ~8-12m down to ~90s in sample runs.
Hypothesis: intermittent burst in sampled-trace volume overwhelmed the ingestion-to-indexing path causing queued writes and delayed visibility. Early evidence: tracing-service queue length spike and indexing write latency increased at shard level. Temporary mitigations (increase workers + collector throttling) reduced delay. Need long-term: apply backpressure, implement alert engine exclusion for backfilled traces older than evaluation window, and add tracing e2e tests for backfill scenarios.
Mitigation completed: increased indexing workers (us-east), implemented collector throttling guard, and disabled trace-based alert for BrightCart during remediation. Follow-ups: merge PR for throttling guard, add alert engine rule change to ignore trace documents with ingestion_timestamp older than evaluation window, and run load test. Customer notified and monitoring set to observe for 72h.
payload.summary: Sampled trace indexing delay causing false-positive latency alerts for BrightCart

comments: 2026-03-11T11:12:00Z Runtime Eng: Observed pattern where large prefix causes multiple kernel context switches and re-serialization of KV shards; candidate hypothesis: continuous caching eviction thrashes finalizer progress under heavy prefix expansion. Adding instrumentation to measure KV hit rate per request.
payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customer reports repeated 504s and abrupt streaming termination when using a dynamically expanded system prompt combined with large max_tokens (>= 100k token budget). The calls initially stream tokens for several minutes then the connection abruptly ends with HTTP 504 or the finalization step fails with a timeout.

Impact:
- Affected DocuBridge production workload: document generation pipeline stalls and fails to produce final output for ~12% of requests during peak windows.
- Customer-visible 504s and truncated results that require manual retry.

Environment:
- Dedicated cluster: dc-dedicated-42 (prod-us-west)
- Customer namespace: docubridge-prod
- SDK: ruby-client v1.8.2 calling /v1/stream with `max_tokens` ~120000 and a system prompt that expands user history programmatically (prefix gets ~300k tokens before generation).

Steps to reproduce (customer):
1) Assemble system prompt by concatenating user history (300k tokens) + task instructions.
2) Call streaming endpoint with max_tokens=120000, model=redwood-v2-large, streaming=true.
3) Observe streaming for ~2-5 minutes, then client sees final chunk never arrives and connection returns 504 or hangs until client timeout.

Logs / Observations:
- Ingress gateway shows long-lived upstream connections with spikes in request latency prior to 504.
- Serving runtime logs show repeated KV eviction / recompute cycles on the request's KV cache just before finalization.
- Finalizer worker reports "finalization deadline exceeded" in several traces.
- No obvious OOMs on GPUs; memory usage oscillates but stays under alloc limits.

Customer request:
DocuBridge requests an explanation and a short-term mitigation they can apply immediately (they prefer not to drop to smaller token budgets if avoidable).
2026-03-11 09:22 - Support (Aisha Patel): Acknowledged. Escalating to SRE and runtime team. Asked customer for exact request IDs and sample payload. SLA: P1, first response within 1 business hour.
2026-03-11 10:05 - SRE (Thomas Nguyen): Collected trace ids: trace-20260311-7f3a and trace-20260311-7f9b. Noticed repeated full KV cache flushes at token ~65k and another at ~110k for same request.

Additional notes:
2026-03-12 08:34 - Customer (DocuBridge - Samir Rao): Provided three request payloads and allowed Redwood to run diagnostics in their dedicated cluster. They reported incidence rate spikes during batch uploads between 02:00-05:00 UTC.
2026-03-13 14:50 - SRE (Thomas Nguyen): Applied temporary routing tweak to send long-context calls to low-concurrency nodes and increased finalizer timeout to 300s for docubridge-prod. Customer reports a reduction in 504s from 12% to ~3% during a short verification run.
2026-03-14 09:10 - Support (Aisha Patel): Following up with next steps and asking runtime eng for longer-term fix ETA.
KV eviction observed: for several traces we see full KV shard evictions at ~65k and again at ~110k tokens — indicates working-set exceeded slot reservation leading to recompute of large prefixes.
Finalizer worker timeouts occur after multiple small recompute windows; finalizer backlog correlates with node concurrency and high prefix size.
No GPU OOMs; CPU-side serialization spikes increase finalization latency — likely from repeated kv-serialize + network chunking.
Hypothesis: automated prefix expansion pattern (customer-side) produces many small updates to the request prefix during generation path that disable effective prefix/KV caching; runtime ends up recomputing large parts multiple times.
We reproduced a similar pattern in staging with synthetic prefix growth and observed the same finalizer deadline exceed behavior when max_tokens > 80k and dynamic prefix updates present.
1) Route customer long-context traffic to a dedicated low-concurrency pool (done). 2) Increased finalizer timeout for docubridge-prod to 300s (done). 3) Recommended immediate customer mitigation: collapse history client-side (summarize) or reduce max_tokens below 40k until fix rolled out.
- Runtime team to implement KV eviction hysteresis: prevent full-shard eviction for requests flagged as long-context (owner: Priya Desai, ETA 2026-03-21).
- Add instrumentation to report per-request KV churn metric and alert when churn > threshold (owner: Observability team, ETA 2026-03-18).
- Postmortem & runbook update: add guidance for routing long-context interactive workloads to low-concurrency pools.
- Follow up with customer on 2026-03-16 to validate and schedule a controlled rollout of KV hysteresis fix.

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customer observed that long-running SSE streaming sessions from our hosted API sometimes reconnect to a different edge proxy instance (ephemeral proxy path drift) and when that happens the resumed stream contains a truncated fragment and the final sentence is duplicated or arrives out-of-order. Impact: partial outputs or duplicated concluding sentences cause downstream ingestion/parsing errors in customer pipelines (JSONL and NLP post-processing).

Observed behavior:
- After a network hiccup and client reconnect, the resumed SSE emits a fragment that appears to be missing the last 8-12 tokens of the previous tail and then replays a short prefix before continuing.
- The duplicated prefix sometimes appears in the middle of the final paragraph, breaking JSONL lines.

Expected behavior:
- Resume should stitch previous tail and resumed payload cleanly: no token loss, no duplicated tokens, and ordering preserved.

Notes: Customer uses Dedicated capacity in us-east, long-running prompts (~30s generation), client-side keepalive 15s, and an intermediary corporate proxy that performs occasional short-lived connection handoffs.
1) Use LinguaTech sandbox account on dedicated pool in us-east to start SSE generation with a long prompt that produces ~600-800 tokens over 30-45s.
2) Simulate a short NAT or path change (client IP rebind) or force a transparent proxy rebind on the path between browser and edge (customer provided repro steps: toggle VPN for 2s).
3) Immediately reconnect the client using same session id/resume token and resume the SSE stream protocol.
4) Observe resumed stream: check final chunks for missing tokens and duplicated short prefixes; capture full raw SSE events and compare sequence numbers/offset headers.
Initial triage: Support verified payload corruption happens only when a client reconnects and the resume path crosses a different edge proxy instance (edge-proxy-18 -> edge-proxy-23).
Hypothesis A: Edge proxy handshake or partial buffer flush leaves last byte as incomplete UTF-8 codepoint which causes serving-runtime to emit a replacement char (�) and then subsequent chunking logic misaligns resume offset.
Hypothesis B: Corporate intermediary rewrites or strips/changes Content-Length/transfer-encoding causing downstream chunk coalescing to occur differently on new path.
Evidence: logs show 'altered Content-Length header' from edge-proxy-23 proxied request and serving-runtime emits 'last-char=�' on resumed chunk. Customer's network team confirmed an inline proxy which performs HTTP header normalization on reconnections.
Repro test: We replayed session with a local proxy that rewrites header and reproduced truncation + duplicated prefix within 3 runs. When header rewrite was disabled, resume stitched cleanly.
Metrics: spike in SSE resume errors correlated with edge-proxy handoffs; dashboard: https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/streams/sse-resume?orgId=1 shows resume-fail-rate increase aligned to 2026-03-10 14:10-14:20 UTC.

Additional notes:
2026-03-10 16:10 - LinguaTech (Customer): Confirmed — our gateway normalizes content-length for connections that re-establish under a different path. We can toggle off for testing.
Root cause: Header normalization by intermediate proxies combined with edge-proxy handoff produced chunk boundary changes and left incomplete UTF-8 codepoints unhandled during resume which misaligned resume offsets and produced duplicated/truncated fragments.
Mitigation applied: 1) Quick workaround documented for customer (reduce keepalive, enable resume-strict client-side buffer). 2) Server-side fix: edge-proxy will now mark resume-capable connections and preserve trailing partial bytes across handoffs (edge-proxy PR https://github.com/redwood/edge-proxy/pull/87). 3) Serving-runtime change to validate and reassemble UTF-8 boundaries on resume before emitting tokens (inference PR https://github.com/redwood/inference/pull/4213).
Rollout: fix deployed to us-east edge fleet on 2026-03-12 10:50 UTC behind feature flag; monitored for 24h — no further repros from LinguaTech after deployment.
Follow-up actions: create guidance page on recommended corporate-proxy settings for SSE/resume and add an SDK helper that validates/trims incomplete UTF-8 suffix prior to resume. Confluence doc created and linked.
This ticket highlights interplay between customer network appliances and our resume semantics; will add a desktop tool to help customers detect dangerous proxy behaviors pre-deployment.
CS will follow up with LinguaTech to schedule a short audit of their proxy behavior and offer configuration guidance.

1) Confirmed correlation between tenant short-session rate and throughput sag via connection telemetry. 2) Scoped issue to same physical reserved shard using allocation traces and nvlink counters. 3) Temporarily rate-limited the noisy tenant's short-lived connection burst at the edge to reduce microburst amplitude. 4) Increased dedicated pool prewarm target by +10% for the customer as a temporary buffer. 5) Adjusted autoscaler cooldown from 120s->60s in the affected region to make it more responsive while we investigate. 6) Gathered additional traces and NVLink kernel metrics; reproduced locally in a staging cluster with synthetic short-connection generator.

payload.description:
Issue summary: During a customer-driven traffic surge and scheduled canary workload ramp (HarborTech), production requests experienced a sudden multi-minute warm-start latency amplification followed by a period of unordered streaming fragments (stream pieces arriving out of sequence or truncated). Impact: Customers reported increased completion latency (p95 for short-chat flows rose from ~120ms to ~2.3s) and intermittent transcript reordering for streamed responses. Two HarborTech endpoints observed duplicated partial chunks and out-of-order final tokens for ~22 minutes, triggering an enterprise escalation. Environment: production cluster serving us-east-1; affected pool: dedicated-dp-ht-02 (reserved capacity).
1) Use HarborTech workload template (conversation payloads averaging 120 tokens, concurrency spike from 50 to 1,200 QPS) against dedicated pool dp-ht-02. 2) Trigger a cold-to-warm transition by spinning up new worker slices with kernel/quantization variant redwood-open-xxl-v1-quantized. 3) Observe request latencies during the first 10 minutes of scale-up and monitor streaming chunk ordering (chunk sequence IDs and chunk timestamps).
Key logs: serving-runtime/worker-127.log: repeated KV-cache eviction events during startup (timestamps 2026-03-11T09:03:10Z - 09:09:31Z). Router traces show request multiplexing reassignments to warm workers with missing seq metadata (router/assign-4632.trace). Observability: p95 token latencies spike in dashboard shard 'dp-ht-02' corresponding to autoscale events; traces linked: https://observability.redwood.com/trace/HT-0311-1, https://observability.redwood.com/trace/HT-0311-2.
Observation 1: Warm-worker startup sequences coincided with autoscale events at 09:02-09:25 UTC. Workers entered warm state but triggered repeated KV-cache eviction heuristics immediately after initialization.
Observation 2: Kernel selector telemetry shows flapping between fast-quantized kernels and compatibility fallback kernels for the same model during first 2-3 minutes after spin-up. The fallback path increases per-token CPU overhead and also delays sequence assembly in stream multiplexers.
Hypothesis: The quantized variant's startup path does not prepopulate required prefix KV entries, triggering eviction heuristics and causing repeated cache misses. Combined with routing reassignment, some stream fragments lost sequencing metadata, leading to reorder/truncation at the router/stream reassembly layer.
Evidence: Heap and KV metrics (serving-runtime/metrics) show KV-miss rate spike x18 during warm window. Router logs show 'missing-seq-metadata' events correlated with worker IDs that recently joined the pool. GitHub trace of kernel selector shows recent change in PR #1248 altered compatibility fallback threshold.
Temporary mitigations tested: 1) Pin to full-precision variant — success, reduces tail. 2) Increase KV cache soft limit on warm nodes — partial improvement. 3) Coordinate ingress routing to avoid reassigning in-flight streams during worker warmup — blocked by router code lacking warmup-tag awareness.
Root cause: Interaction of a recent kernel-selection threshold change (PR #1248) with quantized model warm-start sequence. Newly started workers were allowed to serve before full prefix/KV priming completed; automatic KV-eviction heuristics then triggered repeated evictions leading to cache thrash and delayed token generation. Router reassignment of some in-flight streams to these partially warm workers resulted in missing sequence metadata and reordered/truncated streaming fragments.
Immediate fix: Rolled back dp-ht-02 to redwood-open-xxl-v1 (non-quantized) and increased KV cache soft limits on warm workers. Also disabled the new aggressive fallback threshold in kernel selector for the affected pool. This restored p95 latency and eliminated stream reorder incidents within 9 minutes.
Permanent fix planned: Platform Eng to publish a warmup contract for workers so router can annotate/avoid in-flight reassignment until worker reports 'primed' state. Also revert or refine PR #1248 to include a delayed-serve gating during KV priming. Add a unit/regression test for stream sequence metadata preservation across worker handoffs.
Customer remediation: Provided HarborTech with an incident summary, one day service credit for affected dedicated pool time window, and scheduled architecture review.

ENG-4590: Revert or patch kernel selector threshold with compatibility gating and add integration tests — owner: Omar Haddad — due: 2026-03-22

Billing-98: Issue one-day service credit and confirm invoice adjustment for HarborTech — owner: Priya Nair (finance liaison) — done

Observed behavior: API gateway returned intermittent 502/503s; serving-runtime processes logged SIGTERM/segfault-like exits followed by rapid respawns; edge proxy logs show repeated FIN_WAIT/half-open sockets and ALPN negotiation failures to a small fraction (~0.6%) of upstream handshakes. Expected behavior: sustained tenant traffic should remain under SLA with graceful backpressure and no runtime exits or elevated 5xx floor.
1) Use LexiSearch test harness to replay tenant traffic pattern (mixed streaming chat + batch embedding at 600 TPS peak).
2) Target the dedicated routing tag for LexiSearch in us-east-1.
3) Observe API gateway latencies, edge-proxy socket state counts, and serving-runtime worker process health during ramp to steady-state.

Issue summary:
Customer reports short, high-frequency bursts of 429s that appear to affect multiple API routes simultaneously. The bursts are intermittent (10-30s windows) and do not correlate with a single model or a clear traffic spike at the tenant level. Impact:
- Production inference calls for multiple endpoints return 429s for short windows, degrading user search relevance and causing client-side retries.
- Customer is on a dedicated pool and expects predictable throughput.
Environment:
- Customer using NimbleSearch web service that multiplexes 40+ logical streams over a small pool of persistent HTTP/2 connections to our hosted endpoint.
Observed behavior:
- 429s are grouped by connection/session rather than by logical API key route.
- Bursts start when several short-lived requests from different routes are multiplexed over a reused connection.
Expected behavior:
- Throttling should attribute quota/token usage by API key and logical route, not by single HTTP/2 connection reuse across many logical streams.
1) Customer reproducer: open 8 parallel worker threads each issuing short (50-150ms) generation calls to different named routes (route-a, route-b, route-c) over a single HTTP/2 connection pool.
2) Ensure client reuses connection (keep-alive) with multiplexing enabled.
3) Observe 429 responses under sustained concurrency for 2-5 minutes.
4) Workaround: disable HTTP/2 multiplexing or increase per-route burst credits on tenant — 429s stop immediately.

[2026-03-01T10:14:02Z] request_id=8a2d1f9 route=route-b status=429 reason=quota_exhausted connection_id=conn-174
[2026-03-01T10:14:03Z] request_id=bf9d33a route=route-c status=429 reason=quota_exhausted connection_id=conn-174
[2026-03-01T10:14:03Z] request_id=dd4b6c1 route=route-a status=429 reason=quota_exhausted connection_id=conn-174
Edge-proxy trace snippet:
conn-174: multiplexed streams=12 tenant_id=nimble-562 tokens_counted=unexpectedly_high

Initial hypothesis: token accounting in the api-gateway was applying some burst/quota heuristics at the connection level when http2 multiplexing is enabled.
What we checked:
- Rate-limiter logs show quota deductions that group by connection_id for short windows.
- Edge proxy code path for HTTP/2 reused connections has a fast-path that aggregates per-connection counters for performance.
- Tenant-level metrics show no tenant-wide traffic spike concurrent with the 429 bursts.
- Disabling http2 multiplexing on the client reproduced mitigation.
Intermediate findings:
- Repro script from customer reliably triggers 429s when >6 logical routes share the same connection.
- The connection-aggregated counter expiry was too long (60s), causing short bursts from different routes to be counted together and exhaust burst credits.
- A recent edge-proxy PR that introduced connection-level caching for performance (PR linked above) changed accounting semantics in some corner cases.
Action items:
- Short-term: advise customer to disable HTTP/2 multiplexing or increase per-route burst credits (workaround documented below).
- Short-medium: patch rate-limiter to attribute tokens by logical api_key+route first, only falling back to connection aggregation when route metadata is missing.
- Long-term: add e2e tests for HTTP/2 multiplexed traffic with multi-route accounting.

Eng (Anika): Noted PR 1248 introduced connection-level cache to reduce lookup cost. Will review and propose safe fallback semantics for multi-route tenants.

Customer (Elena): Provided logs and consent for temporary config change. Asked for ETA for a permanent fix and whether this affects other dedicated tenants.
SRE (Luca): Running canary patch in staging with synthetic multiplexed workload. Observed no 429s when attribution changed to api_key+route first. Planning limited production rollout behind feature flag.
Mitigation provided: advised NimbleSearch to disable HTTP/2 multiplexing in their client SDK (immediate) or request increased per-route burst credits while we patch.
Short-term fix: configuration guidance sent (support steps attached) and telemetry added to detect connection-aggregated token spikes.
Planned permanent fix: update edge-proxy rate-limiter to prefer api_key+route attribution, revert to per-connection aggregation only when route metadata is missing; patch scheduled for 2026-03-08 and rollout behind a feature flag.
Follow-ups: postmortem entry and confluence runbook updated, add unit/integration tests for multiplexed multi-route accounting, and notify other dedicated tenants via ops bulletin to check for similar patterns.

Issue summary:
During SummitLedger's scheduled end-of-day (EOD) processing window (approx 02:00-03:00 UTC on 2026-03-10), a high-volume fanout of inference requests triggered cascading timeouts through the routing layer and autoscaler. This led to increased 5xx rates from the serving-runtime, truncated streaming completions for chat flows, and a temporary SLA exposure for SummitLedger (enterprise contract).

Impact:
- Multiple customer-facing APIs returned 500/502 errors and streaming responses were truncated mid-completion for ~28 minutes at peak.
- SummitLedger reported batch job replays and duplicate billing alerts from token accounting.
- Visible spike on customer dashboards and one escalation call with SummitLedger SRE/SPOC.

Timeline (high level):
- 02:01 UTC: Scheduled batch window begins.
- 02:04 UTC: Routing error rates increase; initial alert on gateway 5xx.
- 02:08 UTC: Autoscaler starts scaling but several GPU pools hit allocation failures (no free dedicated capacity).
- 02:12 UTC: Streaming truncation reports from SummitLedger; support ticket opened and oncall paged.
- 02:30 UTC: Mitigation (rate-limited fanout + temporary routing to fallback-small models) applied, error rate reduced.
- 02:35 UTC: Full routing configuration rollback and temporary quota increase for SummitLedger; streaming resume.
- 03:00 UTC: Incident declared over; monitoring resumed and ticket opened for post-incident follow-up.

Environment:
prod - us-east-1, SummitLedger routing policy: heavy fanout -> multi-model multiplexing with prefix caching enabled.

Steps to reproduce (approx):
1) Simulate concurrent EOD job with 12k parallel synth requests using SummitLedger API key and same request prefix.
2) Use long-sequence prompts that trigger KV cache misses to force load on serving runtime.
3) Observe router queue growth, autoscaler allocation attempts and backend 5xx.

Observed logs / metrics (examples):
- gateway: 5xx rate from 0.2% to 8.6% between 02:04-02:20 UTC.
- router: queue depth spike to 17k, per-route tail latency P95 -> 4.3s.
- serving-runtime: "kernel selection failed" occasional traces coincident with memory pressure on quantized variants.
- billing/telemetry: replay window detected ~3k repeat requests for same batch job.

Temporary mitigations applied during incident:
- Enabled an emergency per-customer rate cap for SummitLedger (reduced concurrent fanout by 70%).
- Rerouted a percentage of traffic to smaller, non-quantized model variant to lower memory spikes.
- Increased soft quota for dedicated pool for 45 minutes to allow in-flight replays to drain.

Customer communications: SummitLedger notified via phone and #support escalation channel at 02:20 UTC; formal incident summary shared 03:10 UTC.

Initial root-cause hypothesis: coordinated high-fanout burst from a single customer producing large numbers of cold-kv cache misses, which caused high memory allocation on quantized serving kernels. Autoscaler attempted to spin up additional nodes, but allocation failures and allocation latency led to router queue growth and increased request retries.

Evidence collected:
- Grafana dashboard: https://grafana.redwood/company/summitledger/eod-20260310 (anonymized link included).
- Router logs: multiple allocation_timeout entries around 02:06-02:15 UTC.
- Kernel traces: intermittent kernel selection failures pinned to rwd-7b-v1-quant under long sequences.

Hypotheses tested and outcomes:
- H1 (Autoscaler config limits): rolled out temporary soft quota increase — reduced pressure, median latency improved. (Supported)
- H2 (Model quantization bug under long context): reproduced locally in staging with synthetic load — observed memory growth -> triggered patch to kernel selection. (Supported)
- H3 (Customer job misconfiguration): SummitLedger confirmed batch behavior (identical request prefixes); we recommended jitter and backoff. (Supported)
Immediate fixes applied during incident: emergency rate cap, routing rollback, soft quota increase, and temporary routing to non-quantized variants. Post-incident technical fixes deployed in two releases:
- Routing/backpressure: PR #1428 added per-customer soft fanout limits and early-drop heuristics to the router (deployed 2026-03-12).
- Kernel selection safety: PR #891 adjusted heuristics to avoid quantized path under cold-kv conditions and included a memory guardrail (deployed 2026-03-13).

Customer remediation and follow-up:
- SummitLedger billing team will receive a credit for replayed requests for the impacted window (Finance lead assigned).
- Provided SummitLedger recommended runbook for scheduled EOD windows including suggested request jitter, per-job windowing, and pre-warming KV cache.
- Scheduled a postmortem review with SummitLedger on 2026-03-18 to review changes and long-term mitigation plan.

Current status: incident resolved in platform and customer environment. Monitoring rules updated (synthetic EOD test added) and platform mitigations in prod. Remaining follow-ups tracked below.

Autoscaler team to add capacity allocation timeouts alarm and better retry with jitter (owner: Marcus Lee) - due 2026-03-21
Customer Success to confirm billing credit and send reconciliation to SummitLedger finance (owner: Diego Alvarez) - due 2026-03-15
SRE to add synthetic EOD load test to nightly canary that simulates multi-customer fanout patterns (owner: Marcus Lee) - due 2026-03-22
Docs: publish SummitLedger runbook template for scheduled batch windows (owner: Priya Narang) - due 2026-03-16
Priya Narang (Support) - 2026-03-10T02:22Z: Opened ticket after SummitLedger reported truncated streaming. Included initial metrics from Grafana and request IDs.
Marcus Lee (SRE) - 2026-03-10T02:28Z: Paginated oncall and started live debugging. Hypothesis: sudden coordinated fanout causing autoscaler allocation races and quantized-kernel memory pressure.
Diego Alvarez (Customer Success) - 2026-03-10T02:35Z: Notified SummitLedger CSM and scheduled postmortem call. Customer requested mitigation to avoid replays and billing exposure.
Marcus Lee (SRE) - 2026-03-10T03:05Z: Applied routing rollback and temporary quota bump; error rates back to baseline. Marking incident as contained and creating this follow-up ticket.

Issue summary:
A sustained elevation in 5xx responses originating at the API gateway was observed between 2026-03-12 09:05 UTC and ongoing. Root cause appears tied to an interaction between accept-queue growth and aggressive prefetch / KV warmup on dedicated runtimes, which amplifies upstream latency and triggers GPU preemption (watchdog) on some ephemeral workers.

Impact:
- Customer: VertexDocs (dedicated) reported ~35% failed requests for chat and embedding routes during the window.
- User-facing: increased 5xx and 503/502 responses, elevated tail latency on chat-generation endpoints, degraded throughput for concurrent embedding batches.
- Business: Affected production traffic across a single us-east shard; no billing anomalies reported.

Environment:
- Deployment: Dedicated pool (us-east) serving VertexDocs tenant (dedicated).
- Runtime: inference-runtime v2.14.1 with kernel selection v1.8.
- API Gateway: apigw v3.2.5 behind edge LB.

Steps to reproduce (observed pattern):
1) Sudden concurrent mix of small chat requests (n ~200/s) + large embedding batch uploads from tenant.
2) APIGW accept-queue depth grows > 512 for ~30s; prefetch subsystem begins parallel warmup and KV writes.
3) Serving runtime threads see long blocking latencies (io/warmup) -> backlog -> GPU watchdog preemption on ephemeral workers.
4) Upstream exits / SIGTERM -> APIGW returns 502/503 and hedged retries amplify the load.

Observed behavior / logs:
- APIGW metrics: accept_queue_depth spike to 640, 5xx rate jumped from baseline 0.2% to 18% at 09:06 UTC.
- Runtime logs (ephemeral worker): repeated lines: "GPU watchdog: preempting process (stall detected)" followed by "SIGTERM received - draining" and exit code 137 on a subset of workers.
- Prefetch controller: concurrent_kv_writes = 48 (above recommended 12 for dedicated pool), lock contention traces on kv-shard-17.
- Kernel traces: increased pagefaults and GPU memory fragmentation warnings preceding preempt.

Expected behavior:
- Accept queue should remain within configured thresholds; prefetch concurrency should be throttled before upstream worker preemption occurs. No production-grade runtimes should be preempted by short-lived warmup spikes.

Investigation notes (work in progress):
- Hypothesis A: Prefetch concurrency amplification under mixed small-chat + large-embed workloads causes blocking IO on worker threads, increasing service time and accept-queue growth.
- Hypothesis B: Hedged retry logic at APIGW amplifies already-backlogged requests causing a feedback loop; retries dropped onto the same shard provoke a stampede.
- Observed correlation: workers that hit preemption had higher KV write rates and heavier NVMe iowait.
- Cross-checks: No recent model swap or hotpatch during window. Autoscaler did spawn new ephemeral workers but they entered preempt loops quickly.

Mitigations applied so far:
- Rolled out an immediate temporary APIGW rule to cap hedged retries for the VertexDocs tenant (reduces amplification).
- Reduced prefetch concurrency for the affected dedicated pool from 48 to 8 (config hotpatch) to reduce KV write contention.
- Manually restarted a subset of ephemeral workers after clearing NVMe caches and increasing threadpool IO budget.

Next steps / action items:
- SRE: create a short-term circuit that rejects prefetchs above 16 concurrent per-shard (owner: Ethan Park) - due 2026-03-14.
- Runtime team: add telemetry to correlate kv-write latencies and GPU watchdog triggers (owner: Priya Rao) - due 2026-03-20.
- API gateway: evaluate hedged retry heuristics to avoid retry amplification on accept-queue backpressure (owner: API Platform) - due 2026-03-18.
- Postmortem: capture exact sequence and propose permanent fix (locking/queuing strategy) once full logs are available.

Resolution: Investigating - temporary mitigations in place, traffic restored to ~98% successful for the tenant after mitigations.

Relevant links:
- Grafana: https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/acceptqueue/accept-queue-overview?var=shard=us-east
- Logs (sample): https://logs.redwood.ai/q=SUP-6123456-sample

payload.description:
Issue summary: Multiple dedicated-tenant customers (notably ScribeAI) observed sudden p99 throughput drops during the midday predictive prewarm window. The regression appears as short (2–8 minute) bouts of severe request throttling and queuing on reserved GPU pools, causing inference latency to spike and tail-off in throughput. Impact: Several customers experienced degraded UX in customer-facing flows (chat and embedding pipelines) with 30–60% reduced throughput at p95/p99 and visible client-side timeouts for long-lived streams. Environment: prod-us-east and prod-eu-west dedicated pools, predictive-prewarm enabled, autoscale predictive window 11:30–12:30 UTC. Steps to reproduce: 1) Enable predictive prewarm for a small dedicated customer pool; 2) Run a mixed stream workload (50% short streams, 50% long streams) with ramp to 200 qps; 3) Observe autoscaler prewarm allocations and slot attach logs; 4) During prewarm completion window, send steady background low-CPU health-check streams. Observed behavior: - Autoscaler attempts prewarm allocations but several gpus remain in "allocating" state and do not attach slots for 1–3 minutes. - When allocations finally attach, there's immediate slot serialization: bursts of tiny short streams interleave with long streams producing KV-cache thrash and GPU memory spike; - Platform emits transient "noisy-tenant-eviction" and "slot-attach-timeout" warnings; - Throughput drops even after prewarm completes due to background eviction sweep kicking in. Expected behavior: Prewarm should bring pools to steady-state capacity without introducing eviction sweeps or slot attach timeouts; slot attach time should remain <15s; throughput should ramp without p99 regressions. Logs/metrics referenced: allocator logs (alloc-cycle-2026-03-12T11:29), autoscaler event timeline, per-GPU nvlink/io wait charts, KV-cache size heatmap. Temporary mitigation applied: disabled predictive prewarm for affected pools and applied a short noise-isolation rule (per-tenant short-stream cap) which recovered throughput to baseline within 6 minutes. Next steps: deep-dive autoscaler prewarm/attach path and eviction sweep heuristics; investigate background daemon that triggers eviction sweeps during attach windows; propose a canary change to defer eviction during prewarm window.

Additional notes:
Checked allocator logs: repeated 'slot-attach-timeout' entries at 11:31–11:38 UTC; attach timeouts correlated with increased kernel queue depth on GPUs 2/3 of node.gpu-77 cluster.
KV-cache heatmap shows rapid growth followed by GC spikes exactly at attach retry timestamps; cache growth caused memory pressure and triggered eviction daemon.
Autoscaler event trace: prewarm allocation created, health-check streams started immediately, which kept tiny connections open and increased multiplexing overhead; background eviction daemon has threshold 'inactive-time-seconds' set to 30s which is too low for attach windows.
Network telemetry: no packet loss between control plane and node, but slightly elevated TLS handshake latencies during the period (likely due to node kernel context switching under IO pressure).
Staging repro: synthetic small-stream fanout + predictive prewarm reproduced attach timeout and eviction interplay at lower scale; confirms behavioral hypothesis rather than customer workload peculiarity.
Related PRs: autoscaler backoff change under review (github.com/redwood/autoscaler/pull/112) and allocator attach metrics instrumented (github.com/redwood/realtime-allocator/pull/389).
Cross-check: linked incident SUP-900998 had similar attach-timeout signals but from a different root (training jobs on the same cluster); suggests need for better isolation of prewarm window.
Impact quant: ScribeAI - p99 latency increased from 220ms to 1.9s; throughput (requests/min) dropped by ~48% during incident window.
Emergency mitigation: predictive prewarm disabled for affected tenant pools and a temporary short-stream cap applied to reduce KV-cache thrash. Post-mitigation monitoring shows return to baseline throughput. Planned permanent fix: implement 'prewarm lock' to pause eviction sweeps during prewarm attach windows, increase attach retry backoff, and add an autoscaler feature-flag to avoid prewarm when background eviction load is detected. Canary rollout scheduled for 2026-03-15 02:00 UTC to 5% of dedicated pools, with rollback on p99 degradation. Follow-ups: update prewarm runbook, add alert for 'attach-timeout rate' and 'eviction-during-prewarm' composite signal, and coordinate with capacity planning to ensure prewarm nodes are not co-located with heavy background jobs. Estimated resolution ETA after canary: 5 business days.

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customer (VeloBank, dedicated) reports elevated tail latency and sporadic output token omissions after enabling a tenant-scoped optimizer profile that toggles asynchronous batching, aggressive kv-prefetch, and q4 quantization heuristics. Impact: intermittent 95p/99p latency spikes (+250-600ms) on user-facing generation routes and two customer QA tests showing slight token-drop anomalies leading to classification mismatches.

Impact:
- User-facing latency SLO breaches for a subset of routes (text-generation-chat) seen for ~3 hours during a staged roll.
- Reduced output fidelity in constrained prompts (length ~512) triggering downstream validation failures for two internal tests.

Environment:
- Hosted tenant on Dedicated pool 'db-pool-ve-01' in us-east-1.
- Optimizer profile applied via per-tenant config id: optcfg-20260310-vb (tenant-scoped).

Desired outcome:
- Provide an operational, low-risk reversion plan (orderly reversion) that returns VeloBank to the pre-change baseline with minimal user impact and clear validation checks.

Notes on expectations:
- Customer prefers a conservative, stepwise reversion (traffic gating) rather than an immediate kill-switch.
- Communicate progress in #support and customer Slack channel.

1) Use VeloBank tenant key on prod us-east-1.
2) Send 100 concurrent generation requests with seq length ~512, using model llama-2-70b-q4 on route /v1/generate-chat.
3) Observe 95p/99p latency and final-token omissions in 5-8% of responses.
4) Replay against pre-change snapshot (optcfg-20260307-baseline) to compare.

Instrumentation commands:
- kubectl -n serving-runtime logs -l pool=db-pool-ve-01 --tail=200 | grep optcfg-20260310-vb
- curl "https://api.redwood.example/v1/debug/metrics?tenant=velobank&pool=db-pool-ve-01"

Excerpt (03/10 14:22 UTC):
[serving-runtime][INFO] tenant=velobank raft=ok apply_opt_profile optcfg-20260310-vb
[runtime][WARN] model=llama-2-70b-q4 evict_kvcache miss_rate=0.18 latency_ms=42
[batcher][DEBUG] async_batch: target_size=32 observed=12 timeout_ms=15
[quant][INFO] q4-path loaded kernel=fast_matmul q_scale=0.98
[router][ERROR] route=generate-chat downstream_timeout=500ms failures=3

Initial hypotheses:
- Aggressive async batching with low target_size + short timeouts is causing frequent smaller batches and more context-switch overhead under this workload distribution.
- KV prefetch interaction with q4 quant kernels may cause elevated eviction churn for mid-length prompts (512), leading to repeated cache misses and excess KV recomputation.
- Quantization path may be slightly changing tokenization/decoding around rare tokens resulting in token-drop anomalies for specific prompts.
Evidence collected:
- Trace spans show higher scheduling overhead for batcher (avg scheduling delay +32ms).
- Telemetry shows 18% kvcache miss rate vs baseline 6%.
- Regression only appears on the optimized tenant profile; collocated tenants on same pool unaffected.
Actions taken so far:
- Captured pcap of request timing and a 1-hour perf trace.
- Scoped feature-flag to tenant.
- Notified SRE to observe pool-level GPU utilization.

Short-term mitigations suggested to customer:
- Revert tenant config to optcfg-20260307-baseline (recommended when low-impact window available).
- If immediate revert not possible: reduce async_batch target_size to 8 and increase timeout_ms to 75 to lower scheduling overhead; disable kv-prefetch for this tenant only.
- Route critical traffic to a healthy fallback model variant (redwood-xl-1.0 fp16) while reversion occurs.

Orderly reversion playbook (stepwise, low-risk):
1) Prepare rollback snapshot: verify existence of optcfg-20260307-baseline and capture current live snapshot optcfg-20260310-vb-snapshot for audit.
2) Canary revert: update 5% of traffic for tenant to baseline via traffic-split rule (console -> Routes -> Traffic Split). Monitor latency percentiles and token fidelity checks for 15 minutes.
3) If canary stable: increment to 25% for another 10 minutes, then 50%, then full 100% with 10-minute observation windows.
4) If any regression during canary, immediately abort and restore previous traffic split; capture additional traces and escalate to runtime eng.
5) Post-switch validation: run customer QA test suite (provided by VeloBank) and internal regression prompt-set (regset-opt-512). Confirm 99p latency back within baseline +/- 10ms and zero token-drop regressions in sample set.
6) Hard fallback option: if traffic-split fails or the config is irreconcilable, perform full tenant config replace to baseline and drain running sessions gracefully (allow current requests to finish up to 30s).
7) Communication: update ticket and customer Slack channel at each stage and publish short postmortem within 48 hours.

- Eng: run a controlled A/B experiment to isolate kv-prefetch vs q4 interaction (PR instrumented).
- Runtime: add a temporary debug metric for batcher scheduling delay per-tenant.
- Product: review per-tenant optimizer tuning UI to include preflight simulation and 'revert-to-snapshot' button.
- Documentation: add a 'stepwise reversion' section to the support runbook and link to this ticket.

Additional notes:
2026-03-10 17:05 - VeloBank-SRE (customer): We can accept a staged revert. Please start with 5% and we will run QA. Keeping on-call ready for immediate rollback.
2026-03-11 10:20 - VeloBank-Eng: All targeted QA tests green. Request full revert during low-traffic window 02:00-03:00 UTC.

FinNova (enterprise customer) requests an auditable evidence pack to satisfy an upcoming regulatory review. They need a concise attestation of the retention policy in effect for tenant-scoped audit logs, plus a representative SIEM ingest sample and a per-field redaction/pseudonymization map so their internal auditors can verify compliance with their consent records.

Impact:

Requested deliverables (customer-provided format and acceptance criteria):
1) Retention attestation PDF: clear statement of retention windows for raw audit events, processed SIEM feeds, and long-term logs; include change history since 2024-01-01 and an RFC3161 timestamped signature or equivalent HSM-backed proof.
2) SIEM ingest sample: 24-hour contiguous export covering UTC 2026-02-28 00:00 to 2026-02-28 23:59 (gzipped Parquet preferred). Include manifest.csv with record counts, per-file SHA256, and resume token for replay.

payload.description:
Issue summary:
A sustained burst (t≈14:05–14:22 UTC) of large multipart inference upload requests from a single ScribeAI tenant triggered a rapid elevation in 5xx responses from the API gateway and multiple serving-runtime worker processes in their dedicated GPU pool became unresponsive (hung) leading to cascading failures and elevated error rate for the tenant.

Impact:
- Customer-facing latency and error rate spike: ~40% 5xx for tenant traffic during the window.
- Some long-running streaming sessions failed to resume and required client reconnects.
- ScribeAI reports degraded user experience for end-users ingesting long transcripts.

Environment:
- Redwood hosted dedicated pool (tenant-dedicated) in us-west (prod).
- Customer request pattern: multipart upload of combined prompt+context payloads (~20–60MB per request) with concurrent fanout of 18–24 requests.
- Affected models: rw-v1.2-large (primary), fallback to rw-quant-4bit observed.

Steps to reproduce (observed):
1) Customer submitted concurrent multipart/large-body inference requests (range 18–60MB) over HTTP/2 to hosted API endpoint.
2) API gateway accepted connections and proxied to tenant-dedicated serving runtime.
3) Around the third burst minute, gateway started returning 502/503/504 to client; runtimes showed threads stuck in prefetch and kernel-init.
4) Autoscaler attempted to spin new nodes but warmup + prefetch pressure caused further backpressure.

Observed behavior (logs & metrics):
- API gateway: 5xx rate jump from baseline ~0.5% to 42% for tenant route (14:05–14:22 UTC).
- Serving-runtime: multiple worker processes in dedicated pool reported "prefetch timeout waiting for KV cache" and then entered a "hung" state (no heartbeat) before being restarted by watchdog.
- Kernel logs (host): increased pagefaults and elevated GPU context switching; several processes blocked on epoll for extended periods.
- Autoscaler: attempted adds at 14:08 and 14:12; newly provisioned nodes remained underutilized because existing prefetch/backpressure blocked request progress.
- Client error pattern: repeated retries from client produced retry-amplification spikes.

Relevant log snippets (redacted):
[serving-runtime-2026-03-14T14:09:23Z] WARN prefetch: timeout_wait(15s) waiting for kv-prefetch for tenant t-4321 request r-9d2c
[serving-runtime-2026-03-14T14:09:27Z] ERROR runtime: worker-hang-detected pid=22417 trace=stuck-in-prefetch
[apigw-2026-03-14T14:10:11Z] ERROR upstream: 502 connect error, received reset from upstream
[autoscaler-2026-03-14T14:12:04Z] INFO scaleup: initiated 2 nodes for pool tenant-t-4321

Expected behavior:
- Large multipart uploads should be accepted and either handled by prefetch with bounded memory and queueing or throttled/429'd at the gateway if they exceed per-tenant concurrency/size thresholds.

Business/customer notes:
- ScribeAI (production workload) experienced a user-impacting outage for ~17 minutes. They are on a dedicated reserved capacity plan and expect predictable availability.

Additional context:
- Customer had recently increased concurrency in their client rollout; they were not previously rate-limited by our standard quotas because requests were within per-request size limits but combined concurrency led to resource exhaustion.

Timeline & findings:
- 14:05 UTC: first surge of concurrent multipart uploads (observed from tenant ingress logs).
- 14:07 UTC: API gateway 5xx begins to increase. Threshold hit at 14:09 UTC.
- 14:09–14:15 UTC: serving-runtime workers show repeated prefetch timeouts and blocked IO; watchdog restarts attempted at 14:11 and 14:14.
- 14:12 UTC: Autoscaler started provisioning nodes but warmup sequence requires successful prefetches which were blocked.
- 14:17 UTC: customer reduced concurrency; error rate returned to baseline by 14:22 after gradual recovery and worker restarts.

Hypotheses considered:
1) Prefetch path lock contention + large payloads caused per-worker event loop stalls, preventing progress and causing backlog at gateway.
2) KV-cache memory fragmentation leading to slower allocations for large multipart frames under heavy concurrent churn.
3) Client-side retry amplification (no jitter) exacerbated pressure.

Evidence supporting hypothesis 1:
- Thread dumps show multiple workers blocked in same prefetch code path with identical stacks.
- Heap and GC metrics did not indicate immediate OOMs but allocation latency spiked.

Short-term mitigation applied:
- Support applied an emergency gateway soft-throttle rule for tenant t-4321 at 14:13 UTC to limit concurrent in-flight requests to 6 and enforced a 30s slow-down window for large uploads. This stopped the immediate amplification and allowed the runtime workers to drain.
- Instrumented additional logging around prefetch queues to capture future occurrences.

Next steps (ongoing):
- Engineering: create a targeted fix to make prefetch queueing non-blocking for oversized multipart uploads and add per-worker concurrency heuristics (owner: Marco Nguyen, ETA 2026-03-18).
- SRE: add a tenant-level circuit breaker that returns 429 for large-body concurrent bursts beyond configured safe thresholds (owner: Linh Tran, ETA 2026-03-17).
- Product/Support: review default per-tenant size/concurrency guidance and update onboarding docs to recommend staged concurrency ramp for large uploads.

Aisha Patel (Support) 2026-03-14T14:20Z: Initial triage complete. Applied temporary gateway soft-throttle to stabilize tenant traffic. Escalating to SRE/Eng because runtimes are showing worker hangs.
Marco Nguyen (Eng) 2026-03-14T15:02Z: Confirmed repeated thread stacks in prefetch path. Reproduced high-concurrency local test to validate blocking behavior; filing engineering task for non-blocking prefetch change.
Linh Tran (SRE) 2026-03-14T15:40Z: Autoscaler behavior reviewed; warmup dependency on successful prefetch is causing scale-up to be ineffective under prefetch stalls. Will decouple warmup gating for tenant pools as short-term measure.
Customer (ScribeAI) 2026-03-14T16:05Z: Confirmed that reducing their client concurrency to <=6 reduced errors; requested a postmortem and permanent fix timeline.
Workaround applied: soft-throttle (gateway) for tenant concurrent large uploads and temporary client-side recommendation to cap concurrency at 6 for large multipart payloads.
Engineering action plan: implement non-blocking prefetch queue and add per-worker concurrency limits; add tenant-level circuit breaker for oversized bursts; decouple autoscaler warmup gating from prefetch success.
Follow-up: schedule postmortem with ScribeAI and product to review onboarding limits and SLA expectations. Targeted engineering patches and tests are in progress; hopeful rollback of soft-throttle after deploy if tests pass.
payload.summary: Burst of large multipart inference uploads causes rapid 5xx spike and serving-runtime hung processes in dedicated pool
