Issue summary:
Customer reports streaming requests with extremely large max_tokens (50k-100k) intermittently finish sending early or return HTTP 504/Client deadline exceeded after long periods of partial output. Time-to-first-byte is normal; latencies spike toward the tail of the generation and final chunks are delayed beyond client deadlines.

Impact:
- Affected customer: LexiSearch (enterprise) using hosted API for document synthesis workflows.
- Observed on ~15% of large-output requests during peak traffic windows; otherwise successful.
- Customer observed multiple aborted exports and retries; material impact to their SLA.

Environment:
- Hosted production (prod-us-east-1)
- Streaming=true, max_tokens=80000 (customer-provided), model pinned to redwood/open-llama-13b-quant-v2
- Request pattern: long system prompt (priming ~200k chars) + multi-document context; sustained token emission for >2 minutes.

Steps to reproduce:
1) Create request with streaming=true, max_tokens=80000, context ~120k tokens (multi-doc priming).
2) Send simultaneous 6 requests from a single customer API key (to exercise per-key concurrency).
3) Observe generation progress and streaming frames; measure ttfb, inter-chunk gaps, finalization time.

Observed behavior:
- First ~95% of tokens stream normally with expected throughput.
- Finalization stalls: gap of 30s-90s between last streamed chunk and final chunk, often causing client deadline exceeded or HTTP 504.
- Runtime logs show finisher queue backlog and executor slot starvation; KV-cache evictions spike concurrently.
- Some requests are dropped with 5xx from scheduler when finisher cannot obtain GPU slot for finalization.

Expected behavior:
- Continuous chunked streaming to completion without long tail gaps; graceful fallback to a smaller model variant or throttled continuation if resources constrained.

Logs & tracing:
- Traces: https://console.redwood.ai/traces/trace-431210 (redacted)
- Grafana dashboard (tail-latency): https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/finisher/stream-tail-latency?var-region=us-east
- Excerpt from runtime logs (attached as plain text):
  - "finisher.queue.wait_ms=31234; active_executors=0; idle_executors=2; kv_evictions=43"
  - "scheduler: request_promoted_to_backlog due to executor shortage"

Workaround applied:
- Support applied temporary policy: per-key concurrent request limit reduced to 3 and max_tokens soft cap at 40k for LexiSearch; this restored successful completions but reduces throughput.

Business impact / customer notes:
- Customer experiencing missed nightly exports and has requested timeboxed remediation.
- Account team escalated; customer asked for ETA for a permanent fix.

Additional notes:
RuntimEng Oncall (2026-03-13): Hypothesis: long-lived KV cache for very deep context causing memory compaction and executor preemption during finalization. Captured heap and eviction traces.
Support Manager - Elena Ortiz (2026-03-14): Requesting prioritized patch to finisher queue backpressure and a model-fallback policy for resource-constrained tail emissions. Please attach linked PRs and runbook updates.
Hypothesis 1: Executor slot starvation — finalization requires an exclusive executor and long contexts hold KV resources longer, blocking other finishers.
Hypothesis 2: KV-cache eviction thrashing — frequent eviction during high-context workloads causes page faults and stalls in the finisher pipeline.
Metric snapshots (2026-03-12 22:00 UTC): finisher_queue_length peaked at 37; finisher_tail_latency_p90 = 78s; kv_eviction_rate increased 6x versus baseline.
Reproduced with controlled load: same pattern observed when simulating 4 concurrent ultra-long requests on a medium-sized pod.
Temporary mitigation (throttling) reduced finisher_queue_length to <5 and tail latency p90 to 12s for the customer traffic slice.
Next artifacts to gather: core dumps from executor if preempted, per-request KV cache sizes, and scheduling/placement logs for the affected pod IDs.
Mitigation in place: per-customer throttling and soft max_tokens cap applied (manual override). No code fix deployed yet. Next steps: implement automatic finisher backpressure that will either (a) spill long tail to a lower-cost executor pool, (b) trigger model-fallback to a smaller variant when finalizer wait exceeds threshold, and (c) improve KV eviction policy to avoid thrashing. Target patch PR scheduled for 2026-03-19; runtime team to validate with synthetic workloads and customer test.
payload.summary: Intermittent finisher-starvation causing request timeouts on ultra-long max_tokens streaming requests

payload.description:
Customer reports that Optimize "Enable prefix caching" recommendation shows 65–80% cost savings for their chat workload, which they believe is not achievable given their prompt variability and low cache hit rate.

Issue summary:
- Optimize UI what-if ROI for caching shows very large savings.
- Customer believes actual cache hit rate is low (~10–25%) and that estimates should reflect warm-up / low reuse.

Impact:
- Customer questions credibility of Optimize ROI and Redwood cost methodology.
- Risk: sales cycle slowdown and additional CS time.

Customer context:
- Arcadia LegalTech is evaluating Optimize for a regulated workload with heavy system prompts + per-user context. They report high prompt diversity (low expected prefix reuse).

Observed behavior:
- Optimize ROI card shows large delta in "cache savings" with little/no downside.
- When customer runs A/B manually, realized savings are materially lower.

Suspected root cause (initial triage):
- Cache warm-rate / cache re-use assumptions in what-if projection appear to be effectively set to 1.0 (100% warm), even when workload is not warm.
- Potential mismatch between Optimize input field naming and Cost Model API what-if parameter semantics.

Example (from customer screenshot and our reproduction in prod via internal tooling):
- Baseline: ~2.1M tokens/day, p95 latency steady, no caching enabled.
- What-if: caching enabled; estimated savings ~72%.
- Request appears to omit an explicit cache warm-rate / warmness parameter; backend defaults to a best-case assumption.

Requested outcome:
1) Correct the default assumptions so what-if projections are conservative unless provided workload measurements.
2) Clarify schema semantics and document which fields are required vs optional for cache what-if accuracy.
3) Provide customer-facing explanation and updated estimate using their real cache hit/warm-rate.

Internal notes:
- This ticket is specifically about what-if ROI estimates being optimistic, not invoice mismatch. See SUP-31844 for Console vs invoice discrepancies.

Additional notes:
Action: propose changing default to 'unknown' => returns a bounded range + requires Optimize to pass a workload-derived estimate when available. We also need to avoid breaking Console callers (Console shouldn’t be using what-if today).
Also filing internal follow-up to update schema docs + UI defaults.
1) Cost Model API what-if: change omission behavior from best-case to conservative-default (e.g., warm_rate defaults to 0.2 unless caller supplies, or returns an error/warning requiring explicit input). Prefer returning 'warnings' in response + range.
2) Update schema docs to explicitly define 'cache_warm_rate' and whether it represents (a) probability of warm cache at request start vs (b) expected prefix reuse/hit probability.
3) Add validation guardrails to reject warm_rate > 0.95 unless workload explicitly claims stable prefixes.
Need signoff from Optimize + PM for behavior change (may change numbers).
- assumptions_used: list (as a string list in our logs; for API can return warnings)
- confidence: low/med/high
- savings_range: [min,max] (we can encode as string fields if needed)
Even if v1 doesn’t support full CIs, we should at least surface 'assumed_warm_cache=true' in the response so UI can communicate it.
I’ll coordinate a hotfix to set default to null/unset and show "Using measured cache hit rate" when available.

- Cost Model API team to clarify schema semantics (doc update) and add a response warning when warm-rate is omitted (tracked separately).
Closing this support ticket since customer is unblocked and understands the corrected estimate.

Customer was provided corrected estimates using telemetry-derived cache hit rate (~18% avg; ~10–25% range). Optimize updated to omit warm-rate unless explicitly set or derived from telemetry; schema/semantics documentation to be clarified by platform.
Until the UI fix rolled out, support recommended setting cache warm-rate explicitly to a conservative value (0.1–0.25) in the advanced what-if configuration and interpreting results as steady-state only if the workload is known to be warm.

Add Cost Model API what-if response warnings/assumptions so Optimize can display them (owner: Ethan Park / Jonas Weber).
Add guardrails to prevent best-case defaults in what-if paths and require explicit user intent for warm_rate > 0.9 (owner: Platform team; aligns with policy guardrails work).
Add a small QA test fixture for caching what-if with warm_rate omitted to prevent regression (owner: Leila Farouk).

payload.description:
Issue summary
Aurora Health Systems reports that when they receive overload responses (503 / occasionally 429) from Hosted API, the Retry-After header is not present on some routes. Their client relies on Retry-After for backoff; without it they either retry too aggressively (risking retry storms) or back off too conservatively (causing request latency spikes and user-facing delays).

Impact
- Affected: production traffic; customer reported intermittent failures during peak periods
- Customer-visible symptoms:
  - HTTP 503 with Redwood overload JSON payload but missing Retry-After
  - Some responses include Retry-After correctly, leading to inconsistent client behavior
- Business risk: customer flagged this as an enterprise requirement for safe overload handling and asked whether this is "expected" during the canary.

Environment
- Product: Hosted API (chat/completions + streaming)
- Regions observed: us-east primary; eu-west noted once
- Tenant: enterprise hosted (Aurora Health Systems)

Customer evidence
1) Missing header example (from customer logs)
- Endpoint: POST /v1/chat/completions (stream=false)
- Response: 503
- Headers: includes x-redwood-request-id, missing Retry-After
- Body: error.code=overloaded, error.type=overload_error

2) Header present example (same client, same day)
- Endpoint: POST /v1/embeddings
- Response: 429
- Headers: Retry-After: 2

Steps to reproduce (internal)
1. Generate synthetic overload by applying a low per-tenant concurrency cap in staging OR run perf-canary burst scenario.
2. Issue requests against multiple routes:
   - /v1/chat/completions
   - /v1/completions
   - /v1/embeddings
3. Observe that Retry-After is only reliably set when admission control rejects at gateway; when overload is returned from downstream routing/runtime path, header may be absent.

Expected behavior
All overload responses that instruct clients to retry should include Retry-After with a stable, bounded value per ADR-014 and overload retry contract.

Actual behavior
Retry-After missing for some overload errors (notably 503) depending on where overload is triggered (gateway vs downstream).

Initial hypothesis
Mismatch between overload error mapping layer (gateway middleware) and downstream overload responses: downstream returns a structured JSON error but does not set headers; gateway sometimes passes body through without applying header normalization.

Notes
This is likely related to the ongoing canary rollout for hosted overload protection; customer is seeing the new overload taxonomy in production.

2025-11-19 09:12 PT — Dev Patel (Support) — Opened ticket after Aurora escalation via Support channel. Customer request: "Please confirm Retry-After will always be present when you return overloaded errors; we need a deterministic backoff signal." Added two example responses to internal notes (redacted).
2025-11-19 10:03 PT — Owen Phillips (Escalations) — Confirmed customer is enterprise hosted and running automated retries in a health workflow integration. Asked Eng to treat as canary/GA-blocker candidate because inconsistent Retry-After can cause retry storms.
2025-11-19 11:22 PT — Amara Diallo (Gateway) — Looked at gateway code path: admission-control middleware sets Retry-After on overload rejects it generates. However, when upstream service returns a 503 overload JSON, we currently do not normalize/add Retry-After unless the error is produced by the gateway overload handler. Needs a post-processing step for overload-classified errors from downstream.
2025-11-19 13:40 PT — Christine Wong (Overload Protection) — Correlated with overload metrics: customer requests were shed both at gateway (token bucket) and at runtime saturation (queue depth). Only gateway sheds had Retry-After. This matches customer report (embeddings had 429 w/ header; chat had 503 w/o header).
2025-11-20 08:15 PT — Amara Diallo (Gateway) — Implemented hotfix to apply Retry-After for any response classified as overload_error by error mapper (regardless of origin), unless Retry-After already set. Also ensures x-redwood-request-id present. Opened PR: sources/github/redwood/pr-18472-load-shedding-retry-after-and-client-guidance.json.
2025-11-20 10:07 PT — Ethan Park (Control Plane) — Reviewed and approved approach. Guardrail: do not add Retry-After to non-overload 5xx; only apply when stable overload code is detected (e.g., overloaded, breaker_open, dependency_overloaded).
2025-11-20 15:30 PT — Connor O'Brien (Release) — Rolled out to staging; verified with synthetic overload in chat/completions and completions: Retry-After now present on both 429 and 503 overload responses. Proceeding with production canary in us-east (5% tenants) behind overload_protection.retry_after_normalization flag.
2025-11-21 09:50 PT — Aisha Bello (SRE) — Monitoring canary: no increase in 5xx, shed rate unchanged, p99 stable. Confirmed headers present in sampled logs for overload responses (gateway + downstream).
2025-11-21 14:05 PT — Dev Patel (Support) — Updated customer: fix in progress, targeted rollout by end of day us-east then eu-west. Provided interim guidance: fallback to exponential backoff with jitter when Retry-After absent, cap retries, and respect idempotency keys for replays.
2025-11-22 10:18 PT — Connor O'Brien (Release) — Rollout complete: 100% prod us-east + eu-west. Verified in logs for Aurora tenant: overload 503 responses now include Retry-After: 1–3 seconds (bounded).
2025-11-22 11:02 PT — Dev Patel (Support) — Customer confirmed receipt of Retry-After in recent overload responses and reduced retry-related error bursts. Moving ticket to Resolved; will close after 3 business days if no regression.
Root cause: Retry-After header was only set for overload responses generated directly by gateway admission-control. Overload responses originating from downstream routing/runtime returned the correct overload JSON payload but were passed through without header normalization.

Fix: Gateway now normalizes overload-classified responses to include Retry-After (unless already present) and ensures correlation headers are consistent. Shipped via hotfix PR-18472 and rolled out progressively (staging → us-east canary → us-east+eu-west full).

Customer-facing guidance: Clients should respect Retry-After when present, use exponential backoff with jitter as a fallback, and avoid unbounded retries to prevent retry storms.
payload.summary: Retry-After header missing on some overload (503/429) responses for Hosted API (enterprise tenant)

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customer reports streaming chat sessions (SSE and websocket) dropping to a silent closed state mid-response when overall capacity in the dedicated GPU pool is high. The stream shows steady bytes then connection is closed by server with no final token or error payload.

Impact:
- ScaleChat reports 8-12% of long (>15s) streaming responses in eu-west are cut off or closed abruptly during peak windows; user-facing experience: partial replies with no retry token.
- Affects production customers on dedicated pools using vicuna-13b family.

Environment:
- Dedicated capacity (committed GPUs) in eu-west.
- Model: redwood/vicuna-13b-openai-like (pinned by customer).
- Client types: SSE (EventSource) and WebSocket.

Steps to reproduce (customer):
1) Open a streaming chat request with long generation target (200-800 tokens).
2) Keep generating during 15:00-17:00 UTC (peak).
3) Observe stream producing tokens for ~20-40s then abruptly close (client receives close/no final chunk).

Observed behavior:
- No explicit 5xx returned to client before closure. Socket reports abnormal close (code 1006) for Ws; SSE client sees connection close without last "data: [DONE]".
- Server-side worker logs show SIGKILL or worker process ended around same timestamp for some sessions.

Expected behavior:
- Stream continues until generation completes or returns clear error payload with retry/resume token.

Relevant logs/headers (redacted):
- Proxy keepalive: OK.
- Example server log lines:
  [2026-03-12T16:11:23Z] stream_session_id=abc123 status=producing token_count=124
  [2026-03-12T16:11:55Z] stream_session_id=abc123 status=producing token_count=238
  [2026-03-12T16:11:56Z] scheduler:eviction action=terminate target=worker-17 reason=memory_pressure priority=low session=abc123
  [2026-03-12T16:11:56Z] worker-17 exit_code=137 pid=15234

Attachments:
- Customer provided client timestamps and SDK logs (attached).

Additional notes:
2026-03-12 - Customer (ScaleChat): Provided 12 example session ids and SDK logs showing abrupt close at 16:11-16:17 UTC. Confirmed impact window aligns with their traffic spikes.
2026-03-13 - Support (Aisha): Shared mitigation steps with customer: 1) enable session_priority=high in their routing profile to avoid preemption, 2) enable client-side resume token handling. Customer applied session_priority change for a subset of requests for testing.
2026-03-13 - Engineering (Liam): Deployed hotfix to scheduler (PR 290) to reserve N streaming slots per GPU and to change preemption signal to graceful-terminate then forced-kill after delay. Deployed runtime patch v1.12.3 to ensure worker returns error payload before exit when possible.
2026-03-13 - Customer (ScaleChat): Verified reduced occurrence in subset; long streams continued through peak for sessions with session_priority=high. Observed remaining failures drop from ~10% to ~1%.
Correlated customer session timestamps with scheduler logs and worker exit codes (exit_code=137 indicates OOM or forced kill).
Reproduced in staging by simulating mixed workload: streaming long generations + background batch finetune jobs causing transient memory pressure.
Root cause hypothesis: scheduler allowed low-priority streaming sessions to be preempted immediately under memory pressure; preemption used immediate kill which prevented runtime from flushing final token/error to the client.
Observed that SSE/WebSocket clients do not receive a server-side error when process is killed; proxy connection close occurs without final chunk.
Mitigation validated: reserving streaming slots and making preemption graceful preserves client-visible error or completes generation.
Mitigations applied: 1) Scheduler change merged (PR 290) to reserve 4 streaming slots per GPU and to send SIGTERM to workers before SIGKILL; 2) Runtime v1.12.3 deployed which attempts to emit final error frames on graceful termination; 3) Customer advised to set session_priority=high on critical streaming routes and to upgrade SDK to support resume tokens. Post-deploy verification in eu-west shows failures reduced from ~10% to ~1% for ScaleChat. Follow-up item: scheduler autoscaler policy will be updated (INT-1182) to avoid evicting active streams during scale-down windows.
Postmortem pointer: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/INF/Streaming+Eviction+Postmortem (to be populated by on-call)
Ticket resolved after customer verification and monitoring thresholds established.

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customer is orchestrating a multi-step workflow using the Redwood function-calling feature. Each step invokes an external downstream system via a webhook (payment, inventory, and notification). They want a recommended strategy to guarantee at-most-once business effects when partial failures occur mid-chain and to reconcile when retries or SDK-level reconnects cause duplicate tool invocations.

Impact:
- Intermittent duplicate downstream side effects (double-payment, duplicate shipment record) reported by customer logs.
- Customer has temporarily paused new runs in production while they validate compensation logic.
- Business impact: potential duplicate billing and operational overhead for customer success teams.

Environment:
- Customer runs Redwood-hosted API with enterprise plan and VPC peering to their systems.
- SDKs used: Python 0.9.x for orchestration service, TypeScript 1.3.x for webhooks.
- Region: us-east.

Steps to reproduce (customer-provided):
1) Orchestrator (Python) issues a request to create an order and includes an idempotency_key in top-level request metadata.
2) Model returns a sequence of function calls: charge_payment -> allocate_inventory -> send_confirmation. The orchestrator executes webhooks for each tool call.
3) During allocate_inventory webhook, the webhook endpoint times out (504) while the orchestration client sees a partial network failure and attempts to reconnect/retry.
4) SDK reconnect results in the model re-sending the allocate_inventory tool call in a resumed stream; the webhook endpoint processed the original request but the retry leads to a duplicate inventory booking.

Customer's current implementation notes:
- They attach a UUID as idempotency_key at the request level but do not propagate per-tool call ids to downstream webhooks.
- They rely on downstream systems to dedupe by matching order IDs, but some downstream queues are eventual-consistent (visibility delay) so duplicates slip through.

Logs / evidence (sanitized):
- Orchestrator (Python) trace: request_id=abc123, idempotency_key=order-7f2b, stream_resume=true, resend_tool=allocate_inventory
- Webhook endpoint logs: received allocate_inventory with order_ref=order-7f2b at 2026-03-09T18:22:11Z (processed), then another request at 2026-03-09T18:22:29Z (processed)
- Downstream ledger shows two inventory reservations for the same order_ref; second reservation has different reservation_id.

What the customer is asking:
- Best-practice pattern to ensure at-most-once semantics for chained tool calls invoked by the model when using Redwood streaming + function-calling, across Python and TS SDKs.
- Guidance on idempotency key scoping (request-level vs per-tool) and how to propagate ids through SDKs and webhooks.
- Recommendations for compensation/rollback strategies when partial failure is unavoidable.

Attachments provided by customer:
- sanitized logs.txt
- minimal reproducible orchestrator script (Python)

Orchestrator issues request with top-level idempotency_key
Model returns sequence of function calls charge_payment -> allocate_inventory -> send_confirmation
allocate_inventory webhook times out; orchestrator reconnects and stream resumes
Model re-sends allocate_inventory and webhook processes duplicate

Additional notes:
Customer (J. Reynolds, 2026-03-11): Provided headers: X-Redwood-Idempotency: order-7f2b, X-Tool-Call-Id: (not present currently). Confirmed Python SDK uses automatic stream resume. Mentioned TS webhook service runs behind a queue with eventual visibility.
SRE (Nadia Ruiz, 2026-03-11): Observed increased connection churn in us-east for the customer's VPC connection between 18:20-18:25 UTC. Suggested adding dedupe keys at the tool-call level as a mitigation while investigating network retries.
Hypothesis: Top-level idempotency_key prevents duplicate top-level request processing, but does not prevent duplicate downstream side effects when the model re-emits the same tool call after a streaming resume.
Confirmed SDK behavior: Python SDK auto-resumes streaming and will re-deliver model tool call events when the client reconnects unless the SDK application has already acknowledged processing those events with an explicit marker.
Customer's downstream services do not currently accept a per-tool-call idempotency token; they dedupe by order_ref which can be delayed by queue visibility causing duplicates.
SRE found brief network instability; retries occurred within the SDK which led to replays of tool events. No back-end duplicate suppression at Redwood API layer for per-tool calls in this customer's setup.
Per-tool-call idempotency: Generate and propagate a tool_call_id for every tool invocation. Include it as a header (X-Tool-Call-Id) and as part of the webhook payload. Downstream systems should persist tool_call_id and reject duplicates before executing side effects.
At-most-once pattern: Orchestrator should persist processed tool_call_ids in a local durable store (e.g., Redis, DB) before triggering downstream side effects; if a tool_call_id is seen again, short-circuit and return stored result.
Acknowledgement protocol: Have webhook endpoints return a 202 with a body that includes processed_tool_call_id and a short-lived receipt. The SDK should record acknowledgment before resuming or retrying.
Compensation approach: For non-idempotent steps (payment), implement a two-phase flow or use a dedicated payment 'reverse' operation. Maintain a compensating action log keyed by tool_call_id to drive retries/rollbacks asynchronously.
SDK improvements: Propose SDK change to automatically attach per-tool-call id (UUIDv4) into metadata and expose it on the event object so that client code can forward it to webhooks without extra plumbing.
Short-term mitigation: Customer can disable automatic stream resume in the Python SDK during a critical rollout and instead implement manual resume and explicit ack semantics until downstream dedupe is in place.
Operational: Add a temporary proxy in front of webhooks that deduplicates by tool_call_id for 1 minute window to catch replays caused by transient retries.
Engineering: Draft SDK PRs to expose per-tool-call ids and opt-in ack API (assigned to @eng-llm-runtime).
Support: Share sample Python and TS code snippets to propagate X-Tool-Call-Id to downstream webhooks (assigned to Liam).
Customer: Implement small dedupe cache or DB persistence for processed tool_call_ids (suggested TTL 24h) and enable 202 ack response pattern (suggested owner: Acme devops).
SRE: Continue investigating underlying VPC connection churn and provide timeline (assigned to Nadia).
2026-03-12: Provided customer with immediate mitigations and sample code. Customer implemented short-term dedupe proxy and saw no duplicates in a 6-hour smoke run.
Planned SDK work: Engineering agreed to a non-breaking change to expose tool_call_id on event objects; PRs linked above. ETA for release: 2026-04-02.
Follow-up: Schedule a joint runbook review with Acme Health to update their orchestrator to persist tool_call_ids and to adopt compensation patterns for payment failures.
payload.summary: Guidance for idempotency & compensation pattern across chained function calls (Python + TS SDKs)

Rafael Ortega: Confirmed churn in allocation; requested full allocation traces and node-level GPU utilization profiles.

payload.description:
Issue summary: Customers on a dedicated GPU pool (LexiDocs Inc.) are seeing periodic throughput collapses and p95/p99 latency spikes coinciding with short-lived high-concurrency bursts of tiny microbatches (<=8 tokens). Impact: Multiple end-to-end requests for LexiDocs indexing and chat features failed to meet latency SLOs; observed client retries and increased token cost due to repeated partial responses. Environment: Dedicated pool (reserved) in us-west-2, production, mixed model routing pinned to redwood/rwkv-7b and open/gpt-13b-quant. Observed behavior: - Repeated pulses of queued requests lasting 20-90s producing p99 latency spikes from baseline ~120ms to ~1.1-1.4s. - Aggregate throughput drops by ~40-55% during pulses. - GPU attach/allocate churn: GPUs appear briefly under-utilized (5-10%) then rapidly pinned (90%+) as many tiny worklets hammer the scheduler. - Autoscaler does not add capacity because burst windows are shorter than scale-up cooldown and allocation heuristics consider bursts ephemeral. Expected behavior: Stable throughput with gradual autoscaler scale-up for sustained increases in demand, and fairness across tenants preventing a small-connection flood from causing global queue serialization. Temporary workaround attempted: Apply per-tenant connection throttling at the ingress and enable microbatch coalescing in the serving runtime for the customer's routes. Workaround reduced severity but did not fully eliminate pulses.
1) Run a synthetic client that opens 600 concurrent short-lived streams targeting a single dedicated tenant route with requests that produce <=8 token outputs. 2) Send bursts of 100 requests every 200ms for 60 seconds. 3) Observe queue length, scheduler latency, and GPU allocation metrics via the dedicated pool dashboard. 4) Repeat with microbatching disabled and enabled to compare behavior.

[2026-03-13T09:12:19Z] gpu-alloc: attach start: node=pool-dedicated-37, reqs=18
[2026-03-13T09:12:19Z] gpu-alloc: attach complete: latency=980ms, alloc_failure=false
[2026-03-13T09:12:20Z] runtime: microbatch-coalescer: coalesced=12->1 in-flight microbatches
[2026-03-13T09:12:21Z] autoscaler: no-scale decision: short-burst threshold not met (burst_duration=22s)
[2026-03-13T09:12:22Z] serving-runtime: p99-token-latency=1.28s, throughput_drop=48%
Observed high churn in allocation traces: lots of short attach/detach calls that coincide with request bursts.
Kernel-level GPU utilization shows oscillation (5% -> 95%) on affected nodes, indicating many tiny kernels launched frequently instead of sustained occupancy.
Autoscaler logs show bursts below configured scale-up window (default 60s) and the predictive sensor filters them out as noise.
Hypothesis: small/short-lived streams from LexiDocs (fanout-indexer microtasks) cause scheduler serialization and prevent efficient batching; noisy neighbor behavior results when many concurrent tiny streams from one tenant hold slots briefly and block larger batched work.
Checked RBAC and tenant-routing: no recent config changes. No GPU driver crashes found in the timeframe.
Related PR in runtime (github.com/redwood/runtime/pull/8271) contains a microbatch coalescing improvement but is not deployed to this pool.
Heap of KV-cache metadata for the customer's routes showed rapid churn but not sustained growth (so not a cache pressure issue).
Authored a small load harness to reproduce locally against staging dedicated nodes; reproduction succeeded when using many short streams with default coalescing disabled.

Additional notes:
LexiDocs (Customer): Reported intermittent 502s and saw client-side retries spike during the pulses; asking for ETA on root cause.
Mitigation applied: enabled microbatch coalescing flag for the customer's route and added a conservative per-tenant connection cap at the ingress (worker-level). This reduced the p99 latency spikes from ~1.3s to ~260ms and restored ~80% of lost throughput. Autoscaler tuning: lowered scale-up detection window from 60s to 25s for the affected dedicated pool to be more responsive to recurrent short bursts. Rollout notes: microbatch coalescing enabled via runtime flag rolled to pool-dedicated-37 on 2026-03-14 14:10 UTC; ingress throttling rule deployed 2026-03-14 14:05 UTC. No code changes required for immediate mitigation.
Create a targeted autoscaler policy for dedicated pools that balances responsiveness to short recurring bursts against oscillation risk (owner: SRE).
Merge and canary the microbatch coalescing PR (github.com/redwood/runtime/pull/8271) into the next runtime release and monitor kernel occupancy (owner: runtime team).
Add an observability panel to surface ephemeral-attach counts and average microbatch size per-tenant over rolling 1m windows (owner: Observability).
Customer-facing recommendation: advise LexiDocs to batch index work into slightly larger payloads or add jitter to stagger worker start times for long-running migrations (owner: CSE).
payload.summary: Microbatch saturation causing ephemeral GPU starvation and queue pulses for dedicated pool

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customer reports that streaming chat responses (SSE and WebSocket) occasionally transition to a half-closed state and stop producing tokens mid-generation. Unlike previous 'quiet period' stalls, these incidents correlate with periodic keepalive/heartbeat intervals from the customer's proxy and our load balancer.

Impact:
- Several long-running chat sessions for AcmeHealth (enterprise tenant) truncated without final token or final event; clients receive no explicit error.
- Occurs ~1-2x per 10k streaming sessions, higher on sessions >30s.
- Customer reports user-visible UX degradation in clinician-facing chat UI.

Environment:
- Redwood hosted (prod) routed through our edge LB -> nginx ingress pool -> serving runtime pool (dedicated cluster for AcmeHealth).
- Observed on us-east region only.
- Models: redwood/open-chat-v2 (default), fallback to redwood/gguf-compat-v1 occasionally.

Steps to reproduce (customer):
1) Start SSE stream with long prompt (expected >60 tokens).
2) Keep client idle (no new requests) while generation runs ~30-120s.
3) Observe stream stops emitting tokens; HTTP connection remains open (client sees no FIN) but no more data arrives.
4) After client attempts to reconnect, subsequent requests succeed.

Observed behavior:
- TCP-level traces show duplicate TCP keepalive probes around the time of silence for affected sessions.
- Proxy (customer-side) sends HTTP/1.1 keepalives; our LB also sends periodic pings. Timing collision window ~1s where both endpoints send probes.
- Nginx ingress logs show connection stayed ESTABLISHED; downstream worker logs show request marked as completed with no finalizing event.

Expected behavior:
- Streams continue until model generation completes or an explicit error is returned. Keepalive exchanges should not interrupt chunked transfer or server-sent events.

Immediate customer workaround suggested:
- Ask customer to increase client-side keepalive interval or disable aggressive proxy-level application-layer heartbeats while we investigate.

Attachments / traces:
- pcap snippets (s3://redwood-support/sup-873457/pcap-keepalive-collision.pcap)
- nginx-ingress logs excerpt (s3://redwood-support/sup-873457/nginx-logs.txt)
- runtime worker trace (trace-id: trace-20260312-8432)

Additional notes:
2026-03-12 15:40 - AcmeHealth (primary contact - Rajiv): We applied workaround (increase keepalive) and saw a reduction in incidents in 6 hours. Still want permanent fix; this affects critical clinician workflows.
Findings summary:
- Root hypothesis: race between application-layer keepalives (customer proxy + our LB) and serving runtime's token emission/flush path. When probe collision occurs during a memory compaction / worker preemption, the kernel-level socket state transitions to a half-closed state for the worker process, which then fails to append the final chunk/event.
- Reproducible in controlled environment when configuring both sides to 30s keepalive.
Workaround: recommended customer increase their proxy keepalive to 120s; support applied temporary ingress config changes (disable proxy buffering on streaming routes, extend LB idle timeout to 180s) which reduced occurrences by ~80%.
Next steps / permanent fix: Engineering to harden runtime flush path to tolerate late keepalive probes (task INT-4123). Plan: ensure token flush uses sendmsg with MSG_MORE semantics and adds explicit final event ACK. Also add e2e test simulating keepalive collision window.
Follow-up: monitor SLO for next 7 days; schedule postmortem and update confluence runbook. Customer notified of temporary fix and roadmap for permanent resolution.
- Engineering ticket INT-4123 assigned to runtime team (Lena/Kate).
- Include a load test scenario that injects simultaneous keepalive probes from client and LB during generation.
- Update streaming runbook and add guidance for enterprise customers behind application proxies.
payload.summary: Keepalive/heartbeat timing collision causes streaming connection half-close and mid-generation stall

payload.description:
Issue summary: Customer reports sustained 'rate-limited' responses (HTTP 429) during a scheduled embeddings backfill. This started after enabling a larger autoscale window on their Dedicated pool and coincides with increased background telemetry/health probes from their orchestrator.

Impact: HollowAI's nightly backfill jobs fail intermittently; ~30% of bulk embed batches return 429 and the job churns retries for hours. Customer reported user-facing lag for model-based search updates.

Environment: Dedicated pool (eu-west), tenant ID: hollowai-74, routes: /v1/embeddings (bulk) and /v1/chat (interactive), autoscaler policy: aggressive-burst (scale to 8 GPUs within 90s).

Steps to reproduce:
1) Queue a sustained (200 rps) bulk embedding backfill using their existing API key (shared across services).
2) Ensure orchestrator's heartbeat frequency is default (every 15s) and sidecar healthchecks enabled.
3) Observe burst window over the next 10–30 minutes; watch for 429 spikes on bulk endpoint.

Observed behavior: Intermittent 429s start once autoscaler warms additional nodes; logs show high token accounting for the tenant even though bulk payloads are the only heavy traffic. Health probes and telemetry POSTs from the customer's ingest coordinator are counted against the same burst budget and appear to drain short-window credits.

Expected behavior: Background telemetry and health probes should not push a production bulk backfill into a short-window exhaustion state for interactive or bulk lanes; recommend separation or different priority accounting.

Customer asks: Can Redwood explain why telemetry/health probes appear to exhaust burst credits and provide short-term mitigations and a long-term config for dedicated pools to avoid similar churn?
Timeline:
- 2026-03-10 02:03 UTC: Customer opened ticket after seeing repeated 429s during scheduled backfill.
- 2026-03-10 04:00 UTC: Support reproduced on a small sim tenant using similar config (shared API key + background heartbeats).
- 2026-03-11 09:12 UTC: Instrumented metric: tenant_burst_credit_balance (eu-west) shows sawtooth depletion matching healthcheck cadence.

Hypothesis: Tenant-level token accounting combined with per-route weight means short-window burst budget is depleted by many small health/telemetry POSTs. Autoscaler warmup increases concurrency (more connections from proxies/sidecars) and health probes multiply; rate-limiter charges appear per-request, not exempting small telemetry endpoints.

Logs & traces (examples):
- request_id: r-q7d9-20260310-04, path: /v1/internal/sidecar/health, status: 200, counted_tokens: 120
- request_id: r-x8f2-20260310-04, path: /v1/embeddings, status: 429, counted_tokens: 4096

Dashboards & links:
- Burst budget graph: https://console.redwood.ai/d/tenants/hollowai-74/burst-credit
- Ingress trace (sample): https://traces.redwood.ai/trace/5644c1

Experiment notes:
- Creating an isolated API key for backfill shifted bulk traffic into a different per-key window and reduced 429s immediately (workaround confirmed).
- Reducing sidecar heartbeat frequency to 60s also reduced sawtooth pattern but is intrusive for customer's orchestration needs.

Related PRs/commits considered: PR 4321 (rate-limiter: add per-path exemption config), draft patch for a priority class routing flag.

Additional notes:
2026-03-10 SRE on-call (Elena Kuznetsova): We see a repeated pattern where many short POSTs (health/telemetry) count small token units but multiply across N warmed nodes. This matches the customer's burst dropouts.
2026-03-13 Engineering (Rajiv Menon): Drafted a conservative opt-in flag (route_priority_exempt) for dedicated customers — needs security review and a small ACL change.
Workarounds implemented:
- Customer created a dedicated API key for bulk backfills; immediate reduction in 429s observed.
- Support temporarily advised reducing telemetry sampling rate.
Recommended long-term actions:
1) Configure route isolation: advise customer to route background flushes to a distinct API key and assign to a lower-priority route with separate burst window.
2) For Dedicated customers, we can provision an isolated burst pool (Support/Sales action) to keep large backfills from impacting interactive lanes.
3) Engineering: implement opt-in per-path exemption or a priority_exemption flag for internal telemetry paths for dedicated tenants (SEC review required).
Follow-ups:
- ENG-4321 (internal): implement route_priority_exempt flag — owner: Rajiv Menon — target: 2026-04-02.
- Support to coordinate with Account Exec to propose isolated burst pool add-on to HollowAI.
Current status: Customer backfill stable after key split; ticket will remain open until ENG-4321 Infra change lands or customer adopts isolated burst pool.
This ticket highlights common footgun: shared API keys + background/system probes can amplify token accounting in short refill windows when autoscaling increases parallel probes. For dedicated customers doing large backfills, recommend isolated keys, explicit route separation, or an isolated burst pool. ENG and Security review required before automatically exempting any path from accounting.
payload.summary: background backfill + health-probe telemetry consuming burst credits and triggering rate rejects

payload.description:
Customer reports that when their Go-based service loses a streaming connection to the Redwood API (intermittent network blips), the SDK reconnects but their backend tools (webhook-style function calls) are executed twice. The customer is using the Go SDK with an on-message 'tool' execution flow: the model issues a tool call and the SDK relays that to their internal tool runner. After a reconnect, the same tool invocation appears again, leading to duplicate downstream side effects (order creation, email sends).
1) Use the Go SDK to open a streaming chat session with a tool/call function handler registered on the customer's side.
2) Have the model issue a tool call that results in an outbound POST from customer's relay to internal tool-runner (single-shot operation, non-idempotent on their side).
3) Simulate a transient network drop between client and Redwood streaming endpoint (TCP connection reset or short firewall rule blocking ~2s).
4) Observe that the Go SDK reconnects/reauthorizes and the model's tool call is delivered again; the customer's tool-runner receives a duplicate POST and performs the action twice.
5) Reproduce consistently when reconnect occurs before explicit SDK acknowledgement/receipt confirmation logic is added client-side.

Issue summary:
Customer (AuroraAnalytics, dedicated) reports intermittent 95p+ tail-latency spikes (up to 3.5s) after a recent optimizer profile rollout that adjusted batching thresholds and enabled a new KV-prefetch heuristic on two quantized models. Impact: production traffic across several routes for analytic summarization is affected, user-visible latency spikes and increased error budgets.

Environment:
- Dedicated pool in prod-us-west (us-west-2)
- Models: redwood-mini-1-quant8 (primary), gptj-6b-int8 (fallback)
- Autoscaling policy: reserved 4 GPUs, burst to 6
- Recent changes: optimizer profile v2026-03-11 applied to tenant; KV-prefetch enabled + aggressive batching target 48 ms.

Steps to reproduce / Observed pattern:
1) Normal traffic steady state shows p50 ~120ms, p95 ~420ms.
2) After profile rollout, during moderate burst patterns (10–30 RPS per route) p95 jumps to 2.0–3.5s for 30–60s windows, then recovers.
3) Errors are rare (mostly timeouts for longest requests). No bulk 5xx flash.
4) Reproduced on customer's traffic replay in staging when applying identical optimizer flags.

Logs & artifacts:
- Console timeline: https://console.redwood.ai/aurora/tenant/aurora/timeline?range=2026-03-11..2026-03-13
- Serving runtime traces (sample): trace-id a1b2c3d4 (attached)
- Snapshot of optimizer profile: opt-profile:v2026-03-11 (exported)

Additional notes:
2026-03-13 Support (Aisha): Customer asks for a plan that allows a short safety hold (no config drift for 24h), per-tenant partial throttle, and the ability to snapshot/restore routing quickly if behavior persists. Also wants confirmation that no cold-cache penalty will occur if we change the prefetch concurrency.
Summary of findings:
- Root hypothesis: KV-prefetch concurrency interacts badly with batching windows for long-sequence requests, forming an occasional large-batch admission that exceeds latency SLOs.
- Evidence: Staging replay reproduces p95 spike only when prefetch concurrency >= 2 and batching target aggressive (<=48ms). Lowering either parameter mitigates spikes independently.
- Additional observation: Per-tenant cache warmup after changing prefetch is negligible for our workload; rerouting to fallback model causes brief KV cache misses but not prolonged degradation.
- Risk assessment: Full profile revert has low risk but requires coordination across routes; a per-tenant targeted change is lower risk and allows faster rollback.
- Safety hooks: We validated that per-tenant optimizer snapshots include the full flag set and can be restored atomically via the /v1/admin/tenant/{id}/optimizer/snapshot endpoints.
- Suggested temporary limits: set prefetch_concurrency=1, batching_target_ms=80, kv_prefetch_enabled=false (toggle), and enable a monitoring alert for p95 > 700ms over 5m.
Staged preflight & safe-recovery procedure:
1) Take atomic snapshot: POST /v1/admin/tenant/aurora/snapshots with label 'pre-2026-03-14-preflight' (verify snapshot ID).
2) Apply conservative overrides to tenant optimizer (per-tenant override): {prefetch_concurrency:1, batching_target_ms:80, kv_prefetch_enabled:false} for route group 'summaries'.
3) Deploy for 30 minutes to 1 hour behind a canary percentage (10% traffic) using routing rule 'opt-staged-canary'. Monitor p95, error rate, and CPU/GPU utilization.
4) If canary looks good for 60m -> increase to 50% for 30m, then full.
5) If regression observed at any stage: run immediate atomic restore using snapshot ID and open postmortem.
6) After full stabilization, craft a targeted optimizer profile with gradual prefetch tuning (prefetch_concurrency ramp steps) and schedule a maintenance window for the customer for a clean rollout.
Workarounds provided to customer:
- Immediate: enable tenant-level 'workload-hold' to prevent further auto-rollouts. We applied this at 2026-03-13 21:12 UTC.
- Short term: We applied a per-tenant conservative override (prefetch_concurrency=1) to all 'summaries' routes at 2026-03-14 03:10 UTC; metrics show p95 dropped to ~430ms.
Follow-ups/Action items:
- Ops: Add a fast-restore button to console for per-tenant optimizer snapshots (track in INT backlog).
- Engineering: Add a guard in the optimizer service that prevents prefetch_concurrency > 2 if batching_target_ms < 60ms for quantized models (PR suggested: runtime#5823).
- CS: Schedule a 1-hour post-rollout review with AuroraAnalytics to agree on gradual tuning windows and notifications.
Partial mitigation applied: Conservative per-tenant override pushed and workload-hold enabled. p95 returned near baseline in affected routes. Full targeted rollout scheduled with customer for 2026-03-16. Engineering has an upcoming PR to add cross-flag guardrails. Ticket remains In Progress until the targeted rollout completes and customer signs off.
Do not perform global optimizer rollback without explicit approval from AuroraAnalytics operations. Use atomic snapshot restore for fastest recovery. Documenting this per-tenant playbook as a runbook in Confluence after closure.
payload.summary: Granular optimizer snapshot + staged fallback preflight for tenant experiencing tail-latency spikes

Issue summary
- Customer reports a model version promotion occurred for rw-qwen2.5-72b-instruct, but they cannot find any release notes in Console or public docs. They expected a customer-visible changelog entry with category (perf/quality/bugfix/etc), any breaking changes, and rollback guidance.

Customer context
- Company: Lattice Health Systems (enterprise)
- Deployment: Dedicated evaluation + Hosted API in parallel (per CS notes)
- Why it matters: They have internal change-management requirements and need an auditable record of model changes for clinical workflow reviews. This was flagged as a blocker for expanding traffic to the newer version.

Impact
- No functional outage. Customer trust/operational confidence impacted; they paused rollout to the promoted version.
- Support unable to point to an authoritative customer-visible entry; only internal promotion event existed.

Environment
- Console: prod (us-east)
- Docs: public release notes site

Observed behavior
- Console > Model Catalog > rw-qwen2.5-72b-instruct > Release notes: latest promotion shows “No release notes available”.
- Public docs release notes feed: no entry for the promotion timestamp.

Expected behavior
- On version promotion, a release note should be generated from model metadata + promotion event and visible in Console (customer roles) and in docs (if public). If note is embargoed/internal-only, Console should show a safe placeholder explaining why.

Initial triage notes
- Customer provided approximate time window: 2025-10-09 16:10–16:30 PT.
- Support observed internal admin view showed a promotion event, but customer view did not show any corresponding public note.
[2025-10-09 17:02 PT] Dev Patel (Support) — Opened ticket after Lattice escalation via TAM. Customer quote: “We saw the model version change in our pinned config diff, but there are no release notes. We need to know what changed and whether we should expect output drift.”

[2025-10-09 17:18 PT] Nora Ahmed (Console) — Acknowledged. Asked for: model slug, pinned version(s), region, screenshots. Pulled initial logs for release-notes endpoint for customer org.

[2025-10-09 17:42 PT] Miguel Santos (Enterprise CS) — Confirmed customer pinned to rw-qwen2.5-72b-instruct@1.3.1; promotion was to 1.3.2 on Dedicated pool LAT-DED-03 (us-east) + Hosted alias update. Customer expected entry in Console release notes feed.

[2025-10-09 18:10 PT] Nora Ahmed — Found internal promotion event in control-plane events stream for model rw-qwen2.5-72b-instruct version 1.3.2. No downstream changelog artifact generated for that event ID. Linking Slack threads: #support (sources/slack/support/1743524300.json) and #eng-releases (sources/slack/eng-releases/1743470199.json).

[2025-10-09 18:28 PT] Connor O'Brien (Release Eng) — Hypothesis: generator dropped the event because metadata record missing required public fields (public_summary + category) OR docs build failed to ingest artifact. Noted we recently tightened redaction rules and “required fields” checks are not yet enforced everywhere.

[2025-10-09 19:05 PT] Michael Nguyen (Control Plane) — Checked event payload: promotion emitted correctly. The metadata snapshot referenced by event includes internal_notes and quality_notes but public_summary empty. Generator template expects at least one public entry; otherwise it produces no customer artifact (bug: should produce placeholder + internal-only record).

[2025-10-10 09:12 PT] Nora Ahmed — Confirmed in generator logs: event processed, but rendered output was empty and skipped publish step (treated as no-op). This causes Console feed to show “No release notes available” rather than an explicit “No customer-visible notes for this change” message.

[2025-10-10 10:03 PT] Dev Patel — Updated customer: we’ve identified an issue in our release notes generation pipeline for a specific promotion event; we will publish an entry and follow up with a link and summary.

[2025-10-10 11:20 PT] Quentin Harris (Model Catalog) — Backfilled metadata for rw-qwen2.5-72b-instruct@1.3.2 with a minimal public_summary and category=“Bugfix/Operational”. Marked any sensitive details as internal_only. Requested reprocess of the promotion event.

[2025-10-10 12:04 PT] Nora Ahmed — Reprocessed event; Console now shows release note entry for customer role. Verified RBAC: internal-only fields not visible.

[2025-10-10 12:18 PT] Wei Chen (Docs) — Triggered docs build; public release notes page now includes the entry. Confirmed the URL and RSS/JSON feed updated.

[2025-10-10 13:00 PT] Dev Patel — Sent customer link + summary and noted that the release note is now available in Console. Customer asked for rollback guidance; provided standard guidance and pointed to model pinning controls.

[2025-10-12 09:40 PT] Nora Ahmed — Follow-up: added internal task to change generator behavior to publish a safe placeholder when there are no customer-visible fields (prevents silent missing entries). Also added monitoring proposal: alert if a promotion event doesn’t yield an artifact within 15 minutes.

[2025-10-12 10:15 PT] Dev Patel — Customer confirmed they can see the entry and resumed staged rollout. Closing ticket.
Resolved by (1) backfilling model metadata for rw-qwen2.5-72b-instruct@1.3.2 with a customer-visible public_summary and category per release notes style guide, and (2) reprocessing the specific promotion event so the changelog generator published an artifact consumed by Console and docs.

Root cause
- Changelog generator treated promotions with no customer-visible fields (empty public_summary) as a publish no-op, resulting in a missing customer-visible entry rather than an explicit “no customer-visible notes” placeholder.

Customer-facing outcome
- Console release notes feed now contains the entry for the promotion.
- Public docs release notes page updated and validated.

Workaround (if reoccurs before fix)
- Backfill required public fields on the model version metadata and reprocess the promotion event to regenerate artifacts.
We identified an issue where a model promotion event could fail to generate a customer-visible release note if the public summary fields were empty. We’ve published the release note for rw-qwen2.5-72b-instruct v1.3.2 and it should now be visible in your Console and on the public release notes page. We’ve also queued a fix so future promotions will always produce a visible entry (or a clear placeholder if no customer-visible details are applicable).
File engineering bug: generator should publish a safe placeholder entry when only internal-only notes exist (prevents missing artifacts).
Add monitoring/alerting: promotion event without changelog artifact within SLA window (15–30 min).
Expand CI enforcement so promotions cannot proceed with empty public_summary unless explicitly marked internal_only with approved placeholder behavior.
Document expected behavior in support runbook (what support should check: event exists, artifact exists, RBAC visibility).

Customer (MedicaOne Health, enterprise) requests a one-off SIEM snapshot export for a tenant as part of a pending regulatory review. They require:

- An immutable snapshot (tarball) containing daily audit slices for tenant 'medicaone-prod-42' for the period 2024-12-01..2025-01-31. The snapshot must include a manifest with cryptographic checksums and a per-file HMAC tied to the tenant GUID.
- Evidence of delivery and a simple custodian-proof (who retrieved the archive, timestamp, and MD5/SHA256 checksums).
Impact:
The customer is in active regulatory discovery with a compliance deadline next week and needs the package to satisfy auditors. No production traffic impact reported, but the request has high urgency for legal/compliance.
Environment:
Production (eu-west), tenant: medicaone-prod-42, audit export pipeline via s3-archive connector, SIEM target: Splunk HEC behind customer's firewall (pull stage).
Desired deliverables:
1) Field concordance CSV with example mapping and sample event row.
2) Signed snapshot tarball (sha256) plus HMAC manifest per file.
3) Delivery receipts (S3 presigned URL logs and transfer confirmation) and a short checklist explaining how to verify checksums locally.
4) Short note on redaction: what fields were redacted/omitted (if any) and why.

1) Confirm tenant id and retention window with customer (done in initial call).
2) Trigger on-demand audit dump job for tenant medicaone-prod-42 with window 2024-12-01 to 2025-01-31.
3) Package output into tar.gz, compute checksums (sha256 for files, hmac-sha256 tied to tenant key), and write manifest.json alongside.
4) Stage to secure s3 bucket restricted to support and customer.

Support runbook check: export-job logs show successful run on 2025-02-15T03:12:10Z.
Archive generation: /var/log/audit-export/medicaone/2025-02-15-package.log attached to internal investigation.
S3 put succeeded: s3://support-exports/medicaone-prod-42/medicaone-audit-20241201-20250131.tar.gz (etag: "9f2c...").

Issue summary:
Customer BrightChat reported sudden, sustained 429 responses for interactive chat calls after enabling VPC egress through their NAT gateway. Errors started ~2026-03-12 02:00 UTC coincident with a networking change (move to pooled ephemeral egress IPs).

Impact:
- ~25% of chat API calls returning 429 over HTTP/2 and websocket sessions for BrightChat users.
- Real-time UX degraded; customer reports timeouts and escalations to their engineering lead.
- Background embedding ingestion from the same VPC also observed token usage spikes.

Environment:
- Customer: BrightChat Inc. (private deployment, VPC egress to Redwood edge)
- Regions: us-west-2 (primary), traffic from same subnet NATted through shared ephemeral IP pool
- Models: redwood-chat-v1 pinned

Steps to reproduce:
1) Customer starts interactive chat sessions concurrently with a background embedding ingestion job (low QPS per session, many concurrent sessions).
2) Both flows egress through the same NAT gateway that performs source IP pooling.
3) After NAT change, observed 429s within 1–3 minutes for interactive calls; bulk ingestion continued but contributed to quota burn.

Observed behavior:
- 429 response includes X-RateLimit-Reason: token_bucket_exhausted and X-RateLimit-Scope: per-ip + per-key.
- Edge logs show multiple distinct API keys and websocket sessions mapped to a small set of source IPs (NAT pooling).
- Rate-limit counters for those source IPs quickly hit the short-window burst limit.

Expected behavior:
- Interactive chat should be throttled by API key quotas primarily; source IP aggregation should not cause cross-customer or cross-key exhaustion in private VPC setups.

Attached logs / diagnostic snippets (sanitized):
- edge-proxy request sample: method=POST path=/v1/chat api_key=bKz*** src_ip=34.203.11.7 x-forwarded-for=10.0.2.45
- rate-limiter counter dump: ip_bucket[34.203.11.7].burst=500/500; api_key_bucket[bKz***].burst=320/1000
- NAT mapping snapshot (customer provided): 150 internal sessions -> 8 ephemeral public IPs

2026-03-12 02:08 UTC - BrightChat support: 'After we flipped the NAT pooling config, users started seeing chat failures — looks like 429s even though token usage is low per key.'
2026-03-12 02:22 UTC - Support (Juniper): 'Thanks — can you share a recent request id and confirm whether you run background embedding workers from the same VPC?'
2026-03-12 02:45 UTC - BrightChat support: 'Request id r-0a1b2c3d; yes, background workers on same subnet. We switched to pooled egress to save costs.'
2026-03-12 04:05 UTC - SRE (Ethan): 'Reproduced pattern in edge logs — many keys share the same public IP. We see rate-limiter incrementing against per-ip buckets leading to early exhaustion.'
2026-03-13 09:30 UTC - Support (Juniper): 'Hotfix deployed to edge proxy to prefer original client IP from X-Forwarded-For when upstream is on our trusted proxy list; also scoped per-ip accounting disabled for this tenant as mitigation.'
2026-03-14 11:12 UTC - BrightChat: 'Confirming errors dropped to <1% after hotfix and configuration change. UX restored.'
Checked edge-proxy access logs (us-west-2) — pattern: large fanout of internal client IPs NATted to small ephemeral pool -> repeated increments to same per-ip token buckets.
Reviewed rate-limiter logic: currently enforces layered buckets (per-key AND per-source-ip). In VPC NAT scenarios, source-ip layer can be overly coarse and cause cross-key interference.
Hypothesis: NAT pooling turned many distinct customers/sessions into shared public IPs; with per-ip accounting enabled, short-window burst credits were exhausted by background jobs, producing 429s for interactive sessions.
Tested counter: artificially injected 200 concurrent small requests from separate internal IPs but same public IP — observed per-ip burst counter hitting limit while individual api_key buckets remained under threshold.
Checked trusted proxy list config: X-Forwarded-For was present but edge proxy had been configured to prefer egress IP for per-ip accounting when request arrived from known cloud NAT ranges — this policy caused misattribution in private VPCs.
Related GH PR created to make per-ip accounting opt-in for private customers and to tighten trust->client-ip derivation (see PR #3421).
Per-IP rate limiting layer combined with NAT gateway IP pooling caused cross-session quota exhaustion. Edge proxy configuration used public egress IP for bucket attribution instead of original client IP (and per-ip accounting was enabled for the tenant), producing collateral 429s for interactive traffic.
Immediate mitigation (2026-03-12): disabled per-ip accounting for BrightChat tenant via feature flag; added temporary per-tenant exemption for source-ip buckets to restore chat traffic.
Short-term fix (2026-03-13): patched edge-proxy to prefer X-Forwarded-For when request originates from customer VPC ranges in the trusted-proxy list and to annotate requests with negotiated client_ip for rate-limiter.
Long-term remediation (deployed 2026-03-14): rate-limiter change to require both authentication and explicit per-ip opt-in before applying per-ip buckets; added observability dashboard for per-ip vs per-key bucket saturation and a runbook for VPC NAT scenarios.
Customer validation: BrightChat confirmed error rate returned to baseline (<1%). Monitoring kept on for 72 hours post-fix.
Code/links: GH PR https://github.com/redwoodinference/infra/pull/3421 merged; runbook updated at https://confluence.redwoodinference.com/display/SUPPORT/NAT+IP+Pooling+Runbook
Create a small support KB entry describing VPC NAT pitfalls and recommended config (eg: separate egress for background ingestion or opt-in per-ip policy).
Add automated detection to console: if a private tenant's traffic shows >N api_keys mapped to <=M public IPs, surface a warning and suggested mitigations.
Schedule a postmortem with Networking and Rate-Limit owners to consider defaulting per-ip accounting off for private customers; target decision by 2026-04-01.
payload.summary: Persistent 429s for interactive chat after enabling VPC egress via NAT with pooled ephemeral IPs

Issue summary: Customer runs recurring off-peak batch embedding jobs in eu-west-1 on a Dedicated pool. During the nightly window (23:30-02:00 UTC) a subset of jobs that start in EU are observed to make requests routed to our us-east-1 dedicated pool, introducing ~600-900ms extra p95 latency per request and extra egress/egress-costs. Impact: customer reported increased overall job completion time (up to 30%) and billing anomalies due to cross-region egress. Environment: Dedicated capacity, tenant-specific reserved pool, batch job runner using SDK v1.4.2. Expected behavior: jobs pinned to EU dedicated capacity for entire run when customer uses residency=dedicated and pool pinning. Observed behavior: routing drifts to US mid-run for some long-running batches.
1) Customer schedules a long-running batch embedding job (500k embeddings) targeting eu-west-1 reserved pool with residency=pinned and pool_id provided.
2) Job launches at 23:45 UTC and begins processing; initial requests served from eu-west-1 nodes (confirmed by IP and edge headers).

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customer observed multiple streaming responses that never emitted a terminal event after an upstream reset while the client attempted a resume. The stream contains the last partial text fragment, but the final "end" metadata event is missing and the session appears 'orphaned' on the server side (no further tokens and no close).

Impact:
- Affects LangDoc AI (dedicated tenant in us-west).
- Intermittent: ~3% of resumed streams during 2026-03-04 22:00–23:30 UTC window.
- User-facing: clients hang waiting for finalization; some clients retry and receive duplicated suffix tokens on subsequent resumes.

Environment:
- Redwood Dedicated (reserved capacity pool: dpool-23) in us-west region.
- Edge via customer-configured Cloud NAT + our edge-proxy (nginx-based) in front of api-gateway.
- Model: redwood-rlhf-large-v2, streaming mode SSE and websocket clients both reported.

Steps to reproduce (best-effort):
1) Start a long-running generation that emits several thousand tokens (prefix length ~512, max_tokens 2048).
2) Intentionally drop connection on client during mid-generation (simulate TCP RST or aggressive proxy idle).
3) Reconnect and call resume (client uses resume token header x-resume-id and last-offset).
4) Observe: resume returns last partial fragment but never emits an explicit terminal event ("event: end" or terminal choice).

Observed behavior:
- Server logs show upstream connection pool returned 502/connection_reset from origin during resume; the resume flow logs a successful rebind but no finalization callback invoked.
- The session remains active in runtime's session table with last_write_ts progressing but no emitter for terminal metadata.
- When client retries resume again, some duplicate tokens are produced (identical suffix repeated) in ~40% of retries.

Expected behavior:
- Resume should produce the final terminal event (end+metadata) or produce a clear error allowing client to fall back.
- No duplicated tokens on subsequent resume attempts.

Relevant logs/snippets (sanitized):
- edge-proxy: "upstream reset while sending request body" (2026-03-04T22:21:07Z)
- api-gateway: "resume request accepted: resume_id=rs-72c4, origin_conn=conn-198, origin_status=error:connection_reset"
- serving-runtime: "session rs-72c4 rebind ok, kvcache_offset=14872, emitter_handle not attached (expected on origin callback)"

Temporary workaround provided to customer:
- Advise clients to fall back to reissuing a fresh generation if resume fails to return a terminal event within 8s.
- Increase client-side resume timeout and dedupe tokens by comparing the last 64 bytes of the resumed prefix before appending new tokens.

Notes on frequency and correlation:
- Spike correlated with upstream NAT flaps in the customer's cloud provider between 22:00–23:30 UTC.
- Not all resumes affected; appears if upstream returns connection reset after the Serving Runtime has accepted the resume but before origin finalization callback executes.

Additional notes:
2026-03-05 10:03 - LangDoc SRE (via email): Provided tcpdump capture and nginx error.log snippet showing multiple upstream reset events at 22:20:58Z–22:21:12Z.
2026-03-05 15:40 - Support (Nadia): Shared workaround to customer and asked for more examples of duplicated tokens for analysis.
2026-03-06 08:20 - LangDoc (Customer): Sent two request IDs and transcript where suffix '...the final clause.' was duplicated after second resume attempt.
Reproduced locally with simulated upstream reset by injecting connection reset in origin callback path; reproduces orphaned session in ~70% of trials when reset occurs within 40–120ms after resume accept.
Root cause hypothesis: serving-runtime attaches the emitter in a two-step handshake — accept resume -> schedule origin handshake -> attach emitter on origin callback. If origin responds with reset before emitter attachment completes, finalization callback may be scheduled to a nil emitter and dropped.
Concurrent behavior observed: when client retries resume immediately, the runtime will create a new emitter and replay cached prefix tokens; because the prior orphaned session never recorded a terminal offset, the cache replay can overlap producing duplicated suffix segments.
Edge-proxy configuration: keepalive timeout set to 30s, but NAT devices in customer's environment issue aggressive 15s TCP idle timeouts leading to earlier RSTs when connections are reused for resume.
Telemetry: added additional debug logs to candidate branch to log emitter attachment sequence numbers and origin callback timestamps.
Mitigation applied in runtime branch fix/emit-finalization-guard: ensure origin finalization is enqueued to a fallback finalizer if emitter is not yet attached. This preserves terminal metadata emission even when callback races with emitter attach.
Hotfix PR opened: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/2893 (includes unit + integration tests simulating origin reset during resume).
Canary deployment planned to 2 nodes in dpool-23 for 2026-03-08 02:00 UTC, monitoring resume success rate and duplicate-token metric. Rollback plan in place if duplicate rate increases.
Follow-up actions:
- Add guidance to Dedicated runbook: recommend customers set NAT/edge device idle timeout >= 60s or enable TCP keepalive probes for resume-sensitive workloads.
- Instrument session table with orphaned_session_count metric and alert when > 10/min for a customer pool.
- Postmortem to be drafted after canary.

Issue summary: ClearWave Labs reported a sustained rise in 95th/99th percentile latency and intermittent 5xx errors after enabling a tenant-scoped optimizer profile that combines async-batching, kv-prefetch, and aggressive per-tenant quantization. Impact: Production traffic for several routes saw elevated tail latency (95p >= 1.4s, baseline 95p ~0.45s) and ~1.2% 5xx rate for ~45 minutes, causing degraded UX for multiple customer endpoints. Environment: Dedicated pool in us-west-2, tenant id cw-prod-17, config snapshot applied 2026-03-10T01:22:00Z. Steps to reproduce: 1) On dedicated pool, enable optimizer profile cw-agg-2 on tenant cw-prod-17. 2) Send mixed-length traffic similar to ClearWave's traffic pattern (avg seq len 380 tokens, bursts of 20 concurrent requests). 3) Observe 95/99 p latency increase and occasional serving-runtime OOM/retry 5xx. Logs / traces: - Observability link: https://console.redwood.ai/obs/trace?trace_id=trace-cw-20260310-1 - Serving error snippet: "runtime: KV prefetch miss exhaustion -> worker backpressure -> request retry -> 5xx" - Autoscaler logs show transient GPU utilization spikes followed by worker restarts. Additional context: Customer had previously used conservative optimizer profiles without issues. The new profile was rolled to production via the config-service staged rollout at 2026-03-10T01:22:00Z.
1) Apply optimizer profile cw-agg-2 to tenant cw-prod-17 in prod us-west-2. 2) Replay traffic from ClearWave representative capture (bucket: s3://cw-replays/2026-02-28-main). 3) Monitor token-level latency, kv cache hit ratio, per-worker queue depth, and 5xx rates. 4) Observe that within 10-30 minutes the 95/99p latency climbs and 5xx errors surface.
Selected logs: [2026-03-10T01:45:12Z] worker-23 WARN kv_prefetch: queue_depth=128 threshold=96; [2026-03-10T01:45:16Z] serving-runtime ERROR request=rw-req-4721 retry=1 upstream=worker-23 5xx; [2026-03-10T01:46:02Z] autoscaler INFO reallocate pool: scale_up reason=burst_utilization; trace: trace-cw-20260310-1
2026-03-10 02:05 - Support (Maya): Initial triage completed. Reached out to SRE to check GPU restarts and to ClearWave for traffic capture. Assigned to Rafael for config rollback assist.
2026-03-10 02:20 - SRE (Rafael): Observed worker churn correlated with kv-prefetch saturation and large async batch windows. GPU memory peaks followed by retries. Patching a quick circuit to reduce async batch max_window to 16 for affected tenant could stabilize.
2026-03-10 03:10 - Support (Maya): Customer agreed to a controlled demobilization sequence. ETA to start: 03:30 UTC. Customer noted this is high-impact for nightly jobs between 03:00-05:00 UTC.
2026-03-10 03:36 - Engineering (Priya Anand): Executed soft-demobilize: disabled kv-prefetch for tenant, rehydrated model pin to rw-7b-fp16, and set per-tenant max_async_batch=16. Preliminary telemetry shows 95p reduced to ~0.5s and 5xx dropped to 0.02%.
2026-03-11 09:12 - Customer (ClearWave, Alan): Thanks team — telemetry looks stable this morning. Please provide recommended long-term plan and opt-profile adjustments.
2026-03-12 15:28 - Support (Rafael): Documenting follow-up actions and scheduling postmortem. Leaving ticket open for confirmation of follow-ups.
2026-03-12 16:00 - Support (Maya): Added action item to add per-tenant optimizer snapshot-and-rollback tool to backlog (ENG-issue #4578).

Hypotheses tested: 1) KV-prefetch combined with aggressive quantization and large async window leads to worker memory amplification — observed memory deltas on worker containers match hypothesis. 2) Async batching increased effective sequence concurrency causing KV cache pressure; reduced max_async_batch mitigates tail. 3) Model-specific quantization mismatch (rw-13b-quant-v2) possibly exacerbates decoding memory growth — re-pinning to rw-7b-fp16 reduced memory footprint. Diagnostic queries run: queried per-worker heap, KV hit/miss ratio, and batch size distribution. Key observables: sustained kv_prefetch queue_depth spikes, increased GC cycles in container logs, and increased retry/backoff events in serving-runtime.
Short-term remediation executed: 1) Soft-demobilize runbook applied to tenant cw-prod-17 at 2026-03-10T03:36:00Z: disable kv-prefetch, set max_async_batch=16, pin model to rw-7b-fp16, and apply conservative batching thresholds. 2) Cleared the config snapshot as a new baseline and created backup snapshot id snap-20260310-cw. 3) Monitored for 48 hours; metrics normalized. Long-term actions (accepted by ENG): - Implement per-tenant snapshot-and-rollback API to allow single-command restore of prior optimizer stack. - Add a circuit-breaker that automatically demobilizes kv-prefetch for a tenant when kv_prefetch queue_depth > threshold for 3 consecutive minutes. - Add a regression rule in Optimize that simulates bursty traffic mixes before promoting optimizer profiles to production. - Convert the soft-demobilize procedure into an automated operator action with safe order: (a) reduce async batch, (b) disable kv-prefetch, (c) re-pin to stable model variant, (d) notify customer and re-enable incrementally.
1) ENG to file implementation PR for per-tenant rollback API (ENG-4578) with ETA 2026-04-05. 2) SRE to add automated alert for 'kv_prefetch queue_depth sustained' and a runbook reference. 3) CS to coordinate with ClearWave to schedule a non-peak window for staged re-introduction tests. 4) Product to add a preflight simulator in Redwood Optimize for mixed-length burst tests. 5) Add a KB article in Console docs summarizing safe demobilization steps.
If metrics regress after re-introduction tests, declare a focused postmortem with timelines: - T+0 investigation doc (immediate) - T+48h stabilization review - T+7d customer-impact summary and resolution acceptance. Owner: Rafael Ortiz.
Customer-facing summary to be prepared by CS: We identified optimizer profile interactions that caused KV cache pressure and batch amplification. We applied a controlled rollback to safe parameters and are building safeguards to prevent recurrence. Draft ready; awaiting final metrics confirmation before sending to ClearWave.
