payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customers on Redwood Private deployment report intermittent TLS connection resets between their inference VMs and the Redwood control-plane endpoint when egressing through a managed NAT gateway / NAT GW load balancer. Failures started after a network change on the customer side (introduced source-IP preservation on egress).

Impact:
- Intermittent 5xx/TLS errors observed in customer application causing request retries and failed chats.
- Error rate spiked from ~0.2% to 3.7% during busy windows.
- Affects production traffic for AcmeMusic (private deployment) in us-west-2.

Environment:
- Redwood Private (customer-managed VPC peering + NAT GW)
- prod | us-west-2
- Customer: AcmeMusic (enterprise)
- Affected model: redwood-llama2-13b

Steps to reproduce (from customer):
1) Deploy a short-lived load (concurrent chat requests ~50 rps) from private VMs that egress via their NAT GW with source-IP preservation enabled.
2) Target Redwood control-plane API endpoint (control plane for auth/metrics and model routing) and model endpoints.
3) Observe occasional TLS renegotiation or connection reset after ~20-200 tokens of streaming responses.

Observed behaviour:
- TLS handshake completes for initial connection but mid-stream the connection resets with TCP RST or TLS "unexpected_message" in logs.
- Connection resets correlate with NAT GW logs showing ephemeral source port reuse and asymmetric return path in some flows.
- Client-side logs show: "tls: received unexpected message" and server logs show truncated TLS sessions followed by reconnects.

Expected behaviour:
- Stable TLS streaming connections for the duration of the request (no mid-stream resets).

Initial hypothesis and investigation notes:
- Customer enabled "source IP preservation" on their NAT gateway (to keep client IP visible to destination). This causes egress to reuse original source IP and can change flow hashing behavior on upstream load balancers and firewalls, leading to asymmetric routing or middlebox interference.
- NAT GW ephemeral port reuse combined with aggressive firewall inspection on the customer side appears to drop subsequent packets when a new 5-tuple is seen mid-stream (port remapping/port reuse).
- Redwood control-plane observed connection resets clustered to a subset of customer source IPs and the timing matches NAT port churn windows.

Temporary workaround provided to customer:
- Disable source-IP preservation on the NAT gateway (revert to standard SNAT) OR enable sticky flow mappings on upstream firewalls so the five-tuple remains consistent for the request lifetime.
- Customer confirmed that reverting to default SNAT reduced the error rate to baseline in a canary.

Next steps / action items:
- SRE: add a dashboard showing TLS mid-stream reset counts by customer source ASN / NAT-gateway prefix (assigned INT-4895).
- Networking/Infra: validate that our control-plane accepts connections when client source IPs are preserved and update runbook (if necessary) with guidance for customers using source-IP preservation.
- Support: follow up with AcmeMusic to schedule a controlled test for sticky flows and capture packet traces (pcap) for failed sessions.

Resolution notes (ongoing):
- Workaround accepted by customer; permanent remediation requires runbook updates and a short KB on NAT configuration for Private customers.

Attachments / logs referenced:
- customer-provided pcap snippets (attached separately)
- NAT GW flow logs (customer) and Redwood ingress TLS logs (see Confluence page link)


Additional notes:
2026-03-11 18:40 - AcmeMusic-NetworkOps (customer): Confirmed they recently enabled source IP preservation to preserve client IP for downstream analytics. Will temporarily revert to default SNAT for canary tomorrow morning PST.
2026-03-12 11:05 - SRE-Oncall: Created dashboard query and alert proto (linked in INT-4895). Next action: coordinate with Networking team for formal guidance and update Private deployment runbook.
payload.summary: Private VPC: intermittent TLS connection resets after egress via NAT Gateway (source IP preservation)

Issue summary:
Customer reports that during a scheduled canary traffic shift the pinned model version (redwood-13b-v2) for their route was unintentionally lost after the cluster autoscaler replaced two canary nodes with spot GPU instances. Subsequent traffic was routed to the quantized fallback (redwood-13b-v2-quantized), causing subtle output differences and higher token-level hallucination for their eval set. The customer observed the behavior for ~18 minutes and escalated due to production regressions in generation quality.
Impact:
- User-facing: incorrect/altered responses for a subset of requests (affecting ~12% of requests for the route).
- Business: NimbleDocs classifies this as a high-severity regression affecting SLAs for dedicated customers.
- Scope: Single dedicated pool in us-east-1 with canary weight 10% at time of event.
Relevant contexts: dedicated capacity with spot-backed scaling policy, route-level version pin applied by customer via the API, canary weight adjustments in place, automatic fallback policy enabled to use quantized variants under capacity pressure.
1) Have a dedicated GPU pool configured with spot-backed worker autoscaling and canary pool of 2 replicas.
2) Create a route with model pin to redwood-13b-v2 and enable automatic fallback to the quantized variant.
3) Shift canary weight to 10% and trigger a simulated spot eviction on one canary node (drain + terminate).
4) Observe routing decisions and route metadata via /admin/routes and traffic logs; check if pin is preserved when the canary instance set changes.
2026-03-01T09:14:32Z - scheduler: initiated scale-down of canary-replica-2 due to spot-eviction; draining connections
2026-03-01T09:15:07Z - agent(us-east-1-canary-2): health check failed during replacement; node replaced with spot-gpu-4
2026-03-01T09:15:45Z - routing: decision for route /api/generate -> fallback to redwood-13b-v2-quantized (policy=fallback_on_capacity_shortage)
Grafana dashboard: https://grafana.redwood.internal/d/srv/route-traffic?var-route=nimbledocs; suspicious spike in route latency and increase in quantized-serving-metric
Sentry event: https://sentry.redwood.internal/issue/56422 - small increase in token mismatch score correlated to timeframe
Initial hypothesis: pin metadata is stored on canary node filesystem and was not migrated to replacement node during spot-driven replacement.
Checked /admin/routes state at 09:16: service shows model_pin=null for affected route for a short period (~18 minutes); route metadata subsequently corrected when control plane reconciled.
Control plane logs show a race between node-replacement reconciliation and route-pin persistence: route update event (pin maintained in control-plane DB) failed to propagate to the new agent due to temporary backpressure on the routing service.
Observed autoscaler churn: 2 spot evictions in cluster within 5 minutes leading to increased control-plane load.
Reproduction confirmed in staging with a forced drain sequence: whenever agent bootstrap is slower than control-plane replication, route-level transient unset can occur if the agent queries local cache before full reconciliation.
Customer-supplied evals show small but material output regressions when quantized model served versus pinned float variant.
Workaround applied: Support used the route API to re-apply the pin immediately (customer accepted) and temporarily increased canary replica count to avoid single-node replacement windows. Engineering mitigation: patch landed to ensure route pin is pushed as part of agent bootstrap handshake and to make pin replication idempotent even under transient control-plane backpressure (PR referenced below). Deployment plan: staged rollout to prod canary (us-east) scheduled 2026-03-04; monitoring and post-deploy verification required. Follow-ups: add unit test for agent bootstrap pin sync and an alert when route metadata divergence occurs for >30s.

Additional notes:
2026-03-01 11:22 - NimbleDocs (Customer - Priya Shah): Provided failing prompt IDs and sample outputs demonstrating mismatch. Customer requests permanent fix; temporary pin re-apply worked but they want assurance.
payload.summary: Pinned model version lost when canary shifts to spot GPU nodes causing automatic fallback to quantized variant

payload.description:
Issue summary: Customer requests a near-real-time export stream tailored for their SOC (Sentinel Financial) that includes Sysmon-style enrichment, STIX 2.1 mapping, and deterministic per-record pseudonymization so their security analysts can ingest events into their SIEM with stable identifiers across replays.

Impact: Customer cannot onboard Redwood audit stream into their managed SOC pipeline due to lack of required enrichment fields, inconsistent identifiers after redaction, and missing STIX mapping. This blocks production monitoring for 40 internal services and delays regulatory evidence handover for upcoming audit.

Requested deliverables:
- Continuous HTTPS push or mTLS webhook delivering NDJSON with one event per line, throughput ~200 eps sustained, burst to 2k eps.
- Each event populated with Sysmon-like fields (ProcessId, Image, CommandLine, ParentProcessImage, NetworkConnection fields, UserDomain, LogonId).
- STIX 2.1 JSON envelope per event or a companion mapping file that deterministically maps Redwood audit schema to STIX object types.
- Deterministic pseudonymization scheme: per-customer salt derived from HMAC(KMS-root, tenant_id) and per-entity stable pseudonyms for user, host, process across time windows. Customer requires an allowlist of raw fields (only for legal/forensics) with access controls.
- Resume tokens for guaranteed-at-least-once delivery and idempotent replay semantics.
- Delivery manifest with checkpoints and per-batch HMAC (customer requests RFC 3161-style timestamp included).

Environment / context: Production tenant for Sentinel Financial, dedicated enterprise contract. Customer uses Splunk ES and a managed SOC that prefers STIX translation at source. They have strict evidence requirements for chain-of-custody and replays for incident investigations.

Steps customer took: Enabled audit-export in Console -> Selected "webhook-typed" delivery and attempted a test delivery to their staging collector. Received events but lacked process/commandline fields and identifiers changed after redaction.

Relevant links and logs:
- Console export config: https://console.redwood.ai/tenants/sentinel/export/1432
- Sample received payload (customer provided): https://s3.amazonaws.com/sentinel-bucket/samples/redwood-missing-fields.ndjson
- Customer SOC runbook: https://sentinel.internal/docs/redwood-onboard

Desired timeline: Customer requests a working POC stream and mapping within 7 business days for security onboarding and audit evidence readiness.
2026-03-10 09:14 - Customer (Ryan.McClure@sentinel.com): We need stable pseudonyms across replays for host and user fields; current export gives new uuids each replay which breaks our lookup tables.
2026-03-10 12:03 - Support (Aisha Patel): Thanks Ryan, filing a request with engineering for STIX mapping and deterministic pseudonymization. Can you confirm whether your SIEM accepts STIX bundles or individual STIX objects per event?
2026-03-10 12:47 - Customer (Ryan.McClure@sentinel.com): We accept one STIX object per event, prefer identity objects for user/host with stable ids. Also need a resume token on the webhook body.
2026-03-11 15:21 - Eng (Elena Park): Investigating feasibility of deterministic pseudonymization scheme using tenant-scoped HMAC salt from KMS. Will validate performance impact for 2k eps bursts.
2026-03-12 08:30 - Support (Aisha Patel): Added checkpointing and webhook resume-token work item to delivery backlog. Scheduling POC with customer for 2026-03-18.
Checked existing export pipelines: current webhook export supports NDJSON and per-batch manifests but does not emit Sysmon-specific enrichment fields by default.
Pseudonymization currently uses non-deterministic UUIDs generated at export time; need to introduce tenant-scoped HMAC(KMS) salt to produce stable hashes for identifiers.
STIX mapping present as an internal mapping prototype but not exposed as an export option — mapping needs normalization and documentation for STIX 2.1 compliance.
Estimated runtime cost: adding HMAC per event will add CPU; at 2k eps bursts need to validate worker scaling and possible offloading to native crypto library on serving nodes.
Risk: exposing an allowlist for raw fields requires access-control gating in console and audit logs to satisfy evidence requirements.
Workaround: Provide a near-term patch that augments the webhook payload with an additional 'redwood_enrichment' object containing Sysmon-like fields derived from existing metadata where available, and attach a temporary deterministic pseudonym map generated via a per-request HMAC with a short-lived salt. This will be marked experimental and gated to sentinel tenant only.
POC webhook endpoint that delivers STIX 2.1-compatible objects (one per event)
Deterministic pseudonymization library integrated into export path (configurable per-tenant)
Resume-token and checkpointed manifest attached to each batch with HMAC and RFC 3161 timestamp
Console toggle and access-control for raw-field allowlist
Documentation page and example Splunk ingestion recipe
In progress: Engineering validated HMAC-based deterministic pseudonymization using KMS-derived tenant salt in a canary branch. Next steps: performance test at burst loads, security review for allowlist gating, and schedule a POC with Sentinal Financial on 2026-03-18. Provided customer with temporary enrichment shim and example STIX mapping JSON for testing.
ENG: load test pseudonymization at 2k eps (owner: Elena Park, due: 2026-03-16)
SEC: review allowlist gating and audit trail (owner: Marcus Lee, due: 2026-03-15)
DOCS: publish STIX mapping guide and Splunk recipe (owner: Maya Chen, due: 2026-03-17)
OPS: add webhook resume-token validation to integration tests (owner: Priya Kapoor, due: 2026-03-16)

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customer (Acme Analytics, dedicated reservation) reported intermittent severe throughput drops and elevated p95/p99 token latency beginning 2026-03-09. Sessions see sustained 504s or streaming disconnects for ~30-90s windows.

Impact:
- Multiple production endpoints for Acme experienced request timeouts and 5xx errors during windows.
- Observed end-to-end p95 increased from ~280ms to >3.2s during events; tail hits 10s+.
- Customer SLA: dedicated latency SLO breached; risk of production downtime for key features.

Environment:
- Dedicated GPU reservation: res-acme-us-east (NVIDIA A10G equivalent), autoscaler policy: min_replicas=1, max_replicas=10, scale_up_threshold=65% GPU utilization, scale_down_threshold=30%
- Runtime version: serving-runtime v2.14.1; autoscaler v1.8.0; scheduler v3.2.

Steps to reproduce (observed pattern):
1) Normal traffic baseline for customer for hours.
2) At T0 a background tenant job on the same reservation begins (large-batch client job).
3) Within ~45–90s GPU SM/utilization climbs to >95%, kernel queue length spikes.
4) Serving pods begin to queue; requests hit request queueing timeout and backend returns 504s.
5) Autoscaler does not scale up fast enough due to conservative scale_up_threshold and min_replicas=1; scale-up completes after ~120–200s.
6) During scale-up pods experience GPU eviction signals (kube OOM & device preemption logs), causing additional retry storms.

Observations / logs (high-level):
- Prometheus: GPU SM utilization shows step-change from 40% -> 96% aligned to event windows.
- Scheduler metrics: kernel_queue_length metric elevated to 18–24 for affected GPUs.
- Kube events: multiple Pod eviction events: "DevicePreemption: MIG/eviction-triggered"  (12 evictions in 5m).
- Serving logs: request handler backlog warnings and intermittent "failed to allocate CUDA memory" traces.
- Traces: downstream retries amplify client-side concurrency causing head-of-line blocking.

Hypotheses tested so far:
- Noisy neighbor: confirmed a non-customer batch job (internal CI job from team-data) began large throughput runs coincident with incidents. Logs show job ID ci-batch-887 ramped GPU load.
- Autoscale mis-sizing: min_replicas=1 and scale_up_threshold=65% caused slow reaction to rapid utilization spikes.
- Eviction amplification: when preemption events occur, pods restart and trigger kube-scheduler binpacking which can cause temporary localized hotspots.

Investigation notes / timeline:
- 2026-03-09 10:12 UTC: First customer Slack (Acme) ping to #support reporting elevated timeouts.
- 2026-03-09 10:18 UTC: SRE observed correlated GPU utilization spikes; created this ticket.
- 2026-03-09 10:30 UTC: Identified internal CI job (ci-batch-887) running on same reservation; asked infra-team to terminate.
- 2026-03-09 10:34 UTC: CI job terminated; metrics returned to baseline within ~90s and customer traffic recovered.
- 2026-03-10 02:40 UTC: Repeat occurrence; further analysis showed autoscaler scale-up latency ~160s due to kube-provisioner delays and pod scheduling backpressure.

Temporary mitigations applied:
- Shifted Acme traffic to warm spare reservation res-acme-us-east-b in same region at 2026-03-09 10:40 UTC (manual routing override).
- Bumped reservation min_replicas to 3 for res-acme-us-east to reduce single-point scaling delay.
- Applied node taint for internal CI jobs to avoid landing on reserved pools.

Root-cause (current working):
Primary cause is noisy-neighbor background GPU batch workload occupying SM capacity on the shared dedicated reservation combined with autoscaler policy that is too conservative for rapid bursts. Device preemption/evictions during high contention amplified scheduling instability and restart churn, creating a feedback loop that prolonged throughput degradation.

Next steps / action items (owners):
- (infra) Enforce placement constraints so internal CI and non-dedicated batch jobs cannot schedule on customer-dedicated reservations. Target: 2026-03-13. (Assignee: Priya Nair).
- (autoscale) Update autoscaler policy templates for dedicated reservations: recommend min_replicas >= 2 and lower scale_up_threshold to 50% for bursty customers; add faster scale-up ephemeral slots. Target: 2026-03-16. (Assignee: Leo Martin).
- (scheduler) Investigate pod scheduling latency and reduce provisioning jitter; implement soft-eviction fallback policy to reduce restart storms. Target: 2026-03-20. (Assignee: Jamal Ortiz).
- (SRE/Support) Run retrospective and publish runbook for noisy-tenant detection and automated migration. Target: 2026-03-18. (Assignee: Maya Chen).

Workaround communicated to customer:
- We temporarily routed production traffic to an alternate reservation and increased min_replicas to reduce scale-up dependency. Customer accepted temporary routing and will monitor traffic for 72 hours.

Resolution notes (future):
- Pending: formal config changes to autoscaler and infra placement policy. Once completed, we'll schedule a controlled rollback of temporary routing to original reservation and monitor for recurrence for 7 days.

Additional notes:
Mitigation in place: traffic moved to spare reservation and min_replicas increased. Permanent fixes planned: placement enforcement, autoscaler policy updates, scheduler eviction behavior changes. Target deployment windows listed in action items.

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Aurora Payments needs a production-ready SIEM export that: pseudonymizes user identifiers per-region, packages events into a cross-region envelope (single sequence across regions), and provides a per-batch duplicate-detection manifest (HMAC-based) and signed legal attestation for onboarding with their payments regulator.

Impact:
- Compliance blocking: Aurora cannot complete onboarding until they receive attested evidence that exported events are de-duplicable, pseudonymized deterministically per-tenant, and include tamper-evident manifests.
- Business: Aurora is awaiting a go/no-go for a production cutover scheduled next week.

Environment:
- Redwood prod clusters serving Aurora tenant (tenant-id: aurora-prod-10).
- Exports to Aurora SFTP endpoint us-east-1 and eu-west-1, currently set to per-region delta batches.

Requested deliverables (customer asks):
1) A cross-region envelope format spec that guarantees ordering (monotonic watermark) across regions for a given tenant for the export window.
2) Deterministic reversible pseudonymization spec (per-tenant salt) and sample output demonstrating pseudonymization applied.
3) Per-batch duplicate-detection manifest (per-file HMAC + sequence range + record-count + sample hash) and approach for resumable replays.
4) Signed legal attestation (short form) that the export mechanism preserves order and includes tamper-evident manifests suitable for regulator review.
5) Implementation timeline and any migration steps required for Aurora to switch to the new export.

Steps to reproduce (current state):
1) Aurora consumes per-region SFTP batches from us-east and eu-west.
2) They run an ingest pipeline which occasionally detects duplicates when cross-region replication results in overlapping event windows (they provided a sample of three duplicate event UUIDs).
3) Aurora requests a single canonical export envelope so they can ingest once and avoid cross-region dupes.

Logs/attachments provided by customer:
- three-sample-duplicates.csv (attached)
- sftp-manifest-sample-us-east.json (attached)
- sftp-manifest-sample-eu-west.json (attached)
- onboarding-questionnaire.pdf (legal/regulatory checklist)

Acceptance criteria from Aurora:
- Spec doc describing envelope and per-batch manifest format (JSON schema).
- Working sample export (one-hour slice) with pseudonymization applied and batch manifests that validate with HMAC key provided to Aurora.
2026-03-10 | Aisha Patel (Support): Created ticket after intake call with Aurora. Customer provided sample duplicates and legal checklist. Asking for spec + sample export and short attestation text. Assigned to Diego for SRE/exports analysis.
2026-03-10 | Diego Morales (SRE): Confirmed receipt of samples. Initial hypothesis: duplicates are produced by per-region delta windows overlapping during cross-region DR replication. Need to review the export scheduler and file manifest generation code. Will pull recent export runs from S3 and check sequence watermarks. ETA initial findings by 2026-03-11 EOD.
2026-03-11 | Diego Morales (SRE): Investigation update: found that per-region exporters independently seed HWM (high-watermark) from local ingestion timestamps; small clock skew + retry semantics can create overlapping ranges. Also observed manifests currently contain only file-level checksums, not record-level counts and no HMAC. Attaching S3 prefixes: s3://redwood-exports/aurora-prod-10/us-east/2026-03-09/ and s3://redwood-exports/aurora-prod-10/eu-west/2026-03-09/.
2026-03-11 | Maya Kapoor (Eng, export-format): Proposed immediate mitigation: add per-file sequence-range (min_seq, max_seq) and record_count to manifests and include a manifest-level HMAC using per-tenant export key. For canonical cross-region envelope, propose a top-level envelope that lists ordered file fragments and an envelope HMAC. Will prototype PR for manifest schema and HMAC library.
2026-03-12 | Evan Ross (Legal/Compliance): Reviewed customer's onboarding checklist. We should not provide a formal legal opinion; however, we can provide an attestation template signed by the Redwood compliance team confirming the export format and tamper-evident guarantees given the HMACs and manifest model. Legal needs Confluence spec and sample export to generate attestation language.
2026-03-12 | Aurora (customer contact: Hannah Li): Thanks for fast triage. For pseudonymization we require deterministic per-tenant reversible pseudonymization using a tenant KEK; Aurora will provide public key for encrypting mapping manifests. Also request that HMAC keys be rotated monthly and that rotation metadata be included in manifests.
Checked export-service logs for aurora-prod-10 between 2026-03-09T00:00Z and 2026-03-10T00:00Z. Found overlapping sequence ranges across regions where sequence numbers were derived from ingestion timestamps rather than global monotonic counters.
Hypothesis 1: Clock skew + per-region independent watermarking yields overlapping seq ranges -> duplicates at consumer. Mitigation: move to global monotonic sequence generator or include per-record digest + idempotency keys in manifest.
Hypothesis 2: Retries at exporter can produce duplicate files with same timestamp but different content; manifests currently do not include record_count or sequence ranges so consumer cannot de-duplicate deterministically. Mitigation: include (min_seq,max_seq,record_count,file_checksum,manifest_hmac).
Security considerations: Pseudonymization must be reversible only by Aurora (they requested KEK to wrap per-batch key). Support will not ship any plaintext mappings in the export. We'll provide sample mapping format encrypted with customer's public key or wrapped by their KMS.
Planned deliverables and timeline agreed with Aurora on 2026-03-12 call:
- 2026-03-14: Draft confluence spec for cross-region envelope and manifest schema (Maya).
- 2026-03-17: Prototype export sample (one-hour slice) with pseudonymization and manifest HMACs to Aurora SFTP test endpoints (Diego).
- 2026-03-19: Compliance attestation template completed by Legal (Evan) once sample delivered.
- Post-delivery: follow-up runbook for key rotation and migration steps.

Interim workaround provided to Aurora:
- We recommended Aurora enable idempotent ingest where their pipeline ignores records with identical record_id and sequence number and to block dual ingestion across regions until sample runs are validated. This reduces duplication risk for the cutover window.

Open action items:
- ENG: implement manifest schema changes + HMAC library and prototype (owner: Maya Kapoor).
- SRE: run one-hour production slice export to staging SFTP for Aurora and validate manifests (owner: Diego Morales).
- Legal: draft attestation once sample is validated (owner: Evan Ross).
- Customer: supply public key or KMS wrap info for mapping encryption and confirm test SFTP credentials (owner: Aurora).
payload.summary: Request: Cross-region pseudonymized SIEM export with per-batch duplicate-detection manifest & legal evidence for payment-provider onboarding

comments: 2026-03-12T14:02:00Z Maya Chen: Adding logs and a timeline. We rolled out the sidecar healthcheck alongside a small UX release; spike started ~5 minutes after canary. Healthcheck is configured with a 1s interval and uses ephemeral auth tokens.\n
payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customer reports intermittent 429 responses across several API routes during normal traffic spikes. The pattern is opaque (no consistent client-side spike) and appears correlated with background telemetry probes and a new signed-url callback flow launched last week.

Impact:
- Multiple client processes experience short-lived 429s (seconds to a couple minutes) during what the customer calls "routine telemetry sweeps".
- No clear console quota depletion; console shows available credits but requests still receive 429s.
- Affects their production ingest path for embeddings and a low-latency chat route. Customer worried about data loss and wants a recommended rate-limit configuration.

Environment:
- Dedicated pool (dedicated) in prod-us-west.
- Running redwood-open-7b for chat and embeddings.
- Several short-lived signed URLs used for callback jobs; healthcheck sidecar added to ingestion workers last week.

Steps to reproduce (as provided by customer):
1) Start baseline worker farm (10 workers) with signed-url callback pattern (each worker requests signed URL, posts chunk, and polls for callback).
2) Enable the sidecar healthcheck (1s heartbeat) at worker level.
3) Launch scheduled telemetry sweep across all workers (one background job every 30s).
4) Observe spike window: some routes start returning 429s for a subset of ephemeral keys for ~30-90s.

Logs / Observations sent by customer:
- Sample request IDs: req_usw_20260312_1823a (chat), req_usw_20260312_1823b (embed), callback_req_1823c.
- Example response header (when 429 occurs): X-RateLimit-Reason: TOKEN_WINDOW_EXHAUSTED; X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0; X-Trace: trace-4be2
- Console screenshot shows remaining credits 74% for tenant and 100% for route (screenshot timestamps line up with 429 windows).

Customer asks:
- How should we account for short-lived healthchecks and telemetry probes so they don't cause opaque 429s?
- Should signed URL callbacks be separated into a different route or burst pool?
- What smoothing/refill configuration prevents brief synchronized drain from background probes and client warmups?


Additional notes:
2026-03-12 18:10 - Support (Liam O'Connor): Thanks for the report. We're triaging — asking SRE to check refill pacing and any sudden token bucket drains. Can you confirm whether signed-url callbacks use the same API key as the workers? If not, please include the key prefixes.

2026-03-13 09:35 - Customer (Fleetly Labs - Priya Rao, Eng): Signed-url callbacks use the same tenant key but we create ephemeral tokens server-side per callback; we do not rotate the tenant-level API key. Callback traffic looks bursty (many short-lived posts after ingest completion).

2026-03-13 16:44 - SRE (Jordan Patel): Preliminary check: no global refill outage. Found short windows of token-window exhaustion on a route-weighted layer during telemetry sweeps. The tenant bucket had spare credits but per-route window dropped to zero due to many 1s healthchecks being attributed to the same route.

Checked rate-limiter metrics (tenant/route layers) around provided req ids: trace-4be2 shows per-route bucket refilled every 60s while healthchecks consumed ~40 tokens/minute on that route, causing the route window to empty and reject until next refill.

Edge proxy attribution: healthcheck pings originate from worker IPs and reuse persistent HTTP/2 connections; ingress-sidecar set keepalive was causing many probes to be counted against the same connection/token window, amplifying drain.

Signed-url callbacks: since callbacks are short-lived and immediately follow successful uploads, they create a coincident microburst that aligns with the healthcheck timing, producing synchronized drain.

Console mismatch: console shows tenant-level credits (aggregated) but per-route/show-level windows can be exhausted independently — explainability gap: customer saw tenant credits >0 while route window was zero.

Related runbook: Confluence:RateLimiter-Runbook (section: route-isolation) clarifies per-route bucket behavior and burst pools. Linked PR for future telemetry: github.com/redwood-inference/rate-limiter/pull/642 introduces a telemetry-exempt flag for healthchecks (draft).

Workaround (applied 2026-03-13 20:12): Created a separate route for signed-url callbacks and moved healthcheck traffic to a dedicated telemetry route. This immediately removed the synchronized drain and stopped 429 windows.

Configuration guidance provided to customer:
- Create an isolated route for ephemeral callback and another for sidecar healthchecks; reserve a small burst pool for telemetry to avoid consuming main route token windows.
- Use longer healthcheck intervals (2-5s) or batch healthchecks at the sidecar to reduce per-second token consumption.
- Enable route-weighted burst pools: allocate a dedicated small refill interval for telemetry (e.g., 10 tokens/10s) while keeping main route refill untouched.
- If using ephemeral tokens for callbacks, tag them with a callback scope so they can be mapped to the telemetry route by the edge and not count against chat/embed windows.

Follow-ups (open):
- Engineering: investigate adding opt-in telemetry-exempt headers for healthchecks (related PR #642).
- Product: update console UI to surface per-route token windows more clearly for dedicated customers.
- Support: validate with customer that changes removed 429s and document recommended templates for telemetry/healthcheck configs.

Status: awaiting customer verification on 2026-03-14.
payload.summary: Guidance: configuring ephemeral probe accounting and client-side smoothing to prevent opaque 429s

payload.description:
Issue summary: After a regional canary rollback in us-east, some PhotonPay sessions remained pinned to the canary variant and continued to route to an evicted serving group. The edge route cache honored a stale sticky-pin token with an extended TTL, which caused the routing layer to repeatedly attempt the pinned variant and trigger fallback logic. Impact: PhotonPay reported elevated 5xxs and long tail latency on customer-facing calls (~3–5% error rate for affected sessions) and inability for affected users to reach their pinned model until sessions were cleared. Environment: Dedicated pool for PhotonPay in prod/us-east; canary weight toggled then rolled back during 2026-03-09 22:00–22:15 UTC.
1) Configure a canary for rwd-opus-v1 on PhotonPay dedicated pool with weight 10% in us-east.
2) Establish a long-lived session (session token / affinity cookie) to the pinned canary variant and confirm model responses.
3) Roll the canary back to stable (weight 0) via Console -> Rollouts at 2026-03-09 22:12 UTC.
4) Observe that session traffic continues to include X-Model-Pin header for the canary variant and is routed using edge cache entries with TTL > pin TTL.
5) The serving runtime evicted the canary worker nodes at 22:14 UTC; requests return 502/504 and fallback controller repeatedly tries alternate variants, causing repeated transient 5xx and high latency.
6) Clearing the session (new session token) restores normal routing to stable model.
edge-proxy request trace: requestId=f4c2b3a2, ts=2026-03-09T22:16:03Z, route=photonpay/conv, headers: X-Model-Pin: rwd-opus-v1-canary-20260309
edge-proxy debug: route-cache hit=true, cache-ttl=7200s, pin-ttl=300s, resolved-target=evicted-canary-host:502
serving-runtime: host=evicted-canary-host, health=DECOMMISSIONED, last-heartbeat=2026-03-09T22:14:12Z
fallback-controller: attempted-fallbacks=3, last-error=502 Bad Gateway, latency-ms=1200
customer console snapshot: session_id=photon-usr-19, model_pin=rwd-opus-v1-canary-20260309, created_at=2026-03-09T21:58:00Z
Initial triage by Support (Priya): customer reported persistent 5xxs after canary rollback; reproduces for sessions created before rollback.
SRE (Evan) collected traces and saw edge-proxy route-cache entries with TTL=7200s (2h) while pin tokens had TTL=300s; mismatch allowed stale cache entries to outlive model availability.
Engineering hypothesis: when canary was rolled back rapidly, canary-controller issued eviction but edge-proxy had previously cached route entries that included stamped pin metadata. On cache refresh, a bug in cache revalidation preserved the pin header and extended TTL using cache rehydration codepath (introduced in edge-proxy PR #1259).
Confirmed root cause: route-cache rehydration path inadvertently copied X-Model-Pin from cached metadata during a rollback event and set cache-ttl based on route policy rather than pin expiry. Combined with immediate decommissioning of canary workers, this led to repeated attempts to reach an unavailable variant and triggered fallback loops.
Scope: Customer-scoped (PhotonPay) dedicated pool and a small subset of session tokens created in the 20-minute window prior to rollback. Estimated affected sessions: ~4k, affecting ~3% of PhotonPay's requests during the incident window.
Cross references: Slack #support (https://slack.redwood.ai/support), ops-runbook note, and related ticket SUP-31147 (session-resume-drops-version-affinity-causes-fallback).
Temporary mitigation discussed: avoid immediate decommissioning of canary workers until pinned sessions age out OR invalidate pinned tokens actively on rollback for affected tenants.

Additional notes:
2026-03-11 Customer (PhotonPay - CS): After Support requested session reset, customer cleared sessions via Console and reported error rate dropped to <0.1%. Asked for permanent fix and verification plan.
2026-03-12 PhotonPay (CS): Confirmed normal behavior; requested root-cause writeup and runbook update for future canary rollbacks.
Short-term workaround: Support instructed customer to clear affected sessions (Console -> Sessions -> Invalidate) or rotate session tokens; we provided an automated script to invalidate session pins for Tenant=PhotonPay.
Hotfix: Edge-proxy PR #1287 prevents route-cache rehydration from copying X-Model-Pin metadata when target health != HEALTHY or when a rollback flag is set. Hotfix deployed to us-east edge fleet on 2026-03-12 03:00 UTC.
Migration: Ran tenant-scoped token invalidation job for PhotonPay (job id: mz-inval-20260312-photonpay) to remove stale pins from session-store and route-cache.
Monitoring & verification: Post-deploy dashboard shows 99.95% success rate for PhotonPay requests and 95th percentile latency returned to baseline within 40 minutes.
Follow-ups:
      - Update canary rollback runbook to include explicit pin invalidation step (Confluence: https://confluence.redwood.ai/runbooks/canary-rollbacks).
  - Add unit/integration tests to edge-proxy to ensure pin metadata is not persisted across rollbacks (tracked in GH issue #1310).
  - Consider adding a TTL reconciliation job that ensures pin TTL <= route-cache TTL for tenant-scoped caches.
Customer communication: Customer notified, requested postmortem; assigned to Eng for a brief RCA doc and runbook update. Customer asked for a follow-up review in 1 week to validate rollout safety improvements.
payload.summary: Sticky pin cache TTL exceeded after regional canary rollback causing session fallback loop

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customer MedAtlas observed a sudden increase in tail-latency (95p/99p) and intermittent 502/504 responses after we deployed a tenant-scoped optimizer profile that enabled mixed-precision quant and aggressive KV-prefetch for throughput. They are on Dedicated capacity and requested an automated off-ramp/safemode script that can be run fast to revert only the optimizer flags for that tenant without a full snapshot restore.

Impact:
- Multiple endpoints for MedAtlas returned elevated 95p latency from ~120ms to ~1.8s and sporadic 502s starting 2026-03-10 13:22 UTC.
- Affects critical inference pipelines for clinical summaries; customer reports degraded UX and paused rollouts.

Environment:
- Dedicated pool medatlas-dedicated-1 (us-east-1)
- Serving runtime v1.32.0
- Recent optimizer profile applied: optimizer-profile-2026-03-10-qprefetch-mixed

Steps to reproduce (observed):
1) Traffic runs normal with baseline profile.
2) Operator applied tenant-scoped profile that set quantization=dynamic-mixed, kv_prefetch=true, batch_target=128.
3) Within ~10 minutes, 95p latency climbs and requests start returning 502/504 from workers that show KV eviction churn in logs.

Observed logs / metrics:
- Grafana: https://grafana.internal/redwood/tenant/medatlas/dashboards/optimizer_telemetry (95p spike)
- Sample worker log: "kv_cache: eviction_count=1725 in_last_60s; kv_prefetch_queue_full=true"
- Router logs: elevated upstream 502s with timeout traces to serving runtime containers.

Customer ask:
- Provide a safe, tested script (or playbook) that toggles a per-tenant safemode which:
  * Disables kv_prefetch for tenant traffic
  * Lowers batch_target to conservative value (e.g., 8)
  * Reverts quantization to per-model baseline (int8 fallback) for affected tenant only
  * Optionally drains and restarts a small subset of serving workers for the tenant without taking entire pool offline
- Steps to validate the off-ramp and rollback without impacting other tenants on the same dedicated pool.

2026-03-10 13:40 UTC - Initial triage by support: confirmed tail latency and 502s; notified SRE; customer provided traffic window and baseline config.
2026-03-10 14:05 UTC - Captured heap/KV metrics from medatlas-dedicated-1 workers; eviction_count correlated with the onset of 502s.
Hypothesis: aggressive kv_prefetch combined with mixed-precision quantization increased memory churn and forced frequent KV evictions, which caused cache misses and long downstream kernel latencies under heavy batching pressure.
Rolling down batch_target and disabling kv_prefetch for tenant improved synthetic test in staging (reduced 95p by ~60%).
Risk notes: global profile changes would affect other tenants; need per-tenant toggle. Existing 'optimizer-toggle' endpoint supports tenant flags but lacks an automated multi-step off-ramp script that also adjusts batch settings and drains safely.
Suggested immediate action: prepare a script that atomically sets per-tenant flags and performs targeted worker drain with health-check gating.
Support - Aisha Patel (2026-03-10 13:50 UTC): Acknowledged. Escalating to SRE. Collecting logs and time window.
SRE - Eleni Morgan (2026-03-10 14:12 UTC): Observed KV eviction spikes. Reproduced symptom in small staging cluster. Will draft off-ramp steps and safety checks.
Customer - Rajesh Kumar (MedAtlas) (2026-03-10 14:30 UTC): This is blocking deployment. Please provide something we can run quickly; prefer tenant-scoped change only.
Support - Tomás Rivera (2026-03-11 09:05 UTC): Drafted preliminary safemode script (internal link). Requesting review from runtime team and SRE. CI smoke tests run attached to PR.
Runtime Eng - Priya Shah (2026-03-11 12:40 UTC): Reviewed script. Minor change: add backoff and verify KV eviction rate drops below threshold before completing. Also ensure quant revert uses tenant pin to baseline model artifact.
Support - Tomás Rivera (2026-03-12 08:22 UTC): Prepared customer-facing playbook and one-line command to toggle safemode via admin API. Scheduling maintenance window with customer for controlled run.
Workaround prepared: one-line admin API command and safemode script that disables kv_prefetch, sets batch_target=8 for tenant, and reverts quant to int8 baseline. Script includes health checks (95p latency and kv_eviction thresholds) and a safe drain/restart for up to 2 workers at a time. Scheduled controlled run with MedAtlas for 2026-03-12 15:00 UTC. Post-change monitoring plan defined; full rollback playbook added to Confluence. Follow-up: add a test to CI to validate per-tenant optimizer toggles and add an automated canary gate for future optimizer profile rollouts.
payload.summary: Automated safeguard/off-ramp request for tenant after mixed-quant + KV-prefetch optimizer change triggered tail latency and intermittent 5xx

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customer BrightHome AI observed degraded throughput and elevated p99 latency for their dedicated pool during daytime peak. Symptoms included sudden slot fragmentation (many small GPU attachments that never consolidated), autoscaler repeatedly scaling down after short-lived attach spikes, and brief regional GPU shortages that triggered cross-tenant fallback routing. Impact was limited to the BrightHome reserved cluster but autoscaler oscillation caused transient performance variance for other dedicated tenants in the stripe.

Impact:
- BrightHome AI production routes experienced ~35% throughput reduction and increased failures on batched routes.
- Autoscaler made multiple downscaling decisions that later had to be reversed, causing thrash and occasional 5xx fallbacks for low-priority routes.

Timeline (local times, PDT):
- 07:50 — Support received first alert from BrightHome (console p99 spike).
- 07:58 — Automated alert triggered: reserved-pool-attach-lag-high (us-west-2).
- 08:05 — Support triaged and engaged SRE on-call.
- 08:12 — SRE noted many small ephemeral attachments and high connection churn from BrightHome sidecar hosts.
- 08:30 — Mitigation applied: temporary per-tenant throttle on sidecar connection concurrency; model pin for BrightHome to redwood-open-7b-v2 to reduce model migration.
- 09:10 — Autoscaler damping parameter adjusted for the affected stripe to avoid aggressive downscale.
- 10:20 — Stability confirmed; p99 and throughput returned to baseline.

Wanted: full root-cause analysis, permanent mitigation, and runbook updates to prevent recurrence.
Throughput on BrightHome AI reserved pool dropped ~35% for a 90-minute window; p99 request latency rose from 420ms to 1.3s; single-customer tail event but caused autoscaler responses impacting adjacent tenants.
Collected allocator snapshots, prefetched KV cache usage, and sidecar host connection histograms for tenant=brighthome.
Found that 12 sidecar hosts (cohort) were generating >200 short-lived attaches/min with payloads of ~100 tokens, causing many fractional slot allocations (avg slot occupancy 0.12 GPU).
KV cache grew for the tenant due to many distinct short contexts, preventing efficient reuse and hurting consolidation heuristics.
Autoscaler logs showed repeated downscale decisions triggered 2–3 minutes after transient attach drops; current hysteresis at 90s was too short for this workload pattern.
No kernel-level GPU faults or driver errors observed; GPU contention was logical (fragmentation) rather than thermal or hardware failure.
Cross-checked with console traces; adjacent tenants saw minor p99 blips correlated with autoscaler down/up cycles.
A cohort of BrightHome AI sidecar hosts created high-frequency, short-lived connection streams that led to fractional GPU slot allocation (slot fragmentation). The autoscaler misinterpreted the short spike as a sustained drop shortly thereafter (hysteresis too short) and downscaled, which removed capacity that could have been used to absorb subsequent real traffic. Net effect: temporary GPU shortages and throughput regression in the dedicated pool.
1) Applied temporary throttle on BrightHome sidecar concurrency and recommended batching changes on their side (customer implemented).
2) Increased autoscaler downscale hysteresis for the affected stripe to 6 minutes to avoid reacting to short spikes.
3) Deployed allocator change to prefer consolidation of fractional attachments when tenant KV cache indicates repeated small contexts.

payload.description:
Issue summary: Multiple customers experienced persistent 429 throttles starting ~2026-03-12T04:00:00Z. Root cause appears tied to an orchestrated worker refresh that executed en masse at tenant-local-midnight after a DST/timezone roll event. Impact: Several dedicated tenants (including SlideStream Media) saw short bursts of hundreds of concurrent warmup/keepalive requests that depleted tenant token windows and caused streaming and bulk endpoints to return 429s. Console quota readouts reported 'tokens remaining' that did not match live throttle behavior (console showed ~30% remaining).
Customer-facing errors (429) for streaming and batch ingestion. SlideStream reported 12-minute service degradation impacting live captioning flows. Estimated affected customers: 4 dedicated tenants in us-east; transient soft throttles observed for ~10 other self-serve tenants. Revenue impact under review; multiple escalation calls occurred.
Simulate timezone/DST rollover by advancing tenant-local clock to midnight while cron workers scheduled without jitter start a refresh cycle.
Trigger orchestrated worker restart across a tenant's ingestion pool (simulate multiple workers starting within <30s window).
Send multiplexed streaming warmup + several small batch embed jobs concurrently from same API key.
Observe token-window depletion and 429 responses from /v1/streams and /v1/embeddings endpoints within 5-15s.
Compare console quota readout to real-time /rate-limit headers on responses to see mismatch.
Rapid surge of requests from orchestrated workers (peaks measured at ~85k requests/min across the tenant's pool). Rate-limiter consumed tenant burst credits in under 12s. Responses returned HTTP 429 with X-RateLimit details showing window exhausted. Console displayed quota ~30% remaining due to cached snapshot refresh lag and lack of immediate reconciliation with in-memory token counters.
Tenant-local scheduled jobs should include jitter and stagger to avoid synchronized bursts. Console quota metrics should reflect real-time token counters or flag stale data explicitly. Rate-limiter should handle short synchronized spikes without immediate hard-throttles by smoothing refill or using short grace credits where configured for dedicated tenants.
Edge gateway logs: spike in POST /v1/streams from 10 instances -> 85k r/min at 2026-03-12T04:01:02Z
Rate-limiter metric: tenant_window_tokens_remaining went from 420k -> 0 in 11s
Serving runtime: queue length jumped to 410, per-GPU mem pressure + 18% latency P95 increase
Console metric lag: quota-snapshot.last_refresh 2026-03-12T03:59:00Z while live counters showing exhaustion at 04:01:03Z
Customer logs (SlideStream): repeated 429s with ids: ssm-req-117234, ssm-req-117240
Initial hypothesis: misconfigured cron jitter resulted in synchronized warmups at tenant local midnight; confirmed via orchestration logs showing scheduled jobs with identical cron expressions without jitter for several customer clusters.
Observed refill logic uses UTC-midnight reference for credit refill but token-window consumption is calculated in tenant-local time slice for burst accounting -> mismatch during timezone roll events.
Console uses a cached snapshot persisted to Redis every minute; during burst the cache was stale and did not reflect in-memory token drain.
Confirmed correlated Slack thread: #support (thread t-512) with customer screenshots. See link: https://slack.redwood.io/archives/support/p16234
Telemetry shows pattern repeats for tenants with many short-lived ephemeral workers that rotate at local-midnight. Not common but present in ~0.4% of tenants.
Cross-reference: similar customer-impact pattern to SUP-762318 (tail 429s after dedicated pool scale-down warmup) but root cause here is time-sync + cron-jitter absence.
Applied emergency temporary bump of burst credits for affected dedicated tenants in us-east for 60 minutes (operator action: increase_burst_credit tenant_id: ss-004 -> +150k tokens).
Rolled out a per-tenant short-term smoothing policy on rate-limiter to allow 3s smoothing window for synchronized warmups (feature flag: rl_smoothing_short_burst = true) to reduce hard 429s while permanent fix is deployed.
Advised SlideStream to add client-side jitter to their local-midnight refresh cron as immediate mitigation.

Medium term (2 weeks): update token refill logic to normalize refill windows across UTC vs tenant-local transitions and add DST-aware reconciliation on boundary events.
Medium term (2 weeks): update console to mark quota snapshots stale if in-memory counters diverge >10% and show 'reconcile' button to force refresh.
Long term (Q2): implement adaptive smoothing in rate-limiter that detects synchronized warmup patterns across workers and applies per-tenant soft-grace credits automatically based on historical behavior.
Customer communication: draft status note to affected customers with incident summary and crediting plan (CS to own messaging).
Workarounds applied and smoothing flag reduced number of immediate 429 responses to near-zero within 6 minutes of mitigation.
Burst credit increase prevented further degradation; monitoring shows normalised request rates and token counters were replenished by 04:14Z.
Patch for scheduler jitter merged to main (PR #4491) and queued for staged deploy to production dedicated clusters starting 2026-03-14.
Follow-up: billing team to evaluate one-time credit for SlideStream covering 12 minutes of service disruption; CS owner: Priya Rao.
Postmortem scheduled: https://confluence.redwood.io/display/POST/2026-03-12+Timezone+Rollover+Burst+Incident

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customers (BrightLearn) reported unusually long Time-To-First-Token (TTFB) on chat completions immediately after our 1.4.2 runtime rollout and an accompanying model weight patch (redwood-7b-quant-v2). Impact: interactive chat experiences stall for 2–6 seconds before any token is emitted; after first token stream resumes normally.

Impact:
- Multiple enterprise/dedicated customers observed increased latency in the first token for chat endpoints (not steady-state token throughput).
- Client-side timeouts (5s) triggered for some requests, causing degraded UX and escalations to CS.

Environment:
- Runtime version: 1.4.2 (canary → staged → prod on 2026-03-10)
- Affected models: redwood-7b-quant-v2 (weight layout change + quantization metadata update)
- Regions: us-east (primary), eu-west (partial)

Steps to reproduce:
1) Send a single-turn chat completion request to hosted chat endpoint pinned to redwood-7b-quant-v2 on runtime 1.4.2.
2) Observe TTFB measured by client (start of request → first token).
3) Repeat with multiple warm and cold connections, and measure kernel compilation / logs on the serving node.

Observed behavior:
- TTFB spikes to 2–6s on first token (median baseline was ~200ms).
- Subsequent tokens stream at expected rates once first token emitted.
- Logs show a 1.2–1.8s period of kernel JIT/compilation activity and occasional model weight re-layout steps on the serving node.

Expected behavior:
- TTFB remains within SLAs (<=500ms for these workloads) and no client timeouts on first token for warmed nodes.

Related artifacts/links:
- Grafana dashboard: https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/rt/ttfb-summary?panelId=7 (sharp rise at 2026-03-10 11:22 UTC)
- Slack incident thread: #support (https://slack.redwood.ai/archives/C01234567)
- Canary PR: https://github.com/redwood/serving-runtime/pull/2314

Additional notes:
2026-03-10 12:15 UTC — SRE (Priya Rao): Found compilation cache miss spikes coincident with rollout. Canary cluster had cache cleared by new packaging step. Investigating packaging -> kernel selection interaction.
2026-03-10 13:02 UTC — Eng (Diego Morales): Hypothesis: model weight layout change triggered different kernel selection and forced a JIT/compile path for some GPU kernels. Also saw autoscaler creating fresh instances with empty compilation caches causing first-request stalls.
2026-03-11 09:20 UTC — Eng (Diego Morales): Deployed hotfix v1.4.2-patch01 to avoid compilation path on first inference by pre-warming kernel caches and skipping expensive weight re-layout on serving path. Monitoring.
Instrumented TTFB at ingress and on-serving nodes; delta shows server-side pre-token time is the source (not network).
Node logs show calls to kernel_compiler::compile_and_cache() taking ~1.1–1.8s for a subset of kernels after weight metadata change.
Compilation cache misses correlated with autoscaler events and nodes created after the package change; older nodes with cached kernels were not affected.
Model weight patch introduced a new weight ordering that selected a different GEMM kernel family; runtime attempted a JIT fallback when precompiled kernels were not available for that ordering.
Batching and cache warmers did not trigger for very small single-request patterns; pre-warming was required to mitigate first-request stalls.
No increase in 5xx error rate was observed; errors were primarily client timeouts (4xx category) due to TTFB exceeding client-side timeouts.
Reproduced locally by booting a fresh serving instance with empty /var/cache/serving-kernels and sending single chat requests pinned to redwood-7b-quant-v2.
Telemetry: increased cpu/gpu kernel compiler time and a spike in 'kernel_compile' metric during rollout windows (11:20–11:40 UTC).
Immediate mitigation: Rolled back runtime 1.4.2 in affected Dedicated pools (us-east) to 1.4.1 at 2026-03-10 14:00 UTC; TTFB returned to baseline on those pools.
Hotfix deployed (1.4.2-patch01) that adds: (a) pre-warm routine for kernel caches on node startup for affected models, (b) skip-on-path for weight re-layout during serving (move to background), and (c) gating to avoid JIT fallback when performance-critical flag set.
Changed default first-request batching policy: reduce autoscaling of fresh nodes for single-request patterns and ensure pre-warm runs before routing traffic.
Added rollout checklist item: any model weight layout or quantization metadata change must ship with precompiled kernel artifacts or a warmup job in the image.
Monitoring and alerts: added a dedicated TTFB alert (P1) with 3-minute burn-in window and dashboard panel for kernel_compile metric.
Follow-ups: create internal postmortem (INT-4021) and a task to automate kernel artifact generation in CI (linked PR created).
Customer communication: BrightLearn notified of root cause, mitigation, and timeline; they validated improvement and accepted the hotfix.

payload.description:
Issue summary:
During a staged canary rollout of open-llm-xlarge-v1 -> open-llm-xlarge-v1+tokenizer-fix for customer LexaHealth (dedicated pool), tenant sessions observed repeated fallback between canary and legacy variants. The canary introduces a subtle tokenizer normalization change which causes KV-cache lookups to miss; missed lookups trigger short-lived prewarm + fallback logic that resends requests to legacy variant. This creates duplicate token generation and an amplification loop that increased token consumption and caused a billing spike for the tenant.

Impact:
- Several tenants of LexaHealth saw doubled token billing for a 90-minute window.
- Intermittent mixed outputs: some requests returned responses from canary, others from legacy, causing inconsistent replies in end-user flows.
- Latency increased for affected tenant sessions (~200-400ms p95 increase).

Environment:
- Dedicated GPU pool (redwood-dedicated-us-east-lexa-01)
- Control plane: prod-us-east

Billing spike (~2x token usage) for customer LexaHealth; degraded output consistency and increased latency for affected sessions.
1) Have LexaHealth tenant routed to staged canary weight 10% for open-llm-xlarge-v1+tokenizer-fix.
2) Replay a set of long chat sessions that reuse KV cache (multi-turn > 6 turns) with prompt normalization that includes special punctuation sequences.
3) Observe control-plane logs: canary replies missing KV hit markers followed by fallback routing of same request to legacy variant.
4) Observe doubled token count in per-request accounting and duplicated generation calls in serving runtime logs.
Excerpt from serving-runtime (2026-03-10T14:22:17Z):
- [canary] kv_cache_lookup miss key=conv-lexa:session-9f7a turn=7 len_prefix=512
- trigger_pre_warm(canary)
- fallback_route selected -> legacy variant id=open-llm-xlarge-v1
- generation_start legacy -> token_count accounted: 264
- generation_start canary (duplicate) -> token_count accounted: 258

Edge-proxy trace (same timeline):
- client->edge request-id=abc123 forwarded to canary
- canary returned 502?cache_miss? immediate fallback to legacy per fallback-policy

Billing ledger sample: tenant-lexa token-usage 2026-03-10T14:00-15:30 increased from baseline 1.1M tokens/hr -> 2.2M tokens/hr
Initial hypothesis: tokenizer normalization change caused cache key mismatch. Verified via diffs between tokenizer versions in PR #4492. Found that the canary strips zero-width joiners in prompts, while legacy preserves them, resulting in different serialization for KV keys.

Control plane routing: fallback logic is triggered when KV cache miss coincides with prewarm inability to satisfy latency SLO; fallback fires and replays to legacy. Because the canary and legacy have different tokenizers, the second request results in different token accounting and sometimes different completion shapes.

Observed additional amplification factor: some requests were re-enqueued by the ingress retry (edge-proxy) on a transient 504 from the canary prewarm path; that caused triple-generation in a small subset (~4% of affected requests).

Relevant links and artifacts:
- Slack: #support-lexahealth thread (message link: slack://channel/support-lexahealth/1623)
- Github PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/4492
- Control-plane trace: http://grafana.internal/traces/trace-lexa-20260310-abc123

Additional notes:
Mitigation steps performed 2026-03-10 -> 2026-03-11:
- Canary weight immediately rolled back to 0% for open-llm-xlarge-v1+tokenizer-fix for LexaHealth.
- Added per-tenant fallback suppression flag to prevent immediate legacy replay on KV-cache miss while we validate tokenizer behavior.
- Rolled a hotfix that makes tokenizer normalization changes gated by a model-variant flag and adds a KV-cache compatibility test in CI.
- Throttle configuration patched in edge-proxy to avoid retry storms on transient prewarm 5xxs.
Follow-ups:
- Engineering to add automated KV-cache-key equivalence checks when tokenizer binaries change (owner: Priya Sharma).
- Product to coordinate with LexaHealth on a retro and billing reconciliation (owner: CS Manager Rowan Lee).
- Billing flagged for potential credit to customer for the 90-minute amplification window (ticket created with Finance).
1) Deploy KV-cache compatibility unit in preflight checks (ETA 2026-03-18).
2) Engineering to add telemetry for per-request generation counts to detect amplification loops automatically (ETA 2026-03-24).
3) CS to schedule customer retro and billing reconciliation (ETA 2026-03-15).
This ticket captures combined operational, billing, and model-variant interaction issues. Keeps timeline and artifacts for follow-up engineering and CS actions.
payload.summary: Tokenizer change in canary invalidates KV-cache, triggers fallback loop and billing surge for tenant

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customer reports increased p95/p99 latency (up to 6s) and occasional request timeouts (HTTP 504) since 2026-03-10 09:00 UTC. Root cause appears to be requests routed to an older quantized variant that is in a cold state and triggers expensive cold-starts + slower quantized execution paths.

Impact:
- NovaHealth production workloads experience degraded user-facing latency and sporadic 504s across several endpoints.
- Customer reports elevated error rates during morning traffic ramp (us-east).
- Affects mission-critical inference for clinical decision support; customer flagged as dedicated tenant and requested urgent investigation.

Environment:
- Customer: NovaHealth (dedicated pool)
- Region: prod us-east
- Deployed variants: redwood/llama-3-70b-v2 (primary), redwood/llama-3-70b-quantized-v1 (fallback)
- Traffic pattern: steady ramp 08:00-10:00 local, spikes to 250 rps

Steps to reproduce (customer):
1) Send sustained generation requests at 200-250 rps to the customer's route (route id provided in ticket attachments).
2) Observe increased p95/p99 and occasional 504s between 09:00-10:30 UTC.
3) On our side, confirm that requests intermittently land on quantized-v1 variant.

Logs & traces (collected):
- Trace IDs: trace-20260310-9a1b, trace-20260310-9a2c (attached).
- API gateway logs show 504s with upstream timeout to serving-runtime at 09:15 UTC.
- Router decision logs indicate a fallback policy triggered due to perceived capacity shortage; selected variant: redwood/llama-3-70b-quantized-v1.
- Serving runtime allocation timestamps show container spin-up and long model load times for quantized-v1 (~2.4s additional latency before first token).

Initial hypothesis:
1) Fallback routing policy incorrectly prefers an older quantized variant when capacity signals are transient, not accounting for the quantized variant's cold-start overhead.
2) Quantized-v1 lacks warm cache for KV/collapsed attention paths and has slower kernel-path for this customer's sequence-length distribution causing p99 spikes.
3) Autoscale decision loop may have been slower than expected during the morning ramp, causing router to fall back to variant that was technically compatible but performance-degraded.

Investigation notes:
- Confirmed router logs show a capacity mismatch signal from the dedicated pool between 09:12-09:18 UTC.
- Node-level metrics: GPU utilization was at ~62% on primary pool, but several nodes were being drained for housekeeping; autoscaler not yet provisioned additional capacity.
- Quantized-v1 model artifact was last promoted to prod in Dec 2025 and was not included in the latest kernel selection benchmark; lacks a warmup image.
- Trace analysis shows first-token latency contributed ~2.2s for requests routed to quantized-v1; non-quantized variant first-token latency ~0.3s.
- Customer confirmed they had pinned rollouts to allow fallback to quantized-v1 for cost reasons previously.

Immediate mitigation taken:
- Support temporarily adjusted routing policy for NovaHealth to prefer primary (non-quantized) variant for 1 hour while autoscaler capacity was increased.
- Triggered a rapid warmup job for quantized-v1 in the customer's dedicated pool to pre-load model artifacts.
- Eng SRE patched router scoring to weight cold-start penalty for known quantized artifacts (hotfix deployed to canary 2026-03-11).

Remaining action items:
- SRE/Infra: add warmup orchestration for quantized variants during traffic ramps (ticket INT-412).
- Runtime: add metadata to model catalog that includes estimated cold-start penalty to guide routing.
- Product: create customer-facing doc explaining fallback tradeoffs for quantized variants and recommended pinning strategies.
- Postmortem: link to incident page and finalize by 2026-03-18.

Next steps for customer communication:
- Confirm with NovaHealth that temporary routing change improved latency (requested they monitor 2026-03-12 morning ramp).
- Share planned timeline for warmup orchestration and router scoring changes.

Expected resolution criteria:
- No routing to cold quantized variants during peak traffic without warmup; p99 latency returns to baseline for >=72 hours.

Additional notes:
2026-03-10 12:28 UTC — SRE (Lena Ortiz): Observed node draining in the dedicated pool; autoscaler delayed by 90s due to quota check. Initiated manual capacity increase and warmup job for quantized-v1.
2026-03-11 09:30 UTC — NovaHealth (Customer): Confirmed latency improved after override; seen a single 504 at 09:05 during ramp. Asked for full mitigation plan.
Router fallback policy selected quantized-v1 due to transient capacity signal; quantized-v1 has large cold-start penalty not previously modeled. Autoscaler lag + node drain created a temporary shortage. Confirmed with traces and model load timing.
Temporary routing override applied, warmup job executed, hotfix to add cold-start penalty weighting deployed to canary. Remaining work tracked in INT-412 and a product doc story. Customer confirmed improvement.
Workaround applied and hotfix deployed. Ongoing work to prevent recurrence; ticket will be updated with postmortem link once complete.
payload.summary: Routing to an outdated quantized model variant causing elevated p95/p99 latency and sporadic timeouts

payload.description:
Issue Summary
- After enabling Shadow Traffic (beta) for Aurora Devtools’ Dedicated tenant, our metrics backend began firing high-cardinality alerts and write rejections.
- Primary impact was internal: reduced observability fidelity and increased risk to telemetry stability. Customer-facing API serving remained healthy.

Customer Report (via CSM escalation)
- Aurora enabled shadow experiments on their highest-QPS route to compare control vs candidate variant.
- Within ~20 minutes, their Console “Quality deltas” dashboards showed gaps and delayed updates.
- They also reported that some internal dashboards they rely on (latency breakdown panels) became “partial / missing series.”

Impact
- Telemetry ingestion: elevated series churn and increased dropped samples.
- Metrics backend (Mimir/Prometheus) triggered cardinality alarms; some write paths began rate limiting.
- Console quality panels were missing segments due to aggregation dropping high-cardinality dimensions.

Environment
- Dedicated tenant: Aurora Devtools
- Region: us-east
- Feature: Shadow traffic telemetry events v1 + quality delta dashboards

Timeline (UTC)
- 2026-02-12 16:05: Pager triggered for cardinality threshold breach on shadow telemetry metric families.
- 2026-02-12 16:12: Support engaged Observability + Telemetry (Caleb Johnson, Nadia Rahman).
- 2026-02-12 16:35: Confirmed correlation with new shadow traffic dimension set (per-route + per-target + request fingerprint bucket).
- 2026-02-12 17:10: Mitigation applied: reduced emitted dimensions via allowlist override for tenant; forced bucketing for route identifiers.
- 2026-02-13: Patch prepared to change defaults for all beta tenants (drop unsafe labels, enforce bucketing, cap series).
- 2026-02-14: Verified stability and closed ticket after 24h clean metrics.

Signals / Alerts
- Alert: "mimir_ingester_series_limit_near" (multiple ingesters)
- Alert: "prom_remote_write_samples_dropped" increased
- Internal dashboard: Shadow quality delta panels: missing data for segment breakdowns

Investigation Notes
Findings
1) The shadow telemetry events were being translated into multiple metric families with a label set that included at least one effectively-unbounded dimension under Aurora’s traffic:
   - route_id (string, high variety due to per-team routing keys)
   - shadow_target_id (fine)
   - model_id (fine)
   - experiment_id (fine)
   - prompt_id / request_fingerprint (NOT fine at Dedicated QPS; effectively unique per request)

2) Aurora’s workload had high variance in request metadata headers. Even though we intended to strip most headers, a “shadow_metadata_hash” label was being propagated in one metric path.

3) Existing cardinality guardrails in the Shadow Traffic design were partially implemented but not enabled by default for this tenant (beta config drift). The ADR guidance (adr-shadow-metrics-data-model-and-cardinality) states request-unique identifiers must never become metric labels; they must live in logs/traces with sampling.

Reproduction
- Enable shadow policy on a high-QPS route (>= 200 RPS) with segment breakdown enabled in Console.
- If request_fingerprint/prompt_id is emitted as a label, series count grows ~linearly with traffic.

Immediate Mitigation (2026-02-12)
- Applied tenant-level allowlist for shadow metrics dimensions:
  - Dropped: prompt_id, request_fingerprint, shadow_metadata_hash
  - Forced bucketing: route_id -> route_bucket (stable 128-bucket hash)
  - Limited: segment_key -> {"none", "country_group", "sdk_family"} (pre-approved set)
- Disabled per-request example sampling export for Aurora until patch landed (kept async scoring running; only metrics emission was reduced).
- Confirmed “fail-open” serving path unaffected; no additional routing overhead observed.

Customer Communication
- 2026-02-12: Informed Aurora that the issue is metrics-only (no serving impact), and we’re applying safe default dimensions immediately.
- Shared guidance: run shadow at 1–2% sampling while we deploy defaults; avoid enabling per-request segment breakdowns on day 1.

Resolution
Root cause
- Shadow traffic metrics pipeline emitted one or more request-unique identifiers as labels for aggregation, causing a cardinality explosion in the metrics backend when enabled on high-volume routes.

Fix / Changes Implemented
- Reduced default dimensions for all shadow-traffic quality metrics:
  - Removed request-unique labels from metric paths (request_fingerprint/prompt_id/metadata hash).
  - Enforced a strict label allowlist, matching the ADR and the Quality Metrics Observability Standard.
  - Added hard caps + drop counters when a new label key/value is not on the allowlist.
- Updated dashboard queries to use safe breakdowns only (route_group, model_id, shadow_target_id, rubric_version).
- Added runbook note + Console warning: segment breakdowns are limited to approved low-cardinality dimensions; anything else is sampled and only available via example logs.

Verification

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customers report that dashboards with multiple panels (different queries / route filters) revert their selected time range and panel-level filters to an earlier range after a background retention compaction sweep completes. This appears as a UI "snapback": a user changes the global time range to a recent window (e.g. last 30m), adjusts a panel-level route filter, the panels render correctly, then 20–40s later the global time range and some panel filters revert to the previous snapshot (typically the previously cached 6h window) and several panels show stale tracehook links.

Impact:
- Affects NovaDocs dedicated org (production, us-east) with multiple active dashboards.
- Users lose recently-applied time ranges for live troubleshooting; trace links in affected panels point to pre-compaction runIds that no longer exist in the retention index.
- Workaround is manual re-select of time range and refresh; interrupts on-call investigation and causes longer mean time to resolution for customers.

Environment:
- Prod (dedicated pool) - us-east; org id: org-novadocs-73
- Console version: web-2026.03.10
- Retention compaction job schedule: daily rolling compaction; this issue reproduced immediately following a compaction window triggered for heavy-cardinality tables.

Steps to reproduce:
1) Log into NovaDocs org in us-east.
2) Open dashboard "Service Health — multi-pane" (contains 6 panels, mixed live and aggregated queries).
3) Set global time range to "Last 30 minutes" and toggle panel B route filter to route:analytics-42.
4) Observe panels render with up-to-date metrics and tracehook links.
5) Wait 20–60 seconds.
6) Observe: global time range snaps back to "Last 6 hours" and panel B's filter resets to route:analytics-9; tracehook links update to older runIds and some links 404.

Expected behavior:
- Dashboard retains user-applied global time range and panel filters until user changes them.
- Tracehook links remain bound to the query snapshot used to render the panel and should not revert when compaction background tasks run.

Actual behavior:
- UI reverts to prior cached time range and some panel-level filters are overwritten. Tracehook links reflect the older snapshot and some 404 when the index is compacted and records pruned.

Logs / evidence:
- Browser console logs collected (attached) show a subsequent websocket event "dashboard:refresh_snapshot" with payload referencing snapshot_id: snap-20260313-2100 before the user action.
- Ingest service logs show compaction job started at 2026-03-13T21:00:12Z for table:events_v2-cardinality-high and finished at 2026-03-13T21:00:35Z.
- Query-router logs contain a 200 response for initial queries, then a second identical query issued by the UI with header X-Dashboard-Snapshot: snap-20260313-1200 (older snapshot) at 2026-03-13T21:00:38Z.
- Customer-provided screencast timestamped 2026-03-13T21:00:15–21:01:10 (uploaded).
2026-03-13 21:05 - Support (Maya Chen): Created ticket after phone call with NovaDocs. Initial hypothesis: UI receives compaction event that triggers a fallback to a cached snapshot id. Collected logs and screencast; requested additional console network traces.
2026-03-13 21:20 - SRE (Diego Alvarez): I can reproduce in a staging compaction run. UI emits 'dashboard:request_snapshot' then receives 'dashboard:refresh_snapshot' with older snapshot_id. Attaching trace from query-router and websocket logs. Adding component 'retention-service' to ticket.

Additional notes:
2026-03-14 09:02 - Support (Maya Chen): Customer confirmed impact is reproducible during their daily compaction window; they requested an interim mitigation to prevent snapbacks during active user sessions.
2026-03-14 11:40 - SRE (Diego Alvarez): Applied temporary rate-limiter on compaction heartbeat to avoid emitting snapshot-invalidated events to websocket until client idle or user session flag is cleared. Observed no snapbacks in a 1-hour canary. Planning a patch to snapshot-store fallback logic.
Summary of findings:
- Reproducible in staging when retention compaction completes for high-cardinality tables.
- Root cause appears to be snapshot-store fallback behavior: when a requested snapshot_id is not found (because compaction pruned underlying index shards), snapshot-store returns a 'last-known-good' snapshot id per-org. The console websocket handler treats any 'refresh_snapshot' event as authoritative and forces the client to reapply that snapshot and reset time-range / panel-level filters to the snapshot's stored state.
- Recent change in PR #4729 tightened snapshot TTL and introduced an aggressive invalidation path that exposed the race between user-initiated queries and compaction finishing.
- Query-router evidence shows the UI issues a second fetch after the websocket 'refresh_snapshot' arrives and that second fetch includes X-Dashboard-Snapshot header for the older snapshot.
- Hypothesis: snapshot-store should not return a fallback snapshot for active interactive sessions; instead it should return a signal 'SNAPSHOT_MISSING' so console can choose to keep the user's current view and surface a warning.
- Related: linked issue SUP-271314 documented a similar retention-tied dashboard drift but under different UI code path.
Next steps proposed:
1) Implement conservative fallback: snapshot-store returns explicit "missing" code rather than replacing with last-known-good for interactive websocket flows.
2) Console websocket handler will ignore 'refresh_snapshot' events tagged as 'compaction-triggered' for active sessions and instead surface a toast to user: "Snapshot unavailable — results may be partial. Refresh to reload."
3) Add short-term compaction gating: do not issue global 'snapshot invalidated' websockets to orgs with active dashboards in last 5m.
4) Roll PR with feature-flag and canary on staging/dedicated orgs.
Workaround / Mitigation:
- Temporary: SRE applied gating on compaction-heartbeat to avoid immediate websocket invalidation events for orgs with active dashboards; this was rolled at 2026-03-14 11:30 and mitigated immediate customer impact.
- Customer guidance: if you see a snapback, reapply the time range and refresh; we will notify when the permanent fix is deployed.
Permanent fix plan:
1) Patch snapshot-store to return explicit SNAPSHOT_MISSING code for interactive websocket queries instead of substituting last-known-good. (PR opened: https://github.com/redwood/snapshot-store/pull/53)
2) Update console websocket handler to ignore compaction-triggered refresh events for sessions with recent user activity and to surface a non-blocking warning instead of forcing snapshot revert. (PR opened: https://github.com/redwood/console/pull/4734)
3) Add an integration test that simulates compaction during active dashboard sessions and asserts no time-range resets.
4) Canary rollout to dedicated orgs and monitor for regressions; full rollout scheduled after safety window and positive canary results.
Status: In Progress. Patch PRs created and internal code review ongoing. Estimated ETA for staged rollout: 2026-03-18 pending reviews and QA.
payload.summary: Multi-panel dashboard filters snap back to previous time range after retention compaction
