payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customers (FinScale Labs) reported a reproducible scenario where concurrent clients using different Redwood SDKs trigger retries and the order of function/tool executions does not match the original logical ordering in the prompt. This is producing application-level data inconsistencies for financial flows.
Customer observed that when two backend services (one using Python SDK, one using Go SDK) concurrently call the same conversation with function/tool invocations and experience transient 429s, the final sequence of tool executions can become re-ordered. This leads to state inconsistencies (e.g., 'confirm' processed before 'debit').
Customer encountering incorrect ordering for multi-step function sequences (debit -> confirm). Affected production jobs process ~500 requests/min; ~1 in 400 requests show reorder symptoms after retry storms, causing reconciliation failures and manual intervention.
1) Setup shared conversation id between two services: Service A (Python SDK) and Service B (Go SDK).
2) Service A sends a request that triggers function call 'debit_account' then returns streaming tokens.
3) Concurrently, Service B sends a followup request referencing same convo that triggers 'confirm_debit'.
4) Induce transient 429s at api-gateway (rate limit burst) or drop streaming connection to force client-side retries with exponential backoff.
5) Observe on the backend logs that retry attempts from different SDKs arrive close in time and are routed to different serving instances.
6) Verify final order of tool invocations in audit logs (found confirm before debit in failing traces).
Retries and concurrent requests that target the same logical conversation should preserve the logical ordering of tool/function invocations, or at minimum support deterministic at-most-once semantics when idempotency is used.
In failing traces, 'confirm_debit' executes prior to 'debit_account' because a retried/late message from Service A was processed after Service B's request. The SDK-level and gateway retries appear correlated with request routing to different serving nodes and non-deterministic merging of queued tool calls.
TraceID: trc-20260310-91a2 - Service A (py-sdk) initial request -> request_id=R-1132 attempt=0 routed-> node-srv-07
TraceID: trc-20260310-91a2 - Service B (go-sdk) concurrent request -> request_id=R-1140 attempt=0 routed-> node-srv-12
TraceID: trc-20260310-91a2 - api-gateway returned 429 to R-1132 at 2026-03-10T14:22:03Z, client retried attempt=1 -> routed-> node-srv-12 at 2026-03-10T14:22:04Z
Audit: tool-call debit_account request_id=R-1132 processed at node-srv-12 at 2026-03-10T14:22:05Z (late), confirm_debit request_id=R-1140 processed at node-srv-12 at 2026-03-10T14:22:04Z
Observed that node-srv-12 executed confirm_debit before processing the retried debit_account message; sequence_token logs show missing sequence gap for conversation-id conv-5582.
Initial triage: reproduced in staging by simulating 429 bursts via gateway throttle. Failure only reproduced when two different SDK clients sent near-simultaneous requests referencing same conversation-id.
Checked SDK versions: python 1.4.2, go 0.9.7 - both use client-side retry but differ slightly in jitter backoff and header ordering.
Routing logs show retried messages can land on different serving nodes and are enqueued for per-conversation processing; node-local dequeues respect arrival order per node, not global logical time.
Sequence token implementation relies on per-node in-memory ordering when multiplexed; gap emerges when late retry arrives to a node that already processed a later logical message from another node.
Race condition between inter-node routing and per-node queue ordering: retries arriving at a node after a later message from another node result in out-of-order execution because global sequencing is not enforced at ingest time.
SDK differences (jitter/backoff and header normalization) increase the likelihood of cross-node routing for retries; absence of a conversation-level global sequence gate allows reorder.
Idempotency keys are present but scoped to entire request not to discrete tool invocations, so they do not guarantee ordering when separate calls reference the same conversation id.
Short-term: Advise customer to serialize critical multi-step flows via a single client (stick to a single SDK instance for ordering-sensitive sequences).
Use explicit per-action idempotency tokens in metadata for each tool call (e.g., X-Idempotency-Action) so server can dedupe and enforce application-level ordering checks in customer logic.
Temporarily increase retry-backoff jitter or centralize retries into an orchestrator process to avoid cross-node arrival races.
SRE/Runtime: evaluate adding conversation-level ingest gating or a global sequence coordinator for ordering-sensitive conversations.
SDK Team: add guidance and helper utilities for per-action idempotency tokens and provide a best-practice pattern in SDK docs for ordering-critical flows.
Support: work with FinScale Labs to roll out the temporary orchestrator approach and monitor for reduction in reorders.

Additional notes:
2026-03-10 16:14 - FinScale Labs (Customer): Provided sample traces and said the issue appears during batch settlement at peak traffic windows.

payload.description:
Issue summary: BrightAssist reported a pronounced pre-output idle period for chat completions (high TTFB) immediately after our 2026-03-09 runtime and model cutover. Impact: customer-facing latency increases causing UI timeouts and degraded UX for interactive assistants. Environment: prod-us-west cluster serving BrightAssist's dedicated pool after runtime v2.14 and model rw-chat-7B-q4 repin. Observed since 2026-03-09 22:00 UTC.
1) Send a chat completion request to /v1/chat/completions against BrightAssist dedicated endpoint (prod-us-west) with a 4-turn context and max_tokens=256.
2) Request streaming=true and measure time between request and first token chunk (TTFB).
3) Repeat across 10 requests; observe variability with median ~450ms pre-cutover vs 2.8s post-cutover and p95 > 6s.
4) Toggle model pin to previous model build and observe TTFB change.
5) Force request route to bypass routing affinity (fast-path) and compare.
After the cutover there is a consistent pre-output idle period: median TTFB increased from ~0.45s to ~2.8s and p95 jumped to >6s. Traffic then occasionally times out at the client (client-side 10s). Token stream arrives normally after the idle period; subsequent token emission rate is unchanged.
TTFB should remain within prior baseline (p50 < 600ms, p95 < 1.2s) for BrightAssist dedicated pool when model pinned to rw-chat-7B-q4 and runtime v2.14.
[2026-03-09T22:03:12Z] request_id=abc123 route=prod-us-west pool=brightassist_dedicated step=router_select latency_ms=12
[2026-03-09T22:03:12Z] request_id=abc123 step=serve_prepare_kv_cache duration_ms=1820
[2026-03-09T22:03:12Z] request_id=abc123 step=model_init_check duration_ms=920
[2026-03-09T22:03:14Z] request_id=abc123 step=stream_start duration_ms=30
[2026-03-09T22:03:14Z] request_id=abc123 total_ttfb_ms=2772
Multiple traces show a long gap spent in serve_prepare_kv_cache and model_init_check after routing completes.
2026-03-10 02:00 UTC - Initial triage by Support (Ava): confirmed BrightAssist reports and collected traces and p50/p95 metrics.
2026-03-10 03:20 UTC - Eng (Ravi) reproduced in staging by replaying traffic; reproduced only when routing selected nodes with new kernel-quant dispatch.
Hypothesis A: new runtime build introduced an additional synchronous KV cache validation step that blocks streaming until cache warmup finishes for some model variants. Evidence: serve_prepare_kv_cache durations correlated tightly with TTFB jumps (R=0.87).
Hypothesis B: route affinity change caused requests to land on nodes with cold model shards requiring slow model_init_check (consistent with model_init_check log durations of 600-1200ms).
Correlations: high TTFB aligns with nodes running kernel-quant v3.2 and compiled model variant rw-chat-7B-q4-q.
Observability: Console traces and per-token breakdown show the idle period occurs before stream_start is emitted to client. No 5xxs seen on server; client received 200 then delayed chunk stream.
Next steps: instrument blocking points (KV priming, compatibility check) with finer-grained spans and add sampling for nodes running kernel-quant v3.2.
Applied temporary routing override at 2026-03-10 08:45 UTC to prefer fast-path nodes (bypass kernel-quant v3.2) for BrightAssist pool. Customer reverted to previous model pin (rw-chat-7B-q4@build-20260301) via support guidance which restored TTFB to baseline. Monitoring set up to track regressions.
Workaround in place (routing override + model repin). Root cause still under active investigation. ENG follow-up task created to remove synchronous KV validation and make priming async (INT-678). We will release a non-blocking cache priming patch in next runtime micro-release and validate with canaries before global rollout.

Additional notes:
2026-03-11 09:00 UTC - Customer (BrightAssist - Jason Li): Noted improvement after support changes; requested ETA for permanent fix and rollback guidance for future cutovers.

payload.description:
Issue summary: FinAssist reported intermittent 403 AuthorizationDenied errors for several users after SSO login when calling admin APIs and the customer console.

Impact: Since 2026-02-24 08:30 UTC approximately 12% of auth attempts for FinAssist prod (eu-west) returned 403s for otherwise-valid users. Affects console and admin API flows; regular inference requests authenticated as service accounts were unaffected.

Environment: Private deployment (FinAssist Inc.), control plane in eu-west, identity-proxy v1.7.3, auth-service v2.1.0, RBAC tenant-index. Customer IdP: third-party OIDC/SAML gateway with locale-specific transform rules.

Observed behavior: The identity-proxy receives the principal header (X-Remote-User / preferred_username / sub) URL-encoded for certain users (e.g., 'alice%40finassist.com' instead of 'alice@finassist.com'). RBAC matching is strict and attempts a direct lookup against the tenant user index; encoded forms do not match canonical entries, resulting in 'rbac: no matching principal' and a 403 response.

Steps to reproduce:
1) Configure an IdP to send the subject/preferred_username URL-encoded (simulate locale transform that encodes '@'->'%40').
2) Perform a standard SSO login and call an admin API or open the console.
3) Inspect headers at the identity-proxy and auth-service.
4) Observe 403 and 'Principal not found' RBAC entries in logs.

Logs / examples:
- identity-proxy: "Incoming principal: alice%40finassist.com"
- identity-proxy: "Principal decode check: no match for tenant user index"
- auth-service: "rbac: no matching principal for tenant finassist (principal=alice%40finassist.com) -> 403"

Hypothesis: Some IdP configurations (regional/localization transforms or older gateway proxies) URL-encode special characters in the principal claim. identity-proxy does not reliably URL-decode or canonicalize these values before RBAC lookup, and RBAC matching is implemented as an exact match against the canonical (unencoded) username/email stored in the tenant index. This mismatch yields authorization failures for legitimate users.

Workarounds applied: Support added a temporary ingress rewrite rule on the customer's edge to URL-decode X-Remote-User for affected tenants. We also created a tenant-level mapping entry in FinAssist's RBAC config to accept the encoded principal form while a fix is prepared. These mitigations restored console/admin access for impacted users.

Recommended next steps:
- Engineering: implement a safe URL-decode pass in identity-proxy normalization pipeline (idempotent; should tolerate already-decoded values and avoid decoding harmful sequences), add unit+integration tests covering single and double-encoded forms.
- SRE: patch and rollout identity-proxy v1.7.4 to private control plane and coordinate with FinAssist for a controlled restart of services if required.
- Support / Docs: update private-deploy SSO troubleshooting docs and runbook to include instructions for detecting encoded principals and the temporary ingress rewrite pattern.

Cross-refs: Slack #support (thread FinAssist-encoding-2026-02-24), related PR and runbook links above.
2026-02-25 09:10 (Aisha): Customer supplied raw proxy logs. Noticed X-Remote-User shows percent-encoding.
2026-02-25 10:02 (Carlos): Reproduced locally by configuring a test IdP to emit 'bob%40example.com' as preferred_username. identity-proxy forwarded header unchanged.
2026-02-25 13:20 (Eng): RBAC lookup code uses exact string key against tenant_user_index; no decode/normalize step present. Potential safe place to add decode is immediately after header ingestion but before tenant resolution.
2026-02-26 08:05 (SRE): Customer ingress rule added to decode header as stopgap. Verified 3 affected users regained access.
2026-02-27 11:30 (QA): Tested double-encoded input (alice%2540finassist.com -> alice%40finassist.com -> alice@finassist.com) and verified proposed normalization logic must be idempotent and avoid over-decoding arbitrary %-sequences.
2026-02-24 09:05 - FinAssist (support contact): 'Several admins can't access console after SSO, getting 403. Works for some users. Please advise.'

Additional notes:
2026-02-24 10:01 - FinAssist: 'We're using LocaleGate 2.3.1 (regional transformer) + on-prem SAML gateway. We did a change earlier this week.'
2026-02-26 09:00 - FinAssist: 'Ingress rewrite applied and verifies users can access console again — thanks. Please provide permanent fix ETA.'
2026-02-27 15:40 - Eng (Carlos): 'Patch for identity-proxy normalization in review: https://github.com/redwood-inference/identity-proxy/pull/842. Targeting v1.7.4 rollout next week with tests for idempotent decoding.'
Temporary workaround: ingress header URL-decode rule and tenant mapping applied. Permanent fix: identity-proxy patch merged (PR #842) that adds safe URL-decoding + canonicalization step before RBAC lookup; backported to 1.7.x and released as v1.7.4. Deployed to FinAssist control plane 2026-03-05 and validated. Runbook updated with detection and workaround steps. Follow-up: monitor for similar behavior from other IdP vendors and add an onboarding checklist item to validate principal encoding behavior during Private deployments.
payload.summary: Locale-encoded principal (%40) in IdP assertion leads to RBAC mismatch and 403s in Private deployment

payload.description:
Issue summary: Customer's Private deployment (Direct Connect) is failing TLS handshakes intermittently when the server certificate chain is large and includes an OCSP staple. Impact: model streaming connections fail to establish from the customer's on-prem network to Redwood private nodes; customers observe immediate TLS handshake termination and 5xx errors in our control plane logs.

Impact: Several production endpoints for NeuroDocs' clinical summarization pipeline are unable to connect to our runtime during peak hours; retries temporarily succeed when client reduces TLS max fragment size, but normal clients fail.

Environment: Private deployment over AWS Direct Connect (single DX link to us-east-1), customer-controlled on-prem firewall (hardware appliance), VPC route through TGW attachment to Redwood private node. TLS mTLS not used; server certificate chain includes an intermediate + long OCSP staple.

Observed behaviour:
- TLS handshake fails with 'unexpected_message' or 'handshake_failure' on client side.
- Redownloading with smaller MSS/MTU or enabling TCP MSS clamping at the edge allows handshake to complete.
- New TCP connections after MTU adjustment work; long-lived connections that require handshake renegotiation fail.

Hypothesis: Path MTU blackhole between customer on-prem and Redwood node causes larger TLS ServerHello/Certificate/OCSP responses to be dropped/fragmented and blocked by on-prem firewall, resulting in incomplete handshake and immediate teardown. The OCSP staple increases TLS record size above the PMTU, provoking fragmentation that intermediate gear drops.

Steps to reproduce:
1) From customer's on-prem network, initiate a TLS session to the private node on port 443 with default MTU.
2) Observe client logs showing handshake failure after ServerHello.
3) Lower client MTU or enable TCP MSS clamping on the on-prem firewall and repeat; handshake succeeds.

Logs and evidence:
- Client Wireshark capture (supplied by customer) showing TCP retransmits and fragmented TLS records around the large Certificate message.
- VPC flow logs show established TCP but no application-level ACKs for the large packet.
- Control plane logs: tls_handshake_error entries with TLS_ALERT 40 (handshake_failure) correlated to the customer's IP.
- On-prem firewall inspection log snippets (customer-supplied) showing 'fragmented packet dropped' for packets > 1400 bytes.

Temporary mitigation: Customer enabled TCP MSS clamping on their edge firewall (reduce MSS to 1360) which results in successful handshakes for affected endpoints. As a short-term workaround we suggested increasing MTU on Direct Connect jumbo support path (if available) or configure MSS clamp on the customer's appliance.

Next steps / tasks:
- Confirm exact PMTU along DX + TGW path using traceroute/MTU probes (ENG task assigned).
- Validate whether AWS Direct Connect or TGW attachment is doing any packet-size normalization that could interact with customer's firewall.
- Add a server-side config option in the private node agent to advertise smaller TCP MSS during the TLS handshake (investigate feasibility).
- Customer to provide deterministic pcap for packet-level proof (they already attached one).

Requested outcome: Permanent fix either by documenting PMTU requirements for Private Direct Connect paths and adding a note in the onboarding checklist, or by implementing server-side mitigations so large cert chains / OCSP staples do not fail on common enterprise firewalls.
From customer on-prem host, open TLS connection to private node (port 443) with default MTU
Observe client-side tls handshake failure (handshake_failure) after ServerHello when certificate + OCSP exceed PMTU

payload.description:
Issue summary: During a staged canary with staggered weight shifts and snapshot replay, a subset (~8-12%) of tenant requests remained bound to the previous model variant (legacy/degraded) despite the control-plane indicating successful commit to the new variant. Impact: Customers at DataStream Labs reported increased inference latency (~200-500ms) and lower output quality on streaming endpoints for affected sessions. Scope: Observed in us-east-1 on Dedicated fleet for routes with cookie-based session affinity and prewarm snapshots enabled.
1) Create a rollout for route /v1/chat from redwood/open-7b-v2 -> redwood/align-13b with staged weights: 5% -> 25% -> 60% over 30m.
2) Enable prewarm snapshot mirror and cookie affinity with path / and domain datastream.example.
3) Simulate production-like client reconnects that reuse keep-alive but occasionally re-NEGOTIATE streams.
4) Observe that ~10% of sessions continue to be served by legacy variant after the 25% and 60% steps complete.
Expected: Affinity should bind to the current cohort based on the latest snapshot and model pin. Actual: Persistent binding to previous variant until cache TTL expiry or token rotation.
Note: Reproduction is intermittent and appears correlated with quick successive weight adjustments and edge-side memoization of route fingerprints.
[2026-03-10T14:02:11.342Z] edge-proxy: route-fingerprint=0x7ef3 memo-hit stale=true tenant=ds-102 request_id=aa12b3 model_variant=legacy-202602
[2026-03-10T14:02:11.345Z] orchestrator: commit-snapshot id=sn-8811 status=applied cohort=cohort-25 weight=25
[2026-03-10T14:02:11.348Z] serving-runtime: chosen-variant=align-13b request_id=aa12b3 -> decision-conflict: edge_bind=legacy-202602 controlplane=align-13b
[2026-03-10T14:02:11.349Z] edge-proxy: cookie-scope=/. datastream.example path=/ ttl=3600 token=aff-9c3 expired=false
[2026-03-10T14:09:02.001Z] metrics: route=/v1/chat p50=85ms p95=420ms p99=920ms degraded_requests=9.8%

Additional notes:
2026-03-10 15:01 - SRE on-call (Marta Li): Performed targeted cache invalidation for shard 12 (#support channel: #support). Observed drop in legacy-bound sessions from ~10% -> ~1.4% over 4 minutes. Customer reports immediate improvement on a test cohort but still sporadic on heavy reconnects.
2026-03-12 11:12 - DataStream Labs (CS contact - Priya Rao): Confirmed production tests this morning show stable routing to new variant and quality metrics back to expected baseline. Asked for postmortem and permanent mitigation timeline.
Initial hypothesis: edge memoization combined with cookie path/domain normalization created stale fingerprint that continued to direct traffic to legacy variant despite control-plane snapshot commit.
Evidence: edge logs show memo-hit stale=true at same timestamp as orchestrator commit. Serving runtime logs show decision-conflict where edge bound variant != control-plane chosen variant.
Repro pattern: most reproducible when weight changes are applied within <2m of each other and when clients reconnect with reused keep-alive on multiplexed HTTP/2 streams.
Mitigation tried: targeted cache invalidation on affected edge shard reduced impact quickly. Hotfix added a reconciliation check in orchestrator to clear memo if cookie namespace/path semantics changed between snapshots.
Root cause likely multi-factor: (1) edge memoization TTL longer than snapshot reconciliation window, (2) cookie normalization change that altered matching semantics introduced a month ago, (3) orchestrator did not invalidate edge fingerprints when snapshot cookie metadata changed.
Monitoring added: added histogram of 'edge_conflict_rate' and alerting threshold at >2% conflict over 5m for any route during staged rollouts.
Mitigation: performed targeted edge shard cache invalidation which restored expected routing for DataStream Labs. Fix: rolled out PR to orchestrator (https://github.com/redwood-inference/orchestrator/pull/1267) that enforces cookie-scope and path normalization checks during snapshot commit and proactively emits invalidation signals to edge for affected shards. Follow-ups: INT-2201 to add e2e tests for cookie normalization across canary weight shifts, and a runbook update (Confluence link added). Customer communicated that metrics and quality returned to baseline; monitoring remains active for 72h. Ticket set to In Progress pending postmortem and closing notes.

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customer reports a gradual, low-dollar discrepancy appearing in their hourly billing reconciliation for the last three billing windows. The discrepancy is ~0.1-0.3 credits per hour and aggregates to a visible line-item on their monthly invoice. The customer believes rate-tier evaluation during hourly rollover is classifying a small subset of toolcall requests into the wrong rate class (micro-rate drift).

Impact:
- Visible unexpected charge (~$12 USD/month at current usage) on LuminaAssist's billing export.
- Confusion for finance and internal SRE; customer concerned about correctness of automated-tiering logic for mixed workloads.

Environment:
- Production; us-east-1.
- Org: org-8462 (LuminaAssist).
- Dedicated plan with some hosted fallback traffic during peaks.

Steps to reproduce (as provided by customer):
1) Run a scheduled batch of mixed chat+toolcall traffic that spans the top of the hour (e.g., 00:58–01:02).
2) Export hourly metering CSV from Console > Billing > Usage for the org.
3) Compare per-minute classification between minutes 58–02.
4) Observe ~0.1–0.3 credit difference in the hourly aggregate compared to total of per-minute records.

Logs / evidence attached by customer:
- Usage CSV snippet (lines included here show two toolcall events attributed to hour H but charged at the next-hour tier).
- Screenshot of invoice line for month with small line labeled "micro-tier adjustment".

Immediate ask:
Customer requests explanation of why there is a recurring small discrepancy and whether Redwood will adjust the invoice or provide a credit if a system classification bug is found.

Additional notes:
2026-03-10 11:27 - LuminaAssist (Elena Park): Attached minimal CSV and the two event IDs: pb_23f4 and pb_23f5 (timestamps 2026-03-01T00:59:43Z and 2026-03-01T01:00:01Z). One appears in hour 00, one in hour 01 in our raw logs but both were billed at the higher hour-01 rate.
Hypothesis: The hourly materializer that collapses per-minute postbacks into the hour bucket runs a separate tier-evaluation pass during rollover. When events straddle the boundary (timestamp at or within 1s of the top-of-hour), the tie-breaker for rate-tier selection is non-deterministic due to race between ingestion timestamp normalization and the evaluation job's window assignment. Evidence: traced pb_23f4 (00:59:43Z) and pb_23f5 (01:00:01Z) — pb_23f5 was ingested with corrected timestamp but processed by a delayed worker that used wall-clock hour assignment. Workarounds identified: 1) disable on-the-fly reclassification during the hourly materialize and rely on ingestion-assigned tier, 2) apply deterministic floor(timestamp) assignment (always ceil-to-prev-hour) for boundary timestamps. Engineering ran a replay for sample hour and reproduced the 0.2-credit delta. Linked to race-condition change introduced in commit 1a2b3c4 (metering/tier-eval) rolled three weeks ago.
Mitigation deployed: Added deterministic tie-breaker (prefer ingestion-assigned tier when timestamp falls within 5s of hour boundary) and disabled reclassification pass for the hourly materializer in prod-us-east. Patch rolled to canary on 2026-03-12 and to full region 2026-03-12 02:15 UTC.
Customer outcome: We scheduled a targeted audit for LuminaAssist's affected hours for the last 30 days. Preliminary audit shows ~6.1 credits overcharge which we will apply as a one-time invoice credit. Finance is preparing a credit memo reference CM-2026-0421.
Follow-ups:
- Create a post-deploy job to backfill corrected hourly aggregates for affected orgs (task INT-8102).
- Add unit/integration tests that assert deterministic tiering at hour boundaries (ticket INT-8120).
- Communicate to Customer: summary, credit amount, and timeline.
Status: Customer notified of credit and engineering fix. Pending backfill and formal postmortem.
payload.summary: Dynamic tier evaluation window causes micro-credit drift on hourly buckets

payload.description:
Issue summary:
We need a reliable automated sync that ensures the oncall roster in PagerDuty (or our oncall source of truth) is reflected in the Oncall Slack workspace membership and the Confluence 'Oncall runbooks' space viewer group. Currently these are updated manually by Platform Ops, which causes delays during rotations and leaves temporary gaps in access and audit trails.

Impact:
- Oncall engineers may not receive critical Slack alerts or have access to runbooks immediately after rotation.
- Manual work increases ops overhead and produces noisy audit records.
- Security wants an auditable, least-privilege mapping between oncall role and Confluence viewer group.

Desired outcome / Acceptance criteria:
1) A scheduled and event-driven mechanism that syncs the canonical oncall roster to: (a) add/remove users from the #oncall Slack user group and a dedicated Slack workspace membership list (if relevant), and (b) add/remove users from the Confluence group 'oncall-runbooks-viewers'.
2) All changes are logged to a central audit record (Confluence page + log in S3) with timestamps and the triggering event (schedule vs PD rotation vs manual override).
3) A manual override path for Platform Ops via a Jira internal request that applies immediately and is recorded.
4) Safety: no mass deletions without a manual confirmation step; fallback to a safe read-only webhook on failures.

Current state / constraints:
- PagerDuty exposes an oncall API and we already maintain a small lambda that emits rotation events to a Slack channel.
- Confluence user group API is available via our Okta SCIM integration but requires scoped tokens and an audit trail.
- Slack workspace is standard "redwood" workspace; membership provisioning requires SCIM scoped token and has rate limits.
- Security wants the change history retained for 365 days.

Work items proposed:
- Build a small automation service (lambda or container) that consumes PagerDuty rotation webhooks and scheduled nightly reconciliation.
- Integrate with Okta SCIM for Confluence group changes; use Slack SCIM for Slack user group changes where possible.
- Emit audit events to s3://redwood-internal-audit/oncall-sync/{date}.log and record a short summary to Confluence 'Security/Oncall provisioning audit' page.
- Implement a dry-run mode and a feature flag for initial rollout to a pilot team.
- Add monitoring (CloudWatch + PagerDuty) for failed syncs and rate-limit errors.

Rollout plan:
1) Develop in staging and enable dry-run for one team for 2 weeks.
2) Run reconciliation job nightly for all teams in dry-run for 1 week, surface diffs to Platform Ops channel.
3) Enable write-mode for non-critical teams, monitor for 48 hours.
4) Enable write-mode for all oncall groups.

Dependencies / blocked by:
- Okta SCIM token with group write scope (security approval required).
- Slack SCIM token and confirmation of rate-limit headroom with Enterprise team.
- PagerDuty webhook reliability (we already have event subscription).

Risks and rollback:
- Accidental removal of users from Confluence/viewer groups: mitigated by dry-run and manual confirmation for >5-member changes.
- Rate limits causing partial updates: mitigate with backoff and batching.

Acceptance test examples:
- Trigger a PagerDuty rotation and verify Slack group membership and Confluence group membership updates within 2 minutes in pilot mode, and recorded to S3.
- Nightly reconcile detects a drift and reports a diff; after enabling write-mode the diff is resolved and logged.

Notes for implementation team:
- Prefer serverless (Lambda + step functions) for initial PoC to keep infra overhead low.
- Use existing logging and secrets store (Secrets Manager) and follow the internal service onboarding checklist.
- Add a Confluence runbook with the runbook owner and rollback steps before enabling write-mode.
Checked current artifacts: existing lambda emits PD events to #platform-oncall but does not update membership. Okta SCIM group present: 'oncall-runbooks-viewers' (id: grp-0a1b2c). Slack SCIM provisioning is currently enabled for provisioning users but not for managing user groups. Identified rate-limit of 20 requests/min for Slack SCIM group endpoints — need batching. Recommended approach: event-driven writes + nightly reconciliation to catch missed deltas.
payload.summary: Automate user sync for Oncall Slack workspace and Confluence access provisioning

Issue summary: BrightMart reported repeated 429 throttles (tenant-level) during their nightly bulk sync job after enabling edge-proxy connection pooling and after a dedicated-pool autoscaler rollout. Impact: Nightly backfills fail intermittently, causing downstream sync retries and customer SLA alerts. Environment: Dedicated pool (BrightMart), prod-eu-west, workflow: preflight HEADs -> signed-url PUTs (parallel, chunked) -> websocket progress stream. Steps to reproduce: 1) Start BrightMart bulk-sync with concurrency 48, chunk size 8MB, preflight enabled. 2) Observe series of HEADs followed by parallel PUTs and immediate websocket connections for progress. 3) Watch for tenant-scoped 429s ~5-10 minutes into the run. Observed behaviour: Tenant-level token exhaustion resulting in sustained 429s that persist across requests for 7-20 minutes despite low CPU/GPU usage on dedicated nodes. Expected behaviour: Short-lived per-route spikes with rapid refill; no sustained tenant-wide exhaustion. Attachments: request sample IDs rqt-89f3/ rqt-89f4, logs (attached), dashboard links (rate-limiter ledger + tenant heatmap).

2024-10-15T15:48:00Z - Carlos Mendez (Support): Acked and began triage. Asked for: 1) exact start time of next failing run, 2) sample SDK client version, 3) whether signed-url refreshes are batched. Requested console logs and rate-limiter ledger export.
2024-10-15T17:05:00Z - BrightMart (Customer): Provided logs and confirmed they recently toggled edge-proxy connection pooling in front of Redwood ingress. Also noted an autoscaler change last week that altered dedicated-pool refill epoch window.
2024-10-16T09:35:00Z - SRE (Evan Cho): Investigating. Correlated tenant ledger: high volume of preflight HEADs were being counted under the same route weight as actual PUTs. Observed health-check probe cluster from orchestrator performing 100s of quick HEADs during the run window.
2024-10-16T11:12:00Z - Carlos Mendez (Support): Hypothesis: edge-proxy multiplex + connection-reuse is amplifying preflight fanout and causing token accounting to attribute preflight HEADs to primary route, driving token-bucket depletion. Also seeing refill epoch misalignment after autoscaler rollout causing delayed refill under load.
2024-10-16T14:40:00Z - Engineering (Maya Gupta): Deployed a ledger export and replayed request stream in a staging rate-limiter harness. Confirmed double-counting for multiplexed preflight flows when route tag absent. Proposed mitigation: tag preflight route as low-cost path and separate it into isolated burst pool; align refill epoch across edge and origin; add short-term burst credit increase for BrightMart.
2024-10-17T08:50:00Z - Carlos Mendez (Support): Applied temporary burst credit to customer and pushed config change: route_isolation=true for preflight route, increased dedicated pool burst by 2x for 2 hours. Customer confirmed bulk-sync completed successfully.
2024-10-18T10:05:00Z - BrightMart (Customer): Confirmed stable nightly run for two consecutive days after changes. Requested guidance to avoid recurrence.
2024-10-18T10:30:00Z - Carlos Mendez (Support): Closing loop with recommended permanent config and follow-ups. Marking ticket Resolved.
Ledger analysis showed a sawtooth pattern: large blocks of HEAD requests counted as token usage identical to PUTs between 02:00 and 02:20 UTC.
Edge proxy connection pooling caused single client to open fewer connections but multiplex many logical preflight messages resulting in mis-tagged route classification at ingress.
Autoscaler rollout changed dedicated-pool refill epoch from 60s aligned windows to an offset schedule; under bursty fanout this delayed effective refill by up to 45s causing prolonged exhaustion.
Reproduced locally by replaying customer request sequences in staging rate-limiter harness; enabling route tag prevents HEADs from consuming PUT bucket.
No evidence of node resource exhaustion or OOM on serving runtime; problem is quota accounting and configuration rather than serving throughput limits.
Temporary: granted emergency burst credits to BrightMart and set route_isolation=true for their preflight route; increased dedicated pool burst capacity during their nightly window. Permanent: engineering implemented route tagging to ensure preflight HEADs count against an isolated lightweight bucket and aligned refill epoch for the dedicated pool edge/origin path. Customer advised to stagger preflight/signing refresh by 5s across workers and to use the recommended SDK concurrency limiter. Monitoring: new ledger metric (per-route preflight_token_ratio) added to Console dash and alerting rule created.
INT-4321: Add unit & integration tests for multiplexed preflight accounting (assigned to eng-rate-limiter)
Create KB article for customers: 'Design patterns to avoid tenant-level quota waterfalls for multipart uploads' and link in Console guidance (owner: DevRel)
Add automated audit to detect dedicated-pool refill-epoch drift after autoscaler changes (owner: infra)
Recommend customer-side: stagger worker startup by 3-7s and enable route_isolation on heavy preflight endpoints

Issue summary:
Customer reports intermittent 429 responses originating from a browser-based service that uses a service-worker background sync + signed-url callback flow. The Redwood console shows tenant credits remaining and no obvious quota depletion.

Impact:
- BrightThread is seeing ~10-30% of webhook callback attempts rejected with 429s during scheduled background sync windows (batch size ~200 requests / minute).
- User-facing retry loops cause delayed processing and duplicate attempts in their downstream system.

Environment:
- Tenant: BrightThread (enterprise)

Additional notes:
2026-03-10 10:05 - BrightThread (Customer): Uploaded sample HAR (attached) and reported that the service-worker issues a fetch for an OPTIONS preflight immediately followed by the POST; background sync groups 12-18 parallel fetches per tick.
2026-03-12 16:45 - BrightThread (Customer): Confirms reduced 429 rate to <1% after temporary mitigation. Requests permanent guidance and console reconciliation for why dashboard still reported full credits.
Hypotheses considered:
- Duplicate accounting: OPTIONS preflight being counted as separate tokens on both route and tenant layers during short burst windows.
- Edge proxy connection reuse leading to both preflight and POST being logged against distinct buckets.
- Service-worker parallelism (background sync bursts) exceeding per-route burst pool and triggering route-level rejections while tenant-level bucket still has capacity.
Evidence collected:
- Trace IDs: trace-uw2-20260310-7f9a (see attached trace in ticket).
- Dashboard snapshots: rate_limiter.window=60s shows per-route peak at 320 req/min, tenant peak at 1.2k req/min. Console token balance remained high due to tenant-level smoothing.
- Access logs show frequent OPTIONS then POST sequences with <50ms separation; this causes immediate double-accounting in the edge when preflight is not collapsed.
Tests run:
- Replayed HAR at controlled concurrency: reproduces 429s at configured route burst limit.
- Disabled preflight counting in test edge (internal flag): 429s disappeared while total token consumption remained similar.
Temporary mitigation validated with customer: reducing parallel background-sync workers to 4 reduced 429s to <1%.
Next steps suggested:
- Short-term: apply route-level exemption for CORS preflight counting OR increase route burst pool for BrightThread's webhook route (requires ops window).
- Medium-term: recommend client changes (coalesce background sync ticks, add jitter/backoff, avoid simultaneous preflight fanout).
- Platform follow-up: evaluate collapsing preflight + POST accounting at edge for HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 to avoid double-counting in a single short refill window.
Workaround and final actions taken:
- On 2026-03-12 at 15:30 UTC, support applied a temporary route-level burst increase for BrightThread's webhook route (burst pool +150 tokens for 72 hours). 429 rate dropped to <1% during the window.
- Customer applied client change (reduced background-sync parallelism + exponential backoff). Confirmed successful by customer.
- Follow-up tasks created for infra: create a safe flag to collapse preflight accounting and add an option in Console to show per-route preflight vs primary method token breakdown.
Follow-ups / Owner:
- Product/Console team: Add a per-route preflight token visualization in the dashboard (ticket raised).
- Support: Monitor tenant for remaining 48 hours and keep ticket open until 2026-03-14 for validation.
Customer confirmation:
BrightThread sent final confirmation 2026-03-12 17:02 UTC: "After route bump + client changes we see normal throughput and no further user impact."

Issue summary:
Customers observe SSE streams terminating early (HTTP 200 closed) with a partial JSON payload, then receiving a resumed stream that injects an edge-cache metadata chunk in the middle of the response. The resumed payload has metadata frames interleaved with tokens, which client SDKs mis-interpret and assemble into malformed JSON.

Impact:
- Multiple API consumers at Foodly see truncated recommendations or garbled JSON in ~2-3% of long streaming responses (conversations > 4k tokens).
- Causing client-side JSON.parse failures and repeated retries. Some retries lead to duplicated prefixes.

Environment:
- Dedicated customer tenant on prod-us-east using dedicated routing through our edge CDN (FastEdge).
- Streaming via SSE, client uses our JS SDK v2.3.1 behind a corporate proxy.

Steps to reproduce (observed):
1) Client issues long-stream generation request (max_tokens ~ 4096) using redwood-instruct-7b with streaming SSE.
2) At ~20s into the stream (token boundary varies), edge proxy logs show an asynchronous cache insert for a previous short request on the same connection.
3) Connection is gracefully closed by edge (HTTP/1.1 finish) with 200. SSE client receives partial JSON body up to the last complete choice.
4) Client reconnects with resume token; server responds with remaining chunks but an edge-side cache-insert control chunk (X-Edge-Cache-Insert: true) is appended between token frames.
5) SDK concatenation yields JSON with stray metadata lines, client parse fails.

Observed behavior:
- Partial payloads and then resumed payloads containing unexpected cache-metadata frames (text lines like "EDGE-CACHE-INSERT: id=...;len=128;src=fastedge").
- Client SDK treats these as part of the stream payload; final JSON is invalid.
- Server/tracing shows worker did not re-encode metadata as SSE comment lines ("comment: ...") and the edge inserted raw lines when performing insert-on-the-fly.

Expected behavior:
- Edge should not insert or mutate in-stream content for active SSE sessions. Any edge/insert control must be encoded as SSE comments (starting with ":") or handled out-of-band so client SDKs ignore them.

Logs / snippets:
- Edge traces (fastedge): "cache-insert: attach_chunk id=abc123 connection=conn-77 offset=98123"
- API gateway: "200 finish connection conn-77 cause=cache_insert_flush"
- Serving runtime: "session-resume request_id=rid-9f2 remaining_bytes=2345"
- Client error: "SyntaxError: Unexpected token 'E' at position 12"

Investigation notes:
- Reproduced on our internal harness when we enabled FastEdge caching in front of a dedicated routing pool.
- The edge process performed a synchronous cache insert that wrote an ASCII metadata line without SSE comment prefix, because it re-used an HTTP body buffer path intended for non-streamed responses.
- When client reconnects with resume token, the serving-runtime merges remaining KV cache tokens and appends the buffered edge payload, resulting in interleaved metadata.
- Not observed when traffic bypasses FastEdge or when edge caching is turned off.
- Affected models correlate with longer output sessions; short responses unaffected.

Workaround:
- For immediate mitigation, advise Foodly to disable FastEdge insert-on-write for their dedicated route (edge flag: cache_insert=false) or reduce max_tokens to keep streams short (<1.5k tokens).
- Temporary server-side mitigation: guard in serving-runtime to drop lines matching /^EDGE-.*INSERT:/ on resume merge (hotfix candidate).

Next steps / proposed fix:
- SRE to add an edge change: ensure cache inserts use SSE-safe comment prefix or are buffered out-of-band (edge ticket in progress).
- Runtime: add strict sanitizer on resumed streams to strip non-SSE comment lines and validate JSON boundaries before emitting to client.
- QA: create regression tests in streaming harness that simulate cache-insert events under load.

Please see comments below for back-and-forth and attach request/response dumps if needed.
Create a dedicated route for a test tenant that passes through FastEdge with cache_insert enabled
Send long streaming SSE generation (redwood-instruct-7b) from SDK v2.3.1 (max_tokens 4096)
Observe edge logs for cache-insert events during the active stream
Capture client raw SSE payload: note partial termination, then resumed stream containing lines starting with 'EDGE-CACHE-INSERT:'
Verify client JSON.parse fails or final message contains injected metadata
[fastedge] cache-insert: attach_chunk id=abc123 connection=conn-77 offset=98123
[apigw] conn-77: 200 finish cause=cache_insert_flush
[runtime] session-resume: request_id=rid-9f2 remaining_bytes=2345
[client] SyntaxError: Unexpected token 'E' in JSON at position 12
Reproduced in staging harness when enabling fastedge insert-on-write
Edge inserted ASCII meta-line using body buffer path, not SSE comment path
Serving runtime merged buffer without sanitizing leading lines on resume
Disabling edge insert prevents the issue
Hotfix candidate: strip /^EDGE-.*INSERT:/ lines in resume merge
Disable FastEdge cache_insert for the affected dedicated route or reduce streaming length. Support provided short-term toggle for Foodly tenant.

Additional notes:
2026-03-11 14:10 - Customer (Foodly, James R): Thanks for quick triage. We'll toggle cache_insert off while you prepare a runtime hotfix. Please confirm when safe to re-enable.

Issue summary:
Customer BrightCart reported unexpected split charge lines on their March invoice. Two nearly identical invoice line items appear for the same batch embedding job; one line is attributed to the customer org and a second line appears under an internal staging org ID. Credits were applied to the staging line and not the customer line, resulting in an overcharged final invoice.

Impact:
- Invoice shows duplicate/fragmented line items for the same usage window (March 02 03:00 - 03:30 UTC).
- Credits were applied to the wrong line (staging org), leaving BrightCart with an apparent overage of ~$1,240.
- Customer billing team flagged for correction prior to payment. Customer is on Dedicated tier and needs corrected invoice before payment processing.

Environment:
- Prod ingestion pipeline (us-east), dedicated deployment for BrightCart (org_id: org-brightcart-prod).
- Edge postbacks from batch workers (region: us-east-1).

Steps to reproduce / observed behaviour:
1) BrightCart runs a scheduled batch embedding job at 03:05 UTC that posts usage via the usage-postback endpoint.
2) Multiple postback requests for the same job arrived within seconds, some carrying header X-Org-ID: org-brightcart-prod and others carrying X-Org-ID: org-brightcart-staging (a legacy id from an earlier onboarding script).
3) Ingest service accepted both postbacks and created two usage buckets tied to two org identifiers.
4) Billing aggregation produced two invoice lines; credits attached automatically to staging-line because credit memo mapped to org-brightcart-staging first.

Expected behaviour:
- Ingest should canonicalize org ID and reject or normalize mixed org IDs for a single API key, preventing split attribution.
- Credits should map to the primary customer org when both org ids are linked to the same account.

Logs / artifacts attached:
- Customer-provided invoice PDF (invoice_2026-03-02_BrightCart.pdf) and CSV extract.
- Ingest logs: usage-postback-2026-03-02.log (contains raw headers showing mixed X-Org-ID values).
- Billing trace: billing-aggregate-2026-03-02.trace (high level aggregation steps).

Business impact:
- Financial: immediate overcharge of $1,240 pending correction.
- Reputational: customer escalated to CSM and finance. BrightCart is a Dedicated customer with SLOs tied to billing accuracy.

Requested outcome:
- Issue the corrective credit and regenerate invoice reflecting a single line for the batch job.
- Identify and patch ingestion flow to canonicalize org IDs per API key and prevent future split attribution.
- Provide RCA and confirmation when reprocessed adjustments appear on account.

2026-03-10T09:12:34Z - Support (Maya Chen): Received invoice and logs from BrightCart finance. They're requesting a corrected invoice before the March billing cycle closes. Attached invoice PDF and postback log. Escalating to billing team.
2026-03-10T11:05:10Z - Billing (Alejandro Ruiz): Initial triage complete — I can see two distinct org_ids in the postback log. Opening an ingest investigation. Tentatively marking as P2; customer is concerned about timing.
2026-03-10T13:22:47Z - Ingest Eng (Priya Singh): Reproduced on staging: ingestion accepts postbacks with any X-Org-ID header if API key matches, and we index by header value when present. That allows split buckets. Creating PR to normalize to API-key->org mapping and ignore X-Org-ID when it conflicts.
2026-03-11T08:42:19Z - Billing (Alejandro Ruiz): Ran a one-off reaggregation job for affected window. Created credit memo CM-2026-03-11-BC for $1,240 and produced corrected invoice INV-2026-03-11-BC. Sent corrected invoice to customer and finance.
2026-03-11T16:30:05Z - Customer (BrightCart - Lydia Park): Confirmed receipt of corrected invoice and credit memo. Finance will accept and stop payment hold. Thanks for the quick turnaround.
2026-03-12T10:01:58Z - Support (Maya Chen): Closing ticket after confirm from customer. Follow-up: ingest PR merged and deployment scheduled to prod. Added post-deploy alert to detect mixed-org postbacks.
Ingest service behavior: usage-postback accepts X-Org-ID header and if present treats that header as authoritative even if API key is owned by a different org. This was historical behavior to support certain partner integrations.
Postback logs show batch job had 6 postbacks; 4 used org-brightcart-prod, 2 used org-brightcart-staging. Timestamps within the same window (03:05:22Z - 03:05:31Z).
Billing aggregation iterates over usage rows and groups by org_id found in ingest index. No de-duplication across org IDs was performed. This produced two lines with identical usage details but different org attribution.
Credits service maps credit memos to org ids based on exact org_id match. Credit memo for earlier test runs was tied to org-brightcart-staging and applied to that line because it matched first in aggregation order.
Action taken: 1) Issued $1,240 credit memo CM-2026-03-11-BC and regenerated invoice INV-2026-03-11-BC to merge the two lines into the canonical org (org-brightcart-prod). 2) Deployed ingest fix: PR #742 forces API-key->org canonical mapping and drops X-Org-ID header when it conflicts. 3) Backfilled/reaudited the last 30 days of postback records for this customer to ensure no other split attributions exist. 4) Added an alert to detect mixed-org postbacks for a single API key and a runbook to remediate quickly.

Follow-ups: Engineering to monitor alert for one week. Finance to confirm final invoice acceptance by BrightCart. Documented the change in Confluence: billing/postback-runbook.

payload.description:
Issue summary:
When BrightQube's Go client uses the streaming API to invoke external tooling (webhook actions via function-calling), intermittent network interruptions followed by client resume lead to duplicate external tool invocations. The duplicate occurs even when the client supplies an idempotency key. Root cause appears related to how the Go SDK and serving runtime reconcile the deferred-ack grace window and resume timestamps, resulting in the server re-queueing an already-dispatched tool run.

Impact:
- Duplicate webhook POSTs to BrightQube's downstream task processor (up to 2x in observed cases).
- Side effects: duplicate emails and duplicate records in customer DBs.
- Affects a handful of requests (~0.1% of streaming sessions) during network flaps; customer reports material operational cost and user confusion.

Environment:
- Customer: BrightQube (dedicated cluster)
- Deployment: Redwood Dedicated, us-east-1, prod
- SDK: redwood-go v0.9.4 (BrightQube pins to this version)
- Server: serving-runtime 1.12.3-prod
- Webhook dispatcher: internal webhook-dispatcher service behind streaming-proxy

Steps to reproduce (customer-provided):
1) Start streaming generation with function/tool calls enabled (Go SDK).
2) Ensure function call triggers an outbound webhook from streaming runtime to customer's task endpoint.
3) Simulate a brief network interruption between client and streaming-proxy (~3-6s).
4) Client resumes streaming session using resume token within 10s.
5) Observe two webhook POSTs for the same logical tool invocation (same payload) separated by ~1-3s.

Expected behavior:
- Single webhook POST per logical tool invocation when client resumes, provided idempotency key is present or the server-side pending invocation record indicates prior dispatch.

Actual behavior:
- Server re-dispatches the tool invocation during resume if the deferred-ack grace window calculation marks the prior dispatch as "expired in-flight" due to timestamp skew between proxy and runtime state. This bypasses the idempotency guard under certain resume/timing combinations.

Temporary workaround provided to customer:
- Enable server-side webhook deduplication (BrightQube implemented a per-request nonce check).
- Customer upgraded to redwood-go v0.9.5 (contains additional client-side resume timestamp anchoring) which reduced frequency but did not eliminate duplicates.

Business impact:
- Customer paused rollout of a feature relying on single-execution guarantees. BrightQube requests a prioritized fix and a clear migration path for Dedicated customers.

Additional notes:
2026-03-10 13:20 - BrightQube (Customer): Uploaded full trace and nginx proxy logs (S3 link: s3://brightqube-support/traces/2026-03-09/rq_9c3a.zip). Noted that client reconnection happened at client-side timestamp 2026-03-09T22:31:12Z.
2026-03-12 17:30 - BrightQube (Customer): Confirmed duplicate rate dropped from ~0.1% to ~0.01% after config change. Requests permanent fix and SDK guidance for future resume semantics.
Hypotheses:
1) Deferred-ack grace window computed on runtime differs from value assumed by streaming-proxy resume logic, leading to re-queueing.
2) Go SDK v0.9.4 resume handshake doesn't include a deterministic resume-anchor nonce the server trusts, so server treats resume as a fresh delivery in race conditions.
Evidence collected:
- webhook-dispatcher logs (two near-identical dispatches) matched proxy resume timestamps.
- Serving-runtime metrics show 'tool_dispatch_retry' spike correlated with resume handshake events.
- No evidence of webhook consumer returning retryable error; server retried proactively.
Temporary mitigations tested:
- runtime config to reject replayed dispatches within a 5s window (reduced duplicates).
- upgrade to go-sdk v0.9.5 (client-side anchoring) reduced frequency.
Next steps:
- Implement server-side authoritative resume-anchor check: store 'pending-tool-invocation' state keyed by invocation_id and resume-anchor nonce; treat resume as idempotent if resume-anchor <= last_dispatch_timestamp + grace_ms.
- Add resume 'resumed_since' header in Go/TS/Python SDKs and require server-side honor.
- End-to-end test harness to simulate network blips and measure duplicate rate across versions.
Planned fix (target):
- Short term (hotfix): rollout runtime config flag streaming.reject-replay-within-ms defaulting to 3000ms for Dedicated customers (will be toggled by SRE). Deployed to BrightQube on 2026-03-12 as pilot (observed reduction).
- Mid term (v1.12.4 runtime + SDKs): implement persisted pending-invocation state and resume-anchor handshake. SDKs will add 'resumed_since' header and include invocation nonce in resume frames.
- Tests: add cross-language test scenarios in CI to cover resume-with-replay window.
Rollout plan:
1) Merge server-side PR and tag runtime 1.12.4 (engineering PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/4921).
2) Release coordinated SDK updates (redwood-go v0.9.6, redwood-ts v1.4.2, redwood-py v0.11.0) with resume header behavior.
3) Offer dedicated-cluster patch or config change for customers on earlier runtime.
4) Publish KB article: "Streaming resume best practices and prevents duplicate tool dispatches" and notify BrightQube.
Follow-ups assigned:
- Priya Nair: implement SDK header and tests (ETA 2026-03-19).
- Rafael Ortega: runtime change + hotfix packaging for Dedicated clusters (ETA 2026-03-18).
- Maya Chen: coordinate customer communication and post-incident summary (ETA 2026-03-20).
payload.summary: Duplicate external tool invocations after resume due to deferred-ack grace window mismatch in Go SDK streaming

Issue summary: Several customers on a dedicated cluster (LexiHealth) reported reproducible p95/p99 inference latency spikes and intermittent 504s during sustained steady traffic. Spikes align with ~10s periodicity and frequently occur at the same wall-clock offsets across many connections. Impact: Production inference for LexiHealth experienced ~15% of requests hitting p99 > 2.5s during windows, causing degraded user experience for symptom-check flows. Environment: Dedicated capacity in us-west, serving-runtime v1.3.8, scheduler v2.0.2, adaptive batching enabled with default idle estimator. Observed behavior: Periodic bursts where aggregation window appears to 'resonate' — requests queue up slightly longer than expected, then flush in a larger-than-normal batch causing downstream KV cache misses and transient CPU/GPU contention leading to p95/p99 regressions. Timing shows alignment with the adaptive idle estimator's oscillation interval after a recent optimizer tweak.
1) Provision dedicated cluster with same config as LexiHealth (4 nodes, adaptive batching enabled, idle_estimator=adaptive-v2).
2) Replay production traffic trace (steady 8 qps with short sequences, token length distribution attached) for 20 minutes.
3) Observe latency histograms in serving runtime and scheduler dashboards; periodic p99 spikes at ~10s intervals should appear.
4) Toggle idle_estimator to adaptive-v1 and re-run; spike pattern mitigates in our test runs.
2026-03-12T09:14:02.112Z [serving-runtime] flush_batch: batch_size=28 latency_ms=2103
2026-03-12T09:14:02.113Z [scheduler] coalescer: idle_estimator=adaptive-v2 window_ms=98 oscillation_detected=true
2026-03-12T09:14:02.114Z [kv-cache] miss_rate=0.28 warmup=partial
2026-03-12T09:14:12.218Z [serving-runtime] flush_batch: batch_size=31 latency_ms=2350
2026-03-12T09:14:22.332Z [serving-runtime] flush_batch: batch_size=27 latency_ms=2201
Initial hypothesis: noisy neighbor or GPU saturation — ruled out by per-GPU utilization graphs (no sustained saturation during spikes).
Correlation observed between coalescer window oscillation and latency spikes; window_ms drifts +/- 25ms around a nominal value causing alignment of many connections for a brief instant.
KV cache miss rate increases during flushes due to larger-than-expected batch sizes with mixed sequence lengths; cache warmup couldn't amortize cost for those flush sizes.
Replayed traffic in staging: switching idle_estimator back to adaptive-v1 removed the periodicity and reduced p99 by ~40% under the same load.
A recent change (serving-runtime commit 9f3d2a8) adjusted the estimator damping factor; likely introduced resonance in specific QPS/sequence-length regimes.
Aisha Khan (Support) 2026-03-12: Customer noticed tail latency spikes at roughly 10s intervals after yesterday's autoscaler tuning. Provided logs and sample traces.
Marcus Lee (SRE) 2026-03-12: Reproduced in staging. Attaching trace and CPU/GPU utilization. Suspect adaptive idle estimator oscillation.
Priya Nambiar (Runtime Eng) 2026-03-13: Found commit 9f3d2a8 that changed estimator damping. Putting a rollback candidate together and testing.
Marcus Lee (SRE) 2026-03-13: Applied a temporary mitigation (pin idle_estimator=adaptive-v1) to LexiHealth's config — observed p99 drop back to baseline. Informing customer and monitoring.
Workaround applied: pinned customer cluster's idle_estimator to adaptive-v1 and temporarily increased batch flush jitter to break alignment. Partial mitigation deployed to LexiHealth prod (2026-03-13 22:10 UTC) — p99 returned to baseline in monitoring. Root cause: estimator damping change in serving-runtime introduced a resonance in aggregation window under LexiHealth's QPS / sequence-length distribution. Full fix: PR (serving-runtime #3512) includes adaptive damping with hysteresis and a unit test to reproduce resonance; scheduled for canary on 2026-03-15.

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customer's Redwood Private control-plane is intermittently failing to resolve control-plane FQDNs from inside their VPC, and when DNS does resolve the TLS handshake to our API endpoints times out or drops with an SNI/TLS error. This started after the customer enabled a more restrictive egress firewall policy and a new on-prem DNS forwarder.

Impact:
- Production inference requests fail ~20% of the time across multiple services; observed client errors are DNS resolution failures and TLS handshake timeouts.
- Customer reports model pulls failed during model startup causing 503 spikes and degraded throughput.
- Affects FinEdge Analytics' reporting pipelines and real-time inference for fraud alerts.

Environment:
- Deployment: Redwood Private (control plane + private agents)
- Customer VPC: AWS eu-west-1, private subnets with NAT Gateway behind a transit VPC and on-prem VPN
- Network controls: enterprise firewall (named "FE-FW-1"), internal DNS forwarder (10.12.0.5) that forwards to corporate resolvers, strict egress ACLs allowing only specific IP ranges and ports 80/443

Steps to reproduce (as performed by support):
1) From a private agent EC2 instance in customer's VPC: curl -v https://control.redwood-inference.example.com/v1/models
2) Observe intermittent "Could not resolve host" or long stalls followed by TLS alert "handshake failure" in openssl s_client -connect control.redwood-inference.example.com:443 -servername control.redwood-inference.example.com
3) Meanwhile from a bastion host in same subnet with unrestricted egress, requests succeed consistently.

Representative logs / commands (redacted):
- curl: "curl: (6) Could not resolve host: control.redwood-inference.example.com"
- openssl: "140735058823424:error:14094410:SSL routines:ssl3_read_bytes:sslv3 alert handshake failure:../ssl/record/rec_layer_s3.c:1528:SSL alert number 40"
- tcpdump (captured on instance): repeated DNS queries to 10.12.0.5 with no response for ~15s, then occasional forwarded query out to corp-resolver that returns NXDOMAIN for control.redwood-inference.example.com

Initial investigation notes / hypothesis:
- DNS: The customer's internal DNS forwarder sometimes returns NXDOMAIN or drops queries for our control-plane FQDN; observed correlation between NXDOMAIN responses and curl failures. Potentially due to DNS RBAC/filtering or split-horizon rules not including Redwood domains.
- Egress/firewall: Customer's firewall allows outbound 443 but blocks or drops connections when SNI matches unknown domains (inspection device performing TLS interception). The openssl error and packet traces suggest a TLS inspection device may be terminating or resetting flows when SNI doesn't match an allowlist.
- VPC peering / routing: Not primary — routing between subnets appears correct and bastion host in same subnet can reach endpoints. Points to egress/DNS path or proxy.

Immediate customer-facing workaround suggested (applied by customer):
- Configure internal DNS forwarder to allow/forward queries for *.redwood-inference.example.com to public resolvers OR add a static A record for control.redwood-inference.example.com pointing to our documented control-plane IP set.
- Temporarily bypass corporate TLS inspection for Redwood endpoints by adding exception in the firewall for SNI *.redwood-inference.example.com (customer has applied and saw immediate reduction in TLS failures).

Next steps (Support/SRE owner):
1) Request customer's firewall and DNS team to capture full packet traces for failed flows and DNS logs for timestamps 2026-03-09T08:00Z - 2026-03-09T10:30Z (customer provided initial captures).
2) We will provide a list of canonical outbound FQDNs and current IP prefix list for control-plane endpoints and model storage endpoints (deliverable: control-plane-fqdns-2026-03-14.txt).
3) Verify whether TLS interception causes certificate mismatch by having customer capture TLS cert presented during failures (or run s_client -showcerts) and share.
4) If corporate DNS continues to return NXDOMAIN, advise adding conditional forwarder or static records.
5) Explore long-term options: support VPC endpoints / private-link for control plane or explicit VPC peering to avoid corporate egress inspection for mission-critical traffic.

Notes: customer is on a Private plan with high security requirements and requires written guidance they can give to their network/security teams. They asked for a timeline to resolution and for an interim SLA workaround to avoid production impact.

Additional notes:
2026-03-10 11:45 - FinEdge Network Engineer (customer): Captured tcpdump showing DNS queries to 10.12.0.5 and NXDOMAIN responses for control.redwood-inference.example.com. Will request firewall team to check TLS inspection logs.
2026-03-12 14:05 - FinEdge Security (customer): Temporary firewall exception added for SNI *.redwood-inference.example.com. Observed drop in TLS failures from ~20% to ~2% immediately. DNS NXDOMAIN still observed intermittently.
Customer added temporary SNI exception in firewall and configured static DNS entries for control.redwood-inference.example.com; both reduced errors. Long-term: conditional forwarder or private-link recommended.
For network teams: ensure outbound DNS resolution for *.redwood-inference.example.com and allow TLS passthrough for SNI to avoid interception failures. If egress inspection is mandatory, configure an allowlist for our FQDNs or use our PrivateLink option.
Provide canonical FQDN/IP list to customer (done)
Engineering to scope PrivateLink/VPC endpoint option (linked INT-3310)
Add 'Private deployment networking checklist' step to onboarding for customers with TLS interception devices
payload.summary: Private deployment: intermittent DNS resolution and TLS handshake failures for control-plane egress (customer VPC)

Issue summary:
Customer reports a sudden change in rerank ordering and increased mean latency for rerank requests after a background model swap of the embedding service. The behavior began 2026-03-10 02:17 UTC when a rolling update replaced redwood-embed-v1 with redwood-embed-v2 in the customer's dedicated pool.

Impact:
- Incorrect rerank top-k for ~12% of queries (customer verified via golden prompt set)
- Median rerank latency increased from 120ms -> 520ms for affected tenant route
- Customers on the same dedicated pool (MapleDocs) experienced recurrent 502/504 proxy timeouts during peak traffic spikes

Environment:
- Dedicated capacity pool: dedicated-prod-nyc-2 (MapleDocs reservation)
- Ingress: api-gateway cluster apigw-us-east-1
- Reranker: rerank-lite-v1 served on CPU fallback nodes behind the same pool

Steps to reproduce (observed by customer/support):
1) POST batch of ~64 documents to /v1/embeddings using model redwood-embed-v2 (automatic routing in customer's config).
2) Immediately call /v1/rerank with top_k=10 using the freshly ingested embeddings.
3) Compare top-10 order vs baseline saved earlier (pre-swap).
4) Observe higher latency and different ordering for ~1 in 8 requests.

Observed logs/snippets (anonymized):
- api-gateway logs 2026-03-10T02:18:03Z: upstream_timeout id=... status=504 route=/v1/rerank tenant=mapledocs
- serving-runtime debug 2026-03-10T02:18:04Z: embed-v2: projection_matrix_shape=(768,256) incoming_vector_shape=(512,) WARN projection_mismatch
- reranker warn 2026-03-10T02:18:04Z: scoring_time_ms=430 cache_miss=true fallback_path=cpu_sdk

Initial hypothesis:
- redwood-embed-v2 introduced a different projection/quantization shape (512->256 vs expected 768->256) and the downstream reranker expects 768-dense inputs. The runtime applies an on-the-fly projection fallback that is slower and numerically inconsistent with the original pipeline, producing both latency and quality regression.
- There may be an edge-case in the automatic model-compatibility matcher that allowed v2 to be routed to rerank-lite-v1 without an explicit compatibility tag.

Immediate customer impact and mitigation asked for:
- Customer requests rollback to previous embedding model variant for their dedicated pool and confirmation of data integrity for ingested embeddings during the window 2026-03-10 02:10 - 02:25 UTC.

Notes on urgency and next steps:
- P1 / Sev1 due to production quality and timeout impact for paying dedicated customer.
- Engineering (serving/runtime) engaged to validate projection shapes and compatibility tables.

Investigation notes (so far):
- Confirmed metric spike: rerank median latency +400ms correlates with the rolling deploy window.
- Found runtime warning that projection_mismatch triggers a CPU fallback path that performs an expensive matrix resize + re-quant step.
- Compatibility matrix (model_compatibility.yml) lacked an explicit mapping for redwood-embed-v2 -> rerank-lite-v1; default permissive rule allowed fallback.
- No evidence of corrupted embeddings stored in customer index; embedding size recorded in object metadata differs between pre/post swap.

Open questions:
- Was redwood-embed-v2 intended to be backward-compatible with rerank-lite-v1?
- Did the rolling update include an accidental feature flag enabling permissive compatibility?
- Do any other dedicated tenants share the same pool and need rollback?

Resolution plan (in progress):
1) Support: Requested temporary rollback of model routing for MapleDocs to redwood-embed-v1. (Actioned 2026-03-10 03:05 UTC)
2) Runtime/Servicing: Patch compatibility policy to treat projection shape mismatch as a hard block for model routing; create a canary flow for permissive fallbacks.
3) Engineering: Produce a short post-deploy validation that asserts embedding vector shape metadata matches downstream expectations before cutting traffic.
4) Customer follow-up: Validate that embeddings generated during 02:10-02:25 have not been used for production ranking (or reindex them if necessary).

Expected time to full fix: 48-72 hours for policy + deploy + adding pre-cut validation. Workaround (rollback) should restore baseline immediately once routing changes propagate.

Additional notes:
2026-03-11 09:22 - Customer (MapleDocs - CTO, Jonah S.): Thanks for quick rollback. Can you confirm whether any embeddings generated during the 15-minute window need reprocessing?
2026-03-11 10:05 - Support (Aisha Khan): We're verifying index metadata and will advise. Initial check shows ~3.2k embeddings written with a recorded vector_size=512 during the window; plan: re-run ingestion for those documents and provide a script to map old->new ids.
payload.summary: Embedding projection drift after model swap causing rerank score shift and elevated queueing

payload.description:
Issue summary: Customer Textlytics is seeing repeated 429s during peak traffic windows when their application issues a chain of small synchronous reranker calls per user query (avg 6 calls/query). They are on a Dedicated pool and report the Console shows available tenant burst credits, but the requests are throttled at the route level.

Impact: Intermittent user-facing errors; their search latency spikes and ~8% of queries return 429s during daily 09:00-11:00 UTC window. Business impact: search downtime for paying customers and degraded conversion for query sessions.

Environment: Dedicated pool backed by us-east cluster (gpu-p4d). Traffic pattern: short-lived connections, high concurrency from a serverless fleet that fans out rerank calls per web request.

Customer asks: 1) How to configure Redwood to reliably prioritize low-latency rerank calls vs background batch traffic? 2) Best-practice to reduce per-query 429s (batching, route-weight, concurrency limits)? 3) Any Console or API knob we should change on Dedicated to align observed quota with enforcement?

Expected behaviour: Route-level weights and tenant burst capacity should allow the low-latency reranker RPCs to proceed without sudden 429s when tenant-level credits are reported available.

Actual behaviour: Even with tenant credits available in the Console, individual route requests are being counted against a per-route concurrency/quota window causing 429s.

Attachments: request ids in logs, sample client call pattern, screenshots (uploaded to support ticket attachments).
1) Configure a Dedicated API key scoped to a single tenant and route for reranking (key used by serverless workers).
2) From 100 concurrent worker processes, issue user requests where each request makes 6 sequential reranker calls (small inputs).
3) Observe console showing tenant burst credits not fully depleted, but API returns 429s for a subset of calls.
4) Temporarily scale down background batch job to zero and re-run the traffic pattern to confirm the 429 drop rate.
sample logs:
[2026-03-10T09:03:12.214Z] request_id=ab12cd34 route=rerank-v1 status=429 quota_window=short-window tenant_credit=78
[2026-03-10T09:03:12.216Z] request_id=ab12cd35 route=rerank-v1 status=200 latency_ms=42
[2026-03-10T09:03:12.320Z] request_id=ab12cd36 route=batch-embed status=200 latency_ms=1023
[2026-03-10T09:03:13.110Z] request_id=ab12cd37 route=rerank-v1 status=429 quota_window=short-window tenant_credit=76
Trace: client=svc-search-01 pod=search-worker-a node=gpu-p4d-07
2026-03-10: Initial triage by Support—symptoms consistent with per-route concurrency/quota window exhaustion despite tenant-level credits.
Checked Console: tenant burst credit shows ~70-90 available during the window. No recent quota changes logged for this tenant.
Heap of short-lived connections from serverless fleet seems to create high instantaneous concurrency on the rerank route, which may be hitting route isolation limits.
Hypothesis: Per-route token bucket/refill window is configured shorter/smaller than tenant window; rapid multi-call fanout from each user query causes route window exhaustion and 429s even when tenant credit remains.
Support (Mar 10) - Ayesha Kaur: Thanks for the reproduction steps and logs. We'll validate route vs tenant accounting and check that the Dedicated pool's route weighting is configured to favor your rerank route. Please provide a sample of the client-side call pattern (timestamps and counts per second).
Customer (Mar 10) - Textlytics (Emma Li): Uploaded a 30s capture of production traffic and the sample SDK trace. The pattern shows bursts of 600 calls/sec across 100 workers, where each user query fans out to 6 rerank calls in immediate succession.
SRE (Mar 11) - Marcus Nguyen: Confirmed route isolation rules applied on the pool. Observed short-window exhaustion for the 'rerank-v1' route (config: concurrency_window=10s, per-route-burst=80). Tenant-level burst is larger (per-tenant-burst=1000) but not applied when per-route window is exhausted. Recommend either batching client calls or adjusting route weights.
Eng (Mar 11) - Liam O'Connor: Proposed action: 1) Temporary mitigation: increase per-route-burst to 400 and widen concurrency_window to 30s for rerank-v1 on Textlytics' dedicated pool (requires controlled rollout). 2) Long-term: recommend client-side batching / multiplexing so a single request contains multiple items to rerank, reducing per-query RPC count. Shared RFC/guide link: https://redwood.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/SUPPORT/pages/4356
Support (Mar 12) - Ayesha Kaur: Shared a config snippet and step-by-step guide for Textlytics to test the per-route-burst change in staging before applying to prod. Asked customer to confirm whether changing client batching is feasible on their roadmap.
Workaround provided: suggested temporary per-route config increase (per-route-burst -> 400, concurrency_window -> 30s) for rerank-v1 on their Dedicated pool and guidance on client batching to reduce RPC fanout. Next steps: schedule a controlled config rollout in a maintenance window, and customer to evaluate batching implementation. Case remains open until config change validated in prod.
payload.summary: Guidance on batching & route-weighting to prevent 429s from multi-call reranker workflow
