Issue summary:
Customers using Cordis client library on dedicated pool report intermittent 429s during large parallel multipart uploads over HTTP/3. Failures appear as soft 429s (burst/accounting) rather than hard quota exhaustion.

Impact:
- Several background and interactive upload workers received 429s for short windows (~5-20s) affecting downstream ingestion pipelines.
- Customer seeing increased error rate, delayed ingest completion, and retries causing higher cost.

Environment:
- Dedicated pool (customer-dedicated-07), prod, us-west-2.
- Client: Cordis analytics platform, custom uploader using HTTP/3 (QUIC) with concurrent file chunks (8-16 parallel streams).

Steps to reproduce (observed / customer repro):
1) Start large multipart ingest with 12 parallel chunk uploads using HTTP/3 from a single host behind NAT.
2) After ~30–90s, client triggers connection migration (mobile host sleeps/wakes, or local network switch).
3) Incoming requests succeed briefly, then a spike of 429 responses logged by the client for multiple concurrent chunk requests.

Observed behavior:
- 429 responses include our throttle reason header: X-Rate-Limit-Reason: burst_accounting.
- Server ingress logs show duplicate token-charge entries for the same logical upload sequence_id when connection migration occurs (different connection IDs, same upload metadata).
- Error windows are short and recover when upload retries with backoff.

Expected behavior:
- Connection migration should not double-charge the tenant route token buckets for the same logical session/upload. Uploads should continue or be gracefully rate-limited according to configured burst pools without duplicate accounting.

Quick logs (redacted):
- 2026-03-12T08:12:03Z ingress-edge-01 req_id=uvq9f chunk_id=alpha conn_id=0x7a3a status=200 charges=1
- 2026-03-12T08:12:13Z ingress-edge-01 req_id=uvq9f chunk_id=alpha conn_id=0x9f2b status=200 charges=1  <-- same req_id but new conn_id after migration
- 2026-03-12T08:12:14Z rate-limiter req_id=uvq9f tenant=cordis charges_applied=2 window=1s result=throttle
- 2026-03-12T08:12:15Z client CordisUploader error=429 upload_seq=12345 chunk=alpha

03/12 09:00 - Reproduced locally using Cordis test harness with HTTP/3 and simulated connection migration (netem bring-down/up). Observed duplicate accounting when migration occurred mid-upload.
03/12 10:15 - Hypothesis: ingress-proxy attaches token-accounting keyed by (connection_id, route_key). When QUIC connection migration occurs, a new connection_id is created but request metadata (upload seq, route) remains the same, causing a second charge for the same logical unit.
03/12 11:30 - Rate-limiter pipeline uses short-lived per-connection dedupe caches but TTL is too short to catch migration window; cache miss leads to double charge. Cache hit rate around migration is 0%.
03/12 12:00 - Edge-telemetry shows NAT IP reuse and connection-id churn correlate with 429 spikes for this customer (highly concurrent chunking).
03/13 09:45 - Confirmed non-HTTP/3 clients (HTTP/1.1 over TLS) do not trigger the same double-count behavior under similar migration tests.
03/13 14:00 - Temporary mitigation tested: increase per-connection dedupe TTL to 10s reduced duplicate charges but had memory pressure on edge proxies during mass parallel uploads.
(Short term) Rollback TTL increase to safe level on non-dedicated nodes; keep elevated TTL only for customer-dedicated-07 traffic via route tag (canary).
(Short term) Provide Cordis with client-side workaround: disable QUIC connection migration or implement robust idempotency-key per-chunk that the edge will honor across connection migration.
(Medium term) Implement idempotent accounting key: prefer (tenant, route, upload_seq, chunk_id) dedupe in rate-limiter upstream of per-connection key so migration does not double-charge.
(Medium term) Add safe eviction policy and bounded memory for dedupe cache to handle bursty parallel uploads without OOM.
(Long term) Update docs: Guidance for high-concurrency multipart uploads over HTTP/3 and recommended client idempotency headers.
Workarounds provided to Cordis: 1) disable HTTP/3 connection migration in their uploader (immediate); 2) add idempotency-key per chunk to avoid duplicate accounting across reconnects. Engineering implemented a targeted canary with increased dedupe TTL for route 'customer-dedicated-07' which reduced 429 windows. Follow-up ticket INT-4421 opened to implement robust dedupe by logical upload key and bounded cache with eviction policy. No user data corruption observed; issue root cause: per-connection accounting semantics with QUIC migration.
payload.summary: HTTP/3 connection migration causing duplicate rate-accounting and intermittent 429s during concurrent multipart uploads

Issue Summary:
The new organization policy enforcing resource tags (tag:team & tag:env) on service account creation is blocking the automated cross-project service-role assumption used by the staging->prod debug bridge. This prevents oncall and SRE playbooks that create short-lived service roles in staging and assume them from prod for debugging data-plane issues.

Impact:
- Immediate: Cannot complete planned production-safe debug sessions that require assuming a staging-scoped service role from prod (affects SRE oncall playbooks).
- Scope: Intermittent and reproducible for any automatic provisioning flow that creates service accounts without the new org tags. Affects both GCP and AWS bridging flows when orchestration creates corresponding cloud roles.

Root Cause Hypothesis:
- Org policy (tag-guard) rolled out 2026-02-27 requires tag:team and tag:env on service account/role create. Automated bridge tooling (priv-bridge) creates service accounts via a legacy service principal that does not include tags in the create call, so creation appears to succeed but the resource is non-compliant and cannot be assumed across projects due to deny policies on assume-role/impersonation.

Observed Behavior (examples):
- gcloud iam service-accounts get-iam-policy staging-sa@staging-project.iam.gserviceaccount.com returns policy but Cloud Audit shows a DENY entry tied to org policy enforcement.
- aws sts assume-role --role-arn arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/staging-bridge-role returns AccessDenied with context "TagComplianceFailure" in CloudTrail.

Expected Behavior:
- Automated bridge tooling should create tagged service accounts/roles (tag:team=platform, tag:env=staging) so cross-project assume/impersonate flows succeed and audit logs show compliant resources.

Temporary Workaround:
- Manual creation of a tagged service account/role in staging by a user with OrgPolicy bypass privileges (security-admin) allows assume to succeed. Not scalable and requires elevated privileges.

Proposed Fix:
1) Update priv-bridge provisioning code to include required org tags at creation time for both GCP and AWS resources.
2) Add a preflight check in the onboarding flow that validates org policy constraints and fails early with actionable message.
3) Run a backfill job to detect non-compliant service accounts created between 2026-02-27 and 2026-03-01 and fix tags or recreate them.

Observe provisioning logs (priv-bridge) that show createServiceAccount succeeded with HTTP 200 but audit log contains ORG_POLICY_DENY for tag requirements.
Attempt to assume/impersonate the newly created account from prod: run gcloud auth activate-service-account --key-file=... and then gcloud auth print-access-token or aws sts assume-role equivalent.
Observe AccessDenied and trace id in Cloud Audit/CloudTrail referencing TagComplianceFailure or org policy deny.

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customer reports sustained 429 responses across a set of sliced ingest workers after migrating ingestion to a Dedicated pool. The traffic mix is: low-latency chat calls (priority=high) and large multi-part embedding uploads (priority=background). After the migration, background uploads are intermittently exhausting burst credits at the per-route layer and causing opaque 429s for high-priority short calls during peak windows.

Impact:
- ~30% of short chat requests returned 429 between 09:00-11:30 PDT on 2026-03-10 for Streamly AI.
- Customer reports user-facing errors and retry amplification in their orchestrator.
- Business impact: partial degradation of their real-time features during peak ingest windows.

Environment:
- Dedicated pool: dp-132-usw
- Region: us-west
- Ingest coordinator version: 2026.02.3
- Rate-limiter service version: 1.14.0-canary

Observed behaviour:
- Persistent 429s reported by customer for short-lived chat requests coincident with high concurrency uploads.
- Throttle headers (when present) show per-route-window exhaustion; some requests show no X-RateLimit headers (opaque 429).

Expected behaviour:
- High-priority interactive calls should be isolated into a small burst pool and not experience 429s while background uploads borrow burst credit from a separate pool (or be rate-limited gracefully).

Customer asks:
- Why are small chat calls getting 429s when their load is relatively small?
- How to configure priority classes and burst pools for dedicated pools to prevent this?
1) Use the customer's traffic shape: 100 concurrent short chat requests (avg 50ms) + 20 parallel multipart embedding uploads (avg 45s each).
2) Route both traffic shapes through the dedicated pool dp-132-usw with current priority-class config (default: interactive=high, background=low).
3) Start background uploads in a tight window to simulate a scheduled flush (cron at 09:00).
4) Observe 429s on interactive calls between 09:00-09:30 when background uploads ramp up.

2026-03-10T09:02:19Z - 429 - /v1/chat - key=acct-streamly-01 - throttle: route_window=0/100
2026-03-10T09:02:20Z - 429 - /v1/embed - key=acct-streamly-01 - chunk=12/20 - err=quota_exhausted
2026-03-10T09:05:01Z - 429 - /v1/chat - key=acct-streamly-01 - no-rate-headers (opaque)
Sampler trace: https://observability.redwood.internal/trace/ingest/trace-9832
High - user-visible errors for real-time chat during scheduled bulk ingest; customer is on dedicated tier and requests urgent guidance (P1).
Instructed customer to stagger background multipart uploads and introduce jitter in their flush window. Recommended reducing concurrency of background upload workers to < 6 during peak windows as a temporary mitigation.
2026-03-10 09:20 - Support (Ava Chen): Acknowledged ticket and requested full request IDs and example request traces. Asked customer to confirm whether they use signed URLs for chunk upload callbacks.
2026-03-10 10:05 - Customer (Streamly AI - ops@streamly.ai): Provided request IDs and stated they use signed URLs for chunk completion callbacks and run a cron flush at 09:00 local. Attached sample batch IDs: batch-20260310-0919.
2026-03-10 11:00 - SRE (Liam O'Neill): Checked rate-limiter logs and saw route-level token depletion aligning with the cron flush. Noted some refill events lagged due to burst-pool-weight recalculation on pool attach.
2026-03-11 08:45 - Eng (Maya Patel): Observed a potential priority-class weight inversion in canary release 1.14.0-canary where background ingestion borrow logic could erroneously draw from interactive burst credits under certain attach sequences.
2026-03-12 09:00 - Support (Ava Chen): Shared recommended config changes and rollout plan. Scheduling a brief call with customer for 2026-03-12 14:00 PDT to apply non-breaking adjustments and observe behavior.
2026-03-12 13:30 - Customer (Streamly AI): Agreed to the windowed-stagger plan and will apply client-side jitter for the March 12 trial.
1) Correlation between cron flush start times and onset of 429s is strong (observability traces + rate-limiter counters).
2) Rate-limiter metric rlim.route.tokens.available shows transient negative deltas when background workers register multiple concurrent signed-url callbacks (double-counting observed in edge proxy earlier; needs validation).
3) Canary release 1.14.0 has a code path that recalculates burst-pool weights when a route attaches to a new pool; race condition can allow an attach to read stale bucket state and permit borrow that appears to zero out another pool's credits.
4) Some 429s are opaque because edge proxy returns before rate-limiter headers are populated when under heavy callback fanout. Need to instrument edge path to surface X-RateLimit headers even under backpressure.
5) No evidence of dedicated pool GPU exhaustion; autoscaler metrics are stable.
1) Short-term (apply during call): adjust per-route burst allocation to reserve 20% of interactive burst credits exclusively for priority=high routes on dp-132-usw.
2) Short-term: recommend customer stagger flush windows and add randomized jitter to callback fanout.
3) Medium-term: devs to backport fix to rate-limiter that prevents borrow from reading stale burst-pool state; target patch 1.14.1.
4) Medium-term: instrument edge proxy to always emit X-RateLimit headers even when returning 429 due to callback fanout backpressure.
5) Follow-up: run controlled load test with customer after config change and collect traces for 3 consecutive peak windows.

Issue summary:
A customer on Dedicated capacity experienced inconsistent model responses after a partial downgrade was applied to their pinned model. Some requests continued to route to the previously pinned variant while others were served by the downgraded variant, producing divergent outputs during the same time window.

Impact:
- BrightChat AI reports degraded answer consistency for end-users on two production routes (chat and summarization).
- Customer observed mismatched token billing for identical requests routed to different model variants.
- User-facing functionality was intermittently returning lower-quality summaries.

Environment:
- Dedicated pool: dc-brightchat-us-east
- Region: us-east
- Traffic profile: steady 60 RPS with periodic 500 RPS spikes (batching enabled)

Steps to reproduce (as reported):
1) Customer pinned route "chat/v1" to model rw-infer-rlhf-v2-2026-02.
2) Ops initiated a controlled partial downgrade to rw-7b-ql4-v1 for non-critical traffic using a rollout policy (50% weight).
3) During the rollout window, some requests returned outputs consistent with the older pinned variant while other requests reflected the downgraded model behavior for the same session identifiers.

Observed behavior:
- Split-route inference: Session affinity and version pin metadata appear inconsistent between the read path and the routing layer, resulting in traffic for a single session being split across two model variants.
- Pin persistence: A subset of edge proxies continued to attach the older pin header after the downgrade completed, while controller state indicated the new pinned variant.
- Billing mismatch: Token charges for equivalent requests showed different cost buckets on usage reports.

Expected behavior:
- When a route is pinned, either the pin should be preserved across all request paths until explicitly changed, or the rollout should atomically change pin metadata so all in-flight sessions are consistently routed per the configured policy.

Attachments / Logs / Links:
- Sample request IDs: rq_20260310_aa01, rq_20260310_aa42 (attached logs snippets)
- Routing trace: https://grafana.redwood/trace/route-split/879451
- Billing snapshot: https://billing.redwood/reports/brightchat/consistency-2026-03-10

Initial timeline:

- 2026-03-10 09:28 UTC: Support reproduces evidence of split routing in regional logs.
- 2026-03-10 10:05 UTC: Escalated to Serving Runtime and Routing SRE.
- 2026-03-10 14:40 UTC: Temporary mitigation applied (manual unpin + coordinated re-pin to the intended variant).
- 2026-03-11 02:00 UTC: Customer confirms improved consistency but requests postmortem for root cause.

Investigation notes:
- Hypothesis A: Partial downgrade triggered a race between the pinned-session read cache (edge proxies) and the controller write that updated the canonical pin, leaving stale pin metadata in some proxies.
- Hypothesis B: During weight-based rollouts, the routing policy incorrectly treated pin metadata as advisory and applied fallback routing that ignored session affinity for specific edge nodes during a heavy batching spike.
- Logs show a cluster of edge proxies (edge-redis-group-12) with last pin-refresh > 15 minutes before controller commit for the route.
- Routing service debug logs indicate a fallback decision path taken for ~4% of requests when GPU queue depth exceeded threshold. Those fallback decisions did not carry forward the pin header, leading to downgrade routing.

Immediate actions taken:
- Engineering removed batching-induced fallback for pinned routes in the staging policy to prevent routing decisions that drop pin headers.
- Ops performed coordinated cache flush on affected edge proxies (edge-redis-group-12).
- Manual unpin + re-pin sequence executed for BrightChat to re-establish canonical state.

Workaround (customer-facing):
- For urgent consistency, BrightChat temporarily unpinned the route and pinned explicitly to the desired variant after caches were flushed.
- For future rollouts, recommend using strict session-affinity rollout mode (0->100 step) instead of weight-based split for pinned routes.

Next steps / follow-ups:
1) Route: Implement pin-aware fallback policy that preserves pin headers across all fallback codepaths (owner: routing team; ETA: 2026-03-18).
2) Fix: Add stronger cache invalidation hooks so controller commits propagate pin changes synchronously to edge proxies for dedicated pools (owner: serving-runtime; ETA: 2026-03-22).
3) Monitoring: Create alert for pin-refresh-lag > 60s for any edge-redis-group (owner: observability; ETA: 2026-03-13).
4) Customer comms: Draft postmortem and remediation timeline for BrightChat (owner: Support; ETA: 2026-03-15).

- Confirmation of sessions/clients that saw divergence (session IDs provided).

payload.description:
Issue summary: Customer reports that during high-concurrency usage behind a corporate proxy which rewrites cookies, SSE streaming sessions sometimes end with the last sentence split across two resumed fragments or duplicated. Impact: generated output is split mid-sentence or contains a duplicated trailing clause, which breaks downstream parsers and leads to user-visible corruption in final responses. Occurs on multiplexed sessions when the client reconnects and the proxy rotates cookies mid-session.
Some customer requests return corrupted final sentence (either truncated, duplicated tail, or split across resume boundary). Affects enterprise customers behind proxies that rewrite Set-Cookie (OmniDocs reported ~1 in 1k resume events degraded). Business impact: customer-facing document generation pipelines get malformed outputs and some automated QA rejects outputs.
1) Use a multiplexed SSE session with multiple concurrent stream IDs to the Redwood hosted API.
2) Place the client behind a proxy that rewrites or rotates cookies on short TTLs (simulate corporate proxy behavior).
3) Start a long-form generation (sequence > 600 tokens) which streams via SSE.
4) Force a reconnect mid-generation by simulating a TCP reconnect or proxy cookie swap.
5) Observe resume behavior: some resumed streams present duplicated trailing clauses or the final sentence split across resume fragments and missing closing punctuation.
2026-03-10T09:12:34Z - frontproxy: SET-COOKIE rotated for session_id=abc123 -> cookie_v2; session multiplex mapping kept old session cookie_v1 for pending frames
2026-03-10T09:12:34Z - api-gateway: incoming resume request; resume_token=session_id=abc123|seq=742; cookie header contains cookie_v2
2026-03-10T09:12:34Z - serving-runtime: route resume to worker-17 based on cookie_v2; worker-17 has no KV prefix cache primed for seq=742, requests re-send last fragment from buffer; duplicate fragment emitted
2026-03-10T09:12:34Z - customer-client: received fragment N (partial sentence), then received a resumed fragment with overlapping tokens -> observed duplicated tail and split sentence
Initial triage (Support): Confirmed reproduction with customer's proxy simulator. Hypothesis: cookie rotation causes api-gateway to rebind multiplexed session to different internal routing identity, causing resume_token routing mismatch.
SRE reproduced locally by injecting Set-Cookie rotation in frontproxy; observed routing change at api-gateway layer when cookie changed mid-resume.
Worker-level logs show that worker handling the resumed connection lacked the primed KV cache for that session seq and triggered resend of trailing buffer which overlaps with previously-acknowledged tokens, producing duplicated tails.
Resume handler currently trusts resume_token that uses both session_id and cookie-derived affinity; when cookie changes, resume_token resolves to different worker without reconciling outstanding fragments.
Cookie-based affinity rotation during multiplexed SSE resumes can map the same resume_token to a different routing identity. The new worker doesn't have identical in-memory tail buffer/kv-state, so it replays or emits buffered trailing tokens; client merges resulting fragments and sees duplicate or split final sentence.
2026-03-10 - Support: provided reproduction template and proxy config suggestions to customer.
2026-03-11 - Eng (Diego): instrumented resume handler to log resolved affinity identity and resume_token mapping for affected sessions.
2026-03-12 - SRE: rolled a canary patch to gate resume routing by session_id primary key (ignore cookie-derived fallback) for multiplexed SSE resumes in canary region us-east.
2026-03-13 - Eng: prepared follow-up patch to attach a small per-session durable resume buffer persisted to ephemeral storage for brief handoffs (PR linked).
Mitigations: canary routing change (route by persistent session_id first, cookie affinity second) reduced duplication rate from ~0.1% to <0.001% in canary. Long-term fix: implement authoritative resume-ownership lookup that reconciles session resume_token with a durable minimal resume buffer so workers can hand off mid-resume without replaying overlapping fragments. Patch PR created and under review: github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/1843. Customer agreed to temporary proxy change pending rollout.

2026-03-11 14:20 - OmniDocs: Confirmed we can whitelist *.redwood.ai for cookie preservation. We'll apply the change during a maintenance window tonight.
2026-03-12 09:35 - Diego (Eng) -> OmniDocs: Canary routing change deployed to us-east; please validate generation quality once you flip the proxy setting.
2026-03-13 11:00 - OmniDocs: After whitelist, we no longer see duplicate tails in 48h sampling. Thanks — will await formal fix.
Support note (2026-03-10): Customer observed 1 in 1k resume events with duplicated trailing clause. Repro steps and proxy capture attached.
Eng note (2026-03-11): Added tracing in api-gateway to log affinity resolution. Observed different internal_affinity_id when cookie rotated; confirms mapping mismatch.
SRE note (2026-03-12): Canary shows 98% drop in observed duplication after preferring session_id routing. Recommend patch to resume handler to be more authoritative.
PM note (2026-03-13): Prioritize fix in next minor release; enterprise customers dependent on corporate proxies should be notified of workaround.
Customer confirmation (2026-03-13): OmniDocs validated workaround; marking customer-facing issue partially resolved pending final release.

Issue summary: Customer regulator-equivalent has submitted a fraud inquiry for a set of customer sessions. Legal requests a small, fully redacted sample of inference outputs plus a one-time redaction test run to validate our automated scrubbers.

Background: A regulatory body is evaluating a potential fraud pattern in transactions tied to account hashes. We have agreement from Legal and Privacy to provide minimized evidence for their review, but only after technical controls are validated. This ticket coordinates a timeboxed, read-only extraction of tokenized outputs and a redaction verification job.

Request: 1) Provision ephemeral, read-only access for SRE/Privacy to run a redaction test against a 200-session random sample (seeded by the provided session IDs). 2) Generate output artifacts: raw token sequences (token IDs only), redaction logs (pattern matches, rule IDs), and a fully redacted human-readable sample (PII replaced with <REDACTED>). 3) All artifacts must be stored encrypted, KMS-wrapped, and deleted after certification. 4) Runbook: record commands, PRs, and checksums; capture timestamps and approver list.

Justification: Legal has approved scope-limited disclosure for investigative purposes. Privacy requires validation that our scrubbers remove account numbers and named entities before any human review. Security requires ephemeral access with MFA and session logging for audit.

Data minimization plan: - Sampling: deterministic sample of 200 sessions provided by Legal (list attached in Confluence). - Tokenization: provide only token IDs and hashed session identifiers for RAW sample. - Redacted sample: provide human-readable outputs with reversible elements masked and a redact-certification signature. - Access window: 48 hours from approval.

Access controls & technical constraints: - No raw plaintext customer messages will leave the VPC. - All artifacts remain in the prod-us-east isolated bucket with kms:key-arn set to arn:aws:kms:us-east-1:123456789012:key/prod-redaction-key. - Access via bastion for SRE/Privacy only; disable after window. - Audit trail to be exported to SIEM.

Approval checklist: - Legal ack: present (Sara Goldstein) - Privacy ack: pending (Privacy review required) - SRE scheduling and runbook owner assigned: Lina Chen - Security ack for KMS & bastion: James Ortega - Data retention & deletion verification: Compliance automation to run post-delete.

Success criteria / Done: - Redaction test run completes with zero high-risk escapes for account numbers or email-like tokens. - Artifacts produced and validated by Privacy. - Deletion confirmation recorded and signed-off by Compliance.

Attachments and artifacts: See related Confluence page for session list and runbook template. Also link to PR for redaction rule updates in infra repo.

Next steps: - Lina to confirm time window and test runner (expected by 2026-03-12). - Privacy to provide acceptance criteria and regex/rule whitelist. - Security to create ephemeral IAM role and key policy changes.

Issue summary:
- During a planned KMS rewrap and Vault transit key rotation a subset of ephemeral worker pods failed to claim GitHub App installation tokens and remained in a "pending/CrashLoopBackOff" state. The failure window corresponds to the rewrap and subsequent short TTL mismatch between Vault response and the runner controller.

Impact:
- Multiple release jobs in the nightly cutover failed (approx 18 jobs) and several release gates were delayed by ~45-90 minutes. This affected internal release pipelines only (no customer-facing endpoints).

Environment:
- Prod cluster: k8s: cluster-autoscaler v1.30, runner controller v2.4.1, Vault transit rewrap initiated from infra-ops in us-west-2.

Steps to reproduce (observed):
1. Trigger Vault transit rewrap of the "github-app-transit" key with short rolling window.
2. Start a burst of ephemeral runner pod bootstraps (concurrent 120 pods).
3. Watch controller logs: tokens returned by Vault sometimes have an issuance timestamp that is ahead of controller's lease table leading to immediate rejection on claim validation.

Observed behavior:
- ~15% of pods failed to progress past "Init" and logged 403/invalid-claim-like errors from GitHub App token exchange. Some pods retried and succeeded after 30-60s; a cohort never recovered without manual restart.

Expected behavior:
- Controller should accept the token issuance window despite small clock skew / token epoch drift during coordinated rewrap and should queue or retry gracefully rather than leaving pods unregistered.

Logs / artifacts:
- controller logs (snippet):
  2026-02-25T01:12:03Z controller runner claim: token-claim failed validation: issuance_ts 2026-02-25T01:12:05Z > lease_epoch 2026-02-25T01:12:03Z
- Vault audit: transit rewrap started 2026-02-25T01:11:59Z, rewrap completed 2026-02-25T01:12:04Z.
- GitHub App exchange traces: 403 entries correlated to pod ids: runner-7f9c, runner-8g2p, runner-93kd.

Initial hypothesis: clock skew between controller nodes and Vault caused tokens to appear issued in the future relative to controller's lease table.
Checked NTP/chrony across controller fleet — clocks within 20ms, so not a pure NTP drift issue.
Observed that Vault returned tokens stamped with microsecond-level future timestamps occasionally due to async rewrap commit ordering in transit plugin.
Controller compares token.issuance_ts against its local lease_epoch and rejects if issuance_ts > lease_epoch + acceptance_window (currently 0s).
Reproduced locally by running a mini rewrap and starting 200 ephemeral bootstraps — saw similar 403s when issuance_ts skew > 30ms.
Traffic pattern: burst of concurrent claims amplifies race because some controller workers update lease_epoch only after their local cache refresh; tokens minted in-between fail validation.
Controller code path: token validation occurs in claim_validation.go, function ValidateTokenEpoch. Acceptance window is hardcoded to 0 and should be configurable.
SRE mitigations tested: manual leader restart + controller cache flush allowed stuck pods to complete registration; suggests caching/timing problem rather than permanent token invalidity.

Additional notes:
2026-02-25 05:15 - QA (Nora): Confirmed that restart of controller leader clears pending pods; adding e2e to reproduce burst registration during rewrap in staging.
Workaround applied: hotfix changed controller acceptance window to 100ms and performed a rolling restart of controller replicas. Manual restart of affected runner pods recovered remaining stuck jobs.
Permanent fix plan: (1) PR merged to make acceptance window configurable and add exponential retry/backoff in ValidateTokenEpoch (PR#12245), (2) controller will refresh lease_epoch before rejecting a claim and will enqueue claims that fail soft validation for 2s retry, (3) update runbook with steps for coordinated Vault rewrap (add pre-roll cache flush and graceful restart), (4) infra-ops to stagger rewraps or use a cross-cluster rekey plan for high-concurrency periods.
Postmortem action items assigned: Diego (implement and roll out fix), Ravi (merge PR and add e2e), Marta (update Vault rewrap runbook), Aisha (communicate to release ops).
Rollout PR#12245 to prod during low-traffic window on 2026-03-04 (Diego/Ravi).
Add an automated stage in the Vault rewrap runbook to pause large ephemeral bootstrap waves for 5 minutes (Marta).
Add e2e test to CI that simulates high-concurrency bootstrap during transit rewrap and assert no stuck pods (Ravi/Nora).
Notify Release Coordinators of mitigation and updated runbook (Aisha).

Issue summary:
During a staged canary prefetch for redwood-chat-7b-v1 we observed a subset of Cartwheel tenant traffic being silently routed to the legacy tokenization variant (redwood-chat-7b-v1-legacy-tokenizer). The divergence was not visible at routing policy configuration (no explicit pin change) and manifested as mixed-quality outputs, higher 5xx spike rate, and user-reported hallucination/formatting regressions.

Impact:
- ~6% of requests for Cartwheel (enterprise dedicated account) returned responses produced by the legacy-tokenizer variant over a 42 minute window.
- Customer reported elevated error rate (5xx) and malformed structured outputs in checkout assistant flows.
- Business impact: intermittent customer confusion and increased chatbot failures during a peak campaign window.

Environment:
- Prod - us-east-1, dedicated capacity pool dc-prod-7b-01 assigned to Cartwheel.
- Canary rollout for redwood-chat-7b-v1 (weight ramping 5% -> 25%) using prefetch/batched mirror strategy.

Important notes: routing rules in Console show model pin intact; no manual pin change recorded in audit log during the window. Edge proxies show a subset of sessions with legacy tokenizer header present (x-rt-tokenizer: legacy), but the header was not present on the original client request.
1) Create a staged prefetch canary for redwood-chat-7b-v1 with prewarm mirror enabled.
2) Target a dedicated tenant (Cartwheel) with session affinity enabled and model pin to redwood-chat-7b-v1.
3) Trigger bulk prefetch traffic via load test or real traffic ramp.
4) Observe edge logs for x-rt-tokenizer header and compare model hash returned from orchestrator.
5) Correlate timestamps with serving runtime traces and KV-cache keys for the tenant session.
Intermittent routing of some requests to redwood-chat-7b-v1-legacy-tokenizer leading to tokenization mismatch, malformed JSON outputs, and a 5xx spike (~4.8% baseline -> 12.6% during window).
All pinned sessions for Cartwheel should route exclusively to redwood-chat-7b-v1 during the promotion window; prefetch should mirror traffic without altering tokenizer headers or shifting live requests to legacy variants.
Customer-facing regressions in checkout assistant; elevated error rate and several enterprise escalation messages to CS. Estimated affected sessions: ~9k during 42-minute window. Billing not impacted but service quality degraded.

orchestrator trace: trace-id=orch-5581 - route-resolve: resolved_variant=redwood-chat-7b-v1-legacy-tokenizer - decision_path=mirror-prefetch-fanout

Lucas Chen: Temporarily paused prefetch mirror for Cartwheel tenant at 2026-03-13T19:02Z UTC — error rate reverted towards baseline within 3 minutes.

Paused prefetch/mirror for Cartwheel (applied at 2026-03-13T19:02Z). Manually enforced header sanitize rule on edge for tenant Cartwheel to drop x-rt-tokenizer header for server-to-server mirror traffic. Customer routed to full-weight pinned variant until fix is deployed.

Orchestrator PR #2220 merged to ensure mirror payloads do not carry runtime-only tokenizer headers. Post-deploy monitoring shows 5xx rate returned to baseline and no further legacy-tokenizer responses observed for Cartwheel. Follow-up: permanent test added to prewarm e2e suite to validate header isolation; postmortem scheduled.
Postmortem scheduled in Confluence: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/OPS/2026-03-13+Cartwheel+Prefetch+Partial-Divergence

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customer reports intermittent stalls when streaming large model shard downloads and long-lived gRPC/http2 connections from their Private deployment. The problem started after an on-prem network change from their transit provider two days ago.

Impact:
- Models fail to fully stream for larger shards (>64KB) causing inference requests to stall and time out after ~30s.
- Affects production traffic for FinData Analytics (private deployment, single VPC peered to our control plane).
- Observed in us-east-1 only.

Environment:
- Private deployment (customer-managed VPC) peered to Redwood control plane via TGW.
- Worker nodes: t3.large-equivalent instances with custom MTU 1500 by default.
- Presigned S3 artifact fetches used with range requests (HTTP/2 multiplexed).

Steps to reproduce (observed by customer):
1) Trigger a model load that requires range fetches (large model shard).
2) Observe initial TLS handshake completes. HTTP/2 connection established.
3) After a few KBs, the download stalls and the HTTP/2 stream is left in a half-open state; no further DATA frames from server are delivered.
4) Retry with smaller range window or reduce request size -> succeeds.

Observed behavior:
- tcpdump on worker shows server sending TCP segments but client stops ACKing after a certain MSS-sized segment. No ICMP "Fragmentation Needed (Type 3, Code 4)" is seen reaching the customer edge.
- When we instrumented a capture at the customer-VM side we do see an ICMP type 3 code 4 originating from the downstream router, but it disappears before reaching the customer's transit provider egress (suggesting provider filtering/rate limit).
- HTTP/2 stream state: initial SETTINGS/HEADERS exchange ok, partial DATA frames delivered, then stall; client eventually times out and triggers a reconnect.

Expected behavior:
- If path MTU requires fragmentation adjustments, ICMP "Fragmentation Needed (Type 3, Code 4)" should be delivered to endpoints so PMTU can adjust and streaming continues without stalls.

Additional logs / captures:
- Attached pcap snippets (provided by customer): "pcap_worker_side.pcap" shows server DATA up to a segment then no further ACK progression.
- Worker logs: serving-runtime reported repeated stream timeouts with code 14 (UNAVAILABLE) and downstream transport errors referencing ECONNRESET after timeouts.
- Console trace: Model shard fetch request id=shard-20260312-34 produced 0 bytes after 18s then retried and succeeded with MTU reduced.

Immediate customer workaround performed:
- Customer set worker node MTU to 1400 (temporary) — this prevented the need for ICMP fragmentation and streaming resumed successfully.

Notes:
- This only reproduces on large sequential downloads (range-based) or larger gRPC frame payloads; small requests and embeddings flows unaffected.
- The control plane auth and presigned URL generation are not implicated (we can generate working presigned URLs that still stall when path MTU issues present).

2026-03-12: Initial triage by Support (Aisha). Collected tcpdump + HTTP/2 trace. Customer confirms transit provider changed perimeter firewall/policy on 2026-03-11.
2026-03-12: SRE (Marco) requested pcap from customer and reproduced stalls by issuing range requests to the same object; pcap at worker shows missing ICMP fragments and stalled TCP sequence progression.
2026-03-13: We set up controlled repro from an EC2 in the customer's VPC and instrumented packet captures at three points: (a) worker VM, (b) customer edge router, (c) provider egress (captured by customer but provider did not provide mirrored capture). The VM saw ICMP type 3 code 4 originate from edge router; there is a gap at the provider handoff.
2026-03-13: Opened inbound ticket with customer's transit provider (ticket TP-44821) — provider response indicates they apply ICMP rate-limiting and drop some Type 3 messages under heavy NAT; they are investigating.
2026-03-14: SRE confirmed MTU-lowering on worker (1400) is an effective mitigation. We tested increasing TLS record granularity (server-side capping to 1200) and that also mitigates but requires runtime change.

Hypothesis:
- Transit provider's egress filtering/rate-limiting is preventing delivery of ICMP Fragmentation Needed messages to the customer's VMs, causing PMTU discovery to fail and resulting in a blackhole for packets larger than path MTU. HTTP/2/HTTP/2-over-TLS tends to push larger frames which triggers the failure more evident for large shard downloads.

Next steps / action items:
- SRE: Collect signed pcap evidence to include in provider escalation (assigned Marco Alvarez).
- Support: Document workaround steps for customer (MTU 1400 or server TLS record size cap).
- Customer: Keep transit provider ticket open and request allowing ICMP Type 3 Code 4 or otherwise enable PMTU transparency.
- Product: Consider adding an automatic fallback to smaller TLS record sizes for private deployments when PMTU probes fail (follow-up RFC).

Additional notes:
2026-03-13 08:23 - FinData NetOps (Customer): Provider confirms a firewall policy change on 2026-03-11 and acknowledges ICMP rate-limiting. They've opened TP-44821 with provider. Can confirm MTU workround helps.
Workaround: Customer lowered worker MTU to 1400 which restored streaming. Alternative workaround: cap TLS record sizes/server-side chunking to avoid packets exceeding Path MTU.
Root cause: Provider-level ICMP (Fragmentation Needed) filtering/rate-limiting preventing PMTU discovery; provider ticket TP-44821 opened by customer.
Follow-up: SRE to push escalation to provider with signed pcap evidence. Product team to evaluate automatic TLS-record-size fallback for private deployments if PMTU probes fail.
payload.summary: Egress transit provider dropping 'fragmentation-needed' ICMP causing large HTTP/2 model-shard streams to stall in private deploy

payload.description:
Issue summary: Customer reports intermittent gRPC keepalive timeouts from serving nodes in their private deployment. Timeouts primarily impact KV cache heartbeats and short-lived streaming connections, resulting in transient 5xx/connection-reset observed by application.

Impact: Approximately 8% of requests to the customer's serving tier experience ~5-20s stalled tokens or gRPC keepalive timeouts during nightly batch window (higher packet sizes). No model corruption observed, but increased latency and occasional fallback to lower-tier model variants.

Environment: Private deployment (VPC peered to GreenField Health on-prem via site-to-site tunnel). Multi-AZ serving fleet in us-east-1. Customer uses IPv6-only internal addressing on the on-prem side with NAT64 for egress to some external services. Redwood control plane connects over the peered path for artifact fetch and kv heartbeats.

Steps to reproduce:
1) From a serving node in the customer VPC, trigger a large-shard presigned range download or a prompt with long context to force >1200B MTU segments.
2) Observe gRPC keepalive and control-plane heartbeats during sustained transfer (nightly batch).
3) Failures are intermittent — reproduce rate ~1 in 10 under load.

Observed logs/traces:
- serving-node logs: "gRPC: keepalive timeout, closing connection" followed by "kv-cache: heartbeat failed, retrying"
- tcpdump captures show ICMPv6 "Packet too big" messages from an intermediate router but no subsequent PMTU discovery adjustment from the on-prem client stack.
- traceroute6 shows a jump in MTU-limited hop and then subsequent silence on large packets.
- No TLS handshake failures were observed; failures are at gRPC keepalives/stream stalls.

Customer-provided artifacts: attached pcap, traceroute6 output, and sample serving-node logs (uploaded to ticket attachment).
2026-03-13 09:15 - Customer(ops@greenfield): We're seeing intermittent failures in production during nightly shard fetches. Tokens stall and we see keepalive timeouts. Happening only since last Friday after a router firmware upgrade on the branch site.
2026-03-13 09:42 - Support (Marcus Lee): Thanks for the data — we've triaged and see ICMPv6 'Packet too big' in the pcap. I'm escalating to Network/SRE to verify PMTU behavior across the site-to-site tunnel.
2026-03-13 11:05 - SRE (Priya Nair): Reproduced locally by sending large TCP segments over the tunnel. Observed that intermediate appliance drops fragments for IPv6 and does not forward ICMPv6 PMTU messages to the host. Requesting packet captures from the customer's tunnel egress and the branch router config dump.
2026-03-13 14:20 - Customer(ops@greenfield): Provided router config and tunnel device logs; firmware shows 'frag-offload disabled' option toggled during upgrade.
2026-03-14 08:10 - SRE (Priya Nair): Implemented temporary workaround: forced MSS clamp on the Redwood-serving NAT gateway for this customer route to 1200 bytes to avoid large IPv6 datagrams. Observing immediate reduction in keepalive timeouts in canary nodes. Planning permanent remediation with customer network team.
2026-03-14 12:30 - Engineering (Diego Morales): Reviewed possibility of adding aggressive PMTU probing on our side for IPv6 sessions to detect path MTU changes faster. Raised infra task INT-75921 for a follow-up enhancement.
Initial inspection focused on TLS/OCSP and presigned artifact downloads; TLS was healthy. Packet captures revealed ICMPv6 'Packet too big' originating from an on-prem transit appliance but on-prem host did not send subsequent smaller packets. Hypothesis: on-prem router's firmware upgrade disabled fragmentation/fragment forwarding or suppressed ICMPv6 PMTU messages toward the client (or rewrote them). Without PMTU feedback, client's IPv6 stack continued to send larger packets leading to silent drops of gRPC keepalive packets during large transfers. Correlation: spikes coincide with nightly large-shard transfers and were reproducible when forcing >1280B payloads over IPv6. Verified that when we clamp MSS to 1200 on egress NAT, failures disappear for canary nodes. Also validated no issues when traffic took IPv4 path (dual-stack fallback). Logged kernel/sysctl state on host — clients didn't respond to PMTU change because ICMPv6 replies were not visible to them. Checked control-plane metrics for KV cache retries and saw spike matching customer reports.
Analyzed customer pcap and traceroute6 outputs
Reached out to customer network team for router config and firmware notes
Reproduced issue in staging by sending large IPv6 payloads over a mirrored tunnel
Applied temporary MSS clamp (1200) on Redwood egress for affected route
Monitored canary nodes for 6 hours — keepalive timeouts dropped from 8%->0.4%
Opened internal follow-up INT-75921 to consider proactive PMTU probing for IPv6 and a runbook update
A site-to-site transit appliance/branch router firmware change disabled proper IPv6 PMTU propagation (or dropped ICMPv6 'Packet too big'), causing a path MTU blackhole. Hosts continued sending oversized IPv6 datagrams, resulting in intermittent gRPC keepalive/stall behavior during large transfers.
Short-term: temporary MSS clamp to 1200 applied on the Redwood egress NAT for the affected customer route which mitigated the symptom across the fleet. Long-term: customer will coordinate with their network vendor to re-enable ICMPv6 PMTU messages / fix fragmentation behavior. Redwood to add a defensive will-have: optional MSS clamp per-customer-route for private deployments and an IPv6 PMTU probing enhancement (INT-75921). Follow-up actions recorded in the ticket.

Rollout notes: MSS clamp was deployed to the customer's dedicated egress route in two waves (canary then full) during a low-traffic window; no downtime expected. Monitoring dashboards show KPI recovery.

Customer communication: Informed GreenField Health of root cause and remediation steps; awaiting confirmation from their network vendor for permanent fix.
Customer to validate vendor firmware patch and re-enable PMTU/fragmentation behavior
Engineering: implement optional per-route MSS clamp toggle in control plane (INT-75921)
SRE: add IPv6 PMTU detection probe to private-deploy health checks
Docs: update private-deploy runbook for IPv6 PMTU troubleshooting
payload.summary: IPv6 Path MTU blackhole on site-to-site tunnel causing intermittent gRPC keepalive timeouts and KV cache heartbeats in private deploy

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Customer Quillify reports an unexplained 20-35% sustained throughput reduction in their dedicated pool during midday peak windows despite autoscaler headroom. P90 latency increased modestly and P99 spike frequency increased; many short-stream requests experienced attach delays.

Impact:
- Dedicated reserved pool dc-805 serving Quillify saw reduced throughput and elevated latency for ~45 minutes across the US-East window.
- Customer-facing traffic experienced degraded tail latency and 5xx spikes tied to delayed GPU attach/slot allocation.

Environment:
- prod-us-east dedicated capacity (dc-805)
- Node type: A100-80GB mixed cluster
- Tenants: multiple short-stream, high-fanout tenants including Quillify (dedicated slice)

Observed behavior vs expected:
- Observed: throughput drop with autoscaler still showing available capacity; allocator logs show attach delays and slot fragmentation. NVMe IO queues show short high-amplitude bursts coincident with optimizer jobs.
- Expected: autoscaler should allocate/attach GPUs to meet demand without the attach delay cliff seen.

Initial temporary workaround suggested to customer:
- Route critical traffic to a fallback model variant pinned to a different dedicated cluster or use hosted API fallback for high-importance endpoints while we investigate.

1) In a prod-like dedicated pool, schedule the background optimizer/prefetch-optimizer (service 'prefetch-opt') compaction with default concurrency during midday traffic spike.
2) Generate high fanout of short streaming requests (50-200ms per request typical) from a tenant pinned to the pool.
3) Monitor autoscaler, allocator attach latencies, and NVMe io util (iostat/pmem).
4) Observe transient nvme_io_wait spikes, kernel preemption logs, and delayed GPU attach leading to queuing and p99 latency spikes.
2026-03-10T11:42:03.214Z [allocator] WARN attach_timeout tenant=quillify slice=dc-805 attach_ms=4782
2026-03-10T11:42:03.216Z [kernel] ERROR cpu_preempt: task_preempted pid=4421 iowait_ms=312
2026-03-10T11:42:03.220Z [nvme-monitor] INFO nvme_io_wait=0.78 device=/dev/nvme0n1 window=1s
2026-03-10T11:42:02.998Z [prefetch-opt] INFO compaction_start batch_id=970 concurrency=8
2026-03-10T11:42:03.500Z [serving-runtime] ERROR kernel_sched_delay gpu_id=2 nvlink_io_wait=120ms

Additional notes:
Telemetry correlation: NVMe io wait bursts line up within +/-200ms of attach_timeout and kernel preemption logs across multiple nodes in dc-805.
Prefetch-opt behavior: compaction jobs run every 15 minutes by default; concurrency=8 produced highest observed IO envelope. Lowering concurrency to 2 reduced nvme spikes by ~70% in test cluster.
Autoscaler decisioning: autoscaler was using overall GPU utilization and not NVMe IO signals for short-term scale decisions; allocator was thrashing due to attach delays even though logical capacity existed.
Hypothesis: background compaction creates short-lived IO bursts that lead to kernel-level scheduling preemption and cause critical threads in the GPU attach path to be delayed, resulting in slot fragmentation and queuing at the allocator layer. This is a noisy-neighbor type interaction but driven by infra-service IO behavior rather than tenant compute alone.
Customer impact estimate: ~20-35% throughput loss over the affected 40-50 minute window; increased request latencies for short streams; some host-level 429s/attach_timeouts observed.
Temporary mitigations applied (2026-03-11):
- Reduced prefetch-opt concurrency on dc-805 from 8 to 2 during peak hours (immediate partial relief).
- Adjusted autoscaler weighting to make short-term NVMe io spikes less likely to trigger slot reclamation/shrink operations.
- Recommended customer route high-priority endpoints to a fallback cluster while fix rolled out.
Permanent fix planned (actionable items):
- Merge PR to run prefetch-opt compaction under I/O niceness (ionice) and add adaptive backoff when allocator attach latency > 500ms (PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/3021).
- Update the ops playbook to schedule heavy compaction windows outside customer peak windows or to perform compactions at lower concurrency for dedicated pools.
- Add an autoscaler signal that directly monitors allocator attach latency and NVMe io microbursts to avoid oscillatory behaviour.
Status: mitigations in place; monitoring configured to watch next three midday windows. Work on PR in review. Customer notified and monitoring dashboard shared.
1) Runtime Eng to land PR adding ionice + backoff (owner: Priya Nair) - target: 2026-03-15.
2) Ops to add prefetch-opt concurrency tuning to dedicated pool runbook and to update maintenance scheduling UI to allow per-customer quiet windows (owner: Diego Morales) - target: 2026-03-20.
3) Telemetry team to build short-window NVMe microburst alerting and autoscaler integration test (owner: Mateo Ruiz) - target: 2026-03-22.
4) Follow-up call with Quillify to confirm resolution and remove fallback routing once two clean midday windows observed (owner: Ava Chen) - target: after PR merge and one-week validation.
5) Link this incident into postmortem board and add ops playbook snippet (owner: SRE) - target: 2026-03-25.
payload.summary: Midday throughput erosion in dedicated pool correlating with background optimizer I/O bursts

comments: 2026-03-12T09:18:00Z Priya Kapoor: Customer called in after spike of model pull errors. Asked for immediate tcpdump/dig output.

payload.description:
Customer reports intermittent failures where agent instances in their private deployment fail to resolve control-plane hostnames or resolve to different IPs that intermittently reject TLS handshakes. Symptoms began after a recent network change (added a second transit attachment and enabled ECMP for egress). Failures cause model pulls to fail and gRPC streams to drop for bursts of ~30-90s before recovering.
1) From a node in the customer's private subnet run: dig +short control-api.internal.finedge
2) Repeat the dig command several times in quick succession and note alternating A records
3) curl -v --resolve control-api.internal.finedge:443:<ip_from_dig> https://control-api.internal.finedge/health
4) Observe TLS certificate common name and occasional connection resets when dig returns alternate IP
5) Reproduce from multiple AZs/subnets to see AZ-correlated behaviour.
Customer-provided dig/tcpdump snippets:
- dig outputs: 10.0.5.21
10.0.8.42
10.0.5.21
- tcpdump on node: DNS requests (udp/53) source=10.0.5.50 -> 172.31.2.10 and -> 172.31.3.11 (alternating)
- openssl s_client -connect 10.0.8.42:443 shows certificate CN=control-api.external.redwood.ai (mismatch)
- kube-agent logs: "x509: certificate is valid for control-api.private.redwood, not control-api.external.redwood.ai"
- Control plane logs show successful connection attempts from IPs in resolver-1 subnet and rejected/handshakes-from resolver-2 subnet
Initial hypothesis: split-horizon DNS (resolver sets in two AZs) returns different record sets (one view returns private IPs tied to internal LB with private cert, the other returns an internal CNAME that resolves to an external-facing IP/hostname that presents external TLS cert). Enabling ECMP for egress caused packet flows to be hashed across two NAT paths which send DNS queries to different forwarders / resolvers based on path. Result: same client sometimes gets IP A, sometimes B within TTL window => TLS mismatch when client picks IP with external cert.
What we did:
- Pulled route tables and observed two active NAT gateway paths with equal-cost routes for 0.0.0.0/0 and DNS traffic to resolver endpoints flowed to different forwarders depending on ECMP hash.
- Captured tcpdump showing DNS queries from same source to two different resolver IPs within 5s.
- Compared resolver responses: resolver-A returns 10.0.5.21 with cert CN control-api.private.redwood; resolver-B returns a CNAME that ultimately resolves to 34.x.y.z (external) with cert CN control-api.external.redwood.ai.
- Reproduced by temporarily forcing egress to a single path: DNS responses stabilized and TLS handshakes succeeded consistently.

Additional notes:
2026-03-12 10:05 - Customer (FinEdge): Provided pcap and dig output, noted network change at 2026-03-11 22:00 (added second transit attachment).
2026-03-13 08:41 - FinEdge NetOps: Confirmed two NAT gateways + route table entries with equal cost; resolvers are different firewall-forwarders with independent view configs.
Mitigation validated: customer changed route preference to pin DNS egress to resolver-A (single path) and restarted agents on nodes. After change, DNS responses stabilized to the private-only view and TLS handshake failures stopped. Root cause: ECMP-induced path selection caused DNS queries to hit two different forwarders with inconsistent split-horizon views.
Permanent fix planned: customer will (a) reconfigure forwarders so both present identical internal views, and (b) update network design to avoid ECMP across resolvers for control-plane traffic. Redwood SRE to add documentation guidance for Private deployments about resolver consistency and ECMP pitfalls.
Create KB entry: private-dns-and-ecmp-runbook (assigned to SRE)
Add validation to onboarding checklist: verify resolvers return identical views from all AZs
Add an outbound-route recommendation to Private deployment docs
Engineering: consider agent-level resolver pinning toggle to prefer a configured resolver IP (feature request filed)
payload.summary: Split-DNS views + ECMP path selection causing intermittent service discovery flapping in private deployment

Issue summary:
Customer reports repeated 429 responses during a nightly bulk ingest run that stages objects via signed cookies. Failures started after a safe restart of their ingest fleet and coincide with a scheduled canary of a proxy-side keepalive change. BrightFleet uses ephemeral worker pools that refresh signed cookies frequently (~every 90s).

Impact:
- ~20% of ingest batch requests receiving 429s intermittently across a 2 hour window (2026-03-09 03:00–05:00 UTC).
- Customer sees backlog and retry storms causing delayed downstream processing and SLA risk for enterprise tier.

Environment:
- Customer tier: enterprise, VPC peering to prod us-west-2, using pooled edge proxy IPs and signed-cookie approach for pre-signed uploads.
- Ingest orchestrator uses 200 concurrent ephemeral workers per region; each worker refreshes cookies from control-plane every ~90s.

Steps to reproduce (reported by customer):
1) Start parallel uploader with 200 workers using signed-cookie refresh schedule identical to production.
2) Observe steady-state for 10 minutes, then trigger a restart of a subset of workers (simulates canary).
3) Measure HTTP 429s from /upload endpoint and ambiguous throttle headers.

Observed logs / telemetry (customer-provided):
- Repeated 429s with X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0 and X-RateLimit-Reset drifting between 10–60s.
- Ingest orchestrator logs show bursts of signed-cookie refresh requests to the auth service clustered at restart time.
- Edge proxy traces show keepalive connections sticky to pooled IPs; some cookie refresh POSTs get routed through a small subset of origin instances.

Hypothesis / initial triage notes (Support):
- Likely interaction between signed-cookie refresh fanout and token-bucket accounting at the route layer. Ephemeral workers renewing cookies simultaneously can concentrate accounting at the ingress proxy and momentarily exhaust per-route refill credits.
- Proxy keepalive change may have reduced upstream affinity churn, inadvertently concentrating refresh requests to fewer rate-limiter partitions.

Immediate mitigation requested:
- BrightFleet asked for guidance to avoid enqueueing large simultaneous cookie refreshes and whether a server-side smoothing/fanout backoff is possible.

Requested action items:
- SRE: check proxy partitioning/affinity metrics around 2026-03-09 03:00 UTC and correlate with rate-limiter partitions and refill windows.
- Auth team: inspect signed-cookie issuance logs to confirm refresh clustering and whether refresh endpoints are rebalanced across origins.
- Support: provide customer with recommended client-side jitter/backoff pattern and short-term bypass options (e.g., stagger refreshes, use slightly longer cookie TTL while testing).

Notes on customer posture: BrightFleet is sensitive to any required code changes but can deploy a staggered refresh patch to their ingest agents if recommended by Support.

Expected next updates: SRE to post partition metrics and a short tracer link; Support to propose a safe stagger pattern and verify whether an infra-side fast fix (refill smoothing) can be staged for canary revert.

2026-03-10 | Sofia Martin (Support): Acknowledged. Escalating to SRE and Auth. Please attach raw trace ids if available. First response ETA within 1 hour.
2026-03-10 | Riley Tan (SRE): Looking at proxy partitioning metrics for us-west-2. Initial signal: 3 proxy upstreams received ~85% of cookie-refresh traffic during the restart window. Adding router traces to this ticket.
2026-03-10 | Elena Park (Auth): We see a cluster of POST /auth/signed-cookie that align with the worker restart time. Origin distribution skewed; investigating why load balancer didn't round-robin across auth pool.
2026-03-11 | Riley Tan (SRE): Confirmed refill window exhaustion on route weight 42. Rate-limiter partitions used by those 3 upstreams had aligned refill epochs; recommend changing client jitter and scheduling a short-term refill smoothing flag. Filing INT-3315 for infra rollout path.
2026-03-11 | Sofia Martin (Support): Recommended client workaround to BrightFleet: add randomized jitter 30–120s to their refresh schedule and increase ephemeral cookie TTL to 5 minutes when running bulk ingest. Customer accepted and will deploy patch to canary tonight.
2026-03-12 | BrightFleet (Customer): Applied jitter patch to their canary; observed 99.8% successful uploads during the 2 hour test window. Will keep monitoring and requests follow-up on permanent infra mitigation.
2026-03-12 | Riley Tan (SRE): Scheduling infra action: enable 'refill-smoothing' experiment on affected rate-limiter partitions during next maintenance window. Linked INT-3315 and related PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/rate-limiter/pull/221
Workaround applied by customer (staggered refresh + temporary longer TTL). SRE confirmed refill-window exhaustion as root cause due to partitioned accounting and proxy affinity. Infra mitigation planned (refill-smoothing experiment) and tracked via INT-3315. Customer to monitor; follow-up in 72h to confirm closure.

payload.description:
Issue summary: Customer reports intermittent elevated tail latency and occasional 502s after they applied a combined optimizer profile (aggressive batching + prefix KV caching + 4-bit quantization) to their production route. Impact: Several business-critical endpoints for MedAlign show 95th/99th latency spikes affecting real-time triage flows; customer requests a safe, tested way to cut optimizations without impacting throughput more than necessary. Environment: Dedicated pool (customer-owned node group) in prod-us-east serving two pinned model variants. Recent change: Applied optimizer profile v2026-03-09-agg which enabled aggressive batch grouping, enabled KV prefetch, and switched quantization profile to q4_main. Customer asks for: 1) immediate mitigation steps to stabilize latency and error rate; 2) a recommended circuit-breaker procedure (safe exit) that minimizes cold-cache penalties; 3) a checklist for future experiments to avoid similar disruption.
1) Use the customer's production route (medalign-triage-v1) and send representative traffic with 1-3 sentence prompts at 40 rps sustained.
2) Apply optimizer profile v2026-03-09-agg which sets batch_size: 48, max_batch_delay_ms: 50, kv_prefetch: enabled, quant_profile: q4_main aggressive packing.
3) Observe metrics on Console: per-route p95/p99 latency jumps after ~10 minutes and occasional 502/504 spikes.
4) Reproduce by toggling kv_prefetch on/off via customer config change and watching tail latency delta.
5) Re-run with traffic split: 10% to profile-on, 90% baseline and inspect per-split latency and error rates.
2026-03-10T14:22:11Z ERROR serving-runtime: request_id=abc123 path=/generate status=502 backend_timeout
stack: timeout waiting for kernel exec
CloudWatch link: https://console.aws.amazon.com/cloudwatch/home?region=us-east-1#logsV2:log-groups/log-group/medalign/stream/2026-03-10
Console trace: https://console.redwood.ai/tenant/medalign/traces?from=2026-03-10T14:00&to=2026-03-10T15:00&filter=optimizer-profile%3Dv2026-03-09-agg

Additional notes:
2026-03-11 MedAlign (Customer): Provided traffic profile and representative prompt set. Notes: the issue is intermittent, appears more often during clinical report uploads that include longer context.
Hypothesis 1: Large batch sizes cause kernel scheduling contention on our dedicated pool GPUs; q4 packing increased compute density and increased end-to-end kernel latency leading to timeouts.
Hypothesis 2: KV prefetch interacts poorly with packed quantized weights and LRU eviction on tenant cache causing frequent cache churn and higher memory churn.
Metrics observed: spike in gpu_utilization and gpu_memory_free dips correlated with p99 latency peaks. Scheduler queue length rose to batch_size/2 during peaks.
Dashboards examined: per-tenant latency (Console), GPU telemetry (Prometheus), scheduler queues (Grafana link: https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/optimizer/scheduler?orgId=1&from=now-1h)
Short tests: reducing batch_size to 16 reduced p99 by ~45% in canary; disabling kv_prefetch reduced 502s to baseline but increased average token cost by ~6%.
Risk assessment: Full immediate disable of optimizer profile will result in cold-kv-cache misses and a transient latency bump for first requests; long-term throughput is expected to settle within 10-30 minutes depending on traffic volume.
Mitigation taken (2026-03-11): Applied 'soft-fallback' profile for medalign-triage-v1: batch_size=16, max_batch_delay_ms=10, kv_prefetch=disabled, quant_profile=q4_main (unchanged). This stabilized tail latency and eliminated 502s. Noted throughput drop ~12%.
Circuit-breaker playbook (recommended):
  Step 1 - Snapshot: Export current optimizer profile and persist tenant KV cache snapshot via admin API snapshot/tenant/medalign before any full disable.
  Step 2 - Canary: Create a 5-10% traffic split to a 'safe' profile (batch_size=8-16, kv_prefetch=off, quant_profile=q4_safe) for 30 minutes and monitor p95/p99 and error rate.
  Step 3 - Ramp: If canary stable, increase split by doubling every 15 minutes while watching p99 and GPU memory trends; abort if p99 > threshold or errors rise > 1% of baseline.
  Step 4 - Full switch: Once at 100%, keep monitoring for 1 hour to allow KV caches to warm gradually; run a background cache-prewarm job if available to reduce cold miss window.
  Step 5 - Re-introduction: To re-enable optimizations later, run the inverse: canary enable one knob at a time (first quant_profile change or batch_size increase, then kv_prefetch) and observe for 2x the expected latency window.
Follow-ups assigned: Implement admin API to take atomic tenant optimizer snapshots (INT-404), add a per-tenant prewarm helper in the console (ENG-881), update runbooks with the above playbook (Confluence page link provided).
Outcome: Customer accepted the soft-fallback and requested the formal playbook. Ticket remains open until snapshot tooling delivery and runbook updates are completed.
payload.summary: Optimizer circuit-breaker guidance for tenant batch/cache/quant experiments

payload.description:
Issue summary:
During a customer traffic surge against their dedicated pool, a canary throttle event caused the orchestrator to move traffic away from the normal model variant into a degraded quantized variant instead of the configured higher-capacity fallback. Impact: customer observed variable outputs and ~2.2x token latency increase for 80% of requests over a 22-minute window.

Impact:
- ScaleApps reported elevated error rates and latency spikes affecting their chat product.
- A subset of requests returned responses from the quantized variant that produced shorter outputs and tokenization mismatches.
- No billing discrepancy reported, but customer-facing SLAs were breached for 18 minutes.

Environment:
- Dedicated pool (customer-dedicated-44) in us-east, running 4 x A100-equivalent nodes.
- Canary rollout of redwood-7b-v2 -> redwood-7b-quantized-v2 was in progress with traffic weighting 5% -> 95%.

Steps to reproduce (observed):
1) Synthetic burst simulated by customer at 13:12 UTC (replay dataset attached in support ticket).
2) Orchestrator applied canary throttle policy due to observed per-node token processing lag.
3) Edge routing service routed sessions to fallback group; policy should have chosen warm-hot variant (redwood-7b-v2-warm) but instead selected quantized variant group.
4) Requests returned shorter completions and an increased per-token latency median.

Logs / Observations:
- Edge-proxy logs show header X-Route-Variant: quantized-v2 for affected sessions.
- Orchestrator metrics: canary_throttle_rate spiked to 0.42, batch_queue_depth increased.
- Serving runtime traces show kernel selection falling back to int8 path for variant grouped as "fallback-quantized".
- No node OOM or GPU eviction events reported.

Attachments:
- sample request/response pairs (anonymized)
- edge logs snippets (13:10 - 13:40 UTC)
- orchestrator telemetry graphs link

Hypothesis 1: route-controller snapshot staleness caused wrong fallback group mapping under surge conditions.
Hypothesis 2: canary throttle logic prioritized available capacity groups by a fallback_score that mistakenly favored quantized groups when 'burst-safe' flag present.
Telemetry checked: route-controller apply timestamps, edge routing logs, orchestrator throttle metrics, serving runtime kernel path logs.
Partial finding: route-controller cache TTL was set to 5m; in a rapid update window a stale snapshot remained active due to leader-election lag. This allowed an older fallback mapping to be used until forced refresh.
Additional finding: fallback_score computation treated lower expected latency as higher preference; quantized variant had lower nominal latency in profiling but poorer quality, leading to incorrect selection during throttle.
Consequence: customer saw degraded outputs and latency; orchestration did not follow configured 'prefer-warm-over-quantized' policy.
Immediate: forced route-controller snapshot refresh and pinned ScaleApps cohort to warm variant (redwood-7b-v2-warm). Applied temporary override to fallback scoring.
Permanent: merged fixes in route-controller to (1) reduce snapshot TTL jitter, (2) ensure fallback_score includes explicit customer-tier and quality_weight, (3) add a canary-safe flag that prevents quantized selection for dedicated pools. Two PRs merged: route-controller/pull/834 and serving-runtime/pull/2191.
Customer communication: incident summary, timeline, and goodwill credit provided.
Follow-ups: add runbook entry for forced snapshot refresh, add a monitoring alert when fallback_score differs from policy expected for >2 minutes.
payload.summary: Traffic redirected to degraded model variant after canary throttling during dedicated capacity burst

payload.description:
Issue summary:
Security monitoring flagged potential exfiltration of a long-lived service token tied to a fleet of ephemeral CI runners. Alert originated from log anomaly: identical token used from two distinct datacenter IP ranges within a 5 minute window. Impact: potential unauthorized access to private repositories and deployments; immediate mitigation required for release pipelines scheduled tonight.

Impact:
- Nightly release pipelines (release-nightly) and a handful of ad-hoc build jobs are at risk of unauthorized usage.
- No confirmed production changes yet, but token reuse pattern suggests credential may be leaked to an external CI job runner.

Environment:
- prod control plane, primary runner pool in us-east-1, ephemeral runners launched via autoscaler with service-account tokens minted by internal token-service.

Steps to reproduce / observed sequence:
1) 2026-03-13T18:02Z: Security alert (Evidently: auth-anomaly-20260313-17) flagged token XXXXXX-XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX used from IP A and B.
2) Investigated runner logs: token XXXXXX appears in runner bootstrap logs for runner-id r-3487 and r-3491.
3) Token issuance log shows token minted by token-service for service-account ci-ephemeral-deployer at 2026-03-13T17:58Z with TTL 24h.
4) Access patterns include git fetch and artifact upload attempts to s3-bucket "ci-artifacts-prod".

Immediate requests:
- Rotate all active tokens for service-account ci-ephemeral-deployer and issue short-lived replacements (1h TTL) for any upcoming scheduled jobs.
- Block any outstanding runner sessions that present the old token.
- Audit artifact uploads and git pushes between 2026-03-13T17:50Z and 2026-03-13T18:20Z.

Timeline and hypotheses:
- 2026-03-13T17:58Z token minted by token-service (log id ts-98231).
- 2026-03-13T18:02Z security alert for token reuse from multiple geo-ip blocks.
- Hypothesis A: token printed into a job log or artifact and then scraped by a scanning service or malicious actor.
- Hypothesis B: compromised runner bootstrap image contained a hardcoded token (unlikely, but check image digest).
- Hypothesis C: token-service issued a duplicate due to race and same token reused on two runners (race condition in token-service code).
Findings so far:
- Runner bootstrap scripts do not print tokens intentionally; however, one community script in customer templates folder was discovered in an older job that echoed env on error (CI job id 77312).
- Image digests for r-3487 and r-3491 match the current official ephemeral-runner image: sha256:fdc9..., no unauthorized modifications.
- Token-service code review shows a retry path that can return the same token if request ID deduplication occurs; engineering hypothesis plausible.
Logs & evidence locations:
- token-service logs: /var/logs/token-service/ts-2026-03-13.log (search ts-98231)
- runner audit: gs://redwood-ci-logs/runner/audit/2026/03/13/
- security alert: SIEM event auth-anomaly-20260313-17 (Slack #sec-alert archived thread)
Ava Martinez (reporter) 2026-03-13: Raised after SOC flagged token reuse; requesting immediate token rotation and kill of affected runners.
Samuel Cheng (assignee) 2026-03-13: Acknowledged. Initiating emergency rotation for ci-ephemeral-deployer; will create short TTL tokens for scheduled jobs. Requesting SRE to isolate runner pool.
Lena Ortiz (SRE) 2026-03-13: Isolating runner subnet and revoking existing tokens at the gateway level. Patching autoscaler to stop spawning new ephemeral runners from that SA until rotation completes.
Morgan Patel (Security) 2026-03-14: Found one suspicious artifact upload attempt; quarantine copy saved to secure bucket for forensic analysis. Suggest scanning artifacts for leaked secrets and checking access logs for third-party IPs.
Samuel Cheng 2026-03-14: Short-lived tokens issued (1h TTL) and deployed to release-nightly job definitions. Documented mitigation in runbook and linked a follow-up engineering ticket to fix token-service dedupe retry path.

Mitigation steps executed 2026-03-14:
1) Revoked all active tokens for service-account ci-ephemeral-deployer in Vault and invalidated tokens at the gateway layer.
2) Issued new short-lived tokens (1h) and patched CI job definitions for release-nightly and related pipelines.
3) Quarantined suspicious artifact and initiated forensic scan.
4) SRE temporarily drained and reprovisioned the affected runner pool with fresh images.
5) Created follow-up engineering ticket INT-738211 to implement token-service fix (prevent duplicate token issuance under retry) and another task INT-738212 to add automated token-leak detection on artifact uploads.
Post-mortem/next steps:
- Engineering to harden token-service by 2026-03-20 and add extra logging for request IDs.
- CI config update to set default TTL for ephemeral tokens to 1h.
- Add a pre-flight check to runner bootstrap to redact env prints and fail if dangerous debug flags are present.
- Security to run backward scan for other service-accounts to ensure no further exposures.
Status: mitigations completed; further engineering work scheduled.
payload.summary: Runner service account token exfiltration alert: rotate tokens and validate CI access paths
